paragraphs.text: On the divine revelations that came to Abraham

First Memra / for the First Sunday of the Annunciation / On the divine revelations that came to Abraham. / Response: / The Watcher appeared to Mary and announced to her that from you will dawn / the light of the world. My brothers [?]

Wonder of mind struck me with amazement, that I should turn to learning
and walk in the path of the study of the books, which I had left off.
In the study of the divine books my mind used to be occupied,
and the pure word of their meaning was dear to me.
In their meanings I used to search out how lofty they are,
and I did not neglect to seek out the mysteries within them.
Over the mystery of their words my mind was worn night and day,
and I longed to know the force of their rules.
In this study my mind was occupied, grazing on the words;
then the Evil One took me captive and held me back from it, though I did not wish it.
In negligence, as in sleep, my thoughts sank,
and drowsiness came in like raiders and plundered my study.
The senses of my limbs inclined toward the snares of silence,
and their movements ceased from the study in which they had been occupied.

Amazement at these things wore me down exceedingly, beyond measure,
and like one waking from sleep I rose at the voice of learning.
That learning called me and roused me from my negligence,
and, as one urges a child, drew me on toward its study:
"How long, lover of sleep, will you lie in slumber?
Arise, listen to the voices of the books of the Spirit, which are full of wonder."
Great wonder fills the revelations of the books of the Spirit,
and Moses bears witness, who was the firstborn at the head of the revelations.
He recounted how creation was set in order in the beginning,
and he informs us of the origin and the course of our race.
In his book he showed the road that guides mankind,
and along it, like milestones, the kinds of covenants were set in order.
As a foundation he laid Adam, the head of humankind,
and so, hand in hand, until it reached Abraham.
Twenty generations he counted from Adam to Abram,
and with Abraham he changed the order of the course of his discourse.
With Abram the course of his words came to a bound, though it was not bounded,
and he began to show the kinds of revelations that were granted to him.
The Spirit of revelations revealed to him, by the Spirit, spiritually,
and revealed and taught him about the Creator and his ministers.
Through Abraham the Lover of mankind accomplished his will,
and promised him that in him the peoples of the earth would be blessed.
Father of nations the Creator called the friend of his love,
and set the confession of his faith before the seers.
He gave his faith as the treasury of the promise of his words,
that it might tread a path to his Being for all who believe.
Moses said that by his faith he knew the God of all,
and righteousness that came of free will was reckoned to him.
The will of his soul became a guide to the course of his labours,

and he set out and reached promises loftier than himself.
By promises the Lover of the just bound his friend,
and his friend asked him how and when they would come to be his:
"How shall I know that the words of your love will be fulfilled with me,
and that you will give me the inheritance of the land, as you promised?"
By a sacrifice the Lord showed his servant the sign of his love,
and by animals he revealed and taught him about things to come:
"Take for yourself, Abram, three animals to confirm my words:
a heifer three years old, a ram three years old, and a she-goat three years old.
Of the birds take two, according to the promise,
and with a turtledove and a young pigeon set your soul at rest.
Divide the bodies and set the parts one opposite another,
and in their division depict the sign of what is to come.
Lay the bird down without dividing it into parts,
and in their wholeness stretch your mind toward the fulfilment."
By these things the good Lord taught him the kinds of his will,
that he might extend the [?] of his mind toward things to come.
The righteous man [?] his Lord's bidding and prepared the sacrifices,
and divided them into twelve parts.
He laid down the turtledove and the young pigeon also without division,
and waited for fire to come down and consume his sacrifices.
With vigilance he guarded his Lord's sacrifice,
and did not let the birds eat of his sacrifices.
All day long he guarded his sacrifice from harm,
and at sunset he was found worthy of a divine revelation.
He saw a furnace from which a flame went up,
and a torch of fire that passed over and consumed the portions of his sacrifices.
Great wonder fell suddenly upon his mind,
and he marvelled how ordered was the course of his sacrifice.
The power of the Creator gave him wisdom to know the mystery of the revelations,
so that he would know that the time of the things he had seen was far off.
Now that the sequence of the written words is complete,
let us turn and recount the force of the meaning hidden in the words.

I have heard the words that Moses set down in the book he wrote,
and the words were covered by words as by a garment.
A garment of words was spread over the words of the Spirit,
and I sought to know the reason they were covered.
That they were not plain made me seek to search out what is in them,
that I might know, and make known to my friends, meditations on spiritual things.
Come, hearer, hear the meaning of Abram's sacrifice,
and look and see how lofty are the kinds of the sacrifices.
By three animals he taught him to know the enslavement of his seed,
and through their enslavement he showed him the order of the number of the tribes.
Into twelve tribes this seed of the righteous man would be divided,
and beforehand he divided it through the division of the three animals.
For three generations it would be enslaved by foreigners,
and he depicted for him the labour of its toil in mute creatures.
In its youth it would be yoked under the yoke of slaves,
and for this reason he commanded him to sacrifice a three-year-old heifer.
By sacrifices it would honour the name of the Creator,
and he made his sacrifice a guide before the generations.
Under the name of animals he mingled for him the kinds of mercy,
and depicted a type for him, that he might clearly see his Lord's sign.
The whole order of the Law he depicted for him in his sacrifices:
in sheep and ox, in turtledove and young pigeon.
From the animals he taught him three trials,
and from the birds two, fulfilled in their names.
By the creatures that walk on the earth he showed him its labour in the house of foreigners,
and by the winged ones he revealed to him that it would be lifted out of servitude.
By the turtledove he depicted for him the life of the wilderness,
and by the young pigeon its rest in the land of the Canaanites.
By the lover of the wilderness he was teaching him of the wilderness outside,
and by the young pigeon of the peace in which it would lead peoples and cities.
For this reason he did not divide them when they were sacrificed,
because the people was not mingled with the nations, whether in the wilderness or in peace.
While Abram guarded the bodies from harm,
he was contemplating his Lord's help toward his offspring.
By the bird he named the harmfulness of the Egyptians,

and showed that the power of his help would be stronger than the Egyptians.
That servitude in the house of the Egyptians he depicted and showed him,
and for this reason he set each part opposite its fellow.
They could not help one another;
on this enslavement the One who knows all was looking.
And beforehand he likened three generations to three animals.
At the close of the day he showed him the time when they would be redeemed:
when they were worn out, then they would be freed from servitude.
By the acceptance of his sacrifice the redemption of his seed was made known to him,
in that fire consumed his sacrifices with favour.
By the fire he showed him how bright the redemption of his seed would be,
for before the eyes of all it would be freed from servitude.
Two things he depicted for him in the vision of the torch:
the freedmen of his people and the harsh taskmasters of the Egyptians.
In the brightness of the fire he saw the acceptance of his sacrifices,
and in the smoke the violence of the oppressors.
With discernment he watched how, as though without discrimination,
it gladdened and it distressed the two sides.
With favour it consumed the sacrifice of Abram,
and thus it passed from one to the other like one who discerns.
The righteous man too was astonished and amazed at this discernment,
how it discerned and how it kept order in its eating.
Moses said that amazement fell upon Abraham,
because his mind was led to look upon distant things.
Distant were the things he saw through the revelation,
and for this reason he was astonished and amazed.
The voice of the revelation gave him wisdom to perceive hidden things,
so that he would know that the vision was true and its time far off.
"Know for certain," the Lord said to his servant,
"that your seed will be a sojourner in the house of foreigners.

"Four hundred years," he says, "it will be a slave to slaves,
and from enslavement to its equals it will learn my lordship.
I, even I, have inscribed the name of servitude among earthly beings,
and set it as the yoke of Shem, son of the free, upon Ham the slave.
By that servitude with which the righteous man subjected the despised Ham,
by it I will yoke your seed, as if it were not in my service.
In this way I set the name of servitude on the earth,
to make known my lordship, that I am Lord of slaves and of free.
Upon Shem I set the honoured name by the mouth of the righteous man,
and in Ham I yoked under the yoke of my lordship all that is made.
Behold, I have marked out for you, Abram my friend, a fair road:
travel rightly by the things revealed toward the things hidden.
Behold, I have shown you the servitude of your seed and the freedom of your seed,
that by both of them it may learn the order of slaves and of free.
Through trial I teach it the kinds of my commandments,
that it may know how to keep order between me and man.
In the furnace of servitude I test the inclination of its soul,
that in its labours it may seek provisions that will give it rest.
For three generations it will be a slave to the slave of slaves,
and the fourth will loose from it the yoke of its labour."
With these words the Lord confirmed Abram his servant,
and then showed him kinds of revelations greater than this.
Greater is a sight seen by the eyes than words,
as much as the light of the sun is brighter than darkness.
For those words that were spoken at the time of the sacrifices
were as far from the events as a great mountain.
In this revelation an open vision was made known,
and it carried new tidings of conception and child.
At the time of noon this revelation was made known,
at the hour when the light of the sun is at its strongest.
With the eyes of the body the righteous man saw the vision,
gazing by a light upon the Lord of light.
Three likenesses of three men the righteous man saw,
and they walked in keeping with the likenesses they had put on.

As at men Abraham too looked at them,
and did not know that it was a sight without composition.
Without composition is the nature of spiritual beings, and without body,
and when they are sent to earthly beings they show a body.
They do not truly acquire a body in their change,
but show an uncompounded likeness in the air.
Great power they possess in their creation from the Hidden Power,
and by that very power they show the power of the Godhead.
His power moves with his designs as far as he wills,
and beyond everything among the powers on high he wrought this:
He composed spirit without compounding it, by the Spirit of revelation,
and came in to Abram in three bodily likenesses.
Three men he suddenly saw coming to meet him,
and he was very eager and received them as men.
With great love he went out to meet them, as befitted their greatness,
in the same manner in which all his life he had received men.
As men the righteous Abram received them,
and then he was made wise that they were not men but spirit.
The spiritual beings put on a bodily form,
and came in to the servant to announce to him new tidings.
The Lord and his servants came in to the servant who loved his Lord,
and they were clothed in the likeness of servants and of the Maker.
The likeness of a servant the God of all was to take,
and beforehand he depicted what was to come through Abraham.
From Abraham he was to set mankind free,
and by what he did he trod a path for what was to come.
The Word, the Offspring of the Father, was to take a man,
and call him by his own name [?]: God, King and Lord.
A visible body he was to make the dwelling of his love,
and in it, in bodily likeness, he came in to Abram.
He knew the seed of Abram, that it was contentious,
and beforehand, by his entering in, he cut off the excuse of its inclination.
He was persuading those who say, "How can a man become God?"

and he showed this in the form of a body, the body that gladdened Abram.
In a human body Abraham saw God;
it was not a body, but in a manner that resembled a body.
It was not a body that the righteous man saw, as he thought he saw,
but a body resembling a body, though there was no body.
Abraham too was divided in mind in this way:
was it a body that appeared to him, or was it not a body?
His faith made the righteous man righteous,
and he saw the Hidden One in a visible body and believed that he is.
He saw three who were clothed in one form,
and he left the two and spoke with one as with the Lord.
"My Lord," the righteous Abram called the righteous Lord,
and begged him to come in to him as to his servant.
The Creator, too, heard his request as he pleaded,
and came in with his servants to depict a bodily type.
In a human body he was reconciling all things to his majesty,
and he led two spirits with him and came in to his servant.
The sentence that was given in Paradise he now annulled,
and reconciled to himself the heavenly and the earthly.
All of them together he brought with him to Abraham's house,
and seated them at supper with his majesty.
Heaven and earth he invited and called to Abraham's house,
to show them the greatness of his love toward man.
The greatness of his love he revealed to spiritual and bodily beings
by that entrance in which he came in with his servants to his intimate.
The wall of enmity between himself and man he loosed in the house of a man,
and he called the heavenly beings as witnesses at the door of a man.
At the door of a man they too became lovers of man,
and rejoiced that there was one equality for them and for man.
One equality the Creator made for all, all together,

and seated them at the supper that Abram made.
He with his own came in to his own, hidden from all,
and heaven and earth were astonished with wonder at him.
Rational and mute beings were amazed, in speech and in silence,
seeing that he who has no limit was reclining on the earth.
O the spiritual and bodily table-fellowship,
at which the Lord and his servants reclined in one equality!
O the meal that was prepared in Abraham's house,
and was eaten and yet not eaten by those who ate it!
O how great was that arrangement which the righteous man made,
that his food sufficed for heavenly and earthly beings!
Heaven and earth reclined in the house of the righteous man:
the God of all, who is without limit, and his own within limit.
That order which is kept on high he revealed to Abram
by that meal at which he reclined with spirits.
In the Son of Abram he was to set bounds to the will of his love,
and he revealed this in the great love he showed to Abram.
His great love he showed to the righteous man when he came in to him,
and depicted for him a type of distant things through near ones.
At the end of times he will be, in love, all in all,
and he showed this by his love for Abram, the friend of love.
The house of the father of nations was made a second heaven,
and earthly and heavenly beings dwelt in it.
A new thing that had never been happened suddenly in Abraham's house,
and the spiritual beings marvelled at it with the greatness of its wonder.

At the greatness of its wonder the powers on high were amazed:
"What is this that the Hidden One has done in the house of earthly beings?
We have not seen this happen since the day we came to be,
nor have we heard that the Being showed himself to his servants.
Behold, it is some thousands of years, less a little, until now,
and he has not told us of the hidden greatness of his love."
For the sake of man the Lover of man revealed his love to us,
and more than to any man he showed this to Abraham.
Two spirits he chose out of all for his ministry,
and they came in to Abram in the likeness of visible men.
As men Abraham too received them,
and he paid honour to the form that appeared.
Fine flour and a calf, milk and butter he prepared and made ready,
thinking that these befitted the ways of love.
The Creator too in love accepted the goodwill of his love,
knowing that this helps earthly beings.
O that Power which heaven and earth cannot contain,
which bounded itself, though not bounded, for the sake of man!
For the sake of man he came in to a man whose name was Abram,
and ate and drank, he who is a stranger to food and drink.
His Word was to take one of mankind
and accomplish by his hands what is to come at the end of times.
He was making that Son of Man one with his love,
and inscribed human things in his divinity.
That Son of Man would make use of food and drink,
and beforehand he ate, that by his eating he might confirm his bodily nature.
In body and soul the Son of Abraham was being formed,
and in his father's house he was clothed in the kinds of limbs.
Abraham too was examining his bodily nature:
was what he saw a body, or not a body?
And he also reckoned, in the childlike understanding of that time,
that even spirits need human food in order to live.
Perhaps this too was reckoned as human;
and for his love's sake he did this, though he did not do it.
For he did not do it, nor is it done, nor does it exist at all,

because the Being is higher than bodily likenesses.
His nature has none of the natural properties of earthly beings,
and it was not bounded, nor is it bounded, by the work of his hands.
He has no limit that confines him within his limit,
for he is outside all and beyond all, and all is on this side of him.
In love he shows the hiddenness of his love to the lover of his love,
to stir zeal in the lovers of his love, that they may gaze upon him.
In Abram he fixed the sign of his love before the seers,
that they might see the Hidden One in the visible, while not seeing.
In love Abraham too saw him, while not seeing him,
and his own voice bears witness that no man sees him and lives.
Abram did not see the One hidden from all, O sons of Abraham!
See that you do not err and lead people astray on account of Abram.
Abram was righteous, and his love was true indeed,
and yes, he truly saw likenesses without composition.
Without composition he saw a sight that cannot be comprehended,
and him who is without limit he beheld in a likeness that cannot be likened.
This is the custom of the God of all, to act thus,
because created beings cannot see his divinity.
In this likeness he was shown for twenty generations,
and in the tenth he decreed the sentence and destroyed all.
From Noah he began again in peace toward mankind,
and turned and counted ten generations up to Abram.
In Abram he completed twenty generations of the human race,
and began to show kinds of calm and kindness.
In a calm vision he revealed his will to the friend of his love,
and kindly spoke with him according to his mind.
In his speaking with him the sentences of decreed judgment were abolished:
the transgression of the command, the destruction by waters, and the division of speech.
To him alone he gave a promise that would not prove false,
that through his seed the peoples would turn to the fear of the truth.
With this thought he lowered himself to come in to him,
and came in without coming in, because his nature enters into nothing.
The nature of his Being is not bounded in any place,
since there is no limit to his eternity, which has no beginning.
Without beginning or end, he wholly is, and is;
and how shall one say what he is? For the speech of whoever speaks falls short.

By his word I too have said what I have said,
and my mind cannot grasp the limit of what I have said.
I have said that it is written that the Creator came into Abraham's house;
it was not within a bounded limit, but in a vision.
In the vision of a man Abram, a man, saw God,
and received him in his house as a man who could be seen.
I said that he received him as a man, not in his nature,
for in no way can the eye see the Godhead.
Not his nature did Abraham see in the vision he saw,
but a mystery that was spoken in the body that was to come from him.
Through the body that was from him he was turning all to the knowledge of him,
and beforehand he announced to him the tidings that fill man with life.
The life of man was hidden from all in the God of all,
and he revealed it to the eyes of all creatures through Abraham.
All creation gazed upon the vision of Abram,
and was not sated with seeing the sight that cannot be seen.
Rational and mute were amazed, in speech and in silence:
"What is this, that the world is gathered to Abram's house?"
The rational beings were the more amazed at this wonder,
since they possess a mind to gaze clearly upon things not revealed.
With them he who orders all made a partnership in the mystery of his revelation,
because they are faithful to keep the mystery between him and them.
For it was a mystery hidden from all creatures,
and he revealed it to two rational natures, the Watchers and man.
To two Watchers and one man he revealed his will,
and showed them in mystery the mystery of his hiddenness.
The mystery of his love was to be revealed through a Son of Man,
and for this reason he led spirits with him and came in to Abram.
That entrance was a wonder, and exceedingly wondrous,
and though it was revealed, it was not revealed to those who saw it.
Neither did the spirits perceive the force of its meaning,
nor did Abraham know what it was or concerning whom.
Its appearance alone they beheld, in a human way,
but its meaning they could not approach.
The will of the Hidden One was instructing the servants of the Hidden One,
that they should not wear themselves out seeking the Hidden One who cannot be comprehended.

By the power of His will they were searching without being sated,
and they did not cease from pursuing inquiry concerning Him.
The bonds of love were pressing upon the mind within them:
when would the hidden sign bring forth the power of its hiddenness?
The Watchers and Abram longed to understand the matter,
and were waiting to see something according to their desire.
In this desire both their sides were worn out:
what is this, that He was bounded though He is not bounded,
and entered with an invisible appearance into his house?
Why did He accept that every kind of feast be prepared for Him,
when the nature of His being does not receive bodily things?
Behold, without food He sustains by His power even our nature;
how then did He do this which He did? It is wholly a wonder.
The word that Moses spoke is full of great wonder:
that the Lord of creation was being nourished by His creatures.
The word that the son of the Hebrews spoke cannot be spoken:
that the Being who is above all reclined on earth with His creation.
Abraham set out visible kinds of food for the Invisible One,
and who would not marvel that food enters one who is without composition?
With their senses and their stirrings the beholders too were searching,
and though they were seeing, they were not truly seeing.
What took place in Abraham's house did not take place in literal truth,
but in a mystery that cannot be spoken by speakers.
The nature of Being cannot be spoken by speakers;
so what was spoken did not happen as it was spoken.
For they are words without composition that Moses wrote,
and they were composite, yet not composite in a bodily way.
It was not a body that Abram refreshed with food and drink,
but an appearance that was formed without a body.
It was not a body that had bodily hands,
but a Spirit whose power is finer than spirits.
The kinds of food were not being swallowed by the senses,

but the bodily food was vanishing into the air.
For it was a divine power that did these things,
He for whom it is a simple matter to fashion all things out of nothing.
He gratified Abram by what He did in Abram's house,
so as to fulfil with him the promises of His words through deeds:
the turning of the nations, which He had promised him through his seed;
and He showed Himself to him as far as a man is able to see.
The one who was made could not see his Maker,
and therefore He depicted likenesses before his doors.
They were likenesses that Abram saw with the eyes of the body,
not exact likenesses, but a semblance.
For everything that happened in that revelation was semblance:
the appearance of a man, the speech of a man, and the food of a man.
It was the God of all who did this wisely,
as His power is wont to act in all generations.
He came to visit the creation He had made, through Abraham,
and showed it His love in that same form in which He showed it to Adam.
Great love He showed to Adam within Paradise,
and because Adam strayed from His love he died through sin, and he and his children were condemned.
He came to repay Adam's debt in Abraham's house,
and put on the semblance of that form of the region of Eden.
The commandment that had been made void by that eating passed away,
and death began to be scattered through the conception of Isaac.
Two died in Eden by eating the fruit, Eve and Adam,
and two He revived on the day of revelation, Sarah and Abram.
For Sarah and Abraham were dead in the barrenness of the body,
like that death of Eve and Adam through eating the fruit.
Abraham heard the good news of the resurrection of all
in that voice: "Sarah your wife shall have a child."
That voice which called to Adam, "You shall be dust,"
is the one that called to Abram, "Behold, I revive the deadness of your body."
The whole race of Adam came to life in Abraham,

because through his seed the nations turn to the Creator.
The turning of the nations was being sown in the vision of Abram,
and great peace between the Creator and His creatures.
Great peace filled the house of the father of all,
and heaven and earth were serving at his feast.
The Lord of creation reclined at the head of His hosts,
and the companies on high were at peace with the earthly ones.
All rejoiced with all at the wedding feast of love,
and created natures were praising the name of the Maker.
"Praised be the Creator!" the spiritual beings cried out in Abraham's house,
"who has shown His love and made us at peace with Him, and us with all."
Worthy of praise is He by whose bound the worlds are bounded,
who humbled Himself and reclined with us at table.
To Him heaven and earth owe one thanksgiving,
for He proclaimed to us the words of peace when they had not sought Him.
O how great a new thing the Lord of creation has done:
that He who bounds all bounded Himself in one place!
O that power which holds all by a sign of its power,
which showed itself like a poor man before its creation!
O that treasure from whose gift the worlds are fed,
which asked alms of a member of its household like a beggar!
Abram offered the alms of love to the One who sustains all,
and He repaid him with a child as his reward, one who gives life to humankind.
The life of humankind was hidden in Isaac, Abram's child,
and was handed on from one to another like a pledge.
Generation to generation handed down Abram's pledge,
until it reached the generation of Him who is the beginning of our life.
The beginning of life was to be shown forth from our humanity,
and He sowed it beforehand through the revelation He showed to Abram.
This is the cause of the whole story we have told,
and in it the first things and the last are bound together.
This is the bound by which worlds and generations are bounded,
and within it is enclosed the structure of height and depth.

Paul testifies that everything is enclosed in the law,
and that the end of that law is Christ, who bounds all.
It is Christ who was spoken of in Abraham's house,
and in the mystery of His peace the Lord was reclining with His creatures.
This peace, which came at the end through one from humankind,
He depicted beforehand at that supper in Abraham's house.
That deathless delight which is on high
is what the Lord and His servants made among the earthly ones.
In the haven of peace the Hidden One settles all with all,
and He gave a pledge of what is to come in this which took place.
Behold, all these things came from the Lord of all through Abraham;
come, let us examine closely the cause that lies in them.
Behold, the hidden Being has trodden a path to travel to His appointed meeting;
come, let us learn wisdom to keep the order of hidden things.
Behold, He has revealed and shown us the greatness of His love through a man;
come, let us hasten to bind our love to His will.
Behold, He has willed and called us to delight in His glories,
and given us a type in the food that He ate in Abraham's house.
Abram prepared bodily food for the Bodiless One,
and it was said that He ate, though He did not eat, because of His love.
That He did not eat, rational and mute beings bear witness to us,
in that they are persuaded that the Hidden Nature is without composition.
He did not reveal His nature in the revelation to His servant;
He made His servant wise, that he might look to the goal of His love.
He called Abraham a good lover because of his love,
and taught him to keep the order of love toward his Creator.
Many times He tested the righteous man, though He knew him,
so that the generations to come might know the kinds of his testing.
He promised him a child, gave him a child, and confirmed His words;
then He turned and asked that the child become a sacrifice for the fragrance of His will:
"I desire that you offer me a sacrifice, Abram, my lover;
satisfy my will with the sacrifice of your son, whom you love.
By trial I have learned your love, that you are a good lover,
and that the comfort of those you love is far sweeter to you than your own self.
The food of your love was sweeter to me than anyone's,
as I found by trial at that feast within your house.

In that feast I openly revealed my delight before the eyes of the spiritual beings,
and now, between me and you, I wish you to satisfy my will.
A great mystery has been hidden in me from eternity, together with my Godhead,
and I am preparing to reveal it now between me and your love.
Something has been laid up with me from the beginning that has no beginning,
and I hasten to show it to you as to a friend.
My mind prepares a new creation, which I shall create a second time,
and I call you to partnership in fashioning it.
Through a man I will accomplish the hidden purpose of my will,
and I will make Him the one mediator between me and humankind.
Through His mediation I will show my love before the eyes of all creatures,
so that the first creation and the children may live by that ordering [?].
In the image of man I revealed my hiddenness in the beginning, when I created:
that I am, and that there are three Persons in one nature.
By this nature, which was not made by craftsmanship,
I named the image of man when I fashioned it.
For his sake I created all things, hidden and visible,
and set him as steward over my works.
Through him even now I complete my love in deeds,
and renew the creation that has grown old in mortality.
Death corrupted the beauty of my creation because of man,
and through a man I renew all things along with man.
To put the demons [?] to shame [?] I accomplish what I have said,
so that they may not boast that they overpowered my strength through Adam's errors.
Through Adam himself I show them the authority of my lordship,
and through one condemned I crush them, to show how low they are.
They condemned to death Adam, the image that depicted my hiddenness,
and through death I loose from him the yoke of death.
Sin made death a death over mortals,
and through mortality I quench it from mortals.
By the counsel of the evil one, sin and death gained dominion,
and it does not please me that my creatures should be slaves of others' slaves.
All that exist are mine, rational and mute,

and I do not neglect the creation that my hands have made.
From nothing I created everything, as befits me,
and now I renew it with something, so that it may never perish again.
In man I sealed that creation which came to be in the beginning,
and through a man I renew all things along with man.
From you, Abram, I choose this man,
because of the love you have shown me above all who have ever been.
I call you the father of humankind, of all who have been and will be,
because you loved me and hated the errors of the Chaldeans.
I make your son lord and king over my creatures,
so that everyone may know that the name I give you is true and chosen.
I have called you, Abram, father of nations among the earthly ones,
and through the child who comes from you I seal your name with deeds.
Through the child who comes from you I fulfil all my will,
and as in a temple I make rational and mute beings dwell in him.
I make your child, Abram, the temple of my kingdom,
and through him I receive the worship of love from all creatures.
Through him the creation I made from nothing worships me,
and I give him the honoured name, the name of my Godhead."
These things the Voice [?] spoke with Abraham,
not openly, but in a mystery that cannot be spoken.
The mystery of hiddenness cannot be spoken by the mouths of speakers,
and though it was very difficult, He spoke these things with Abraham.
The Hidden One, who cannot be spoken, spoke with Abraham,
and taught him the order by which he was to offer Him the sacrifice of his son:
"A sacrifice of love I ask of you, my lover;
offer it to me as the order of love requires.
I am to take the pledge of peace from his offspring;
tread a path for him by a sacrifice in mystery, for the sacrifice of truth.
I know your seed, that it is given to reproach,
and they will reproach me when I fulfil my will through your Son.
By a sacrifice without blood I rebuke their contentiousness,

so that they may not reproach me when the sacrifice of truth is performed.
Take, then, your son Isaac, your child whom you love,
and make him a burnt offering for me on the mountain of which I will tell you."
O voice, how beloved it was, and how hard!
It was spoken, and yet not spoken as it truly was.
It was beloved in love, according to the divine command,
and very hard for the weakness of human nature.
To one who was weak by nature the Lord of nature gave strength,
to make known that he could overcome his nature through love of his Lord.
Abraham's Lord made him a furnace of testing,
and in him human weakness was tested and gained strength.
The mind of this son of mortals gained great strength,
and though he was mortal, in his mind he became immortal.
O mortal one, who forgot the nature of his mortality,
and trampled with his will the hard afflictions of mortality!
O sufferer, who brought his sufferings under his mind,
and drove them on in the arena of his endurance!
O patient one, who reined himself in as with a bridle,
and subdued the sufferings of his body and the stirrings of his soul!
O mind, wholly yoked to labours,
that threw off the weight of its sufferings as though it were not yoked!
O how his nature was bridled within him by the stance of silence,
so that he was still and silent from the course of headlong running!
Did his mind not ponder, as it was wont to do:
"What is this new thing that the God of all has asked of me?"
Did the stirrings of his soul not give birth to all kinds of thoughts:
"When has a man ever offered a man as a sacrifice to the Hidden One?"
A hidden power strengthened the mind of the one endowed with mind,
and he did not falter in the contest of the sufferings of body and soul.
The sweetness of the love with which he loved his Lord pressed upon nature,
and took the taste from the bitterness, the bitterness with which natures are mixed.
O you, Abram, good lover of faith,

who forgot the beloved things that nature holds dear!
Rightly, then, did He choose you, He who chose you out of all peoples,
and made you head of all who imitate the affection of your love.
Out of love for his Lord the zealous one fulfilled his Lord's will,
and led his son to go to the place that had been shown to him.
In a distant place the voice commanded him to make his sacrifice,
so that he might be proven before the eyes of earthly and heavenly beings.
Before the eyes of all creatures he was showing the endurance of his soul:
how strong it was, and how it did not falter in the toil of his journey.
Three days he travelled, keeping silent, without wavering,
and did not reveal the mystery of his Lord's will to his household.
From everyone he hid the mystery between himself and his Lord,
and not even to Sarah did he reveal the intention of his mind.
Between himself and his Lord he kept his Lord's mysteries hidden,
so that the truth of his love might be wholly true to the Lord who had chosen him.
His Lord's command was more precious to him than anything,
and he shaped his own will according to His will.
By this will the stirrings of his soul were bound,
and he waited for what would be at the end of his journey.
The count of his journey, three days, was completed,
and he raised his eyes and saw the place, and rejoiced to meet it.
With the eyes of the body He showed him the place of his son's sacrifice,
and in the mind He revealed to him the type of what was to come.
The sacrifice of truth was to take place in the place of the mystery,
and He showed him the place, so that the mystery might hand over to the truth.
In this place Christ was to be the sacrifice,
and He sowed it beforehand in the mystical sacrifice, before the deeds.
For the sacrifice of Isaac was a mystery of that of Christ,
and it was most fitting that sacrifice should resemble sacrifice.
The power of the Creator was shaping the purpose of His love,
so that those who heard the words might not be divided over the deeds.
With this intention came the journey of three days,
so that sacrifice might bear witness to sacrifice, and type to truth.

Abraham, too, set his mind on this goal,
and his soul found rest at the place of the sacrifice that his Lord had shown him.
At the place of sacrifice he fulfilled his own will and his Lord's will:
he built an altar, arranged the wood, and bound his son.
He drew the knife, and with the knife he drew out his will,
and the voice stopped him, that he should hold back his hand from his beloved.
"Abram, Abram!" the spiritual one called to the bodily one,
"hold back your hand and refrain from slaying your son as a sacrifice.
Refrain from the sacrifice of human blood that I asked of you,
and take and offer me silent blood instead of speaking blood.
I do not want human blood at this time,
for it is not able to blot out with its blood the bond of debts.
The debt of humankind is not repaid by human blood
until there comes from humanity a perfect man.
I know the time that is drawing near to perfection,
and I do not forget when a man will redeem humankind.
I have revealed to you, Abram, the redemption of humankind by means of a sacrifice,
so that all may know to watch for the time of humankind's redemption.
In this, towards you, I have trodden a path for what is to come,
so that humankind may travel to the appointed goal of the hope of death's abolition.
For this reason I devised occasions and asked for a sacrifice:
to reveal to humankind the hidden purpose of my will towards humankind.
Through you, Abraham, I have revealed to creatures my will, which is over all;
hear, and grow wise, and make humankind wise from your wisdom.
But do not think that I have rejected your sacrifice as imperfect;
behold, I grant you to fulfil my will with the sacrifice of a lamb.
I give you a mute lamb instead of a speaking one,
and by a silent one I teach you the kinds of sacrifices.
Three sacrifices I ask you to offer me:
two speaking and one silent, type and truth.
In type I have received the death of Isaac, in the place of the truth,
and instead of Isaac the silent blood of the quiet lamb.
Behold, I have charged you to keep the order of the fulfilment of the times;
I have fulfilled your desire by the sacrifice of the time: wait for the time."
By a revelation of the Spirit He signalled to him to look at the top of a tree,

and suddenly they saw a lamb hanging there, in the mystery of the Crucified.
And in the marvel that was being worked for Abram,
the kinds of its likenesses were strange beside all other likenesses.
All the lambs on earth graze on the ground,
but Abram's lamb was being fed at the top of a tree.
At the top of the tree hung the lamb that was shown to him,
and instead of nails the branches of the wood were fixed in its body.
The type of the Crucified was set in the likeness of the truth,
and the whole of it was fastened all over, as if for death.
The death of the Cross was to be the loosener of death,
and He hung the lamb at the top of the tree to proclaim His death.
And if one should ask what the reason was for the lamb on the wood,
and who hung it there, outside the order of the kinds of dumb beasts,
for dumb beasts are wont to roam the earth unaided [?],
and what is this, that it alone was hanging on the wood:
that it did not bind itself to the wood is plain,
and that another bound it and hung it there is not true.
The truth bears witness, and its truth does not lie,
that a hidden sign hung it on the tree in the mystery of the Cross.
The Lover of our race showed us beforehand the mystery of our Redeemer,
so that when He redeems us we should not marvel at how He redeemed us.
By the death of a man the children of Adam were to be redeemed,
and He depicted beforehand the mystery of our redemption in the death of a lamb.
John, too, called the Redeemer of our race a Lamb,
because He was to redeem our life by the sacrifice of His death.
From among lambs was the lamb that redeemed Isaac's life,
and from among humankind was the man who by His death redeemed humankind.
The silent one who delivered Isaac trod the path of His death,
and this is what He said: "Abram saw me and rejoiced on the day of my death."
Abraham saw the day of His death, not that he saw it with his eyes,
but he saw the day of His death through revelation.
His death was hidden in the death of the lamb that Abram sacrificed,
and in the redemption won by its slaughter lies the life of every person.
And if someone says that the discourse I have spoken is a mere composition of words,
then let him speak something of his own, and I will accept it;
let him show me, from the Scriptures, the power of the meaning of their words,

and I will grant him that he was right to blame me as a fool.
No, O man! It is not foolishly that these things are written,
nor did I invent from my own mind the meaning and the power within them.
My thoughts have looked to the goal of the Scriptures,
and from reading them I learned to speak about their meaning.
I did not establish my words on a type that is untrue,
but on mysteries that look very plainly toward the truth.
The truth bears witness that my word has not strayed from the truth,
and I have not exchanged the truth of its words for false words.
From the truth itself I learned to speak the discourse about it,
and I gave my mind to be its disciple, as to a master.
I am a disciple of the books of the Spirit, which the Spirit wrote,
and I hold it true that my mind has not strayed from what is written.
Trusting in the power within them I have followed after them,
and through their help I have gained help to speak words.
The words within them have been my meditation all my life,
and it does not please me to cease from their study or neglect it.
By experience I have come to know the meditation within them,
how abundant is the meaning of the words of their interpretations.
I have received a good loan from them, with which I trade,
and I do not cease to repay its kindness, if only in words.
I am eager to repay my teachers' kindness with words,
lest I be found guilty as one who borrowed and defrauded.
I am a debtor, and I do not deny the debt of my debts,
and I strive to repay in words instead of deeds.
I saw that the words of the books cost their readers toil,
and I sought to know what the cause of this toil might be.

A longing stirred me to toil with them in the labour they contain,
and to learn well the power of the meaning that is within them.
The power of their meaning drew me on to become their companion in discourse,
and to occupy my life with the good meditation that gives life.
The power of the Spirit interpreted them through the mouth of the flesh,
so that beings of flesh might meditate on spiritual things.
This meditation drew even me, weak in thought,
so that I occupied my mind with words full of the meditation of words.
In the book of Moses I saw that this subject was taken up,
and it was set down so that whoever meditates on it might meditate on it again.
The story of the righteous was placed in it as in a treasury,
and better than all of them was the story taken up of the family of Abram.
The story of Abram stirred in me a longing for this story,
and from his account I cried out in entreaty to seek what is hidden.
About hidden things a thought came to me, to search out
what the reason is that words are hidden from those who speak them.
Why are they not open, as open as the power within them,
so that the mind would run [?] to uncover what is not open?
If the power of their meaning were as easy as their reading,
everyone would readily love the meditation of excellent things.
The One who knows all knows for what benefit He did this,
that He hid the power of the words of the Spirit beyond understanding.
He honoured learning and magnified it in the sight of learners,
so that the eyes of the flesh would not despise it for being open.
Whatever is revealed to fleshly sight is despised,
and whatever is hidden from beholders is honoured and loved.
This is the reason for the hiddenness of spiritual words,
and by their hiddenness the power that interpreted them is magnified.
The power of the Spirit interpreted them through the mouth of bodily beings,
and therefore their meanings are not easy for the hearing to grasp.
It is very hard for the tongue of flesh to speak in the Spirit,
just as the nature of mortals is alien to the Immortal.
The Immortal was destined to take on the nature of mortals,
and He chose Abram and made him the head of new life.
In the son of Abraham all things together were being renewed,
and in Abraham himself He depicted a figure of what would come about in his son.
For this Abraham too was longing:

to see in his son the vision of the renewal of humankind.
Abraham saw the renewal of humankind in the sacrifice of his son,
who died without dying and depicted a figure of death and life.
He was counted as dead from the moment his father bound him,
and he lived in a mystery by the will of the God of all.
It pleased the God of all, and He asked that he become a sacrifice;
then He accepted his sacrifice as though it had taken place.
Not out of regret did the One who knows all do this,
that He asked for a sacrifice, then turned back and said, "I do not want it."
It was not the proof of Abram's love that He learned, as it is written,
nor was it His own need He sought to fill when He asked for a sacrifice.
He knew Abram and all things before anything existed,
and there is nothing among the works that were and are that He does not know.
The works He made within His bounds bear witness to Him,
and He is within all and outside all, without bound.
Let no one, then, think in a simple way
that He asked Abraham for the sacrifice of his son because He did not know.
He did not learn the love of the righteous man, as is supposed;
He taught humankind to acquire a love like Abram's.
For the sake of humankind He did all that He brought upon Abraham,
and for the sake of humankind He chose him out of humankind and called him His friend.
To humankind He showed the mystery of the renewal that will come at the end,
so that they might reflect on what was to come at some time.
What was to come He showed in the death of Abraham's son:
that through the death of one man humankind lives.
By two deaths human beings die, and by two they live:
one in the baptism of the mystery, and one in reality.
In a mystery Isaac died, and in a mystery he lived,
and he depicted for us the death of baptism and the life that comes from it.
The death of truth our Saviour died at the place of the Skull,
and the life of truth He lived in reality and gave life to all.
So we die both in mystery and in truth,
and we are destined to live the incorruptible life of truth.
For Christ, it says, has risen from the grave and dies no more:

then the whole of nature rose with the Son of its kind.
The nature of Adam is one in all who belong to Adam,
and if a portion of it has risen, the whole of it has risen.
He brought us up with Him to where He ascended, Paul said,
and if this is true, our whole nature ascends there.
Our old man, it says, was crucified with Him;
so we have died with Him, and we live with Him, and we reign with Him.
With Him in death, with Him in life, and with Him in glory —
who, then, can separate us from His company?
If God is for us, as it is written,
who can hinder the salvation of our lives?
The Creator Himself swore by His own self to His friend Abram:
"In you shall all the peoples over whom My name is called be blessed."
See, He fulfilled in deeds His words to Abram,
and the nations became sons of Abraham, as had been promised.
By this hope all the peoples were held bound,
and they waited for when they would become sons of Abraham.
The sons stumbled over the story of Abram,
and did not want the nations to become brothers to his seed.
The envy of this thought the Seer of all saw,
and He rebuked them through the change of Abram's name.
Abram was called the father of one people only,
and after a time He called him Abraham, father of nations.
The first name his father gave him was lowly and small,
and for this reason his Shepherd changed his name.
With the Creator's name the Creator called the son of the Chaldeans,
because He was going to raise his seed to the height of His name.
He was going to give an honoured name to the son of Abraham,
and beforehand He honoured Abraham's name with the name of the One to come.
Because of his offspring the Lord of Abram honoured Abram,
so that he would know that the blessing was not his own.
The peoples of the earth were not blessed in him and in his children
until One of his seed came and blessed humankind.

With soul and body let us sing praise with our whole humanity
to the One who made us worthy to praise the name of His majesty.
In these things let us occupy our soul with an occupation that never has its fill,
and give our impulses no room to wander in confusion.
Confusion is the wandering of earthly desires;
let us not be stirred by them, lest we be condemned with the guilty.
The night of bodily desires has passed,
and the light of the life of immortal beings has dawned.
As in the light let us show our soul to the eyes of those who see,
and let them give thanks with us to the One by whose light we see light.
The great light is the dawning of our Lord, who dawned upon the earth
and drove away the error of idolatry from earthly beings.
Come, earthly beings, look and examine in the fear of truth
how His light is brighter than the luminary that gives light to the earth.
Light and fire our Lord also called His preaching,
and by it earthly and heavenly beings were enlightened.
See, the world has been lit by the great light of the Creator's name;
let us abide in His light, so that we are not cast into the darkness outside.
On the divine revelations that came to the fathers and the prophets

Second memra / For the Second Sunday of the Annunciation / On the divine revelations that came to the fathers and the prophets / Response / Blessed is he who teaches us, guides us and makes us his own, my brothers:

The Creator fashioned the images of his revelations in the mind of man, / and men began to fashion spiritual images. / He set life in a nature full of mortality, / and in their thoughts they gained a life that does not die. / In their thoughts he spoke with them as with beings of flesh, / and taught them to meditate on his hidden things. / Spiritually he showed them the ways of his will, / so that through things revealed they might see things not revealed. / Things not revealed he revealed to their nature from the beginning, / and made them wise to perceive the power of his greatness. / The power of his greatness he revealed in the moulding of Adam's clay, / and taught him to tell the manner in which his formation was composed. / From dust was the composition of the son of dust, / and once he was composed, he breathed into him a spiritual soul. / Of himself Adam spoke concerning the forming of the rib taken from him, / and began to say that from him came the portion of Eve. / By the spirit of revelation the learner learned this; / it was not in his own power to tell a cause hidden from him. / Hidden from him was the mystery of the salvation of his body and his soul, / yet from the way he was fashioned he gained discernment to see himself. / With the eye of the spirit he gazed at his nature, how it is constituted, / and praised, magnified and thanked the one who had fashioned him. / Behold the beginning of the work of the spirit of revelation, / by which the Lord began to reveal his love to earthly beings,

to teach them how greatly he loves the race of man. / The tenderness of his love he showed to man through his revelations, / and though he is hidden, he spoke with him in the ways of his hiddenness. / A power from him spoke with that hidden mind within them, / and they began to speak spiritually after his likeness. / In two likenesses he spoke with them, in body and in spirit, / according to their nature, which is both bodily and spiritual. / To the house of Abraham he appeared bodily, / and they gazed on him as on a man in the choice of his words. / Bodily he rebuked Adam for his folly, / and like the voice of a man Adam heard his footsteps in paradise. / In their own language he answered them as they conversed with him, / and taught them to offer sacrifices of love. / Sacrifices of love he taught them to offer to him, / that through sacrifices he might teach them that he knows all. / By sacrifices he tested the hidden impulse of their minds, / and rebuked Cain, whose inmost soul was not pure. / With an open voice he spoke with the one whose soul was defiled: / "I do not accept a sacrifice that is not clean of stains." / Wicked Cain turned the rebuke to evil, / and instead of sorrow and repentance of soul he brought forth murder. / The murderer killed and hid his brother's innocent blood, / and a voice called him bodily: "Where is Abel?" / Bodily it demanded the bodily blood, / and showed that there is a time for it to return to life. / Two requitals were heard in the blood that spoke: / the shame of the demons and the joy of the heavenly hosts. / In this marvel he gave a voice to what has no voice, / to make known that he exists and that he created the nature of man. / The nature of man the Good One made wise in all generations, / and for their instruction he fashioned revelations in every form. / For their sake he translated Enoch and kept him alive, / to lighten for them that sentence pronounced in paradise. / Here at once he gave them to hear of resurrection, / and fashioned a proof in a single man that they would not perish. / The hope of man's renewal Lamech too marveled at, / and he revealed it and showed it in the rest that would come through the child born of him.

In Noah the harsh season [?] of the flood of waters came to an end, / and the curses of paradise too were being loosed. / With an open voice he made them hear of their destruction, / but they despised and scorned that voice that warned them. / Noah alone heard the voice and its meaning, / and believed and affirmed that its sentences would be fulfilled. / The righteous son of the righteous feared its sentences, / and made a house that preserved the remnant of the world. / A small remnant was left of the dumb creatures and of those who speak, / and he brought them across to a fair and peaceful land. / With a bodily voice he informed Noah of these things, / how they should go into the ark and how they should come out of it. / With that same voice he spoke with him after a time, / and taught him the rule for eating the flesh of animals. / With a bodily voice he too blessed his offspring, / and then placed the two under the servitude of fair Shem. / From Shem he showed that hope would dawn for the nature of man, / and therefore he turned his sons to dwell with him. / From him Abraham, the son of the promise, was to come, / and in him the wearisome course of twenty generations would find rest. / By this marvel a sign drew him out of Babylon, / to be head of the chosen people and a promise to the nations. / By the Spirit he commanded him: "Go out from the land of your birth," / and he received and accepted that voice which spoke with him. / By voice and by silence he guided the good servant, / so that, being made wise, he might bring his sons under his Lord's yoke. / He confirmed him by that promise concerning his seed, / and he longed to learn clearly when it would come to pass. / When and how it would come to pass Abraham asked, / and the Lord answered him with an open voice and spoke with him: / "Take animals and make sacrifices to my honored name, / and I will teach you how my promise to you will come to pass. / With three animals portray the servitude of three generations: / that your seed will be among foreigners and then be set free.

Take three young ones, fit according to the law, / for so must lawful sacrifices be. / Divide them, and set each part opposite its fellow, / and portray their servitude as they are ground down one against another. / Through a turtledove and a young pigeon, which are not divided, / portray their dwelling in the wilderness and in peace. / By the bird that comes down on the parts you divide, / portray the injuries that tyrant nations will inflict on your sons. / In that you are diligent and guard your sacrifices from the birds, / be reminded of my care, how careful it is for your offspring. / By the setting of the sun, and only then the acceptance of your sacrifices, / gain understanding that the time of my promise to you is far off. / When fire has consumed and pleasingly devoured your sacrifices, / see that the will of your love is sweeter to me than sacrifices." / These things chosen Abraham learned by an open voice, / and believed and affirmed that a time would come when wonders would be wrought. / Here, by night, came the interpretation of the things I have recounted; / it was not in a dream, nor in a spiritual vision. / He revealed it by a command in which the bodily voice had a visible form, / as distinct as one human body is from another. / Bodily he showed him the ways of his revelations, / at a time when bodily nature was accustomed to be tested. / In this form he came in to him and to those with him, / and though he has no body, there he showed the appearance of a body. / Three men the righteous one saw at the door of his house, / and received them as men, according to their form. / What was to come he revealed to the just one by what he did: / that his Offspring would one day dwell lovingly in Abraham's son. / The son of Abraham was to be a dwelling for his love, / and he went ahead and trod the path of his dawning before he dawned.

Of his dawning he gave instruction by his entry into his servant's house, / so that when he dawned, the truth would not be estranged from the mystery. / He was appointing a body of his own for his embodiment, / and showed it in a mystery before it came to be in bodily form. / Abraham called upon him by the name of his majesty when he sacrificed, / but he inclined his love and called himself by the name of a man. / As at a man Abraham too gazed at him, / and he was pleased that the righteous should honor and refresh him. / In the appearance of humble men the Lord and his servants were clothed, / and they were awesome and beloved in the eyes of the just one. / With great love he received them as just men, / and refreshed them with bodily food and drink. / They showed the man of body the appearance of eating, / and while they ate, they did not truly eat. / Their love refreshed Abraham's love by the eating they displayed; / not that they ate, but they taught him the tenderness of their love. / The tenderness of his love the Good One showed in what he did, / that he entered his servant's house bodily without being embodied. / Two spiritual beings he embodied with him in that visit, / not that they became embodied, but to keep the manner of the appearance. / For it was an appearance that appeared in bodily form, / and this is the wonder: that having no body, he fashioned a body. / A great wonder the Creator wrought with Abraham, / that he showed himself bodily while not showing himself. / He showed a body, though his divinity has no body, / and ate and drank, though his nature receives no food. / His nature has none of the natural properties that natures have, / for even the name of "natures" is foreign to his nature. / For want of names we call him by the name of natures, / since what is made is accustomed to be named by something [?] it knows. / By this custom the Lord of natures named his nature, / for he came in to man in the form of man, under a borrowed name.

Under a borrowed name took place what took place in Abraham's house, / and let no one think that it happened literally as it is written. / Moses wrote down that visit as he was commanded, / and placed it in his book as a foundation for the building of truth. / For the building of truth the Lord did all that he did with his servants, / and above them all this which he did with Abraham. / In the seed of Abraham he was to work the redemption of man, / and he honored the just one with the mystery of the redemption that would dawn from him. / Let no one, then, think a foolish thought about the Creator, / as heretics think, misleading the [?] of heart. / I have heard the foolish thought they think about such things, / and therefore I mention them in the midst of my words. / Because of them I walk the path of recounting words, / for I know the hateful turmoil of their thoughts. / It does not escape me how they confound the path of their words, / and how it is their way to twist what is straight. / At their crookedness my thoughts gaze at all times, / and they have not ceased, nor do they cease, from struggling with their wickedness. / Their wicked reputation I have recounted many times, / not to boast, but to rebuke their lack of discipline. / Without discipline they forever walk the way of the Scriptures, / and confound the conduct of man with their disputes. / With their disputes they have dragged me too at all times, / and do not let me walk quietly in the way of my words. / In the path of divine visions I long to walk, / that I may know and make known the cause of their diversity. / Their diversity, I see, is adorned with every beauty, / and they tell the word of truth in body and in spirit. / In body and in spirit Isaac too heard the speech of the Spirit, / which reminded him of that promise made to his father. / In his father's promise the son of the wise man was tested, / and he hastened to hand on the promise of life to his sons. / Like an athlete he prepared himself for the blessings, / and wished to give, but a divine sign held him back. / To Esau the firstborn he wished to give the blessing full of blessings, / but that command which rules over all did not permit him.

As in a contest the just one was thrown by the turn of his words: / he wished to give, yet was held back, and stood between divisions. / O the wonder that was wrought with the righteous one! / He longed to give, yet could not accomplish what pressed upon him. / And though he did not wish it, the Creator did his servant's will, / and gave the promise of Abraham's house to the one worthy of it. / Here he lovingly urged the upright one to do these things, / and most just was what was done between the two brothers. / Jacob had been seen by that will which sees all, / and it chose him beforehand, before he came out of the womb. / Just, then, is the choice that the God of all made, / and it was worthy to keep the treasure of the promise of life. / The promise of life Jacob carried in the stirrings of his soul, / and he hurried on his road, and saw a vision at the start of his journey. / He saw a ladder standing on the earth with its top in the height, / and the God of all above the height of its length. / He saw angels ascending and descending swiftly, / fulfilling the will of the Lord who sent them. / This was a dream that Jacob saw, not a waking vision, / and while he slept he saw the appearance that is not seen. / Not with his eyes did he see the ladder or the spiritual beings, / nor could he see the Lord as a man. / For it was an appearance that displayed the kinds of service, / and gave instruction about his going down and his coming up. / The ascent and descent of the spiritual beings encouraged him, / and taught him not to grow weary in the toil of his journey. / And if the spiritual beings are hard pressed in their ministries, / how much more fitting for him not to falter before hardships! / The vision he saw taught him the message of the Spirit, / and that whoever endures will receive the reward of his toils. / With faith and hope and love it strengthened him, / and therefore he called the place the House of God.

House of God he named the place of the vision he saw, / and vowed a vow to render there the full measure of tithes. / Again he saw a vision like this one at the completion of his labors, / which taught him what it had taught him at the start of his journey. / In haste he fled as he went out from Laban's house, / and it was much like that going down to Beth-Nahrin. / In his very flight he saw a camp of heavenly beings, / reminding him of the vision he had seen at Bethel. / He saw the awesome sight of ranks that were ministering, / and drew near and seized their chief as one would a man. / The valiant wrestler grappled with the spiritual one, / and strove to receive from him the power of blessings. / "Bless me," said Jacob to the spiritual one, / and he asked him, "What is the name of your person?" and he said, "Jacob." / "No longer shall this title be given you, / but your name shall be Israel: he saw God." / Isaac's son did not see God bodily, / but a vision that was spoken in the name of God. / With his senses the just Jacob saw this vision, / and as with a man he grappled with the hands of the spiritual one. / That spiritual one taught him to wrestle, / so that when he was strong he would know that he could prevail over his brother. / This is the reason for the wrestling that took place here, / which bore witness to that vision of the ladder. / One was the aim of that command and of this I have recounted: / there it was a dream, here a vision in waking. / Awake, he saw that camp of heavenly beings, / and named the place after the event of the vision. / Penuel he named the place of the vision shown to him, / because he saw the spiritual one face to face. / It was a spiritual being that he saw and grappled with bodily, / and not the nature that created creation out of nothing. / That Being is not seen by those who see, / nor can seers gaze into his hiddenness. / To the just he taught, in the form of a vision, the name of his Being, / to kindle zeal in those who are not just to become just. / Jacob was just, and his ways were beloved,

and fittingly he gave him the name "seer of the Godhead." / With the eye of the spirit he showed him an appearance without body, / and taught him the way to portray its likeness before seers. / Great power had the vision that was shown to him, / and he gave it to his sons as an inheritance from God. / By the Spirit the just one blessed his sons as he was commanded, / and revealed and gave instruction about the end of their deeds. / Spiritually Joseph too gazed at things far off, / and interpreted the vision of the sheaves and the lights. / The greatness of his rank and his brothers' humbling he portrayed in his dreams: / that he would be exalted and his brothers would descend to the rank of servants. / In every form the Lord made his servants wise, / that they might be witnesses of his care for man. / One of the witnesses of his care he made Job, / and the name of witness suits him better than anyone. / A chosen witness was the son of Esau, who earned his rank, / and he showed that the sons of the wicked can be just. / Job was just and his faith was true, / and the prophet fittingly set his name in the roll of the just. / By the just the hidden Will was honored in all generations, / and he fashioned their justice in the likeness of an image before seers. / The just Will fashioned the image of his justice in Moses, / and set him to be the skilled scribe of his hidden things. / More than anyone he revealed to him the mysteries of his hidden things, / and raised his rank above the ranks of his fellows. / He made him chief of the seers of his hidden things on earth, / and taught him to portray what is unrevealed as if revealed. / An appearance of fire he fashioned for him on the mountain, at the bush, / and from it [?] he brought him the sound of his name. / In a lowly form he saw the appearance that was shown to him: / in a thornbush, which is despised and bears no pleasant fruit. / By a lowly thing the Creator is accustomed to show his power, / to teach man that he created creation out of nothing. / Something is better than nothing, however lowly it may be, / just as a real substance that stands is better than a shadow. / In the lowly bush he showed Moses a wondrous sight:

fire and bush, and the bush in the fire, yet not consumed. / A sight and a voice gave instruction from within the fire, / and bodily he was tested by sight and by scrutiny. / "Moses!" the voice called to the Israelite, / and showed him that it knew who he was and whose son, and declared his lineage. / "I am the Lord of the house of your fathers," it said to him, / "and I have come down to redeem the seed of Abraham from slavery." / These things were heard by the senses of the one who perceived, / and in body and spirit they were seen by the one who saw. / By a bodily sign he taught him the power of the name of his lordship, / and changed the staff and made it truly a serpent. / With this staff he chastised the Egyptians with ten plagues, / and with it divided the sea, and the people crossed as on dry land. / It was not the staff that possessed the power of the name of his lordship, / but divine power did these things through it. / By this same power he sweetened waters that were bitter, / and at his command brought up quail and brought down manna. / With it he split the rock and made water flow from the flint, / and filled the people's need for drink, and the fullness [?] of love. / The power of his greatness he showed to all in what he did, / and conveyed these things through a man slow of speech and stammering. / The stammering man he chose from the whole of mortal nature, / and revealed through him the power of his Being and the ordering of all things. / The Lord set one of mortal nature on earth as a second lord, / and gave him power to recount in order the ordering of the worlds. / The ordering of the worlds he showed him spiritually on the mountain: / how creation was ordered in the beginning out of nothing. / The tenderness of these things stirred the mind of the Israelite, / and he began to entreat: "Show me the glory of your Godhead." / Moses thought that he was seeing him as a man, / and did not know that that hiddenness cannot be seen. / As a friend he showed him, instead of his hiddenness,

and fashioned a token of the greatness of the glory of his face. / The appearance of his glory he made for the stammerer, glorious above all, / and eyes of flesh could not gaze upon it. / It was not God that the mortal saw in the flesh, / for this is hard, and beyond the grasp of those who speak. / His glory showed him a power hidden from all creatures, / so that he might know that his Godhead is beyond comprehension. / It was an angel who ministered in the Lord's place, / and he showed a wondrous sight to radiant eyes. / His were all the things that took place on Mount Sinai, / and there was no voice Moses heard that he did not speak. / Paul testifies that it was an angel who gave the law; / not that he gave it, but that it was spoken through his hands. / The angel was moved by a divine sign, / and conveyed the kinds of the law into the ears of Moses. / Moses was made a mediator between him and the people, / and he explained and spoke spiritually. / As on an instrument the Spirit struck through his mouth, / and spoke glorious words in the ears of the people. / O that power that has no perceptible voice, / yet conveyed the kinds of his will through the work of his hands! / Three times over he performed his service: / toward the spiritual beings, toward Amram's son, and toward the sons of his people. / From one to another he passed on the word that was with him, / like a king who commands others, and those others others. / He, like a king, was served by spiritual beings, / and the spiritual beings carried his words to earthly ones. / The place of his feet he showed on the mountain as if he had a body, / and though without body he fashioned bodily likenesses. / He gave a new [?] to the instrument he showed in his name, / for it was written on two tablets, on this side and on that. / Aleph and Beth were written on them as the firstborn letters, / and they came before all the letters in all books. / He made Moses chief of teachers among earthly beings:

and he was the first to spell out His words in written letters. / That command which formed creatures out of nothing / itself wrote them, not with hands but by a sign. / The Creator does not possess bodily hands, / though it is written that the hand of the Lord wrote them. / The figure of hands is customarily used in every kind of figure, / because men too perform their tasks with hands. / In this figure He worked with Moses and Joshua son of Nun, / and hand in hand with the righteous of every generation. / One angel He made the envoy for His service, / the one whose name was called Michael and Azazael. / Of him He spoke to Moses on the mountain when He persuaded him: / “Behold, My angel goes before you and leads you.” / By His own name He named the minister of His Godhead, / and commanded Moses to fear him as one fears the Lord. / It was he who showed himself to Joshua son of Nun in the appearance of a man, / girded with visible weapons. / It was not a man who appeared, as it is said, / but the likeness of a man, though there was no man. / “I am the commander of the army of hosts,” he said to him, / “and I have come now to teach you the order of my leadership. / I, I am the one who wrought all that came about by the hand of Moses, / and I am working these things that come about by your own hands.” / This man who called himself by the name of man / is he who fought all the wars of the Canaanites. / He took the land of Palestine and gave it to Israel, / and fulfilled and completed that promise made to Abraham. / He showed Gideon a sign with the fleece and the dew, / that he could destroy the Midianites without weapons. / Without weapons he taught Gideon to fight, / so that when he won he would not boast in weapons. / He also announced to Deborah that she should call Barak / to go out and put to shame the might of Sisera, the mighty in strength.

It was he who taught Jael as well all manner of stratagems, / so that under the guise of love she might hunt the cunning one who was oppressing the people. / By the hands of women he humbled the might of the kings of Hazor, / so that it would proclaim the power of the One who sent him, whose strength is able for all things. / It was he who revealed to Manoah’s wife the reason for Samson, / how he would overpower the Philistines by the sign of his hair. / In the head of his limbs he showed the sign of his might, / so that it would be known that the strength of his greatness was not human. / Again, he condensed the thin air and made it solid, / and brought down rain as Samuel the priest had asked. / With the voice of thunder he rebuked the people who had asked for a king, / to teach them that their desire had not been rightly fulfilled. / The Creator did all that He did through the spiritual being, / yet no spiritual being was able to do things higher than himself. / Through spiritual beings His power worked among creatures, / not because He needed them, but to make known that He is the Lord over all. / His power did not need the help of the work of His hands, / and creation bears witness that He alone called it and established it. / Not by their hands did the Maker of all do all that He did, / for there is no number to the things He has done without them. / There were revelations to the righteous in generation after generation, / yet it was not the angels who ministered their revelations. / Behold, righteous David sang his prophecy by the Spirit, / and not one of the orders of ministers came near it. / The power of the Spirit mingled with the soul of the one pure of soul, / and composed the sounds of spiritual songs. / He did not hear with the senses the speech addressed to him, / but with a mind that knew how to listen to the speech of the Spirit. / Spiritually the skilled psalmist sang all that he sang, / and there is nothing in his singing that was without the Spirit, / nor did an angel interpret for him, and yet he sang. / The power of the Spirit played upon the harp of his soul, / and the senses of his body spoke in the harmony of strings. / As with a pen, the Spirit held the tongue of his mouth, / and wrote with it all kinds of spiritual songs. / By this order his words are distinguished from those of the prophets, / and are not called by that name of prophecy. / The title “Psalms of Songs” is inscribed on his book,
