Go, rest a little from the strife of your blasphemies.
Far be it from us to yield to you rather than to the truth.
Neither death nor life will separate us from our trust.
Light does not mingle with darkness, which is alien to it,
and the confession of our soul is not mixed with that of falsifiers.
One confession of one God is fixed in our soul:
that he is from eternity, as he is, without change;
and that he has an Offspring begotten of him is written in our heart;
and that there is no time between him and his Offspring is certain to us;
and that there is also the Spirit, a hypostasis from him, undivided,
and equal with him in all that he possesses as God.
We confess also this, which took place at the end of the ages:
that he redeemed us through his Son and reconciled height and depth with us.

By "his Son" I mean the Word from him and the body from us,
one spiritual and one bodily, the hidden in the manifest;
two in natures, the form of the servant and of the Maker,
one in the Being who willed it and honoured what was his own in himself.
To him, the Fashioner of all, all acknowledgments are fitting,
who wisely led his own to the knowledge of him.
On my Lady Mary

Memra 4 on my Lady Mary. / This is also the fourth memra, / which is recited on the eve of the commemoration of my Lady Mary. / Responsory: / Blessed [?] Mary, mother and virgin: through you all creatures rejoiced, / and by your giving birth watchers and human beings were redeemed. / My brothers…

In the greatness of His love the Creator willed to be revealed in human beings,
and He made the heavenly ones hear a voice: that He would make man.
He created all things from nothing and took no counsel,
but in the case of man: "Come," He said, "let us make man in our image."
He made the spiritual beings, yet did not will them to be [?] the image of His Being,
but in the fashioning of lowly dust He revealed His hiddenness.
In fashioning [?] all He sought no help and no counsellor,
but for the lowly one He asked help and counsel of all.
He brought into being a creation that had not existed, and did not call it His image;
then He took from it a small, cut-off portion and called that His image.
In one member He enclosed [?] the hand that had wrought so wisely,
so that through it He might make the works of His hands wise enough to know His name.
The name of His Being He willed to set forth [?] in the image of man:
that while He is One, there are with Him equal hypostases.
In mystery He revealed to His servants the power of His hiddenness,
and what they could not grasp He showed them in a visible image.
That He alone exists He taught the world through His works,
but how He exists He did not will to reveal until now.
For the end of His labor He kept the mystery of distinction in the persons [?],
and taught all the power of His Being and the Power that is with Him.
In the sight of all He made heard that voice, that He would make man,
and the hosts on high were astonished at it: what it was, and about whom.
In great wonder the spiritual beings stood as they listened to it,
and at its single "Come" they marveled and could not be satisfied:
"What is this new thing that the hidden Nature has made us hear,
and whom does it call as a helper with it in fashioning its image?
With whom does it take counsel, and how does it make the image of its Being,
and how can a work of His hands resemble Him?
Who is there with Him who possesses the power of making,
that He should invite him to fashion the image of His image?
It seems that He has other hypostases with His Being—
otherwise what is this that has come: 'Come, let us make'?
Had He said 'Come' in the singular, it would be understood of one;
now that He has said 'Come' in the plural, it is understood of two at least."
Not openly did the spiritual beings learn these things I have said;
they pondered [?] who the power was that lay hidden in the word "our" [?].
They only heard it with the mind, in mystery,
but the force of its meaning they could not grasp at all.

This alone the Creator willed to make known to them:
that there was with Him something hidden along with His hiddenness.
He revealed a mystery to them, not the explanation of the mystery,
so that when it came to be examined it would not seem strange in their eyes.
For their sake He made heard a voice that was no mere sound,
and for their instruction He drew out His labor over six days.
In six days He completed His creation and sealed His words,
and on the seventh He rested, though He neither rests nor grows weary.
On the sixth day He made heard that voice, "Come, let us make,"
and He made an image and bound in it rational and mute creatures.
In body and soul He composed His work with skill,
that it might resemble both the heavenly and the earthly.
As an image He set him in the world, the royal city,
so that rational and mute creatures might look lovingly upon Him in him.
Like a furnace He built it for the simple one, to test everything,
so that in its heat He might try the discernment He had set in rational beings.
In a beautiful place, Eden, He set him, that all might feel zeal over him,
to see who would rejoice in His love and who would be grieved at his rank.
Among the assemblies on high He made trial with the honor of the earthly one,
and from among them was exposed whoever was counterfeit gold in his thoughts.
He set him a boundary, knowing that he would not keep it,
so that through this his inclination might be revealed, and those who desire evil.
He withheld him from a single fruit of the tree, that he should not approach it;
the Evil One sensed it, grew envious, led him astray by it, and made him a laughingstock.
Envy blinded the discernment of the prince of the air,
and he did not care to see the fair beauty that was in the image of man.
It was not man he envied, with an envy such as envy might befit,
but the Being who had named man with the image of His image.
The hidden Being the rebel envied presumptuously,
and since he could not harm the Inaccessible, he harmed His image.
Like a spy the cunning one came upon the perfect one,
despoiled his riches and stripped him, leaving him naked.
In insulting him he supposed he was insulting the name of the Creator,
and did not know, blinded by envy, that he was harming himself.
As though at the image of the King of kings he was hurling stones at him,
and instead of stones he cast at him words of insult:
"Out of envy," he said, "the Creator has withheld you from the tree,
lest you become a co-heir with Him in His divinity.
Divinity is gained from the tree He has withheld from you;
if you eat, you will become a god like the gods."
These words the Evil One cast at the image of the Good,
and he overturned him and threw him down, and mocked and laughed at his fall.
The Good One, full of goodness, also looked on this contempt,
and took pity on His image, which had been despised by the rebel.
He chastised him for having erred, and turned His grace upon him in mercy,
so that the cunning one who had wickedly overturned him might not boast.
He decreed [?] death for his folly,
and made his body a fountain from which life would flow for his race.
Streams of mankind flowed from his body to the four quarters,

and filled the earth with rational fruits from his limbs.
Living fruits blossomed from him who had been slain by food,
and the Hater saw it, and groaning seized him at his reversal.
He had supposed that if he ate from the tree he would die for ever,
but the Good One did not will that the Evil One's desire reach its fulfillment.
The medicine of life He placed from His own life in the body,
that it might run on with its line of descent without end.
In the seed that Adam bore He kept the name He had given him,
so that the name of His greatness would not be stripped from his offspring.
The name of His greatness He drew on the tablet of his formation,
and when the Evil One effaced it, He drew it again in Seth, a second time.
Of Seth it is said that he resembled Adam in everything,
because in his body lay hidden the mystery of the succession of his race.
Cain and Abel Scripture did not call the image of Adam,
for the one was to die, and the other to perish by a sentence of judgment.
In [?] whom Adam begot, life dwelt,
and the son of Amram rightly named him too the image of Adam.
The image of Adam the Lord of Adam was to take;
He set it beforehand, from the beginning, in Adam and his sons.
Like a foundation He laid His name in the building of mankind,
so that they would build, one upon another, the image of the One who was to come.
In this sense He was taking counsel to make man,
and in this order He was calling him the image of His hiddenness.
One from among mankind was to become a dwelling for His love,
and beforehand He called the fashioning of man the image of the Hidden.
From the beginning He placed the name of His Being on man,
so that it would not be divided when He fulfilled it in the event.
For the end of times this thing He wrought was kept for Him,
and beforehand He wrought it in mystery until He fulfilled it.
And lest anyone say in answer to my words:
"In what does the image of man resemble the Godhead?
How can a hidden nature without composition
be resembled by a nature that is made and composite?
How can the made be like the Maker,
and how can the bounded be sufficient for the boundless?
How can it be true that man is the image of the Godhead,
when the Godhead has neither bound nor composition?
And granting that he is the image of the Hidden, as is written,
where is it? For behold, it was corrupted and returned to its earth.
In every generation death corrupts, and again they are corrupted;
where then is the image? For there is no likeness among the children of men.
And if someone says it will be so when it is renewed,
behold, even there it cannot be likened in being."
No human being is a visible image of the Being,
nor can transient creatures resemble the Immortal.
In love alone can human beings resemble the Hidden [?],
and by love the Maker, too, makes His own like Himself.
In love He named the image of man the image of His hiddenness,
and in grace He called him by names higher than himself.
In grace He gave him, at the beginning of times, the name of His Being,
that he might depict the mystery of what was to be at the end of times.
At the end of times He confirmed for him the name of the image,

for the sake of what He had earlier depicted in figures of things to come.
By this end he was named from the beginning,
and in this hope He was exalting his formation.
For this reason He chose for Himself one people from among the peoples,
and set it apart from all, that the leaven of life might be kept in it.
For this reason He honored the righteous, one after another,
that they might keep the mystery hidden in their limbs.
The righteous, too, in this sense handed it on to one another,
and carried and passed on the leaven that was in them from one to the next.
Adam gave it to Seth, who was named with the name of the image,
and from Seth it went to Enoch, to Lamech, and to Noah, who pleased God.
Noah prophesied and gave it to his son through blessings:
"Blessed," he said, "be the Lord, the God of Shem, who has given us peace through his name [?]."
From Shem it passed by succession to Abraham,
and Abram kept it with diligence, more than anyone.
The Creator, too, who saw him diligent in keeping His image,
chose him and appointed him steward of the treasure of His name.
Through him He willed to reveal the great treasure He had placed in his fathers [...],
and through him He promised to bless all in the seed that came from him.
For his seed He established a great covenant that does not lie,
and sealed His covenant with oaths that are not annulled.
This is the reason for the election of Abram and his offspring:
that he might keep the treasure of life until it was revealed.
Otherwise, the One who magnified Abraham hates the nations;
for why did the Creator choose him above all?
Why to him alone did He give the law that confers life,
and estrange the nations from the law that is hidden within it?
If the whole race of Adam is His,
why does He choose one and reject others with partiality?
It is partiality to magnify one and diminish others,
and not justice, when, though they are one, they are not treated as one.
If it is the Creator to whom the people and the peoples belong,
why is His creating not as even as He Himself is [?]?
No equality is seen in the election of the people
unless the nations are allowed to delight in its goodness.
No, son of Abram, do not divide the equality of our race,
and do not stir up a quarrel between us and our Maker.
Your election is the cause in which the treasure of life lies hidden;
let our mortality be comforted by the life that comes from you.
For the life of humankind the Creator chose you and made life dwell in you;
why are you grieved that people live through the revelation of your life?
For the sake of all was the election of Abram and his sons,
that like guides they might show humankind the way to life.
Life was hidden in that dispensation of the law,
and was passed from one to another in mystery.
From Abraham the succession grew strong and settled in David,
and from David it came and reached as far as Mary.
In Mary the course of the way of the succession of life came to its end,
and into her limbs it entered, rested, and dwelt as [...] in a harbor.
A harbor of peace the daughter of man became for the race of man,
and no more did the waves of mortality's troubles wear it down.
Like a ship she carried it in her bosom, our whole race,
and brought it out and set it on the shore of the kingdom on high.
A spiritual being came down from on high, from the presence of the Hidden,
and set her course to travel lightly to the appointed place on high.

Good tidings and new things he dropped into her ears, the daughter of mortals,
and she marveled greatly at the newness of the voice that spoke with her.
A new conception without union the Watcher announced,
and she received it in faith without doubting.
In faith Mary yielded to the heavenly one,
as the earth yielded in the beginning to the Creator's voice.
The command that signaled to the earth, and it conceived Adam,
the same He depicted in the earth whose body bred the second Adam.
The Craftsman who took dust without hands
composed in her a body like that first one.
The Being that breathed into Adam the breath of life—
that same was in the daughter of men, who is sister to her of the beginning.
In a new manner, alike and yet not alike, He fashioned Adam,
so that Adam might resemble Adam in all that is Adam's.
From the Adamic clay itself His Will took,
and composed and made it skillfully into body and soul.
The image of that image which death had corrupted He renewed by His hand [?],
and in its likeness He drew it on a bodily tablet.
The medicine of life He kneaded by His nod into its features,
that it might be able to give life to dead bodies.
Like a temple He built him, a dwelling for His divinity,
that in him He might receive the worship of love from all creatures.
With all creatures He blended him in the clay of his formation,
that in him He might bind in peace all that the transgression of the command had loosed.
Rational and mute creatures He gathered into the enclosure of his body and soul,
that they might look on Him in him as in an image that holds every likeness.
As a tabernacle of love He made him, for Himself and for all,
that the creatures might dwell in him in love, and He in will.
His divinity He revealed to His servants by what He did,
that they might see the true mark of the distinction in the persons [?].
The hypostases with Him, which had been hidden in Him, He distinguished through him,
and as with a finger He pointed them out through his composition.
His hidden Offspring He proclaimed on earth through the conception of her womb,
and taught that He has an Offspring equal with His Being.
By the name of His Offspring He named the offspring of the second Adam,
that he might tread the way of fatherhood and sonship.
Son of the Most High the Watcher too called him, as he was commanded,
that by his name it might be revealed concerning that Offspring who is beyond comprehension.
To the high rank of the Word of the Father he was to ascend,
and beforehand He depicted that rank by his name, ahead of the events.
One with the Offspring without beginning he was to be,
and He set on his head the name of His Being like a crown.
Crown and rank He gave by grace to the son of mortals,
and in a divine way He exalted his conception and his birth.
For the sake of all He chose him from all as a first-fruit,
that in him all might be reconciled with Him, and He with all.
As the cause of peace He called him, and set him between Himself and mankind,
that by the peace of his name he might bring peace to the division of mankind.
Peace too Gabriel gave his mother at his conception,
and he made ready the power of the Most High and called it to come down upon her.

The Spirit and the Power together overshadowed her who bore him,
and fulfilled toward him the great name that belongs to the hidden Son.
It was not the hidden Son who came to the bodily birth;
it was upon the son of the daughter of man that the will of the Hidden came down.
The will of the Hidden came down from on high, not the hiddenness,
and dwelt in the womb, not by nature but by love.
To fashion the bodily image His will came down;
it was not that He fashioned His own hypostasis, which is eternal.
To sow life in mortality He overshadowed another,
not so that He Himself should gain a reckoning of life by being fashioned [?].
Otherwise, how could He become what comes into being
and not be emptied of what He is? How then could He become?
A new becoming is the dissolution of all that was before,
which cannot remain as it was while it is being fashioned.
Eternal is His Offspring, everlasting, beyond time;
and if He came to a second birth, He ceased from what He is.
He is without composition and without limit, like His Begetter;
if He were bounded in the womb, He became flesh like any man.
All that the Father has, He too has without beginning;
if He was fashioned by the Holy Spirit, He is wholly a made thing.
The Spirit, Scripture says, formed in the womb the one who was in the womb.
If so, then He was formed, and not a maker.
No—there is no maker that makes itself,
nor can the Word of his mouth [...] him like a flame [?].
No nature that is eternal can turn and come to be,
nor can the unbounded take a bound upon its boundlessness.
Far be it from me to say that the Eternal received becoming,
and God forbid that I should affirm that He whom no limit holds was bounded in flesh.
I do not accept a thing that is too hard to be accepted,
nor do I assent to the incongruity of the Hidden being fashioned.
I do not believe that the One without beginning became a beginning,
nor that the Fashioner of all fashioned Himself in the flesh.
It was flesh that His nod fashioned in a fleshly womb,
that He might renew through it the flesh worn out by mortality.
Flesh He composed in a new manner, without union,
and the Spirit filled him, that He might bring forth a man spiritually.
By the power of the Spirit He completed his conception and his birth,
and made him holy, a temple of holiness for the will of His love.
From the beginning of his formation His love dwelt in him,
and it did not depart from him, nor will it ever depart or withdraw.
With him went that Will which fashioned him in the womb,
and by the might of His power he overcame all powers and reigned over all.
One I call him and the Power that made all things through him—
one, though not as separate things become one when I mingle separate natures.
One I call the will of the Hidden and the visible body,
and yet even so I do not mix the hidden with the visible.
I am not mistaken in holding that there is a distinction between the one and the other,
for the made nature is less than its Maker.
I do not confound the proper order of the hidden nature,
nor do I dissolve the properties of the visible body.
The hidden is hidden, however much you mingle bodily things with it,
and the body is body, however much you mix spiritual things with it.
The hidden nature is not mixed with the body except in love,

and the visible is not mingled with the Hidden except in name.
In name it is possible for one to call them one in being,
so long as the one who calls them does not confuse their distinctions.
In this sense I have called them so; but the two are one in love:
the Son of the Being and the son of humanity, one person.
The Son of God willed His will in the son of humanity,
and gave him what was His and took what was his, though not in nature.
By His own birth without beginning He honored his birth,
and by His authority without end He exalted his rank.
To the high rank of His divinity He called and raised him,
to fill the place of the Hidden for the works of His hands.
In place of His hiddenness came the visibility of the visible image,
that through his visibility the Power wholly hidden in him might be proclaimed.
Like a trumpet He called creatures to his visible birth [?],
concerning that Offspring begotten eternally, without beginning.
His is the conception and the bodily birth [?],
while the Word of the Father does not share in his bodily things.
His is the conception, his the birth, his the childhood,
and it is he who offered a sacrifice to the Hidden for his fashioning.
He sucked milk, and him the knees carried, and he kissed the mouth,
and it is he who crawled with the children through the streets.
He grew up by measures, little by little,
and again it was he who received the power of wisdom by the power of the Spirit.
He fulfilled the righteousness of the law for a span of thirty years,
and he paid the debt to the God of all, and pleased all.
It is he who was baptized like one in need by John,
and the herald buried his limbs in the tomb of the waters.
It is he who received the power of the Spirit in the sign of a dove,
and over him the voice of the Father bore witness that His love is true.
He fasted and was hungry, for nature required it of him,
and it is he who seized the [?] with a mighty sword.
His is the hunger, his the thirst, his the sleep,
and he grew weary and sat down and asked for water to slake his thirst.
His is the visible body that receives sufferings,
and his the soul laden with the weight of discernment.
His is the fear, his the sweat, his the prayer,
and he was strengthened by a spiritual being so that he would not grow faint.
He was in the upper room, he in the court, he at Golgotha,
and it is he who received unclean spittle from the mouths of the unclean.
His is the cross, his the nails, his the spear,
and it is he who bowed his head upon the wood and gave up his spirit.
It is his body that lay in the tomb three days,
and his soul that went to Eden and returned to him.
It is he who raided the house of the dead without harm,
and he was raised by the power of the Creator who was hidden in him.
In him lay hidden the great power of the Word of the Father,
and by the might of His power he was strengthened to endure his sufferings.
In him the Son of God dwelt by will,
and though hidden in him, He did not share in his weaknesses.
In him from the moment the Watcher announced it to his mother,
in him by a will beyond searching out, as to how and how far;
in him before the sufferings and after the sufferings, without change,
in him on earth and in him in heaven, without end.
I do not say that the power of the Being departed from him,

neither in the body nor when he put off mortality.
One with the Eternal I count him because of his rank,
and one I call him, Son of God and not a part [?].
I do not say "two," as the simple-minded say;
"one" I say, however much the liar wrongs me.
O wrongdoer, do not wrong me as you are accustomed to do;
you have not heard from me that the Son is [?] and [another] Son belongs to God.
O all-presumptuous one, do not presumptuously find fault with me;
do I not see you walking off the road?
O contentious one, do not trouble yourself against my words;
you do not understand me, and you have always strayed from what is fitting.
O forger, do not accuse me before forgers;
I have no need to test you whether the testimony of your words would be accepted [?].
What is it to you, my fellow, blinded by envy without cause,
that you listen idly to my words as though you were in the right [?]?
What have I to do with you, a quarrelsome man full of disputes,
that I should stir up words in anger to fight with you?
By your protection, O Hidden One, whose love dwelt in our visible body,
judge [?] the presumptuous who insult you with their passion.
By the protection of your Being, O Eternal One who are without beginning,
silence the voices that confine you in a womb of flesh.
Because of you the people of disputes cry out against us,
for calling you by the living name that befits your name.
Against your life they strive every hour to make it die,
and since they cannot, behold, they put you to death falsely.
They long for your death, these many dead of iniquity,
and do not perceive that your nature is higher than harms.
Why do you love, you who are full of anger, to kill Life,
when there is no way they could make Life cease from His life?
Why do you weary yourselves to imprison the Spirit within limbs,
when heaven and earth cannot contain Him?
Why do you hate the one who says that the Eternal does not die,
for whether he says it or not, He does not die?
Why do you despise the one who exalts our lowly body,
for whether he magnifies it or not, it reigns in glory?
What do you gain by making the Immortal die,
and what do you lose if our body reigns with the Being?
Why is it not plain that the Eternal is above harms,
and who does not know that mortality means suffering and death?
Perhaps, if the mute had mouths of reason,
they would be our companions in holding that the Eternal does not die.
Perhaps, if there were discernment in the undiscerning,
they would despise the one who makes the hidden nature suffer.
Come, elders, judge justly with these speakers,
who cover over the visible truth with obstinacy.
Be ashamed, and restrain yourselves [?] at least a little, you masters of words;
cease from musing on the passibility of the Impassible.
Be still; do not cry out presumptuously against the Being,
lest you become partners in judgment with the slanderer.
The slanderer is what the zeal of your thoughts resembles.

who, in the guise of love, also blasphemed the worshipped Name.
Why do you become companions of the evil ones, devoid of reason,
and estrange yourselves from blessings that have no end?
Flee, you weaklings, from the business of the murderer of mankind,
and come, take refuge in the life that is hidden in faith.
Let us believe that the Being, by his will, put on a body from among us,
and perfected it through sufferings, and through it decreed life for the whole of it.
As the cause of life he took it from us as a first fruit,
and called it by his name, that in his name he might give life to all.
Through a man from among us the will of the Hidden One gives us life,
and he is the man who died and was raised, and lived and gave life.
He it is who loosed the bonds of Sheol from the departed,
and went forth and proclaimed the new tidings of the resurrection of the dead.
He died and lived by the power of the Life that dwelt in him,
and while he was in death, the Life of his life was above death.
The Will that accompanied him did not abandon him,
nor did it neglect to help him in the time of suffering.
With him at the trial, with him on the wood, with him in the tomb;
and though it was wholly with him, it did not share in his weaknesses.
The nature of mortals received, in what is its own, what belongs to its nature,
and the nature of the Hidden One remained in what is its own, without change.
It was not changed, and again I say that it was not changed;
and if anyone is angered, let him be angered again: it was not changed.
What was changed was the nature of humanity, which was subject to suffering,
which put off sufferings and put on the glory of the immortals.
It was the mortal one who suffered on the cross, apart from the Word,
and by the power of the Word he overcame death and dispensed life.
He was mortal, and again I say that he was mortal;
and though this is so, I call him and the Word one.
In his trial he bore the humiliation by which we are humbled,
and in his temptation he learned to help those who are tempted.
Through his innocence he gave acquittal to our guilt,
and through his fasting he wove a crown of glory for our nature.
With great glory the Power that dwelt in him crowned him,
and invited [?] watchers and men to glorify him.
To watchers and men he showed his glory and the greatness of his rank,
and gathered them to gaze on him on the day of his ascension.
Forty days after he rose He left him on the earth,
that in his bodily form he might put to rest the doubt of his race.
To assure his race he showed in his body the nails and the spear,
and ate and drank after he had become immortal.
In all things the hidden Power that overshadowed him made him perfect,
and when he was made perfect, it raised him to the height above all.
The day of his ascension was far more glorious than all days,
and splendid was the road he trod toward the heights.
Company upon company the spiritual beings stood to gaze at him:
how could a body fly through the air, which is not its wont?
A new thing watchers and men saw in him, the head of humanity:
that he opened the gates which had been shut in the face of men.

The gaze of all creation was fixed on him in spirit,
until he reached the place where there is no means of seeing.
A hidden sign brought him through, before him [?] of the height,
and he entered and beheld that order which is not corrupted.
He entered the great and perfect tabernacle to minister,
and no longer hands over his office to others after a time.
With the Being he holds an authority without end,
and for ever and ever his scepter reigns over all and in all.
Who would not marvel at the greatness of the divine rank,
that he made us heirs with him in his glory and his authority?
Who would not give thanks for the incomprehensible wisdom of truth,
which exalted the work of his hands and set it with his own greatness?
Who would not praise the craftsmanship of the Maker's power,
which bound the world together in one son of man and invested it with his name?
One son of man his will fashioned in the likeness of an image,
and raised him and set him above all, to judge all.
Like a mirror he set him on high above all,
that in his visibility they might see the beauty of the Hidden One's hiddenness.
In his bodily form he willed to show his love to all,
so that they would not wear themselves out seeking to inquire into his hiddenness.
In him he set a bound for all against searching into what cannot be searched,
and turned the gaze of all toward him, so that they wander no more.
He made his body a second heaven in that order,
to fill both the place of the light and the place of the eyes.
He is wholly light to anyone who gazes on his radiance,
and nothing that shines can be reckoned against the measure of his light.
In the sphere of his body is the Will that is hidden from all,
and it makes him beautiful in appearance to the eye of those who behold him.
Like rays, the wisdom of truth goes forth from him,
and makes all wise with that knowledge which cannot be comprehended.
It is not wisdoms that the Master of masters teaches there;
he gives discipleship rest from its toils, so that it is not worn out.
In a haven of peace he settles men and spiritual beings,
and they no longer ponder the things that belong to [?] the dwelling of time.
Beside him the rush [?] of words and of deeds comes to rest,
and there is no one who asks, “What is this, and why?”
No one seeks where the Hidden One is, who cannot be searched out,
for the inquiry concerning him is uprooted from the mind.
There the made one cannot speak about the Maker,
for the gate of the unchanging Will is shut in his face.
He is not torn in doubt over how He is hidden from all,
for love calms his impulse, so that he does not doubt.
In the Visible One he sees the Hidden One, though not by sight,
and in him the desire of his soul is filled without lack.
There is fulfilled what is written, that man is an image,
in whom the image of the Being is discerned by the eye of all creatures.
There he became Lord [?] in them [?]:

who reigns over all, and all is made subject under his authority.
There the demons who scorned his lordship are put to shame,
and they bend the knee and hallow him against their will.
There the divisive schisms of the heretics cease,
who no longer persist in their ignorant doctrine of suffering.
There the war they waged against the Hidden One falls silent,
and there the assault they mounted against the Revealed One comes to rest.
There they confess two true likenesses:
the likeness of the servant and of the Maker, one person.
One person all tongues confess there,
and one “Holy” they repeat always to the Word and the body.
The body and the Word they worship always in one equality.
While they perceive that they are two, yet are proclaimed as one,
they see a great wonder there through their worship:
that with the Maker the made one receives the worship of love,
a thing worthy of wonder, and the mind is too small to marvel at it.
For how creation worships itself in the temple of the body,
who is able to examine this precisely?
And who can say how great it is, and what its power is?
The power of the Being alone suffices to say how great it is,
and he knows it, for he fashioned it with skill.
This craftsmanship is his own craftsmanship,
that Craftsman's who created creation out of nothing.
Skillfully he composed his work according to his purpose,
and it was settled with him from eternity how he would fashion it.
At the end he fashioned it, knowing it from the beginning,
and it was seen by him, before it came to be, just as it came to be.
At the fullness of the times [?] his will, perfect in his Being,
and he poured out his love on all and in all abundantly.
The great wealth of his divinity he revealed to his works,
and appointed a man to govern what is his by what is his own.
One ruler he chose from humankind according to his will,
and sealed him with his name and gave him the rank to reign
and to judge. In the place of his love he called him and set him before his ranks,
to fill the place of his invisible self.
There he fills the place of the Being for watchers and men,
and in the sight of his body sight comes to rest and inquiry falls silent.
This is the reason for the greatness of his rank and of his authority:
that he might proclaim the power of hiddenness through visibility.
Two causes are hidden in his name, and they are very precious:
one of the Being, and one of the love toward all.
It was not possible for the made ones to see the hidden Being,
and he comforted them with the sight of his body, so that they would not wear themselves out.
They were also deprived of divine communion,
and he made an ineffable means [?] and shared, and made them partakers.
Very great and incomprehensible is the cause of our life,
and however much we say, we fall short of saying what it is like.

Heaven and earth, if they were to become mouths in our place,
could not suffice to recount it as it is.
And though it is very great and incomprehensible to all creatures,
the quarrelsome have reckoned it as not even being anything.
Iniquity is upon you, heretics! How unjustly you have acted,
in that you have wronged the Good One, whose love has no measure!
You contenders, who never withdraw from disputes,
why do you tear down the great height of the edifice of truth?
You crafty ones, craftier even than the evil ones,
why do you rend apart the concord of humanity and divinity?
The Godhead willed to honor man with what is its own;
what harm is it to you that men have become sons of God?
The Being made the work of his hands a partaker in the greatness of his rank;
what injury is it to you to share freely in grace?
Cease, you quarrelers, from striving against this,
and look and consider that watchers and men marvel at it.
See the heavenly myriads who extol it,
and have never ceased praising how glorious it is.
Beautifully was it ordained that men should become divine,
and no one is able to repay the grace to the One who ordained it.
Beautifully did he make the made nature reign with the Maker,
and there is none among the made ones who can reproach him: “Why so?”
Do not, then, reproach, witless heretic,
that Knowledge which has done well in all that it has done.
Come, if you will, praise and magnify, with all creatures,
that Craftsman who made his handiwork share in his greatness.
On the Epiphany
Discourse 5 of the Epiphany. / The fifth discourse: / To its own melody, that of the Epiphany. Refrain: Blessed is the Spring / that came down upon our Jordan, and Adam drank, and his thirst [?].

The Creator willed to fashion Adam as a rational image,
and he mixed spirit with the colours of his lowly clay.
First he put together a vessel of earthenware from the mire,
then anointed it with spirit, and it became wholly a living soul.
He formed the limbs with the beauty of visible clay,
and breathed an invisible spirit into what is visible.
O Craftsman, who hid the power of his craft
and set the beauty of his image's comeliness within the tablet!
By his craftsmanship the outward natures are made beautiful,
and they show beholders the beauty of their adornments.
By the craftsmanship of the Godhead the inward natures are made beautiful,
and the outward ones serve as a covering for the inward.
A wondrous vessel he made [?], fashioning the whole:
a visible body and a hidden soul, one human being.
The Creator made from lowly mire a thing of humble appearance,
and within, in hiding, he fashioned the greatness of his power.
He placed a precious thing full of life in a despised, dead thing,
that by the power of its life it might give life to mortality.
The inner one sang like a comforting pipe in the limbs of the body,
and the clay grew beautiful with the melodies of the living spirit.

Life gave praise with a voice of glory in the temple of its clay,
and [...] the rational and the dumb creatures gathered to the sound of its melodies.
The mortal stood like a statue within a palace,
and at its features spiritual and bodily beings marvelled.
Full of colour, the beauty of the image endured for a time.
Then iniquity rose like filth over its features,
and dimmed the colours of its comely beauty through desire for the fruit.
By eating from it, it took on the colour of mortality;
sin smeared the life-giving name of the image of the King.
It stamped [?] its own name, corruption and death, upon his limbs;
over the length of time it corrupted and wore him out through mortality.
Death trampled it and ruined the beauty of its rationality;
it darkened it, and even mocked its Painter through its abasement,
and cut off hope that it would ever be renewed from its ruin.
The Word saw that wicked ones had darkened the painted image,
and had pity on his image, that it should not be dishonoured by the insolent.
An image proclaims the authority of the king by being seen,
and by its features it displays the beauty of the one who set it up.
In the image of Adam the authority of his Lord was shown,
and through its features the power of his hiddenness was made known.
And because Adam fell and death corrupted the image of his features,
the King sent grace and mercies to raise him up;
two envoys of peace he sent for the honour of his image.
They proclaimed on earth a message of renewal to mortality;
through his creation he revealed to his creatures the power of his hiddenness,
and by its renewal he showed them the wealth of his love.
He exalted the renown of its renewal far above its creation,
so that the heavenly beings should marvel at how far his mercy reached,
for through his creation they had been held fast from the beginning.
By its renewal he gladdened those who had been sad;
his will came down to his creation in a love that befits him.
He painted on the tablet the body of Adam, the second Adam;
after the pattern of Adam he painted Adam with the paint of the symbol.
He renewed Adam and his offspring through the son of Adam;
the second Adam came forth from the womb as the first came from the earth.
He wholly resembled that first one whom the earth brought forth;
in body and soul the second Adam was his equal.
Yet in authority he was Lord of Adam and of his offspring:
equal in nature, but greater in honour than all who have ever been.
The Watcher who announced his conception bears witness and called him Lord;
in many things the second Adam is greater than Adam.
He is not to be compared with created beings in the rank he attained;
exalted is his conception, for it was not mingled with human seed.
Glorious was his birth: heavenly beings were his heralds;
he alone received and inherited the name of lordship,
that heavenly and earthly beings alike should obey him.
His nature testifies that he was an earthly one born of earthly ones,
and the name of his authority cries out and proclaims that he is divine.
He is earthly because of the body and soul of a man,

and he is heavenly, for he became a dwelling for the God of all.
Earthly beings marvelled and were amazed at the greatness of his rank.
The Father and the Spirit sealed it with voices and showed that he is the Son.
He chose envoys from among spiritual and bodily beings,
that heaven and earth should be mouths to announce his coming;
he honoured them also as envoys of his proclamation,
and raised them up to make him known [?] before the eyes of beholders.
From the earthly ones he chose John, the Voice of which it is written.
He sent the Watcher, and he announced an unlooked-for conception:
that same envoy who proclaimed the conception in Mary's ears
also made it known to Zechariah concerning John;
one spiritual being brought the tidings of both servant and Lord.
He proclaimed conception to virginity and to barrenness.
The barren old man's turn came to serve as priest in the Holy of Holies;
he fulfilled his office, and heard the voice of the Watcher proclaiming;
in great glory the spiritual being revealed himself.
The barren old man trembled and was dismayed at his fair splendour,
but the Watcher heartened the earthly man with a gentle voice:
"Do not fear, for my coming to you is for peace;
the Hidden One has accepted the sacrifice of your hands and arm.
He has sent me to you to repay you the wage of your labours;
receive fruit in return for your sacrifices and your prayers:
from Elizabeth, the barren old woman whose limbs are dead."
The barren old man heard tidings of an unheard-of conception,
and he doubted greatly in his mind how it could be.
The spiritual one saw the bodily one, who was looking to his own nature,
and restrained him with silence, so that he should not doubt what he had heard;
the Watcher bound two of his senses, speech and hearing,
so that his silence and his deafness should be witnesses to the child.
It was not out of anger at his doubt that he kept him from speaking;
he bound him for this reason: that everyone might believe what was revealed.
It was not fitting that he himself should recount the vision he had seen,
lest he be like a herald of his own glories;
silence taught the children of his people the hidden vision
and confirmed them, so that they should not doubt what was being explained.
For nine months the Watcher held him with the bridle of silence,
until the barren womb bore fruit according to his promise
and the words he had heard from the spiritual one were fulfilled in deed.
Then he received the fruit, and spoke and heard, and gave back praise;
he gave him the name he had learned from the revelation:
"Hannan", which proclaims the mercies that pity mankind.
John went forth as an envoy before the King.
A sign drew him to spiritual discipline;
for thirty years he was raised in the wilderness, away from the world,
meditating on the hidden things of the proclamation.
In this way a sign drew him out of the midst of quiet,
that he might lead his life with godly thoughts;
apart from men he was raised by the power of wisdom,
until the Spirit of revelation called him to proclaim,
to shine forth from silence like the sun from its sphere.
It drew him to the world for the light of his proclamation,

and at the river Jordan he opened the treasure of the One who sent him.
As he cried out, "Repent, sinners! Receive forgiveness!"
by the forgiveness of iniquity he woke those who slept in iniquity,
and natures were stirred at the sound of a forgiveness that cost no toil.
His voice was like a trumpet in the people's ears,
and gathered them [?] to the promise of the forgiveness of iniquity.
He promised to give them birth in the womb of the waters,
and to renew them by repentance as in a furnace.
He cast the net of his words over all [?],
and shut them in within the hearing of his proclamation;
by forgiveness he hauled them in like a dragnet.
And how, and by what means? What was the cause [?] of his words?
[...] from silence, and he changed his voice in the people's ears:
"I am a servant and minister of the One who chose me;
I am an envoy before the King of whom it is written that he will come,
and he sent me to proclaim that, behold, the hope has arrived.
With water alone he commanded me to grant forgiveness of iniquity,
until he comes and gives the Spirit together with forgiveness.
With water and Spirit he abolishes the [?] of mortality,
and sows a spiritual seed that brings the dead to life.
In the furnace of the Spirit he recasts the image that iniquity disfigured,
and gives the beauty of the heavenly beings to the earthly.
In the womb of the waters he begets man spiritually,
as he is built up with a new name as a firstborn of the Spirit.
He frees the body from the slavery of mortality,
and delivers the soul from the turmoil [?] of the passions.
He forgives iniquity and gives the Spirit as a pledge,
so that the children of his inheritance may not doubt his promises.
One stands among you who is hidden from your eyes;
not even I, who proclaim him, know him.
A sign has revealed to me that I should proclaim his dawning in the house of darkness,
that through my words they may see the light of righteousness.
I am a lamp, not the sphere of the sun in its greatness,
and the gleam [of the sun] is not to be compared with his greatness.
I am beyond all measure, beyond all reckoning, smaller than he,
and I am not worthy even to loose the sandal of his feet.
From the gift of his great wealth he gave me a little,
and my senses grew rich from the hidden treasures of his love.
For a small drop that flowed from him my thoughts were found worthy,
and I gained strength to proclaim his hidden things.
Revelation pressed me beyond the ordinary course of proclamation:
even from within the womb I was eager to come out and fulfil his words.
Yet though he chose me for the mission of his proclamation,
he did not wish to show me the splendour of his face except in a mystery.
Not by the sight of the outward senses do I know him;
by the Spirit he gave me a clear sign, that I might learn who he is.
The One who told me to proclaim the Virgin's Child
sketched the figure of a dove and showed it to me in the spirit of revelation.

This he revealed to me in a mystery, as to one of his household:
'The one on whom you see it come to rest, he is the Lord.'
And this is why I proclaim and baptize:
that I may prepare a road for men to come down to his revelation.
Behold, he has drawn near and come close; from now on his light is dawning.
Let each one scour the filth from his soul, so that he may not be [?].
The sword of the Spirit is held in his hand to test men,
and whoever withholds the fruits of praise, he cuts down with it.
Living is his word, and sharper even than a sword;
it enters and searches within the senses, among the stirrings of the soul.
He is Lord over all, and also Judge of the living and the dead,
and by his testing he will separate the good from the wicked.
Under the authority of his headship every authority is placed,
and his command reigns over spiritual and bodily beings.
Come, let us enrol soul and body to him with the poll tax,
and offer him purity of soul instead of tribute."
O herald, who encouraged and who struck fear!
Love and zeal filled the words of his proclamation.
He spread abroad mercies by his name and by his voice in everyone's ears,
and cast the bridles of a judgment decreed upon the mouths of the presumptuous.
He was brandished like a rod against the iniquity that dragged men along,
and by his name he proclaimed hope to the hopeless.
His name is interpreted "Grace", which pities men freely,
and the sword of the word of his mouth is sharp like [?].
By his name he tore up the bond of humanity, which was in debt to sin,
and enrolled men to become servants of the One who sent him.
His words came down like rain upon the earth of mankind,
and watered [?] them through the word of his mouth to bear fruit.
He cried out from silence, by the spirit of revelation that spoke with him:
"Behold the Lamb who cleanses blemishes and forgives debts!
This is he of whom I said: he comes after me, yet he was before me;
and I do not know how to reckon him, who is both old and young.
He is younger than I in the [?] of his birth in a bodily frame,
and he is older than I in the [?] of his mysteries."
Who is younger than John, you uncircumcised of heart?
And how is he old, and yet comes at the end? Reveal it and tell me!
Whom does he call [?] the man who comes after him,
and whom does he name the living Lamb who takes away iniquity?
If the Only-begotten came down, was embodied and became flesh,
what need compelled him to cleanse our iniquity through flesh?
Why did he not take away the iniquity of our race by his divinity,
rather than lowering his great glory to lowliness?
Or had the flesh perhaps acquired a power greater than his own,
and was that why he changed himself, so as to conquer through what is lowly?
Far be it that we should say this, or [...]
that the power of his being has need of the power of lowly flesh!
It is the flesh that was magnified and gained power through the divine Being;
it is not the Being that gained help from the mortal.
The divine will put on the bodily one,
and it conquered and justified its fellows by the power of the One who took it.
Him it was that the son of Zechariah named the pure Lamb,

who by his sacrifice cleanses the blemishes of the children of his race.
He named him no further, but called him "the man who comes at the end",
who at the consummation of the ages judges and sets all free.
For his sake he became a harp for the Spirit of revelation,
in which the age-worn sayings of prophecy were sealed.
The Spirit revealed him to him; he saw him coming and hastened to meet him,
and rejoiced to see the hope that prophets and kings had longed for.
He saw him coming to him like everyone else to be baptized by him,
and began to urge him that he should baptize him, and not be baptized by him:
"I need to be baptized by you, as one in want;
it is not for you to come to a poor man to be enriched by him.
You are the fountain that gives mortality life to drink;
why do you need to be filled by a mortal?
You are holy, and by you the defilements of the soul are cleansed;
how can you seek cleansing of soul, you who cleanse blemishes?
Yours is the treasury of all wisdom and hidden things;
why should a great master learn from his own disciple?
You are the Luminous One who lights all with the light of his face;
what need have you of the small lamp of a word?
Yours is the abundant sea of mercies that washes away iniquity;
who can bathe you, so great in glory, in common water?"
"Let it be so now," the King answered the herald;
"thus it is fitting that righteousness be fulfilled in me.
Let it be so; do not reveal my greatness and my honour to the eyes of onlookers
until I have done and accomplished all that is written.
Let it be so: I am baptized as one in want, in need of mercies,
that in my own person I may make up the need of the human race.
I am of the race that is in debt to sin;
let it be so: I am paying off the bond that Adam wrote in Eden.
My frame is of the clay that the passions swept away;
let it be so: I am firing the softness of its mud with fire and Spirit.
I am of the stock that death swallowed, standing over its life;
let it be so: in a mystery I go down to the waters, and I bring it up.
I am a son of the race that the Evil One took captive through its freedom;
I will bring out and return our captive people from the rebel.
My fathers wrote the bond of death and became debtors to sin,
and I have resolved [?] to pay it off first in a mystery.
The comely image that is the frame of our body was corrupted and worn out;
I will go down and wash the filth of iniquity from its features.
In the furnace of the waters I recast it, the likeness of our image,
and instead of fire I breathe into it the Spirit of life.
If I do not wash its filth in my own person, it is not cleansed,
and if it does not go down with me to the [?], it is not pardoned.
The Creator chose me from among mortals as a firstfruit,
and appointed me to be a ransom in place of their lives.
In me, as a sacrifice, he willed to be reconciled with his servants;
he accepted my offering, and by my hands decreed peace for all.
And because he willed it, and set me apart from all for the sake of mankind,

it is right that I repay love on behalf of all to the God of all.
By the second birth I tread out for it the road of peace,
and I walk like everyone who comes to the mystery of renewal.
For my coming you were chosen for a mission and called a Voice,
to summon man to the birth that takes place by my hands.
Let it be so: I am baptized in water by your hands as in a grave,
and I bring mortality down with me, and bring it up again.
I am baptized now as one in need of cleansing,
and after a time I will show my power in the cleansing of the defiled."
The herald yielded to the One who sent him in what he heard,
and the priest consented to lay his hand on the High Priest.
O John, who ministered in the outer sanctuary,
and was found worthy to enter the Holy of Holies, which was not permitted!
As a son of the race, needy and in need of forgiveness,
he opened the treasure that had been hidden from former generations.
It was not to the sanctuary of the high priests that John came:
he trod, in a mystery, the entrance to the sanctuary of heaven.
He completed the order of priestly service according to the law,
and began to serve as priest in a mystery, in a higher rank.
He left the ministry of the washings of the house of the Jews,
and began to walk within the rule of pardon for the nations.
He came near to baptize the great sea that washes away sins,
and opened the door that had been shut in the face of man.
The High Priest went down to the waters, baptized and sanctified them,
and gave them the power of the Spirit to impart life.
The Holy One drew near to the weak and mute element,
and made it a womb that gives birth to man spiritually.
He went down and sank into the womb of the waters as into a grave,
and rose and was raised, and raised Adam in a mystery.
He came up from the bosom of a new and unaccustomed mother,
and the Spirit came down and anointed him with divine power.
With the Spirit he anointed him, not with the oil of the law:
a chosen anointing, which surpassed that of his fellows.
In the form of a dove the Spirit came down and remained with him,
and by a visible sign he showed what was hidden in him.
By the dove he showed that he had received the whole wealth of the Spirit,
and that it remains in him without change in the order of its dwelling.
Through a bird that loves peace he depicted a sign,
that in him the peace of all remains unshaken.
In the sign of peace the hidden power rested and remained in him,
and the Father sealed it with a voice: "This is my beloved."
He anointed him with the Spirit like an athlete for the contest,
and sent forth a voice to the spectators of the struggle.
The spectators heard only the voice that the Father proclaimed,
and did not perceive the anointing in the likeness of a dove.
He anointed him in secret, before the eyes of the one alone who ministered,
for thus the great rule of anointing commands:
it permits the oil to the priests alone, to consecrate,

since they are tried as members of the household in the greatness of their rank.
So John too, as minister and friend of the Bridegroom,
was found worthy through revelation to perceive the Spirit that came down.
He alone saw the gift in the likeness of a dove,
and testified and said that the vision was true and the One composed was great:
"I saw the Spirit, a hidden nature, in the mystery of a bird,
which came down and remained, hidden yet in the open, in perfect love."
The mediator who was ministering testified that the Spirit came down,
and the Father sent forth a sound with his voice in the mystery of our renewal.
Now that the rite of the waters is completed and the Father has sealed it,
let us inquire who it was that received the Spirit and the name of Son.
Who is it in whom it came down and dwelt in the mystery of a bird,
and whom did he name the Son in whom he was pleased and on whom he fulfilled his love?
Who is it that went down to the womb of the waters as one in want,
and who is it whom the Spirit anointed with love and endowed with power?
If it was the Word himself who took a body and became flesh,
why did he not anoint his flesh in his own person?
Why did he not give power to the frame of his body,
rather than the Spirit coming down and strengthening his body with anointing?
If he is equal to his Begetter in love and power,
why did he add to him the name "Beloved" as though to one in want?
If he is spiritual and a Son of the essence of the Father and the Spirit,
why does another come down and testify, and how is he magnified?
How does one come down to his fellow, when they have no limit?
And how does a Being anoint a Being that is in no want?
The purpose of anointing is the greatness of a rank of glory,
so that whoever is chosen through anointing receives rank.
If, then, the Holy Spirit anointed the Only-begotten and filled him with Spirit,
then he received the rank of great glory as something new.
And if he received greatness at baptism through anointing and voice,
where then is his being equal to his Begetter, and the Spirit that is from him?
But if these things I have said are not fitting, as indeed they are not,
then let us inquire who it was that was magnified through anointing.
The one who lacks nothing is not blessed by one who is less,
and who that is holy has need of anointing?
The Unlimited is not contained by a womb of waters,
nor does greatness of rank magnify the One who is higher than all.
For he is, and he is, and in his being he remains forever,
and the nature of his being does not change from what he is.
Whatever is perfect by reason of its being does not change;
and if it changes, it possesses being under a borrowed name.
Whatever is made has need of the power of its Maker,
and cannot stand without the command of the One who established it.
Whoever is magnified by measures, another magnifies him;
and if he were great, he would not be magnified beyond what he is.

There is nothing in nature that loses its own by means of what is not its own;
how then did he change himself, so as to magnify all by means of what is ours?
Far be it that we should say or think, as the wicked do,
that the Word of the Father lost his own in taking what is ours!
It is the one taken who was magnified through anointings, not the One who took him;
it is the lowly one that gained an exalted name by the power of the One who took him.
The image that was corrupted by the filth of iniquity through desire for the fruit,
that is the one the Spirit recast in the furnace of baptism.
The potter took a lowly vessel of soft clay,
and turned his work into a vessel fit for glories.
The Creator took the very nature of Adam's clay,
kneaded it with water and fired it with the Spirit, and it gained beauty.
Our nature was in debt and was pledged to death and to the Evil One,
and in that very nature of ours the Creator paid the debt of our race.
The ugliness of our soul ruined the beauty of our comely image,
and our Painter restored it with spiritual colours.
The envious Evil One smeared our outward features,
and now he changed it and painted them within the tablet.
Our race lay cast out in exile like a stinking thing,
and when it was brought low, he pitied it in mercy, and a voice loosed it.
It was imprisoned in Sheol, with the cords of death cast upon it,
and the mercies that formed it took pity on its lowliness, and came down and redeemed it.
It was wholly rotting and festering with the sores of iniquity,
and Grace bound it up and washed from it the stench of its iniquity.
He chose one member from the whole body of mankind,
and taught it by the Spirit to heal the pains of the children of its race.
One man he formed in a unique way, beyond the natural order,
and with his own hand renewed the [?] that had worn away in mortality;
he did not paint him with the colours of human seed.
With the paint of the Spirit he mixed his painting in body and soul;
in body and soul he composed his work in the likeness of Adam,
so that through him the body and soul of his fellows might be renewed.
He composed his work as a pure dwelling for the will of his love,
so that by his composition he might bind all in his love.
In the temple of his body he willed to receive the worship of mankind,
and openly to show all the power of his hiddenness.
For thirty years he raised him in body and in human concerns,
while he grew before the eyes of onlookers and before his face.
After a time, when the growth of the body was complete,
he willed to make known the renewal that is accomplished in him;
he chose a herald from his race and sent him before him.
He went out and proclaimed the Voice that is written in prophecy;
he gathered and brought back the children of Jacob who had been scattered.
He announced to them, who were poor, the good tidings of the King,
and invited them to the wedding feast of the spiritual King.
At the feast [?] they received the King, though they were unwilling;
he named him the Lamb, and called [?] him the sacrifice that pardons all.
In his baptism he depicted death and life and the renewal of all;
he likened him to a bridegroom because of his love for mankind,
and called the children of his race, who were joined to him, a bride.
The Bridegroom accomplished it through the wedding feast of faith.

And he joined to himself the church of the nations, the betrothed of holiness;
instead of purple robes he clothed her in the garment [?] of baptism.
He set on her a crown woven all through with the seals of the Spirit;
by the splendour of the Spirit he showed her glory to the eye of the beholders.
For though he was earthly, he was given the crown of the kingdom on high;
the Father [?] exalted him above everyone
through the testimony, "This is my beloved, who fulfils my will":
the Father cries out, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends.
Three witnesses who set their hand to the authority of the king:
it was the son of our race who was baptized and gained the name of sonship.
To him were given the leadership and the crown of the height;
it is he whom the Spirit anointed with power and on whom it remained.
And the Father bore witness about him with a voice that his love was true;
it is he who was found worthy and became a dwelling for the Word of the Father.
And he was honoured with the name of the Being who is above all;
he too bore witness to the deeds that took place with him.
For they were done with human beings, as to a man;
his baptism was a man's: it was a body that was baptized by bodily men.
And he trod a path for the children of his race toward [?];
the rank and the name that he inherited proclaim that he was one of the mortals,
and that by grace he became heir and lord of height and depth.
The Spirit that he received in the sign of the dove revealed and showed us
that he too is of our race, which is lacking and in need.
Through grace he filled up and made good his lack,
and made the children of his race sharers in the wealth of the Spirit.
He was baptized like every bodily person in physical water,
and the womb of baptism gave birth to him spiritually.
In the name of the Being, the three names, he was baptized and sanctified:
the Father by the voice, the Son by love, and the Spirit by anointing.
By three names they perfected in him the name that he received,
and he grew great in name and in deed and reigned over all.
At the announcement of his conception the name of sonship was promised to him;
[...] in mystery through the spiritual birth.
"Son of the Most High," said the Watcher, "he is destined [...]";
for it was a man who received the Spirit in the likeness of a dove.
It was a man whom the Spirit anointed with hidden power,
so that by the power of [?] he might drive out demons and heal pains.
He was a man in body and soul, apart from iniquity;
the Spirit glorified him, and he became in the body God and man.
I call him by the name "man" because of his body,
and I give him the name "God" because of his rank.
One [...] I [...] the body [...] the Word, the Son of God;
one in the Being that is not split apart by divisions.
The natures I have distinguished by the name of two, not as [two] sons:

one [...] the Son of the Being and the body that is from us.
I call him Christ and Son for two reasons:
because he was anointed with the Spirit, and because in love he became Son together with the Word.
Word and body, when I say they are two in nature,
are like body and soul within one human being.
Soul in body and body in soul are distinct yet united,
and everyone bears witness that they are two and are named one.
The Word in the body is after the pattern of the word within the soul,
which is in the soul and goes outside it without separation.
On this pattern is laid the building of the confession of my words,
as I join two that are distinct into one perfection.
And if the heretics wrong me with slander,
let them show who it was that was baptized and whom the Spirit anointed.
Let them plead their case before a judge who listens well,
and bring witnesses from the archives of the words of the Spirit.
Let the parties stand one against the other, as in a court,
and let there be a sign from an advocate who hears both sides.
In court let them show to whom these things I have said belong;
and if they are vindicated, it will be plain that they were right to wrong me.
Without quarrelling let them reveal the power hidden in the words,
and if they hit the mark, then they are true.
If they contend with me before the judge, I am not afraid,
for the king's order puts a bridle in the mouth of the troublemaker.
Whoever flees from the law, the charge against him is plain,
and before the court I convict him by his own defiance.
I do not stray from the divine laws,
nor do I exchange the court of the Lord for another court.
See, I stand before the Judge who sees in secret;
let whoever accuses me show it openly by deeds.
Why do they hide the falsehood within them under the guise of truth,
and whom do they deceive, posing as champions of what is true?
Why do they boast [in the great number of their party] [?],
when the strength of the unlearned is feeble before anathemas?
Even if they win by tumult, it is no victory,
but the force of arrogance that wins by [...].
[... in] insolence against the truth,
and he humbled the truth for a time [?] before [...].
The victory of the insolent does not earn the name of justice,
and justice has never been defeated [...].
[...] they led them astray with their words by cunning,
and persuaded them that they were champions of the truth.
For deceitfully they wear the skins of [...] lambs,
but in their deeds against the truth they are wolves.
Which of them [...] stripped off his falsehood and was not exposed?
And who has won by just judgment rather than by arrogance?
See, the masters who taught them were defeated and exposed,
and the pure Church drove them outside her gates.
The Paulianists [?] and the Eunomians are uprooted and cast out;

those of the house of Arius and of Novatus [?] have become strangers.
And the teachers of error too: their words have gone flat.
What are their disciples reckoned? Babbling dogs.
I do not fear the Eutychians, for that one inclines toward [?];
nor am I brought low by the Egyptian, who won by force [?].
Nor am I weakened by the heirs of their runners [?],
who are stammerers and babblers when it comes to teaching.
They only cry out when they are stirred up like Legion,
and the voice of Jesus silences them as it silenced Legion.
At the noise of their disorderly wrangling my thoughts were shaken,
and wandered far from the path on which they had been travelling.
On the king's highway I had set out to go forth in the king's company,
and the cry of robbers who fear the truth held me back from my course.
It was not out of fear of their words that I turned aside from my discourse;
I turned against them so that they might not trouble my course of truth.
I was indeed roused against the [?] of their thoughts,
since, though unlearned, they seize the rank of teacher.
By these things I have recounted I sought to make the childlike heart wise,
so that it may not be led astray after the reports of turbulent voices.
My thoughts have painted the image of the king on the tablet of words,
and in my verses I wished to show it to the eye of the beholders.
It was granted me to paint the image of the promise of his words,
who gave forgiveness by the seal of his name to the children of his house.
Resurrection of the body and redemption of the soul he counselled and promised,
and he wrote them on two tablets, of water and of Spirit.
In baptism he set up a target of life for the hosts,
that they might aim at the perfection of the kingdom on high.
In the water he set up the new target, the birth of the Spirit,
so that whoever conforms himself to it by free will receives it.
See, the promise of the kingdom on high, which does not lie;
come, let us be eager to receive freely the wealth of the Spirit.
See, the target is set before the learners, that they may be conformed to it:
let the heart believe, the mouth confess, and every movement aim at it.
See, the king himself has trodden a new path in his own person;
come, let us travel on it toward the goal while there is light.
See, open is the womb that gives birth to humankind spiritually;
bury mortality in baptism and gain life.
Let everyone hear that voice from heaven, "This is my beloved,"
and cry out in love to him who gave life to humankind in love.
With John let us cry out the confession with one voice:
"This is the Lamb of God, who cleanses all blemishes."
On Saint John the Baptist
Memra 6 [?], on Saint John. / [?] of six [?] / on Saint John the Baptist. / Responsory: / Glory to him who revealed the mystery of his will to the one who loved his will. / [?]

until One who was victorious came, and the one Victor gave them the victory.
In the contest of hidden labours they were toiling,
until the Truth came to light and gave them rest.
In the study of hope they meditated on this hope,
until they touched him with open senses, and then they were comforted.
In every form they longed for what was to come,
until it came, and then the course of their contests came to rest.
From one to another they handed down the hope of their promises,
until a single revelation about a single just man brought it to its end.
One revelation brought their revelations to a close,
and a voice bears witness that it stilled the voice of their revelations.
From a voice from heaven they heard this proclaimed with an exalted voice:
that in John the revelations of prophecy were fulfilled.
The Law, it is said, and the mystery of the revelations of prophecy
received through John the fulfilment of their meanings.
His birth stilled the course of mysteries and parables,
and revealed and explained the mystery by spiritual interpretation.
In the birth of the just one, grace revealed the power of its goodness,
and trod a path by which people might travel to the meeting-place of life.
Like a guide [?] was the son of the Hebrews to the barrenness of mankind,
and they began to bear fruits of praise to the Creator.
The Spirit of revelation revealed to his father the mystery of hidden things,
and he gave thanks and said, “Blessed is the Creator, who has visited his people.”
The Spirit made wise the radiant priest, son of the Hebrews,
and he revealed and showed that the time of mankind’s redemption had drawn near:
the horn of salvation for mankind that had been made known to him,
by which the unclean demons who had gored our race are gored.
Through the occasion of his birth he revealed to us the mystery of the redemption of our lives;
[?] he revealed to us the mystery of the salvation of our lives in the Lord of all.
And he named his son “Grace,” for he shows grace to us debtors:
the name John is the name of the grace that has pity on mankind,
and his embassy portrays the image of the King of kings.
As an envoy the herald went out before the One who was coming,
and showed his dawning to the heavenly beings and to those on earth.
Beyond the order of nature he hastened along the path of preaching,
and while still a babe he began the labours of maturity.
Oh, the mature one, who, while not yet mature in the senses of the body,
was perfected by the Spirit for the embassy that goes before the King!
Oh, the untaught one, who, though he had not walked in the study of books,
made wise the minds of the wise and of the learned!
Oh, he who had the stature of an unknowing infant,
yet imparted the savour of experience to every age!
Oh John, conceived in nature beyond nature,
for your very conception proclaims the conception without union!
Without union was he conceived whose envoy you are,
and from your mother’s womb you revealed the order that is beyond order.
In your mother’s womb you saw the mother of the King of kings,
and you revealed to your mother that she should call his mother “Mother of the Lord.”
Your mother called Mary “Mother of the Lord” [?],
and gave thanks to him who had revealed to her the mystery of hidden things.
Oh, the wonder that was wrought among the daughters of Eve,
who bowed down to give thanks to the infants within them!

Who ever saw women with child, beyond all custom,
who prophesied about the [?] of the infants within them?
Who has examined the one marvel of the two women,
who conceived in a hidden way, beyond the order that holds among women?
The wonder of them was spoken of among the Hebrews,
and they marvelled at the new and unaccustomed conceptions.
Beyond hope the mother of the servant and the mother of the Lord conceived,
the one in barrenness and the other in a manner without union.
Here was fulfilled what is written about Abraham,
that beyond hope the daughters of Abraham hoped in hope.
Elizabeth gained good hope through an unhoped-for child,
and her child gave hope to the hopeless.
Good tidings John carried on the tip of his tongue,
and called on people to [rise?], take heart and gain hope.
To the hopeless he announced the tidings of life,
and interpreted kinds of good things that he himself had not seen.
Oh John, small in limbs and perfect in [soul?],
who became a voice to [?] men and heavenly beings!
Oh you, the man who, while not yet grown to the stature of men,
became an envoy from God to our humanity!
Oh, how wondrous is the story told about you,
and no one knows how to recount all the ways of your story!
I wished to recount the ways of your conduct before the hearers,
and my mind was afraid that it would not suffice to set your story in order.
It is a great [fear?] to recount the ways of your story,
and it is boldness to rise to the height of your story.
Your story is greater than all the stories of the children of flesh,
and your [?] is lofty, since you are exalted above all who are born.
There is none among creatures who can tell of you as you are,
except the One whom you proclaimed before the multitudes.
Before the multitudes you revealed the mystery of mankind’s salvation,
and as in an image you portrayed the dove of his sacrifice.
The Spirit of revelation drew you to the wilderness; concerning this story
I sought to know what was the reason you moved to the wilderness.
I heard those who share your labour recounting the story about you,
and my mind was caught up to listen well to what is beautiful.
I saw the image of your conduct as the fishermen portray it,
and I set my mind to examine the beauty of your labours.
In toilsome labours the Spirit taught you how to live,
and, though mortal, you portrayed the likeness of the immortals.
The power of the Spirit was your teacher and [instructor?],
and taught you an order greater than the order of those who set things in order.
You became a disciple of spiritual mastership,
and it gave you the lofty rank of teacher.
Come, hearers, hear the wonder concerning John,
who was raised without the rearing of guardians.
People pass on to one another and impart customs and ways of life,
and this is the wonder: that no one was anything to him.
More than anyone’s was the order of his upbringing perfect in the wilderness,
and perhaps even the wilderness marvelled at the wonder concerning him.
In great wonder he dwelt in the wilderness without comfort,

and like a discerning man he marvelled at the calm of his peace.
Oh John, who brought peace to the undiscerning wilderness,
and turned back and calmed the discernment that had gone astray!
The dwelling of men was like a lifeless wilderness,
and was bereft of the good things of the love of truth.
People were full of the thicket of iniquity and the thorns of wickedness,
and human life was choked, and no one perceived it.
Nature was breached, and the law of the spirit was made void,
and passions and wild demons were wasting it away.
John’s voice tilled the world with the plough of [?],
and instead of seed sowed in it the hope of the forgiveness of iniquity.
Through excessive iniquity the race of Adam had died,
and at the voice of forgiveness it stirred from its iniquity as from sleep.
The debtors, sons of debtors, heard the voice of forgiveness,
and rose up to tear up the bond of the debts they had incurred through sin.
The bond of debts Adam had written in the land of Eden,
and his sons increased it with the interest of hateful deeds.
In shameful deeds the human race went about,
until they heard the voice of John, and then they were ashamed.
On this condition the One who chose him for his embassy chose him:
that, as an emblem of peace, he should calm the turmoil [?] of the worlds.
For this purpose he raised him in the wilderness, apart from men,
that he might know how to reconcile the divisions of mankind.
Skilfully [?] did the One who knows all accomplish this,
that through his servant he might [win back?] his servants to his lordship.
The divine will set on him the emblem of peace,
that he might stand against the stirrings of the soul and the senses of the body.
The Spirit clothed him wholly in the armour of the Spirit,
so that none of the arrows of the Accuser should pierce him.
The Accuser stood ready to do battle with his thoughts,
but [God] girded him in the Spirit like a mighty man in weapons of armour.
Mightily he gave himself to the struggle;
even unto death he braced himself in the conflict with the adversary.
