At his strenuousness the companies on high marvelled,
at how firmly he stood and did not slacken in the contest of his labours.
At his zeal the tyrant demons were astonished,
at how he overpowered the might that was in them amid the provocations of his body.
In two hard conflicts he was waging battle:
the war of the wild demons and the passions of his body.
The demons schemed with guile to weaken him,
and so did the stirrings of the soul through the provocations of desire.
By the power of the Spirit he was strengthened in body and soul,
and by it he overcame his own desires and the desire of the Evil One.
Nature silently demanded of him what is natural,
and the demons with guile laid snares of guile for him.
Two adversaries were contending with his freedom,
and he alone did not slacken from the struggle.
With toils he toiled in body and soul,
and this is the wonder: that, toiling and worn down, he fought and won.

Meagre and less than usual was his body’s nourishment,
and the conduct of his life was lofty and higher than that of bodily beings.
On lowly locusts and wild honey he was fed,
and the power of the Spirit sustained him on scant food.
The power that strengthened great Moses in his redoubled fast
was the power that established in him endurance of soul in the face of provocations.
That command which gave Elijah strength through food
was what strengthened him to trample on the passions of desire.
Forty days Elijah walked on scant food,
but John thirty years on little food.
Thirty years the righteous one walked a wearisome road,
and though he grew weary, the road became for him as though it were not hard.
Oh you, the man who walked a road full of fear,
and the kinds of evil, the terrors of the road, did not shake you!
Oh, the fervent one, who was set aflame with the love of his Lord,
and did not grow cold in the struggle for his Lord’s sake!
Oh, the discerning one, who was armed with the armour of labours,
and did not put off his armour night or day for thirty years!
Oh, the athlete who joined battle with incorporeal beings,
and the claws of the spirits did not [fasten?] on the frame of his body!
Oh, the contest that has no equal among those on earth,
and perhaps even the [hosts?] of heaven fall short of it!
Oh, the mind that endured so much in toils,
and did not slacken over the length of time, though beaten and worn down!
Oh, the limbs, how they bore the weight of their provocations,
and did not falter or give way in the contest of unaccustomed labours!
Beyond all custom John walked the road of labours,
and the ways of his conduct were strange to mortals.
There is no mortal who walks a road like this,
nor any earthly one who stood firm in the conflict in which he stood firm.
Without distraction he gave his soul rest in good meditation,
and who would not marvel that weariness did not wear him down?
Without comfort he comforted himself with things not seen,
and who would not say that the Spirit bound him in hidden ways?
Where, then, were the strong passions of mankind,
that they could not stand against the power that fought in him?
How did the desire of the body, the fire of [?], grow cold,
and the [?] of its heat not flare up in the body of the just one?
Where did the love of money, the fount of evils, vanish,
so that its course did not reach the height of the soul of the valiant-souled one?
Who bound the love of money, crafty in strife,
so that its claws did not lodge in that swift-winged mind?
Who stilled the agitation of turbulent pride,
so that it did not [overcome?] the steady mind of the steadfast man?
Who put the bridles of [?] on the passion of anger,
so that he did not turn savage, as it is stirred to trouble the soul?
Who abolished envy, the slayer of mankind,
so that it became dead within John as in a tomb?
As in a tomb the turbulent passions were buried in him;

though alive, they were not alive to the freedom of his soul.
As if lifeless they dwelt in his mortality,
and he did not give the desire within them power over his limbs.
They had power to stir him as they stir a man,
but the power of the Spirit roared at them and they trembled before it.
Trembling and fear were cast upon the passions in John,
and they were terrified to approach him as they were accustomed.
He felt them as one who feels the passions of his soul,
and through his endurance he rose above their passions.
By endurance he overcame the passions of mankind,
and though he was a man, in his conduct he became as one who is not a man.
As one who is not a man the righteous one lived apart from men,
until the time came for the dawning of the King who chose him.
In the fullness of times the One who fulfils the times dawned out of silence,
and he began to cry out that the time of mortality was ended.
“The time is fulfilled!” the herald cried to the age of the world,
“and the time has come for the time that has filled its time to depart.”
“Repent!” said the son of Zechariah to sinners, sons of sinners,
and he taught them to wipe away iniquity by baptism.
The son of the barren woman opened the baptism for the forgiveness of debts,
and began to give birth to new people from within the waters.
The voice whose voice is a trumpet proclaimed the mystery of renewal,
and the dead of iniquity stirred from iniquity as from sleep.
In the sleep of iniquity the sons of Abraham were [sunk?],
and the voice of the herald, the son of Abraham, awakened them.
In the name of Abraham the dull-minded people boasted,
and the just one rebuked them because they boasted in names unjustly.
“Do not boast in the name of Abraham, sons of Abraham,
and do not trust in a name that is bereft of love [?].
You are bound to show the fruits of labours;
repay in purity the debt of love to him who loved you.”
These words John sowed in the ears of the people,
and everyone began to tear up the bond of his debts.
He showed them how to blot out the bond of debts in water,
until the One should come who blots out iniquity and gives the Spirit.
With water alone he blotted out the iniquity of the people,
and he taught them about the One who would come after his words.
After his words dawned the Dawn that gladdens all,
and he began to seek him and to show him to the eyes of the beholders.
Openly he showed the greatness of his rank, how great it was,
and how lowly he himself was when compared with his greatness.
“He is great,” he said, “[?] as the heavens are higher than we,
and I am not worthy even to untie the sandal of his feet.
He is the King over all, and also the Judge of watchers and men,
and there is none among creatures who does not worship him as Lord.”
The power of being gave him names that fall short of him;
that is why I said that watchers and men worship him.
Not by nature did he gain the title of being worshipped by all;
the Nature that is above all made him to be honoured above all.

At the greatness of his rank I, who am his servant, am amazed;
behold, I am ready to reveal to mankind the greatness of his rank.
For mankind’s sake the Lover of mankind honoured him with a name,
that he might forgive the iniquity of men by the sacrifice of his body.
The iniquity of mankind had troubled the peace of human beings,
and he willed through one man to reconcile watchers and men.
These things the good servant proclaimed before the Lord of all,
and as a debtor he rendered thanks to the Lord who chose him.
These words the Hebrew sowed among the children of his people,
and prepared them to receive the King who had dawned.
These means the just one devised in the presence of the wicked,
that by every means they might hate the iniquity that had made them hateful.
He wished to transform the ugliness of mankind by the beauty of his words,
and he sanctified the waters and absolved them of their debts.
The Forgiver of debts taught him the order of the forgiveness of debts,
that he might prepare the way for that forgiveness, perfect and good.
Not wholly perfect was the forgiveness that John gave,
because he was not able to give the Spirit with the forgiveness.
With water alone he promised forgiveness,
and showed that there is a forgiveness greater than his measure.
“Behold,” he said, “a man comes after me who is very great,
who forgives iniquity, bestows the Spirit and gives life.”
He grants mankind the possession of undying life,
and they no longer fear the change that mortality brings.
By his death he breaks the dominion of death that corrupted mankind,
and overthrows the lofty pride of the tyrant demons.
The demons cast the human race down into the pit of death,
and a Son of Man arose and cast them into the pit they had dug.
In the depth of iniquity Satan struck the head of our humanity,
and a man turned and broke the sting of his bitterness.
Through the whole race the gall of his bitterness had spread,
and from our own race came the Healer, who healed our wounds.
The Lover of our race chose from our race a skilful physician,
and taught him to heal the wounds of his race with the medicine of the Spirit.
The divine will gave him the medicine of the Spirit,
and with it he healed every kind of evil in a divine way.
Like the sun his revelation dawned among those in darkness,
and drove away the error that had spread over all and in all.
John’s voice cried out on earth concerning his coming,
and error trembled, and the foundations of the edifice of iniquity were shaken.
Like a sword the son of Zechariah made his word flash,
and the demons were astounded at the sharpness of the words of his mouth.
As with a sword he laid waste the faction of error,
and the ranks of truth were strengthened by his zeal.
The King chose for himself a zealous soldier and sent him before him,
and girded him with a power whose strength cannot be overpowered.
In his armour the girded soldier, son of the Hebrews, gloried,
and he did not slacken from the struggle against the adversary.
In every struggle he defeated the Enemy,
and as he conquered he fought on victoriously.
Insatiably he ran along the road of labours,

and did not weary of the struggle against iniquity.
Against iniquity his weapon was [raised?] night and day,
and the conflict of labours was sweeter to him than delight.
The righteous one hated the hateful wickedness of iniquity,
and strove to wipe out its very name from humanity.
He loved mankind for the love of the Lover of mankind,
and longed to bind mankind in the love of his Lord.
To the love of his Lord the good servant’s love was yoked,
and he awaited that voice from heaven: “Good servant.”
John became a good servant to the good Lord,
and the Good One, seeing the goodness of his labour, sealed him with his name.
With his name he sealed the son of Abraham, already sealed by circumcision,
and placed in his hand the sword of the Spirit to lay iniquity waste.
Human iniquity had raised a rebellion against righteousness,
and through John he willed to humble its tyranny.
The just one, who hated iniquity, longed for the slaying of iniquity,
and did not cease from the struggle against evils.
Even unto death he gave himself to the struggle,
and he died, yet did not die, for his portion is the hope of the raising of the dead.
In the conflict with iniquity the righteous one died unjustly,
and his death became a [?] witness to his preaching.
Against a tyrant king of iniquity he armed himself,
and raised his word, and exposed and laid bare his wantonness.
Wantonly the wanton-souled one conducted himself,
and zealously the holy one rose up against his iniquity.
He was exalting himself above the divine Law,
which had decreed that the bond of marriage should not be [?].
The wicked man wrongfully entered into union with his brother’s wife,
and John was zealous for the Law that had laid this down.
For the Law the zealot of the Law was zealous,
like Phinehas, who was zealous and grew fierce against the fornicators.
Against fornicators the Law is fitted to the mouth of the righteous,
and it ever lays waste every kind of fornication by the hand of the just.
Zimri, who committed fornication, he slew with the sword of the Law,
and Herod with the boldness of the word of the Spirit.
In Phinehas the law of the Spirit showed great zeal,
and in John the strength of reproof.
There it exacted the iniquity of the wicked with blood,
and here by a word that was sharper than a sword.
The just one raised the sword of his word against Herod,
and was not abashed by the authority and the crown upon him.
John remembered that saying which David uttered,
and zealously rebuked the king who was bold in sin.
Herod committed an evil sin, worse than all others,
in that he wronged his brother by union with his brother’s wife.
Over his brother’s wife the contemptible fool was running mad,
and when the just one saw it, he was zealous and grew fierce against his baseness.
Oh, the upright one, how he aimed at the mark of uprightness,
and openly rebuked falsehood before the eyes of many!
He knew the falsehood of the Edomite,

and he exposed [?] it beforehand, until it brazenly killed him.
In prison the most unjust of all shut up the just one,
and schemed how he might fulfil the lust of his inclination.
He longed to kill him and awaited the day of his death,
so that when the just one was dead he might bring his wantonness into the open.
Herod and Herodias made a wicked agreement
to extinguish the light that had exposed the iniquity in them.
The wicked forged a plot of iniquity among themselves,
to silence the trumpet-voice that silenced iniquity.
The crafty laid snares of guile for the guileless [?] soul,
and did not know that, in hunting him, they themselves would be caught.
For his birthday the king kept the [guile?] of his heart,
so that on the feast day the guile hidden in him might be revealed.
Hateful guile lay hidden in the Edomite’s heart,
and he was eager for the moment when he might reveal the wickedness of his inclination.
With the [?] of iniquity the wicked one made a feast for his officers,
and invited and summoned the chief men of the people to rejoice with him.
The wicked one spread a show of dancing over his lewdness,
and the daughter of the shameless woman over whom he was running mad came in and danced.
The lewd dance pleased the lewd man in front of the guests,
and he boasted in his promises beyond all measure.
The fool set aside half his possessions for the daughter of the shameless woman,
but she would take nothing except what she desired.
The wicked girl desired an evil thing, as one [?],
for she opened her mouth and asked for the head of the one who hated iniquity.
Woe to you, wicked man! How wicked you are, and your iniquity is plain,
and you are not ashamed of the hatefulness of your iniquity!
Oh, how the [?] of your impudence [?] among your hearers,
and shamelessly they fulfil the lust of your wantonness!
“Give me the head of the just one on a platter,” the shameless girl asked,
and she was not ashamed to speak a word full of disgrace.
Great disgrace and redoubled iniquity were hidden in her word,
and this is the wonder: the hearers of her word were astonished and dismayed.
She asked for the death of the just one as the wages of her wantonness.
And the king, it is said, was grieved when he heard the request for death.
Oh, the grief that was no grief, of the crafty heart,
which was wrapped in a show of grief while rejoicing and exulting!
Oh, the show that covered [joy] with a show of sorrow,
while it hastened to shed blood savagely!
Falsely the king grieved over what grieved him,
and Scripture did not wish to reveal the guile of the crafty one.
Thus falsehood knows how to lead mankind astray,
and with a show of good things it hides the counterfeit of its falsehood.
The liar spread falsehood over his wickedness,
and sent to cut off the head of the just one as though unwilling.
He was most willing for the thing that happened, as he had wished,
and covered his wickedness with a show, as with a garment.
For the sake of [the oath?] the twisted-minded one was acting craftily:
“It is not fitting,” he said—O wicked one, wicked in everything—
“[to break?] your word”—or that you should shed innocent blood?
So then, crafty one, in whom there is no purity or clarity and [?]

Which evil is worse, falsehood or [?] murder?
Wretched liar! Even if it is wicked for a man to lie,
still it should not have gone so far as to shed the blood of a holy man.
Iniquity put on the guise of oaths like a garment,
and concealed and deceived, though its wickedness was plain to see.
O deceitful [?] and vile pretense,
which was not ashamed, but feigned grief over a crime full of foulness!
O the cruelty of a hard heart, like stone,
which was not softened by an outrage harsher than all outrages!
Alas for the woman full of the brazenness of wantonness,
who was not ashamed to shed blood before many!
O the wanton hands of a lustful soul,
which carried the head of the righteous man, the bearer of victory!
O the bold pupils of haughty eyes,
which were not ashamed but gazed upon the blood of the righteous man!
O the cruelty of the king and the woman, full of brazenness,
who were turning innocent blood about [?] amid their finery!
With finery they carried the head of the righteous man,
and were not moved by the righteousness with which it was clothed.
O how silent justice too kept at this wickedness,
and did not reveal the strength of her zeal as is her custom!
For she could have shaken the earth so that it swallowed them,
as she did to the camp of Dathan and Korah.
For they deserved that new punishment which then took place,
and more besides [?], in keeping with that iniquity which has no equal.
The loathsome iniquity which the lustful committed has no equal,
since there is none greater than the man against whose blood they sinned.
Among those born of women there is none greater or more exalted than John;
therefore the requital of his blood is harsher than all requitals.
I saw the blood of the holy one flowing over unclean hands,
and outrage seized me: who, then, is pure of wrongdoing?
A filthy woman was carrying the head of the righteous man
and mocking it: "Where now is all your zeal?"
On the platter of food it went in with the food that nourishes the living [?];
and this is the outrage: how could they eat that banquet?
O the banquet that was mingled with innocent blood,
and like wine they lapped up the blood of the pure one!
Herodias did not thirst for a cup of wine
as she longed to hold the head of the righteous man in her hands.
There was no desire so suited to her wantonness
as the desire to see his blood flowing on the ground.
In shedding his blood she fulfilled her bestial desire,
and like a beast she was tearing [?] his body with her hands and her movements.
O the licentiousness of one who was licentious in the lust of the flesh,
and when she was [?] sated, began to eat human flesh!
O the struggle of one who struggled against the truth,
and did not rest [?] until she had gone down into the blood of the upright!

O the foolish woman, foolish in her lusts,
who poured out her bitterness on him who would have drawn her out of folly!
Hear, you women, the outrage that a licentious woman committed,
who became a bitch and bit the body of a righteous man.
[Turn away, foolish women, from a folly like hers,
lest you be named "Herodias, slayer of the righteous."]
Marvel and beware, you women [?] who are captive to desires,
lest the captivity that took Eve captive in Eden take you captive.
Desire for the fruit took Eve captive as into captivity,
and she estranged us from the delight of Paradise.
There is no exile of which you women were not the cause,
and no captivity of desires has taken captives without you.
Who drove the head of our races out of Paradise?
Was it not the insatiable desire of your mother Eve?
Who destroyed every people, with everything, in the mighty waters?
Was it not the lust and wantonness of the daughters of Cain?
Who shut righteous Joseph up in prison?
Was it not the licentiousness of one of you, full of brazenness?
Who counseled righteous Job to break into murmuring?
Was it not a daughter of Eve, whose counsel resembled that of Eve her mother?
Who made Samson, mighty in strength, a laughingstock?
Was it not a whining [?] and nagging woman who knew no shame?
Who set a blemish on David, pure of mind [?]?
Was it not the sight of a loose rib from your ranks?
Who made Solomon, wiser than every king, a fool?
Was it not the bewitchment of wanton women who clung to him?
Who made Ahab a hater of what is good?
Was it not Jezebel, a hateful fountain of abominations?
Govern the course of the impulse of your soul and of your eyes,
so that travelers on the road may not stumble because of your eyes.
Look modestly, and adorn yourself with chastity,
lest you be left outside the door with the foolish virgins.
Prepare oil and go out in the company of the wise,
lest the lamp of your love go out and you become a laughingstock.
Do not adorn yourself with outward adornment of the face,
lest those who gaze be beguiled [?] by it; be fair in the beauty of your soul.
Restrain your steps and your eyes from what is hateful,
lest they call you [?] a lewd Chaldean [?] in the marketplace.
Look and understand that your eye and the adornment of your face are a snare,
and in you senses and impulses are caught as in nets.
You are wholly a snare hidden in the ground before passers-by,
and no one knows how [?] he falls into your traps.
The nets of your desires are woven with cunning knots,
and it is very hard to escape your wiles.
You are like the partridge that calls those of its own kind to death,
and by its cries kills its companions and dies itself as well.
Like a partridge you spread out your appearance to the one who looks at you,
and with your allure you catch the simple like birds.
A twofold death is shut up in the cage of your evil impulse,
and it calls a man to destruction as though to peace.
The speech of your mouth before the simple is like scattered bait [?],

and when they have been lured to it, every one of them dies, and in sin.
There is no hunter more skilled [?] than you at catching men,
and no bird that calls as sweetly as your allure.
You are very cunning in the craft of catching men,
and no one knows how to recount your wiles.
Your impulse is wise at reading in the books of the slayer of men,
but your heart is simple when it comes to meditating on the wisdom of truth.
He has been [?] your great teacher [?] from the beginning,
and in his writings you read and meditated, and sinned and made others sin.
Leave off the study of the crafty scribe who teaches falsehood,
and come, meditate on the books of the Spirit, which bestow life.
Do not be like Eve your mother, who carried out his counsel,
and ate the fruit and gave birth to death for the house of Adam.
Behold, his hope is cut off and death is slain by the Fruit that came from you;
do not stir up the bitterness of death again through your wiles.
It is enough that you killed us by eating the fruit your mother desired;
do not kill us with the lust of your body as with the fruit.
Stop! Do not be a snare of iniquity before those who look on,
for behold, all [?] are bound fast in the net of your face.
Would that you were as ugly in the look of your face as in your mind,
so that the simple-hearted might have turned away in loathing from your ugliness!
Would that you had not so much adornment of gold and pearls;
perhaps the lovers of adornment would have neglected your company!
Who will put a halter [?] on your eyes and your steps,
and bring you in and shut you up in an enclosure [?] with the wild beasts?
Who will set the seal of silence on your tongue?
Then perhaps it would cease laying waste the ranks of truth.
Blessed is he who stopped his ears and did not listen to your words,
and became deaf to the converse of your wantonness.
Blessed is he who [?] with you, yet was not with you,
and dwelt with you, yet guarded himself from the harm you do. Bless[ed]
is he who did not forget, in your company [?], the goal of his words,
and was not troubled by the wiles [?] of your wantonness.
What was the cause of this, of all that I have said?
Was it not the brazenness of Herodias, which surpassed all?
Because of this I have recounted the tale [?] of your crimes,
to reveal to people how evil is the wickedness of women.
The wickedness of women has grown and risen beyond all measure,
and I have mingled the story of your abominations with the story of the righteous man.
The story of the righteous man compelled me to recount the ways of foolish women,
how foolish they are and how cunning in abominations.
The death of the righteous man called me and woke me as from sleep:
"Rise, O man, and see a man who died because of a dance [?]."
The wicked one made a banquet of iniquity for his hosts,
and like wine the blood of the righteous man was mixed, cruelly.
He who chose him for his embassy saw the mixing of his blood,

in the same way as he sought requital for the blood of Abel.
Of the voice of Abel's blood he said that it cried out to him;
how much more was the blood of John crying out than that!
John is greater than all the righteous who have been and who are;
therefore his death is more precious and more grievous than all deaths.
Grievous was his death, for he died at a banquet full of lewdness,
and wanton women, a daughter and her mother, were mocking him.
A daughter and her mother were carrying the head of the righteous man
and cruelly dishonoring his dignity.
O cruel women, how cruelly they acted and how licentious they were,
that they mocked and derided the priest who served two at once!
Two at once John accomplished in his embassy:
he completed the earthly course and revealed the spiritual.
Between the two the herald stood and spoke the truth;
he sealed the one and gave a beginning to the one to come.
With the seal of his word he sealed the course of the law,
and opened the book of the spiritual covenant.
Book for book the skilled scribe of scribes exchanged,
and proclaimed life in place of the requitals of the law.
New ways the scribe who makes scribes wise revealed to us,
and he trod the road before him who comes to give life to men.
As in an image he portrayed the mystery of our salvation,
and went before him and called him by the name of Lamb because of his sacrifice.
By the sacrifice of his death, death and iniquity were being abolished,
and he made them plain before the events, just as they came to pass.
Behold John, searcher of mysteries, revealer of hidden things,
who revealed to mankind that the death of a man abolishes death.
Behold, great one, the greatness of the grace that was given to you,
that you revealed the mystery that was hidden from all creatures.
Praised be the will of him who willed it, and made you a son of his will,
and all the power of his working served through your hands.
Worthy of praise is he who revealed to you the mystery of his will;
and let Watchers and men lift up their hands to him who is worthy of praise.
On the Commemoration of Peter and Paul
Fourth Memra / On the Commemoration of Peter and Paul / Response: Blessed is Christ, who chose his apostles and filled them with the riches / of his wisdom, my brothers.

Good One, who shared out the riches of his love among the children of his house,
grant me to be worthy of a small portion of your gift.
King, who clothed his hosts in the armor of the Spirit,
direct my thoughts toward the goal of your preaching.

Great and skilled Master, who gave understanding to the childishness of humankind,
make my mind wise, that it may keep pace with your words.
Giver of life to mortality through death,
revive my senses to hear the voice of the word of life.
Scribe, who traced the book of the Spirit for bodily beings,
let my tongue run, together with my thoughts, in the bosom of your word.
In you let the senses and the movements, the eyes and the mind, meditate,
that they may be kept back from vain pursuits.
Of you I ask the help of the Spirit, which profits all;
give me of what is yours, that by what is yours I may recount your wise deeds.
You enriched the poverty of our despised race,
and through you the created world grew wise and gained understanding.
Your voice trod out the way of life among mortals,
and your command became a guide for our ignorance.
By the apostleship of the children of your race you willed to reconcile
heaven and earth, which had been divided because of our iniquity.
Twelve men you chose from an earthly stock,
and gave them the power of the Spirit to strengthen all.
Through them you humbled the tyranny of Death and the Evil One,
and through them you subdued height and depth beneath your authority.
Twelve stones your will hewed from the mountain of humanity,
and you made them foundations for the building of your love.
With twelve, like the months that serve the year,
you completed and perfected the establishment of immortal life.
To the four corners you sent them, two by two,
and they tilled the earth and uprooted from it the forest of iniquity.
Again you chose seventy and filled them with the Spirit of life,
that they might breathe on the face of the world the breath of the spirit of life.
And when height and depth were revived by the voice of your command,
they blossomed and bore fruits of praise to the name of your majesty.
Great was the harvest of the fruits of your seed that you sowed in our land,

and few were the laborers of the Spirit to gather it in.
Your will gave a sign to the ministers of your preaching
to entreat you to send out laborers to thresh your seed.
You spread the riches of the power of your gift over all nations,
and called good and evil alike to the banquet of your love.
You chose from among the good, that the good might bear the work of truth,
and you called the multitudes, that those without hope might gain hope.
Through the righteous you revealed your justice, that you love truth,
and through sinners you showed the riches of your kindness.
Through those who turned of their own will you revealed our freedom,
and through those who rebelled you showed and [?] your power over all things.
Twelve clung to you by their own will and by the power of signs,
but your persecutor your command compelled against his will.
Saul rebelled against the words of your preaching,
and against his will your sign bent his neck under the yoke of your love.
He was a zealot, zealous beyond everyone for the law,
and he looked for the reward the law repays.
He was an athlete who strove ever according to the law,
thinking he would win by an earthly race.
In earthly fashion he contended in the contest of labors,
and did not know he would never be crowned without the Spirit.
He was strengthening himself by bodily observances,
going down daily into the arena with the senses of the body.
He wore, like everyone, the armor of obligation on his limbs,
and the will of his soul was hindered from winning.
He carried within himself a great aim, the name of the Creator,
and held a single confession in his mind.
All other worship he counted superfluous,
for he would accept no foreign god, but only the One.
With this aim he persecuted the preaching,
because he thought it foreign to the God of all.
The zealot heard the new tidings of the distinction of persons,
and burned with zeal and grew fierce to avenge the insult to the name of the Creator.

He saw lowly men bringing [?] new things into the land,
and he put on armor to destroy them like [?] garments.
He could not bear to see the name of a son of man prevail,
and the name of one who was made praised by every mouth.
His zeal blazed fiercely in him like fire,
and he sought to burn up the purity of sinners like a forest.
“Why,” he said, “do they make a created nature equal to the Maker,
and why do they bring in another power alongside the Godhead?
Why do they offer the worship of the Hidden One to a bodily being,
and how is a crucified man honored with the name of God?
I cannot bear the great insult to the name of my God,
that men give the name of his majesty to the work of his hands.
It is not right for me to keep silent and hold back from my duty,
lest I be accused by the law, which warned against this.
Moses revealed to me, ‘You shall have no foreign god,’
and he taught me that the festivals [?] of what comes into being are not true.
All gods that did not make and establish heaven and earth
shall perish utterly, and their memory shall not be recalled.”
With this thought the hard and ardent zealot was clothed,
and he persecuted the name of Jesus as something foreign.
He persecuted his name, so that it would not be preached among the Hebrews,
and he drove its preachers out of the people.
And when he saw that the preaching had gone out to the gentiles,
his zeal inflamed him to seize it among the nations too.
He took authority from the blind chiefs of iniquity,
and went out to persecute the light that had chased away the darkness of our error.
The zealot set out on the road of the nations to persecute the light,
and from above a ray flashed out, struck him, and threw him down.
With a rod of light the Kind One struck that zealot,
to show him that he was being scourged by the very thing he hated.
He shot an arrow of light at him and struck him on his eyes,
and took away his light, since he wished to persecute the light of all.
With light he scourged the persecutor of light upon his eyes,

and struck him on his face and shook the persecutor of his name.
The light of his outer eyes was swallowed up and blinded,
and from above a hidden light dawned within his mind.
He saw a Radiant One whose light surpasses the sphere of the sun,
and heard a voice sweeter and dearer than all voices.
“Saul, Saul,” he called him gently, as one who knew him,
and showed that he would win him over in his zeal to accept his words.
“Why do you persecute me, you who are circumcised in body and uncircumcised in heart,
and why do you drive out the name of my lordship as a foreigner?
Why have you oppressed my preachers so fiercely,
and why do you thirst for the blood of those who proclaim me, though they have done you no wrong?
Why do you seek to tear down the height of the building of love,
and disturb the peace that came to reconcile the divided world?
Why do you struggle with the Mighty One, who is mightier than death,
and why do you shoot the arrows of your wrath at the Victor over all?
It is hard for you, man, to kick against the goads,
and you cannot enter the arena with the senses against spirits.
Your nature is too weak to rise to the height where I am,
and it will not let you come up to me while you are of flesh.
Why have you persecuted me, inflamed with zeal, as though I were dead,
and why do you mock my precious name before the eyes of onlookers?
Why are you zealous for the law, young scribe?
Leave childhood behind and come, draw near to maturity.
I am not dead, as you suppose, but living,
and by me living kings and the peace of all are sustained.
Though I died unjustly at the hands of the rebellious,
yet I live in a new life that has no end.”
These things the living Voice spoke with the mortal man,
and dread seized him, and he trembled and was terrified at the voice and the light.
By two witnesses the Living One showed his truth to the dead man:
by voice and light he revealed his life and his authority.
By the voice he taught him that he was not dead, as he had thought,
and by the light he showed the truth of his preaching.
The zealot thought he was persecuting a murdered man,
and he saw him holding a crown on high and reigning over all.
In great glory the Kind One showed himself to the eyes of his persecutor,
as in a type of the revelation at the end.

He showed that glory in a mystery to the mind, not to the sight,
for the body cannot see that glory with the senses.
It was not the person that his bodily eyes saw,
but the mystery of the revealed image of the One hidden on high.
By the light from above he and his companions alike were made to gaze,
but the meaning of the words was interpreted to him alone.
They too saw the Radiant One and heard the voice, as he did,
but to them it was an echo whose meaning lay hidden in the sound.
O the wonder that befell Saul:
he heard a voice that was hidden and revealed, he and his companions!
O hearing that was equal and yet not equal:
one understood, and the others stood like the deaf.
They heard a voice that was articulated as if it spoke to them,
but its force was hidden from their hearing and from their mind.
One was hearing the sound, and with the sound its meaning too,
while the others heard a sound whose sense was concealed.
Saul heard and learned the force of what he heard,
but to his companions it was a marvel, a change in the voice.
With him alone it conversed in a mystery,
as with a member of the household who knows how to keep his master's secret.
The voice taught him that he was waging a vain battle,
and showed him plainly that it was not fitting for him to struggle.
He too received and heard and surrendered to the hand of the one he heard,
and answered the one who had called him kindly.
“Who are you, Lord?” Saul replied to the one who had called him.
“Who are you, who are hidden, yet your voice is revealed through deeds?”
“I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” the Kind One answered him.
“I am the one who died, and the Power that in its love put me on brought me to life.
I am the one whom the seed of Abraham crucified on the top of the wood,
and with me they nailed up mortality, which I brought to life by my life.
I am the one who went down, in the likeness of my own person, to the depth of Sheol,
and released from it the captives of long ages whom Death had imprisoned.
Me you mocked as a dead man who had died and perished;
see and observe that I live with a life without end.
Behold, I have shown you the power of my victory by a deed;
cease, do not chase after a power stronger than you.
See from where I have spoken with you kindly,

and I have kept no grudge against you for the insult you hurled at my person.
Enough! You have persecuted me without pity through my preachers;
restrain your sword and cease from destroying my ministers.”
The ardent man saw the flame hidden in the words,
and the heat of his zeal cooled; he grew quiet and was calmed.
He came down from the height of the foolish pride in which he had stood,
and put on the garment of humility and lowered himself.
He changed his voice from scorn to confession,
and began to compose the plaintive sounds of a contrite soul.
“Who are you, Lord?” he said, calling him Lord without compulsion,
and the Voice of the one who had come to life answered him of its own accord: “I am Jesus.”
“Who are you, whose words have a fearful voice that terrifies the soul,
and whose sign is swifter than lightning to act?
Who are you, Man of light, whose light runs before your command,
and who scourge with streaks of fire the one who hates you?
Who are you, who dwell in the place above while your word is on earth,
and whose sign commands the heavenly and the earthly?
I did not know that you were in heaven rather than on earth;
I did not imagine that you were among the living rather than in death.
Forgive me that I sinned in persecuting your name and your preachers,
and do not punish me for withholding the glory that was your due.
Ignorance made me blind to understanding,
my movements grew dark, and I did not gaze on the beauty of your light.
From now on, since you willed it and your love has called me to know you,
I serve not according to the law but in your love.
I have abandoned the law and its observances, which made me blind,
and which gave no reward to my will that bore its honor and its zeal.
Under your lordship my mind will serve spiritually,
and toward the goal of your preaching my movements yearn.”
The Kind One saw him, he who saw in foresight
that he would scourge himself more than with the scourge upon his eyes.
He saw that he was ready to labor with him in senses and movements,
and he sealed him with his name and called him his own laborer of the Spirit.

He saw that he was scourging himself for the sins he had committed,
and he pitied him with mercy and revived him with the hope of repentance.
He encouraged him with the thought that the iniquity he had committed against him was forgiven,
and gave him the hand of fellowship toward his preachers.
“Rise, Saul,” he said, “and go into the city to my preachers,
for there you will learn the hidden mysteries that are too hard for you.
Rise, go in, and see the persecuted whom you drove out from among the people,
how the power that is in them triumphs among the nations.
Go to the men whom you counted as deceivers,
and learn from them the plain truth of the power of the Creator.
Go, while the rod that struck you still remains upon your eyes,
and show them the sign of my lordship, and they will receive you.
To them I have given the key of mercy and of passing judgment;
go, entreat them, and they will open to you the door of light.
Them I have made stewards of the treasure of the Spirit;
draw near to them, and they will receive you at the door of my lordship.”
The zealot submitted to what he had heard from the Kind One,
and went in, blind, to the disciples, as he had been commanded.
Three days he fasted, searching and lamenting himself,
and pleading that the light of his eyes might be restored to him.
At the end of his fast he was found worthy of a vision of the Spirit's revelation,
and a preacher was sent to him to heal his pain.
He was shown a man whose name proclaimed his healing,
and who by the gentleness of his hand drove the suffering from his eyes.
In a vision he revealed it also to the physician whom he sent to him:
“Go,” he said, “revive Saul, the dead man who persecuted the Living.
Go, open for him both his eyes and his thoughts,
that with his eyes and his mind he may see the light of my teaching.
Go, make him hear the voice of renewal and refreshment,
and behold, the senses of his body and the movements of his soul are being awakened.

Go, make wise the skilled scribe of the covenants,
and teach him to read the Scripture spiritually, in the newness of my words.
Go, tell the runner of the legal race
that there is no prize in the stadium of observances.
Reveal and teach the wrestler who prides himself on circumcision
that the seal of the body does not give you the crown of victory.”
Ananias heard that he was sending him to his persecutor,
and was amazed, and hesitated whether a wolf could be changed into a lamb.
“My Lord,” he said, “I have heard from many about this man,
how many evils he has inflicted on those who proclaim you.
How shall I go to the persecutor who persecutes your name,
and how shall I reveal the mystery of your love to the one who insults you?
How shall I make one who thirsts for blood hear the voice of comfort,
and how shall I sow hope and love in the disturber of our peace?”
“Rise, go,” the Lord said to Ananias,
“for he is not a wolf, as you suppose, but a lamb.
The wolf's appearance is wrapped about him in outward form, not in truth;
though he persecutes, he is not a persecutor but one persecuted.
He is zealous, thinking it is for the sake of the truth;
he is seeking a sign, and behold, he is drawing near to maturity.
He is a chosen vessel, whom the hidden will has chosen and tested,
and there is no blemish in the pure gold of the clarity of his soul.
With the trumpet of his voice he will proclaim my victory in the four quarters,
and show my power by deed to the eyes of the onlookers.
By his words he will loosen the fence of the law of observances,
and bring the nations into the brotherhood of the house of Abraham.
By the thunder of his voice he will make the earth eager to yield fruit,
and by his utterances he will revive the slain who died in sin.
I know him, how ready he is to endure sufferings,
and I do not forget that he dies daily for my preaching.
I have tested his love beforehand, how true it is,
and I know him: he does not slacken before trials.
He is a good lover, whose love is bound to his beloved,
and his ardor does not cool in hardships.
He is a contestant who knows how to win spiritually,
and does not let the will of his soul be distracted by earthly things.

He is a sturdy laborer who fights constantly against the adversary,
and does not strip the hidden armor from his mind.
And because I saw the strength of his soul, how true it is,
I chose him and stamped him with the seal of the Spirit, as is fitting.”
The disciple heard the testimony of the skilled Master's words,
and received it, and agreed that they were true, as had been said.
He took courage from what he had heard about the persecutor,
and went to him, that he might be further confirmed through deeds.
He went in and said to him in a gentle voice, as he had been commanded:
“Saul, my brother, our Lord has sent me to come to you.
He has sent me,” he said, “the one who called you, ‘Saul, Saul,’
that by my coming near the light of your eyes may be restored to you.”
The sick man sensed the physician of the Spirit who had been sent to him,
and hastened to meet him, for he heard a voice like that of the one who had called him.
The physician too saw the sick man rejoicing to meet him,
and did not delay to apply the medicine of light to his eyes.
He laid his hand on his eyes, which were sick,
and peeled from them the garment of darkness that had spread over the light.
By light he had been blinded in his eyes and his light darkened,
and the Light that had made him blind turned and gave him light.
O Radiant One, who gives light to all where he wills,
and darkens the light of the one who hates him by his rays!
O wonder: while the Radiant One gives light to eyes,
he blinded Saul's eyes with the brightness of his light.
The Radiant One stripped the persecutor of light of his light,
then returned and gave him light doubly, in eyes and mind.
At the gentle touch of the hand of the Spirit's physician the darkness fled,
and the light returned and gladdened the eyes and the mind.
He saw and perceived in what he had heard how choice it was,
and wrote it with the pen of the Spirit upon his thoughts.
He was baptized and purified, and stripped off the honor of the observances,
and put on the garment of kindness that the Spirit had woven for him.
He broke the seal with which he had been sealed according to the law,

and sealed himself with the new seal of the name of grace.
The persecutor turned and began to tear down what he had built,
treading the opposite way to his former words.
Out of the law he accused Judaism,
and showed how inferior it was to grace.
Through deeds he proclaimed the help of the Spirit,
and interpreted the power hidden in the preaching.
The circumcised people saw the circumcised man persecuting its name,
and trembled and was terrified lest the time had come for the people to be abolished.
The sons of Abraham saw a son of Abraham who had left his people
and begun to reconcile the scattered nations to the love of Abraham.
The circumcised and the uncircumcised stood amazed at his change,
and both sides were filled with great fear of him.
The people marveled at how he trod against his own people,
and the disciples too feared him, lest it be a trick.
Through deeds he showed the truth of his preaching:
that he had undergone the change not in appearance but in truth.
In truth he put on the beautiful garment of faith,
and spiritually he was adorned with it in secret and in the open.
With love and mercy he gave himself to the service of truth,
and put on armor and stood in battle against our error.
He saw that his struggle was not against visible flesh,
and he armed himself spiritually against spirit.
The King gave him the armor of the Spirit to fight with,
for he knew his love, that he wished to fight spiritually.
Like a skilled general he set him over his armies,
for he saw him clad against the sufferings of body and soul.
Through his eagerness he wished to show the greatness of his power:
that if a son of his house conquers through what is his, how much more does he himself.
He made him fight spiritually against everything,
and he himself won in him, and gave him a reward as a victor.
He set the world on one side and him alone on the other,
and all nations were defeated before the truth, and the Apostle won.
He entered the arena against spiritual and bodily beings,
and subdued and terrified every terror, while he raised his voice.
Earthly and heavenly beings gathered to gaze at him

as he fought against all sufferings, hidden and visible.
He would not come out of the contest night or day,
until the evening of death came and gave rest to his labor.
He did not take off the armor the King had given him to fight in,
until he had laid waste and finished off the ranks of the Evil One.
He did not sleep or slumber as he sailed on the turbulent sea,
lest the wealth he had gathered among the waves should sink.
He was awake every hour and guarded his treasure from harm,
and encouraged his companions with the sound of his words.
His body and his mind were sound in faith,
and by his words he healed the pains of the body and the blemishes of the soul.
By the garments of his body he healed bodies that were sick,
and by the breath of his mouth he drove iniquity out of souls.
He raised the fallen and gave a hand to those who had fallen,
and applied the medicine of repentance to the wounded.
He called the slothful [?] and roused them to rise and prosper,
and supported and raised those who humbled themselves in repentance.
With all and in all he became like them, to give life to all,
and he shared with all nations through his help.
Abundant was his love, and he lavishly gave the wealth of his words,
and he enticed all the needy to grow rich from him.
He left no people with whom he did not share his treasures,
and no kingdom in which he did not store the power of his wisdom.
In every region he made his voice heard like thunder,
and people gathered to him from every corner to listen to him.
Sweeter was the sound of his melody than all sounds,
as he sang the Trinity in the ears of everyone.
O harp on which the song of the Spirit was plucked,
which gladdened spiritual and bodily beings!
O flute that played daily and did not tire,
and even when weary was refreshed as it played!
O trumpet that was confined to one place,
yet made its sound heard in every region as if near!
His limbs and his mind set out for the four quarters,
and he gathered them to hear the wonder of his preaching.
Through deeds his testimony to his Lord was brought to completion in him.

that he was the chosen vessel, chosen and tested in the furnace of the Spirit.
The Will to which all things are revealed before they come to be chose him,
and entrusted into his hands the treasure of the Spirit of his preaching.
He wiped out circumcision, the seal of the corruptible flesh,
and sealed it with the Spirit, that it might serve spiritually.
He changed his name, for he had been called by the name Saul,
and was called Paul, "the persuaded one," who was persuaded and persuaded others.
By his name he expressed his mind, which matched his name,
and by deeds he fulfilled both his name and his election.
In every form he stripped off the name of Judaism,
and in everything he put on Christ, the precious name.
Above all things he loved the Name for which he changed his name,
and set nothing beside Him who chose him, but Him alone.
In the name of Christ he gloried in all afflictions,
and by it he would advance and overcome error and its worshippers.
That very Name he laid as the foundation of his preaching,
and upon it he completed the building of the people who believed in His name.
Glorious is his building, wondrous and desirable the height of his words,
and no one builds the building of truth better than he.
"I," he says, "as a wise builder lay the foundation of truth;
let each one see how he builds on to completion."
O builder who laid the foundation of faith,
and on it, as on foundations, completed and built hope and love!
O athlete who took up the contest against everything,
and counted everything loss beside the gain of his faith!
O warrior who armed himself spiritually,
and fought and pressed on with all his strivings toward the goal, Christ!
Who is sufficient to recount in words the victory of your labours,
and who can portray your beauty in writings?
There is no mind able to reach the height of your labours,
except one that resembles you in its senses and its impulses.
No one ascends to where you ascended, as you have said,
unless he strips off mortality after the pattern of your way of life.

To the third height the divine Command drew you and spoke with you
words that are hidden and are not spoken in the tongue of flesh.
O creature of flesh who, while still flesh, flew through the air!
O mortal who was counted worthy of the voice of the immortals!
O you who were honoured with glories higher than yourself,
yet humble yourself as though you did not know you were worthy of anything!
O traveller who reached Eden without walking,
and heard a voice which, though spoken, is not spoken!
What is this you have said, chosen Paul? It is hard to grasp:
how did one hear what it is not lawful to hear?
Reveal to us plainly what you said, for it is hard to hear:
with what senses were you alone counted worthy to listen to it?
If it was not lawful to be spoken, why was it spoken?
And if it was spoken, then it is lawful to hear it.
If you were worthy to hear something that is not spoken,
then you also received the understanding of what you heard.
"Yes," he says, "I heard, and I learned the force of what I heard,
but it is hard for fleshly beings to hear it in this way.
I too, who heard, did not hear with the senses of the flesh,
but in the mystery of the language which the immortals possess.
In the mystery of that voice with which they give praise in that order,
by it I heard what I heard; it was not in the body.
In the spirit I heard the assemblies on high, mystically,
praising spiritually the power of the Divine Being.
Glorious and wondrous was the sound of the melodies of their praises,
and the mind was never sated with hearing that sweetness.
The ear of flesh is not sufficient for that hearing,
nor could the tongue speak as their language does.
This was a new thing, which happened to me alone, yet not for my own sake,
that I was counted worthy to see that order mystically.
In me first He willed to show the riches of His mercies,
to give through my hands a good hope to mortality.

For this reason I was counted worthy of things higher than mortals,
that through me the human race might take heart in the hope of life.
And for this reason the Command drew me as far as Eden,
that I might go and see, and bring back the tidings of that order.
That I went I know, but how I went I do not know,
for the Command did not will to explain to me how I went.
It did not will to reveal to me whether my limbs held together with my soul,
and this too it did wisely, that I might know my nature.
Beyond the natural order it willed to appear to me, as to one untimely born,
and, lest I forget my nature, it kept me, abased, from knowing this.
That I heard a voice, and understood it too, is certain to me;
but whether I was there in the body or in the spirit, I do not know.
And if this escaped even me, who heard those things,
what explanation [?] can there be for one who asks how I went?
I went and arrived where I have said; believe it and confirm it,
and do not be divided over the things I heard and have related.
It is not glory that urges me to recount my labours;
zeal against [?] compelled me to boast of things higher than myself.
For this reason I willed to explain the things I saw:
that I might give hope to the hopeless in the good things beyond."
Who will not love the word of Paul, who was persuaded and persuaded others,
who did not hold back and cheat his fellows of what he heard?
Who will not meditate in books on the words of the scribe of the Spirit,
who explained and made hidden mysteries shine before his disciples?
Who will not fix before his mind the goal of his teaching,
he who pressed on toward victory with all his strivings and all his limbs?
Who will not scour away the ugliness of his soul by the beauty of his words,
and see its blemishes in the mirror of his beauties?
Who will not build upon the confession of his faith,
against which the winds of harsh sufferings blew and could not shake it?
Who will not put on the armour of the Spirit after his manner,
he who did not slacken from the struggle until death?
Who will not journey on the road he travelled toward the presence on high,
which he hastened along and reached, the presence on high, without weariness?
Who will not bind the impulses of his soul by his faith,

and write down hope, and meditate on a love that does not perish?
How can one who reads his writings keep silent,
and not repay him at least with words in return for his deeds?
How can it be that one who runs toward his goal
should not be repaid the crown of victory as he deserves?
Who fought in the contest of truth like Paul,
and who was more worthy than he of the crown of glory?
Who grew wise in spiritual things like his mind,
and who told of things to come as he wrote?
Who resembled him in running toward the goal the King had set,
and who pressed on toward victory in his likeness?
Who laboured without cost, as he laboured,
and did not take human provisions as wages?
Who ran in the spiritual stadium
and did not let the will of his soul be entangled in earthly things?
He hired himself out to the labour of the Spirit at the hour of morning,
and counted his toil as a single day for the whole of his life.
He began the race of preaching in his youth,
and finished his course in chains and in his old age.
Paul, aged and a prisoner for the sake of truth,
what mouth is able to tell of you as you are?
Feeble is the mind to run beside you swiftly,
and weak its wing to fly beside you to where you are.
One alone knows how to repay you the crown of victory:
He whom you loved above all things, as befits Him.
The Command that chose you is able to repay you the reward of your love,
He who sees the deeds of all before anything came to be.
The love of His love loved you, held you dear, and called you His own,
and gave you power to conquer by His strength as though by your own.
It was not in you to conquer sufferings without His power,
for the nature of mortals is far too weak to conquer by its own.

It was not in you to teach the hidden mysteries,
for created beings cannot gaze into what is hidden.
His love revealed them to you, as to a true lover of His love,
and He explained to you the force of hidden things higher than you.
He showed your faithfulness by the silver He gave you to trade with,
and, as to a faithful man, entrusted into your hands the treasure of His mercies.
True is your love, and worthy of the treasure He entrusted to your hands,
and no one knows how to manage it better than you.
You proclaimed the name of the Divine Being in the ears of all,
and you showed the equality of the Father and the Spirit.
You explained that the Son is not younger than His Begetter,
nor is the Spirit less than the Father and the Son who is from Him.
You taught us that the Divine Being is not bounded in Itself,
and you showed us that It is not touched by suffering.
By the Spirit of revelation you revealed the mystery of our life's redemption:
that the hidden Will was fulfilled and accomplished in the visible body of ours.
On the lyre of your soul you sang the distinction of the two likenesses,
the form of the servant and of the Maker, hidden and revealed.
Your tongue became like a pen in the hand of the Spirit,
and traced signs in the human mind: the Word and the body.
The Word and the body your voice proclaimed among mortals,
two that are distinct in their natures yet equal together.
Distinct and equal, hidden and revealed, and called one:
the Son of God, who made the man He took share with Him.
Paul did not bring in a distinction of son and son,
lest the heretic stumble at the distinction in his words.
He distinguished the natures, in that they are distinct one from another,
and gathered them in unity into one person.
He distinguished them because of the sufferings and the glories,
and made them equal because of a love without division.
He divided them, yet did not split them one from the other,
and made them equal through the Will that willed this.

He gave to each of them its own, according to what it is,
lest the Divine Being be lowered to sufferings by taking what is ours.
He made the Exalted share in the weaknesses by a borrowed name,
and the lowly in the glories by the very deeds themselves.
And if Paul, whom the Spirit chose, distinguished and made equal,
what heretic will dispute with the chosen vessel?
Paul has spoken: who has the right to dispute with Paul?
And whoever disputes with the Spirit that chose him becomes guilty before It.
Be silent, then, heretic, and do not dispute,
lest you be condemned by the harsh sentence of the Spirit.
Be silent, do not cry out against the true ones, you workers of falsehood,
for you have blotted out human peace by your contentions.
I am persuaded that you greatly hate the name of Paul,
and I am in no doubt that the distinction in his words gives you no rest.
The medicine of his words stings sharply the sore that is in you,
and for this reason you hate him as a stranger.
Hatred of the man has blinded the eye of your minds,
so that you do not look into the light hidden within his words.
It gave you to drink the cup mixed with the bitterness of its wrath,
and in you it troubled the serenity of the peace that brings peace to all.
It taught you to climb up on high to the Divine Being,
and it showed you the hateful path of passibility.
It estranged you from understanding the word of Paul,
who saw and proclaimed that the hidden nature is not bounded.
This is its own device, which it found and taught to those like it:
to bring down the Hidden One and to rob our body of the height.
In this way it accomplished its will through your words,
and threw into confusion the orders the Spirit ordained through the preachers.
In you it hid its falsehood as in a garment,
and entered and concealed itself within the flock as though it were true.
You it sent as spies into the households,
and through you it plundered the preaching like raiders.
In you it avenged on the true ones the disgrace of its scorn,
for you have despised the sound body of the faith.
From your hatred of Paul one learns this:
that you armed yourselves with devices against his words.

O the impudence of the heretics and slanderers,
every one of whom toils to confound the orders of the Spirit!
A great outrage the impudent have committed, together with the rebellious,
who trampled and despised the pure holy thing with their blasphemies.
For Your own sake [?], O King who redeemed our race, have pity on our race,
which, after it was set free, turned back and was enslaved to the slavery of death.
People have abandoned the road of Your love, full of peace,
and held to the road full of the loathsomeness of discord.
They hated the preachers who proclaimed truth and faith,
and loved the lie of falsehood that gave birth to evil.
Forsaken is the name of Paul and of his fellow labourers of the Spirit,
and everyone weaves crowns of victory for the workers of the lie.
No one brings the testimony of words from the true ones,
for the invention of error has been founded in the minds of fools.
If anyone repeats a saying of Paul or of Christ,
to hear it is strange, and it is not received in hostile ears.
They greatly hate meditation on the words of the Scriptures,
and among the impudent, studying them is reckoned superfluous.
"It is not good," they say, "to meditate much on glorious things,
lest the heart go astray through meditating on the words of the Spirit.
Inquiry teaches strife over words and unsettles the soul,
and makes the mind drunk with perplexities as with wine.
'Do not eat much honey,' cried the wise man;
see," they say, "he showed that you should not inquire into what is written.
"And the servant who knows his master's will and does not do it
is swallowed up by harsh lashes, because he knew and neglected it."
Behold the teaching of the great fool to his disciples:
he traced letters and turned them back from Taw to Alaph!
Behold the interpretation of the crafty scribe to his hearers:
he darkened them, shutting them off from the knowledge of the word of life!
Behold the venom of the man-slayer, which he cast into men,
and led them astray, outside the road of the Spirit's words!
The Spirit trod the road of life by the mouth of the preachers,
and the hateful one in his cunning filled it with ambushes before the travellers.
He cast fear and frightened them away from instruction:
"Do not," he says, "keep to the road of the books, lest you go astray."
Come, preacher, chosen vessel, who proclaimed truth,
see the devices the evil one has contrived against your words!

Come, teach us from the wisdom the Spirit placed in you,
that by it we may pull down the building of falsehood the crafty one built.
Speak in us, that we may tell what is yours to the wrongdoers
who have greatly wronged you by the slander of their blasphemies.
From the treasuries of your writings rebuke them,
and by your sayings let the falsehood of their opinions be exposed.
Let us repeat your saying: "All Scripture that the Spirit wrote
yields the profit of life to the one who meditates on it with toil.
It makes perfect and complete the one who meditates on it,
and he becomes fit to minister spiritually."
Come, you false ones, see the profit of the Spirit's words,
which perfect a man in spiritual things and give life.
Let us repeat also the word with which you urged your disciple:
"From your childhood the Scriptures have taught you the way of life."
The haters of meditation on the Spirit are put to shame and refuted
by the voice of the skilled master to his disciple.
Do not dispute falsely against the building of his words,
which is strong by the power of the Spirit and wisely built.
The Spirit testifies of his building that it is beautifully established,
and It rebukes the building of falsehood in your minds.
Let the Spirit be advocate in the judgment between me and you,
and let Its command lay bare the hidden cunning of their thoughts.
Let It rebuke you, who have wronged the labour of his love,
he who stood in the contest and was victorious and made his fellows victorious.
Tell me, you hostile ones, so hostile to plain things:
what light is so wondrous in its dawning as the name of Paul?
What road is so smooth for running as his sayings,
and who grows weary on the path of his words, laden with treasures?
What good things are not stored up and hidden in his name?
Whenever a man opens and reads Paul, he is enriched and made victorious.
What medicine is there that is not tempered and blended in his epistles,
and for every pain help is found in his admonitions?
What rule that gains life has he not laid down,
and what class of people has not been helped by his canons?
He laid down laws for youth and for old age,
for slaves and free, to be subject under one Lord.

He brought every measure under the canon of his preaching,
and yoked husbands with their wives in the yoke of love.
He gave victory to the striving of the upright will,
and strengthened and supported in their weakness those who had fallen.
He set in order the ranks of authority, inner and outer,
and showed everyone how to render what is due.
He yoked the world in the gentle yoke of his Lord's love,
that each might labour in the field of spiritual life.
He drove the darkness of the power of evils from humankind,
and drove man toward the light of his preaching.
With the sword of his word he cut off and cast away the love of money,
and showed everyone the bitterness hidden in its fruits.
With the lance of his love he brought down the height of the love of glory,
and humbled the pride and haughtiness of soul that do not befit man.
The envious serpent, whose venom tears and kills man —
at it he shot the arrow of the word of peace, and its venom lost its strength.
He called the angry to repent and to cease from anger
before the sun of life, which fulfils its time, should set.
He cast fear and pronounced judgment before sinners,
then turned and encouraged them: if they are justified, they are not condemned.
He revealed the riches of the kindness of the God of all,
which He shows in the fullness of the times to all and in all.
O the depth of the great riches that cannot be contained,
which nourish the world with its inhabitants and are not diminished!
O scrutiny that enters with its inquiry into senses and impulses,
and does not forget even a glance or the smallest hint!
O knowledge that shut up all in ignorance,
that it might give life and revive in goodness the work of its hands!
O mighty one, to whom the Command gave the keys of the Spirit,
and who opened the treasure of secret things hidden from all!
O disciple whom the rank of mastery reached,
who learned and taught through meditation the three Persons!
O you who were schooled from the Law for the kingdom on high,
and were enriched, and enriched both the people and the peoples from your treasures!

In you was fulfilled through deeds the power of the riddles,
for you gathered up the riches of the Law and of the Spirit.
You are worthy of blessing from every mouth, O preacher,
who proclaimed truth and turned all to the fear of truth.
Let the crown of victory be rendered to you from every tongue,
for you taught man to sing glory to the name of the Divine Being.
In the path of your words all classes ought to walk,
for you trod the road of the body's resurrection and the soul's freedom.
Upon the building of your word let the lovers of truth build,
for you completed and built one confession that cannot be shaken.
Toward your goal let everyone press on, in body and soul,
for you died to creation, and creation too was dead to you.
Every day you were crucified to desires, as one not living,
and the living world was reckoned by you as dead.
Blessed are you, Paul, the persuaded one, who was persuaded and persuaded others,
for the crown of victory is kept for you for the contest of your labours.
Plead for us, O persuaded one, as you are wont,
that your lovers may be counted worthy of the good things the Command grants to you.
Refrain: Thanks be to the Gracious One, who teaches the kinds of mercy to the lovers of His uprightness.
On the Apostles

Memra 8, on the Apostles. / The one before it is complete. / The eighth memra, which he composed on all the apostles; it is recited at the commemoration of the Evangelists. / Response: Blessed is Christ, who clothed his apostles / in the armor of the Spirit, and by it they triumphed and were victorious. / Another: Blessed is Christ, who promised and swore: / a reward for the righteous and judgment for the wicked. / My brothers,

The King on high made a spiritual banquet,
and sent his servants to call all to the wedding feast of his love.
He invited and called the heavenly and the earthly,
and sent his servants to call all to the wedding feast of his love.
He invited and called the heavenly and the earthly,
and prepared spiritual food that does not perish.
He seated them in the visible temple of the body,
and showed them the might of his greatness through senses that are manifest.
On the head of a son of man he set the crown of divinity,
so that men [?] spiritual beings might see the hidden in the manifest.
It was not possible to see the Son and gaze upon him,
and so he showed his glory in the body to the eye of those who behold.
He showed his glory to the eye, his adornments, not his essence;
the might of his greatness he revealed to his works, not his hiddenness.
The Will, the Word that is from him, put on the garment of the body,
and through it he made known the force of the search into his hidden things.
His love fashioned a harp of spiritual flesh,
to delight with it the spiritual and the bodily.
On the strings of the body his will played, as with a finger,
and men and spiritual beings marveled at the sweetness of its sound.
Beautiful was the melody the Hidden One made for the work of his hands,
and very pleasing as he sang his hiddenness on the flute of flesh.
For the work of his hands he made the banquet, not for his own need,
for he lacks nothing, since his goodness is with his essence.
He honored his image by what he revealed of his Being.
He added nothing to his nature by what he acquired;
he has nothing to increase or diminish of what he is,
nor does his nature come to rejoice or grieve by being made known.
He willed to renew rational nature through the things he visited,
and through it, again, he made known the power of the wisdom of his love's hiddenness.
To the image of his image he gave honor above all, as to an image,
and through it he gladdened the sorrow that had driven away peace.
The sin of men had troubled peace and loosened love,
and through human beings he willed to bring all into peace with his love.
One from among men he chose by his will and called him by his name,
and through him he turned rational nature toward knowledge of him.
For the affection of his love he called [them] to the banquet he had made for his [?]

and gathered to himself the heavenly and the earthly [?].
The sons of his own race he made servants and envoys,
and invited all to the wedding feast of spiritual life.
He spoke his intimation in the tongue of flesh with the bodily,
and taught them how they should catch men for life.
His power strengthened the weakness of their minds,
so that they might bring the divided world to peace by the sound of their words.
He mixed his love like medicines into their words,
so that by their utterances they might heal the pains of body and soul.
He clothed their minds with his truth as with armor,
so that they might overcome the error the Evil One had sown in the land of humanity.
The grace of mercy anointed their limbs like athletes,
so that the hand of the demons might slip off them in the contest of labors.
He gave them the sword of the Spirit to destroy iniquity,
to put the Enemy to shame, and that men might slay the one who had slain them.
He clothed them with the might of his help as with breastplates,
so that the arrows of his cunning might not lodge in their limbs.
He held faith before them like a shield,
so that with it they might shelter body and soul from harm.
Spiritually he clothed them with the weapons of war,
so that they might be skilled in joining battle with the hosts.
With all things and in all things he trained them in the exercise of labors,
and through trial they gained the discipline of spiritual things.
The power of the wisdom of every craft they learned from the Spirit;
they grew rich, and from their treasures they made the poor rich.
Light and salt they were in creation by their deeds:
they gave light to the dim and gave savor to the tasteless.
They pursued error with the glorious brilliance of their way of life,
and made the light of righteousness dawn in the house of darkness.
They uprooted paganism, the false building the demons had built,
and built the firm, pure truth of the Creator's name.
They overthrew the temples of idolatry that the demons had adorned,
and brought love and faith to perfection in the minds of men.
They drove the gloom of the name of gods from all peoples,
and the world saw the beauty of the one God springing up.
Their voices were like thunder among the earthly;
the sunken were stirred and the weighed-down arose at the sound of their words.
Spiritually their limbs wove the net of love;
they spread it over all, and it caught from all, the good and the bad.
They fished from the sea and fished from the dry land a rational catch,
and offered them as an offering to the King on high.
That King, too, named his preaching a net,
which his love spread over all peoples by the hand of his servants.
In deeds the apostles fulfilled that heavenly voice:
"Make disciples and baptize all the peoples in the name of the Being."
Three names they received from him like a seal;
they sealed men with it and marked them spiritually.
They inscribed the Trinity on limbs and members,
that everyone might learn to hallow the worshipped name.
With a living mark they marked the flock of the human race,
and gathered it and brought it into the fold of spiritual life.
In the pasture of the Spirit they fed the rational sheep,
and by the springs of the drink of rest they made them lie down.

They shepherded rightly, set in order and visited wisely,
and made rams and ewes wise in the love of truth.
They visited their rams, bound up the broken, sought the lost,
nourished and kept the whole flock as one body.
Like a mirror there stood always before their minds
that word to Simon: "Do you love me?"
With great love they girded on the will of the Shepherd of the sheep;
even to death they pressed on into sufferings for love of humanity.
They loved humanity above all things, as they had been commanded,
and for humanity's sake they spurned their own lives and loved death.
They honored humanity because of the love of him who loves humanity,
for they saw that he loved humanity above all things.
They saw that in his love he put on, by his will, the likeness of a servant,
to raise humanity from the blemish of its stain to greatness.
In his love they imitated him and loved humanity, those called by his name,
and taught them to turn to him by the way of truth.
According to his will they mixed medicine for their sicknesses,
and gave them to drink grace and mercies that do not wear away.
With mercies they healed the sick who had lingered in the pains of iniquity,
and with compassion they bound up the dead whom evil had crushed.
Grace soothed the bruises of senses and limbs,
and they washed them in the gentle waters of baptism.
As into a furnace they brought body and soul to refine them,
and scoured from them the hateful filth of loathsome iniquity.
Like potters they broke the rational vessels
and renewed them through repentance into a new molding.
O mortals, a nature of clay, prone to breaking,
whose members were turned, renewed, and became gold!
O earthly ones, children of the serpent [?], contemptible to look upon,
who made the despised lowliness of humanity gain a heavenly body!
O poor ones, whose father sinned and sold them,
and who bought the world with the wealth they gathered by their labors!
Rich from the treasure of the One honored with the name of Creator,
they enriched humanity with what was not theirs as though it were theirs.
With what was not theirs they freed what was theirs from slavery,
and wrote them a charter of freedom free of death.
Spacious armor they received from the spiritual King,
and in it they triumphed in the eyes of the spiritual and the bodily.
The captives of humanity they ransomed from death and from Satan,
and freed them from bondage to the worship of iniquity.
They waged war with the Strong One who enslaves humanity,
and recovered from him the captives he had led off from their ranks.
With the sword of the Spirit they cut down the camp of the Enemy,
and laid low the ranks of his forces before bodily men.
The strong one who enslaved men was defeated; humanity triumphed,
and the demons were distressed by the voice of men clothed with the Spirit.
By the Spirit the spiritual ones waged war with the bodily,
and men clothed with sufferings conquered the impassible.
A great wonder did endurance work in the love of the righteous,
who despised the visible body for the sake of the Spirit.
Glorious is the combat they displayed on earth through their labors,
and the mouth is too small to tell the tale of their victories.

The course of their conduct is longer than any measuring,
and the mind is too feeble to journey with them to the end.
Fearful is the contest in which they fought with the hosts,
