and the heart shrinks from recounting their sufferings.
Fear and love fill the passage where they are read:
labors to be feared, all crowned and glorious indeed to the one who loves.
Through love the mind is able to read their deeds,
and it shows the lover the path of their labors.
Through faith his mind is able to journey with them,
and it encourages him not to slacken from the things promised.
Hope urges the hidden inclination toward hidden things,
and it strengthens him to tread on sufferings through endurance.
Love and hope and faith the victors put on,
and with them they fought against all powers, hidden and manifest.
With them they were strengthened, as with armor, against evil,
and by them they fought with spirits and with bodies.
In their simplicity [?] they went down into the contest of harsh labors;
they trod upon sufferings and despised life as though they were not human.
Like the impassible they showed their love in what they endured;
they hated life and loved death, against all custom.
Beyond all order they despised life and its bonds;
they became haters of earthly things and loved what is above.
What is above they loved, though it is hidden from those who see,
and hated what is below, though it is manifest to senses and limbs.
In the love of the love of things to come they despised what is on earth,
and taught men to hate earthly things.
The hidden things were before their eyes as though manifest,
and they saw them, as in a mirror, before them and with them.
As with a finger they pointed them out to the earthly,
so that mortals looked and saw the beauty hidden on high.
As children they drew humanity toward the things promised,
and as with milk they nourished them with the food of the Spirit.
The medicine of life they cast upon the land of mortality,
and the dead of iniquity began to live at the sound of their words.
New voices mortals heard [from mortals]:
men crying in the ears of humanity the abolition of death.
A new hope men brought to mankind:
the resurrection of the body, the redemption of the soul, and the renewal of all.
As from sleep they awakened mankind,
and the sunken were stirred at the voice of the renewal of body and soul.
They taught all to meditate on the name of the Being:
three persons that are not torn apart by change.
The unlettered wrote a new book for rational nature;
they taught them to read: Father, Son and Spirit.
Three names they wrote on the tablets of their minds,
one Being whose eternity has no beginning.
The nature that put on a body they marked with a letter,
so that they might read the Word and the body, the hidden in the manifest.
The likeness of the servant and of the Maker they inscribed in their hearts,

so that everyone might see the image of hiddenness in the manifest senses.
Divinity with humanity their voices sang,
and their song delighted the spiritual and the bodily.
Son of the Being and son of humanity they called one child,
one from the height and one from the depth, the Word and the body.
The hidden and the manifest they proclaimed and taught to mankind,
so that through what is seen they might gain hope toward the Being.
With their mouths, with the body as a door, they set bounds to senses and motions [?],
so that they would not wear themselves out searching for the Hidden One who cannot be grasped.
They held bodily nature in their hands like a mirror,
and showed the world the power of hiddenness in senses that are manifest.
The name of God they painted on a bodily page,
and named the Son of Man with a divine name.
God-man they called the Being and the humanity,
the Son of God, whose love dwelt in the temple of our body.
The hidden Spirit revealed to them the hidden mysteries,
and taught them to ponder the two natures [?] as one person.
He revealed to them hidden mysteries they had not known,
and made them wise in how they should confess the Word and the body.
They distinguished the natures one from another as they are,
so that the nature of the Being might not be diminished in our body, which it put on.
To each of them they justly gave what it possesses,
so that everyone might learn that the Being is not mingled with our body.
To the Being they gave a revelation above all, as befits it,
and they called the body visible, as it is.
The impassible they exalted and set above sufferings,
and the mortal they covered with the garment of mortality.
They distinguished, and spoke of the two alike, as those who know,
so that those who travel the way of their words might not be troubled.
They were afraid that someone might stray from the truth,
and the course of the perfection of the Creator's name be diminished.
They were anxious for the cultivation of spiritual life,
lest the thicket of error spring up in the good seed.
They were very careful in building love and faith,
lest crafty workers build with hay and straw.
With a hidden eye they gazed at things to come:
that there would be men who conceal the truth and build falsehood.
It was revealed to them that some would put on wolves' skins in the likeness of sheep,
and bite the lambs of men in their disguises.
They looked into the wickedness of the heretics' minds,
who [?] the beautiful garment of faith.
They saw that men would wrong the body that is from us,
and beforehand they uprooted the thorny thicket of their thoughts.
The name of humanity they sowed first in the ears of men,
and afterward [?] concerning the Being that is hidden from all.
Wisely they taught the manifest truth:
the will of the Hidden One and the temple of the body, two that became one.
From lowly things to glorious ones they led them by steps,
for so the proper order commands the one who teaches.
They gave men bodily nature to drink like milk,
and then they offered the solid food of divinity.
These nets the fishermen spread in creation

and caught the world in the meshes of their words.
With these ploughshares they ploughed the earth full of thorns,
and its womb brought forth fruits of praise for its Owner.
These words the spiritual farmers sowed,
and the seed of their faith sprouted in the land of men.
This is the way the guides of faith marked out,
and cities and humanity began to travel to the place of peace.
By these voices they reconciled men with spiritual beings,
and trained them in the good exercise of a living mind.
By this power they prevailed in the combat with Satan,
and exposed the mysteries the demons had taught mankind.
By this help they conquered and were crowned in the hidden and the manifest,
and gained the rank of mastery in both worlds.
The name of the Creator they put on like armor and fought with all,
and counted the heights and everything that is as refuse.
They traveled with their limbs and their bodies to every place,
and healed pains, raised the dead, and drove out demons.
They divided peoples and cities among themselves for their ministry,
so that each of them might show his proven worth through deeds.
They journeyed relying [?] on that voice which had chosen them:
"Behold, I am with you forever."
Simon proclaimed among the Romans the new hope:
the divinity that put on a body that gives life to all.
The fisherman went out first to catch the peoples;
he cast his net and caught the mother of cities.
The head of the disciples caught the city of dominion,
brought it in and enclosed it within the fortresses of faith.
The firstborn, who first confessed the Son as the Son of God,
was the first to offer the sacrifices of the conversion of the peoples.
He laid his confession like a rock at the foundation of the house,
and built and completed the peoples, joined together by the sinews of love.
In it he made Rome complete; the buildings of idolatry shook,
and the error the demons had adorned for the building of falsehood fell.
At his voice the demons trembled, and men, the servants of demons,
and they despised the worship of the name of gods and honored the truth.
John too raised his voice to the Ephesians;
as from sleep he awakened them to the worship of life.
Like thunder was the echo of his voice in the barren land,
and he watered its womb with the living rain of the word of his mouth.
He cast into it the good seed of faith,
through deeds befitting the name he was called by.
He made the sound of his preaching heard like thunder,
the son of thunder, whose voice raised those who had died in sin.
He showed them a new way that gives life to the dead.
Matthew taught the Trinity among the Hebrews [?].
He sealed the voices of prophecy with his preaching,
and confirmed them through the promises made to the righteous.
They made known to them that the mysteries were fulfilled and the truth had dawned.
He gladdened Abraham, that the peoples had become brothers of his beloved,
and made David rejoice that from his seed had arisen the King who was written of.
He recorded his conception, that it was by the Spirit, without union,
and like a root Mary sprang up from the land of thirst.

In this temple of the body he showed that the will of the Hidden One dwelt,
and called him by the name of the Son of God, exalted above all.
To this goal Luke also attained, the physician of the Spirit,
and as with medicine he healed the Egyptians with his words.
A skilled physician was sent to a sick people,
to bind its wounds with divine medicines.
In the [?] of God the son of Shem visited the son of Ham the slave,
and laid on his mind the medicine of the soul's freedom.
In the pain of iniquity the seed of rebellious Ham lay,
and the Hebrew bound it up by the Spirit and covered its iniquity.
He loosed it from the yoke of slavery to the iniquity of the [?],
and stamped it with the Spirit to be a soldier of the King on high.
Beautiful were the voices [as he cried out in the land of Egypt
and silenced the voices] of error by his preaching.
Great was the outpouring of the word of his mouth, greater even than Gihon,
and the movements of his soul surpassed the silent ones [?].
His voice was fearsome to the Egyptians, more even than Gihon [?],
and the freedoms of his people exceeded those of Israel.
Moses freed his people, who died in sin, and led them back;
Luke freed his people and turned them back with hope and life.
Freedom and life the Hebrew counseled to the sons of his race,
and proclaimed to them the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the soul.
Mark nourished the seed that [?] Cephas among the Romans,
and with his words watered the rational fruits with the sweetness of his voice.
He built his teaching on the confession of Cephas the chosen,
and did not slacken under the blasts of the winds of error.
Like the sun the truth of his words dawned among the Romans,
and drove away the darkness of the sorcery Simon had taught.
He exposed and laid bare the craft of that deceiver,
and made his bitterness tasteless by the sweetness of the name of Jesus.
He uprooted his tares and cleared the thicket of his [?],
and sowed in men the good seed of his faith.
In faith he began and finished, like his companions,
and joined his book to the testaments of his fellows.
In four books the King sealed his preaching,
and set the hand of seventy-eight [?] to the redemption of the peoples.
Like a garment he spread his teaching to the four quarters,
and clothed the naked world with the garment of his [?].
The name of Christ they bound on their hands and their limbs,
and as with a seal [?] they sealed men with it against harm.
They regarded one another as a single body, though they were many,
and bound the love of their minds to the head, Christ.
Beautiful was the gathering of their members, the Christians,
and very precious was the honored name they bore.
Like an image Christ was painted before their mind,
and they gloried in the stamp of his name as in a crown.
Nothing was in their eyes but Christ,
and on him the hidden gaze of their minds was fixed.
They did not reckon this dwelling in time to be anything,
nor did they think there was any gain in earthly things.

Paul, the chosen one, friend of the King on high,
who was dead while living and alive while dead, despised and glorious.
He was dead to the world, for he took no joy in its desires,
and he lived in the hope of that renewal which will come at the end.
He longed without being sated for converse with his Lord, and waited
to see him face to face, without a veil.
For he was with him in the life of time in a hidden way,
but he longed to be with him in perfection.
In this matter the heralds of the word of life were lovers,
and while they were on earth they were not on earth, but with him.
For his love's sake they left everything and honored his love,
and became witnesses of his preaching among humanity.
They proclaimed his conception and showed forth his birth and the growth of his body;
they depicted his passion and portrayed his resurrection: that he rose and ascended.
They heard the voice that commanded them to make disciples and baptize,
and lovingly fulfilled his love, the word of his mouth, in the ears of all.
They went out into the streets and along the roads after men,
and gathered and filled the banquet hall with good and bad;
they seated them at the spiritual table.
They gave them to drink the medicine of life in a mystery that bears a likeness;
with the body and blood they nourished them in a hidden way,
so that all might learn that the body and blood are his who was bodily.
With the food of the Spirit they accustomed the weary peoples;
they spurned the table of idolatry and honored the truth;
with the robe of glory they clothed the naked.
They checked the course of their frivolous conduct;
with hope and life he confirmed them in the promises,
and taught them not to slacken in the sufferings of time.
The promise of life they set as a goal before their eyes,
so that they might press on in faith toward the things to come.
By their own example they urged them to [?],
and they set out like teachers before disciples.
They went first into the contest of labors before the athletes,
and showed the weapons of battle to the warriors.
They overcame every power by the power of divine help,
and burned and scorned the rage [?] of demons and men.
They despised wars and trampled on the threats of tyrant kings,
and derided and laughed at judges and their authorities.
They undid the teaching that error had written by the hand of men,
and wrote books of the one teaching of the God of all.
Beautiful was their voice as they cried out among the earthly:
Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one Being.
Lovely was the song of their spiritual harps
as they sang of the Word and the body, the Son of God.
Their words were pleasing to cities and to men
as they sowed the new hope, the cause of peace.
The hosts of heaven marveled at the power that was in them,
as they prevailed over every teaching by the power of Jesus.

The spiritual beings stood in wonder at their contests, / for they saw that the world and its might had been brought low by painters. / They saw that they were clothed in the nature of corruptible flesh, / and they marveled greatly at how they overcame the passions within them. / O beings of flesh, who scorned nature and its bondage, / and showed the likeness of those beyond suffering before their oppressors! / O earthly ones, who lived on earth in the frailty of the body, / and were not stained by the hateful sores of its weakness! / O merchants, who travelled a road full of terror, / and the great treasure of their thoughts was not plundered! / O sailors, who sat in the ship on the raging sea, / and their faith did not sink amid the storms! / O harps that sing [?] to the Trinity, / whose strings of thought never lost their tuning! / O athletes, who wrestled in the arena with serpents, / whose limbs the hands of their captors could not bind! / O farmers, who sowed life among the dead, / while paganism was a forest that the demons had made grow [?] among men! / O disciples, who kept the love of Christ the Great, / whose gaze of love never turned away from their Lord! / Love is too weak to give an account of your thoughts, / and the mind cannot paint the image of your victories. / The tongue is pained that it cannot reach the height to which you rose, / and the mind waits to reach the haven of life with you. / One alone can paint the image of your love, / and he knows how to count the labors of your contests. / To him it is revealed how much you suffered for love of him, / and it is he who decides how to reward your devotion. / In his vineyard you labored from the beginning of his preaching [?], / and he pays you the denarius of life that does not perish.
On the Commemoration of Saint Stephen

A [?] homily on the commemoration of Saint Stephen.
Response: Glorious is your death, firstborn of the martyrs, Stephen, beloved of Jesus, who trod the way for the blessed martyrs, so that they might follow you to the kingdom on high. My brothers.

The King on high, who by the Cross conquered the Evil One and Death, chose a laborer for himself and sent him first, ahead of his camp.
Ahead of the camp a champion of the contest went out and stood among the troops of the King on high against the Adversary.
The King sent Stephen ahead of his camp, so that he would be the first to join battle with the rebels.
The King sent him in the wondrous rank of the [?], so that when the hosts on high saw him they would marvel at him.
He anointed him with the Spirit and girded him with armor so that he would not be defeated, and before the band of the apostles he triumphed in the contest.
The King gave him the whole armor of the warriors, so that he might wage war on the rebels without fear.
The sword of the Spirit was put into his hand at the bidding of the One who sent him, so that he might cut down and overthrow the wicked who had rebelled against righteousness.
Faith, the shield of truth, he held in his hands, and with it he caught the sharp arrows of his adversaries.
When the arrows of iniquity were shot at him to wound him,

he caught them on the shield of hope and was not harmed.
He wrapped the breastplate of righteousness about his limbs, so that they could not strike them and he would not become a laughingstock to their hosts.
He put on the helmet of salvation and life that the King had given him, so that by it he might protect faith, the head of his life.
He was strengthened wholly and entirely in faith, and there was no place in it where he could be stripped of the truth.
Faith was reckoned to him as the head of his life, and he hid it under the helmet so that they could not strike it.
The King warned him and his companions and commanded them: "Be like serpents in your cunning."
Wise is the serpent, which guards itself so that they cannot strike it, for as long as its head lives it is not destroyed by blows.
In this way it is right for you to guard your faith, for as long as it is kept you need not fear harm.
The steadfast laborer held fast to this commandment and guarded it like a head, so that it would not be harmed.
Like a shield he held faith in his hand, and he shod his feet with the readiness of the gospel.
He rode on the word of holiness as on a horse, and, light of wing, on the humility of righteousness.
He rode on the word, took up the sword, put on truth, set on the helmet, and shod his feet with his Lord's readiness.
He cried out like a general in the camp of the Adversary, and they began to tremble at the sound of his voice, which was like thunder.
The King sent him ahead of the troops of the hosts on high, to tread the way for his fellows so that they might be like him.
He was the first to tread the way of witness to his Lord, and he became the firstborn of the martyrs of Jesus, the King on high.
The hosts of the prince of the air were thrown into turmoil when they saw the warrior who was scorning them.
They saw that they were too weak to fight against his might, so they hired the sons of Abraham and brought them to be with them.

The sons of Abraham and the hosts of the Evil One became a single troop, to defeat Stephen, the laborer of truth.
The sons of Abraham hired themselves out to the Adversary, and as the wage of their hire they received the judgment to come.
Through the Hebrews the Evil One made war on the laborer, just as through their chiefs he had made war on the King.
Stephen was full of power and of grace, and he was working signs in the land of Judea.
Men arose from the wicked synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians with their companions, to dispute with him.
The enemies of the truth could not stand even a little against the Spirit that spoke in him.
They were defeated by the words of the good laborer and put to shame, and see, their defeat is proclaimed in all generations.
In their insolence they sent men and taught them to say, "We heard him blaspheming in his words against God and against the king."
They seized him and brought him into the midst of the assembly of the workers of iniquity, to put him to death as one who had blasphemed against God.
With the arrows of his words the witness of Jesus scourged them, the sons of Abraham who were not heirs of Abraham's hope.
The Just One recounted to the sons of Abraham the election of Abraham, whom the One who beckons chose from among the Babylonians, in order to shame them.
The One who beckons chose the sons of Abraham out of all the peoples, and honored them with his intimacy above everyone.
He let no one wrong them or harm them, and he delivered them from the Egyptians and from the Babylonians.
"Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in your hearts, you have set yourselves against him and against the Holy Spirit who is from him.
The jealousy of your minds is like that of your fathers, who persecuted the just and killed the righteous whom the One who beckons sent."

With these words he struck them as with a rod, and confronted them with unsparing bitterness.
The gall of anger leapt up in their hearts, and they could not withstand the sharp arrows of his words.
The good laborer defeated the laborers — the snares [?] — of the Evil One, and they were embittered at finding themselves on the losing side.
In anger they hurried, since they were being defeated by the truth, and they seized him, brought him outside the city, and began to stone him.
They could not withstand the force of the word of the athlete of truth, and they saw a way to put him to a temporal death.
The temporal death that the victor died is not for ever, and so he received death with joy.
He had learned from his Lord, who conquered death and broke its sting, and so he scorned it and was not afraid.
For those who stoned him he pleaded with the Lord who had chosen him, not to hold against them this sin they were committing against him.
The laborer of truth was becoming like the Lord of all, who pleaded with his Father to forgive his crucifiers.
The laborers of iniquity drew up their ranks as for battle, and instead of armor they armed themselves with stones and rocks.
The steadfast servant did not falter before their wickedness, and did not draw back from the fight against iniquity.
The King who had chosen him was encouraging him so that he would not falter, and he opened the heights above before him so that he might take still more courage.
In a revelation he saw the heavens opened, and he saw Jesus standing at the right hand.
The chosen martyr saw Christ standing, standing like one who wishes to come down to him.
In this way Christ was showing himself to him, like one who wishes to come and rescue him from their hands.
The athlete saw the unspeakable love of Jesus, who showed himself not sitting but standing.
This is the way of those who watch over their loved ones: they cannot be persuaded to hold back from them while they are being wronged.
The King's beloved was being beaten by insolent men, and the King saw his beloved overwhelmed and showed himself.

Through a revelation he showed himself to the lover of his love, and his face shone like the countenance of an angel of light.
The athlete saw the light of his glory in the midst of the contest, and his eyes shone as he gazed into the kingdom on high.
Into the kingdom on high the beloved of Jesus was gazing, and so he scorned and despised every suffering.
The light of Jesus' radiance shone upon his face, and the light of his soul was mingled with the radiance of his face.
The light of his face was mingled with the radiance of Jesus' light, and the light of our Lord's glory and his own were one.
Christ was on high and Stephen among the earthly, yet the glory of his Lord on high and his own below were one.
He was not like his Lord in unspeakable glory; but He gave him a portion of his glory, and he was in glory.
The King on high clothes his servants in glory on high, but Stephen he clothed in glory while he was still on earth.
While he was still on earth He gave him the glory of the immortals, to confirm what is to come at the last.
"When our lowly body is changed," says Paul, "he will make it like his glorious body."
In this way He acted now with Stephen too: while he was still on earth, He honored his face with His own radiance.
What a wonder was displayed in Stephen: death roaring, and he scorning the echoes of its voice!
Who ever saw a dying man whose face rejoiced as Stephen rejoiced as he died?
What laborer's cheeks ever shone in the hour of battle, except this laborer of truth who was found worthy of it?
Who ever saw arms hurling stones, and the face of their target shining so that it amazed his killers?
All of them gazed at him, as it is written — the whole assembly — and they were amazed at the sight of his face, wondering what this was.

At his face the laborers of iniquity grew embittered, and they brought down on him a rain of stones, as on Abel.
Envy stoned him with stones of wrath as it did Abel, and more than Abel's did the athlete's blood cry out in truth.
The envy of his brother unjustly stoned Abel, and Stephen's brothers unjustly stoned him.
They gathered a cloud of stones of wrath over the victor, and buried him in them, like Abel whom Cain killed.
Cain killed his brother Abel and buried him under stones, and raised a heap of stones over him so that it would not be known.
In the same way they too acted against the blameless one,
and like Cain they now await the payment of their wages.
Alas for the excellent one who was not wrapped for burial with honor, whose radiant body was despised beneath a heap of stones!
Alas for you, head that was consecrated by the laying on of hands, and that unjustly bore a crown of stones in iniquity!
He was consecrated by the laying on of the apostles' hands, and the sons of iniquity heaped stones on him in their insolence.
The Spirit hovered over him and consecrated him by the power of his grace, and the sons of iniquity spattered his person with his own blood.
The blessed band of the apostles laid their hands on him and set him apart to consecrate the mysteries of holiness.
He was a minister of the awesome and divine mysteries, and by his ministry he portrayed the pattern of the angels.
Deacons in the Church take on this pattern, becoming like the hosts on high through their ministry.
This rank the athlete attained in this life here: the rank and the appearance of being, in truth, a Watcher in the flesh.
A nature of flesh and a face of fire were seen together, a wondrous sight in a human nature that resembled the Watchers.
Therefore his Lord honored him with the radiance of the Watchers, so that when he rises he may be in a glory like theirs.
The body of the children of light resembles the body of our Lord, in that state in which mortality is taken away.

The laborers of iniquity were not deterred by the light of his face, and insolently, in their audacity, they stoned the Just One.
The wicked servants in the vineyard of my beloved saw a shoot sprouting on the stock [?], and in anger they cut it down.
The insolent saw a shoot that bore good fruit,
and they cut it down at once so that it would not bear sweet fruit.
The vineyard of my beloved is the people of the house of Israel, and the wicked servants are the heirs who mocked the Lord of the vineyard.
The Lord of the vineyard sent his Son to collect the fruit, and they seized him, brought him outside the vineyard, and killed him unjustly.
The unjust pronounced a true judgment when they were asked what the Lord of the vineyard would do to those servants.
"He will miserably destroy those servants," they said, "who beat his servants, insulted his laborers, and killed his son."
And the Creator, seeing that the vineyard gave no fruit, broke down its fence, uprooted its tower, and withheld its watering.
Prophecy, from which it used to drink the water of the Spirit, ceased, and the [?] of its idleness closed around it.
He uprooted the tower, the holy temple built within it, in which they used to press out the mute sacrifices of the law.
He took a single vine from the stock of this vineyard, and left all the rest to bear brushwood and thorns.
The Creator took the vine of life from this vineyard, so that all who wish might nourish their souls on the life that comes from it.
The vine of life became, in creation, the head of our race, so that with the sweetness of the wine of his love he might fill his servants to overflowing.
"I, I am the true vine," he said, "and you are the branches,

and I have set you in the world so that you may go and bring fruits of glory.
My Father is the husbandman of this vineyard, and every branch on which no fruit is found, he takes away.
See that you do not slacken in bearing good fruit, lest you burn like branches that burn in the fire.
A withered branch is gathered at once and thrown into the fire; so it will be with you too if you do not abide in love for me.
I, I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the husbandman; bring fruit and give thanks, so that you are not cut off."
These things the good Lord said to the servants he had chosen, and he warned them not to stray from his love.
In him they too planted their love truly, like a branch whose root is set in the vine.
From its life, life flowed into their planting, and from it they drank its waters of holiness.
Their stature rose above all the peoples of the earth, and they shielded them from the sickness of mortality.
They cast shade over every corner of the earth's regions, and protected them from the scorching heat of sin.
They gathered all the sweet clusters of their way of life, and everyone ate, and the palate that had been bitter grew sweet.
Everyone's palate had been bitter from the poison of death, and they sweetened it with the good hope of the resurrection of the dead.
They taught them to proclaim the resurrection of the dead on earth: that everyone will rise from the dead as he rose.
In this vine, like his companions, the chosen one was planted, and the laborers of iniquity cut him off with the pruning knife of their insolence.
Into this vine he grafted himself with great love, and he bore early fruit and put out leaves for the healing of mankind.
He fed them teachings like food, and by the power of the Spirit he healed them of their pains.
Like his companions he came to bear fruit through the drink of life, and his leaves rejoiced in a great and unspeakable wonder.

The cluster of his soul was full of the wine of Jesus' love, and the enemies of grace saw its beauty and grew embittered.
They became messengers of the Slanderer, the enemy of mankind, and gathered over him a cloud of wrath and a hail of stones.
With a hail of stones they beat down the sweet fruit, so that those in need of drink might not delight in its sweetness.
They put the Just One into the winepress of envy, and trampled him under the heels of hostility.
They poured out his blood like wine in a winepress, and pressed his body down under stones like heavy weights.
Even as they hurled at him the stones of wrath they were carrying, the blood of Christ had not been washed from their hands.
The Redeemer's blood still defiled the tips of their fingers, while the stones of iniquity in their hands were raining down on him.
Like wolves they rushed upon the shepherd and tore his body, and bared their jaws at the lamb to overcome him.
The defiled were not sated with having shed the blood of the Lord, and again they were eager to shed the blood of the lover of his love.
They were stained with drops of the Lord's blood when they came to overcome the beloved lamb.
The wolves of evening were drunk on blood beyond measure, and their rage was bitterer than that of wolves.
They took the blood of the Lord upon themselves and upon their children, and they are stained with it for ever, world without end.
The wicked mingled the blood of the servant with the blood of the Lord, and bore it upon themselves to convict them of their guilt.
The blood of the holy one was poured out like his Lord's, so that he might be with his Lord in glory in the kingdom on high.

When the wicked iniquity of the sons of iniquity assails us, let us call on this saint to deliver us from the unjust.
Whoever is oppressed and takes refuge in him with love and hope is no longer harmed by the unjust who oppress him.
Whoever is persecuted by the Slanderer, the enemy of mankind, let him take refuge in him, and the enemy will flee from him like smoke.
In his life in time he used to drive out the insolent demons, and now in his death they tremble all the more before the might of his power.
In his life in time they could not look at him, and now in his death they cannot even enter his dwelling.
And if they do enter, they enter in fear, for all their insolence, proclaiming their defeat by their very fear.
Trembling and fear truly fill the rebels when they see the dwelling of the Just One, even from afar.
The shrine of the Just One is set in their minds as a strong city that cannot be taken by assault, whenever they see it.
They stand far off on the mountaintops and gaze at it, because they cannot come near the face of its wall.
Power goes out from the treasured relics of the Just One's bones, and they see him as a general and flee from him.
Come, let us hasten on the day of the commemoration of the radiant martyr, so that he may help us and we may not be harmed by the rebels.
Come, let us hasten with prayers on the day of his feast, so that we may be with him in the kingdom on high, in the promised blessings.
On the Greek Fathers and Teachers

Homily 10: On the Greek Fathers and Teachers.
Again by the same author, the tenth homily, which is on the Greek fathers and teachers.
Response:
Thanks be to him who revealed the treasure of his wisdom to the loved ones he chose.
My brothers.

A just zeal on behalf of the just has pressed me hard
to ask why the reward of their labours has been withheld from them.
I have seen their excellence despised among the people of the earth,
and I have grieved deeply at how, and how greatly, the just are wronged.
The insolent have done a great wrong to those who know the truth,
and they have bitterly mocked and scorned their words.
In their words humankind saw the truth revealed,
and those who are not true were darkened by the light of faith.
As with salt they purified the world by their understanding,
and the dull of heart found the savour of the word of life tasteless.
They trod the way of life in creation for mortal humankind,
yet those dead in iniquity were not raised from their sins.
The haters of life were deranged in their madness,
in that they hated the word of truth spoken by those who know.
The true loved the word of truth above all things,
and the sons of error named them haters of truth.
The revealed truth proclaims the power of their words,

and the foolish cry out that the discourse of their thoughts is false.
Truth cries out like a trumpet in their books,
but the ear of the foolish was like a stone that will not soften.
The true set their course toward the goal of the divine Scriptures,
and diligently they interpreted the force of their meaning.
The rebel, the hater of humankind, saw the truth that was in them,
and he incited people to hate them as if they were mad.
The Crafty One cast an evil zeal into the minds of the foolish,
that they might fight against the word of truth spoken by those who know.
His is the seed of this teaching that has spread across the earth,
which makes the learned hateful in the eyes of the foolish.
Through the mouth of the unlearned he belches out his bitterness against those who know,
for he knows that their heart longs eagerly to listen to his words.
Through the crafty the Crafty One is ever striving,
and through them he shoots the arrows of his deceit at the company of the just.
Through their mouth he wages battle with the true in every generation,
and by their tongue he lays waste the ranks of the faith.
This has been his aim from the beginning of man's making:
that by the hand of man he might array battle against men.
In bodily form he has always fought against bodily beings,
since his own nature is without composition and invisible.
Through the bodily serpent he first drew near with speech [?],
and by its tongue he sowed error in the ears of Eve.
By the hand of flesh he slew Abel, the firstborn of the just,
and through the envious man he fulfilled the will of his envy.
Through the mouth of an insolent one he reviled the just man who was pure of iniquity,
and a contemptible son mocked and laughed at his father.
Through the brothers, in envy, he sold Joseph,
and made him a slave to the seed of Canaan, the servant of servants.
Through an Israelite he drove Moses out even from the house of Pharaoh,
and Moses hired himself out to a diviner, a priest of demons.
Through Saul, a demon, a dwelling of demons, he pursued David,
who suffered and groaned as he sojourned among foreigners.
Against all the just the Crafty One has acted thus in his craftiness,
and there was no modest man whom he did not mock through the mouth of the insolent.
Through the mouth of the insolent he has done his will in every generation,
and he has never ceased or grown weary of his struggle with the true.
One alone from among men brought his warfare to an end,
yet afterward he turned again to the battle of his cunning.
He loves to wage the battle of iniquity with the people of the earth,
and see how he contrives artful schemes to fulfil his desire.
He who is wholly a liar wars without ceasing against the true,
and through liars he displays the power of his skill.
Through the mouth of forgers he expounds his false forgery,
and by their tongue he lets loose mockery upon the chaste and the just.
His aim is set on waging war against the just,
for he knows that they can bring down the high building of his falsehood.
The true have brought down his falsehood by the power of their words,
and therefore he barks without ceasing at their sayings.
Like a dog his cunning barks through the mouth of the insolent,

and stirs up the hearing of the foolish with his eagerness.
The dog-like one has taken on the habits of dogs, a dog endowed with speech,
and whenever he sees someone who will not heed him, he snarls [?] and grows furious.
Even now he has seen three men who walk aright,
and he has begun to howl as he did in that time before our Lord,
when the just apostles pricked him with a goad like this one,
and he trembled and was terrified at the severity of their words.
The labourers of faith shot three arrows at him,
and taught him the power of the Godhead hidden in a man.
In faith they laid open the mystery of faith,
and revealed and showed it to the heavenly and the earthly.
The Self-Existent set a man of our humanity before humankind,
so that people might be inclined to call him Word and Body.
Men of skilled mind proclaimed the Word and the Body,
and see how fierce demons and foolish men are enraged.
The just set forth one Essence which is three,
and joined to it one Son of Man in union.
By one name the true called the Word and the Body:
Son of the Essence and Son of Man, one Person.
One is the Word, begotten of the Father without beginning,
and one the Son of Man, from Adam's humanity.
Two in nature is all that belongs to the Self-Existent and to the Son of Man;
one in honour and authority is the Son of God.
The Son of God is one Person, not one in nature,
for the Self-Existent is the Self-Existent and the man is a man: two who became one.
This is the word the just proclaimed in the ears of men,
and foolish men heard it and spurned its comfort.
Toward this goal the three I have spoken of set their course,
and they did not slacken at the mocking voice of demons and men.
Demons and men reviled them as madmen
because of the word of faith which they proclaimed on the earth.
They put on faith like a shield against every voice,
and the arrows of insult did not pierce their limbs.
They were armed in the spirit while they were in the body,
and in their bodies they withstood the war of sufferings.
A great wonder, full of the struggle of their victories:
that while mortal they did the deeds of the immortal.
They were mortal by nature, formed from dust,
and this is the wonder, that by their nature they overcame their nature.
The spring of sufferings did not hold back the course of their limbs,
and their heart poured forth a pure discourse of pure truth.
A pure discourse sprang from men pure of soul,
and evil demons and foolish men muddied its drink.
An evil bitterness corrupted them, the haters of their own souls,
and they would not receive the sweet drink of faith.
By faith the soul beholds the faith,
and faith makes it wise to see a sight that cannot be seen.
The true laid open [?] hidden things by their revelations,
and showed them as in the light to the eye of those who see.
Hidden was the mystery of the one Person of the Self-Existent and the man,
and it was concealed from the minds of the unlearned.
From the unlearned the mystery I have called hidden was hidden,
because they do not know how to look rightly at things unrevealed.
To those who know, everything hidden is revealed,

and they searched out clearly the mystery of hidden things.
Clearly they showed the mystery of faith,
and set it up on the earth like an image before those who see.
Men showed the wondrous sight to humankind,
but the brutish did not look into its glory.
Glorious was the good word they proclaimed among the people of the earth,
and gloriously the men who love truth heard it.
Only the foolish refused to accept the persuasion concerning it,
and did not look rightly at the glory of the comeliness of its beauty.
Bitter envy blinded the blind of soul,
and they did not see the light that shines brighter than all lights.
The light of the sun, however bright it is, is nothing
when compared with the brightness of the word of truth.
The word of truth pursued the darkness of the error of the Two,
and see how evil men who reject peace come to its aid.
The just drove the fear of demons out into the desert beyond,
lest the dwelling of men be troubled by its assault.
Our dwelling was assailed, and the conduct of our life was troubled,
until the Peacemaker set all things right in one son of man.
That Power which formed man chose one from among men,
and gave him power to be the reconciler of all with all.
For the peace of humankind the Restorer of all chose him from all,
and nothing remained that he did not reconcile in him with his majesty.
He revealed the power of his majesty in our nature, lowly creatures,
and in his glory he honoured our race, formed from dust.
Contemptible dust forgot its Creator and its Fashioner,
and began to bark like a dog at the Lord who formed it.
At the Lord who formed us the dull men of our days bark,
through the blasphemies their mouths belch out against the true.
Through the true he revealed his will, that he wills our life,
and through them we grow wise to know the mystery of his hidden things.
He placed the treasure of his love in the hands of those who love his love,
that they might lovingly distribute it to our need.
Our race was needy and stripped of every good,
and he set his will in our fellows, that they should nourish us.
According to his will the just fed our poverty,
and without envy provided for our life with spiritual things.
Spiritually they showed the power of spiritual things,
and through revealed things they portrayed for us the likeness of hidden things.
Hidden from us was the mystery of the inquiry into the Son and the Spirit,
and we did not know that they are Beings without beginning.
The just made wise our ignorance and our want of revelation,
and they taught us to call upon three names in order.
This order the dull men of our days have confounded,
and they have wronged the labours of the men who set it in order by their labours.
The diligent laboured wearisome labours in this order,
and the corrupters have named them crafty workers.
The crafty workers have called the workers of good liars;
and who would not be dismayed at this outrage, fearful even to hear of?
At this outrage I marvelled greatly, and I marvel still,
and because of it I was strongly compelled onto the path of words.
I saw the word of the just wronged by wrongdoers,
and I sought to know what the cause of this wrong might be.

I chose three men from the whole company of the just,
that through their cause I might reveal the cause of all.
The wrongdoers have wronged the just in every generation,
but more than all those I have spoken of they have heaped wrong upon these.
Beyond measure the sons of madmen have reviled them,
and surely it was from demons that they learned this kind of blasphemy.
The demons cast a foolish zeal into foolish men,
that they might fight against the word of truth with a tongue of flesh.
With a tongue of flesh the demons are ever blaspheming,
and through creatures of flesh they cover the falsehood of their blasphemies.
I have seen that their blasphemies are hateful and utterly abominable,
and I was moved with great zeal to demand from them satisfaction for the insult to the just.
On behalf of those who know I contend with the unruly,
who have become partners of the Slanderer in his war against them.
It is a great war that men wage against men,
and there is no one who asks what the cause of this struggle may be.
All the dull [?] are sunk as if in sleep regarding this matter,
and see, I wish to rouse them to search it out.
Openly, then, I set forth the matter of my words,
so that those who listen to words may know the sense of words.
Foolish men, I said, have wronged just men;
it is right that I reveal who is wronged and who the wrongdoer.
The wronged are those who served the priesthood well and freely:
one Diodore, one Theodore, and one Nestorius.
These are the wronged of whom I spoke at the beginning,
and their wrongdoers are demons and heretical men.
The heretics saw that their falsehoods were exposed by them,
and the men clothed with truth put on armour.
Those clothed with truth laid bare the error of the erring,
and above all others Diodore was armed for battle.
He fought against the bands of the heretics,
and exposed and revealed their falsehood before every man.
With the sword of his word he laid waste the words of the crafty,
and they could not stand firm before the force of the word of his mouth.
There were wolves he scattered with the voice of his sayings,
and he gathered the flock that their madness had scattered.
In the city of Antioch he began the war against the erring,
and after a time he completed his victory in the region of Tarsus.
In the city of Tarsus his lot fell to serve as priest,
the place where the herald of all the nations was born.
In this city the teaching of the splendid priest prevailed,
and in it he was crowned as a victor whom they could neither defeat nor bring low.
The Chief of victors strengthened the stalwart labourers,
and set them as light and salt for the benefit of humankind.
Theodore he sent to a city sick with sin,
which was named by the vain name of Mopsus, a demon.
A demon set up an idol to his own name and called it Mopsus,
and that city too was named Mopsuestia.
From one city went forth three torches of light,
and the light of their conduct shone in three cities.

The birthplace of all three of them was one city,
and from the time they were brought up they began the war for truth.
Truth armed them like labourers with its power,
and sent them to wage war with Satan.
Love cast the lots of love for the three of them,
and each went to the region that a sign appointed for him.
A hidden sign was hidden in the words of Theodore,
and he expounded hidden mysteries to the Mopsuestians.
The people of Mopsuestia were called Mopsuestians
after the name of that demon in whose name a dumb idol had been set up.
The skilled mind stripped those hateful names from them,
and made them pure vessels for the name of the Creator.
In the name of the Creator the just man bound the demon of the city,
and taught it to confess three names, one Essence.
The labourer of righteousness took hold of the three names
and shot them like arrows at the heretics.
Fearful was his voice when he cried out against their divisions,
and they could not bear to hear the meaning of his words.
At the meaning of his words the hosts of demons were astonished:
"What is this, that a son of man shakes us with his voice?"
The Creator worked a great wonder through the members of his household,
and demons and men were defeated by the voice of their words.
Demons and men heard the echo of the trumpet's voice,
and they gathered and came and arrayed battle against his words.
A fountain of spiritual words burst forth from his mouth,
and like a flood swept away the strength of the heretics.
Like bubbles the Arians and Eunomians floated off,
and with them perished the Dimoerites and the Apollinarians.
Like chaff he scattered the divided schisms,
and they fled and hid in the clefts of their lairs.
The bands of the sons of error fled in terror
before the man who expounded the pure truth.
The liars heard the pure truth from the true,
and they trembled and were seized with alarm like a woman in labour gripped by pain.
He showed the power of signs to humble labourers,
and they cast off the armour of their teaching and fled naked.
O how fearful is the power of the might of the labourer of the Spirit,
before whose voice the hardened assemblies the demons had gathered were defeated!
O how fearful was the meaning of the words of his treatises,
which laid bare the kinds of artifice of every teaching!
O how skilled was that mind, more excellent than every skilled one,
which left nothing veiled that it did not reveal and show!
O how keen he was in searching the divine books,
who interpreted the voices of prophecy and of the apostles!
O how the movements of his soul raced along with his limbs,
and he brought the course of all the books to completion within his words!
O that soul, skilled of mind and mighty in strength,
which endured and won two wars, against demons and against men!

The athlete of righteousness overcame demons and men,
and did not slacken in any struggle with any passion.
He fixed a sure goal in creation for those who strive,
that they might incline toward the fear of truth after his likeness.
His sayings were salt and light among the people of the earth,
and men learned to purify the thoughts of humankind.
Through his understanding humankind acquired a good taste,
and despised and cast away the perversity of the fear of demons.
This man, mighty in strength and skilled of mind,
was hated by men who hate their own souls and are full of ruin.
The word of truth made him a herald of truth,
yet the foolish called him divided of mind and a teacher of falsehood.
O the perverse! How perverse is their perversity,
who called the luminous one darkness, and darkness light!
The dull deserve the woe of the prophetic word,
for they have perverted the order of right things into perversities.
Perverse haters of their own souls loved perversities,
and they loathed and hated men who love the faith.
The just proclaimed the faith that is not defiled:
Diodore and Theodore, and with them Nestorius.
In the three of them the Trinity showed its power,
and taught them to tear down the fabrication of the teaching of error.
It set them as chosen priests in three cities,
that they might heal hard pains by their words.
The true were physicians of humankind in every city where they were,
and they diligently tended the flock of rational sheep.
That voice which came to Simon the diligent heard,
and they made disciples and taught men and women and children.
By their deeds they fulfilled the very name of shepherding,
and each of them tended his flock without neglect.
Diodore, skilled in disputation, shepherded the people of Tarsus;
he made them wise to loose the knots of the heretics.
Theodore, the searcher of mysteries, shepherded the Mopsuestians,
and taught them to look rightly at things unrevealed.
Nestorius, keen in his movements, shepherded the Byzantines,
and made them wise to meet the war with the heresies.
The royal city fell to his lot to govern,
and in keeping with his rank he showed the fruits of his teaching.
Wisely he built the foundation of the word of truth,
that the turbulent waves of the heretics might not shake it.
The heretics hated the lover of truth without cause,
and mounted stratagems of falsehood against his words.
The lying Cainites forged crafty stratagems
to bind words that cannot be bound by the hand of falsehood.
Falsely the insolent plotted against the true,
and without cause they fabricated a cause of lies.
They gathered lying false witnesses at the trial of the just man,
in the same manner that Jezebel used at the trial of Naboth.
A woman killed Naboth the just because of his vineyard,
and women drove the true man from his priesthood.
Women hired priests of falsehood for a trial of falsehood,

and made them scholastics of lying.
For gold they sold the pure truth that cannot be sold,
and in the marketplace they wronged the just like merchants.
Mute silver drove the just man out of peace,
and though it is utterly mute, it raised its voice against justice.
O justice, how silent you fell from your claims,
and did not rebuke open falsehood as you were wont!
O how great was the iniquity that priests worked through priests,
and they did not tremble or fear before the priesthood they exercised!
Come then, priests, see what the company of priests has done,
that drove a priest from the priesthood unjustly.
Insolently they drove the just man from his priesthood,
and unjustly they passed sentence and sent him into exile.
And if anyone says that I have not said these things justly,
let him show it openly, and I will pay the debt of my words.
Come, show me, you man who would contest my words,
what the cause of this man's guilt may be.
Reveal and set out clearly for me the kind of folly he committed,
and I will grant you that you rightly condemned him as one who had erred.
I said these things to his revilers, and I say them again:
let them show us the kind of folly for which he was condemned.
There is surely no one who can speak words against my words
without knowing how to walk in the way of answering words.
You do not know how to compose a persuasive argument;
if you wish, listen to me and I will tell you what you do not know.
I will tell you the cause of this struggle,
and from where the slander against this man sprang.
The evil envy of evil men hated the diligent one
because of the matter of faith which he expounded well.
The head of Egypt was sick and tried in this matter,
and when he heard the voice that cut into his pain, he grew zealous and fierce.
The Egyptian saw the cut of his word that heals well,
yet the word full of every kind of healing did not please him:
"Why, then, does he proclaim two names, Word and Body?
And to whom does he ascribe the saying about death, to the made or to the Maker?
Why does he not say that Mary is the mother [...] of the Godhead,
who bore the Self-Existent in the flesh when he became flesh?"
This is the cause of the Egyptian's envy,
and for this reason he hated the diligent one as a madman.
Envy sent the envious man forth against the just,
because it had fallen to his lot to govern the royal city.
Envy in its cunning forged the snares of craft,
and placed them in the hands of men to trample down the truth.
He gathered an assembly of liars and brought it against the true,
and called it by the name of synod, chosen and pure.
This assembly drove the priest from his priesthood,
in partnership with women who abetted the folly [?] of priests.
This is the cause by which the innocent was condemned,
and the report of his condemnation went forth falsely.

The crafty hid crafty snares for the one pure of soul, / and for no reason they reviled him as a hater of the faith. / See, I have shown the cause of the trial of the wronged man, / whom deceitful men condemned unjustly. / See, I have also exposed the envy of the envious one, / who for no reason wronged the worthy priest in unworthy ways. / It was not just that the priest should be put out of his priesthood, / nor was it right that the deceitful should take his rank. / See, O people, how many well-ordered things the envious have overturned; / look and consider how evil envy is. / See, the cloak of falsehood worn by the false has been pulled away, / for they unjustly claimed justice in the sentence they passed. / And if anyone says that I have not told the story truly, / let him tell me in what I have strayed from what is proper. / What have I said that I did not tell as it actually is? / Let anyone who has a plain word show it openly. / You have no man who can turn words against my words / and show that the judgment which condemned the just man was just. / And should someone say, "Look, priests passed the sentence," / why do they condemn as guilty those who were never condemned? / Look, Diodore and Theodore are just men; / there is no one who says that any human court accused them. / Why do the dull of heart revile the learned, / and why do they flee from the wisdom of their commentaries? / Look, no inquiry of words sprang up against their words / until evil envy sprang up in evil men. / Look, in their days there was no synodical assembly, / nor any command that gathered priests for inquiries. / Three assemblies took place in the land of the Romans, / and for each of them the time is known and the cause is plain. / One assembled in the days of the emperor Constantine, / because of the wickedness that suddenly sprang from the mouth of Arius. / The second, again, took place in the days of Theodosius, / because of the hateful fabrication that Macedonius begot. / The third took place under the rule of two emperors, / and its cause was the envy of the Egyptian. / See, three synods took place at three times, / and not one of them concerned the three men I have named. / At the first, Diodore and his companions had not yet been born, / and who can pass judgment on the unborn? / At the second, again, they had not yet attained to leadership; / so it is plain that the assemblies did not summon them to judgment. / At the third, they had already departed from among the living, / and who is so mad as to accuse the departed for no reason? / See, the matter that the various insults call into question has been made plain; / let us ask, then, why they revile the just. / Why do contentious men fight against the upright, / and those hateful of soul pour scorn on the excellent? / Why do they call the books they wrote untrue, / when the rising of the sun is not as bright as their words? / Why do they falsely allege words of a synodical anathema,

when there is no assembly that accused them of anything odious? / And if they cite that ecumenical synod, / what has it to do with men who were already dead? / And if they bring up the affair of Nestorius at that time, / he did not even hear the case that decided his sentence. / He was not present before the judges who condemned him for no reason, / since he was [?] before he ever came before his judges. / Who has ever heard of such a thing as the priests did, / that a sentence was passed while the accused was not present? / The judges of this trial acted with partiality, / and they were ashamed to his face to show the plain truth. / The wise, men of understanding, were ashamed before the Egyptian, / and fear of [?] terrified them from speaking the truth. / And yet they were persuaded of the drift of the Egyptian's words, / though they did not assent to the anathemas so rancorously written. / Rancorously they pronounced anathemas against those who knew the truth, / and their rancour was not hidden from their own eyes. / Look, they too anathematized the anathemas he had fabricated, / and not only his anathemas: they bound him too with anathema. / See, this is what is written in the document of their faith: / that anyone who speaks of a "mixture" is anathema. / And see, the Egyptian has set an anathema against this: / that no one is permitted to say "body and divinity." / What then is one to do who hears these things, / when both the one who confesses rightly and the one who does not are anathematized? / See what partiality did among men of intelligence: / they judged justly, then turned and condemned unjustly. / Just was the anathema that undid the Egyptian's words, / and it was not just that the man who struck them down should be ruined. / The envious one waged a great war on behalf of his anathemas, / and they lumped together the one who loosed anathemas and the one who bound them. / The ecumenical assembly mixed anathema with anathema, / and cast strife among the learned and the unlearned. / No one can loose one anathema by its opposite, / since both anathemas are bound under a single anathema. / This confusion has muddied the world with its turbidity, / and see, love is divided and there is no concord between one and another. / There is no concord at all among the people of the earth, / and least of all among the people Christ chose for his name. / Among Christians divisions beyond number have multiplied, / and no one knows how to walk rightly on the way of truth. / The way of truth I have seen deserted by travellers, / and I marvelled greatly at what the wickedness of women has done. / I saw that the wickedness of women had troubled the community of men, / and I said to myself that it would not be right to look on and keep silent. / I put myself on trial, as one gifted with speech is able to do: / why had I neglected the inquiries carried on by means of words? / It is very easy for one who possesses speech to check injustice, / and a small thing for him to silence evils of every kind.

Evils of every kind I saw spread among the people of the earth, / and my mind counselled me to pass judgment in just words. / I have a judgment of words to pronounce against the speakers: / why are they silent from words that judge words? / I heard foolish men speak unjust speech, / and I composed words against words that are not good. / I saw just men wronged by the ignorant, / and it did not please me to hear the mockery of the intelligent. / I read the books they wrote and pondered how excellent they are, / and I marvelled greatly at how wronged they are by wrongdoers. / I sought to accuse their wrongdoers with the voice of my words: / why do they wrong those who lack nothing of righteousness? / Why, you wrongdoers, have you so greatly wronged the pure of soul, / and rejected the good study that comes from their words? / What is the wrong the just have done—though they did no wrong— / that they are persecuted for their words like wrongdoers? / If it is wrong for a person to meditate on the faith, / then all the just completed their lives in this meditation. / And if it is a disgrace to speak the truth without disguise, / then the heralds, the apostles, trod this very path. / Look, the head of the Twelve himself cried out to the Jews / that Jesus is a man, a human being from God. / Look, Paul too, the choicest of the apostles, agrees with this, / and calls him the one mediator between the Self-Existent and us. / Luke and Matthew wrote his story without disguise, / and set out his forebears one after another. / The son of thunder too revealed his humanity in a plain voice: / that when it is destroyed, the divine power raises it up. / Let whoever would reproach, then, reproach the heralds themselves, / for in their books is written the distinction of the Word and the body. / Our Lord himself would have to come under blame, / for he showed in his body the place of the nails and the spear that pierced him. / He and his disciples trod the path of this distinction, / and revealed and examined the nature of the divine Being and the nature of mankind. / They distinguished the natures so that their order would not be confounded, / and gathered them into the unity of one person. / One person the heralds called the Word and the body, / and to this same aim the teachers of true religion inclined. / To the aim of their fellows Diodore and Theodore inclined; / so what is this, that fools reproach them alone? / There are other wise men who meditated on this subject, / and no one reproaches any commentaries but theirs. / It is only heretics who have hated this teaching, / and refused to accept the one confession of the Word and the body. / With these who have gone astray, then, the ignorant agree, / and following their thinking they walk a path that is not true. / Not true is the path the heresiarchs trod, / and I will show from their own books that it is not true. / The Simonians reckoned bodily existence a dream, / and explained the human things as fantasy.

The Borborians wronged the Word and the body altogether, / and composed a fabrication of hateful things that cannot be spoken. / The Menandrians erred altogether, saying there is no divine Being, / and gave the name of Creator to angels. / The Photinians called the three one person, / and confused the order of fatherhood and sonship. / The Paulianists confined the Son under a beginning, / and made his divinity begin from the daughter of men. / The Marcionites [?] fled both from the one side and the other, / and brought in an alien Self-Existent, foreign even in name, under the name of the divine Being. / The Valentinians [?] did not come near persuasion even in word, / since they removed the name of the divine Being from their books. / The followers of Bardaisan reckoned everything as nothing; / they tore down, and built a building of falsehood that cannot stand. / Valentinus's blasphemy surpassed all blasphemies: / he acted wickedly and said that it was not a body that Mary bore. / Sabellius wronged both humanity and divinity: / he abolished the hypostases and corrupted the order that exists in the divine Being. / The Arians separated the Son from his begetter, / and called him a servant and minister like all creatures. / The Eunomians called him Offspring in name only, / and abolished the name of fatherhood and sonship. / The Dimoerites confined our Lord to half a man, / and did not allow him to be complete, not even in soul. / Macedonius corrupted the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, / and estranged it and cast it outside the [?] of the Father and the Son. / The followers of Severus wronged the body he took from us, / in that they said it was not a man that suffered and was tempted. / See the confession of the heretics, hateful of soul; / see, you ignorant, how full of blasphemies their teachings are. / Look carefully how alien they are to the faith, / and how they strive to unsettle what is firmly established. / Discern justly, as discerning men, you who possess reason, / how many differences there are between the just and the wicked. / Very just are the men on whose behalf I have pleaded, / and true and pure is the truth they proclaimed among men. / For their sake I have recounted the record of the heretics, / to show people how far these are from righteousness. / I sought to show their wrongdoing before the wrongdoers, / to make them know that they unjustly wronged the upright. / They have called those who know the truth heretics, / and that is why I have recounted the charge-sheet of their wrongdoing. / My discourse has set the truth that is in those men beside the liars, / to show people how foreign truth is to falsehood. / It is the plain truth that men of understanding proclaimed on earth, / and fools reckoned it like the error of heretics. / The true waged a great battle against the false, / and this is the wonder: that they called them by the name of the false. / Theodore lived ninety years and a little more, / and he never rested or kept silent from the struggle against those in error.

The just man wore spiritual armour all his life, / and contended with the bands of heretics. / With the sword of the Spirit he laid waste the children of error, / and exposed the many crafts of their teachings. / Skilfully he contended with the heresies, / and shrewdly he untied the knots of error. / Like an athlete he grappled [?] with them, / and pointed out their guilt as if with a finger. / Like a [?] he showed himself in his feints, / and threw falsehood to the ground before the eyes of the onlookers. / The many kinds of contest seemed to him like a theatre, / and he never fell short of victory all his life. / From his youth he began the discipline of the athlete, / and did not rest or cease until death brought his running to a halt. / He reckoned the course of the years of his life as a single day, / and for him the day of youth was no different from old age. / In grinding warfare the days of the armed soldier were completed; / valiantly he began and finished in the service of his Lord. / Love of his Lord pressed the upright man to contend, / and he did not slumber or sleep until he attained victory. / He longed for the victory of which Paul's word speaks: / "I run toward the goal of the victory on high." / O victor, who bore the [?] of the race so well, / and neither the weakness of the body nor the sufferings of the soul held him back! / O diligent one, how watchful he was over the possessions of life, / and gave the enemy no room to plunder his possessions! / O wise one, how wise he grew in seeing hidden things, / and not one secret thing was hidden from his mind! / O merchant who traded with the talents of the Spirit, / whose profits doubled [?] his preaching! / The good servant received talents of the Spirit from his Lord, / and diligently sowed their profit in the ears of all. / In every place the profits of his soul's labours sprang up, / and no people remained that was not seasoned with the savour of his words. / Like light his insights shone among the people of the earth, / and drove away the error that lay hidden in human minds. / Through his sayings humankind saw the light of life, / and learned to gaze through what is revealed at what is not revealed. / People had ceased from study as if asleep, / until the morning of his words dawned and woke them. / A covering of sleep was spread over the books of the Spirit, / and he lifted it by the good study of his soul's stirrings. / The readers of the books pondered them without understanding, / until they read his writings, and then they grew wise. / It is fitting to call the one skilled in understanding the scribe of scribes, / and were it not for him there would be no scribe who teaches well. / From the treasury of his writings everyone who grew rich grew rich, / and from his explanations they gained understanding for explaining. / From him I too have learned, I who have learned only to stammer, / and through his teaching I acquired the habit of studying words.

His study became for me a guide to the Scriptures, / and it raised me to an understanding of the books of the Spirit. / In return for his benefits I contend with his detractors, / and I show that they have unjustly wronged his benefits. / Men clothed in arrogance have done him a great wrong, / and I was very zealous to exact from them requital for the insult to him. / The requital of his insult moved me to seek out a discourse of words, / and for his sake I have travelled the road of rebuttals. / I saw that heretics revile him and his companions, / and I undertook to pronounce a just judgment on their words. / My discourse looked to their words from the beginning, / and again with them I bring the subject of my discourse to its close. / I accuse those who accuse the words of the learned, / who, though ignorant, attack and revile men of understanding. / Great is the understanding that the skilled in mind displayed on earth, / and no one knows how to grasp their insights. / Wisely they wrote all that they wrote in the books they wrote, / and there is no wise man who could find a blemish in their explanations. / Only fools have reviled them as if they were evil, / because they are too sick to grasp the force of their words. / The dull are sick with the hard pains of ignorance, / and they do not wish to hear the news of the soul's healing. / Sick in soul are those sick of soul, beyond consolation; / that is why they hate those who cut away the soul's hard pains. / They know well that their gangrene cannot be healed; / that is why they are clothed in wrath without reason. / The ignorant have conceived bitter wrath against the learned, / because they distinguish the natural properties of the Word and the body. / The Creator, the Word of the Father, took a body from us, / and in love called it Son of God in his own rank. / He gave it what was his, while he himself was not lessened from what he is, / for his nature can neither be diminished nor increased. / His nature is exalted above injuries and changes, / and the properties of human nature do not touch it. / The humiliations of human nature came to the human nature, / not to the nature that is exalted and lofty above injuries. / Human are all the things written about the man: / conception and birth, and growth too, and suffering and death. / This distinction of the Word and the body the true have revealed, / and fools fight them: why did they reveal what is not revealed? / This is the cause that made them enemies of the just, / and because of it they are despised and hated among the people of the earth. / And yet it would have been right that for this very thing they be loved, / in keeping with the inquiry into hidden things that they displayed on earth. / Worthy of praise is he who reveals what is not revealed, / and treads a path for humanity in its infancy to seek out hidden things. / The wisdom of the word in the learned made humanity's infancy wise, / and who would not find it strange that fools have wronged this benefit? / The lovers of truth bestowed [?] two twofold benefits: / the word of truth and the excellence of their conduct. / Glorious was the labour of the conduct of the men of understanding,

and no one knows how to recount properly all the kinds of their labours. / In labours Diodore, mighty in strength, toiled, / until the senses of his body were worn out by humility. / Theodore's labour is too great for telling: / his eyes grew dim in the study of the books, yet he did not stop or slacken. / Nestorius too laboured more than all who labour, / giving his [?] no room to go idle. / See how the labours of the just men prospered, / and see how high the wickedness of their wrongdoers rose. / See, O people, how men have risen up against men: / ignorance against fountains full of wisdom. / The true were sweet springs for human thirst, / and whoever drank from their springs forgot his troubles. / Fools refused to accept the drink they offered, / and see, they are tormented by the strife of their own thoughts. / O the blind, who see yet are blind to understanding, / and the blindness of soul with which they are afflicted is pleasant to them! / The dull are like bats in their brutishness, / for they love the darkness of the nights more than the light. / O rational nature that has made itself deaf, / and abandoned the course of discernment that was set within it! / There is no remedy for the ignorance of the "knowing," / nor any escape from the sentence our Lord's word has decreed. / The word of our Lord has cut them off from within the Church, / and cast them into exile with the outsiders. / He commanded us to regard them as tax collectors and pagans, / and not to mix with the hateful things of their thoughts. / Paul too cut off their ways with the sword of his words, / and handed them over to be companions of the Slanderer. / Haters of the truth are like the Slanderer, / for they slander the lovers of truth as Satan does. / And so Satan has kept them busy with this business, / that they might fulfil his desire by insulting the just. / He hates the just and wages war on the true at every turn, / and he has no wish to see a just man at all. / He saw every kind of righteousness in just men now too, / and in envy readied himself for war against them. / It is his war that fools wage against the wise, / and through their mouths he hurls the arrows of his wrath at the ranks of truth. / He seeks to lay waste the ranks of truth through the mouth of the rabid, / but the power of truth does not allow him to fulfil his desire. / The bitter one displays only the wickedness of his [?], / and his soul's desire never rises to fulfilment. / Were he able to accomplish his [?] as he intends, / there would be no name of righteousness on earth at all. / And were there an opening for his schemes against the true, / he would have blotted out the name of Diodore and his companions from among the living. / This band he has hated, and hates more than anyone, / because he knows they are able to untie the knot of his craftiness:

all the wiles of the Deceiver—these wise men— / and they displayed his falsehood to the eyes of earthly and heavenly beings. / In the heretics the kinds of his error lay hidden for him; / the shrewd of soul exposed them before the eyes of all creatures. / The base one chose base workers for himself against the just, / and they were not able to prevail in waging war against the true. / As with a sword the just laid waste the camp of his falsehood, / and few remained to be witnesses of his guilt. / The guilty one, full of sins, saw his guilt, / and see, he grows embittered and spews his gall on the ignorant. / He seeks to exact requital for [?] from the victors, / from Diodore and Theodore and Mar Nestorius. / No, guilty one, you have no strength to contend, / for you have learned by experience the armour of the armed soldiers. / See, you [?] them in the war they waged against your bands, / which [?] and hid, and could not prevail on the day of battle. / If not, show which of your soldiers defeated the true, / and when and where and in whose days your victory took place. / Where is Simon, the firstborn who led the way in your hateful works, / and, one after another, all who were schooled in his deceit?
