/ See, all the schisms he begot on earth have perished and faded away, / and nothing of them is left but a remnant, to your disgrace. / To your disgrace a small remnant of the heresies remains, / lying in wait like wolves for the gathering of the sheep. / At the gathering of the sheep heretics are always assembled, / and they are not abashed that they are rejected and cast out as corrupt. / The word of the just has driven them away from the sheep, / and above all the just zeal of Diodore and his companions. / Diodore and his companions humbled the pride of every heresy, / and the books they wrote bear witness to their labours. / In their writings is inscribed the record of their victories: / when they began and when they finished the war against them. / In the days of Valens their struggles began, / in the days of the man who supported the falsehood of the Arians. / He lifted up the bowed head of the Arians, / and drove the just priests away from the sheep. / In this time—and hard was that time—the true were there, / and truly they humbled the time and its hardness. / The Lord of times sent them to meet the times, / like a king who chooses soldiers for hard wars. / Hard was the time of the three armed soldiers, / and it was the beginning of the heretics' strife. / Against all order the party of Arius fought, / and the contentious emperor supported their strife. / Emperor and people stood up together against the just, / and they could not prevail against the just. / O the victory that earthly men displayed on earth, / who overcame the world and trampled mortality into the ground! / O mortals who displayed the success of immortals:

and left on earth the name of their victory for the generations to come. / O guides who trod a path whose labour is hard, who taught people to journey well to the place on high! / To the place on high journeyed the wise, who made people wise; and this is a wonder: while they were on earth, they visited heaven. / The conduct of these earthly men is full of great wonder, yet earthly men did not look closely at their conduct. / Their conduct compelled me to recount their struggles, and the wrong done to them made me rebuke those who wronged them. / Let those who wronged them bear the judgment for the wrong they did, for though they were innocent, they condemned them falsely. / For this wrong I sought to take vengeance on the wrongdoers, and my mind compelled me to bring forth words of rebuke. / The words of fools have made me one who answers back, and though unwilling, I have told the story of the conduct of the upright. / Let everyone whose conversation is upright love the conversation of the upright, and by their conversation let him train his soul all his life. / Study in the company of the true acquires a life that does not perish; come, let us meditate on the meditation of life that comes from their words. / Above all things the true loved the life of human beings, and for the sake of human beings they endured contempt from the insolent. / In the Lover of mankind they saw that He humbled Himself for the sake of humanity, and they set themselves a goal: to imitate the goal of their Beloved. / The athletes of righteousness saw the goal of their Beloved; come, let us take courage to look upon the goal of their conduct. / Let us set their conduct like an image before our mind, and let our soul take heed lest it become hateful through hateful iniquity. / Let us always scour the filth of iniquity from our mind, so that we may not be put to shame in that trial whose testing is just.
On the wickedness of the times, suitable for a service of supplication
Sixth homily: On the wickedness of the times, suitable for a service of supplication

I tell of the evil of the scourges that have swallowed our land.
Come, people of the earth, listen, and groan at how much has swallowed us.
It has swallowed us greatly, to match our wickedness, which has grown very strong,
and perhaps there has been no generation whose scourges were as many as in ours.
In our generation what is written about the Hebrews has been fulfilled:
“I struck them, and they would not accept any kind of discipline.”
The Creator has disciplined us severely in all that He has disciplined us,
and without comfort our mind has looked on the harshness of His scourges.
He disciplined us out of love, like a father who disciplines his children,
but to the evil of our inclination His loving discipline was not pleasant.
Our nature was running like a brute after shameful things,
and would not accept the gentle yoke of its Lord's service.
When the Creator of the soul [?] our soul as if under a yoke,
it bellowed and kicked and broke the yoke of the commandment of His words.
The living power of our reason went its way like a beast,
and bit at the words of those who taught it more fiercely than a beast.
Like dogs our thoughts barked in our musings,
and our mind could not tell the master of the house from a stranger.
A dog knows its master's face and fawns on him,
but our heart did not discern, and does not discern, the things that are just.
And because we did not discern, as beings endowed with reason and speech should,
the Giver of speech raised His hand and struck us hard.
Hard did that Commander whose commandment is just scourge us,
and He brought our shameful deeds unmistakably into the open.

In our scourges He portrayed the evil of the inclination within our soul,
and uncovered it and showed it to the eyes of earthly and heavenly beings.
Heaven and earth became witnesses of our shameful deeds,
and through our chastisement they learned of our iniquity, which had been hidden.
In the harshness of our scourges, rational and mute creatures saw it plainly,
and weighed our iniquity as if in scales, to see how wicked it is.
The chastisement of our days became like a mirror,
and the evil of our shameful deeds was made known all the more by our scourges.
Our evils grew stronger than our countless blows,
and our heart, heavy with the weight of its iniquity, did not reflect.
And because we did not reflect, as befits those endowed with knowledge,
the scourges goaded us like a beast, without comfort.
Like a beast the divine will goaded us,
and what was spoken by the wise man was fulfilled in us:
with rod and goad the wise man disciplines the foolish [?],
and one threat is decreed for the mute and for the speaking alike.
Like a beast our soul was goaded by every kind of blow,
yet it was not restrained from the wickedness of its shameful deeds.
Famine starved us, yet the haughtiness of our spirit did not bow;
sickness struck us, yet our arrogance was not weakened.
Death swallowed us and shut us up in the pit of Sheol,
yet our heart was not shaken by a terror full of terrors.
As it is written, the corpses of men fell like dung,
yet the height of our pride did not fall from its loftiness.
The earth held back and did not give us fruits and crops,
yet the spring of our frivolity did not cease from its flowing.
The air passed through every kind of change for which it is known,
yet the heat of our provocation did not change from what it is.
Thunders and lightnings out of season shook the earth,

yet our inclination did not budge from its hardness.
Hail shattered the vines [?] and the fig trees, with every kind of fruit,
yet the sight of the wrath that was upon us did not terrify us.
Signs appeared, each more fearful than the last,
and our mind did not ask what the reason for their visitation might be.
There came ravages of locusts and creeping things such as we had never seen,
and we did not ask why our scourges are so many.
Lowly, senseless creatures ate up our food,
and we did not search out who it is that gives us food.
Our sustenance ran out, our labor came to nothing, and our lives perished,
and there is no one among us able to stand up for us and help us.
Woe to us, lest our race come to an end in the harshness of the scourges,
and no survivor be left to us among the living on earth.
Woe to us, lest the things that once happened befall us too:
the fire of Sodom, and the pit that swallowed the household of Dathan.
Every kind of evil I have recounted is found in us,
and the pains that have swallowed our land bear witness that they are in us.
From the pains of our land I perceive that they abound in us,
and now I make ready to set them out before my hearers.
Come, you hearers, hear the story of every kind of pain we suffer,
and tremble and groan over the blows of our evil generation.
Our evil generation has done more evil than any generation,
and so its scourges are thicker than those of any generation.
The Will that sees all saw the ugliness of our iniquity,
and turned the face of His kindness away from our hateful deeds.
He who is without wrath showed us the face of wrath,
and the earth quaked and came near to becoming an abyss.
Our iniquity in its wickedness shook the whole of creation,
and nothing was left that was not shaken by our shameful deeds.
The sight of our shameful deeds made the whole world loathsome,
and made heavenly and earthly beings alike recoil from us.
The spiritual beings saw the shameful sight of our hideous iniquity,
and were zealous and strengthened themselves to scourge it with the upheavals of the air.
Those who see clearly looked upon our insolence and examined it,
and put on armor to humble our tyranny.

That Commander who set them over our service
commanded them to set their hand to the writ of our scourges.
The King who is above all wrote out the list [?] of scourges,
and gave it to the hosts of heaven to bring upon us.
Like birds His winged ones flew at the command,
and swiftly carried out in deed every kind of blow against us.
They saw that the verdict concerning our blows was urgent,
and with haste they performed the will of the One who sent them.
With thongs [?] of the spirit the kinsmen of our race stretched our race out,
and with the whips of hunger and thirst they lacerated our body.
Their bodiless hands grasped the combs of pain,
and they raked our body with the sharpness of their combs.
Like a robber before the judge they hung up our people,
and it began to wail at the harshness of the scourges upon it.
Like a criminal it was swallowed up and torn all over,
and it wept and wailed, but the King's servants would not listen to it.
The King over all commanded, concerning our iniquity-loving people,
that they should scourge our insolence without pity.
Without pity the heavenly hosts have scourged us,
and perhaps they will not cease from chastising us until the end.
They looked, and they look continually, at the greatness of our iniquity;
therefore the hand they hold is raised over our backs.
Surely they know that we do not turn back from our hateful deeds,
and so they are clothed in wrath to exact what we owe.
The sum of our debts has grown very great, beyond all measure,
and now they demand from us every kind of interest that has built up against us.
Our humanity owes a bond of debts beyond anything human,
and because we did not pay it, we now pay against our will.
Our will has dealt unjustly with the sum of our debts;
therefore our blows are harsher than those of any generation.
Because we were not eager, as debtors should be, to pay back the principal,
now we pay even interest compounded upon interest.

Interest is demanded of us in keeping with our wickedness,
and rightly so, as wrongdoers who have done great wrong.
Great wrong have we done, and our inclination testifies that we have done great wrong,
and perhaps even demons do not commit a wrong like ours.
Demons do wrong, but they reflect that they have done wrong and know that they have sinned;
we neither reflect nor accuse ourselves of our shameful deeds.
And because we did not reflect, as befits beings endowed with knowledge,
behold, mute creatures chastise us by their very natures.
And because we would not judge ourselves by our own judgment,
behold, the just Will, whose scrutiny is just, judges us.
The Chief of judges has handed our case to the justice of His will,
that it may be known that He also has a justice that cannot be overcome.
Most justly has He examined the case of our wrongdoing,
and passed sentence according to the evils of those who are scourged.
In the balance of His scrutiny He placed our iniquity,
and since it weighed down [?] greatly, He set scourges against its weight.
To each kind of iniquity He apportioned the scourges meant for the iniquitous,
and requited each of them with the scourge that suited it.
The love of money He uprooted with the mattock of poverty,
so that it might no longer sprout again and bear the fruits of coveted money.
The love of glory He cut down with the axe of humiliation,
so that it might no longer contrive to snare [?] a man with the sting of glory.
Greed He cut away with the iron of want,
lest the swelling that comes from it spread through the whole body.
On pride He laid the cautery of lowliness,
so that it might not lift itself up and take on the habits of a beast of prey.
Falsehood He bound with the armor of a single word,
so that it might not grow used to speaking more than is needed.
Into the mouth of envy He put the muzzle of silence,
lest it bite a man with the fangs of its strife.
Theft He shut in with fortresses that cannot be stormed,
so that it might no longer rob people's lives of their possessions.
Adultery He struck with the blow of dimmed eyes,
so that it might not look wantonly at what is not its own.
Rage He silenced with the voices of the forces that pass sentence,
so that it would have no room to rush about like a brute.
All the passions He chastised justly with the justice of His scourges,
and wisely showed His power in those who are scourged.

Everything trembled at His blows and everything stood condemned,
and dread reigned over everything that exists.
Everything was shaken by what came upon everything,
and nothing was left that was not tried by the sufferings of mankind.
Because of mankind these things came upon mankind's dwelling place,
and through man's wickedness rational and mute creatures bore evils.
Because of him the earth swallowed harsh scourges,
and her womb dried up and gave no sprouting of crops and fruits.
Because of his iniquity she would not bring forth the offspring of seed,
and though she is one who bears, she became barren and bereft.
The undiscerning earth looked upon the barrenness of mankind,
and withheld her womb from the course that had been set within her.
Her neighbors, the elements of water and air, followed her example,
and did not run well along the smooth path of their changes.
The silent ones that had been set in order ran without order,
and threw into confusion the world that had been ordered from the beginning.
Man's iniquity taught the insensible elements
to walk in a path full of dread and disorder.
Man himself threw into confusion the order of all creation,
and by his [?] loosened the bond that holds height and depth together.
In him height and depth had been bound together in a single harmony,
and because of him everything has lost its savor and fallen from what it is.
His provocation provoked to anger the Power that is never wont to be angry,
and He chastised the world with harsh wrath, without pity.
Pitiless has been the chastisement of our days,
and perhaps no human wickedness has ever devoured as ours has.
Let us inquire of nature and of Scripture
whether there is any generation the Just One has chastised as He has ours.
The ancients were swallowed up by harsh scourges, as it is written,
and He made known to them the reason for the scourges that swallowed them.
Us He has scourged with every form of every kind of scourge,
and has not shown us the reason for the harshness of our scourges.
This is what is harder than anything for those who are scourged:
that while they are being scourged they do not know the reason for the scourge.

Our iniquity has hidden the reason for the scourge from our mind;
it is our iniquity that has blinded our soul to comfort,
and she does not understand, even as she is debased by shameful deeds.
It is iniquity that has put the muzzle of silence on her power of speech,
and kept her mind idle from pondering what is good.
It does not allow her discernment to discern rightly,
and though she is discerning, she has taken on the habit of the undiscerning.
This habit has made her blind, without comfort;
she has swallowed scourges, yet would not know the reason for her scourges.
Our soul, sharp of mind as she is, has swallowed harsh scourges,
and however many she swallowed, the scourges were to her as no scourges.
How many the scourges were, yet those scourged did not suffer or feel them!
The blows were doubled, yet those struck only grew bolder.
How many earthquakes there were! The earth trembled and mountains fell,
yet our heart was not moved by the cry of the once-tranquil earth in travail.
Dwellings fell and became graves for those who lived in them,
yet the haughtiness of our spirit was not humbled from its full measure.
The earth was bereft of produce of every kind,
yet the wickedness of our inclination did not cease from fashioning hateful things.
Trees withered, leaves fell, and crops were scorched,
yet the hateful spring of our shameful deeds did not dry up.
The locust devoured us, the [?] stripped us bare, the cricket struck us,
yet the bitterness [?] of our soul did not depart from what it is.
Fierce gales blew in summer and in winter,
yet the harsh blast of our shameful deeds overcame them.
The air [?] and let fall rain as stones of hail,
yet our wickedness did not change the course of its iniquity.
The silent things were shaken by the sound of thunder and the sight of lightning,
yet our sluggishness [?] did not awaken from its slumber.
Spiritual beings painted every kind of sign across the face of the heights,
and we saw them and forgot them as if they were a dream.
They were true, they were certain, they were clear,
and yet to our wrongdoing our hateful deeds were not laid bare.

The powers on high showed them to us in our wrongdoing,
and we saw them, yet did not see them with a sound mind.
All that happened in height and depth happened because of us,
and we did not ask the reason for their changes.
And because we would not inquire into the cause of every kind of scourge upon us,
the Creator gave a sign to His ministers to scourge us.
The Watchers, our kinsmen, received the command against our wickedness,
and stretched out our heart for a harsh scourge to match our heart.
Because our heart did not feel the scourge the earth swallowed on our account,
the just ones struck us on our limbs and on our thoughts.
And perhaps those who reflect well considered this concerning our insolence:
that it is not fitting [?] that the one who mixed the cup should not swallow it.
It is customary [?] for a man to hand out all there is without mixing it himself;
let the one who [?] swallow it, then, and he will grow wise.
Let him taste for himself the taste of the harshness of the scourges,
and he will know how to keep the order of his reason.
To this end our limbs have been swallowed up in harsh pains,
and our despised body is torn with bruises.
In this way the just ones hasten to scourge us,
and they have not ceased, nor do they cease, from striking us, summer and winter.
In every form the just ones chastise the perversity of our heart,
and when we did not repent, death came and swallowed us suddenly.
Beyond all order greedy death lays waste among us,
and pitilessly and cruelly tears our body apart.
Like a captor it pursues every one of our race,
and its captivity surpasses the captivity in which man takes man captive.
Men took us captive, and death took us in a double captivity,
and the captivity of our shameful deeds surpasses both the one captivity and the other.
The captivity of our iniquity has surpassed captivity by men and by death,
and perhaps it was this that trod out the road for the two captivities.
Woe to our people from the captors that never leave it,
that finish it off, while it is not restrained from its hateful deeds!
Woe to us, for we have become a mockery and a disgrace before all creatures,
and rational and mute beings alike reproach us for the greatness of our shame.
Woe to us, for an evil report of us has gone out to the four quarters,
and there is no one in creation who does not tell the story of our iniquity.
The demons, who are more evil than we, tell of our wicked name,

and though they are exceedingly evil, they are exceedingly astonished at our evils.
And if the evil ones marvel at us because we have done evil,
then rightly have our evils grown strong and our pains multiplied.
Rightly do famine and pains pursue our lives,
and perhaps they keep our wickedness back from doubling its iniquity.
The Just One chastises our wickedness with famine and pains,
and teaches us not to run like brutes after iniquity.
Let us inquire what the reason is for the harshness of our scourges,
and why the sustenance of our life has grown scant and meager.
Why is our time more troubled than any other time,
and why is there no season when the course of our life is calm and fair?
Why are the seasons of the year gloomy in their courses [?],
and why is there no change whose order resembles the proper order?
Everything is in turmoil, everything is confused, everything is gloomy,
and the world has become like a wilderness to those who dwell in it.
Creation has put on deep mourning over our evils,
and weeps for us as over a dead man whose mourning is bitter.
Bitterly, bitterly the earth grieves on our account,
and if she could, she would cry out like a mother over her beloved.
And if she had a speaking mouth like those who speak,
she would weep for this evil time of ours with the sound of lamentation.
And if the mute elements could feel the sufferings of our soul,
they would not cease from dirges over our humiliation.
We have been brought very low, down to the earth, as it is written,
and instead of to the earth our soul has cleaved to mockery and disgrace.
Our evils have blown like a whirlwind in our evil time,
and stripped our branches [?] like trees in winter.
Like leaves, good things have fallen from the mouths of men,
and men have become as if they were not men in their deeds.
Mortals have been swallowed up in harsh sufferings, even to death,
and have been scorched and withered by the distress of the pains of famine.
The sword of famine has gone out against our people, a flock [?] in sin,
and has laid us waste and cast us down like beasts left unburied.
In us has been fulfilled what was written concerning the ancients,
that the corpses of men will fall like dung.
Behold, the bodies of men have fallen without burial,
and men have walked over men without restraint.
Famine has shut the door of compassion in the face of loved ones,

and man has trampled on man as if he were not a man.
Famine has forced nature by the power of its might,
and has begun to do violence to what belongs to nature and to Scripture.
Because of famine, wretched nature has forgotten its nature,
and has enslaved itself to eating unnatural food.
Against all custom men have eaten human flesh.
Woe to us! What has befallen our nature, so full of ruin!
Woe to us, lest the end of the world be completed in our time,
and everything written about the consummation be fulfilled in us.
It is written that women ate their children in a time of famine,
and beloved infants of the womb became food for the belly.
Behold, this has happened in our own evil time:
women have eaten their offspring, and even the price paid for them.
For paltry prices fathers gave up beloved sons,
and ate food full of anguish, and died amid lamentations.
For a morsel of bread a mother took the price of her darling,
and her eyes streamed and her soul melted with grief.
Alas for that food which nature bought, against all custom,
and so forgot the natural bonds that had been set within it!
Alas for nature, which is wholly bound by love of its own,
yet sold its own for love of a single hour's food!
Alas, what has befallen our race, the head of all races,
that it has debased itself with indignities lower than all!
Alas for our nature, called by the name of the One who formed it,
that it has become lowly, and the lowly have jeered [?] at its lowliness!
Alas for him who was exalted above all and glorious above all in name and rank,
whom sufferings have trampled, pains have humbled, and death has swallowed!
Alas for him who held the whole world within his body and soul,
and has become more hateful than anything because of his iniquity!
Because of his iniquity, rational and mute creatures alike have come to hate him,
and behold, they buffet him with harsh scourges of every kind.
Harsh famine, crowding pains, and hasty death—
and there is no comfort between one chastisement and the next.

Like waves the scourges rush in, one after another,
and give us not even a little quiet and rest.
The sound of wailing thunders in our land at all times,
and our life has become like a wilderness, night and day.
Weeping in the streets, wailing in the houses, dirges everywhere;
the mouth wails, the eyes shed tears, and the ears listen.
Weeping and lament are what everyone hears from every mouth,
and there is no one who does not utter the cry of woe.
“Woe, woe,” says one man to another about a man
whose good things are gone, whose mourning has multiplied, and whose groans have doubled.
Each hears the sound of groaning every hour from his companion,
and there is no utterance not mingled with human grief.
Everyone is grieved, everyone is distressed, everyone weeps,
and there is no face bright and cheerful toward its neighbor.
Every man is dismayed [?] at the gloomy look of everyone,
and everyone is astonished at the distress that reigns over the land.
Everyone asks whoever meets him about the distress:
“Is there, then, any place free of distress?”
Every people, all of it, is full of distress upon distress,
and kings and lowly folk alike bow their heads before distress.
The rich man is in distress, the poor man is in distress, the slave and his master,
and everyone has gone out begging for the needs of his life.
Beggars and those who were never beggars have gone out begging,
and famine has overturned the great order that stands between one person and another.
Famine has taught the freeborn to beg,
and behold, they go about asking for alms like beggars.
The trade of begging has spread throughout the land,
and there is no hour when the cry of begging does not ring out.
People compose mournful strains before their fellows,
so that, weeping and lamenting, they may make their hearers weep with them.
Like animals, everyone howls along with his fellows,
and they moan and twitter like doves and swallows.
The sound of their dirges does not even resemble a human voice,
for famine has altered their words and their melodies.
The wretched man varies his mournful strains according to his need,

so that whoever hears the kinds of his tunes may grieve all the more.
For he cries out without restraint and begs with [?] and shamelessness;
he swears and takes oaths: “Unless I get something, I will not leave.”
What has the wickedness of our bitter-natured inclination done!
It has rooted out from us the freedom of the soul and sown shamelessness.
The soul possesses freedom together with its very make-up,
and this is the wonder: hunger has mastered it even in one who is not hungry.
Hunger has made the soul that was free no longer free,
and it has become a handmaid serving the needs of the body.
The body's needs have harnessed it under the yoke of the body's needs,
and it has begun to compose choked cries to beg for alms.
Iniquity has done a great wrong in our wicked generation,
in composing choked cries to beg for alms.
Iniquity has done a great wrong in our wicked generation,
in troubling the beauties of body and soul.
Beautiful were the natures that were set in it,
but iniquity, the tyrant of evildoers, has corrupted them.
Iniquity is the cause of these things I have told and will tell;
it is what has chastised us with hunger, pains and plague.
It is what has stripped the fair earth of good things,
so that it has not given us fruits and seeds as it used to.
It is what has bred the locust, the creeping thing and the cricket,
and changed the air, and brought down fire instead of raindrops.
There is no harm that has ever befallen us that it did not cause,
no loss by which our race has been diminished that it did not bring about.
So it is right for us to put the blame on our iniquity,
and not on our God, who made us just and freeborn.
It is our freedom that ought to condemn its own lack of freedom:
why has the freeborn become one who is not free?
And because it did not discern as the discerning thing it is,
sufferings have followed it, a harsh consequence: losses.
Harsh are the losses our soul has suffered in this time,
and there is no weight whose value rises as high as our loss.
The loss of every generation is small beside our loss,
and the afflictions bear witness how much our soul has swallowed, how much we have lost.
The kinds of our blows cannot be told by a human tongue;
too small is a mouth to recount them as they are.
A speaker can say only that they happened;
but how, and how great they were—can a tongue set that out?

That they happened I too have said, I who wished to tell of them,
but my mind was not able to reach the full measure of them.
Their great number made me search into them,
and I was greatly amazed, and fell far short of what I was seeking.
My thoughts put together a composition of words in the way of words,
and I wished to go down, with words for my companions, to the events.
I wished to recount the kinds of events that happened in our land,
but when I saw how tangled they were, my speech went lame.
In fear my speech too faltered at the start of its words,
lest it give way and fail to reach the end.
I saw the long stretch of words it was about to compose,
and I grew very weary at the composing of so many kinds of words.
Powerful are the words that are spoken about blows,
and the tale of the harshness of afflictions never ceases to be retold.
The compulsion of afflictions forced me to speak a discourse on afflictions,
and my mind constrained me to weave a garment full of afflictions.
By means of words I wished to portray the afflicted,
so that they might be set out before the eyes of beholders who see clearly.
I saw that those who see clearly are eager to behold much,
so I painted the image of the kinds of afflictions for them to gaze upon.
Come, you beholders who see clearly, behold our blows:
how much we have swallowed, and how much we have endured in the face of our afflictions!
Our mind before our blows is like a wild beast:
they press it down, yet it is not subdued to the end.
As afflictions have goaded our boldness like a beast,
the more it swallowed, the more it grew strong to endure.
Hunger set a pain at the mouth of our wickedness,
yet our wickedness did not cease from running after its evils.
It stretched our body out like veins of stone before the blows,
and it swallowed much and endured much, as though it felt nothing.
The one that feels became unfeeling in the time of sufferings,
and its nature forgot the nature that was fashioned in mortality.
Pains drew near the afflicted, even to death,
and the soul trembled and fled and went out from within its dwelling.
The soul used to dwell as mistress in the temple of the body,
but pains demolished the temple of its love, and it fled from it.

And if the soul has fled from us in the time of our afflictions,
let everyone know that the blows we swallowed were many.
Death is the end of life for the afflicted;
so it is plain that our blow is harsher than other blows.
And already whoever hears says, “It is death.”
But let him hear that there is a death worse than death.
Our death is worse than all the deaths that have been and are,
for we have seen our death, and so we die a double death.
We saw the sight of death in what came upon our spirits,
and before we died we were dying at the sight of the harshness of our afflictions.
Hunger and pains became guides for a swift death,
and it ran and swallowed us as a dragon swallows a beast [?].
In every form death has swallowed our mortality,
and still the remnant of life has not departed from our humanity.
Every trial has passed over our soul, which possesses life,
and already the spring of life is failing and our body is perishing.
Life, which corruption did not gain a hold upon in its being from the Creator,
lives by its own vitality and, being the stronger, keeps our body going.
And had it not kept us by the strength of its vitality,
the human race would have become as though it were not human.
We have become as though not human in the aftermath of every ruin,
and creatures rational and dumb are amazed and stunned at our ruin.
Heaven and earth weep and wail over our ruin,
and we alone do not feel the ruin of our race.
Because of our hateful deeds the course of summer and winter is sad,
and the great order of the months of the year is confused and disturbed.
Because of us creation is clothed in garments of mourning,
and mourns for us as for one dead whose mourning is bitter.
The mourning of the day of our distresses is bitterer than all mournings,
and the day of our death is more restful than the days of our harsh afflictions.
In afflictions and pains the days of all the days of our life have perished,
and there is no day in our life that was at rest from distress.
Pains have raised us from our youth, as it is written,
and as we grew, the blows upon our limbs grew too.
From the very beginning of our race pains have fastened upon us,
and distresses have become a guide for the course of our life.

A poisoned life we have lived on earth since the day we came to be,
and the hard wars of envy have never ceased from us.
We have had evil neighbors in the land of our sojourning;
they plundered our [?] and enslaved our lives with hard labor.
In the captivity of iniquity the enemies of our race took our race captive,
and made us slaves to the desires of their affairs.
Our fathers went out from paradise as exiles
and dwelt in a land full of thorns and pains and death.
The captivity of the waters drove them out even from this,
and would that it had been a captivity, and not a pitiless ruin!
Without pity the captivity of the Flood ruined us;
it swept away the dust that made up our bodies and buried it in the earth.
Captivity hands us over to captivity, carrying us from one to the next,
and it does not let us stay in the place of our sojourning.
The first captivity carried us off from the beautiful place of Eden,
the second from the inheritance full of thorns.
Another captivity carried us off from Babel through the dividing of tongues,
and scattered us to the four quarters, over sea and dry land.
Three captivities, each worse than the last, carried off our race,
and One from our race set our race free from slavery.
An evil habit has grown old in our race from the beginning:
the slavery of slaves is sweeter to it than freedom.
The freeborn does not love freedom but the service of slaves,
and has no wish to lift his head out of slavery.
This habit has made him swallow harsh afflictions,
and now he is despised for the wounds of body and soul.
In his body and soul he multiplies his sinning and multiplies his swallowing;
everyone is stretched out for harsh afflictions and is not deterred.
The harshness of his afflictions has walked with him through all generations,
and in our generation above all the blows have been doubled.
Harsh afflictions now surround us on every side,
and now they swallow us, and the kinds of our evils have no end.
Our evils and abominations have multiplied beyond number,
and afflictions have chastised our boldness beyond measure.
Our afflictions have been harsher than all afflictions in every generation,
and there was no interval between one and the next, at a signal:
a hidden signal gathered them to the meeting-place of our life
and taught them to wage war against our wickedness.

They waged a great war, and set against us the afflictions of our own people,
and pierced our people with the sharp arrows of hunger and thirst.
Like an army, pains surrounded us on every side,
and no limb escaped being struck with wounds.
Our whole body became one sore without health;
it rejected remedies, and they could no longer bind it up.
Hunger and pains have wasted his body and troubled his soul,
and cut his life short of food and of vitality.
There is no vitality in a man's life, none at all;
and if there is, there is not, for there is nothing to sustain his life.
The food that sustains life has run out from the mouth of the living,
and his life hangs in doubt, for life is cut short before his doors.
Everyone looks to the end of his life and makes light of life,
and broods and fears that his appointed time may have drawn near.
In the evening he says, “Will I be alive till morning?”
and at morning he asks his friends whether the sun has set.
All day long he is occupied with thoughts of distress,
and his need is doubled as he counts the hours of night and day.
Woe to the wretched nature of man, how troubled it is,
and how tangled are the sufferings of his soul and the pains of his body!
Woe upon woe to him who is more wretched than all, in all generations,
and more wretched in our generation than in all generations!
In our generation every man is wretched and distressed;
woe is doubled, affliction is multiplied, and need is great.
Great is the need that our eyes have seen and our ears have heard;
pains have pursued us, and man has pursued us, both together.
Our humanity, bitter of nature, has borne the captivity of hunger,
and the captivity of man, which is worse than hunger and all evils.
The captivity of the sons of Hagar is harsher even than hunger,
and the blow they deal is more bitter than diseases.
The blow of the sons of Abraham is like the bite of a serpent,
yet there is a remedy for the bite of reptiles, and for them there is none.
Would that the sons of the Egyptian woman were not called by Abraham's name,
for now those who do not know find fault on account of this name.
Would that that righteous man had not gone in to that foolish woman!
Then those who stumble would long since have been free of their stumblings.

Would that they had a foreign name, foreign to Abram!
They would be called barbarians, like their father.
The Creator called the head of their tribes a wild ass of the wilderness,
for he knew that he could not keep the order of man.
The life of the wilderness befits the one called son of the Egyptian woman,
and let the name of Abraham, the lover of men, be taken away from him.
Abram is a lover of men and a lover of his Lord;
so it is right that the sons of the just one should be just.
Abram is not to blame for having begotten wicked and barbarous sons;
the wicked are to blame, who did not walk in the way of Abram's love.
I too, in blaming, have put my word on a level with all who blame,
when I said, “Would that Abram had not gone in to Hagar the handmaid.”
Fathers cannot fashion the freedom of the soul;
it is the freedom of the soul that makes men just or unjust.
These things I have said to those who blame Abram, and I say this too:
if the Hagarenes have taken us captive, why blame others for nothing?
Are the Qadishaye, then, brothers of the sons of Hagar,
they who plundered the world with a plunder more grasping than the Ishmaelites' [?]?
Did the ruin wrought by the Tamuraye come down from Abram,
they who made Assyria, mother of kings, like a desolation?
So let us blame neither the fathers nor the sons,
but the inclination that chooses between the two ways [?].
Let us always blame the evil inclination of the sons of Hagar,
and above all the beast-like people of the Qadishaye.
The nature of beasts is not so barbarous as the Qadishaye,
and what they have done shows how savage they are.
The sons of Hagar did not commit such outrages as they committed,
nor did the Tamuraye work such ruin as these worked.
Their ruin spread to the borderlands and to the northern peoples,
and still there is no evil to compare with the evil they did in our land.

In these afflictions our land, full of iniquity, has been swallowed up,
and through evildoers worse than we are has our chastisement come.
The Creator has chastised us by the hand of the wicked, who are worse than we are,
so that when iniquity is punished by iniquity it may come to despise itself.
Iniquity has raised three tribes against our wickedness:
the Ishmaelites, the Tamuraye, and the Qadishaye.
Three elements have swallowed up our soul, full of arrogance,
through three tribes far more arrogant than we are.
Just is the Creator, who has chastised our iniquity through the unjust,
and it is just for us to confess how justly our chastisement came.
For our good that Ruler who has authority over all has chastised us,
and in his wisdom he has cut away the pain of our abominations.
Come, then, let us give thanks to that wisdom which bound up our pains,
and bring it gifts of praise, for it chastised us and won us for itself.
On Supplication and Fasting
Sixth Memra / Seventh Memra / On Supplication and Fasting / Responsory (to the tune “That which befits”)

O Physician who healed the pain of our race with the balm of His mercies,
have pity on our sins, as You are wont to visit us.
O Good One who pitied the wickedness of our nature though He hated it,
bring to completion the good will of Your kindness in the turning of our lives.
O King who redeemed us from bondage to the Evil One and to death,
redeem our nature from the wounds of the guilt of its debts.

O Son of God, who turned back our captivity from the captor,
set our lives free, that they may never again return to bondage to the Evil One.
For by the yoke of death our race was bound from the beginning,
and One of us died and broke from us the yoke of death.
O Power that overcame the Evil One and death through the Son of our race,
give us strength to be strong in the contest of toils.
Into the contest of the toils of the body's sufferings we are thrown every hour,
and there is no time when the war of our desires ceases.
A spring of sufferings flows from us by nature,
and with its turbulence it troubles the course of our lives.
Like a whirlwind, turbulent are the passions that whirl us about,
and they trouble our soul as a tempest troubles the sea.
It is like the sea when it is stirred up by its blowing,
and it gives forth the roar of its desires like a whirlwind.
Like waves its gusts race within a man,
and body and soul are shaken by it, lest they be drowned.
The sea of the two passions of the body that dwells in our body
shakes like a whirlwind the ship of our bodily nature.
In its turbulent sea sails the ship of our mortality,
and the dread of its fierce winds shakes it.
Our race, full of wounds, is afraid of its wounds,
and constantly seeks the embrace of the One full of grace and mercies.
Grace and mercies every man of mortal nature asks,
that he may be delivered from the wounds that are constant to him.
I see that the kinds of its wounds have greatly multiplied,
and I have composed words to go down with him to the harbor of peace.
To the harbor of peace, the forgiveness of debts, he longs to come;
let Your grace be pilot for the course of his life.
Let the oars of Your mercies be oars for his heaviness,
and let them draw him up, lest he sink in the sufferings of his soul.

With Your great name let him bind his life as with a [?],
and in You let him take shelter from the blows of turbulent passions.
Turbulent passions trouble his mortality every hour,
and hold him back from the journey to the meeting with Your name.
In Your name he seeks to take refuge, weak in strength;
give him a hand, that by You he may be drawn up out of his guilt.
By the guilt of his debts he is drowned and thrown as into the sea;
behold, he longs for mercies to draw him up to the height.
To mercies he looks, that they may help him in the contest of his toils,
for he knows that his nature is weak and despised before the passions.
At his weakness I too, weak in thought, have looked,
and I have set my mind to go down with him to the meeting with mercies.
Let mercies be like a guide before his steps,
and show him the path of forgiveness for which he hopes.
For forgiveness of debts he hopes, and eagerly he runs in fear;
forgive him his sins, that he may take heart in the course of his life.
Short is life, the life of a debtor full of sins;
have pity on his sins before the lamp of his life goes out.
A lamp is the course of the life of his life, which is short of life,
and it burns lightly, and the oil of mercies fails it.
The fire of passions consumes his life as it consumes oil,
and suddenly quenches and extinguishes the light of his reason.
Death covers over the cave of his body by nature,
and it becomes a corruption, corrupted, without life.
Without life it waits in Sheol, corruptible,
until it hears that voice which is the voice of the resurrection of the dead.
Of this corruption he is wont to be reminded at all times,
and he is distressed lest he depart in the guilt of his debts.
He ponders his debts; therefore he asks for grace and mercies;
have pity on his sins before he departs to the house of his fathers.
To the house of death the fathers of this son of mortals departed,
and likewise he too prepares provisions for his journey.
A great journey is the journey of death for the children of Adam,

and they travel it every day, and it never lacks for travelers.
On this journey of necessity they are worn down every day,
and they ponder lest they go to Sheol guilty.
O Pitier of debtors, have pity on the sins of our guilt,
for behold, the guilt of our debts has grown strong through all generations.
We have incurred much debt, and there is no counting our guilt,
and the interest on the bond of our debts has doubled beyond what we borrowed.
An evil loan of iniquity we borrowed from the Evil One,
and behold, he multiplies it upon us through the interest of our shameful deeds.
In shameful deeds our race began from the beginning,
and in that habit it longs to complete the days of its life.
Habit has overpowered man, and overpowers him all his life,
and in his own eyes he is loath to hate the habit of his shameful deeds.
O Lover of mankind, have pity on man, who hates his own life,
and give him strength to overcome the war of his desires.
Give strength in his helplessness, You, to him who is weak in strength,
that he may not grow slack before passions and fierce demons.
Into two wars the wretch is thrown, more miserable than all:
the sufferings of his soul, and demons who confound his weakness.
Strengthen the movements of the one weak in strength, who asks and entreats,
and drive away from him the evil demons who thirst for his blood.
Do not, my Lord, grant the evil ones their desire to be fulfilled,
lest they exalt themselves and mock Your great name in him.
By Your great name You called us, O Good One, from the beginning;
complete in deed the calling of Your name in the lowliness of our race.
The names of Your name You set upon our head when You fashioned us;
confirm them through deeds that befit Your name.
Your name is precious and cannot be uttered by speakers;
let not Your name be despised through the names of our worthlessness.
If we have done wrong, we have wronged ourselves and not diminished You;
to You neither loss nor gain draws near.
You are as You are; You are, and You are without change,
and with all creatures Your will goes forth without wearying.
The iniquity of the wicked and the unjust does not weary You,
nor does the praise of the upright and the righteous exalt You.
Blasphemers do not dishonor the name of Your righteousness,
nor do exaltations raise the rank of Your perfection.

Praise and contempt are alike to You, compared with Your greatness,
since Your Being admits neither of these.
Your nature has not even this name of "nature,"
and for lack of names we call it by the name of "nature."
No other nature gave You Your nature, O You who give nature to creatures,
and the name of a thing that has received its nature does not fit You.
Let creatures therefore call You only as befits You,
and let not borrowed names that lower You fly at Your name.
There is no title that befits the name of Your eternity,
but only "the One Who Is," who exists without beginning.
By this title it befits everything that was made to call You,
this which You taught the work of Your hands, that they might call You by it.
To Moses Your servant You revealed the name of Your eternity;
it is plain, then, that Your name has no other title.
Praised be Your will—how it loves the work of its hands,
and in that very work shows the power of its eternity!
On this will my speech has gazed; my speech has loved words,
and has begun to bring forth words of suffering for sinners.
A sacrifice of words my speech offers on behalf of speakers;
accept its sacrifice, You who accept sacrifices and prayers.
Its sacrifice is an entreaty full of complaints;
have pity on its words, even if they are unworthy of acceptance.
Complaining, it pleads with You in weakness of strength,
like the widow with that cruel judge.
You composed that parable to make known the weakness of our race,
and You painted an example in the importunity of her stubborn [?].
And if her entreaty overcame the cruelty of that cruel man,
how much more will Your mercies incline toward sinners!
If the cruel one became merciful, as You have shown,
show openly the power of wonders toward our wickedness.
If an unjust man demanded justice for the wronged woman,
how much more will You, the Just One, judge our wrongs justly!
We are wronged, my Lord, by the passions and by Satan;
avenge us with the vengeance that befits Your judgeship.
Two adversaries have been for us the cause of all evils:
our evil inclination, and the Evil One who hated us from the beginning.

The Evil One became for us the counselor of shameful counsel,
and man went out to seek the counsel of his shameful deeds.
By his shameful deeds he defaced the beauty of the comeliness of our image,
and it became loathsome to heavenly and earthly beings.
In the comeliness of our image we shone before our folly,
and once we had become foolish they were turned and amazed at our ugliness.
O Fashioner of our image in the likeness of His own image, which is without composition,
have pity on our image for the sake of Your image, which is without composition.
You have no image that has taken on composition, as mortals do;
and this is the wonder: You named us, though You Yourself are not named.
By the name of Your greatness You called us, O Good One who are wholly good;
let not the name of Your goodness be changed by the wickedness of our iniquity.
Far be it! It does not happen, nor can it be,
that our iniquity should seek to overcome the power that holds all things.
What is the iniquity of demons and men compared with Your mercies,
or the wickedness of all creation before Your compassion?
Your grace is greater than the creatures that came into being from You,
and Your mercifulness cannot be compared with the work of Your hands.
At the target of Your mercies the thoughts of those who love entreaty have gazed,
and they have begun to aim toward the target of the greatness of Your mercies.
The target of Your mercies You fixed in the house of the statutes of Scripture,
and behold, for nearly six thousand years it has not changed.
Mercifully Your will has gone along with all generations,
and it has not diminished from what it is, nor will it until the end.
You decreed upon Adam the sentence of death when he sinned,
and Adam lived after he sinned nine hundred years and more.
You pronounced upon Cain sevenfold vengeance of seven punishments,
and You did not carry them out in full as You had pronounced.
You said, "I will blot out all that I have made, without pity,"
and behold, all creation stands, with all that came to be.
You cursed Canaan to be a slave, a slave of slaves,
and from him reigned harsh kings who subjugated peoples.
You went down, though You did not go down, to the Babylonians to make war,
and You changed them into instruments of Your armor for peace.
You decreed upon the land of the Philistines that no one should remain in it,

and great multitudes of its inhabitants remained without chastisement.
You raised Your hand against the Egyptians and struck them,
and there was no chastisement in which a little grace was not mingled.
You swore that You would destroy the Israelites with a mighty destruction,
and after You had sworn, You provided for them lovingly.
Lovingly, we see, You have chastised whenever You chastised,
and there is no chastisement in which You did not mingle kindness.
In Your kindness we have been tested and are tested,
and we do not cease from pleading over our sins.
In the greatness of Your love we take refuge at all times,
like children who always cling to their fathers.
To Your fatherhood we look, the only Father,
and we do not lovingly call "father" those who begot us.
We know no other father but You,
for there are no fathers whose love is like Your fatherhood.
You, You alone are Father and Lord and also Judge,
for You have all these together with Your beginningless Being.
Without beginning You possessed, as God, all that You possess,
and You have nothing that has not been eternally.
To You, our Lord, it befits every man to lift his eyes,
and from You to ask food in its season and forgiveness of iniquity.
Have pity on our lives, O Fountain of life that does not die,
and give us a season full of peace, and the sustenance of life.
We have sinned greatly, and our iniquity has gone over our head,
and we are near to drowning in the depth of our debts.
The number of our shameful deeds has grown beyond number,
and our guilt cannot be measured by any known measure.
We have swallowed many and severe blows,
and our inclination has not ceased from thinking on evil things.
The weight of our great scourges [?] because of our hateful deeds,
and we have not tried to hate our iniquity, not at all.
If our iniquity testifies against us, my Lord, as it is written,
have pity and forgive, for the sake of Your mercies that cannot be measured.
Your mercifulness cannot be measured by measurers;
and if this is so, what is our iniquity, a despicable thing?

Despicable indeed is our iniquity, however great it may be;
cast it like a pebble into the great sea of Your kindness.
Do not be angry with us because we have sinned like sinners,
for You, O Good One, understand better than all the nature of our sinfulness.
You knew us before we were fashioned and after we came to be,
and You understand our evil inclination, that it is bent toward evil.
For You fashioned it, and You gave it the task of meditating;
so from You it learned to meditate between good and evil.
And if You are the master and it is the disciple of Your teaching,
perfect Your disciple according to the will of Your mastery.
Take a tablet for the young child who has become Your disciple,
and spell out before him the words that give him life.
Write the letters of the name of Your Being upon his mind,
that he may read with understanding and keep the order of his life's conduct.
Again, inscribe for him another law, the love of man,
that he may bind his love with the Alaph of the One Who Is and the Taw of humanity.
And once a man has learned to read well,
it is easy for him to write, and to meditate on it in the freedom of his soul.
With freedom of soul You filled the soul when You fashioned it,
and the Good One gave it authority to discern the two with discernment.
Discern, O discerning one, this discernment set in your nature,
and know your nature and your Maker, who set the two in you.
You have two things, O soul, mistress of good and evil;
judge justly which of the two is right.
With the palate of the flesh you tell sweet from bitter;
discern your own nature as you have discerned what is not yours.
What is yours is fair to behold—fair, if you have done fairly—
and what is fair for you, the beauty of your soul, is set in your choice.
Set in choice is every human being who possesses a soul,
and it is his to tell the hateful from the fair.
Rightly, then, do the mute natures contend with us
and condemn us, for they are not liable for our guilt.
If the divine command had truly governed us

and changed the seasons outside the order of their changes,
just would be our affliction and fitting the scourge for our insolence,
and moreover we deserve to be scourged with doubled scourges.
With doubled scourges our inclination deserves to be scourged,
for it knows that it sins, and does not remember that judgment will be required.
It has heard of the judgment that will come at the end of all things,
and it is not afraid of the threat of the name of Gehenna.
Woe to us, how far our mind has strayed from reason,
that the demand of judgment is for us both true and not true!
If it is true for us, why is the evil inclination not ashamed,
and why does it make light of something true and proven?
True is Your judgment, great Judge, who judge all,
and what shall we do, who have made the decree of Your judgments false?
Falsely we heard the name of Your just judgment,
and had we heard it truly, we would not be sinning.
We have sinned as we have sinned, because our nature clings to sin;
O Lord of natures, have pity on our nature, that it may not be condemned.
Over our sins we are troubled all our lives,
and behold, we devise means, seeking release from sins.
Release our sins, O Lord, who have authority over our sins,
and blot them out from the record of the book of Your judgments.
Take them out of the archive of Your judgeship,
and tear them up before the eyes of angels and men.
Let not the bond that Adam wrote remain with You,
lest the enemies of Adam boast in the sins of Adam.
The bond of debts was written in Eden by the eating of the fruit,
and because it was not repaid, Satan rejoiced in the guilt of his debts.
The interest on that commandment grew upon his offspring,
and they gave their bodies as a pledge to greedy death.
Like pledges, death has gathered their bodies to itself,
and behold, it cruelly wears them away in the pits of Sheol.
Devouring Sheol has swallowed the children of dust,
and there is no one made of dust who considers the dust of his fellows.
O Moulder of our dust, have pity on our dust, which has become dust,
and raise our dust from death and from sins.
By two deaths of the Evil One each of us dies:
by the corruption of death, and by the shameful deeds of our evil inclination.

Raise our lives, O Lover of our lives, from both of them,
and open before us the door of resurrection and forgiveness of iniquity.
Death and iniquity have seized the door before us with their wiles,
and behold, they scheme to drown us with no resurrection.
You are the path of resurrection and the forgiveness of debts,
and You taught us that death is abolished and iniquity silenced.
Through One of our race, who trod the way of our race's renewal,
grant us to go down to the fitting meeting of the renewal of our lives.
With the life of His life He sealed the gifts of our life,
and we trust that You will not prove false in the promise of Your words.
The hostage of peace whom You created from our race, full of sins,
behold, is adorned with the glories of Your divinity.
More praised than all You made Him with You, the head of our life;
honor our life for the sake of the life of the One whom You chose.
Great, unspeakable love You showed toward Him,
in that You raised Him to the great height of Your name.
Let the Son of the right hand of Your divinity entreat You, then,
that You be reconciled with us, because we have wickedly angered You.
He offers You prayer [?] on behalf of sinners;
behold, it is the time that the order of prayers requires.
Lovingly He is wont to pray for His beloved;
accept His words with the love that befits Your kindness.
Lovingly You love Him with the desire of Your name;
fulfill in deed the entreaty of His words on our behalf.
On our behalf the head of our race prays with us;
O Lover of our race, hear the Son of our race and have pity on our race.
Listen to our petition, which the Son, the Son of our race, offers You,
and give us the hand of forgiveness of debts, which we ask of You.
Hear us, O Good One, You who hear even the babble of our words,
and be persuaded, though our entreaty before You is small.
Small is our entreaty compared with the greatness of our guilt,
and that it does not persuade You—this too is guilt.
Into the contest of sufferings over our sins each of us is thrown,
and whether he persuades is a fear, and whether he does not persuade is again a doubled fear.
It is fear that persuades, though You have no need to be persuaded,
and fear is afraid lest it fail to persuade concerning our folly.

You have no need of the entreaty of the words of those who plead,
since the entreaty of every man is heard by You before he entreats You.
Seen by You is the iniquity of all generations, before all creatures;
and what am I saying—generations and times, beside Your Being?
Together with Your Being, in Your heart You are the end of all things that come to an end,
and there is nothing in creation that exists which does not exist in You.
With You is the record of the books of what was and what is,
and among deeds there is nothing hidden from Your knowledge.
Our iniquity is revealed to You, and the righteousness of Watchers and men,
and weighed out by You is the recompense of reward for the good and the wicked.
And while everything that is and is to be is good in You,
we cannot but plead over our sins.
For our guilt we beseech You before Your greatness;
forgive our sins and blot out the bond of our great iniquity.
Have pity, O Merciful One, on our wickedness, which has grown very strong,
and we are near to becoming companions of the Sodomites.
Let no room be given for iniquity to dwell in us,
for if even a little of it dwells in us, our judgment demands the vengeance of Sodom.
Let us not, my Lord, be companions in judgment of the Sodomites,
lest the name of our wickedness be [?] like theirs.
Withhold from us the scourge like that of the Sodomites,
and do not trace in our land the hateful likeness of the land of Sodom.
Waste and void is the land of Sodom since it burned,
and desolate and empty of the produce of seeds and fruits.
Let us not see that chastisement, not at all,
and let not the name of its deeds be remembered in the conduct of our lives.
Short is life, and full of debts, the life of our humanity;
O Lover of mankind, have pity on our lives, full of debts.
Do not condemn us with the guilt of the sin of our debts,
for behold, we were sentenced to but light scourges for our sins.
Enough have the visible things chastised our wrongdoing;
do not add doubled scourges upon us, lest we perish.
Lift Your rod from the blows upon our body and our land,
and rebuke the heavenly hosts, that they may not strike us.

Calm them, that they may not show us faces of wrath,
and calm the air, which is troubled because of our iniquity.
Give a sign to the ruler who holds the course of the months of the year,
that he cast the reins of peace upon the turbulent seasons.
Call and warn the wind that holds dominion over the wind,
that the gusts of the movements of the air may be checked from their harshness.
Set an order for the one who orders the confused seasons,
that he may teach them to keep the order of their changes.
In their disorderly changes everything has dwindled,
and nothing is left that has not been impoverished from what it was.
Poor and needy of all good things is the life of man,
and despised are the food of the body and the meditation of the soul.
Rest of body and of mind has fled from us,
and our humanity stands like a tree in the days of winter.
Like dark winter is the course of the months of the year,
and there is no comfort that rightly gives hope.
There is no memory at all of anything restful and peaceful,
only the sound of shameful deeds that thunders on the earth.
The sound of iniquity alone thunders among the dwellers on earth,
and the sound of good things is still, like a dead man without life.
All kinds of good things have died, like a dead man without a shroud,
and those who cared for them have forgotten them, as one forgets the dead.
Good things have died, and the kinds of shameful deeds have come alive;
woe to us, for we have become dead to truth and alive to iniquity.
We have raised iniquity from the dead by our wrongdoing,
and by our cruelty we have killed the infants of righteousness.
We have made our righteousness barren of offspring,
and have not let it raise the fruits of love.
Like Pharaoh is our cruelty toward truth,
and even more cruel than the Egyptians is our lack of peace.
Pharaoh drowned the bodies of infants in the waters of the river;
we drown the life of the soul in the flood of iniquity.
The life of the soul, which does not die, a man puts to death—
not that it dies, but that it becomes dead through iniquity.
Worse than all deaths is the death of the deadness of iniquity,
and the voice of the Reviver of the dead, who explained these things, bears witness.

Death, they say, is not what kills only the body,
but what destroys body and soul together.
Body and soul together it destroys on the day of judgment;
woe to us, for near is the day of judgment that will call these things to account!
Woe to us, for here our body has wasted away in hunger and pains,
and we are destined to be tormented in body and soul.
Woe to us, who are worn down by poverty in the dwelling of time,
and in the time to come we shall be stripped of all good things.
Woe to us, for we lived, yet did not live well in the conduct of our life;
we shall be raised, yet shall not be worthy of our rising.
We dwelt on earth and did not prove upright in our sojourn there;
how then shall we fare in that way of life of the heavenly ones?
So we have no place where there is a house of labor,
but only that Gehenna where no labor is done.
Woe to us, lest the dwelling of our life be there,
in that labor full of weeping and gnashing of teeth!
May what I have said not come to pass as our sins deserve,
and may we not be deprived of the good things here and beyond.
May we not go out of this world naked,
and go on to be in need of glory in that splendor.
May we not be estranged from that glory which glorifies the good,
nor be cast out like the one who was cast out of the wedding feast.
Blessed are the good things you promised our race through one son of our race;
let not the promise of your words be proved false through our slackness.
We are very slack and idle in the labor of truth,
and it wearies us to work even a little at good deeds.
Great and abundant is the wealth of immortal life,
yet we do not desire to take from it even a single portion.
Fearful is the judgment that will be there in that way of life,
and it will not remit us even a jot of our sins.
Even for the idle word that is heard he will require an account at our hands;
yet we do not think to stop, nor do we ponder that trial.
That trial came upon my mind, which feeds on words,
and it trembled and was dismayed, and began to compose a plea of words.
My foolish mind wanted to compose a plea,
knowing that it is too weak to compose a way of life.

Entreaty is easier for those who entreat than works,
and for this reason my mind chose what is easy.
The sluggard does not wish to go down into labors,
for he knows that the conduct of the spiritual life is wearisome.
From the hunt for spiritual labors my mind too has fled,
and see, it stitches together a garment of words to cover itself.
Naked it saw itself, naked,
and it took words and spread them over its face for shame.
With words it chose to cover its nakedness,
because it has heard that words cover those who are like it.
It heard the voice of the wise man who rebukes the sluggard,
and rouses the slack to labor as if from sleep:
"How long," the wise man cried to the sluggard,
"will you sleep and neglect the labor of righteousness?"
He portrayed the ant for the idler weary of labors,
that he might look at it and it might rouse his mind to labor:
"Look at the ant, speak with it, you who are heavy of heart,
and learn from it the ways of diligence and wakefulness of soul.
See how wakeful its lowly soul is for its labor,
and rouse your impulses toward the labor of good things.
See how it prepares its food for its life before the season,
and you too prepare provisions that will provide for you.
See that there are neither commanders nor commanded among them,
and persuade yourself to labor before others persuade you."
These words were heard by the thoughts that hate labors,
and they set their hand to the labor of persuasive words.
The plea of words laid a foundation for those who labor,
so that out of words they might build an edifice of labors.
The edifice of labors I wished to show to the builders of labors,
that they might build their conduct upon my words.
O builders of the edifice of spiritual labors,
build upon my words the labors of your conduct!
Come, you who plead for the forgiveness of every kind of iniquity,
mingle my words with your words in suffering and tears.

Come, you who are as perfect in your conduct as one can be,
sprinkle your labors like mercy upon sinners.
Come, sinners, who have sinned and gone astray like sinners,
go down with words that are full of meditation on sinners.
In meditation in words on sinners my speech has meditated,
to teach them the way that is full of grace and mercy.
Grace and mercy my mind mingles in a medicine of words,
so that through words people may drink grace and mercy.
In the drink of words I mingle the medicine of the pardon of debts,
and I long that everyone may drink it and forget his iniquity.
With this aim I have given it the title "Petition":
that I may ask and plead for my debts and those of my companions.
Come then, my companions, be my companions in the plea of words,
and let us together entreat the One who has no need of entreaty.
He seeks entreaty, not because he needs it, as I said,
but to teach those who entreat to entreat him.
Like a teacher, his sign stands over our head;
he makes our childishness wise, yet our childish soul does not grow wise.
Make mankind wise; have pity on mankind, dull of heart,
who despise the books of your teaching, full of life.
See how weak is our nature, beset with weaknesses,
and do not be angry with it if it always sins out of its defects.
You fashioned it from dust as it pleased you,
and with its dust you mingled the defects of a slack inclination.
Its slack inclination—mingle your sign with its dust,
for its dust cannot brace the slackness of its dust without you.
Pressing sufferings oppress its life all its life long,
and do not let it be girded for the labor of its life.
Like gnats, [?] stand over its back
and distract it from care for good things.
Night and day it is worn down by the pressure of toils,
and there is no time when its whole mind is gathered in.
Summer and winter it toils and is harried by want;
it works constantly, and its want is never filled.
Like a beggar it too goes about begging for its life,
and is always knocking at the doors of every craft.
Every day it seeks new discoveries of other labors,
so that it may find provisions for the span of its life.

The weary one wearies itself inventing new labors,
and the more it toils, the stronger its poverty grows.
O poor one, child of the poor, who is poor and foolish,
and does not consider keeping the rule of his poverty!
O beggar who goes about constantly, summer and winter,
and the need of his soul is not filled by alms!
O hireling who hires out his life in toils,
and works every day, and is cheated of his wage without knowing it!
Not knowing has made him cheated and a beggar too;
the more he goes about, his labor grows and his reward dwindles.
It has dwindled, and Adam's dust has been spent in toils;
O you who fashioned his dust, have pity on his dust before it perishes!
The particles scarcely hold together in its frame,
and see, the winds of sufferings drive them from place to place.
Sufferings whirl it about continually as in a whirlwind,
and pile it up like heaps on the seashore.
Like water and wind are his sufferings, full of sufferings,
and what they pass over becomes like dust before the feet.
The foot of suffering passes over it by the force of its mortality,
and does not let its dust rest in one place.
See, swept and scattered is our dust in all our places,
and there is no place in creation that is not sown with our dust.
See, we are scattered like seed in the bosom of the earth,
and have been made food for creeping things and birds.
One thing is lacking to the wickedness of our bitter inclination:
that it should remain in the earth and our dust become a portion for the dust.
No, O Gracious One, may what I have said not happen to us,
and may the word that empty hope gave birth to not be fulfilled.
May our great hope in your majesty not be emptied,
and may the truth of your name not be proved false through our falsehood.
You are true, and through you the truth of your name stands firm;
our falsehood does not harm you at all.
Fulfill, then, the promise of your words to our race,
and give us a hand, that we may rise a little from our fall.
We have fallen deeply into countless shameful deeds,
and if your help does not reach us, we have fallen forever.
You are forever, O Lord, our Lord and Lord of all,

and through you heaven and earth and all that is in them stand firm.
Not to us, Lord, not to us—do not be angry at the greatness of our iniquity—
but to your name give glory, as befits your name.
Honor your name through the salvation you work for us,
so that demons may not blaspheme your name because of our iniquity.
Because of our iniquity demons have blasphemed your great name;
cut off the pretext of those who seek pretexts by forgiving iniquity.
Forgive our iniquity, and let its name not be remembered at all,
and see, the pretext of those who seek a pretext is cut off.
Cut off this too: that I should be offering you entreaty always,
for see, I have wearied you with my tiresome words, though you never weary.
See, my words too are spent and worn down from composing,
and can no longer compose further kinds of petition.
See, the eloquent word that gives birth to words has grown weary,
and no longer wishes to keep company with the mind.
See, the mind too has withdrawn into itself,
and no longer wishes to meditate on the business of words.
See, there are no words about forgiveness that have not been said,
and however much anyone says, whoever says them says the same.
See, they are said and repeated by every mouth;
and what profit is there, when there is no profit in wearying with them?
See, our whole nature, bereft of everything, has raised its finger:
Lord of natures, have pity on our nature, full of debts!
On Jonah the Prophet

The eighth discourse, on Jonah the prophet, to be recited at the Rogation of the Ninevites. Response: Blessed is he who has shown his glories in his works, and has fulfilled and completed his mysteries, my brothers.

The Creator placed a great treasure within the Scriptures
and hid it in mystery until it should be fulfilled as He had decreed.
He spread parables like a veil over the signs,
so that the eyes of the flesh would not despise the treasure of the Spirit.
He hid His wealth from the childishness of ignorance
until it should come to maturity, and then He would open the door of His mercies.
He set guardians over those who knew His covenants,
so that the power of wisdom might grow greatly before their eyes.
He did not give the childish of heart authority over His hidden things,
lest His precious things be despised through shallowness of soul.
The heir was a child and was not able to manage his wealth,
and, as to strangers, in His goodness He gave us of His [?].
And when He had examined His hidden things well through His dispensations,
for the salvation of our life He hid it in mystery until the end.
He chose one people and called it by His name as heir,
so that through it He might open the treasury of His mercies to all peoples.

But the son, who saw that he was called by the Name and set apart from all,
was carried off by pride without discernment and despised all.
The childish of mind looked upon the signs with the eyes of the flesh,
and did not search out the power of the hidden things with the movements of the soul.
The child thought that the wealth was his alone,
and despised and scorned his fellows with foolish pride.
He did not know that he was honored above all for the sake of all,
and that the One hidden in him reconciles all with the Lord of all.
In this way of the people's election even the righteous walked,
and they reckoned the course toward the peoples superfluous.
The Law, too, strengthened them in what is written,
and inflamed them with love of their people to hate the peoples.
They did not desire that the uncircumcised become like members of the household,
lest the chosen people should go out of its inheritance.
They found no rest in the mission to the peoples,
and Jonah bears witness: when he was sent, he fled and hid himself.
The Hebrew heard the voice of the resurrection that would give life to its dead,
and was greatly grieved lest they should live and his people die.
The new tidings fell into the ears of the son of the Hebrews,
and sorrow seized him at the new good news of the peoples' turning.
He put on a grief without consolation at what he heard,
and thought to flee and not be sent on the road of the pagans.
The circumcised of flesh heard that the uncircumcised would live freely,
and instead of the veil he rent his mind with division.
The Revealer called him and spoke with him in mystery:
"Go out and gather for Me the rational sheep into the fold of life.
Arise, go, proclaim the voice of salvation in the house of the drowning,
and awaken with the voice of your words those who sleep in iniquity.
Come, travel the road of preaching to the house of the strangers,
and set them on the new road of the worship of My lordship.
Come, go, reconcile the angry ones who went out from My household,
and shepherd them by grace toward righteousness.
Come, go and visit the sick who are afflicted with the pains of iniquity,
and by your words heal the fever of their minds.

"Take for yourself medicine from the treasury of My hidden lordship,
and bind them up with repentance unto forgiveness.
With grace and mercy cleanse and water their minds,
and with the medicine of sweetness wash from them the stain of iniquity.
Take the lamp of the light of My knowledge and set it before their eyes,
and drive from them the darkness of error that has blinded them.
Season those who are without understanding with the salt of My knowledge,
so that through your hands they may acquire the sweet taste of the one Creator.
First show them harsh words before the deeds,
and comfort those who feel them with the voice of forgiveness.
Arm yourself with the power of divine help,
and go down to the contest and trample sin, which has killed humankind.
Grasp the sword of the word of the Spirit on the tip of your tongue,
and destroy the tyrant iniquity that rebelled against righteousness.
Uproot the edifice of the name of the gods that error built,
and set the confession of the one God in the mind of humankind.
Arise, go to Assyria, the city of kings that rebelled against Me,
and instead of arrows hurl at it words that sound a threat.
Call to it and shake the city full of pride with the voice of your words,
and cast into its ears: 'A harsh overthrow, behold, is hastening!'
Go and say to it: 'Behold, I shake the earth beneath you,
