and hasten the news of the day of your fall to all the peoples.'"
The son of Amittai heard the voice proclaiming a harsh overthrow,
and again he shrank from going on the road toward the peoples.
He looked upon the grace of his Sender, which overcomes wrath,
and thought that perhaps he would speak words and they would not be believed:
"I know that You are merciful and spare iniquity,
and that Your great love changes the harshness of wrath.
If I go and proclaim terrifying words to the Assyrians,
I shall be made a liar, for You do not act according to Your threats."
Two doubts multiplied the road, the road before Jonah:
lest he be proven a liar, and lest the chosen people go out [of its inheritance].
At the outset of his road the one who was sent was being tested:

the claim of his people and the doubt about his words were terrifying him.
He chose flight for himself, so as not to be sent on the road of the peoples,
lest the fence of the Law be broken down through his going.
Jonah rose to flee and to hide from Him who knows all,
and to dwell in a place where he would not hear revelations.
It was not flight in the sense that the preacher fled from God;
he changed his place in this way so as not to be sent.
For he knew that the power of the Creator is in all things,
and that the work of His hands is not hidden from God.
He changed his place according to the testing of prophecy,
supposing that revelations dwell in Judah alone.
The son of Amittai thought that those who go far from it are neglected,
and that he would no longer hear the voice of revelations to go to Assyria.
He chose for himself a route by the wide sea to the land of Tarshish,
so that the farther he went, the farther he would be from the voice of the Creator.
He hired a ship so that the salvation of the peoples might not be traded,
and left his land so that the peoples might not be favored over the people.
He fled from the dry land so that the heart of the uncircumcised might not be appeased,
and traveled by sea so that the voice of his words might not be proved false.
The fugitive went down into the ship and slept from his grief,
and the command went out like a messenger and stirred up the sea.
The storm became like a fisherman and spread its nets,
and Jonah fell with the sailors into the snares of the waters.
With the rod of the wind the command lashed the sea for his sake:
"On whose behalf have you hidden the servant who fled from Him who knows all?"
It struck the silent and moved them to speech,
and taught the mute to speak with the Creator.
Wind and waters pressed one another because of Jonah,
to hunt him down for the preaching to the peoples.
Beyond all order the sea was troubled over the son of Amittai,
while the hurrying waves sought him whom [?] was hiding.
That tempest was not like those of every day,
and the rush of its course was different from the usual.
The lashing did not stretch over the whole expanse of the sea;
only around Jonah's ship was it lashing.

A great wonder was seen among the waves:
while the sea was calm, it was troubled over Jonah and quiet over all.
How the command gave discernment to those without senses
and stirred them to speech, for it sought him who wished to keep silent!
How wise the silent ones, bereft of reason, became,
so that half was quiet and half stirred beyond all order!
The sea was calm for the sailors as they traveled,
yet it raged with harsh waves at Jonah's place.
The air was still, the waves at peace, and everyone traveling,
while Jonah's ship was being battered by the storm.
The fence of the command divided the sea around the sailors,
and they saw the wonder: while all was calm, it was stirred over Jonah.
The portion of the sea was being lashed within the veins of the command,
and the lashing of the wind did not cross the boundary of the command.
It brought the ship down to the depth, yet it was not broken,
and raised it to the surface of the sea, yet it was not overturned.
The command was careful of it, while the rod of the wind lashed it,
and it rose to the height and sank to the depth, yet the wind did not destroy it.
In the lashing of his ship the sailors were overwhelmed by harsh lashings,
and gave up hope, thinking they would not be rescued from the tempests.
They took counsel together that each should cry to his god,
that perhaps they might be delivered from the tempests and see life.
The chief of the sailors woke Jonah: "Get up and entreat,
pray and ask your God that perhaps He will give us rest."
In the heaviness of sleep Jonah was sunk in the hold of his ship,
and did not feel the lashing of the sea that was on his account.
The fugitive rose and saw that the sea was troubled with waves,
and his thoughts judged that the tempest was on his account.
He did not pray with the sailors that the sea might be stilled,
for he knew that he had offended, and if he entreated he would not be received.
He kept silent from prayer, like a discerning man who had despised a command,
who, even if he calls, is not answered by the one he despised.

The sailors saw that their petition had become futile,
and took counsel to search out the iniquity of their deeds.
They reckoned the sea's pressing around them to be because of sin,
for they saw that it was calm, yet against them it came on like a destroyer.
In the lashing of the sea they gained discernment, and distinguished and knew
that it was because of iniquity that the tempest had stirred half the sea.
The tossing of the wind became great for them and made them wise;
they considered among themselves who had offended, that his sin might be revealed.
In the furnace of lots they examined one another like discerning men,
so that the deceit hidden within the mind might come to light.
They cast lots, so that the lots might search out who had sinned
and give judgment for the folly by which he had stirred the sea.
The command descended into the midst of the lots and chose among them,
and the lot of the son of the Hebrews came up before the sailors.
The uncircumcised asked the circumcised in body, "What have you done?
Reveal your deeds, tell us your people, and show us your land."
Jonah answered the sailors, "I am a Hebrew,
and I am a servant of the God of all, who established all.
From God who knows all I fled and hid myself,
and His command has hunted me down in the harsh net of the shifting waters."
O preacher who sought to hide his preaching,
yet against his will searched out and revealed the fear of his Lord!
In this way he was sent to the house of the strangers,
to go and proclaim one God for the abolishing of error.
He fled from the people, and the peoples caught him, the hater of peoples,
and, unwilling, he became a preacher to the peoples whom he hated:
"It is the one Lord, who holds all things, whom I fear,
and He governs sea and dry land according to His will."
The uncircumcised learned from the Hebrew that the good servant
had fled from God who knows all and hidden himself.
The sailors were alarmed when they saw the wonder that was because of Jonah,
and wanted to turn back to the dry land, but the sea would not allow it.
The ship was bound fast in the sea so that it could not travel,
and when they turned it toward the shore, the command held it back.
The tossing of the wind shook it on every side,

and the waves armed themselves against it like horsemen.
The tempest was drawn up and surrounded it like a camp,
and the tossing of the wind was fenced before it like a wall.
The sailors fell into deep thought because of Jonah;
they weighed his death and his life, how hard both were.
"What shall we do to Jonah?" they said in despair.
"Deliverance is hard and your death is grievous; do not lay the blame on us."
Jonah answered the sailors like a discerning man:
"Take me and cast me among the waves, and behold, the sea will be calm.
For an eager lion, the mouth of the waters, is seeking me;
give him his portion, and he will not rage against your lives.
It is at me that the great deep roars with the voice of its surging,
and it was after me that the storm too went out and stirred the sea.
Because of my folly the wall of wind is fenced before you;
it is watching for my descent, and behold, it will loosen the fence of its waves."
The sailors cried to God in great despair:
"O Creator, do not hold us guilty of innocent blood.
You are the Lord who rules over all on sea and dry land,
and if You will that this should happen, accomplish Your will."
The sailors took Jonah and cast him among the waves,
and the tempests ceased, and the men marveled at the power of the Creator.
They vowed vows and afterward fulfilled them,
namely, that they would be servants of the God of all.
The fugitive fell into the snares of the waters, and the waves bound him,
while the mute creatures judged his discernment in silence.
The Judge gave the sentence after his lashings,
and broke the reed of the verdict that he should go down to Sheol.
He dug a grave for the living dead man in a living body,
so that He might keep his bodily life within a living body.
The command went down after a fish and drew it upward,
and it rose and received the living man and buried him within itself.
The son of [?] entered the fish, a grave within a grave,
and the command held the door shut before the living dead man.
The fugitive went down into the prison house full of darkness,
and his feet were bound in the wide stocks of the fish's entrails.

He fled from the dry land, and the sea caught him and gave him to the fish,
and it brought him in and confined him, a grave within a grave: the deep and the fish.
How wondrous the thing that was wrought in the son of Amittai,
that he went down alive into two graves and was not corrupted!
How the departed was escorted, still alive, to Sheol!
How the earthly one was covered with dust in the full shape of his body!
How the mortal was wholly buried, and alive as he went down!
How the prisoner was wholly bound, and journeying in the grave!
It was not by the strength of the power of life that the mortal lived;
the command kept him in the manner of infants within the womb.
A man's life does not endure without air,
yet without air the bodily man lived like spiritual beings.
It was not his own doing that he fled to hide and not be sent,
for the great mystery that was to come was already being depicted in him.
It was not that he should die that the One who knows all buried him in the fish;
through his descent He traced the parables of things to come.
Through a son of man He was going to make life for all,
and through a man to free all from slavery.
Through the death of a man He was going to loose the dominion of death,
and He buried Jonah, as in a mystery, before the deed.
The body of our Lord was not to see corruption in Sheol,
and He kept Jonah without corruption in the mystery of our Savior.
Three days He buried Jonah in the belly of the fish,
so that he might be a type of the truth, hidden while it was being searched out.
A living fish became the grave of the one who depicted the mysteries,
and a new grave received the body of the One who fulfilled the mysteries.
A new thing in mystery was wrought in the catch of the son of Amittai:
when the fish swallowed his body, it kept it alive.
New, too, was the fulfillment of the mystery of Jonah:
the body that greedy death swallowed was not corrupted.
New and full of wonder are the mysteries of things to come:
a body buried in the grave of a body, and it lives and walks.
A new road the son of Amittai trod before the deeds,
so that what was fulfilled might not seem strange in the eyes of the beholders.
For the sake of the truth of the peoples' salvation were the parables given,
so that when humankind was saved by a man, they would not doubt.
But let the circumcised of flesh and uncircumcised of heart say:

What is the power hidden in the mystery that Jonah served?
What was it that compelled him to be three days in the fish
and to live a life foreign to the life of a man?
And if it be that he offended by despising the command and word of his Lord,
why did He not pursue him with other lashings, but with a fish?
When did He ever draw any of the children of His house as He did Jonah,
and who was ever imprisoned alive in Sheol like the son of Amittai?
At what time did He send His preachers to the house of the strangers,
and when did He send a prophet to the peoples apart from the people?
Why did he not prophesy in the land of Judah,
but the voice set him apart from the people to go to Assyria?
Uncover the veil that is cast over your face, son of Abraham,
and look upon the truth hidden in the mystery that Jonah served.
Take away the curtain that Moses spread, and leave off your vexation,
and see openly the image of the King, as He truly is.
My son, look with discernment into the books of the Spirit,
and behold, you will learn that the mysteries were fulfilled in the hope of the peoples.
Raise your mind to the new mystery that the son of Amittai depicted,
and see that all the mysteries were fulfilled in Him whom you crucified.
Lift your thought to the great height of his preaching,
and compare his road to the house of the peoples, who turned back.
Let Nineveh be like a mirror to the eyes of your heart,
and see that the voice of salvation went out to the four corners.
Travel with Jonah and go down to the deep in his company,
and behold, at the end of your road you will reach the height above.
The son of Amittai went down and dwelt in Sheol in the mystery of our Savior,
and the command kept him from becoming food for creeping things in the belly of the fish.
Buried in the temple of the fish, the discerning one prayed;
his thoughts judged him, and he sought and sought and pleaded to return to life:
"Hear the voice of my petition, God of all, and listen to my words,
and bring my life up from destruction to life.
I know that I sinned in not serving You on the road of the peoples;
behold, by my life, which You have preserved, You have taught me that You love humankind.

For the salvation of humankind You called me to go, and now it pleases me;
redeem me from my captivity, that I may go out and bring the dead back to life.
I did not know that Your love overflowed toward strangers;
I thought that You had acquired one inheritance and that it alone was Yours.
I thought that if the uncircumcised peoples entered into Your inheritance,
the inheritance You had chosen might go out from Your house.
I judged this according to the will of the Law,
which estranges the unclean peoples from its fellowship.
Now that I have heard from its Lawgiver that He calls the peoples,
I do not shut the door of my mercy in the face of the wicked.
Let my petition come before You, my God, and I shall live by Your word,
and my life will be a sign of life to those dead in iniquity.
In the grief of my life I said that there was no salvation;
if You will, I shall once again see Your face.
Grant me to pay the vow of my lips in the land of the living,
for if I come up, I will not be silent from proclaiming life."
How the prayer, confined in a grave within a grave,
broke through the wall of the fish, the water, and the face of the heights!
How the prisoner in his exile in the depth of the waters
stretched out his will, in place of his footsteps, toward Him who had bound him!
How the buried one pleaded with the one who had buried him,
and loosed his grave with the voice of his words and returned to life!
The scribe of the Spirit wrote a letter in the depth of the waters
and gave it to the mind to go in and read before Him who knows all.
Spiritual movements carried it and gave it to the Hidden One,
and brought back to him the voice of hope that he would return to life.
The command drew along the grave that carried the living dead man,
to bring up the body buried in its belly to the place of the living.
The fish hastened as it went up to the shore of the dry land,
for the command that had ordered it when it swallowed him pressed it to give him back.
The cords of the command pressed it to repay what it had taken,

so that the mystery might not be delayed in the grave beyond the truth.
The ship came up, laden with the mystery of the salvation of the peoples,
set down its wealth on the shore of the sea, and returned to its place.
Where it had been laden, when it was ready to go down to the depth,
there it came out, as the command of power drew it.
In the very harbor where it had been made ready, there it came down,
for the Chief of the sailors, who stood in it, steered it there.
In the place where the fish had swallowed Jonah, there it set him,
so that there he might hear the heavenly voice from which he had fled.
The son of Amittai came out and saw the light, and heard a voice
entirely like that first one, that he should go to Assyria:
"Come, go and proclaim new tidings to the uncircumcised peoples,
for you have become a mystery, and your mystery is fulfilled through the deeds.
For this I buried you alive and opened [the way] before you,
so that you might open the door before the strangers to enter to Me.
Through your resurrection you sought that I should revive the living who are buried;
behold, I have taught you the salvation of your own life: save the lost.
Come, go and proclaim the salvation of life to those long dead,
and revive them with the living hope of repentance.
Plow the land of hearing, the ear of their minds,
and cast into it the good seed of the fear of truth.
Uproot the tares of paganism that the Evil One sowed,
and sow the word: One Creator rules over all."
Thus He taught him the road of the peoples while he was unwilling,
and thus He taught him that it was right for him to love the peoples.
The son of Abraham acquired the discernment of wisdom,
so that he called the peoples into the kinship of the house of Abraham.
He began to travel, set apart from the peoples, to the house of the strangers,
and went on the road to the appointed place, Assyria, as he had been commanded.
The voice taught him how great the city of Assyria was,
so that for three days he traveled within Assyria, preaching in it.
It revealed and showed him also that its greatness was from God,
and that through Him it had come to abundance of wealth and people.
He began to go in, a day's journey, through the midst of its streets:

and as he went, he began in a voice full of threat.
He proclaimed, and spoke in everyone's ears a word of wrath: / "Nineveh the city is being overthrown upon its inhabitants!"
He set a term of forty days to confirm his words: / if they turned back, well; if not, He would punish as He had decreed.
The son of the Hebrews did not proclaim overthrow alone, / for see, he also mixed mercy into the overthrow of the term that was set.
With fearful words he terrified the hard of heart, / to bring them down from haughtiness to humility.
With hard iron he cut away the sore of their deeds, / so that iniquity would not linger like a disease in the stirrings of the soul.
He laid a strong medicine on the inflammation of their minds, / to root out from them the mark of the iniquity that had slain them.
The herald cried out like a trumpet in Nineveh the city, / and the waves of the sound of his words stirred it until it was filled with turmoil.
The mighty winds of the word of his mouth blew through it, / and the whole city trembled, for it was near to falling.
His voice terrified kings and lowly ones and every rank, / and gathered them to the new hearing of his preaching.
He was not held back by the power of authority, / nor did he show favor to wealth, or to the crown that is honored above all.
People and king heard his words, and trembled and were dismayed; / and though he was despised and scorned, his voice terrified the kings of Assyria.
Assemblies were made ready to hear his word, / and he cast the net of his preaching and subdued them.
His word caught youth and old age alike, / and swiftly bound the course of all the ranks.
The sound of his preaching reached the king of Assyria, / and he left his crown, despised his rule, and honored his word.
He proclaimed a word full of grief to all the people: / "Let each one turn from his deeds to supplication.
Let us hate iniquity, the loathing of our soul, which has made us unclean, / and let us love the truth, which is fair in its name and in its deeds.
Let us curse the sin that has spread its darkness over our mind, / and let us see with the understanding the light of the word of the son of the Hebrews.
Let us afflict our soul with the labor of fasting from [?],

and restrain the force of levity by sobriety.
Let us keep our mouth from the food that nourishes the body, / and restrain our soul from the service of wickedness.
Let the beasts too fast with us from nourishment, / and let the dumb creatures weep with us, because we have provoked Him.
Who knows whether the God of all will have pity on us, / and turn the heat of His wrath from us and not destroy us?"
The Good One saw that those who had seemed to Him worthy of blame, / the wicked, had repented, and He changed His wrath to gentleness.
He made them hate iniquity, though they had not wished to, / and stirred His mercies toward the discernment of the repentant soul.
He drew them by a hidden sign to the knowledge of Him, / and gave His sweetness as the reward for repentance.
Did not the Ninevites tread the way of repentance? / The Hidden One in His love revealed His hidden purpose to the members of His house.
In them Jonah traced the figures of things to come: / that the nations would be shown pity at the end of times through the second Adam.
The herald saw that the Good One had mixed mercy into His wrath, / and it grieved him greatly that the sentence of his words was not fulfilled.
He resolved to go the way of his own nature, as before, / and began to recount: "This is the reason that made me flee.
Was this not my word, O Lord, while I was in my own land? / That is why I made haste and fled, so that I would not be sent.
For I knew that You are a God abundant in mercy, / and that when people repent before You, Your love turns to forgiveness.
And now that I have become as a liar before foreigners, / command that I die, and let me not be called a false prophet."
"Is it right for you to be grieved?" a revelation called to him and spoke with him; / and he answered his Lord, "My grief has reached even to death."
The Hebrew saw that the blind had turned back, and he consented to die, / for the life of the dead of the unclean nations was not sweet to him.
Grief over the soul's distress wore him down beyond measure, / and he chose death as better than life, so as not to be proved a liar.
He left the city and went out to dwell alone, / watching whether the sentence he had pronounced would be fulfilled.
He made himself a booth to dwell in for the appointed time,

with this intent: to see whether what had been decreed was already coming to pass.
The Knower of all saw his thought, what he was seeking, / and his Lord drew him toward compassion by means of a trial.
The divine command swiftly made a gourd vine spring up, / and spread its leaves over Jonah, and he rejoiced in it.
In the leaves and fruits of the lowly gourd the son of Amittai rejoiced, / for he saw the wonder: it had sprouted suddenly and borne fruit.
He forgot his grief in the pleasure of his love for the fruit; / it is plain what the reason was that it sprang up suddenly.
The command bound him with love of the gourd so that he might again be made wise, / so that whatever befell it he would feel keenly and learn its reason.
The command that had given it suddenly and bound him with love of it / turned about [?], and suddenly it withered, and he grieved over it.
The command signaled to a harsh heat, and suddenly it blew, / and the gourd withered, its leaves were scorched, and its fruits fell.
The sun beat fiercely on Jonah's head, / and he groaned, and his soul was grieved, and he asked for death.
The heat that came upon the herald was not the usual one; / the Sign had kindled it to a fever beyond measure.
The command that stirred up the sea in an unusual way / is the same that kindled the blaze of the sun beyond measure.
By the sea it taught him not to stand in the way of the nations, / and by the gourd it rebuked him, that he should not grieve over people's life.
The stalk of the gourd became his great teacher and made him wise, / and bound him with love toward sinners, though he was unwilling.
The rational one became a disciple of the dumb, the prophet of the gourd, / and he learned his lesson and gained comfort from the silent one.
The heat fixed itself upon his limbs, and grief in his heart, / and through the trial he began to soften toward compassion.
The mystery of love and mercy in the silent one taught him,

and explained them through a revelation, so that he would not be grieved.
The Sign spoke to him in a single utterance, as in his own tongue: / "Why are you grieved over a silent thing that sprang up suddenly?
Why are you bound with perfect love to weak things, / and do not draw near to the glories that people gain?
Why do you love what is not yours, and hate what is yours, / and why are you angry at people's life as though you were not human?
Why do you not enter into judgment justly with your thoughts, / and judge yourself, with your own mind, in these matters of yours?
Where is the wakeful nature of your discernment sunk, / that you do not feel for your fellows as for your own?
You are grieved over the ruin of a dumb gourd; / how much more should I grieve over rational beings fashioned by my own self!
Visible heat in the outward body distressed you, / but the hidden iniquity of people's destruction wears me down.
You have had pity, and great grief, for a lowly thing; / how much more shall I pity the precious ones who turn to me?
See the twelve myriads of little children, / and stretch out your mind to the number of the whole.
Have pity, son of Amittai, so that the great city may not be destroyed; / become like me through compassion toward your neighbors.
What do you gain from the ruin of a place that wrath destroys? / No one confesses the name of my being within the grave.
Set your will straight toward the aim of my mercies, and have pity on it, / for this is why I called you to me: that you might be like me.
I made you a model, that you might turn the nations who have strayed back to me; / spread out your words like nets for the catching of people.
The net of love I am about to spread over all the nations, / and through the Ninevites I have traced in your hands the redemption of all.
To the four quarters I will stretch out the worship of my lordship, / and see, I have shown it through the deeds of Nineveh, which turned back.
One of your race I am about to set as a mighty champion, / and see, I have tested through your victories my victory that rests on him.
Through a son of man I bring all back to faith in me; / in his type I called the Ninevites to the preaching.

He gathers the nations and the people together in love toward me, / and I have trodden the way before his coming, on the road to Assyria.
In him I loosen the fence of the law that stands before the nations; / with this intent I called you and sent you to the house of foreigners."
The Hidden One comforted the son of the Hebrews in a mystery, / so that he would not grieve at the return of the nations who lived through him.
Through what was his own He taught him to love what is His, as one discerning, / and through him tested the redemption of the nations that was hidden in the people.
He showed him the new way of preaching, / and through him trod the path of peace to the meeting-place of life.
In this way He extended the course of prophecy: / He set its boundary in the people, and through the son of Amittai brought it out to the nations.
All were looking toward the fulfillment of his preaching, / and through him He showed the beautiful image hidden in mystery.
Blessed is He who traced for us, through the son of Amittai, the return of our life; / thanks be to the Hidden One, who in what is ours revealed His hiddenness.
On Humility
The Ninth Demonstration: On Humility, which is fitting for fasting and prayer

Weak is mortal nature
to draw near to perfection,
for flesh and blood cannot
inherit the life to come.
The inclination of its thought is set
on evil from the beginning,
and however much its will loves good,
its inclination draws it toward evil.
And though there are set in its nature
two thoughts opposed to each other,
its inclination overcomes its nature

and drags it toward the passions.
It enslaves the will of its freedom
to the servitude of the desire of the flesh,
and, wholly led captive
by the sufferings of mortality,
it cannot accomplish
the good that it wills;
but the evil it does not will
its inclination forces it to do.
It is cast into a contest at all times,
struggling with its inclination,
and it fights against the passions
with the weapon of its free will.
Every man sins through his inclination
and is enslaved to the desires,
and the strength of his will does not prevail
before the onslaught of the desire of the flesh.
Every human being is [?],
for he is at war with himself.
Who can deliver him
from the sufferings of mortality?
To the One Righteous alone belongs the victory
that justified our guilty race:
he whom mortality had weakened,
He strengthened with the armour of the Holy Spirit.
Both things befit You, Lord,
for Your treasure [?] and Your bidding are the bidding of Your grace:
a fashioning out of nothing
and a renewal that does not decay.
Your fashioning was not to blame
that our inclination is called evil;
our inclination is to blame for being so evil
that it fights against our will.
You did not bind into our nature
the good and the evil that are in our nature,
but to the freedom of our will
You gave them both.
It is our will that drags us
toward the sufferings of mortality,
and when our will so wills,
it rises above the sufferings.
It is our freedom that bends
to the servitude of the desire of the flesh,
and if it pleases, it is set free
from the bondage of the passions.
And since our freedom possesses
authority over both,
our nature is too weak for this:
to be justified by itself alone.
By the power of Your love You justified us
when our guilt had grown strong,
and You roused it within our will
to a victory of great power.
And if, when our folly had grown strong,
Your love did not spurn our iniquity,
how much more now will Your merciful grace
heal our sins!
And if, while we were dead in our sins,
while we were dead in our sins,

Christ died and gave life to us all,
how much more now shall we be justified
by the blood that sanctified our uncleanness!
And if, while we were enemies,
You reconciled us by the death of Your Son,
how much more now, through His reconciliation,
shall we become sharers in His life!
Where our folly grew strong,
the power of grace prevailed.
Therefore the hope stands firm
that mercy is shown to sinners.
Our iniquity, Lord, has fenced off the road
that leads to Your refuge;
let Your mercies tear down the fence
that our wickedness has set before us.
The darkness of the desires
has covered our discernment;
let Your grace lift the veil
that our errors have spread over our heart.
Ignorance of what is fitting
has blinded our mind;
let the dawn of Your knowledge shine,
and in it we shall see the blindness of our soul.
The passions of the desires
have scattered the salt of Your teaching;
let Your grace win back for our mind
the sweet savour that we lost.
Your love needs no persuading,
for before we plead You already know.
You are not appeased by words,
as though we still had to speak to You on our own behalf.
It was not anger at our offences
that stirred You when we did wickedly,
for You had searched out our inclination
before it came into being.
The sufferings of our nature were revealed
to Your knowledge before they existed,
and our hidden and secret things
lay clear before Your scrutiny.
You knew that the inclination within us
enslaves us to the desires,
and You were persuaded that, by means of death,
it returns our dust to its own nature.
You looked upon the needs of its life
before the fashioning of our clay,
and You filled our race with life
with the delight of the fullness of time.
You knew that two dwellings
were needed for our nature:
the earth for the childhood of our mind,
and heaven for its perfection.
The mystery of our salvation was hidden
in Your knowledge, together with Your hiddenness,
and when the time You had decreed arrived,
You revealed the hidden counsel of Your will.
You knew that You would take One
as firstfruits from our race,
and by the sacrifice of His body would annul
the decree of judgement and death against us.
The exaltation of our despised race
was hidden in the hiddenness of Your knowledge,
and You revealed it after a time
to make ready the hidden things of Your love.
And if these things were revealed
to Your knowledge before they were,

You looked all the more upon our inclination,
that it does not prevail against the passions.
It was You who brought us into being
and honoured us with speech;
You turned us from wandering
to the way of the hidden things of Your Lordship.
Through the feebleness of our soul
the honour of the greatness of Your image was diminished,
and Your help raised us up
from lowliness to greatness.
Our wrongdoing changed You
from mercy to severity,
and Your love became mediator
and reconciled us with His majesty.
Yours are peace and mercy,
for You reconciled us with Yourself.
Our nature has no place of refuge
but Your grace, which upholds all things.
For our sake You were called
by names that are foreign to You,
and though they do not befit Your nature,
You took them on because of Your love.
Your nature was not diminished
by our weak names;
You magnified the lowliness of our race
when You called Yourself by our names.
The nature of Your Being has
no place where it may be confined or dwell,
yet because of Your love toward us
You came to us in Your nature.
Your hiddenness is not seen
by the sight of eyes of flesh,
yet in our body, as in a mirror,
we have seen the glory of Your majesty.
Your nature, the bound of all things,
neither descends nor ascends,
yet by the descent of Your will
You honoured us as one who had come down.
Joy does not gladden You,
nor does grief distress You,
yet You rejoiced at our return
and kissed us in the younger son.
Between two heirs You divided
the great treasure of Your wisdom,
and You did not reckon against us, with our weakness,
the squandering of Your possession.
To seek us who were lost
the will of Your Being went forth,
and when You found us, You made
Your joy the joy of the heavenly ones.
With a robe of glory You covered
the nakedness of our hateful iniquity,
and with the seal of faith
You confirmed Your covenant with Yourself.
We received the seed of Your word,
and it set in us the fruit of life;
do not let the Cunning One
sow his tares in our soul.
You called us Your sons
by love and not by nature;
let the name of sonship You gave us
be confirmed in us by deeds.
You invited us to the life above

and to kinship with the spiritual beings.
Let not the iniquity of our soul drown us
in the abyss of great torment.
The hope of the greatness of Your promises
gives our soul consolation,
for however strong iniquity may grow,
Your grace overcomes our sins.
With oaths that cannot be broken
You sealed Your promises;
by Your great nature You swore,
and You do not lie by Your nature.
On this [?] You have built
our petition before Your Lordship.
For it is a sign of repentance You seek,
and You do not exact the former debts.
In trust in Your grace
all who sin make supplication;
open the door to our supplication,
which knocks at the door of Your goodness.
Stand firm in Your gentle justice,
that You may not be embittered by our iniquity;
let the love of Your will reconcile You
to do as You have promised.
Let not Your knowledge search out
our sins with exactness,
and do not bring us into scrutiny
in that judgement which tries all.
For the word of our petition is short
and does not reach the height above;
stretch out to us the hand of Your grace,
and by it we shall ascend to forgiveness.
For heavy is the wing of our mind,
and it cannot fly toward Your love;
let it be lifted on the wings of Your mercies
from the depth up to Your majesty.
For dim is the light of our knowledge
for discerning what is fitting;
let the light of Your knowledge dawn
and show us by it the blemishes of our soul.
For iniquity has made us strangers
to the inheritance of sons;
let us be fed in the rank of dogs
from the crumbs of Your grace.
For we have not borne the burden of the day
in labouring in the vineyard of Your knowledge;
let not our thanksgiving be defrauded
of the wage that is given by grace.
However great our folly,
it is very small beside Your grace;
and though our wickedness has no measure,
beside Your goodness it is like a shadow.
Yours are grace and mercy,
and the wealth of Your love has no measure;
the multitude of Your works bears witness
that You fashioned them in mercy.
Your goodness cannot be measured,
nor is the treasure of Your mercies exhausted;
for though those who take from it take abundantly,
it remains as it is.

From it the spiritual beings grow rich,
and the hosts cry out in its service;
by the power of its word they are strengthened
and fulfil all its wishes.
By it the needs are supplied
of mortals clothed in a body,
and by its help they rise
above the sufferings of nature.
To every side it is distributed,
to heavenly beings and earthly,
and it feeds the rational and the dumb
and is not diminished from what it is.
Let not the door, then, be shut
upon the great wealth of Your grace,
nor let our petition be held back
before the door of our folly.
Do not, Lord, exact the deeds
of the wickedness of our nature's inclination;
for however much flesh may be justified,
even when it is justified, it is guilty.
Our whole fashioning is a clod of earth,
and our clay is kneaded with sufferings;
and the portion of the living that it acquired
it has dragged after its passions.
The waters of the sufferings soften
the dust of our mortal body,
and the flood of iniquity sweeps it away
and brings it down to humiliation.
The power of life within the soul
draws it toward good things,
but the inclination of its heart drags it down
to the great depth of evils.
It is cast into battles with itself
and struggles with its own thoughts,
and the bow of mortality
shoots arrows into its members.
It conquers and is conquered at all times,
and never ceases from the struggle,
and it is trampled all over
by the blows of sins.
The mortality of its nature
stands upright against its desire,
and the passion of its members
drags its mind along.
With these snares it is fettered
by the inclination hidden in its members,
which binds it with a chain
forged out of desires.
Let the key of the bidding of Your grace, Lord,
set its captivity free,
and let Your goodness wash from it
the filth that has stained its thoughts.
Let the prisoner whom his own will has bound
go out into the relief of Your mercies,
and be consoled in his grief
by the hope of the greatness of Your promises.
Let Your grace be a guide
to the stranger lost in ignorance,
and teach him the way by which to walk
to the dwellings of the kingdom on high.

Let Your mercies go out in search
of the lost one who has gone astray in his soul,
and let Your love turn him to the persuasion
of the knowledge of faith.
Let Your bidding quench the fever
of the sick man who lies in iniquity,
and with the sponge of Your sweetness
let the blemishes of his soul be wiped away.
If Your help does not overtake him,
he is nearer to death than to life,
and if Your medicine does not heal him,
there is no cure for his wound.
Human drugs have lost their savour,
and bodily remedies too,
and the pain of our iniquity day by day
grows, festers and gains strength.
Our pains have defied the skill
of earthly physicians,
and healers spiritual and bodily alike
have raised their finger from our iniquity [?].
Our nature has no physician
like the hope of Your mercies,
and none can heal its wound
like the knowledge of Your hiddenness.
It was not You who neglected our pain,
so that our folly grew so strong;
it was we who let our wound fester,
and gangrene took hold of our members.
It was not that the power of Your grace
had lost its savour for helping;
the sick did not wish to lay
the medicine of mercy on their sores.
Not on You does the blame [?] of iniquity fall,
that we have wallowed in sin;
ours is this sickness,
that we would not let the medicine of life refine us.
It is we who struck our own selves
with the wounds of the arrows of our mouth,
and many are the gashes in our body
from the stones our lips have thrown.
It is we who lost the knowledge
of the discernment of our nature,
and the word of our understanding lost its savour
in the business of frivolity.
Our weakness opened the door
of sight and hearing and speech,
and enemies came in and plundered the wealth
of the treasures of the words of the Spirit.
The sluggishness of our mind
did not rouse us from early morning,
and the day went by with its hours,
and we gained no profit from it.
Our stinginess did not allow us
to win mercy for Christ's sake,
and the lamp flickered and went out,
the light of the hidden places of our soul.
Sloth buried
the talent of the word of teaching,
and did not distribute to the needy
the silver of the word of Christ.

Through our wickedness we did not receive
forgiveness for our great iniquity;
for because we did not forgive our fellows,
Justice saw it and was grieved.
On the rock of our hardness of heart
the word of teaching fell,
and when the sun of the passions grew hot,
the seed of our soul was scorched and withered.
Beside the path of our mind
the word of life was sown,
and the Enemy, like a bird,
snatched it away from among our thoughts.
Among the thorns of our desires
the ear of life sprang up,
and the thicket of our sins grew up
and choked the spiritual seed.
The passions within us did not let us
walk on the narrow way,
and we went off with the many
on the broad way of destruction.
The heaviness of the sleep of sin
sank our light mind,
and our sleep was not roused
to receive the blessedness to which it was counselled.
These things have loosened the bond
of our peace with Your Lordship,
and after reconciliation had been made,
our wrongdoing provoked You.
Do not, Lord, let our corruption prevail,
and let us not be drowned in it by sin.
Draw us out of the depth of evils
as You drew Simon from the sea.
You named us sons and heirs
in the wealth of the greatness of Your promises;
let not Your promises prove false,
nor let us become strangers to Your wealth.
Let not the Envious One rejoice over us
when we forsake Your inheritance,
nor let him boast that by his strength
he plundered the wealth You gave us.
Let not the Rebel exalt himself
that with his weapon he overcame Your gift,
nor let him say that he took them captive
and no one stood up against him on behalf of their heirs [?].
Let not the unclean demons rejoice
at the humiliation of our evils;
let not the prince of the air say
that his authority still reigns.
Let Your love incline to be persuaded,
and let the Enemy be put to shame for ever.
For it is easy for Your grace
to heal the pains of our iniquity,
and it is simple for Your goodness
to wipe away the stains of our sins.
Do not hold it against us that we have sinned,
for You knew before we sinned
that flesh and blood cannot
be cleansed of sins.
And though our petition is not worthy
to have its requests granted,
have pity, because You have begotten us
as sons and heirs of Your majesty.
Let sweet love persuade You
and reconcile You to us, wicked as we are.

Let Your grace be mediator
and bring us a sign of peace.
We do not know how to pray
as is fitting for forgiveness;
let goodness be persuaded on our behalf
by supplication, as You have promised.
Let the Firstfruits from our race
prevail upon You, together with Your goodness,
for it was for the sake of our salvation
that You made Him equal to Your majesty.
Receive our supplication by His hand,
the Mediator You chose from among us,
and let there come back to us a voice
of reconciliation and forgiveness.
For our iniquity You humbled Him,
that by His passion He might lift up our humiliation;
and now that He has ascended and been exalted,
let Him take up our cause before You.
You chose Him for our salvation,
that our deadness might live in His life,
He who is equal with You in honour
and in the authority of Being.
Let the might of His authority make us worthy
to receive forgiveness freely,
for He became a temple for Your hiddenness,
a dwelling of His own will.
To receive forgiveness freely,
for He became a temple for Your hiddenness,
a dwelling of His own will.
Let the will of His love dwell in us
and cleanse us from sins.
By the eating of His body let the stain
of iniquity be wiped from our heart,
and let the drink of His blood calm
the turbulence of our mind.
He gave them for the sake of forgiveness
and as a pledge of good things;
let both be confirmed in us,
forgiveness and the pledge of life.
By His passion He abolished sin,
and by His death He slew death,
so that our slayers may not be roused
at the cry of the evils of our deeds.
By the hope of these promises
the aim of our petition is held fast;
let not our trust prove false,
nor the Evil One who watches us rejoice.
The faith of our mind
has given us two sureties:
hope and love, which do not forget
the affection of those near to them.
On strong love our confession rests,
and on hope our trust is set,
and faith is a surety
whose promises do not prove false.
Let mercy come to them
because of these promises,
lest the Destroyer take them captive
and make them liars.
Let not our good things be turned
into evils because we have sinned.
Stand firm in Your sweetness,
and turn us to the will of Your love.
The wealth of Your knowledge has no need

of our petition and our pleading,
for all good is Yours:
have pity and forgive, as You have promised.
The creature has nothing
that is not from the treasure of the Maker;
for even the pleading he begins to offer
he learned with help from Him.
Yours is the power of wisdom
that dwells in the soul of rational beings,
and from You they received the gift
of understanding and discernment.
Through Your treasure the wise grow rich,
and through Your help the righteous.
Your grace brings back those who stray
and increases hope for the lost.
There is no good that is not Yours,
and no gift that is not at Your bidding;
for even this, that we call upon You,
You called us to and taught us.
"Turn to Me, and I will turn to you,"
the Spirit declared through the prophets;
"I do not desire your death,
but the salvation of your lives."
The mortal has no meditation
but the desire of mortality,
and the fleshly man takes no pleasure
in spiritual thoughts.
The care of Your love draws him
from darkness to light,
and lifts from him the veil
that is spread over his mind.
In Your light he sees light,
and through Your knowledge he gains life;
from You he learns to interpret,
and with what is Yours he teaches others.
Whenever he meditates on You,
his wealth grows and abounds;
but if he forsakes Your care,
he falls into debt and his treasures are impoverished.
His wealth is bound up with Your goodness,
and his poverty with justice;
if he is justified, he triumphs,
but if he sins, he is overthrown.
And since both things are plain,
that it is by what is Yours he grows and fails,
the mortal is clothed in pride
and boasts of what is not his own.
However little good he has done,
his pride lifts him up to heaven,
and when he stumbles into sin,
it cuts off his hope altogether.
Whoever gains understanding
[?] is contemptible, more wretched than any man,
or lower even than his abasement [?];
for whatever wealth he gathered by his labours
he scattered through the weakness of his mind.
Through our folly our wealth was lost,
and through our weakness our treasures,
and we lessened the honour of our image
by the craving for the love of evils.
Our wealth is in heaven,

yet we set our thoughts on earthly things.
We were invited to the feast of joys,
yet our mind wanders in the dust.
All our labour is in sin,
and we busy ourselves with vanities,
and the hours of night and day
are not enough for our toil.
Our humanity labours unceasingly
in a field [?] of fruits,
and though the harvests cheat it,
it does not cease from its labour.
So too the body and the movements of the soul
are under the hard yoke of sin;
this is the labour of them both,
and they do not perceive how crushed they are.
There is no idle member
that is not diligent for the desires,
nor any slow movement
that does not run after the passions.
So, then, the whole man
is at war with himself at every moment;
he is wholly divided against himself
and shoots arrows at his own person.
The heart is divided against the members,
and the members against the mind,
and they falsely hide
their deeds from one another.
Without order, at every moment,
the members and the movements of the soul run on,
racing in a stadium
without reward or crown.
The gaze of our eyes is frivolous,
and the hearing of our ears is false,
for the speech of our lips is lying,
and our words are not true.
With a double heart
the judge speaks with his neighbours,
and the inward parts do not agree
with outward deeds.
Our tongue offers peace,
while guile lurks in our mind;
kisses are on the tips of our lips,
and a sword is hidden in our thoughts.
False report finds its way in
and sends out a messenger of wrath;
it condemns the innocent
and acquits the guilty.
Painted eyes are sent out
in pursuit of the prey of lewdness,
and the greedy body is fed
by defrauding its fellows.
By the [?] of the weak eye
the inclination is set like a bird,
and instead of a voice, with a single sign
the weak inclination is stirred up.
The inclination of lewdness lies in wait
behind the panels of the doors,
and exchanges messages by signs,
by whose snares the prey is caught.

O eye, the lamp of light, / the lamp of the outward senses,
which has become the cause of stumbling / for thoughts and for limbs!
The heart signals to the tongue / that it should speak falsely,
and though the thing does not exist / it renders it as if it did.
On the harp of the mouth the heart / strikes with the finger of the tongue,
yet the sound of the strings does not accord / with the signal of the craftsman's finger.
He plays on it as on a flute / sweet melodies,
and the hearing is pleased at first, / but the end of the word is evil.
The mouth too, the [?] vessel / that pours out a drink of speech,
whose drink has turned from sweetness / and become the bitterness of evils.
O advocate of fraud / who turned and became a defrauder,
and sold the freedom of his authority / into the slavery of fraud!
O tongue, the messenger / trusted by two kings,
which has cast strife among the limbs / and divided them against the soul!
O speaking harp / whose melodies have fallen into confusion!
O contriver of cunning, / who schemed and forgot what is fitting!
The soul is at odds with the body, / and the body does not agree with the soul;
for in the soul there is one thought, / and the mouth expresses the opposite.
The laxity of our will has trampled / on nature and on the law,
and nature and Scripture have become / superfluous to our insolence.
The course of nature has ceased, / and the voices of Scripture,
and nature does not run in its order, / nor in the commandments of Scripture.
In getting there is fraud, / and in marriage corruption;
in eating gluttony, / and in drinking drunkenness;
in looking lewdness, / and in hearing falsehood.
Slander is on the lips, / and death is set on the tip of the tongue.
There is rivalry in love of money / and strife in amassing wealth,
as each vies with his fellow / over who will defraud the more.
All mortals go down / into the contest of love of glory,
and when they think they have won and risen, / glory runs off and condemns them.

There is no victory for their contest, / nor any reward for their labors,
for they do not look toward the goal / of the spectacle of the contest.
Fasting is wronged by vainglory, / and prayer by praise;
the working of alms has ceased, / and there are no fruits of the forgiveness of iniquity.
The body is sick with fleshly lust, / and the soul with love of praise;
the eye of the mind is blind / and is not examined by truth.
The outward senses are weak, / and the inner movements are diseased,
and the course of both has ceased / from the way of uprightness.
In the harsh fever of iniquity / limbs and thoughts lie prostrate,
and soul and body are sunk / under the weight of the love of evils.
O man full of sufferings, / who will rescue you from sufferings?
Seek and implore, if you can, / that mercy may come to your help.
If mercy does not heal you, / there is no healing for your fracture,
and if grace does not stand by you, / your hope of uprightness is cut off.
O Good One, who fashioned our nature / and made it in his image and likeness,
redeem your image, the work of your hands, / that what you fashioned may not be corrupted.
For the sake of the name of your precious image, / look on us with favor because of your image.
You have called us children; let us not be / strangers to your household.
Our nature is too small for this / and is not worthy of the name of your image.
In you let our redemption be completed / like our first fashioning.
For your slightest signal, renewal / was as easy as fashioning,
and your will is not hindered / by the evil of our corruption.
In mercy and love you fashioned us, / without petition or persuasion;
now too, in mercy and love, / renew and revive, have pity and forgive.
For our petition is not worthy / to win forgiveness by persuasion.
Let mercy and love prevail / in our renewal, as is their custom.
No petition is needed / by a Giver who is never impoverished,
nor does persuasion avail with him / who knows all things beforehand.
He had heard the voice of our petition / before ever it came to be,
and the persuasion had dawned before his knowledge / before ever it was composed.
He was looking on us continually / and examining us at all times,
and all that is ours, and all things, were revealed / to the hiddenness of his divinity.

It is not petition that persuades / the power whose wisdoms are such as these.
He wished to show us / that it is the will that sins and repents.
By petition he teaches us / that it is not by compulsion that he makes us sin:
just as we choose to pray, / so it was easy for us not to sin.
That same inclination which did wickedly and sinned / is the one that discerned and was justified,
and to it belong the guilt / and the merit of the soul's repentance.
This is the teaching which the Creator / [?] imparts to us through petition:
that our will should not be blamed / in our fashioning, as though it were evil.
And since the Good One knows our nature, / that both are his,
he does not neglect to set us right, / because of his love toward us.
To our inclination he gave the victory / for the sake of the will of our freedom,
and since our inclination is freeborn, / he teaches us how we may prevail.
You, my Lord, have placed in our nature / the knowledge to consider these things;
you have taught us how / our inclination holds sway over our soul.
You have made us know as one who knows, / and made us wise as one who is gracious.
Accept, then, our petition, / on which the image of your wisdoms is imprinted.
To you we give of your own: / receive from our hands your gift.
Take what is yours and give us what is yours, / for it befits you to give of your own.
In petition toward your hidden greatness / the word of my weakness has looked up,
and it has longed to become worthy / of a small crumb of your gift.
Through the abundance of your love I have lifted / the gaze of my poor mind,
and I have resolved to ask, if I may, / to receive forgiveness freely.
Trusting [?] in your grace, / my lack of learning has grown bold.
Show me the way by which I may go / to the dwellings of perfection.
Stretch out a hand to the one who is sunk / and longs to come up out of his iniquity.
By the power of your help let the broken one be strengthened / who has begun to falter.
The longing of love awakens me, / like a sleeper from sleep.
In the morning of your signal let there be driven / the sleep of iniquity from my mind.
Before the light of your knowledge / the movements of my thoughts swim.
Uncover the veil of darkness / that is spread over my mind.
O spiritual law, / make straight for me the goal of victory.

Let my movements, together with my words, / come alive toward truth, the goal of life.
At the spring of the word of instruction / I sought to quench the thirst of my mind.
With the drink of the Spirit let there be watered / the dryness of my thoughts.
With the silver of your word I wish / to trade, if I am able.
At the eleventh hour I hire myself out, / that I too may receive a denarius.
Since I have not borne the burden of the day, / let the favor of your grace give me rest.
Since I have not toiled in deeds, / let me be counted worthy of the wage through words.
By the labor of words I wish / to be called among the workers in your service.
Hear my words, though they are despised, / that I may be a laborer in your vineyard.
I have sought to gather the invited / to the spiritual wedding feast.
Let mercy cover my limbs / that are stripped of modesty.
Let your love go out with my words / after the lost sheep,
and let them be gathered from every quarter / into the fitting fold of your mercies.
Help by my hands, as you are accustomed / to help by the hand of sinners,
and let me become a source of profit / to myself and to the lowly like me.
The hunter calls toward death / and snares his companions for destruction;
at the reading of my words let there live / the dead who died in their sins.
At the sound of my words let them awaken, / the sleepers who sank in sin,
and let them shake off the weight of their debts / at the summons of the second dawn.
Let your own will persuade you on my behalf, / for I am not able to persuade you.
Let your love wipe out my debts, / that I may hear the voice at the door [?].
Let the dew of your mercies come to us / and the drops of righteousness,
and let the shoot of repentance blossom / among the roots of our mind.
Let spiritual seed sprout / in our soul, which is fallow ground,
and let our heart, which yields thistles, / bear the fruits of joy.
Let the dull hearing of our mind / be watered by the voice of your commandments,
and let our ear become a road / for the voice that brings in comfort.

Through the lewd gaze / the lamp of our mind has grown dark.
Let your truth be a mirror, / and let the ugliness of our soul be polished away in it.
The mouth that has become a ferry / and a bridge for lewd words,
let the voice of your will sing in it / thanksgiving without division.
Let the temple of our body be sanctified / and the movements of our soul be cleansed,
and let hope and love dwell in us / in the perfection of faith.
Let judgment speak to our humanity, / body and soul together,
and by the decree of upright judgment / let the inclination that does wrong be condemned.
Let our discernment justify it, / if victory is won,
and let it be accused as guilty / if it slackens its striving in the contest.
Let the voice of the comforter come to us, / which strengthens the camp of our body,
and let our limbs gain strength / in the struggle against sufferings.
For the armor of our mind is weak / before the assaults of our [?].
When it is armed with faith, / patience accepts afflictions.
By the power of your help let there be condemned / the violent and lustful inclination,
which wars against our soul / with the weapon of our will's freedom.
Turn them back, Lord, to the fold of life, / for your grace seeks the lost;
and let the Watchers, who minister to your will, / look [?] upon our restoration within it.
Let your sweet voice call out: / "Return, you repentant children!
Strip off the iniquity that made you hateful / and put on the garment of uprightness."
Our iniquity stripped off our modesty / and lessened the name of our honor;
let it be covered with the garment of your mercies, / and let our lowliness grow great in your name.
Sin killed our nature / and veiled the face of our freedom;
by the signal of your power let it be raised / from iniquity, the grave of both.
Through our sins we sold ourselves / into the slavery of mortality;
by the silver of your love let us be freed / from the bondage of sin.
Our ugliness has made ugly the beauty / and seemliness of height and depth,
and through our evils heaven and earth / have dried up and lost their fruits.
Through the harshness of our iniquity / the elements have changed into constraint [?].
Because our mouth dried up from praise, / the seed dried up together with the fruits.
Because our mind became barren / of the fruits of righteousness,
the earth has grown gloomy over its fruits / and bears no sustenance for us.
Because we exchanged truth for falsehood / and do not abide in truth,
see, the changes of summer and winter / run out of their order.

Winter is gloomy out of order, / and summer beyond what is fitting,
as they chastise our wickedness / with cold and heat out of order.
Hunger and thirst lash / the insolence of our mind,
and our sunken heart does not feel / the lash that has swallowed our mind.
Our body is bound at all times / in the chain of sufferings and pains,
and greedy death hastily / leads us to the house of the dead.
The rod of authority is raised / and tosses us about in distress,
as it greedily demands of us / poll tax and new levies.
Kings issue new decrees, / and rulers are without pity,
and with the amassing of wealth / iniquity grows great and strong.
Were it not for the abundance of your love / and the wealth of your many mercies,
the world would long since have been swept away / in the flood of our harsh iniquity.
Your love overcomes at all times / the multitude of our evils,
and our lewdness is covered / with the fitting garment of your help.
To you, Lord, it is fitting to bear / the burden of our evil inclination,
for the treasure of your mercies is never exhausted / and your goodness cannot be measured.
You are the strong place of refuge / and the helper of our nature,
and there was no time when our race was guilty / that your help did not justify us.
In every generation, with their courses, / your sweet grace runs on,
and it grows according to the measures / of youth and of old age.
Your goodness holds fast with us / and does not keep away from wherever we are,
as it pursues our iniquity / so that it may not return and dwell with us.
Who is there for us like you, / gracious and loving our race?
Who bears our afflictions / as your sweet love does?
From whom can our need / be filled as from your treasury?
Though we did not repay you first, / your gift abounds in mercies.
Toward the goal of your love for us / the word of our petition looks,
for how eager you are to accept / persuasion on behalf of sinners,
who sleep and are heedless as they petition

for the needs of their lives.
And your grace cries out like thunder: / "Rise, you lowly ones, and grow rich freely!"
It is not our will that seizes for us / the boldness to ask for forgiveness;
you drew us on to offer / even words in place of labors.
Let the words of our mouth / be spoken to you according to your will,
and those that are stripped of deeds, / let your help clothe them.
Who can perceive / the slips of mortal nature?
And who is able to be justified / from the hidden faults that are not revealed?
You have placed understanding in us, / that we may grow wise about our hidden things.
You teach us how / we may compound a remedy for our sickness.
Help our weakness, / which has nothing apart from your help.
Do not neglect to help us, / lest we perish forever.
Our soul has been tried in the struggles / of labors for uprightness,
and in every generation that held us / our limbs have been swallowed up in wounds.
And if there were in our nature / limbs that were not corrupted,
it was your help that stood before them, / and they were not swallowed up by the arrows of the evil one.
To you, the Good, / the good and the wicked are alike in debt:
for if they are justified, it is your doing, / and if they sin, they find pity in you.
Yours it is to forgive iniquity / and to bring righteousness to completion.
By your power let the righteous run, / and sinners by your help.
Do not cut off our brokenness / for the slips of ignorance,
since our inclination easily leads us to sin: / it sins and does not feel it when it sins.
Do not reckon, along with our weakness, / the wrong of transgressing your commandments.
For if you exact recompense, / no man can avoid sinning, / and no mortal can be justified.
For he was fashioned from dust, / and dust loves its own.
In his dust the creature of dust thinks, / and to his dust he returns every day.
His life dissolves like vapor / and does not endure to completion.
Mortality chastens him, / lest he wear himself out over earthly things,
and sufferings and pains chastise him, / yet his fever is pleasant to him.
Let your grace pursue the sicknesses / of our nature, which loves pains,
and let its insipidity be seasoned / with the sweet taste of your commandments.

Let your signal open the door / that its weakness shut in its face,
and let it loosen from it the chain / that iniquity cast upon its neck.
Let your sweet voice awaken / the sleeper sunk in sin,
and let him sing, with the spiritual beings, / praise to the One who gives life to sinners.
On Human Nature
The sixteenth memra, which is recited during fasts and at times of supplication. Response: Our Lord, in your mercy turn to your servants; accept our prayer and grant our requests.

O God, hear our petition, for you are one who hears,
and in your mercies answer the request of our soul, by which you are entreated.
You who abound in grace, show your love, as is your custom,
so that the hater of humankind may not mock the work of your hands.
You who are richer than all, open the house of your treasure to our need,
so that we may not grow poor and our soul hire itself out to the deceiver.
Mighty One of the ages, uphold your handiwork with the strength of your power,
for see, it is shaken by the harshness of sufferings and demons.
Being by whose being heaven and earth are filled,
fulfil your will, and let your holy name be hallowed in us.
You whose nature is hidden from spiritual beings and from bodily ones,
reveal your power in us and show the riches of your kindness.
You who set all things in order, who created creation out of nothing,
spare your work, that it may not be destroyed because of our iniquity.
You who freely feed and sustain in your goodness both the speaking and the dumb,
stretch out your right hand and satisfy our soul from your gift.
You who lack nothing, from whose fullness your works are filled,

open to our plea the door of your will that is shut in our faces.
You who are perfect in your being, whose eternity has no beginning,
bring to completion in deed the beginning of your words toward our race.
You who painted the world with the pigment of your love, which never fades,
wipe the filth of ignorance from our images.
You who compose bodies and breathe a soul into the limbs,
strengthen our nature, that it may not grow slack before the passions.
You who honour humankind above all things for the sake of your love,
spare the image of your honour, that it may not be disgraced.
By the name of your being, which is not composite, you named our composite nature;
let not your precious name lose its savour through our insipidity.
In us you showed your great love toward your creatures;
do not show in us a sign of wrath toward the work of your hands.
In us you set the seal on the great name of your craftsmanship,
and in our composition you joined together the earthly and the heavenly.
In us you compounded height and depth as one body:
the mute in our body, the speaking in our soul — a great wonder!
Do not, my Lord, dissolve this composition that your love has compounded,
and let not the great spectacle that your command bound together come loose.
On this composition my speech, weak in strength, fixed its gaze,
and sought to travel along the way of the words that are bound up in it.
At this bond my mind stood still, lacking understanding,
and marvelled greatly at the craftsmanship of the command that bound it.
In this handiwork my thoughts wandered and my running fell short,
and words made themselves ready to build a narrative before the hearers.
With this hope my speech set out in pursuit of words,
that I might go and bring the hope of your name to the work of your hands.
With this intent I went down into the inner chambers of the Scriptures,
to meditate on humankind in the great story of your creating.
In this form I painted words with the reed of my tongue,
that everyone might gaze on the beautiful image of your craftsmanship.
I beheld the image of your handiwork, so wisely wrought,

and I longed to draw out the loveliness of its beauty before the beholders.
In the fashioning of our image I saw that all creation is bound up,
and I called humankind to come and see everything in our nature.
Nature drew me on to see the natures that are bound up in it,
how, and how far, a feeble being is able to take in the whole.
In this very nature of ours I saw the wisdom of your Godhead,
and I reflected that there is hope for man, however much he sins.
I saw the name of your being dwelling in him as in a temple,
and wonder seized me: how can the lowly contain the Hidden One?
He is very lowly, and you honoured him beyond all measure;
who would not marvel that you chose his lowliness far above all?
And if your love chose him out of all and called him by its own name,
then let it stand firm that you will not reject the choice you have made.
If your Lordship made him lord over all that exists,
what would not bow its neck to the yoke of toil for his livelihood?
If your knowledge called him and brought him near to the lofty rank,
who would not confess that his rank is secure, and the name of his authority?
If through his manifestation you revealed your hiddenness to your servants,
who would not gather in his gaze from all else toward his composition?
If in him you laid open the great mystery of the Son and the Spirit,
who would not draw near to the wisdom hidden in his name?
If in him you showed your kindness to Watchers and to human beings,
who would not take refuge in his body, which pleads on his behalf?
If the Word, the Child who is from you, dwelt in him in love,
who would not call him the one who holds the bounds of height and depth?
If in him you fulfilled your providence on behalf of all,
who would not hold fast to his care, which never ceases?
If through him you are to judge the earth at the end of the ages,
who would not fear the testing that takes place at his hands?
And if through him you give blessings to the good and punishments to the wicked,
who would not entreat you to be an advocate for his sins?
And if he is the one who rules over this world and over the world to come,

who would not believe that he stands second to the Godhead?
I saw that our lowly nature was raised to these ranks,
and my mind urged me to go down in words to its lowliness.
The greatness of its rank compelled me to venture beyond due order,
and to set out on the way of the Great One [?] with my words.
To your hiddenness, which is in his manifestation, I wish to draw near;
stretch out your hand to me as to Simon, that I may draw near and plead.
Into the sea of words on behalf of our life my thoughts have gone down;
let your command draw me up, so that I may not sink unfittingly.
I have drawn near to plead for my needs and those of my fellows;
strengthen my movements, that they may not grow slack until they are heard.
At the door of your mercies my will is knocking, longing for our life;
open to us, that we may enter and receive alms like the poor.
Poor and needy beyond all is our lowly race;
support its lowliness with a small crumb of your gift.
It is very weak at gathering for itself the food of the season,
and cannot till the earth by its own strength without your strength.
Great fear fills his labour, however hard he labours,
and there is no confidence about his food, however plentiful it may be.
Pains and griefs attend his toil in summer and in winter,
and every kind of harm is constant to him, to him and to what is his.
Great is his labour and small the wage returned to him;
great is his weariness, and lowly and meagre the food of his life.
He sows much and reaps little out of much;
he is driven about and worn down, and before he can enjoy it, death swallows him.
In fear he sows, and in dread he gathers the fruits,
and his heart is not confident that he will rejoice in his labour and his harvest.
He casts his bread on the face of the field so that it may come back to him,
and he is afraid and anxious lest it perish and his life come to an end.
He tills the ground and worries lest blight come upon the fruits;
he journeys on the road, and death sits waiting for him.

Like a woman in labour he waits for the fruits as for a child,
and the pangs of death strike his understanding every hour.
A great war is set in array at all times against his nature,
and if he sleeps and slumbers, the passions come in and plunder his freedom.
The feeble one is cast into two misfortunes, each worse than the other:
in the pains of his body and in the food of his life — grievous punishments.
He is scourged as with whips by the hand of his own nature,
and there is no place in him not filled with the fullness of pains.
He suffers and is distressed by his pains and by his labours,
and there is no time when he does not groan bitterly.
If the sun is hot, his mind grows hot over his seed;
if the rain is withheld, his thoughts wither with his plants.
If heat prevails, thirst kills him;
if cold increases, he perishes from nakedness.
If he becomes poor, he grumbles without ceasing and breeds discontent;
if he grows rich, pride and arrogance clothe him.
If he becomes righteous, he mocks and laughs at sinners;
if he is a sinner, he despairs and decides there is no more hope.
If he grows wise, he forgets the nature of his lowly clay;
if he boasts, he becomes like a beast without understanding.
In much and in little his pains multiply and his iniquity grows,
and what is he to do, and where is he to flee, despised in his life?
Caught between too much and too little, he is in want altogether;
how can he keep his life free from harm?
It is very hard for human beings to live well,
and the course of righteousness is not easy for bodily creatures.
A body is a body, however much it may desire spiritual things;
even its desire is not its own, but another's.
Another dwells in him, in the temple of corruptible clay,

and in his life he flickers for a little while until he decays.
He is wholly corruption, however much a portion of life there is in him;
and even this portion has too little life to keep him alive.
And if the life that is in him falls short of life,
how can he live amid a corruptible life?
Let your mercies come, my Lord, to the help of our lowly race,
for see, it has grown weak and lost the strength of its life in the contest of pains.
Stretch out your hand to the wrestler whose mind has grown slack,
for see, he has raised his finger and cannot hold out openly in the arena.
Cry out and hearten the soldier who is wasting away,
for see, the arms of his hands have grown too slack to strike the mark.
Command the rational natures to help him,
for see, his hand has failed to grasp the bow of truth.
Call the heavenly legions to support him,
lest he fall and become a laughing-stock to his adversary.
Write and send him the decree of your name, which is greater than all,
and see, he will be strengthened to bear his pains in the hope of your name.
Set your hand to the documents of the salvation of his life,
and see, pains and demons will be terrified to look at him.
Rebuke the ranks of the soldiers who fight against him,
and see, they will be thrown into confusion by the command of the name of your being.
Send one Watcher, as in the days of the Assyrian,
and see, the armies of the Evil One that surround him will be scattered.
Send your command, as you sent Isaiah to Hezekiah,
and instead of figs let it lay mercy on his wounds.
Let us too hear that voice that came to Hezekiah:
'In place of life, see, I add forgiveness of iniquity.'
Yes, my Lord, turn our faces toward the health of good things,
that we may not be despised among the companions of our shameful deeds.
Come forth at our petition, as befits the craftsmanship your love composed,
and let us enter and pasture in the fold of spiritual life.
Make your face shine, and in your mercies seek out our lostness,
that the beauty of our clay, which is stamped with your name, may not be spoiled.
Rejoice at our plea as at the younger son,
and proclaim with us the life of the hope with which we are sealed.

With the deceiver we laboured for nothing and lost our wage,
and among the ruins of desires we have lived wickedly.
We sinned and provoked you — far be it that you were provoked or are provoked! —
and we are not worthy that our souls should be called sons of your name.
Grant us to be like hired servants in the service of your house,
and to receive alms like the poor from your table.
And if it be possible, complete in deed the power of your craftsmanship,
and bring into the open the mystery you composed for our sake.
Say to us too: 'From death I have now brought you to life,
and from the ruin of ignorance I have turned you back to me.'
Command your grace to cover our shame with a robe of glory,
and to put on our hand the pledge of life like a signet ring.
Let your command be appeased and prepare before us the sacrifice of your Son,
and by its eating let it drive the bitterness of death from our limbs.
And if anyone begrudges our salvation and our service,
let your love sweeten the bitterness of his nature with the life of life.
Call the angels and gladden them at our return,
so that those who were grieved that we sinned may now confess that we are justified.
Give pleasure to those who were angry because of our iniquity,
and turn them back to the ministry of the needs of our life.
Let them stir the air by the power that comes from you, as they are wont,
and make it firm, that it may carry the waters upon its back.
Let them put into its mouth bridles of silence and of gentleness,
that it may not rage through its changes beyond due order.
Let them be like charioteers upon its back,
and drive it over the face of the earth at the full speed of its course.
Let them watch its running like spectators in a stadium,
and weave for your name a crown of thanksgiving in which we may rejoice.
Yes, my Lord, accept the composition of our words, though they be lowly,
and grant a reward to the meditation of our soul, though it be insipid.
Yes, my Lord, make the words of our mouth worthy of an answering word,
and let us hear from you: 'For sinners who repent there is hope.'
Yes, my Lord, gladden the air, which is sad because of our iniquity,

and place in its mouth a crown of raindrops, that it may be reconciled to us.
Yes, my Lord, let the voices of our mouth be keys to your treasury,
that we may open it and take forgiveness of debts and food for the season.
Do not, my Lord, disregard the petition of our poverty,
lest our hope in you grow slack in despair.
Do not, my Lord, turn your face from us in the time of wrath,
lest the proud demons mock, as is their custom.
Do not, my Lord, cast us off from your help as you do the wicked,
