lest the evil ones exalt themselves over our lowliness as before.
Do not, my Lord, be unmerciful, for you are merciful —
God forbid, my Lord! Not that you are not; I have spoken only according to our need.
Do not, my Lord, let the name of your greatness be lessened because of our iniquity —
yet it is not lessened, even if thousands upon thousands do wickedly.
Do not, my Lord, be poor in help and needy in treasure —
ah, what a falsehood I have spoken about your being!
Do not, my Lord, be like a stranger in your own creation,
nor like a traveller who turns aside to lodge in what is not his.
Do not, my Lord, be like a human being, for you are God,
nor like a man who cannot save, for you are the Saviour.
And if our debts are greater than the debts of all generations,
you, have pity for the sake of your precious name, by which we are called.
If our hateful deeds have darkened the face of the clear air,
do not show the face of anger, which does not befit you.
If our wickedness has withheld good things from the mouth of the wicked,
do not change the name of your goodness, which never changes.
You are wholly good and wholly just, and you hate iniquity,
and neither your goodness nor your justice can be measured.
No one knows how to call you by a name befitting your name,
for all names are small beside the greatness of your glory.
Should we call you Good? The voice of your justice thunders on the earth.
Should we call you Just instead? Heaven and earth are full of your mercies.

Should we call you Hidden? Your deeds are revealed to the eyes of all creatures.
Should we call you Revealed? There is none among the things made that can see you.
Should we call you One who hears? You heard our voice before we called you,
and before we pleaded, your love had already forgiven us and our iniquity.
We know neither how to pray nor how to praise,
and we are afraid to speak words that do not befit you.
How shall we pray to the One who lacks nothing, who is wholly perfect,
and how shall we praise him who abides in his glory for ever?
If by being praised he grows greater, then it is by praise that he grows;
and if he grows greater by glory from us, then through us he becomes perfect.
Is his greatness insulted by the slighting of his praise?
If he is hallowed by our mouth, does he add to his praise?
If he is angered, then the insult of the wrongdoer had been hidden from him;
and if he is reconciled, then we have shown him the path of reconciliation.
And if, by repenting, he considers something after a time,
then the times have compelled him to learn something he did not know.
And if he does not know this, which the mouth dares to say,
what more has he gained in knowledge about his creatures?
No, you earthly ones, do not think earthly thoughts!
In the Being there is nothing that is less than Being.
Being entire — its very name is proof of its eternity,
and as it is, so its knowledge also is with it.
Before all things it is, and it is just as it is,
and nothing that is or that shall be escapes it.
Thus it is fitting for the made to think about the Maker,
and thus the one who speaks is bound to repay the Giver of speech.
A debt of love we owe to our Creator;
let us take care, then, to repay a little out of much.
It is not repayment he seeks from us, as one in need;
he contrives occasions so that we [?] may be enriched from his treasures.
The treasure of life that never fails is gathered in his nature,
and he greatly desires to give of it to the children of his house.

He called our nature children of the inheritance of his Son's love;
therefore he chastises us and makes us wise in love.
Let us then bear the kinds of discipline that come from his discipline,
and let us not loathe the punishments of hunger and of sickness.
If the name of sons is truly upon our mind,
then it stands firm that our discipline too is for our profit.
Without complaint let us receive the punishments from our Maker,
and without murmuring let us understand the misfortune of changing times.
This alone let us ask of him in the time of punishments:
'Do not, my Lord, rebuke us in harsh wrath according to our deeds.'
Like the son of Jesse let us plead loudly for our iniquity,
and by way of his words come to the meeting-place of repentance.
Yes, my Lord, make us worthy of that voice that came to David,
and let us turn back, as he did, to the rank of forgiveness of iniquity.
Yes, my Lord, take away the folly of your servants as you did your servant's,
and let them hear the voice of forgiveness that the just man heard.
David was just, yet he coveted wickedly and did wickedly,
and he confessed that he had sinned, and from his heart wiped out the name of wickedness.
And if confession wiped out the name of the wicked and wrote them down as good,
then hope is established for the wicked to become good.
Good One, who forgave adultery and murder at a word of the mouth,
forgive the offences of our shameful deeds as you forgave.
You are the one who forgave that lawless offence;
you, now too, forgive our sins, which are beyond all order.
You are the one who revoked the sentence you had passed on murderers;
now too withhold the punishments you have prepared for our wrongdoing.
You are the one who mixed mercy with wrath in all generations
and did not let the enemies of our people mock us.
You are the one who stirred up the greatness of your love toward the righteous
and made them worthy to plead with you, though you are in no need.
In your love you pardoned the sins of our people from the beginning,
and gave this as the reward of your kindness to the will of the just.
For the sake of the just you forgave the offences of earlier generations,

and see, it was forgiven before you, so that they might plead with your kindness.
You stirred up zeal in human beings to plead with you,
so that, when they plead with you, they might see that they can obtain pardon for iniquity.
Moses prayed, and you pardoned the iniquity of the people who worshipped the calf,
and you said to him: 'See, I forgive, as you have pleaded.'
Joshua prayed, and you held back the course of the sun and the moon,
and placed the halting of their courses in the charge of Joshua's word.
Samuel prayed, and your command answered him with the voice of thunder,
and at his word you turned back the rain that had come out of season.
David prayed when he saw the Watcher who was destroying the people,
and the spiritual being drew back at his petition, being held back by you.
Elijah called on you, and you made the winds strong and they carried rain,
and you showed [?] the people that the word of the just man could bind and loose.
Elisha called on you, and by his hands you brought the dead back to life,
and counted to his prophecy a victory over the mouth of death.
Hezekiah called on you, and you laid waste the thousands of the Assyrians,
and because he believed rightly, he conquered by the sword of the Watcher.
Daniel too, by the power of your help, revealed hidden things,
and for his will the Babylonians wove crowns of praise.
In all generations the just prayed and you answered them;
in our generation, which is bare of the just, you plead with yourself.
Greater than all the just is the pleading of your kindness,
and the treasure of your mercies cannot be compared with creatures.
Your love drew the will of the just to plead with you;
and since there are no just, let your will take care of us without the just.
Yours is the pleading, and the words of those who plead;
why lay the burden on others? Your goodness toward the children of your house is your own.
Let all goodness be yours, as indeed it is,
and care for us as you cared at the beginning of the ages.
Who persuaded you to create creation when it did not exist,
and who counselled you to bind the world together in the composition of humankind?
Who was your counsellor, that you should call humankind your image,
and who showed you how to complete your work in our composition?
And if in our coming into being, and in that of all things, you sought no help,
why do you seek help over our iniquity, a contemptible gnat?

Our iniquity is a gnat beside the greatness of your Godhead,
and it is full of absurdity if it is compared with the sea of your mercies.
The sea is great; your grace is great, and greater than the sea,
and height and depth are very small beside its greatness.
That your grace is great, heaven and earth cry out,
for when they did not exist, you spoke, and they came to be out of nothing.
Out of nothing you created everything for our sake;
how then can you disregard us in the time of wrath?
And that you are exceedingly good and cannot be measured by those who speak:
your love clothed us, raised us up and set us in the rank of your name.
By the name of your being you called our name, with a borrowed name;
and now let it remain in its rank through these very deeds.
To the lofty rank that is with your being our [?] has ascended;
let it not be brought down from its height because of our iniquity.
At your right hand our body sits, clothed in glory;
let not its glory be disgraced by the shame of our rebellion.
Let not the rational natures despise it for its weakness,
for you honoured it with the great name of your Godhead.
Do not, my Lord, give the proud demons cause to boast,
saying, 'See, they were made kings, and their hands have lost their power.'
Do not, my Lord, let the enemies of our people rejoice, as is their custom:
'Where is he who ascended to the lofty rank of the immortals?'
Already they have scoffed and mocked at the name with which we are honoured;
silence them, that they may not exalt themselves against your lordship.
Through us they wish to mock your great name,
and so they think to lift themselves up above your greatness.
The enemies who have become enemies of your name hate our image,
and because they cannot overcome you, they insult you through us.
Do not, my Lord, let the deceivers reach the height of their desire,
and let not the building of falsehood in which they boast be completed.
Rebuke it at the height of their thoughts, and let it fall to the ground,
and raise the head of our lowliness to the rank of your name.

Deliver our nature from the hands of the destroyers,
for see, it is worn down [?] and spent in the hard war against their ranks.
Spread your hand over our camp, which is poor in strength,
for see, it has dwindled in the number of those who love the truth.
Let your face shine on our despised dwelling, full of troubles,
for see, the fair light of righteousness has faded from it.
Set your command as steward over our slackness,
for see, it has squandered the treasure it received from your gift.
Call the spiritual beings and command them to help us,
for see, demons and sufferings have broken into our inner rooms [?] and plundered our treasures.
Send the Watchers to wake us from our slumber,
for see, we have sunk into our vile deeds as into sleep.
Send angels to bring peace to our turmoil,
for see, all our ranks are thrown into wars of discord.
And if the hosts on high cannot wake us,
let the Son of our race plead, and reconcile us with your majesty.
He is able to help us in our turmoil in the contest of toils,
since he is your only Son and also our mediator.
He knows how to plead lovingly for the guilty,
since he took upon himself the trial of the sufferings of mortality.
For he was tested in all things, having taken on the nature of mortals,
and all the more he knows how to help those who are tested.
For the sake of peace you chose [?] him out of all to reconcile all;
fulfill in deed the choosing of his name, for the sake of our peace.
Now is the time for him to show in us the greatness of his rank,
just as he showed it at the time when our guilt grew strong.
If, while we were enemies of your name, you reconciled us through him,
how much more will our discord be brought to peace by his mediation!
If by his hand you redeemed us from death and from the Accuser,
how much more will you rescue us from vile, testing quarrels [?]!
If by his cross he uprooted paganism and Judaism,
how easy it is for him to hold back the sufferings that oppress us!
If he will carry out the judgment of all at the end of the ages,
how much more is he able, before the end, to ease the harshness of the scourges!
If he has authority over the treasury of your Godhead,

then he has authority to give freely to the children of his race.
Grant this good thing to our weakness, as you promised,
and give us victory through the Son of our race, who holds your treasury.
A Homily on a Certain Person

Again, another homily by Mar Narsai: on a certain person.
Responsory: The priest asks mercy for the world, which has taken refuge in [his] bones.
My brothers.

Mortals heard the mighty voice that proclaims life,
and they hated the world and its passing desires.
The teaching of life fell on the ears of the children of earth,
and they left the earth and looked to heaven, toward spiritual things.
They heard the voice that calls people to the house of God,
and they put away [?] from themselves the weight of the world and looked to the height.
The teaching of the Son of God dawned in their minds,
and with discernment they quickened their running on the road on high.
The discerning heard that there is a world that does not perish,
and they despised this temporal world whose course comes to an end.
The just wisely exchanged one world for another:
this one that passes away for the one that endures and does not perish.
The wise hated this brief life, full of harms,
and loved the world full of blessings that does not change.
The saints, with discernment, conceived a great desire,
and exchanged the earth for the great dwelling of heaven.
O the reward of the house of God, which they gained [?]!
They exchanged mourning for the pearl of the kingdom on high.
They gave nothing and acquired wealth that cannot be taken away:
for a dream that passed away, truth and life without end.
They heard the voice of the Son of God and [hastened] [?] to meet him,
and became disciples of his teaching and good servants.
They saw that his great treasure was opened before mortals,
and they ran to him and drew from it spiritually.
They heard what he said: “See that you acquire nothing on earth,”
and they withdrew their hands from possessions and from worldly pursuits.
They left their labors and went out [stripped] of their pursuits,
and hurried on their course toward the possession of righteousness.
They left fathers, abandoned brothers, renounced kinsfolk,
and took up the cross of good labors and of [?].
They abandoned wives and despised bodily pleasures,
and like spiritual beings they lived, bodily creatures clothed in suffering.
The saints clung to the good Lord, full of mercies,
who in his great love called them to his teaching.
That gracious one, full of mercies, was not ashamed
to call even sinners to himself with great love.
“Come to me, you weary ones, burdened with heavy loads;
find rest with me and cast off the weight of your sins.”
O goodness, wholly full of compassion!
O humility that exalted the lowliness of earthly beings!
He did not say, “Cast off your burdens, and then come,”
lest they grow weak on the journey toward life.
Why did he not command, “Cut off the burdens of your sins”?
Lest they grow slack and, with hope cut off, remain on the earth.
“Come with the burdens of your sins,” the Gracious One commanded,
“and I will forgive you and pardon you your debts.”
The door is open to the wounded and to sinners,
and the love of the master of the house abounds toward all who call.
After this good sower, full of mercies,

the saints have walked, generation after generation, and inherited life.
While he was on earth, and after he ascended to his Begetter,
he filled the way on high with bands of bodily beings.
As he was passing along the shore of the Sea of Tiberias,
he caught fishermen and made them partners in his discourse.
He led simple men and filled them with the wisdom of life,
and sent them to the four quarters to preach.
He dissolved a tax office and brought its owner out of his business,
and supported his life with the possession of righteousness.
Another tax collector the apostle full of beauty made his own,
and all he possessed he gave to the needy, and clung to him and followed.
A harlot heard of his goodness and scattered [?] her possessions,
and clasped his feet and received from him forgiveness of her sins.
Men clung to him, and slaves and free ran after him,
and every [?] who saw his radiance grew humble.
He received tax collectors and was not ashamed of sinners,
and filled assemblies for the way that looks toward the height above.
Men and women ran and clung to him lovingly,
and for the sake of his love he endured the labors of righteousness.
And when he ascended and sat at the right hand of his Father,
the way on high was made all the more ready among the children of Adam.
He caught Paul while he was threatening his saints,
and made him a target for all the trials of his coming.
His light dawned on the house of the centurion Cornelius,
and he made his household a great church for the glory of his name.
He raised up elders from the lowly and from the honored,
and sent them out across the dust of the earth.
He called youths from pleasures and from luxuries,
and furnished them with toilsome fasts and prayers.
He cast his glance upon brides in their chambers,
and they left mortal bridegrooms and went after him.
He brought kings down from thrones of finest adornment,
and made them run on foot on the road on high.
He stripped them of silks and fine garments,
and clothed them in the worn garments of poverty.
He dawned upon kings, and his love led them,
and made them fit for his preaching.
The children of the palace he led out into the barren desert,
and made them partners in the discourse of heaven.
He filled mountains and caves with ranks of praisers,
and in the [barren] desert he arrayed troops of the children of light.
High cliffs and mountaintops are full of his saints,
and from them thunder the sweet voices of the power of his wisdom.
The Son of God cast the fire of his love upon the earth,
and melted the world with the love of spiritual life.
With the fire of his love he burned up the desire for earthly things,
and drew [?] the world to that delight that does not perish.
He lightened for it the weight of [?] full of [?],
and yoked it to his yoke, which is pleasant, sweet, gentle and smooth.
He laid on its shoulder the spiritual load that is good and light,
and set it running on the road that leads up on high, to the kingdom.
On this path the saints have walked, generation after generation,
and labored carefully with God, and acquired life.
On this same path walked the holy one, as long as his Lord willed [?];
earnestly he labored in the field of righteousness.
From his youth—
from his youth alone [he chose] the way of righteousness,

and walked uprightly in the [?] of holiness.
He stretched out his neck and took up the yoke of the Son of God,
and diligently he plowed the field of righteousness.
He cast off from his shoulder the load of the world, full of harms,
and took up the burden of the Son of God, full of life.
[?] the good one, like [?], from the captivity of the foolish world,
and like a bird he escaped from the snares of desire.
He fled from the world that strangles its children with its desires,
and became a companion of the just who labored with God.
He restrained his mouth from earthly conversations,
so that his lips meditated on spiritual songs.
He crushed his thought away from earthly concerns,
and made it a [?] for spiritual hallelujahs.
He closed his sight to the beauties of this world,
and gazed instead at the good things of the house of God.
He shut his hearing so as not to listen to bodily sounds,
and purified and polished it to hear spiritual voices.
He weaned his heart from joys that do not last,
and poured into it and filled it with every heavenly joy.
He guarded [?] his sense of smell from bodily scents,
and was perfumed with the pure fragrances of righteousness.
He cleansed his mind of the filth of earthly things,
and raised his understanding to the lofty order of spiritual beings.
He gathered his soul away from bodily thoughts,
and filled it abundantly with divine concerns.
He sent his knowledge toward that knowledge of the Godhead,
and gazed upon that life which has no end.
He gave his limbs to toilsome vigils and prayers,
and sanctified [his senses] in the whole course of righteousness.
His movements shone [?] with the great light of the Crucifixion,
and he shone wholly with the Sun, Christ, who is all light.
He sanctified his soul, purified his body, polished his thoughts,
and became wholly a pure vessel for the Living One on high.
He bore the cross of labors humbly on his shoulders,
and pressed on at great speed along the way of the kingdom.
He bore his cross according to the command from the mouth of God,
and indeed he was crucified to the whole world (and its desires).
Like an eagle the blessed one flew above the snares,
and [beat] [?] his wings toward the height above, to the assembly of the firstborn.
The pious one was diligent in good works of righteousness,
and insatiably he rose higher in holiness.
With lofty desire he who counted himself among the sons
labored diligently in the estate of his hidden Father.
He did not labor diligently like a slave before his master,
nor did he think himself a hireling as he labored.
A slave labors when driven by authority;
a hireling, too, looks to his wage and takes his hour's pay.
But a son labors diligently as one to whom it belongs,
and the inheritance of his father's house is truly his.
The slave waits for the sun to set, and the hireling too,
and both labor as under compulsion [?], and not out of love.
The heir labors hard and fervently

for his possessions and his flocks, at all times, diligently.
In this way labored the holy one of whom I speak,
and all his life he toiled purely with God.
All his days he stood in the contest of righteousness,
and in the spiritual battle his time was spent [?].
Against the ranks of passions and demons the victor stood,
and fought the battle and conquered and came out valiantly.
With the inner man and with outward foes he joined the fight,
and broke their ranks and came out victorious from the contest.
The ranks of passions surrounding him he overcame by his rigor [?],
and the holy one put the horde of demons to flight with his prayers.
For he was a laborer whom the immortal angels befit [?],
and he strengthened his whole walk [?] in the judgment of righteousness.
He was clothed with the strength of faith, which is true,
and the pious one was girded with the breastplate of righteousness.
On his head he had set a helmet whose forging
is the living cross, at which evil demons tremble.
In his hand he held the great bow of careful fasting,
strung with the strong bowstring of good works.
He carried the arrows of prayers with strong feathers,
and took aim at the contests of the rebellious demons.
In his hands he grasped the hope of the fire of his Lord's love,
and in his right hand the spear that pierces with pure love.
On his feet he was shod with a zealous and upright readiness,
and like lightning [he fell] upon the ranks of the children of passion.
He was hardy and girded, diligent and nimble, watchful and swift,
skilled and victorious, and in victory his [?] were made complete.
Demons and passions turned back when the victor stood firm [?],
and were driven off before that laborer of righteousness.
The heavenly ranks clothed in light marveled at him
as he wrestled and overcame the demons, the children of darkness.
The heavenly hosts rejoiced in him and gave him strength
in that battle with the powers, the children of harm.
He fought and conquered by strength in the battle,
and behold, the house of God has prepared for him a crown of greatness.
He was a sailor who steered his ship wisely
through the hazards of the sea, turbulent and full of storms.
He gathered the wealth of righteousness by good works,
filled his ship with it, and looked to the harbor of the house of God.
On the great sea traveled the trader of faith,
and he was the owner, the sailor and the pilot.
He fastened the anchor of faith, the mistress of treasures,
and provided toilsome, careful fasts and prayers.
He spread the linen of a pure heart and a clear mind
on the lofty mast dyed with the blood of the Son of God.
The living Spirit blew [?] rightly upon his ship,
and the harsh waves of desires did not shake it.
He flew over the billows, soared, and passed over the hazards,
and by his trade he was supplied for the harbor of heaven.
His ship is kept safe in the harbor of the garden full of blessings,
until the day of resurrection dawns and he opens his treasures.
Before the eyes of angels and of men he will present his wealth

in the great assembly in which all generations are gathered.
There he will open the great treasure of righteousness
before that King to whom heaven and earth belong.
He will render the wealth of his good works to the Lord of wealth,
and receive from him life and blessings without end.
In the humble company of the wise virgins
the holy one has joined, with the lamps of his good works.
Since the Bridegroom delays to come in his glory with his angels,
he has slumbered and slept until that coming dawns.
At the end of time the pious one fell asleep in righteousness,
and behold, he waits for the Bridegroom to come, and to go out to meet him.
See, his vessel is full of compassion, the pure oil;
he has trimmed his lamp, and it shines, and its light will be found burning.
He makes ready, for the Bridegroom is about to come; when he hears “The Bridegroom has come,”
he will take up his lamp and go out to meet him with unveiled face.
He will enter with him that delight that does not perish,
and recline at the wedding feast of spiritual life.
He is the good servant, faithful and just, and wise as well,
whom his master set over the provision of his household.
He received authority in the great house of the Godhead,
and provided spiritual wealth for the members of his household.
In due season he gave out the portion of life spiritually,
and did not fall short of the spiritual rule.
Watchful, diligent, careful and upright was he in his service,
and in the balance of righteousness he weighed out his provisions.
That thought full of wickedness did not overcome him:
“Tomorrow the master of the house will come; rest a little.”
He kept his eyes on that coming full of dread,
and the day of reckoning was always set before his eyes.
He did not strike his fellow servants or the maidservants with blows,
nor did he eat and drink with the dissolute [?] and the drunkards.
With fitting order and humility he managed his life,
and in piety he fulfilled his service, a son of the bridal chamber.
For he was waiting for his master to return and see his diligence,
as he stayed watchful and strong, and his [lamp] [?] shone with holiness.
Blessed is he: kept for him is what was spoken by the pure mouth,
and he will receive it before the eyes of spiritual and bodily beings.
The talents he received from that immortal Lord
he traded with diligently, and doubled their profit.
He did not dig in the ground and hide the spiritual silver,
nor did he scorn the authority of the Lord he had seen.
He did not shut his eyes to the trade that is full of life,
nor was he idle about the profit of righteousness.
He traded diligently with the talents he had received,
and he is about to repay them with their profit when the Face is revealed.
When he presents the talents he received, with their profit,
his Lord will rejoice and pour great love upon him.
He will hear from him that voice full of blessings:
“Good servant, enter into the joy that never ends.”
At that voice spiritual beings will fly toward him,
and receive him and escort him to the bridal chamber of light.
At their Lord's will, the servants clothed in light look on,

and stand ready for service in great awe.
From the moment they hear that voice full of life,
with awe and love they escort the just to the house of the kingdom.
And they become companions to the just who lived well,
and by their hands these crossed over the pit and inherited life.
Mingled with them spiritually is the soul of the just man,
and when they rise with them he will enter that delight.
Behold, the reward of his labors awaits him at the gate on high,
and his place is appointed at that wedding feast that never ends.
In good garments the pious one will enter the wedding hall,
and he will feel no shame when the King visits the guests.
Blessed is our community, which has a father among the saints,
and by his prayers our ranks are guarded from harms.
Behold, his tears flow in the place of the house of mercy,
and his atonement is marked on the horns of the holy altar.
His body is with you, and his soul among the heavenly ranks;
his bones are in our place, and his spirit in the garden full of blessings.
Behold, his good labors have become a school for us,
and his prayers a high wall for the assemblies of his children.
Behold, his dust is laid up as a treasure for our poverty,
and his prayers drive away pains and sicknesses from us.
Blessed is our community, which is honored by his radiant body;
he has become heir to the great dwelling of the just who have risen.
O my beloved, let us take refuge in his prayers,
let us shelter in him, and with him walk to the place of light.
We are children of a pious father full of goodness;
after our father let us lift up our wings to the house of God.
Like disciples let us be spiritual servants,
so that our father may rejoice spiritually in the assembly of his children.
Behold, his holy tears, good signs,
are laid out along the way that leads up to the height of the house of God.
Behold, his footprints on the straight way of righteousness;
let us walk after him and set our steps in his tracks.
By the good marks of his holy steps
let us hasten our course to the spiritual meeting place.
Let us direct our lives in the way of our father with discernment,
and with him enter the delight that is prepared for him.
Like a guide our father went before us, my beloved,
to show us the way on high in brightness.
Behold, at the end of the road of righteousness the pious one has encamped,
and he looks to his children, that they may walk after him in holiness.
Behold, in the harbor where there is no harm the merchant has unloaded,
and to his disciples he points out the goal, that they may journey to him.
He came up from the sea with his spiritual merchandise,
and looks for the ships of his spiritual household.
He ran the course with toil, a son of the bridal chamber,
and at its end, behold, he rests and is free of all harm.
The holy one has prepared that other lodging at the end of his road,
and made ready a place for the assembly of his spiritual children.
Whoever walks the straight way after the pious one
will rest with him and fly with him to meet his Lord.
Let us ask for his prayer, and run in his footsteps with love,

so that when we rise and put on glory, we may be covered by it.
May the prayer of the just one, and your prayers, his diligent children,
gather the scattered to the way that leads to the new life.
With you may I be gathered at that time when the worlds hasten on,
and may the King's servants not cast me out of your company.
When the troops of fire hasten down to the earth
before the King's Son, who comes to comfort our despised race;
when the companies of the hosts of Gabriel are drawn up
before that Power which descends to summon those who lie in the dust;
when the seraphim fly and soar before the coming
of the Lord, who comes to give out life to the dead [?];
when the cherubim carry in splendor that chariot
upon which the Judge of the living and the dead is exalted;
when the last trumpet sounds the resurrection of the dead,
and trembling falls, and the dead stir within the dust;
when the great horn of the house of the kingdom sounds
and calls the generations from within the earth to the resurrection;
when the departed who died in Christ rise first,
and strip off and cast away mortality, and fly in the air;
when all generations are gathered to that judgment seat,
and trembling falls, and silence fills all creation;
when the flocks are separated, to life and to torment,
and the ranks are divided, to the kingdom and to Gehenna:
at that time may our whole community find mercy,
and with the pious one, our just father, inherit life.
Make us worthy, our Lord, of that delight at your right hand,
and with the saints, the children of your kingdom, to you be praise.
Responsory: Glory to you, whose fatherhood has no equal; the Son for whose hope the just have looked.
A Homily on the Departed and on the Resurrection of the Dead

Homily 11: On the departed.
Again by the same: the eleventh homily,
suited to the Friday at the beginning of the Fast,
which is called the Friday of the Departed.
Responsory:
Blessed is he whom the Lord of the world has chosen out of this world for mercy.
My brothers.

I wished to marvel at the beauty that befits the image of man,
but while I sought to see his beauty, I saw his humiliation.
I saw how his crown was bound on, on earth, as he ruled over all,
and I turned and saw that he was cast down into Sheol, apart from all.
I saw him giving commands, and the speaking and the dumb obeyed him,
and after a little while I saw a moth crawling through his body.
I saw him seated on chariots, his appearance awesome,
and again I looked at him as he bowed his head at the door of the grave.
I saw that he was adorned in garments of fine linen and silk,
and after a time I saw that his face was overlaid with [?].
I saw him sending the voice of his command swiftly to his fellows,
and death ran and swallowed him suddenly and silenced his voice.
I saw him building and enlarging his dwelling beyond measure,
and on the day of his death no one let him dwell in it.

I saw that he had prepared fine garments for the day of the wedding feast,
and death hurried and bound him in Sheol, a bridal chamber of mourning.
I saw him running to gather wealth without ever being satisfied,
and at his departure he was seen to be poor in good things.
Without any gain the mighty one went out of his life,
and he took no provisions for the journey to which he was summoned.
He went out of his life just as he came out of the womb:
naked he came and naked he went. A great grief!
A grief, for his lowliness grieves my mind more than all his injury,
and I grieved deeply over the humiliation of our despised race.
I saw that his exaltation was uprooted from him like a shadow,
and I saw his lowliness and his own humiliation, which lingered long.
In his lowliness I watched how he rotted in Sheol and was turned to dust,
and I pondered how and when he would return to life.
I pondered how life could be sought out of death,
and how his despised dust would return to its exaltation.
Who will build the temple of the body that death has torn down,
and who will bring the soul back to it, so that it may give praise in it?
Who will open for him the door of Sheol that is shut in his face,
and who will bring him out of the strongholds of greedy death?
What power will breathe the breath of life into his face
and give voice to dead senses to sing praise?
What sign will go out and run into the four quarters
and separate the dust of men from the dust of the earth?
Who is it that can separate the dust of men from the beasts
that ate them and died, so that bodies were mixed with bodies?
How great, then, must that command be that commands them to rise,
since there is no counting the thousands of men who have become dust!
How many thousands of heavenly beings, then, go forth to seek
those who perished in the sea and [?], in every form!
From where, then, will flesh and bones return and come,
since no trace of the body's [?] remains in the dust of the earth?
For it is the dust of the earth that becomes a body,
and who can separate dust from its own kind?
These things I pondered foolishly, in the person of the fools,
and I set out their thoughts as one who had joined them.
I set out the thinking of fools from my own mind as though it were theirs,
and Paul listened to me and reproached me along with them as a fool.
The herald of the Spirit, the proven witness that the dead live,
heard the doubt as to whether the dead live, and he was zealous and stirred.
"Fool," he called me, in the person of the fools who are divided in heart,
"why have you voiced the thinking of fools in the ears of men?
Fool," he says, "look at the nature of the seed you sow, whoever you are:
unless it dies it cannot live and bear fruit.
Look at the grain of wheat, the seed you cast into the earth,
how it dies completely and so lives, in the mystery of the resurrection."
It is that very grain that falls and dies, in the likeness of the body;
it is that very one that springs up from its decay in great splendor.

In this order the body dies and the body lives,
and it is the very same body, though corruptible, that puts on glory.
It is the same body that acquires visible senses like its former ones,
and its own soul returns and sings on the lyre of its limbs.
In body and soul each one rises, just as he is:
the body with its [?], and the soul with movements of lightness.
The body becomes immortal instead of mortal,
and the soul strips off the grievous garment of soiled vessels.
The very body that became dust becomes a body again;
the very soul whose voices had ceased gives praise within it.
Paul bears witness to its corruption and to its renewal:
that it is corrupted and it is renewed by the power of its Creator.
"This corruptible," he says, "is destined to put on glory,
and this mortal to live in a life that does not die."
Do not let nature, worn out by mortality, grieve you,
and do not doubt the renewal of body and soul.
Rise, listen to the voices that announce the resurrection to you,
and take hold of a hope that will be a hope for your mortality.
Hear the prophet who cries out by the Spirit to dead bones,
and whose voice proclaims new tidings in the house of the dead.
Hear him crying out like a trumpet beside the silent ones
and gathering the whole army of the body for renewal.
One renewal his voice proclaimed for body and soul,
and he gave them to drink the cup of comfort: that the dead live.
Listen again to the voice of the Renewer of mortality,
who points out the renewal of man as if with a finger.
Hear him rebuking the Sadducees, divided in heart,
and contending with them from the divine laws:
"You are in error," he says, "for you do not know how to read the Scriptures,
and you do not discern the force of the meaning of their words.
In the resurrection," he says, "there is no distinction of men and women,
for their nature becomes immortal, like the spiritual beings."
See, our Lord has trodden the new road by which the dead live;
come, let us walk on it toward the renewal of body and soul.
See, he has proclaimed good hope to us by the voice of his words;
let us believe that he is able to fulfill for us the promise of his words.
See, he rebuked death, the bold lion that ravaged our race,
and took three bodies away from it and brought them back to life.
See, he too went down into its lair, where it swallows men,
and gave it his body, and it swallowed him and quickly spat him out.
See, he rose and raised our whole nature from its fall,
and tore down the walls that death had built in the face of the dead.
See, he went out and brought back mankind's captives from the strong one,
and took his armor and plundered his camp and made him a laughingstock.
See, he took captivity captive, ascended, and reigned above all,
and he is destined to come and renew all things by the voice of his words.
See, the time draws near when he will descend to earth as he ascended,
in a visible body and the hidden power of divinity.
See, heaven and earth, Watchers and men, wait for him
to set them free from the bondage of corruption.
See, all creation sighs over mortal beings:

when will they be immortal and beyond suffering?
The speaking and the dumb alike are clothed in garments of mourning:
when will they strip off the hateful garment of mortality?
Hard pangs strike the earth like a woman in labor:
when will she bring forth the bodies of men from her womb?
Men and spiritual beings bear great pain:
how long until they see the truth in the event of mankind's renewal?
In hope the good servants wait for the master of the house:
when will he return from the wedding feast and give the reward?
In hope the wise virgins hold their lamps:
when will the Bridegroom from on high shine forth, so that they may go in with him?
The hosts of heavenly beings wait for the fulfillment of hope:
when will hope shine forth openly and put an end to fear?
They wait every hour for that divine revelation:
when will the gates on high be opened, so that they may receive him?
The ear of their minds is inclined toward that voice:
when will it [sound?], so that death trembles and the Evil One is put to shame?
The ranks keep watch for that command which they serve:
when will he command, so that they call out the cry of salvation over the earth?
At the King's gate all the members of the palace stand waiting:
when will he come out, so that they may receive him with their hosannas?
With the hands of their movements they weave a crown of victory
to offer it to the King of kings, who conquered by the wood of the cross.
The longing of their minds' love cannot be put into words,
how much they long to see his glory and to praise him.
Fear and love reign together over their ranks,
and they hasten all the more, yet do not slacken in their readiness.
They love much, and long much, and fear much,
and like athletes they are thrown into the contest for the promised life.
In spirit they run in the spiritual stadium
to receive the prize of that victory which can never be overcome.
See, the time for the reward of their contests has arrived,
and the time has drawn near for them to receive the gifts of their struggles.
See, the kingdom on high of the King on high has drawn near;
come, let us adorn ourselves spiritually and go out to meet him.
See, the gates on high are lifted up before his coming,
so that he may descend to earth and take up with him those who serve him.
Great wonder and blessedness and suffering on the day of his revelation:
wonder at his shining forth, blessedness for the good and suffering for the wicked.
In splendor and glory he shows himself to Watchers and men,
and heaven and earth alike are filled with his praise.
The sign of his power lifts the veil from the face of the heights,
and the light of his great brightness shines over all and in all.
Like lightning its light shines out in the four quarters,
and any light that can be seen is small beside the measure of his light.
The light that flashes from his face has no measure,
and there is no way to show the swiftness with which his sign runs.
Lightnings, however swift, come forth from his command,
and the light of the sun's orb is darkness compared with him.
The greatness of his glory cannot be told by a human tongue,

and the mouth of every creature is too small to say how great it is.
Awesome and hard is the hour of his shining forth, sudden beyond all suddenness,
and there is no being, bodily or spiritual, that is not terrified.
A great amazement falls suddenly on all creatures
at the voice of the command whose sound rushes on more mightily than the sea.
Like a herald his sign runs before his face
and sets up the ranks of heavenly beings, troop upon troop.
In order the spiritual beings stand before his majesty
and acclaim him with a voice of praise that has no measure.
Thousands upon thousands stand before him in fear,
and myriads upon myriads repeat his praise without ever being satisfied.
His love reigns over the thousands of heavenly beings,
and they hasten all the more to repay him the debt of love.
The Cherubim bear him, the Watchers acclaim him, the Seraphim cry out:
"Holy, holy, holy is the King who dwells in glory!"
"Holy" they cry spiritually in the tongue of the spirit,
like that language Paul heard, which cannot be spoken.
That voice cannot be uttered by a tongue of flesh,
the voice with which they praise the God of all in a divine way.
With hidden movements they openly sing praise to the Hidden One,
and their sight fails before the bodily door.
They see a body being borne in procession on the chariot,
and hidden within it the divinity that cannot be seen.
The Hidden One, made manifest, suddenly commands their hosts
to sound the voice of praise for the renewal of all things.
They all cry out the voice of renewal in the ears of men,
and the earth shakes at the awesome sound of their trumpets.
Thunders of voices they all become, as many as they are,
and as many as they are, so many are the sounds of spiritual horns.
Splendid is their appearance and glorious the utterance of their words,
and the swiftness of their ministries is far quicker than lightning.
Above them all comes the King Messiah in glory,
and they acclaim him with a voice of praise worthy of his name.
The archangels carry the standard of victory, the Cross,
and display it to the heavenly and earthly beings.
Before him comes the standard of his passion and of his victory,
so that those who were insolent and the rebellious demons may be put to shame by it.
To its assembly the troops of Watchers and angels run,
and they gaze on it with the hidden eye of their minds.
The King and his standard descend to the earth on which he suffered,
and he avenges the insult done to him and gives gifts to those who received him.
The voice of the divine horn sounds out before him,
and the dead and the living gather and come to the assembly of his name.
The last horn sounds at the end, at the completion of the times,
and by it the gates of Sheol are opened before the departed.
The hidden sign runs together with that voice,
and in the blink of an eye raises and renews the bodies that had worn away.
Voice and sign suddenly cry out in the ears of death:
"Give back the captives, and give account of the bodies that perished!"
A great groaning falls on Sheol, the mother of the dead,

and terrible pangs overwhelm her like a woman in labor.
The womb of the barren mother becomes a fountain of men,
and as much as she [?], so quickly does she give back.
The sign sprinkles the dew of mercy on the face of the earth,
and like seed the bodies sprout up from the dust.
The body rises, whole and entire, with visible senses,
and the soul returns with its wisdom to give praise within it.
There is no limb of the body that remains behind in Sheol,
nor is any of the soul's movements lost that does not return to it.
Body and soul rise together in the blink of an eye,
and they strip off and cast away the garments of suffering and put on glory.
The dead rise, and their nature becomes immortal,
and so too the living are changed into that likeness.
One command raises the dead and changes the living,
and no one is lost, neither of the dead nor of the living.
The resurrection is the same for all bodies and for all souls,
and the good and the wicked rise alike in body and soul.
The whole nature of Adam's dust returns to life,
and there is no one among those born who remains in Sheol and is not raised.
One alone is lost there from the number:
he who, by a spirit of error, goes astray and leads mankind astray.
The son of perdition is the only one lost from humanity,
and mercy does not deem him worthy to enter the number of men.
In his face alone the sign shuts the gate of resurrection,
and the face of the King who commands the rising is not shown to him.
With a terrible weapon he binds his body and the movements of his soul
and sinks him in the pit of Sheol, without end.
In him a great wonder is shown to reason:
how a living nature can perish from life.
In him spiritual and bodily beings gaze
on a man in his body and a Watcher in his soul, both of which come suddenly to an end.
A new thing happens in that renewal full of wonder:
all are renewed, and one is destroyed without pity.
A great wonder on the day of the revelation of the King of kings:
that he judges everyone, and one he abandons without inquiry.
Joy and distress on the day of resurrection for the two sides:
blessedness for the good, and for the wicked doubled scourges.
Crowns and scourges are made ready by command before the Judge:
crowns for the righteous, and scourges for the wicked who sinned in the contest.
The sign holds glory and shame as though with a finger,
and gives glory to those who conquered and shame to those who failed.
Like a magistrate before the command at the gate of the [?],
he brings one in and puts one out into the outer darkness.
In the furnace of judgment he brings in rational beings and refines them,
and gathers the gold, the manifest truth, and casts away the dross.
With the King's seal he seals the good for the King's service,
and the wicked he rejects and casts into Gehenna.
He holds an outstretched staff in his hand and visits his flocks,
and sets the sheep at his right hand, as he promised.
Great is the distinction that will be made there among rational beings,
for though they are one in the one renewal, they are not one.
One is the nature of the rationality of Watchers and men,

yet they are not one, because of the difference in their deeds.
"On that day," he says, "if two are in one bed,
one will be lifted up toward the heights and the other left behind.
If there are two women grinding at the mill at that time,
one will be taken and the other left as she was."
See, our Lord's word has shown that distinction,
how he separates the righteous and the chaste from the wicked.
He showed that this distinction would hold among all kinds,
and that as he chooses males, so also females.
And though there is one nature of men and women,
he showed that some are left behind both from these and from those.
Like lightning the sign passes through their kinds,
and leads one and leaves one, from every kind.
A great order, full of distinctions, it separates,
and according to deeds it gives reward and also pardon.
With one and the same distinction it deals equally with men and spirits,
and tests together the truth and the counterfeit of both sides.
Into the bridal chamber on high he brings the chaste, clothed in love,
and here on earth he leaves those who fell and did not adorn themselves.
On earth remain the lovers of the earth, where they loved,
and those who long for what is above are raised on high on the wings of the Spirit.
On earth they receive doubled scourges, as they deserve,
and there they are repaid the debts of their deeds.
The earth becomes Gehenna for them, for the children of earth,
and they themselves chastise themselves for the sins they committed.
Their own inclination scourges itself, each one separately,
because they neglected what was fitting in this life here.
They condemn the evil within them, and that they are guilty,
and they lay it bare in the furnace of the memory of their thoughts.
"A great judgment!" they say there, along with their sins,
and before everyone they lay bare their hidden blemishes.
Bitter beyond all scourges are the scourges with which one is scourged
when the side of the just is crowned and his own is put to shame.
The wicked see a great wonder in the side of the good:
how they fly up lightly toward the heights.
It is a great wonder, and how much greater than a wonder, to say
that despised flesh should sprout the wings of flight!
That command which fashioned it in the beginning from the dust
strengthens it for flight, to fly through the air.
He who breathed into it the breath of life, so that it became a living soul,
makes it a temple of the Spirit that does not decay.
He who lovingly humbled himself to the level of his creature
exalts its lowliness and renews it in mercy.
In love and mercy he fashioned it in the beginning and called it by his name,
and again, in it, at the appointed time, he confirms toward it the promise of his words.
In his image he formed it from the beginning, when he set it in order,
and at the end he descends in his image and raises it.
In his image descends a hidden sign, though he is not hidden,
and he gives immortal life to mortality.
In the second Adam, whom he humbled himself to put on in love,
in him he is humbled without change at the completion of the times.

The body that he put on by the will of his love and called by his name,
in that he wraps himself willingly and descends to earth.
He who ascended before the eyes of angels and of mankind
is the one who comes to judge men and spiritual beings.
The Watchers saw him in a visible body as he ascended,
and at that sight they said that he would come as he ascended.
With his manifestation his sign descends swiftly
and renews all things, and takes them up with him to the place above.
The hidden sign sounds openly an awesome voice
and shakes the earth and stirs the ranks of heavenly beings.
With a voice he commands heavenly and earthly beings:
"Arise, be renewed, and put on glory that does not decay!"
The voice of his command wakes the earthly from sleep,
and they shake themselves and rise as if from a heavy sleep.
One voice full of wonder cries out over the earth,
and the speaking and the dumb tremble at it and obey it.
All listen to it and all fulfill it without delay,
and by it height and depth and all that is in them are renewed.
The speaking beings ascend to a high rank that has no measure,
and the dumb rest from their servitude to human labor.
The sun ceases from the course of its swiftness,
and the moon rests from its changes in every month.
The stars fall, and the light of their rays is quenched,
and the blowing of the winds of the air ceases and stirs no more.
Darkness comes to an end, and the order of night and day passes away,
and hours and weeks and the months of the year are no longer counted.
The fountain of Sheol's womb dries up from all its fruits,
and cattle cease, and wild beasts [?] and creeping things come to an end.
The sea rests from the turmoil of raging waves,
and thousands of men no longer race across its back.
All is changed and all is renewed in the renewal of mankind,
and over all and in all reigns the light of the one Creator.
All is set free from servitude to men,
and the Son of Man dwells in a place where there is no fear.
By a small sign all is changed and all is renewed,
and its swiftness cannot be told, how and how great it is.
That command is swifter than anything,
and if there is anything very swift, it is slower than it.
There is no delay between descending and ascending,
not even as long as a man takes to blink his eye from moment to moment.
On the chariot of the back of the air the King goes forth in procession
with the chosen laborers who drew near and conquered for love of him.
His sign yokes one spiritual chariot,
and on it he seats earthly and heavenly beings alike.
It is his sign that becomes both cloud and chariot,
and it is what carries and leads all things to the heights.
It is what serves rational beings in place of everything else,
and by it Watchers and men are raised to the place above.

He it is who goes forth like a commander before their ranks,
and he again gathers other ranks to the assembly of his name.
The King goes forth at the head of his camp toward the height,
with thousands of Watchers on his right and on his left.
With him go forth the children of the palace to the place of light,
that they may be heirs with him in the kingdom on high.
Very great is the company of his host, beyond all hosts,
and the splendour and glory with which he is arrayed cannot be told.
With him is all rational creation,
thousands of Watchers and myriads of human beings.
All of them carry the crown of praise for the day of his victory,
and offer it to him by the hand of spiritual impulses.
Heaven and earth recount his glory by the mouth of rational beings,
as they repay him the debt of love, the voice of praise.
By the greatness of his love he kindles [?] the gaze of their minds,
as they long for the moment when he will open the gates of the height.
They hasten eagerly to see the way that has been prepared for it,
that they may enter and receive spiritual rewards and gifts.
The sight of the King does not satisfy their minds,
and the more they see, the more they long to gaze.
Before their movements the Sign runs swiftly,
and passes on and enters ahead of them at the gates of the royal house.
The King opens the great gate before his entry,
and enters and takes his rest within the palace, he and those with him.
Wonder and anguish fill the sight of that entry:
wonder for those above, and anguish for those below who are not raised up.
He is good beyond all good things; even the wicked gaze upon him,
and this is their anguish: that seeing him, they are deprived of him.
In anguish their mind gazes without being satisfied,
as the gates of the height are opened and as they are shut.
A strange sight men see among men:
that while they are one, one is raised up and the other brought low.
Strange too are the spiritual hosts of demons to behold:
though they are spirit, they cannot fly like spiritual beings.
In amazement stand wicked men and cruel demons,
as they gaze at the gates of the height while they are being shut.
They weep and lament for themselves with a roar like thunder,
for they see the gate of forgiveness closed before their faces.
In anguish they weep, with thunderous groans,
and without ceasing they utter the cries of remorse.
Anguish lashes the nature within them with discernment,
and remorse judges the faults of their own selves.
They judge themselves together with their sins, wisely,
and as in a furnace they assay the dross of their thoughts.
In their minds they weigh the weight of their offences,
and in proportion to their wickedness their anguish bitterly increases.
Bitter and harsh is the just judgment by which they are crushed,
and the severity of its scourges cannot be told by human tongue.
Great and deep is the pit into which they fall,
and very hard it is to escape from its severity.
With the rich man, each one cries out to Abraham:

"Have pity, merciful one, and plead for mercy on our behalf;
ask and entreat the hidden Sign, as is your custom,
that it may sprinkle a little dew of mercy upon our wickedness."
"Sons, it is not possible to prevail," Abraham answered,
"to cross the gulf that lies between us and you.
Remember that you loved earthly things and the goods of this age,
and you did not look, you did not hope, for the kingdom of spiritual life."
Abraham tells these things to his sons, but not with a voice;
I have spoken the words as they happened, according to what is written.
For they do not call upon Abraham to have pity on them,
nor can Abraham speak apart from the Sign.
It is the Sign that has shut the gate of the kingdom before their faces,
and it is the Sign that cries through Abraham's mouth, "Be trampled down and tormented."
It holds the rod of scourges, though not with hands,
and distributes the scourges to the condemned according to their deeds.
And while it holds the treasury of good things on high,
it gives a reward to the lovers of love according to their love.
The scourges of those who did wrong without knowledge are not equal to the others,
and the glory of those who were strong in the contest of labours is greater still.
The Sign distributes good things and scourges according to the will,
and lessens and deepens them according to wickedness and righteousness.
And although there is nothing at all lacking in that delight,
Paul said that one glory shines more than another.
In great and ineffable glory dwell those on high,
and in unspeakable torment those below are cast down.
In the place of light dwell the righteous, Watchers and men,
and in darkness dwell the wicked and the demons who did wrong.
In the company of the King the saints dwell spiritually,
and with him they delight in the feast of the Spirit that does not decay.
Their seasoning is glory, whose sweetness never cloys,
and their converse too is a voice of thanksgiving without end.
They are clothed in glory and cry out glory in holiness
to the one who in his holiness willed to make the work of his hands a partaker with him.
The righteous see the hidden one, who is hidden and revealed in his glory;
they do not dispute how it is that they see while not seeing.
In the visible one they see the glory of him who is hidden from all,
and through the revealed one the vision of their minds descends.
In the temple of the body they offer the sacrifices of their minds,
and they are not permitted to gaze into the Holy of Holies.
The Holy is the visible body, the firstfruits of our race,
and the Holy of Holies is the Godhead that is not seen.
Yet the Holy and the Holy of Holies are one in union,
one God in the temple of the body that he chose for his love.
One thanksgiving men and spiritual beings offer
to the hidden one in the revealed, and to the revealed one for the sake of the hidden.
In one love all are bound to the one who is revealed,
and he, in one being, is one lordship and one authority.
Over all and in all the hidden one is enthroned [?] there in the revealed one,
and in his manifestation he judges all according to his promise.

For this reason too he chose it out of all and subjected all to it,
that those being judged might see who this is.
For the children of the kingdom and the children of darkness had need
to see who it is that distributes gifts and inflicts scourges.
They wished, moreover, to see something, however hidden it was,
and yet it could not content them as they desired [?].
Wisely did he who orders all accomplish all that he accomplished,
and the wisdom of his love cannot be told, how great it is and of what kind.
Marvellous is his ordering, great his renewal, and perfect his love,
and however much our tongue may magnify, it falls short of his greatness.
He showed his love in that he created all and renews all,
and makes all partakers in the fellowship of the love of his Godhead.
To the wedding feast of his love he invites, calling the children of his house,
and gladdens them in that well-ordered kingdom on high.
In the place above he distributes the riches of his delight,
and sits granting a charter of freedom to the work of his hands.
Men acquire the riches of life that does not die,
and without toil they dwell in a place raised above sufferings.
In the harbour of peace the ships of their limbs come to rest,
and the waves of suffering no longer wear down their minds.
By the power of grace they gain strength to sing glory
to him who in his love made them partakers in his praises.
There is fulfilled what is written concerning man:
that he is a visible image which proclaims the hidden one through its visibility.
There men on earth see the one who is hidden from all,
and they no longer weary themselves in the search for hidden things.
There one will reigns over all and in all,
and there is none who resists the repaying of the debt of love.
There Watchers and men become one in concord,
and strife ceases, envy comes to an end, and wrath is done away.
Love and peace reign over all and subdue all,
and one will governs all according to its will.
The hidden one holds the rod of wrath in the hands of the revealed one,
and governs all toward the hidden one who is in the image of men.
To the assembly of the Man run men and spiritual beings,
and when they draw near to the gate of the Man they render thanksgiving.
As in an image they gaze upon him in the image of man,
and in his manifestation they see the might of the power of the Essence.
The eye of rational nature does not see the Essence,
but the visible image that resembles the hidden one.
"Resembles," I said, in greatness of rank, not in nature,
for among things made there is none whose nature resembles the nature of the hidden one.
In love he deemed the work of his hands worthy to be made like him,
and in goodness he called it and set it in the rank of his name.
This is a divine dispensation that cannot be explained:
how he wisely honoured what is his own through what is his own.
This is the discovery of that will which has authority over all,
which skilfully bound the world to his Godhead.
To him be praise for his wisdom that cannot be comprehended,
who ordered all and renewed all in love and mercy.
On the Perfection of Conduct
65. On the perfection of conduct. / By the same author, the sixty-fifth discourse. / On the perfection of conduct.

One victor overcame sin, which had killed humankind,
and in his victory he made humans and heavenly beings partners.
One hero went out to battle against evil,
and by his struggle earthly beings learned the ways of struggle.
One athlete went down to the contest of righteousness,
and by his courage mortals gained good hope.
One athlete revived [?] the contest of righteousness,
and by his courage mortals gained good hope.
One warrior joined battle with the strong one,
and by his endurance the dust-born braced [?] their minds.
Over all and in all he spread [?] the help that comes from his gift,
and he invited good and evil alike and called them to the banquet of his love.
Like a hero he cried out in creation, the mighty hero:
"See, the world has been won; let every man rise and trample on his head.
Rise and take courage, you earthly and heavenly beings,
and take victory through the victory that has come about by my hands.
Come, rest in my harbour, you who are weary with the toil of amassing,
and do not be worn away amid the storms of desires.
Come, take back the inheritances of your runners [?], which had been plundered,
and lay hold of the laws that were snatched from your lives.
Come, hasten to acquire spiritual life,
and despise the service of earthly things, which are not true.
Come, grow rich by meditating on the good things hidden in my person,
and hate and cast away the hateful feasts of passing things."
True and choice is the promise of life that is spoken through me,
and without distinction he gives a reward to whoever believes in me.
The Power of the Creator willed to make his power known through my hands;
through me he dispenses the wealth of his love to the work of his hands.
A debt of love the works he made owe him,
and above all those endowed with the word of discernment.
Come, rational beings, repay the thanksgiving you owe
to the Power of Being, who proclaimed his power in the war I waged.
Come, gaze at the true mark at the top of the wood,
and learn how the war against passions and demons was won.
The passions have made the beauty of your minds loathsome to [?];
scour the filth of your armour from your hearts.
Plundering demons have seized the inheritance of your possessions:

do battle with them and lay hold of the laws of new life.
Wage war in the spirit against your enemies,
in the same way that they fought with you and plundered your goods.
Against the harshness of harsh passions put on endurance,
and bring them low, so that you are not brought low beneath their feet.
Like the cunning of crafty [?], acquire composure,
so that you are not [?] by their stratagems as before.
Clothe the whole person in the armour of righteousness,
so that the sharp arrow of the Accuser does not pierce him.
Let body and soul join battle with the passions,
and strenuously keep their eyes on the goal of the promise of life.
Let the motions and senses of the body keep their eyes on the goal of the righteous,
so that together they may be worthy to receive the imperishable reward.
It is time, then, to show the warriors
the kinds of struggle, full of war against the passions.
Openly let us state the reason for the discourse we are preparing,
before listeners who love to hear spiritual things.
Brightly let the radiance of the words of our mouth shine
for the eye of spiritual people, who see the meaning of words well.
Without shame let it paint the story our soul longs for
on the page of the mind, which knows how to gaze on things to come.
I have wanted to speak about the dwellings of things to come,
and I have desired to recount the imperishable order.
At the victory of the King who conquered on the wood I marvelled greatly,
and longing has driven me to reveal his victory to the eyes of his worshippers.
In the contest of the toils of chosen labourers my thoughts have wandered:
how strong they were against the wars of desires!
I saw that his way, and the way of the sons of his house, is narrow,
and I said I would walk, if only in words, toward their paths.
I have heard that promised blessings are hidden in its narrowness,
and my mind has compelled me to proclaim them, if only to proclaim them.
I have surely heard that the way of this company is good,
and I have reflected that whoever has walked in it has profited from its gain.
Come, travellers who love the way of life,
journey with our story and take hold of the hope of new life.
With love let us hear the story of spiritual lives,
and with understanding let us listen to the meaning of hidden things.
With hope let us confirm what is said about things to come,
that even though they are hidden, they are truer than the sun.
These are the three that Paul spoke of,
for truly these are mighty to accomplish all things.
Hard for bodily beings is the conduct of spiritual things,
but where these are mingled with it, it is light and well ordered.
Our Lover too explained and revealed the power that is in them,
that they can overcome the war of the soul and of the members.
"Everything," he says, "that is impossible for men
is possible with God through faith."
Faith is a second sun for the eyes of the body;
come, let us see in it the beautiful splendour of things to come.
Better than the sun it shines on whoever gazes toward it,
and while still on earth he sees what is kept above in heaven.

The conduct of faith is full of great wonder;
come, let us marvel at it and learn the order that is spoken of in it.
Abundant treasures fill the deeds of its working;
let everyone draw near and freely take what his life needs.
At the door of its house even the wise will long to stand,
and see, their needs are filled without lack.
Come, all you merchants with all your trades, grow rich alike
from the treasury of faith, which has no limit.
By faith let us fulfil the mysteries of faith,
and in its confidence let us place our confidence in things to come.
By its light let us see what is not revealed to the eyes of the flesh;
its meditation is a meditation that rouses our soul to glorious things.
A great glory beyond all speech fills its meditation,
and it is gloriously praised with praise by the lovers of its love.
By it the prophets were glorified in the mysteries of things to come,
and by it the apostles triumphed through the power of mighty deeds.
Upon its building the just and the chaste built their labours,
and the height of their conduct reached up to the height.
They began to build truth in a weak world,
and they set people to build labours upon their labours.
On its foundation Simon Cephas laid his confession,
and received the crowning reward of blessings that do not perish.
"Blessed are you, Simon," said the mouth full of blessings,
"for you were worthy to learn the hidden mystery from the mouth of the Hidden One.
Not flesh and blood," he says, "revealed to you that you should confess rightly,
but the Father, who has a Child resembling his image."
The beautiful Image without composition revealed it to Simon,
that he should confess the Father who has a Child of two likenesses.
Like Simon let everyone confess who confesses the Son,
and let him not be divided over how Word and body are one.
The apostles received in love and handed on what had been done:
that the Word dwelt willingly in a body for the salvation of our lives.
For the sake of our lives he dwelt willingly in a body [?],
and freed our lives from bondage to evil and death.
By sufferings he accomplished what became for us the cause of life;
by sufferings he guides to completion the course of the conduct of our lives.
From him let us learn how through these sufferings he won the victory,
and how he made light of the passions of desires.
From his heralds let us hear of his labour and of the endurance of his soul,
for these labours he modelled in his own person ahead of their labours.
They too will recount the pattern of their own conduct:
how strong they were in their own persons against sufferings.
With the body they fought against the passions of fleshly desire,
and with the mind they joined battle with their motions.
Through their senses they strengthened the watchmen of sensation,
and through [?] they gave strength to mortal nature.
With food they fed the toil of the spirit to their minds,
and even in sleep they drove cessation away from their understanding.
By nature itself they conquered nature and its passions,
and though they were in it, they were like people who were not.

They heard that they would come to be in immortal life,
and they despised the life of time as no life at all.
They saw that they had been mystically renewed in baptism,
and they clothed their senses in the likeness of spiritual things.
They saw that the time of reward for their contests was drawing near,
and they portrayed beforehand what is to be, before it came to be.
The true ones portrayed the world to come in their conduct,
and set it up like an image on earth before those who looked on.
Like pigments they made pure the labours of every form,
and with strokes [?] they traced a showing of hidden things.
By fasting they showed that the body can live without food,
and by prayers that the soul's converse is in the spirit.
By vigil they taught that mortal nature no longer sleeps,
and with ceaseless songs it sings praise.
By despising possessions they proved the wealth hidden on high,
and by humility they traced a path toward glorious things.
They fasted from bread, not because the food from it was hateful,
but to gaze on that conduct which is without food.
They gave up marriage, not because union in it was unclean,
but to be as they will be there.
They despised pleasure, not rejecting what is needful,
but to be worthy to delight in what has no end.
They subdued passion by the [?] of body and soul,
though they themselves were bodily and of the soul.
They hated the pursuit of earthly things while they were earthly,
and loved the meditation of spiritual things while they were far off.
They did battle with every passion, hidden and revealed,
and did not slacken from the hope of things to come.
They bridled anger, humbled pride, swept away envy,
and did not let [?] run as it pleased.
They cast chaste bridles on the desire of the body,
and, since it is light, they made it run steadily.
They sprinkled cold water on the fire in the members,
quenched its strength, and it did not fight as is its wont.
As on horses they mounted their impulses upon their senses,
and ordered the course of the whole person so that it would not be thrown into confusion.
They put the bit of peace in the mouth of the horse of words,
and the soul rode like a charioteer upon its back.
To the eyes they granted, in due order, to look upon visible things,
and to the ears they allowed, in measure, to let in fitting hearing.
They taught the hand to sow the seeds of righteousness
and gather for itself the fruits of glory through its almsgiving.
For the foot they marked out the way to walk toward people
and visit them with spiritual visits.
The whole human body they purified in the service of life,
and occupied its life with the pursuit of a life foreign to it.
They compelled every nature to resemble what is not its nature,
and it abandoned its own and began to resemble what is not its own.
The nature of the body always desires bodily things,

yet they made it forget its own and meditate in the spirit.
The nature of the soul is wont to think on natural things,
yet they turned the soul's meditation toward glorious things.
A great wonder did human beings show to human beings on earth:
that in their bodies they made war against their bodies.
A new way the sons of clay traced in creation:
that they joined battle with the [?] of their members.
Contrary to custom, mortals wrought in mortality,
portraying newness while bound in the cords of death.
Who has ever seen corruptible members
making war against their passions through the senses?
Who has looked on swift and wavering impulses
joining battle with the feeble changes within them?
To whom has valour been given as to humankind,
that while guilty they won a victory not to be won?
A man is a man, however much he conquers what is not his own,
and this is the wonder: that he conquers in others as in his own.
Something new befell the sons of Adam, the clay of the earth:
in their conduct they turned dust into the gold of the Spirit.
Adam of clay, moulded by a hand that is not composite,
what has made you forget your nature in what is not your nature?
Your nature is dust, and your dust testifies that your dust is dust;
yet the conduct of life you have now taken up is higher than your dust,
and, as if in reverse, the passions are overturned by its perception [?].
You are a being of senses, and passions are woven into the garment of your body;
who will not marvel at your perception, that it has prevailed over them?
Come, beings of sense, marvel and be astonished at your brothers,
who by their will overcame the passions of their own persons.
Come, mortals, see how mortals proved heroic:
they died before they were dead, and lived before they came to life.
Come, earthly ones, look at the earthly, how wise they became:
they judged their deeds justly before the day of judgment.
They set just judgment like a target before their eyes,
and took great care to disdain the faults of their own selves.
Before the testing they entered into the examination of their thoughts,
and accused and rebuked the disgraceful things of body and soul.
For the [?] within them they appointed a judge between good and evil,
and they praised truth and censured falsehood without negligence.
Without negligence the true ones judged like the just,
and showed that human beings can judge truth justly.
There is no excuse, then, for lovers of excuses to excuse themselves,
for see, human beings from among humankind have judged justly.
You have no one, O man, to open his mouth in defence of your deeds,
nor can you say that the course of righteousness is hard.
It is very easy for you, if you wish to be justified,
as your just brothers were justified in generation after generation.
Stretch your mind toward the conduct of the sons of your race,
and see the truth of what I have said about their deeds.
Travel in the company of the books of the Spirit on the feet of the mind,
and walk well toward the just gathering of the labours they contain.

Take the road from the very beginning of humankind,
and set a mark at the lodging-places of their conduct.
Enter the archives of the writings of the King of kings,
and read the histories filled with hundreds of human victories.
Take up the chart on which the story of Abel is inscribed,
and look at him as he sacrifices a pure lamb and purity of soul.
Polish your mind of the filth of foul deceit,
and offer the sacrifice of purity of soul that resembles his.
Open your hearing to listen to the report of the day of his departure,
and listen to the voice that demands [?] for his youth.
Let the voice of the blood weigh [?] on the endurance of your soul,
and do not be grieved when you are wronged unjustly.
And when you have been comforted by the hope of the death of the firstborn of the dead,
turn the page and see his neighbour Enoch, who was translated.
Hear of a man clothed in corruptible members
who spread his wings and flew in the air above the passions.
