See a new wonder that befell a human being:
by his translation he [?] the order of humankind.
After his story, read the passage in which Noah is inscribed,
who by his gentleness calmed the threat that had decreed judgment.
The commandment had gone forth that decreed pains and sufferings upon humankind,
and with Noah the severity of the earth's chastisement subsided.
O soul filled with the rest of righteousness,
in whom humankind found rest from the turmoil of toilsome life!
From Noah let whoever wishes to learn rightly learn
that a human being can conquer the passions, even though he is a creature of senses.
Noah, gentle of soul, was a creature of senses like the men of his generation,
and in that very nature he won the war against passions and waters.
He also set his own goal [?] before him and gazed upon it purely,
and by his purity he became worthy to receive a high rank.
Through his blessings he annulled the curses of the decree of judgment,
and people began to be blessed in the name of the Creator.
With his offspring flowed the blessings his father had given him,
until they reached Abraham, the father of nations.
Upon Abraham rested the blessings that flowed down from Noah,
and in him the uncircumcised nations shared in the blessing of the just one.
By the Spirit of his will the Fashioner of all accomplished his will,
and made humankind share in the great wealth of his sweetness.
The wealth of his mercies the Merciful One gave through Abraham,
and he apportioned the wealth of the greatness of his love to his household.
With purpose he bound his will to his ordinance,
to make humankind zealous to walk in the way of his faith.
The Lover of humankind cast zeal upon humankind,
to bind them in the love of his name so that they would not forget him.
From Abraham his will passed on and came to dwell in Isaac,
and with him it expressed the voices of love and of [?].
Isaac was raised in his father's will toward his Lord,
and became heir of the promise of life, which does not lie.
In faith the righteous man fulfilled the voice of the promise,

and when he saw that it was true, he gave it to Jacob to be sustained by it.
Jacob made light of all the [?] of the harshness of sufferings,
and eagerly pressed on toward the rank of the house of Abraham.
True to him was the voice that calls, "Abram, Abram,"
and he arranged his ways so as to be a companion of that voice.
He bore and endured every affliction, full of forbearance,
so as not to be estranged from the promise of his fathers' house.
For twenty years the blameless one served for the wage of wives,
so that through wives he might become worthy of the wage that comes from God.
The Creator apportioned a good wage to human nature,
and the true ones were zealous to carry it on from one to another.
True to them was the voice of the promise, though very far off,
and they gazed at it in its distance as though it were near.
By their labours they proved the love of their minds,
how greatly they loved the name of the Creator, who honoured them.
The labour of Joseph is a witness, a revealer of revealed truth:
he became a slave, yet was not enslaved to desires.
His envious brothers sold him from lordship into slavery,
and he did not dispute how, or why, so unjustly.
:: 5: The Stranger ::
In the house of strangers the son of the household of faith served,
and while still a slave he received authority over the lords of the land.
Let Joseph be a beautiful mirror for those who are worn down,
how sufferings and people wore him down, yet he did not sin, but was humble.
The son of Jacob won the war of women and its [?],
and proved and revealed that a human being is master of his freedom.
Like a trumpet his labour cries out through all generations,
that humankind might hear of the victory of a human being in a human being.
Moses too, the companion of Joseph, won the war of sufferings;
he was persecuted and endured the sufferings of oppression.
The labourer of truth hired himself out to worshippers of demons,
yet the purity of his soul was not stained in an unclean dwelling.
Truly the true one served in the house of liars,
and did not grow slack through the falsehood of the fear of demons.
After his labour he saw the vision and heard the voice
that was interpreting new voices among earthly beings.
The voice that in the beginning called creation called the upright one,
so that by his hand he might proclaim the greatness of the power that made its works.
Like a painter it painted the world by its utterance,
and put in its colours before speakers, that they might gaze on it.
The tongue of the upright one became a pen for the hand of the Spirit,
and he painted the creatures in the form they had from the beginning.
A book of the Spirit he wrote for rational beings, beyond speech,
and made them meditate on how the world was established.
Like a sophist he interpreted [?] in human ears,
and made them hear the name of the Creator who made humankind.
The ascetic of the Spirit took up the task of teacher of the fear of truth,
and began to instruct the childishness of humankind in the fear of truth.
The great and skilful one raised his hand against the Egyptians,
and by their chastisement he cast fear on all peoples.

With harsh [?] the mouth of the Spirit's mouthpiece wrought devastation,
so as to confirm bodily beings all the more through spiritual things.
Like a physician his voice went among mortals,
and he bound up the labourers who were festering with the pains of their error.
Who will not marvel at the power of divine help,
that by a man's hand he healed human beings of their pains?
Through Moses he healed the sickness of iniquity in the sons of his people,
and showed that a man can heal human beings.
The righteous became physicians in generation after generation,
and their words were like medicines for the sores of iniquity.
Moses handed on his craft to Joshua son of Nun,
to heal the pains of the Israelites with the medicine of his words.
The skilful disciple of the great one took up the iron of the Spirit,
and cut the people off from the uncircumcision of body and soul.
The fervent one put on harsh zeal against iniquity,
and by his cutting he set free both members and mind.
See the deeds of just men who were of our race;
let us rise and become like the good likeness they showed on earth.
Let us look rightly to the good course of their conduct,
and walk upon the earth of our sojourning as they walked.
The life of time they reckoned an earthly dwelling;
like travellers they lodged in creation and soon moved on.
Job cries out that the good things of time are not true,
and sealed it by saying: "Naked I came, and naked I shall go."
Naked the righteous stood, without adornment,
and showed everyone that there is no profit in visible things.
The name of the Creator they loved and cherished above all things,
and set nothing visible alongside his hiddenness.
They gazed on what is invisible as if it were in plain sight,
and regarded revealed things as though they were not revealed.
O earthly one, who left the earth though he was earthly,
and ran toward heaven though he had not seen the dwelling above!
O son of man, clothed in corruptible members,
who made his body like adamant before trials!
Job was a son of man, a human being, O you humans,
and though he was human he won the struggles of turbulent sufferings.
Like waves, trials tossed his body and his soul,
yet he did not sink in the storms of despair.
Good hope held him fast like [?] in the grip of his tempests,
and steered his soul to the harbour of peace of his Lord's word.
As if at sea the victors lived amid sufferings,
and without fear they steered the ships of their minds.
The sailors of faith looked to the haven of peace,
and believed and affirmed that their rewards would not be withheld.
By faith they endured every suffering, hidden and revealed,
and left the pattern of their conduct to those who came after them.
One after another they journeyed on the paths of toilsome labours,
and came to rest and reached the dwelling full of blessings.
In Moses and Joshua, Barak [?] was formed, and Gideon was raised,

and in their service Jephthah and the great Samson laboured.
Samuel spread the wing of his course and passed beyond them,
and received the rank of prophecy and of priesthood.
From his youth he set out on the course of righteousness,
and with the number of the years of his life he lengthened his endurance.
He bore a true witness about himself before God,
that his judgment had not been stained by partiality.
David too, pure of mind, saw the path of his service,
and prepared himself to walk in spiritual labours.
Spiritually he was chosen, the labourer of the Spirit, to give pleasure,
and with spiritual beings he longed to please the Countenance on high.
He was eager to live according to the will of the One who chose him,
and had he not dozed a little and slept, he would have been perfect in his love.
Sin overcame him, as sleep overcomes a wakeful mind,
and though he was very [?], he erred once and grew wise not to err again.
Through his sin he learned the crafty devices of sin,
and no longer gave it room to enter his thoughts.
An evil thing, however evil, became for him a good occasion,
and he roused himself never to sleep again and let it make sport of him.
The trial proved a great and skilful master to his skilful mind,
and he guarded his treasure so that it would not be robbed by harms.
Come, all you traders, just and chaste and sinners,
and see how the upright one showed himself a hero against his folly.
Come, listen to his voice as he groans over his fall
and weeps for his iniquity with a voice like thunder.
The just one composed laments in prophecy,
and mournfully he wailed and wept over his folly.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" he said to his Lord,
"and removed from me the salvation of life because of my foolishness?"
O soul that knew the devices of the soul's repentance,
how you laboured to bind up the pains of your guilt!
O valiant man, mighty in strength, who fell into sin,
how valiantly you strove to take from yourself the name of the guilty!
O David, lover of righteous judgment,
how strictly you pursued the judgment of your own soul!
No one knows how to judge his own deeds so
as David judged himself in the things in which he sinned.
He sinned, and the garment of his soul was stained with innocent blood,
and he rose and washed it in the waters of thundering tears.
Once he erred, though he had not wished to err at all,
and without number he multiplied the sighs of the soul's repentance.
He turned back, and pleaded, and sought, and made amends for his folly,
and he remained in his rank and uttered the voices of prophecy.
Through his mouth the Spirit of revelation proclaimed his Exalted One,
who had let him hear the promise concerning his seed;
in his seed he received the promise of a life without end:

and he believed and affirmed that it would be, and it came to pass as he had prophesied.
The word he had uttered [?] in the stirrings of his soul came true in deed,
and from his seed arose a man who gives life to humankind.
His seed is the one who became for us the cause of life,
and his seed bears witness that he lives and has given life to those who believed in him.
Is there anyone, then, who perceives this salvation from the house of David,
and knows how to look at the conduct of the righteous who painted his likenesses?
Is there anyone persuaded by the revealing Spirit of prophecy,
whose mind is awake to understand the meaning of its mystery?
Is there anyone healed of the sickness of ignorance,
whose heart is steady enough to take the food of faith?
By faith the ancients looked to those who came before them,
and they strove and took on the likeness that each received from his fellow.
Hezekiah saw the likeness of David in his writings,
and took its image upon his limbs and upon his mind.
Precisely he painted the features that David's labours had pictured,
and [?] he passed on to perfection through his craft.
Josiah too strove manfully over what is written,
and of his own will he longed for everyone to be like him.
The righteous completed the fair [?] of the love of truth,
and longed to paint it in the human mind.
They left in the world a good cargo of their way of life,
so that those in need of a dwelling might trade with it and gain life.
They showed the kinds of spiritual commerce,
and people learned to trade in the things of the Spirit.
They built ships of love and bound them together in their minds,
and launched them on the stormy sea of bodily sufferings.
They brought a new craft among earthly beings,
so that people might become labourers in the heavenly land.
The diligent practised seamanship on the sea of the mind,
for without timber they cast [?] amid sufferings.
Like a [?] they bound their movements to their heads,
so that they might be [?] of strength for the course of the Spirit.
They steered the voyage of their deeds toward the meeting place on high,
and as if by a star they gazed at and searched out the things to come.
On high they made their faith fast like an anchor,
so that it would not be shaken by the blows of the winds of suffering.
The sufferers saw the harshness of sufferings, how harsh it is,
and they devised many means that help to overcome sufferings.
Skilfully they entered into battle with their sufferings,
and with gentleness they brought low the height of their [?].
Like athletes they went up from a world full of contests,
and came to rest in the harbour of the good hope of their promises.
In hope they finished the wearying course of their contests,
and that hope, the hope they had set on him, made them firm.
Into his hands, as faithful men, they committed what they had to entrust,
so that he might keep it for them until the day of recompense at the end.
Come then, O people, let us entrust our lives to the good Hope,
so that they may not be plundered by crafty thieves.

Let us lay up the treasures of our souls' labour in the place above,
where there is no passion, the moth [?].
Like a moth the passions corrupt the garments of our soul;
let us shake them out with the report of a life free from passion.
Bodily existence is a filthy dwelling, and our life [?] it;
let us wash it in the waters of the word of truth, the sweet spring.
Our body is earthenware, a glass vessel full of produce;
let us not bring evil habits near it, lest it be broken.
A pretext is what they seek against the crystal vessels of our senses,
and as if against earthenware the passions make ready to strike them.
The stones of the passions knock against our limbs at every hour,
and were they not fired by the Spirit, they would have perished.
By the power of the Spirit what remains of our worthless clay is kept safe,
and by his help life wells up within its sherds.
It is nothing without the power of the One who strengthens it,
and if he leaves it, it [?] and departs from life.
By the vitality of immortal life it lives and walks,
and if it is let go, it returns to its earth and becomes clay.
Our clay is clay, and our frame is kneaded with the waters of the passions;
let us not add more of the waters of the passions to it, lest they soften it.
Let the strength of our conduct prevail over its wateriness,
so that it is not lost through the slackness of its wateriness.
By faith let us bind up the looseness of our slack mud,
so that it does not dissolve and become spilled water.
With love let us wipe away the hateful sweat of our passions,
so that the stench of iniquity, odious to [?] the fair, may not linger in us.
With hope let us strengthen the building of our soul as with [?],
so that the plunderers of the passions may not strike it with [?].
Let us build truth on the foundation that the ancients laid,
and let us order the course of the words of our mouth after the pattern of their labours.
Let us imitate them in the labour of spiritual life,
and paint the image of their conduct in our own selves.
The First Sunday of the Fast

Tenth Discourse / for the First Sunday of the Fast / Refrain: Blessed is he who by his fasting has trodden out the road for us, so that we may journey [?] / to the place to which he has invited us. My brothers,

My mind took counsel with me and pronounced judgment on my thoughts,
that they had loved negligence and hated the discipline of the word of life.
My own nature rose against me in judgment and reproved me:
"Why have you hated spiritual profit?"
My thoughts rose up to plead the cause of truth
and condemned me severely for how far I had failed to give what was due.
My impulses became like creditors for the sins I had committed:
"What is the reason you have stood like a mute when it was time to pay your debt of words?"
The discernment within me spoke to me as if at a trial:
"Why have you sinned against yourself, keeping my senses from comfort?"

As if from sleep, the watchful mind called me and woke me:
"Rise, you who are sunk in sleep, and shake off the heaviness of your long sloth.
How long will you sleep and hold back from work?
Hear the voice of the morning that reproves the sluggard.
Enough! You have spent the days of your life in idleness;
leave off negligence and busy your soul with the labour of truth.
Come to the work even now, at the end of the day,
that you may still be found worthy to receive wages, as by grace.
And if the strength of your senses has grown weak through your affairs,
still pay back words as you can, as a debtor."
Then the mind, your witness, called me in secret and said to me:
"See that you do not hear that voice spoken to the wicked servant.
Behold, I have shown you the way of life; hold fast with the good.
Do not join the wicked who walk on the broad way.
Grieve over yourself, and rebuke the faults of your fellows,
and teach them to hate iniquity, which kills a man.
Lead them in the labour of love and faith,
and encourage them to gain the hope of what is to come.
Rouse them with the voice that promises the kingdom on high,
and stir them with the delight of the promises of life."
With these words the mind judged me as a debtor,
and I know that it counsels me well to turn to the way of life.
Come, mortals, let us walk in the path the righteous trod,
that we too may arrive at the fulfilment of the promised life.
Come, let us imitate their conduct in the impulses of the soul,
and set the goal of their striving before our minds.
From them let us learn what the Lord asks of His servants,
and in what things the will of Him who orders all things takes delight.
Let us ask them, as teachers of spiritual things,
to lead us from childhood to maturity.
Let the labours of their victories be our mirror,
and let our soul look to see whether any ugly stain of iniquity is upon it.

In body and soul they gathered spiritual wealth;
with visible senses and hidden impulses they won the victory.
They subdued the senses amid the natural passions of the body,
and calmed their impulses by striving against desires.
With due order they gave the body food, lest it grow brutish,
and in due measure the mind ran together with the members.
They cast the bridle of fasting on impulses and members,
and ran, senses and impulses together, to the appointed place of life.
By fasting, while it tames the body, it puts it under a yoke,
so that it may labour in the field of spiritual life.
This they had already learned in a mystery from the hidden Power:
that fasting serves to overthrow the lusts.
The help of the Spirit taught them the power of wisdom,
and like men of knowledge they governed body and soul well.
And if it is so, that the hidden Sign made them wise,
let us learn this from the son of Amram, who began with fasting.
He was the first to tread the way of fasting so longed for,
and at the end of his fast he received the wealth of the Spirit of revelations.
From it he first gathered the fruit of fasting that brings life,
and sowed it among men, that they might delight in eating of it.
He tilled it with the husbandry of spiritual fasting,
and received as his wages the rations of the world to come.
He went down first into the stadium of the lusts,
and wrestled with the desires in the craving for bread.
Forty days he stood in the contest, night and day,
and because he prevailed, the Sign gave him the crown of its secrets.
O mortal who forgot the nature of his mortality
and sought to be like the immortals, who need no nourishment!
O bodily one of flesh, who made light of the lusts
and busied his soul with the conduct of spiritual life!
O earthly one, who scorned the ways of the earth
and, while on earth, lived by the life of heaven!
O creature of dust, whose clay was kneaded with the waters of the passions,
yet whose valour proved not too weak to master the passions!
By fasting he first tested his members like an athlete,
and knew that he could wrestle in body and soul.

The One who watched his athletic prowess saw that he was ready,
and opened before him the stadium of hidden things.
Because he had searched the treasuries of the Spirit with the mind of the Spirit,
he touched the hidden things that are grasped by none but the Spirit.
The Sign revealed to him the power of the Being who is eternal,
and his strength was equal to the account of the making of all that came to be.
By the Spirit it was revealed to him to see the order His hands had made,
and he saw it with the mind and told in speech the ordering of all things.
With a hidden mind he read and meditated on hidden things,
and interpreted them in a clear voice to his fellows.
The Sign wrote a new book for him upon his thoughts,
and he copied its writing onto tablets of stone for the instruction of mankind.
Three times the letters of the Book of Life were inscribed,
so that whoever reads much and meditates again may become wise:
once upon the heart, once upon tablets, and again upon tablets,
twice by the Sign and once by the hand of men of flesh.
Here is the spiritual meditation which the Spirit taught;
come, disciples whom the Spirit has discipled, read and understand.
Here is the victory which the athlete of truth displayed by fasting;
come, you who fast, fix his zeal in your minds.
Here is the reward the King gave to the new labourer;
put on strength of soul as armour, draw near, and win.
By fasting the Knower of all tested the good servant,
and so repaid him wages that surpassed his diligence.
Why then did He keep him from bodily food
and make him live in the likeness of the immortal life?
Through him He depicted a mystery for bodily beings clothed in passions:
that in the place of the kingdom on high they will not live by food.
This, for the discerning, is also the reason for fasting:
that in the world to come men will be like him through their zeal.
Without food they will live when they are raised,
and he taught them to keep this in the life here below.
Renewal comes to mortality in that state,
and he depicted it as a mystery before their eyes, that they might grow like it.
By fasting he revealed to them the renewal of their members:
that they will strip off the garment of mortality, along with the outward form of eating.

And if fasting has revealed to us the mystery of the renewal of our body,
who would not hate earthly things and love the love of it?
If the making of all that came to be was searched out through it,
who would not strive in its toilsome labour, to be found worthy of mysteries?
If it made the son of Amram, who loved it, radiant with glory,
who would not despise earthly things and be tested by it?
If a mortal acquired radiance in the mystery of the Creator,
who would not scorn everything and long for it?
Moses set up fasting like a mirror,
and the eye of men of flesh flinched from gazing into it.
O members that were fearsome above all members!
O pupils from which the light of eyes fled away!
O shining one who chased away the light by the splendour of his own light! [?]
O lips, the doorway of a mouth of flesh,
which, when they opened, shook and terrified body and soul!
The face of that bodily man was fearsome and frightened bodies,
and the sound of the words of his mouth shook senses and impulses.
Come, see a wonder in the body of a man,
who fasted and shone so brightly that men feared to look at him.
By the fast of Moses let us gain hope of our renewal,
for if we fast from evils, our hope is sure.
Let us restrain our heart, together with our lips, from evils,
that we may be glorious like the son of Amram in body and soul.
Let the mind fast together with the members from all that is hateful,
and keep the impulses from desires, as from bread.
A human being is one person in body and soul,
that he may be wholly complete for the labour of life.
Let the impulses fast from pride, fury and anger,
as the members do from earthly food.
Let us wash from our heart the ugly envy that defiles the soul,
as each one washes away the dirt on his members.
Let not the mouth fast from food while the heart runs loose;
let not the outward senses abstain while the impulses wander.
With fasting let us heal the pains [?] of our body and the blemishes of our soul
before Him who knows the difference between hidden things and open.
Let us show Him the pains of our whole person, within and without,
for His power is enough to heal the body and cleanse the soul.

He is the good Physician who heals the sick freely,
who binds up with mercy the wound of iniquity and gives life.
He mixes grace and mercy and gives them as medicines,
and gives hope and love to drink in the cup of faith.
His cup is pleasant to whoever drinks it in faith,
for the sweetness of endless life is hidden in it.
He is a sweet spring that flows for all continually,
and those who drink never tire of the sweetness of its water.
Come, minds that the heat of iniquity has dried up,
quench the thirst of your thoughts with the cup of sweetness.
Come, you dissolute who ran riot and strayed from what is fitting,
draw near to fasting and gain the taste of discernment.
Come, you envious whom foolish jealousy has troubled,
and change the anger of the nature within you by the sweetness of fasting.
Come, you oppressors, wicked in your deceit,
repay with alms the groans of those you have oppressed.
Come, you fornicators who defiled the holiness of your members,
receive purity by sharing in the labour of fasting.
Come, you thieves who plundered treasures unjustly,
fast and humble yourselves, that you may yet find mercy through contrition of soul.
You proud, bring low the hard height of your minds,
and put on fasting, that chaste garment wonderful to behold.
You gluttons, mourn over the greatness of your belly with the voice of moderation,
and when it craves, shut the door of fasting in its face.
You lovers of money, scatter money in the land of fasting,
that you may carry off the wealth of righteousness that does not perish.
You lovers of glory, flee from glory, that deceitful snare,
and expose its deceits in the light of fasting, which gladdens the soul.
Fast, O faster, from food and from glory too,
lest love of glory creep in and undo your fast.
Keep your lips from murmuring as from bread,

lest the words of your mouth destroy the labours of your soul.
Spread the veil of pure fasting over your eyes,
that you may not look lewdly with an ugly glance.
Keep from your eyes the wanton drink the body craves,
and give them to drink the chaste cup of holiness.
The eye is weak, and a weak gaze is set in it;
shut in its face the door of a chaste will.
Wash your eyes, O women, in the clearness of fasting as in a mirror,
and polish the blemishes of your minds as you do your faces.
Make chaste the gaze of your thoughts as with garments,
that the will of the soul may match the form of the body.
Do not adorn yourself with outward garments, O daughter of Eve;
put chastity on your mind as you put it on your ornaments.
Order the running of your heart's eyes like your steps,
that the broken-hearted may not stumble through your wantonness.
Reduce the adornment on your members and adorn your mind;
polish your thoughts, as you do your face, with purity of soul.
See that you do not become a cause of stumbling through the adornment of your faces,
lest you receive a double judgment, for sinning and for causing others to sin.
Hear from the Law the charge of your great iniquity,
which reproaches the wickedness of your nature for every iniquity.
Behold, I have shown you from the Law, from the pure One:
fear the punishments and ask for mercy while there is time.
Put on the strength of fasting as armour, men and women,
for there is no distinction in the new mystery that He depicted for us by His hand.
Fasting revealed to us the single equality of that state,
how the body puts off corruption and its outward form as well.
Let us fast purely, as befits the mystery of renewal,
that the truth of the mystery may not be belied through our weakness.
In body and soul let us fast alike from all that is hateful,
lest the fasting of the mouth be hindered by the mind.
Let no iniquity be mixed into the sacrifice of our fast,
for if it is defiled it is not accepted by the Knower of all.
The Knower of all takes no pleasure in sacrifices of iniquity,
nor is the body's fasting without the soul's pleasing to Him.

The Jews fasted and offered sacrifices and were not accepted,
for the fear of demons was mixed with their sacrifices.
The Hebrews fasted with the outward senses and not with the impulses within,
and the One who sees all gave no reward to the empty fast.
They humbled the body, but the heart did not come down from its pride;
they appeared fair outwardly, and He sent them away empty of reward.
The insolent falsely demanded the reward of fasting,
and the prophet rebuked them in the Spirit: "You are utterly astray."
"Why," they said, "have we fasted, and you do not look at the fasting of our body?
Why have we humbled ourselves, and you did not regard the affliction of our soul?"
O deceitful work of boasting, idle at all times,
which yet demands wages from the Lord of the vineyard like a diligent worker!
O foolish pride, which is outwardly bare of fruit,
yet argues impudently with the Husbandman: "Look, you have wronged me!"
The revelation of the Creator's mystery spoke forcefully through a tongue of flesh
and rebuked them, for they had fasted and humbled themselves falsely.
"Do not fast," it says, "with such a fast"—so the prophet interpreted—
"I do not want humiliation of body together with pride of soul.
This is the fast my will asks of those who fast:
to loose the bonds that iniquity has tied within the mind.
If you want your fast to be pure of blemish,
show pity to your neighbour with love and mercy, and behold, I have accepted it."
See, the prophet of the Spirit has taught us the kinds of fasters,
that we should not be like the Jews who fasted and were sent away empty.
See, the Hidden One has shown us openly how we may please Him:
by purifying our soul together with our members before the eyes of the Hidden One.
See, through Isaiah He has made plain to us the will of His love,
that at all times we may be ordered by His will in the things that please Him.
Let us hate boasting, which destroys the labours of body and soul,
and love the goal of humility, which heals freely.
Let us root out from our mind guile, bitter with thorns,
and plant peace, which calms all things within our thoughts.
Guile is a snare hidden in the soul as in a trap,

which hunts man down like a beast for the destruction of death.
In the name of righteousness guile leads astray as with bait [?],
and draws our nature down to eat the bitterness of death.
Let us then cast out [?] the guile that is hidden within our mind,
and so draw near to the labour of fasting with purity of soul.
Let not guile be hidden in our fast as in a garment,
as the men of Jezreel did, who fasted and played a part.
Let not slander serve in our abstinence,
as that foolish woman did to Naboth the pious.
Here let us see the great outrage that guile committed,
which cloaked itself in the form of fasting and served murder.
Tremble, you who fast, at the report of a murder committed during a fast,
and fear lest guile be hidden in your minds.
See that there is no one who wishes to defraud like Ahab,
and forges guile to kill his neighbour and inherit his goods.
And even if the one who defrauds like Ahab does not kill,
to the Searcher of hearts he is a murderer, because he coveted.
To the will of the soul are assigned both reward and Gehenna;
according as it wills, it is justified or condemned.
The son of Omri too willed and coveted what was not his,
and the sword of the soul's will killed his neighbour.
By his will he killed Naboth, not by the sword;
he was the king, and he killed not with his hands but with his heart.
Jezebel hid Ahab's sword in a sheath,
and so put it in the hand of guile, and it killed the pious man.
She concealed the murder in letters, so that it would not be discovered,
and stamped them with the king's seal, so that they would not be exposed as false.
"Proclaim a fast," she says—O foolish woman, who hated fasting!—
"and seat Naboth at the head of those fasting"—thirsting for blood—
"and bring witnesses of falsehood against the truthful man,
and let them put out the report that he cursed the king and God."

O will that blasphemes the God of all at every moment,
which through guile seeks insult in the guise of love!
When did you ever love the name of the Creator, O foolish woman,
and how did you honour the king's commands lawfully?
O how cunning is your guile, cunning creature that begets murder!
There is none like you except yourself or your crafts.
O how deceitful you are, evil worm of the mind,
who in the guise of love spew bitterness like a dragon!
Come, see, O race of Eve, the wickedness of Eve,
who decreed a fast and shed blood in the name of righteousness.
Hear and lament bitterly, O rich women,
over this outrage that a king's wife committed on earth.
Women, give good counsel to your husbands,
that you may not be condemned like Jezebel, who counselled murder.
Men, do not be persuaded by the counsels of wanton women,
lest you be exposed like Ahab, who coveted and was exposed.
Let no one mix guile into his fast like the wicked,
lest he be condemned by the sentence passed on those who shed blood.
Let each be zealous with a righteous zeal like Elijah,
who rebuked guile, exposed iniquity and avenged blood.
In his fast let lovers of fasting imitate how strong he was,
who fasted from bread and from desires, was zealous and prevailed.
He too was like Moses in his fast of forty days;
night and day he fasted, as he travelled to the meeting place of peace.
At the end of his fast he was found worthy of revelation like the son of Amram,
and the voice taught him love and mercy, as it taught Moses.
Behold, these are fasters who fulfilled the fast in deeds;
come, let us imitate their deeds, even a little.
See, the hidden Word has taught us through two men
that whoever is seen to labour as they did receives a crown.
Let their conduct, then, be the target for our soul,
and let us become like them through a will that is clear and pure.
Let us humble our soul like the son of Amram, who hated boasting,
and rebuke iniquity like Elijah, who was rightly zealous.
They bore the burden of the day like diligent workers;
come, let us labour, even now at the end of the day.
And if the pace of our journey falls short of the ancients,
come, let us join those in the middle, whose way is easier for us.

If the labour of Moses and of Elijah is too hard,
here is Daniel, whose fast is easy and whose labour is gentle.
For three weeks Daniel fasted in body and soul,
and purified his heart, together with his members, from hateful things.
At the end of his fast he too received the reward of his labour:
the Spirit of revelation, which announced the changes of the nations.
O gift which, though greater than those who receive it,
is not diminished when divided into portions!
O receivers who took their reward from a single treasury,
and grew rich, while the treasure remained as it was!
He made the children of His house equal in a single reward,
lest they be grieved if one were honoured above another.
They received one gift equally from one treasury,
because their wills were directed toward one target.
It is fitting for us to imitate them in the labour of fasting,
and to run always in the footsteps of their conduct.
Let us hold to the way with them by a spiritual will,
that they may lead us to the consummation of the renewal of all things.
In the way of fasting let our body walk together with our mind,
with the few who journeyed and reached the place of life.
Let no one keep company with the many on the broad way,
lest with the many he hear, "Go to destruction."
Christ our Head trod the narrow way for us by His words;
come, let us walk in it, that we may hear from Him, "Come, rejoice."
He too walked in it first by fasting, with vigour,
and journeyed and arrived at the fulfilment of perfection.
In the manner of servants He too became like them, and fasted, and was tempted; [?]
and after His fast He defeated the hosts of the spirits. [?]
Forty days, night and day, He stood in the contest
and in the [?], being proved in the strength of His soul.

He limited His fast to forty days, like the ancients,
so that no one would think His nature was merely spiritual.
In the manner of His brothers and fellows He resembled them in His fast,
so that He would not seem strange to the eyes of those who saw Him, as though He were not a man.
He was human, from a humanity clothed in passions,
and it was fitting for Him to be like a man in every respect.
It is not I who rashly call Him by the name of man;
Paul showed that His nature and ours are one.
"One," he says, "is He who sanctifies man, and man who is sanctified,
and for this reason He was not ashamed of the name of His brothers."
Elsewhere he again named Him with the name of a son of man,
calling Him one Mediator and one son of man.
And if the heretics stumble at the word of Paul,
let them hear from Him that He too called Himself a man:
"What," He says, "do they say of me [?]—that I am a man?
And why do you seek to kill a man who proclaims the truth?"
See, He called Himself and His brothers by the name of man, according to His nature;
why then do the heretics wrong Him over the name of humanity?
With hatred they hate the nature of our body, as Mani did,
and for this reason they quarrel with us as though we were strangers.
They too have fallen into that sickness of denying the resurrection,
and whoever preaches the resurrection of the body sets himself against them.
Even now I have turned to look at the sickness [?] of their minds,
and my word has strayed from the course of the way of fasting.
From the beginning my word held to the way of fasting,
for love of the men who conquered through their fasting drew me on.
Lightly my thoughts ran over their stories,

so that I might set them like a mirror before those who fast. / The reason for the fast of the King's servants has drawn my mind / to recount the story of the King and of his servants, who fasted and triumphed. / I wished to show the powers of fasting before those who fast, / and I have brought the King and his servants as witnesses to confirm my words. / It is fitting, too, for one who judges according to the law / to confirm his words with documents from the archives. / Let the treasuries of the King's judgment recount every deed, / and see, the words of our mouth are confirmed to the hearers. / This is the reason for the daily fast, for the discerning: / that as one fasts from bread, so one should fast from wickedness too. / It is also a symbol of that incorruptible state / in which bodies live without food, like spiritual beings. / There is in it also a reason for restraint from evil deeds: / that when the body is humbled by fasting, it may set its course in order. / The forty-day fast is a remedy that the spiritual physicians / devised for the health of humankind. / For they saw that human nature was worn down by the daily round, / so they purified it, and gave it a short season like a medicine. / At a fitting time they set the bounds of the fast for humankind in its infancy, / and bound people to self-denial through longing for the feast. / They laid the fast down as a foundation for the building of love, / so that by a good way of life each might build the temple of his soul. / Like a roof on top of the building they completed it with the feast, / so that each might delight in the spiritual temple of the mystery of the resurrection. / The reason for the feast is the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the soul, / and they rightly taught that body and soul should fast together. / Inscribed in it, too, is the victory of the King on high, / who conquered and gave victory, who rose, was raised, and will raise all. / At the end of the forty-day fast he set the seal on his victory, / and taught his servants to remember him on the day of his victory. / In his fast he revealed his victory to them, so that they might become like him, / and by his victory he taught them to prevail over sufferings.

He set the bounds of the courses of perfection at forty days, / so that the journey might be light for anyone travelling to the meeting place beyond. / He made the feast of his victory like a haven of life, / which those who travel the way of righteousness reach. / On the day of his resurrection he encouraged those who are in the body / not to grow slack when their limbs grow weak. / At the end of the fast he showed them the mystery of the resurrection: / that when they do battle with the [?], they will rise with him. / “Put to death, then, your members,” Paul proclaimed, / meaning that we should put to death the deeds done by the members. / So let us bury the passions of our body in the tomb of the fast, / that at the end of the fast, on the day of resurrection, we may be found worthy of life. / Along with the lips, let the impulses and the senses fast together, / and let us lay the deeds of mortality as if in a tomb. / Let the eyes fast, so that they do not gaze frivolously, / and the hearing too, so that it does not take in slander. / Let the tongue, the advocate of the impulses and the members, fast, / and let it render praise as a pledge for its companions. / Let the hands fast from the work of theft, / and the feet with them from running to take what belongs to others. / Let the mind fast from thoughts, both the intellect and the heart, / lest passions enter the soul as food enters the belly. / Let us fast from bread and from all passions, hidden and open, / so that the Hidden One may give a reward to our body and our mind. / This is the fast that the Creator has chosen and loves: / when body and soul are estranged from everything hateful. / So it is fitting for one who fasts with discernment / to cast away from himself all shameful deeds. / This is the fast of which he said that it can drive out demons, / and that, like an athlete, it does not turn away from the crown of victory. / By this the heralds of the word of life also triumphed, / and the power of the Spirit exalted them in the eyes of those who saw them. / Come, you mortals weak in strength, take refuge in it, / for its strength is able to give strength in weakness. / Come, take up its armour and arm yourselves with it as is fitting, / so that by its hand you may conquer the Adversary and his hosts. / With its armour let us fight the Strong One who fights against us, / and with its help let us tear down the height of his rebellion.

Let each one say, with the mouth of those who fast, to the Rebel: / “Go away, Evil One; your strength is weak against the fast.” / Let us shoot the arrows of the fast into the ranks of the Slanderer, / and see, his hosts are scattered from our camp. / With soul and body let each one give praise in the Spirit / to him who trod out for us the way to the heights through his victory. / Response: Blessed is he who by his fast set us free from slavery to corruption.
On the Generations of Our Lord

Memra 12: On the Generations of Our Lord. / Again by the same author, his twelfth memra: / on the generations of our Lord. / It is recited on the Wednesday at the beginning of the Fast. / Refrain: / Blessed is he who by his fasting trod out for us the path by which to walk to the life that has no end. / My brothers,

Satan heard new words among mortals,
for men and heavenly beings were telling of peace for mankind.
The rebel heard from Gabriel of peace for mankind,
and dismay seized him: what is this new thing that has happened?
The chief of the angels greeted the daughter of mortals,
and the envious one trembled at the good news sent to mankind.
"Peace be to you, Mary," the spiritual one cried in Mary's ears,
and the Evil One wailed, and the demons gathered at the sound of his wailing.
"Our Lord is with you," the angel cried to the daughter of mortals,
and the Accuser's groans were doubled at the peace of mankind.
The messenger called the son of the daughter of men "Son of the Most High,"
and the Hater was put to shame, and his hosts sat down in mourning.
The man of the Spirit announced these things among earthly beings,
and the demons shook, and Satan, the head of their ranks, trembled.
One spiritual being announced his conception to one woman,
but on the day of his birth many cried good tidings to mankind.
Spiritual beings cried good tidings to bodily beings,
and the rebel died at the sound of the tidings of life for mankind.
The sound of good tidings was spoken from every mouth;
men and spiritual beings rejoiced, while the demons grieved.
Simeon made a clear voice heard: "This is he who is to come,"
and as in a furnace he tests men by the dawning of his light.
Anna the prophetess was telling of the manner of his redemption,
and the Hebrew women made response after her words.
The voice of the barren woman's son thundered louder than thunder,
as he cried out that the time was fulfilled and the time had come.
"The time of the law has come to its end," he prophesied,
"and the time of the spiritual way of life has drawn near."
He named the Pure One a pure Lamb who cleanses blemishes,
by whose sacrifice iniquity is blotted out and life is given.
The messenger called the one who sent him "Lord of mysteries,"
and showed that he is Lord and also the Judge who tries all.
These words men and heavenly beings proclaimed,
and the Father set the seal of his voice on them and sealed them.
These words the rebel, the hater of mankind, heard,
and he grew bitter at words that were strange to him.
New words were spoken by speakers
about a son of man who resembled a man and was higher than man.
The rebel too looked on him as on a man,
and grew bitter at words that were strange to him.
The rebel, the hater of mankind, stood between two things,
and did not know what to call him, man or God.
To call him man—the words spoken about him were higher than that;
to call him God—his bodily nature testified that he was a man.
The makeup of his body showed him to be wholly man,
and the power of his words proclaimed him to be divine.
His conception and his birth told of his humanity,
and his heralds told of the Being who dwelt in him.
Satan too was probing the power of that Being:
how is he a man, and how is his power higher than man?
The senseless one was astonished at the greatness of his power,

and he was tormented over the two in the one man.
A womb conceived him; his birth was seen by the senses; knees carried him;
and this belongs to man, to have senses that can be perceived.
He was conceived from a word, without bodily union,
and this is higher than a son of man of flesh.
He sucked milk, received nurture, grew weary from toil;
to this natural things bear witness, that he is of man's nature.
He was baptized like men, by a son of man, as one in need,
and this is plain: there was need, so far as his humanity was concerned.
The Holy Spirit came down; the Father proclaimed, "This is my Beloved";
here is a divine power that is mightier than man.
One son of man came up from the water, in body and soul,
and the Spirit came down and stayed with him, never departing.
The second Adam was led by the power of the Spirit,
and the Adversary was astonished at his hidden power.
Cruel pangs were striking the Accuser,
and he debated whether to approach him or not to approach.
Like a woman in labour the one bitter in [?] was in anguish,
and he pondered by what devices he could bring his [?] to completion.
The rebel nursed hateful desires in his mind,
and longed to approach him as one approaches a man.
"Who will grant me to approach him?" he mused,
"and test through sufferings whether he can suffer?"
He looked on the son of Adam as on Adam,
and hoped to lead Adam astray as he had led Adam.
After Adam's fashion he thought to do battle with him,
yet he was afraid of the Hidden One who shone forth in him.
He counted him one of the righteous, a vessel of wrath against him,
and he was bitter enough to bring his case against him openly.
For thirty years he was tormented by the words spoken of him,
until he heard that voice: "This is my Beloved."
That voice cast trembling among his hosts,
and they began to cry out from the anguish of their minds.
As if from sleep, the sunken ones were startled at the Father's voice,
and gathered together to knot a plot against the mystery of our life.
The rebel and his hosts knotted a plot of iniquity,
to wage a contest with the champion who was stronger than he.
The deceiver armed himself with the weapon of his deceit,
and began to stir up trouble as at that time in Paradise.
He likened this time to that time,
and did not know that the one time was not like the other.
He called the second Adam "Adamic,"
and in that same likeness he tempted him with the passions of the body.
He kept reminding the bodily one of the passions of the body,
and offered him all kinds of appetites, as to one who loved them.
He longed to go out with him into the wilderness—he who loves the wilderness—
where no food for the hour is to be found for earthly beings.
Like an athlete he was luring him to the fight,
to see whether there were in him the kinds of appetites that were like Adam's.
He armed himself with all the passions of Adam,
for he feared that perhaps he might escape his temptations.
The words spoken of him were driving him on to the fight,

and he contrived to approach him with skill.
Skillfully the craftsman worked the implements of his armour,
and gathered stratagems, and so brought against him every kind of combat.
Crafty stratagems he set out like weapons in his mind,
and he marshalled his strength and hid the weapon of his cunning.
He sought a time in which to show every kind of his wiles,
and to suit the time he devised stratagems held in reserve behind stratagems.
He readied the devices of his deceit for the time,
and he longed, and yet feared, to reveal his deceit.
He drew near himself before he would join open battle,
and examined himself while he probed, lest he be brought low.
The war brought him face to face with a warrior stronger than he,
and he worried that he might become a laughingstock to men.
These things the hater of man pondered within himself,
while the Lover of man made ready a man to do battle with him.
With the armour of the Spirit the Spirit armed the man who is from us,
and sent him to wage the contest in the wilderness with the mighty ones.
To match the Adversary's preparations he prepared him for the match,
and the athlete went out to where the chief of wrestlers had sought him.
Like an athlete the athlete of righteousness went out,
girded wholly, in every part, with the armour of the Spirit.
The Power that had chosen him sent the hosts of the height with him,
to be witnesses and spectators of his contest.
The Lord of the world made the world like a theatre,
and the hosts of the height were judges of the contestants' match.
It was a contest—on behalf of the world was the contest—
and it was fitting that he gathered the heavenly beings to praise him.
They had been in sorrow since the time Adam was defeated,
and were waiting for when Adam would win the victory in Adam.
Those who loved our race were preparing for the day of victory,
and longing for our race to win through the son of our race.
For forty days the wrestlers stood one against the other,
the chief of the air and the man who is from us—a marvellous sight.
A marvellous sight was shown to the eyes of the spectators,
as spirit and body fought without hands.
Without hands the bodily one fought;
spiritually he held fast the chief of the air.
He chose toilsome fasting as the weapon to fight with,
lest the Accuser think his strength came from food.
Without food he went into battle with the mighty one,
so that the demons might see that, though he was a man, he was higher than man.
Through abstinence he was teaching the dull-witted
that he had with him another power, stronger than all.
The head of their ranks was probing the greatness of his power;
therefore he prepared combat of every kind and every form.
The rebel set out every form of attack that is used against men,
lest he escape his wiles and he himself become a laughingstock.
Great was the contest that suddenly confronted the warrior,
and it was not like the contest he had waged with every generation.
Great dread was terrifying the bold-souled one,
and he was afraid to grapple with the bodily one.
In his dread and his audacity he went on testing the bodily one,
and the bodily one gave him an opening to approach him in the guise of hunger.

For forty days the Faster fasted from appetites,
and at the end his nature demanded what is natural.
In that nature Adam's nature was being tested;
therefore he limited his fast to the fast of his fellows.
Satan too took heart from this point,
that he had not exceeded the number of days that the fasters had fasted.
The rebel looked at the hunger in the bodily one's body,
and drew near him and saw that it was a body overcome by hunger.
He saw that the senses of his body had weakened, like those of all bodies,
and thought to himself: "Now is the moment for the body's appetites."
He recalled that moment in Paradise
when he saw Adam longing to eat the fruit.
He looked on the son of Adam as on Adam,
and in that same likeness he offered him the desire for fruit.
He stirred up the body's appetite in the body of the bodily one,
and, as one would a body, urged him to ask for food.
By food he had persuaded the house of Adam to go astray with him,
and he thought he would persuade the Son too, as he had them.
The persuasion of bread he took up first, as his opening hold,
and began to show his adversary the forms of his privation.
"Say a word, so that it becomes bread," the cunning one declared,
"and see, it will be known that you are truly the Son of God.
Command the senseless natures as Creator,
and do something worthy of the name by which he called you.
Change the stones from the hardness that resides in them,
and give them the nature of bread that can be eaten.
Through deeds show the proof of the words spoken about you,
and see, the greatness of your rank will be revealed to the eyes of the onlookers.
Before the eyes of many the Father proclaimed, 'This is my Beloved':
if you are the Beloved, work a wonder and confirm that you are loved.
Thousands heard that voice: 'You are the Son of God';
[?] your name by a deed that comes from you.
Do, like your Father, a work that resembles the work of his hands,
and let rational and mute creatures raise their hands at the tribunal of your authority.
Speak a word full of wonder before the onlookers,
and let those who behold the wonder of your words' power praise you.
You are in the wilderness, and food for the hour is not found with you;
command the natures, and let them feed you as befits a lord.
You are Lord, according to that voice that came to you;
accomplish your will by the perfect power of a spoken word.
See to your need, as the righteous, your fellows, saw to theirs,
and do something by which your body's need may be supplied.
Your fellows too fasted a fast like this one of yours,
and after a time they obtained the means to supply their needs.
Yours is greater: the election of your name far surpasses theirs;
work a wonder that befits one who is greater than his fellows.
It greatly befits you to make one thing by changing another,
so that your deed may be a proven witness to the word of your mouth."
These things the chief of the air declared to the head of our race,
thinking he had brought him down to his enticements.
This hold the deceiver took first,

and he was badly mistaken: his nails found no grip on the anointed body.
The one practised in contests waged this contest first,
and the bodily contestant made him a laughingstock.
In this combat he tested the strength of the one proud of his nature,
and the nature clothed in mortality brought his strength low.
The Spirit brought the bodily one into the contest of the spirit,
and the spiritual one lost, and the body, weighed down with senses, won.
Out of bodily desire he fashioned the enticements,
and offered them to the bodily one in the guise of gifts.
Contemptible gifts the contemptible one offered to the one wise of mind,
and he turned them back with contempt and shame upon the one who deserved them.
The second Adam flung the Evil One's gift back in his face,
just as the Creator also dealt with Cain's offering.
He trampled the deceiver's counsel like dung,
and mocked and laughed at his insipid wiles.
Wisely he gave the senseless one an answer,
and from the law he stopped the blasphemer's mouth.
By the law he settled the case of the Evil One's guilt,
so that he would know he was contending with him according to the law.
With one word he untied the knot of ten thousand words,
in what is written: "Not by bread does a son of man live."
"Not by bread does a man live," he answered the cunning one,
and the crafty stratagems of every form vanished and came to nothing.
The Creator is able to keep a man alive without bread,
and a word in the Creator's name suffices in place of everything.
The shameful ones were put to shame in the confidence they had boasted of,
and he moved off and fled to devise other stratagems.
Stratagem for stratagem he kept changing against the contestant,
thinking perhaps he had found some hope for his cunning.
The guilty one hoped a vain hope against the innocent one,
and did not know that his hope of victory was cut off.
The shamefaced one was fighting for victory,
supposing that there were stratagems that work against man.
The deceiver stretched cunning snares for the one perfect in soul,
and hid them under comely beauty that captivates the eyes.
In an eye-catching display he set out every comely kind of beauty:
gold and silver, beryl too, and pearls.
By illusion he set out everything when there was nothing,
and made them stand there when they did not truly exist.
Because he looked on the man who is from us as on a man,
he set out likenesses of what man loves.
The love of money is greatly loved by mortals,
and so he kept its allure for the second contest.
In the first contest he fought him with the desire for fruit,
and in the second with the love of money, the sea of his ruin.
In this sea he had seen that the mind of man is drowned,
and he spread his [?] upon the dry land before our Redeemer.
With a flood of silver he covered the earth like water,
and did not know that the one wise of mind was mocking him.
In that same guise he set out his phantoms,
while the One who sees what is hidden and what is open scorned every kind of his baseness.

He set out, as if they were real, comely kinds of beauty that did not exist,
and drew near the contestant to probe his strength.
He opened a theatre full of evil hidden things,
and the fool went in and stood among golden things, though there was no gold.
The one proud of mind cried out insolently to the humble one:
"Come, see, O man, something not easily shown.
Come, see, O man," said the Evil One to the man who is from us,
"the whole world, which I hold under my authority.
Mine is the world and the glories within it,
and I give it to whomever I wish, if he worships me.
Only worship me as a lord who rules over all,
and take the world in return for the confession of your mouth.
Acknowledge my lordship and call me Lord with love,
and I will give you a good reward: the world and its wealth.
The world and its wealth I give you for a single word;
and you, return to me the worship of love, lovingly.
Take the world, O man who belongs to the world,
and leave with me as a pledge the word of your mouth that you worship me.
Give me your mouth for a moment as a pledge,
and take for yourself something boundless
in [its] revenues [?].
See how great is the greatness of the rank of the whole world,
and how small the worship of a word that you pay me.
See how lavish I am in my love toward man, O son of man,
and I demand nothing burdensome of those who love me.
Love alone is what I require of the one who obeys me;
obey me, and see how generous I am to the one who obeys me."
These words the Evil One spoke in the hearing of the son of our race,
and the son of our race was roused to zeal against the deceiver's deceits.
The Zealous One, the Good, put on zeal for what is fair,
for the Good One heard a servant seeking the worship due to his master.
The Mighty One shot at him the arrow of rebuke,
and pierced his heart, and the gall lodged in him poured out.
Evil gall was lodged in the evil-minded one,
and our Lord exposed it with the plain word of his mouth.
From the Scriptures he returned an answer to the adversary,
and taught him the proper order, so that he would know he was nothing.
"Have you heard that it is written—or have you not heard, O rebel—
that the Lord is One, and to him alone the worship of all is due?
One is the Lord who rules over all as God,
and no other has any share in his divinity.
The name of God does not befit one who is not God,
nor may a thing that was made rise to the rank of the Maker.
You too are a thing that was made, O arrogant one who burns with pride;
know your nature, and do not exalt yourself against your Maker.
Know that you are made, a servant made by his Maker,
and do not arrogantly seize for yourself your Lord's rank.
Cease, O rebel, from the speeches of your arrogance,
and do not recite to me the hateful fabrication of your ingratitude.
I know you, and the speeches of your cunning,

and I do not forget that you go astray and lead mankind astray.
Go away, deceiver; go astray in your deeds, as you are accustomed,
and take the illusion of your heap of silver—dash it in your own face.
You gave nothing, and you will receive nothing of what you plotted;
you offered phantoms, and your combat has been in vain.
Go, fight your fight with yourself,
and take as your wage the shame of your guilt.
Go, guilty one, see how loathsome you are in yourself,
and keep away from contests with the true, lest they expose you to disgrace.
See, your guilt has been exposed in two contests;
go, prepare yourself another contest, and lose a third time.
Three witnesses raise their hands in every case,
and for the third time I convict you, in three rounds."
The wrestler withdrew from the contest of two rounds,
and changed the place and the styles of his wrestling.
He fled from the wilderness to where he thought he would win,
and began to set out battle in the inhabited world before the eyes of spectators.
In the midst of the inhabited world he wanted to display his combat,
saying: "When I win, men will be witnesses of my victory."
The one full of guilt was fighting for victory,
and did not know that he was heaping defeat upon defeat on himself.
The unclean one went up to the holy temple to fight,
where everyone could plainly see his guilt.
The lowest of the low brought the Lord up to a great height,
and stood there raving with the madness he was used to.
"Throw yourself down," he said, "from this height to the depth below,
and if you remain unharmed, you are a true Son.
God called you 'Son of God' before the eyes of many;
fly upon the air, as befits a Son of God.
You are a righteous man—the voices that came to you bear witness;
come down from the height, and see, the hosts of the height will receive you.
It is written of the righteous that they reach the ground unharmed,
guarded by spiritual angels.
You are one of the righteous, and your rank is even greater than the righteous;
test your righteousness by the care taken over your righteousness.
Test your power by the care of the heavenly beings,
who will receive you on their hands, as it is written.
They will not leave you in hardship, however hard it may be,
since they have been commanded by God to keep you.
Test the help of your guardians through deeds,
and see, the company of the righteous will take heart to walk in righteousness.
Tread the way, by a trial, toward hardships,
and show everyone the crown of reward that comes from your righteousness."
Oh, the cunning one—how he schemed to hide his snares!
Oh, the nimble one—how he leapt over the hidden snares!
Oh, the trickster—how he toiled to weave his stratagems!
Oh, the wise one—how wisely he cut them through!
Oh, the fighter—how he fought to fulfil his desire!
Oh, the discerning one—how he took thought to win in due order!
Oh, the spiritual one—how his stratagems flew in spiritual fashion!
Oh, the bodily one—how he braced [?] his senses and mastered them!

O the contest that took place on earth, unexpectedly, / that one of the world [?] should wrestle with a spiritual being! / One of bodily nature made contest with a spiritual one, / and men began to contend in the spirit. / By the power of the Spirit the bodily one overcame the one mighty in strength, / and the hosts of heaven [?] marvelled at the victory of a man. / Host upon host, the spiritual beings stood by at this contest, / and they wondered how the body could overcome the spirit. / Great astonishment was voiced among their hosts: / “What is this new thing that has happened in our midst?” / They saw that a mortal had contended with the strong one, / and they marvelled and were amazed that mortality had defeated the tyrant. / They gazed on the victory of the man and the defeat of the evil one, / and praised the power of the Creator who had given victory to a man. / “Glory to the power that gave victory to a man!” the spiritual beings cried out, / “He has reconciled the world to his majesty through a son of man.” / One son of man made contest with Satan, / and Satan was defeated, and a man won and won the victory for mankind. / The son of man won in the struggle he waged with the strong one, / and the strong one was defeated in the contest with the son of man. / The hosts on high were watching this contest, / and they wondered at the unexpected victory. / Unexpectedly they saw victory and defeat, / and they acclaimed and magnified him who had exalted the race of man. / The race of man had been defeated and handed over in pledge to Satan, / and a son of man arose and paid the debts of the children of his race. / Through the desire for the fruit Adam had been defeated by the counsel of the evil one, / and through hunger the son of Adam overcame Adam's conqueror. / The wrong [?] done to Adam, Adam required of Adam's enemy, / and he humbled him and loosed him from the power of his tyranny. / Before the spiritual beings he wrestled with him openly, / and lifted him and threw him down and made him a laughingstock and a byword. / He entered with him into the stadium full of sufferings, / and kicked those hard goads aside with the feet of reason. / The rebel set all the sufferings before the bodily one, / and divided them into three bouts. / Three bouts the fool wrestled with the wise one, / and in all three the son of Adam won and Satan lost. / Through the craving for bread he bound up every desire that men desire, / and the son of man despised human desires. / Through the love of money he laid out every kind of money, / and the athlete of truth bound them up as nothing. / Through the love of glory he hid all the snares that lie in wait for man, / and he leapt over them and passed them unharmed. / Unharmed the athlete came up from the contest, / and he was acclaimed by the spectators of the games. / Victoriously the bodily athlete triumphed, / and in defeat the spiritual one, the prince of the air, was overthrown. / The prince of the air made contest with a son of man, / and the man won, and the strong one who had made man guilty was defeated. / Now that the course of the contest and the defeat is complete, / let us inquire how the contest came about and what its cause was. / Its cause is this: the struggle that took place in the land of Eden,

in which a human being was defeated and the evil one had been winning until now. / By the debt of its sins the race of Adam was bound, / and the tyrannical demons were exalting themselves over its sins. / He who had called it his own image saw its guilt, / and it did not please him that the demons were trampling on his image. / That very image which had been defeated in Eden, he now / fashioned anew in the form of the first one. / Without coupling he fashioned Adam from the dust, / and without the joining of union he fashioned the last Adam. / From the race that had been defeated by sin he loosed sin, / through a son of man whom he fashioned by the Spirit without coupling. / By the power of the Spirit he fashioned a son of man from a daughter of man, / and filled him with the Spirit and called him by the name “Son of God.” / “Son of God” God called that son of man, / and Satan trembled at the name of a son of man who was higher than man. / This title made him come to the contest, / and he was burning for the moment when there would be room for his scheming. / In the fire of his scheming he was scorched as if by fire, / and he did not know how to bear its flame. / “Who will grant me to come near him?” he was thinking, / and he chafed at the divine command. / “Who will let me bring before him all kinds of enticements, / so that I may show him that he too is a man full of passions? / Who will drive him out to the wilderness, far from mankind, / so that I may go out with him and test his strength with the sufferings of man? / He is a man, wholly of human nature, full of passions; / how is it, then, that he tramples on passions, though he is subject to them? / Who will persuade the power of the Creator to withdraw its help from him, / and give me room to go in to him as one goes in to a man?” / These things the hater of man was pondering within himself, / while the lover of man forestalled the desire of his malice. / He saw him preparing to make contest with the son of Adam, / and armed the son of Adam with the Spirit and sent him out to meet him. / It is written that by the Spirit he went out from the settled land to the wilderness outside; / so it is plain that he was led by the power of the Spirit. / The power of the Creator signalled to him to go out there, / and when the enemy saw it he went out with him to see the outcome. / The Spirit revealed to him the law of the spirit that wages the struggle, / and taught him stratagems to break the stratagems of the slanderer. / It showed him that the enemy who had defeated Adam would join battle with him, / and anointed him with the Spirit so that the hand of the spirit would not prevail against him. / It taught him how he should wrestle spiritually, / and how he should go down into the stadium full of sufferings. / By the power of the Spirit he did all that the athlete of the Spirit did, / for the will of his soul clung to the Spirit he had received. / He with the Spirit, and the Spirit with him, waged the contest, / and he repaid the defeat of that fall which took place in Paradise. / That fall which Adam fell he repaid to the evil one, / so that he might know that in the son of Adam there is the power of victory. / The son of Adam won and acquitted Adam of his debts,

and Satan was defeated, and the camp of demons was defeated with him. / A hard overthrow the son of Adam turned back upon his adversary, / and the enemy could not give word in reply to word. / Three times the cunning one questioned the wise one, / and with one word he unravelled the snares for him. / Three bouts the champion wrestled with him, / and in all three he dashed him to the ground as if to death. / Three blows the son of Adam struck the son of Gehenna, / and he howled and cried out, and his legion of forces was shaken. / Three arrows the bow of righteousness let fly, / and three times he finished the contest with his adversary. / Three names he was going to proclaim among the earthly, / and he proclaimed them in a mystery in the contest he waged. / By the mystery of that power which was hidden in him he won the battle, / and he set it forth beforehand in a mystery, to show it after his death. / This is the cause of the contest he waged with Satan: / that he might redeem his race and reveal the mystery of the power of Being. / Hidden in him in a mystery were these things that came about: / the redemption of man, and the power of the Being that cannot be comprehended. / In the contest he waged he revealed them both by the power of him who chose him, / and confirmed them through the victory by which he defeated the evil one. / By the power of him who chose him he defeated the tyrant who had made men guilty, / and [?] that victory well through his privation. / Through privation he overcame the habits of human passions, / for that will which had chosen him out of all clung to him. / A hidden will dwelt in the temple of his bodily frame, / and through him was doing the work that befitted the Maker of all. / It befitted the Maker of all to do a fitting work, / and the son of man to fulfil the love of the one who sent him. / To the enemy of the Maker men had been captive from the beginning, / and a man went out and brought back the captivity of his fathers' house. / He went out to the wilderness to visit his race, he the lover of our race, / there where that captor who had taken his race captive sought him. / The captivity of man the son of man redeemed from the rebel, / and he despoiled his power and made him a laughingstock and a byword. / He, the man, defeated the tyrant who had defeated man, / and by his victory he exalted men and brought the devils low. / He brought the devils low in the contest he waged with the chief of the devils, / and took from them the armour they had taken from his fathers. / He left them standing naked, the enemies of his race, / so that they would not arm themselves to make contest with a son of man. / A great contest the son of man waged against their ranks, / and the spiritual hosts marvelled at the power of his victory. / The power of his victory the spectators of the games saw, / and they gathered to him as to a king, to acclaim him. / Crowns of victory they plaited and offered to the human athlete, / and they praised and gave thanks for the might of his power in the contest of sufferings. / Over all sufferings the athlete of righteousness was victorious, / because the evil one had summed them all up in three bouts.

In the three bouts with the strong one the son of our race prevailed, / and humbled the enemy who exalted himself over the generations. / He it is who humbled that strong one who had humbled our race, / he together with the power that strengthened his lowliness. / The power of the Creator enabled him to defeat the adversary, / while the Creator was hidden in the glory of his handiwork. / In his faithfulness the Hidden One was faithfully hidden, / and his power, which came from him, was helping the man who is one of us. / The man who is one of us contended with Satan, / not the Creator, as the dull of heart imagine. / For it was not the Creator who contended in bodily sufferings, / and witnesses testify that they waged the contest with a son of man. / The demons testify with whom they joined battle in the wilderness: / with a son of man whom hunger overcame after his fast. / He was hungry after his fast of forty days, / and the enemy knew that his hunger bore witness to his humanity. / He saw that the bodily frame had grown weak from want, / and he drew near to him to offer him bodily desire. / He saw that his body had been weakened by hunger, which weakens the body, / and he thought he was already able to lead him astray through the desire for bread. / The desire for bread he was stirring up in the body of the second Adam, / in that same way in which he had led Adam astray through bodily desire. / His crafts failed, his devices were cut off, his wiles came to an end, / and no place was left to him free from defeat. / Utterly the rebel and his forces were defeated, / and utterly the son of Adam won and won the victory for his race. / The race of Adam is therefore bound to repay praise / to him who exalted Adam's race through a son of its own race.
On the Generations of Our Lord

Homily 17: On the Generations of Our Lord. / Again, another by the same author: / the seventeenth homily, on the generations of our Lord. / It is recited during the Fast. / Again, another by the same author: / the seventeenth homily, / on the generations of our Lord. / It is recited during the Fast.

Adam, the speaking image,
whom the Voice composed from dust:
the honour given to the lowliness of his clay
cast jealousy among the spiritual beings.
The words that were spoken
about the fashioning of the mortal
kindled with the fire of envy
Satan, the prince of the air.
The care taken over his fashioning
stirred up the Hater with envy.
The name "image", with which he was honoured,
provoked him to wage a contest.
"Who," he said, "is this despised one,
whose nature is from filth,
that counsel is taken over his fashioning,
and he is brought into being like this?
And the One who is great and beyond measure,
exalted above all that is made,
calls a vessel moulded from clay
his own image!"
His bitterness stirred up the envious one,
and he made himself ready for combat.
He put on the armour of wiles
to do battle with the simple one.
From the beginning the Creator
was watching his deceit being prepared,
and gave him room to contend
with His image, to test him.
His bodily image was defeated
by the cunning of the deceitful one,
who bound him with the yoke of sin
and made his freedom a slave to death.
His fall became for him
a great [?] to his childishness.
He turned and accused his will,
which had enslaved itself though it was free.
He went to judgement with his freedom,
and accused and rebuked his thoughts:
had he stood firm in the contest,
he would have taken the crown of glory.
In a single span of time the mortal was defeated,
and quickly the rebel gained the rule;
but the cause of his folly became
instruction for those who came after him.
The fall of [?] the head of our race
greatly taught the children of his kind wisdom,
for through sin they gained the comfort
of becoming haters of sin.
The Creator turned to profit
the folly of the head of our tribes,
for through it He made plain our freedom,
so that He would not be blamed for the way we were made.
Before He fashioned us He knew
that this would help our nature:
that once it had been defeated by the will of its freedom,
it would ask Him for victory.
And though the victory is His,
He gives it into the power of its freedom,
so that it may learn how much He loves
our nature for the sake of His image.
Through our freedom He made us wise
from the beginning of our fashioning,
and from our own nature He gave us
a Saviour at the end of the ages.
In fashioning the first Adam
He called us by the borrowed name "image",
and in forming the second Adam
He confirmed that name in deed.
From our own nature He composed
an image that resembles the first,
to show that He had not rejected
