our nature because it sinned.
Under sentence He cast our nature
into the exile of sin,
and in mercy He took pity on our race
through a Mediator, a son of our race.
He did not send spiritual beings to us
to turn us back to the knowledge of Him;
He Himself reconciled us to Himself
through the mediation of our firstfruits,
to confirm the name "image"
with which He honoured us from the beginning.
He fashioned an image within the members,
and the image of His Being [...] dwelt in it.
He did not paint it with pigments

that resemble human seed;
by the power of the Spirit He composed His work
from human clay itself.
He composed a body with the faculties of bodies,
and breathed a soul into it by the power of the Spirit.
He made it complete in all that belongs to nature:
in conception, birth and growth.
He tested it with sufferings and passions,
with hunger and thirst, like everyone else,
and made it ready to wage the contest
with the Strong One on behalf of its race.
In all that is Adam's he had a share,
in the likeness of the first Adam;
sin alone he did not serve,
for he prevailed by the power of the Spirit.
The new words that were spoken
at his conception, his birth and his baptism
greatly troubled the envious one,
and the ranks of his hosts were shaken.
At the honour shown in Adam's fashioning
he envied Adam and made war on him;
and at the glories of the Son of Adam
he was embittered and took up his armour.
The voice of Gabriel distressed him
when he spoke with the one who would bear him,
saying that she would conceive
in a new manner, without seed.
The tidings that the spiritual beings
proclaimed on earth on the day of his birth
lodged like arrows
throughout the whole strength of his camp.
Again he heard the voice in the wilderness:
"Behold the Lamb who cleanses stains,"
and he made himself ready for combat,
so that sinners might not be justified.
The voice of the Father stirred him up
more than the earlier voices,
for it proclaimed: "This is my beloved,
the Son who fulfils my will."
New were the words his heralds
spoke in their revelations,
and the signs at his appearing
were beyond anything human.
These goaded the deceitful one,
and the new tidings unsettled him,
and he began to burn with envy
more than the first time.
His mind within him was astonished
at the things that had been spoken,
for when he saw a human body,
he heard words loftier than it.
"Who then is this despised one,
a mortal clothed in sufferings,
about whom such extraordinary things are said,
unlike anything said of his fellows?
Nature bears fruit from nature
by means of marriage,
but a voice sowed him in the womb
apart from human seed.
With the borrowed name of sonship
He called the members of his race,
but with the name of His own sonship
He went further and called him 'Beloved'.
He gave grace to those [?],
but it stayed with them only for a time;
this one, however, received the gift
with a promise that it would not be taken away.
He is a man, born of a human being,
and like a man in all that he is,
however exalted his fashioning.
It is not fitting for me to slacken
because of the unusual things said about him.
With the weapon of the desire for food
it is fitting for me to fight him,
for I am convinced that his nature
is bound by desires."
With such counsels the Hater
was consoling the distress of his mind,
seeking to wage the contest
with him in the wilderness.
He remembered the desire for fruit
with which he had seduced the first Adam,
and thought that through the desire for bread
he would overpower the second Adam.
The Creator gave him room,

as at the first time,
to contend with the Son of Adam:
He led the athlete out into the wilderness,
as the murderer of men desired,
and gave him an opening through the fast
of forty nights and days,
for he was eager to tempt him with bread.
With that seduction by which he had fought Adam,
and whose deceit grace had seen,
grace armed him with fasting against him
for forty days in the wilderness.
He was readying the weapon of his deceit,
and waiting to shoot at him
the arrow of the desire for food.
For forty days he held
the arena of the athlete's contest,
until the spiritual beings had gathered
as spectators of the athletic struggle.
At the end of the forty days
the wrestlers went down into the contest:
the athlete of righteousness
and the envious prince of the air.
At the end of the fast He allowed
the rebel to join the bout,
to show the power of His victory
in limbs that hunger had weakened.
On the pretext of bread he approached
the body that hunger had worn down,
thinking he could draw him
through his distress towards food.
"Behold," he said, "now is the time
when the Father's care for you is needed.
If you are a true Son,
show your sonship in deed.
You are in a wilderness, a stranger
to any dwelling that could fill your need;
your body is worn down by hunger,
and there is no food to be found for you.
Command the stones, which obey,
to supply your need.
Change the stones into bread,
so that you do not perish of hunger.
Speak a word with authority,
as befits the things said about you,
so that your need may be filled
and the things said about you be confirmed.
It is not hard for the power you possess
to make one thing out of another,
for even the righteous of old
gave commands to natures, and they were changed."
O the wiles of the deceitful one,
in which unbelief is hidden,
while, alongside the truth, he lets down
his own errors upon his hearers!
O the schemes that deceit devised,
and the True One laid them bare!
O the snares that the impostor hid,
and he cut them quickly!
The bodily athlete went down
into the contest with the spiritual one,
and the light spiritual one was defeated
by the heavy bodily one.
With abstinence from food
he fought him through the stirrings of the mind,
and the heavy one, clothed in limbs,
trampled the light one on the ground.
The spirit seized the limbs;
the winged one seized the one heavy of body;
and its grip [?] could not withstand
the bodily one, who possessed a composite frame.
With a single word
the bodily one rebuked the spiritual one,
and the prince of the air was confounded
by the answer of the one made of dust.
A word overthrew the rebel,
and his foot could not stand on the ground:
"The Creator's word is able
to keep people alive without food.
I know that the Creator's power
supplies the needs of mortals;
but it is not right to ask for help
by way of putting Him to the test.
Go and learn from those of old
who tested Him when they demanded food,
and whom the testing that came
from their divided minds destroyed.
Do not offer me enticements
in the guise of one who loves compassion.
I know that your counsel
begets death for whoever listens to it.
Do not, in your wickedness, hand me

the deadly poison that killed Adam.
Your table is a table of falsehood;
go and regale yourself on what is yours."
The Strong One was defeated, who had triumphed
in battles with many,
and one of the guilty conquered
by a spiritual weapon.
The rebel came up in shame
from the first contest,
and changed the place of combat
and the weapon for the second bout.
He was waiting on an empty hope,
going from contest to contest,
thinking that the passions
that ensnare the light-minded still held.
"If he has scorned bread
and trampled hunger with abstinence,
with the root of the love of money
I will weaken the power of his abstinence.
And what if he has despised hunger
and spurned the desire for food?
He is a mortal, a son of mortals,
who, though he won once, will lose another time.
Many have conquered through fasting,
and mammon has condemned them.
Many have spurned wine,
and I have made them drunk with envy.
With the root of the love of money
it is fitting for me to fight him,
for from it evils sprout
and bear the fruits of sin."
With the love of money he wanted
to wage the contest with him,
and he longed, on the top of a mountain,
to show him the beauty of possessions.
The Creator granted him his desire,
for He knew that this was what he sought,
and brought the athlete up the mountain
to grapple in a bout with the Evil One.
The rebel made, as is his habit,
illusions by deceiving the eyes,
and showed the beauty of possessions,
the crown and the authority of kingship.
It was not reality, nor real things,
that the Hater showed to the All-Seeing,
but in an unreal semblance
he gathered the world and its goods.
In a fantasy he showed him
likenesses that were not real,
while the All-Seeing bore patiently
with the impostor's contrivances.
He kept showing him likenesses,
thinking that perhaps he would lead him astray,
while Christ, with a hidden eye,
was examining his imaginings.
He arrayed gold, though there was none,
and set out a crown, though it was not real,
and set up ranks and authorities,
though there was no voice to give orders.
"All these I will give you
if you will fall down and worship me,
for this authority has been handed over to me,
and I give it to whomever I wish.
One thing only I ask of you:
honour me, if you are willing;
worship me and take the crowns,
and reign over all your dominion."
The spiritual one seized the bodily one
with the holds of the love of money,
but the hand of the spirit could not keep its grip
on the body that the Holy Spirit had anointed.
The bodily one raised up his will
and brought the spiritual one down to the ground,
and the heavenly hosts marvelled
at the bodily one who conquered a spirit.
The bodily athlete was raised
above the armour of the Strong One,
and the one heavy of limbs trampled
the light prince of the air.
With a single word the one clothed in a body
shook the light-winged one:
"It is written: You shall not worship others,
but the Lord alone.
Get away, Hater," he said to him;
"do not snatch the Creator's name.
A creature is not permitted
to take the worship due to the Maker."
With the word of the Creator's name
he made the bitterness of his wickedness insipid,
and poured out the cup that the Accuser
had mixed for him with wiles.

"It is written," he said, "You shall worship the Lord,
and serve Him alone."
With this one saying he pulled down
the building the impostor had raised.
Through worship of the impostor he had sought
to drag him after his enticements,
but he reminded him of the name of God
and rebuked him, for he is not God.
"To One alone," he said, "thanksgiving is due,
and Him it is fitting to worship at all times.
Do not snatch for yourself, rebel,
the true worship that is not yours."
By the power of the Spirit and the name of the Godhead
the bodily athlete triumphed,
and humbled the pride of the arrogant.
Before the eyes of the spectators of the contest
he had grappled with the bodily one
in one bout over the desire for bread,
in another over the love of money,
and one bout more after those contests.
The wicked athlete came up
from the contest in shame,
and began to devise wiles
to change the place of the bout.
One hope alone was left him,
and on it he had set his trust,
and he kept it for the end of the contest,
that by it perhaps he might win the victory.
"If hunger did not snare him,
and the love of money did not bind him,
there is a hidden snare,
and he will not notice when he falls into it.
If he has trampled the arrows of hunger
and broken the bow of mammon,
with the spear of the love of glory
I will hurl him down from his height.
A cup full of deadly poison
I will mix and give him,
and if he tastes even a little of it,
it will loosen his limbs [?]."
To the height of the love of glory
the envious one longed to drag him,
for he was convinced that the height of glory
is a pit for whoever climbs it.
The Spirit brought the athlete up
to the place [?] the rebel wanted,
and he opened the contest of combat
above the temple of atonement.
The athlete went down into the contest
with the weapon of the love of glory,
and set as his target for victory
the one who had mastered the love of money.
In the bout of the love of glory
he was confident that he would defeat the Lord,
and he did not know that he would be caught
in the fineness of the nets he had cast.
In a word, as an envoy for his life,
he hid glory and sent it to him;
he sent him a saying
in which an empty hope was written.
The rebel hid deadly poison
in the arrows of glory and shot at him,
but the shield of salvation,
which the Holy Spirit had put in his hand, caught it.
"If," he said, "you are the Son,
and the things said about you are true,
throw yourself from here to the ground,
and so seal your sonship.
For it is written that angels
give help to the righteous,
and guard him in hard places,
so that his steps do not stumble.
Come down from the height to the earth,
and let us test the strength of your authority;
see, the spiritual beings will carry you
and lift you up in their hands.
Why do you hide your authority
and block the way of its glory?
Reveal your glory and show your power,
and see, you will be praised by all."
O the snares that deceit hid,
and the nets that cunning spread,
which he cut quickly
with a saying, the word of his mouth!
With a multitude of weapons the spiritual one fought the bodily one,
and with a few words he overthrew him

and brought all his wiles to nothing.
Against the wiles of the deceitful one
he returned him an answer,
and with the testimony of Scripture
he stopped the mouth of the insolent one.
"It is written," he said, "that you shall not test
the Maker with a divided mind,
lest He shut the door in your face
and your requests be turned away."
O the schemes that deceit devised,
and the wiles the impostor forged,
which the All-Knowing laid bare
in the furnace of the Spirit that tests all!
O bodily athlete,
who grappled with a spirit!
O passible one, whom the Strong One
who enslaved mankind could not overpower!
O nature clothed in sufferings,
which conquered the passions in its nature!
O son of captives, who showed valour
and led the captor away captive!
O warrior who fought
and set the subjugated free!
O son of a race of sinners,
who freed his race from iniquity!
Three times the bodily one
grappled with the spiritual one,
and with the stirrings of the mind
the passible overpowered the impassible.
Three arrows he drew and shot
from the bow at the target,
and with the third he proclaimed
victory and the [?] of the Evil One.
In the first bout were broken
the bow and the spear of the Strong One,
and not one of his weapons
was left him sound and whole.
In the second bout the limbs
of the warrior were loosened,
and the arms of the spirit were broken
in the combat with the bodily one.
With many weapons the rebel
fought the Son of Adam,
and with the single weapon of the Spirit's power
he overpowered him and abolished his dominion.
With every art the Strong One
contended with the passible one,
and the bodily one, with a word alone,
undid the structure of his wiles.
With three strongholds the captor
held fast the son of exile,
and the exile breached them,
the rebellious walls of sin.
In three snares he hid
all the passions of mortals,
and he passed quickly over them,
the passions that ensnare many.
In the desire for bread he offered him
desires of every kind,
and the rebel concealed them
in the guise of bread, as in a garment.
In the love of money he gathered and heaped up
the kinds of all evils,
and with the name of crown and authority
he adorned the hatefulness of his designs.
In the cup of the love of glory
he mixed and blended deadly poison,
and hid glory, like sweetness,
on the rim of his bitter cup.
In three bouts he [...]
all the passions without and within,
and set them up like a target
in the combat with our Saviour.
On his own side he set up
the whole world, from end to end,
and the whole camp was defeated
by One who conquered by the power of the Spirit.
Every scheme he devised and forged,
and put them on like armour,
and the Son of David broke them,
the instruments of his armour, with a word.
The rebel was put to shame with his armour,
and his forces were scattered,
and the whole left side sat
in mourning over the humiliation of the Strong One.
The Accuser completed all his temptations
against our Lord,
and departed from him for a time,
until he should whet the sword for killing.
The battle ceased and the combat rested
between the passible one and the prince of the air.

And the spectators of the contest rose
to acclaim the athlete of truth.
Wonder had gathered them all
to the stadium of the athletes,
to see a new contest
of the bodily and the spiritual.
A new sight they were seeing:
two wrestlers face to face;
for never had flesh dared
to join a bout with a spiritual being.
The spiritual beings were scrutinising
the weakness of the passible one:
with what weapon, then, could
a weak nature conquer the Strong One?
For their fellow had not become [?]
like the one clothed in limbs,
and they knew that he had triumphed
in battle against many.
For this reason they gathered,
to see the end of the contest,
so that whoever won the victory
they might crown with a crown of praises.
For the end of the contests they kept
the crown of their praises,
to set their acclamations
on the head of whoever triumphed.
And when they saw that the bodily one had conquered
their spiritual fellow,
they adorned with the crown of their acclamations
the athlete of righteousness.
Words of glory they rendered
to the passible one for the victory,
crying out in their companies:
"Blessed is the Power that conquered in the body!"
Here their voices were reconciled
with our race, with which they had been angry,
and they gained the hope of renewal,
that with us they would rest from toil.
The spiritual beings wove a crown
for the bodily athlete,
for they saw that through his greatness he had removed
the barrier between those at enmity.
They cried glory to him with hosannas
as he came up from the contest:
"Blessed is he who as Mediator established
peace for us and for all!
Thanks be to the Good One, who by His might
strengthened your body in the contest!
Blessed is he who by his nod humbled
the tyrant who took Adam captive!"
They were drawing near him in love
after the end of his contest,
and they ministered his hidden things
in revelations to the earthly ones.
Their companies were going up and coming down
to honour the Son of mortals,
and they rejoiced at the sight of him,
and the sound of his answers delighted them.
They marvelled greatly at his contest
and were amazed at his abstinence,
for though he was of a guilty race,
he conquered the tyrant through his sufferings.
It was not with human weapons
that the passible one won the victory;
his victory came by the power of the Spirit,
and the Spirit credited it to his will.
In the name of the Son, which [...] in him,
he triumphed and conquered the passions,
and was found worthy of great honour
and of praise from the spiritual beings.
Now that the contest is finished,
let us ask whose contest it was:
was it the passible one's, clothed in limbs,
or the nature's that does not suffer?
Who was it that hungered and was tempted,
and whose need did the Evil One perceive?
And to whom did the rebel offer
the enticements of the desires?
Who was it that went down into the contest
and grappled in a bout with the Evil One?
And who was it that conquered the Strong One,
and to whom was the victory reckoned?
The contest proclaims a clear distinction
to those who understand:
it was the Son of Adam who was tempted,
in the likeness of the first Adam.
It was he whom the Spirit led out into the wilderness,
and it was he who hungered and was tempted,
for nature demanded it of him.

food to sustain his life.
The Rebel kept urging him to change stones into bread,
for he saw that his limbs had grown weary and fasting had loosened his sinews.
He kept showing him likenesses of wealth and of the greatness of dominion,
for he saw that he wore the limbs of mortals, who covet silver.
He offered him the poison of death in the cup of the love of glory.
The Evil One tempted the bodily one, not the Power of the Godhead,
for he knew that the nature of the Self-Existent is not tempted by food.
It was not to the Only-Begotten that he showed wealth and the greatness of dominion,
for he knew that the greatness of his glory scorns the wealth of mortals.
It was not from the Knower of Hidden Things that he hid the snares of glory,
for even the Enemy himself knew that his wiles lie open to the Godhead.
He was not doing battle with the Power that holds all things,
for it was plain to him, a creature, that his strength is feeble before his Lord.
How would the Creator do battle with his own handiwork?
And what need had the Victor of a victory over the guilty one?
He was not fighting his equal, so as to test his strength,
for the nature of a creature is too lowly to be compared with its Maker.
And if it was for the sake of salvation that he joined battle with the Evil One,
he could, without any contest, have brought back the strays by his nod.
When has the Maker ever accomplished his works by means of combat?
And what power of opposition stands firm before the Godhead?
How could the Rebel be able to stand against the Creator?
And with what senses did the crafty one probe the simplicity of the Godhead?
How could he move the One who holds all things from place to place?
And by what movements could he draw him wherever the Rebel wished?
Why was it not his own will that led him out to do battle?
For it is written that the Holy Spirit led him out into the wilderness, to go out and be tempted.
Who is it, then, that was tempted by the will of the Spirit and performed mighty deeds?
For see, otherwise his will would be made lower than the will of the Father and the Spirit.
How could he suffer through hunger who by his nod gives life to all?
And how could the Rebel tempt the One who holds the sum of all wisdom?
If it was because he put on a body that his nature was tested by suffering,
then he is capable of being tempted both within a body and without a body.
And if the Only-Begotten was tempted in those things in which it is written he was tempted,
then the Father and the Spirit also share with him in the temptation,
if indeed the nature is one, in the equality that belongs to the Godhead.
It is impossible for one to be tempted while the others remain free of suffering.
Whatever belongs to the nature belongs to the hypostases of the Godhead;
whatever touched the one, the whole nature would share.
And if the Offspring of the Father suffered the sufferings that mortals possess,
then the Father and the Spirit also tasted the suffering that touched the Only-Begotten.
But far be it that this should be, and may those who know never accept it,
that the impassible nature

should be tempted in what is ours.
It was our nature that was tempted and received sufferings in its own nature,
and the nature that dwelt in it raised it by victory above sufferings.
It was the son of our race who fought against the strong one on behalf of his race,
and by the power of the Spirit he triumphed and brought back the captor's captives.
To him, the lowly son of mortals, belong the [?] of death,
and to the nature that assumed him belong praises, as befits it.
And if the heretics quarrel with us, as is their custom,
it is not right for us to bring the Godhead down to the sufferings of the body.
Their strife is our boast, and their reproach is our praise.
Since they hate us for the sake of the truth, their voices do not grieve us.
The echoes of their revilings do not shake our [?],
and we do not accept a teaching that diminishes the Self-Existent from his full measure.
Our confession roars within us like the Ocean in the midst of the sea,
and when their waves beat against us, we bind them by the power of the Godhead.
In the matter of the Godhead we prevail, for it was in no way diminished;
and over the assumption of the manhood they wrangle, asking why it was exalted.
Over the distinction of the natures they arm themselves against those who know;
at the passible and the impassible they loose the arrows of their words.
By mixture and blending they seek to blot out the natures,
while with their bitterness they trouble the peace that reconciled the estranged.
As for us, let us boast in nothing but this distinction,
confessing that our nature, his garment, is preserved with the Self-Existent.
Through the [?] of the firstfruits of our body we look for the redemption of our bodies,
and since it shares with the Godhead, its honour is our exaltation.
Our whole race has been honoured by the good gifts of the [greatness?] of his glory,
for his honour stood surety for us in our peace with the Maker.
We call his garment “Son” together with the Word, without division,
while confessing that it does not share with the Godhead in all things.
We do not [?] his nature, nor do we forget his humility;
we do not defraud his salvation, nor do we falsify his promises.
We confess his weakness and worship his glories.
We honour the body that is from us out of love for him whose garment it is.
We confess the hidden One in the revealed, and the revealed for the sake of the hidden,
while we gather our confession into the one person of the one Son.
Those who defraud the body of our nature, let his humility accuse them;
and those who make the Word of the Father passible, let his sovereignty humble them.
The passible one, who suffered in his nature and was tempted, has rebuked them;
he bore suffering on behalf of all, his garment apart from the Word.
By his temptation he showed us plainly that temptation touched his nature,
and by his victory he made it shine for us that he triumphed by the power of the Spirit.
Because of the folly of Adam the second Adam was tempted;
where the first was defeated in the contest, the last overcame by his victory.
Through the defeat of the first his race was condemned and became barren,
and through the victory of the last both the first and the last conquered [?].
Because of the folly of Adam

death entered and enslaved his race,
and by the endurance of the [second?] Adam death died and the dead came to life.
Adam slipped and fell and [?], and the pains of his limbs grew strong;
and the second Adam rose [?] and lived, and by his suffering gave life to many.
The son of Adam did battle for Adam with the strong one,
and repaid him the wounds he had inflicted on Adam through the craving for the fruit.
With the very weapon by which the first was defeated, the last triumphed.
Adam was defeated by craving for the fruit; Christ conquered by self-restraint.
The first Adam, who was from the earth, pledged himself to sin;
and the second Adam gave himself as a ransom and set his race free.
Because of Adam death entered and held sway over many,
and through the second Adam it was abolished, and he made life reign over all.
Adam was set free through Adam, the earthly through the heavenly,
who loosed his frame from death and adorned it with heavenly life.
The Rebel tempted Adam in combat, on account of Adam,
for he saw that he had put on his nature and resembled his fellow in all things.
With the son [of Adam?] the strong one fought, he who had despoiled [?] Adam,
and it was not with the Power of the Godhead that the Rebel joined battle.
Let the haters of the Godhead cease from ascribing temptation to the Godhead,
for see, the son of our race has shown us that the temptation is his own.
Let him say to the heretics, the disciples of the Accuser:
“Do not tempt the Power of the Godhead, as your master Satan did.
It is I who went down to the contest and joined battle with the Evil One,
and I overpowered the one who overpowers all by the Power that clothed me from the womb.
Do not bring the Only-Begotten down to the lowly things of mortals,
for I, who went down to the contest, received the victory by his Power.”
See, the son of our race proclaims to us whose contest it is.
Listen and hear, you heretics: the Godhead is not tempted.
Let the prophet cry out in every tongue and rebuke the proud:
“I, I am the Lord God, and I have not changed from what I am.”
The Sunday of the Third Week of the Fast
Memra [?] / For the Sunday of the Third Week of the Fast / Responsory: The Creator has promised us new life, and has given a pledge through his own life. / [Tune:] "Of Elijah": My brothers

The path the Tishbite trod for me, that I may travel it in words,
I have sought to follow toward the deeds of his preaching.
The zealous one has kept me for the teaching of the words of the Spirit,
he who bound and loosed as he willed and did not prove false.
He held back the clouds and dried them up like barren women,
then turned, prayed, and made them fruitful by a hidden sign.
He went down like a lion to the lair of greedy Death,
and took from it the sentence passed on a man, by the help of his Lord.
He waged a contest with the gods and their worshippers,

and error was destroyed, and the power of the Hidden One triumphed by his hand.
He won the contest by the power of divine help,
and put the no-gods to shame in the name of God.
And so that a mortal might not be misled about his own lowly nature,
he lost heart before her and trembled at the voice of a feeble woman.
The Tishbite learned two things from this:
the lowliness of his own state, and his Lord's love for mankind.
He showed his zeal for the Hidden One by his going away,
and at the end of his way he heard a voice full of mercy.
The zealous one set out in his fervour like an exile;
he asked for death, lay down, and sank in the grief of his heart.
A revelation called to him: "Arise, Tishbite, and be nourished,
for the road you have set before you is too hard for you without food.
See, a hidden sign has prepared visible food for you:
take it, be strengthened, know your nature and have pity on your race."
The zealous one rose and saw the table of the sign was set;
he ate and drank, and turned and sank down again, for he was grieved.
Twice the spiritual one called to the bodily one:
"Arise, mortal, and nourish your soul with the food of the sign."
That Commander who had fed him mightily through silent creatures
now also gave him food through one who speaks.
The speaking and the dumb are His, before Him, for His use,
and without toil the dull creature lived [?] in return for the truth.
He ate and drank the food of men and the drink of the earth,
and gained the strength of heavenly beings through earthly things.
Why then did He give him hidden power through visible food,
and why did He bind the power of His help to eating?
By the food He gave him He showed that man has need of food,
and by His help He revealed that it is His power that sustains man.
Through eating He taught men that they live by food,
and through His sign He revealed that, if He wills, He gives life with ease.
Not that it is hard for Him to sustain life without nourishment,

but to make known that the life of this age is bound to food.
The arrogance of the foolish did not escape the Knower of all,
who would come to be misled about a man in their imaginings.
The presumption of their thoughts was plain to Him:
that, though mortal, they would snatch at the rank of the immortals.
Through Elijah He cut off beforehand the love of glory,
lest mortality grow insolent toward the height of life.
In one day's food He gave him strength to live for days,
and on the meal of a single time he journeyed great distances.
The Tishbite set out and walked by means of that meal
forty days, night and day, as far as Horeb.
"In the strength of the meal," it says, he journeyed, not as men do,
teaching us that the power of His help dwells in His servants.
Forty days the zealous one journeyed, being strengthened,
and every day he fought a hard battle against the insolent.
He reached the lodging-place at the end of his way,
and heard a voice questioning him as though it did not know:
"What are you doing here, Elijah?" it said to him.
"Who drove you out of peace into the fearful wilderness?"
O the greatness of the hidden depth of the God of all,
who asks the Tishbite, "What are you doing?"
He kept him by a sign, that he might turn toward Him in calm,
and sought to learn the reason for his journey as though He did not know.
He asked him, "What are you doing?" as though He did not know,
to open a path for the prophet to come to his own words.
The righteous one answered the Hidden One: "I have been very zealous,
for the great covenant of Your hidden love has been forgotten.
They have abolished the sacrifices that were due to be paid to Your name,
and offered them in the name of demons that are alien to You.
They have killed Your prophets and shed their blood without mercy,
and I alone am left, and see, they seek my life as they did my companions'."
A revelation called to him, making him hear the hidden will:

"Go out, arise, listen and see and learn, and rest from your anger.
See, I am making wind and earthquake and flame,
and I am shaking the earth before you as you would wish."
The Commander gave a sign to the senseless things and set them rushing;
fire and wind clashed together, and the earth quaked.
He held them back with rebukes and shook them before the zealous one,
so that the fire of his wrath against the people's iniquity might die down.
By earthquake and fire He laid bare his inclination, that this is what he wanted:
to shake the earth and burn mankind with fire and wind.
He showed him the wind, then stilled the earthquake, and then the fire,
and made him hear a voice: "I do not wish to do these things.
You, being a man, seek like a man to destroy mankind,
but it does not befit Me to be like you in destroying mankind."
After the fire He made him hear a gentle voice,
teaching him His will: that He loves mankind.
Elijah trembled at the hard things set before him,
and covered his face from the terror of the hard vision.
A second voice spoke with him: "What are you doing?"
and he too answered as at first: "I have been very zealous."
He bent his soul away from harshness by the gentle voice,
and set before him a peaceful aim toward mankind, that he might show it mercy:
"Turn back, then, to your way, to the deeds of prophecy,
for see, I have left Myself seven thousand who obey Me."
The zealous one thought that he alone was prophet and righteous,
and the voice taught him that he had companions in the fear of his Lord.
"I have left," He said, "seven thousand who did not stray and worship,"
making known to us that His sign had guarded their minds.
By His help He left a few out of the multitude that was swept away,
and the flood of iniquity did not carry them off to the worship of error.
Through the remnant that He left, who took no part in the worship of Baal,
He taught the righteous one the aim of His mercies toward mankind:
"Go then and anoint a king, and a king, for the people and the nations,
that they may cut down the arrogance of the wicked people.
Anoint also and raise up a prophet of the Spirit to be in your place,
so that whoever escapes justice may be punished by him."
The zealous one turned from harshness toward gentleness,

and journeyed by the way of sweetness toward [?].
He anointed the prophet and set up a king for the people and the nations,
and joined words to deeds in his preaching.
For this reason the sign drew him as far as Horeb,
that through discipline he might acquire love toward his neighbours.
When the zealous one set out to bring complaint against the insolent,
the voice taught him the way of peace toward mankind.
He turned back from the wilderness to the people at home who hated peace,
and saw that the people and the king were sick with the disease of iniquity.
Because of their iniquity he had left the people and hated the king,
and when he turned and came back he saw that the people and the king were sick.
The fever of Baal worship had been checked for a long time,
but the disease of greed that lay hidden in the soul broke out.
The greedy king looked, and coveted what was not his,
and covered the falsehood hidden in his heart with the name of justice.
To Naboth he said, "Give me your vineyard for good silver,
or I will give you in its place a vineyard better than yours."
And because his greed was not heeded in the way of the world,
his thoughts were troubled with grief of soul beyond comfort.
Ahab lay down, grieved, and would not eat,
because of the word of just judgment with which Naboth had answered him.
Jezebel heard that the greedy one had been humbled before justice,
and by craft she sharpened a sword against truth.
"Why are you grieved, and your heart crushed?" she said to Ahab.
"Why are you humbled at the sound of a rebuff in the name of justice?
Why are you not bold in the deeds of greed,
and why are you asleep to the crafts of gathering silver?
You are slack and feeble too in the work of iniquity,
and you are not fit to be king over Israel.
Arise then, eat and drink and rejoice, and let your heart be glad,
for I will give you Naboth's vineyard though he does not wish it."
She forged the weapon of deceit in her thoughts,
to shed blood lawfully, in the name of justice.
She tempered the sword that deceit had sharpened within a letter,

and bound falsehood within a tablet of writing.
She wrote iniquity and sealed the lie that deceit had devised,
and the scribes of falsehood set them forth with partiality.
O letter written in the name of justice,
in which lay hidden deceit giving birth to murder!
In the name of justice the foolish woman wished to commit murder,
so that the evil of her deceit might not be exposed before onlookers.
In a seemly, lawful tablet she covered her iniquity:
that whoever blasphemes the name of God shall die by stoning.
In this way too she wrote to the false ones,
that they should seat men, witnesses of iniquity, opposite Naboth:
"Proclaim a fast, then, and put on mourning like men set apart,
and avenge the insult to the name of God and to the king of the people.
Let the fast and the mourning be witnesses against the blood of Naboth,
that he deserves death, for he has reviled the king and the God of all."
The men of Jezreel, the elders and the nobles, did
as it was written: murder by deceit against the innocent one.
They gathered the people, proclaimed a fast, and set the deceit in motion,
and condemned the blood of the pure in heart by false witness.
O testimony whose sound was never sown in the ears,
yet the heart conceived it by union with deceit and gave birth to murder!
O mind, fair radiance of reason,
whose light grew dark through false testimony against innocent blood!
Speaking men grew dumb to what was right, more than the dumb,
and condemned blood that was not guilty, and did not examine it.
The innocent one died by the sword of stones that deceit had sharpened for him,
and the greedy one seized the inheritance of his house to be his own.
A revelation of the hidden sign called to the Tishbite:
"Arise, zealous one, and avenge the blood that deceit has shed.
Show your zeal like a strong man toward the wicked,
and require from his hands the blood of the wronged, and do not hold back.
Go and say to him: Thus says the Knower of all:
You have killed and taken possession, not justly as you supposed.

In the blood you have shed I will bathe your own blood upon the earth,
and I will avenge the blood of My prophets on account of Naboth."
The good servant armed himself with the weapon of the Spirit,
to go and fight with the wicked one who had trampled justice.
The zealous one saw the hard-hearted man who was eager for blood,
and drew the sword of the word of the Spirit and showed it before him:
"See then, you have carried out murder by deceit and taken possession of a vineyard,
but the desire of your deceit will not come to completion.
The divine judgment has gone ahead of your evil inclination,
and has shed your blood for the blood you shed, before the event.
The Judge has pronounced the sentence of death against you,
and the executioner, the hidden sign, has drawn the sword.
In the place where you shed Naboth's blood, your blood will be poured out,
and there Jezebel will become a sacrifice for the greedy dogs.
And because iniquity has prospered in your hands more than in all who have been,
in you also justice will triumph in hard judgment."
The wicked one was put to shame by the righteous one against his will;
he took off his crown, put on sackcloth, and walked barefoot.
He grieved and was ashamed over the lawless deed:
that he had coveted, been greedy, seized, killed, and trampled the commandment.
A word of the hidden sign came to Elijah,
teaching him how much the soul is longed for:
"Have you seen how Ahab the king has been ashamed before Me,
and put on mourning in his mind over what he did?
Because he was ashamed before Me and knew he had sinned against a man's blood,
I will not bring the evil upon his offspring in his days.
In the days of a king who loves iniquity like his father,
I will require from the house of Ahab the blood of My prophets."
The sentence of the hidden sign upon the wicked one was fulfilled,
and he readied himself for war with the Edomites.
The presumptuous one was swallowed up by a hard arrow which the sign shot,
and the word of the righteous one was fulfilled in him as it had been prophesied.
The wicked had shot arrows of stones at Naboth the righteous;
so the presumptuous one too was swallowed up by evils, in the manner of Naboth.
The wicked one died and lost his hope of justice,
and handed on his crown to a wicked heir who resembled his father.

And because he ran lightly in the way of iniquity,
he fell suddenly into the snare of affliction into which the sign tipped him.
The fool sent to inquire about his [?],
to see whether there was a remedy to heal his severe fracture.
The messengers set out to inquire of the no-god,
and the Tishbite went out on the road to meet them.
The zealous one laid bare to them the deceit of the heart of the son of the wicked,
how bound he was in the love of [?], like his father:
"Go and say to him who is senseless and steeped in sin:
Is there no God among the chosen people to heal your pain?
Because you have mistaken the God of all for no-gods,
your life will be cut short, and the demons you loved will not pity you."
The messengers turned back to the wicked one who had sent them,
and brought news that cut off hope for the hopeless.
He asked them, "Who has turned you back so quickly?"
and they told him, "The one who hates your father held us back from our way."
The sick man, though cast down by two afflictions, steeled himself,
and sharpened the sword for war against the righteous, like his father.
He armed a feeble force in a contest against truth,
and his force was defeated by the hidden power of the Spirit.
The captain of fifty went up, threatening Elijah,
and in his arrogance he tried to hurry the Tishbite:
"Come down quickly, prophet of the Spirit, and do not delay,
for the king wishes to see your face at once."
The prophet, who heard the voice of arrogance from the presumptuous man,
shot arrows of fire at him, and he burned with his troop.
The fire of the hidden sign consumed the horses of the men,
and burned the armour along with the garments of those clothed in arrogance.
The disaster that had happened did not move the son of the wicked;
he turned and sent a captain of fifty like the first.
The presumptuous one went up to the zealous one in the madness of his heart,
and began to hurry him: "Come down quickly, for the king wishes it."
And because his arrogance had climbed to the great height of prophecy,
he came down in shame to humiliation, like the first.
The hard-hearted man, sunk in earthly things, persisted in his obstinacy,

and turned and sent a captain of fifty for the third time.
The humble one saw that the armour of arrogance had brought his companions low,
and put on the armour of humility so as not to be condemned.
The humble one went up and pleaded, seeking to appease him humbly:
"Let my life be precious, and let not the sin with which I have come [?] harm me."
And because he had not armed himself with arrogance like those before him,
the revelation signalled to the zealous one: "Come down, go with him."
Elijah put on the hidden armour of prophecy,
and went down and killed the son of the murderer with the sound of his words.
Thus he said: "You who have provoked Him with a no-god,
from the bed you have gone up on you will not come down again, nor see life."
He cut off his hope of life with the sword of the Spirit,
and sealed his words by deeds against the house of Ahab.
He completed and finished the great height of prophecy,
and the ship of his preaching came down into the harbour of peace.
The Hidden One signalled to him through one of His spiritual revelations:
"Come, weary one, rest in the harbour of life that is above death.
Come, delight in the new mystery of the immortals,
and dwell in life in the new order of the kingdom on high.
Come, enter and see, as in a mystery, that kingdom
to which you invited the people and the nations by your words.
Ahead of the event I show you the restoration of life;
My will is ready for spiritual and bodily beings alike.
In new life without end I will keep
Watchers and men, rejoicing spiritually.
In you I give a sign of peace to the human race;
let your life be a pledge of immortality.
In you I give surety for your whole race that it will live with you,
and by your removal I seal the promise of My words.
In you I tread a path to life without end,
which greedy death does not cut off from the count of your life.
In you I multiply good hope for the hopeless,
that they may not slacken in the confidence of their freedom.
I show by you that the dust of Adam is not loathsome to Me,
for see, I have honoured the lowliness of its nature through your departure."

Elijah heard that the sign was removing him while alive,
and he wished to hide in silence this preeminence of a man.
The zealous one thought this befitted his humility,
that a lowly nature should not boast of what was not its own.
The Knower of all, who saw him, saw his intention,
and revealed the mystery of man's preeminence to the minds of men.
It was also right that the cause of our life should not be hidden,
so that, being openly revealed, it might be confirmed in things to come.
In this way the Creator revealed the departure of His servant,
to bind man in love of the life without end.
Elijah, too, not as one who begrudged us the preeminence of our life,
wished to hide the departure of his life from our minds.
The zealous one took care lest the way of life become
a cause of arrogance, and also of reproach, for those after him.
He set out on the way and contrived a pretext for his disciple:
"My God has sent me on a journey, that I may travel alone with Him."
The sign made the departure of his life known to the minds of men,
and revealed it before everyone to Elisha as the truth.
"As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives," Elisha answered Elijah,
"I will not leave your great love until the end."
"To Bethel," he said, "the Lord has sent me, in a mystery,
to the place worthy to be called by the name of God."
The hidden sign revealed the reason for his journey to the prophets,
and they came out to meet him, to see him by the spirit of revelation.
The seers of things to come said to his disciple,
"Do you know, then, that today the Lord will take your master?"
And he answered them by the spirit of revelation, as one who knows:
"This mystery has been revealed to me; be silent about it."
For Jericho too he put forward a pretext to his disciple,
and he cut short his pretext by the name of God and the life of his soul.
There too prophets came out in the spirit to meet the righteous one,
prophesying his departure from among men.
"Do you know, then, that today the Lord will take your master?"
the prophets asked Elisha, and he said, "Be silent."
The zealous one saw that the Spirit had revealed the mystery of his departure,
and put forward a pretext to his disciple a third time:
"The Lord has sent me as far as the Jordan, to go and come back,"

but the fervent-hearted one was not deterred by pretexts.
The Spirit urged him to go out and see the great wonder,
as the dust of Adam was carried off by spiritual beings.
Elijah set out on a new way, beyond what is human,
and struck the waters, and the mute element trembled before him.
He lifted his mantle and struck the river and divided it in two,
and the senseless things did not resist his word.
The mute element feared the sign hidden in the mantle;
it ceased from its running and kept an order not in its nature.
Elijah crossed with his disciple as on dry land,
and the river returned, as before, to the running of its course.
The master stood to set forth a fine charge to his disciple,
and to explain to him the mystery hidden by the pretexts:
"What do you wish? Ask, and I will give you the riches of the Spirit,
before I am led to where the sign has appointed me to go."
The disciple asked of his modest master a double armour,
to go and fight by its help against error.
The master, seeing that he had asked much, beyond measure,
held him back from it until he was removed, and then he would give it to him.
Not out of envy did he withhold the gift from his disciple;
the disciple had been very bold, and he set him a condition:
"If you see me when the sign removes me from you,
take the gift as you asked, and honour its rank."
It was not doubt about his departure that divided his mind,
but [?], lest his remaining should be brief.
"If the hidden Commander leads me beyond the human,
may the power of the Spirit be with you as you wish."
The master finished his words of counsel to his disciple,
and the hosts of the heavenly ones arrived to remove him.
They displayed an array of horses of fire, yoked together,
and a strong chariot too, with reins of fire.
Wheels of fire could be seen beneath the chariot,
and the horses had wings of fire like flying creatures.
That chariot which was seen was not fire,
nor did the horses have senses, or riders.

For it was a vision, and not a body, that was shown:
an appearance of fire, and the form of horses without riders.
Spiritual beings showed horses as if escorting him,
and the chariot was harnessed for the exaltation of the Tishbite.
The hidden sign hastened them toward the deed,
that by fearful things they might show the vision of man's exaltation.
The spiritual beings depicted a great mystery to the earthly ones:
that see, the lowly nature is raised up to the heights.
By means of the chariot they traced the departure of the dust of Adam,
which the sign will honour at the end through understanding.
In one who was removed and was not swallowed by greedy death,
he depicted for us the mystery of the new life without end.
Through Elijah the Creator revealed immortality,
that hope stands firm for the hopeless at the end of the ages.
He accomplished his departure through spiritual beings in a great vision,
to make known to us our own departure toward the heights.
The chariot too was carrying off the Tishbite;
the sign was pointing it toward the face of the heights for its course.
The bodily one became like a charioteer above the wind,
and flesh held the reins of fire and was not harmed.
O bodily one, who rode the wind and reined in fire!
O fleshly one, who was not scorched by the flame!
O honoured one, who acquired wings for flight!
O mortal, whom the hand of death did not touch!
The sign set him, through spiritual beings, above the horses,
and he left his mantle behind as a pledge for his disciple.
In the mantle from his body he gave him a sign that what he had asked
he had received twofold, in the visible and in the hidden.
The fleshly one rode on the wind and flew through the air,
and at the end of his way the sign directed him to the land of Eden.
To Eden the Tishbite was removed, and not to heaven,
and on earth the sign kept him alive, and not in the firmament.
For the feet of flesh did not tread the way to the heights,
nor was that entrance to immortality opened.
One alone among mortals ascended to heaven:

He who dwelt there had opened the firmament,
that he might minister in the Holy of Holies on behalf of mortals.
He it is who ascended by the same will by which he had come down to it,
and he was exalted above all, that he might fulfil all.
By his own word, which cannot be undone, our word is bounded:
that no one has ascended from among mortals except him.
The symbol drew the Tishbite toward the heights,
and when he was lifted up it set him in Eden, in the fair place.
There it kept him with his kinsman Enoch, who had been translated,
that there they might be, free from suffering, in the mystery of the kingdom.
In them it showed us a sign of the peace toward our race,
and by their life it promised life unto immortality.
It held them as pledges of love for the peace of humankind,
and so long as they are in the place of life, our hope stands firm.
The freedom of the soul and the resurrection of the body were promised to us,
and it made them like sureties on the bond of our life.
It laid its hand on the covenants of our bodies' renewal,
in that their bodies are kept unharmed.
It divided the time of the life of time into portions,
to sow the hope of the life of the dead in all generations.
It translated Enoch in the tenth generation of those who corrupted order,
and by his translation it taught them about his wrath.
In the middle of the generations he chose Elijah and kept him alive,
and by his exaltation revealed the glory of the immortals.
At the end of the ages he took one of us as firstfruits,
and through his sacrifice reconciled all to his majesty.
Not as he kept the servants alive apart from humankind did he keep him;
for the servants are on earth, but he, as Lord, is above in heaven.
Enoch and Elijah are kept on earth, in the place of Eden,
but he in heaven reigns over all with the One who assumed him.
Within paradise he made the good servants dwell,
as a pledge of that restoration which knows no corruption.
The righteous did not receive the life of Eden as their recompense,
for the reward of their crowns is kept in the kingdom on high.
For he who knows all looked beforehand to the help of our life,
and kept them in a mystery, for our sake, for the promise of the just.

For us he looked, and so fulfilled the promises of his words,
that together with them we might receive the freedom of our bodies and the redemption of our souls.
See, the cause of the just has trodden a way to life for us;
come, let us walk, as in a mystery, toward the end.
See, through the translation of two men he has shown us
what translates us toward the incorruptible restoration.
Come, let us set before us the goal of the just and strive toward it,
and let each one look to the strength of their thoughts.
Let our lowliness be roused by the sweet sound of their words,
and let it drive the weight of desires from our mind.
Let us wash our thoughts clean of the filth of the hateful world,
and let our soul see itself in the mirror of their conduct.
Like sentries, let each one keep watch around the camp of our race;
let none grow slack, lest evil break into our ranks.
Let us train ourselves always by their conduct toward perfection,
today and tomorrow, for the end of our life is drawing near.
By faith the victorious overcame the sufferings that befell them;
in it let us take refuge in all the battles of body and soul.
It is a shield that receives the arrows of the adversary,
and the fiery sword cannot prevail against its firmness.
In it human minds are tested as in a furnace,
and the seething of sufferings shows up the dross of the soul's vileness.
Let the mind of our soul be gold in the furnace of its testing,
and not grow slack before the provocations of our evil inclination.
Let us look to Jesus and become like him in the strength of our soul,
for he is both the beginning and the perfecter of our faith.
Instead of joy, he endured the cross for our sake;
let us wait in the love of faith in him, that we may reign with him.
Refrain: Let our fast be to the Messiah a hyssop to whiten our stains.
For the Sunday of the fourth week of the Fast
Twelfth Discourse / For the Sunday of the fourth week of the Fast / Responsory / Come, let us flee from iniquity, and love the life that does not perish, / my brothers

In the dwelling of time, a time of suffering, mortals dwell,
and for a short time each one lives the life of this world.
Time runs on in a single, ceaseless change that hurries it along,
and together with time men become like a shadow.
The world in its course and its changes is like a dream,
and like a vapour the life of mortality comes to an end.
Man is vapour, and the life of time is vanity of vanities,
and time and the changing of life bear witness that they are vapour.
Time passes on to time and hurries like a courier,
and time gives way to time so as not to be held back.
Generation hands on to generation the continuance of life,
and death runs like a guide ahead of all the generations.
Time goes on without delay, and the generation with it,
and, though mute, it cries out to the rational being not to delay.
Time in its course is always reproving rationality:

"Why do you wear yourself out for no fitting gain?"
Like one who speaks, the mute cries out to the discerning:
"Look and examine the change of time and the alteration of life:
where is the time whose course has stayed without change,
and when have men remained in a life without alteration?
Who is it that has held back the sun so that it should not change,
and who has put fetters on death so that it should not come near him?
Who has given silver and pearls and bought life,
and who has hidden his body in secret from sickness?
Where is the king who guarded his life from harm,
and when did his crown remain, once he had died, and not decay?"
There is no mortal who bears the name of man who is not mortal,
and there is no creature of dust whose sufferings are not kneaded in with his clay.
And if he is mortal, and his mind is clothed in the garments of the passions,
why does contemptible dust boast in the life of time?
See, his departure cries aloud about his corruption,
that man is dust and returns to the dust of his clay.
Like a hired labourer he lives on the earthly land,
and like a passer-by he waits for death as for evening.
At birth he hires himself out, as at morning, to work the land,
and at evening time death gives him rest, as in sleep.
He acquires nothing that does not perish along with his corruption,
and he, together with what is his, always returns to contempt.
Why then is the proud mortal haughty over what is not his own?
For see, he does not profit his possessions, nor do his possessions profit him.
Time changes what is his during his life, while he looks on and is silent,
and death carries him off to Sheol, and what is his falls silent.
Do not, then, rejoice, you who acquire possessions, as though you had acquired them,
for see, you are estranged from what is yours, and what is yours from you.
Call your possessions and stand them up at the time of your death,
and see whether any of them opens its mouth and persuades death.
Gather your servants and clothe them in armour of strength,

and let them shoot arrows at the ranks of death so that it may not wound you.
Arm the movements of your soul as well, and go down to the contest;
engage sickness in battle, and overthrow it and cast it out.
And if that which weakens the strength of your limbs comes through the struggle,
prepare silver and give an offering, and save your soul.
Riches have none of these things you have recounted,
nor is death persuaded by bribes to show you favour.
If you wish, judge truly as a discerning man,
and bring my words to the scrutiny of your soul, and see that they are true.
Look carefully with the clear eye of discernment,
and see that the span of our life is vapour and lies under dread.
Our life bears witness to our changing, that it is not ours,
for it wraps us, along with all things, in one and the same change.
Do not, then, rejoice, O son of man, in the possessions of time,
and do not exalt yourself over the poor man whose living is meagre.
Do not in your pride overthrow the man who is bitter of soul,
lest you be overthrown by the sentence of the judgment that is just in its scrutiny.
Do not deal harshly with the one who is in need,
lest you be sunk with the rich man in the pit of Sheol.
Remember his torment and his groans in Gehenna,
how much he pleaded, and his words were in vain.
Do not take your delight alone, as though in what is your own,
lest you be estranged from the fellowship of the promised blessings.
Do not pamper yourself with earthly things beyond due measure,
lest countless manifold punishments be multiplied for you.
Give yourself rest as is fitting for the life of time,
and give the surplus to whoever lacks sustenance.
The wealth you have acquired is not yours but your Lord's;
manage your soul and your fellows like a steward.
You are a steward in all these things that you have acquired,
and you will have to give the master of the house an account of your property.
The master of the house is the God of all, who established all things

and entrusted the wealth of his kindness to the work of his hands.
He gave wealth to those who are rich in earthly things,
to test them with what is not theirs, whether they are faithful.
He likewise diminished the sustenance of time for those who are poor,
to test them in want as in a furnace.
He could have given wealth to everyone alike,
but this would not have helped rationality.
For he knew, before he established all things, how he would give,
and kept what is fitting for a discerning nature clothed in passions.
To one he gave wealth, to test his mind with what is not his;
another he made poor, that through trial he might train his life.
It was not that he needed to learn about them, as one who does not know,
but to make known the strength of the freedom he placed in rational beings.
By abundance and by want he willed to test the wealth of the soul,
to show how far its discernment is exalted above the animals.
For an animal great wealth and poverty are alike;
it is neither puffed up by much nor consumed by little.
The soul of man is a treasury of discernment,
and it has authority to rejoice in much and to grieve over little.
In the treasury of its mind the Establisher of all placed his wisdom,
so that by its own choice it may dispense the treasure entrusted to its hands.
It is clear that our Lord gave both to our scrutiny,
so that we might be witnesses in the judgment against our own wickedness.
You have, then, no answer to give, O rich man,
nor can you win when you are called to account for why you did wrong.
"It is not because you acquired," says the Judge of all, "that I contend with you,
but because you were stripped of mercy and became a hater of man.
For man's sake he who enriches all gave the wealth,
and you hid it away and stripped men of their life."
On the sustenance of time hang the lives of men,
and whoever withholds the life of man is a murderer of man.
Who would not weep over the rich man stripped of mercy,
who in the wickedness of his mind became a companion of the murderer of man?
If there is nothing greater than man in all that has come to be,
then there is nothing more evil than a man who hates man.
"Why have you hated me, O rich man, like the Evil One,

and become a hater of man, who is the image of the Creator?
Why have you estranged yourself from the peace of man, you hater of man,
and made yourself void of mercy, like the Evil One?"
Turn away from the region of pride, a desolate mountain,
and dwell in the land of humility, whose tilling is pleasant.
Occupy your soul with the company of men who love peace,
and subdue your mind under the gentle yoke of humility.
Sow your almsgiving in the land of man, which does not defraud,
and wait in hope for the fruit in whose eating life lies hidden.
Give to the needy, stoop to the distressed, give rest to the orphan;
make your face bright, and do not be grieved when you give.
See that you do not give while it pains you and your heart is distressed,
lest you hear that voice which came to Cain:
he too offered a hateful sacrifice that seemed good to him,
and the Just One, who saw that his heart was gloomy, rejected it and cast it away.
Do not, then, sow the seed of your alms in despair of hope,
lest the fruits of your labours be cheated of their reward.
There is no reward for fruits that come from grudging sorrow,
and hateful sacrifices are not accepted before the One who sees all.
The one who gives and is gloomy incurs two losses:
he loses what is his, and confines himself under accusation.
In a double judgment he is accused through his very gift,
and he does not perceive to whom he gives and against whom he sins.
He gives, and grieves the Giver who gave to him and to all,
and does not perceive that it is toward Him, over what is His own, that his eye is grudging.
For God of all is the one who possesses kings and the lowly,
and from his gift men and heavenly beings are made rich.
It is right to give to him what is his, with pure love,
lest we be accused over what is not ours, as though it were ours.
And if the wealth is his, and the life, and the reward of the wage,
why does contemptible dust boast because gold has been put into it?
Paul laid down that no one who is made should boast,

and if one boasts, let him lift up his mind in the Lord alone.
Let each one lay [?] before the Maker whatever he has acquired,
except iniquity, which is our own and is practised by us.
For it is our own mind, and not another's, that is the iniquity of our soul,
and though it be very wicked, whenever it wishes it can turn its iniquity to righteousness.
It bears witness for itself to the authority of its discernment,
that by its own will it wins or is guilty in the things it has acquired.
Come, mortals, set in order the course of your wills,
for see, it has been revealed that it is our will that rules over all.
Let each one blame his own will for whatever grows slack,
and let him examine his own person and reprove his iniquity.
Let the mind be like a judge over all our deeds,
and bring iniquity and righteousness to its scrutiny.
Every rational being is bound, as by a debt, to know these things,
and if he does not repay it, his own mind reproves his wrongdoing.
Let not, then, the strength of the wisdom hidden in our soul lie idle,
nor let it give birth to an irreconcilable murmuring against our Maker.
Let us not boast when wealth and power abound for us,
nor let it grieve us when our life is despised and our body weak.
Let us not be exalted by the greatness of a rank of leadership,
nor be ashamed to be subject to good order.
Whoever commands, let him soften his words with peaceable speech,
and whoever obeys, let him repay kindness as one in debt.
Whoever is a head, let him be a head in deeds,
like the head by which the whole body is given light.
Whoever is obedient, in the place of the feet,
let him always walk toward those who command him, like feet.
Whoever is bright of mind to discern well,
let him show the way to those who are in darkness without comfort.
Whoever is weak of hearing in his understanding when it comes to obeying the truth,
let one raise a voice for him like a trumpet in dull ears.
Whoever is sharp with the sword of his word to slay iniquity,
let him lay waste the ranks of the Adversary with his sayings.
Whoever is wise and knows the order of the word of life,

let him give savour to those who are insipid and lack what is fitting.
Whoever is true in the love of his soul in faith,
let him soften the spiritual food for those who are still infants.
Whoever is whole and free from the stains of the desires,
let him wash the limbs of his fellows clean of hateful things.
Whoever is holy and free from the impurity of the lust of the flesh,
let him sprinkle his words like dew upon sinners.
Whoever is occupied with good meditation on spiritual things,
let him help his companions by the good report of his way of life.
Whoever is learned and wishes to teach the unlearned,
let him measure his words to their minds, and so teach.
Let the master say to his disciple, "Look at me and learn,"
and let the disciple in turn attend to the aim of his master's words.
Let the master not be lifted up in arrogance over his disciple,
nor the disciple scorn the master who makes him wise.
Let the master be in the place of the eye for the senses of the body,
and let the senses walk after the eye toward learning.
Let the word of the mouth fulfil its office toward the limbs,
and let the limbs listen to its voice without ever having enough.
In the order of the body let our love be bound one to another,
just as the body is held together by its members and is one whole.
The body is one and is not divided by the distinction of its members,
and though they are many they are equal, in a harmony that is not torn apart.
Christ is one, the head of the Church, the pure body,
and it is fitting that Christian members abide in one love.
If the members are distinct and yet equal in what is visible,
how much more should the hidden movements be bound together in hidden things!
The feet are distinct from one another in their tasks,
and yet the course of their service to the one body is the same.
There is no member that envies its fellow for its skill,
nor do they quarrel and cheat one another of the food they need.
In the order of the members let us look to one another as discerning beings,
and let each one, like the members, be alike in our deeds.
Let the sound of mind give heart to the one who is weak,
and bind up his suffering with the medicine of a hope that is not overturned.
Let him restrain the light of soul, lest he grow frivolous,
and let the lover of peace quiet the heat of the wrathful.
Let the shrewd help the one who lacks understanding to know the truth,

and let the one skilled in labours rouse the slack to the work of life.
Let the owner of possessions manage his wealth wisely,
and let the one who lacks property guard his soul from murmuring.
Let the one sound of limb not despise in his mind the one who is afflicted,
and let the one sick in body not lose heart through despair.
Let the one full of comeliness not mock the ugly of face,
and let the one who is unsightly not grieve over why he is so.
You who are skilled in conversation, keep your words in order, free of boasting,
and restrain your speech, keeping your tongue from blasphemy.
You who are quick in your movements, see that you do not run after hidden things,
and you who are dull of understanding, do not hang back from learning.
Lover of money, do not strive to take what belongs to others,
lest the books of the Spirit call you a second Ahab.
Lover of praise, do not paint your works for the eyes of onlookers,
lest you share in that voice of the Pharisee.
Nazirite who abstains from wine, see that you do not mix anger into your drink,
lest you become drunk on the drink of wrath and your understanding go astray.
Constant faster, keep your mind from hateful things,
lest you be thrown into hunger both here and in Gehenna.
You who are busy in prayer, pray in secret, as you were commanded,
lest empty praise empty out the works of your soul.
You who are chaste of gaze, do not be dazzled by the beauty of faces,
lest you be entangled in the snares of the lust of the flesh.
Through a hateful glance the honoured have fallen from their ranks,
and the mighty have been found guilty through the stirrings aroused by meeting faces.
The glance of eyes bound Samson, the mighty man of strength,
and the beauty of a face ensnared David, bright of understanding.
And if the mighty and the men of understanding fell through sight,
who would not guard the gaze of his eyes from stumbling?
The eye is a frail thing, and a store [?] of wounds is shut up in its spring,
and if they burst open, they flood the body and lead the soul astray.

Keep the door of your eyes chastely and guard your gates,
lest the treasure you have gathered with care be plundered.
Do not be dazzled by the beauty of faces throughout your time,
lest you be found unsightly in the bridal chamber on high.
You too, Eve, cover your face with a chaste garment,
lest the chaste be caught in the traps of your hateful glance.
Set in order the course of the mind of your soul, and your gates,
lest those who pass by you stumble on the road because of your eyes.
Look properly, and adorn yourself with modesty,
lest you remain outside the door with the foolish virgins.
Prepare oil and go out in the company of the wise virgins,
lest the lamp of your love go out and you become a laughingstock.
Do not paint yourself with the outward colouring of faces,
lest those who are sound and fair in beauty of soul mock you.
Restrain your goings and your gates from hateful things,
lest they call you a stumbling stone thrown down in the marketplace.
Look and understand that your eye and the colouring of your face are a trap,
and by you senses and movements are caught as in a net.
You are wholly a trap hidden in the ground in front of the paths,
and no one knows how he falls into your snares.
With cunning knots the nets of your desires are tied,
and great is the toil of escaping from your wiles.
You are like the partridge that calls the members of its own kind to death,
and by its cries kills its fellows and dies itself as well.
Like the partridge you display your appearance to whoever looks at you,
and with your allurements you catch young men like birds.
A double death is hidden in the perversity of your evil mind,
and it calls a man to destruction as though to peace.
The speech of your mouth before the simple is like fruit for the picking [?],

and whoever has longed to eat of it has been counted among sinners.
There is no hunter more skilled than you at hunting men,
and no bird that calls as sweetly as your allurements.
You are exceedingly cunning in the art of hunting men,
and no one knows how to recount the kinds of your wiles.
Your mind is wise to read in the books of the murderer of men,
and your heart is foolish when it comes to meditating on the wisdom of truth.
He has been your skilled teacher from the beginning,
and in his writings you have read and meditated, and sinned and caused others to sin.
Leave the instruction of the crafty scribe who teaches falsehood,
and come, meditate on the books of the Spirit that grant life.
Do not be like Eve your mother, who listened to his counsel
and ate the fruit and gave birth to death for the house of Adam.
See, once again you make the bitterness of death spring up through your wiles.
Is it not enough that you killed us by eating the fruit your mother desired?
Do not kill us through the lust of the flesh as through the fruit.
Cease to be a snare of iniquity before onlookers,
for see, people of every stature have been caught in the nets of your face.
Would that you were as hateful in the look of your face as you are in your mind,
so that the young of heart would have recoiled from your hatefulness!
Alas! If you had not so much colouring of face and so many pearls,
the lovers of colouring would long since have grown indifferent to your dealings.
If only someone had put a halter [?] on your eyes and on your goings,
and shut you up in a cage [?] like the wild beasts!
If only someone had bound your evil mind fast at all times,
the voice that troubles men's peace would long since have fallen silent!
If only someone had set the seal of silence on your tongue,
it would long since have ceased from laying waste the ranks of men!
Blessed is he who stopped his ears and did not listen to your words,
and became deaf to the converse of your wantonness.
Blessed is he who, while he was with you, was not with you,
and lived with you yet guarded his soul from your harms.
Blessed is he who did not, through dealings with you, stray from the aim of his words,
and was not troubled by the shifts of your wantonness.

In speaking of you I have turned aside from the course my words were taking,
for I saw that the snares of your wiles were beyond number.
Talk of you has drawn me away from the subject that concerns every man,
for I saw that the whole world is bound up in the business of loving you.
It was not out of malice that I accused you, as you supposed,
and it was not you I blamed, but your mind, which sins and causes others to sin.
Nor did I blame your mind itself as evil,
but because, though it is good, each one makes it evil for himself and for his fellows.
Your mind is not bound by nature, like the dumb creatures,
nor are you alone in having movements that tend toward the stirrings of passion.
The choice of your discernment is equal to that of a man,
and if you please, you fall short of him in nothing in your labour.
One is the mind of discernment in men and in women,
and one the strength and freedom of the soul that wins or sins.
It was not the company of women that was hateful before the One who knows all,
but the mind of brazen women that cannot be restrained.
It is not the business of modest women that makes a man sin,
but the seduction of wanton women that leads young men astray.
The union of the fellowship of faithful wives has not defiled,
but evil is the lustful drink of lawlessness.
A woman is pure when she is far from lewdness,
and holy and pure is union with her, and the child born of her.
She is equal in labours and in reward, she and her husband alike,
and together they inherit the life of time and the kingdom on high.
Here they are distinct from one another in their forms;
beyond, there are neither males nor females, for there is one nature.
And if they are one in the place that is pure of harms,
let no one separate anything that God of all has made equal.
One is the nature of men and women, and one is the Creator,
and it is fitting that they look to one goal in their deeds.
The man is not apart from the woman in faith,
nor is the woman apart from the man in the fear of truth.
Let the man fill the place of the head for the women, who are the feet,
and let the woman walk in the order that befits the feet below.
Let the man be like a tongue, a harp of strings,
and let him always sow chaste sounds in people's ears.
Let the women listen to the sound of his words in faith,
and bring forth the fruits of purity of soul: hope and love.

Let not the sounds from the mouth of the one who sows be cheated,
nor let the hearing turn dark toward the seed of the word of life.
Sow, O man, the word of life in the ears of women;
and you, women, receive and listen to the testimony of the men.
We are bound by the debt of love toward one another:
repay one another, and the Creator, as is fitting.
Pure love is able to repay the debt of man,
and it makes us lovers of the hidden One, and spiritual beings.
Love, O men, one confession of one Creator,
and love, O women, one equality of one God.
Confess rightly, as is fitting for the mind that is in you,
one essence and one authority, three persons.
Confess that there is an equal nature that is not divided,
and that he is everlasting, just as he is without beginning.
Confess that there are the Father and the Son and the Spirit who is from him:
one Begetter, one Begotten, and one Proceeding.
Confess the Father, for whom there is no "when" at which he was not Father,
and believe in the Son, between whom and his Father there is no time.
Praise and magnify the Spirit, who is one in essence,
and not less or smaller than the authority of the Father and the Son.
Call rightly upon the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,
a nature that is equal and not divided by change.
The God of all does not change from what he is,
nor is the nature of his being confined within limits.
No eye can see him [?] by the outward senses,
nor does he have a voice perceptible to the senses, as bodily beings do.
He is wholly being, wholly hidden, wholly equal,
and wholly perfect in his divinity and in his power to make.
His sign established heaven and earth and all that is in them,
and from nothing he created everything, hidden and revealed.
