He set a time for making his creatures, as it pleased him,
and when he willed, he brought the hidden depths of his love to light.
For his love's sake he created all things, not for his own rest,
and to his creatures he showed his power, not his essence.
He established all things from nothing by the power of his will,
and he will renew all things at the end of the ages in the image of his Image.

To him belongs the first coming-into-being out of nothing,
and the renewal that is in the One is his as well.
In the beginning he made things out of nothing, as a Maker,
and now he has renewed his handiwork, as a Wise One.
He made all things and renewed all things wisely,
as befits the power of his being, which is hidden from all.
In the image of man he completed his work at the beginning of creation,
and through the Son of Man he renewed and gave life at the end of the ages.
In the making of man he gathered everything together as in a house,
and in the image of man his will dwelt as in a temple. (a)
In man he bound up all the power of his creative work,
and through the Son of Man he renews all and judges all.
He called the image of man by the name of his own image when he made all things,
and in it he is shown, as in an image, when he judges all.
In the image of man both humans and spiritual beings see
the one who executes judgment and searches out iniquity, who rejects and chooses.
In the temple of his body all worship the God of all,
and in his visibility all see the One hidden from all.
With the outward senses they see the visible body,
and through the inner movements of the mind, the Godhead that is not seen.
In his body their questions come to rest as in a harbor,
and they are not worn out searching for the Hidden One who is hidden within him.
In his love earthly and heavenly beings are bound together,
and in him they praise the one Creator with a single thanksgiving.
Come, let us draw near in faith to the temple of his body,
and offer in it sacrifices of love that repay his love.
Come, let us worship in him as in a divine temple,
and in him give divine praise to the God of all.
Come, let us see in him, by faith, the One hidden from all,
and believe in him, revealed and hidden, here and there.
By faith the mind is able to know these things,
for faith reveals to it the hidden and concealed mysteries.
By its hand the mind sees things far off as though they were near,
and they are as certain to it as things that have already taken place in deed.
In its hidden treasury faith has stored up the life to come,
and from it both spiritual and bodily beings grow rich.
It is like an anchor fixed for ever in the sea of sufferings,
that it may not be torn loose amid the surging waves of desires.

Come, let us moor the ship of our soul to it as to an anchor,
and keep love safe amid the turmoil of the stormy waves.
Come, let us hold fast to it as to a guide who knows what lies beyond,
and with it reach the consummation of the kingdom on high.
Come, let us examine in it the nature of our soul as in a furnace,
and reject iniquity and choose the love that loves the truth.
Come, let us uncover to it the blemishes of our bodies and our minds,
and with its medicines heal our pains within and without.
It is a good physician who knows the remedies for the afflicted,
and there is no help that is not prepared and stored up in its treasury.
It knows how to heal the rich and the poor,
and the just as well as the wicked stand in need of its help.
Come, rich man, uncover to it the sores of your extortion;
give alms, and take the medicine that heals your iniquity.
Come, poor man, take refuge in the strength of its help,
and labor with it without ceasing for the denarius of life.
Come, righteous one, lay up treasures in the storehouses of its love,
and set the seal of its truth upon your mind.
Come, sinner, write out repentance of heart and bring it to it;
offer suffering and tears as a pledge, and receive forgiveness.
Come, frivolous one, make your soul chaste through its humility,
and put the garment of holiness on your limbs.
Come, thief, give up theft and walk in its way,
and hope in its hope, that it may tear up for you the bond of your debts.
Come, adulterer, sanctify your body by its holiness,
and sprinkle over your whole self the pure waters [?] of the mystery of forgiveness.
Come, humble one, walk in the company of its humility,
and reach with it the harbor of peace that knows no sorrow.
Eve, broken one, come, grow wise in faith,
and acquire understanding to guard yourself from your accuser.
Like a mirror, set its purity before your mind,
and scour the filth from your thoughts with the loveliness of its beauty.
Strip off the covering of ignorance, that outward adornment,

and adorn your soul with the lovely garment of modesty.
Put on the clothing of chastity, over your body and over your mind,
and instead of a snare be a mirror to people's eyes.
Set the judgment of the world beyond as a target before your doors,
and look and gaze upon the royal reward and upon the torment,
the sure and certain judgment that is coming upon the good and the wicked,
in which each receives, without end, what is fitting.
Without end the good rejoice and the wicked weep,
and according to the deeds the delight is full and the punishment doubled.
Come, let us trade while there is still opportunity and while it is the time for trading,
lest the time of the end come and our labor fall short.
Come, let us win friends for ourselves here with the mammon of this age,
that they may receive us into their tents that are never taken down.
With love let us visit our neighbors and our Maker,
for love is able to make human beings divine.
Let us judge rightly with our mind the things in which we have sinned,
and let our nature reprove itself like a discerning judge.
Let each one repeat to the nature of his own soul that saying:
that the word of the God of all is living and just in its scrutiny.
Let our nature, together with the tongue, interpret the things to come,
and explain to itself the mysteries hidden in the place on high.
Let the mind show to the eyes of the body the lovely likeness
of that delight whose sweetness never cloys.
With the mind let us behold it and long for it with the love of the soul,
that at the end we may receive its riches face to face.
Response. Glory to you, forgiver of debts, thousands upon thousands of times.
On Poverty
Thirteenth Discourse: On poverty, and how it befits prayer

Wretched is the age that has befallen me in my sojourning,
and in it the gaining of spiritual life is held in contempt.

Evil is the way of life that I find has become second nature among the earthly,
and it is very hard for anyone who wants to live well.

Troubled beyond all other days is the life of this week of my days,
and there is no order in it befitting beings endowed with speech.

Darkened is the light of discernment, the light of the two [?],
and there is no one to set the foolish right with the word of truth.

Weak is the building of faith, which bears all things,
and no one teaches how to build up well the purity of one's soul.

Cold is love, whose glow is warmer than fire,
and everyone seethes with harsh anger against his neighbour.

Weak is the hope that holds the gate of the kingdom,
while the body is robust in the impulses of the soul, in earthly lust.

Despised and scorned are the lives and the books of the wise among men,
and the pursuit of discernment and of the Scriptures has come to a halt.

The study of spiritual things is reckoned as nothing,
and everyone ponders earthly things without ever being satisfied.

Scarce is the conduct of holiness, the pure vessel,
and beloved is the waywardness of wantonness, a foul mire.

Despised is marriage, the proper order of creation,
and everyone runs along the shameful road of adultery.

Deceit, murder and adultery have multiplied upon the earth,
and the fruits of love have perished and vanished from humanity.

Sorceries, divinations, enchantments and vanities have grown strong in creation
and have driven truth away, so that it may not rule among mankind.

The dominion of the cruel demons stretches out in their deeds,
and they have weighed the world down with the harsh yoke of their blasphemies.

The company of the ministers of righteousness has dwindled,
and everyone works the earth continually, without ceasing.

Few indeed are those who love to meditate on spiritual things,
and there is no counting those who love earthly things.

With earthly things the earthly are busy night and day,
and the mind cannot lift its gaze to the heights.

For those who are invited, who are called to the kingdom on high, seek what is below,
and long to stay here in this earthly dwelling.

Mortality has bound them with the cords of suffering,
and to everyone the prison house of mortality is pleasant.

No one feels how harsh is the weapon of our capacity to suffer,
and no one hopes to escape its harshness.

In an oppressed life full of loathing they long to remain,
and they do not yearn for that restoration which does not decay.

The gaining of the things of time is precious to them and dearer than their own life,
as though the delight of the promised life were not counted true.

No one hopes for that hope so full of blessings,
unless it is in words that he speaks of it, and not in deeds.

In words they recount all the good things that cannot be uttered,
and though they are true, to their minds they are not true.

The reality of the world to come is reckoned a tale,
and everyone fears, while not truly fearing.

True things are not true to those who are untrue,
and in their deeds they deceitfully display their rottenness.

Lowly in the members is the love of the love of truth,
and the impulses of the soul are laid bare and let loose without purity.

The body is adorned like a tree laden with fruit,
but in the mind there is no cluster of faithfulness.

The vineyard of my Beloved flourishes with leaves as though it were thriving,
but among its branches are hidden wild grapes that cannot be eaten.

The age that has come upon me among the earthly is like winter,

and men, like trees, have been stripped bare of good things.

The barrenness of iniquity has seized the land of reason,
and the husbandmen have ceased from cultivating what is fair.

The snow of wickedness has fallen on the impulses as on mountains
and blocked the road, and no one walks toward righteousness.

Love of money has beaten the soul like hail,
and the leaves of faith have fallen from the mind.

Hatreds have blown like a whirlwind in the heat of the mind,
and the skilled pilot, the will, has been shaken and confounded.

The harsh frost of desires has bitten into creation,
and thoughts have come to the point where they no longer build the edifice of love well.

Oppression has scorched the earth with inequity;
peace has been burned up, compassion has dried up, and mercy has been cut off.

The love of truth [?] has entered and burrowed among the thoughts,
and like a locust it has struck and withered the root of the soul.

Tyrannical pride has rebelled on the crag of a haughty spirit
and has begun to wage war against the ranks of humility.

Gnawing envy lies in wait on the roads before the travellers
and has bitten the world with the harsh teeth of its bitterness.

Like a [?] destruction has crept into the minds of men;
it has eaten the fruit, stripped the leaves, and left only the root.

Like a bare root the mind has remained, without virtuous conduct,
and only a little of the life of life still persists in it.

In its winter the rational vineyard of Adam has been laid waste and dried up,
and demons have trampled it in its bareness [?] like passers-by.

Not a single cluster remains in it that has not been damaged,
and if one does remain, there is no wine of delight in it.

Woe to us, lest the Lord of the vineyard bring his case against us
and indict our wrongdoing as he did that of the Jews.

Woe to us, lest he prepare and summon the mute natures
to be witnesses against our wickedness, which has wronged his love.

Woe to us, let us say with the herald, the prophet of the Spirit,
for men have become like the gleanings of summer, as it is written.

There is no cluster in our vineyard pleasant enough to eat,
nor any first-ripe fig in which the planter's mark can be seen.

Our Lord says, like the voice of prophecy,
‘The godly man has perished, and there is no longer anyone upright among men.’

In their heart is deceit, and on their lips falsehood,

and like hunters they hide snares in their tongues.

The man who has gained power shamelessly makes unjust demands,
and the judge too exacts mercilessly and to excess.

The great man speaks as he pleases and is not restrained,
and to his haughtiness men are reckoned as no men at all.

He who teaches, teaches out of pride and not out of love,
and he who learns strives against his master out of love of rank.

The teacher does not keep to the aim of Christ, the great Master,
nor does the disciple walk in the order of discipleship.

Darkened among disciples is the light of mastership,
and insipid in the mouths of masters is the taste of discipleship.

The arrogant master teaches words and not deeds,
and the disciple too hears words and not understanding.

With eyes of flesh he spells out the words of the Spirit to the young
and shows the bodily members the powers of hidden things.

The flesh looks carnally on spiritual things,
and the examination of things to come is reckoned a shadow.

Man busies himself with the senses of the body as though he had no senses,
and wanders among the divine mysteries as in a dream.

In our generation the truth, when it is told, is like a dream,
and to fools a dream is indeed truer than the truth.

To the untrue a dream is true, though it is utterly false,
and when it is told they wander along its path rather than that of truth.

Truth cries out in the Scriptures, and no one listens,
and the ear of the earthly inclines to hear earthly things.

It runs on continually, but only among the letters,
and great is the crowd that walks the broad road of iniquity.

Its radiance is brighter than the sun to those who see clearly,
but to the dark, darkness is dearer than its light.

The study of it is more desirable than gold and pearls,
yet lovers of money do not even sense that it exists at all.

It is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to the palate,
but to the wicked its drink is bitter and unacceptable.

To those who love it, the study of it is beloved and its food pleasant,
but to wrongdoers even the mention of it is harsh.

The prophet proclaims that it is more precious than all things and sweeter than all,
but to the dissolute its taste is insipid and the study of it despised.

David undertook to keep its words with care,

and the perverse of heart fled from him, away from evil.

Evil men have reckoned the study of truth an evil thing,
and they have retched at its drink as at a drug with a powerful smell.

Mortals lie stricken with the grievous diseases of the passions,
and so the word of truth upon their sores seems harsh to them.

Men sick in soul are like a sick body
that is loath to reveal the trouble of its pain to physicians.

Sinners, too, chafe at their sins,
yet they do not draw near to the door of truth, the physician who heals for nothing.

They are ashamed to show the pain within them,
and do not understand that a pain grown old is hard to heal.

In their ignorance they cover up the sores of their deeds,
and do not consider that after death there is no healing.

They are badly mistaken in hoping that mercy pardons freely,
and do not reflect that if there is mercy, there is also justice.

If there is mercy, it exists for you, O man;
so accept, then, that there is justice which cannot be overcome.

If mercy prevails in judgment, there is no justice,
and if the Just One judges justly, there is no pity.

If he is just, accept then that he is just in his testing,
and learn well that he is just and good, but not indiscriminately.

Every created being rightly acknowledges that the Creator is just,
and his love toward our race testifies that he is merciful.

With discernment it is fitting to call him just and good:
good to the one who repents, and just when he exacts payment from the one who does not repent.

It is plain to us that our will holds power over both,
and if it so pleases, it turns punishments into pity.

And if the treasures of life and death have been placed within it,
why is our will rashly blamed as evil?

Our will holds the gate of the kingdom, if we so wish,
and it is the will that lets in and the will that lets out as it pleases.

That Voice, too, which trod the way of the kingdom on high,
cried out that the kingdom is within men and dwells in them.

And if the kingdom full of life dwells in man,
then there is no one more foolish than a man who hates his own life.

How is he not a hater of his own life, a hater of the truth,

who forsakes the way that gives life and walks in the wilderness?

Man stands against his own will and against the truth,
for though he knows, he wrongs both himself and his Maker.

Great is the wrong that mortals have done to the life within them,
for they despised the law that the Creator laid down for their ordering.

They forsook the commandment that had exalted them above all things,
and loved the love of the Accuser, which brought them low.

They despised the Name that honoured them with its glories;
they gave the honour of the name of majesty to what is not God.

They trampled on the law, which is light and salt and guide as well,
which treads out the way, gives savour, and enlightens the mind.

They breached its commandments, the high wall that stands against iniquity,
and wild beasts, evil habits, came in and ravaged its fruits.

Wild asses, wolves and lions, evil kinds of every sort,
fell upon the vineyard of the law, the husbandry of mankind.

Gnats, locusts and flies, despised creeping things,
gathered on its leaves, stripped off its fruit and scattered its yield.

Like creeping things, thoughts crept in [?]
and clung on until they reached the great height of the law of the Spirit.

Body and soul ran riot and were inflamed with desires,
and gave no thought to the shamefulness of their minds.

Fornication has put on the face of a dog against the truth,
and however much it is rebuked, it stays in its wantonness just as it is.

Theft has caught the shamelessness of the greedy wolf,
and even if crowds cry out against it, it is not restrained.

Envy, the unruly beast that gives birth to murder, roared like a lion
and raised its voice against the judges [?] and their threats.

Oppression has become like a [?] bear,
and the more it drinks the blood of the oppressed, the more it thirsts.

Love of greed has hidden snares on sea and land
and has caught peoples and cities into its bosom.

Love of glory has stopped its ears against consolation,
and like an asp it has scorned the power that is in the books.

Falsehood, the daughter of the Evil One, whom he begot in Eden,

has surpassed her father in the craft of slander.

She is like a fox in her deceitful twistings,
and burrows into the earth as if in holes so as not to be exposed.

Arrogance, the wild ass that roams the desert without rest,
has broken free of the yoke of humility, the bridle of man.

Gluttony, an insatiable Sheol,
has swallowed the world, and no one knew that it had eaten anything.

Murmuring, the [?] whose appearance is contemptible and whose damage is grievous,
has passed over the field of discernment and destroyed its fruits.

Anger has flared up like fire in the thicket of the soul,
and senses and impulses alike have burned in its heat.

All that was fair has been scorched and singed as in fire,
and no fruit of sweetness is left in the vineyard of man.

The passions have come like beasts into the judge [?],
have eaten his fruits, and left him bare as in winter.

A harsh winter of desires has spread over creation,
and the world has ceased from spiritual husbandry.

The darkness of error, the night of the two [?], has overpowered the truth,
and the lie has risen to a high rank above the truth.

Like the days in the winter months, good things have grown short,
and like the long nights, evils have grown strong.

In our generation there is nothing like summer in the husbandry of life,
and no one stands firm against the passions as in the warmth of summer.

As in winter, the mind is shut up in the temple of the body,
and the barrenness of iniquity holds back its fruitfulness.

In passing things the earthly find summer pleasant,
but in the things to come they are content to stay in a gloomy winter.

For the work of iniquity the turning of the months of the year is too short,
but for the pursuit of righteousness not even a single day is given.

In shameful things they spend summer and winter, and no one grows weary,
but in good things only half a day, and with much grumbling.

For the provisions of time there is no satiety in gathering,
while the pursuit of acquiring life is hidden away as superfluous.

Fools reckon the study of the Spirit superfluous,
and, as if it were night, they are heedless and idle about good things.

As in sleep, the body is sunk down together with the mind,
and they do not wake at the call of the [?] that brings life.

The sleep of iniquity is very dear to the sluggish,

and they do not care to hear the voice at the hour of dawn.

The children of the poor long to stay in poverty,
and do not yearn for the great wealth hidden on high.

In the place on high is hidden a delight that does not decay,
but to the earthly the earth is dearer than the heights.

He counselled our nature toward heavenly things that are not seen,
but those of the dust want to remain in the dust.

On high he fixed the goal of the life his words promised,
and no one can even find words to compare anything with it.

By the power of the Spirit he interpreted the things to come,
and pointed to them, as it were with a finger, through his heralds.

As on a tablet he painted blessings and punishments in scrolls,
so as to enable eyes of flesh to see hidden things.

Like an image he set his commandments in the Scriptures,
so that men might see the truth of his name through revelations.

Within the palace of the Scriptures he traced his hiddenness,
so that everyone who enters may look upon his being through the letters.

The greatness of his love wished to show itself to the work of his hands,
so he wrote a book and lovingly taught them to read it.

The might of his greatness he portrayed in letters, but not his being;
his workings he confined in scrolls, but not his hiddenness.

For the comfort of men he built the palace of the Scriptures,
and brought in and laid up in it the memorial of the mysteries of his hidden things.

He made the spiritual law like a treasury,
and gathered and filled it with the decrees of judgment upon the wicked.

He built himself a palace on the earth, full of all creatures,
and gave men authority to dwell in it in holiness.

In it, as in a storehouse, he placed the boundless treasure of the Spirit,
enough to suffice for both the earthly and the heavenly.

He made the children of his love, who are called by his name, his treasurers,
so that they might distribute it wisely, as people of knowledge.

The keepers of the divine treasure became thieves
and exchanged the wealth of glorious things for paltry ones.

The children of the palace carried off the mysteries of the King of kings
and raised their hand against the Creator who had honoured them.

The servants of the king fled from the King who reigns over all
and bound the mysteries to the rebel, so that they might be his.

The children of the kingdom abandoned the concerns of the palace
and began to talk of the business of farming.

The bridegroom's guests have come to hate the spiritual feast
and have gone out, wandering the roads to trade.

The sons of God, who were worthy of the name of immortals,
have come down from their divine rank and taken their stand on the earth.

The mortals who had been surnamed immortals have died,
and have cut off the hope of ever returning to the name they lost.

In everything they have wronged the hidden sign that honoured them;
they have despised his law and made light of his words, which cannot be undone.

By the law he tested them, to see how much they hated him,
and by the Scriptures he tried the falseness of their minds.

As into a furnace he brought them in through his commandments,
and refined them, but they were not refined of their hatreds.

Come then, let us say, like the voice of prophecy,
that the Spirit has refined us in vain in the furnace of the law.

Let us recount our disgrace, as Jeremiah did to the children of his people:
that discipline has been of no profit against our wickedness.

Our wrongdoing closely resembles that of the Jews,
and our mind has rebelled against teaching even more than they did.

They did not hate the words of the Spirit as we do,
nor were they divided as we are over what lies ahead of us.

The Israelites did not despise and reject their masters
as much as the Gentiles have mocked and insulted those who know the truth.

The Creator's name was not blasphemed among the Hebrews
as much as by the taunts with which the pagans have mocked our faith.

That people was a child with respect to the conduct of perfection,
and, for the measure of its time, not greatly to be blamed for what it dared.

The Gentiles, who have received the perfect wage of the kingdom on high,
have turned to frivolous habits more than children do.

They have let go of the food set down in the incorruptible book
and have turned to sucking the weak milk of observances.

They constantly mock Judaism and paganism,
and do not understand how much more contemptible they are than both.

They condemn those who stray from the truth,
and do not consider that they stray more than those who stray.

The pagans honour their gods as good beings,
while the God of all is despised in his honour by his own worshippers.

The teaching of every heresy is dear to its hearers,

while the teaching of truth is despised and scorned by its ministers.

The Jews are busy with observances that are not true,
and though they are much despised, they are zealous, like members of the household.

The Manichaeans keep the rule of their masters
and do not slacken in their conduct, though it is utterly false.

The Marcionites repay their teachers with love,
and though they are false, they wear the semblance of true things.

The followers of Arius are very zealous over our Scriptures
and build energetically on a foundation that is not true.

The Magians are bound fast in magic, an invention of demons,
and boast of it as of something real, though it is nothing.

There is no people in creation that forgets the one it worships,
or exchanges the worship of the lord it serves.

Let us then rouse the son of Hilkiah, whom the Voice chose,
to rise and astonish the mute natures as before.

Arise, Jeremiah, and judge justly as you are wont,
and call heaven and earth as witnesses against our wickedness.

The Gentiles too, like the people, have committed two evils:
they have forsaken meditation on spiritual things and loved earthly ones.

They have forsaken the law, the sweet fountain that gives life,
and have dug broken cisterns, the inventions of falsehood.

In the Gentiles that word too has been fulfilled which asked, ‘Is the people a slave?’
for they have forsaken truth and desired the pursuit of empty things.

It is fitting that lions too should roar against them,
for they have opened the mouth of demons to blaspheme.

Against the Hebrews roared the Babylonians and Assyrians;
against us now roars the Accuser, the rational lion.

The people that sinned was despised by the Gentiles, who are worse than it,

and we, because we have sinned, see how sufferings and demons trample us.

That people received the punishment for its iniquity at the hands of the Gentiles,
but the punishment for our iniquity is reserved for the day of examination.

Our punishment, then, exceeds that of the Jews,
for he punished them at the hands of men, but us by himself.

His punishment is far harsher than that of man,
and Paul testifies that it is a great terror to fall into his hands.

His word is living and sharper than a sword,
and as with fire it tests the falsehood within the soul.

It enters into judgment with the thoughts that have desired evil things
and exposes them before the eyes of angels and of men.

He has a great case against our discernment,
which has wronged itself and the echoes of his holy words.

With just judgment he tramples down the iniquity of our insolence,
which despised his words and was not restrained by his commandments.

Wisely he inflicts punishments for our evil deeds,
for we have trampled on the order set down in nature and in the Scriptures.

Skilfully he weighs deeds in the scale of his decree,
rejecting what is worthless and collecting what [?] in full.

His commandment is full of severe retribution and stern punishments
for the insolent who did not first heed the decree of his judgments.

He exacts [?] retribution for his great love and for his threats,
for he showed beforehand both his love and his punishments, yet they did not discern or understand.

In proportion to his counsels he increases his demands on his household,
who did not long to wait for the life to come.

The counsel of life without end he traced in his writings,
so that men might see in the Scriptures that which has no end.

He laid out through his prophets a smooth road full of peace,
so that everyone might walk by the waymarks toward our appointed goal [?].

He set the law among the earthly like a mirror,
so that they might look into it and see the blemishes of their persons.

Through the law he showed two things to whoever looks into it:
promised blessings, and severe punishments for whoever despises it.

On both counts he judges us and punishes us:
we desired the blessings and hated the punishments, as people of discernment.

It was for our discernment to distinguish which was fitting,
and because we did not distinguish, he is about to separate us from his promises.

Truth ought to have been required of our speech; and because it was not required, see, it is now being required in just judgment. / Our debt was bound to repay praise; and because it did not repay, see, it is now being exacted without pity. / For we deserve that judgment should come upon us harshly, since we did not accuse our faults by judging our own souls. / Who is as blind to comfort as we are, that we did not judge ourselves before the fearful judgment came? / Who has gained a heart of stone like ours, that we were softened neither by promises nor by threats? / Tasteless things became harsh to our rebelliousness, and excesses became mild to the sloth of our souls. / Heralds are not lacking in the Scriptures, yet no one listens, and the strength of their tongues has grown faint [?] from crying out. / The likenesses and figures have been fulfilled, yet our iniquity stands; visions and revelations have ceased, yet it remains as it is. / The embassy of the heavenly ones has worn out the road, yet the rush of our insolence has not ceased from hateful deeds. / Only mute creatures were sent on the embassy, and see, it is quite evident that not even they have ceased from this. / They have become silent witnesses to us, mute as they are, and instead of a voice they have spoken to us by their changes. / The sun, which grew dark at our hateful deeds, hid its light; and the moon, which was dimmed by our insolence, our insolence turned to blood. / The lightnings that kindled fire, our heat set them blazing; and the thunders that shook things, the sound of our blasphemy made them grow stronger. / The earth that quaked, our iniquity weighed heavily on its shoulders, and as if with a mouth it cried out our reproof through the tremor. / The summer that scorched the fruits with heat, our impudence set it alight; and the winter that lingered long in cold, our murmuring drew it out. / The sicknesses that multiplied, the wickedness of our nature gave birth to them; and death that came in haste, we ourselves hastened it to carry off our souls. / The people that drew near against us, we are the ones who called it; and the king who was brought low and condemned in battle, our sins condemned him. / Through us the excellent order of leadership was thrown into confusion,

and through us the lofty rank of the priestly name was afflicted. / Through our license strife came in and reigned on the earth, and see, priests and kings fight one against another. / Openly and in secret each one wages war against his fellow, and there is no end to their battles night and day. / In a harsh and unequal war they hurl themselves against every troop, and on every side hidden snares lie before those who walk. / In fear and dread one thought keeps apart from another, and no one trusts even that his love is true in others. / With a double heart each one speaks to his neighbour, and the heart is weary, because the words do not agree with the heart. / His tongue is smooth, his speech close, his voice bright; but his heart is twisted, his voice angry, and his look dark. / Smiling and cheerful is the meeting of face with face, but mournful and gloomy is the inner disposition, as if over the dead. / Mouth kisses mouth, giving its portion lovingly, while the deep mind hides snares cruelly. / It is a great fear to go down to the gathering of the waters of life, for passions lie hidden, as in sleep, in the sea of the soul. / Who can hold firm on the road to the kingdom on high, when thoughts lie in ambush and hide like robbers? / Rightly, then, I have called evil the time that has come upon me, for it is evil and contemptible, and full of fear for anyone who walks in it. / Rightly I have pronounced woe on myself at the beginning of my words, for the sustainer of life has perished and ceased in the years of life, in the years of my life [?]. / In my days what is written has been fulfilled: “The godly man has perished,” and there is no one in creation whose soul repents in his mind. / I too have recited a discourse, though I have not done the deed, and I am more bare of good works than my fellows. / A forest of sins fills my thoughts, as it does my companions', and there is no fruit in my mind to please the lord of the vineyard. / I have put words together like a debtor before the judge, in the hope that mercy may incline in judgment toward my guilt. / On the pretext of words I have come in, to hire myself out at the end of the day, since by now I may be found worthy of a small portion [?] of the wage that is paid.

I heard a voice, the echo of the voice that went out to seek labourers, and it urged me to hire out my tongue for the labour of words. / The command that ordered the wage to be paid, a denarius to each, said to me: “Arise, work hard, you lowly labourer.” / May the mercy that hired the lowliness of our race for the labour of truth count me also worthy to receive the wage, the denarius of life.
For the Fifth Sunday of the Fast
[?] Fourteenth / For the Fifth Sunday of the Fast / Responsory / O Good One, who reconciled the world to himself: make peace in our [?], which is troubled by his envy, my brothers.

On the road of the King I was running
toward the goal of the kingdom,
and blind Envy met me,
led along by the evil inclination.
At the crossroads Envy was standing,
going around the evil ways,
and it was asking those who passed by
which road was the good one.
It was wrapped in the guise of compassion,
and asked as though out of love,
and the bitterness of death lay hidden

beneath the smooth [?] garment of its lips.
On the broad road it wished
that many should travel with it,
and that is why it was asking:
to find company for destruction.
The evil inclination was leading
Envy, blind in both eyes,
and blind was leading blind
to the place of the gate of Gehenna.
Envy hired the worker of falsehood
for the service of evil deeds,
to be constant in its labor
at the hours of night and of day.
It fixed for it a denarius of falsehood
stamped with the image of death,
and promised it a reward
if it would go astray and do much wickedness.
From the morning of the beginning, iniquity
took up its service,
and it has stretched out its bitter labor
until the evening of the end.
It does not weary of the long years
from beginning to end,
nor do its works weary or cease,
or slacken from their labor.
It is renewed, ever renewed,
day by day like the eagle,
and with the renewal of its hatred
it makes its bitter shoot flourish.
It does not fear old age,
nor is it brought low by sickness;
even one who is old and feeble
is young and vigorous for envying much.
However old the envier may be,
at envy he is a boy, as from infancy;
though he is lacking in knowledge,
for evil jealousy he is full-grown.
The envier is blind in both eyes,
deprived of the light of truth,
and like night and day
are falsehood and truth alike to him.
The envier is deaf and dumb,
he does not hear the voice of the commandment;
he is deprived of hearing and of speech
by his own free will and not by nature.
The envier is sick, gravely ill
in his impulses and not in his limbs,
and while he thinks he is wholly sound,
he is wholly wasting away and does not know it.
His soul is sick with envy,
and he burns every day with jealousy,
and he does not feel the flame
that is kindled within his mind.
The fire of wrath the evil inclination
sets ablaze in him, in the mind,
and heats him with the fuel of anger,
so that man burns up man.
Hot is its flame,
hotter than the fire of nature,
and it burns the hidden soul

and not the outward body.
Its sword is harder than a sword
or a razor with two edges,
and there is no number to the slain
it casts down among men every hour.
It is accustomed to the blood of men
and thirsts for the slaughter of humankind,
and it ruins impulses together with senses,
soul and body alike.
Many are the slain of the sword,
yet not as many as the slain of envy,
for the sword [?] openly.
Who then is this Envy,
hidden and yet revealed in its deeds,
which, though it has no being of its own,
destroys beings every hour?
In seeking it my thoughts wandered,
that I might find what its beginning is,
and where the root is that bears
its bitter branches and fruits.
Who is it that tends
the evil soil of its tares,
and who gathers its crops
and provides for its forces?
With what armor does it engage
with spirits and with bodies,
and with what senses does it fight
against the athletes of righteousness?
Who is it that arms it
and gives it strength in secret?
And how, though despicable, does it play the mighty one
and overpower the ranks of the mighty?
At its victory, won without justice,
my thoughts were astonished and amazed:
how does the despicable conquer
and bow the head of the victorious?
My mind urged me to examine
and to make a search for Envy,
whether it conquers by its own power
or perhaps by what is not its own.
The inclination counseled me in secret
and showed me a road to travel by,
and became for me like a guide
to the place where the journey ends.
The help of the Spirit set up for me
a goal full of victory,

that I might encamp against it with my impulses
and strike down loathsome Envy.
As though in a mystery there spoke with me
the great power of grace:
"If you wish to learn,
take the road from the beginning.
Travel with the books of the Scriptures
in company with the words of the Spirit,
and they will bring you to the harbor
of what your thoughts have sought.
Keep company with the son of Amram
and go with him to the beginning,
and he will show you from where
the bitterness of Envy sprang.
In the bosom of the sixth day
read and understand with care,
and there your mind will find
the meaning of the cause you have sought.
See there the fashioning of man,
and hear the voice of the name 'image',
and at the end of that word
see the beginning of Envy."
Envy heard the voice of 'image',
as he was named with the image of the Hidden One,
and the bitterness of death was stirred in it
at the voice of the fashioning of the one made of dust.
The fire of its inclination blazed
in the tyrant, the chief of the air,
and set him wholly ablaze with envy,
and he set fire to humankind.
He opened the quiver of his hatred
and shot his bitterness at man,
and stained the garment of creation
with the poison of death that the fruit [?].
He loosed the bond that the Hidden One had bound
in his hidden knowledge,
and troubled the peace that was blended
in the love and mercy that set all things in order.
He divided the dwelling of equals
and tore them one from another,
and made them, who were brothers,
strangers to one another.
With envy the Evil One sowed
his error among mortals,
and brought forth sin in their senses,
and they blossomed with fruits of deadly poison.
He tore down the precious image
and threw it to the ground like something worthless,
and gave it to death for a dwelling,
and mocked and laughed at its fall.
Behold the beginning of Envy:
you who would know, read and consider.
See its cunning and learn its cause,
what it did from the beginning.
Read its story with your mind,
and see, you have discerned its devices;
hear its deed with understanding,
and see, you have come to its secrets.

It corrupted the beauty of the form
made by the Artist who adorned all things,
and turned to revile him as though evil,
him whose wisdom holds back all evil.
It brought forth the bitterness of evil deeds
and made the worship of gods spring up,
and reviled the One who Is in his fashioning,
as though he had been fashioned imperfect.
Behold the foundation of its building,
the crafty worker of falsehood:
see, you builders of truth,
and flee from the evil of its labor.
Behold the signs of its meditation,
the great folly of the left:
see, you disciples of the right,
do not meditate foolishly.
Behold the cup of the bitterness of its death
which it mixed and gave our nature to drink:
there is no one who has drunk it
who is not corrupted by death.
Behold the open road which the slayer of man
has trodden with his devices:
see that you do not travel in its company,
you travelers on the narrow road.
Behold, the book of the Spirit has revealed to you,
O mind, the search you sought.
Travel within the bosoms of the Scriptures
toward the goal set before you.
Put on the armor of the word of truth
and fight spiritually,
and shoot words instead of arrows
at the crafty ranks of Envy.
Mix spiritual food
for the mind that evil has troubled,
and sweeten the bitterness of evil deeds
with the sweetness of the sound of your words.
Calm the angry
with the word of peace that has calmed all,
and call them to the concord
that the love of creation once beheld.
Encourage the afflicted
with the promise of the kingdom on high,
and repeat to them that heavenly voice:
"Whoever endures shall live."
Read to those slain by envy
the passage on the death of Abel,
and make them hear the voice
of the blood that cries out from the ground.
Open the archives of the kingdom
and read in the decrees of judgment,
and show the punishment of murderers
inscribed with the King's reed.
Go out to the field with the brothers
and see Envy as it conquers,
and the crafty inclination of the insolent
assisting its victory.
From there learn its devices
and the depth of the snares of its cunning,
and prepare subtle stratagems

that lay bare the secrets of its cunning.
Envy had put on the guise of love
and drew near to Abel.
With the sign of peace it led him astray
and brought him out to the wilderness to be slain.
It saw the fair beauty of his victories,
and it grieved it;
for it is a hater, and has no wish to see
anyone whose mind is fair.
Envy brought forth the fruit of murder
in the land of curses,
and by its hand first carried out
the sentence decreed over the tree.
The cup of blood it poured, it gave
to the grieving earth, and she would not accept it;
for she was sick from the blows
she had swallowed for the transgression of the commandment.
She was revolted and cast out the blood,
for she was not used to drinking it;
and that blood did not stay in her,
but cried out and rose up from her bosom.
O silent blood that cried out
with the voice of senses that speak!
O precious one who was lifted up
on the wings of the Spirit on high!
O you slain and buried in the earth,
whose voice spoke like thunder!
O you hidden and concealed,
who went out after your murderer!
O Envy, blind in both eyes,
poison upon poison in its deeds!
While it thinks its cunning is hidden,
it is revealed to righteousness like the sun.
O crafty one, who in pretending
exposes itself and does not know it!
O shrewd one, who in playing the wise
shows the poverty of its mind!
Envy killed the blameless one
and hid him under the garment of its devices,
and the One who knows all revealed the secret
of the covering of its craft.
He exposed and revealed its hatred
by the decree of judgment on the murderer,
and showed it to generations and families
by the punishment of its iniquity.
Come, you envious, examine
the great crime of Envy,
which shed innocent blood
and hid it from the One who knows all.
Come, you haters, who hate your brothers
without cause, like Cain,
and hear the blood that speaks
and answers the hidden secret.
Come, examine the punishment
of the murderer who killed without cause,
and take a proof of righteousness,
how fitting it is for murderers.

Let the strokes of the crafty one be
a proof to the evil inclination,
that it may not run recklessly
in the paths of murder.
Let them be as a mirror to it,
the seven strokes upon Cain,
and let it see itself in secret
in the trembling and shaking upon his body.
Let the mind say to the inclination:
"See that you do not envy without cause,
lest you be condemned to punishment
sevenfold upon sevenfold, seventy times."
Let everyone hate envy,
for it is envy that gives birth to murder;
and let everyone flee from murder,
for bitter is the punishment of murder.
Envy is the root of murder,
and from there its branches spring,
and whoever eats of its fruits,
the bitterness of death blossoms in him.
Envy began in creation
a new and a first murder,
and the envious began to walk
in its footsteps with one mind.
Envy set up a crafty target:
to shed innocent blood;
and it taught the crafty
to shoot with the bow of devices.
It blinded the light of the soul
and made blind the impulses of the mind,
and the whole of man grew dark,
bereft of the light of discernment.
It made the reasoning faculty
like the dumb beasts,
and the discerning inclination lost
the wisdom of its reason.
Envy armed the mind
to make war on those it loves,
and it did not perceive with understanding
that it was destroying its own companions.
In its armor the envious triumph
and overpower the ranks of righteousness,
and in the night of its darkness
shoot arrows at the shining one.
It makes the envier clever
at contending with the truth,
and teaches him the ways of warfare,
to fight in the guise of love.
In the guise of love the envier
fights like one who is zealous,
and though he is a hater of truth
he is taken for a lover of peace.
Envy has put on zeal
like a claimant of what is due,
and shows its zeal in falsehood
while tearing down everyone's due.
It has acquired an unbridled anger
at the report of good things,
and though the good have done it no wrong,
it accuses everyone and grumbles.
O you who hate righteousness,
why do you quarrel with the true?
What have the blameless done against you,

that you slander every one of them?
O you who are blind of will,
why do you fight against the light?
How have the rays of its beautiful light
wronged your blindness?
If your own will has deprived you
of truth, the light of both your eyes,
why do you foolishly cast blame,
when the light has done you no wrong?
Your evil has shut the door
in the face of the light of your eyes,
and you yourself have deprived yourself
of the light of righteousness.
There is no cause for your cunning,
no reason why you envy;
for even your cause is no cause,
but a false pretext.
And to show you that you are false
and bring false accusations,
I will bring from deeds
a proof of your injustice.
What is the cause for which you hated
the pure law of revelations?
When did it revile you as you revile it,
and where did it disgrace you as you do?
When did it in truth repay
the evil debts you lent it?
Show openly how it has wronged you,
and then there will be room for your grumbling;
and bring witnesses who will seal
the deed of your falsehood.
But far be it that this should happen,
that your falsehood should conquer truth.
You have no cause, loathsome one,
against the party of the true.
You envy the upright without cause,
though they have not wronged your evil;
without cause you are always jealous,
and disturb the peace of the humble.
The evil inclination incites you
against the flock of the lovers of righteousness,
and with the sword of slander
you destroy the ranks of the right.
Abel you deprived of life,
that he might not sow the word of life;
and Rachel's son you sold,
that the freedom of his soul might not flourish [?].
Jacob you drove from the dwelling
of his fathers to another land,
and Jacob's son you removed
from his brothers to the house of the Egyptians.
Job, the diligent laborer
who worked in the vineyard of truth,
you stripped of his runners
and of the soundness of his limbs.

It was you who carried off his possessions,
and you who loosened his frame.
By your counsel his friends reviled him,
and he became hateful to his kinsfolk.
Who would not flee your company,
Envy, hater of those it loves?
Who would not hate your dealings,
destroyer of fair things?
Who can be like you,
and who is as deaf as you are?
For the light is darkness to you,
and sound hearing is cunning.
You see a sight and do not see,
and listen to sound without understanding;
you call the good evil
and name the evil good.
There is no likeness in all that is evil
that can rise to match your evil,
for you turn the sweet to bitter
and embitter the sweetness of truth.
There is no people you have not divided
in strife, one against another,
and no kingdom you have allowed
to remain at peace for a single day.
You tore the garment of concord
that was woven in the love of all,
and you uncovered the modesty of mankind
and made them contemptible.
Woe to you, disturber of peace
and undoer of the love of all,
for you have divided those who were equal
into portions of every kind!
Woe to you, slayer of man,
who destroys life by death,
for you have made rational beings
warriors against their own lives!
O harsh one without mercy,
what have mortals done against you,
that you incite them with jealousy
ever to destroy their own ranks?
By your graces, King of righteousness,
deliver our feeble nature,
which its bitter inclination has taken captive,
so that it enslaves its very self.
Come, Grace, to us,
and stand before us as you are wont;
for if your help does not reach us,
our nature will drown in envy.
Spread the wings of your sweetness
and shelter our race from our inclination,
for see, it seeks to consume us
with the hard teeth of envy.
Envy has made us strangers
to the household of your help,
and it has driven us out of the inheritance
you won for us from the beginning.
Envy sold our freedom,
and we became slaves to sin,
and it brought us down from greatness

to the lowliness of mortality.
The bitter inclination imprisoned us
in the prison house of curses,
and set before us a guard [?],
that we might not escape its bondage.
Who is as blind as we are
to the understanding of what is right,
that our murderer dwells within us
and we do not perceive him in our dwelling?
Who is as deaf as man,
who will not listen to the medicine of his life,
so that each one consumes himself
with the envy of his evil inclination?
The envier has sharpened the sword of his mind
against his own soul,
and when he thought he had struck his fellow,
his sword turned and struck him in the heart.
For he thinks he is slaying his companion
with the blows of his tongue,
and does not perceive that against himself
are turned the arrows scattered from his lips.
He stirs up strife at every moment,
that there may be room for his envy,
and he multiplies and composes pretexts
to bring his deed into the open.
He throws jealousy at the simple
like a fowler before a bird,
and spreads his murderous nets,
and overturns every measure.
In the guise of cunning
the envier leads his companions astray,
and as one who counsels what is good
he presents himself to men.
He puts on sorrow of soul for everyone
and wraps himself in the name of compassion;
he answers "peace" with his lips
and sharpens a sword in his mind.
He grieves and suffers for his fellow
as one who pities his own limb,
and watches for when he will find
an opening to accomplish his will.
Let Saul be named
the double envier, who hates his brothers,
who soothed while calling out
"my son David" in cunning.
Tears of cunning Saul poured out
before the son of Jesse,
and his mouth was full of sighs
while his mind was sharpening a sword.
With his lips he called him "my son"
and hated him in the secret of his thought;
his tongue spoke fair words,
but twisted was the speech of his mind.
He called out: "Come back, do not fear,
my son David; I will not harm you,"
and he sharpened his intent
like a thief bent on murder.
The eyes weep with sighing,
and the mouth cries out with cunning;
the face is sad in pretense,
and the heart exults toward blood.
The inner impulses signal
to the outward senses of the body,

which multiplied and composed pretexts
in guises of falsehood.
The mind is spurred on toward murder
like an executioner,
while the tongue softens its voice
like a lover toward his beloved.
O Envy, how bitter you are,
and there is no measure to your cunning,
and the iniquity of the whole world
is not enough to match your evil.
O cunning that is wholly cunning,
with no place in it for simplicity!
O deceiver, who always pours out
bitterness in the guise of sweetness!
O lyre that is strung
with strings stretched taut by devices!
O flute of the jealous,
that sings the sound of deadly poison!
Sweet and desirable is the sound of its melodies
when it sings deceitfully,
but hidden at the end of its dirges
is the bitterness of death for its hearers.
The sound of its song stupefies
every ear that listens to it,
and when its voice reaches the soul
it troubles it and carries off its calm.
It takes on the guise of a lover
at the outset of its first speech,
but the end of its word is evil,
that of a hater and a murderer.
Let it see its evil in Saul,
how much of it he poured out upon David,
and though it was as plain as the sun,
he hid it under the guise of sorrow.
Let the envious look at Saul,
whom envy blinded in his mind,
so that he did not see the beauty of the victories
of the son of Jesse, how desirable they were.
In him let the cruel examine themselves,
who hate their brothers without cause;
for because he went far and hated much,
the merciless one was slain by the uncircumcised.
Let David be a mirror
to the envied in their afflictions,
for he endured insult and persecution
and took up his crown in a single [?].
In the goal of his love let them be like him,
the lovers of spiritual love,
for he composed songs of lamentation
over his murderer with sighing.
In Saul alone let everyone learn
the evil end of envy,
and in David let them see the fruits
of love, how sweet they are.
In king and king let each examine himself:
the one who envied and the other who was envied.
The envier was slain by envy,
and the envied was kept alive by love.
Envy in Saul has shown us
how much one hates his kin,
and love in David has taught us
how much one loves his friends.
Behold, its hidden cunning has been revealed to us

in the death of Saul the envier.
Let our mind not be overturned
by the hidden nets of its devices.
Behold, the son of Jesse has taught us
how to overcome those who lie in wait for us.
Let us sweeten the bitterness of the envious
with the sweetness of love, as David did.
Let love say by the mouth of David
to Saul, the double envier:
"What have I done against you, envier,
that you persecute me like Saul?"
Let the wronged bring his case
before the Searcher of secrets,
for he will condemn the envier
to punishment, as he did Saul.
In the death of Saul was proclaimed
the harsh punishment of the envious,
and in the exaltation of the son of Jesse
the crown of victory of the wronged.
Do not be grieved, you who are wronged by envy,
at the sound of the envier's reproaches.
Endure and be silent like David,
that you may reign with him at the end.
Do not boast, envier,
in lying slander,
for your sword is destined to enter
your own heart, as it did with Saul.
Do not think, envier, that you have conquered
the humble by your arrogance.
You overcame them without their willing to fight,
for they were strong against your devices.
You are guilty for having prevailed,
and you have not won the victory;
for your victory is a disgrace,
and your triumph a shame to your face.
When has your deed ever prospered
except in a loathsome gang?
And where has your hateful cunning triumphed
except in a reckless crowd?
You are blind, deprived of light,
and you do not search out the truth;
fair things are hateful to you,
and evil things are dear to you.
The speck in your brother's eye
you see as a beam,
and the beam in your own eyes
you do not even think is there.
Cast out first, envier,
the harsh anger of your mind,
and then judge your companion
concerning the lack in his soul.
Why do you strain out gnats
and swallow beasts?
Why do you cleanse your limbs
while the inner impulses are defiled?
Why do you contend with sinners
as though you were the perfecter of righteousness?
When have you ever shown your concern
in punishing for the sake of truth?

Woe to you, deceitful one,
how far you stray from the truth!
For though the truth hates the crafty,
you carry its banner craftily.
Woe to you, doubly blind,
to whom light and darkness are the same!
For while the light gladdens all,
you are gloomy toward its rays.
Let the discerning learn from you
how bare you are of truth;
and let the knowing weep over you,
that while alive you are doubly dead.
Your life is no life,
for by your life you destroy life.
Would that you had died at the beginning,
and death had ceased with your death!
You are the one who first trod
the road of death for mankind;
and had your arts let go,
the Rebel would no longer have reigned.
Tell me, hater of humankind,
how has our humanity wronged you,
that you killed us from the beginning
and are not sated with our ruin?
Tell me, you who thirst for human blood,
why are you so eager for our destruction?
Spare us a little of your cruelty,
and ease your hostility toward our nature.
Why are you inflamed with jealousy
and burning against our salvation?
Hold back the heat of your flame,
lest you destroy us utterly.
Who will tear up your root
and cut off the spring of your wickedness,
so that you no longer bear fruits
that embitter the sweetness of good things?
Would that your seed had perished
and your form had never been put together!
Would that she who bore you had not opened
a door for your coming forth!
Your wickedness has not multiplied for you alone,
but for everyone alike;
even the one who accuses you
acquires stumbling blocks in dealing with you.
In dealing with you my thoughts have worn me out,
as I laid bare the hatefulness of your wickedness;
your bitterness made me harsh,
and I went beyond due measure.
I was astonished at the contempt of your craft,
and I blamed the one who fashioned you;
and while I supposed I was not reproving
myself, I became liable to rebuke.
O how your wickedness strikes
your lovers and your haters alike!
If anyone praises you, it is torment;
and if he reproaches you, he is blameworthy.
I blamed the one by whom you were fashioned
when I saw the sword of those you slew.

But my mind repented when I remembered
that your wickedness does not come from nature.
Your son, O Creator, is a freeborn son,
and your servant is master of his own will;
and both are yours:
to tell truth apart from falsehood.
Do not, my Lord, hold this against me,
that I rebuked so boldly,
and accused the evil inclination
that stirs up bitter envy.
Envy has no being of its own,
so that I [?] rightly blamed its prompting:
it is our inclination that makes each one envious
of one another's good things.
Our inclination gives birth to envy
and rears it with cunning arts;
and when its wickedness is full grown,
it throws the world into turmoil with one of its fruits.
Yet our inclination too does not exist
as a being of its own apart from the soul:
it is the soul's power of discernment,
which works in every form.
The soul is mistress of a person,
ruling over the impulses and the senses;
it governs our being
as its will desires.
In our soul both are set,
good and evil alike,
and it chooses, as it judges,
to set the one above the other.
The soul rides upon the body
like a charioteer upon a chariot,
and governs the person
by the reins of its hidden impulses.
The outer senses run
like horses in a stadium,
and the mind restrains and gives rein
with the hands of the soul's impulses.
The body is yoked and runs always
wherever the charioteer wishes;
and the impulses and senses are driven
as the rider wills.
The mind calls every one
of the senses that carry it,
and orders the whole body
as a general orders his camp.
See, we have learned from our soul
that our freedom belongs to our soul,
and our humanity is not in bonds,
so that there is ground for blaming us.
See, our will shows us
that it is our will that sins and repents,
and no force drives us
where our will does not wish to go.
See, our discernment [?] makes plain to us
that wisdom is His,
and that it chooses to bear what is good
or to envy wickedly.
To it belongs blind envy,
which is bare of the light of love;
to it belongs foolish jealousy,
which cannot tell what is fitting.

To it belongs the spring that pours forth
the drug of life and the gall of death:
it sows the sweetness of peace,
and from it strife springs up.
So let us blame our will,
and not the one who fashioned our nature;
for it is our will that makes hateful
the beauty of our free soul.
Let us accuse our freedom,
and not the giver of wisdom;
for it is our freedom that resolves
to do what is good or what is hateful.
Come, then, let us hold a trial
with the freedom of our will's form [?],
and let us accuse our discernment
by the laws of our nature.
Let us say to the freedom of our soul:
"Why do you envy within yourself,
and why do you wickedly hate
the brotherhood of your neighbors?
Why do you tear down the building
that is bound together by the sinews of love?
Why do you loosen the bond
whose tightening brings all to peace at a nod?
Why do you not judge truly,
as befits your discernment?
Why do you not reprove yourself
as you blame others?
Why do you not see your hateful deeds
in the clear mirror of the mind?
Why do you not scour your stains
with love, which cleanses every blemish?
Why is your voice raised high
when you accuse the one who does wrong,
while you are deafer than the deaf
to the charges against yourself?"
Why do you, envious one, blame
the one who envies foolishly?
Utterly hateful, why do you hate
the one who hates his fellow?
Confused as you are, how do you take it upon yourself
to set right the one who is disordered?
Full of blemishes, how can you seek
to wash away the filth of others?
Judge yourself first,
and enter into an examination of your deeds;
and see that you are wholly guilty
and in pawn to your sins.
You are slain by the sword of your envy
and do not feel it in your wound;
you are dead and buried while alive,
and are not convinced of your deadness.
The lamp of your mind is bright
for seeing the faults of others,
but you have made yourself wholly blind
to examining your own wickedness.
You are as cunning as a sophist
in censuring your fellows,
and more ignorant than the ignorant

in accusing your own hateful deeds.
You are a hypocrite instead of a truthful man
when you reprove falsely,
and an oppressor when you exact retribution
beyond the commandment, in your folly.
With insolence you condemn others,
and with rashness you justify yourself,
and falsely you pronounce
sentence on yourself and on your fellow.
There is no truth in your judgment;
envy, be silent, do not reprove!
For it is not fitting to judge
for one who is crafty and crooked.
Who set you up as a judge,
wicked one, wholly wicked?
You have been a liar since you came to be,
and the gate of truth has never seen you.
In the guise of a lover of justice
the envious one always cloaks himself,
and with a zeal that passes for truth
he sharpens his bitterness.
He envies the one who excels,
saying that he clings to the truth;
and again he hates the one who falls short,
in the guise of a lover of excellence.
He is harsh [?] toward the one who studies
and meditates on the words of the Spirit,
and scorns the one who does not meditate,
as though he were concerned for learning.
He mocks the one who shows honor,
because, he says, he flatters too much;
and he insults the one who shows contempt,
because, he says, he does not know how to honor.
On teachers he fastens faults,
and on disciples reproaches:
"See," he says, "everything is in confusion,
for one loves and others hate.
They have dissolved," he says, "the elements
that lead to perfection,
and their way of life does not
incline toward the goal of uprightness."
In these guises envy leads astray
every rank,
and throws into confusion the lowly and the chief,
those who command and those who obey.
There is no place where the nets of wickedness
are not spread for envy;
there is no spot where crafty snares of cunning
are not hidden for it.
There is no people that it does not enslave
under the crafty yoke of its service;
there is no kingdom that does not carry
the crafty banner of its hatefulness.
On sea and on dry land it has cast
a net woven with traps,
and over mountains and over heights
its long cords are stretched.
Among rich and poor
it has set out a full stock of merchandise,
while profits come in to it
from the envious and the envied.
The envious scatter its seed

in the souls of those who listen to them,
and the envied stir up murmuring
at the sound of the reproaches of the envious.
Over all and in all is spread
the snare of the Accuser,
and the world sits in envy
as in a dark night.
The light of righteousness has been darkened
by envy, the darkness of error,
and the salt of propriety has lost its savor
through the foolish jealousy of the wicked.
In every corner its heralds have appeared
to announce its coming,
and they have thrown the whole inhabited world into turmoil
with the bitterness of their voices.
There is no place where the humble one
who loves peace may take shelter,
for envy has driven concord
out of human dwellings.
Where can the loving one live,
whose love is bound to mankind?
For jealousy has torn equality apart
and divided the world against itself.
The band of those who love the truth has dwindled
under the tyranny of envy,
and the envious help it
to lay waste night and day.
Its forces never sleep,
nor do they put off the armor of its craft,
for they find it sweeter to shed blood
than to sleep in rest.
It has made war in every form
against the priests, generation after generation,
and shed the blood of the pious
with a cruelty that knows no pity.
It destroyed the former prophets,
who bore wonders,
and it killed the apostles too,
who brought forth the power of hidden things.
It dared to climb higher than mankind,
to the very cause of mankind's salvation,
and poured out its murderous gall
upon the Peace that brings all to peace.
O envy, mad dog
that barks night and day
and bites without distinction
both household and strangers!
O tyrant who is not restrained
from shedding innocent blood!
O murderer who gives no thought
to the corpses of all he casts down!
O asp of cruelty
that will not heed the voice of the charmers,
and into whose bitter hearing
the voices of love never fall!
O murderous dragon
that lies coiled in the abyss of the inclination
and forever troubles our thoughts
with the bitterness of its twistings!

O insatiable oppressor,
O greed that is never filled,
whose cruelty has grown and reached
even to the cause of all good things!
It drove Adam from his inheritance
and killed Abel, who was righteous;
it assailed Jacob because he was humble,
and Joseph because he had grown wise.
It envied Job when it saw that he had grown great
in the wealth of body and of soul;
and it hated Moses because he was called
a god among those of earth.
But why should I recount its wrath
against servants who were righteous,
when it dared to rise up in tyranny
even against the Lord of the servants?
Through Judas envy accomplished its will
against the cause of our salvation,
boldly supposing
that it would cut off the cause of our life.
From this let us learn the cruelty
of envy, the hater of mankind:
how bare its wickedness is
of mercy and of pity.
The crafty one has no reason
for hating the good;
it is its own reason,
and with cunning it puts reasons together.
And if among the servants there is a reason,
since all creation is guilty,
in the One who is pure and holy
what reason is to be found?
And if the guilty gave reason
to one another, as guilty men,
what did you see in the Innocent One
that you shed His blood for nothing?
See, it has been shown by deed
that you hate the fair for nothing,
and with reason and without reason
you have poured out your bloodshed upon mankind.
It is not only the good that you hate,
O envy, hater of mankind,
for upon good and wicked alike
your gall is smeared equally.
Not only on the knowing
does the affliction of your wound fasten,
for see, on the wise and on the foolish
the marks of your craft are set.
Against the just and the unjust
your false bow is stretched,
and you strike every limb
with the sharp arrows of your jealousy.
Through the whole body of humanity
the gall of your wickedness has spread,
and there is no sound limb
that does not fester [?] from your bites.
O how evil is your evil,
envy, evil and hateful!
There is no evil as evil as you,
even if there is one who is your disciple.
O how twisted is your craft,
and there is no comparing your cunning!
And if anyone is crafty and wily,
it is in the devices of your craft that he has studied.

The mouth is not enough to tell
in how many ways you lead astray,
nor can the mind gather up
the schemes your craft gives birth to.
One alone knows how to expose you
and reveal the faults of your hateful deeds:
the One you hated because He laid bare
your hidden things to the eyes of the beholders.
He can cut off your root
from the soil of our soul's life,
and pluck the branches of your fruits
from the tree of our mind.
By the sweetness of His love
may the gall of your bitter cup be turned,
and by the light of His dawning may
the fog of your hateful darkness be lifted.
At the dawn of His word may they awaken
who have sunk deep in jealousy,
and begin the labor of love,
even at the eleventh hour.
Come, mortals, let us take shelter
in the strong fortresses of love,
for see, envy like a raider
has gone out in pursuit of our humanity.
Come, let us flee to the place above,
where wrath does not reign,
for see, jealousy has spread like a canker [?]
and seized the whole inhabited world.
Come, let us seek help for ourselves
from the mercies that took pity on our nature,
for see, the tyranny of our evil inclination
has brought our nature low.
Let us give our hand to Goodness,
that it may help us in the contest,
for see, the whole man has been condemned
by the arts of envy.
Grace is moved to let all live
who consent to the truth,
for see, the wickedness of our inclination has troubled
the sweetness of the peace that brings all to peace.
Our inclination has loosened the bond
of our peace with the Maker,
and it is up to us, if we will,
to tighten again what it loosened.
Our inclination stained us with sin
and defiled the purity of our mind;
yet if it wills, it is in its power
to cleanse our soul once more.
Our inclination troubled us with envy
and cast strife among us;
and it is up to it to reconcile us
with one another and with the Maker.
I too have assailed our inclination
and reproached it as wicked,
because, though it has discernment,
it has made itself deaf in one of its wills.
I have given it names
that point to its discernment:
envy and wrath and jealousy
are fruits that belong to it.
It is the father of envy,
and jealousy is its offspring;
if it wills, they grow,
and if it does not wish it, they do not exist.
It is the one that rides upon the seeds [?]

like a charioteer upon horses,
and it drives the outer senses:
eyes and ears and tongues.
At its nod the inner senses are yoked,
and by its authority the outer ones;
if it wishes, they run in order,
and if it wants, they run wild.
To it belongs the power of wisdom,
and the lack of consolation;
where it wishes it is a sophist,
and a moment later a simpleton.
It taught me to speak with it
about why its freedom is despised;
and it revealed to me that to it belong
both cunning and brokenness of heart.
It prompted me to restrain and reprove
the impulses that serve envy,
and it urged me to shoot words
like arrows at the ranks of craft.
It examined for me the device
that it puts together in its cunning,
and showed me the deadly snares
that are hidden under the guise of a gift.
I awoke at the sound of melodies,
as it sang the songs of peace,
while strife lay hidden
within the garment of its lips.
I heard it changing its voices
craftily, like a bird,
and greatly bewildering its hearers,
like a decoy partridge calling to death.
I saw it, marvelous in its form,
and thought that it was wholly fair;
then it turned and revealed to me
that its true aspect was foreign to its deeds.
O inclination, how wise you are,
and how cunning your deeds!
O how just you are, if you wish,
so as not to take your own side!
You are skilled in every device
wherever you wish to multiply;
and there is none more simple than you
when you wish to help.
I marveled greatly at your wisdom
and at the authority of your freedom,
how easy hard things become
for your will wherever it wishes.
From you disciples learn,
and through you teachers grow wise;
to your door the poor run,
and to your treasury the rich.
See, the inclination of our soul has revealed to us
that both are ours:
to love the love that gives us life,
and to hate the envy that has killed us.
Come, then, as discerning men,
let us expose the craft that is in our inclination;
for see, the inclination within us has shown us
that peace and wrath are ours.
Come, let us speak truly
to our inclination, master of our will:

"Do not exchange the sweetness of love
for the bitterness of envy."
Come, let us recount from what is its own
and expound it from its own books:
"See, inclination, do not trouble
the peace of mankind with your envy."
Rise up, you envious, and say
to the inclination in your members:
"Cease, inclination, do not burn us
with the flame of envy."
Recall to it the affliction of the rich man,
who was cruelly tormented
and begged the one he had hated
to cool him from his burning.
Let the envious, who hate for nothing,
remember that saying:
"There is a great chasm, which none can
cross over to Abraham."
Our Lord overthrew Satan,
who had troubled our race with his envy.
Sixth Sunday of the Fast
[?] / For the Sixth Sunday of the Fast / Responsory / Give thanks to the Bridegroom who has made his friends great and brought them into the garden of his kingdom, my brothers.

Beautiful is meditation on the words of the Spirit set down in the Scriptures,
and good is the study of the writings for the one who meditates on them.
The proclamation of the kingdom on high is full of teaching,
and His love bestows good blessings on whoever loves it.
A great treasure lies hidden in the letters; meditate on His words:

whoever reads them with love of soul grows rich, and for ever.
The lines of His writings are like the dawning of light,
and whoever gazes without wavering sees everything.
Like a guide His fame runs before the mind,
and whoever loves the company of His love reaches heaven.
Lovingly He calls a man to draw near to Him,
and whoever draws near lovingly is filled with His love.
Like a great teacher He urges a man toward His teaching,
and whoever accepts discipleship to Him becomes a master.
I see that the mastery of the skilled Master is skilful,
and my mind counsels me to become His disciple, if He will have me.
Have me, great Master, who makes a man wise by Your mastery,
that my tongue may grow in discipleship to the meditation of Your words.
My speech longs to be taught to study Your words;
write for me the line of the alphabet, that I may spell it out.
I see straight lines traced in Your writings,
and I greatly long to learn the order of their meanings.
Fulfil my desire, Good One, who are full of all good things,
and grant me what I need: the meaning of the words in Your writings.
I was turning over the parables that are traced for You,
and my mind urged me to seek the hidden power in them.
The kingdom on high, He says, is like ten virgins
who were waiting with their lamps to meet the bridegroom.
Five of them, the wise, took oil, He says,
and the foolish did not trouble to take oil.
Time passed, He says, and the bridegroom delayed his coming,
and sleep overcame them, and all ten of them slept.

At midnight, He says, the sound of the trumpet cried out,
announcing the coming of the bridegroom from on high.
They rose, He says, and the prudent trimmed their lamps,
so that with lights they might receive the bridegroom who dwells in light.
Foolish and wise rose together;
alike as they were, they were not alike in everything.
Oil was lacking in the lamps of the simple ones,
and they began to ask their companions for a share as a kindness.
“Lest there not be enough for us and for you,” the prudent answered,
“go rather to those who sell, if it can be bought.”
They heard, He says, and went to buy the oil that cannot be bought;
and the bridegroom came, and the prudent went in, and those did not go in.
Outside the door remained those who had neglected what was fitting,
and they began to knock and knock, trusting in their way of life.
“Open to us, our Lord, the door of the treasury of the house of Your kingdom,
that we may go in and receive the reward for the labours of our virginity.”
“I do not know you,” the voice of the bridegroom answered them,
“nor am I in any way persuaded by the virginity you kept for me.”
Now that the living Mouth has finished the word of its mouth,
let us draw near and seek the power hidden within its sayings.
Power fills the saying that is framed in the figure of women:
why did He set aside the class of men and speak of women?
And if His word looks to nature, in that it is one,
why, when He has virgins who are alike, are they not all alike?
Why did He make the virgins equal in name
and separate them by their deeds into two sides?
Why, when they were pure of the stains of degradation,
did He exclude them from being placed in the greatness of His love?
Why did sleep overpower them all, while their toil was left [?],
and again in waking, when they were of one appearance?
Why, when all their lamps were lit,
was oil left only to the wise?

If they practised the way of virginity equally,
why the difference between wisdom and folly?
If they were as alike as they were in body and soul,
why did one not lend a share to her companion as a kindness?
Why did the wise send the foolish away,
when they knew that oil is not bought for a price?
And if it is true that oil was bought for a price,
why did those not sell oil and take the price?
