And if those who were rich did not sell,
who would take the sustenance of his life and give it to others?
But if the needy went to buy oil,
why did the bridegroom not wait, so that they might all go in together?
Why did He answer them, “I do not know your deeds,”
when He knew that they had kept themselves from defilement?
And if they had not acted according to the will He desired,
why did He not say, “Go to the fire and the darkness”?
The different word He made them hear stirred me greatly:
why is the punishment of those who are punished not equal?
My thoughts marvel at the inequality of the sentence passed on them:
how did they not fall into the pit of fire with the rich man?
And if they remained outside, on the earth, in the honour that was theirs,
how can it be that they are not tormented by their wants?
And if they did not enter and see the place they were waiting for,
what profit was there in the loss of their virginity?
Why did they wear out body and soul with sufferings,
and on the day of judgment receive a crown of thorns instead of a crown?
Why did they struggle against the stirrings of their nature,
and, though they were victorious, fall under retribution with the guilty?
Great grief fills the end of their deeds:
how they began and could not complete fine things!
Let us begin, then, to seek the power that lies in their deeds,
for the pain of the story told about them is painful indeed.
Let us seek how it is written that the kingdom was likened to them,

when they were not able to resemble its likeness.
Why does He not say of them that they resemble that glorious one,
since it is more exalted in its glory than all that is created?
The kingdom on high, He says, was likened to the virgins:
a great wonder, that the one likened is the lesser thing!
Beautifully does the One who is praised liken with praise those who praise Him,
for He is able to liken, and they are not able to liken.
In the kingdom on high and in the unspeakable delight,
it resembles them in that it calls them to its delight.
With this purpose it was likened for us who are of earth,
that through its likeness we might seek the likeness of glorious things.
Very fitting is the likeness that He drew, teaching truth,
and there is no painter who could paint its likeness exactly.
Beautiful is the image whose symbol He composed and set in His gospel,
and it is right to look closely at the splendour of its beauty.
Come, beholders, look carefully at the word of our Lord,
which painted humanity and the kingdom on high in the image of deeds.
In His gospel the Renewer of humanity painted the deeds of humanity,
and fixed them like an image before the beholders.
His gospel itself He called the kingdom which is like women,
because the gospel announces the kingdom on high to humankind.
By its nearness people learn to seek what is above,
and by its revelation they see the beauty of hidden things.
Of it He said that it was likened to virgins,
in that it shows a way of life without marriage.
By the name of virgins He called the congregation that believes in Him,
teaching us that He requires purity of His servants.
In the figure of women He painted the likeness of the will of His love,
for in women the figure of meekness is despised.
Men and women He joined together [?] in the word of His mouth,
teaching that both kinds are able to live in purity.

Had He painted the likeness of His word in the figure of men,
it would perhaps have seemed that He rejected the class of women.
Wisely He painted females in the image of His word,
so that one equal nature should not be divided into parts.
He painted our whole nature, and in it He showed us our nature,
that it might be clear to us to choose the good in all that we possess.
Our beauties and our ugliness He revealed in His parables,
and the blessings and punishments that await us He painted and showed us.
Into two classes He divided the course of our way of life,
and to the one He gave the name wise, and to the other foolish.
In the wise He represented the course of perfection,
and in the foolish He depicted deeds that fall short in love.
The deeds themselves He called lamps that were being made ready,
in that they had laboured, even if they had not laboured equally.
It was the inequality of their deeds that made the oil run short,
for had they been equal, nothing that was equal would have been lacking.
By the oil that ran short through the meagreness of their deeds He showed us
that they were debtors and not diligent in love and mercy.
Mercy He named by the name of oil, Christ, the Anointed, who showed mercy,
that as He showed mercy, so we should show mercy to our fellows.
To oil He likened the one who shows mercy to his fellows,
for like oil he soothes the thoughts as well as the senses.
Without oil He painted the likeness of the insolent women,
whose words did not soothe the burning of wrongdoing.
With oil He made pure the way of life of the wise,
who showed mercy and compassion and were diligent in body and soul alike.
Because of the oil of mercy in which their way of life was diligent,
they held out and were not hindered by the delay of time.
Even painters bear witness to this by what they do:

by means of oil they keep their images from decay.
The painter of images mixes oil with the pigments,
so that by it his image may last unchanged.
And if painters know how to preserve borrowed images,
how much more fitting was it for a person to preserve the image of his own likeness!
Our Saviour scorned those who are idle about their likeness,
under the name of the foolish, who took no oil among their provisions.
The diligence of a good will He praised and magnified
in the wise, who mixed oil into their deeds.
Within the number of the ten He bound up all that is done,
longing greatly that they should receive Him on the day of His revelation.
The day of His revelation He called the coming of the bridegroom who is coming,
and the virgins who go out to meet him are all the perfect.
The sleep in which He says they all slept together
is death, which made good and wicked equal in one corruption.
The cry that came at midnight and stirred the sleepers
is the voice of command, which calls at the end and raises all.
At midnight, He said, the bridegroom who betrothed us comes,
because bridegrooms too take their betrothed by night.
That those of whom He wrote rose alike, according to their deeds,
shows everyone the resurrection of everyone: that everyone rises.
By the five lamps that went out He pointed to the merciless:
if they do not show mercy, they will not receive mercy in the judgment to come.
That the wise would not sell to the simple
openly reveals to us that there is no place there to ask for mercy.
That they answered and said, “Lest there not be enough for us and for you,”
makes known that our deeds here are small beside our reward.
That they sent them to buy oil from wherever it could be found
shows that there was a place for showing mercy, had they shown mercy.
That the bridegroom came while they were returning from where they had gone
is the knowledge that we do not perceive when he comes.
That the wise went in with the bridegroom and the door was shut:
the righteous are those who enter and rest in the haven of peace [?].
That the foolish remained outside the door of the house of the kingdom:

the wicked are those who remain on the earth to be tormented.
That it is written that the foolish cried, “Lord, Lord,”
implies that they already beg mercy for their sins.
They were reflecting on their deeds, which were not in harmony,
for perhaps that Just One would not deal unjustly with their way of life.
That they cried out and He answered them, “I do not know”:
love not mixed with compassion for one's fellows He does not wish to know.
“I do not know you,” He said to the foolish,
“you did not know how to fulfil my will through pity.”
The door was shut in the faces of those outside, and they did not go in with Him:
it is the firmament above, which a sign closed once the good had entered [?].
That sign becomes a furnace of testing for good and wicked,
and separates the just from the unjust by the burning of His love.
Great is the separation that will be there between the one and the other,
and the distance between height and depth cannot be measured.
Lofty and exalted above all heights is the height of the just,
and deeper than all depths is the pit of the wicked.
The appearance of those who love love is fairer than everything fair,
and the colour of the deceitful is uglier than everything ugly.
There is no measure to the glory of the children of light,
nor again any likeness for the ugliness of the children of darkness.
Light and darkness show each person
in what deeds he spent himself in the life here.
The appearance of the body becomes a witness against the mind,
and rebukes it for the things it did falsely.
From the body itself spring both glory and the crown,
and it becomes for itself the one who bestows blessings and brings on [?] punishments.
The man himself punishes his soul for the things in which he sinned,
and like a judge he despises his mind for its ugliness.
Each one sees the blemishes of his own soul and of his fellows,
and no one is hidden, neither from himself nor from his fellows.
A person gazes on the whole of nature in its fullness,
and everyone gazes on him in that bright form that is his.
All are examined exactly in one man,
and that man stretches his mind out toward all who see him.
Among those who have passed over, none can hide there from his companion,

nor again can his colleague and companion be hidden from him.
Sight runs swiftly to the four quarters,
and takes them in from within the brightness that is within the body.
O the wonder that comes to be in a man from his Maker,
who makes him take in height and depth with his understanding!
The whole of him, body and soul, is contained in one place,
yet he is far from all, and all are near to him as one who is near.
He is in every place while he is in one place,
and this is the wonder: that he is with all and is not with all.
He resembles the Godhead in the order that is within him,
which is in every place, and how it is cannot be comprehended.
Through the perfect deeds within him he gives forth a voice
that man is the image of the One who formed him, and greatly resembles Him.
He resembles Him in this, that he is in every place while he is not,
and examines hidden things within his own mind and in all.
Like a maker he tests the wickedness hidden in the soul,
and by his testing separates the ugly from the beautiful.
Who is able to recount in words the greatness of his rank,
that a creature of clay makes his sign reign with all and in all?
Who knows how to paint, together with his greatness, his lowliness as well,
that while there is in him what reigns over all, there is in him what is despised by all?
Who would not marvel at the one separation that will be in him,
that part of him is in the height and part in the depth, in glory and in shame?
Who would not rejoice, and who would not grieve, over both,
over what is examined in the blessings of the good and the punishments of the wicked?
Who would not say, “Great is man, and despised is man,”
seeing him in the kingdom on high and in Gehenna?
I saw his glory and his shame painted on the pages of the books,
and I rejoiced and grieved over his abasement and over his exaltation.
In two colours the symbol painted the likeness of his image,
and taught him to meditate on his glories and on his disgraces.
In a parable He revealed to us the separation that will come at the end,
so that he may resolve to choose well before that day.

By the virgins He taught him the course of righteousness,
that he should practise purity of soul without neglect.
Through the parable He traced for him the path of praiseworthy deeds,
that he may travel well toward the appointed place of life, to the end.
By the wise He encouraged his heart with the hope of the kingdom on high,
and by the foolish He terrified him with a harsh report.
By their virginity He proclaimed that he is able to live in purity,
and by their deeds He showed that he possesses freedom of soul.
By their taking oil He showed that he has a nature that shows mercy,
and by their not taking it He revealed that his wickedness is not compelled.
He revealed his freedom by the lamps that burned and that went out,
for had he wished, he could have lit all ten.
The same will that lit five with the oil of mercy
was able to light five as well as the other five.
The wise and the foolish share one nature,
and had he wished, he would have been wise entirely, in everything.
By hardening himself without pity toward his neighbours
he made known that he has both together, good and evil.
That the insipid ones asked oil of the prudent
is itself a reproach to him, that he ought to have shown mercy to his fellows.
That the wise would not lend to the foolish
openly scorned the hardness of soul of the merciless.
That they said to them, “Go, buy from those who sell,”
is wholly a reproach to the one who did not work in the time that has passed.
Every man is able to work well as long as he is on earth,
and it lies with him to reach the rank of perfection.
Because he did not work lovingly here, as was fitting,
the lights of their lamps grew dark on the day of the feast.
Because they did not spend of their deeds on the one who was in need,
the wise too withheld from them a share of the oil.
Because they did not listen to the voice of those who pleaded for forgiveness,
they heard a voice: “I do not know your deeds.”

Because they shut the door of the spoken word before those who would learn,
the door of the house of the kingdom was shut before their requests.
Because they made their love a stranger to concern for others' good,
the King did not wish to make them equal to the concern of His love.
Justice repaid them for the corruptions they had cast off,
and by that measure of their deeds He took their reward.
They condemned their own persons before the judge,
and by the verdict of their own thoughts they settled their deeds.
The judge did not wrong their deeds in the reward;
it was they who did not wish to repay His love wisely.
It was not justice that shut the door before their faces;
they shut it themselves, because they did not open their love to others.
Had they opened the door of their will before the needy,
the bridegroom would not have kept them outside the door.
Had they anointed the wounds of wrongdoing with the oil of the word,
the oil of mercy would not have run short in their lamps.
Had they poured out the love within them on the afflicted,
their companions too would have been persuaded to help them.
They themselves fenced off the road of mercy before them,
and could not walk with the prudent by their deeds.
From them let us learn about the way of life here,
and in their reward let us picture the reward of the judgment beyond.
For our sake He wrote the parable of their way of life,
and for our teaching it runs in lines as though it already were.
I do not say “as though it already were” to mean it is not,
but that it is not yet in deeds, as it is written.
It had not come to pass in fact when it was spoken,
but it is certain to come to pass without doubt.
For the parable, in so far as it bears the likeness of truth,
depicts in its likeness deeds that lie beyond this time.
It is like a shadow in its swiftness and lightness,
and, as a shadow does of a body, it shows the truth that is in deeds.
It is wont to run ahead of the deeds in its writings,
and it anticipates something that is to be at the end.

It shows distant things near to the one who gazes on it,
and though they are distant it tells of them as if near.
Like a painter it paints words that are not yet deeds,
and depicts them in that form of image and likeness.
The parable painted in the virgins is like an image,
and the nature of man and the way of his life are tested in it.
In it the greatness of love of the pure in soul is proclaimed,
and in it the meanness of the merciless is scorned.
The pure in soul it called wise, and possessors of oil,
and the mean it named foolish, and sellers of oil.
The oil is mercy, which those who are full of mercy sell,
and the one who did not sell showed that it was not then to be bought.
It made known that buying too has its own appointed time,
for outside its time nothing is bought from one by another.
In the world of toil there is a time for buying,
but in the world to come selling ceases, together with buying.
In this way the wise did not sell,
so that the great order of that arrangement should not be confused.
Both worlds, this one and that, are ordered in order,
and wisely the orders proceed in their arrangements.
The world of time is suited to buying and selling,
and the world of eternity to rest and tranquillity and delight.
Come, buyers and sellers, buy and sell
in the world in which it is granted to buy and sell.
Let no one undo the great order of the two worlds,
and leave off buying here in order to buy there.
No one is permitted to bring merchandise into the house of the kingdom,
and if anyone dares, his daring turns back upon himself.
And if one who scorns an earthly kingdom receives judgment,
how much heavier is the judgment of one who scorns the kingdom on high!
On high is that kingdom which is never dissolved,
and there is no place in it for earthly dealings.
Those of earth are not permitted to enter there
while they still carry with them the taking and giving of earth.
By the five virgins whom He kept from entering
He barred and kept out everyone who is stripped of pity.
That He gave no reward for the toilsome labours of their virginity
shows that He rejects every way of life that does not come from love.

They were virgins, and their conduct was true,
but they were losers, gaining no profit from their labors.
Their conduct brought no profit to those who had it:
since they gave nothing of it, they did not receive the reward they hoped for.
For the sake of the reward she endured the [?] of desires,
yet they did not aim well at that goal, the Lord of the reward.
The beloved goal showed them that they should resemble it,
and because they did not resemble it, he withheld the crown from their heads.
They were eager to receive from him the crown of victory,
and now angels and men mock them.
O how evil is the evil of a merciless disposition,
which makes labors as if they were no labors on the day of recompense!
O how hateful it is for a man not to share his good with another,
for even when he has good things, his soul is stripped of good things!
O how foolish it is for a man to profit himself alone,
for even if he owns the whole world, he owns nothing!
He owns nothing who owns only himself,
because his self cannot stand without the many.
Without the limbs the soul cannot stand in the body,
nor does it receive the recompense for its labors without them.
The soul needs the limbs, soul though it is;
how much more does one human being need another!
A man finishes the course of his righteousness through another man,
and if he is made righteous apart from others, he is not human.
A man cannot be a man apart from others,
and his uprightness apart from others is no uprightness.
Do you want to be upright and good, O man?
Do for your neighbor what you will one day need done for you.
Do you want to receive the reward due to you on the day of recompense?
Repay your fellow the debt of love, and see, you are repaid.
Do you long to meet the Bridegroom on high with lamps of light?
Let your face shine to meet your fellow, and see, you have met him.
Do you mean to enter that delight with the wise?
Make the foolish wise, and see, you enter at the head of the wise.
No one enters unless he brings others in with him,

for this is what that order requires of whoever enters it.
Is there anyone with you who asks at the door for the one who enters?
Whether he enters or not, he stays outside the door.
Come, you who would enter and long for that entrance:
hear what is required of anyone who wants to enter and see it.
Come, wise ones, see the wisdom of the wise virgins,
who knew how to choose and take with them provisions of mercy.
Virgins, come, listen to that voice that came to the foolish,
and renounce for yourselves the name of folly, so that you never hear it.
Lovers of meditation and searchers of hidden mysteries,
complete in action the meditation your thoughts have brought forth.
Interpreters of the meaning of parables before your disciples,
do that very thing which you teach, in your own persons.
Guests of the Bridegroom, keepers of the promise of that kingdom,
stay awake from the sleep of ignorance.
Response: Glory to your mercies, Lord of all, which freely showed grace to sinners.
On the Raising of Lazarus

Homily 20. On the Hosannas.
The twentieth homily,
on the raising of Lazarus, recited
on the night of Hosanna Sunday.
Response:
Blessed is the Glorified One, who on the day of his entry stirred the children
to praise him with hosannas.
My brothers.

With the yoke of death the Evil One bound the human race
and subjected it to the servitude of his bitterness.
The yoke of his toil he laid upon all, unjustly,
and without pity made good and wicked alike labor in slavery.
He made the whole race mortal and corruptible,
and shut it up in the fortresses of Sheol, never again to come out.
The whole of nature, a free-born child, he cruelly carried off into captivity
and sold it into the slavery of death, a grievous master.
Because of death, mortals became slaves to death,
since the poison of death had been mixed into their nature.
Death lay quiet in nature as if asleep
from the moment it heard the sound of the sentence of death.
The commandment was broken; that called it and woke it as one asleep,
and it began to roar and to demand the sentence, the full measure of its inheritance.
Like a lion death rushed upon men and swallowed them,
and like a wild beast it went in and hid in the clefts of Sheol.
Sin called it and urged it to rush to the slaughter,
and she taught it to break men without pity.
Like a harlot she went out and stood in the streets of Eden,
and, as one does with youths, she drew Adam to his slaughter.
She demanded a heavy wage of the one who played the harlot with her;
he gave his body, and she pledged it into the hands of death.
Greedy [death] took the pledge from the harlot
and ground it down until it left in it no true remnant.
The Creator saw the emblem of his image in man's garment torn,
and took pity on his work, that it should not be scorned by the arrogant.
Love drew him toward the compassion that his hands had worked,
and he set about renewing the garment worn out by mortality.
As if it were purple, his will put on the garment of flesh,
and he showed his glory in a thing far smaller than his greatness.
A human being is smaller than the Maker beyond measure,
just as a woolen garment is less than the one who wears it.
In a woolen garment the King showed the greatness of his love,
[and] the Word of the Father in Adam's body [revealed?] his hiddenness.
To abolish death he put on the corruptible garment,
so that in human form he might rescue men from the mouth of death.
His will went out after death on feet of flesh;
it ran and seized it and took from it the captive host of men.
In the form of men he hunted the lion that hunts men,
and with human food he quietly gave it something deadly to eat.
With humanity his will grew strong to hunt down mortals,

and he proclaimed on earth the good news of the resurrection of the dead.
Like a fisherman he stood upon the sea of mortality
and cast the net of the word of his mouth and caught death.
The food of the flesh he first threw before it as bait;
it rushed and swallowed it, and so he drew it to dry land.
In a single limb [?] the Lover of mankind visited it, by way of our humanity,
so that through a man he might abolish death from mortals.
Skillfully he caught the world by [?]
and subdued it under his lordship, never to stray.
The hand of the Man cast its sign over sinners
and drew them like beasts to bear his love.
He hunted sinners in his will with bodily members
and spoke with them gently through a mouth of flesh.
Humbly he went in among the fishermen, sons of the earth,
and drew those fishermen as one draws youths, by his teaching.
He bound a bond of love with them in mystery
and made them friends of his love and children of his mysteries.
First he chose for himself three friends from among mortals,
and so spread his love richly over all.
Jesus, it is said, loved human friends:
Martha and Mary and Lazarus, three siblings.
He who loves all did not love them more than anyone,
but he did it to stir up zeal in mankind to love his name.
He stirred zeal in both orders of mankind
in choosing friends for his love, men and women.
Through Martha and Mary he drew women toward purity,
and through Lazarus he urged men to keep love.
In the three he revealed the aim of his love to our whole race,
and set their love before the onlookers like mirrors.
In them the power of his greatness triumphed as among friends,
and through them he tested the armor of the Spirit in which he fought.
He armed himself against death and the tyrant Iniquity,
and shot two arrows at the mark and aimed true.
Sin and death were bitter against his justice;
he was moved and grew strong and subdued them against their will.
The mark was set for him to aim first against iniquity,
and he shot and struck it through the forgiveness of Mary's iniquity.
Against grievous iniquity he tested the armor the Spirit had given him,
and then he turned to look at death, and bound it and shot it down.
He kept great order in the battle with the arrogant:
the first he killed was [missing], which had pronounced the sentence,
and fittingly he first loosed the arrows of righteousness against it.
Sin was wounded and bore the fruits of righteousness,
and when death saw it, it trembled and was afraid to swallow men.
In Mary sin was ruined first, and its leaves fell;
and in Lazarus death too swallowed a hard arrow.
Through two siblings death and the Evil One learned his strength,
and were greatly amazed: what is this new thing that has happened?
They thought it strange that one full of iniquity should hate iniquity,
and that a dead man who was buried should return to life without being born.

Through iniquity the human race was made to be overthrown,
and along the road of death their nature went, one after another.
According to this custom death, the fearsome lion, looked about,
and opened its mouth and swallowed the friend of the One who gives life to the dead.
It carried him off and went down to the depth of Sheol to bear him away,
not knowing that it would quickly give back its food.
Like a hawk it swooped upon innocent doves,
and like a chick it snatched the brother from his sisters.
The peaceful doves moaned and cried out loudly
over the tender chick that had become food for death.
The chaste women put on deep mourning for their brother,
because death had split the united household of the company of siblings.
They sent and made known the secret of his illness before he departed
to the good Friend who loved them for his love's sake.
'Behold, our Lord,' the innocent women sent word to our Lord,
'your friend is ill and near to death; come, save his life.'
In faith and love they sent to persuade him,
as one sends to a friend whose love for his beloved is true.
He in turn looked to the aim of his own thoughts and said
that this illness was not unto death but unto glory.
He called death 'glory' because of his friend, foreseeing
that for what he would raise up all would glorify his name.
The All-Loving heard that his friend was ill and about to die,
and did not hurry to go and see him before he departed.
He reined in the love of his sweetness with the bridle of the Spirit
and did not let it run quickly to bring healing.
Wisely the Wise One, who makes men wise, made his visit,
and as one who knows the future he revealed his power.
For he knew that he would wage war with the strong one
and turn back from him the captive host he had taken from mankind.
It pleased him to conquer and humble death the tyrant;
therefore he lingered rather than going quickly.
It was not fitting that he should go to fight with an illness,
for that was nothing to the strength of his might.
Nor would it have helped for him to fight without cause,
lest greedy death think he was stirring up pretexts.
It was not right, while the captor had not yet gone out and taken captive,
that he should go out and stop him and give him no room to get in.
Thus it befitted the greatness of the power with which he fought,
that what greedy death had swallowed he should take away from it.
Thus it befits a warrior who wages war
to fight with the enemy within the enemy's fortresses.
Thus it is fitting for a spiritual contestant
to show his contest in the stadium before the eyes of the onlookers.
This is greatness: that while the strong man dwells in his city,
the hero should come in and take from it the captives he has captured.
This befits the great wonder and the glory:
that from within the very house of death he should plunder the spoil of man.
Therefore the Life-Giver remained where he was
until death had swallowed his friend and hidden him in its clefts.
He framed his words before his disciples as one who did not know,

to make known to them that he knew well what was to come.
'Come, let us go to the land of Judea,' he said to them,
and they protested strongly, thinking the time of his passion had arrived.
'Look, the Jews are very eager to kill you;
why do you want to go and cut off the hope of our life?'
He was going to rescue a dead man from the mouth of death,
and they were thinking that death would swallow him as it does everyone.
He was preparing to wage war with the strong one,
and they supposed that men weak in strength would overcome him.
And because they had not learned the might of his greatness in mystery,
he framed a reason more plainly revealed than the first.
'Our friend has fallen asleep,' he said to them of Lazarus;
'come, let us go and wake him from his sleep, and call him, and he will rise.'
'If he has fallen asleep,' the young men said to the One who knows,
'he will rise, as the order of sleep requires.'
He spoke of the sleep of death, which is very harsh,
and they spoke of ordinary sleep, such as everyone sleeps.
He saw that they had not stirred from the sleep of ignorance,
and he woke them with the word: 'Lazarus has died.'
'Lazarus has died, and I am very glad I was not there,
so that through his death you may gain the strength of faith.'
'I was not there' — hear, [?], who it was that was not there:
the Word of the Father, of whom heaven and earth are full!
How then, when height and depth cannot contain him,
was he not in Bethany, as he said?
Flesh cannot acquire such a make-up as to be everywhere,
for it is not possible for what is bodily to be everywhere.
And if he was where he was and also in Bethany,
then it is confirmed that it was not a visible body.
And if there is no visible and bounded body,
why was it said, 'I am glad I was not there'?
Be silent, arrogant one; this is not the time to argue with you;
do not hold us back from the fair course of our way.
It was bodily that he said he was not where he was not;
and so it is that whatever is made is not in every place.
The One who Is is everywhere, in every place, without end,
and the nature of his glory was not far from Bethany.
Two days he stayed there where he was,
so that in his delay death might rush upon his beloved.
Four days he gave it room to rejoice in its food,
and then he shook it with the new voice of the resurrection of the dead.
Then Christ set out and arrived and came to rest at Bethany,
and the innocent doves heard and went out to meet him.
Martha first went out alone to meet him,
and when she met him she wept and told him of her brother's death.
'If you had been here,' she said to him loudly,
'greedy death would not have rushed in and destroyed my brother.
If you had visited him while he was still alive here,

the fountain of life that flowed in him would not have dried up.
If your pure body had drawn near to his limbs,
the bitterness of weeping would have turned into the fragrance of your body.
If you had seen him while he still saw the light of day,
he would have looked at you, and the suffering that pained him would have changed.
If he had heard you speaking as you used to,
the sweet voice of the words of his mouth would not have fallen silent.'
These things the broken dove said without understanding,
supposing it would be hard for him to raise her brother.
'If you believe,' he said to the believing woman,
'you will see the great glory that is hidden in my words.'
'Yes,' she said, 'it is certain to me that you are the Christ,
and that you are the Son, that fountain which pours out life.'
She spoke a word according to a mind schooled in the Law,
and it was not the truth that befits the divine name.
She said, 'You are the Christ who comes into the world,'
not distinguishing the likeness of the servant from that of the Maker.
This had not been revealed to men or to spiritual beings
until the Spirit showed it to mankind in the form of light.
His friends called him Christ and Son,
as prophets and kings were called anointed by grace.
In this sense Martha called him Christ and Son,
not knowing that he was Son of the Essence and Son of humanity.
These things she said in grief of soul and the affection of love,
and went in to call Mary her sister: 'Our Master has come.'
Mary heard the report of our Lord and went out to meet him,
and fell and worshiped and also said her sister's words.
Mary repaid with worship of love the One who forgave her iniquity,
for the affection of his love was greater to her than anything.
He asked them where they had laid his friend's body,
not in order to learn but to show that he knew where.
He asked them as one who did not know, in order to make them understand,
and they answered, 'Come and see the place of the grave.'
He went with them, walking in suffering,
and as he walked the tears of his eyes poured out.
Suffering and weeping wore him down over his beloved,
and he wept, as nature demanded of him.
Nature in its distress clearly demanded it of him,
and the bitterness of his suffering made its way along the path of his eyes.
For it was nature that wept over its beloved,
remembering to what end the nature of rational beings had come.
Human nature looked and sighed bitterly
that death destroys its beauty and it becomes dust.
That nature which death had taken captive he too had put on,
and by nature he grieved at the humiliation of the children of his race.
He too was formed from that dust which is softened by sufferings,
and with his make-up the poison of mortality was stirring.
From it came that confusion which breeds pains, flowing on as its inheritance,
and, as with everyone, grief [?] darkened him in what was his own.

Therefore he wept chastely over his beloved,
so that all might learn that it was the likeness of the servant that wept.
And since the suffering of passibility wore him down,
in the manner of the servant he grieved and lamented meekly.
Chaste groans he gave in his movements and in his eyes,
and he comforted himself with the good hope of the resurrection of the dead.
At his chaste weeping the dull of heart were amazed and astonished,
and did not discern how wisely he was acting.
'Could not this man, who raised other dead,
have rebuked death so that it would not come near the one he loves?'
He paid no heed and kept silent, as if he did not know what they said,
and did not answer the foolish murmuring of their thoughts.
He drew near to the grave and lifted his gaze toward heaven,
and began to entreat the Hidden One within him to reveal his power.
'You have already heard me, and again I know that you hear me;
reveal your power in me, so that all may know whose Son I am.
It is not to boast that I have asked for his power to raise the stricken,
but to reveal the power of your hiddenness to the eyes of the onlookers.
It is not because I need help that I have called on you now,
but to reveal that it is by the power of your strength that I conquer.'
Who is it, you who wrong our body, who began to weep over Lazarus?
And who is it who prayed and asked for power from the Maker?
And who is it who wept aloud over his beloved,
and who ended his weeping with the hope of the resurrection of the dead?
Who gave thanks to whom for hearing him and hearing him still,
and to whom, from whom, was entreaty in words offered?
The Word of the Father did not pray to the Father who begot him,
for he is equal with him in divinity, as [?] proclaim.
Equal with his Father, he does not need the strength of help,
and, having no senses, he does not weep tears of suffering.
Higher than sufferings, he does not suffer in the sufferings of men,
and knowing all, he does not ask where the grave is.
It was a son of Adam who began to grieve over his beloved,
and it is he who wept over the corruption of his fellows.
It was the likeness of the servant that saw its nature captured by death,
and asked and entreated to raise its life from destruction.
It was the man who prayed to the Hidden One who dwelt in him,
to redeem man's soul from the mouth of death [?].
The Hidden One was hidden within his limbs without [?],
and by the power of his strength he cried out to death, and it fled from him.
By the power of his help he was moved and strengthened against the arrogant,
who were going to see the wonder and despise him.
Jesus, it is said, was moved, being strengthened by the power of the Spirit,
and he troubled himself and cried out to death indignantly.
Why then was the Sea of Peace moved and stirred,
and against whom did he raise a loud voice, he who is full of calm?
Against the Jews, who wronged his power, he was stirred,
for he was raising a dead man who had rotted in the grave, and still they would not [?].
For he had his eye on them before he offered entreaty to his Father,

and he prayed first in order to shut the door on their words,
lest they count him as an opponent of God;
therefore he first ascribed to his Father what was to come.
The Wise One built a wall of words before them
and gave no room for the slander of their thoughts to feed.
By his thanksgiving he showed that he is equal with his Begetter,
and by deeds he taught that he has power over all things.
He raised his voice [...] and called the dead man as one who was weary,
so that all might hear that at his command he lived and rose.
An open voice resounded in the earthly land,
and greedy death trembled and was terrified at the sound of his voice.
'Lazarus!' the Mighty One cried into the ears of death,
and dismay seized it: who is this who calls the dead?
It heard the voice of a man calling a dead man as though he were alive,
and began to writhe like a woman in labor at the time of giving birth.
The captor heard a new voice from a son of captivity,
and cried out and wailed: what is this new thing that has happened?
'A new thing has befallen me,' said death itself [?]:
'a man who cries out and shakes the strength of my might in Sheol.'
'Who are you, man?' said death to the voice that called him,
'and who are you who cry with confidence, "Come out, dead man"?
Who are you who despise my might? Have you acquired power,
and do you seek to remove man's captive host from the house of my hands?
Who are you who seek to undo the order of mortality
and open the door which Adam shut in the face of all?
You seem to me not to be from mankind, you who are clothed in sufferings,
and you are like a stranger to the kinship of mortality.
Have you not heard the story of man from mankind,
that ever since they came under the subjection of my lordship they have been placed there?
Have you not asked by what cause men became mortal,
who placed them there, who sold them to be slaves?
And if you do not know what is the cause of your race's slavery,
hear it from me and learn how it came about from the beginning.
Your father incurred a debt of debts through the Evil One's word,
and since he did not pay it, he handed over his children for his debts.
The Slanderer handed you over to me as a pledge,
and behold, all the generations of your heirs serve me.
I hold man as a pledge within my fortresses,
and unless they pay the bond of your debts, they will not escape.
If you wish to set free your race's pledge,
pay their debts, and then you may take back their [?].
The debt of debts of their deeds cannot be paid off,
for it is mortality, however much you may pay.
Enough for you to cast terror into the ears of the dead
and stir them with a new voice to which they are not accustomed.
Who appointed you steward of mortality?
For behold, the governance of the end of life is placed in my hands.
Who is it [?] who dares [?] to plunder the house of man from me?
For whether they will or not, they obey me.'

'I do not allow men to be outside my lordship
until they pay the debt of debts of their deeds.
If you are just, judge justly between me and them,
and examine and see that it is for debts they are imprisoned with me.'
These things greedy death said without speaking,
for it did not speak; rather, it was the very sense of mortality.
I have set out the meaning in the person of mortality:
'Because of iniquity you were made [?] slaves to the Evil One and to death.'
'Give me what you took,' our Lord said to the one who spoke;
'give me men, and I will pay the bond of their debts.
Give up the pledge which the tyrant, your companion, [?] with you,
and I will pay the debt of debts in which you take pride.
Since you have cruelly worked the garment of our body
and made our limbs like a couch beneath your [?].'
These things the Second Adam answered death,
not with an outcry but with silence, in mystery.
'Come out,' said the Man to the man whom he called,
'come out and be a witness to my words among mortals.
Come, mortal, whom death swallowed as it does everyone,
show mankind the pledge of the life that I proclaim.
Come, departed one, attended by voices that cut off hope,
lay hold of the resurrection of the dead that is proclaimed through me.
Come out, proclaim good hope to mankind,
and encourage them not to be frightened by the voice of death.'
The mortal heard the voice of the Passible One who resembled him,
and stirred from quiet at the voice mingled with creative power.
At the [?] of the Soul, the soul of Lazarus that was with him heard,
and turned and entered the temple of its body to dwell in it.
It plucked its will on the lyre of its being as before,
and the dead senses acquired feeling voices.
Where is the wonder that was proclaimed in Lazarus,
that he listened to the voice while the senses of his body were silent?
Where he had hard fetters cast on him and was bound in Sheol,
he broke them, and not by human hands.
Where he was imprisoned in the rebellious fortresses of mortality,
he broke them open, and was astonished, and laughed at his guards.
The mortal heard a new voice from one of his own race,
and began to leap like John in the womb of Sheol.
A great wonder came about through a man for mankind:
by the voice of a man the buried dead gained life.
Who ever saw such a marvel of a word,
a man who commands the dead, 'Come out,' and is not hindered?
Even if men have brought men back from the house of the dead,
it was not in the manner of what happened at our Lord's hands.
Elijah and Elisha raised the dead,
but they asked much and entreated, and only then accomplished it.
For they were servants, and entreated the Creator,
and he honored them as servants, for his love's sake.
Christ, who is from us, though he is of our race,
did not ask and entreat like a servant and only then raise the dead.
Though he entreated as a petitioner, it was no petition.
If you had visited him while he was still alive here,

I would not [?] the fountain of life that was at work in him.
But the words are full of the power of his exalted rank:
"You have heard me," he said beforehand
in his prayer, and again, "You hear"; and yet
his hearing had already been more than persuaded to hear.
"Because of the crowd that is standing here," he said, "I said these things";
so it is clear that he did not rise to pray out of any need to pray.
He entreated and asked, as befits one who was made,
and he called to Death, and it brought out and gave him the dead man he asked for.
The buried dead man heard the voice that called him by name,
and he stripped off mortality, cast it away, and put on life.
Lazarus came out, wrapped tightly in the garments of his grave,
bound all over, and yet he walked with ease.
The departed one came out with the limbs of his body bound,
shackled from head to foot, and yet running with his whole body.
The crowds marveled at the might and greatness of the one who [raised?] him,
for he did not loose his bonds until he had brought him out of the tomb.
He commanded the onlookers to take his wrappings off him,
so that they would not be divided, thinking perhaps it was not he but another.
He commanded the Jews to roll away the stone of his tomb,
to rebuke them, for they had seen his body dead and decayed.
They themselves opened the tomb that they had shut at the time of his death,
and they themselves removed the wrappings they had put upon his limbs.
Their doubting was what put the Knower of all to the test;
that is why he said, "Take away the stone," and "Unbind him and let him go."
It would have been easy for the sign that raised him from inside the tomb
to remove his wrappings as well, and so bring him out to the onlookers.
It could have rolled the stone away beforehand from the mouth of the tomb,
and likewise loosed the bonds of death from his limbs.
He brought back to life a dead man who had lodged in Sheol four days,
and made those who buried him witnesses of his death and of his life.
The Jews gathered, crowd upon crowd, to look closely
at the dead man running while his hands and feet were bound.
The onlookers saw a great wonder, and not with weeping,
and though the wonder delighted them, what had been done was beyond them.
For it was a wonder, and however much one might say, it was a wonder still,
that a buried dead man stretched himself out like a living man.
Who has ever seen a departed one like Lazarus,
carrying his grave clothes on his shoulders and bringing them out with him?
Who has ever looked closely at the dead limbs of a dead body
that were bound and yet not hindered from walking?
The body was bound all over with the cords of the wrappings,
and the door before his eyes was shut, and yet he did not stumble.
He ran, coming out of his dwelling with ease,
and the crowds ran eagerly to [?] him.
The eyes of everyone were fixed upon his coming out,
and could not have their fill of seeing the body that Death had spat out.
Insatiably their eyes searched his body,
and the more they gazed, the more they gazed again, whether it was he or not.

They all set him before their eyes like a target,
and the more they looked at his face, the more they looked again.
Eyes were drawn to his face, marveling at his eyes,
which turned and saw, and ears at his ears, which listened to the voice.
Eagerly they pressed to listen to him
as he told how he had heard the voice that called him.
And straightway the mortals of the world asked the dead man who had come to life:
"What order did you see in Sheol among the departed?"
And fittingly the dead man who had come to life answered the living who die:
"The order in Sheol is silence and stillness without [?].
A great silence, without life, over the limbs,
and a quiet rest, without activity, in the motions of the soul.
The body is silent, as one deaf, according to its deafness,
and the soul is alive, according to its life, but without work."
He cast a good hope into the ears of the living,
[to turn] them to the teaching that sows life.
Our Lord was sowing new life in the house of the mortals,
and he showed it to them as a pledge through Lazarus.
He reigned over all nature and confirmed it with seals,
and he sealed his word with three dead whom he raised and brought to life.
Three witnesses he set as a signature on the bond of our life:
Lazarus, the widow's son, and the daughter of Jairus.
Three hostages he led away from Death, the destroyer of man,
until he claims from it all its captivity at the end of time.
Through their lives he taught it the power of his might,
so that it would not be in doubt about the victory at the end.
He revealed a letter to us at the start of the war he waged with it,
so that it would know that the Redeemer of man would claim them from its hands.
He set it a limit from the day that Lazarus rose:
"Keep for me the captives who come back to you until I come.
See, I have shown you that the captivity of man is not yours,
and you are not master of their lives as you supposed.
You are the nurse of their limbs until the fullness of time;
see that you do not lose a single hair from their heads.
And you too, captives who have returned from slavery, see to it:
keep the promise of the resurrection of the dead in your minds.
See that you do not go astray as you went astray at the beginning,
so that the yoke of death may not press upon your necks again.
See what a great war I waged on your behalf
with the two strong ones, who are called Death and the Evil One.
See how by my own death I went down to the depths of Sheol,
and broke the gates and cut the bars to redeem you.
Behold, Death is undone, and the Enemy is shut in the prison house;
do not grow slack, lest their bonds be slackened.
See, I have shown you by what men are condemned and how they win acquittal;
make ready the weapons that are needed for the war into which you are cast.
Put on the breastplate of good hope that does not deceive,
and take up the shield of faith that is not loosened.
Set the helmet of great love upon your heads,
and take up the sword of the word of truth [?].
Draw near and overcome the desires of the passions and of the flesh,
and look for the reward that crowns with a life without end." Finished.
Another, for the Feast of Hosannas

Another, for the Feast of Hosannas.
Response:
With the eye of the Spirit the children beheld you
as you were entering, and they gave praise.
My brothers:

A great wonder is the providence of the God of all,
and at every hour it stirs the discerning to praise.

No mouth, passing as it is, can tell his glory,
through whose goodness these blessings have reached our race.
Our race was steeped in the leaven of mortality
and enslaved to tyrant death as to a king.
Everyone served the lusts of mortality,
and greedy death had prevailed over our humanity.
It did not please the Maker of all to leave us in our bondage,
so he sent his Son and raised our race from its fall.
From the field of our dust he uprooted all sufferings
and granted us the honour of sonship, full of blessings.
And when he had in every way been brought to completion, as was fitting,
he ascended to heaven and sat at the right hand.
And as it pleased him, he freed our race from slavery;
when he had made it strong, he left his memorial in the holy Church.
In the world he set the chosen Church in the likeness of a body,
and within it the feasts, like limbs, one after another.
It did not please him to leave his Church without festivals,
lest his bodily economy be forgotten by it.
And as the working of the body is known from its limbs,
so his economy is made known to us from the festivals.
The body can do nothing without limbs,
and each limb shows only what is its own.
If one limb could nourish the whole body,
the many limbs in it would be superfluous.
And if one limb does not suffice for the whole body,
neither does one festival show everything to the Church.
The feast of our Lord's birth cannot show
the things he did on the day he was baptized by John.

Nor can the feast on which he was baptized make plain
that victory over the evil one at the end of his fast.
Nor can all the glorious feasts within the Church
show everything that was done on this day.
On this day the testing of prophecy was fulfilled,
that of Jacob the elder, of David the king, and of Zechariah too.
On this day the word of Jacob the righteous was shown forth,
the word written generations ago about our Savior:
“The sceptre of rule shall not depart from Judah,
nor a lawgiver who is a prophet from between his feet,
until he comes to whom the eternal kingdom belongs;
and then prophet and king shall cease from Judah.”
His is the eternal kingdom that has no end;
he is the end of the mysteries and the hope of the nations.
And as Jacob his father prophesied generations ago,
there is in Judah no prophet or king from itself and over itself.
So the Jew has no ground to open his mouth
and say that Christ was not the king of whom Jacob the elder spoke.
He cannot show that he has a king from himself and over himself,
and he has nowhere to show a prophet among his people.
And since prophet and king have ceased, as indeed they have,
then it is he in whom Jacob's word was fulfilled.
And perhaps he says: because we have been scattered through all our lands,
[?] we have no prophet, nor yet a king to govern us.
At what time did you go out from your land, O wicked one,
when there were no prophets and kings for you before our Lord?
In Egypt, where you were, Moses and Miriam were prophets for you,
and in Babylon, those of the house of Hananiah, with Daniel.

These three he gave you in Babylon, with Ezekiel,
and Joshua the priest and Ezra the scribe, with Zerubbabel.
Why now are prophets and kings shorn away from you,
and why are you not honoured before God? Because of your wickedness.
The Spirit taught Jacob the elder to bless,
and he set the limit of your honour until our Lord.
The honour that was among your people has been taken from you,
and you will not be raised again to the greatness from which you have fallen.
Where is the time when your captivity led you away to the lands,
when a reckoning did not fix for you the sign of the years you would remain?
Four hundred years he fixed for you to be in the land of Egypt,
and in Babylon seventy years, and then you were delivered.
But now, when you suppose you are in captivity outside Zion,
how many years are fixed for you to be there before you return?
Be still and do not be troubled, O wicked one: your honour has passed,
for the King has dawned on whose account you were honoured.
Do not be divided, you circumcised in flesh and uncircumcised in heart;
come, examine with discernment the words of Jacob.
See the signs he foretold concerning that king
who was to come and take prophets and kings away from you:
“He will bind his foal to the vine-branch of the vineyard,”
and the foal will not shy and break the branches.
By this sign he shows the might of him who subdues all,
and how he brings tyrants under his lordship as if they were foals.
And when he wished to prophesy about his death,
he foretells what he would do at the time of his passion:
“He will whiten his garment in pure wine, the king who comes,
and in the blood of grapes the robe in which he is wrapped.”

Hidden is the blessing with which you bless, Jacob the righteous:
how are garments whitened in wine, which stains vessels?
If his robe is one that was made, and all can see it,
then perhaps its wearer is greater than the kings who were before him.
Not everyone understands every word you spoke in the form of a blessing,
and not everyone knows how the garments you spoke of are whitened.
Yet Jacob's word is not hidden from the discerning,
and great is the strength of the faith of the Orthodox.
The wine is death, which stains the human race;
but the body he put on, greedy death does not stain.
And because he humbled himself and gave himself up to the suffering of death,
he ascended to heaven and sat at the right hand.
He whitens in wine the garment he put on from our humanity,
and in the blood of grapes the robe that is from the house of David.
This is what he said in prophecy about his death;
it is a great blow to Cyril, the apostle of falsehood.
What will he say, the one who makes the Godhead suffer,
against Jacob, who assigned death to the body that is from us?
In the creed he made there is an anathema at the end,
and in it he set Jacob at the head of the anathema, for making him suffer, Jacob [?].
Do not be grieved, Jacob, by the counsel of Cyril:
along with you he anathematized everyone who says that Christ died.
The deluded one anathematized the Holy Spirit and the apostles too,
and even our Lord himself, while he is held fast in his anathema as in his prison.
Which garment does the wine whiten? Let the deluded one hear:
the one from Mary, or the one woven by hands?
If perhaps you say that Jacob spoke of the garment he wore,
garments are never whitened in wine, as you understand it.

Wine leaves a stain on whatever garment it reaches;
so about which garment did Jacob say it is whitened?
You do not concede it is about the body he took from us;
to which, then, does your mind incline to interpret it?
For I know that, as your rashness is accustomed,
your mind hands the Only-Begotten over to suffering.
O interpretation full of every rashness!
O blasphemy that does not shrink from the truth!
Far be it from us to say this, that God suffered,
or to be mixed with the band that made the Only-Begotten suffer.
Let our assembly rejoice, which Zechariah the prophet gladdens,
and let the Church exult in place of the daughter of Zion, who spurned him.
The prophet brought the daughter of Jerusalem the good news: “Your king is coming,”
so that when she saw him she would go out to meet him and receive him.
“Exult, then, and rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem,” the herald cries,
“for behold, your king comes to you, exalted, and he gladdens you.”
The daughter of Jerusalem did not ask him what his sign was,
but he began to persuade her of his economy, as he had been commanded:
“Your king is lowlier than all kings, by his own will,
and rides a foal, and his command rules over height and depth.
Lighten yourself of the weight of the sufferings that surround you,
and do not grow weak before the multitude of nations encircling you.
Righteous indeed is he, lowly too, and a saviour,
and he speaks peace even with the nations, for they are his.
From Jerusalem he destroys the swift horse,
and from Ephraim the lofty chariot, so that it shall be no more.”
O herald of good news, who brought good tidings to the children of his people,
he gladdened them and grieved them by his proclamation.
For when he said, “Your king is coming,” he gladdened them,

but when he showed them his economy, he saddened them.
When he prophesied that he would ride a foal, they were not glad,
thinking that a foal cannot wage war.
And when he announced that he destroys horse and chariot too,
they thought that their precious things would be taken from us.
And because he proclaimed that he speaks peace even with the nations,
they understood that perhaps the nations would become members of the household.
Zion, the house of divisions, the lover of strife, rose up
and sneered at the sign of the king that the prophet proclaimed by the Spirit.
“How shall I rejoice in this good news?” answered Jerusalem,
“that horse and chariot are destroyed from within my streets?”
In what should the lover of strife exult, O herald,
when the king whose good news you bring rides the foal of an ass?
In this good news you announce, let the nations rejoice,
for he speaks peace and calm with them, as you prophesied.
If you want him to speak peace and calm with you,
behold, you have heard his sign: when you see him, go out to meet him.
Had you not been taught his appearance long beforehand,
perhaps you would have had an excuse when he calls you to account.
The words the prophet spoke by the Spirit were fulfilled in deed,
and Zion saw her king who had come, and did not receive him.
He rode on a colt, the foal of an ass, and entered Jerusalem,
so that the word the prophet proclaimed by the Spirit would not prove false.
His power stirred the multitude of the crowds who thirsted for blood,
and they went out to meet him with olive branches to praise him.
Not every time our Lord entered Jerusalem
did they go out to meet him as they went out on this day.
On this day the multitude of the crowds went out to meet him

to see his glory and Lazarus, whom his command had brought to life.
They were not persuaded in their own minds why it was
that a hidden power moved them to go out to meet him.
Some carried olive branches and gave praise,
and some spread their garments on the road where he was going.
There were women singing before him with lyres,
and the sound of the hosannas of their songs stirred Zion.
The Pharisees and scribes shut their mouths against his praise,
and in their place nursing infants praised him.
The praise of the nursing infants surpassed that of the fathers,
for they cried out a new praise that no one had heard.
Beyond nature the nursing infants spoke
a new voice with which no tongue of flesh had ever praised.
The children sang a new praise to the new King
with a new mouth from which no other word had come.
“Hosanna indeed in the highest!” the children cried,
“and Hosanna also to the Son of David, who is glory!”
A great wonder took place in Jerusalem on this day,
and the foolish people of the Jews did not understand it.
One wonder: that her king rode the foal of an ass,
he whose divine glory the cherubim bear in procession.
Another wonder: the crowds went out with olive branches
and did not know why their ranks went out.
They knew only that they should go out in great numbers,
but what they should say as they went out they did not know.
Another wonder, at which heaven and earth were amazed:
that babes nursing at the breast cried out Hosanna.
The children rebuked the scribes and priests with their hosannas,

and with a tongue they had never spoken they spoke.
The scribes and priests in their envy could not bear
the new praise that the mouth of nursing infants proclaimed.
The wicked heard the sound of praise the children uttered,
and envy grew strong in their hearts against our Savior.
They saw boys and girls singing praise,
and began to rage like a woman in labour seized by pain.
Children and crowds cry out and say, “Blessed is our God!”
and they call to our Savior, “Rebuke your disciples!”
“O blind ones, blind of heart,” cried our Savior,
“they are your own children, who are not persuaded about me by the senses of the body.
For their ears have not yet heard the sound of my preaching,
nor have their eyes seen the signs my hands have done.
You saw the dead whom I raised from within the graves,
and even against the dead man whom my will brought to life you decreed death.
You heard the sound of the oracles of prophecy
of Jacob the righteous and David the king and Zechariah too.
Jacob blessed the fruit that came from him and announced concerning me
that prophets and kings would come from him until my coming.
He gave a sign that I would ride in procession on a foal,
and behold, it has been fulfilled on this day, and you have not believed.
And the very sign that Jacob gave in the form of a blessing,
Zechariah gave too, so that when you saw him you would not be divided.
And also concerning the children who gave praise, though not by habit,
David showed by the Holy Spirit that you would again be proven wrong:
‘Truly, from the mouth of boys, children and infants
you have perfected the praise they sing to the Lord, our Lord.’
And long before, David saw by the Spirit your vindictiveness against me,

and explained and said that the children gave praise because of you.
And perhaps you will say in your mind, you lovers of strife,
that it was poverty that made him ride a despised foal.
It was not because I had no swift mount
that I rode a foal, walking gently before your crowds.
For heaven and earth are mine, and all that is in them,
and my will rules over beasts and over birds.
The ass's foal that he sent me did not belong to him;
the power of my lordship moved him, and he did not refuse.
And just as I moved the man who owned the ass's foal,
I could also have moved one who owns a herd of horses.
This I did on this day, riding a foal,
so that what the prophets prophesied about me by the Spirit would be fulfilled.
This one thing I did to bring the prophecy to its completion,
and I gave my ministers an example of humility.
For if I, who am Lord, rode a foal,
how much more should they not ride in procession on chariots!
All the kings who rode in procession on chariots
gained no calm for the earth by their riding;
but I, who chose to ride a foal in my humility,
through me heaven and earth are at peace and are not shaken.
To whom are you saying, ‘Rebuke the children who praise me’?
Silence them yourselves; perhaps they will be silenced by your words.
And if you are annoyed by the sound of the hosannas with which they praise me,
teach them; perhaps they will fall silent, as you are.
But if you tell me to rebuke the children who sing praise,
the stones will cry out another praise greater than this.
And if perhaps the stones sing praise to the God of all,

you priests of the daughter of Jerusalem, whom do you envy?”
All these things our Savior did on this day,
as his prophets, whom he taught, prophesied by the Spirit.
The crowds went out to meet our Lord with olive branches;
let us, too, cast out from us envy, the offspring of the evil one.
Let baptism, the spiritual mother, no longer give birth
to a child that does the will of the evil one, the accuser.
And let whoever sucks the precious blood that the spear pressed out
complete his life according to the will of our Lord Jesus.
And let whoever runs the race that befits righteousness
make errors flee from the sound of his voice wherever he preaches.
And let whoever has been chosen in the holy Church to serve as priest
shepherd his flock according to the will of the Chief of priesthood.
And let everyone entrusted in this world with [?]
satisfy from them whoever is in need of sustenance,
so that on that day, when the King on high comes in his glory,
he may be worthy to enter that kingdom which was promised to us.
Of the Hosannas

Memra 21: On the Hosannas. / Also his: the twenty-first memra, suited to the Hosannas. / Response: / O Son, who was praised by the mouth of children, strengthen us to receive You with Hosannas. / My brothers.

The glorious Radiance who is from the Father, / the Son who is no younger than His Begetter, / the eternal Word of the Father, / who exists together with His Father, / shone like the sun in our humanity / and filled the world with His glory. / He drove away and put out the darkness / with the rays of His glory. / And since the eye could not see Him / or gaze upon His nature, / He first put on [a body] from us / and veiled the splendor of His greatness. / He showed His glory to His creatures, / not as His hidden nature is, / and made known to us the power of His lordship, / not by the measure of His being. / In His love the Word of the Father put on / the garment of our body and dwelt in it, / and through it He interpreted to rational beings / the mighty discourse of His wisdom. / His love fitted for itself a lyre of flesh / for His revelation, / so that with its melodies He might gladden / spirits and bodies. / On the strings of the mortal body / He played the will of His hiddenness, / and men and angels marveled / at the sweetness of His melodies. / He fashioned the image of His own being / and honored it above all through His love, / and through it He gladdened creation, / which had grown dark in sin. / Through the iniquity of men the peace / of the whole inhabited world had been troubled, / and His glory dwelt in a man / so that creation might find peace in Him. / The hidden mystery of wonder / came to light in His mercy, / He whom the heavenly and the earthly / longed to see. / The scriptures of truth spoke of His coming / and taught us that He was going to come; / and He completed and fulfilled the words / of the prophets who proclaimed His mysteries. / He came to be in the womb, as He had determined, / and was revealed from the seed of David, / as had been spoken generations before / by the mouth of all His holy ones. / By His birth He set us free from our error / and sanctified us in the mysteries of His baptism, / and He shaped for us a pattern of purity / in His radiant and holy fast. / And when He saw how the demons / had grown arrogant against our race, / He willed, by the pattern of His humility, / to bring to nothing the pride of the rebel. / So He rode on a humble colt / and entered the city of Jerusalem. / Children, boys and little ones / carried branches in their hands, / crying out "Hosanna" / to the King who shone forth from David. / For on this day was fulfilled / the word of Jacob the righteous, / who prophesied long before / of His coming to us: / "The scepter shall not depart / that ruled over Judah, / nor the interpreter of hidden things / and the prophet from between his feet, / until He comes to whom belongs / the authority of the kingdom." / And then, he says, king and prophet / shall cease from Judah. / For His is the eternal kingdom, / which has no end through all generations; / and He is the fulfiller of mysteries / and the hope of all the peoples.

And just as Jacob prophesied, / as he had learned by revelation, / so, according to his word, there is in Judah / neither king nor prophet. / Judah cannot say / that he has a king from his own race, / nor can he show / that he has a prophet among his people. / If from now on prophet and king / have passed away, as indeed they have passed away, / then in this was fulfilled / the prophecy of our father Jacob. / Do not be divided in your thoughts, / son of Abraham, sealed with circumcision. / Examine carefully / the words of Jacob the righteous. / See the signs he gave beforehand / and set down for you about the One who comes, / that He would come and bring to an end / prophets and kings from your people. / For he said that He would tie His colt / to the vine, His donkey's foal; / and that, he says, colts would no longer [?] / and cut off a shoot from it. / By this sign he showed us / the might of the One to whom all is subject, / and that, as with the colt, He subdues / tyrants beneath His kingdom; / and that He would ride on this day / upon a colt and enter Jerusalem, / so that the word should not fail that / the prophet spoke in the Spirit generations before. / Zechariah the prophet, son of Jacob, / also expounded like his father / and proclaimed concerning Him, saying / plainly in his prophecy— / he tightened the strings of his lyre / and lifted up his voice, saying: / "Dance and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, / and shout, for your King has come to you! / For behold, your Savior is arriving / and riding on a donkey's foal. / Open your gates to Him, Jerusalem, / for the Savior has come to you." / Dance, then, daughter of Zion, / and cry out to Him fitting praise; / take His yoke upon you gladly / and worship Him with a sincere heart. / The daughter of Zion did not ask him / what the sign of this King was, / yet he began to persuade her with His words, / which He would accomplish at His coming: / "Your King is humbler than all kings, / and became humble by His own will; / He rides on a humble colt / though He rules the height and the depth. / Lift from yourself every burden / and the afflictions that surround you, / and do not grow faint with fear / because of the peoples who hate you. / Righteous, humble too, / and a Savior is your King, / and He speaks peace with the peoples, / for they too are His." / And he said further that from Jerusalem / He destroys the swift horse, / and from Ephraim the lofty chariot, / and destroys it so that it is no more. / For Jerusalem became a house of divisions / and loved iniquity / when she heard the sign of the King / that Zechariah proclaimed to her in the Spirit. / He fulfilled in deed the words / expounded about His coming: / He came to enter Jerusalem, / and the children of Zion did not receive Him. / So the elders withheld the glory / of the King who came to them, / and the children were stirred with wonder / to praise Him with Hosannas.

The children paid Him the praise / that the elders of the daughter of Zion owed Him, / and there the hymn was made ready / that was due to His honor. / The wicked shut their mouths, / priests and scribes and Pharisees, / and children stood in band upon band / to shout to Him with Hosannas: / "Blessed is He who came in the name of the Lord!" / The pure of soul cried out to Him. / The road of the King's Son thundered, / for they praised Him with a new praise. / The trees bowed down to offer Him / branches of olive and of palm, / so that with their fruits might be adorned / the road of the heavenly Bridegroom. / The children wove crowns of praise / and offered them with the branches of their tongue, / rejoicing in the Messiah / whom they beheld among their throngs. / Not every time our Lord entered / Jerusalem did they go out to meet Him / as the children went out / on this day to give praise. / On this day [?] / the throngs of the crowds went out to meet Him, / to see the glory of His greatness / in Lazarus, the dead man who came to life. / Yet they went out not knowing / what the reason was for their going out; / for it was His power that stirred them / to go out to meet Him with hosannas. / Some carried branches of olive / and some fronds of palm, / and some again spread their garments / on the road where our Lord walked. / There were young men there too / who sang with lyres, / and at the sound of their hosannas / the city of Zion was stirred. / Pharisees and scribes held back their mouths / from praising our Savior, / and the boys praised in their place / with an indescribable wonder. / The praise of infants at the breast / astonished the fathers, / for they cried out a new praise / that men had never heard. / Beyond nature the boys / spoke before the Messiah, / a new voice the like of which / no human tongue had ever spoken. / The boys sang a new praise / to the new King from David, / with a fresh mouth from which, until then, / no word had come out. / "Hosanna in the highest!" / the children cried with their cries; / "Hosanna also to the Son of David!"— / and its meaning is "praise." / Zechariah called the daughter of Zion / to give praise with the children, / but the foolish bride did not heed / the longed-for voice of the prophet. / For she had gone mad over carved images / and was vexed that He had come; / and for this reason she did not consent / to receive her Betrothed. / For her heart was captivated by the calf, / and she loved it shamefully. / That is why she did not listen / to the prophet who cried "Rejoice!" / For in the image of the four faces / the daughter of Zion was entangled, / and she would not open the gate / to the Messiah who came to her. / She was anxious for her idols, / to serve them in fear, / and she cared nothing for her Lord's glory / and turned her face away from His splendor. / She bowed down openly to Astarte; / she made mourning for Tammuz; / she loved Milcom, the lie, / and offered sacrifices to Baal.

With Egyptian songs / she was taken up with Amon, / and she had no leisure to sing / praise to the Son with the boys. / She was eager for the sacrifices of demons, / to prepare them without delay, / but she did not go out to carry branches / with the children with hosannas. / Children were blessing and praising / the King who humbled Himself to come to her, / while Zion was a bitter image, / raving over her idols. / The prophets knocked at her gates, / waking her from sleep, / but she lay asleep in her sin / with the evil demons she loved. / "Dance, daughter of Zion!"—but she did not dance; / she loved calves and carved images, / and cried out against Him who came / to her city, the pure Bridegroom. / For she knew that He would expose her, / and so she hated Him without cause; / and the wicked woman did not want / Him to be praised by the boys. / Her heart was blinded with envy; / she was struck dumb and kept silent from praise. / She was anxious about the praisers, / to silence them from His praise, / and she would not praise / the King who came for her redemption. / She was eager to put an end to / the praise the boys raised to Him. / They praised with joy, / and she was angered by their voices; / she threatened them to make them be silent, / and the boys shouted all the more. / She wanted only that they be silent, / and longed for it in her anxiety, / and sought ways, as she desired, / to silence their hearts. / The praisers did not cease / from the praise of the Son of David, / for truth stirred them / to praise with their voices. / His entry was a marvel / and an amazement to the discerning, / such as neither heavenly nor earthly beings / are able to tell: / the crowds exulted in its joy, / and the children were bold in it, / and leapt before the King's Son / as David did before the ark. / The boys sang a new / and fitting hymn to God, / and to the Son of David, who in His love / raised up our lowliness by His [?]. / With David His father they clapped their hands / for the Son of David in their hallelujahs, / and shouted with their trumpets / in the melodies of the Watchers on high, / with the great sound of horns, / with harps and lyres, / with [?] and kinds of song, / in the strains of their sweetness, / with lutes and ringing cymbals; / on sweet strings they sang / to Him who was exalted in His humility / and trampled the strongholds of the rebel, / with their branches in their hands / and their hosannas in their mouths. / With myrtles and olives and every tree / they recount the praise of His greatness. / For it was like a feast for them, / to give honor with their cries [?]. / With fronds of palms, he says, / and with citrons they went out to meet Him. / He received praise from the boys / and hallelujahs from their crowds, / and the angels thundered in heaven / at the wonders of His entry. / In great wonder the Watchers stood / on the day of our Savior's entry, / when they saw Him riding on a colt / and passing through the streets of the city. / The heavenly beings gazed and saw Him, / how humble and calm He was in His gentleness / among the crowds of children:
