and they marveled at His humility. / The angels were amazed at these things, / that He was praised on two sides: / on high by their companies, / and below by children and boys. / So they all were gazing / at His great throne in heaven, / and saw Him in the robe of our body / being praised with hosannas. / He rides the heaven of heavens in His hiddenness; / He rides on a colt in His humanity; / and the authority of His divinity / reigns in the height and in the depth. / In heaven His lightnings bow low, / and on earth the garments and the branches, / as they cry Hosanna to Him, / Watchers and men alike. / Cherubim and seraphim are stirred / to bless Him on high, / and below in the depth children and boys / cry out His praise without fear. / But the daughter of Zion, who saw Him, / envied Him as He was praised, / and wanted His praise to cease / from every mouth and every praiser. / She agreed neither with the heavenly beings / nor with the earthly ones who praised. / She lay in wait [?] on the road of our Savior, / which was full of wonder and amazement. / For the crucifying city toiled greatly / to silence the children, / but because truth filled their mouths, / their voices were not silenced. / The ranks of angels praise / the Son in His holy place, / and in the streets of the daughter of Zion / voices rang out in hosannas. / With the [?] of His praise / He was being praised by the boys, / and they reproached Him: "Why / have You seized praise that was not Yours?" / They rebuked Him over the children, / so that they would desist from His praise, / thinking that if they were silent, / the praise of His honor would depart. / O wicked Jews, / haters of the true light, / how can His praise cease, / of which heaven and earth are full? / Though you restrain disciples and children / in your contentiousness, / behold, He has throngs on high / who praise Him without ceasing: / myriads upon myriads of angels / and thousands upon thousands of seraphim. / Behold, they sanctify Him with their voices, / surrounding the throne of His glory. / Is it then too great a thing / that He be praised by the earthly ones, / for whose sake He put on a body / to redeem them from death? / The discerning heard and marveled / at the insolence of the crucifiers, / how they burned with envy / and hated their Savior without cause, / for His praise from crowds, / from children and little ones. / Listen and hear, you haters of the soul, / and [?] to endure it. / With an evil and bitter heart / they came to Him who brings peace to all, / saying to Him, "Rebuke the children, / for it is not fitting that You be praised like this." / Our Lord answered and said to them, / "Have you never read what is written, / that from the mouth of all the children / the praise of the Lord is perfected? / Order requires that they praise, / all [?]. / And if these, then, are silent, / these stones will cry out." / And so it is in truth, / as our Savior said: / if these crowds were silent,

the stones would speak His praise. / It was a time when it was fitting / for the Son to be praised by all, / and if the children had kept silent, / the stones would have cried out His praise. / If the children and little ones / had not praised with palm branches, / the senseless foundations would have praised / at that hour of His entry. / The Lord of kings humbled Himself / and in His humility rode a colt, / and the crowds were stirred to offer praise / for His humility on our behalf. / The heads of the peoples in Jerusalem, / together with the crowds, were bound / to speak of His praise / at the time He came to them. / And because the priests [?] His praise, / which they were bound to sing, / the children cried out hymns to Him, / their hosannas to the King's Son. / And had the praisers kept silent, / praise would not have ceased there, / for the stones, shaken, would cry to Him, / "Hosanna to the King of kings!" / All creation marveled / at the humility of His coming, / and was stirred to offer praise / with a loud voice in hosannas. / For to those who truly know, / the word our Savior spoke is plain: / that had He commanded, walls / and stones would have cried out the praise of His greatness. / He said it to the one who hated / the demonstration of the truth, / for from what was manifest it was easy for him / to perceive what was hidden. / When He was hung upon the wood / the praisers fell silent, / and stones and rocks cried out the praise / owed to His divinity, / in place of the disciples and children / who did not praise Him as He hung on the wood. / The dead came out of their graves / and gave praise to His honor. / All the natures of creation / do not withhold the praise of our Lord, / for behold, they are stirred to praise / His lordship at all times. / Even from stones and from wood / it is easy for His power to speak, / for at His signal natures are stirred / to cry out the greatness of His praise. / The speaking, with the silent, / behold, sing in their own forms / the praise befitting His honor, / hiddenly in their natures. / At the wonder that took place today / the speaking and the dumb were amazed, / yet His power was not perceived / by the foolish people of the Jews. / One wonder is this: / that our Lord rode on a colt, / He whose lordly praise / the cherubim on high proclaim. / And another wonder is this: / that they went out to meet Him with branches / and did not know why / they were [?] Him. / A third wonder is this, / at which heaven and earth marveled: / that children, infants at the breast, / were crying out to Him with hosannas. / The boys rebuked the priests / and the scribes with their hosannas, / for though they had never yet spoken, / they proclaimed new things with their voices. / With unutterable praises / the crowds praised Him today, / the King who triumphed in battle / against death and Satan. / And today the spirits / praised the Son with the crowds, / for they saw that He humbled Himself / by riding a lowly and humble mount. / And in place of Zion, who hated Him

and would not cling to His love, / behold, all the peoples praise Him / in the holy Church of His love. / The peoples who turned to His knowledge / leap for joy at His holy feasts, / and celebrate His coming / in place of the wicked who did not receive Him, / as they praise Him with their branches, / young men and old men and children, / and in the melodies of the Holy Spirit / they sing praise to His lordship. / Thus the crowds redeemed by the Cross / have come to understand this, / and have learned the mystery of His truth, / which He accomplished today for our sake. / For when He rode on a colt / it was not because He had no steeds, / but to give us a pattern, / that we might become like Him in His humility. / By His riding He set the mirror / of His beauty before our eyes, / so that we might see the blemishes of our conduct / and not be puffed up with empty glory. / For He has invited us to His kingdom / through His coming to us. / He has prepared the wedding garments / so that we may enter His bridal chamber with Him. / Pure garments are required of us / on the great day of His revelation. / Let us clothe ourselves in purity of soul, / that we too may see Him in purity, / and with ceaseless hallelujahs / let us exalt His holy name, / and let us all cry out together: / "Hosanna to You in the highest! / Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who came in the name of the Lord!"
Against the Jews
It is recited at the Feast of Hosannas, and it is / Against the Jews. / Response: / Blessed is the Lord, who from the mouth of boys chose praise / for His honor. My brothers:

Come, Jew, you who pride yourself on bodily names,
reveal and explain to me the reason for your people's election.
Why were you chosen out of all by the God of all,
and honored in name and rank above the nations?
Why were you set apart from the families of the whole world,
and do not mingle with the nations of Adam's children?
Why do you hold yourself aloof like a stranger from the sons of your own kind,
when you are from the same clay of humanity, formed from dust?
One is the nature of Adam's descendants, O son of Adam,
and one the power that fashioned Adam and his offspring.
Nature testifies that there is one nature and one Creator;
and if they are one, why the distinction between the people and the nations?
If one command created everything from nothing,

why do you divide an equal creation without equity?
If the power that created the speaking and the mute is just,
why is his dealing not equal toward his creatures?
Why did he choose you from all peoples and reject the rest,
and why did he make a promise with you and not with everyone?
Why did he bind the course of the spirit of his revelations to your people,
and confine and restrain prophecy within your tribes?
Why did he give the law of life to you alone,
and keep the nations away from the sweetness of his great spring?
Why did he show through you the power of his signs and mighty deeds,
and chastise nations and rebuke kings on your account?
Was it perhaps because your love for him was greater than anyone's,
and for this he paid you a reward worthy of your love?
Or perhaps because he honored his love for Abram's love,
and therefore made you the heir of his great love?
Then let us inquire why he chose Abraham,
and what reason the Hidden One had for loving him in his kindness.
If you say that his love made him beloved of the Hidden One,
lo, his election came before his love, and Moses testifies to it.
The spirit of revelation called him from Babylon before he believed,
and after it had called him he left paganism and honored the truth.
So the boast is not yours, nor your fathers',
for your election belongs to another, who chooses and rejects.
And grant that Abram was chosen because of his love:
lo, there were those who loved, before his election, more than he.
Abel loved and showed his love by deed,
and his murder testifies: it was envy that slew him for his love.
Noah too was pleasing in a hateful generation that had corrupted its way,
and lo, the testimony to the purity of his soul is in the book of Moses.
Melchizedek too served as priest and was exalted before his God,
and, let us note, Abram bowed his head before his blessings.

Lo, there were righteous men, son of Abraham, who were like your father;
why was your father the one with whom the promise was made, and not they?
Why did he promise him that in him the nations of the earth would be blessed,
and yet, as you hold, did not wish to fulfill the promise of his words?
I said this, that he did not wish to fulfill it, according to your way of thinking;
to me it is certain that he has fulfilled it in deeds.
Why did he change his former name and call him by another,
and why did he give him fatherhood over all peoples?
Abram is a father who rules over one people alone,
but the name Abraham is a fatherhood over many.
His first name had no faith in it,
and once he was established in faith he became Abraham.
The Divine Being revealed the meaning of the power of his name,
and by its understanding marked out the path on which the nations would walk.
His faith made him the father of nations;
and what is to be done, since his election came first, in his very name?
I ask you, son of Abraham, about your father's election:
what is it, and why is your race honored above all?
Reveal and explain to me, as one of the household, his election and his name,
and I will grant you that you walk well in his faith.
If the Creator chose him alone out of all who were,
his love is not just, which chooses one and rejects others.
Why did he not choose another righteous man like him,
for [?] the company of the righteous was growing great and wickedness was trembling?
And lo, those who came from the righteous man were not righteous, as this would require;
the wickedness of Abram's sons, alien to Abram, testifies to it.
And grant that he chose him as he did, since he had the authority to do so:
why then did he change his name and call him father of nations?
And if a father truly becomes a father according to his title,
his election and his name are the causes of his fatherhood.

What do you say, son of Abraham, about Abraham?
How is your father a father to you and to the nations?
Then you have nothing more than they in the name of Abraham,
for lo, the nations too are his sons, as it is written.
It was because of the nations that Abraham rose to a high rank;
so it is plain that the nations were the cause of his greatness.
Come then, son of Abraham, praise the nations, your brothers,
for had they not been sons to your father, he would not have been great.
Small would that father be, however much you might say,
just as his people is small among all the peoples.
Had his fatherhood been confined to one people alone,
his name would not have matched the deed after which it was named.
Small too would have been the authority of the Lord who chose him,
and even the gods would have had more dominion than he.
And if only Abraham's children had been children to Him,
the fatherhood would have been turned over to the pagan nations.
If the Creator had ruled only over his own offspring,
mute idols would have despised his lordship.
A small portion of what was his would have been given to him,
and voiceless things would have been called lords.
To the nations a host of gods without number,
and to the God of all a small people, despised and enslaved!
No, son of Abram, do not belittle the Maker of all,
for the nations who reject your contentiousness are his.
Your father's election shuts the door in the face of your words,
for whoever is a son of Abraham is a son of God.
You have gained nothing more than anyone else in the name of the Creator,
and you have no authority to shut the door in the face of the nations.
They are your brothers, O circumcised one who pride yourself on the seal of the flesh;
why do you not consent to the brotherhood of the house of Abraham?
By the name of his own Being the Creator swore to your father and theirs
that in you the nations would be blessed and become sons of your inheritance.
Is the word he swore by himself true or not true?
Have they been blessed, or is it perhaps still to come?
If it has happened, lo, the nations have become sons of his inheritance;
and if it has not yet happened, it is going to happen—and what will you do?
Affirm that it has happened, and the books testify that their words are true;

and if it has not happened, then the truth in them is false.
The nations have not become sons of Abraham, as you say?
Then why does Abraham love them better than you?
Were they not blessed by that heavenly voice, 'In you shall they be blessed'?
And why have they gone in while you have gone out?
Who turned the dullness of their hearts away from error,
and made known to them the plain truth of the name of the Creator?
Who laid on their necks the yoke of peace,
and yoked them under the lordship of Abram's Lord?
Who became their counselor, counseling them to hate the Evil One,
and planted in their hearts the good meditation of faith?
Who occupied their thoughts with the meditation of love,
and took from them the hateful bitterness of idolatry?
Who beat out for them the fair road of the body's resurrection,
and taught them to walk in the hope of the kingdom on high?
Who tore up the edifice of falsehood that error had built,
and swept away the temples that demons had adorned for their pleasures?
Who revealed to them that one Creator created all things,
and received and fulfilled the writings of the words of his mouth?
Who wrote for them a new book that they did not know,
and lo, they meditate on spiritual things night and day?
What power fortified the world in its nakedness,
and brought it in and shut it within the fortresses of the word of peace?
Who subdued the four quarters by the name of one man,
and lo, instead of tribute they raise to him a voice of thanksgiving?
Who yoked the West with the yoke of the name of Jesus,
and lo, it yields him fruits of praise without being sated?
Who planted in the East the plants of faith,
so that it no longer runs shamelessly after paganism?
Who bound the harsh North with the fortresses of love,
so that it no longer wages the war of wickedness against righteousness?
Who sowed good seed in the barren South,
and lo, its bosom bears fruits of praise to the One who restored it?

Who abolished the borrowed names of those that are no gods,
and established on earth the precious name of the Divine Being?
Where are the mute idols that the demons fashioned?
Lo, they have vanished, and their memory has ceased from human lips.
Why have you too turned your mind away from them,
and no longer sacrifice your sons and daughters as before?
Why are you idle, and pour no libations on the high places,
when there was no time at which the righteous did not recount accusations against you?
At what time did you ever leave off the sacrifices of idolatry,
as now you have refrained, out of zeal against the nations?
Your zeal is foolish, and it is not out of goodness that you have refrained from sacrifices;
or else show when you ever remained without libations.
The murder you committed has restrained you from error against your will,
and lo, it has turned the uncircumcised nations, to your shame.
But speak, if you have the strength to speak:
what is this, that error has ceased and he is victorious?
Who cast such zeal on the earth among mankind,
that they choose death and hate life for the one whom you killed?
How could a crucified man win over creation,
and who taught creation itself to listen to his words?
How did he subdue the world, when his power lay in lowliness,
and as for the world, who persuaded it not to [?]?
With what weapon did he wage war against all the powers,
for lo, he possessed no visible weapon such as earthly men have?
How could despised laborers who followed him
wage war against paganism and Judaism?
I ask you, son of Abraham, about the son of your race:
how did he do battle with weakness against hardship?
It was the son of your race who did these things I am telling you,
and the words of prophecy testify that they were fulfilled in him.
Is he of your race or not, O Jew?
Did you crucify him in Judah, or did you not crucify him? Reveal and explain to me.
And if he is, from whom does he come, and what is his lineage,
and what is the reason for his crucifixion and for his preaching?
That he is, heaven and earth testify, which tell his glory,
so that you cannot deny it and say his preaching is untrue.

If he is, this is what I asked you, and I ask again:
by what power was he able to overcome creation, when he was himself a creature?
And if, on the other hand, he is not, this too I ask you:
how did his name conquer creation when he does not exist?
How can one say so when there is nothing at all to him,
and how can one confirm that everyone believes in nothing?
What is this, that the nations have abandoned their gods
and swear by the name of a man who, as you say, does not exist?
If he was a deceiver, and you crucified him as one who went astray and led others astray,
how, once dead, did he by his death lead astray those who know him?
And grant that he went astray, as you say—God forbid that he went astray—
who would believe that a deceiver, and a dead man, could lead everyone astray?
Many have gone astray and led many astray in their names,
and after a time the masters and their disciples came to nothing.
His 'error'—it is more or less five hundred years now—
grows great and gains strength in every region.
Who ever led others astray and had his falsehood stand as his has?
And who seized the name of the Creator and was not exposed?
There is no teaching that has endured on earth like his teaching,
nor any discipleship that has borne increase like his discipleship.
Not even Moses, who set down the law from the mouth of the Hidden One,
was able to bring rebellious nations under his commandments.
People did not worship the name of Moses or his writings,
nor did they adorn temples for him on earth as they did for Jesus.
And lo, the Lord called him a god among earthly beings,
yet none among creatures called him by the name by which he was named.
Lo, he shone, and people could not look upon him,
and though he was very great, no one says 'Glory to Moses.'
The glory of great Moses has ceased, son of Abraham,
and there is no one who praises the carnal observances.
But let every Jew who has something to say, say it:
where is Moses, and who among mankind has fulfilled his commandments?
Show openly, Israelite, the glory of Moses,

as the nations show the glory of the man you crucified.
That Moses is great I confess more than you do,
but he is immeasurably less than the name of Jesus.
Less than Jesus—and again I say, much less—
not in nature, but in divine rank.
That he is greater than Moses, the course of his preaching testifies,
which has outrun the sun and the moon in its swiftness.
Lo, in every region the voice of his preaching thunders,
and all tongues, every one of them, weave the crown of his victory.
Lo, the Greeks race toward the goal of his crucifixion,
and even barbarians bear the yoke of his faith.
And if you will not see with the visible senses,
stretch your mind to the four quarters and see his power.
See how all tongues cry glory to his name
and offer him the gifts of their minds' love.
Come then, O Jew, compare mine with yours,
and show whether there is power in your words as there is in mine.
Without contention let us look into the case that lies between us,
and let whoever is guilty concede to whoever is innocent.
Which are your books? Let us argue from them, one against the other,
and let every word of mine and of yours stand upon what they say.
I will grant you whatever you say from the Scriptures,
and I do not reject the words of the spirit of prophecy.
Let Moses come, the firstborn of the divine scribes,
and let us inquire among his signs into the case of this one who has come.
What do you say, Moses, great in spiritual things?
Reveal and explain to me the force of the meaning within your books.
'A great prophet like me will arise from among mortals,
and much greater than I, as high as heaven is above us.
He is a great prophet, and his rank is greater than the prophets',
and everyone must serve him as Lord.'
Is Moses truthful or not, son of Abraham?
Has his word been fulfilled, or does a time remain for it to be fulfilled?
Has the prophet who is written of arisen from your people, or not yet?
Has it come to pass in deed, or do you say it is yet to come?
If it has not come to pass, and you suppose it is yet to come,

who is this who has come and led both you and the nations astray?
For it was not only the nations he led astray, but you too.
You first did this one lead astray, who came and whom you killed,
and twelve voices testify that it was from you that they turned.
Moses wrote that a great prophet would arise from you,
and that in him the nations would be blessed and become sons of Abraham.
'By myself I have sworn,' the Lord said to righteous Abram,
'that in you the uncircumcised nations shall be blessed and become your seed.'
Who is this who has blessed the nations in the name of Abraham,
and how did the words come to pass and issue in deeds?
If it is not he whose story great Moses wrote,
how is it that what has been done resembles what is written?
All the nations cry out together that this is the one who came,
and to whom shall we listen—to you alone, or to creation?
All creation testifies, by receiving him, that he has come,
and you alone do not assent to the words of your own books.
But reveal to me, as one of the household, when he is to come,
and what is the time when the nations become Abram's brothers.
And grant that he is still to come: when he comes and the nations enter,
why have you, who are of the household, gone out of your inheritance?
Why are you rejected like something putrid, lo, for so long,
and priest and king and interpreter have ceased from you?
Why have you been scattered to the four quarters, as if in wrath,
while nations goad you with toil and kings with tributes?
Why does no prophet arise from among you as before,
to explain to you the reason for this servitude?
There was never a time when the voice of explanation ceased from you,
neither when you were in your land nor when the nations led you captive.
In Egypt there was Moses, in the land of Canaan Joshua son of Nun,
and among the Babylonians one a king's son and one a priest's son.
Nor did the spiritual ones ever cease or grow slack in helping you,
until this one came whom you killed, and he restrained them.
Why does that angel not carry off the firstborn
and avenge your humiliation as he did in the land of Egypt?
Why does Michael too not do battle with your enemies

as he did battle with the prince of the kingdom of Persia?
Where is the love of the heavenly beings that was with your fathers,
that they do not help you as they helped generation after generation?
There was never a time when they fell silent and were still as at this time,
nor did your scattering among the nations last so long.
Lo, it is five hundred years less a little that you have been rejected and cast out,
and the longer it lasts, the further it stretches over you.
And if you say that your punishment lasts long because of your wickedness,
lo, your wickedness is no greater now than before.
Compare and see that your wickedness is less than before,
and your sin lighter than what you committed in earlier generations.
In the wilderness you provoked him with the worship of the calf and with the daughters of Moab,
and in the land of Canaan you went astray and ran mad after stones and wood.
For all your afflictions there was healing, and mercy pitied you,
but this affliction has lasted with you beyond all measure.
And lo, you are not sick with the fear of demons as before,
nor do you sacrifice the fruit of your womb to unclean demons.
Your affliction has lasted long, and still there is no remedy for your wounds;
or else show when you ever remained without healing.
In Egypt for two hundred years and more you lay in fever,
and Moses came and drove toil and wickedness away from you.
In Babylon for seventy years you were sunk as if in mire,
and Daniel arose and prayed, and you went up according to the promise.
In every region your people found physicians,
and the medicine of the Spirit was never withheld from among your people.
In this time, why is there no physician to bind up your wounds,
nor any interpreter to comfort you in your sickness?
Perhaps you will cite the scripture whose time has passed,
that priest and king and the one who applies remedies shall cease from you;
and lo, this was fulfilled in Babylon, and your orders ceased,
and you returned and went up in the days of Cyrus with great pomp.
In the days of Cyrus, and under Zerubbabel, you went up, as it is written;
or do you deny this too, as you are accustomed to do?
Then Zechariah and Haggai lied, and Malachi too,

and perhaps Jeremiah too composed a fabrication,
and Ezekiel saw shadows that were not true.
Then Daniel did not go down to the land of the Babylonians,
nor did he pray and win, at the end of the seventy years, the return.
Did you return or not? Answer me as I asked you.
Did the Lord stretch out his hand a second time, or will he yet do so again?
A second time is written, that the Lord would add; there was no third.
Whom shall we believe—prophecy or the deniers?
This is the custom of Judaism: to deny in this way,
and to wrong the voices of prophecy out of contentiousness.
You are ever accustomed to deny, son of Abraham,
and the calf testifies that when you clung to it you called it god.
By the power of God Moses redeemed you from Egypt,
and you ascribed that redemption to molten gold.
And perhaps you did not cling to it as to God?
Why then did Moses test you in the crucible of water?
And perhaps you will say that lo, the nations too do this,
and sully the name of Jesus by their deeds.
I accept from you the point you cleverly turn about,
and I counsel you to listen to my words with discernment.
It is not because you sinned that I have spoken, or speak, against your people,
but because you deny against the light, as though it did not shine.
But show me what is hidden in our teaching,
which heaven and earth justify, and which you deny.
On this second point I have counted out your offenses from Scripture,
to show you your contentiousness against the truth.
You are contentious and are not persuaded by those who instruct you,
and the righteous testify that you slaughtered them because they reproved you.
You fight against the things revealed in the books,
and will not accept the truth that is in them.
You returned from Babylon, and this is clearer than the sun,
and when they reprove you, you [?] and say, 'I did not go up.'
If you did return, why do you stubbornly deny it?
But who built you a house in the land of Judah?
Zechariah and Haggai will rebuke the stubbornness of your contentiousness.

who set their hand to the writings of the day of your return. / With just judgment Daniel too will enter into judgment with you, / who showed you beforehand the mystery of the coming of the King you rejected. / By the spirit of revelation he counted weeks and set them in order, / and at their end he portrayed His passion as in an image. / Tell me: is the destruction of your city written as bound to His killing, or not? / Then it is plain that, if it has not been destroyed, it is yet to be destroyed. / If the one you killed was not He, His killing still lies ahead, / and you will kill Him, and He will destroy the temple of your sanctuary. / Prophecy did not force your will, / so that whether you wished it or not you would kill your King. / It did not foretell your zeal so that you would kill your Liberator, / but to lay bare the wickedness of your heart, which rushes after blood. / It saw you with a hidden eye, that you are bent on blood, / and drew your evil plot in advance on the page of the books. / It is not I who have called you the killer of your King, son of Abraham; / your prophets cry out like trumpets about the day of His killing. / Jacob your father saw in Judah the suffering of His death, / and his visionary eye saw His blood as like the wine of the vine. / The son of Jesse too saw the fierce crowd gathered against Him, / and pronounced a sentence full of wrath upon His killers. / Isaiah marveled at His lowliness and His slaughter: / that He bore it and kept silent and did not open His mouth in the hour of suffering. / Zechariah saw Him dyed in the blood of His covenant, / setting the prisoners free from the waterless pit. / Are these your prophets, whom you recite, or perhaps not? / Did they speak by the Spirit, or from what their own minds devised? / If they are true, grant the truth of their words; / or else say that they are not true, and let the dispute end. / Either recite with me from their books and I will answer you, / or show me, and I will give way to your words. / I assent to all the voices of prophecy, / and I do not turn away from the meaning of their words. / From them I learned to confess the King who dawned from you,

and they showed me how to walk in the way of faith in Him. / If your heralds revealed to me the mystery that was among you, / why do you envy me for becoming a member of your household? / It was not I who chose to be a fellow heir with you; / they gave me a portion with you. Why does it grieve you? / Your King redeemed me from bondage to the Evil One and to death, / and His love brought me under His lordship. With whom are you quarreling? / He came to His own, and His own did not want to receive Him; / and when He saw that they scorned Him, He chose your people instead and rejected His own. / Did He come to you or not? Speak the truth. / Did He choose the nations or not? Tell it as it is. / If it was not He who came to you, who is it you set aside? / And if He did not choose the nations in your place, why do they confess Him? / That He came is plain, and there is no light brighter than this; / and that He chose the nations, the nations and their gods bear witness. / The nations that received Him confess that He came, and you deny it; / their gods surrendered to Him, and you run away. / What do you say about the worshipers and the worshiped, / when even the hosts of heavenly beings tell His praise? / The speaking and the mute tell of Him, by voice and by silence, / and you alone have shut your mouth to His praise. / Evil envy has blinded the eye of your discernment, / and you do not want to see the light of the greatness of His glory. / The wickedness of your will has made you blind beyond consolation, / and though you see, you do not see even what is ordinary. / Had you perceived that you are a stranger to these blessings, / you would already be calling on heaven and earth to weep for you. / Had you been persuaded of the judgment kept in store for your insolence, / you would be weeping night and day and would never cease. / The blessings are hidden from you, and the punishments from your mind; / you see neither the things that are present nor those to come. / Who, then, is blind and deaf in a stupor like yours? / For you are reckless and heedless, and do not perceive why. / You have become a stranger to the heavenly and the earthly,

and cities and people shun you, and you are not ashamed. / You are thrown out like dung, and everyone tramples on your head, / and you do not ask what the cause of your soul's disgrace is. / The way of the heavenly ones to you has been cut off, / and you do not discern why they have abandoned your service. / Divine revelations have ceased from your heralds, / and there is no one to bring a remedy to your pains, not even with bread. / If only you knew to inquire into the greatness of your fall, / and would sigh over your lawless death! / If only you saw the hatefulness of your soul, how loathsome you are, / and would refrain even a little from your hateful deeds! / If only you listened to the voice of reproof from your teachers, / and opened your mind so that the word of life might enter you! / If only you looked into the hidden things within the books, / and saw that their power was fulfilled in this One whom you crucified! / His Crucified One has swept you away from the dominion of your high rank, / and rejected you and cast you out from the inheritance of your fathers' house. / His death, which is the cause of life for the dead and the living, / has prepared for you strangling and bitter blows. / You are destined to enter into bitter blows on the day of testing, / before that King whom you judged cruelly on earth. / Without pity He will lash blows upon your wickedness, / not because you killed, but because you wronged His preaching. / With just judgment He will require at your hands vengeance for His servants, / whom He sent to you after His killing, and you did not listen to them. / Through them He punishes the great wrong that you committed, / and exposes you before the eyes of angels and of men. / Response: Blessed is He who uprooted Zion the crucifier, / and planted the faithful Church within her borders.
On the Canaanite Woman

Memra for Tuesday, on the Canaanite woman.
Response: Blessed is he who brought back our captivity from the Hater / through a son of our race, who conquered and made us conquerors.
My brothers…

The Hater of mankind wronged mankind unjustly, / and corrupted the image that had been called by the name of the Divine Being.
The slayer of men was drunk with envy against mankind, / and he clouded them with the hateful smoke of his bitterness.
The rebel put on the zeal of wrath against mankind, / because earthly beings were called by the name of the Divine Being.
The slayer of men was drunk with envy against mankind, / and he clouded them with the hateful smoke of his bitterness.
The rebel put on the zeal of wrath against mankind, / because earthly beings were called by the name of the Divine Being.
With the armour of cunning he armed himself to destroy them, / and with his crafts he whetted his sword to devour their blood.
In every guise he made himself ready for battle, / to sate the urge of his bitterness through their deaths.
He contrived crafty stratagems against their lives; / he dug deep and hid the snares of death to kill them.
The net of iniquity he wove skilfully in his thoughts, / so that it might catch the prey of mankind into his bosom.
Over sea and dry land he spread his thoughts like nets, / and he hunted all the peoples and made them food for death.
Through them he fought against their own lives while they did not perceive it, / and he sent them out as spies and hunted their companions.
By their hands he engaged their ranks and overpowered them, / and with the swords of their own thoughts he trampled them.
He cast the strife of his warfare into their thoughts, / and urged them to fight one another.
They destroyed one another like strangers and did not discern, / and trampled the bodies of their own members as though they were not human.
He taught them the kinds of warfare that belong to his bitterness, / and made them skilled in how to wage it without mercy.
A crafty book he wrote upon the tablet of their minds, / so that they would read wickedly, according to his will.
He saw that they were eager to meditate on his writings, / and he set himself to consume them shamelessly.
He dwelt among them and lived with them, and they took pleasure in him; / and while they loved him dearly, he hated them and overthrew them.
It was not out of love that he loved the company of earthly beings, / but to trouble the peace that was in them through his company.
In the guise of love he furnished them with what was not truth, / and with flatteries he darkened them in the confusion of his words.
Demons ran riot and made sport of men, and men of demons, / and the world, sea and dry land, reeled as in drunkenness.
The Creator saw that the evil one had troubled the peace of mankind, / and he sent his sign to bring man back to the peace of his name.
He sent his sign by an embodied messenger, / that through him he might interpret the word of peace to humanity.
On the parchment of the body he wrote it, at the will of his love, / so that embodied beings might see the hidden openly.
With visible members his will was girded, / and it came to them to teach them to drive back their hunter.
He composed a body with writings, like a letter, / and set on it the hand of the power of his hiddenness, and sealed it with his name.
He taught the body, that in it might be read the mystery of hidden things,

and that it might interpret to its fellows the meaning of the mysteries.
Like a commander of an army he armed him and sent him against the evil one, / so that by his victory his race might obtain release[?] from their debts.
The Embodied One went forth with the divine will, / and raised his hidden voice openly, and the demons trembled.
The rebels heard a new voice crying out in a body, / and they shook and were dismayed at the newness of a voice they were not used to.
The power of the Divine Being shone out in creation through the mouth of a mortal, / and the ranks of the evil one's hosts trembled, and insolent Death.
The sound of the name of Jesus resounded on the earth like thunder, / and the demons howled, for they could not bear the greatness of his voice.
By his voice alone he shook those full of arrogance, / and against their will they began to move out of their dwellings.
The sound of his name was heard by Legion, the head of their ranks, / and groaning seized him, and he howled and wept bitterly.
The fame of the name of Jesus went out to every region, / and peoples and city-dwellers gathered to hear his word.
A hidden sign gathered them to the harbour of his love, / that they might come and bring their minds into subjection to the peace of his name.
They heard that by his word he drives out demons and heals pains, / and from every side they longed to receive medicine for their sicknesses.
A woman went out whose daughter a demon inhabited, / to ask him for the spirit's medicine for the pain the demon caused.
Her thoughts, together with her members, were girded to follow Jesus, / and her movements and senses began to incline toward the goal of his name.
Who, then, taught the daughter of Canaan, the slave of slaves, / to go out and ask freedom of soul from the son of Abraham?
Who revealed to the Canaanite woman, daughter of accursed Ham, / that the son of Shem can loose the seal set by the righteous one?
Who made known to the servant of demons, whom demons had defiled, / that at the voice of Jesus demons move out of their dwellings?
Who wrote for her a new book of the name of the Creator, / for a soul grown old in the company of demons who hate the truth?
Who showed her who daily beheld the gate of demons / that she should walk in the way of faith in the one God?
A hidden sign signalled to her mind mystically: / “Despise the worship of idols, and believe, and live.”
That sign girded her with faith as with armour, / that she might go out and engage the rebel who had taken her daughter captive.
With faith and hope and love she girded her soul, / and as with a sword she cut off the evil one by the word of her mouth.
Faith clothed her mind like a breastplate, / and she held hope like a shield in the hand of her movements.
Toward the goal of love her thoughts, with her members, inclined, / and she went up and stood—stood—on the lofty step that bears the name of the pure.
With hidden armour she armed her soul spiritually, / that she might be able to join the hidden battle with the hosts of the evil one.
She knew that the Hater of mankind who fought with her was hidden, / and she prepared spiritual armour to match his hiddenness.
In secret she forged faith within her mind,

and gained strength to fight with the strong one.
With faith her members were girded to follow her will, / and her senses and movements raised their voice to ask for mercy.
Mouth and mind together, with a humble voice, / took on the boldness of faith that cannot be defeated.
Like a trumpet the mind cried out through the outward senses, / and the mouth announced the grief of the inward sufferings.
The mouth became their advocate for their movements before the Judge, / and the mute faculties, in place of speaking ones, uttered choked cries.
The daughter of the accursed cried out like thunder before the son of the righteous: / “Have pity, Son of David, and free my servitude from captivity.
Have mercy, son of Abraham; rouse your love toward the daughter of Canaan, / and redeem my life from the bondage of servitude to the evil one.
The father of our fathers cursed my fathers with a hidden mouth, / and bound them with a harsh yoke of slander.
Noah cursed our father, who mocked and scorned insolently, / and blessed our fathers, who honoured him and wisely covered him.
As with a rod the righteous one chastised the arrogant of heart, / and see, the scourge strikes his offspring until now.
Has not our boldness been swallowed up by the scourges of our father, / so that we have become slaves to a slave who rebels against the Maker?
Does not the tyrant of iniquity enslave the freedom of our soul, / and scorn our [?] against the right order of human nature?
But if the seed of insolent Ham is bound to servitude, / let them be slaves to the son of righteous Shem, and not to the tyrant.
Even righteous Noah interpreted it so in his prophecy: / that Canaan should serve Shem in servitude, as a lord.
To you, then, falls the debt of love, as one who owes it, / for you are of that seed in which the freedom of mankind is inscribed.
You are the Son of David and the son of Abraham, son of Shem, son of Noah: / free your servants from the cruel one, and they will be yours.
I have heard of living testimonies that David your father received; / seal his words with deeds, as is fitting.
The divine sign has sent you for the peace of mankind; / complete it with deeds—come, show it toward us on our side[?].
I heard your fame, that it went out in the land and the rebels trembled, / and I went out to see the truth openly by experience.
I heard that in the name of your authority men drive out demons, / and I came to take the good news of your name and bring it to the demons.
A tyrant demon has entered and hidden himself in the soul of my daughter, / and strives in torment to loose her life from life.
Without pity he crushes her body and distracts her soul, / and unless your commands drive him away, her life will come to an end.
Send your sign swiftly, like a messenger, / and the demon will be restrained before he strives to shed blood.
Give me the seal of your authority and I will show it to him, / and see, he will be dismayed like a woman in labour seized by her pangs.
Write a letter and set on it the hand of the power of your help, / and if he sees it, he will no longer dare to defy your commands.”
With a choked voice the daughter of Canaan was pleading,

and the All-Knowing kept silent toward her as though he did not hear.
At the boldness of her voice the disciples marvelled at how she persisted in asking, / and they came and urged the Physician to free her by the power of his help:
“Give her the medicine of your word, as she demands, / and let her go and heal the pain of the demon that torments her daughter.”
The Master turned wisely to his disciples: / “I was sent only to heal the sons of Jacob.
For the lost sheep of Israel I went out to search, / that they might return and enter the fold of life of the name of the Creator.
For it is not fitting to give the bread of the freeborn children / to Canaanites, shameless dogs who have not had their fill of iniquity.”
The daughter of Ham heard that the master of the house called her a dog, / and she took hope that she too might live in the rank of the dogs.
The ewe saw the Lord of the flocks who visits his sheep, / and she pressed to enter the fold of his sweet words.
She saw that even dogs seek food, like the heirs, / and wisely she asked for nourishment from the master of the house:
“Yes,” she said, “it is so, and you have spoken well, good Lord, / for I am a dog and not worthy of the name of heirs.
Yes, freedom of soul belongs to the freeborn children, / and to us belong the sinners too, the dogs of peace[?].
Give nourishment to the freeborn children, as they deserve, / and let the dogs live on the crumbs from their tables.
Grant me by your help to live in the rank of the dogs, / just as you give life to mute natures along with speaking ones.
Grant me to be worthy of a small crumb from your good things, / for there is nothing among created things that does not live from the treasure of your love.
Grant me to receive, with the dumb creatures, what my life needs, / and I will live by grace, like all the creatures your sign nourishes.”
O wisdom, which made fruitful a heart that had strayed in error, / so that it learned, and taught, how to speak wisely!
O knowledge, which a mind occupied with sin recounted, / and instead of falsehood spoke truth before the All-Knowing!
O mind grown old on earth in the service of iniquity, / which loved the company of spiritual beings it had never seen!
It was not that he saw her for the first time and marvelled at her as one who did not know her, / for her faith was visible to him before she spoke.
He was watching her until she should compose the cry of entreaty, / and he heeded the words of her mouth, and they thrust back her captors.
He was willing to heal her daughter's pain with the medicine of his sign, / and it was plain to him that he would drive out the demon by the power of his help.
It was not to test her that he treated the woman so[?], nor that he did not heed her words: / he wished to show the truth of his love to those who did not know.
It was not out of contempt that he spurned her and drove her from his pasture, / the lamb that bleated after the love of the Shepherd of all.
It was not as one grudging the healing that he held back and kept silent, / but to give men boldness to ask for mercy.
Through her boldness he also taught that everyone should be bold in seeking his help, / and not grow slack if he does not receive it quickly.
Through his delay he provoked to jealousy, by grace, the circumcised people,

which boasted of belonging to the household of the name of the Creator.
He shut the door in the face of the murmuring of the rebellious, / lest they say: “Look, he has turned away the sons of Abraham and visited the heathen.”
He was searching the hateful seed of their thoughts, / and he forestalled its root before it could sprout and bear fruit.
It was clear to him that if he answered the daughter of Canaan, / they would quarrel with him: “Why has he taken pity on the servant of demons?”
He knew of the woman that her love was true, / and that she would be healed even if he delayed and did not answer her.
For this reason his sign did not answer her quickly, / so that her sincerity might be revealed and he might rebuke the arrogance of the hard of heart.
The sound of her words pleased him more than other voices[?], / and he was waiting for her to sing yet more choked cries.
By his delay he stirred up the well-tuned heart / to strike yet more, on the lyre of the mouth, the strain of its petition.
Through her petition he provoked the People to jealousy and taught the peoples / to see the light of faith in the daughter of darkness.
Through her petition he provoked the People to jealousy and taught the peoples / to see the light of faith in the daughter of darkness.
She was of the people whom demons had robbed of consolation, / and she [?] her hunters, and gladdened with her light those in darkness.
Like a torch her mouth blazed with the truths of her soul, / and outshone the sphere of the sun in its brightness.
Like a herald her voice rang in the ears of everyone: / “Come, all who are in need, compose your cries and receive help.”
The master of the house saw that she was eager to live, and she lived, / and he made her voice a guide toward reward.
By the word of his mouth he revealed the reward of the things to come: / that thus he enriches the one who asks without ceasing.
“O woman,” he said, “great indeed is your faith, / and the whole world cannot compare with the truth of your love.
Your mind has gained great strength against the evil one, / and you are not overpowered by the strong one who fights against you.
Wise is your heart and skilful your nature in fighting, / and no one knows how to wage war better than you.
Subtle is your thought and skilled your mind to discern well, / and there is no bird so light of wing as your movements.
There is no athlete who knows how to wage war like you, / nor a bow that bends toward the mark like your strength.
Because your love was strong and its pleading did not slacken, / see, I pay the wage for the labours of your faith.
Because you persisted and knocked at the door of divine mercy, / see, I open the door to your voice: enter and take your delight.
Because you counted yourself, a perceiving nature, in the pack of dogs, / see, I hold out the crumb of mercy to your hunger.
Because your mind discerned wisely and called me Lord, / see, I write you down, no longer as a stranger[?], under the name of heirs.
Because you loved and longed to be a lamb in the fold of my sheep, / see, I set the seal of my lordship upon your mind.
Because you believed and trusted that my help suffices to drive out demons, / see, I seal with deeds the truth of your soul.
See, I write the power of hidden help in my words,

and I seal it with the hidden sign and give it to you.
Go, show the demon the seal of my person, / and see, he will be dismayed, leave his armour, and flee naked.
Go, tell him that Jesus has said: ‘Go out of your dwelling, / and go, be tormented in the desert, far from humankind.’
Go, announce to him his fall, he who casts mankind down, / for see, the height of the building he built on earth is torn down.
Go, explain to him the power of the meaning of my precious name: / that the name of Jesus saves mankind and overthrows the wolves.
Go, tell him: ‘See, the King has gone out after what is his own, / to bring back the captivity: give an account of those you have destroyed!’
Take up a shield on which the divine hand has been laid, / and go, show him that his authority over the tyrant slave is ended.
And if it is true, and the power of my words does not lie, / see, the words have already been joined to deeds, even at a distance.
See, the demon has gone out before he could see the truth openly, / and has left his dwelling like a fugitive before the strong one.
Go, test the truth of my words by experience, / and receive proof of the greatness of the power of my authority, as is fitting.
See, my will has pronounced sentence on his wickedness, / and he has begun to scourge himself in madness.
See, he has heard the report that I am at war with his rebellion, / and he cried out and howled before the dreadful scourge reached him.
See, the body that he crushed in his bitterness is at rest, / and the mind that he distracted in his warfare is restored.”
The King from afar declared war on the rebel, / and cast him down ahead of the bearer of the writings.
While the messenger was waiting for the King to set his hand, / the crafty one fled, lest his lie be exposed openly.
Who, then, taught the evil demon the manifest truth, / so that while the judges were still far off he condemned himself?
Who revealed to the cunning one all his schemes, / so that he hid himself from disgrace in the sight of everyone?
Who made known to the crafty wolf, destroyer of mankind, / that the Son of David had gone out to hunt him, as his father did?
Who showed the cunning fox the path of the lion, / so that he trembled at the gate lest he be undone by the strength of his voice?
A dreadful sign shook his heart and weakened his strength; / terror seized him, and he left the inhabited land and loved the waste[?].
His mouth was full of weeping and wailing as he went out, / for he saw that harsh exile was being sent against him.
In the dwelling of man he had delighted in his shameful deeds, / and when he saw that they were driving him out, he grieved and concluded there was no consolation.
He saw that the daughter of Ham the slave had been freed from her slavery, / and he knew that the yoke of his toil had been lifted from mortals.
In the Canaanite woman he learned the proof of the greatness of his disgrace: / if the daughter of the accursed has broken his yoke, who will reckon him anything?
Great was the groaning that seized the evil one at this deed,

for a weak rib had defeated his crafts and trampled his arrogance.
Great is the wonder that she too [?] by strength, / and waged war with the strong one and was not defeated.
The daughter of Ham fought a great contest with the rebel, / and like arrows she shot words of faith at him.
O strong one, overpowered by the voice he took pride in / when he fashioned the sound of his melodies in Paradise!
O mighty one, cast down from the might that had won him victory in Eden, / and bound by the very hands he had bound with the eating of the fruit!
By the eating of the fruit he bound Eve, who listened to his word, / and in turn the Fruit from her members [trod] his head into the earth[?].
By the armour of the fruit the guilty one won and made Adam guilty, / and through the Son of Adam he was condemned, and it was shown that he was not the victor.
On the lyre of Eve he sang his melodies of the bitterness of death, / and through the daughter of Eve he heard the good news of the abolition of death.
In Eden he composed eloquent songs like a victor, / and here he howled laments like one condemned.
With bitter suffering he groaned when he heard / everyone call Mary blessed, who bore the Fruit.
He mourned himself as for the dead[?], Mary's [?], / as he fled from the echo of the name of the Son of David.
He heard the woman's voice as she cried out after Jesus: / “Son of David, deliver the daughter of your house from the strong one.”
Fitting was her voice as she asked mercy for her daughter; / it weighed heavily[?] on Satan, the hater of mankind.
At the sound of her laments the hosts of the height marvelled, / and the herd of demons was saddened and mourned, cast out of their ranks.
As often as the name of Jesus came again to the tip of her tongue, / the wretched demon was bitterly embittered.
As boldly as she pleaded for help, / so the demon groaned and wept over his fall.
O humble woman, who gained strength to overpower demons, / so that the oppressors of mankind trembled with quaking at her voice!
O enslaved woman, who had been bound in the service of error, / and who freed herself from servitude to a cruel master!
O huntress, whose soul's dwelling the demons had laid waste, / and whose voice brought peace to her daughter's temple, which they were overthrowing!
O merciful mother, how great is your love, / that you put on armour against the evil one who took your daughter captive!
O woman, who by the sacrifice of your faith / pleased the King and brought back your captive from captivity!
O how you believed, how you loved, and how you endured, / and the strength of your soul did not slacken from trust!
O nature, how well it kept the rule of its bond, / that it turned back and repaid the love that befits human nature!
Nature goaded the Canaanite woman like anguish, / and she suffered greatly over her beloved daughter, whom the demon crushed.
The crafty spectator[?] tormented her daughter with the anguish of his cunning, / and his bitterness flew into her daughter's soul and mind.
She counted her own suffering as the suffering of her daughter's members,

and she was not consoled until the Hater had moved off to the desert.
In great mourning she sat as if over the dead, / so long as the rebel raised his voice in her daughter's temple.
Weeping and wailing filled her mouth at all times; / she kept hearing the deranged cries of the demon's babbling.
With bitter suffering she was tormented night and day, / as she saw the wasting of the body and the confusion of the soul.
Her mouth did not cease from bitter lamentations / until her daughter's body was at rest and her members at peace.
The flow of tears from her eyes and her thoughts did not stop / until she saw that the spring of the evil one's bitterness had dried up.
She did not strip the armour of mourning from her mind / until she heard the report that the demon had gone out.
She did not think she was in the house of the living, though she was alive, / until the voice of Jesus raised her as if from the grave.
By his voice he raised her from grief and from the mouth of the demon, / and she came back and saw the life of time and the life without end.
He cast the medicine of life into her soul like seed, / and the fruit of faith blossomed within her mind.
She came alive from the death of the demon's ruin, she and her daughter, / and put on the garment of faith that does not wear out.
Two benefits the ewe gained by her faith: / the expulsion of the demon, and a place in the household of the name of the Creator.
Through the rod of the demon that scourged her daughter she gained comfort, / and learned the way to walk on the road that leads to the Hidden One.
To the demon, too, a doubled pain was added, / for while he thought he was the chastiser, he was himself scourged in turn.
Into the pit he had dug the rebel fell without knowing it, / and his cunning in turn came down on his own head, as it is written.
He sought to make his own dwelling secure and to destroy man, / but the sign overthrew the building he had raised and made man secure.
In the smoke of his wrath he wished to embitter the sweetness of peace, / but peace wiped his bitterness away from mortals.
As with wine he made them drunk with his warfare, / but since [man] was given the drink of the Spirit, his gall [ran dry][?].
Like slaves he was enslaving the earthly ones, / and one of them arose and freed them from his slavery.
As if they were the despised, he mocked the children of the earth, / and one embodied raised his voice, and he trembled before him.
He had been confident and at ease in the dwelling of man, like a king, / and he heard the report of a man's authority, and shook and was dismayed.
The pangs of death seized him suddenly, like a woman in labour, / when he saw men driving out demons in the name of the Son of Man.
“What is this?” one demon asked another, his companion, / “that our hosts are dismayed at the voice of a man?
When did the power of the strong ever bow before the weak, / as now the earthly ones chase off the spiritual?
When did those sick in body heal the members of others, / as now the garments of a body heal sick bodies?
When did a slave free others from slavery,

as now Jesus gives freedom to mankind?
Already that which is written about the Son of Man is fulfilled: / that when he conquers he will tread on the head of our hosts.
Already the time has come for the fulfilment of the words of Balaam the soothsayer[?], / and this is the one he called the Star of light that enlightens mankind.
Already the utterance of that spiritual being's words has proved true, / who announced his conception and called him Lord and Son of the Most High.
Never before has it happened as it happens in this time, / that men call on the name of the Son of Man and demons tremble.
It was never heard that the dead came to life without entreaty, / as this one wakes the dead as if from sleep.”
These things the haters of mankind said to one another / when they saw a man bringing men back from their hunters.
They saw that the crafty nets of their tumult were cut, / and that the prey they had hunted from Adam until now had escaped.
They saw that even the bird with feeble wing had broken the snare, / and flown up high above the fear of their harms.
In the Canaanite woman they saw the fall of their own persons: / how a weak rib had overpowered the might of demons.
Take heart, then, feeble race that has incurred guilt through sin; / put on spiritual armour, and engage, and conquer.
Take up the shield of faith in your minds, / and set the helmet of saving life on the head of your understanding.
In secret arm your thoughts wisely, / and learn the order of battle for fighting with spirits.
It is not in flesh that the Hater fights against your lives, / but as a spirit he wages war with hidden movements.
To match his hiddenness, prepare spiritual armour, / and engage and conquer through the strength of your minds.
May the Living One keep us in our aim, that we may see the evil one and drive him off[?].
On the Prodigal Son

By the same author, again: the twenty-third memra.
On the Prodigal Son.
A memra recited each night in this Week of the Passion.
Response:
Fitting for the Passion.
My brothers…

I sought to become a disciple of the teaching of the books of the Spirit,
and I began to meditate on what is written [?] about a man and his sons.
At the head of the passages a story met me about the dividing of possessions:
a father who bequeaths the wealth of his love to his two children.
I heard the younger saying to his begetter:
"Give me a share, that I may have authority over my inheritance.
Give me, give me, that I may be master of my possessions and manage what is mine,
as it befits free sons to hold authority.

"Give me, that I may gain the name of sons, not of servants,
and let everyone know that from my lineage I possess freedom.
If I am an heir, let the name of heir be made complete in me,
and let my mind be tested by the experience of managing my life."
Though the father knew that his child was not upright,
he did not decline to fulfil for him the desire of his soul.
And since his son's error was not hidden from his kindness,
he did not think to give more to the one lacking in sense.
And though it was in his power to give more to the one who was worthy,
he gave equally the great wealth of his kindness.
In equal measure the Father of mercies divided the wealth among his sons,
and took no account of the worthless one who shamelessly asked.
The rich man's sons took the inheritance and assumed its rights,
and with their division they parted and became strangers to one another.
The younger gathered the wealth that came to him from his father's house,
and went far away and settled in a land remote from those who knew him.
Along with his property he also parted his love from his begetter,
and loved and was fond of dwelling among strangers.
He forgot his dealings with the fine things of his father's house,
and began to wander in ways unfitting for free sons.
In soul and body he went out and became a stranger to the sons of his kin,
and along with his possessions his thoughts were dragged after error.
The prodigal took all the wealth and went out with it,
and the hideous one did not leave him his love for his kinsfolk.
He left peace and loved strife full of loathing,
and busied himself with prodigality and worthlessness.
His thoughts conceived hateful desire at the urging of iniquity,
and his mouth brought it forth, and his eyes raised shameful fruit.
Worthlessness took captive the mind of the wise man's son,
and like an exile he went out and was humbled before the lowly.
He forgot his wisdom and despised the name of his honour,
and did not remember who he was, whose son, and what his lineage.
He ate the food of prodigality with prodigals,
and busied himself with shameful drink among worthless men.
His mind was drunk with the desires of body and soul,
and his eyes ran after his impulses without restraint.
He grew wanton and was inflamed by the lust of the flesh, the food of death,
and did not perceive that by his food he was destroying the possessions of his life.
He destroyed his wealth and squandered his possessions in the house of harlots,
and became destitute of possessions and of comfort.
He [?] and ate, and his prodigality was not sated;
he fell into debt and poverty, and hired himself out for a day's food.
He hired himself to a deceiver, to labour for nothing,
and the hater [?] him with the hard yoke of his bitterness.
He suffered cruelly under him without pity,
and as if in contempt he made him a herdsman of unclean beasts.
Unclean swine he sent him to tend, him who was more honoured than all,
and from the carob pods he gave him food as to dumb beasts.
The hater who hired him made his life equal to the beasts'.

And with the silent beasts he bound the course of his discernment.
His food was less even than that of the dumb beasts he tended,
and the sustenance of his life was scantier than he needed.
For he ate despised food without being satisfied,
and longed to fill his belly with carob pods.
Hard suffering was added to his hunger,
and he perceived that while his food was despised, scanty and meagre,
the suffering of his soul tormented him far more than hunger:
how he had lost his wisdom along with his possessions.
In his suffering and his hunger I wished to inquire with discernment
what its cause is, and why it is written in the Gospel.
Its story perplexed me from the start, when I came upon it:
whether it is a parable, or perhaps it really happened.
I was eager to know whether its story is true or not,
and whether he took wealth from his father's house as it is set down.
My thoughts stood divided over its reading,
whether I should call it a parable, or reflected that it was an event.
I marvelled greatly at the book of the Spirit that wrote its story:
it recorded his memory in his worthlessness and placed it among [?].
Like a statue it set him up facing the public squares,
that everyone might see who he was, whose son, and to whom he hired himself.
Therefore it is right not to be divided over what it relates,
for behold, the herald of the Spirit showed that its story is true.
It is a parable, not a bodily event;
and though it is indeed a parable, its story is true and its inquiry great.
Great wealth is hidden in its story, even if it is a parable,
and in it the power of the Maker and the work of his hands are examined.
The man who is written of is God, who fashioned all things,
and his two children are the ranks of the righteous and of sinners.
The wealth that he divided is discernment, which he gave to rational beings,
that they might discern the power of the Maker who honoured them.
The elder son is the perfect, who love his love,
and the younger son those who desire the love of earthly things.
To the good and the evil the Creator gave the power of his wisdom,
and he set comfort among the righteous and the wicked.
The righteous kept their treasures and their possessions in love,
and the slack of heart squandered the wealth of their will.
These are the sons who remained in their father's house
and repaid the debt that men owe to the one who made them.
The younger, who took the wealth that came to him and went far away,
are the wicked, who hated the love of spiritual things.
They are the ones who strayed and went out from beside the truth,
and went far off and settled beyond the peace the Creator established.
They are the ones who squandered the wealth and the mind within them,
and the sustenance of life was ruined and ceased from their knowledge.
They are the ones who ate and drank prodigally,
and the hateful desire of their thoughts was not sated.
And they are the ones who served for nothing with the deceiver,

and fell into debt and poverty through their desires and their deeds.
For he who hired them, and they laboured with him and he gave no wages,
is the murderer of men, who is wholly bare of joy.
With him that free son hired himself in order to gain authority,
and he it is who made him empty of the possessions of discernment.
He is the deceiver who made him a herdsman of vile things
and gave him the food of prodigality without satisfaction.
He it is who busied him with the shameful drink of worthlessness,
and as with wine he was drunk with sin and forgot his mind.
To the Accuser the sinner clung through his deeds,
and to him he hired himself in desires without profit.
The swine, which it is written that he tended for nothing and without nourishment,
are the labours of iniquity, from which he who labours at them has no profit.
Again, what it said, that he longed to fill his belly,
is the evil desire for vile things that are never sated.
The carob pods are the kinds of prodigality,
which, however far the heart wanders after them, never satisfy it.
So the deeds of sin are always near those who come close to her,
to entice the heart to rush into what is unseemly.
Like a harlot she shows a face of worthlessness,
and instead of the body she goes in and commits fornication with the mind.
Her lust is more abhorrent than worthless beasts,
and her clinging more unclean than a brute that knows no rest.
With her the prodigal son who squandered his possessions committed fornication,
and she defiled him in a lawless union.
Her love parted his soul's love from his begetter,
and in dealing with her he forgot the dealings of his father's affection.
She impoverished him of comfort as well as of possessions,
and she enslaved him to the servitude of iniquity in the house of strangers.
The free son laboured at the labours of slaves with her [?],
and she yoked him with the beasts in toil and feeding.
Without pity the Evil One worked the son of exile,
and his humiliation did not grieve him, that he was despised and scorned.
In his ignorance he even honoured the one who disgraced him,
and did not discern or know how he toiled and for whom he laboured.
The impulses of his soul were sunk as if in sleep,
and he did not feel the weight of his hard toil.
As with wine his heart was drunk with desires,
and he did not perceive the vile things of his self-hatred.
Like a dead man he lay in the iniquity of his self-hatred,
and the moth of sufferings was eating him, and he did not feel it.
He rotted and was corrupted wholly in desires,
and no share of life or of health remained in him.
He sank and fell silent in the hard pain into which he had hired himself,
until nature cried out to him in silence and spoke with him.
Like a goad nature pricked his discernment,
and he started up from heedlessness and saw himself, how hateful he was in iniquity.
He saw that his body and his soul were corrupted by the sickness of iniquity,
and he grieved and groaned over the corruption that had no pity.
He wailed and wept with the sound of thundering groans,

and he said to himself: "Where are you, my faculties of discernment?
Where are you, my understanding, who acquired the wisdom of discernment,
that you became mute and did not perceive the contempt of your soul?
Where are you, my mind, brother of the Watchers, ever watchful,
that thieves came in and plundered your wealth, and you neither grieved nor felt it?
Where are you, intellect, pilot of the body's senses,
that the course of your swiftness has ceased and you were defeated in the contest?
Where are you, soul, spring that gives the body life to drink,
that the streams of your wisdom have dried up and the drink of your eloquence has ceased?
Where are you?" So the dead man asked, who had died in iniquity:
"Am I among the living or among the dead? I do not know."
In great suffering he groaned over his humiliation,
and began to reproach the iniquity that took him captive and plundered his wealth.
"Woe because of iniquity!" the sinner cried out bitterly,
"for it squandered my possessions and made me a laughingstock among my kin.
Woe because of the hater, who hates and makes hateful whoever clings to him,
for he made me hated and vile of face in the eyes of those who see me.
Woe because of the defiler, who is wholly defiled and defiles everyone,
who defiled my impulses through dealings with his vile things.
O how bitter is the labour of iniquity, and how heavy its yoke,
and how empty the toils of whoever hires himself to its cruelty!
O how blind is ignorance, and how evil its dealings,
that it blinds the whole man to what is fitting!
Ignorance made me blind and lacking in mind,
and it squandered the wealth that came to me from our father's house.
It emptied me of my inheritance and of comfort,
and behold, I live on despised food from carob pods.
How many hired servants who live without cost are in our father's house,
while I here am perishing of hunger through ignorance!
How many there are who eat of the leftovers of my father's table,
but I am in need of sustenance, and no one has pity.
I will arise and go to that Father who is mine and his and everyone's,
and I will say: I have sinned against heaven above and before your face.
I have sinned, I confess, not a little but greatly,
for I forgot your love and squandered the wealth of your kindness.
I have sinned, I will tell him, and I am not worthy to be called your son;
make me from now on like the hired servants, and let me live by your grace."
These things the prodigal son said to himself,
and he began to come down in repentance of soul to his begetter.
Fear and love filled his heart as he came down:
fear frightening him, and love drawing him to be bold and ask.
The fear of his sins was terrifying him from returning,
and his father's affection was urging him not to delay.
The affection of love prevailed far more than the fear,
and it took his hands and strengthened his impulses, that they not grow slack.
The lost one turned back on the road by which he had left his father's house,
and fixed repentance as the goal at the end of his journey.
Mercy saw him as he was coming down to the meeting place of peace,
and went out to meet him, to comfort him in his grief.
He saw in him that sign which he had seen in him before he went out,

and he ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him lovingly.
He saw that he was wearied, worn out and crushed by the toils of iniquity,
and he felt for his lowliness and his humiliation in the house of strangers.
He saw that he was corrupted by the wounds the Evil One had dealt him,
and he bound him up with mercy and washed from him the filth of iniquity.
He saw that his body and his soul were stained with desires,
and he sprinkled over all of him the pure waters of the mystery of forgiveness.
He saw that the boldness of his speech was lame,
and he began to interpret the words that came from the core of his heart.
"This one," he says, "my son, was dead, and he has come back to life and returned;
the lamb that was lost from the pasture, behold, I have found it."
The broken-hearted heard the word of hope that his father proclaimed,
and began to sob thunderously before his begetter.
He heard that there is hope that those [?] who have died in sin may live,
and he began to plead that perhaps he might be relieved of his hateful deeds.
"My father," he says, "I have acted wickedly and sinned greatly beyond measure,
and I am not worthy to call myself by the name of heir.
The name of sons does not befit one who is not free-born,
nor is it fitting for the slave of iniquity to be set free.
Freedom of soul does not become one who hates his own soul,
nor does it become the ignorant to hold the sceptre of leadership.
I am far too small to be called heir and son,
and I am not able to receive a rank that never dies.
Let me labour for each day's bread like a stranger,
and receive a portion with the hired servants who are in your house.
And if I cannot hire myself out, labour and receive wages,
count me worthy to receive alms by your grace like a poor man.
For I know that I have sinned greatly beyond all order,
and I am not able to repay the debt of my sins.
It does not escape me that my folly is too great to be forgiven,
and the sea is too small to wash away the hateful blemishes of my person.
There is no other remedy that can heal the sore of my pains
except the mercies of the Father who begot me as the work of his hands."
With these words he wept over the deadness of his soul,
and did not cease from groaning over his offences.
He made great mourning over his iniquity as over a dead man,
and with groans he wept thunderously over his sin.
Great weeping filled his mouth and his mind,
and tears of suffering poured from his eyes.
At the sound of his groans his begetter marvelled, and the hosts on high;
he sent grace and mercies to him to quiet him.
"Be quiet, sinner," the mercies cried to him, but he would not be quiet;
"for behold, your father has commanded that they tear up the bond of your debts.
Be quiet, do not weep, but rejoice, you and your begetter,
for behold, your father too has grieved and groaned over your groans."
His begetter saw that the mercies were not able to quiet him,
and he himself went out and urged him: "Cease from weeping.
Cease, do not weep over the loss of what was before,
for in your father's house there is great wealth without end.

Cease, do not grieve over the offences of your ignorance,
for however great the iniquity, I count it as nothing to blot it out.
For I knew before you went out that you would meet with a blow,
and it was revealed to me that you would lose the wealth you took.
My will was watching your going out and your return as well,
and I was watching over you as you went in and as you came back.
With you went out to the house of strangers the mercies that pity you,
and they counselled you to return to the peace of your fathers' house.
Come, take your delight as an heir in your inheritance,
hold its rights, and manage what is yours wisely."
Then his father gave orders to those of his house concerning his exaltation,
that they should crown him with the name and the rank of his begetter's title.
"Bring out the robe that the mercies wove, and let him be clothed in it,
and let everyone know from how well it suits him whose son he is.
Put on him the ring of his father's seal, which is truer than all,
