that slaves and free sons may see that he has returned to his rank.
Let him put on his feet the pure truth that does not deceive,
and trample the head of the adversary who plundered his inheritance.
Kill also the ox, that he and those with him may feast on it,
and that the hater who gave him food from carob pods may be put to shame."
The servants carried out his father's words swiftly, as he commanded,
and servants and free began to rejoice on the day of his return.
But his brother, who was older than he, was not there,
for he was in the field, faithfully labouring at his father's labour.
He too came on the day his brother returned,
and saw that a great feast had been made on the day of his return.
The brother was greatly displeased when he saw his brother's return,
and he was angry and turned back to his labour and would not go in.
But his father heard and went out to him to entreat him,
just as he had gone out to meet his brother with love and mercies.
"My son, do not be displeased that your brother has returned to his fathers' house,
and do not estrange yourself from the fellowship of the day of his return."
He too turned to his begetter, in answer to his urging,
and showed his love, how much he had valued his father's will:
"See how long I have served you with the labour of slaves,
and never have you honoured me with a kid so that I might refresh my friends.
For this one, who squandered the possessions of your house in the house of harlots,
now that he has returned you have killed the ox, which he does not deserve."
"My son, all that is mine is yours," his begetter answered him,
"and you have authority over my inheritance as the elder.
It was fitting for you to rejoice today and to give praise,
that your brother, who was dead, has returned and been relieved of his childishness."
He too grieved his father greatly, far more than his brother did,
in that he reproached him for having pitied the straying one who returned.
The kind one bore great vexation from his children,
and beyond measure he carried the trouble of their thoughts.

Both of them grieved him by the unlikeness of their deeds:
one by sin, and the other by objecting to the forgiveness of iniquity.
One distressed him by the ruin of his life and the squandering of his possessions,
and the other reproached him because he received repentance.
Kindly he bore with them, as one who knows,
and taught them to become like him and gain life.
Now that the story depicted in mysteries is finished,
let us ask what power is hidden within its words.
Let us ask what it means that is written of the prodigal,
that he thought to turn back and go to his fathers' house.
The mystery of sinners is depicted in the younger and in his repentance,
and in his dwelling in the house of strangers, the thicket of demons.
In his going out is depicted the distance from God,
and in his return, the repentance that stands beside righteousness.
In the plea of his words, when he counted himself among the hired servants,
it is discernment that judges itself for what it has sinned.
The hired servants are those not baptized, who have only believed
and have not shared in the mystery of the spiritual birth.
Again, what he said, "I am not worthy to be your son,"
is the mind, the [?], which judges rightly concerning its own deeds.
The father who went out to meet his child and ran to meet him
is the mercies that pity everyone who sins.
By going out, embracing him and kissing him lovingly,
he showed how much he desires that men should return to him.
The fitting robe that clothed his body and covered his disgrace
is baptism, which blots out iniquity and gives freedom.
The ring is the pledge of immortal life,
which the Spirit gives to those who have acquired the name of sons.
The fatted ox is the great mystery of the Body and the Blood,
by whose sacrifice the world was reconciled with his Majesty.
And rightly he called the sacrifice of his body the [fatted] ox,
for it was nourished with the food of the Spirit and the drink of wine.
And that he killed it on the day his son returned from his error
is a sign of the love toward our race that cannot be measured.
By the voice that proclaimed, "My son was dead and has returned to life,"
he taught us how much he rejoices at our repentance.
And that he urged his son, who reproached him for pitying the lost,
is the rebuke that comes to whoever is vexed at the forgiveness of iniquity.
It is not the righteous who err there in that fault,
but whoever here reproaches the mercies that pity.
Before the testing he examined beforehand what is to come,
so that if anyone is angry at acts of pity, he may correct his inclination.
He showed two things by his saying concerning the elder:
that the righteous one who is faithful in the labour of truth is not to be reproached;
and that the one who reproached was in the field, as is written in the Gospel,
making known to us that he was always busied beside righteousness.
The field is a mystery of the labour of the spiritual life,
and through the likeness of earthly things it represents what is above.

The kid that he said his father never gave him to make merry with
shows that he was fenced off and kept back from the business of dissipation.
The kid stands for the iniquity that strays and leads a person astray,
since kids, too, each wander off away from the flock.
The kid is very bold in its grazing and dark in its colour;
it is like iniquity, which roams in herds [?] and darkens the soul.
The Creator's mercy is the nature that existed before sins [?],
and nature claims what is its own, however much it longs for spiritual things.
For nature loves what is its own, insofar as it is earthly,
and, as though in a contest, it sets the two against each other, body and spirit.
His father had kept him from the desires of bodily lust,
and promised him the riches of the Spirit, so that he might take his delight in them.
"Everything that is mine is yours," he said to the elder,
showing us that good things are his possessions.
In a parable he portrayed our whole nature in the likeness of an image,
and brought it and set it within the palace of the lofty order [of iniquity?].
In the order of the senses he set the world as his two sons,
and good and evil alike were gathered to him beneath his love.
In the younger son he called sinners to repentance,
and in the elder he encouraged the righteous with the payment of a reward.
The Lord of natures called our nature sons and heirs,
and he became a Father to us: a great wonder, beyond words!
O how far beyond the telling of the tongue is the story
in which the One who orders all things named himself Father to man!
O how highly the nature of the children of dust has been exalted,
that it became worthy to be heir and son to its Maker!
O how, and in what way, shall one say that this has come to pass,
that he became our Father and we the heirs of his divinity?
A great, unspeakable love has visited our race
and stirs the mouth of every creature to tell how great it is.
How can a silent mouth suffice to recount the greatness of his love,
who made us, together with him, to be worshipped by all creatures?
How can anyone repay him the debt of love,
when even spiritual beings rejoice at our repentance?
Why else would the assemblies of heaven rejoice
over a sinner who turns back and repents of his folly?
And if angels rejoice with us at our repentance,
then heavy is the penalty of anyone who finds fault with mercy.
If spiritual beings long to see us justified,
then harsh lashes are owed to the one who hates his brother.
Are the heavenly assemblies glad that we live,
and does it grieve you that mercy has pity on man freely?
Do natures that cannot suffer suffer over our loss,
and does it please you that someone should remain in Sheol without [?] mercy?
Do they long for the time when we shall reign together,
and are you angry with one who runs as they desire?
Have I too, who have been sunk so long in the sleep of iniquity,
[?] risen at the call of forgiveness to seek for words?
The story of the one who strayed urged me to seek the force of parables,
and at his return my thoughts turned toward learning.
His story drew me to read the book of his writings
and to learn the hidden power in the words the Spirit interpreted.

I went out with him when he left his father's house,
and I came back with him to see him reconciled with his father.
I saw him squander his wealth in the great house of harlots,
and again I watched him as he turned to go toward forgiveness.
I heard him put together pitiful words over his folly,
and I suffered greatly over the iniquity of my own self, which is like his.
I heard him say, "I am not worthy of the name of heir,"
and groaning seized me, for I have walked the path of squandering as he did.
My conduct is very like the path he walked in,
and I too, like him, have squandered the gaining of life.
With that loathsome man to whom he hired himself out I too have served,
and like him I have lived on the carob pods of desires.
Ignorance has left me, too, stripped of mercy,
just as he lost what was his without a thought.
May the mercies that pitied him and went out to meet him on the day of his return
plead for me before the Judge who searches all things.
May the voice that said, "My son was dead and has come back to life,"
make me worthy to hear that this sinner has received forgiveness.
May the hand that spread the robe of glory over his nakedness
cover my face, so that it is not laid bare to the eyes of onlookers.
May the sign he placed on him as a ring, the pledge of life,
strengthen my movements to look toward the kingdom of life.
May the mouth that calmed the anger of his brother, who found fault with mercy,
rebuke the tyrant iniquity that draws near to my thoughts.
May the Watchers who rejoiced on the day of his return and praised his Father
be my helpers before Justice, in place of my guilt.
May the finger that painted the image of his [?] and his return to life
paint on my mind the image of [?] that bestows life.
Yes, my Lord, let me be a companion in the land of the dead man who came to life,
and let what was spoken at the close of his story be fulfilled in me.
Yes, my Lord, by grace make me worthy with him of the banquet of your love,
and may mercy receive me at the judgment, as he was received.
For the Thursday of Passover

Nineteenth Memra, to be recited on the Thursday of Passover.
Response: You who put an end to wars from the ends of the earth, put an end for us to the wars of the Deceiver.
My brothers, [?]

The Mighty One went out to battle, to deliver the captives from the Evil One,
and he put on bodily armour to wrestle with the spiritual one.
The athlete armed himself for the contest with the strong one,
and set his authority upon his shoulder to show the power of his greatness.
At the top of Golgotha he opened his contest in the arena,
so that angels and men might be spectators of his feat.
The Adversary saw and was embittered that the athlete had come down into the arena,
and with the weapons of the Accuser he made himself ready to kill.
With the semblance of armour the rebel grew bold in his wiles:
"To me mortals owe service, as to a lord."
The athlete of righteousness was watching the aim of his cunning,
as he said, "Behold, the ruler comes to plead his case."
"Now indeed is the great judgement, in which the Accuser goes to law with me,
and as from everyone he demands at my hands the debt of death and of sin."
The ruler of the world cried out

with the tones of battle cries, supposing he would terrify the Son of Adam as he had Adam:
"Do you not know that to me was handed the whole world and its dominion?
Are you not convinced by my might, that I have enslaved your whole race?
To me you have rendered service from the beginning to the end.
Have you not heard of the contest that I once waged with Adam?
How I overpowered and defeated the living image of the Creator?"
With words full of the poison of death he tried to frighten the athlete,
and he did not know that he was being mocked, while the other laughed at his wiles.
By means of death he supposed that he would defeat him as he had everyone,
and he did not know that by his death he would rescue the captives from his hands.
He fulfilled the will of the presumptuous one and gave himself into the hand of death,
and the dead one upon the wood turned and overthrew him and annulled his dominion.
Mortality died in its own nature, and the power that dwelt in him raised him,
and by the victory of his resurrection he brought the captives back from the Evil One.
He stripped off and cast away mortality and was exalted above sufferings;
he tore up the bond of the debtors and by his blood made peace for those at enmity,
and he bound the rational beings in love toward the Creator.
His death became the cause of life for mortals and immortals,
and rational and dumb creatures alike gained hope and joy.
The dominion of the rebel who had enslaved humankind faded and was abolished,
and he began to speak, crying out, "What have we to do with you, Son of David?"
The heralds of the words of the Spirit pierced him with voices from every side,
as they pursued the deceiver so that he would not disturb the peace of humankind.
The searchers of hidden things revealed to the rebel his torment,
and cast into his ears tidings of the flame that is never quenched.
And when he saw that his dominion was abolished and torment prepared for him,
he grew bitter, raged and went mad, and gave himself wholly to opposition.

He saw that his wiles were exposed by the light of the dawning of Christ,
and he began to act brazenly in the open and to snatch for himself the honoured name.
By the name "Christ, angel of light" the presumptuous one calls himself,
and he calls those who do his will "angels of righteousness."
He heard that the coming of Christ is to be at the end of times,
and the counterfeit began to lead astray in the name of the revelation of Christ.
Long ago he laid his scheme, and he plots it in his bitterness,
and his desire burns like fire to bring his will into the open.
A sign of the Creator's power holds back his bitterness,
until the end brings on the time appointed for his end.
He knows how long the span of the times must last;
and when he takes away the sign that restrains, then iniquity dawns.
At the end of times he lets him loose to display his bitterness,
and the presumptuous one rises and climbs to the height of the name of Christ.
In everything he imitates him, in outward form and not in truth,
performing mighty works in his likeness by illusion, without substance.
The rebel does not accomplish his coming in spiritual form;
through a son of man he carries out his error among the lost.
After the manner of the dawning of Christ the Accuser imitates him,
when he chooses for himself a son of man and fulfils in him the full measure of his wickedness.
In the likeness of the Word from the Father the rebel makes himself out,
who came down by his own will to the dwelling of our humanity.
He imitates that greatness which accomplished the life of our redemption:
he too puts on a son of man, and through him hunts humankind to death.
One son of man he chooses for himself from the mortal race,
and clothes him with the spirit of falsehood, and works in him the powers of his error.
He gives him the cup of his gall to drink and makes him drunk with the [?] of his wrath,
and with his bitterness he stirs up the foolish, that they may become like him.
All his will the presumptuous one fulfils in that son of man,
as through him he steals the honour, through him he steals the honour

of the greatness of Christ's glory.
He sends messengers before him, thousands of demons to every quarter,
as they throw creation into turmoil with dreadful reports of his coming.
Rumours full of terrors they sow in the ears of all peoples,
so that they leave their labours and go out to see the deceiver.
Disasters and bitter reports run through the whole earth:
"Behold, the hope has now dawned! Go out, receive the king who is coming!"
The host of demons throws the world into turmoil over its inhabitants,
as they gather from every quarter to see the killer of men.
Dreadful visions appear to dreamers by night,
and while awake by day, reports that trouble their thoughts.
A band of demons draws humankind after the counterfeit,
as they gather in throng upon throng to worship the iniquity of the rebel.
With thousands of demons he is borne in procession, that vessel of all error,
while the rebels cry out to him, "Hail, O king!" they cry, "O ruler!"
He makes himself fly in the air as he is borne along on the clouds,
and to the eye of the onlookers he appears, by a spirit of falsehood, as one flying.
The unclean demons hallow that unclean one as the pure one,
as they weave acclamations for the presumptuous one as the pure one.
He opens his mouth and speaks in tones full of peace,
as he draws humankind with the semblance of love and concord.
With lying promises he draws all nations after his words,
as he promises resurrection and rising to the corpses that have fallen asleep.
He raises dead men who have no body, by phantoms and likenesses,
and gives the lame the power to walk while they do not tread upon the earth.
Falsely are the signs of the deceiver performed,
and by a spirit of error the counterfeit leads astray the son of perdition.
He multiplies, devising every scheme, to lead astray all nations in great numbers;
he plots deeply and hides every snare, to ensnare many of every [?] stature.
He dissolves the authority of judges, so that his own authority may reign;
he abolishes kings and their crowns, so that they may call him alone king.
He removes burdens and servitude, and the poll tax and tribute,
so that those who have grown weary of servitude may hold fast to his works.
He proclaims peace and concord

as a king who loves peace,
so that for the sake of peace he may confine all nations in his nets.
Messengers travel before him to prepare lodgings for him,
and from place to place he moves after the manner of a king and of rulers.
By the name of God the rebel is called by his ministers,
as he enters the holy temple and they worship him as Lord.
As the Creator the presumptuous one is honoured by the oppressors,
for he calls himself Christ, the counterfeit, the vessel of falsehood.
In the temple of atonement sits that unclean one who loves iniquity,
and receives the worship of iniquity from the wicked, wickedly.
"I, I am the Christ who is awaited!" this the oppressor proclaims.
"Let mysteries and types and parables now cease and be no more!"
He abolishes the liturgy, so that he alone may be served;
he removes the word of teaching, so that his own word may be received.
He silences the holy voices, the heralds of the words of the Spirit,
so that they may not read in the ears of the people, nor let them listen to the message of life.
"It was about me that the heralds searched, as they prophesied my coming.
Leave the vision of parables and look upon the true person!"
He forbids the baptism of water, so that sinners may not be justified,
and opens the spring of his hatred and with it defiles the pure.
"I, I justify sinners and forgive iniquity and sin;
my words give atonement instead of water, to body and soul."
He abolishes the table of atonement, so that it may not be consecrated according to the rite,
as he proclaims in the ears of all the abolition of the living Mystery.
He robs the sweet spring from the lips of those who drink it,
and that spiritual food he withholds from those who receive it.
The presumptuous one cries out with arrogance words full of blasphemy:
"I, I am the truth and its meaning; leave the mysteries and honour the truth!"
Alas for the disaster, bitter in its report, that the rebel is to work,
that he calls his own mystery the Mystery of the Body of the giver of life to all!

Let the discerning now wrap themselves in mourning over this disaster,
and let those who test the counterfeit against the truth pour out tears of grief.
Let the lovers of meditation and teaching compose voices of lament,
for the counterfeit abolishes the study of the words of the Spirit.
Let the unclean who were sanctified in the washing of baptism weep,
for the rebel silences the spiritual birth.
Let all alike mourn, the partakers of the living Mystery,
for they are robbed of the medicine of life, the children of Christ's table.
Let the priests who minister in the sanctuary be clothed in garments of mourning,
for the Accuser dissolves the canon of their orders.
Let all nations, of every stature, sing voices of lament,
for the voices of praise cease and are no longer sung in the sanctuary.
Who will not weep and sigh over this bitter disaster,
that the worship of the Creator ceases and is offered to the Accuser?
The presumptuous one throws all ordinances into confusion on the day of his revelation,
and dissolves rites and laws, so that his own error may be honoured.
With the signs of the deceiver he draws the simple to his side,
and by changing appearances he leads astray the heart of the knowing.
He abolishes the worship of the gods and dismisses priests and diviners,
so that he alone may be served, as priest and king and prophet.
Before the end these things come to pass, which our Saviour spoke:
reports of wars and battles, and then iniquity dawns.
There are earthquakes and plagues and disasters full of terrors,
and nation rises against nation and kingdom against kingdom.
The world ceases from its labour in harsh and bitter winters,
and the rod is stretched out over everyone, and famine lays low the mighty.
In a time that is crushed and wretched, when wars and battles grow fierce,
in that time the presumptuous one dawns for the revelation of his bitterness.

And for this reason he bewilders everyone, and his error multiplies among the lost,
for they see the times change and wars fall away from the earth.
He brings battles and contests to an end and increases peace for all peoples,
so that they may not be hindered from running to the work of his bitterness.
With these nets he catches humankind and binds it fast,
so that when they see peace in counterfeit they may receive it as true.
With the semblance of seeking peace he draws all peoples to his side,
as they leave their labours and bear him in procession as king.
Every nation, untroubled, strays after his teaching,
for even the elect, if it were possible, he would turn and draw to his persuasion.
With love and compassion the wicked murderer of men conducts himself,
and the hater of all justice answers "Peace" to everyone.
Only the elect does he hate, who give him no obedience,
as he loads the assemblies with wrath against the just, that they may not spare them.
From place to place he moves to crown himself over all his dominion,
as the rebel exalts himself above every object of worship and every god.
It is not the error of the religions that the erring one dissolves and abolishes;
he devises schemes to wipe out the religion of truth from the earth.
With the semblance of peace he loosens the love toward the Creator;
with the semblance of righteousness his ministers run before him,
and bring tidings of peace: "Behold, the Saviour has now come!"
Cities go out to meet him on his way with songs and praises,
as they cry out to him "Hosanna! Glory to the king who has dawned upon us!"
Into great mourning he turns the joy of the church of the nations,
and the vessel of holiness is corrupted by the iniquitous worship of the counterfeit.
Lips that cried "Glory" and kissed the mysteries of the medicine of life
cry out words of blasphemy and kiss the Accuser.
Mouths that sang praise in the sanctuary, the psalms of the words of the Spirit,
defile the holiness of their mouths with the songs of the deceiver.
With the voice of praise the presumptuous one snatches for himself the worship of his Lord,
as he brings humankind down from the heights to the depths.

The rebel accomplishes all his will in the son of perdition,
and then the Creator gives a sign of mercy upon the earth.
Elijah dawns suddenly and holds back the violence of the deceiver,
and stops him in his course, so that he may not lead astray and make everyone stumble.
For this reason Elijah is sent at the end of times:
to come and set everything in order before the revelation of Christ.
Elijah comes beforehand to silence the voices of error,
and to turn the heart of the fathers, that they may be set right by their children.
The King sends to the world a messenger full of peace,
so that by the frankness of his words he may sober the drunkenness of the wrathful one.
Like a lamp he enlightens through him the darkened, toward knowledge,
and like a guide he turns through him the wanderers to the way of life.
At the tones of Elijah's voice the voices of the deceiver fall silent,
and his nets are cut from the captives, and they turn back from iniquity.
Elijah sows abundantly the tones of the soul's repentance,
and with the dew of his words he makes the repentance of the people and the peoples grow.
In the manner in which John ministered before his earthly dawning,
in that manner Elijah comes before that heavenly dawning.
Two bodily heralds he chose for himself in his two revelations,
to prepare for him on earth lodgings of love in his two revelations;
to prepare for him on earth lodgings of love in the soul.
John proclaimed his birth, and Elijah his revelation,
and the aim of the two of them is one: to bring the lost back to him.
Elijah warns abundantly: "Behold, the end is now near!
Turn, you who have strayed, from wandering to the fair way of my words!"
The presumptuous one persists in his brazenness, as he strays and leads humankind astray,
until the flood overflows the face of the whole earth.
For that revelation he keeps the wicked one, and so destroys him,
so that men and angels may see the requital of judgement that he receives.
Before that day the signs that our Saviour gave appear,
and all that is written is fulfilled, and the world ceases from its course.
The sun's rays grow dim, and the moon does not show its light,
and the stars fall like leaves, and the course of the luminaries ceases.
Thousands of the ranks move in procession

of the heavenly hosts,
as they perform their offices to escort the King of the height.
Christ, the Lord of glory, opens the gate of the firmament,
and dawns suddenly in his revelation and veils the luminary.
Compared with the light before him, the light of the sun is darkness,
and against his swift dawning the flash of lightning is slow.
There is no comparison for that glory in which his revelation appears,
nor any likeness for that greatness in which the Watchers bear him in procession.
Thousands of spiritual hosts recount the praise of his greatness,
and seraphim without number hallow him on every side.
Their voices are not uttered in earthly tongues,
nor can mortals listen to the melodies of their praise.
They shake the earth with their voices and heaven with their trumpets,
as they run to the four quarters to announce the voice of redemption.
The sound of the horns makes the world tremble over its inhabitants,
and dreadful trumpets cast quaking into the heart of those sunk down.
Above them all is borne in procession Christ, the Lord of glory,
as they cry out to him with their voices, "Holy is our pure King!"
The chief of the angels bears in procession the living standard of the Crucified,
and with ineffable glory shows it to the eye of the beholders.
Before him comes the victory of the King who conquered by his cross,
and the spiritual beings hallow him in return for the insults of the oppressors.
The daughters of the house of Israel are pained at the sight of him,
and in mournful melodies they recount voices of lament.
With great splendour he displays that standard on which he suffered on earth,
so that when his crucifiers see the greatness of his glory they may be pained by it.
With his standard our Head is borne in procession by the spiritual beings,
and heavenly and earthly beings see the glory of his greatness.
In his very nature he appears to spiritual and bodily beings,
and he who ascended on the clouds is the one who comes at the end.
The angels announced beforehand, at his ascension, concerning his revelation,
that in the form in which he ascended, in that form he comes in his great glory.
It is not the nature of the Godhead that moves and travels in its own nature;
it is the bodily one who comes to judge, who received judgement and authority.

The Godhead does not have it by nature to move from place to place;
it is by will alone that the self-existent Word travels with the body.
A descent without movement comes down with him from on high,
and by it he renews rational beings and by it he tests their deeds.
In great splendour he appears, as he dawns like lightning,
and shows his appearance from end to end of the earth.
The chiefs of the angels cry out with spiritual trumpets,
and at the end of their trumpeting the horn of resurrection calls.
The chief of the angels sounds the last horn of resurrection,
and with dreadful words commands the earth to bring forth the departed.
Birth pangs strike the earth, to bring forth instead of seeds,
as the command presses upon her that no dead one remain within her womb.
The dreadful voice terrifies Death, the master of the house of Sheol,
as it demands of him an account of the number of Adam's children.
Not one dead person is forgotten in Sheol, and not one limb remains in it.
One is the voice that raises the good and the wicked alike.
The resurrection is the same for all; the appearance of each is not the same:
it is the will that shows one body more glorious than its fellow.
Suddenly his revelation strikes, the King of the height, upon the earthly ones,
and he abolishes the darkness with the light that flashes from his body.
Amazement falls upon all at the sound of the angels' shout,
and the earthly beings are terrified at the sight of the spiritual beings.
The heart of men is dismayed at the voice that is like the sea,
and pangs and anguish seize them with a quaking that drives out souls.
The dreadful voice terrifies the Accuser, the rebel,
and all his dominion ceases at a single nod, in the blink of an eye.
With chains of fire he binds him and casts him into the flame,
as the onlookers marvel at his silencing without end.
But the son of man whom he chose and filled with the desire of his wickedness,
him he removes from life, in the destruction of his body and soul.
He does not allow him to remain with his master in torment;
he brings him to a complete end and removes him from life.

The Creator works a new wonder in the son of perdition:
that with the destruction of his limbs the dissolution of his soul is added.
He shows rational beings a great disaster in the abolition of his life:
how a soul, a nature that does not die, is wiped out from life.
That vessel of all error deserves to become a terror,
who led men astray from the truth, so that men may see his destruction.
To the grief of the Accuser he destroys him from life,
because his will dwelt in him, so that they may be tormented by the destruction of his life.
Severe blows await the rebel in Gehenna,
for the temple of his will is laid waste, and he is tormented for ever.
Before spiritual and bodily beings he destroys that son of man,
and to heavenly and earthly beings he shows the abasement of the presumptuous one.
First he binds the rebel and casts him into Gehenna,
and then he opens the gates of the height and gathers his own to himself.
He makes a great separation when he gathers the elect:
the just fly up to heaven and the wicked remain on earth.
Here what was prophesied beforehand about the pure comes to fulfilment:
that some are taken and some are left, that the good are separated from the wicked.
The departed rise first and strip off mortality,
and then the living are changed into the likeness of the immortals.
Then the word of Paul the herald is fulfilled:
that the living whom the end overtakes do not sleep the sleep of death.
The dead and the living are changed and become like spiritual beings,
and body and soul are renewed and no longer fear sufferings.
One voice rouses and raises the dead from the sleep of death,
and with the resurrection of the departed the living gain transformation.
In a small nod all these distinctions are accomplished,
and in the blink of an eye heavenly and earthly beings are changed.
Swifter than lightning is that light that dawns suddenly,
and with the dawning of his appearance it changes all and renews all.
The bodies of the just become winged and spiritual,
as they are borne in procession on the clouds up to the gate of the firmament.
Clouds of light bow down

and carry the bodies of the saints. / They are caught up to the Bridegroom's path / to go up with him to heaven. / The voice of command rings out / toward the gate of the firmament, / and it opens before those who enter / the great gate of heaven. / The King enters at the head of his host, / with all who loved his appearing, / and he shuts the gate of the height / in the face of the wicked and the unbelievers. / In that hour the demons / and wicked men are struck with dismay, / for they see the glory of the chosen / as they are borne aloft on clouds. / They knock at the door of justice, / but goodness does not answer them. / They beg mercy from the Judge, / but grace turns away from them, / for they loved the land of curses / and did not long for heavenly blessings. / In the place they loved they are left behind, / harshly scourged. / Grief and anguish of soul / crush them more than the scourges. / There they pass judgment on their own faults / and lay bare their deeds. / There they receive knowledge / and come to discern what was fitting, / and they declare justice to be just / in the penalties exacted from themselves. / There, with knowledge, they see, / through the senses of the swift mind, / the crowns of glory with which / the saints are rewarded in the kingdom on high. / They weep and wail with groaning / as they gaze up toward the height, / and they see the road that lies between, / so hard to cross over to the good. / "Open to us!" cry the wrongdoers / to the Lord whose love they hated, / and a voice answers them: / "I do not know your works." / Countless are the woes / that sinners recount there, / and beyond words the pleas / with which they beg to be spared from torment. / The earth becomes like Gehenna / for the children of the earth, / and in the furnace of their thoughts / they assay the dross of their faults. / With the sight of the mind they see / the hidden things of their deeds, / and in the balance of thought / they weigh the burden of their evils. / The scourge of torment is not the same / for all who are in Gehenna, / for according to the greatness of wickedness / one scourge is more bitter than another. / Nor in the glory of those on high

is the radiance of their splendor the same, / for crowns of glory are given / to the victorious according to their labors. / To stars, bright lamps, / Paul compared their splendor: / that one body outshines another / as one star outshines another. / To each according to his labor / justice weighs out and gives his reward, / and according to the love of the mind / the glory of the diligent increases. / Their dwelling becomes / the expanse of the firmament's vault, / and their canopy the heaven above, / the one established from the beginning. / They dwell in a bright place / where darkness holds no sway, / and there is no measure to the delight / of their spiritual joy. / They do not toil in their rest, / nor grow weary at their banquets; / spiritually they take their delight / in blessings that never fail. / Their works are their praises, / their occupation their hymns of holiness, / and they never tire of the melodies / with which they sing glory to the divine Being. / There is no desire of the flesh there, / nor any change of mind, / for soul and body are raised / above passions and changes. / In the great glory the forms / that set them apart are worn away, / and male and female are equal, / wrapped in a garment of light. / There the distinction / between slave and free is abolished, / for One alone reigns, / and his authority extends over all. / There God becomes / all in the soul of rational beings, / as he is hallowed by all, / by spiritual beings and bodily ones. / There every authority is abolished, / for one authority alone is named, / and he subjects beneath his feet / the whole host of the Rebel. / From the darkness they cry out to him, / the Accuser and the sinners: / "Righteous is your judgment, O Judge, / and upright the verdict of your justice!" / The good hallow him in light / with a glory that never grows dull, / for by the power of the Spirit they are strengthened / to render glory to his majesty. / Over all and in all is spread / the knowledge of faith in him, / and good and wicked alike plainly / confess that the divine Being is one.

There the divisions are abolished, / and the rifts that the disputers brought forth, / and one God is believed in, / in three equal Persons. / They learn the power of the divine Being, / which is high and exalted above passions, / and with unveiled faces they see / the firstfruits that he took from us. / Him they see as an image / with the sight of the outward senses, / and with the mind they gaze / on the Being that has no image, / with the sight of the outward senses, / and with the mind they gaze / on the Being that is not seen. / In him they offer thanksgiving / as in a temple of atonement, / worshipping, through his body, / the Nature that cannot be bounded. / With him they become partners / in the inheritance of the greatness of glory, / for through their kinship with him / they are honored with his glories. / Yet they are not raised by his kinship / to the height of his authority, / for he, together with the divine Being, is honored / by spiritual and bodily beings. / The children of his inheritance are called / by the name of immortality, / and from the light of his great glory / their bodies put on glory. / Let us remember these blessings / and despise the desire for gain; / let us long for that light / and see our foul deeds in the light. / Let that day be to us like a mirror, / and let us gaze into it / and polish away in it the blemishes of our soul / before the scrutiny of justice. / Let us rouse our drowsy thoughts / with the wakefulness of the love of truth, / lest the thief come / and plunder the wealth of our soul. / Before that day let us make ready / oil for the light of our lamps, / so that [?] may not bind us / with the harsh cords of sin. / And let us not be held back from the journey / along the fair road of righteousness, / for narrow is the gate of the kingdom / and the road of life is hard. / With care for our souls let us gain / wings for the honor of our limbs, / for the day of the coming is hidden: / let us guard our treasures in fear, / lest it come suddenly / and find us out like a thief. / Let us order our ways here / carefully, like the wise, / and through the knowledge of the Spirit gain / spiritual riches, / for hard is the gulf that lies between / those above and those below. / Let us hold fast to the company of love, / that it may raise up our honor. / With the [?] of faith / let us moor the ships of our mind, / so that the storms
of the Accuser may not sink us. / Refrain: Glory to your power, our Savior, by which you defeated the Accuser.
On the Explanation of the Mysteries
The Seventeenth Homily / On the Explanation of the Mysteries

On the mysteries of the Church my thoughts meditated in a mystic way,
and I wanted to reveal the heart's meditation in the words of the mouth.
In the words of the mouth I wanted to tell of their greatness,
and in words to paint the image of their glory.
Before their glory my frail mind was dazzled,
and trembling seized me and left me slack and unable to act.
Unable to act I remained, standing back from the beginning,
and I began to cry out in anguish with the son of Amoz.
With the son of Amoz I cried woe on my unclean self,
for in its uncleanness its mind was dazzled by the mysteries of its Lord.
I meditated on these things and turned back in fear,
but the Spirit by his sign urged me to enter the Holy of Holies.
He gave me leave to enter the Holy of Holies of the glorious mysteries,
and to reveal the beauty of their glory to the children of the mystery.
Come then, O child of the divine mystery,
hear the wondrous story of the words of the Church's mysteries.
“My secret is mine, my secret is mine, my secret is mine and my own,” the prophet cries:

wisely, then, hear the mystery that is being explained to you.
Truly lofty and exalted is this mystery
which the priest performs in a mystic way within the sanctuary.
In a mystic way the Church depicts the glorious mysteries,
and shows to everyone, as in an image, the things that took place.
The things that took place at the Son's death she recalls in the mysteries,
and she also reveals his resurrection from the grave before the eyes of all.
A mystery and a sign stand for what has been and what will be,
and in her mysteries the Church signifies only what has been.
The Church celebrates her mysteries hidden from outsiders,
and the priest performs them in a mystic way within the sanctuary.
Only her own children, the baptized and signed, does she gladly allow
to share in these adored mysteries that she performs.
Therefore she cries out to the hearers through the deacons
that they should bow their heads and receive a blessing from the priesthood:
“Bow your heads, O hearers, believers, baptized,
and receive a blessing from the laying on of the splendid priest's hand.”
And after they have been blessed, another call comes to them:
that whoever has not received baptism should go away from here.
“Go, you unbaptized; you may not share in the mysteries of the Church,
for only the household is permitted to share.”
Then another proclamation is made in another manner:
that whoever has not received the sign of life should go away from here.
And whoever has repented and turned from a heresy that distorts the glory
should not share in the mysteries of the Church until he is signed.
And whoever has denied his faith and returned to his vomit
should not share until he is absolved by the Church's sign.
Then another proclamation is made in another order:
that whoever does not receive the Body and Blood should go away from here.
Whoever has been excluded by the priesthood and barred from receiving
may not remain even at the time when they communicate.
Whoever is barred from receiving by the canon of holiness
is not permitted to stand even in the place where they communicate.
But one who is sick and unwell, and by necessity cannot receive,
may stand even in the nave where they are sanctified.

They all go out from the nave in sorrow,
and stand in great mourning in the court of the Church.
They call blessed those who remain in that delight,
and cry woe on themselves for their separation.
By sending them out the holy Church depicts a type
of those who will go out to that darkness of Gehenna.
The king saw a man who was not clothed in the proper garments,
and gave orders, and they bound him and put him out into that outer darkness.
So too the Church searches her assemblies at the time of the mysteries,
and whoever is not adorned with pure garments she casts outside.
After this a cry goes out to the hearers
that they should go and watch the doors of the Church and guard them.
“Go, hearers, and watch the outer doors carefully,”
since they do not share in the mysteries of the Church as the household do.
Of these the prodigal son is a reminder, who squandered his possessions
and humbly asked to be like the hired servants.
Let us put away anger and wrath from us at that time,
and watch Jesus being led to death for our sake.
He goes out to his passion on the paten and in the cup with the deacon:
bread on the paten, wine in the cup, a mystery of his death.
They carry the mystery of his death on their hands,
and when they set it on the altar and cover it, they figure his burial.
They do not bear the likeness of the Jews,
but of the watchers who ministered at the Son's passion.
He was ministered to by angels at the time of his passion,
and the deacons honor in mystery his body that suffered.
Then the priests enter the sanctuary in procession,
and stand there in great glory and comely splendor.

The priest who is set apart to perform that sacrifice
bears in his own person at that time the image of our Lord.
Christ acted as mediator between us and his Father,
and in the same form the priest acts as mediator.
Hear, O priest, to what height your rank has reached,
and fear the Lord, and honor your rank as befits it.
See that you have been raised above the cherubim, above the seraphim;
rise above nature in your conduct, as becomes you.
See that you have been entrusted with managing your Lord's treasures;
be blameless and without fault, as you are commanded.
In this form the priest stands at that time,
and there is nothing to compare with the Majesty to which he draws near.
All the priests in the sanctuary bear the image
of those apostles who gathered at the tomb.
The altar is a symbol of our Lord's tomb, without doubt,
and the bread and wine are the body of our Lord that was embalmed and buried.
The veil that lies over them also depicts a type
of the stone that was sealed with the signet ring by craftsmen and soldiers.
And the deacons who stand on either side and wave fans
are a symbol of the angels at his head and at his feet.
And all the deacons who stand continually before the altar
depict a likeness of the watchers who surrounded our Lord's tomb.
The sanctuary too depicts a type of Joseph's garden,
from which life flowed out to men and to angels.
In another sense it is a type of that kingdom
which our Lord has entered, and into which he brings with him all who love him.
His adored altar is a symbol of that throne of his majestic glory,
on which he will be seen by watchers and by men on the day of his revelation.
The things below and the things above [?] are signified,
and it recalls what has been, figuring spiritually what will be.
And when the priests and deacons stand together,
they begin and recite the faith of the Fathers.

“We believe in one God, the eternal Father,
who holds all things by the hidden sign of his divinity;
who made and established all things visible and invisible,
and brought creation, height and depth, out of nothing.
And in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the Son of God,
Only-begotten in his divinity and Firstborn in his body,
who became the firstborn from the dead for all creatures;
who was begotten of his Father and is without beginning,
and was not something that came into being or was made along with creatures,
since he is God from God, Son from the Father,
of his Father's nature and equal to him in all that is his.
Through him the worlds were brought forth and all that exists was created,
and in authority, worship and glory he is equal to his Father;
who for our sake came down from heaven without change,
to redeem our race from bondage to sin and death;
and by the power of the Holy Spirit he formed a body as his temple from the daughter of David,
and became man and made his temple divine in union.
His body was conceived in the temple of Mary without wedlock,
and he was born in a way beyond human orders.
He suffered and was crucified and underwent death in his humanity,
while Pilate held the governorship.
He was in the grave three days like every dead man,
and rose and came to life again, as is written in prophecy.
He ascended on high to the heaven of heavens to fulfill all things,
and sat in glory at the right hand of the Father who sent him.
And he will come at the end of the ages to make all things new,
and to judge the living and the dead who died in sin.
And we confess also the Holy Spirit, the eternal Being,
equal in essence and divinity to the Father and the Son;
who proceeds from the Father in a manner beyond searching out,
and gives life to all rational beings who were created by him.
And we confess also one catholic Church,
apostolic and patristic, sanctified by the Spirit.
And we confess also one washing and baptism,

in which we are baptized for the forgiveness of debts and adoption as children.
And we confess also the resurrection from the dead,
and that we shall live in new life for ever and ever.”
This the three hundred and eighteen priests sealed,
and they excluded and anathematized whoever does not confess according to their confession.
The Church confesses according to the confession of the Fathers,
and at the time of the mysteries she again serves their faith.
At the time of the mysteries her children thunder out their faith,
repeating it with mouth and heart without doubt.
And when the faith has been recited in fitting order,
the herald of the Church then commands them to pray.
“Pray,” he says, “for the remembrance of the catholic Fathers
and bishops, together with the teachers,
and with them the priests and deacons and all the orders,
and everyone who has departed this world in faith,
that they may be crowned on the day of the rising from the dead,
and that we with them may inherit life in that kingdom.
Pray, my brothers, for the offering we are offering,
that it may be accepted before God, to whom it is offered,
and be sanctified by the hovering of the Holy Spirit,
so that it may become for us a cause of life in the kingdom on high.”
With these words the herald of the Church urges the people
and tells them to pray before God with a pure heart.
Then the priest offers the mystery of our redemption,
full of trembling and clothed in fear and awe.
The priest trembles and is greatly afraid and quakes exceedingly
because of his own sins and the sins of all the children of the Church.
He is the eye of the whole body of the Church,
and he keeps in mind all the needs of his fellows.
He is also the tongue of the whole body of Jesus;
he is its advocate and pleads its cause.
Trembling and fear, for himself and for his people,
fall upon the priest at that time, full of awe.

In a fearful type, in a fearful order, above the seraphim,
the son of dust stands as mediator in great fear.
Fearful is the King who was slain and buried in mystery,
and fearful are the watchers who remain in fear to honor their Lord.
The ranks of watchers surround the altar at that time,
as Chrysostom testified, who saw them.
In this meditation the priest stands to perform his priestly office,
in sorrow, in great fear and trembling.
Like Jacob he bows three times, and three times more,
and then draws near to kiss our Lord's tomb.
Jacob honored his brother Esau with bowings,
and the priest with bowings honors the Lord of Jacob.
With love and affection he kisses the holy altar,
and trusts that he will receive holiness through his lips.
He asks for the prayer of the deacons who surround him,
that through his humility he may receive mercy from the Gracious One.
Then he prays before God with an aching heart,
and confesses his own sins and the sins of the body of the Church.
The priest asks for hidden power and for help,
so that he may carry out his gift according to His will.
And to everything the priest says before God
the people assent, sealing his ministry with “Amen.”
With “Amen” the people lift their hand together with the priest,
and join with him in his prayers through their voice.
Then the priest blesses the people at that time
with that word which gives life to the mouth that has sinned.
“Peace be with you,” the priest says to the children of the Church,
for great is the peace in Jesus our Lord, who is our peace.
Peace be with you, for death has been abolished and corruption undone
through the son of our race, who suffered for us and gave life to us all.
Peace be with you, for sin has passed away and Satan has been condemned
through the son of Adam, who conquered and made the children of Adam victorious.

Peace be with you, for the good Lord has been reconciled to you
through the death of his Son, who suffered on the cross for our sake.
Peace be with you, for you have been made at peace with the angels
through him who was given authority over the angels and reigns over all.
Peace be with you, for you, the people and the nations, have been made one,
and in Jesus the dividing wall of all hostility has been broken down.
Peace be with you, for new life is kept for you
through him who became the firstborn of all creatures in incorruptible life.
Peace be with you, for you have been invited to the kingdom on high
through him who went first to prepare a place for us all.
The people answer the priest lovingly and say,
“With you, and with that priestly spirit of yours.”
By “spirit” they do not mean the soul that is in the priest,
but the Spirit which the priest received by the laying on of hands.
By the laying on of hands the priest receives the power of the Spirit,
by which he is enabled to perform the divine mysteries.
That grace the people call the priest's spirit,
and they pray that it may have peace with him, and he with it.
This shows that the priest too depends on prayer,
and it urges the whole Church to be diligent on his behalf.
Therefore they cry out that he too may have peace with his spirit,
so that through his peace alone the peace of all her children may increase.
For by his virtues he greatly profits the whole Church,
and by his faults he does great harm to the whole body.
“Peace be with you,” the people say to the splendid priest;
“may peace be won with your spirit in all your conduct.
Your peace, by which the mysteries of the Church are performed—
may peace be with your spirit, and with you, through your way of life.
Peace be with you, for great is the gift that has been given you;
may the peace of your spirit grow through your spiritual successes.”
Then the herald of the Church commands all the people
to give peace to one another in the love of our Lord.
First the priests give peace within the sanctuary,
and then the people give it in the nave in the same way.
It is fitting for whoever gives peace to his brother in the Church

to wash his heart clean of all wrath, anger and evil inclination.
This is the peace in which watchers and men will be in harmony
on the day when the glorious Bridegroom comes to judge all.
This is the peace in which there is neither deceit nor hatred,
but all of it is light upon light and perfect love.
Blessed is he who gives peace to his brother in love,
for he receives perfect peace within his mind.
Peace is the name of Christ, who reconciles all,
for it is he who made peace between the earthly and the heavenly.
Blessed is he who makes peace in his heart at the time of the mysteries,
for all his sins are forgiven him, and his hatreds too.
Here it is fitting to recall the word of the Lord
that warns us so earnestly about wrath:
“If you remember that your brother holds anger in his heart,
leave your offering and go and be reconciled to him, and then offer.”
“Go first and be reconciled to your brother,” our Lord said,
“and then offer the sacrifice you are offering.”
Even though the priest has been made mediator to offer,
he should still offer in peace with all the people.
He who offers this offering, then, is bound
to forgive the debts of his fellows, and then offer.
But if the one who holds anger against him in his heart is far away,
let him forgive his debts before God in his mind.
If the priest tramples on this command of the Lord of the worlds,
let him know that he has neither prayer nor offering.
While peace is being given in the Church from one to another,
they read the book of the two names, of the living and the dead.
The Church commemorates the dead and the living at that time,
to make known that the living and the dead benefit from the offering.
And on behalf of all the Catholics the people join in
with a response that answers what the reader of the book proclaimed:
“For all the orders who have departed from the holy Church,
and for those who have been made worthy to receive this offering,

for these, and for your servants in every place,
accept, O Lord, this offering that your servant has offered.”
Then the herald of the Church cries out and admonishes everyone
to give thanks to the Lord and to make their petitions to him with a pure heart:
“Stand well; look with your minds at what is being done;
great is the mystery at which you are ministering, O mortals.
Behold, fearful mysteries are being consecrated in the priest's hands;
let everyone be in fear and awe until they are completed.
The priest alone has now drawn near to pray;
pray with him, that your peace may increase through his mediation.
Bow the gaze of the eyes of your hearts to the ground,
and lift on high the hidden gaze of your minds.
And with earnestness ask and entreat the God of all
at this time, which is full of trembling and great fear.
Let no one dare to speak a word with his mouth,
for whoever speaks transgresses and breaks the command.
Whoever prays, let him pray in his heart and not with his lips,
and ask for mercy in his mind and not with his tongue.
Stand in stillness and in fear,
for behold, the peace that surpasses all understanding is with us.”
At this time the priest uncovers the adored mysteries,
and casts aside the veil that lies over them.
This removal does not signify the resurrection,
for even before the stone was moved the resurrection had taken place.
After the resurrection the angel [?] rolled away the stone,
and so the priests lift the veil from before his mystery.
Then, before anything else, the priest blesses the people
with that canon by which he makes his voice heard to the faithful:
“The grace of Jesus our Lord, and the love of the Father,
and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us.”
That grace which our Lord gave us through his coming—
may it give us boldness of face before his Majesty.

The love of the Father, who sent his Son to us—
may it open to us the door of mercy on the day of his coming.
The fellowship of the Holy Spirit, of which we have been made worthy—
may it sanctify us and cleanse from us the filth of our debts.
Then he carefully prepares the people and says,
“Let your minds be on high at this hour.
Where Christ the King sits at the right hand,
do not busy yourselves with hateful earthly thoughts.
Look on him who is now slain in mystery upon the altar,
who sits on high and asks mercy for sinners.”
The people answer, “To you, O Lord, our minds are lifted up,
God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the glorious King.”
The glorious King whom the righteous and the patriarchs praised,
and in whom they were glorified, and whom they praise without end.
The priest goes on: “This offering, acceptable and pure,
is now being offered to the Lord, the Lord of height and depth.
This is the Lamb who bore and still bears the sin of the world;
he is now sacrificed, to blot out and forgive your sins.
Behold, it is offered for angels and for men,
that all together may delight in it in body and soul.
Behold, it is offered for sinners and for the righteous,
that by it they may be cleansed from the stains of their sins.
Behold, it is offered for the departed and for the living,
that all the nations may find mercy through his sacrifice.
Behold, it is offered to the God of all as a pledge,
that he may deliver us from the torment of Gehenna.”
The people answer, “It is fitting and right, worthy and proper
to offer this offering on behalf of all creatures.”
Then the whole body of the Church falls silent,
and everyone sets himself to pray from the heart.
The priests are silent and the deacons stand in silence;
the whole people is calm, still and quiet.
The altar stands crowned with splendor and glory,

and on it lie the Gospel of life and the adored Cross.
The mysteries are laid out, the censers give their fragrance, the lamps shine,
and the deacons hover and wave their fans in the likeness of watchers.
Deep silence and calm peace dwell in that place;
it is full and overflowing with radiance and glory, splendor and strength.
The splendid priest, the tongue of the Church, opens his mouth,
and speaks with God in mystery as one of the household.
He recounts the glory of that Being who cannot be comprehended,
who is the cause of all things known and perceived;
who cannot be comprehended, nor searched out, nor traced,
and is not known by bodily beings nor by watchers;
one essence, one lordship, one authority,
one will that never changes from what it is;
one Creator, who by his sign established height and depth,
whose name the watchers praise on high and men in the depth;
one God, who through Moses made known that he is,
and through Jesus our Lord revealed and showed us his Trinity.
The Church has learned from our Savior three persons:
Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one Being;
three names, none of which is before or after another,
with no distinction among them except only in their properties:
fatherhood, begottenness and procession;
one will, one glory, one lordship;
a mystery wholly hidden, concealed and covered from all,
whose hiddenness the watchers bow down to marvel at.
The priest goes on to say that all the watchers stand in fear
to glorify the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
The angels too offer worship to that Majesty,
and the myriads of hosts raise glory without ceasing.
The cherubim praise, the seraphim hallow with their Holy,
and the principalities and dominions with their praises.
All of them together cry out and say to one another—
and the people answer—“Holy is the Lord, who dwells in light.”
“Holy, holy, holy Lord,” the people answer,
“of whose praises heaven and earth are full.”
This cry of “Holy” three times signifies:

while the "Lord" declares the single nature of the Self-Existent.
Holy is the Father, who possesses the property of fatherhood,
who is the cause, the Begetter, and unbegotten.
Holy is the Son, who possesses the property of sonship,
who was begotten of the Father eternally, without beginning.
Holy is the Spirit, who possesses the property of procession,
who proceeds from the Father and is beyond all times.
With these words the whole Church cries out and then turns to stillness,
and the priest bows down to converse with God.
He gives thanks for the mercy and goodness that visited us
in the one revelation of the Word, revealed in a body taken from us.
A body from us the Creator took (adored be His honor!)
to renew in it the image of Adam, which had grown old and corrupt.
The Holy Spirit built a rational temple in Mary's womb,
and by its will the whole Trinity was joined in the work.
He was laid in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes as a man,
and the Watchers praised Him with their hymns as God.
He offered sacrifices according to the law as a man,
and received worship from the Persians as God.
Simeon carried Him in his arms as a man,
and called Him the Merciful One who pities all, as God.
He kept the law perfectly as a man,
and gave His own new law as God.
He was baptized in the Jordan by John as a man,
and heaven opened to honor His baptism, as God.
He went in to the wedding feast in the town of Cana as a man,
and changed the water so that it became wine as God.
He fasted in the desert forty days as a man,
and the Watchers came down to minister to Him as God.
He slept in the boat with His disciples as a man,
and rebuked the wind and stilled the sea as God.
He went out and withdrew to a desert place as a man,

and broke bread and fed thousands to the full as God.
He ate and drank and walked and grew weary as a man,
and drove out demons by the word of His mouth as God.
He prayed and kept vigil, gave thanks and bowed down as a man,
and forgave debts and pardoned sins as God.
He asked water of the Samaritan woman as a man,
and laid bare and searched out her hidden deeds as God.
He reclined at table in the Pharisee's house as a man,
and forgave the sinful woman her sins as God.
He went up Mount Tabor with His disciples as a man,
and before their eyes revealed His glory as God.
He shed tears and wept over Lazarus as a man,
and called him, and he came forth by His great power, as God.
He rode on a colt and entered Jerusalem as a man,
and the children acclaimed Him with their hosannas as God.
He came to a fig tree and showed that He was hungry as a man,
and withered it by the quiet working of His power as God.
He washed the feet of His Twelve as a man,
and called Himself Lord and Master as God.
He ate the Passover of the law as a man,
and exposed the treachery of Iscariot as God.
He prayed and sweated at the hour of His passion as a man,
and shook and terrified those who seized Him as God.
The guards took hold of Him and bound His hands as a man,
and He healed the ear that Simon had cut off as God.
He stood in the court and endured mockery as a man,
and declared that He would come in glory as God.
He carried His cross on His shoulders as a man,
and revealed and foretold the desolation of Zion as God.
He was hung on the wood and endured suffering as a man,
and shook the earth and darkened the sun as God.
Nails were driven into His body as a man,
and He opened graves and raised the dead as God.
He cried out on the cross, "My God, my God," as a man,
and promised Paradise to the thief as God.
His side was pierced by the spear as a man,
and at His bidding the curtain before the door was torn, as God.
They embalmed His body and He was buried in the earth as a man,
and He raised up His temple by His great power as God.

He remained in the tomb three days as a man,
and the Watchers praised Him with their hymns as God.
He said that He had received all authority as a man,
and promised that He is with us for ever as God.
He bade Thomas touch His side as a man,
and gave them the Spirit as a pledge as God.
He ate and drank after His resurrection as a man,
and went up on high and sent the Spirit as God.
This, then, is the confession of the apostles and the fathers,
and whoever does not assent to their faith has no hope.
This is the truth that the fathers proclaimed and taught;
confess it with them, that you may receive life that does not die.
Our Lord Jesus has departed from us to the place above,
so that at His coming He may take us up with Him to the kingdom on high.
And since He went to a place far beyond our knowledge,
He willed to comfort us with His body and blood until His coming.
And since He could not give His own body and blood to His Church,
He commanded us to perform this mystery with bread and wine.
Blessed is the Christian people: what it possesses,
and what hope is kept for it on high, without end!
For when the time came for His passion, which gives life to all,
He ate the Passover of the law with His disciples.
He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to His disciples,
and said, "This is My body," in truth, without division.
And He took the cup, gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to His apostles,
and said, "This is My true blood, which is for you."
And He commanded them all to take and drink of it,
that it might be atonement for their debts for ever.
That He gave thanks and blessed is written in the Gospel, the word of life,
but what He said, the chosen apostles did not make known to us.
Theodore, greatest of teachers and interpreters,
handed down thus what our Lord said when He took the bread:
"Of all glories, all thanksgivings and all praises
the nature of Your Godhead is worthy, O Lord of all,

for in every generation You have fulfilled and accomplished Your dispensation
for the life and salvation of humankind.
And though they were exceedingly unjust in their deeds,
You in Your mercy did not neglect to help them.
And to accomplish the salvation of all and the renewal of all,
You took me from the nature of Adam and joined me to Yourself.
In me all promises and all counsels will be accomplished,
and in me the mysteries and types given to the righteous will be fulfilled.
And since I became blameless and fulfilled all righteousness,
through me You uproot all sin from humanity.
And since I died without guilt and without fault,
through me You decree the resurrection of the body for all nature."
With this intent the Son of Mary gave thanks to His Father,
and spoke these words as He gave His body and blood:
"This indeed is My body, which I have given for the debts of the world,
and this again is My blood, which I willed to be shed for sins.
Whoever eats of My body in love and drinks of My blood
lives for ever and abides in Me, and I in him.
Thus you shall do in remembrance of Me in your churches,
and you shall receive My body and My blood in faith.
Bread and wine you shall offer, as I have taught you,
and I will perfect them and make them body and blood.
Body and blood I make them, the bread and the wine,
through the hovering and working of the Holy Spirit."
Thus spoke the Life-giver of the worlds to His disciples,
and He called the bread and the wine His body and His blood.
He did not call them a type, nor a likeness of death,
but body in reality and blood in truth.
And though their nature is far removed from Him who is beyond all measure,
yet in power and in union it is one body.
Watchers and men confess You, my Lord, faithfully,
O Christ our hope, who gave Yourself up for our sake.

One in power is the body that the priests break in the church
with that body which sits in glory at the right hand.
And as God united to Himself the firstfruits of our race,
so Christ unites to Himself the bread and wine upon the altar.
Therefore the bread is truly the body of our Lord,
and the wine is His blood, in the Lord's own way and in truth.
Thus He commanded the children of His mystery to eat His body,
and thus He charged the children of His house to drink His blood.
Blessed is the one who believes in Him and trusts His word,
for if he dies he will live, and if he lives he will not die in his faults.
The apostles received their Lord's command with care,
and they diligently handed it on to those who came after them.
To this day it has been kept in the church, and it is still kept,
until He brings His mystery to rest at His dawning and revelation.
With this intent the priest gives thanks before God,
and at the end of his prayer raises his voice for the people to hear.
He makes his voice heard and with his hand signs the mysteries that are laid out,
and the people join in with "Amen," sealing the priest's prayer.
Then the herald of the church commands the people, saying,
"Be praying in your minds; peace be with us."
In mind and thought they should be intent at this time,
for behold, a great peace is being accomplished in the completion of the mysteries.
The priest begins to entreat earnestly before God
that in His love He may be pleased with the living sacrifice offered to Him.
He sets out the orders of the church one after another,
on whose behalf the church offers the adored mysteries.
He remembers first the glorious Church in every place,
and asks that they be of one mind and one faith.
He remembers the priests, the visitors and the ministers,
and pleads that they may live in holiness and purity.
He remembers the martyrs, the confessors and the teachers,
that their names may be commemorated in the church at the time of the mysteries.
He remembers the kings and judges in every place,
that they may judge uprightly throughout the world.
He remembers in his words all who mourn and the humble,
that their prayer may be accepted every day before God.

He remembers the upright and the righteous in every place,
and asks that they keep perfectly the covenant they have taken up.
He remembers the children of the holy Church in all their ranks,
and asks that they keep their faith with care.
He remembers too the departed in every place,
who died and passed on in the faith without division.
He remembers himself, who has been made worthy of this mediation,
and asks mercy for all creatures in humility.
He remembers those who give alms generously to the poor,
and asks that they receive a double reward for their almsgiving.
He remembers the fallen, the sinners and the wrongdoers,
and asks that they turn to repentance and the pardon of debts.
He remembers those for whom he offers the sacrifices,
that they may find grace and forgiveness of the debts of their faults.
He remembers the pagans, the unbelievers and those who stray,
and pleads that they may come to know the faith of the holy Church.
He remembers the whole world together and its inhabitants,
that wars, demons and upheavals may cease from it.
He remembers the air and the seasons of the whole year,
and asks that the crown of the year be abundant and blessed.
He remembers his own land and all lands together,
and asks that there be peace and tranquility in their dwellings.
He remembers those who travel the seas and the islands,
and asks that all of them be delivered from storms.
He remembers those cast into afflictions and persecutions,
and asks that there be relief and rest from their oppressions.
He remembers those cast into prison and in chains,
and asks that they be freed from chains and cruel fetters.
He remembers those sent into exile far away,
and asks that they escape from hardships and from trials.
He remembers those who labor in sicknesses and pains,
and pleads that they gain bodily health together with healing.
He remembers those whom accursed demons torment,
and asks that they find grace and mercy from the Lord.
He remembers in his words also the adversaries of the holy Church,
that there may be pardon for their faults before God.
He remembers the debts of the whole body of the Church,

and asks that they be made worthy of the forgiveness of debts and faults.
All these the priest remembers before God,
likening himself by his supplication to Mar Barsamya.
With this intent the priest prays before God,
and asks Him to be pleased with the sacrifice he offers Him.
In place of everything that is sacrificed is the living sacrifice within the church,
and this offering helps and profits all creatures.
By that supplication which the priest makes for all the ranks,
all his own sins and faults are forgiven him.
After these things the priest gives thanks before God,
as our Lord Jesus taught His Twelve.
"Behold, we commemorate in mystery," says the priest, "and we remember
the passion and death and also the resurrection of our Lord Jesus."
These things the priest says softly [?] and with humility,
and he draws himself up to his full height and spreads his hands toward heaven.
Toward heaven the priest gazes with boldness,
and calls on the Spirit to come and complete the mysteries he has offered.
He asks the Spirit to come and hover over the offering,
and bestow on it divine power and efficacy.
The Spirit descends at the priest's entreaty, even if he is a sinner,
and completes the mysteries through the mediation of the priest who consecrates.
It is not the priest's purity that completes the adored mysteries,
but the Holy Spirit completes them by His hovering.
The Spirit hovers not because of the priest's worthiness,
but because of the mysteries laid upon the altar.
As soon as the bread and wine are laid upon the altar,
the mystery depicts the death of the Son and also His resurrection.
Therefore the Spirit who raised Him from the grave
descends now and completes the mysteries of the resurrection of His body.
Thus the Holy Spirit accomplishes them by the hands of the priest,
and without a priest they are never, for ever and ever, completed.
The mysteries of the church are not completed apart from a priest,
for the Holy Spirit has not permitted anyone else to complete them.
The power of the Spirit the priest received through the laying on of hands,
and by it all the mysteries within the church are fulfilled.

The priest sanctifies the womb of the waters of baptism,
and the Spirit bestows the adoption of sons on those who are baptized.
Without a priest a woman is not betrothed to a man,
and without him their wedding is not completed.
Without a priest even the departed is not shrouded,
and he is not lowered into his grave without a priest.
Unclean waters are not sanctified without a priest,
and if there is no priest, the whole house becomes unclean.
These things the Holy Spirit accomplishes by the hands of the priest,
even though he be wholly given to debts and faults.
When priests perform them, they complete them, even if they are sinners;
those who do not hold the rank cannot complete them, however upright they are.
The righteous do not bring down the Spirit by their purity,
nor do sinners by their sinfulness hold back His descent.
Here [?] the Spirit is long-suffering toward the priest who sins,
and by his hand completes the glorious, ineffable mysteries.
In the world to come He will judge him severely,
and take from him that gift which was given him.
And whoever did not honor the greatness of his rank as befitted it
will be despised there and become a laughingstock before all creatures.
Hear, O priest who has no deeds that match his rank,
and tremble and fear the torment in Gehenna.
Of every stern reckoning you will be required, sinful priest,
because you did not serve the rank that came to you as was due.
In the world to come there are neither ranks nor measures,
but Christ alone is all in all.
The priest invites the Spirit, and He descends upon the offering,
and the priest bows down with trembling and fear and awful dread.
Then the herald of the church cries out at that moment:
"Stand in silence and fear; peace be with us."
In fear let the whole people be at this moment,
in which the adored mysteries are fulfilled by the descent of the Spirit.

Then the priest makes his voice heard by all the people,
and signs with his hand over the mysteries, as before.
He signs them now not because the mysteries need the sign,
but to teach by this final sign that they are complete.
Three signs the priest makes over the offering,
and by them he completes and fulfills it in mystery.
Three bows the priest makes before God,
and in them he worships with boldness before His majesty.
In one he praises, in one he gives thanks, and in one he prays,
and calls on the Spirit to dwell upon the offering and overshadow it.
Three days our Lord remained in the womb of the earth,
and on the third He rose and was raised in great glory.
In its likeness the priest bows three times,
and by the third he signifies the resurrection of our Lord Jesus.
The priest also kneels three times,
and by these he depicts our Lord's stay in the tomb.
Three times he kneels before the descent,
and then kneels no more, since the mystery of the resurrection has been fulfilled for him.
The mystery of the resurrection the priest completes in the completion of the mysteries,
and no longer signifies the mystery of His death by kneeling.
The three hundred and eighteen priests laid down a command
that on Sundays and on all feasts there is no kneeling.
Therefore no one is permitted to kneel during the mysteries
except the priest, who by his kneeling depicts the mystery.
And even the priest may kneel before the descent,
but after the descent of the Holy Spirit he may not kneel.
Then the priest lifts the living bread in his hands,
and raises his gaze toward heaven and gives thanks to his Lord.
He breaks the bread in the name of the Father and the Son and the Spirit,
and unites the blood with the body and the body with the blood.
He signs the blood with the body, making mention of the Trinity,
and signs the body with the living blood with the same invocation.
And he unites them, the body with the blood and the blood with the body,
so that everyone may confess that the body and blood are one.
Then the priest, once all the rites have been completed,

blesses the people with the very words with which our Lord blessed.
Then he begins to break the body with his hands,
