so that it may be ready to be shared among all who receive it.
The priest signified the resurrection of the Son in the completion of the mysteries,
and now he duly breaks His body so as to distribute it.
For our Lord too, when He had risen from the tomb in glory,
appeared to the women and the disciples ten times:
once to Mary Magdalene alone,
and once to Luke and Cleopas as they walked on the road,
and once to the company of the Eleven in the upper room,
and another time by the sea of Tiberias.
To all of them He appeared and assured them of the resurrection,
and to Thomas too He showed His side, the place of the spear.
And on the Mount of Olives our Lord blessed His Eleven,
and parted from them and went up in glory to the heaven of heavens.
And now He is seen by the children of the Church in the medicine of His body,
and they believe in Him and receive from Him the pledge of life.
Then the herald of the church cries out and raises his voice,
that we all may approach in fear the mystery of the body and blood.
In faith let us remember the passion of Jesus our Lord,
and take comfort also in His resurrection from the dead.
For our sake the Only-begotten of the God of all
took a perfect man and accomplished His dispensation.
He suffered on the cross, died, was raised, rose and ascended,
and in His love gave us [His body] and His blood as a pledge,
that by them we may remember all the benefits He has done for us,
and confess, worship and praise Him at all times.
Let us, then, with pure love and faith
draw near to receive the treasure of spiritual life.
And with one pure and clean prayer and contrition of heart
let us partake of the adored mysteries of the holy Church.
Let us lay the sighs of repentance before God,
and grieve and sorrow over the loathsome deeds we have done.

Let us ask mercy and forgiveness of debts from the Lord of all,
and let us too forgive the faults of our companions.
The people answer: "Lord, pardon the sins of Your servants,
and cleanse our conscience of division and quarrels.
Lord, pardon the faults of those who praise You,
and purify our soul of hatred and slander.
Lord, pardon the sins of Your servants who confess Your name,
and make us worthy to receive this holy thing in faith.
Lord, pardon Your servants who call on Your name every day,
and grant us, Lord, to be Yours according to Your will.
And may these divine mysteries be for us, my Lord,
boldness and openness of face before Your majesty."
Then the priest prays and asks of God
that He sanctify us and blot out our sins in His goodness,
and make us all worthy to stand before Him blameless,
and all to call Him with boldness, "Abba, our Father."
Then the people answer and say earnestly
the prayer that His living mouth taught the children of His love:
"Our Father, who dwells above in heaven and in every place,
hallowed be Your holy name among us by all peoples.
Your kingdom come to us, the kingdom You promised us,
and may it grow sweet to us through its pledge from this time on.
May Your loving will come to be, rest and be fulfilled in us,
and may we be worthy to do all things according to Your will.
And as in heaven all other wills cease from us [?],
so on earth may Your will alone be pleasing.
Give us bread and every bodily need
in this time of our sojourn in this world.
And forgive our debts and pardon our sins, in which we have sinned
through our slackness, our passions and our weakness.
For we too have forgiven from our heart all who are in our debt,
and we keep no grudge in our heart against anyone.
And do not bring us into temptation or into trial,
for we are weak, and without Your power we are nothing."

"But deliver us from the wickedness of the crafty Evil One, / and do not let him come near us through his wiles.
For yours is the power and the kingdom also, / and to you praise is due for ever and ever."
Then the priest says to the people, "Peace be with you," / and the people answer, "And with you, O priest, and with your spirit."
With our Lord's Prayer the priest begins at the start of the mysteries, / and with it again he concludes, now that all the mysteries are completed.
"Peace be with you," says the priest at this moment, / and he calls to our mind the resurrection of our Lord from the house of the dead.
"Peace be with you," said our Lord to his Twelve, / when he appeared to them and brought them the good news of his resurrection.
"Peace be with you," said our Lord to the children of his mystery, / "for see, I am risen, and I raise up all of nature."
"Peace be with you," he said to his brothers, his close companions, / "for see, I am going up, and I am preparing a place for you all."
"Peace be with you," said our Lord to the Twelve, / "for I am with you until the age that has no end."
And this peace the priest gives to the children of the Church, / and he confirms them in love and hope and faith.
And when the children of the Church have made ready to receive the mysteries, / the priest cries out, "The holy thing is fitting for the holy."
For all the holy, sanctified by the Spirit who established adoption as sons, / holiness is fitting, according to the tradition of the fathers.
For all the holy whom baptism has sanctified, / holiness is fitting, according to the law of the Church.
Other bands, those who have been driven out of the Church, / shall have no share in receiving the divine mysteries.
The people answer, "One is the holy Father, / who exists for ever, without beginning and without end.
And he has made us worthy to acquire holiness by grace / through the spiritual birth of baptism.
One is the Father, and one also the Son and the Holy Spirit, / one in three and three without change.
Glory to the Father, and to the Son who is from him, and to the Holy Spirit,

the Eternal Being, who exists for ever and ever without end."
Then the priest himself is the first to receive the holy thing, / to teach the people that the priest too stands in need of mercy.
The priest who has consecrated needs to receive the adorable mysteries, / so that he too may be made worthy of a share in the pledge of life.
The priest goes before the bishop in receiving the mysteries, / if it was the priest who consecrated them and not the high priest.
Then, one from the hand of another, the priests and ministers receive, / and after them the people, men and women, small and great.
And as he comes out, the priest blesses the people and says, / "The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you."
The holy thing comes out on the paten, and the cup, with splendour and glory, / attended by priests and in a great procession of ministers.
Thousands of Watchers and ministers of fire and spirit / go out before the body of our Lord and escort it in splendour.
All the children of the Church and all the people rejoice / when they see the body coming out from within the sanctuary.
And as the apostles rejoiced in our Lord after his resurrection, / so all the faithful rejoice when they see it.
Great, my brothers, is this mystery, beyond all speech; / whoever finds himself equal to it, let him tell it, if he is able.
"My secret is mine, my secret is mine," cried Isaiah, amazed at the cherubim, / at the divine revelation he saw in the temple.
If I wished to write anything about this field, / all the papyrus in all this world would not suffice me.
For the perfect and the mature, meat is fitting; / for infants, milk, until they reach maturity.
"Whoever eats my body abides in me, and I in him, / if he keeps all my commandments with care."
"Whoever eats my body and drinks my blood while unworthy / eats and drinks to his own condemnation, without profit."

The one who comes forward to receive the body stretches out his hands, / raising his right hand and placing it upon its fellow.
In the form of a cross the receiver crosses his hands, / and so he receives the body upon a cross.
Upon the cross our Lord Jesus was mocked, / and by that same cross he flew up and was raised to the height above.
In this form the one who receives comes forward to receive, / and the priest who gives says to him, "The body of our Lord."
He receives in his hands the adorable body of the Lord of all, / and he embraces it and kisses it with love and affection.
He hides the leaven of life within the temple of his body, / so that his body may be sanctified by receiving the body of our Lord.
It pardons his sins, cleanses his blemishes, heals his sicknesses, / and washes and scours his stains with the hyssop of its mercies.
And while the body and blood are being distributed to all who receive, / the Church cries out in honour of the mysteries and says these things:
"Behold the medicine of life, behold, it is distributed in the holy Church! / Come, you mortals, take, and be pardoned of your sins.
This is the body and the blood of our Lord in truth, / which the nations have received and by which they have been pardoned without distinction.
This is the medicine that heals sicknesses and festering sores; / take, you mortals, and be cleansed by it of your sins.
Come, take freely forgiveness for offences / in the body and blood that bear the sin of the whole world."
And once the whole assembly has shared in the body and blood, / they go on to say with joy and gladness:
"Our Lord Jesus, King adored by all creatures, / take away from us all harms by the power of your mysteries.
And when you shine forth at the end of the ages for the salvation of all, / may we go out to meet you with boldness and with hosannas.
And we will give thanks to your name for your grace toward our race, / for you have pardoned our sins and blotted them out by your body and your blood.
Both here and there may we be found worthy to offer up to your divinity

fitting glory with thanksgiving for ever and ever."
Then the herald of the Church cries out in his proclamation, / and urges the people to give thanks, and speaks thus:
"All of us who have been made worthy of the gift of the mysteries, / let us give thanks and worship and praise the God of all."
And the people answer, "To him be praise for his gift, / which can never be repaid, for ever and ever, amen and amen."
Then the priest prays and gives thanks to the God of all, / who has made our race worthy of the glorious mysteries beyond all speech.
And he asks and entreats that he strengthen us to be pleasing before him / in thoughts and words alike, and in deeds.
Then the prayer which that life-giving mouth taught / all pray together, in the sanctuary and outside it, in the congregation.
With it they begin every prayer, morning and evening, / and with it they conclude all the mysteries of the holy Church.
For this is the prayer that embraces all prayer, / and without it no prayer at all is complete.
Then he comes out and stands at the door of the sanctuary, / and stretches out his hands and blesses the people, saying...
The priest blesses the whole people at that moment / after the pattern in which our Lord Jesus blessed his Twelve.
On the day of his ascension the great High Priest raised his hands, / and blessed and ordained his Twelve, and so was taken up.
The mystery of his resurrection the priest signifies at the completion of the mysteries, / and the mystery of his appearing before his disciples in their distribution.
Stretching out his hands, the radiant priest, facing the height, / pours out blessing upon the whole assembly and speaks thus:
"He who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heaven, / may he now also bless us all by the power of his mysteries."
By this blessing with which the radiant priest blesses us, / he portrays the mystery of what is destined to awaken us.
When we have risen from the house of the dead and have been clothed anew, / we shall be raised up to heaven with the Saviour.
There all sufferings will cease from our humanity,

and we shall delight in longed-for blessings without end.
In this world, where we dwell amid every suffering, / may he guard our lives from harms both hidden and open.
And as he has made us worthy to receive his mysteries by his grace, / may he make us all worthy to become temples for his divinity.
And with every breath let us give thanks and worship and praise him / for his gift, which the tongue of flesh cannot tell.
Upon us the radiant priest pours out his blessings, / and with his right hand he signs the assembly with the living seal.
These are the glorious mysteries of the holy Church, / and this is the order by which they are performed by the priesthood.
Blessed is the one whose heart is pure at that moment / when the awesome mysteries of our Lord's body are consecrated.
The Watchers on high call the children of the Church blessed, / who have been made worthy to receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus.
Glory to your name for your gift beyond all speech! / And who is able to repay glory worthy of your divinity?
Come, then, O child of the mystery, one of the children of the Church, / learn the order by which you should draw near to the priesthood,
so that you do not draw near [?], as the apostle Paul has ruled. / With a pure heart draw near to the body and blood of our Lord, / which pardon you of the stains of the sins you have committed.
They do not turn away from the sinner who wishes to repent, / nor from the defiled one who mourns and grieves over his defilement.
On this condition they receive the defiled and the sinners: / that they make a covenant not to return to their former deeds.
Pray with the priest in love at that moment,

for the One who receives you gives life and forgives sins.
Take care, then, that you do not go out of the sanctuary / at that moment when the awesome mysteries are consecrated.
Who is this who would willingly make himself a stranger / to that banquet to which Watchers and human beings are invited?
Who is this who, though placed among the portion of sons, / sets himself among the strangers whom the Church has driven out?
This is the time when one ought to stand like the angels, / at that moment when the Holy Spirit overshadows.
This moment gives life to the one who stands within it; / this moment distributes gifts to the one who receives it.
Blessed is the one who believes in it and receives from it, / for if he dies he lives, and if he lives he will not die in his offences.
Thus far our ship has reached the harbour, and our net is full; / so let us fall silent, for what it has gathered was our aim.
I confessed from the start: do not condemn my weakness for its lapses; / and now, in love, pass lightly over my shortcomings, if you find any.
Glory to your name, for you have completed with us what began with you, / and thanksgiving to your Father and to the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.
Wednesday of the Passion (Holy Wednesday)

Yilēh kad dilēh [?]. / Memra twenty-seven. / And again, for Wednesday of the Passion, an antiphon [?]: Blessed is he who by his own slaying slew sin, / and by his humility calmed the wraths. / My brothers.

A human being is a vessel of clay
in which a treasure of life is placed.
The greatness is not its own,
but belongs to the power of its maker.
In a lowly vessel are stored
the precious things of the house of Adam,
and though it is very lowly in its nature,
glorious things are kept within it.
In a vessel of [?] that was broken
are stored treasures for mortals,
and in a body that brings forth sufferings
dwelt the Being who does not suffer.
Lowly clay is a human being,
and lowly in his nature like clay;
yet that he might become a dwelling for his Creator,
He made him a precious vessel.
Glorious and beautiful was his fashioning,
though he was utterly of dust.
But whoever heard the words of his deceiver

despised the lowliness of his own nature.
[...] it did not please the Creator
that the Evil One should [?] His fashioning,
lest the envious one should boast
that by his power he had overcome Adam.
He took up the vessel that had been corrupted,
of the earth of mortal Adam,
and kneaded it with the Spirit instead of water,
that its fashioning might be firm.
Because death had broken its nature
and corrupted the beauty of its form,
He cast it in a spiritual furnace,
that it might not be ruined by sin again.
The Creator took up His image
and made it a temple and dwelt in it,
so that the envious one, who had defiled
the temple of the King, might not have dominion.
One from the race of mortals
the Being chose for Himself and dwelt in him,
and by the composition of his fashioning
He bound His love to creation.
From the clay of the house of Adam
He composed an image like Adam,
and perfected it through mortal sufferings
by the power of His Godhead.
By the power of the Spirit He kneaded it,
without the seed of union,
that it might resemble in everything
Adam, the first image;
so that, just as through Adam
death entered and corrupted his race,
through Adam, the second image,
those held captive might be set free from death.
In all the things of Adam
the man, the second Adam, shared,
and since he was subjected to sufferings,
he redeemed mortals from death.
Nine months, as is the order of nature,
he dwelt in a womb of flesh,
and in the pangs and sufferings of birth
he came forth from the womb of her who bore him.
He sucked milk like an infant,
to show that he was of our race;
and he offered sacrifices like everyone,
that he might repay goodness in return.
Circumcision was laid upon his body,
that the promise might be confirmed in him,
that the nations should become heirs
to the abundance of Abraham's blessings.
He was brought up as a child,
for he was truly a child,
and through the power of grace
he advanced step by step to perfection.
He drew near to baptism in water
to tread a path for his fellow mortals;
and while he was pure in his own person,
by his baptism he purified the unclean in his person.
With him from the beginning was
the only Word of the Father;
with him it was, and in him it dwelt,
and it did not share in the humiliations.
He in his nature was growing
in wisdom and in grace,
while the Being in His own nature remained
without change or alteration.
Among men he lived his life,
the man, the second Adam,
to turn men from their error
toward the counsel of life which they had lost.
He healed the pains of the body
without human medicines,
and cleansed the blemishes of the soul
by the power of the Holy Spirit.
With clay he opened the eyes
of those whose sight was blinded,
and from the garments that were on his limbs
the stricken woman gained healing.
He gave limbs to the lame
and steps to the paralysed;
he opened stopped ears,
and they heard the sweetness of his words.
He drove out visible pains
and healed hidden sins,
and by the visible he showed
that he had authority over the hidden.
With his voice he commanded death

to give back the dead it had swallowed,
and at the seal of his words
the dead returned to life.
The dead who were raised became
true witnesses to him of the sign,
crying out about the resurrection,
that henceforth death is abolished.
Demons he drove out by his word,
to remove them from their dwellings,
while the rebels cried out to him,
"Do not torment us, Son of David."
Even they, though unwilling,
proclaimed his authority beforehand:
that he would call hidden things to account
in the just judgment of his testing.
By healing the body he showed
that he also heals the sins of man,
and by the three dead whom he raised
he proclaimed resurrection to the broken.
By the demons he drove out of men
he dissolved the authority of the deceiver,
and turned back the captives of the captor
by the man whom he rescued from his hands.
The envious one cried out and was embittered;
he shrieked and wailed with weeping
that a mighty man had gone out to battle
to take away the captives of the captor.
The tyrant gathered the forces of his dominion
against the Victor,
supposing that he would overcome,
through death, the one who gives life to the dead.
In the battle against Adam
the serpent put on armour and fought,
and now against our Saviour
he fought through Adam with Adam.
The children of Abraham, who had been freed
from slavery to the Egyptians,
became weapons for the deceiver;
he put them on and fought against our Lord.
At the feast of Passover the tyrant stirred up
the labourers he had chosen for himself,
so that the insolent might help him
with the swords of their tongues.
The children of Aram became labourers
for the deceiver against Adam,
and he fulfilled his desire by their hands
as by the serpent against Adam.
It was not his will
that he should be brought to death at the feast;
it was Christ who fulfilled in deed
the dispensation of his humanity.
At the feast he gave himself as a sacrifice,
that many might see his death,
so that when he was raised from the tomb
they might be witnesses of his resurrection.
For the Passover sacrifice was prepared
the living Lamb of God,
that through the sacrifice of his own person
he might reconcile the world with its Lord.
He kept the Passover according to the Law,
and by the Passover revealed his own Passover.
He divided his body among his disciples,
a pledge of life for mortals.
By deed he showed his love,
the son of Adam, for the sons of his race,
in giving his body as food
before the suffering of his crucifixion.
He prophesied what was to come,
his suffering and his humiliation,
and revealed and disclosed his betrayal,
that Judas would hand over his master.
By the power of the Spirit he was strengthened
against the wickedness of the insolent one,
yet the bitterness of that man was not dulled
by the sweetness of the mystery he received.
He made him a partaker in the mystery,
yet he did not turn from his murderous thought.
The Giver of life to all washed his feet,
and the wicked one was not shamed.
The deceiver was known to him,
even before he chose him, as a murderer;
yet he sheltered him with his kindly love
and did not expose his deceit.
By night the false one went out
to hand over his master to the insolent,
for the deceiver was urging him on
to accomplish his will by his hands.

The envious one had longed to kill him
from the day of his birth,
and through Judas as a go-between
he brought his intention into the open.
Judas became like a messenger
for the Accuser, the envious one,
and he sent the band of the insolent
to hunt down the Life for death.
For a price the thief sold him
who buys back the worlds from death.
He took his price, a price that would strangle him,
and sold the Life to the house of the dead.
O seller of the Life to death,
who did not consider whom he was selling!
He gave a gift beyond compare
and took a contemptible price.
For thirty pieces of silver he sold
the liberator of our nature,
and the word of the prophet was fulfilled,
who saw it in the Spirit generations before.
The Giver of life to all fulfilled
all things in his own person, for the sake of all.
He prophesied his humiliation
and the disposition of his disciples:
"All of you will stumble
when the time of suffering draws near,
and you will leave me alone
and not stand firm in my afflictions."
In his love Simon boasted,
and said to our Lord,
"Never will I deny you,
nor will I weaken before sufferings."
With an "Amen" the Giver of life to all sealed his answer
to the boast of the ardent one:
"Three times you will falter
in denial at the time of suffering."
He showed his disciples
that he bore suffering by his own will,
and that he was not forced
toward the humiliation of the cross.
"Rise, let us go," he said,
when the time of suffering drew near,
making known that by his own will
he gave himself up to his persecutors.
He went out to pray alone,
and took his disciples with him,
to teach them by his prayer
that in affliction they would need mercy.
Three times he prayed in suffering,
and this he said in his prayer:
"If it is possible, let me not drink
the cup of all-swallowing death."
In suffering our Saviour prayed,
before his suffering, as one who suffers,
and drops of sweat gathered on his limbs
from his fearful anguish.
There appeared to him from heaven
an angel to strengthen him,
that he might not weaken in the contest
whose victory he would win.
With words full of encouragement
the angel strengthened him:
"[...] the cup of death gives you
a crown after your victory.
Do not weaken in weaknesses,
you who are of flesh, of the race of Adam,
for the cross brings you to glories
at the end of your contest.
Bear sufferings, you who suffer,
and drink the cup of the house of Adam,
for you will be exalted to the height
after suffering and humiliation."
Let the erring now come,
the Eutychians and the Manichaeans,
and show how they explain
the prayer and the suffering: whose are they?
Who is it that prayed before the suffering,
O wise man lacking understanding?
And whom did the encouragement strengthen?
Reveal and disclose your understanding to me.
Ignorant one, as you suppose,
you are rising to the height above,
yet your blasphemy subjects to suffering
the Being, the Word from the Father.
O unspeakable blasphemy!
O iniquity not to be forgiven!
That the Fearsome One who holds creation
they make weak in the contest!
O insolent will,
how far it has dared and gone astray,
that He who made His angels spirits

should be strengthened by a Watcher!
Why would the Word pray,
or was he deprived of [...] comfort,
he who possesses authority in his being
in the likeness of the Father who begot him?
How could he lose through sufferings
that power which bears all [?]?
And from whom would he ask help,
he, the giver of good things?
Who helped him in creating
when he brought everything into being,
that now in the suffering of the crucified
he should call an angel to his help?
Spare us your blasphemies, insolent one;
we have no need of your interpretations.
Our confession is a good seed;
do not mix your tares into it.
Do not subject the Word of the Father
to the sufferings that mortals incur,
nor make the Only-begotten [?]
for the help of his own creature.
Who has spoken iniquity like this?
Who has dared error like this,
that the power which strengthens encouragers
they think was weak on the cross?
Do not err, insolent ones;
the Word was in no way less than his Father,
nor did the Creator ask for help
from a spiritual being.
It was a bodily one who prayed,
one who needed help;
a sufferer who feared sufferings,
for sufferings accompany his nature.
The son of our race was entreating
for himself and his companions,
for he knew that help would come to him
at the time of suffering.
He it is who feared suffering,
for his nature was seen to be mortal,
and for this reason the angel strengthened him
at the time of suffering.
In truth he prayed and feared,
and not falsely, in appearance only;
and in truth the angel strengthened him,
without pretence [?].
If he did not pray in truth,
then he was not a man,
and then our trust is vain.
Do not drown, insolent ones,
our nature in the abyss of death!
Let our hope be exalted
in honour with the son of our race.
The sufferer prayed in suffering,
and the Being accepted his petition,
and he handed himself over to his captors
to fulfil the will of his Father.
The band of the insolent arrived,
with Judas as their guide,
and he drew near and greeted the Gracious One,
and the deceiver kissed the Kind One.
O false disciple!
O friend whose love was deceit,
who carried a sword in his mind
and kisses on his lips!
Because of what he brought he spoke to him,
for he called him a lying friend:
"Do what you will, insolent one;
why do you kiss me in pretence?
With a kiss do you betray me,
a disciple selling his master?
Why do you cover with a greeting
the sword hidden in your mind?"
"Whom do you seek?" he said
with power to the band of the insolent,
and he threw them to the ground
to show the strength of his greatness.
The disciples took up swords
when they saw [...] the insolent,
and Simon the zealous rushed forward
as if to fulfil his promise.
He cut off an ear, thinking
he was fulfilling his love for his master.
But the All-knowing turned to him:
"Enough; your help suffices."
The Kind One showed his love,
as befitted his coming,
and put the ear back upon the body,
yet the band of the insolent was not ashamed.
They dragged him off to the court and went,
to have him questioned as a guilty man,
and his disciples left him and fled

and did not stay with him in his suffering.
Simon followed after him
to see the outcome of his trial.
His love drew the zealous one,
and he went in with his master to the court.
Those present asked the perfect one,
"Are you not also a disciple?"
His ardour had cooled [?],
and he forgot all his promises.
Fear of death shook
that head of the Twelve,
and he faltered and his will was overcome
in denial three times.
At dawn our Saviour looked at him
as he came out of the court,
and with his look he rebuked him:
"Where is your boasting, zealous one?"
Simon groaned and remembered
how his master had reminded him of his promise,
that he had promised, "I will not deny,"
and then swore, "I do not know him."
The Master did not hold [?] the folly
against the head of the disciples,
for this was why he let him falter,
that his word might be fulfilled.
The foundation stone of his teaching
he made head of the apostles,
and by his denial and his repentance
he trod a path for the lost.
Before Pilate they set
the innocent one as a guilty man,
inciting the judge against him,
that he wished to seize the kingship.
And about this Pilate
questioned him as he judged him:
"Are you a king, as they say,
the sons of your people and your fellows?"
But he gave no answer,
for silence befitted his humiliation,
that his word might be fulfilled in deed,
that he did not open his mouth in his humiliation.
Before Pilate they were crying out,
the wicked sons of Abraham:
"Crucify him, who is guilty of death,
who has stirred up our people and shaken it!"
The judge, who was not of the people,
acquitted him and cried that he was innocent,
while the people who knew God
covered up justice with a lie.
The wicked took his blood upon themselves,
to be required of them,
for they had made it a cause for his murder,
for which their children would be held guilty.
The judge washed his hands
and declared himself clean of his murder.
The wicked led him away and went out
to torment him on the cross.
They devised a deceitful plan
with their master, the Accuser:
that he deserved to die on the cross
as one who had transgressed the Law.
They arranged it with robbers,
so that the insolent might [?] him,
that the onlookers, seeing him,
would count him among the wicked.
On top of the wood they fixed him,
to be a spectacle for onlookers.
Yet he for his part was fulfilling all,
and openly proclaiming his death.
By the priests he was mocked
and by the people he was derided,
he who was the dwelling of the Godhead.
And the Godhead was shaking
creation over his humiliation.
Heaven and earth and all that is in them
put on garments of mourning
for that holy body
which was being tormented by the unclean.
The sun set and shrouded its light,
and the moon was turned to blood,
so that the wicked might not take pleasure

in the beauty of their light.
An earthquake made the earth tremble,
splitting rocks and stones,
as the silent things rebuked
the hard heart of the insolent.
The Spirit tore the front of the gate
and dishonoured the temple of atonement,
showing that he was forsaking and leaving it,
for he tore the garment of its holiness.
The tombs of the righteous were opened,
for the command shook them,
that the dead might be heralds
of the resurrection of the one who gives life to the dead.
With nails the insolent destroyed
the [?] which the Word had composed for himself,
and the Word shook the silent things,
that they might join the speaking in judging them.
In the midst of robbers they fixed him,
as a doer of evil deeds,
and unwillingly they sealed
the fullness of prophecy.
The robber on the right
wonder drew to repentance,
and he rebuked his companion
to keep him from his blasphemy.
With words full of groaning
the robber made his entreaty,
asking for forgiveness,
that he might be granted mercy on the day of judgment.
With the hidden eye of his mind
he saw the kingdom of heaven,
and to our Lord he said,
"Make me worthy to see your kingdom."
O wonder, that through a robber
it was told to the earthly
that of one crucified, who was crucified with him,
he was asking for the kingdom!
Yet the Giver of life to all did not deny
the robber the reward for his words;
he turned and gave him a recompense,
the kingdom in return for confession.
By deed he fulfilled for him
what he had confessed to him:
he brought him in with him, by his soul,
into Paradise at the time of his death.
O wonder at Golgotha,
spoken through a mortal:
that the body fixed on the cross
was treading the way to Eden!
O dead one whose death proclaimed
the life of the dead to the departed!
O bound one who on top of the wood
loosed the bonds of sin!
In the sufferings of death was suffering
the body, the garment of the Only-begotten,
yet he did not leave it or depart from it,
even at the time of his humiliation.
To him the mortal one committed his soul
when it grieved him:
"Into your hands I place my soul";
he turned it toward its dwelling in peace.
He bowed his head on the cross
and handed over his soul to the Creator,
bearing witness, by the departure of his soul,
that his death was not under compulsion.
Here is a testimony which shows
whose the suffering and the death are,
as the son of our race teaches us
that the Word does not share in his sufferings.
"Into your hands I place my soul":
let it be asked whose soul it is.
Is it of the one Word who is from the Father,
or of our fellow, the son of Adam?
The Godhead has no soul,
heretic, do not err;
for the life of the Godhead
is not sustained by a soul.
The soul belongs to the mortal
who was clothed with limbs,
and when sufferings came upon his limbs
it departed from him in affliction.
For there was a soul in that body
which the Word chose for his dwelling,
and it is a witness by its departure,
for it left him at the time of suffering.

It was a sufferer who suffered
in the harsh sufferings of the cross,
as he cried out with groans,
"My God, my God, do not forsake me."
It was not the Word who entreated
his Father, being one with him.
The divine one has no God;
Eutychian, why do you contend?
It was not the Word who bowed his head
and handed over his soul on the cross;
the fountain of life does not die.
Spare us your blasphemies, insolent one.
It was not into the Being that they drove
the nails, and the spear into the side.
The Only-begotten has no limbs;
heretic, do not be so bold.
It was one of flesh whose body
was [?] on the wood of the cross.
He it was who offered petition,
who stood in need of help.
It was a bodily one who bore death,
who was mortal by his nature,
and he entreated the Only-begotten,
who [?] his soul.
He bowed his head on the wood
and handed over his soul to the Creator,
and while his soul departed to Eden,
his body remained within the tomb.
The Word of the Father did not leave
[...] the pure dwelling which it chose for itself;
and though it was in him from the beginning,
it did not suffer in his humiliations.
Never did it depart from him,
not in sufferings, nor on the cross,
and never did it suffer in its nature
in the sufferings the bodily one bore [...].
Death swallowed the mortal one,
yet he did not see corruption in the house of the dead,
for prophecy did not allow
death to prevail over his body.
With a spear they pierced his side,
and blood and water flowed from him,
yet they did not break a bone in his limbs,
according to the mystery that Moses wrote.
The insolent divided his garments
and cast lots among themselves,
and the word was fulfilled in deed,
the prophecy of his father David.
They took his body down from the wood
and laid it in the tomb.
Yet his death did not corrupt his body,
for he was not bound over to the house of the dead.
Three days he remained
within the tomb, the Life-giver of the dead,
and he pronounced judgment on death
and loosed and abolished its authority.
The Word who had put him on was with him
while he lay at rest within the tomb,
yet it did not suffer through his sufferings,
for its nature was higher than sufferings.
With angels the Word honoured
his holy body,
and the spiritual beings awaited
the sign of the Giver of life to all.
The only Word of the Father
fulfilled his promises to him,
and when death had released his body,
he raised him on the third day.
O dead one whom death swallowed,
and his slaying turned against his slayer!
He broke its bitter sting
and freed humankind from its [?].
O one of dust, who wrestled
with the spirit and prince of the air,
exposed the demons by his victory
and put them to shame in his own person!
The son of our race waged war
with death and the Accuser,
and by the power of the One who put him on he conquered
the two tyrants who had grown arrogant.
It was the war in which Adam had been defeated,
and all his kind defeated with him.

The Divine Being truly put on the Son of Adam, / and through him gave victory to the children of his race. / For three days he stripped off / the mortality of his nature. / In his flesh he slew sin / and gave victory to mortals. / By the power of the Being who dwelt in him / he went down into the contest and was victorious. / By his own power he overcame / death and abolished its dominion. / He was with him while he suffered, / yet did not share in his humiliations. / And once he had been tested in all things, / he made him perfect through the suffering of his own person. / The outward temple of his body / death destroyed at the hands of the insolent. / But the Word rebuilt it and dwelt in it, / a building that will never again be shaken. / It was of this temple that he said, / "Destroy it, and I will raise it up," / teaching his hearers / that the destruction was of the body alone. / The Godhead is not undone, / for the Godhead has no beginning. / What is undone, the body, is mortal, / and it alone tasted death. / By the undoing of his body he taught / that it was a human being who suffered; / and by rising on the third day / he showed the power that raised him. / Our mortal nature was too weak / to become its own saviour; / so the Being put on our nature / and through it set our whole race free. / The Exalted One in his love lowered himself / to raise up mortal Adam, / and with the very weapon by which Adam was defeated / the Being gave the son of Adam victory. / He willed to exalt the lowly one; / it was not he himself who came down to humiliations. / He lifted up and raised the one of dust / to the honour that is with his majesty. / The [?] for breaking the commandment / was owed by the race of Adam, / and since his mortal offspring had not paid it, / the Being paid it through the son of Adam. / The mortal one died in his nature, / while the Being remained in union with him; / and by the power of the Godhead / the mortal one conquered and was raised. / It was not the Maker who suffered / the pains of death upon the cross; / it was the son of Adam who paid / by his suffering the bond of Adam's house. / He fulfilled the dispensation in him, / in the bodily one, on behalf of mortals, / and in his death and his resurrection / our whole nature died and came to life. / He made his garment a veil for his hiddenness / and a mirror for us mortals, / so that by the movements of the soul we might see / his hiddenness in the garment of our body. / He took the [?] of rational beings / as a firstfruits from all of us, / to bind up in him the love that Adam / had loosed by transgressing his commandment. / The whole nature of rational beings / he honoured by assuming it; / those who are akin to us in nature / he made partners in his honour. / This greatness, which reached / rational beings through the son of our race, / the perverse and the contentious have robbed / by the twisting of their words. / They will not allow our nature / to be honoured with praises, / nor permit the one he took / to be exalted together with God. / Two impious evildoers / conceived and gave birth to heretics, / who brought the Being down to lowly things / and robbed our body of life. / They are enemies of the body / and divided over the Godhead, / for they ascribed a beginning to the Being / and robbed the body of its assumption. / Their war is waged against the Godhead, / which they wound with their words,

and their battle is with humanity, / which they do not deem worthy of majesty. / With the books of the Spirit's words / every one of them wrangles and butts, / for these show us the distinction / of two natures that became one. / The heretics will not listen / to the heralds of the Spirit's words, / who cry out like trumpets / about the exaltation of the son of our race. / Let the chief of the apostles come / and refute the folly of their words, / and, together with the Jews, their companions, / accuse those blind men. / Let Cephas say to the perverse, / the new Jews who have sprung up, / that God made Lord and Christ / our body, which he took. / Whom did he make Lord? / Simon, firstborn of our confession, / explain to us the force of your [?], / so that by it we may refute the heretics. / "The Being," he says, "the Word of the Father, / took our nature and dwelt in it, / and made it Lord and Christ / in honour together with his majesty. / This Jesus whom you crucified / (hear, you double-minded Jews!) / the Being made a partner in glory, / and he exalted his dominion." / He is the firstfruits of our nature: / let him refute the perverse, / he who after his resurrection showed / the structure of his body to his disciples. / Their quarrel is with the disciples, / since they deny even his humanity. / "For a spirit has no limbs," / as he showed his disciples. / "Touch me," he says, "and examine / the body and the bones I have, / and proclaim this among all peoples, / that in body and bones I have risen." / See, he showed us openly, / after his killing and his resurrection, / that it was the bodily one who endured death, / and the Word did not share in his sufferings. / And if they will not say openly, / wounding the Being with their words, / that it was the Creator who showed / flesh and bones in his own nature, / then let the reproach for the reckoning / of all I have recounted fall back on them, / for they confused [?], and proclaimed a distinction / that the body of the Godhead proclaims. / With two beginnings they confined / the Creator who has no beginning: / one from the womb of a daughter of man, / and the other from within the tomb. / Oh, the boldness of the insolent, / how presumptuous and haughty they have grown, / that the Godhead, which cannot be comprehended, / they have bounded in a womb and in a tomb! / Come, my brothers, like men of discernment, / let us sort the wheat from the tares, / and wash the garment of our confession / clean of the filth of the heretics. / Let us cut them off from our body / like diseased and sickly limbs, / for see, the plague of their words has spread / and gangrene has seized on many. / Let us drive away from the flocks / the wolves that have trampled the pasture, / who in the guise of lambs pass for sheep / while they are strangers to the truth. / Let not the tares of their words / be mingled with our truth, / for they lead everyone astray into divisions / in the confession concerning the Godhead. / Let us bind the love of our mind / to the faith of the apostles, / for they made our humanity strong / by the confession of faith. / On the confession of Simon let us build / the edifice of our faith, / and in the company of Paul let us run, / who trod the road to heaven, / in fellowship with the Twelve.
Let us confess with them, like Simon, / that the Creator made Lord and Christ / our body, which he took. / Finished.
On the Robber
Twentieth Homily: On the Robber, delivered on the Saturday of the Resurrection. Response: Give thanks, my brothers, to him who trod out a way to the Kingdom through a shedder of human blood.

A new creation the Creator created at the top of Golgotha,
and showed the power of his artistry in the crucified Man.
The crucified Man was seen by the earthly and the heavenly,
and they gathered to him to see the wonder that was spoken of in him.
All creation gathered from every quarter
to gaze on the artistry atop the wood.
With skill the Lord of the world painted his image for the world,
and raised his likeness on the top of the wood for all to see.
On the tablet of the visible body he painted all creatures,
that the rational and the dumb might gaze on his artistry in him.
In man he completed the work of his hands at the beginning of time,
and in a son of man he perfected his design at the end of time.

A man he chose, in whom to renew the worn-out world;
he polished him with sufferings and showed his beauty to the eyes of all creatures.
On the wood he fixed him like a mirror for the eyes of those who look,
that they might gaze on him and see the blemishes of their own selves.
As Moses lifted up the serpent, so he too lifted him up,
to heal mankind from the bites of the wicked demons.
The demons had bitten the human race with venom,
and a Man was hung at the top of Golgotha to give life to man.
To him he turned the gaze of all in love,
that whoever looks on him with loving affection might wound the demons.
In love the rational and the dumb looked on the crucified body;
they suffered with his suffering and gained hope in the redemption of man.
In love the world looked on him for the redemption of its life,
for it saw that the time had come for the renewal of its old age.
It saw him in great disgrace, standing among thieves,
and grieved deeply over his unjust humiliation.
At his love the natures marveled, the dumb and the speaking alike,
that he consented to die for the renewal of their natures.
A hidden sign made them wise to stand in amazement
at the crucified Man, with whom the world and its iniquity were crucified.
O the wonder of the power of the ineffable Creator,
who [?] the world and its lusts in a single son of man!
A great wonder the creatures saw in a single son of man:
that they were crucified with the Mortal One atop the wood.
At this wonder the thief on the right marveled,
and remorse seized him over the lawless deed.
A great and bitter suffering he put on over his sins,
for he saw that creation was mourning in pain.
He saw the natures that were darkened at the time of the passion,
and he suffered and sighed over his hateful deeds beyond number.
He saw the luminaries wrapped in garments of mourning,
and was greatly astonished at the change in their order.
He saw a quake shaking the earth as if to make it fall,

and he trembled and was dismayed at the harshness of his mother's scourging.
He saw the hard rocks split and the people dismayed,
and instead of a garment he rent his soul over what had happened.
He saw the insults heaped on the Man crucified with him,
and he pondered what the cause of his death and the cause of his mockery might be.
Wisely he pondered and reasoned like one with discernment:
“Surely it is for this that the luminaries have darkened and the earth has shaken.
Why then are darkness and quaking seen together,
and on whose account have both grown so heavy in a single hour?
Who then has torn the dumb natures from their roots,
so that, see, they are dismayed like a woman in labor gripped by pain?
Who has changed the clearness of light into darkness,
and who has shaken the face of the earth with trembling?
Who has put a bridle on the sun, so swift in its course,
and who has turned the bright moon into dark blood?
For whom do the dumb natures mourn as never before,
and for whom do they weep, as for a firstborn bitterly mourned?
Why does the earth shed tears thunderously,
and for whom do the eyes of its face pour down tears of trembling?
Is he then just, the crucified Man who is crucified with us,
and is it for his sake that the dumb natures have put on mourning?
Perhaps they crucified him in envy and wickedness though he was not guilty,
and slandered him and drove nails into him though he did not deserve it.
Perhaps the priests envied him and hated him wickedly,
because he worked mighty deeds higher than their rank.
Why do they revile and insult him as one guilty,
when, see, his name for helping shines bright, spread through the land?
Why does he drink disgrace and mockery like a guilty man,
when, see, the dead bear witness to his triumph, for he gave them life?
If my iniquity has crucified me according to my sins,
why is he who did not transgress wickedly condemned?
If debts that I owe to justice have bound me,
why does he who is innocent bow his head upon the wood?
If, because I sinned, the snares I hid in the earth have caught me,

why does he by whose words sinners have lived now die?
I have heard of the mighty signs he worked in the land,
and it is not justly that men have repaid him with the pangs of death.”
These things the man on the right was pondering about him,
and like a judge he examined the deed that he saw on the wood.
With discernment he entered into just judgment with his own nature;
he condemned his own iniquity and acquitted the Just One crucified with him.
As in a furnace he tested the truth and rejected falsehood,
and showed the beauty of the word of truth to the eyes of the onlookers.
And though the pain of the body's sufferings was still afflicting him,
he paid no heed and did not fall back from the contest against iniquity.
With the armor of truth he was armed at the time of the passion,
and he drew near valiantly and conquered as none had done before.
A hard fight he fought quietly at the top of Golgotha,
and eagerly he gave himself over to the contest.
He set his soul as if for death while he was still dying,
and he scorned and made light of all pains as one who felt nothing.
Two contests he waged as he stood at the top of the wood:
against iniquity, and against the mockery of the insolent.
Like the athletes, the robber of men stood crucified,
and took up battle with his hateful deeds and with the mockery of the people.
Iniquity and the people stood against him like an army,
and he alone conquered sin and the crucifiers.
O how wondrous was the battle that the weak mind waged,
that at the moment it had lost hope it carried off the victory!
At the hour of death he entered the battle stripped of armor,
and naked he overcame all pains, outward and inward.
The armor of mockery the people put on against our Lord,
and they were hurling words of disgrace like arrows.
By the mouth of the unclean the Sanctifier of all was mocked,
and reviled by the insolent as a villain.
Even the thief on the left was mocking him,
and more than the people he was hurling at him the darts of disgrace.

Insolently the insolent one behaved, [?] in his folly,
and instead of a sword he drew his tongue to hurl disgrace:
“If you are the Christ who is to come,” the wicked one said,
“save yourself, and save us too from torment.
If you are a king and David belongs to you,
command your armies to arm themselves against your crucifiers.
If you are the Son, the Son of God, as you say,
come down from the wood, and see, the name of your sonship will be confirmed.
If the mighty works you did for mankind are true,
show your power in saving yourself, and you will be believed.
If you are innocent and men have crucified you on the wood,
call on God and let him avenge the disgrace of the wrong done to you.”
O how the rabid dog barked at that gentle one,
and the despicable soul felt no shame before the Holy One!
O how the mouth of the insolent blasphemed the humble one,
and the shameless was ashamed neither of iniquity nor of his own suffering!
O how the hidden sign bore with his insolence,
and the fire of wrath did not fiercely consume him!
At the sound of his blasphemies the man on the right was stirred with zeal and grew strong;
he forgot his pains and began to fight against his disgrace.
A just battle the righteous man waged with the wicked,
and wisely he loosed at him the arrows of repentance.
The wise one called to mind the name of God before the godless:
“Do you not fear God, who is just in his judgment?”
Like a judge he said to the one condemned to death:
“Why do you pour out the iniquity of your mouth upon the innocent?

Why do you insolently mock the one who has no blemish,
and multiply the lashes of the sentence upon your folly?
Do you not know that the iniquity of our souls has hung us on the wood,
and our insolence has made us die without pity?
Justly the hidden sign has exacted judgment from us,
and according to our deeds has paid us the wage of a small death.
This man is innocent and holy and pure of stains,
and without cause the people, blinded by envy, crucified him.
Why do you want to be a partner in the blood of the wronged one,
and bind yourself under the sentence that falls on murderers?
Is the former blood you shed in vain not enough for you,
that you must add a doubled iniquity to the first?
Is the death in time in place of your iniquity not enough for you,
that you must die the hidden death that has no end?”
O new teacher, who proclaimed the truth on earth
and openly rebuked wicked iniquity with the word of his mouth!
O wrongdoer, who openly exposed the wrong he was used to,
and proclaimed a truth he had not known how to meditate upon!
He rebuked his companion for insulting the Just One unjustly,
and turned thunderously to plead for his sins.
The memory of his iniquity rose upon his heart at the time of suffering,
and he began to judge himself for what he had sinned.
As from sleep he started up from his debts, the slumber of iniquity,
and saw that he was stripped of good things as of garments.
He saw his body and his soul laid bare, naked,
and he suffered and sighed bitterly over his sins.
In great suffering he scourged himself painfully,
and with thunderous laments he wept over his folly.
A house of mourning he made on the wood all by himself;
the quakes became his wailing women, and he composed the strains.
As for a dead man he wept for himself at the top of the wood,
and he wrapped and buried himself in repentance.
A double mourning he made over himself and over his torment,
for he saw that he would die and be raised again for the rigor of judgment.
Two reckonings of two deaths he weighed justly,
and remorse seized him that his debts had bound him to two judgments.
The judgment beyond terrified him more than the one here,

and he counted the death at the top of the wood as nothing.
That endless torment he kept in mind,
and as with eyes he saw it in his hidden mind.
That order of the kingdom on high he saw in secret,
and he longed, thinking that perhaps the friends above might count him worthy.
At the royal blessings he gazed closely with his mind,
and like a poor man in his need he took courage.
Great boldness the bold one took, as before,
in the same manner in which he used to rob so boldly.
Unashamed of his thieving, he stretched out his hands,
struck [?], and began to break into the royal house.
In this way he made bold and asked of our Redeemer
whether he might plunder the spiritual treasure.
His former habit drew him on to grasp greedily;
he trampled every voice and went in to plunder, as was his custom.
“Remember me, my Lord,” he began to say to the Lord of the treasure,
“in that kingdom on high that is hidden from those who look.
Have pity on my need with a single spiritual coin,
and I shall live by grace on a little drop of your gift.
Forgive my sins, blot out my debts, and cleanse my blemishes,
and in your mercy blot out the bond I owe to your justice.
Redeem my lostness, pity my need, and revive my deadness,
and paint in me the image of death abolished and iniquity undone.
Tread in me a path of repentance for generations to come,
that they may follow after me in repentance toward forgiveness.
Let the light of your faith dawn within my darkness,
and drive from my soul the darkness of iniquity that has led me astray.
Bring me back to you from the captor who carried me off from you,
and free me from my slavery, that I may serve with you and be yours.
Yours I am, a captive carried off from your lordship;
redeem the son of your house, and let all know the power of your lordship.
Enough that I have served in the house of strangers until now,
and my days have been spent in the service of my error without profit.
The day has ended and the sun of my life's day has set,
and if your help does not reach me, I am nothing.

Let me not perish, my Lord, from the company of Adam's dust,
nor be shut out from fellowship in the raising of the dead.
Sprinkle on my deadness the dew of mercy hidden in your words,
that I may perhaps revive on the day of resurrection and give glory.
Make me worthy to walk with the few on the way of the just,
and to enter and rejoice in that delight that does not perish.”
Who revealed to you, dead in your sins, that you should know these things?
And who explained to you that the crucified Man is King over all?
Who showed you that a man holds authority on high,
and how he can have power over the things to come?
Who taught you that he can free man from iniquity,
and from where he has undying life to give?
Tell me, man: when has a man given life to a man,
and when have earthly beings shared out the kingdom on high?
That a man should give life to a man is indeed written,
but that a man shares out the kingdom on high we have not heard.
Who led you astray, you who wandered in the delight of lusts,
into thinking that a crucified man gives life and forgives iniquity?
See, son of my error, perhaps your mind has strayed in error;
examine well, and only then ask what is higher than you.
Perhaps in the severity of your body's pains you have strayed and grown confused,
and your mind wanders as in a dream, without revelations.
It was not in error that the thief erred in his request;
the composer of words erred, and mocked him according to his deeds.
The speaker recalled the greatness of his iniquity and his abominations,
and wished to mock: whence did the erring one get the truth?
Who then taught him to understand all things, to know the truth,
and who trod for him a path to walk before the height?
Who copied a new book for him, the disciple of falsehood,
and who became his master in the study of things to come?
Who expounded to him the power of the explanation of hidden things,
and who told him that there is a kingdom that is never dissolved?
Who became a counselor of counsel for him who wandered in error,
that at the time of terror he might benefit his soul?
With what eyes did the seer of hidden things see
that order on which the eye of flesh has not looked?

With what ears did the precious listener to iniquity hear
that daughter of the voice which is not heard by the senses of clay?
With what mouth did the stammerer, a stranger [?] to truth, utter
that praise which cannot be spoken by a tongue of flesh?
With what palate did the parched one taste the sweetness of life,
and how, and how far, was he able to receive the food of the Spirit?
And grant that he perceived there is a hidden kingdom on high:
what authority does a crucified man have over its delight?
And grant that he supposed that mercy is shown to sinners:
what can a man do to help a man?
And grant that he believed that the one he pondered could do these things:
who put in him the thought of these things he had not seen?
Not with fleshly thoughts did the fleshly one ponder,
nor was it in him to ask lovingly about what is above.
The hidden sign drew him secretly to see hidden things,
and it raised him to the explanation of secret things.
The power of the Spirit spoke with him spiritually,
and it expounded to him hidden mysteries that had been hidden from him.
It placed in him the power of the wisdom of things to come,
and it explained to him that there is a kingdom and a sentence of judgment.
It told him that the crucified Man crucified with you,
his is the kingdom on high and the judgment to come.
It revealed to him that he can blot out man's iniquity,
and write in his name a deed of freedom in place of slavery.
The bond of the guilty he wished to tear up by his demonstration,
so that if a guilty man carried off the victory, who could doubt?
He opened the kingdom on high to the earthly by his entry,
so that if the thief entered first, who would be left outside?
The exaltation of our race he revealed in the promise he made him,
that if a son of our race has won the kingdom, blessed is our nature.
The undoing of our folly he showed in himself, which entered Eden,
that we are destined to enter with him into the kingdom on high.
In the likeness of an image he painted in him our iniquity and our repentance,
and raised and fixed it at the top of Golgotha for the eyes of the onlookers.
In this way he forgave him his iniquity at the time of the passion,
that we might learn that it was for our sake he suffered on the wood.
In this figure he chose for himself a man more sinful than all,
that in a sinner he might show his power, which is mightier than all.

Through the shedder of blood, full of iniquity, he [?] the kingdom,
that he might tread the way of repentance for those who had done wickedly.
The bond of debts of Adam's race he came to pay,
and first he set free one debtor who owed much.
The nature worn out by mortality he wished to renew,
and he visited it in a man who was dead, wholly in hateful iniquity.
He gave a sign to the natures and darkened them over his humiliation,
and they showed that he is Lord and Son of God who rules over all.
Through the silent and the speaking he proclaimed his power,
and like heralds the creatures cried out his authority.
He did not darken the senseless as though they had sense;
rather he gave the senseless a mind of the Spirit.
Sun and moon he clothed in garments of mourning,
and he urged the thief to interpret the greatness of his power.
As with a mouth the silent ones cried out by their changes:
“For the sake of the Man hung among us we are in pain.”
The earth by its quaking spoke with the children of the earth:
“My children, you have greatly hated the Blood that wrings my pains.”
The voice of the thief, louder than thunder, thundered in creation:
“Look, mortals, to the Life hung at the top of the wood!”
Already heaven and earth had listened to the beauty of his voice,
and the people alone stopped their ears from hearing.
The signs came to rebuke the people's hardness of heart,
and for its sake the luminaries darkened and the earth shook.
Because of its iniquity he urged on the thief, and he repented of his iniquity,
that it might see, and repent, and seek, and plead for its folly.
His divinity he revealed in his humanity to the eyes of all creatures:
that though he suffers as a son of man, he is the Son of God.
The Son of God in the body the Jews crucified,
not God the Word of the Father, who was begotten of him.
Into the composite body they drove bodily nails,
not into the Being whose nature is above all harm.
A visible body the thief saw at the top of the wood,
not the hiddenness that is seen only by the mind.
By the mind the Spirit of revelation showed the man on the right
that the Man whom the people mock in his disgrace is the Son of God.

To shame the people and condemn the demons he made truth strong in him,
that the Enemy and those at his side might be shamed by his preaching.
At the voice of his confession the rebel who had taken Adam captive was put to shame,
for at the top of the wood he took from him the captives he had taken.
Him he shamed by a single son of man whom he turned to himself,
and the rebel could not stand and hold him back from confessing him.
Him he exposed through the promise he made the thief,
and he sealed his redemption with “Amen” upon the word of his mouth.
With “Amen” he swore a word, which is the seal of truth:
“Today you will be with me in Eden, in the manner of the soul.”
“You will be with me in the place of Eden,” he said to him;
and why in Eden, and not in heaven, where he had asked him?
The kingdom on high the thief requested, and not paradise;
royal blessings he asked of him, and not trees.
What is this? The thief too could have said:
“I asked you for the kingdom, and not paradise.
If you are Lord, and height and depth are yours,
why do you delay to fulfill the promise of your words?
I asked that I might inherit the things above that are never dissolved;
what are you giving me, an inheritance of earth whose dwelling is mean?
Paradise too is a portion of the earth, however beautiful,
and the food of its fruits is perishable, however pleasant.”
He who judged truly did not argue these things in his mind,
for the sign that had pity on him did not permit him to demand them.
He who revealed to him the mystery of the invisible kingdom
put on him the bridle of silence, so that he would not doubt.
In faith he asked the kingdom of the one who was leading him,
and the one who had been far off he brought into Eden as one chosen [?].
He could not enter with him at this time,
lest the great order of that design be thrown into confusion.
In due order that entry will take place at the end of time,
and together the Watchers and mankind will enter, a great assembly.

And so as not to let him enter with him, which was not fitting,
he brought him in hope into the mystery of the entry into the kingdom.
In soul he brought him into the place of Eden, not in body,
into that delight which can receive spiritual beings.
To his rational soul he gave a pledge of things to come,
that he might know the hope into which he had entered is not false.
A pledge of life he gave in Eden to the son of mortals,
that he might undo the death that had enslaved Adam and his offspring.
Where the head of humanity sinned and death killed him,
there he brought the [?] in the delight of theft.
After the custom of his father, the son of a thief entered to dwell there,
and the Enemy saw him and wailed and wept, for it did not please him.
The place whose fence the commandment was broken through by Adam,
into it Adam entered through the thief who entered with our Lord.
The soul of our Lord and that of the thief entered together,
and he opened the gate before the souls of the just [?].
The fence of wrath had been set before us so that we might not enter,
and our Lord broke it down and brought us in with him by his entry.
To the shame of the demons he opened paradise before mortals,
the demons who had rejoiced that we went out estranged, now shamed by our entry.
The prince of the air he exposed and shamed by what he did,
for he had driven Adam from the inheritance his Lord had given him.
The envious one thought that Adam would never return to his place,
and suddenly he was put to shame when he saw him in Eden in two souls.
Two entered first, one righteous and one a sinner,
that he might know that from now on the good and the wicked enter.
Over the thief he suffered and groaned more than over our Lord:
how had the shedder of blood broken through the gate of the wall that was built?
In his counsel the proud-minded one supposed that paradise was fenced off,
and when he saw they had opened it, remorse seized him and he lost hope.
He saw that a path to Eden had been trodden for men to follow,

and he wailed and wept that he alone was left in disgrace. / "What shall I do?" said the one bitter of soul, / "for the king whom I cast into exile has reached his kingdom. / Where shall I go?" the evil one asked his evil nature, / "for Adam has taken hold of height and depth through his offspring. / I drove him far away from paradise so that he would never inherit, / and now no place is left on earth that is not his inheritance. / Better for me had he kept the inheritance of the earth that he acquired on earth, / and that this new report had not reached me, that he is going up on high. / I had wished that he would possess the earth to the full, / and not be called heir of the heights and son of the kingdom. / I would have been at rest if he had inherited height and depth alike, / and had not been raised to the lofty rank of divinity. / This one whom I fixed on the top of the wood is his kinsman, / and look, he is promising heaven and earth to his fellows. / He hangs on the cross with nails driven into his body, / and swears 'Amen' that he is able to give the kingdom of the heights. / He is thrown into the contest of suffering and is near to death, / and one wretch rises up and begs him, 'Give me life.'" / Hard blows were added to the Slanderer / by that voice: "Remember me, my Lord, when you come." / The more the robber pleaded on the top of the wood, / the more the other groaned, and groaned bitterly. / The more the Giver of life to all promised, "With me you will be," / the more fiercely he was consumed in the fire of his own nature. / As he swore and sealed his word with "Amen," / the other wailed like a woman in labour seized by pain. / As if by arrows the envious one was pierced by what had happened, / and from every side the robber's voice was goading him. / And if the robber, his own disciple, goaded him like this, / what will he do to the One on whom heaven and earth call? / If his own confidant has exposed and laid bare his craft,

where shall he go from the One whom Watchers and men praise? / If a murderer has received the promise of the kingdom of the heights, / with what eyes shall he look on as our whole race enters in? / O robber, who cut off the hope of the adversary, / and through the forgiveness of his wickedness won and created hope for the hopeless! / O you who stood condemned and had pledged yourself to disgrace, / and by a single word received back for nothing the bond of your debts! / O you who were defiled through and through with loathsome wickedness, / and sprinkled over it all the pure waters of repentance! / O you who all your life plundered and seized the things of earth, / and on the day of your death plundered the good things of heaven! / O you from whose wickedness travellers hid along the road, / who trod out the road of repentance before sinners! / O idler [?] who ended his days in emptiness, / who spoke one word and received as his wage the kingdom of the heights! / O how much, and how, shall I paint the image of the forgiveness of your wickedness, / which he sealed with "Amen," granting rank upon rank to the rank you reached? / My tongue is too small to depict your story, you who broke through walls [?], / and I do not know how to uncover the hidden things of your craft. / You were trained [?] in everything, and craftily you led your life; / you sinned as you wished, and turned back and appeased as it pleased you. / He who forgives your wickedness alone knows the folds of your heart, / and he who knew you was not wearied by the greatness of your wickedness. / Wisely he painted your story on the page of his sufferings, / so that everyone might learn to go down through sufferings to what is prepared for us. / Response: Glory to you, who turn back those who stray, / to the knowledge of the greatness of his glory.
On the Mysteries of the Church and on Baptism
Twenty-First Homily / On the Mysteries of the Church and on Baptism

Our Lord has opened for us the sweet spring of baptism,
and given our race to drink the sweetness of life that does not die.
In the heat of iniquity our mind had dried up and its fruits had fallen,
and he sprinkled his gift like dew and refreshed our soul.
The hard thirst of mortality had killed our body,
and he buried it in the waters, and life crept into its mortality.
The rust of the passions had eaten away the beauty of our discernment,
and he recast our image with the medicine of the Spirit that does not perish.
O how he has purified, with the medicine of our race's renewal,
by oil and water and the power of the Spirit, mightier than all!
The great Craftsman has brought forth a new craft:
that men should fashion men without intercourse.
The divine will has found a discovery never found before:
that without seed a man should be born from within the waters.
Where was such a thing ever done, or when did it happen,
that a womb of water gives birth to babes without union?
To whom was it ever heard that a kind gave birth to what is not of its kind,
as a mute nature now gives birth to speech?
Though the waters brought forth creeping things and winged things,
it was never heard that the waters brought forth a man.
This is a wonder, and how much more is it full of wonder,
that a womb of water should conceive and bear full-grown babes!
All of it is new, and great is the ordinance ministered in it,
that in a brief hour the whole course of conception and birth takes place,
beyond the order set in nature, which follows its own order

and is not held back by growth that comes little by little.
Come, hearer, hear the wonder of the new birth,
in which both conception and bearing take place in a single hour.
Come, beholder, behold the Fashioner who fashions babes,
and while the word is still turning in the mouth they come forth from the womb.
Come, discerning one, discern and examine with discernment
the power of the Being who gives power to the weak.
And come, you mortals, look at a nature laden with mortality,
which strips off its passions in baptism and puts on life.
Come, let us search diligently into the mysteries of our renewal,
and learn what is hidden in the visible waters.
Come, let us draw near to the priesthood, the salt of the earth,
and see how it purifies men spiritually.
Let us go in with it to where it goes in to heal,
and incline our mind to listen to the voice that speaks with it.
Let us listen how the power of the Spirit whispers with it,
and makes it wise to give power to the despised waters.
The hidden will interprets the hidden mysteries to it,
and it explains them in a clear voice before the hearers.
It performs before it the craft of the new birth,
and shows it how to fashion a spiritual image.
The priest becomes like a pen for the hidden power,
and with his hands writes names upon the waters.
O scribe, whom the Spirit makes write on a soft tablet,
the ink of whose words is not blotted out in the dissolving waters!
O how great is your craft, son of mortals,
and no one knows how to search it out as its greatness deserves!
O how fine is the pen of your mind for depicting mysteries,
and there is no painter who can make likenesses like your images!
O you priest, who serve as priest on earth in the Spirit,
whom spiritual beings are not permitted to resemble!
O you priest, how great is the rank in which you minister,
at which the ministers of fire and spirit tremble!
Who is able to say how great is the greatness of your rank,
by which you have surpassed the heavenly ones in the name of your authority?
Fine and glorious is the nature of the spirit, more than yours,
yet it is not permitted to depict mysteries as you do.
Great is the angel, and how much greater than you,

yet when he is compared with your ministry he is less than you.
Holy is the seraph, and beautiful the cherub, and swift the watcher,
yet they cannot run with the freedom of the word of your mouth.
Glorious is Gabriel and great is Michael, and their names bear witness,
yet beneath the mystery at work in your hands they bow like everyone else.
They gaze on you when you draw near to minister,
and they wait for you to open the door to their hymns of holiness.
They stand bearing voices of praise at your right hand,
and when you have completed the mystery of your redemption, they cry out in glorification.
In love they bow beneath the will hidden in your mysteries,
and honour you because of the ordinance ministered through you.
And if spiritual beings, who feel no passion, honour your ordinance,
who would not weave crowns of praise for the greatness of your rank?
Let it be marvelled at always, how great the greatness of your rank has grown,
which has bowed height and depth beneath its authority.
Over height and depth the priests of the church have taken authority,
and they give commands to the heavenly and the earthly.
Between God and man they stand as mediators,
and by their words they bind away iniquity from mankind.
The key of the divine mercies is placed in their hands,
and according to their will they distribute life to the children of men.
A hidden power has empowered them to perform this,
that openly they might show his love to the work of his hands.
He showed his love in the mystery he handed over to the earthly,
that men might show grace to men from his gift.
The power of his gift he handed over into the hands of the priests of the church,
that by it they might strengthen the weakness of men condemned by sin.
The priest pays the debt of men through his ministry,
and erases the bond of his race in the waters and renews it.
As into a furnace he casts bodies into baptism,
and as with fire he burns up the thicket of mortality.
He casts the medicine of the Spirit into the waters as into a furnace,
and purifies the image of man from filth.
By the heat of the Spirit he polishes the rust of body and soul,
and instead of clay they acquire the colour of the heavenly ones.

He prepares the font of waters and sets it like a furnace,
and then he draws near and reveals the power of his faith.
With beautiful garments he covers his body outwardly,
and a robe of the Spirit adorns his soul inwardly.
Wholly adorned he stands before the eyes of beholders,
that through his adornment he may reveal to men the things to come.
He becomes like a mirror to the eyes of his fellows,
that they may look at him and gain hope of being glorified.
In the garments he wears he sets a sign before their eyes,
that they may long to be adorned spiritually.
This he teaches by the adornment on his limbs:
that the mystery in his hands clothes with glory whoever approaches him.
In his hands is placed the treasure of life hidden in the waters,
and unless he approaches and distributes it, it is not given.
He stretches out the key of his word and opens the door of the gift,
and with the sound of his voice he distributes gifts to the King's servants.
He too stands as at the sea, like Moses,
and instead of a rod he lifts his voice over the silent waters.
With the word of his mouth he strikes the waters like the son of Amram,
and they listen to his voice better than to the voice of the son of the Hebrews.
They heard Moses—though they heard him well, they were not sanctified;
they obey the priest of the church, and acquire holiness.
Moses only split the Israelite sea in two,
and by the power of the wonder he could not cleanse his people's iniquity.
For the priest's office is great, and has no equal among the things that have been,
for it gives the power to forgive iniquity to the senseless waters.
He fixes his gaze on that will which created creation,
and learns from it how he should create a new creation.
He too images it in the pattern in which the world came to be,
and sounds a voice like the one that cried out in the beginning upon the earth.
Like the Creator he too commands the despised waters,
and instead of light the power of life dawns from them.
The Creator's voice created the luminaries out of nothing,
and he creates something from something by the Creator's power.
The creation he creates in the womb of the waters is not his own,
but belongs to the will that created creation out of nothing.
That command which spoke, and speaking and mute creatures came to be—

by it he gives command, and men come to be a new being.
That word which the waters heard and brought forth creeping things
is the same they hear from the priest's mouth, and they bring forth men.
Greater is the offspring they bear now than that,
by as much as a speaking man excels the silent creature.
Like seed he casts his word into the womb of the waters,
and they conceive and bear a new child, not in the accustomed way.
His mouth interprets the utterances of the Spirit to the silent water,
and it acquires power to give life to rational beings.
