The mute hear a new whisper from those who speak,
like that whisper which Mary heard from Gabriel.
And he too lets good tidings fall into the ears of men,
like that hope the watcher proclaimed at the birth of the Son.
He fulfils his office in the watcher's place, and does better than the watcher,
for he gives hope to the hopeless by the sound of his utterances.
Between the Being and mankind he stands as mediator,
and through his words confirms the covenant between the two sides.
With gentleness he persuades the Hidden One, who was hidden and was revealed in his love,
and brings down his power from him, and it accomplishes his words.
In the name of the Being, three names, he sanctifies the waters,
that they may be sufficient to cleanse the unclean completely.
Men's uncleanness is cleansed in the waters—not by the waters,
but by the power of the name of the Being who dwells there.
The power of the Being dwells in the visible waters,
and by the power of his might they dissolve the strength of the Evil One and of death.
The Evil One and death are abolished in baptism,
and the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the soul are proclaimed in it.
As in a grave, body and soul are buried in it,
and they die and live in the mystery of the resurrection that will be at the end.
It performs the rite of the grave for men mystically,
and the voice of the priesthood is like the voice of the trumpet at the end.
In the grave of the waters the priest buries the whole man,
and raises him by the power of life hidden in his words.
At the door of the grave of baptism he stands armed,
and there he completes the mystery of death and of resurrection.
In a clear voice he proclaims the power of the hand that is at work:

how a man dies in the waters and comes back to life.
Openly he reveals and shows to the one who is baptized
in whose name he dies and lives again in a moment.
He calls to mind the name of the Being, and says it three times:
Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one equality.
He repeats the names in a clear voice, saying thus:
"So-and-so is baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Spirit."
He does not say, "I baptize," but "is baptized,"
for it is not he who baptizes, but the One set in the names.
The names give forgiveness of iniquity, not a son of man,
and they sow new life in mortality.
In their name the one who is baptized is baptized, as in a grave,
and they call him and raise him from his death.
Three times he bows his head in their names,
that he may learn the doctrine that they truly exist as three.
The womb of baptism becomes a mystery of our Saviour,
after the pattern of the three days within the grave.
Three days our Saviour was among the dead;
so too the one baptized goes down three times, for three days.
He truly dies in the mystery of that death which died and gave life to all,
and lives again in the likeness of the life that has no end.
He strips off sin and death and casts them away in baptism,
after the pattern of the grave-clothes our Lord left in the grave when he came out.
Like a babe from within the womb he is lifted from the waters,
and instead of swaddling clothes the priest receives and embraces him.
He is like a babe when he is lifted up from within the waters,
and everyone embraces him as they would a babe.
[?] they put garments upon his limbs,
and adorn him like a bridegroom on the day of the wedding feast.
He too fulfils the manner of the wedding feast in baptism,
and by his adornment depicts the glory that awaits him.
By the beauty of his garments he proclaims the beauty of the world beyond:
here a mystery, and there the truth that does not deceive.

He invites and calls to the kingdom on high that is not dissolved,
and depicts beforehand the mystery of the true one's ordinance.
In the mystery of that glory that does not perish he puts on garments,
that he may image the things to come mystically.
In mystery he dies, and rises, and is adorned,
and mystically he images the life that does not die.
His birth is a mystery of that birth which will be at the end,
and the conduct of his life a mystery of the conduct of the kingdom on high.
He begins to walk in the way of spiritual life,
and like spiritual beings he lives on spiritual food.
Spiritual is his mystical birth,
and according to his birth is the nourishment prepared for him.
New is his birth, and very strange to earthly beings,
and there is no weighing the greatness of the food on which he is nourished.
Like milk he sucks the divine mysteries,
and they lead him step by step, like a child, toward the things to come.
The mother of the Spirit prepares for her children the milk of the Spirit,
and instead of breasts she puts the Body and Blood into his mouth.
With Body and Blood the church gives life to the children of her womb,
and reminds them of the great love of her betrothed.
Her betrothed gave her his body, and his blood as a pledge of life,
that she might acquire power to give life from her own life.
He commanded her to give life to her children with the food of his body,
by means of the parables he composed beforehand in mystery.
The fatted ox he called the sacrifice of his bodily nature,
and he offered his sacrifice through the return of one of her children.
In her children she who had been grieved by the story of the one who strayed was made whole,
for his love went out and received them in baptism.
In love and mercy he went out to meet them and received them,
and embraced them as the dead who had returned and come to life.
He explained the force of his parables and revealed it before their eyes,
and gladdened them with spiritual food and drink.

He gave a pledge, the ring, which he called the power of the Spirit,
and clothed them in the robe of glory of baptism.
He sacrificed his own self, the fatted one, spiritually,
and fed them a food in whose eating life lies hidden.
He shod them with the good swiftness of a life well conducted,
that they might not stumble on the path of mortality's deceit.
He invited and called the heavenly ones on the day of their renewal,
and gladdened those who had been sad over their debts.
The womb of the waters bore them spiritually,
and the power of his goodness filled up and supplied their needs.
Watchers and men rejoiced, and still rejoice, at their repentance,
for the words in the parables have reached their fulfilment.
Heaven and earth are glad that they have returned to their Father,
and have taken hold of the laws of their course, which had been plundered.
Demons plundered the inheritance of men wickedly,
and one man rose up, pronounced judgment, and exposed them.
He pronounced a just judgment against the deceivers,
and took from them the spoil they had snatched from his Father's house.
Through Adam the deceiver led astray, he who sowed error in the world,
and the son of Adam was zealous and avenged the disgrace of his whole race.
The Kinsman put on great zeal on behalf of his brothers,
and accepted death, that they might not be called slaves of the evil ones.
Like an athlete he went down to the contest on behalf of his people,
and grappled with Satan, and overpowered him and defeated him.
On the summit of Golgotha he joined battle with the slayer of men,
and made him a laughingstock in the sight of angels and mankind.
By the victory of the wood he swept him away and cast him down from his confidence;
in the very thing by which he thought death would enter, death swallowed and was put to shame.
The wicked mind had been boasting in the death of men,
and through the death of one man his boasting was brought to nothing.
One man died crucified on behalf of mortals,
and taught them to walk in the way of his death and his life.
Men depict his death and his life in baptism,
and those who died with him rose and were raised mystically.
In the new way of the Living One [?] the dead walk with him,

and in the conduct of the heavenly ones they become like them on earth.
By the food of his body they drive death from their bodies,
and with his living blood they give their minds life to drink.
Body and soul are nourished by the food of his body and blood,
and they overcome Satan and death by the power of his gift.
By the power of his gift they were washed and sanctified from their debts,
and acquired strength to contend against the passions.
From the waters they put on a hidden power as armour against the passions,
and began to scorn the might of the enemy.
Like athletes they came up from the font of baptism,
and watchers and men received them lovingly.
The earthly and the heavenly cried out the shout of their victory,
and the demons heard and trembled, and were confounded by the new shout.
Height and depth wove crowns for them by the hands of men,
for they saw that they had won a great fight against the strong one.
They received from the King gifts worthy of their labours,
and he honoured them gloriously above the host.
Within his hidden palace he made them recline,
and set before them a table of life that does not die.
He prepared a beautiful bridal chamber on earth in the mystery of the one above,
that they may delight in it mystically until the end.
He built himself a sanctuary, that in it they might hallow his holy name,
until they ascend to the Holy One hidden on high.
He chose himself priests to minister in it in holiness,
and instead of sacrifices to offer the sacrifice of the mystery of his Son.
All offer the mystery of his Son before his will,
and by it they heal the iniquity of men who call on his name.
He placed the silver of his word in their hands by way of [?],
that they might trade with it for the possession of spiritual life.
As in a furnace men recast the children of men,
and polish away from them the hateful rust of hateful iniquity.
Quietly, from within the waters, they acquire a beautiful colour,
and the light of their minds shines brighter than the sun.
They become rays of light on earth by the light within them,
and the world shines with the beautiful rays of their conduct.

They suck the Spirit after the birth of baptism,
and according to that birth is their nourishment, lofty and exalted.
Like fledglings they lift the wings of their conduct,
and enter and rest in the beautiful nest of the holy church.
Like an eagle the priest hovers over their faces,
and prepares the food of perfection to nourish them.
He prepares a living sacrifice and sets it before their eyes,
and invites them to gaze on it with the love of the soul.
He begins to depict a fearful mystery spiritually,
and like painters he blends words before the beholders.
With the pen of his word he depicts the image of the crucified King,
and as if with a finger he points out his suffering and his exaltation.
His voice proclaims death and life in the ears of the people,
and he distributes the forgiveness of iniquity, giving it in bread and wine.
He shows the mystery of death first, for the sake of mortality,
and then reveals the power of life hidden in his words.
As for one dead, he spreads a bier with the holy vessels,
and lifts up and lays down the bread and wine like a corpse.
He keeps the King's day of commemoration mystically,
and sets servants on watch for the display.
He sets two deacons in order, on this side and on that,
to guard the mystery of the King of kings.
Fear and love are cast upon the movements of their minds
as they gaze on the bread and wine as on the King.
A radiant form is wrapped about their faces from within,
and by their garments they show the beauty of their minds.
With their stoles they depict the sign of the serene ones
who were wrapped in beautiful garments in the shrine of the tomb.
The disciples saw two angels in our Lord's tomb,
who honoured the place of his body as they would his body itself.
And if spiritual beings honoured the place of his body with fear,
how much more should bodily beings honour the mystery that has honoured them!
After the pattern of those two watchers, two deacons
now stand to hover over the mysteries.

The priest fills the place of the mouth on behalf of all mouths,
and as a mediator interprets his voice to the Hidden One.
He calls on the Hidden One to send him the hidden power,
that it may give power to the bread and wine to give life.
He turns the gaze of all minds toward the hidden,
that they may look on hidden things by means of things revealed.
"Your minds on high!" he cries out and says to the earthly ones,
and they answer, "To you, Lord, who are hidden on high."
He repeats and says: "What is the reason for looking upward,
and what is it that calls men to his fellowship?
Look then, O men, at the offering of the sacrifice on your behalf,
which the Being receives in love on behalf of your life.
Look carefully at the bread and wine upon the table,
which the power of the Spirit changes into body and blood.
See the revealed things with the revealed senses of your limbs,
and picture the hidden things with the hidden movements of your minds.
Remember your death in the sign that is full of death and life,
and give praise and draw near to the one who gives power to the weak."
As with a seal they seal his word with their voices:
"It is fitting and right, and beautiful and holy, the sacrifice of our life."
He, like a pen, writes words on the tip of his tongue,
and they set their hand to it with the words, "Yes, it is true."
As witnesses they attest the words spoken on their behalf,
and instead of a seal they seal the mystery of their life with "Amen."
He plainly writes a bond of thanksgiving through his utterances,
and they stand surety: "Yes, we pay the debt of praise."
With their voices they pay the praise that is in his writings,
and he carries it to the divine will.
With the offering the priest lifts up the prayer of the people,
and sanctifies it by participation in the living mystery.
In great anguish he prays for himself and for all,
that his word may be an acceptable sacrifice before the Most High.
In his words he resembles the spiritual beings as he makes supplication,
and in holiness he teaches men to cry "Holy."
He repeats for men the voice of the heavenly ones' hymn of holiness,
that they may cry, "Holy, holy, holy Lord."

That voice which the Seraphim cried out three times
is the very one he sounds in the people's ears at the time of the mysteries.
Like Isaiah he too is moved when he sounds it,
remembering how lowly man was, and how great he has become.
The sign which the prophet saw in a mystery
is proved in deed, through faith.
Isaiah saw a coal of fire drawn near to him,
which a Seraph of fire held in a hand of fire.
It came to his mouth, yet did not truly come to it,
and it truly took away the iniquity of his body and his soul.
It was not a vision of the senses that the seer saw,
nor did the spiritual being bring a bodily coal near him.
In the coal he saw a sign of the mystery of the body and the blood,
which, like fire, consumes the iniquity of mortality.
The priest explains the power of that mystery the prophet saw,
and as with tongs he holds in his hand the fire in the bread.
In the Seraph's place he ministers to the people, as to Isaiah,
and by his ministry takes away iniquity and gives life.
The Seraph of spirit did not hold the Spirit in his hand, even in a vision [?];
and this is the wonder: that a hand of flesh holds the Spirit.
The light-winged one could not bring food into the belly,
but the heavy body stretches out its hand even to the soul's impulses.
He nourishes body and soul with the food of the mystery's power,
and out of mortals he makes man immortal.
He silences the authority of death over mortals,
and loosens the grip of the Evil One and removes it from mortals.
By food the Evil One killed us in the beginning and made us slaves,
and by food the Creator has willed that we should now live.
By the hand that plucked the fruit in Eden in sin,
by that same hand he has wisely held out to us the fruit of life.
In Adam he cursed us and gave us as food to greedy death,
and in the Son of Adam he opened to us the spring of his sweetness.
In our own nature he fulfilled his will and showed his love,
to confirm for us that word which called us his image.
To us he has given the pledge of life in our mortality,
so that we may govern our souls as we will, by the power of his will.

By the power of his will the priest distributes life in the bread,
drives out iniquity, and makes the Spirit dwell within the members.
The power of the Spirit comes down upon the son of mortals,
dwells in the bread, and hallows it by the greatness of his might.
O wonder! Though the Spirit fills all things,
yet until the man of dust commands, he does not draw near.
O gift! Though it was given from the beginning,
yet until the son of dust entreats, it is not received.
The Spirit is with all and in all, in height and in depth,
and he is hidden; yet the priest reveals him by his words.
To the height above he stretches out his hands, and his mind with them,
and invites him to come down and fulfil his soul's request.
It is not in his nature that the Spirit, the unseen, comes down;
it is the power from him that comes down, visits, and accomplishes all.
His power overshadows the visible altar
and imparts power to the bread and wine to give life.
His power strengthens the priest's hand to hold his power,
so that the trembling flesh is not consumed by his live coal.
The bodily one holds in his hands the Spirit in the bread,
and lifts his gaze to the face of the height, and so beseeches him.
He breaks the bread, puts it into the wine, signs it, and says:
"In the name of the Father and the Son and the Spirit, one equal nature."
In the name of the one Being, three Persons, he completes his words,
and raises up the mystery as one raises the dead, in the form of truth.
In truth the Lord of the mystery rose from the tomb,
and without division the mystery acquires the power of life.
At once the bread and the wine acquire new life,
and at once they give forgiveness of iniquity to those who receive them.
He makes the bread and the wine one in communion,
since the blood is mingled with the body in all the senses.
He pours wine and water into the cup before he consecrates,

since in the blood too water is mingled with the other elements.
With these the priest completes the mysteries of the consummation,
and then he sounds a word full of love and mercy.
Love and mercy are hidden in the word of his mouth,
that the creature should call the Maker his own Father.
In the path of his voice the voices of the hearers run,
as they make ready to call the hidden Being "our Father."
O gift to man, past all comprehension,
that he has freely received a name the world cannot match!
"Our Father," the sons of dust call the Maker of all,
and ask of him holiness and the kingdom on high:
"Your holy name be hallowed in us, Maker of all,
and the pledge of life without end be confirmed in us."
Together they ask for holiness and the help of the Spirit,
for the hidden will, the food of the season, and the forgiveness of iniquity.
By their requests they show the love of their minds,
how they long to share in the things to come.
With the word of thanksgiving they seal the words that complete the mysteries,
and render holiness to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit:
Holy is the Father, holy his Offspring, and the Spirit who is from him,
and to them belong holiness and praise from every mouth.
After the word of holiness and the rendering of praise,
they stretch the gaze of their minds toward the gift.
In senses and impulses alike they hasten to draw near
to the bread and wine, in which forgiveness of iniquity is hidden.
By faith they gain the power to see hidden things,
and reverently, as for a king, they hold the holy gift in their palms.
They lodge within themselves the body of the King, which dwells in the chosen bread,
and in it the life of the dead is proclaimed to the one who eats of it.
The priest too says "the body" to the one to whom he gives it,
and names the mixed wine in the cup "the blood."
He gives the bread and says, "The body of the King, Christ,"
and gives the wine to drink, and with it, in like manner, "the blood of Christ."
He believes that the bread and wine are the body and blood,
and truly it is good for the giver and for those who receive.
With it he proclaims the forgiveness of iniquity and the life of the dead,
and though these are not seen, they are most pleasing to faith.
Faith shows the soul a hidden vision

and teaches it not to be divided over what is seen.
The eyes of the body's senses see bread and wine,
but the soul's impulses see the power of the Hidden One, who is mightier than all.
With the impulses of the soul it is right for us to look upon the mystery of our salvation,
and let faith set the goal before our mind.
Let us take the bread and believe that it can forgive iniquity;
let us drink the wine and confess that by its drinking it gives life.
Let us honour them as the body and blood of the King,
that they may make us worthy of the glories of the house of the kingdom.
Let us believe that they can give life to our mortality,
and let us stretch our mind toward the hope and expectation that is in them.
With a hidden mind let us look in a hidden way upon what is seen,
and not be divided over the renewal that lies in visible things.
The seer does not look at the bread, nor at the wine,
but at the power that hallows the bread and wine.
Bread and wine are set as a sign for the body's eyes,
that it may share with the mind in what is not seen.
The body cannot see hidden things as the mind does,
nor search out secrets as thoughts do.
For its sake the gift came through bread,
so that through visible things it might gain hope of the hidden.
For it and for the soul is promised the delight hidden in the mystery,
and for its comfort were the visible things of food and drink given.
See, through visible things it is quickly consoled from its sorrow,
and so that its Lord's comfort may not be strange to it, it comes in bread and wine.
In bread and wine he has set for it a goal toward the things to come,
that it may look toward the renewal he is preparing for it.
Come, mortals, let us look to the goal hidden in our mystery,
and not slacken from the expectation of the promised life.
Come, let us take refuge in the power of his spiritual help,
that he may help us in the struggle with the brutish passions.
Come, let us hasten to draw near to him in holiness,
to receive from him the medicine that heals our wounds.
Let us apply it always as a medicine to our senses and impulses,
that it may drive from us the sickness of the body and the weakness of the soul.
It is a good medicine, whose power heals by grace,
and there is no illness, hidden or open, that withstands it.
The Physician on high has given it to the earthly,
that by its help they may heal the pains of their minds.

In faith let us all lay it upon our wounds,
that we may gain from it the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the soul.
On Baptism
Memra Twenty-Two / On Baptism / Refrain: / Blessed is the spring that flowed over the Jordan: Adam drank, and his thirst passed. / My brothers

Who is able to repay love to the Restorer of all,
who came in His love to give birth to man spiritually?
Too small are the mouth and the mind to give thanks with us
to the power of the Creator, who renewed our image and blotted out our iniquity.
As in a furnace He cast our image in baptism,
and in place of clay He made us spiritual gold.
Spiritually He willed to fashion us without pigments,
so that the beauty of our image would no longer be corrupted by mortality.
O Painter, who paints images on a surface of water,
and whose art is not hindered by what is contrary to it!
O Artist, who breathes spirit without hands,
and sows undying life in mortality!
What a command, for which all difficulties are easy,
and which gives strength to the weak by the power of its greatness!
What a will, whose sign came before its work,
and which, before it created, saw in its knowledge what it would create!
This will had seen its sign, which it showed toward us,
and on it He was gazing before He created us in the beginning.
Before He fashioned us, the image of our renewal was depicted before Him,
and along with His being it existed in His mind that He would do this.

In wisdom He carried it out, as befits the One who knows all,
and wisely He fulfilled His will and showed His power.
A second creation He created for the creation He had created in the beginning,
and shook off from it the agedness of mortality.
The corruption of iniquity He willed to wipe away from mortals,
and His sign put the sponge of the Spirit into the hand of our body.
Who is it that set the will of His love toward our race,
and made our lowliness master of His wisdom?
From our clay He made treasurers of His hidden things,
and from it He appointed stewards to give life.
Priests He chose for Himself, as mediators between Him and our people,
and He sent them as an embassy to mankind.
To them He gave the great seal of His divinity,
that with it they might seal the work of the renewal of all.
To them He entrusted the wealth of the Spirit, which is never diminished,
that they might distribute it lovingly, as befits His greatness.
A spiritual art He taught them,
that they might paint the image of life on a surface of water.
O bodily beings, painters of spirit without hands!
O mortals, who give birth to life in mortality!
O priesthood, how exalted it has become above all,
and has taken authority in height and depth by the power of Him who chose it!
O wonder, at whose greatness astonishment itself is astonished:
that mortality should give itself life as though by its own power!
O will, which humbled itself beside the things it had fashioned,
and placed its wealth in the hand of flesh, that flesh might enrich itself!
O Creator, who came and was zealous for His work of creating,
and handed a pen to the work of His hands to paint itself!
Who would not be amazed at the greatness of the love of His kindness,
that He made our clay a creator of creation in His own likeness?
Who would not give thanks for His care toward our race,
that He exalted our lowliness along with His incomprehensible being?
To our nature He gave authority together with its renewal,
that it should itself create a new creation free of death.
The power of life He breathed into our body, which gives birth to sufferings,
and it began to interpret spiritual things which it does not see.
The craft of His creating He showed to our soul,
and it gained power to create a creation like the Creator.

By the word of Him who fashions man in the womb of the waters
and puts him together spiritually without hands —
this is a craft whose examination is beyond amazement,
and only a hidden will could tell it as it is.
In purity of soul the mind can gaze upon it,
and instead of eyes it sees its preciousness with the intellect.
Precious is its story, and it cannot be told in a bodily way;
it is too lofty to search out, and cannot be grasped in an earthly way.
Spiritually is composed the story of the renewal of our image,
and except by the Spirit the mouth cannot speak of its account.
In heavenly fashion the medicine cleanses the sore of our iniquity,
and unless the intellect rises to the height, it does not see it.
For the Master of masters is reserved the explanation of the meditation of our life,
and unless the one who learns draws comparisons, he does not understand.
Come, disciples of the great Christ, let us look carefully
at the spiritual writings of baptism.
Come, heirs of the testaments written in blood,
see the wards of your inheritance with the eye of the Spirit.
Come, gaze with the affection of love upon your wards,
and praise and extol the enriching of man from treasures.
Come, pure children of baptism, let us all together
depict the voice that cries out over the waters so that they gain power.
Come, let us gaze discerningly at the hand of flesh,
which buries bodies and raises them up swiftly.
Let us make ourselves ready to see the wonder in the temple of holiness,
and the powers of the height who celebrate the mystery of our salvation.
Behold the time when order requires of those who look on
that each keep the gaze of his mind on what is being said.
Behold, the priest makes ready to enter the Holy of Holies,
to open the door of the kingdom of the height before those who enter.
Behold, he draws near to the door of the royal house,
to receive power to complete the mysteries performed by his hand.
Behold, the King of the height stretches out to him the hand of the Spirit,
and places in his hand the seal of His name, to seal His lambs.
Behold, He clothes him in an undying robe of glory,

that with it he may cover the shame of men who sinned and were exposed.
Behold, He allows him to tend the sheep entrusted to him,
and he raises his voice and calls his lambs by their names.
Behold, lambs and rams and ewes are gathered together,
and he casts upon them the seal of life of his Lord's word.
Behold, he brings them in by their own words as into a fold,
and requires of them one confession of the name of the Creator.
Like a pen the sign is held by him spiritually,
and he writes body and soul clearly in the book of life.
As with a rod he drives away from them, by the word of his mouth,
the darkness of error that had blinded them from understanding.
He raises his voice and says: "Renounce the Evil One and his power,
and his angels, and his service, and his error."
First they renounce the lordship of the Evil One who enslaved them,
and then they confess the power of the Creator who set them free.
Two things, he says, are required of one who draws near to the mysteries of the Church:
renunciation of the Evil One, and faith in the Maker.
"I renounce the Evil One and his angels," he cries aloud,
"and I have no fellowship with him, not even in word."
Like a mediator the priest stands and asks him:
"Whom do you wish to serve from now on?"
From him he learns whom he wishes to call lord,
and so he enrolls him in the number of the firstborn of the height.
From Satan and from his angels he turns his face,
and so he paints the image of the Being on his forehead.
He renounces the Evil One as one whose purpose is evil,
and his angels as haters of the word of truth.
The word of truth hates the Evil One and those on his side,
and it is right that one who loves truth should hate them.
"Those who hate You, O Lord, I have hated," he says with the son of Jesse,
and he exacts from him vengeance for the insults to the Creator's name.
Whoever draws near to baptism has a war
with Satan, and with his angels, and with his service.
Now his angels are men clothed in falsehood,
who serve him with abominations full of wickedness.
One of his angels is Mani, the crafty wolf,
who has put on the likeness of the rams of the flock and leads the sheep astray.

Another of his angels is Valentinus, the wronger of truth,
who obscures the resurrection of the dead with his perversity.
His angel too is Arius, loathsome of mind,
who cast men into the sickness of inequality, more evil than a lion.
His angel too is Eunomius, the crafty serpent,
who by his bites corrupts the souls of his hearers.
Among his angels is the foolish Apollinaris,
who builds falsehood upon the building of truth and is not ashamed.
Among his angels is Paul, perverse of mind,
who in his insolence scorns the power of the Word of the Father.
Among his angels let us also count Eutyches,
the madman who raved in love of the suffering of the Impassible.
The Man of the Chapters has learned the art of chapter-making,
mingling, for all, the living nature with the sufferings of the body.
Greater is his wickedness than the wickedness of his fellows,
and he aids the Accuser more than his companions do.

Through these the Hater of man leads mankind astray,
and through them he casts the bitterness of his deceit into the mind of man.
They carry out the kinds of his abominable service,
and even enlarge it with lying inventions.
His service is that service in which they take pride,
and his mysteries, not those of truth, are spoken in it.
To him the heretics [?] in every guise,
and by his crafts they go astray and lead others astray in their hatred.
It is right, then, to flee from them as from the unclean,
and not to mingle in the abominations of their deeds.
Let him call them unclean and evil, them and the Evil One,
and let him turn his face from their mysteries full of wickedness.
Full of wickedness is the invention of the Evil One and his hearers,
and the pains of iniquity lie hidden in it through the error of his craft.
His inventions are the circus, the stadium and the theatre,
and the riotous sounds of the songs he composed and wrote.
His errors are auguries and divinations of every form:
the twitching of the eyes, the ringing of the ears, the meeting on the road.
These the disciple of truth renounces when he becomes a disciple,
and so he draws near to the confession of faith.
The truth of his soul he reveals with an audible voice:
"Behold, I have turned from the side of the Evil One toward the Creator."
He puts the demons to shame with the voice of the word of his mouth:
"Listen, rebels: I have no fellowship with you."
He gladdens the hosts of the height with the words of his faith:
"Come, spiritual ones, rejoice with me, for I have been saved from perdition.
I am your companion and a fellow servant in your works,
and the Lord whom you serve, I long to serve."
A fellow servant of the kingdom of the height he names himself,
the wanderer who has returned to take refuge with the King of kings.
The stewards of the holy Church he first entreats

to bring him to the King's gate, that he may speak his words.
The stewards are the priests, ministers of the mysteries,
to whom belongs the administering of the treasury of the Spirit.
To one of them the wanderer, the exile, draws near,
that they may free him from the slavery of the Evil One who took him captive.
Like a captive he stands naked, without covering,
and shows him the hardship and toil of the house of his captors.
"By your favour with the King," the captive cries to the King's servants,
"draw near to the King and plead for me, that He may be reconciled to me.
Go in and tell Him that one of His servants has returned from captivity,
and behold, he begs to see His face in love.
"I was taken captive by a servant who rebelled against Your lordship;
free my life from his slavery, that he may not fall upon me again.
I am Your servant, good Lord, and the son of Your handmaid;
why should I serve an evil servant who rebelled against You?
Enough that I have served unjustly the one who is wholly injustice;
redeem me from him, that I may be Yours, for I am Yours."
These words the wanderer composes on the day of his return,
after the manner of that story of the younger son.
For his sake the parables were given in deed,
and it was fitting that he speak his words in the manner of the penitent.
He it is of whom it is written that he strayed, went out, turned back and came,
and the day of his going out and of his return is marked in the Gospel.
On this day what is written becomes truth,
and abundant mercies go out to meet him and receive him.
At his return the heavenly hosts rejoice [?],
and celebrate him as a dead man who has come back to life.
The Accuser alone grieves at his return,
for he has broken free of his snares, shattered his traps, left him and fled.
From the slavery of his bitterness the sinner has fled,
and taken refuge with the good Lord whose love is sweet.
From his captivity the captive has returned to his own country,
and behold, he begs to go in and see the face of the King.
By his petition he brings an accusation against his captor,
and accuses him from the divine law.
To the King's servants he gives the pen of the word of his mouth,
and they write it and present it before the Judge.

He asks the priests, as advocates, [?] to take up the case,
and they plead the case on his behalf while he is silent.
As in a court of law the priest stands at the time of the mysteries,
and accuses the Accuser on account of the sins.
Like a poor man who has been wronged, the sinner too stands,
and begs and entreats that mercy may help him in the judgment.
Naked he stands, stripped, before the Judge,
that by his abasement he may move mercy to cover him.
Without covering he pleads his case against his adversary,
that the King may see him and swiftly take up his cause.
He bends his knees and bows his head for shame,
for he is ashamed to look up at the face of the height, toward the Judge.
He bows himself on sackcloth, and so draws near to ask for mercy,
remembering his slavery to the Evil One.
Two things he depicts by the kneeling he performs at the time of the mysteries:
one, his fall; the other, that he pays as a debtor.
That fall in Paradise he now remembers,
and he pleads his case against Satan, who led his father astray.
Of him he is afraid, and so his face looks to the ground,
until he hears the voice of forgiveness, and then he takes heart.
He waits for the priest to bring his words before the Judge,
and to return to him the deed of freedom with oil and water.
The sponsor too leads him along to the house of the laws,
to go in and bear witness to the readiness of his soul's love.
In love of soul he entreats that he may persevere in love of the truth,
and his companion stands surety that the testing of his soul is genuine.
He becomes like a guide to his words and deeds,
and shows him the spiritual conduct of life.
By his name he calls him and presents him before the guardians,
that they may name him heir and son and child of the kingdom.
In the records the priest asks for the name of the lost one,
and brings it in and places it among the archives of the King's books.
Like a lamb he sets him at the gate of the sheepfold,
and signs his body and mingles him with the flock.
The sign of the oil he holds in his hand before the onlookers,
and openly proclaims the power of the things he beholds [?],

and as in a type he shows to the eyes of the bodily senses
the hidden power concealed in the visible sign.
O dust that signs the sheep with the sign of its Lord,
and seals the name of His hiddenness with a manifest sign!
O creature of dust, who holds the Spirit on the tip of his tongue,
and cuts away the iniquity of soul and body by the word of his mouth!
O mortal, in whose mouth a great fountain is fixed,
which gives the children of his race immortal life to drink!
O poor man, son of poor men, who suddenly became rich,
and began to distribute the wealth of the Spirit which his fathers never had!
O creature of dust, whose dust bears witness to his lowliness,
who has received power to create a new creation himself!
A new creation the Good One taught the children of His house,
that they might renew it by the craft of His creating.
The iniquity of man tore down the building His hands had made,
and He gave mankind authority to build it again.
He saw His works grown old and worn out by mortality,
and His craft devised for Him a means of immortal life.
He saw that the foundations of His house were tottering through passibility,
and He laid its foundations in the depth of the waters and made them firm.
In soft waters He willed to make firm the soft bodies,
and by the power of the Spirit to strengthen the motions prone to fall.
A furnace of water His sign prepared in mystery,
and instead of fire He heated it with the Spirit of the power of His will.
The Maker appointed for Himself a craftsman over His workmanship,
that he might cast it in the furnace of water and the heat of the Spirit.
Come, see a wonder in mortality:
it dies and lives through the mediation of its own ministry.
Come, let us gaze on the mystery of our death within the waters,
and see the wonder that is performed in us in mystery.
Come, let us draw near to the treasurers of the Church's treasures,
and hear from them how they give life in water.
Let us enter with them into the mystical Holy of Holies,
and learn from them the explanation of the mysteries of death and life.
Death and life are the mysteries of baptism,
and both together are performed by the one priesthood.
Through the priesthood the Creator willed to reveal His power,

and to it He entrusted the great wealth of His goodness.
Priests He appointed as stewards over His wards,
that as faithful ones they might distribute wealth to the children of His house.
To them He gave the seal of the name of His incomprehensible being,
that they might seal mankind with the holy name.
The seal of His name each of them casts upon his flock,
and in threefold manner men sign men.
The iron of the oil the priest holds at the tips of his fingers,
and signs the body and the senses of the soul with its sharpness.
With the words of his mouth the mortal whets the oil,
and sharpens it like iron to cut away iniquity.
The three names he recites in order, one after another,
and in threefold manner he completes and fulfils the mystery of our salvation.
O weak one, how great is the wonder performed through you!
Too small is the mouth to tell how great the power of its testing is.
O lowly one, how exalted your lowliness has become!
The mind cannot ascend with you to where you have reached.
O man — it is of the priest that I have said what I have said —
how great the authority you have been given, that you are a giver of life!
Life the priest gives to his fellows through his ministry,
and he treads out the way for those of his nature toward the things to come.
The office of the mouth speaks to the motions and the members,
and on behalf of each it utters the words of the forgiveness of iniquity.
Oil and water he lays down first as foundations,
and by his words he completes the building of the name of the Being.
With oil and soft water he casts the body,
and in place of clay he changes it and makes it pure gold.
Who would not be amazed at the power our poverty has acquired,
that it should itself grow rich from a gift beyond comprehension?
Like a treasurer the priest stands at the gate of holiness,
and puts in the keys of the word of his mouth and opens up life.
The three names he casts upon the oil and sanctifies it,
that it may sanctify the uncleanness of man by its holiness.
With the name of His hiddenness he signs the visible body,
and the power of the name's sharpness enters even to the soul.
O wonder, that man performs what is not his own:
he signs bodies that are prone to fall and passible within!

After the manner of a physician he too attends to the members,
touching from outside and perceiving the suffering within.
To body and soul he brings the remedies of his art,
and heals the visible and the hidden by divine power.
Divinely he softens the medicine he applies with his hands,
and heals all pains by its power, and it never fails.
Like a shop he has opened the door of the temple of holiness,
and he treats diseases and binds up the pains of those of his nature.
By the sign outside he touches the hidden pains within,
and then applies the medicine of the Spirit by the sign of the water.
With a manifest voice he proclaims the power of his hidden things,
and with his tongue he distributes spiritual wealth.
He makes words heard in the ears of the sheep as he signs it,
and it listens lovingly to the three names as they are proclaimed.
In the name of the Father and the Son and the Spirit he seals his words,
and confirms the one who is baptized in their names.
The three names he paints on his face like a shield,
that the tyrant may see the image of the Being on the person's head.
The shaming of the demons is the reason for the sign on the forehead,
that when they look at the person's head they may flee from him.
For their sake the mysteries of oil and water exist,
to be armour against the war of their onslaughts.
The oil with which the earthly are anointed is armour,
that they may not be harmed by spiritual beings in the hidden battle.
It is the great seal of the King of kings, with which they are sealed,
that they may do service in the spiritual contest.
On their foreheads they receive the spiritual seal,
that it may shine before the eyes of angels and men.
Like eager labourers they stand at the King's gate,
and the priest at their head like a commander at the head of his flock.
As for war he draws up their ranks at the time of the mysteries,
that they may shoot sharpened arrows at the Adversary.
Arrows of words he fashions and places in their mouths,
that they may prevail [?] against the Evil One who enslaved them.
A target is set before their eyes for them to aim at,
and like a bowstring he stretches the words upon their tongues.
They enter into testing at the start of the war for which they have enlisted,
as they are proved by the confession of their minds.

As in truth the priest stands at the head of their ranks, / and shows them the target of truth, that they may aim well. / They renounce [?] the Evil One, his power and his angels, / and so the King's mark is painted on their foreheads. / They renounce and confess, two things at once and without division: / renunciation of the Evil One, and the heart's confession in the name of the Divine Being. / Through the priesthood they make a covenant with the Divine Being, / that they will never again turn to Satan in their deeds. / To the priest they give the pledge of the words of their thoughts, / and he brings it in and reads it before the divine will. / The door of the archive of the royal house is held in his hands, / and he has authority to enroll men by means of [?]. / He calls the servants of the King by their names and sets them up, / and passes them one by one and stamps on their faces the stamp of the oil. / By the sound of his utterances he proclaims the power hidden in his words: / whose they are, and by whose name they are stamped. / “N.,” he says, “is the servant of the King of kings above and below, / and is stamped in his name, to serve according to his will.” / He mingles the name of the Divine Being with the oil in his hands, / and signs and says: Father and Son and Holy Spirit. / “N. is signed,” he says, “with the three equal names, / among which there is no distinction of elder and younger, one from another.” / “It is not I who sign,” says the priest, “but he is signed,” / for the stamp he sets is not his own but his Lord's. / He is the mediator, chosen by grace to minister, / and through what is not his own he drives out iniquity and gives the Spirit. / By the outward name he shows the power that is in the names, / which can strengthen a man's weakness without being seen. / He repeats the three names with the oil over the whole man, / so that demons and tyrants and passions may not harm him. / It is not the oil that protects a man from harms; / it is the power of the Divine Being that gives strength to the feeble. / The oil is a sign that proclaims the divine power, / and by outward things [?] it strengthens the servant in hidden ones. / By its power body and soul acquire strength, / and no longer fear the harms of mortality.

Like athletes they go down and stand in the arena, / and join battle with the feeble [?] that are in them. / This power the oil of anointing imparts: / it is not the oil, but the Spirit that strengthens it. / The Spirit strengthens the anointing of the soft oil, / and it becomes firm through the use to which it is put. / By its firmness it hardens the body and the motions of the soul, / and boldly they engage in battles against the Evil One. / The demons see the sign of his name upon a man, / and they tremble at him, for in his name they see a precious name. / The name of the Divine Being gleams from the sign on the forehead, / and the eyes of the deceivers are ashamed to look upon it. / The Sun of [?] has dawned from on high upon the head of man, / and by its rays has driven away the errors of the darkness of [?]. / Come, O man, give praise and offer it to the one who honoured you, / who by his gift made your body a sun of [?]. / Come, debtor, pay thanks to your liberator, / who redeemed you and freed you from the bondage of sin and death. / Come, mortal, give glory to the power of the Divine Being, / who gave you strength to sow life in mortality. / Let the whole race of earthly Adam, with every mouth, [?] / him who raised you from the dust to his own greatness.
Sunday of the Holy Week of the Resurrection

Another, by the same author. / Memra thirty-one. / It is recited on Sunday of the Holy Week of the Resurrection. / Response: / Blessed is Christ, who on the day of his resurrection acquitted our nature and condemned the tyrant. / My brothers.

The King of the height put on an earthly form, / to bring the captive soul of mankind out from the strong one. / His will went forth in the form of a man, to give life to mankind, / and the Evil One saw him, but did not perceive the power of his hidden nature. / The Creator took the likeness of a servant to set all free; / he hid his glory within the garment of mortality. / From the race that the Evil One had taken captive he chose a mighty one, / and armed him with a spear, to go out and redeem the children of his people. / He gave him divine armour to fight with, / so that once he had won he might gain, by his own strength, the name of victory. / The mighty one of the body put on the King's armour, / and set the helmet of the salvation of life on the head of his mind. / Spiritually he put on the armour, in keeping with his hidden nature, / and braced his soul for the contest on behalf of the limbs. / With the stirrings of the soul the bodily one armed himself, / for he saw in the Spirit that his adversary was a spiritual being. / In the Spirit he joined battle with the spiritual one, the prince of the air, / so that he would not be tripped up through his earthly limbs. / In body and soul he bore the armour the King had given him, / and he wore it with love, with the senses of the body and the stirrings [?] of the soul. / A hidden war the mortal waged with a hidden power, / and he won the victory for body and soul and set them free. / The Evil One had taken his race captive, and Death the tyrant who had rebelled,

and he gave himself up to the struggle on behalf of his people. / He went out to battle against the Evil One in combat and defeated him, / and readied himself for the struggle with greedy Death. / He grappled with the strong one in the struggle of the fight, / and bound him and threw him down with force from beneath [?]. / The spiritual one was overcome by the bodily one through the power of the Spirit, / and the body that sufferings had trampled overcame the prince of the air. / The despised body mocked and laughed at the strong one, / and stripped him of his armour, so that he would fight with mortals no more. / 'Go, Evil One, to your partner,' he said to him; / 'go and prepare yourself other armour, for the cause of Death. / Go and set yourself snares of death by means of mortals, / for on your own your strength proved weak in the struggle. / Go and gather the children you begot through your crafts, / and arm them with every slander, as you are accustomed to do. / Call your companions in falsehood to help you, / for you are a liar, and with liars [?] you win.' / He let the deceiver go from the struggle for a short time, / so that he might go and contrive a means of death in the guise of a lawsuit. / He knew that he would plead his case by the law, / and he sought to win by reminding him of what had gone before. / The transgression of the commandment enjoined in Paradise, / and its folly, he held on to as testimony. / In the case over the fruit he pressed his claim like a guarantor, / for the fruit had stood surety for him for the bondage of mankind, which he had bought with a word [?]. / He showed him the signature of Adam and Eve: / 'See, your parents sealed it and consented; read and understand. / Adam wrote me a bond when he fell into the debt of sin, / and since he did not repay it, his children are pledged for the interest. / From the beginning I gained authority over mortals; / they did not write it in secret, and they were enslaved as debtors. / Not by force did I take your race captive, but by debt; / they willingly agreed to be slaves. / Not only Adam and the children of his generation are in my debt, / for the whole of nature is bound by the bond of mortality. / And if you are made of dust and share in the sufferings of the body, / look at your nature and know that you are bound by the bond of [...] my lordship. / There is no bodily being with limbs who is not mortal, / and if he is mortal, he is under my servitude and that of Death. / Or else show me that you are not mortal, and I will fall silent before you. / But if you are mortal, your nature settles the dispute over your words. / Show the token the King gave you that you are not mortal— / though even this I would not accept of one made of dust. / You are bodily: why should words be needed in the trial? / The very nature [?] of the body is wholly the corruption of mortality.' / These things the Accuser was turning over in his mind, / smarting from the defeats he had suffered at the hands of the body. / He clung to mortality like a shield, / thinking that through it he would win, as Death had. / The hater spoke these things secretly in his thoughts, / and with a searching mind he pored over them as though in haste [?]. / And because the hidden Mind saw the scheming of the Evil One, / he revealed the hatred of the evil-minded one to the beings who were watching. / With an open voice he spoke out the hidden things: / 'See now, the Accuser has come to plead a case. / See, the ruler and seizer of the world demands at my hands

the full dues of mortality, as from mortals. / In the form of a lawsuit he has spoken against me as against a man: / "You are a son of man; pay like a man who is liable to judgment." / With subtleties he has disputed with me too, as with Adam: / "You are an Adamite, a stock that the flood of my cunning swept away. / Why are you proud of words that happened to be at your side? / Do not boast of what is not yours, for you are dust." / He looks at my nature as at a despised thing, this hater of our race, / and does not perceive the power that clothed me from the womb. / The manifestation of my descent to mankind is hidden from him, / and he does not know the dispensation that has come about through me. / I too in silence hide my greatness from him, / until the struggle of his deceit is complete in the death he plots against me. / Now, in court, I will show him from the laws / that he has slandered wrongfully through mortality. / If mortals are liable to him because they sinned, / who can go to law with me, who am pure of stains? / And if Adam sinned and was pledged because he listened to his counsel, / who will fight against me, whom he did not overcome even with a hint? / Then it is clear that he wrongfully [?], / and that he does not justly wield his sceptre over mortals. / And when it is clear besides that I am free from his servitude, / I willingly accept the death of his deceit. / With death he threatens me and frightens me, being Death, / and by means of death I will throw him down from his dominion. / With the armour of the sufferings of mortality he wages war on me; / by the suffering of my own person I will teach him that his strength is weak. / By the very thing by which he supposed Adam and his children were pledged, / by that I will wipe out the bond of his lordship over mortals. / With death he sealed the bond of the debts of the human race, / and through death on the top of the wood I will tear it up. / Before the eyes of spiritual and bodily beings I will annul / the sentence in which he boasts as victor. / To the heavenly and the earthly I will show / the salvation of life and the renewal accomplished in me. / I call heaven and earth as my chosen witnesses, / and in the hidden name I seal the covenant of my words. / Speaking and dumb things shall be mediators between me and the Evil One, / that without justice the hater urges on greedy Death. / And if he has done wrong, and thirsted for wrong, and thirsted for blood, / let them justly rebuke his wrong and expose his deceit. / See, I accept the sentence of his wicked judgment, / and I show that Death did not overpower me by force. / See, I go down into the depth of Sheol as into the sea, / and swiftly I proclaim the name of my victory. / See, I fulfil the types and mysteries the just traced out, / and I pay his wage to Jonah, who died on my account. / By deeds I show the meaning of that descent, / when he went down and came up and proclaimed my victory in a mystery. / In a mystery the fish swallowed Jonah without his dying; / me Death swallows in very deed, and cannot corrupt me. / Let the gates of Sheol now lift up their gate before me, / for I will enter [?] and bring Adam's captive people out from the strong one. / I will go down with the blood of the new covenant of my own person, / and set free the prisoners whom Death has shut up in the pit of Sheol. / With my blood I write and seal the salvation of mankind,

for death is the witness that confirms a testament. / On the top of the wood I write it with the blood of my own person, / and I tear up the bond of the debts they owed to sin.' / He went down, struck everything, and plunged into Sheol, the sea of the dead, / and like a living fisher [?] he caught them in the dead waters. / With a living net he stirred up those without sense, / and set thousands of the dead moving toward the meeting-place of life. / With silent stirrings the mighty one cried out in greedy Death, / and a groan seized it at the new tidings of the return of the dead. / 'Give me the captives [?] of the children of Adam whom the Evil One gave you, / for you have enslaved the freeborn under your hard yoke.' / Death the tyrant trembled and was confounded at the sound of his words, / and released mankind's captive people from its grip against its will. / The prisoners came out from the pit where there is no life, / and proclaimed to those without hope the hope that the dead will live. / The dead brought a new hope to the living dead, / and the living did wrong to the new message the dead had spoken. / The tombs became messengers, showing the dead alive, / and he made the good news of the voice of salvation heard in everyone's ears. / At the voice of the departed, those dead in wickedness were raised, / as they saw the renewal of the body and the return of the soul. / The dead were telling the dead the new thing that had happened: / how death overcame Death and raised the dead. / A great wonder was spoken of in the land of Judah, / as a dead man would meet someone [?] he had known. / It was not the departed who had died long before who came to life at the cross, / so that each one might be recognized by his brother and by his kinsfolk. / For he did not raise any of the ancients who were long removed, / lest the eye of the flesh should falsify the testimony of truth. / From the generation that was then alive, / from it he raised them, to be witnesses of his preaching. / O mighty one, who went down to Sheol by the road all take, / and cut off the road by which men travel to the house of the dead! / O buried one, whom Death swallowed, yet he was not corrupted! / O bodily one, the frame of whose body was not dissolved! / O athlete, who wrestled with the strong one, / and let him think he had fallen, then turned and threw him and raised up his own race! / He fell as he willed, in body and soul, like the guilty, / and he rose and was raised, and raised up the body and set the soul free. / On this condition he grappled with the strong one: / that by his victory he would free his race from slavery. / By his death he defeated the one who defeats all, and struck the one who strikes all; / by the very thing by which he thought mankind condemned, he was brought low. / With death Adam and his children wrote him a bond of servitude, [?] / and through death Adam set free Adam and his children. / The mortal, the second Adam, died for the sake of Adam, / and the son of Adam rose and gave life to Adam and his offspring. / The bodily one died who had been composed with the sinews of the Spirit, / and he rose and was raised by the power of the craftsman who destroyed and built him. / At the raising of his body the earthly and the heavenly rejoiced, / and he gladdened those who had been grieving over his death. / The spiritual beings rejoiced that by his death he had overcome greedy Death, / and they came down and [?] his body in the tomb as a victor. / His body was made a royal temple for the heavenly beings, / and they praised with a voice of victory the one who overcame death. / They cried glory to him as he came up from within the tomb:

'Blessed is he who by his death killed Death, which corrupts mankind.' / They had grieved greatly over his [...]ing, as over a king, / and he clothed them in a lovely colour on the day of his resurrection. / Through white garments he displayed the heavenly beings, / to teach them about the renewal that comes about through him. / The Watchers showed a wondrous sight to the earthly ones: / the beautiful garment that bodies will put on at the resurrection. / By the beauty of their clothing they taught them / that by a sign of peace he had sown in their ears the voice of salvation. / 'Whom do you seek? The living among the dead?' they said to the women. / '[?] that he has risen and been raised and has overcome Death.' / They rolled the stone from the mouth of the tomb at a hidden sign, / and opened the door before their eyes, and the women went in and saw. / Why did the Watchers lift the stone that had been sealed? / Was it hard for the conqueror of Death to lift the stone? / See, the resurrection, which is very hard, he accomplished with a sign; / how then would he not lift a stone, which was easy? / His body escaped from the mouth of Death, the raging lion, / and for the stone, a contemptible thing, he called spiritual beings to lift it. / That command which raised his body would not have found it hard / to lift the stone from the door and let him go out. / It was for the sake of the eyes of bodily beings that he lifted the stone, / so that they might see the tomb and the grave clothes and gain hope. / To assure mankind he opened the tomb before onlookers, / so that they would not be divided over his resurrection, saying he had perhaps not risen. / That he truly rose is clearer than the sun, / and the swift course of his preaching to the four quarters bears witness. / And though his resurrection was made plain to all by deeds, / to the slow of heart and the haughty of soul it was not true. / That he rose and was raised—see, here is the proof of the greatness of his power: / that he abolished error and loosed the bonds of mortality. / He rose on the third day, and the promise of his words did not prove false, / and he fulfilled the mystery the son of Amittai traced out in the belly of the whale. / For three days the prophet was in the deeps, as a mystery, / and he fulfilled the mystery of the three days in deeds. / In Jonah the mystery died without dying and stayed alive; / here, in deed, he truly died and was not corrupted. / The son of Amittai came up out of the sea as he had gone down, / and traced out a figure of death and life and of the turning of the nations. / On this condition he sent him with a sign to the nations: / to trace out the mystery of what took place at the end of the ages. / So too the firstfruits, who died on behalf of all and for the sake of all, / rose and was raised, and proclaimed life to the people and to the nations. / He came out of the tomb and left his linen clothes as a testimony / that he has now stripped off mortality and put on glory. / He made two things known, wisely, by the linen clothes he left: / that he has no need of them, and that they serve as witnesses against the wrongdoers. / Plain to him was the impudence of the sons of Jacob, / that they would cover up with slander the laying aside of his clothes. / By the clothes he left he exposed the deceit of their thoughts: / for how could they have left the clothes in the tomb if they had stolen his body? / His body had been embalmed with myrrh and aloes and carefully laid out; / would it have been easy for those carrying him off to strip [?] the clothes? / And if they stole him like fugitives clothed in fear, / how did they separate and roll up the clothes at their leisure? / Troubled envy blinded the slanderers,

and they did not look at the clear light of the resurrection [?] of his body. / With silver they wanted to cover up his preaching, / but it tore up the cloth that deceit and its [?] had woven. / With silver they bought him from Judas for the slavery of death, / and when he had been raised they suppressed his resurrection with deceitful silver. / But what can deceitful silver do against manifest truth, / when it is proclaimed as by a herald from the mouths of silent things? / Stones and tombs and [...] the veil of the door cried out to those who speak: / 'Rise, you who are sunk down, and accept the hope that the dead will live.' / And if silent and mouthless things proclaimed his victory, / then the deceit of the silver is void and is not believed. / Speaking and dumb things were witnesses for him before the wrongdoers, / and set their hand to the testament of his death and his life. / The skilled scribe, the mighty one of the Spirit who set down victory, / gave a demonstration through the veil of the door, which he tore in two. / He showed that he had abandoned the temple of the sacrifices for the people's atonement, / and no longer desires blood [...] for the reconciliation of mankind. / By the veil of the door he revealed his resurrection, which [?], / for if a silent thing [?] and was silenced, how much more the speaking! / The lash of wrath that the guilty deserved turned to discernment: / it raised the rod and struck the cloth instead of the mind. / He sheathed the sword that had decreed his sentence within his compassion, / and raised his hand to bring down his rod, but his love held him back. / 'I do not exact vengeance for his death as from the guilty'— / for it was not fitting that the Life-giver of men should destroy men. / 'For the life of men,' he said, 'I have come, not for destruction,' / and he confirmed his words by his deeds. / He died for all and gave life to all, as he had promised, / and he fulfilled and completed the work on behalf of all. / The second Adam died in his nature, like mortals, / and crucified mortality with himself, and gave it life by his life. / He restored the building of the temple of the body that the wicked had destroyed, / and the Word of the Father completed and built it, as he had promised. / He went down in a nature that gives birth to sufferings and plunged into Sheol, / and brought up with him a catch of men to new life. / He broke down the pit that Death had built before the dead, / and trod out a path for mortality toward life. / He raised his voice like a mighty man before his labourers: / 'Rise and take courage, for I have conquered Death and the Evil One. / I wrestled with a hidden one in a visible body, / and overcame the strong one in the contest and plundered his wealth. / I pleaded a just case against him before the Judge, / and so condemned him for wrongfully taking our race captive. / I brought out the unjust bond and showed it before the laws, / that it had not been sealed with the signature of chosen witnesses. / And when the falsehood of the hidden one was exposed [?] in his words, / the King rebuked him and gave orders, and cast him into exile. / Now that I have won and the strong one, the hater of our race, has been condemned, / I make my fellows sharers in the greatness of my victory. / The Spirit has given me the power of immortal life; / with it I arm what is passible against sufferings. / See, spiritual armour has been forged for those of flesh; / put it on, you mortals, and fight and conquer spiritually. / By the sentence of the judge [?] of death you were indebted and pledged; / come, take back the bond of your debts freely, and gain life. / By the death of my own person I have trampled the Death that corrupts mankind,

and through my victory the prince of the air has been condemned and exposed.' / O victory that, even as it was being won, overcame the tyrants! / O fall of the bodily one, who fell and raised up! / The mortal temple of flesh, built by the Spirit, fell, / and the will of the King who dwelt in it renewed it and built it again. / Who is it, you lovers of death, that fell under Death, / and who is it that paid off the bond of debts as a debtor? / Who is the dead one who died in his nature and rose in truth, / and what is the resurrection whose heralds even silent things became? / Reveal, then, the wound of your thoughts, so that a remedy may be found for it: / why do you want to call [?] the descent of the one who conquered Death? / Which nature fought with suffering and also won the victory? / Reveal it and examine it for us, you seekers of truth. / If it was the Word, the offspring of the Father, who suffered in his nature, / then our nature did not suffer with him in the death of his being. / And if it was not our despised nature that died and was raised, / then the hope that the dead will live is false and empty. / If Death had swallowed the impassible nature, / how then did he suffer in it—in his own nature, or in ours? / If he tasted suffering in his own nature—and this is wickedness— / did all of him suffer, or did he suffer in part and was put to the test? / Yet there is nothing that is neither impassible nor passible, / so that in part he would suffer and in part remain unaffected, without being [?] whole. / If the Only-begotten fell in his nature under Death, / then he has cut off [?] of the name of Being. / And if he fell as the Word, and not as one of us, / who raised him from his fall and gave him life? / That he should raise his own fallen self is a hard thing to say, / and if others raised him, he is needy and lacking as well. / If it was the Spirit and the power of the Father that [?] him, / see, it turns out that he is far lower than the Being. / And if he is less than the Being—I do not say so— / why do we quarrel with Arius as with a stranger? / For this reason the Church drove him out beyond its doors, / because he makes the Son small and lowers him beneath his Begetter. / And if this is so—which it is wrong even to say— / weave a crown for the Interpreter, who interpreted well. / To you I said that you cannot do this; / between us and them is a great chasm that cannot be crossed. / We do not surrender ourselves to heretics, like a torn garment, / and we do not put good wine into the wineskins of error. / We do not give the pure holy thing of our faith / to [?] dogs who do not understand the power of Being. / Why should we cast the pearl of our soul's confession / before grazing herds that love dung like beasts? / We do not walk in the path of confusion with those who stray, / and we are not dragged along the road of the falsehood of passibility. / We do not bring down the one exalted above all to humiliation, / and we do not put to death that Life which gives life. / It was the [?] that fell into Sheol, being subject to death, / through the mortality in which he died in his nature, to abolish death. / Death was knocking against a rock formed out of dust, / and its formation turned into a [?] of all, spiritually. / It is he who dwelt three days with the departed, / and he it is who was raised on the third day and raised up our race. / Blind envy blinded the slanderers,

and they did not look at the clear light of the resurrection [?] of his body. / With silver they wanted to [?] his preaching, / but it tore up the cloth that deceit and its [?] had woven. / With silver Judas sold him into the slavery of death, / and when he had been raised they suppressed his resurrection with deceitful silver. / But what can deceitful silver do against manifest truth, / when it is proclaimed as by a herald from the mouths of silent things? / Stones and tombs and the veils of the doors cried out to those who speak: / 'Rise, you who are sunk down, and accept the hope that the dead will live.' / And if silent and mouthless things proclaimed his victory, / then the deceit of the silver is void and is not believed. / Speaking and dumb things were witnesses for him before the wrongdoers, / and set their hand to the testament of his death and his life. / The skilled scribe, the mighty one of the Spirit who set down victory, / gave a demonstration through the veil of the door, which he tore in two. / He showed that he had abandoned the temple of the sacrifices for the people's atonement, / and no longer desires blood [?] for the reconciliation of mankind. / By the veil of the door he revealed his resurrection, which [?], / for if a silent thing was confounded and fell silent, how much more the speaking! / The lash [?] of wrath that the guilty deserved turned to discernment: / it raised the rod and struck the cloth instead of the mind. / He sheathed the sword that had decreed his sentence within his compassion, / and raised his hand to bring down his rod, but his love held him back. / 'I do not exact vengeance for his death as from the guilty'— / for it was not [...] that the Life-giver [?] of men should destroy men. / 'For the life of men,' he said, 'I have come, and not for destruction,' / and he confirmed his words by his deeds. / He died for all and gave life to all, as he had promised, / and he fulfilled and completed the work on behalf of all [?]. / The second Adam died in his nature, like mortals, / and crucified mortality with himself, and gave it life by his life. / He restored the building of the temple of the body that the wicked had destroyed, / and the Word of the Father completed and built it, as he had promised. / He went down in a nature that gives birth to sufferings and plunged into Sheol, / and brought up with him a catch of men to new life. / He broke down the wall of Death before the dead, / and trod out a path for mortality toward life. / He raised his voice like a mighty man before his labourers: / 'Rise and take courage, for I have conquered Death and the Evil One. / I wrestled with a hidden one in a visible body, / and overcame the strong one in the contest and plundered his wealth. / I pleaded a just case against him before the Judge, / and so condemned him for wrongfully taking our race captive. / I brought out the unjust bond and showed it before the laws, / that it had not been sealed with the signature of chosen witnesses.' / He it is who went down to the lowest parts of the earth, / and he it is who went up above all to exalt all. / Into the frame of his body they drove spears, nails and lance, / and by his renewal he wiped out the bond of the body's sufferings. / He came down upon the lion in its lair with the armour of the Spirit, / and removed the sentence on the race of Adam, which had been [?]. / He cried out within Sheol like a mighty one, and its foundations shook, / and he broke its gates and cut through its bars and plundered its spoil. / 'Lift up your gates, the veils of the gates!'—as he was coming out, / and the spiritual beings were praising the power of his victory. [? five [?] [?].] / Heaven and earth became mouths for him in place of the wrongdoers,

for the living did wrong, the departed cried out, and the dumb set their seal. / The hosts on high [?] to the honour of the earthly one, / and [?] his death, and proclaimed his life to his fellows. / The Watchers brought the hope of life to the house of mortals: / 'Rise and take courage, you who are made of dust, at the abolition of death.' / They cried out and said to the destroyer of your limbs: / 'Where is your sting, O serpent, that killed us through eating the f[ruit]?' / Recount it and mock him, laughing at his snares: / 'What did you do, that Life has cut off these [?]?' / In riddles they spoke of his name, in the manner of Samson: / 'The body you swallowed became for him a spring that brings forth life.' / Out of the eater came forth spiritual food for us, / and out of the strong one [?] who breeds sufferings flowed sweetness. / Let heaven and earth, the speaking and the dumb, rejoice with us, / for the sacrifice taken from among us has reconciled the Lord with his creatures. / One firstfruits of our race has drawn near to the Godhead, / and given us through himself the sign of peace and the renewal of all. / With us let the earthly and the heavenly give thanks: / Blessed is he who in our body showed his love toward his creatures. / The end.
For the Friday of the Confessors
Memra twenty-four, / for the Friday of the Confessors. / Response: / Praise to the Power that strengthened his martyrs, so that they triumphed and conquered / by the power of his love. My brothers.

Mortals heard the voice of victory from the top of the wood,
and gained hope of wrestling in the spirit.
One of the race that had fallen through sin was victorious on the cross,
and the guilty rose up at the voice of his victory and put on armour.

In soul and body the Second Adam won the victory,
and so did the sons of his race, by the senses of the body and the motions of the soul.
The earthly heard that echo which cried out on earth:
"Arise, take courage: I alone have conquered on the cross."
The bodily had no hope of even the name of victory,
and the voice proclaiming the One who conquered gave them courage.
Mortality could not stand firm against sufferings,
but when it saw the body that hung on the wood, it gained courage.
The weak body could not bring itself to hate life,
but when One in a body despised it, the body girded up its senses.
The earthly did not know how to go up to the height,
and One who was earthly trod the way before their eyes.
They could not be persuaded to wrestle with the senses of the body,
and One showed them, by his endurance in abstaining from food.
They did not know how to trample silver under their feet,
and One taught them, when he bound it and trod it into the ground.
The deceitful snare of the love of glory was hidden and covered over,
and One ran lightly and exposed its deceit.
Body and motions of the soul were taken up with earthly things,
and among the earthly there was no glimmer of spiritual things.
They struggled in the stadium of the athletic contest,
and there was no one to award a crown of victory for their toils.
At every hour they went down to wrestle in human things,
and whenever they struggled they lost the contest, and the reward was lost.
But when the guilt of the human race grew strong,
and the wicked demons made light of their sufferings and laughed at them,
the Merciful One took pity when he saw his image being mocked,
and anointed him with the Spirit to meet the sufferings of the flesh.
By the power of the Spirit he strengthened his image as with armour,
that by the might of the Spirit he might go forth and conquer the spiritual powers.
He tested him in every bodily battle,
that by his testing the body might be trained for victory.
In him, as in a target, he taught his fellows
to aim toward the perfection of the kingdom on high.
As a mirror he set his victory before the contestants,

that in motions and senses they might become like him, toward perfection.
By his sufferings they learned to wrestle with the passions,
and by his endurance they despised and spurned the desires.
They saw his body fastened with nails by wrongdoers,
and they gave their bodies to every affliction in his likeness.
By his death they received the good hope of the resurrection of the dead,
and they hated life and loved death, that they might live with him.
