While they suffered they would remember how, at the time of his death,
he forgave those who crucified him and entreated his Father for their forgiveness.
They recalled that echo which cried out on the wood:
"Father of mercies, forgive the folly of ignorance."
In this they made themselves like him, while they suffered the sufferings of time,
and exchanged the life that is bounded by time for one without end.
The bodily crucified their bodies to the desires,
and earthly things became dead before their eyes.
They died to the world while living in it as though not living,
and they in turn reckoned the world as though not living.
They walked on earth in the manner of a spiritual way of life,
and by their labours fashioned a perfection that does not decay.
With the sufferings of time they bought the kingdom without end,
and with despised things they gained the exaltation of the rank above.
They went down to the contest and wrestled with the Strong One,
and grappled with a spirit by means of visible limbs.
The hand grappled with the incorporeal spirit,
and the light of wing lost and was overthrown before the heavy one.
O corruptible nature that sins every day,
that grew strong and conquered in battle the one who conquers every day!
O dust, whose very dust testifies to its lowliness,
that conquered the spirit whose name proclaims its lightness!
The Rebel saw the Second Adam, and that he had conquered,
and he cried out and wailed over the unexpected victory.
He saw the powers being driven out by the name of Jesus,
and amazement seized him: how does a body put a spirit to flight?
He heard that demons were driven off by a voice perceptible to the senses,
and he trembled and was dismayed that the impassible fled from a voice.
Amid the wars the Arrogant One stood over what had happened,
wondering whether it was a dream or something real [?].
For in his stubbornness he supposed that he could not be humbled,

and he reflected again on the mortals, who could not be redeemed.
But when he learned from events of the redemption of man,
he fell from his height and began to devise hateful schemes.
He stripped off the armour of wickedness with which he used to fight,
and armed the captive race itself and set one against another.
He set the world at war, so that it would fight against itself and lose,
and he became for it a spectator of the battles.
He incited the sons of earth to the struggle,
and stood there mocking as they were defeated, one by another.
He clothed mortal nature itself in his armour,
and it began to despise its own corruptible self.
He spread a covering and blinded them from understanding,
so that they would not consider why man strikes man.
He clothed them in the lying spirit of his warfare,
and made them like avengers of truths.
He made them drink the dregs of the cup of his bitterness,
and drenched them with desires as one waters a meadow.
He cast zeal for the name of God into their minds,
and made them avengers of the insult to the errors they themselves had begotten.
The Rebel heard that the voice of the Creator's name
had destroyed the edifice of iniquity, the name of "gods," which he had built for himself.
He saw that the one confession of the one God was being proclaimed,
and he hired the servants of idolatry to help him.
He saw that nature, weak in the contest against sufferings,
had begun through endurance to triumph over sufferings.
Amazement seized him: how does the body that hates death
now turn and seek its destroyer, to come near to it?
Among the [?] he lay cast down and crushed, pondering
why those who love life should hate life.
Why indeed have the earthly scorned earthly things,
and why, unexpectedly, have they disdained the passions?
Why have the earthly trampled on the desire of the flesh,
and why have they made light of their comforts as superfluous?
Why has the nature bound in desires become a stranger to them,
and yoked itself to a way of life that is foreign to it?
This has never happened, nor been heard of among mortals,
that mortality should hate life and love death.
The race of the sons of Adam has no other hope

but a lifetime bounded by time, and the life of time.
Men have never hated human things as though they were not human,
nor have the sons of dust become strangers to the tilling of the earth.
The earthly have never served the service of the Spirit,
nor offered corruptible fruits to the impassible.
The earthly have not gone up the way to the regions on high,
nor has the body, heavy of wing, flown with spirits.
The earth is their mother, and on earth they are born upon the dust,
and like infants they suck the milk of earthly things.
They fall far short in spiritual training,
and cannot take the solid food of the word of life.
It is a new thing that has suddenly happened on earth to the sons of earth,
that they have hated the earth and their kinship with earthly things.
By these sufferings the hater of man was tormented,
for he saw that men had begun lightly to trample on sufferings.
The envious one saw that men had come to hate his love,
and he stoked the fire of his evil inclination to destroy them.
He saw that the creatures of dust had armed themselves against his power,
and he too changed his armour, to ensnare men.
The ruler of the air armed himself with crafty schemes,
for he saw that the simple had learned stratagems against his deceits.
It was the sons of earth themselves that he armed, one against another,
and he goaded them through strife, one against his fellow.
The Rebel divided the very nature of Adam's clay,
and from it raised up a help to the side of his forces.
The deceiver called those simple ones to help him,
and sent them out like spies against their fellows.
He taught them the various kinds of warfare of crafty schemes,
and busied them with the murder of iniquity, to pour out iniquity.
Despised nature was commanded and given power over its own members,
and it began, without understanding, to despise its own self.
They went down to a fleshly contest against flesh,
and despised dust grappled with its own kind.
The Rebel and those of his side stood on its left,
and the host of the Hidden One and the sons of truth on the right.
The spectators of the athletes, the powers on high, gathered
to see men struggling with spirits.
Demons and men wrestled with senses and motions,

men perceptible through the senses of the body, and demons through motions.
Spirit clothed itself in a hand of flesh for the motions within them,
so that through visible limbs they might carry out their desire.
The impassible laid hands upon the passible,
and maltreated the bodily garment that lies outside the [?].
The hand of the adversary touched the garment of flesh,
but suffering did not reach the motions within the limbs.
The Rebel grappled with the visible senses of the body,
but the edge of the sword of his deceit did not reach the mind.
His crafty schemes struck the despised vessel that held the treasure of life,
but the motions hid the wealth of the Spirit in the strongholds of the soul.
Through open means the Arrogant One thought he had prevailed and conquered,
and he did not take account of the host of the Hidden One within the soul.
Though the weak body lost its limbs in the contest,
yet the soul was not overcome by his crafty schemes.
On the weak body the envious one fixed the arrows of his wrath,
but the right mind received them on the shield of the Spirit.
The visible limbs were swallowed up in temporal things,
but the impassible motions remained without change.
Nor did the body lower itself when it was despised,
for though passible it overcame nature beyond the ordinary.
It was a marvel in its endurance against sufferings,
and it was mighty indeed when it was cut to pieces without pity.
O passible one, whose nature testifies to its corruption,
that forgot its nature and became like the power of the impassible!
O dust, grains of scattered sand,
that gathered itself toward spiritual perfection!
O mortal, fashioned wholly in mortality,
that changed its clay into a composition foreign to its name!
O earth, weak of body, moulded in the ground,
that suddenly became a pearl possessing beauty!
O glass, a frail nature, quick to break,
that sufferings struck as if it were adamant, and it did not break!
The despised stone that was not set in the building of truth
has become the head of the building of the King's temple.

The clay that the waters of the sufferings of passibility swept away
girded itself and became a rock that withstands sufferings.
The weak mind girded itself like a hero,
and sought to triumph over the strong one who had trampled its nature.
Who then taught the heavy of body the kinds of warfare,
and who girded him to wrestle with spirits?
Who showed the short-lived how to hate his life,
and who gave him the hope of life without end?
Who roused from his drowning the one asleep in vanity,
and who made straight the way to the height for the lover of the depth?
When did the bodily ever love spiritual things,
and where have the earthly ever resembled the heavenly?
Who revealed the reward to the one without hope,
and who brought him the good news of the renewal of body and soul?
A hint touched him from the One who cast the fire of his love into him,
and taught him in secret to wrestle with the passions.
By the host of the Hidden One he girded himself for battle,
and by it he became a hero, grew bold, and triumphed over his foe.
By the Spirit of revelation he gained understanding to hate his life,
and by it he grew wise to exchange life for life.
Like discerning men they compared life with life and weighed them,
and the scale of the life here proved light against that of eternity.
They weighed the endurance of the life here against the kingdom on high,
and the labours did not come up to the reward of what is to come.
The sufferings of body and soul are small beside the promises,
and fire and sword are not to be compared with the crown of glory.
The body cannot by its sacrifice suffice to gain entry,
nor the soul by its endurance to be the cause of peace.
In goodness they reckoned that gift, the cause of peace,
and did not boast that they had won the victory by labours.
The King's servants recalled that echo:
"When you have done all that you were commanded, do not be proud."
They called to mind that herald who proclaims to the peoples
that the sufferings of time are not worthy of the good things promised.
They marvelled at the labours of his soul, how praiseworthy they are,
and were astonished at his words, so full of fear.

"I fear," he says, "lest I, who have sown the word of life,
should myself become a stranger to the treasure of life."
And if he whom the Spirit chose was full of fear,
who will boast that for his labours he will be made equal to the good things?
If the athlete of righteousness humbles himself,
who will display the beauty of his labours before the spectators?
The athletes too reflected on the aim of his words,
and considered that suffering is small beside the reward.
And for this reason they bore sufferings with delight,
for they looked on crowns far greater than their labours.
They laughed at swords, scorned the iron combs, and trod on fire,
and mocked and made light of the stubbornness of the Evil One and of death.
They broke the sword with the hard edge of their minds,
and cut through the instruments of torture by the endurance of the soul.
They conquered the fire by the warmth of the love within them,
and it grew cold, and its fierceness faltered before their earthen vessels.
O nature, destroyer of bodies, that lost to bodies!
O devourer that became food for those it devours!
O bodies always burning with desires,
that silenced the strength of the flame by their endurance!
The athletes overcame fire by the fire of their minds,
and the motions within them were not grieved by the burning.
In them was fulfilled in deeds that saying of Scripture:
"When you pass through the sea and the fire, I am with you."
They went through fire and water and were tested by persecutors,
and the fire grew cold and the waters lost their force, and they stood in a place of relief.
O creatures of dust whom the flame heated,
and they became vessels of the treasure of life that cannot be stolen!
O dust, soaked at every hour in the waters of sufferings,
as sufferings passed through its limbs like fire!
A vessel woven of corruptible threads of wool
washed itself in the flame and was not scorched.
One might call the bodily ones "asbestos,"
for they washed the filth of their limbs in the flame.

For that substance is a corruptible body like all bodies,
and yet the garment made from it is not destroyed by fire.
So too the bodily possessed a corruptible body,
and yet the garment of love that they wore was not destroyed.
The fire of the waters of sufferings washed the filth from the body,
and the body grew beautiful and the soul shone at the voice of renewal.
Mortals heard the voice of renewal that spoke on earth,
and they demolished the body built in sufferings, that it might be made new again.
They saw that the composition of their limbs was small and weak,
and they hastened to demolish it through the readiness of their minds.
They demolished it not through the compulsion of their persecutors,
for it was open to them to drive sufferings away from their bodies.
They reflected on the shame of the corruptible body,
and brought it into the furnace of sufferings that it might gain beauty.
Compulsion did not overcome the freedom of their minds;
like discerning men they judged this fitting.
With a pure mind they saw that their bodies were being tested,
and they cast off the garment of weak clay and gained spirit.
Like wise men they judged and weighed the two sides:
that death bounded by time is profitable, but not that which is eternal.
They entered into judgment with the motions of the soul and the senses of the body,
over which it is right to suffer, the light or the harsh.
"Which is easier?" said the motions to the senses of the body:
"the sufferings of time, or torment without end?"
"Whom should we fear?" said the soul to the dwelling of its life:
"the slayer of one part of a man, or of both?"
The mind had already read the decree of that saying:
"Do not be afraid of the slayer who kills the body,
but fear rather, and tremble like discerning men,
before him who can cast both soul and body into the fire."
They reflected on that torment without end,
and on that judgment which enters into the motions of the soul.
"Living is the word of God," they all read and meditated,
"and its judgment is far sharper than a two-edged sword."
On the tablet of their heart the victors wrote the books of the Spirit,
and in the spirit they meditated on hidden things.
When torments came upon them, and eyes saw, and limbs trembled,

their thoughts read the things to come and comforted them.
And when the dread sword flashed above the body,
the mind put on the redemption of life like a helmet.
When the flame was kindled with the fuel of wrath,
endurance came down like dew upon the limbs.
In their minds the victors went down the road to Babylon,
and there they saw the fire that lost and the body that conquered.
In the mind they saw that flame, how high it rose,
and how a hidden sign drove back the height of its blaze.
It was fearsome indeed when it was let loose in the fuel of wrath,
yet it became contemptible, and suddenly its blaze was overcome.
Fierce indeed was that command that gave it fuel,
yet the force of its working grew faint and weak, against the order of nature.
That which destroys everything corruptible
forgot its nature, and the strength of its fierceness lost its edge.
The mouth of the lion, which is never satisfied in its greed —
they threw it a morsel, and it did not open its mouth to its food.
What the Babylonians had brought about in the trial
the victors pictured like a mirror before their eyes.
There they stood and gazed with the eyes of the heart,
while the peoples gathered to watch the destruction of men.
They awaited the outcome of that event, and it was fulfilled,
as fire was kindled with the fire of wickedness.
They too answered their slayers in the same way:
"We are not anxious to give up our spirit at our destruction.
That command which bridled the mouth of the flame
will rescue us from the torment of your afflictions."
They heard that promise which does not lie, and took heart:
"He who endures to the end shall live forever."
The hope of life strengthened them in their afflictions,
and they did not grow slack as they suffered from the [?].
A wondrous vision was shown before their eyes,
and the warmth of love was [?] by love.
By the yearning of divine love was uprooted
the yearning of the love that is set in mortal nature.

O will, possessing the freedom of discernment,
that overcame the compulsion of the bondage the Creator set!
O nature, wholly bound in the life of time,
that the love of yearning for immortal life overcame!
O you who pledged your nature to death for its folly,
and began to pay off the bond of debts by the sufferings of the body!
O you who were sold to the Accuser for the eating of a fruit,
and proclaimed liberty through endurance against desires!
With all and in all they fought bodily battles,
and over all they triumphed, and all they defeated; they prevailed and conquered.
Through sufferings of the body and motions of the soul they won the victory,
and despised and made light of the desires of body and soul.
Though of a twofold nature, they conquered the Watchers through endurance,
and trampled nature itself and passed beyond its straits.
The desire of the body, a spring that flows unceasingly,
they cut off from overflowing into the limbs, that they might not lust.
The love of money, the mother that bore all evils,
they laid in a grave, that it might never again yield fruits for death.
The love of glory they imprisoned in the strongholds of humility,
and held shut before it the doors of love, which are strongly secured.
The wicked envious one, who went about and triumphed over all who suffer,
they humbled, the strength of his might, by the word of peace.
Anger, which is a living beast that cannot be tamed,
they bound and fettered with gentleness as with a chain.
Pride, the lion that prowls with a pack to crush men,
they brought in and shut up within the [?] of humility.
The evil inclination they cut down and tore out by the roots,
that it might never again sprout and bear fruits of bitterness.
They humbled the height of the desires of motions and senses,
and subjected them to the will that loves truth.
In the armour of the Spirit they overcame all the forces, within and without,
against which the soul's will fought as though with its own.
Without what was its own, the will conquered as though by its own,
and the victory of the host was reckoned to it as though its own.
It was not by its own strength that it conquered the sufferings fixed within it:

but that of the Power who gave him power to endure his sufferings. / The fire of love, which the Spirit set within the mind, / blazed up and burned the hateful thicket of desires. / The will looked to the promise of undying life, / and love drew it on to go and fulfil its soul's desire. / By hidden stirrings it rose and [?] to the height above, / and with the mind it saw that order which does not perish. / On the wings of the Spirit earthly beings flew and entered heaven, / and there they heard the voice of praise that cannot be uttered. / In company with Paul, the chosen vessel, the victors journeyed / and reached the place where praise is offered in the Spirit. / The sign that chose him brought them near through their will, / to hear the voice that cannot be spoken by a tongue of flesh. / With him they ascended to the third height in hidden thought, / and hid the beauty of their victories within his boasting. / They were always like those who conquered, keeping to the straight goal, / and pitched their camp close beside it through the discipline of their thoughts. / The death of Abel was always pictured before their eyes, / and they looked upon his killer as he was being punished. / At the voice of his blood their thoughts were roused, / as it cried out to the All-Seeing against his killer. / The silent one offered a great sacrifice against the insolent one, / and gave it to the sign, that it might go in and summon him before the Judge. / The Judge saw the offering of blood, was zealous and grew stern, / and passed sentence on the killer according to his folly. / He subjected the shedder of blood to seven harsh scourgings, / so that by the decree of his sentence man might be terrified of murder. / [?] the chosen martyrs gave up their bodies, / and did not demand of their oppressors the outrage of their afflictions. / They were edified by the blood that cries out like a speaker, / and gladly they poured out their blood, that it might gain a voice. / Through the harsh scourgings laid on the insolent they were avenged / for the wrong of death done by the killers who condemned them. / They did not reproach their persecutors, "Why do you do this?", / for they were persuaded that this affliction was the cause of life. / They did not grieve over the destruction of their limbs,

for the resurrection of the body was always pictured before their eyes. / They were not distressed at the parting of body and soul, / for they saw that through death they were passing over to life. / O mind, how strong it was, how it scorned nature, / closing its eyes and keeping silent at the parting of the two sides! / O freedom, how it despised bondage, / and counted the love set within nature as though it were nothing! / O the struggle that the soul waged with itself, / enduring and overcoming the tyranny of harsh impulses! / It joined battle with the impulses, and the impulses with it; / then it, together with the impulses, gave its hand to the power of freedom. / The power of the freedom of discernment triumphed in the contests, / for it had the hidden sign that brings all to completion. / With the armor of the Spirit freedom overcame nature and its sufferings, / like a valiant commander who conquers by the power of the kingdom. / In the power of this armor bodily beings were wrestling / with spiritual and with bodily foes, in secret and in the open. / Through deeds they received proof of the power of its help: / whoever fought with it gained victory, grew great and reigned. / With the hidden eye of faith they looked upon / that athlete who put it on and fought against the Strong One. / The suffering of Job was always set before their eyes, / and they imitated his self-discipline on the way to victory. / They fixed his struggle before them like a mirror, to see with the mind / how a bodily being fights against a spiritual one. / They looked upon the seen and the hidden as though it were all in the open, / seeing that the body triumphs and the spirit is defeated. / At the sound of the victory of despised flesh they took heart / to join battle with the Strong One in the senses of the body. / That answer which Job returned to his wife / they returned to the Accuser, leaving his hope empty. / Job reckoned as a foolish woman the rib that clung to him, / who had lent her ear to the voice of the one who whispered through her. / The Fool played the harlot in the lust of impulses with the foolish woman, / but the righteous man uprooted the thicket that sprang up in the soil that clung to him. / "Away with you, Evil One!" the victors cried out with the righteous man;

"go and play the fool with foolish women, as is your custom. / You will not cheapen the chastity of our soul by your hateful embrace, / and we will not receive evil seed into our thoughts. / Go, arm yourself with bodily beings against our soul, / for without flesh your strength is too weak for the struggle. / Go, gather your companions to help you, / for from the beginning it is through us that you have fought against our humanity. / Through the rib of our body you joined battle with the head of our race, / and as with a sword you slew Adam by means of his own limb. / With Eve's bow you shot the arrows of your deceits at Job as well, / but he caught them on the shield and breastplate of faith. / On Joseph you cast the hard fetters of fleshly lust, / but he snapped them with the nimbleness of chaste impulses. / And because you learned by experience to conquer with our own weapons, / see, you seek to wrestle with us by means of what is ours. / You are a deceiver: in the guise of a man you lead man astray, / and without a man you do not fight against humankind. / Through the childishness of man you fulfilled the desire of your bitterness, / and through him you make his fellows taste the gall of death. / Come with the fleshly army you have gathered, / and join battle through fleshly beings with our limbs. / Go in, hiding the hatefulness of your soul in visible flesh, / and fulfil your desire through fleshly beings against [?]. / We do not fear your wiles, however harsh they are, / nor do we flee at the twang of the bow of your deceit. / We will not strip off our armor until we have defeated you, / and we give you no room to break the ranks of truth. / We do not cease from the struggle as long as it is day, / until the evening of death comes and gives rest to our bodies. / If you wish to learn the aim of our valor, / fulfil your will by bringing death upon us, and see our deeds. / If you desire to test our strength by deeds, / bring on the scourges, kindle the fire and sharpen the sword. / For neither height nor depth counts for anything with us, / nor can heavenly powers defeat us.

"Nor, if some other creature should fight against us, / will it loosen our soul's love from him who created us." / O athletes of righteousness, how valiant they proved, / who conquered on earth and began to prevail over those in heaven! / They held out against the [?], and through their sufferings brought down his power; / they mocked and laughed even at death, which all men fear. / They hated their lives and spurned earthly comforts, / and invited body and soul together to the wedding feast on high. / That feast which is never dissolved they beheld in secret, / and they adorned the mind with endurance as with garments. / Fear and love always filled their minds, / as they remembered the man whose soul's garments were foul. / They gazed on him as he was cast out of the feast, / and in his torment they considered how bitter it is. / They remembered that [?] of the virgins, / and did not cease gathering the oil of mercy. / And though the wealth of sufferings they had gathered on earth was very great, / they feared lest the flame of their suffering should fall short. / With the eyes of the mind they searched the Scriptures, / and advanced step by step toward the goal of perfection. / For they were persuaded that labor is void without love, / and cannot enter the gate of the height except with it. / The word of Paul made them ponder this: / that he declared glorious gifts void without love. / If prophecy, which is greater than all, remains behind on earth, / how will lesser labors ascend to the height above? / If he counted the gift of tongues as sounding brass, / who will stand firm before the scrutiny of righteous judgment? / Faith that masters mountains he called nothing; / how then can anything lesser suppose that it is something? / Even if sufferings and almsgiving abound, / who can gather the wealth of the great love? / To the harbor of love the victors journeyed on the stirrings of the soul, / and in it, as in a [?], they laid up the treasures of their possessions. / They saw that no good things can compare with its greatness, / and they spurned everything and loved love above everything.

Through their sufferings they proved its greatness, which cannot be overcome, / and in their afflictions they sought no other help besides it. / It was fitting for them, the lovers of love, to love love, / and for love itself to help the children of its mystery. / Because they loved it greatly and did not slacken in their devotion to it, / it loved them and helped them beyond their strength. / Because they journeyed by it and did not fall behind it in their deeds, / it brought them to the harbor of life without end. / Theirs is the victory, with a reward that does not perish, / for they hated this life and loved a hope that does not lie. / Theirs is praise from every mouth as victors, / and ours is shame, that we do not resemble them in their goal. / To lowly heirs they left [?] from their sufferings, / and these squandered them on earthly desires. / To the greedy they handed over the wealth that came from their labors, / and these did not relieve with it the poverty of human life. / Slothful sons took up the spiritual inheritance / and sold it for nothing, receiving no spiritual price. / Not truly did they become heirs to the wealth of the Spirit; / falsely they cherished the truth and loved it in pretense. / For love of earthly things they clung to the truth, / and because they coveted leadership they put on the habit. / For love of glory they adorned and built shrines for the righteous, / and made them a house of trade for the love of money. / The ministers of holiness set snares of silver in the sanctuary, / that hateful silver might fall as prey to the love of silver. / For silver's sake they overlaid the walls with deceitful silver, / so that everyone might see the beauty of the silver and bring silver. / For love of money they displayed the bones to the outward senses, / and in their minds they kissed money without ever being sated. / For love of money they displayed the bones to the outward senses, / and in their minds they kissed money without ever being sated. / They made the dead bones take on a bodily voice, / to demand money from humankind by means of visions. / Those who hated money, who cut the snares that money spread, / the love of money turned into bait for money. / By the power of the bones greed sought to devour much, / and through its handling of them it profited from the authority to drive out demons.

Not in truth did it drive them out, but in pretense, / and the rebels fled at the sound of money, not of truth. / The love of money hired them as laborers for its vineyard, / to work the estate of iniquity as though in truth. / The demon serves the love of money in the senses of the body, / and ministers to it in desires as to a master. / Come, discerning one, take its measure and marvel with discernment / at how far the love of money has flown on wings of silver. / In the yoke of its toil it has harnessed men and demons together, / and neither height nor depth can fill its want. / It has overcome the shrewd and the simple in their ways of life, / and gained a rank of mastery above everyone. / Even the athletes who triumphed and conquered in the contest of truth / it has overpowered, in the guise of love for their bones. / It demanded a wage of love from the bones of the chaste, / though it loved them in appearance and not in truth. / For money the greedy made much of money and honored it, / and demanded the wage of a false show as though it were genuine. / The bones of the righteous did not seek to be honored, / nor did they depend on our hymns and our service. / Those radiant in soul had no need of incense from us, / nor did those clothed in light need the splendor of temporal lamps. / It was fitting to honor the righteous with love of soul, / just as they too loved God with the stirrings of the soul. / In secret they were pleasing, as discerning men, to the One who sees in secret, / and the Hidden One honored them in secret and in the open. / Our Head too, who trod the way in life toward the height, / pronounced blessed the one who believed in his name without seeing. / It was right for us to draw near to his goal with our inner stirrings, / and not to display our beauty to our fellows by outward show. / It was not fitting for us to honor ourselves with the honor of the righteous, / nor was it right for us to demand of them the wage of our labor. / Freely they gave that gift by which they had been enriched, / and in the same way it behooved us to serve.

Gluttony has entered and settled among the dead, / and for this reason human life is troubled and worn down. / The love of [?] has spread nets among earthly people, / and everyone has fallen into the snares of fraud. / Empty glory has humbled itself under the name of sweetness, / and given the children of men the gall of death to drink. / Hateful envy has blinded the soul to knowledge, / and the world has grown dark and begun to grope at walls at noon. / Understanding has passed away from the rational mind, / and the stirrings of discernment have ceased from [?]. / And if the help of the divine sign does not reach us, / even the promises made to our race are made void and proved false. / Come, debtors, let us quickly pay off the bond of our debts, / lest the weight of our iniquity grow heavy and sink us. / Come, let us take refuge in the harbor of the righteous, as the righteous do, / that they may help us with love and mercy before the Judge. / Come, let us make friends for ourselves here while we are alive, / that they may receive us into their tents that are never taken down. / Come, let us trade spiritually with the diligent, / that we may be worthy of the wage of the laborers who bore the burden of the day. / Let our mind, like discerning men, judge the things in which we have sinned, / that we may become companions of those who bore scourges in love. / Since we cannot endure the sufferings of the body, / let us suffer a little in the stirrings of the soul instead of the limbs. / Since our strength is too weak to stand firm before trials [?], / let us call on the stoned ones, who suffered in our nature, to help us. / Response: Blessed is the Lord, in whom his servants rest, and who magnifies their memory.
On the Martyrs
Memra Twenty-Five / On the Martyrs / Refrain: Blessed is he who has magnified the memorial of his helpers, here and above / in heaven. My brothers.
In every place Jesus raised up witnesses to his [?], / and in every region the standard of his cross was received. / Over the whole world the sun of his preaching dawned,

and by its rays it drove the darkness from the inhabited earth. / He cast the net of his teaching into the sea of humankind, / and within it he gathered all peoples together with all kings. / He left no city on earth to rebel against his teaching, / nor was there any corner of the earth where he did not triumph. / His preaching had wings and flew over the earth, / and in every region it swiftly took hold of the laws. / Over sea and dry land his word ran swiftly, / and yoked the world with the gentle yoke of his teaching. / With great love people received his preaching, / and for its sake they endured tortures and every affliction. / For love of him sons left their fathers, / counted them as strangers, and clung to him. / For his sake fathers too renounced their sons, / and handed them over to every kind of death without pity. / He cast a great rift upon the earth on the day of his coming, / and cut off that love which came down from father to father.

Brother handed brother over to death for his sake, / and there was no house that was free of strife. / The daughter was unwilling to accept her mother's error, / nor was the mother persuaded to confess him as her daughter did. / Jesus is the cause of all this division, / as he himself also teaches us plainly: / "Do not suppose that I came to cast peace upon the earth; / for I did not come to cast peace, but a sword. / I have come to proclaim a new hope to humankind, / and whoever is persuaded and receives me becomes hated. / Whoever confesses me and my words renounces his father, / and whoever receives and believes in me leaves his mother. / He renounces all the members of his household, and they renounce him too, / and he crucifies his body to the world night and day. / He carries his cross upon his shoulder and goes out with me, / and [?] family and all his kin, and clings to me. / If he is rich, he despises his wealth and becomes poor, / and once he has been stripped, then he is worthy to become my disciple. / If he is wise and draws near to the simplicity of my teaching, / let him first renounce the wisdom of the world, and then come. / If he is a ruler and wishes to come under my authority, / let him in fitting humility become a disciple of my lordship. / I have come to open a narrow door for humankind; / it is very slender, and not everyone is able to enter it. / Only the little ones can enter by the door that I have opened, / and it is the slight who can walk the way that I have trodden. / The door is slender, the way narrow and very toilsome, / and not everyone finds it easy to walk in it. / Not everyone who wishes to come is able to come, / for a person completes my discipleship only with great toil. / Not everyone who calls himself my disciple / is able to complete the discipleship that I require. / I have come to teach humankind a life of toil, / and he is worthy who hears and keeps my words. / He renounces his brothers and estranges himself from his sisters too; / he leaves houses and villages and possessions, and so draws near to me."
This seed our Saviour sowed among humankind,

and the martyrs received it with a wondrous love for his discipleship. / They became strangers to all that they possessed for his sake, / and counted the world and its good things as nothing. / They hated comforts and loved [?] and peace, / and while they were on earth they were not on earth, but on high. / While they lived, they were dead to the whole world; / for they lived to him, not to the world that does not endure. / They hated their lives and loved death without compulsion; / the death that everyone fears, they accepted. / On the road of death they saw blessings, and were not anxious or afraid, / and though its taste is very bitter, they did not shrink from it. / They weighed the life of time against eternal life truly, / and with discernment despised the one and chose the other. / In that true balance of the mind they had been trained, / and weighed well the passing world against the eternal. / They did not slacken in the contest into which they had gone down, / nor did they draw back or give way under the harshness of sufferings and tortures. / They cared nothing for wealth and the gifts that fill this age, / and were held back neither by kin nor by family. / This one aim alone was set before them with discernment: / that for Jesus' sake they should choose death and hate life. / They saw that the death of Jesus became the cause of our life, / and they gained the strength to despise every kind of death. / They saw that he hung on the top of Golgotha for our redemption, / and they repaid the debt they owed: the blood of their necks. / They looked on our Lord hanging on the wood with the robbers, / and understood that he consented to die for humankind's sake. / They saw the robber who received from him the forgiveness of his sins, / and reckoned that his mercies were revealed upon them also. / They saw the elements that were changed on the day of his resurrection, / and understood that he is Lord of them and of all. / They saw the natures that have no speech crying out, / and perceived that he is Lord of height and depth. / They saw mute natures crying out to rational humankind,

and they knew and perceived why he had tasted death. / They too ran and took refuge in him like the robber, / and asked of him forgiveness of sins and new life. / They counted the life of time as nothing, / and believed this world to be like a single day. / They hated the world and all the works of creation that are in it, / and waited to inherit new life in the kingdom on high. / They hated and despised all beauties and possessions, / and longed for the world to come and the promised blessings. / They despised perishable gold that brings no profit, / and hated silver that cannot redeem any of its owners. / They cast off from themselves every form of idol worship, / and cried glory to the one God who is higher than the heights. / They hated and despised the glory of a passing dwelling, / and loved and longed for the glory on high that does not perish. / They forsook the idols which the Evil One set up for humankind's error, / and drew near and worshipped with the worship of love before the Judge. / Here they let go of all possessions and all beauties, / and ran after the pearl more glorious than all. / The Master of the house was made known to them through his creatures, / and like trumpets they gave praise to the Maker of all. / They let go of the craving for Magianism which the Evil One had sown,

and cried glory to the one Creator and Maker. / They understood that the sun and moon are creatures, / and that it is not fitting for them to seize the rank of divinity. / They understood that it is not right for what are not gods to be called gods, / nor for the worship due to God to be offered to them. / They saw the Son who trod out the way of life for our race, / and as over a bridge they crossed over death to the place of life. / Very fearful is the hour of death, and very painful, / and how desirable to a person is this life of time! / Very dear to humankind is the life of time, / and even the righteous who part from it are sorely distressed. / See: when Hezekiah was told of his departure,

he turned his face to the wall and wept bitterly. / With great weeping the king wept when he heard that he would die, / until he heard the hope of life from Isaiah. / And if a righteous man feared and was terrified of the cup of death, / who could bear its pains lightly? / The martyrs endured the pains of death and were not terrified, / and died a temporal death with Jesus so as to live with him. / The death of Jesus made death become a sleep, / and by his resurrection he abolished it and freed us from its dominion. / How could the weak body, a child of the earth, / withstand and conquer and overcome sufferings and tortures valiantly? / How could our race, wretched and full of sufferings, / willingly approach and overcome the pains of death? / There is no strength in the weakness of Adam's dust; / how then could it endure pains without labouring? / Who granted the body this, to hate its own life, / and how is it able to despise the cup of death? / By what power did it overcome scourgings and combs, / and who strengthened its weakness so that it did not slacken? / The death of Jesus gave bodily beings a helping hand, / and in it they glory and mock the dominion of death. / Had Jesus not died and come to life, who could, / being mortal, hate the life that is loved above all things? / Had Christ not imprisoned death in the tomb, / humankind would have had no hope of new life. / Jesus invited our whole race to new life, / and the martyrs ran and went to him, to where he had gone. / He went ahead first to prepare a dwelling on high, / and then those who love him go up with him to the royal house. / On this hope the martyrs die without compulsion, / and for this reason they despise the life that does not endure. / The just looked to another world to find delight, / and for this reason they die here, so as to live there. / Let everyone hasten to look closely at these just ones, / for by their deaths error was abolished and truth triumphed. / In them the teaching of the preaching was also made victorious, / for they bore witness to him not with words but with death.

For see, whoever believes with faith alone / is not deprived of the reward for the confession of his words. / Paul cries out that if you confess the death of Jesus / and also believe that he rose from the tomb, you will inherit life. / If the confession of the mouth alone gives life, / how much more will the martyrs inherit, who believed and were also crowned! / If the robber entered Paradise by a word alone,

into what place will the martyrs enter, who despised their lives? / Christ alone is sufficient for this reward, / and he repays the martyrs with crowns for their [?]. / Who is sufficient to praise these just ones, / except that good Lord for whose sake they died? / See, their deaths are more glorious than life in every place, / and in every region their feasts are held high. / See, from everywhere people run to the day of their feasts, / and every day their memorials are glorious in the four quarters. / Walls cannot guard cities / as well as the prayer of the martyrs guards the whole world. / There is no king who can help us / as the prayer of the martyrs is able to help us. / There is no ruler who can rescue the one who takes refuge in him / as the martyrs are able to rescue from afflictions. / Who will not rejoice in these just ones and gladden his heart, / and who will not honour their memorials and their feasts? / These are the ones who became like sacrificers of their own selves, / and offered themselves as offerings to the King whom they loved. / These are the ones who hated the whole world and its delights, / and loved sufferings and death for Jesus' sake. / These are the ones who renounced family and wealth and power, / and would not live the life of time, for Jesus' sake. / These are the ones by whom the party of the pagans was condemned and brought low, / and the teaching of Jesus conquered and triumphed in the house of unbelievers. / These are the ones who did not bear witness with the testimony of words alone, / but doubly sealed and confirmed what they had received. / With words they bore witness to the teaching of the preaching, / and by their deaths their words too were confirmed.

All these things the martyrs cried out before the persecutors: / "The death of Jesus is true to us, and his resurrection too. / We confess of him that he truly died and truly rose, / and the good Lord will not separate us from his lordship. / We see him who rose from the tomb in great glory, / and he is not exchanged for another lord, for he is true to us. / And if you are in doubt about our words, O persecutors, / deed is a witness to our words, if you are willing. / It is not with words alone that we confess the lordship of Jesus, / for see, we are making ourselves ready for every suffering for Jesus' sake. / It is not with the word of the mouth alone that we confess him, / for by death we bring our love for him to completion. / The sword cannot cut off our love for Jesus, / and there is no affliction that can put a blemish on our faith." / All these things the athletes pleaded before the persecutors, / and they did not waver or give way before the persecutors of righteousness. / With a loud voice the martyrs cried out before the judge: / "We do not serve the sun and moon, natures that were made. / The one God who created the height and fashioned the depth, / him we serve, and to him we offer the debt of love. / Him we reckon Lord, exalted, King of all, / and to him we offer songs of praise at all times. / The Lord of the height, who came down to earth to give life to the world, / we confess him without division, as it is written. / That Saviour who came down and redeemed the race of Adam, / to him we sing songs of praise night and day. / That Saviour who died for our sake, so that we might live with him,

him we worship, and to him we sacrifice the sacrifices of our bodies. / 'Whoever [?] my words and [?] his life, / let him take up his cross and come after me and rejoice with me.'" / They put wicked kings to shame with their answers, / and cried out to them: "We do not worship any creature. / Let the sword come, and let fire come with its burning, / and let us see whether they can part his love from us. / Until now we have borne witness in words to him whom we love; / from now on let deed be a witness to our words. / With a testimony of words a person may perhaps lie,

but who can make a deed void? / Deed, then, is a witness that does not lie; / let it too now come and bear witness for Jesus. / See, we enter into every affliction for his sake, / and we make ourselves ready for every scourging for love of him. / And if you say that you do not accept a testimony of words, / then see, accept the testimony [?] that lies in deeds. / Our body bears witness, and our limbs too as they are cut off, / that Jesus is true, for whose sake we are being destroyed." / The martyrs endured temporal death in the hope of life, / and their memorials will never be blotted out. / The memory of their persecutors is wiped out, while theirs endures, / for Jesus, for whose sake they gave up their bodies, is one. / See, the pagan kings who tortured them have come to nothing, / while the just who endured every torture triumph. / For the memorials of renowned kings are not on the earth, / yet see, the feasts of lowly people are held high. / In this there is no reproach to the human race: / that, though they were human, they despised the life of humankind. / The weak race of humankind is a lover of life, / and it has no strength to stand firm against sufferings. / Our body is dust, and how could [?] be in dust, / which is the offspring of powder, and nothing is weaker than it? / This earthly race is more wretched than all, / and from it come the martyrs who scorned every kind of death. / They gave their necks to the slaughter of the sword for Jesus' sake, / so that from their Lord they might receive a reward for their toils. / They are convinced that they will not be wronged by the Creator, / and they are certain that they will receive from him the reward of their labours. / On that hope of new life they endured every evil, / so as to enter and dwell in the haven of light in the place above. / On the hope of the kingdom on high they gave up their necks, / so that on the day of judgement they might receive from him the crown of victory. / In return for confessing our redemption they gave up their bodies,

and see, they wait for the day of his revelation to receive their reward. / That Jerusalem which is on high they sought to inherit, / and for its sake they despised the delights of the dwelling below. / They are worthy to take pleasure in that spiritual delight, / and therefore they renounced the idols and confessed the Son. / They longed to share in the life of that royal house, / and for its sake they despised gold and silver and hateful dross. / They longed to cry "Holy, holy" with the Watchers, / and therefore they loved and longed for the dwelling above. / They longed to eat from the table full of life, / and therefore they spurned earthly delicacies. / They longed to drink from that spiritual cup,

and for its sake they gave up the drinking of earthly wine. / The martyrs longed to receive the crowns of glory, / and for their sake they let go of the perishable glory of the earth. / The martyrs longed to delight with the Bridegroom; / for his sake they despised all the adornments of this dwelling. / There is one who gave up his life to the sword at the hands of the persecutors, / and he is to receive the unfading wreath of glory. / There is one who was cut up limb by limb by the persecutors, / and this was a wonder: half of him was alive and half dead. / There is one who ended his life under tortures, and one under combs, and one / in prison, and one in afflictions, and one under torments. / Hail to the athletes of righteousness, who triumphed and conquered! / Hail to the victors who conquered and made the race of Adam victorious! / Hail to the guests of the Bridegroom on high, who does not perish, / who gave themselves up to every affliction and every scourging! / Hail to the rays of the great Sun of righteousness, / who were not destroyed by the gloom of the hateful darkness! / Hail to the lamps of righteousness, who gave their light / so that it shone on the earth and drove out the dismal darkness of error! / Hail to the valiant ones who did not slacken in their afflictions, / who conquered tyrants and kings and rulers! / Hail to the Nazirites who stood in the contest against the Evil One, / and conquered all the troops of the children of darkness! / Hail to the race of Adam: how high it has been exalted,

so that it has become lord over what is in the height and what is in the depth! / The wicked demons howled and cried out with a voice of wailing: / "Woe to us, for the great crown of our headship has come to nothing! / The headship of our leaders has now come to nothing, / and we no longer have an opening of the mouth over what has happened. / The teaching of our words has now ceased among our disciples, / and see, the whole world has become a disciple of the name of Jesus. / All creation is filled with the words of the Spirit, / and everyone hastens to take refuge in the Galilean. / See, the whole world has become a disciple of the name of Jesus, / and even the disciples of our words' teaching have taken refuge in him." / In these just ones let our whole race rejoice and be glad, / and through them let the weakness of our whole body be made strong. / Thanks be to the Lord who made his servants triumph in the contest of toils! / To him be praise, and to them acclaim, from every mouth!
On the Martyrs
Memra Thirty / On the Martyrs / My brothers.

O Power who went down with the athletes into their contests,
it was through you that they were strengthened for the beautiful gift of their victories.
O Son, for love of whom the martyrs endured such torments,
grant me a word fit to recount their praises.
O you, by whose love they grew drunk like men and trampled upon death,
let your love give me to drink, that through you I may speak their praises.
O Slain One, who trod the road of sufferings before his armies,
let your passion rouse me [?] to tell their stories with discernment,
O slain Bridegroom, at whose wedding feast the demons were cast down.

Grant me to mingle the sweetness of your slaying into your banquet.
Through you, my Lord, I will draw near to speak of their sufferings,
for unless it is through you, their victories are not known.
You are the beauty of all who have drawn near to perfection,
and you are the crown of all who have triumphed in their contests.
For the sake of your own passion the martyrs gave themselves up to their sufferings,
and because they had seen pains in you, they endured their afflictions.
Grant me, our Lord, to weave the beauty of their crowns
from your treasury, which is full of riches for whoever draws near to it:
these who bore the honour of your passion on their bodies,
and by their wounds lifted up your image to the cross;
these who were burned upon the blade and upon the coals,
and trod upon the embers in the fervour of love for your sake;
these who bowed down to meet the sword as they were slain,
and boldly gave their limbs to be cut off;
these who ran to meet slaughter with great eagerness,
and received the sword as a gift full of blessings;
these who became food for fire and for beasts,
and did not tremble or falter when they were destroyed for your sake;
these who left the world and their kin for your sake,
and hated homes and brothers and families so as to draw near to you.
A true friend is proven only by truth,
and if he does not die for his friend's sake, he does not love him.
This is love, and there is none other greater than it:
that a man should go rejoicing to death for the sake of his friend.

By a pleasant life, by honours and by delights,
one who loves is not proven in his love, in the judgment of the discerning.
Fire tests pure gold, whether it is fine,
and death amid sufferings tests love, whether it is true.
If gold does not enter the furnace and is not refined in it,
there is no way for the image of the king to be stamped upon it;
and if a man does not draw near to affliction, even unto death,
the image of the love of the Godhead is not stamped upon him.
Gold in the furnace receives a seal, so that it becomes an image,
and a man in sufferings establishes in himself the image of the Godhead.
Gold is beaten many times upon the anvil,
and so they make of it ornaments for the crown, that it may gain beauty.
In the same way the martyrs found beauty through their wounds,
and lo, they are woven into the King's crown as they triumph.
The tyrants of men became skilled craftsmen who forged
men by sufferings and set them in the royal palace.
They put the body of the martyrs into the fire like gold,
and made of it a wondrous crown for the great King.
With scourges they forged it, and with wounds they laid beauty upon it;
the fire tested it, and it received a form that does not decay.
They were beaten like gold and gained beauty like ornaments,
to be the adornment of the bride at the wedding feast.
The slain Bridegroom invited them to the wedding feast,
and they brought their blood with them as their gifts [?].
A banquet of light full of the mangled—lo, I see it!

Necks severed, bodies sawn apart, limbs torn with combs;
heads slain, and the [?] of every limb—
and the great hall of the wedding house was full of them.
And among these the virgin bride boldly reclined,
and the hideous sights of their mutilations were dear to her.
This one scourged, this one split open, this one slain;
this one mangled, this one combed, this one flayed.
Some bound, and some slain by the persecutors;
one pulled apart, and one torn by the beasts.
And there is one whose fragrance rises to Him from the fire like incense;
another is dismembered as he is torn by the wicked.
That one was rent, that one mangled, that one cut to pieces;
all of them unjustly endured every affliction.
The great banquet of the Crucifixion is mistress [?] of sufferings,
and whoever enters it, the wine of pains is pressed out for him and he drinks.
The guests whom the Bridegroom on high invited had gone in with him;
the sword met them in the hidden chamber [?] of his wedding house:
fire that burns, with the sword that thirsts for blood,
the battering of stones and the gnashing of lions' teeth,
with the great smoke that rises from the burning,
and the fury of the pagans, which in its waves is like the great sea.
In sufferings of this kind the saints were well practised,
and boldly they endured pains without murmuring.
It is easy for love not to murmur when it is afflicted,
for it bears all things and endures everything, as it is written.

Pains and sufferings, with afflictions and scourges, the martyrs endured
in their love, while they were mocked by the wicked.
The cluster of life, which the Jews pressed with a spear,
made the martyrs drunk with its wine, so that they forgot their afflictions.
They drank deeply from that vinegar [?] of the Crucifixion,
until they did not even feel the fire in their contests.
The wine they drank from the cup so affected them
that they walked upon coals rejoicing.
Blood from the side of the King Messiah anointed them for the contest,
and the uplifted hand of the adversary slipped away from them.
The wretch who drew near and cast Adam down among the trees
strove to cast the martyrs down before the judges.
The spirit of falsehood that sang deceit into Eve's ears
enticed them to deny by its cunning.
But they did not accept the evil king and his hateful word,
for they were more cunning than the dragon who sought to lead them astray.
From the skilful teaching of Jesus they had grown wise,
and they had been trained in shrewdness and in innocence.
He in his gospel commanded them and taught them
to be like doves, and like serpents too.
In innocence they resembled doves, as they had been taught,
and while they were slain they were quiet and guileless among their killers.
If there were anger in the dove, it would not dwell
with the one who presses upon its young to kill them.
And because this is a fine thing, the disciples too acquired it,

so that they would not be enraged when they were destroyed by the wicked.
He held up as an example [?] the serpent, which guards itself from harm
and lives warily every day, like the wise.
For in its cunning it knows how it is caught:
that its head is crushed; and so it flees from its hunters.
For if its body is seized so that it is beaten, it hides its head
and surrenders its whole body to sufferings and blows.
The head of the soul is faith, as the discerning know,
and this the martyrs guarded in their trial, so that it would not be struck.
Their firm truth alone they took care to guard,
with the cunning of serpents, which are full of gall.
Faith, the head of life, they held fast with care,
and gave their limbs to cutting and to mangling.
The serpent's life is in its head, and if it is crushed
it loses its life; therefore it always hides its head.
And the life of the soul hangs upon faith and is kept by it,
and if faith is harmed, life is lost.
So it is necessary to guard faith from stumbling blocks,
just as the serpent hides its head from blows.
In this way the martyrs guarded faith with fear,
and though they were struck by the judges, it was not struck.
The martyrs perceived another life that was to come,
and therefore they gave their bodies to bear sufferings.
By the sufferings they endured and by their wounds they shook the earth,
showing that God has another world, greater than this one.

They endured sufferings because of the pagans, until the pagans believed
and confirmed that there was something hidden which the martyrs perceived.
The persecutors saw how bold they were in the face of death,
and great amazement moved them to give praise.
And they began to reason that if there were no other life,
men would not so despise their own lives:
"They boast in something great and hidden while they are slain,
and so they run to meet the sword with a pure heart.
These perceive a good hope, glorious and hidden,
and so they scorn every blow and every threat.
Who is this Jesus, that they die for his sake?
And why do these boast in his name while they are slain?
Why do they confess him lovingly even unto death,
and endure sufferings, and not deny him in their afflictions?
They say he was crucified, they proclaim that he was slain—why then
do they boast in him, worshipping him before many eyes?
Why do they worship him, if he was a man who tasted sufferings?
And if he is not living, how is it that they die for his sake?
There is great power in that one who was crucified by the Jews,
and in his love he makes men worthy to believe in him.
Whether he is God, or a man, the Son of God,
there is power in him that draws men to faith in him."
Because of the afflictions the martyrs endured from their persecutors,
the pagans who saw their torments said these things.
And through these pagans, who honoured the Crucifixion,

the martyrs, by their sufferings, gathered a people for the preaching.
The onlookers marvelled at how they endured every blow,
and seeing that they were not struck for nothing, the whole world believed.
In their afflictions the martyrs became witnesses for the Son of the [?],
that he has another life to give to whoever loves him.
With their blood they wrote down faith in the God of all,
and by their deaths they became teachers of truths.
It was not by their words that they won acceptance from their hearers,
but by deed, showing how true their faith was.
From the blows and sufferings they bore on their bodies
everyone knows that the toil of their contests was not in vain.
Lo, their testimony is painted in the sufferings of their own persons,
and their teaching is written in the scourge-marks on their bodies.
And everyone affirms their testimony and accepts it,
because they sealed it with their blood and received their rewards.
The martyrs died in the hope that they saw: that there is a resurrection.
Blessed is the Messiah, who crowned his martyrs in their contests!
Its conclusion: Glory to you, Lord of all, for those who glory in you are not put to shame.
On the Renewal of Creation

Homily Twenty-Six
On the renewal of creation; it is suitable for New Sunday.
Response:
Blessed is he who built us, and overthrew us and destroyed us, and who will build us again
and will not destroy us again, my brothers.

One Creator created creation from nothing,
and He renews it, from lowly things to glorious.
One Will established the world, toiling in trouble,
and He sets it free from bondage to toil.
One is the Lord who began with a work in which there was no toil,

and He brings it to perfection, lacking nothing.
One is the Nature who established both the rational and the mute,
and in the harbour of His love He gives His creatures rest, so that they are not worn out.
One is the command that sustains the world through things seen,
and that will give life to things seen through what is unseen.
One Authority orders the course of Watchers and of men,
and from His treasure-house distributes gifts according to their wills.
One is the Hidden One who hid His nature and revealed His work,
and while He is hidden, His works cry out about His hiddenness.
His works bear witness to His incomprehensible hiddenness,
for from the time they came to be they cannot behold His eternity.
Eternally He is, and He is without beginning,
and He willed that the works He made should endure without end.
In His eternity He willed the works He made to share,
so that by enduring they might be witnesses to His eternity.
It was fitting that the One who Is and His work should both endure for ever,
so that as He is, so His creation too might be everlasting.
It was not for time that the Creator of creation created creation,
but that by its permanence it might preserve time itself as well.
Alongside its constitution the times have run from when they came to be,
and the times pass, but it does not pass from what it is.
Without end run the orders of its permanence,
and even when it comes to its end, with its end comes also its renewal.
My mind drew me to turn to speak of its end,
for I saw that it is far more beautiful than the time of its beginning.
Beautiful is its end, in that renewal too is joined to it,
and of renewal itself I have said that it is more beautiful than the beginning.
Beautiful was its beginning, when it was established quietly from nothing,
and far more beautiful its renewal, which comes about quietly.
In the very manner in which it came quietly from nothing,
something comes to be at the last more beautiful than the first.
It befitted the Good One to renew the creation He had created,
so that in its renewal it might endure with Him without end.
He desired from the beginning that it should be without end,
and He fulfils His love's desire for it on the day of the end.
This will was His continually, without beginning:

that it should be, before time was filled up, and so for ever.
He knew this will before all things,
and it was not as something new that He willed to fashion it and so fashioned it.
He was fully assured also of the renewal that would come after the times,
and it was no deliberation that pressed Him to renew what He renews.
That thought of His involves no deliberating, for it is not thought out;
nor is there willing in that will which did not first not will and then will.
He had already thought out what He did before He did it,
and He willed the will that He willed, and things came to be.
It was not as something new that He did all He has done and will do,
for He had with Him everything that has come to be before it came to be.
Wisely He made a beginning for the work of His hands,
and gloriously He renews His work at the end of the times.
Times and orders He made for His works, He who is glorious in His work,
and His work cannot tell how glorious and well-ordered He is.
Glorious and well-ordered is the order He made for two worlds:
to one He gave a fixed time, and the other He made everlasting.
In the one He set an order that all should persist in toils,
and the other He made so that, without toil, it gives rest to those who toil.
The one He furnished with kinds of training full of toils,
and the other He filled with delight in which there is no weariness.
With the hidden eye of His treasury He looked upon them both,
and ordered them as befits the One who knows all.
He knew that the lifespan of time was perishable,
and He prepared its heart beforehand by the renewal He promised it.
By promises He drew its mind toward His knowledge,
that it might believe what He knew: that He is able to raise its fall.
As one would a fallen man, He held it with hands of flesh,
and propped up its frame and lifted its gaze to the heights.
By a human hand the Lord of the world took hold of the world,
and cried to it: “Arise, and be strengthened from your sickness.”
A clod [?] taken from itself He gave it as a medicine,
and it drank of it and shook off the bitterness of mortality.
The dead world lived and was revived in mystery,
and learned the order by which it will be revived again in very deed.
He trod out a path for it to look toward the constitution on high,
and sent before Him one of His own as a guide.

One Messenger He sent from one world to the other world,
to prepare a perfect world for the toiling world.
As high priest He commanded him to enter the sanctuary above,
to make atonement there for the sins of the toiling world.
A covenant of peace he received from the Lord of all for all,
so that, while he is with Him, all might believe that he will return from His side.
He fixed a time when he will return from beside the One he loves,
and behold, earthly and heavenly beings watch for him.
For that delight the world, toiling in sin, waits,
to receive from him release from the debts it owed its God.
For that Messenger whom He sent before Him it waits every day,
that he may come and bring it the good news of the renewal of its old age.
Already the light of the world has dawned from that world,
and the darkness of earthly toils flees before it.
With the light of his face he takes away the mourning of its sorrow,
and lifts from it the heavy yoke of suffering.
With the sound of the trumpet he rouses it from the sleep of its ignorance,
and it springs up and stands, as from a bed of the distress of its pains.
Wholly and entirely he renews it, quietly and without delay,
and no place remains in it that is left without renewal.
All creation is renewed in that renewal,
heaven and earth and all that is enclosed within their bounds.
Rational and mute alike rest from their toils,
and no longer weary themselves in the labours of their needs.
That world gives rest to all together from every burden,
and there is none of those who pass through it whose weariness it does not relieve with its ease.
It is that rest which is written in the books of the Spirit,
and in it the weary voices of prophecy find rest.
In its rest there is no toil that wears down the one who rests in it,
nor does anyone any longer grow weary of the change between good and evil.
There is no shifting between good and evil in that renewal,
nor anyone who waits in expectation, hoping for yet another hope.
In it are bound up all the expectations of Watchers and men,

and in it the first things and the last are brought to their end.
In the harbour of its peace the hosts of heavenly beings rest,
and are no longer worn out by governing heaven and earth.
In it they rest from their labours on behalf of men,
since the course of men and their deeds also comes to an end.
Men rest from the weariness of human things,
and are no longer in want because of earthly sufferings.
The freedom of men gives the spiritual beings rest from toil,
and men and heavenly beings come to share one way of life.
In wearisome labours the spiritual beings toil on behalf of humankind,
and once he is set free, commanders and commanded alike rest.
For his need they now command and are commanded,
and when he has become rich, they no longer command or are commanded.
In the riches of immortal life he reigns there,
and with him rest also the ministers who served the needs of his life.
Perfect, unchanging rest receives the weary,
and natures no longer wear themselves out or are worn out for his sake.
All creation rests with him, and he with all,
and rational beings, speakers though they are, abide in quiet and silence.
His sufferings of soul and body cease,
and he is no longer tormented, nor do sufferings struggle against him.
Sin is extinguished, and death is extinguished for him,
and the hard war that was waged against him ceases from him.
In his rest even the rebels who assailed him without cause find rest,
and they are with him in the one will of the one Creator.
One will reigns there over all and in all,
and there is no adversary, no hindrance, nothing at all.
It is he who reigns with the will that set the crown upon him,
and it is he who judges by the will that gave him judgement.
All judgement the Son, the son of our race, received from the Father,
and it is he who gives gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked.
On the day of his revealing he shows the might of his sovereignty,
and subjects all and renews all by the strength of his authority.
For that renewal which comes by his hands creation waits,
and sighs: when will the time of its renewal come?
Like birth-pangs, sufferings strike at its suffering:

when will it bring forth children of immortal life?
Like a woman with child it bears the burden of mortality,
and that day will relieve its distress and take away its mourning.
Already it is putting on the garment of renewal in a hidden sign,
and like a bride it stands in glory incorruptible.
In great glory it beholds how glorious it is,
and the eyes of its soul are never sated with the sight of its face.
Insatiable is that joy for those who rejoice in it,
above all men and heavenly beings who served well.
Men and Watchers rest there in that delight,
and they become heirs of blessings without end.
The Watchers rest from ministry on behalf of all,
and are not worn out by the constant course of the changing times.
The motions of their minds rest from change,
and they no longer desire a hateful desire as the demons do.
The course of those who strayed from their ranks comes to an end,
and they all come to accord in the one will that fashioned them.
The demons cease from the wickedness of their blasphemies,
and instead of insult they render glory, though unwilling.
No longer do they wage a war of mockery against men,
nor do they presume to revile the name of the Godhead.
One will of love comes to be for all, with all,
for heavenly and earthly, for good and wicked.
Good and wicked acquire a love that does not turn back,
and though they are far apart in their deeds, in love they are at one.
In perfect love Watchers and men are at one together
to offer one praise to the one Creator.
Good and wicked cry out glory, each as they are,
and there is no end to the voice of praise of those who praise.
Glory is the delight in which they abide for ever,
and it is an everlastingness without interruption and without toil.
Without toil whatever happens there happens,
and no mouth, so long as it is mortal, can say how it is.
How can mortality recount in words
the life of that immortal constitution?
How can the tongue of corruptible flesh
depict the image of that beauty which has no likeness?

That life has no likeness in this life,
nor is there any demonstration that can show it exactly.
It alone resembles the likeness of its own exactness,
and it alone can tell of the breadth of the greatness of its glory.
Its glory drew me to recount in words its gloriousness:
how glorious it is, and how glorified by those who are worthy of it.
I saw those who praise, who are destined to be glorified,
and wonder seized me at the greatness of that ineffable glory.
Ineffable is the praise of that day:
how creation becomes another in place of what it is.
It is not that creation becomes another creation there,
nor does something else stand in place of the first.
That very thing which came to be in the beginning from nothing
is what becomes a being more glorious than the first.
It is the nature of the spiritual beings that acquires glory,
and by nature they endure together without change.
It is the race of bodily beings that inherits life,
and in their very nature they acquire immortal life.
To body and soul the resurrection of the revived gives rest,
and without ceasing they sing glory to the Renewer of all.
To the Renewer of all the renewed give thanks,
since nothing at all remains that is not renewed.
Everything is renewed without losing its former nature,
and everything is changed, and its change admits no further change.
The rational are enriched with blessings beyond what speakers can tell,
and the silent too rest in an indescribable order.
The heavens endure in the stability in which they were established,
neither moving nor being moved from their pillars.
The course in which sun and moon persist comes to an end,
not that they cease to be, but that they rest from their courses.
From their courses the mute bodies rest [?],
and they turn and become that light which came to be in the beginning.
The gathered light of their spheres turns back into light,
and in its own nature a light without end endures.
Not one of the luminaries is lost, not a single ray,
nor is anything diminished of the beauty of its brightness.
There is nothing in its nature that loses anything that is in its nature,
nor anything that remains as it is without change.

That change compels all things to be changed,
and what has been changed endures in an order that does not change.
The blowing of the swift motions of the air ceases,
since earthly beings no longer need the use of its blowing.
As into a harbour it enters and rests from its changes,
and the spiritual beings no longer wear themselves out moving it.
The spreading of its subtle body is no longer required,
nor that it take up gentle waters and sprinkle them on the earth.
The nature of the gentle waters also ceases from flowing,
and is no longer stirred up turbulently as before.
The blowing of the winds no longer wears down the yielding body,
nor does that yielding body run in the order of its pouring.
Worn-out natures are no longer worn by their changes,
since none has need of the change that comes from the elements.
There are no elements in that spiritual life,
none that serves or is served by its partner.
One is the power that preserves all without all,
and by the strength of His power earthly and heavenly beings hang.
By His power He strengthens rationality, that it may not change,
and muteness, that it may keep the order of quiet and silence.
In quiet and silence the mute endure in their nature,
and are no longer required to honour the possessors of speech.
The possessors of speech acquire a power that has no need,
and there is no need for the service that comes from the silent.
Who needs the rising of the sun for those who have no toil,
and of what use is the course of the moon to those who have no time?
What benefit is there in the rays of the stars of light
for one who has no need of light from the luminaries?
Why the blowing of the motions of the air for those without distress,
and for whom are cold and heat, for those without sufferings?
Why the falling of rain and dew for those who lack nothing,
and for whom are times or seasons, for those without times?
Why the changes of summer and winter for those without change,
or the counting of months and days for those without end?
Why the yield of seeds and fruits for those who do not eat,
and for whom are creeping things and beasts, for those who need no threshing?
Why anything at all that can be eaten
for one who has no need of the strength that comes from food?

Why messengers and envoys to humankind,
where the will is bound fast in the affection of love?
Men are bound in the affection of love in that constitution,
and have no power to be changed toward the opposite.
Along with man all things rest from all toils,
