and in his building everything is preserved without destruction.
Let no one say that anything of all that has come to be perishes,
for behold, everything endures and is preserved in its own nature.
In its very nature of brightness light endures,
not by a bond, but by the order in which it was established.
In its very nature of subtlety the air endures,
not blowing, but in a quiet without change.
In its very nature of darkness darkness is preserved,
not in the arrangement of this present distinction, but otherwise.
There is no distinction between light and darkness,
since there is no sun to divide night from day.
And there is no day, since there is no toil for those who have no toil,
nor any longer night, since there is no sleep for those who do not sleep.
Without sleep and toils and sufferings man lives;
what need, then, has he of the course of night and day?
For the needs of his life the things that came to be were made and established,
and in his delight the course of his ministers comes to rest.
The earth rests from the tilling of summer and winter,
and is not worn out yielding fruits to those who till it.
It endures in the order in which it came to be in the beginning,
and is neither dissolved nor corrupted from its composition.
In the very composition in which it was composed when it was not,
in that it is preserved, together with the natures that dwell in it.
With it natures rest from weariness,
and with it they keep the order of quiet without change.
With it the wearied seeds cease from yielding,
since those who eat no longer need food from them.
With it the yield of all the trees also falls silent,
and they no longer sprout or wear themselves out in growing.
In it the nature of fire is hidden, whole as it is,
and though its use is abolished, it itself does not cease.
Upon it the loosed waters are poured out, as they are,

while they neither run nor are moved by the blowing of the air.
In it are buried the kinds of species that sprang from it,
and they abide in quiet and silence without suffering.
To it returns every formation that was made from it:
gold and clay, the glorious and the despised, are buried in it.
In it is everything, and upon it all things, and it is with all,
and in its preservation everything is preserved without destruction.
In it are all that can walk upon its back:
creeping things and beasts, and the winged birds as well.
In it the mute natures are made to cease from life,
not perishing, but ceasing from generation.
Already the mute kinds have ceased from generation,
and this is a rest that gives rest to the world, not destruction.
There is no destruction at all for anything that perishes,
for behold, everything turns to earth and is hidden in it.
There is none among the rational and the silent that perishes utterly,
except one rational nature and one silent one.
One who perishes wholly and entirely, in body and soul,
is that man who becomes a vessel for the Slanderer.
One it is who perishes from the life of the rational living,
and is sold to the beastly life of the dead which falls to the body [?].
In his body and soul that lost one perishes utterly,
and his perdition becomes a spectacle to all creation.
All creation examines his perdition,
and marvels at the mercy that in mercy preserved it from destruction.
In that one who perishes it learns the power of its Establisher,
who fashioned it in mercy, preserved it by His love, and renewed it in grace.
Through his perdition it sees a sight it had never seen:
a living soul whose life is cut off [?] from life.
Kinds of incorruption the soul acquires in its very being,
[?] the wonder that the plunderer stealthily [?] its life.
The nature of spirit is not corrupted, not at all;
who then would not marvel at how this comes about by the power of the Creator?
It is the power of the Creator that destroys the soul of one man,
that men may learn how evil is the wickedness of men.
The wickedness of that man's evil teaches everyone

that had men not lived by mercy, they would not be alive.
By His mercy toward all He shows the power of His goodness,
and in the one who perishes He proclaims the truth of His justice.
Two things He teaches through the destruction of body and soul:
that He is good and that He is just, toward speakers and silent alike.
Rational and mute learn alike about both:
that neither His goodness nor His justice is diminished.
In justice He condemns that guilty one who condemned himself,
lest His mercy be found lacking in order.
A great order He shows to all through the lost one:
not so as to make a show, but to make known that he deserves to perish.
It is not to show the strength of His justice that He does this,
but to put to shame the Enemy, who supposed that through him he would overpower all.
To shame the Enemy, that man perishes utterly,
lest he boast that in humankind he began and finished his work.
Through men he led astray from the beginning, when men came to be,
and through a man he completes his deception, yet does not complete it.
The desire of his soul, bitter of soul as he is, is not fulfilled,
because the temple in which he wishes to hide perishes from him.
In a tower of flesh he sets up the dwelling of his bitterness,
and his tower is ruined, and he is fettered in bonds of fire.
Into fire he falls whose heat is fiercer even than fire,
and into a darkness whose darkness overwhelms those who are dark.
In the harshness of his punishments creation sees a new thing:
that though he does not feel, his sufferings press about him and his punishment is doubled.
At his punishments earthly and heavenly beings marvel:
how bitter and how just is the requital of his wickedness.
Wickedly he strove to seize for himself an honoured name,
and justice, most justly, decreed his sentence.
Just is the Creator, and just the trial that decreed his sentence:
He [?] a few, and many live, that He may make all wise.
In justice He [?] the wicked who despised His commandments,
and wisely He gives gifts to those who keep His love.
Wisely He destroys one man out of all,
and mercifully gives life to all through His life.
He gives a sign to the rational and to the mute,
that they may see that He has power over all things, as Lord of all.

He is Lord over all, and all things rational and mute are his, / and to him belongs the name of Being and of Godhead. / It befits the Existent One, who created creation out of nothing, / to keep the order of his creating without confusion. / It is a great order that he renews his creation, / so that by its renewal he may set forth a showing of his kindness. / In his kindness he shows all, through the renewal of all, / so that all may learn the effortless ease of the Lord who is over all things. / By his effortless ease everything came to be out of nothing, / yet the works he made would not acknowledge his ease. / He willed to make his works wise at the end of the times; / for this reason he brings about that renewal and just judgment. / Through the renewal they learn the power of his creating: / that it is he who created, and he who renews creation a second time. / Those who would not learn from the beginning of the One who set all in order / will learn the power of his Godhead on the day of the end. / This is the purpose of that renewal at the end: / that creation may learn the power of the Creator who created creation. / Great is the lesson creation learns in that renewal, / and she herself marvels at it, how much greater it is than what she is. / She reckons the time of that training as nothing / when that perfection is compared with this one here. / Not even that it exists, though it truly exists, enters her thought / when she contemplates the everlastingness of that which is forever. / At its everlastingness, which has no end, her mind is held suspended, / and her soul's love cannot have its fill of its delight. / At its delight my own mind too was amazed as it journeyed in [?], / and it roused itself to gaze well on the comeliness of its beauty. / "Look well," I counselled my mind—the mind— / and it began to travel a road it had never seen. / On the new road of the renewal of all my thoughts set out, / and they were amazed and astonished at how wondrous are the things beyond. / They stood in astonishment, though they did not truly see what they saw, / and they grew weary and concluded that they could not see the sight they sought. / Good hope encouraged them not to lose heart,

and they began to make for the goal they sought to depict. / I set a goal for the speech of my mind, that it may [?] toward it, / and now I seek to make for it well, if it is able. / The mind is able to see beautifully the things that are beautiful, / and nothing hinders it, if it is willing. / The beautiful things I wish to recount before those who are fair of mind, / so that they may set themselves to gaze well on the beautiful things. / The beauties of the day of renewal I have recounted, as I recounted them, / and again I recount them, so that people may be stirred to [?] them. / Who would not love to hear again words full of wonder, / and who would not meditate on the glories that glorify him? / Wonder and glory fill the discourse of those who meditate on it; / therefore I have meditated, and I still meditate, on meditations about these things. / On them I long to meditate without being sated, / so that perhaps I may keep my heart from dwelling on shameful things. / By trial I have gained experience of the mind, / and I have learned that good meditation is very good for the one who meditates on it. / Come, O mind, meditate fittingly on things that are fitting, / and with love repeat once more the words of the renewal of all. / Come, look well how beautiful is the renewal of all, / and praise and magnify the Renewer of our oldness. / He who created us looked upon our oldness before he created us, / and depicted beforehand the day of our renewal, together with our perfecting. / As one comforts a child, he willed to comfort the childishness of our soul, / so that it might not grieve in the oldness of the toilsome world. / In the likeness of an image he painted likenesses of things unseen, / and showed them to the hidden mind that is hidden in our soul. / In the mind he showed us that renewal at the end, / and though it is very far off, he placed its proof in things near at hand. / Through things near he showed us the power of things far off, / and through things revealed he taught us the order of things hidden. / Openly he revealed to us the hiddenness of his Godhead, / and made a tongue of flesh the herald of his secrets. / With a tongue of flesh he spoke with us about things to come, / since flesh is accustomed to hear things of the flesh. / To the one of flesh he taught the spiritual mystery,

and flesh spoke in riddles, and those of flesh listened to a new riddle. / A new riddle the one of flesh spoke with those of flesh, / and perhaps whoever hears will ask, "Who is it that spoke the riddle?" / "Who spoke the riddle?" you wish to hear, O hearer: / hear from me and learn that it was a man who spoke in riddles with humankind. / It was a man in whose soul the Spirit spoke in riddles, and he spoke with humankind; / he listened to hidden things and interpreted them through human means. / He became as a mediator between humanity and the Creator, / and through his [?] he reconciled the Lord with his creatures. / By his mediation he dissolved the strife between all things and all, / and proclaimed on earth the good news of a peace that does not change. / This is the man who reconciled all with the Lord of all, / and he it is who trod the new road of the renewal of all. / He made known to us the renewal that is to come at the last, / and he showed us the path of the journey of faith. / He taught us that in him our oldness is renewed, / and he painted for us a type, that we might resemble him in mystery. / He showed in his own person these things of ours, / so that we would not doubt the hidden things promised to us. / He was the first to strip off the garment of mortality, / and in his very nature he ascended and was exalted above death. / As though pointing with a finger, he showed humankind the renewal of his body, / so that mortals might gaze upon a body that had become immortal. / For this [?] the divine power raised him, / that by his resurrection it might set forth a showing of the renewal of all. / He renewed all creation with him in mystery, / and in him he renews it in truth at the end of the times. / In him that renewal which is beyond words comes to pass, / and in him that judgment which cannot be spoken of is pronounced. / The Lord of all chose him out of all as first-fruits, / that he might fill his own place for the works of his hands. / He fills the place of the Existent One for all through his visibility, / and creation rests in the senses of his body as in a harbour. / In him the unbridled motions of rational beings are given bounds, / and they no longer wear themselves out searching after the hiddenness of the Hidden One. / He becomes for all the holy temple of the One who holds all, / and in him the worship of all is offered to the Lord of all. / All creation enters with him before the Lord of all,

and offers him one undivided thanksgiving. / This too is the purpose of his election and his exaltation: / that he might be a harbour giving creatures rest from their toils. / He it is who gives the weary world rest from its weariness, / and by the breath of his mouth drives from it the cloud of sufferings. / On the day of his revelation he reveals the strength of his might, / and creation sees the power of the Being that is glorified in him. / Suddenly the light of his dawning shines upon all creatures, / and there is none among created things that does not marvel and take refuge in him. / The Lord of all turns the dwelling of all toward him, / so that they may see him judging all and renewing all. / Swiftly he gives his sign to the things that are to be done, / and at once the work [?] his sign without delay. / A single cry he cries upon the earth, and all hear it, / and before it has ended, everything is complete, at rest and set in order. / By that command by which creation was suddenly called forth in the beginning, / he too acts in likeness and renews all by the power of the Lord of all. / That very power which made everything out of nothing / renews in him heaven and earth, rational and mute. / Rational and mute he gives rest from toil and from change, / and no longer do they labour, nor are they worn down with labours. / He began in himself that renewal which knows no corruption, / and he completes it with a completeness that has no end. / He was the first in the life that is beyond all harm, / and he gained power to give life to others as well. / The mortal one inherited the possession of the immortals, / and in his inheritance he makes humans and spiritual beings partners. / It is written that we have become, and are becoming, heirs of his inheritance; / therefore the promise of his words is true and not false. / The spiritual beings saw the truth made manifest through the earthly one, / and they rejoiced and praised the One who revealed in him the truth of his hiddenness. / The hosts on high raised the sound of praise on earth / to the Hidden One who openly showed his love to the members of his household. / His great love he revealed to creatures through a human being, / and he taught them that among created things there is none greater than man.

He made man chief of the chiefs among the works of his hands, / and see, the natures serve him in the rank of ministers. / Creation bows to his lordship as to a master, / and honours him because of the power that shines forth in him. / The Creator's power willed to raise him to the height of his own name, / and see, he is called by a name with which no other compares. / A creature has no claim at all to the name of Maker, / and this is the wonder: that a creature was made worthy of the name of Maker. / The Creator of creation honoured his creation by what he did, / in that he took a portion of it and honoured it with his glory. / That human being who came to be among these things is a portion from all, / and in him, through his honour, all are honoured with the Lord of all. / His soul is a portion from the spiritual and impassible beings, / and they are close to him in kinship and in exaltation. / His body is a portion from all corruptible bodies, / and they are akin to him in kinship of body and of renewal. / From all creatures there is a portion in him, the first-fruits of our life, / and in his exaltation lies the exaltation of all creation as well. / How then can anything among creatures perish, / when see, everything is gathered up and kept safe in one of our race? / How could it be that, while the first-fruits dwells in glory, / the lump from which the first-fruits came should remain in disgrace? / No, O hearer, do not divide the love for all, / and do not tear the whole lump away from its oneness. / Do not doubt, asking how this can come to be; / believe that the Creator's power is equal to all things. / To the Creator's power everything, hidden and revealed, is easy, / and it is never hindered when it wills to do anything. / It pleased the Creator to act in this way, / and it had already been done by the will of his love before he did it. / It was not as something new that he chose one man for the renewal of all; / he had chosen him before he created creation in the beginning. / Together with his being, this which he did existed in him— / not that it existed as such, but that it was not hidden from him. / Without beginning he had confirmed this decree, / and it existed for him just as it exists now that time has come.

And if this is so, and true just as it is, / let us not doubt the work that exists from eternity. / The Existent One, who brought all into being, is from eternity, / and in him all things that came to be were hidden, whenever they came to be. / As far as he was concerned, the world was created before he created it, / and it was renewed before he announced its renewal. / A second time he renewed it, by the will of his love that delights in our life, / and he taught us the order of his eternity and his creating. / It is us he taught, by these things he did for our sake, / how greatly he loved us and how greatly he honoured us with his glories. / He loved us and created us though he knew we would hate him, / and he renews us and grants us much though we are unworthy. / We are unworthy—and how unworthy, one might say— / to receive a rank so high and exalted above all created things. / The nature of the Creator cannot be compared with creatures, / and who would not marvel that he made us his counterpart by exalting us? / His will chose one of mankind, and he was well pleased with him, / and he placed his will in the hands of that man's will, to govern all. / Into the hands of his will he placed the divine will, / and there is no will that is not fulfilled in him, willingly. / In him the world of time and the world everlasting are upheld, / and he it is who governs the earthly and the heavenly. / He sustains all from the treasury of the One who was pleased with him, / and he orders all according to the will of the One who sets all in order. / One of our own race orders all and gives life to all, / and though he is a human being, he holds a divine rank. / His nature shows that the rank he received is higher than itself, / and he too testifies that his rank is higher than his make-up. / Come, then, let us marvel at the rank our lowly race has attained, / and let us repay with thanks the One who raised us to the height of his name. / Come, let us be amazed at the power and authority of the son of our humanity, / who renews all and judges all as Lord of all. / Come, let us marvel at him when he appears from where he is, / dawning suddenly and veiling the light with his own light. / Come, let us remember that descent when he comes down to earth, / and returns and ascends with all creation with him. / All creation, I said, ascends with his ascension,

because rational and mute are bound up in his body and his soul. / Come, let us make ready for the preparation he is preparing for us, / and wait for that hope which comforts us. / With love let us keep the pledge of the life of that renewal, / so that we may not grieve when heaven and earth are renewed.
On the Ascension of Our Lord

By the same author. Homily thirty-six, on the Ascension of our Lord.
Responsory: Blessed is Christ, who on the day of his ascension raised us up and seated us with him in heaven.
My brothers.

I have marvelled greatly at the lowliness of our dust, how great it has become:
though it is only dust, it has gained authority and reigns over all.
My thoughts have gazed on the lowly clay, how highly it has been exalted:
what once suffered so much has come to glories.
I have searched out mortality, which endured sufferings, to contemplate it:
how it suddenly became a spring that makes life flow for all.
My mind has wearied itself over the moulded clay of which our body is made:
how it gained wings to fly toward the height.
Our lowly nature beckoned to me in silence: 'See a wonder,
how great the humility of Adam's dust has become!'
Passible nature, which endured sufferings, called out and urged me:
'Look at the nature that was [?] and is now clothed in glory!'
The feeble dust, worn down by sufferings, called me and roused me:
'Arise and contemplate the son of dust who has reached the [?]!'
The discernment within me nudged me as one nudges the deaf:
'Let your palate [?]; render thanks to the one who has magnified your race!'
The impulse of my own self whispered to me in silence, mysteriously:
'Make a reply; give exaltation to the Bridegroom on high!'
My mind counselled me: 'Lift your gaze toward the height;
look at the firmament, which has opened its gates to the new King!'
My thoughts were stirred at the voice of the spiritual herald,
who cries out in the Spirit and shows us the image of victory.
I listened to the new book of the New Testament,
which interprets through revelation the fulfilment of our life.
I saw the Twelve, the chosen witnesses, gathered together

and asking about the restoration of the kingdom on high.
The children of the palace gathered around the King to ask him:
'At what time will you show the crown of your sovereignty?
Reveal and explain to us whether the promise of your words is near,
and whether you will give the reward to the seed of Abraham, as you have promised.'
The skilful Master saw the thought of those who were children in heart,
and held them back from their worldly question.
In a fleshly way the children asked about the kingdom,
and he [?] led them on to maturity.
'It is not for you to know the time of the end of the ages;
do not weary yourselves probing the power of hidden things.
This is yours: to receive the power of preaching,
and to be witnesses of the new way that I have trodden in my own person.
Of you I ask that, by the laying on of hands, you seal
the covenant that is written in blood for the sons of Adam.
You I send as envoys to the four quarters,
to turn the nations to kinship with the house of Abraham.
You I clothe with the armour of the Spirit, who strengthens all,
to join battle with the strong one who enslaved mankind.
Through you, as by light, I chase away the darkness of error;
by the lamps you kindle I give light to the blind world.
Through you I strip away the covering of iniquity that the Evil One spread,
and I tear the hateful garment that he wove in Eden.
You I set like mirrors before those who look,
that people may see themselves and hate iniquity.
Through you I open the treasury of the Spirit, who enriches all;
go out, give letters of freedom and life to mortality.
Through you I complete and fulfil mysteries and types;
explain them, and make the force of the parables shine in every ear.
Through you I tread the way of the Spirit for those of earth;
show them the path of the order that is not corrupted.
Through you I reveal stern judgements and abundant mercies;
warn and reprove, that they may not be condemned at the sentence of judgement.'
The Master gave his disciples fitting instructions,
and began to travel the new road toward the height.
He fulfilled the will of the One who sent him for the redemption of mankind,
and completed the work of his stewardship on behalf of all.
He won the victory before the eyes of spiritual and bodily beings,
and rational and dumb creatures escorted him and bore him with fitting love.
The earthly and the heavenly gathered to accompany him,
as he set out to go and receive the kingdom on high.
The hidden Command harnessed a chariot with the harness of the wind,
and bridled the air for the King, who had conquered and ascended, to ride.
It spread clouds of light like linen over the chariot;
the King took his seat, and the Command set a crown upon his head.
Rational and dumb creatures yoked their voices beneath the chariot,
and escorted the Hidden One in the Revealed, the Being in the body.
The charioteer turned the steeds of fire toward the height,
and taught them to run on a road never trodden before.
A command sounded like a trumpet in the ears of the dumb creatures:
'Open the gates, that the King may enter in glory!'
The Command lifted the veil of waters from the face of the gate,
and opened the gate that was set in the planks of the waters.
The Command opened a new gate for the new King,
which no human foot had ever trodden, save through the Word:

he alone trod the road of the kingdom on high,
and entered to serve as priest in the Holy of Holies, as high priest.
It befitted him to minister spiritually in the sanctuary of the height,
in a pure place that is not stained by earthly things.
Ah, our nature, grown great in name and in deeds,
that has ascended and reigns above principalities and powers!
Ah, our dust, that has gained the rank of sovereignty,
and has made rational and dumb creatures subject to its authority!
He walked upon the earth and took captivity captive from the strong one,
and led it up to a place secure from harm.
He humbled and cast down the tyrant who rebelled against his lordship,
and clothed his own forces with spiritual armour.
He taught them the art of spiritual combat,
that they might aim at the mark by which he himself had conquered.
He showed them the path of ascent on the road to the height
by the sign of his body, carried in procession above the air.
He drew them to gaze at him with delight,
that they might see his glory and gain hope in his promises.
Before their eyes he gave the air a body, like a chariot,
and the visible body rode the wind and reached the height.
He sent to them some of the spiritual beings who were escorting him,
and the disciples were amazed at them, at the white garments they wore.
In a garment of light he showed them the heavenly ones:
if his envoys are wrapped in light, how much more he himself!
He set a veil of light before their faces, that they might not weary themselves,
for they longed to see what was not permitted.
Two thoughts drew those of earth,
and for two reasons they were gazing toward the height:
they looked to see whether they might see the gates as they were opened,
or perhaps whether the composition of his body would be changed.
For they were pondering how a body ascends to the height,
and how a thing with a composite form enters through a gate that is shut.
For this reason he sent the spiritual beings to them,
to dispel their fear and the doubt of their minds as well.
They stood suddenly before their eyes and amazed them,
for they did not approach them gradually, but all at once.
They addressed them by a plain name, 'Galileans',
and showed them that they had been given leave to speak of him who had ascended.
'Why do you stand and gaze into the height above?
Why do you weary yourselves with what is too hard for children of flesh?
Learn from us, as from those who are certain of hidden things:
this Jesus will come in the same way as he ascended,
in the very appearance in which you saw him with the senses of the body.
In it he remains, without change in body or soul;
in that same appearance he remains, in beauty beyond words,
and at the end of the ages he will come to test all.'
In that same appearance of the visible body he remains, though hidden,
he who ascended and reigned with the Will that chose him out of all.
In that same appearance, however much the heretics may dispute,
in it I confess him, and I do not deny the testimony of the Watchers.
I do not make liars of the spiritual beings, the chosen witnesses,
nor do I alter the plain imprint of the sound of their words.
I do not transgress the sayings of the King's servants,
nor do I resist the stewards of the hidden Command.
True and tested is the record of the ascension of the first-fruits of our race:

the spiritual beings too laid their hands on it, sealed it and delivered it.
They too walked in the way of the word of him who ascended,
who revealed and made plain in what nature he rose from the tomb:
'Touch me and see the place of the spear and the place of the nails;
know and understand that a spirit does not have flesh and bones.'
Flesh and bones he showed to the witnesses of his death,
that they might not doubt his resurrection, thinking it a mere semblance and not he.
He showed the nails and the spear in his body to the children of his mystery,
after it had become immortal and impassible.
After his death he showed a new thing, beyond the order of nature:
he ate and drank with his heralds and confirmed them.
He constrained his nature, whose passibility glory had swallowed up,
and showed it suffering and taking food like one in need.
That he showed suffering in what was impassible is certain to us;
how he showed it, he alone knows.
That he ate and drank, we do not make his words liars;
how he ate is known to him who testified that he ate.
He sealed the promise of his words beforehand by what he did,
for he said that he would eat with them in the kingdom on high.
Otherwise, let them tell us, those who efface the body and make the Word suffer:
how are we to understand that he showed sufferings, and ate and drank [?]?
Come, interpret for us the new books of the preaching:
what is the body that received sufferings, and that hands touched?
If the Hidden One came into the visible and became flesh,
why did he show us sufferings in his body after he had risen?
Was his nature perhaps passible before his coming,
so that he showed sufferings to confirm his passibility?
God forbid! It was not my will that gave birth to this boldness;
the foolish zeal of the minglers forced me, and I said it.
It was not from my own desire that I undertook to ascend to the height above;
it is they whom I wish to bring down to earth, for they have been so presumptuous.
It was not vainglory that carried me off to probe hidden things;
I sought to cut short the [?] words of their blasphemies.
It was not the rank of teacher that I sought to seize for myself;
the simple-minded cried out [?], and it did not please me.
They have overturned the mark that he set at the head of his victory,
and for this reason I have shot the arrows of my words against them.
They sought to lay hay and straw on the building of truth,
and my thoughts grew hot, as with fire, to burn them up.
Otherwise, let them show by their deeds how they build,
and I shall learn the aim of their minds and how they aim at it.
If they belong to the body of the Church, as its members,
why do they hate the name of Christ, the head of the body?
Why do they disown the name 'Son of Man', which is set down in the Scriptures,
and why do they efface the name of honour that our race has received?
Why do they confuse the hidden nature, which cannot be confused,
and why do they mingle hidden things that cannot be mingled?
The hidden nature is not confined in the visible body:
how can what has no end be bounded in what is bounded?
The One who holds all has no place that could hem him in [?],
for outside all and within all his nature reigns.
This is why I take up arms with the weapons of my words,
to lay waste the ranks of those who make the Word suffer and efface the body.
They bring the Word down to the passibility of lowly flesh

and thrust the body away from the honour it shares with the Being.
The Watchers cry out that he ascended and reigned in that very nature,
and the mouth of the perverse of heart is stopped, without comfort.
They revealed to the apostles that in it he will come again at the end of the ages,
yet these do not listen to the preaching of the spiritual beings.
It is the son of our race who ascended and reigned with the Being;
it was not the Being that came down to earth and so ascended.
It is our nature that rode the wind and bridled the air,
and rational and dumb creatures escorted and bore him for the sake of the Hidden One.
He it is who trod a new road through the [?] air,
and grew wings for flight, though not by his nature.
He it is who opened the gates of the height before those of earth,
and entered to minister as priest in the Holy of Holies for their life.
It was not according to the order of the Law that he entered to serve as priest,
but with the blood of his own new covenant.
It did not befit him to minister with earthly things, like the priests;
he entered heaven to make atonement for all by the sacrifice of himself.
Once for all he entered and was received into the Holy of Holies,
and time no longer cuts short his [?] or the greatness of his rank.
He entered and appeared before the One who sees all, who had seen him beforehand,
and He gave him rank and set on him the crown of the name of the Being.
By the power of the hidden Command He brought him near to the rank above,
to that greatness which bears no comparison with created things.
He subjected all things to him, and by the power of the One who took him he reigned over all,
and received authority to judge spiritual and bodily beings.
In his judgement he tests the discernment of rational beings,
and [?] deeds and words and the glances of the eyes.
Through the visibility of his body I see, with hidden movements of the mind,
that Hidden One who is concealed from all and to whom all is manifest.
In him they gaze with the outward senses, as on what is visible,
and with the mind on the power of the Being hidden within him.
In the yoke of his love Watchers and men are yoked together,
and they escort him as the image of the hidden King.
In his body bodily beings see their own members,
and spiritual beings, in his movements, see themselves.
They repeat their praise spiritually with the voice of the senses,
and hallow him with the delight of their minds.
At every moment they worship, in the temple of his body, the One who is hidden in it,
and offer him the hidden sacrifices of their minds.
In the haven of his body the movements of their thoughts come to rest,
when they weary themselves seeking the Hidden One, who cannot be comprehended.
That is why the Establisher of all chose him out of all,
that in the visibility of his body he might fulfil the need of all.
The creature needed always to seek what is hidden,
and to learn the power of hidden things and their explanations.
And since the hidden nature could not come into the visible,
he set the bounds of their questioning in the visible image.
At every moment they run in the stadium of the name of the Being,
and when they reach the door of his body they carry off the victory.
He it is who gives to the contest of their minds
the crown that the Hidden One holds out by his hand in return for their labours.
By the hand of his body the Lord of the vineyard gives wages
to the labourers who toiled in the hope of new life.
Through him the talents of the Spirit are entrusted to the good servants,

that they may take the silver, manage it well, trade, and grow rich.
From him the wicked servant hears that saying:
'Why did you hide the talent that I gave into your hands?'
With him the wise virgins enter the Bridegroom's chamber,
adorned with a garment of glory that does not decay.
He it is who answers the foolish virgins, who had acquired no oil:
'Go, take your delight from your labours, as you have loved.'
At the sound of his words those who keep his love gain hope,
and go out to meet him, to receive the reward for their labours.
With him they fly toward the height on wings of the Spirit,
carried in procession on the chariot of the back of the air.
By the visible sign by which his own body was taken up,
by it are raised the bodies that have become a dwelling for his love.
A cloud bore him like a chariot as he ascended,
and the hidden Command drove it like a charioteer.
In the same likeness, clouds of light will bear the bodies,
by that command which bridled the air and [?] his body.
In it he depicted our weaknesses and our glories,
and inscribed them like writings on the tablet of his body.
In it he showed us how grievous our fall was,
and in it he made plain to us how exalted our redemption is.
By his conception he depicted our fashioning from the dust,
and by his birth showed that the earth bore us without union.
Through his upbringing among earthly things he revealed that he was one of us,
and by enduring sufferings he showed that his nature was from mortals.
By his death he proclaimed the breach that had come about by his hand [?],
and by his resurrection he undid sin and abolished death.
By his ascension he trod for us the road by which to ascend to the height,
and by his procession he raised our body up from the dust.
He became for us like the dawn, that the earthly might shine,
and the close of the day was the course of his journey toward the height.
He went out from the morning and [?] through sufferings the course of our body,
and came to rest in the haven of the height above, as at evening.
By his ascension he opened for us the gates that had been shut,
and brought us in with him into the Holy of Holies, which had not been permitted.
Our dust ascended with his exaltation to the Being,
and our dust sat in the rank of a King who holds authority.
It took the sceptre of sovereignty and reigned over all,
and began to command what is not its own, as the Maker does.
Ah, the dust, how great it has become through what is not its own!
Ah, the mortal, who distributes life from what belongs to another!
Ah, the one of earth, who left the earth, the mother of his body,
and entered to dwell in the bosom of a mother not of his own nature!
Ah, the one of dust, who left his place, a dwelling bound by time,
and ascended to the place whose permanence has no end!
Ah, the son of Adam's stock, fashioned from the earth,
who has gained the rank and the name of the authority of the Godhead!
The heavy one rode the wings of the wind and flew through the air,
and amazed the hosts on high with his lightness.
The hosts of the heavenly ones stood in great wonder,
as they saw a body flying, which was not usual.
The Watchers wove a crown of praise for him as he ascended,
for they saw that he had trodden a road for men to their own hosts.
They became envoys to the disciples, who were downcast,
and gladdened them with the white garments they wore.
Through his ascension they gained love and affection for our race,

and began to run the course of peace toward our humanity.
They had grieved greatly over our fall into captivity,
and when they saw our rising through the son of our race, they rejoiced again and were comforted.
He [?] the decree that had blocked the road between us and them,
and by his blood he undid the sentence of judgement that our many sins had brought.
By his mediation he made peace for all through [?],
and by his ascension he confirmed the peace that renewed all.
He set free the captives who were shut up in the fortresses of [?],
and comforted them with the glories that he received and inherited.
He himself became a mirror of beautiful things,
and wove them into crowns fitting for the head of his victory.
At his conception there was 'Glory to God' from all his ranks,
'and peace on earth, and good hope' for the hopeless.
At the offering of sacrifices came the voice that explained the prophecy:
'Behold, he is set for a sentence of judgement and for a sign of peace.'
His baptism cried out like a trumpet about his greatness,
and the Father's voice proclaimed his love and the greatness of his rank.
His fast proclaims his victory in the wilderness,
where with bodily senses he overpowered the one who had overpowered all.
At the time of his death even the silent became speakers,
for the hidden Command compelled them and they gained power.
The sound of his [?] killed death and trampled sin,
and the dead cried out in the ears of death: 'Where is your sting?'
On the day of his ascension he called those of earth and those of heaven,
and showed them a new road by which to travel to the height.
Spiritual and bodily beings went out to escort him,
to see his body, how it flew spiritually.
The sight of his body was delightful to those of earth,
and the converse of his soul was dearly loved by those of heaven.
The eye of flesh was not sated with gazing
at the features of his body as it was carried aloft on the chariot.
The spiritual beings would not consent to be left behind him,
and hastened eagerly to see who would outdo the others in love toward him.
Fitting and desirable, too, was the season in which he ascended,
and the course of his journey outran the sphere of the sun.
Together with the victory of the great sun he won his own victory,
and spread the light of his preaching to the four quarters.
In the month when light conquers darkness he conquered sin,
and chased away error, the hateful garment that the Evil One wove.
In June light conquered, light the servant and light the Lord,
and darkness was vanquished together with the dark night of error.
The luminary stood at the upper point of its course,
and set the darkness at the lower point, as in a grave.
The Sun of righteousness, too, ascended to the height above,
and swept error and its [?] down to the depth below.
By the three hours that light took from the darkness
it cut short its course and confined its length to the lower point.
Our King, too, gave three names to his Twelve,
and by them they cut off the road of death that the Evil One had trodden.
His rays came down upon all the earth like rain;
they watered her bosom and ripened her fruits with his warmth.
Through our first-fruits the Creator sprinkled the dew of mercies,

and the fruits of righteousness sprang up in the land of our soul.
In the month that yields fruits and seeds for the life of time
came the first-fruits that bestow life without end.
He was conceived in Nisan, the month that is the firstborn of the year,
and born in Kanun, the month in which light plunders the darkness.
He fasted and was tempted in the gloomy month, bare of fruits,
and offered the first-fruits of his soul's [?] from [?].
He sacrificed himself at the season when Adam sinned by eating,
and by his sacrifice he reconciled the Lord and his servants, and gladdened them.
In the month in which Adam's guilt grew strong in Eden,
in that month the second Adam, who conquered death, was victorious.
At the time when the [?] heir went out from his inheritance,
the diligent one entered the place of life that does not decay.
By his victory he paid off the bond of our debt,
and wrote us down with him as equals and heirs of the wealth he received.
He brought back our captivity from the strong one who had taken our race captive,
and led it up to the place where the weapon of his deceit cannot overpower it.
He placed our spiritual wealth in the height above,
where it is not ruined by the harm of the passions.
He drew the mind toward the treasures where our soul is laid up,
that it may travel in what is ours and not stray into what is not ours.
He showed us what is ours, that we may love what is ours as the wise do,
and not be fettered by what is not ours, as the ignorant are.
He [?] our soul through the promises of things to come,
that the senses of the body may not bind us with desires.
He set up for us milestones of peace along the road he travelled,
and taught us how far and how we should travel to the [?] of life.
By two roads he showed the course of two directions,
that each may travel in whichever he wishes, by his own freedom.
The road of life he called narrow, because of its toil,
and the road of destruction he called broad with desires.
He himself completed the course of the road of life,
that whoever sets out after his words may not grow slack.
Behold, the King has set out on the new road of the kingdom on high;
let us travel with him, that we may not be stripped by robbers.
Behold, he has set up a mark for his forces in the [?] of the height;
let us aim at it with the movements of the soul instead of the limbs.
Behold, he has opened the gate of the stadium to the royal palace;
let us join battle with [?] with a hidden mind.
Behold, he has forged spiritual armour for soul and body;
let us take up the sword of the word of the Spirit on the tip of our tongue.
By his sufferings he tilled the land of our body, which was full of thickets;
come, let us sow good seed in it and [?] life.
By his blood he cleansed the blemishes of our soul and of our members;
let us not be stained by the desires of our evil inclination.
By his sacrifice he reconciled height and depth with the One who sent him;
let us not make the peace of all lose its savour through our slackness.
By his ascension he raised up our body, heavy in its senses;
let us gain wings through the movements [?] of the soul, to go where he is.
Paul cries out in his epistles like a trumpet
that he raised us with him [?] at the right hand.
We died with him, and he gave us life with him, since he is one of us,
and he raised us with him, as members together with the head of the body.
That he rose, was raised and gave life to all, our heart believes;
that he ascended and reigns above all is certain to us.
With the love of our soul let us keep his love, as is fitting for him,

and let us not doubt his promises, as though they were far off.
With the spiritual beings let us bear witness always to his ascension:
that he will come in the same appearance in which he ascended.
On the Day of the Feast of Pentecost

Homily twenty-seven, on the day of the Feast of Pentecost.
Responsory: O mortals, let us repay our debt to the one who has magnified our race by the power of his wisdom.
My brothers.

The Creator opened the treasury of the Spirit before mortals,
and enriched them from the treasures of the greatness of his might.
In a vessel of little worth he who enriches all placed his wealth,
and though it was despised, he kept in it the treasure of glories.
Feeble clay he made the treasurer of his hidden things;
he kindled it with the Spirit, and set a glorious Spirit in what was despised.
Like a harp, it sang hidden things on the strings of its body,
and with its voice imitated earthly and heavenly beings.
Like a trumpet, the commandment cried out with a tongue of flesh,
and spiritual and bodily beings gathered to it.
A broken reed became a flute for the living Spirit,
and gladdened all with the sweetness of its songs.
In one born to suffering dwelt the power that gives life to all,
and he began to pour out life for all by the breath of his lips.
The sick man who had long lain in the pains of iniquity
began to heal the pains of the body and the blemishes of the soul.

The wood that had dried up in the harsh heat of desires
suddenly blossomed and bore fruits of sweetness.
The vine that had been robbed of tending and had brought forth thorns
suddenly yielded early clusters of wine and bore glory.
The heir who had squandered in prodigality the wealth he had taken
turned back to his father, and his father longed to meet him and gave him his wealth.
In love and mercy the Creator reached out to meet our life,
and embraced our race through the first fruit that he took from us.
He covered our shame with the robe of glory that mercy had woven,
and gave the power of the Spirit as a pledge, like a signet ring.
He invited and called us to the feast of life without end,
and to the banquet full of blessings that never cloy.
In a mystery he betrothed us to fellowship in his love;
he opened his treasury, and sealed his words by deeds.
From our race he chose one body as a first fruit,
sanctified it by the Spirit, and accepted its sacrifice as redemption.
He made it the treasury of hidden and awesome things,
and put the rule into its hand, to enrich all from his gift.
Through it he made a covenant with the sons of his race, an inheritance of life,
and made it the fountain that gives his own to drink from his life.
He filled it with the undiminished power of his divinity,
so that it might give power to mortal nature, weak in power.
He promised and covenanted with the ministers of his preaching
to enrich them from the fullness of the power he had taken.
He encouraged them as he was going to the one who sent him:
"Behold, I am going, and I will send the promise of my Father."
He named him "Paraclete", the wealth of the promise of his words,
who is able to console the poverty of the grieving soul.
He called him "promise", so that they might hold hope in their thoughts
of when they would see his wealth openly distributed.
He called him also "power", hidden in the height above all,
who can strengthen all and give all victory by the might of his greatness.
You, remain in the land of Judea where I suffered,
until I give the power of the Spirit to your members.

Remain in Zion, as in the proving ground of prophecy,
from which goes forth the one who is able to forgive iniquity.
He wished to do away with the iniquity of the nations by means of the people,
and made this the reason: for Jacob's sake iniquity is turned away.
In Zion he showed that his light is there and his judgement decreed,
as he enlightens all and accuses by his testing.
In the place that he chose and called by his name, where he set his laws,
there he expounds the power of wonders and the hiddenness of mysteries.
To Mount Zion he invited and called the tribes of the nations,
and gladdened them with the feast of the sacrifices of the law.
In Zion he expounds also the wonder of that banquet
to which earthly and heavenly beings gather.
There he commanded the lovers of his love to wait for him,
so that he might repay them the reward of the love they had shown him.
He bound them with the bonds of a spiritual reward,
so that they would not grow slack when they parted from one another.
He placed upon them the seal of the Spirit in a mystery,
and signed them with the breath of his lips, that they might be his own.
By the breath of his mouth he showed them the power of his gift,
from which comes the payment of the reward of the wealth he promised.
He breathed on their faces and confirmed them in the promise of his words,
and taught them to forgive sins and to judge iniquity.
He put into their hands the key of mercy and the decree of judgement,
to open the door to both sides, to the good and to the wicked.
He departed to receive the kingdom on high that had been destined for him,
and charged them: Remain in Judea and proclaim my victory.
Remain there, in the land where I bore suffering and shame,
for there I will display my greatness to those who shamed me.
Before many I bore suffering from the insolent,
and before the eyes of all I will show my awesome power.
Where the base mocked and laughed at my humility,
there proclaim my invincible might.
Those who counted me despised, full of sufferings and rejected by all,
I will teach through the deeds of my wisdom.
Those who robbed me of the glory that was my due as the innocent one
are put to shame, behold, as every tongue sings to me.

Those who did not praise me on the harp of David's making,
I will sing my victory on twelve strings taken from their tribes.
Like a harp of twelve strings he arranged them,
so that they might praise him with twelve voices, as on strings.
And because they did not render him the voice of thanksgiving they owed,
he plucked his victory on the harp of his Twelve.
Twelve voices cried out his victory like trumpets,
while the tribes fell silent, though the strings of their members should have sounded [?].
At the glorious feast he sacrificed himself in the manner of the lamb,
and at the festival of Pentecost he sealed his victory.
He set all free in the mystery of the redemption from Egypt,
and distributed his wealth like the wonders on Mount Sinai.
At the feast when he wrote tablets of stone for the heart of stone,
he engraved spiritual letters in the stirrings of the soul.
On the day he gave an inheritance to the people of the flesh,
he distributed spiritual wealth to the spiritual.
At the time when he wrote the covenant full of death,
he sealed promises in the covenant that gives life.
In the wonder of the voices and trumpets on Mount Sinai,
he suddenly made heard the voice of the Spirit who makes all things new.
There, a voice full of fear that terrified servants;
here, a voice that grants hope to soul and body.
There, fire and smoke and violent quaking;
here, light that was distributed in the sign of fire.
There, servants ministered to servants with fearful voices;
here, he calls with a gentle voice full of peace.
There, an adornment of earthly things for the earthly;
here, the beauty of spiritual things for the heavenly.
There, in great fear, dwelt the mediator as well,
who carried words to a people whose heart was divided.
Here the head of the Twelve dwells in joy,
and makes peace reign in the minds of his companions.
Moses cries out that fear and terror fill my thoughts;
and Simon proclaims hope and love and faith.
Moses tore [?] the garment that the bridegroom had sent to the bride,
and Simon clothed the assembly of the nations in the robe of glory.
He steeled his resolve to put the betrothed to death, and broke the tablets,

and openly exposed the disgrace of the King's bride.
Here the lovers of the bridegroom cry out like trumpets,
and show the hidden beauty of the holy Church.
The bodily heard that voice [?] and recoiled from it;
here the spiritual heard it and longed to meet it.
They cried out to Moses, "You speak [for] God" [?],
for the Creator's voice was not pleasant to those without God.
In the chamber of the spiritual bridegroom every one longs
for the time when he will hear the new tidings of the Creator's voice.
In this hope labourers went out and hired themselves into the vineyard,
to receive a reward, a pledge in place of a denarius.
Girded labourers heard the promise of the King on high,
and readied their movements and their members to put on armour.
Suddenly a trumpet sounded ahead of the King's coming,
and gathered the hosts by a signal to meet the King.
He made a sound heard, shook the earth and showed fire,
as he rebuked and encouraged with fear and with mercy.
By the quaking he showed fierce wrath against the insolent,
and through the fire he revealed his wealth that never diminishes.
Suddenly, it says, there came a sound like a mighty wind,
and the wonder of his [?] filled the dwelling of men.
They saw tongues distributed like fire,
and he set them on their heads as a hidden sign.
In the sign of fire he gave the spiritual wealth,
so that it would not diminish when they took of it in abundance.
In the brightness of the light the King distributed to his hosts
spiritual provisions that do not spoil.
Through tongues like fire he revealed his wisdom,
and taught them a new learning that they had not known.
In the vision he also depicted the power by which they would conquer:
that like fire they would set alight the thicket of mortality.
With hidden armour he armed them as for battle,
and handed them the sword of the Spirit to lay waste iniquity.
He changed his wealth into portions of every kind,
so that they might distribute it according to the hearing of those who received it.
They were sent to tongues that they had not known,

and they wrote books and read them spiritually.
They wrote spiritual letters on the tablets of the heart,
and the bodily mouth interpreted the power of their knowledge.
Their members became like strings for the finger of the Spirit,
and the Spirit secretly plucked the sentient instrument in the body.
O organ that had acquired the voice of mortality,
that changed its voice and sang life in the ears of the dead!
O harp whose strings were corruptible flesh,
that composed songs free of suffering, beyond its custom!
O flute of a broken reed that played sufferings,
whose voice drove suffering away from those who suffer!
O unlettered men who mocked and laughed at the sophists,
and with plain words cut short the course of rhetoric!
O fishermen who fished for perishable food,
who caught the food of greedy death and drew it toward life!
O poor men who lacked a dwelling and begged for alms,
who suddenly became rich and distributed life from their treasuries!
The weak in strength went out to battle with the strong,
and with visible members won the victory.
The broken-hearted acquired spiritual wisdom,
and gave savour to human wisdom, which had grown insipid on earth.
The blind of heart, deprived of light, groping on the earth,
became lamps, drove out the darkness and gladdened the earth.
The bodily, who bore the weight of earthly things,
became spiritual and acquired the wings of flight.
The earthly, sons of dust, offspring of the earth,
began to encamp [?] in the stillness of the heavenly.
Mute fishermen went out to catch eloquence;
they cast the net of preaching and enclosed the earth.
From sea and from land they caught every tongue,
and invited them to eat spiritual food.
They kindled the fire of preaching in the thicket of iniquity,
and burned the thorns of desires that wickedness had brought forth.
In the sign of fire they received authority to till the earth;
they burned the thicket and sowed wheat, the good seed.
In the flash of fire they acquired the wisdom of every tongue,
and gave it as a sweet savour to the foolish nations.
By the power of the Spirit all the nations gathered to see the marvel,
seeing the new thing that had happened beyond all custom.

They were astonished and amazed at one another,
hearing distinct voices from a single people.
Mortals saw a great marvel in mortality,
as a thirsty nature poured out streams of water.
There the divided nations received one concord,
for a new hearing of answering voices made them equal.
Syrians cried out to Greeks as in their own speech;
wrath subsided, anger ceased, and peace reigned.
Cushites spoke one word in a foreign tongue with Romans,
and sang praise with one tongue to one Creator.
Medes signed to Alans, "What is this?"
and a mouth interpreted and spared them from asking.
The uncircumcised asked the circumcised people as though they were of their household,
"Has this ever happened in the house of your tribes?"
The people told the nations, "It has not been seen by me,
nor has this happened among our people until now."
In one tongue Abraham received and handed down to his sons,
and in it the wonders of prophecy too were composed.
A hidden sign resolved the questions of both sides,
and taught them what this was that had happened.
That commandment which gave tongues and divided the nations,
it is he who spoke in one tongue with many.
The scribe who taught a new learning to that childhood,
it is he who brought it to maturity in what has now happened.
The pen that inscribed words on the heart in that clumsiness,
it is he who enlarged the dull heart and interpreted well.
The key that opened the doors of the soul full of arrogance,
by it humility opened the treasury of the Spirit.
There arrogance seized the mind to climb to the height,
and a voice swept it away and cast it to the earth, so that it should be arrogant no more.
There the insolent drew up for battle against the hidden one;
and here the hidden one sent down his will to the humble.
The flood of waters that had swept over the earth frightened them,
and they began to build a building of iniquity in which to be saved.
The heart of rebellion was united in building the iniquity,
and a voice tore apart that unity, scattered it and cast it down.
The sign came upon them like evening and gave them rest,
so that they would not wear out their lives at the hand of toil.

They had longed arrogantly to climb to the height,
and he who knows all bound them with earthly things.
He gave tongues in the manner of wrath, not because he was angry,
but to put the bridles of fear into the mouth of the insolent.
For their benefit he brought about that rebellion by which he scattered them,
and in it he depicted the mysteries of what has happened at the end of the times.
In all that he has done may he be blessed by every mouth,
who before the times foreknows, and so acts.
For he knew that by one sacrifice he would pardon all,
and he first depicted it, for the atonement of sins, in the sacrifice of the lamb.
By this he persuades us that he gives the Spirit through tongues,
and depicted its likeness in what happened among the ancients.
He revealed the power of his being to his servants and made them wise,
that the first things and the last are his.
He distributed wealth and gave tongues in the sign of fire,
and taught them that it was he who divided here and there.
There he divided them and occupied them with earthly things;
here he divided them and trained them in spiritual things.
There he concealed the reason why he divided them;
here he declared and revealed the meaning of both that and this.
Then, as with children, he raised the rod and frightened them;
here he opened the door of his mercy to their maturity.
Since it is he, the Good One, who struck there and made wise here,
he varied them by means of threat and of strengthening [?].
There he frightened and here he encouraged, like physicians,
and mixes them like drugs for the soul's drink.
There he hid the power of hidden things, so that they would not be despised;
here he declared and revealed the wealth of his great glory.
He showed his glory in those who received his preaching,
exalting them beyond all measure in the eyes of the beholders.
He revealed his hidden things in the frame of a visible body,
and made the voice of the greatness of his power heard in a tongue of flesh.
Movements and senses became mouths for him in place of his hiddenness,
and he completed and perfected his work in soul and body.
He who lacks nothing wished, through those who lack,
to fill the lack of bodily and spiritual beings.
O lacking ones, who distributed the wealth that lacks nothing,

and visible ones, who proclaimed the hidden one with manifest senses!
O sons of earth, born on earth and dwelling on earth,
who by their words trod out the road to the kingdom on high!
O nature that daily returns to its nature of dust,
yet in love became a dwelling for the unchanging Spirit!
In a temple of dust the Creator wished his love to dwell,
and in what suffers he showed the wealth of the greatness of his power.
In the visible he revealed his hiddenness, hidden from all,
and among the poor he distributed the wealth of his sweetness.
By the mouth of the weak he speaks the mysteries of his hidden things:
that he has an Offspring wholly like the Father of his Offspring.
With a tongue of flesh he cried out concerning the Spirit who is from him:
that as the Son is equal to him in nature, so also is the Spirit.
On the harp of fleshly words they heard of the equality
that the Son and the Spirit have in person with his being.
They were hidden with him, since they are without beginning,
and he declared them in the image of man, to magnify his image.
In the visible image he revealed the proof of the Son and the Spirit,
and showed them to heavenly and earthly beings.
Through a mouth of flesh spiritual and bodily beings learned [?],
through the ministry of the name of the being, three persons.
"Go," he said, "make disciples of all the nations and baptize them
in the name of the Father, and of the Son who is from him, and of the Holy Spirit."
And if the earthly were baptized and sanctified in the name of the being,
what profit, then, did this name bring the heavenly?
Let us call on Paul, that we may learn from him as a treasurer,
who with the key of the mystery in his hand opened the treasury of the Spirit.
"Through the Church," he says, "the God of all revealed his wisdom
to the rational powers, who did not know it."
And if spiritual beings learned the power of the hidden things in the Church,
who would not confess one being, as the Church's mouth does?
If the authorities of heaven were made wise by her,
who will not learn from the wisdom she learned and revealed?
The Church gave birth from her great Betrothed, the Lord of lords,
and wrote a book in which her children may meditate.
The apostles received the power of the Spirit; they grew rich and inherited,
and from it they provided for the poverty of the human race.
Freely they received that gift full of blessings,

and freely they spread it out before those who would receive it, as they had been commanded.
The heralds went out across the untamed world,
and bowed its neck under the gentle yoke of the Creator's name.
In love they heard that word, "Make disciples and baptize,"
and fulfilled it in words and deeds without hesitation.
They proclaimed and confessed the name of the being, three persons,
one equality that is not torn apart by division.
Girded labourers rode upon steeds, the rebellious nations,
and yoked them beneath the chariot of the King of kings.
With the armour of the Spirit they overcame all the powers that bore the name of gods,
and taught mankind to call on the name of the one God.
They uprooted paganism and Judaism, which gave no fruit,
and planted truth, a fruit pleasing to the lord of the vineyard.
They burned the thicket that wickedness had brought forth in the field of mankind,
and sowed the seed of the word of life in souls.
They uprooted the law of idolatry which error had built,
and laid the foundations of the building of truth of the one heir [?].
They drove away the darkness that had been spread over humanity,
and toil fled before the radiance of righteousness.
Twelve lamps shone in the creation that had been dark,
and it put off its mourning and put on the garment of faith.
In the order of the months they served the earth through all its changes,
and mixed spiritual food to suit each mind.
They went out to the paths and the highways, as they had been commanded,
and gathered and filled the banquet hall with good and bad.
On sea and land they journeyed with mankind to give mankind life,
and in every ear they sowed the hope of the life of the dead.
They spread the net of preaching to the four corners,
and it gathered and filled a catch of men, pleasing and beloved.
Like springs they watered the earth with the fullness of life,
and the dead pit of its dryness brought forth life.
They cast lots and divided the nations and the lands,
and each of them went to the region the sign assigned him.
Simon made a new voice heard in the land of the Romans,
and taught them the door to the lordship of the one Creator.

The head of the disciples reached the mother of cities,
and, as at the head, fixed in it the eyes of faith.
Like a trumpet, the son of thunder cried out to the Ephesians,
and gathered them to hear the wonder of his preaching.
He expounded his name through the deeds of his zeal,
for all perceived it in him as he cried, "Come, take life."
At the thunder of his voice the human heart was stirred,
and was softened to yield fruits, hope and love.
Matthew tilled the land of Judea with the voice of his sayings,
and cast into it the seed of life, and it bore glory.
The land that had grown sick from being drenched with wonders
was set right by the drink of the explanation of the mysteries, and it gained strength.
The circumcised people, who boasted in the seal of the flesh,
saw the nations sealed by the Spirit, and its seal was broken.
He made the people complete, as one lacking what it needed,
and gave it spiritual food: three names.
Like a child it meditated on the name of the Father,
and when it had grown wise he taught it three equal persons.
The heralds sowed the Trinity in every ear,
and one confession of the Creator's name sprang up on earth.
Mark was drawn by the voice that called him to the Romans,
and there he interpreted the power of the deeds of preaching.
He made the good news of a new king heard in the king's ears,
and the king marvelled that there might be a king above him.
King and people listened to his sayings, being chosen,
and they received and confirmed that there is a King who reigns over all.
Luke poured out the drink of his words in the land of Egypt,
and like the Gihon spread the hope of life over all.
The Syrian spoke in a strange tongue with the Egyptian, a foreigner to him,
and they gathered to him, for they heard that his speech was like their own.
In his voice he was like a bird calling to its own kind,
and he caught them in the snares of his preaching.
In their own tongue he spoke and made them hear the voice of redemption,
and roused them, as from sleep, to the labour of life.

In this way he enriched them with the power of tongues,
so that each might receive the good hope in the speech of his own mouth.
By the gift of tongues he taught them
to travel the road of preaching to every land.
With new speech they laid the foundations of the building of truth,
and from all peoples they completed and built one confession.
Paul the chosen one sought pure, true gold for it,
and urged everyone to consider how to build wisely.
He cries out to everyone about the heretics, those crafty workers:
“Do not build hay and thorns into this building!”
It was fitting for him to warn the household,
for he knew how to tell apart the timber of the building of iniquity.
Like a general at the head of the camp he spurs them on at every hour,
that no one should strip off the armour of the Spirit and so be found guilty.
He teaches stratagems for how we are to fight in the spirit,
and shows us that our adversary is a spirit.
“Put on truth, wear the helmet of salvation and life,
and grasp the sword of the word of the Spirit in your thoughts.”
See, the servant of the Spirit has taught us the kinds of warfare;
come, let us make ready to put on armour in his ranks.
See, the servants of the King have trodden the road of preaching;
come, let us travel it to the meeting-place of endless life.
See, they went out and tilled the land of thorns through their sufferings;
let us uproot from it the weed that sprang up amid sins.
See, they opened the doors that had been shut in people’s faces;
come, let us hasten, lest we be shut out through the slackness of our souls.
See, they wove the robe of faith in the womb of the waters;
let each one cover with it the pains of his body and the blemishes of his soul.
See, the armour has been forged for the battles of righteousness;
let no one grow slack before the wiles of the Accuser.
See, they taught us how to conquer, and with what
to receive the arrows of the guilty one on the furnace-tempered shield of faith.
See, they opened the treasury full of blessings before those who would take;
let us take freely and give freely, and live and give life.
See, a spiritual drink has sprung up for those of the earth;
let us give our souls and our fellows to drink of its sweetness.
See, the Sun of righteousness has dawned in the darkness;

let it drive the dark error of the Two from our mind.
Since we are not equal to perfection as the preachers were,
let us cast words in place of deeds, like a mere listener.
Since our speech falls short of reaching the height of their conduct,
let us follow along with them in the love of a soul whose wing is clipped.
Let us cry out with them one confession to the one Creator,
who has enriched all from the gift of the greatness of his power.
On the parable of the labourers for his vineyard
Again by the same. / The sixty-eighth homily, / which he composed on the parable of the man who went out early in the morning to hire [?] labourers for his vineyard.

The trumpet-call of our Lord's dawning cried out upon the earth,
and the world awoke as though from the sleep of sloth.
In sloth the mortals were lying as in sleep,
and the voice of our Lord woke them though they did not wish it.
Those lying in iniquity did not wish to hate iniquity,
nor were they pleased to see the Sun of righteousness.
The night of error was dear to them, the children of error,
and they had no desire to listen to the voice of the dawning of truth.
In love of the darkness of ignorance they were bound,
and the prison of shameful deeds was pleasant to them.
An evil habit had grown old among the sons of Adam,
and they loved and cherished shameful things as though they were fair.
Sluggishness held them back in the silence of error,
and they had no wish to acquire the wealth of good deeds.
Without the labour of good deeds they had been since they came to be,
for without the toil of the love of truth they walked in creation.
Sluggishly they went about in their affairs,
and they were needy and stripped of every good thing.
There was no glimmer of good or of doing good in their dwelling,
and however much they sinned, they sinned again without being sated.
Iniquity upon iniquity was mingled in the life of their conduct,
and there was no place left that was free of hateful things.

As though they were not human they conducted themselves in their ways,
until one Man came and made them wise.
One Man arose from among humans sick of soul,
and healed them of the disease of ignorance.
With the medicine of his words he revived them from their sins,
and showed them the path of the new life of good deeds.
In good deeds he busied them to meditate,
that they might no longer turn to meditate on iniquity.
Away from iniquity he fenced them off [?],
and toward uprightness he drew them to draw near.
In good meditation the good Lover busied them,
and like labourers he hired them for good toil.
For the labour of humans there came a Man who is of humanity,
and he raised his voice and made them hear the kinds of his labour.
In a parable he set out the labour and toil of his preaching,
and in a mystery he called [?] to the invitation of his love.
The voice of his invitation that called humanity: hear it, my thoughts,
and rouse yourselves from the silence in which you lay as in sleep.
From the sloth in which the motions of my mind were lying [?],
arise to listen to the voice that proclaims a good wage.
At the voice of the wage my mind awoke, shy of toils,
and began to compose a little of the words of the kinds of diligence.
As in a dream it saw the truth being interpreted,
and thought it could labour at toils in an ordering of words.
It heard words from that Mouth that interprets life,
and drew near to listen to the sound of the words, the labour of toils.
To the labour of toils the Lover of our race called our nature,
and sent us one of our race to call us to himself.
With parables he hunted us like a hunter for the gathering,
and shut us in within the words of his preaching.
The bait of words he cast on the ground before our minds,
and enticed us as a lure draws to food.
The snare of parables bent our heart, which loves to wander,
that it might no longer wander after desires as before.
He knew of us that we were accustomed to the wandering of error;
therefore he shut us within the nets of his teaching.
Skilfully his love hunted us as though for prey,
and closed before our faces the door of the teaching that fills his mouth.
At the time of morning he went out to hunt us for his teaching,
as a watchful man goes about the land for labourers.
In the morning everyone who hires in the earthly realm hires,
and by this same custom our Lord too called us to the labour of his love.
Morning he likened to the beginning of the parable of his preaching,
and as in the morning he called us to the work of labour in his vineyard.
To night he likened the former time, from him backward,
and to day the time of the parable of his teaching.
As one day he set the course of this dispensation,
night and day, as Moses called it in Genesis.
Into two parts he divided the time of all generations,
and to one he gave the hours of night, and to one those of day.

The age of the earthly [?] he called night because of its darkness,
for as in darkness men were blind to what is good.
His own time he called day because of truth,
for as in light men saw in it the manifest truth.
Manifest truth proclaimed its voice in the ears of men,
and humanity listened to it as to a man proclaiming truth.
By the name of "a man" he called his own person, a man from among us,
and his preaching he called the kingdom of the One hidden on high.
The kingdom of the height, he said, is like — the King of the likeness [?] —
a man who went out at the time of morning to hire labourers.
He agreed with the labourers on a denarius for the work of the day,
and sent them to labour in the vineyard he had planted.
He went out again at the third, the sixth, the ninth and the eleventh,
and hired them on the terms of the wage like the first.
At the eleventh hour he hired them as in the morning,
and in the wage too he made them equal with one equality.
At evening he called the steward to give the wage,
and he gave the last a denarius each, as he was commanded.
The first labourers saw the gift he gave the last,
and thought that he would give them more in proportion to the time.
They too received a denarius each, like their fellows,
and began to rehearse kinds of [...] grumbling in their minds.
They broke into murmuring, amazed at the gift:
why had he made equality in the payment of the wage?
"We," they said, "bore the burden and the heat of the whole day,
and these who were hired for one hour have received the same as we.
The wage is not just if it is set against the labour,
and the toil of one hour and of the whole day are not equal.
The whole day we laboured at the work without slackening,
so what is this, that the toil is great and the wage the same?"
The master of the house saw the labourers breaking into murmuring,
and he called one of them and persuaded him before his fellows.
"My friend," he said to him — and he called him his friend sweetly,
and showed him the sign of the greatness of his love toward humanity —
"I do no wrong in paying the wage, as you supposed,
nor do I defraud one who [?] lovingly.
For one denarius you agreed with me, and you complain?
Take what is yours and go, and cease from words full of murmuring."
Here end the words that our Lord interpreted in a mystery;
let the soul seek with a hidden search into their interpretations.
Searching is required by every interpretation that lies in parables,
for unless searching illumines the words, they are not illumined.
The light of discernment [?] is the searching that words require,
and as by light it shows the light of the meaning of words.
There are no treasures greater than the light of the words of the Spirit,
nor any wisdoms possessing power like their wisdom.
They are not weighed against beryls and pearls,
nor compared with anything whose worth is precious.
Everything is less when compared with the beauty that is in them,

and every beauty that resembles their desirability is as no beauty.
They are far more desirable than all that is desirable in the earthly realm,
and so the desire for them has captured the world to desire them.
The desire for them has captured the earthly and the heavenly;
they scorned all else, and loved and cherished meditation on them.
Meditation on them I too love, though I do not love it,
in words I love it, though I am far from deeds.
Desire has made me desire words without deeds,
