that perhaps from words my mind may turn toward deeds.
As a child my mind draws me toward learning,
that from learning I may learn the power that is in learning.
To the school of the great Teacher I wish to draw near,
for I have seen that the utterance of his word is more skilful than all teaching.
A good saying I have heard that he spoke in the ears of men,
and I am pressed to know and make known the saying I have heard.
The good news of the wage he gave the hired has reached my ears,
and I wished to hire myself, even a little, at the end of the day.
In the morning I heard that he hired labourers for the labour of his vineyard,
and agreed on one denarius for one hour and for twelve.
At the equality of the wage the thoughts of my feeble mind were amazed:
what is this, that the wage is not in proportion to the labour?
Who ever agreed on a denarius for twelve hours [?],
and what labourer toils thus and receives thus?
There is no rich man who hires labourers at every hour,
nor a hireling who hires himself out at every hour in the middle of the day.
Strange is the report of this labour to all labours,
and it has no likeness among all the labours of the earthly realm.
Its unlikeness urges me to wear myself out in searching about it:
why is its likeness so different from all likenesses?
Its likeness draws me to paint its likeness with the colours of words,
since by means of words he revealed to men the kinds of its likenesses.
The likeness of his works I have seen inscribed in the Scriptures,
and from what is written I wish to reach toward what is not written [?].
In the Scriptures I have seen the name of the kingdom running,
and with it the name of a man who hired labourers for his vineyard.
To one who hired labourers he likened the Man who proclaims truth,
and his preaching he called the kingdom that is on high.
The kingdom of the height he called the hope he proclaimed on earth,
because it shows the way of the kingdom to those who seek it.
The word of our Lord traced on earth the way of the kingdom,
and taught men to walk with it to the place where it is.
The order of the height was going to be revealed to the earthly,
and he depicted its likenesses in the earthly realm until it should come to be.
It was laid upon him to occupy men with labours of the spirit,
and he occupied them in bodily fashion with deeds.
In bodily fashion he showed a bodily likeness before bodily beings,
and showed men how to walk in the way of spiritual things.
The labour of the spirit he traced in a sight perceptible to the body,
and men began to see the sign of the One hidden on high.

O the wonder that came to pass on earth in the earthly realm,
that earthly beings loved a labour that is not earthly!
A new voice the earthly heard from an earthly one,
proclaiming on earth a new hope that had never been proclaimed.
With the promise of a wage he enticed the children of the earth,
and they ran to him, and he received them lovingly.
His love drew him to the labour of the sons of his race,
to hire them for the labour of spiritual life.
The kinds of spiritual labour he taught them,
that from their labours they might acquire immortal life.
In this way he went out from the morning of the beginning of his dawning,
when he named his dawning morning and the beginning of the day.
He named himself a man, because he was indeed also a man,
and his teaching he called the kingdom full of life.
The time of morning was the beginning of his preaching,
and the labourers of the morning were the twelve apostles who were hired with him.
They were hired at the morning time of the preaching,
and they are the ones who bore the burden of the whole day.
A great burden the heralds of the word of life bore,
because the beginning of the time of preaching was hard.
Hard was the time that all the chosen apostles endured,
and very fierce was the war of pagans and Jews.
Judaism was strong in its observances,
and paganism too was ardent in its love of demons.
In love of demons the pagan peoples were bound,
and the love of demons was the foundation of their minds.
Two contests the athletes of righteousness waged,
with paganism and with Judaism, lofty cliffs.
On a lofty height the head of Judaism was set,
and paganism too was fortified as in strongholds.
Strong was the name of gods that are no gods,
and the apostles overthrew them on earth by the name of one Power.
The name of one Power the earthly proclaimed on earth,
and all the names of the no-gods shook and were confounded.
The no-gods the godly uprooted from the earth,
and as seed they sowed the name of the one God.
Like ploughmen they cleared the forest of error,
that the seed of life might not be choked as it grew.
For the growth of the seed the good labourers were diligent,
and like dew the words of the Spirit watered it.
With the words of the Spirit they tilled the vineyard of humanity,
and waited for it to yield spiritual fruits.
With fear and love they drew near to its labour,
that they might not be despised by that Lord who hired them.
Like pruners they cut away from it the kinds of evil,
that the root of the roots of its faith might be firm.
In faith they laid the foundation of its faith,
that the storm and wind of desires might not harm it.
Very eager they were to guard it from harms,

and they were urgent that it should not lack the drink of the Spirit.
With toils they tilled it, and with discourses they propped up its branches;
they made its leaves flourish, and it bore the fruits of purity of soul.
Pure fruits the vineyard bore that had been stripped of fruit,
and men and heavenly beings marvelled at the goodness of its fruits.
A great marvel was the change of season in the vineyard of the peoples,
that it gave good things instead of the carobs it used to grow.
Kinds of carobs it bore in the time of idolatry,
but since it gave itself to the labour of the spirit it has borne blessings.
The pillars of apostleship tilled it spiritually,
and drove from it wolves and bears and every kind of evil beast.
Every kind of evil one had trampled it like wild animals,
and they multiplied in their face kinds of good things that are not withheld [?].
A high fence they made for the divine vineyard,
that cruel demons might not hurt it with their harms.
A tower of glory they built in its midst for giving glory,
that it might guard the fruits of glory with which it is adorned.
A winepress of baptism too they made for the disciples,
in which the blemishes of bodies and of minds are cleansed.
Truly [?] they placed in it every kind of good thing,
that not one good thing should be lacking in it for the one who labours there.
The power of the Spirit made them wise to accomplish these things,
and gave power to their minds to cultivate men.
To labour in his vineyard the lord of the vineyard sent them,
and according to his will they fulfilled his will in the labour of his vineyard.
All the care of the lord of the vineyard the labourers fulfilled,
and began and finished with one will, without ceasing.
Their minds were not cut off in their labours,
for they were looking to a reward far greater than their toils.
Small was the toil when compared with the reward,
and twelve hours were not equal to one denarius.
One denarius was a good agreement for good labourers,
and well were they fitted to labour in the vineyard of reason.
In a rational way the labourers of righteousness laboured,
and guarded its fruits, that they might not be spoiled by harms.
Three names they made into a wall to guard its life,
that the building of the life of its immortality might be firm.
They knew that the make-up of its body was changeable;
therefore they set three names for it like sinews.
With the sinews of the Spirit the builders built the building of humanity,
and strengthened its foundations with the name of the unchangeable Being.
The name of the Being they laid first as a foundation,
and upon it they completed the whole height of humanity's confession.
One confession of one Creator they built in creation,
and one naming they proclaimed on earth to their hearers.
In this naming they made disciples, taught and baptised men,
and bound all creation beneath the authority that rules over all.
From every authority they gathered the scattered peoples,

and taught them to honour one authority.
In one authority they bound every authority of height and depth,
and within it they enclosed all creatures, rational and mute.
Within the hearing of their discourses they enclosed everything,
the earthly, and the heavenly who are without composition.
O mortals clothed in a corruptible body,
who enclosed the world within the words of the Word that was in them!
O earthly ones bearing the burden of mortality,
who ascended and subdued the hosts of the height beneath their word!
O hunters who hunted food to feed the body,
who hunted rational beings and fed them the food of the spirit!
O unlettered ones, innocent of all learning,
who trained the world in an eloquence it had never seen!
O you who were created with one tongue and one speech,
who spoke with all according to the speech of their tongues!
In every tongue the halting of speech spoke,
and to every people they explained the power that was in their words.
At the power of their words the peoples possessed of speech marvelled,
how much stronger was the power in them than every power.
Every people beside them fell back before the power of the fishermen,
and no people remained that did not yield its hand to the power in them.
The wise were defeated, the learned were ashamed, the eloquent fell silent,
and the voice of the unlettered thundered on the earth like a trumpet.
Pride was humbled, boasting fled, idolatry ceased,
and the praise of humility was sweet in every tongue.
All the teachings the demons had invented were as though they had never been,
and in truth there stood one teaching which the simple [?] taught.
The studies of poetry and of rhetoric fled,
and they could not answer the word of truth of the fishers of fish.
The brilliance of the philosophers, proud of name, was darkened
before [?] the light that was in the words of those innocent of all learning.
Those innocent of all learning taught something greater than anything,
and raised a finger toward priests and kings and their rulers [?].
One authority they set up like a standard before all peoples,
that all tongues might bow at the gathering of his name.
The name of the Being who is and who is they proclaimed on earth,
and they counted twice and thrice a Trinity that is not divided.
Three names they assigned to the hypostases, as they had been commanded,
and joined them to one authority, the name of the Being.
With the Being they counted also the mystery of the embodiment,
that the Trinity might not become a quaternity.
In one naming they bounded and enclosed the name of humanity:
Son of God and son of man, one person.
One person, as it is written, is the name of the Son:
the Word of the Father who is from eternity, and the man from among us.
Two in their natures, as natures they are two,
and one person, as a number that does not change.
The number of Father, Son and Spirit does not change,

and the nature of the Being is not mixed with the nature of man.
In what is its own the nature of the Being abides with humanity,
and humanity too is preserved [in its own nature] with the Being.
The properties that belong to the natures are not mixed,
and above all the nature of the Maker with what is made.
The nature of the Maker the bold have mixed with what is made,
and very greatly has the will of man dared.
The will of man urges me to change the course of my words,
and I have left my discourse and walked in the way of the Word and the body.
The Word and the body the bold have mixed without discernment,
and my discourse was zealous to distinguish things that are not mixed.
This zeal has been in my mind in every discourse,
and it does not let me walk on any road but its own.
The road of the parable of the labourers who were hired lay before me,
and when it turned me aside to the path of mixing, my discourse strayed from it.
I left my discourse to rebuke the word of the makers of words,
and turned to walk again in the path of the discourse I had left.
Come then, my discourse, to the matter that lay before you,
and walk in the road the labourers trod in the labour of the vineyard.
In the company of the labourers who laboured well I long to be seen [?],
that perhaps I may share in the wages they were promised.
Their promises draw me to hire myself out alongside their toils,
that perhaps I may become a speaker of words for the sake of life.
For the sake of life they toiled in the work of the lord of the vineyard,
and bore the burden of the hard toils of the whole day.
In the morning they were hired, as the order of the wage requires,
and with the course of the hours of the day they stretched out their toils.
The whole day they laboured, diligent in their labours,
and at evening they rested from toil and received the wage.
For the sake of the wage they bore every toil,
labourers labouring, and to one goal the first and those after them looked.
One after another they drew near to the work they had been taught,
and in one equality laboured at the labour that gains life.
The apostles were hired at the morning time of our Lord's dawning,
and bore the burden of the hard contempt of the People and the peoples.
Those of the third hour are another generation that arose after them,
and walked in the road of the well-trodden toils of apostleship.
Those of the sixth, again, are the ones hired after that time,
who portrayed the likenesses of that way of life in their own way of life.
Those of the ninth hour are the just who lived generation after generation,
and received the burden of afflictions like the first.
Those of the eleventh hour are those who come at the end of the ages,
and gain a love that does not slacken in the face of its afflictions.
The love of love mingled them with the first,
and they received the wage with the blessed ones of their own mind [?].
In their minds they longed greatly to labour greatly;
therefore they received a wage greater than their labour.
To the aim of their love the master of the house gave the reward,

that through their love he might draw humanity to love love.
He drew men on with the good wage of one hour,
that they might not slacken, even a little, during the time of their lives.
It is love he seeks, in few days and in many,
and according to love he gives the wage to the lovers of love.
For love's sake he honoured the last labourers,
and gave them the reward without demanding the toils of deeds.
Far less was the small toil of one hour
when compared with the reckoning of the twelve.
O love that is in those who love, how precious you are,
that you give a wage to small toils as to great!
Small was the toil of the labourers hired at one hour,
yet love set it on the balance with the twelve.
Who ever weighed like this, with one equality,
so that the scale of twelve hours and of one hour came up even?
In one equality the reckoning of much and little came up,
and this is the marvel, that the balance of the scales did not tip [?].
Here let the one who knows how to look well marvel
at how far the greatness of love surpasses everything.
The greatness of love has pressed together the reckoning of much and little,
and has made equal the course of the whole day and of one hour.
The likeness that love has made in this deed resembles
that deed which Moses did in the gathering of the manna.
A measure for each head Moses commanded to gather of the manna,
and the greed of the belly gathered much beyond the measure.
With the measure he tested the greedy will as in a furnace,
and exposed and laid bare the gluttony that was hidden in it.
When gluttony grew greedy and gathered much,
it came to the measure, and its labour became as no labour.
O gathering that was gathered without being sated,
and when they measured it, much and little became one!
O command that goes with all and makes all wise,
and brings muchness and littleness to equality!
Much indeed was the great labour of the whole day,
and much less the small labour that saw but an hour.
That command tests the toils and searches after them,
and weighs them in the same fashion as the measure of the manna.
With the measure of the manna I have compared the wage of much and little,
not that it is equal to it, but that it resembles it by way of illustration.
Not like the fools who greedily gathered did they toil,
nor did the victors labour little, like those who gathered properly [?].
There they gathered out of love of the belly, for the sustenance of the body,
but these were strong in hard toil on the terms of the wage.
On the terms of the wage the first and those after them toiled,
and according to love they received the rewards of their will.
The will of the soul the lord of the vineyard also examines,
and to that will he gives the reward that bears the name of a denarius.
In the name of a denarius he gave them rest from their toils,
and comforted them for the grief of the sufferings they had borne.

He called the evening hour the rest of the resurrection of the dead, / for when they are raised they rest from the labours of mortality. / In the night the toil of the earthly world comes to an end, / and in it there dawns again the life that knows no death. / In that state he gives the wage to the weary labourers, / and weighs the labours according to the will of those who laboured. / According to their will he promised the reward to the many and the few, / and gave to the few as to the many, a denarius each. / A denarius each the last received before the first, / lest perhaps they be grieved over the labour of one hour. / Small was the labour of one hour beside that wage; / who will not marvel at the greatness of love in the one who gives the wage? / At the greatness of love in the giver of the wage the first marvelled, / and [?] that he would give them more, in proportion to the time worked. / By the time they had worked the weary labourers were reckoning, / and they were expecting a wage greater than the agreement. / According to the agreement they too received a denarius each, / and they were deeply aggrieved that their hope did not reach to the reward. / The impulse of envy gave birth to foolish grumbling: / “Why was there equality in the paying of the wage?” / Over the equality they were blaming the master of the house: / “Why has he made [?] little equal with the much? / Why then have you made the last labourers, of one hour, equal / with us who [?] the burden and heat of the whole day? / Why have you given those who did not toil a wage in the same measure as ours, / and made one hour equal to the running of the whole day? / It was right for us to receive more, for we toiled more; / for this is just: that the reward too should match the toil.” / The lord of the wage saw the reproach that confronted his love, / and turned to win over the reproachers with love. / With love and sweetness he answered the reproacher, / and called him his friend, as one worthy of that title: / “My friend,” the master said to his servant, “I do you no wrong, / nor am I false to the terms of the wage I agreed with you. / For one denarius I agreed with you, and you yourself are witness; / take what is yours, and do not find fault with the greatness of my mercies. / If I am good, and it pleases my will to give much, / what grieves you, that you complain beyond what is fitting?” / The reproacher did not truly reproach the lord of the wage, / nor did the master in turn blame the hired men, as it is written. / It was not as it is written that the exchange of words took place and was spoken, / nor did those who spoke them render them as things that had actually happened. / They rendered them according to the thoughts of mortals, / so that they might restrain the [?] of reproachers, that none should reproach. / He restrained all reproachers by the form he gave to the words, / so that if anyone reproaches, he may hear the words and reproach no more. / With this aim he presented the figure of labourers who grumbled: / not that they grumbled, but so that no one should give birth to grumbling. / By the figure of grumbling and the voice of blame he taught people / not to reproach when others are shown mercy by grace.

By grace the master of the house made the members of his household equal, / and he did not keep account when he gave the wage in one equal measure. / He gave the labourers their wage equally, not without cause, / but because he saw an equality of heart, sincere and pure. / The Seer of hidden things saw an equality of love, / and gave a reward to the small labour together with the great. / Short was the time of the labourers who toiled for one hour, / but the wage was great, according to the will that was ready. / “No one hired us,” they answered when they were asked, / as though one were saying, “We were not there at the time of labour.” / And [?] they were saying to the master of the house, “If only it had been possible! / Had we been there at the start of the day, we would have laboured much.” / It was to the readiness of this will that he gave the wage, / and he showed that the readiness of love is worthy of a doubled wage. / A doubled wage the last received together with the first: / one denarius of the fullness of life that does not perish. / The promise of undying life he called a denarius, / which is given to the just as a wage for their labours. / For their labours they receive the wage justly, / and to each of them his reward is multiplied according to his will. / According to their will the last and the first received the reward, / and they learned the order by which the Lord governs his servants well. / A great ordinance all generations have learned from this ordinance: / that they should not grow slack when they hire themselves out to the fear of the truth. / To the generations to come he gave hope through the equality of the wage, / and gave them still more courage in that the last received first. / It is said that the last received the wage before the first, / not that they actually received it so, but to enlarge the faint of heart. / One is the sign by which he gives the wage to all together, / and there is no delay between one gift and the next. / For there is no first or last there at the time of judgement, / for one is the judgement, one the reward, and one the separation. / All that is told of that day is told in a sign, / and nothing compares with the swiftness of that command. / A single command he gives suddenly to those he commands, / and everything stands just as it was commanded from the beginning. / Come then, let us listen to that Commander whose command is great, / and keep good order before that day which sets all things in order. / Come, let us hire ourselves out with the labourers in every kind of good work, / and tend our souls as the just tended people. / The just tended people purely, as one tends a vineyard; / [?] come, let us at least tend our own souls with good things. / With good things let us keep our soul busy together with our members, / and not grow slack in the work of good deeds. / In body and soul let each one work the work of life, / with the outward senses and the hidden impulses of the one human being. / Our soul together with our members is one human being:
with one mind let us cultivate goodness [?].
On the Rich Man and Lazarus
Homily Twenty-Eight / On the Rich Man and Lazarus

Our Lord painted the image of the parables on the panel of his words, and set them within the palace of his preaching. He arranged the words of his mouth as in a portrait, and named them with the names of deeds, as though they had happened. Fittingly he compared words with words, and set on them the stamp of parables, so that they would not be despised. In every form he likened them to what had happened, and covered them with the fine garment of the name of parables. With the name of parables he covered the power hidden in his words, so that they would not be despised by the minds of the slack of soul. He had in view the wakefulness of the slack of soul when he painted the image of the deeds of the good and the wicked. To the good and the wicked he showed the beauty and loveliness of his words, and roused them to hear words full of wonder. Great wonder was hidden in the words of his preaching: they were shown, and yet, strictly speaking, they were not seen. They were seen as though they had happened in deeds, and they were not seen, because the deed in them was far off.

The deed completes what is lacking in words, and shows the beauty of beautiful things as if in light. Beautiful things fill the words of preaching, and he hides the power of their sayings as in a treasury. Great power is hidden for whoever seeks to search it out, but unless he seeks with the affection of love he does not find it. The affection of love called me to read in the book of our Lord, and from the reading a parable drew me toward understanding. The reading itself enticed me to make a search of the words, and from beside the words there came to me the meditation on what is hidden in the words. I saw the hidden things of the words covered with the garment of words, and my mind enticed me to uncover the words behind the words. I went in and stood within the door of the scriptures, and as in a portrait I saw the signs of the image I was seeking. In the fair fold of the parables I wished to examine why the name of parables is set upon the signs. I saw the name of parables running through the house of signs, and I wished to know the meaning along with the naming. I saw two persons painted in the colours of words; though they were alike, figure and figure, they were not alike. The name of a rich man and the name of a poor man were inscribed on them, and they were distinguished by their names and by their deeds. The name of the rich man was inscribed first, at the head of the panel, and at its end the name of the poor man, who was poor and needy. The image of the one who had acquired wealth was painted in fine garments, and that of the poor man in a wretched form covered with rags. Splendid was the appearance in the features of the one who was not fair, and hideous was the sight of the face of the one fair of soul. Bright were the many colours of the image of the loathsome one, and dark with darkness were those of the fair one. O the wonder that was seen in the two images:

that they were fair and, in truth, not fair! The rich man was not as fair as he appeared, nor was the poor man as ugly as his loathsomeness made him seem. Outwardly the appearance of the humble of soul was loathsome, and inwardly the proud of mind was loathsome and ugly. In himself the loathsome one, loathsome through and through, was loathsome, yet in his mind he was splendid, desirable, wholly fair. Outward beauty disgraced the one ugly of soul, while the ugliness of the body adorned the one fair of soul. In his body the poor man was loathsome, loathsome of feature, and in his mind the one splendid of limb was repulsive and ugly. On the limbs of the one, the loveliness of beauty was seen; within his soul was a sight more loathsome than anything loathsome. The one loathsome of mind showed himself in garments of fine linen, and revelled in countless luxuries. His garments were splendid and his adornments desirable too, and he was never sated with indulging himself in the abundance of his goods. His wealth was lavish and the provision of his life extravagant [?], and there was no room left between one luxury and the next. Goods were heaped up in great abundance on top of goods, and the many kinds of adornment never left their place. That pleasure-seeker delighted himself in every adornment, and the more he delighted, the more he longed to delight again. No kind of delight departed from his table, for while the first was departing, another came ahead of it. The house of the dissolute of soul was made like a festival, and the sound of merriment always thundered like thunder. By the sound of his merriment the poor man was tormented, and he composed sounds of mourning over his distresses. Over against the merriment of that merry man the afflicted one was afflicted, and his laments matched the number of the other's songs. One sang and the other wept bitterly; who would not marvel at such joy of soul and such grief of soul? One danced, and the other lamented as over a dead man; who would not wonder at deeds that were not just?

One did wrong, and the other laboured in righteousness; who would not say that their recompense was not just? Unjustly that cruel man exulted, and wrongly was that humble man tormented. Inequality was seen in their conditions, and contrary to what was fitting one delighted and the other was tormented. That cruel man did not deserve that delight, nor did that humble man deserve that torment. An evil time overturned the time of the good and the wicked, and unfittingly honoured the one and despised the other. Unfittingly the lover of truth was tormented, and the lover of falsehood luxuriated in glories. The one wholly bare of mercy dwelt amid fine good things, and had no pity on that poor man who lay at his gate. At the cruel man's gate lay the gentle one, poor even in his name; he longed, and no one relieved his want. He was in need and lacking every good thing, and his poverty and his sickness were doubled. He was sorely afflicted by two grievous pains: by poverty, which humbles a man, and by loathsome sores. He was full of loathsome sores, covered with them all over, and there was not a healthy spot free of blemishes. The body of the pure of mind was made a spring of sores, and loathsome pus flowed from it that sickened the soul. Drops of pus streamed down from his limbs, and the stench of foulness that flowed from him troubled him. Greedy dogs drank the pus of his body, and were fed from the delights of his fellow. At the smell of his foulness those greedy of soul held back; they would visit him and recoil from his wounds. Alas for the man who, though a man in body and spirit, was made a stranger to the visits of men! Alas for the bodily one whose body was loathsome to bodily beings, so that the eyes of his own kind fled from the sight of him!

Alas for that soul which dwelt in a dead body, and made its home in it without the life that is in the limbs! Alas for limbs that, while they existed, did not exist, which the soul moved with a lifeless life! Alas for that soul which bore the weight of the body, and did not slacken in that toilsome and hard struggle! Toilsome and hard was the contest the just man endured, and there was nothing to compare with the endurance of that mind. Who ever saw a contest so toilsome, and who ever beheld a contender like this one? Who waged war in the body when there was no body, and who held a contest with the senses without the senses? That athlete had no senses with which to contend, since they had been quenched by the corruption of the hardship of pain. The pure of mind was tormented by harsh pain, and though he suffered, through endurance he did not suffer. He did not suffer, because he looked to the end of his labour; and he suffered keenly at what he saw in the decay of his body. In body and soul he was tormented in the contest of his labours: his body by pain, and his soul by the suffering of weariness. Weariness crushed the one who did not grow weary, as he saw the kinds of his own torment and his fellow's delight. He gazed at the abundance of the rich man's goods, and longed, and no one relieved his need. O how needy was that one who was not needy, who was needy in his name, and how doubled was the wealth hidden in the end of his labour! O how at ease was that rich man, splendid in his titles, and how doubled was the torment withheld from him! O how cruel was that crafty man who possessed cruelty, who looked upon that pitiless torment! O how harsh and hard his heart was, beyond all harshness, that he gave no relief from his crumbs to the humble of soul! O how serene too was the humble man in his humility, as he looked on the abundance of that reveller! The sight of good things crushed him more than his pain,

and he was doubly tormented and shed tears. Wailing and weeping filled his mouth night and day, and he sighed at the sound of the revels of that dissolute man. As much as the dissolute man indulged himself in desirable things, so much did the mourning over his pain and need increase. As much as the cruel man hardened himself in his harshness, so much did the other grow and humble himself under insults. As much as the proud man was exalted by the abundance of his riches, so much was the humble of soul abased in beholding his lowliness. As much as the loveliness of that unlovely man increased, so much did the ugliness of the pain of that fair man grow strong. As much as the dishes of that tomb of food were set out, so much was the one in need of food wrapped in kinds of torment. As much as the kinds of good things gladdened the greedy one, so much did pain and hunger trouble the chaste and pure one. Alas for the contest, how it crushed its contender! Alas for the luxury, how slack was the one who enjoyed it! Alas for the sickness, how sound was the one who lay in it! Alas for the health, how odious was the one who dwelt in it! Alas for the sight of two images set one against the other, in colour without measure, a contrast beyond measuring! Without satiety that rich man delighted himself, and without measure that poor man was tormented. In their inequality I was observing how different they were, and how doubled were the delight of the cruel man and the suffering of the just. I saw delight and suffering joined together in the account, and I drew near to see the sight full of inequality. The inequality pressed me to make a search of the words, and see, my mind is in labour to bring forth words about what it has sought. Come, my mind, approach the search of what you have sought, and set forth openly the kinds of explanation that are ready for you.

What is the reason for the name 'rich man' and the name 'poor man', and why is the record of their deeds inscribed? Did their deeds really happen as they are written, or perhaps are they really to come to pass in time to come? Did the rich man really rejoice and the afflicted man suffer, the one exulting and the other tormented until death? Did the time really come to an end, with the joy of heart and the grief of soul, and did death dismiss the delights and the distresses? Did the poor man really go to the bosom of Abraham, and the rich man remain tormented in the flame of Sheol? No, my hearer, this did not happen in deeds, nor was it fulfilled as the account of the words about it tells. No rich man delighted and exulted in pleasures, nor did pain and need crush a poor man. Only in words did the account come about in what was written, and the writer wrote kinds of parables for teaching. For the teaching of people the Lover of people painted parables, so that through parables humanity might hunt its way toward his teaching. Like a painter he arranged the words of his preaching, and painted it for the world in two images of two orders. Two persons and two orders he painted in his gospel: soft wealth, and poverty that bears the just. Soft wealth he painted in the figure of that rich man, and poverty in the name of Lazarus, the name of a poor man. With the name Lazarus he named the side of poverty, and joined to his name the strength of soul that is not overcome. With the name 'rich man' he called those at ease [?] and the children of wealth, and in his luxury he painted the luxury of the luxurious. In his pitilessness he portrayed the cruelty of the unmerciful, and in his wickedness he rebuked the disposition of the crafty. In the greatness of his arrogance he humbled the arrogance of the lofty of soul, and taught them not to grow proud in human things. Through his dissoluteness he exposed and laid bare the greatness of the belly, so that it should not be greedy, lest severe punishments be multiplied for it. Severe punishments he decreed for the greedy through that greedy man: that if they show no pity, they will not be pitied, as he was not.

That cruel man was ungracious all his life, and did not bend to pity the one at his gate. It is written that the poor man lay beside his gate, so that everyone may know how evil cruelty is. He rebuked cruelty in the name of that cruel man, and comforted need in the name of that poor man. In the name of the poor man he bound up the pain of poverty, and put on it the medicine of patience of spirit, which is not overcome. In his poverty he portrayed the life of poverty, and in his endurance the kinds of mind that do not slacken. In the endurance of his soul he encouraged the souls of those who bear pains, and through the name of his sores he lightened the weight of their pains. In that he was in need, and longed, and did not eat, he signified to need that it should stand firm before want. In that he was cast down and despised before the cruel man's gate, he called the despised among people to look at the contempt he suffered. By his patience of spirit he gained patience for mankind, so that no one should bring forth hateful murmuring on the day of his trial. Through the foulness of his sores he called the sick as with a voice, to bear with constancy the struggle against pains. In that the pus of his body was wiped away by dogs, he offered comfort to the [?] so that they might gain hope. Through all that he bore in his poverty and the hardship of his pain, he sowed good hope in the weak, so that they should not slacken. For the weakness of man he willed to be strong through a son of man, so that those tried by infirmities should not slacken. The whole order of poverty he called by the name of Lazarus, so that they might come and see the image of their lives in one poor man. He painted his story like an image before the poor, so that from his paintings they might hunt out hope for their minds. Like a mirror he set his endurance before their eyes, so that those tried by insults might look upon it. In the parable of that man he clothed all who suffer pains, and in his endurance all minds that are strong in suffering. Fittingly he painted his trial for those who are tried, and crowned him with a crown for the labours that had come upon him. He wove a crown of reward for the labourers who resemble him,

and decreed harsh punishments for the wicked who hate the good. In him and in his fellow the great Painter painted all the orders: in one the poor, and in the other the order of the possessors of wealth. He put the possessors of wealth to shame through the rebuke of that rich man, so that they might abhor cruelty like his. He shamed his cruelty with rebuking words, so that everyone might learn to humble himself in repentance of soul. Through his death he warned of the day of death and frightened the wicked, and through the end of that poor man he showed the rest of the good. Death is rest for whoever is wearied with toils, and the voice that gave a reward to the name of Lazarus bears witness to it. Lazarus died; the writer wrote of Lazarus that the hosts on high carried him up and set him in the bosom of Abraham. Beside Abraham went up the poor man who resembled Abraham, and rested in the haven of the one who in his lifetime gave rest to the weary. Abraham the just gave rest to the labour of that diligent man—not that he has given him rest, but that he will give it on the day of resurrection. It is not Abraham who gives the weary rest from their labours, nor is it he who pays the reward to those who resemble him. It is the Lord who is over all who pays the wage for crushing labours, and by the decree of his judgment punishes the wicked who showed no pity and gave no relief. The recompense did not happen; it is yet to be, as was spoken, nor have the punishments that the judgment decreed yet come upon the wicked. What took place mystically will come to pass at the end, and at the consummation the power hidden in its mystery will be drawn forth. Mystically the poor man who rested from his labour is portrayed, and in the same way also the rich man who remains in Sheol. It is said that the rich man remained in Sheol, being tormented, because the wicked will remain in the place below. In the place below the wicked remain to be punished; that is why it is said that the rich man remained and stayed in Sheol. That cruel man who had no mercy remained in Sheol, and was not raised up with Lazarus to the place above. The weight of sins [?] hung upon the soul of the heavy of heart, and he could not fly through the air with the light one. The body of the one sick in body sprouted wings of the spirit,

and like a bird he flew from the earth to the face of the heights. The limbs of the one clothed in fine linen were like lead, and he sank in Sheol like lead in the depth of the waters. The beauty of his garments became snares for the proud of soul; suddenly they caught him and gave him as food to greedy death. His food became to him like a gaping gullet for the one who had swallowed up his fellows, so that he could not escape from the mouth of death. Death swallowed that glutton of delights, and the rebel did not remain among the living. From the height of his delights he fell into the depth of Sheol, and began to wail over the distresses that had suddenly surrounded him. A great groaning came upon him suddenly at what had happened to him, and he was astonished and amazed at the change of time. An evil time had brought him to an end without consolation, for he had not discerned the time, and its evil rebuked his pride. Without consolation he looked back on the time of his prosperity, and his own soul despised him without restraint on the day of torment. On the day of his torment the senseless man was put to shame, and he did not know that the time for repentance of soul had passed. In himself he made the same error he had erred in all his life, supposing that persuasive words would avail him. The ignorant man wished to compose persuasive words, and began to persuade with a persuasion empty of profit. 'Father Abraham,' the boorish man called to Abraham, and Abraham answered him with a voice that rebuked his boorishness. The compulsion of suffering forced the proud man against his will, and he spoke a word far removed from his deeds. He called Abraham the just his father, he who was wholly unjust, and it did not occur to him to distinguish iniquity from justice. He named himself a son of Abraham, he who was a son of sin, supposing that he could deceive Abraham and Abraham's Lord. The free man remembered the kinship of the family of Abraham's house, and did not consider that the wickedness of his disposition made him a stranger to the family. The wickedness of his disposition had made him hateful to Abraham, and he heard a word full of groaning that cut off hope. The proud son of Abraham relied upon Abraham; that is why he called much upon Abraham to come and help him.

In the bosom of Abraham the cruel man saw that poor man, and he asked and pleaded that he might come down to relieve his distress. 'Send to me my brother Lazarus,' he said to Abraham, and he was not ashamed to call him by names that were foreign to him. The names he called were foreign to the wickedness of his disposition, and the name was utterly foreign to his deeds and their doing. His impulse drove that man of bitter disposition, and he sought to soften the harshness of his punishments by the name of Abraham. The invisible flame crushed him greatly, and he pressed to obtain the relief of mercy for his burning. The cruel man asked for waters of mercy through Lazarus, to lighten the heat of the flame from his tongue. The tip of his tongue was tormented more than all the rest of him, for it had been the advocate of words against the truth. The hard of mind had contended against the truth; now truth itself shut the door in the face of his words. Truth would not persuade Abraham to pity his son, and Abraham answered him with a reply that cut off hope. 'Remember, my son,' said the father to his son who was no son of Abraham, 'that the day of judgment has cut short the course of the day of your good things. Much you delighted in that bodily delight; come out and be tormented in proportion to that time of your pleasures. Remember that time in which the kinds of your good things abounded; weigh it well against the recompense that has been set aside for you. Judge rightly that the testing which has tested your falsehood is just, and has wisely given you a wage equal to your labour. The Greatest of judges has decided the judgment against your wickedness, and no one dares overturn the word that his judgment has decreed. By the decree of his judgment he has set bounds and kept us from converse with you, and none of us can come down to where you are. There is a great chasm in the middle, between us and you, and there is no one among creatures who can make the crossing over it.' These things Abraham set forth, not in deed:

but in words, suited to the mind with which he was speaking. / The father spoke to the mind, though he did not spell it out, / and the rich man heard what he heard according to the words. / The rich man heard a fearful report from Abraham, / and began to devise other schemes so that he might escape. / The erring one devised other schemes to suit his own mind, / and did not know that the door was shut against his schemes. / Using his brothers as a pretext he multiplied the pretexts of his folly, / and turned to make an appeal full of falsehood. / "I have five brothers," said the merciless one, / and he made a show of being deeply concerned out of love for his brothers. / He lied when he said that he had five brothers, / for he had never had the aim of seeking brotherly love. / For his brothers' sake he was pleading with Abram, he who was no son of Abram, / that someone from the dead should go and proclaim the reckoning of judgment. / "No one knows the reckoning of judgment that has been renewed in me, / and someone must go from the dead to bear witness to the living. / The ignorant need witnesses to the things that are here, / lest they too come to this torment into which I am cast." / Then, rich man, when and how did you become merciful, / that you are now so concerned to keep a man from torment? / Was not one poor man in want cast down at your door, / and your nature had no pity on the misery in which he lay? / When, wicked one, did you show your love toward the afflicted, / that we should now believe you do not wish a man to perish? / The envious one put together a semblance of pity for a human being; / he pleaded and he begged, and his words ran to excess. / Out of excess came the jumble of schemes he brought forth, / when he heard the word that demolished the height of the words he had built. / The son of Abram heard a word of hurt and of despair, / when he told him that there were [?] — let them persuade them. / "There," he said, "they have the great Moses and his fellows: / let them teach them what is fitting there and here."

Moses and the word of his fellows suffice for a man's instruction, / and there is no need for someone from the dead to come out to the living. / The dead cannot persuade the living as the living can, / nor will the living listen to a report from those who are not alive. / A great fence is set up before those who have departed, / and none of them can breach its strength. / Strong is the wall that death has built before the dead; / so why do you weary yourself over a thing so hard to win? / The appeal of that rich man proved unpersuasive; / his words came to an end, but the lashes his sentence decreed did not. / Harsher judgment was added to him at the end of his words, / and he fell silent in Sheol, where stillness and silence reign. / Now that the rich man's voice has ceased and his words are done, / come, let us draw near to the meaning hidden in his story. / The meaning of the words lies hidden in the pleading of the words about him, / and only through words is the veil over words uncovered. / Words are spread over its story, which multiplies words: / let us stretch out words and lift the covering that lies over the words. / From the beginning of the story his words have urged me / to learn and to make known the reason his words were put together. / Its reason is this: a man's instruction is hidden within it, / and no other reason is needed to make its reason known. / For a man's instruction his delight and his torment were written down, / so that people may learn to keep the order of the two worlds. / The parable of two men has shown me world and world: / one rich and one poor, the reality and the order. / The reality and the order of the two worlds lie hidden in the two of them, / as do the lowly things and the glorious things of this world. / The world of time proclaims the time of that rich man, / and the world to come displays the toil of that poor man. / That world was likened to the poverty of this world, / and the wealth of this world to the poverty of the one that lasts for ever. / For whoever is poor here without ceasing is rich there, / and whoever gains wealth and is haughty of spirit is poor there. / Whoever loses his life, as it is written, finds it there, / and whoever finds it in this state loses it in that one.

That rich man had great possessions on earth, / and on the day of his death he left his goods behind and inherited woe. / That Lazarus lacked every useful thing, / and in that world he gained goods that do not decay. / The ruin of his body prepared for him a bliss without ruin, / and wealth without end sprang from the depth of his poverty. / His adornments doubled bitter woe for the wearer of fine linen, / for out of his pleasures he gained the torment of the flame. / Things fell out in reverse for the two men, / and not for the two alone, but for everyone who resembles them. / These things befall those who have wealth and poverty, / and they receive the reward of their deeds twice over. / Whoever is rich and merciless, his torment is doubled as a rich man; / and whoever is needy and toils, his delight overflows as a poor man. / Poverty puts heart into whoever has become poor, / and the greatness of wealth makes the rich man's judgment heavier. / That echo of a voice which the burning man heard from Abraham / is heard by those who possess wealth and are merciless like him. / In the haven of rest where Lazarus rested from his afflictions / those weighed down by the burden of their labors find rest. / Through Lazarus our Lord gave rest to the weary who toil, / and in the person of the rich man he [?] mercilessness in its course. / He exposed wealth for what it is when mercilessness goes with it, / and for unceasing need he wove crowns. / It is mercilessness that remained in Sheol in the torment of fire, / and it is poverty that went up and rested in Abraham's bosom. / Abraham gave rest to the poor all his life long, / compassionate and full of mercy toward the needy. / In his dwelling on earth he gave rest to men and to spiritual beings, / and in that dwelling above, through Lazarus, to all who are afflicted. / In Sodom he pleaded that, if there were righteous men, it might be left for mercy's sake, / yet he cannot pity the rich man in his distress. / "It is not possible," he answered the afflicted man, "to cross over to you"; / and this belongs to mercy, not to a reckoning without pity. / It was not a reckoning without pity that called the merciless man to account, / but a judgment full of justice and faithfulness.

The poor man did not inherit a delight granted out of favoritism, / but a reward equal to the labors of his diligence. / For the things that befell the two who are written of were fitting, / and no one knows how to weigh a judgment as their judge does. / Just was the judgment that judged the two of them with two judgments: / torment for one, and for the other delight with Abraham. / To Abraham he invited and summoned all who are afflicted, / and with the rich man he cast into torment all who live in luxury. / Through the one who lived in luxury he set a limit to the life of time and laid it bare, / and through the one who was afflicted he taught everyone self-denial. / Through Lazarus, who was tormented, he encouraged the afflicted, / and he marked out the luxurious by the reckoning of the luxurious man. / All that came about from the One who brings things about was for people's benefit, / and he arranged it wisely, as in a treasury. / He hid these things that came about among his hidden things, / and taught people to seek them out with love. / The Lover of humankind cast the fire of his love upon people, / and showed them how to make known the blaze of its light. / He skillfully fashioned the power of his teaching, / so that it might be firmly founded in the stirrings of the soul without being shaken. / He planted it in the soul like a foundation in the depth of the earth, / and sprinkled his sayings like dew upon seeds. / Like a husbandman he took upon himself the cause of the needy, / and weeded out from them every kind of evil like weeds. / The thorns of every kind of iniquity that the wicked bore / he cut off like branches from trees. / As one clears a thicket, he cleared the thicket of foul things, / so that the good seed he had cast among people might not be spoiled. / Like a physician he went in to those who were stricken, / and on each of them he laid the remedy that helped him. / He cut back the great growth of iniquity with the iron of the sentence of judgment, / and strengthened weakness with the hope of things to come. / On mercilessness he laid the cautery of the name of Gehenna, / and gladdened the merciful with the name of their [?]. / He encouraged diligence with a reward of abundant bliss, / and put the sluggish to shame through one who was put to shame.

He gave every people everywhere a taste of beautiful things, / and as with salt he purified them by the sweetness of his words. / He gave the sweetness of his words to drink to people sick of soul, / and shook off from them the hateful weight of foul things. / Behold his good medicines, which healed our mortal race: / come, let us examine them with loving affection, by the power that is in them. / Behold the commandments of the great and skilful One who made our souls wise: / come, let us hasten to keep the order he ordained. / Behold the path of peace that he showed to people in his own person: / come, let us walk in it by the measures his love has set. / Behold, he has set before us two states, that of time and that to come: / come, let us long for that state which has no end. / Behold, he has told us the good news of the kingdom he has on high: / come, let us adorn ourselves in garments fitting for the day of his banquet. / Behold, everything is prepared and kept for our sake: / come, let us be diligent to take wealth that never becomes poor. / Behold, there is nothing that has not been explained before our minds: / come, let us be confirmed in the sense of the words that have been explained to us. / Behold, every kind of hidden thing that had not been revealed has been explained: / come, let us meditate deeply on the power of their explanations. / Behold, the course of preaching has gone out to the four quarters: / let everyone listen to the good report that gives life. / The heralds of preaching sowed the good report, / and made the fruits of righteousness blossom among mortals. / Come, mortals, let us grow the fruits of righteousness, / while there is still time to increase every kind of good thing. / With love let us till the field of our soul's will, / so that we may reap immortal fruits that never cloy.
On the Fashioning of Adam and Eve
Homily One Hundred and Twenty-Nine: On the Fashioning of Adam and Eve, and on the Transgression of the Commandment

A king is honoured through his image,
though far away, as if he were near.
The Creator, through the image of Adam,
wished to delight the rational beings.
In the world, the city of the kingdom,
the Creator set up his image,
and through the visible image
he makes known the power of his hiddenness.
Through his image the Creator bound together
the creation as he fashioned it,
so that by love toward Adam
they might be made alike in love of him.
He made him a brother to the angels
by one spiritual soul,
and joined to him the mute natures
through the composition of his limbs.
The Lord God formed
Adam of dust from the earth,
and breathed into him the breath of life,
and made him living and rational.
The Lord God looked,
and behold, all that he had made was complete;
Eve alone was lacking,
a helper who would be for Adam.
The Lord God cast
a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept,
and he took a rib from his sides
and fashioned the woman in his likeness.
He took a member from Adam
and made a human being like Adam,
and made up Adam's members for him
so that he would lack nothing.
Adam saw a new wonder,
a human being who had come from a human being,
complete in every respect,
in body and soul, like himself.
The Maker [?] a revelation in him,
as far as he was able,
and made him know how she was fashioned,
that Eve was a portion of his flesh.
Adam prophesied and said
that Eve is bone of my bones:
"This one shall be called woman,"
she who sustains the dwelling of the age.
In the fashioning of Adam he showed

that he set Adam as head,
and Eve, in the second rank,
fulfils the service of the man.
Eve is equal with Adam
in nature and in fashioning,
but less than he in authority,
for Adam is the head and she his feet.
Outside the dwelling of Paradise
the Creator fashioned them,
and placed them in the land of Eden,
where the rivers rise.
The Lord God led
Adam, the image of his glory,
and set him in the Paradise of Eden
to be its heir within it.
He also laid a commandment on him
that was fitting for him at that time,
so that he might know the power of his nature
and learn the authority of the Maker.
The Lord commanded Adam
and set him a boundary at the tree,
so that through this might be known
the discernment of his nature.
"All the fruits of Paradise
I have given you for your delight;
from one alone you shall not eat,
for death is born of its fruit.
But if you keep my commandments
and do not presume upon the tree,
I will give you the fruit of life,
which your freedom has sought."
To both of them alike
he laid down this law,
so that they would not blame each other
when they transgressed the commandment.
O Fountain of all wisdom,
who knows all that will be!
Though he knows his own creature,
he lays the law on him as though he did not know.
The inquiry into these things has drawn me on
to recount the reason for the tree;
for how can one who keeps silent
come to know wise things?
If he knew that he would not keep
the law he was laying on him,
why did he make him mortal,
subject to death against his will?
And if he had not created Adam,
the head of our nature, mortal,
why did he, the Knower who knows all,
not restrain him from this?
To hear the words of the reading
greatly troubles the simple:
that Adam's transgression of the commandment
made our race mortal.
And if Adam's folly
condemned Adam and his children,
why did he, the Knower who knows all,
let this transgression pass?
Why did he fashion creatures
so well suited to mortality,
and why male and female
in nature, for continuance?
Far be it! It is not fitting to say
this of the Creator's will,
that he did not know we would sin

and anger changed his will.
He knew, when he fashioned us,
that he was making us mortal,
and his creation bears witness to his knowledge
that it was created for mortality.
He made us rational and discerning,
and strengthened us and filled us with his wisdom,
and wished to bring our discernment
to light through a trial.
Adam was formed and adorned
in body and soul alike,
yet his discernment was hidden
until the transgression of the commandment.
The commandment became like a furnace
and brought Adam to the test,
and his discernment was revealed,
that he was not lacking in his nature.
He called it the tree of knowledge,
though it was mute by nature,
because the knowledge hidden in Adam
was revealed by its fruit.
Adam was gold that was tarnished
before he ate from the tree,
and after he ate the fruit
he showed the beauty of his features.
The fruit became like a furnace,
and Adam within it like gold;
the power of the eating blew upon him
and he received the taste of knowledge.
The order of the world to come
he sketched for us in the tree of life,
and made it the place of reward
for the excellence of his will.
Desire for the fruit of the tree
drew Adam's childish mind,
so that when his soul had eaten of it
the fruit of life would renew him.
In speaking of two trees
he pictured both worlds for us,
and, as for children, by means of a symbol
he wished to sketch his hidden purpose.
By the tree of knowledge
he bound him to earthly wealth,
and by the tree of life he pointed him
toward that heavenly wealth.
Adam, being a child at that time,
could not learn this,
and so he drew him by the tree,
that it might lead him to knowledge.
He knew all that concerned Adam,
he who created Adam and all things,
and through the fashioning of a mortal
he wished to sketch his delights.
He barred him from one tree
and drew him to desire the other,
and whether to eat or not to eat
was placed in Adam's will.
In the dwelling of Eden he set them,
the simple ones, and honoured them,

and subjected all that had come from him
to the authority of Adam, his image.
The Lord God created
the cattle and the wild beasts,
and brought them before Adam
to give names to his possessions.
The Maker gave him power,
and he gave as many names as were needed,
thus teaching him
that he had made him lord of all that exists.
The Creator's image was a wonder:
how excellent its fashioning,
that its lordship stretched over all,
and all that existed were made subject to it!
In him are bound together alike
the life of sentient beings and of rational beings,
and by their kinship with him
they honour him as a king.
Height and depth were for his dwellings,
sea and dry land for his provision,
winds and breezes for his life,
summer and winter for his rest.
The creatures rejoiced in him
and obeyed him as a lord,
and the angels assisted
in his service, rejoicing.
In love they gathered round him,
the mute and the rational natures,
and rejoiced that the nature of them all
shared in his glory.
One alone did not [?] himself
to the lordship of love for Adam;
concord did not please him,
for [?] swallowed him up.
He was not compelled by others;
he drove himself into opposition,
for he had been created good in his nature,
like the angels, the members of his order.
There was no cause for his envy,
nor any room for his bitterness,
but only Adam's greatness,
when he saw him honoured by all,
so that his mind stirred him to envy
and he became wholly an adversary,
and he raged against the Creator
for honouring Adam's image.
He was wasting away in his thoughts
with the evil desire that burned in him,
and he contrived every kind of device
to bring his schemes to light.
This hateful thing was his desire:
"Why is Adam honoured?
And why are the mute and rational natures
bound together in love of him?
To me, who am head of the air,
and to all the spiritual orders,
he did not grant even a word of honour
when he fashioned our nature.
Yet in fashioning this despised thing,
the lowly dust of the earth,
he said, 'Let us make man in our image,
and let him be honoured with our likeness.'
He made him a lord on the earth

and called him the image of his hiddenness,
and he is honoured by all that exist,
like the Creator in his creation.
More than that, he subjected to his honour
the heavenly and the earthly.
He is a mortal formed from the earth,
and as lowly in his worth as the earth,
yet the authority of his word reigns
over those above and those below."
The fire of his envy blazed,
the anger of his jealousy burned,
and he sought to hunt them as his prey
and to bring his thoughts to light.
He did not show them his schemes
as he is accustomed to do now,
for at that time he had no power
to appear in the form of a man.
He made the serpent a garment for himself,
put it on, and hid his hatred,
so that they would not be startled from their calm
by a sight they were not used to.
The innocent ones were calm and quiet,
keeping the order of the Maker,
and each was a seemly sight to the other
in the chastity of their minds.
The deceiver began to speak
with a voice, through a lyre of flesh:
"What is the reason you refrain
from eating of all the fruits?"
He questioned them first
as if to learn the truth,
for he was convinced in his own nature
that he could not know hidden things.
He had not heard the commandment
that the Creator had laid on the house of Adam;
therefore he questioned them,
to learn the matter and so lead them astray.
The serpent said to Eve,
the crafty one to her who was pure of mind:
"Has the Creator perhaps forbidden you
the desirable fruits of Eden?"
The young woman said to the cunning one:
"We do not refrain from the trees;
only from one tree [?],
for death lies hidden in eating it."
The deceiver found an opening
and began to sow his tares,
and brought forth the fruit of his will,
which from the beginning was exile.
"You will surely not die,"
the serpent told Eve, leading her astray;
"you will be like gods,
knowing hidden things."
Alas for the hater of humankind,
who troubled the peace of creation!
It was not enough for him merely to deceive;
he also brought in [?] gods.
Here his wickedness came to light,

and by his own words he accused himself,
for he envied Adam and his children
and brought in many gods:
"You will be gods,
and not one God only.
That is why he has forbidden you
the tree, and called it death.
Come near, delight in its fruits,
and behold, your eyes will be opened;
for life lies hidden in eating it,
which will make human beings gods."
The woman looked at the tree,
and it was all desire and delightful to see;
she took of its fruit and ate,
and gave also to her companion with her.
She ate first, it is said,
to snatch for herself the name of gods,
because she was led by the persuasion,
"You will be like gods."
She gave to her husband afterward,
so that she might become a god first,
for a vain hope deceived her,
the promise of the slanderer.
Then their eyes were opened
by eating the fruit, and they saw,
and within themselves they were reproached
by a sight full of shame.
They had known no [?]
before eating from the tree,
but after they transgressed the commandment
they saw that they were stripped and exposed.
They stuck fig leaves together
for shame before one another,
for sin had made them
exposed, and their disgrace a byword.
Discernment had lain hidden
in their pure minds,
and after they ate from the tree
they became discerners of what is fitting.
That is why he called the tree
from which they ate "knowledge":
because the knowledge of their minds
came to light through eating from it.
It did not give knowledge,
for this it did not possess by nature;
but by occasion of it
they learned it, through transgressing the commandment.
They made a covering for their bodies
from the leaves of that same tree:
by occasion of it they gained knowledge,
and with its leaves they covered their bodies.
But he who knows hidden things
did not neglect his blessed one,
for even when he laid the commandment on him
he knew that he would surely sin.
Toward evening the Creator
made the sound of his footsteps heard,
as he came to require of them
[?] for transgressing the commandment.
O Nature without composition,

not bounded by his works,
who gave sound to his steps
as he came to rebuke Adam!
O Fountain of all wisdom,
who holds the end of all things,
who asks as though he did not know
where the son of his house is hiding!
He made the sound of his steps heard
to alarm them for having sinned.
He asked, "Where are you, Adam?"
and showed that he knew where he was.
"Where are you, Adam?" said
the Maker to the image he had fashioned.
"Where are you, heir of Paradise?
Why do you hide your faults?"
O Good One, how greatly he loves
the image of Adam, the creature of dust,
who with choking voice
seeks the one who was lost!
"Where are you, honoured Adam,
whom I made lord on the earth?
Why have you become exposed,
modest one who has stripped off his radiance?"
"I heard your voice and hid myself,"
Adam answered his Maker,
"and I am ashamed to see your face,
for I am stripped and exposed."
"Who made you naked?"
the Lord said to his servant.
"Who stripped off your covering,
honoured one who has disgraced himself?
Perhaps the sight of the tree
drew you toward eating,
and the boundary I set for you
has made you naked, without garments."
"The woman gave to me and I ate,"
said Adam, the child,
thinking that he was showing
that he was far from blame.
God said to Eve,
"What is this that you have done?"
She heaped the blame on another:
"The serpent deceived me and I ate."
But he did not question the cunning one
in the way he questioned Adam,
for he had no excuse for his envy,
that he might say, "Others deceived me."
Then the Creator who had fashioned them
began to pronounce the sentence of judgment,
and he began first with the serpent,
for it had been the cause of the evils.
With the curses on the serpent
he was cursing the slanderer,
hinting at his fall,
that he was loosing him from his authority.
He had been head of the air
and commander of his fellows,
and because he deceived Adam and Eve
he fell to the earth and was brought low.
God said to the serpent:
"Because you have done this and deceived,
cursed are you above all creeping things,
and your steps shall be bound within you.
Dust shall be your food,
and into the earth shall be your return,

for you drove the heir from his glory;
on the earth shall your springing be.
From now on you shall be an enemy
to Adam and to all his children,
for he shall tread your head into the earth,
and you shall strike him when he sins."
After the serpent, Eve
he brought next to the sentence of judgment,
for she had accepted its counsel first
and stretched out her hand to the fruit.
With pains and wailing he cursed her,
and with the pangs of childbirth he bound her,
and gave her in subjection to the man,
to supply his needs.
O devices, how wise they are,
of the Creator toward his creatures!
What he had fixed in nature
he made into a punishment.
Adam, the image of his glory,
the Creator cursed last,
for the severity of the sentence of judgment
he turned upon the serpent and Eve.
The Lord said to Adam,
the Maker to the image he had fashioned:
"Because of you I curse
fruits and seeds and trees.
Because you listened to the voice of your wife
and ate the fruit of knowledge,
you shall be a tiller of the ground,
and only then will it give you fruit.
Dust you are, Adam, from the earth,
and to the earth you shall return, because you sinned.
Because you scorned the commandment I laid on you,
the rational and the mute shall scorn you.
See, you have now become a god,
as the evil one deceived you!
Command the natures to obey you,
if his promise is true."
These words the Creator
made heard as he mocked him:
"See, Adam has become like one of us;
now he has become a god.
Let him go out from Paradise,
the heir who did not discern his glory,
lest he stretch out his hand
and take from the tree of life."
For his instruction the Creator
made these words heard,
so that his folly might loom large in his eyes
and he might hate sin deeply.
And if one who transgressed the commandment
made his own dwelling foreign to him,
how much more ought he to honour
his Creator and sin no more!
How splendid Paradise was,
and how much delight was found in it!
As he was leaving it and going out,
he was reproached by his sin.
The transgression of the commandment, like a master,
made the simple one very wise,
and the sentence of judgment and the punishment
made him hate sin.
Through the tree was revealed

what lay veiled over his mind,
and through desire for its fruit
the freedom within him was made manifest.
Adam began to prophesy
by the power the Creator had given him,
and the things to come in his nature
he spoke of by revelation.
Adam gave his wife the name
Eve, the bearer of life,
for she was to be a mother
and bear humankind in succession.
The Lord God made
garments for the house of Adam,
stirring their thoughts
to cover their members.
Garments of skins
the Creator put on them,
because he had set knowledge to dwell in them,
so that they might supply their needs.
For their instruction were carried out
all the things he had decreed and punished,
and by clothing them he supplied
the needs of their members.
With his voice he commanded them to go out
from the fair dwelling of Eden,
so that they would not delight in the fruits
of the tree that gives life:
"Lest Adam turn back
and take from the fruit of life,
let him go out to where he was fashioned
and till the land of curses."
For one day the creatures of dust
were heirs in the dwelling of Paradise,
and toward evening they moved away
as sojourners to another place.
In the morning they [?] their fashioning,
and at the ninth hour [?],
and on the very day they were fashioned
they ate, and sinned, and went out.
The prophet, by the Spirit, wrote for us
that they were in the land of Eden for a day,
for he said "toward evening,"
and not "toward evening of another day."
Adam went out from Paradise
and dwelt in the land around it,
while the creature of dust grieved
that his dwelling had become foreign to him.
He fenced Paradise off before him
with the sharp edge of sword and spear,
and also set a guard for it,
a fearsome cherub, to keep it.
O wise Creator,
how he loves his creation!
He kept the despised ones away from it,
that they might honour it with praises.
He greatly honoured Paradise
by setting a guard for it,
so that Adam might know his folly
and turn back to seek his glory.
He made him feel his sin,
that he might honour his Lord's commandment,
so that while he tilled the earth by his strength
he would know what he had lost.
Adam went out from Paradise,
and grief was bound to him,

and the hateful one began to boast:
"Adam has become my slave."
The spiritual hosts were grieved
to see the disgrace of the honoured one,
and all of them put on grief
that a son of the free was serving as a slave.
They had rejoiced in his fashioning
and been glad at the sight of him,
for they saw that he was making their nature
akin [?] to his own soul.
Now they put on the suffering of love,
because death reigned over Adam,
and they were distressed when they saw
his soul being parted from his body.
All creation mourned
over Adam's fair image,
for it was bound to him in love,
and sin had loosed the bond.
The spirits turned their faces from him
as from a stranger,
and the elements were unwilling to move
to sustain his life.
The beasts too rebelled against him,
the creeping things fled and hid in the earth,
and all his possessions despised him
because he had scorned his Lord's word.
By his own will he became a stranger
to the lordship that had been given him,
and the lowly ones, grown insolent,
greatly despised the honoured one.
The mute and the rational natures
put on mourning over his fall,
and only one rejoiced:
he who had been distressed at his glory.
In the neighbourhood of Paradise
he gave the mortal a dwelling,
so that he would remember at every moment
both his inheritance and his folly.
By these devices the Creator contrived
to discipline Adam,
and by the severity of his punishment
he was drawing him toward knowledge.
These things had been hidden from the beginning
in the knowledge of him who created all,
and he brought them to light
by occasion of the transgression of the commandment.
He had created Adam mortal
and prepared the dwelling fitting for him,
and made the sin of transgressing the commandment
the cause of mortality.
To the whole of nature he was giving wisdom
by this occasion in the house of Adam:
that if sin has wrought death,
let us hate it now, for it has undone us [?].
The sentence of judgment became a master to him
and greatly disciplined the simple one,
so that he might learn who it is that strikes him:
sin, which cast him into death.
The commandment made him very wise
and made him know his own nature,
so that the creature of dust would not grow proud:

and his nature stray into the abyss.
The Maker firmly set in him,
in his making, every kind of wisdom,
and made him master of his freedom,
to govern himself as he willed.
He planted gentle impulses in him,
desire and love by nature,
so that from the spring of his body
his whole race might be sustained.
Adam knew the partner of his side,
and Eve conceived life;
she bore a child and named him
"Acquired from God."
See the wisdom of our nature,
which the Maker stirred within it:
the gift that He gave first
she counted as her own acquisition.
Eve rejoiced in what she had acquired,
in Cain, the very first firstborn.
After him she bore another
and gave him the name "Breath."
She called Abel "Breath"
because his life would end like a breath,
hinting in her prophecy
at his brother, who would destroy his life.
Eve and Adam saw
that they had gained fruits that speak:
though they had become mortal through sin,
they gained life through their children.
Abel became a shepherd of flocks
and Cain a tiller of the soil,
and they offered the firstfruits of their labour
to the God of all.
Abel offered a lamb,
and his will along with his offering;
Cain offered grass from the ground,
and no will was mingled with it.
Their offerings put to the test
the wills of their thoughts.
The deceitful one was exposed and rebuked
when his offering was turned back to him.
That Maker who rebuked
Eve and Adam when they did wrong
wished to bring into the open
the will of Abel and his brother.
His knowledge became a balance
and weighed the two of them:
the blameless one's side sank down,
and the deceitful one's will was found light.
He received in love the offering
of Abel, whose heart was pure,
and rejected and cast away Cain's,
whose mind was not sincere.
By fire the Creator tested
whose offering was accepted:
Abel's it seized and consumed,
but Cain's it did not touch.
Cain put on deep mourning
and his face grew very dark,
and he grew bitter against his Maker
for rejecting his offering.
Then the Lord said to Cain
openly, in a gentle voice:
"If you make your will good,
I will accept your gift.

But if the bitterness of your thought
is not turned into sweetness,
your sin lies crouching at the door
and will not leave your limbs.
Here is your offering, envious one:
He who grieves you has given it back to you.
You are master over what is yours;
go, manage your own with your own hands."
Cain's will did not change
after this warning,
nor did he accept correction
in the gentleness shown to him.
He swelled with arrogance,
like the Accuser,
and added anger upon anger,
and his mind gave birth to murder.
For the presumptuous man supposed
that if he killed the blameless one
he would grieve the Creator
for rejecting his offering.
Through Abel he would take revenge
for his grudge against the Maker,
like his master Satan,
who through Adam rebelled against his Fashioner.
And Cain said to his brother,
the envious to the blameless:
"Come, let us go down to the plain
and look at the beauty of the land."
The serpent of envy rode him,
the man who burned with jealousy,
so that under pretence of love he would go
and spend his anger on the simple one.
The simple trusted the crafty,
as Eve trusted the deceiver,
and the blameless one went out with him to the plain,
knowing nothing.
