The murderous Cain dared it,
and wronged the tenderness of nature:
he killed his brother out of envy,
thinking by his murder to vex [?] God.
O heart that gave birth to murder,
a new deed on the earth!
O presumptuous will
that trod out a path to the house of the dead!
In Abel the path was trodden out,
and Death began to go down by it.
And Adam learned by experience
that he too is mortal.
Through Cain the Accuser
fulfilled the desire of his envy,
and in the fullness of time he was consoled
to see that Death had gained power.
The master taught his disciple
lying and denial,
and he hid the slain man in the earth
so as not to confess when questioned.
For the murderer supposed
that Abel's blood would stay hidden,
and did not know that He saw him,
He who had rejected his offering.
Cain hid the slain man
and buried his intent along with him,
and sought to hide his deed
from Him who knows hidden things.

The Maker spoke calmly
and called aloud to the murderer:
"O envious and deceitful one,
what wrong did the blameless one do you?"
"Where then is Abel your brother?"
the Lord said to Cain.
And he answered Him insolently,
knowing why He called him.
O Knower of all, who asks
as though He did not know what had happened!
As He had asked in Paradise,
so He asked the murderer.
Once He asked Adam,
"Where are you, Adam?" while seeing him;
and here He asked Cain about Abel,
"Where is your brother?" while knowing.
He asked as if He did not know
so that the presumptuous man might at last repent,
and if he confessed his folly,
He might grant him forgiveness too.
Cain, the first disciple,
was armed with his master's weapon:
master and disciple lied,
and truth bound them both.
"Where then is Abel your brother?"
Yet the presumptuous man would not confess,
but answered wickedly,
"Am I my brother's keeper?"
Insolently he spoke to his Lord,
and the murderer felt no shame:
"If your beloved is lost,
what do I owe you, that I should give you?"
With bonds of fear truth bound
the voice of Cain:
he who would not confess of his own will
revealed it and confessed once exposed.
"What is this you have done?"
the Lord said to Cain.
"Your brother's blood cries out to me
as it pleads its case against its murderer.
From now on you are cursed from the earth,
and the earth beneath you shall not prosper.
Since it received innocent blood,
let it receive curses along with it.
Your body shall shake with trembling
in place of the body your hands destroyed,
and you shall be a terror to those who see you,
because your heart did not tremble at murder.
Since you began with the first blood
and offered firstfruits to Death,
for seven generations I will require
the innocent blood from your hands.
Since you trod out a path to the house of the dead,
by which the multitude of mankind will go down,
in you I set an example
that I require blood for blood."
The curses took effect
and trembling clothed the murderer.
His body shook upon the ground,
and quaking wore him down all over.
With a repentance not of his own will
he pleaded with the Creator,
and begged death for himself,
to be delivered from his torments.

And Cain said to the Lord:
"See, You have driven me from the land.
You have clothed me with trembling and quaking,
which greatly terrify those who see me.
One thing I ask, if You are willing:
deal with me according to Your mercy,
that by death Your curses
may be loosed from my limbs."
"Not so, murderer,"
the Lord said to Cain.
"Not so shall your folly
be punished by death alone.
For seven generations I prolong
the lasting torments of your wickedness,
and the punishment of your murder
shall be spoken of in all the world."
The Lord set a sign on Cain
that he should not die by any man's hand;
when He set this sign,
it was so that He might keep His own token.
He kept the murderer alive
as a warning to generations to come,
so that those who looked at the sign
might flee from murder.
In the fullness of time Eve and Adam
were consoled when they bore children,
for grief had come over them for their children:
they wept for Abel the fair,
whose features Death had ruined,
and they mourned over Cain,
who had been made to tremble in creation.
The Creator bound them
with the love of natural tenderness,
so that the sweetness found in weeping
might soften the grief of their hardships.
In this way the Maker made us wise
from the very beginning:
that through the pains and sufferings of death
we might gain love for Him.
He kept us busy with earthly things
in an earthly order,
so that when we feel ourselves worn down
we might ask for a life without toil.
He reared our childhood on milk,
on weak things suited to our strength,
so that when we come to maturity
we may live in the knowledge of life.
He did not entrust us with riches
while our understanding was childish,
for as long as an heir is a child
he cannot manage his possessions.
In the life of the soul He granted us
to sustain the life of time,
and when we are no longer mortal,
He will keep us by the power of the Spirit.
In all that belongs to our nature
He who created our nature persuaded us,
and wisely He leads us
from lowly things to lofty ones,
so that when we learn by knowledge
who has given us these things,
we may give thanks to the Power that made all
for how greatly He has loved our nature.
On Humility
By the same, likewise: a homily of sixty [?], on humility.

By the word of peace the Lord of the world caught the world,
and bowed its neck under the gentle yoke of His sweetness.
By humility He humbled the strength of height and depth,
and taught them to walk in the way of humility.
The net of peace He cast over all, and it caught all,
and He fed them with the gentle food of the word of His mouth.
The fire of His love He cast upon the earth; it [?] the thorns,
and the forest of mortality was burned up, and life blossomed.
By the light of His name He drove away the darkness of ignorance,
and people saw the power of His being and believed in His name.
By the voice of His commands He cleansed the world that lacked understanding,
and it gained the taste of the sweetness of the life of the One [?].
With the waters of mercy He washed the people whom iniquity had defiled,
and gave them the beauty that befits righteousness.
In the fire of the Spirit He refined His image, He who establishes all,

and renewed its form spiritually, so that it would never again be corrupted.
He overlaid it with the spiritual gold of the name of His being,
and set it on high, so that it would not be harmed by injuries.
By renewing His image He revealed to His servants the power of His wisdom,
for in wisdom He has brought His own near to the knowledge of Him.
In wisdom He brought it about that through His image He would renew all,
and bind humankind together with the spiritual beings in the peace of His name.
A new way of humility He trod before His servants,
for He first travelled it Himself and came to His perfection.
The Word of the Father, who is wholly the likeness of His Father,
willed in humility to reconcile the divided world.
The Creator took the likeness of a servant from mortals,
and humbly showed His hidden self openly.
For He did not show the nature of His being to the eyes of beholders,
lest they think that pride had made Him grasp at it falsely.
The form of a servant He put on by His will, and was shown in it,
and His nature remained what it was, without change.
He hid His being, which cannot be grasped by what He has made,
and revealed His glory and showed His power through a humble one.
In humility He came to teach the children of His house,
and humbled Himself through the lowly one whom He took for His name.
In what is ours He showed His humility and the power of His wisdom,
and not in His nature, which is neither humbled nor increased.
The likeness of the servant humbled itself, for all that it had grown great,
and did not boast in the glories of hidden majesty.
In Himself He set humility up like a mirror,
so that people might see themselves and hate pride.
Even unto death He humbled Himself for people's sake,
and crucified with Him the mortality of His own kind.
He died for all and gave life to all by the power of what He took,
and reconciled the world to the Will, so that all are at peace in Him.
For this reason He humbled Himself and went down to Sheol,
to raise humankind from the lowliness of mortality.
And because He gave Himself up to death and gave life to all,
the Creator honored Him with the name that is above all.
In humility He conquered and was exalted above death,
and taught us too that through lowliness we may overcome sufferings.
And if the Humble One, whose garment is lofty, humbled Himself,
who would be carried away by pride, a fool who destroys himself?
If the Rich One made the riches of His glories poor,
who would boast of what is not his as though it were his own?
If the Son of the free humbled Himself and set slaves free,
who would not render the service he owes to his liberator?
If the Righteous One counted Himself among sinners,
who would not pour out the labors of his soul for His members?
He Himself trod for us the way of humility;
come, let us humble ourselves, so that we are not estranged from the kingdom of life.
He showed us that by lowliness He took the victory,
and raised up Himself and His fellows from lowliness.
He taught us a living goal, that we should be like Him,

bowing in our movements and our limbs down to lowliness.
In humility He sowed His teaching in the soil of humankind,
and people blossomed with the sweet fruits of humility.
In humility He caught the world [?],
and brought His captives within the fortresses of humility.
In humility He cast His net into the sea of humankind,
and the catch of humility, which mercy had caught, [?].
In humility He proclaimed His words in the ears of everyone,
so that the voice of teaching would not weigh heavily on the learners.
A gentle yoke He called His gospel before His hearers,
so that the human mind would not slacken in its labor.
“My yoke,” He says, “is sweet to whoever labors humbly,
and the burden of my words is light to whoever carries it.
And if it is hard to toil under it all the time,
see, the consolation of the reward is better than the labors.
Let whoever is weary of labor become like me,
for I myself toiled in the land of human beings and of spirits.
Let whoever is brought low by afflictions become like me,
for I trod down the sting of insolent death gladly.
From what is mine let him learn, whoever looks to the gentle goal,
and see, he is raised to an exaltation that is never brought low.”
In humility the Humble One won the lofty world;
come, children of the dust, humble yourselves and receive exaltation.
In humility He took captive the tyrant who despoiled humankind;
come, let us weave Him a crown of victory in humility.
In humility He trod down death, which tramples our nature;
let us tread down [?] in humility, after His likeness.
In humility let us bind our love to His lowliness,
so that it does not slacken because of the possessions of wealth.
In humility those perfected in His love fulfilled His will,
and He made them partners in the glories that He received and inherited.
In humility Abel offered a humble lamb,
and he was humbler in the will of his soul than his offering.
The humble-souled, whose will was pleasing along with his offering,
raised up his sacrifice and the will of his soul to the gate.
Humility set Enoch above death,
and made the wings of the immortals blossom toward life.
O mortal, whose whole food was mortality,
who escaped from the mouth of death, the insolent lion!
Noah too, the gentle, subdued his impulse by humility,
and by his steadfastness won the battle of the turbulent waters.
O honored one, whose dwelling was sunk in the waters of suffering,
whose honor the waves bore up, and it did not sink!
In this way of humility Abraham also walked,
and he went on and reached the fulfilment of the reward's recompense.
To humility he gave himself over as to a master,
and learned from it to meditate on the name of the Creator.
O disciple, who learned and taught himself and his own,
and explained the mysteries of the Name of Being to the children of his race!
O rich man, who acquired both wealth and humility,

and was not exalted by earthly things as though they were his own!
Contemptible dust he called himself before his Creator,
and because he made himself small, He made him head of [?] kings.
Let Abraham be like a mirror to the possessors of wealth,
so that they do not exalt themselves over the humble because of wealth.
Do not boast, O possessor of possessions, in the possessions of time,
for time itself, by its changes, makes your pride poor.
Time passes, and wealth passes with its possessions,
and pride comes to nothing, and the lofty neck goes down to Sheol.
Why are you proud, child of mortality, of what is not yours?
Why do you exalt yourself in earthly things that do not remain with you?
You are dust, and your dwelling returns to dust;
consider your nature, that you are about to be [?] from its corruption.
Know your nature and humble yourself before the All-Seeing,
and ask and entreat Him to raise your dust from lowliness.
Put on lowliness like a garment upon your limbs,
so that your body may put on the fruitful garment of the resurrection of His dead.
Acquire lowliness, the great wealth that does not grow poor,
so that your body may put on the fair garment of the resurrection of the dead.
Acquire lowliness, the great wealth that does not grow poor,
so that you may be worthy to receive the wealth of life without end.
Look at Abraham, who acquired wealth and humility,
and grew rich and reigned in things earthly and spiritual.
Be like Jacob, who humbled himself in earthly things,
and acquired the rank of humility and of seniority.
See the wonder that it worked by his hand—
humility—
which overturned the order that the Creator had set for humankind.
His humility constrained [?] nature
beyond its order,
and gave the rank of seniority to the younger.
Who would not love humility, which has acquired power,
whose power has overcome natures and their rulers?
Who would not flee from loftiness, which weakens strength,
whose strength was diminished at the hands of Esau before the humble one?
Esau's pride humbled him; he sinned and became poor,
and gave up the rank of seniority to the one younger than he.
Let everyone flee from [?], the deceitful armor,
which cannot win in battle for the one who wears it.
Let everyone put on humility, the good armor,
which gives strength even to the weak and grants a reward.
In this armor of humility Joseph too was victorious,
and won the battle of desires through steadfastness.
Moses too put on humility like armor,
and at his voice those who wore the armor of sorcery were defeated.
In humility he anointed his mind like an athlete,
and put to shame the [?] contestants whom error had anointed.
In humility he purified his body and sanctified his soul,
and his mouth interpreted the voice that explains hidden things.
He loved humility, set apart from everything else,
and by it he was raised to a high rank above everyone.
See the testimony to his humility in his books:
that the man Moses, it says, was humbler than anyone.
The All-Seeing too saw him clothed in the garment of modesty,
and adorned him with glory, and he became a god among mortals.
O humble one, who humbled himself in a singular way,
and received a reward greater than the labor of his humility!

O child of the earthly race, of contemptible nature,
who put on a glory foreign to the garment of mortality!
O poor one, of meager life and short span,
who acquired spiritual wealth and the name of God!
In Moses let us see how humility is exalted,
how it lends a hand to the victory of one whose strength can do all things.
Let those who serve humility look upon him,
and not slacken in the struggle against pride.
Against pride let the humble-souled arm himself,
like an athlete guarding himself against his opponent.
Pride is hateful, and the enemy of humility,
and it is not fitting for the humble-souled to slacken.
Guard the fortresses of your soul carefully against arrogance,
lest it break in and plunder the treasure of your humility.
Watch for the movements of your discernment, and guard your treasures,
and drive the sleep of laziness from your thoughts.
Put on the coat of mail of humility against pride,
and grip the sword of the word of peace on the edge of your lips.
Do not give the enemy room to watch you closely,
lest he take courage for battle and break in to kill.
Foolish, undiscerning pride is a killer of men,
and no one perceives [?] the slaughter its insolence works.
It is a tyrant [?] that is not softened by the voice of entreaty,
and like a lion it roars continually to break humankind.
It is what broke Cain, the firstborn of arrogance,
and shook his body and turned his soul from uprightness.
It is what spoke in the despised Ham, and he insulted his father,
and bent his neck into the hard chain of the righteous man's curse.
Its counsel made Esau weak, so that he lost his rank,
and through dealing with it he learned to deny his birthright.
With it Pharaoh the king armed himself against Moses,
and, having grown very bitter, he went down into the abyss without pity.
With it the rebels who coveted the priesthood also served,
and went down to Sheol without dying, outside the natural order.
By the power of its boasting Sennacherib raged against Hezekiah,
and shouted down [?] the voice of uprightness and made it a laughingstock.
Pride spoke in the voice of blasphemy through the mouth of the Rabshakehs,
and the voice that explains prophecy stopped their mouth.
Foolish pride took Rehoboam, the foolish king, captive,
and because he spurned counsel, a foreign kingdom came over the inheritance of the tribes.
The Babylonian too subdued peoples in the armor of pride,
and his pride bent his neck under the yoke among the beasts.
Over all peoples he raised his rod and ruled everyone,
and he did not discern who it is that rules him and his fellows.
And because the power of victory ought not to make him victorious,
He rejected him and cast him into exile among the beasts.
See the reward that pride pays to the one who loves it;
flee from its service, you weak ones, for it kills humankind.
See, its hidden cunning has been laid bare by the testimony of the Spirit,
so that no one may stray after its words, while [?].

See, it is shown that the end of its way is shame of face,
and whoever walks with it sinks into the pit.
So do not walk in the way of pride, O man;
leave loftiness behind and go in the company of humility.
Do not boast in the possessions of time, which do not endure;
see how many gathered wealth and left it on the earth.
Do not be exalted by the name of a dominion that passes and is gone;
look and consider the crowns laid down in Sheol.
Which of the kings has saved his crown from the mouth of death,
and who has given wealth and bought life without end?
Do not, O man, do not boast and deceive yourself,
for there is no death that does not turn nature back to its dust.
A man possesses the life of time, and not life for ever;
see, the proof of how short his life is lies at the door of death.
So a man is bound to live in keeping with his life,
and to lead his life to its end in a fitting way.
In the lowliness of his dwelling let the earthly one see how humble he is,
and let him humble himself, so that he is not put to shame even by his dwelling.
Humility befits your name, O earthly one;
why do you exalt yourself in things that do not befit the name of the despised?
You are a child of the race, O man, of upright men;
walk in the path of humility which the upright have trodden.
Keep company with the company full of peace, with the ancients,
and see how pleasant is the company of those who labor in humility.
Be like David, how he humbled the will of his soul,
and did not boast in the greatness of the labor of his humility.
See that the word of peace chose him for a high rank,
and he did not grow lax, as a weak man might, in his authority.
He was anointed by the Spirit to be king and physician,
while the corrupt one went out, wandering, away from the people [?].
His will was made a holy temple for the Spirit of revelation,
and he was continually persecuted by the spirit of falsehood that dwelt in Saul.
He was always striking a hidden melody on the lyre of his soul,
and drove the demons away from the envious man who persecuted him.
When Saul was inflamed and raged with a raging demon,
the son of Jesse struck the lyre of the Spirit and quieted the deceiver.
When the killer of men was set burning with envy,
David cried out by the Spirit of revelation, and the rebel trembled.
And when, again, the one raging with envy brooded in his torment,
he sharpened the spear to shed the blood of his helper.
The foolish sick man, lying in the pain of the demon and of iniquity,
began to fight the physician of the Spirit who tended him with mercy.
Saul lay in two pains without discernment:
poisonous envy, and a raging demon that devours humankind.
David applied the medicine of the Spirit to his sickness,
and because [?] it, he rotted and festered and died in his sin.
In Saul let the proud of heart see, the haughty and the blind,
that envy blinded him and pride slew him with the sword of the uncircumcised.
In David let the humble look, the lovers of peace,
so that they do not slacken at the taunts of rebels.

Do not be grieved, O humble-souled, when you are insulted;
see the son of Jesse, whom Saul repaid with reproach and insult.
Do not repay the one who does you harm according to his offense,
so that you are not put to shame by that voice which says, “Forgive.”
Bind your love in the gentle yoke of humility,
and do not slacken from spiritual labor.
Keep company with the company of the words of the Spirit in the way of the Scriptures,
and walk in them among the laws of humility.
Read and consider the power of the wonders of the preaching,
and learn the parables and interpret the hidden mysteries.
Seek out the passage of the parable written against pride,
and see there two men praying before the All-Seeing.
Look at the Pharisee, the proud fool who praised himself,
and by raising his voice made his pride a thing without reward.
He was not lying in what he said, that he was no adulterer and did not steal,
but because he sought to display his labors, he went down in shame.
See the reward of foolish pride to the one who puts it on:
it strips him of the labor of his upright toils.
The Pharisee was upright in what he recounted, that he fasted and was righteous,
but because he mixed pride with his righteous deeds, his righteousness was made void.
The tax collector, who heard the voice of boasting that destroys reward,
looked into himself and brought himself down to lowliness.
He saw that there are no labors that give a man boldness of speech,
and lowered his eyes so as not to look upon the face of heaven.
He bowed his head and hid his face from onlookers,
and began to plead like a debtor who has sinned and become poor.
He folded his limbs, together with his mind, before the All-Seeing,
and began to beat himself upon the breast.
He saw that he was stained all over with the blemishes of iniquity,
and poured out tears and washed his body and the movements of his soul.
He raised his hand and struck himself with the scourge of suffering,
and condemned himself, like a discerning judge, for the wrongs he had done.
With a choked voice he pleaded before the Judge:
“Have mercy on me, for I have sinned, and do not [?] me, who have wronged your love.”
At the sound of his groans the Judge and the ranks of the King were astonished,
and He sent mercy to release him at the sound of his weeping.
“Be still, sinner,” the mercies cried to him with a hidden sign,
“see, the King has commanded that the bond of your debts be torn up.
For ever is your iniquity forgiven in exchange for your lowliness;
go, rejoicing in the forgiveness of iniquity that mercy has given you.”
Come, you humble, see how lowliness has been exalted,
and has received a rank of primacy [?] for ever.
Come and look, Pharisee, you who are full of blemishes,
how his blemishes were washed away in the baptisms of his self-humbling.
Who was ever justified like his justification, he who was wholly guilty,
upon whom the All-Seeing openly set a crown woven for ever?
Who was made righteous like the sinner whose name was iniquity,
who through lowliness blotted out his name along with his sins?
Who would not look to the gentle goal of humility,
which teaches even the unlearned the ways of victory?

Who would not marvel at the workings of her love, full of peace,
which urges the one who has sinned to ask for mercy?
She taught him the ways of supplication, to cover his fault,
and she shaped for him repentance of mind in place of signs [?].
Come, let him meditate in the books of the words of her who has acquired power,
and read with understanding, and gain life to overcome iniquity.
The power of her help is able to justify the one who is guilty,
and the greatness of iniquity counts as nothing against her persuasion.
Paul bears witness and praises the power of her help,
for it was she who raised him up, and he acquired the rank of headship.
In his humility he looked to the Will that cried out to him,
and first set himself apart for the teaching of His preaching.
With gentle voices he proclaimed his message in people's ears,
and roused them to hear the voice of the word of life.
In sweetness he tilled the land of rational beings,
and it gave fruits of righteousness to the lord of the vineyard.
Humility he taught and implanted and directed and acquired,
and bowed people under the gentle yoke of humility.
Through gentleness he became like the Great One who chose him,
as he proclaimed one confession of one Creator.
In humility he uprooted paganism and built up truth,
and the Truth too called him a wise man who builds well.
Come, you humble, build the building of your conduct
upon the foundation of humility that Paul laid.
Learn from him how one ought to begin,
and set these materials upon the rock of faith.
Let his voice be like a mirror before your eyes,
crying out and proclaiming, so that everyone may see how he builds.
Whoever builds with pure gold, his work endures,
and whoever builds with straw and stubble, his work is burned.
See, he shows us how we should build the building of truth,
and that the judgment tests the materials of both kinds.
Humility is able to teach us to build well,
and by her a person's building is completed, even if he is lacking.
There is no one lacking who is not filled by her fullness,
and no simple person who is not made wise by her shrewdness.
To the weary she is a rest that refreshes soul and limbs,
and without weariness she keeps the labors of righteousness.
By her the temple of the body and the will of the soul are purified,
and a person becomes a pure dwelling for the hidden Power.
“In whom,” He says, “shall I look and choose a dwelling for my hidden will,
but in the gentle and humble who hears my words?”
O Creator, of whom heaven and earth are full,
how can a contemptible human being suffice as a dwelling for your majesty?
“Yes,” He says, “I am in height and depth, and they do not suffice me,
but in the humble I rest, to make a dwelling for my will.
My will loves humility more than sacrifices,
and though I have no need, I long to see the sacrifices of her love.
She brought humble Noah near to me with his offerings; in her I gave rest to my will,

and I received from him sacrifices offered openly.
By her Moses the leader was made wise and gained understanding,
and in his stammering he interpreted my hidden purposes.”
By her Paul the chosen one was made ready against sufferings,
and she saw that he was able [?] one generation [?] measured him by the Spirit.
See, he has shown us the hidden mystery of whom He wills,
and how He dwells in whoever dwells willingly.
In the humble the Spirit, the Establisher of all, chose Himself a dwelling,
and though all is His, He left everything and dwelt in the gentle.
The humble-souled is more worthy of blessing than all who have ever been,
for he alone is worthy that the Hidden One should dwell in his soul.
If there is nothing greater than the Power that establishes all,
then neither is there anything greater than the dwelling that suffices for His name.
Who would not adorn the temple of his soul with humility,
so that it may become a dwelling and the hidden Will may dwell in it?
Who would not hate the business of pride, which lacks understanding,
which always pays evil wages to those who honor it?
Everyone, then, He says, who humbles himself will be exalted,
and whoever is proud in the height of his heart will go down to disgrace.
The very proud of mind is abhorrent before God,
and the Seer of hidden things rejects and hates the conduct of his life.
See, you despised, do not slacken in small things,
lest you become hateful to the Hidden One, who hates pride.
Endure a little in humility, so that you may live much,
for the reward kept for the humble is in proportion to their labors.
Hear the echo of the voice of the Lord of the reward toward the humble:
that He makes the scourge severe upon whoever oppresses the gentle of soul.
Everyone, He says, who causes to stumble and oppresses one who is small,
it would be better for him to be sunk in the depths of the sea.
The humble-souled, who makes himself small, He named “little,”
one who does not boast in the glories of the greatness of his labors.
Him, the little one, He called Lazarus in the word that He wrote,
who was afflicted with two pains of humility.
He was tormented by sicknesses and poverty,
and was despised, and no one relieved his distress.
And because he was in need of earthly things for a [?] time,
he grew rich and was gladdened with delights without end.
In the everlasting life of Abraham's bosom Lazarus found rest,
and trod out the way for the humble to ascend to Him.
Come, you humble, keep company with the companions of the humble-souled,
and rest for ever in the bosom of Abraham with Lazarus.
See, our Lord's parable has trodden out the way as a guide,
so that whoever walks humbly may not slacken.
Like a watchman the parable cries in people's ears:
“Rise, take courage, and keep to the way of humility.”
Like a trumpet it sounds its voice to all who are proud:
“See, O people, do not exalt yourselves like the rich man.
See the good things of that wicked man who spent his time on earth,
and his wealth did not go down with him to Sheol, as he had supposed.

See how he begged, and no one gave him drink in his torment,
and he wished to go back and testify to his brothers, but He did not permit him.
A sign [?] the way before his face on every side,
and barred the door before his petition, so that it was not received.”
See, He shows us through Lazarus and the rich man
how beloved humility is and how rejected pride is.
See, He has taught us about the recompense of that rich man,
and that with these blessings He gives rest to the weary according to their labors.
Let the bosom of Abraham the father [?] be the goal of our soul's will,
so that we may become like him through the steadfastness of our faith.
Let us call Him Father by deeds and not by names,
so that He may open the door of His everlasting love and receive us.
On the Coming of the Antichrist

Homily. By the same.
On the coming of the Antichrist, or rather the false Messiah,
and on the revelation of Christ our Lord.
It is recited on the Sunday at the beginning of the Fast of Mar Elijah.
Response:
Let us arm ourselves with the armor of good works, so that the arrows of the Evil One may not harm us.
Ayaḥ [?].

We have heard a report by night that he is coming at the end of times, / and it is very hard to recount the turmoil he will bring. / A great disaster is about to be spoken of among the dwellers on earth, / and no mouth can tell how bitter the report of it is. / An evil tiding announces evil among mortals, / and there is no one who is not troubled and whose mind does not reel. / What is about to be told is worthy of weeping, / and choked voices are fitting to accompany its telling. / Let whoever listens with discernment listen in anguish, / and let whoever hears aright weep in grief. / Let him lament in his mind and pour out tears in his thoughts, / and in place of sighs let tremors rend him over what is to come. / The slanderer is about to compose a harsh deceit, / and craftily he arms himself against our life. / He wishes to raise up the rebellion of iniquity against righteousness:

and he is preparing to set the name of the Creator beside his own. / The haughty-minded one seeks to climb to the lofty rank, / and in his presumption he utterly scorns the Divine Being. / The fool puts on crafty impudence like armor, / and wickedly marshals war against the truth. / He calls himself by the name of the Just One, though full of passions [?], / and for nothing he snatches the voice of praise that does not befit him. / 'I, I am the Christ,' says [...], and he is not ashamed: / 'in me are fulfilled the mysteries and types that the righteous sketched.' / Posing as the Righteous One, he urges men to receive him, / and he errs and leads astray, until he is exposed by righteousness. / By illusion he leads astray, and by semblances he shows mighty works, / until that voice at the end [?] him. / Proudly he heaps scorn on the anathema of all our voices [?], / and he strives and climbs to the lofty rank, though he does not climb it. / The herald, the chosen Paul, was amazed at his arrogance, / and depicted it beforehand in the scriptures so that everyone might see it. / By 'the rebellion' he named the son [?] in whom it is revealed, / who raises rebellion and holds back the truth so that it is not spoken. / His fame had gone abroad from the very beginning of the preaching, / and people began to make inquiry about his coming. / The apostle heard the inquiry about him from his disciples, / and he instructed them not to be alarmed at the report of him: / 'Do not accept,' he said, 'that the time of the end of times is near, / and do not be deceived, either by letter or by revelation.'

'Unless the rebellion comes first' — so the Knowing One revealed — / the course of earthly life is not complete. / Unless the son of perdition comes to err and lead astray, / the truth of the renewal of all [?] is not proven. / Unless he shows the wickedness of his nature before the eyes of all creatures, / the [?] of his coming is not sealed by deeds. / The Maker has set a limit of time for the work of his hands, / and until it is complete he does not allow the deceiver to lead astray. / The fence of the command stands before him like a wall, / which holds him back from the path of his rebellion's course. / He has long yearned greatly to accomplish his desire, / and he is not permitted until the decree that was decreed is fulfilled. / The crafty one waits for that commandment which set bounds and restrains him: / when will the appointed term be complete, and his falsehood be revealed? / Like a furnace he is heated within himself with the fuel of anger, / waiting for when he may blow up the fire of his wrath and burn mankind. / He is used to hiding the snares of deceit night and day, / and he sits watching for when the hunt for the offspring [?] will come. / Like a hunter he bides his time, twisted of mind, / and constantly watches for when he will reach the summit of his plan. / He likens his nature to a snare [?] within a crafty snare [?], / and he is more eager than the [?] and hastens toward the day of the end. / And were it not that the harsh [?] one were bound by the command of the Hidden One, / he would long ago have striven and swallowed our race at every moment. / By his will we would long since have perished:

were it not that he is restrained by that commandment which called us His image. / It is He who called [?] him, so that he should not exalt himself beyond due order, / and again He restrains him until the day appointed in His knowledge. / Wisely He restrains him within the bound of His hidden command, / and wisely He opens the way before him, and he goes out and leads astray. / The day of his revelation is for our advantage, even if it brings loss, / so that everyone may learn the wickedness of his deceits against mankind. / Two things are taught to angels and men by his wickedness: / his own arrogance, and the power of the Creator who restrains his wrath. / As if with a finger, our Good One shows His love for us: / were He not restraining him, he would long ago have destroyed us from the beginning. / If now, at the end of the ages, he does such evil, / how much evil would he have done had He let him loose from the day we came to be? / He made his nature a furnace of testing for us and for all, / so that through his wickedness the gold of our discernment may be tried. / By him He teaches us the kinds of struggle for the truth, / and by him He makes known to us His help that keeps us. / He has kept him for the end, for the great war prepared for him, / so that men and heavenly beings may see the wickedness of his nature. / Before that day on which He renews the creation He created, / He gives room for his iniquity to come out into the open. / It is not that the Creator longs to harm [?] by letting him loose, / but that his arrogance and the slackness of our souls may be revealed. / As in a court of law He sternly accuses us by him, / that we are not alert in the war of sufferings for the truth.

It is a great war that is prepared for us to wage with him, / and by every device he seeks to lead us astray from the truth. / He saw that our nature was weak, and hurled his might at it, / and behold, he is embittered at how he was suddenly condemned and exposed. / He saw that one of our race dazzled him and made him a laughingstock, / and behold, he schemes to exact his vengeance from that one's kin. / He saw that man was exalted to the lofty rank of the name of the Godhead, / and behold, he plans to overstep his own rank in arrogance. / He saw that angels and men were made subject under His authority, / and behold, he contrives to raise rebellion against His power. / He heard that at the end the Lord of all is going to come, / and he prepares for himself the armor of his iniquity, to come in His likeness. / He heard that He will descend to earth in the glory of the heavenly ones, / and he too prepares troops of demons to escort him. / He heard that in the judgment of the end he is going to be tormented, / and he rages in fury [?] against the Power that will torment him. / He saw that the sentence of the time of his downfall has drawn near, / and behold, he is changed like a murderer at the hour of his death. / He is certain that he will not escape justice, / and having cut off all hope, he scorns and disdains every fear. / He reflected that there is no place where he can hide on the day of testing, / and he is very eager to accomplish his desire wickedly. / The greatness of his iniquity made him commit iniquity without pity, / and his freedom made him do wickedness beyond all order. / The insolent one went out beyond the order of the Maker:

and he sought to exalt himself against the Maker and the work of his hands. / The arrogant one contends [?] against the Power that gave him power, / and he does not realize that by his freedom he is harming himself. / He wages a grievous war against the Will that honored mankind, / and through a man he spews his bile against the Godhead. / Through a man the Creator redeemed mankind, / and through a man he too wishes to destroy mankind. / The God of all chose a man and through him set all free, / and he too has seized [?] one man so that all may be enslaved. / The Creator called the man whom He chose 'Christ' and 'King,' / and after that likeness he names the man who is his dwelling. / Without union He formed Him in the womb to redeem mankind, / and already he too is preparing the same for that deceiver. / From the seed of the house of Abraham He took His beginning, / and it is Jewish blood that becomes the vessel of that deceit. / In all that took place in the Second Adam, he too [imitates], / and he works mighty deeds, though he does not truly work them. / In the very form in which He came to the world bodily, / in that he too comes to the world, in the body of a man. / The crafty one chooses one man from among mankind, / and dwells in him as the Hidden One dwelt in a man. / In a man the enemy of mankind dwells in order to lead mankind astray, / and he calls him the Son of God, as was the case before. / The crafty one calls the son of perdition the Son of God, / and he snatches the name of God with his hand and attaches it to his own name:

he sets the honorable name, as a sacrilege, upon his own vileness. / And he strives to climb to the lofty rank [...] that is not permitted him. / In his boasting the fool scornfully makes a raid upon the Divine Being, / and in his contentiousness he seizes the prerogatives of divinity. / Like a raider he passes through a land full of loftiness, / and he takes men captive to become slaves to his rebellion: / as head of the captivity he leads men out of their senses, / and instead of possessions he plunders the wealth of their thoughts. / He takes the understanding captive and strips the mind naked, / and instead of the body he mocks and torments the soul. / He wages war skillfully with hidden thoughts, / so that he may subject all mankind to his desires. / Skillfully he composes the war that is prepared for him, / and crafty demons prepare the time that suits [?] him. / By the craft of the demons he leads astray those who look on, / and shows to their eyes shadows that are not real. / In the twinkling of an eye he raises up phantoms before their pupils, / and props up the senses on nothing as though on something. / He depicts on the earth the likeness of things perceived, / and makes them seem to exist, though they do not exist. / The demons become a vision that is there though it is not there, / and they confirm it through likenesses that are not true. / They become blind and deaf and stammering and tongue-tied [?], / and the son of perdition heals by illusion, though he does not heal. / They cry out like the afflicted before his vileness:

and he exalts himself and stretches out his hand to heal. / It is not the healing of truth that he gives to those sick with sin; / by the promises of his words he longs to corrupt the health of the soul. / He takes the form of that Physician who came to the world, wrapped in falsehood, / and he calls to men, 'Come, be healed' — that is, 'die.' / The crafty physician's healing is full of bitter death, / and under the form of good he deals out ruin [?] to those who obey him. / In the form of the Messiah the messiah of deceit imitates Him, / and he draws after him the congregations of the peoples to escort him. / Like a righteous man he raises his voice to sinners: / 'Come, take for nothing the bond of your debts' — that is, 'incur guilt.' / Like a humble man he softens his words, which are full of haughtiness, / and humbly sows his word in the minds of men. / And already he says arrogantly, like our Redeemer, / 'Look to me, for I am gentle, and find rest from pride in the pattern of my gentleness.' / And already he, wholly iniquitous, proclaims the forgiveness of iniquity, / and the wicked one, whose wickedness has no measure, rebukes the wicked. / And already he undoes the divinations and enchantments of the Chaldeans, / so as to make his falsehood firm beyond shaking. / And already he becomes the opponent of his own art, / so that his evil nature may shine forth against his Lord. / And already he denies kinship with the children of his own mysteries, / so that he may snatch for his own name the honorable name of one who is a stranger to him. / And already he rebukes the priests who set up the houses of idol-worship, / so that he may establish the intent that he is the one to be worshiped.

And already he repeats, 'Why do you go astray after illusion?' / so that no one may perceive [?] that he is leading men astray from the truth. / O how skilled is the enemy of mankind and of the Maker! / Yet he shows no regard for the Power that gave him power. / O how presumptuous is the tyrant who rebels against the Godhead! / Yet the Existent One, who is and ever is, he cannot subdue. / Against the Godhead the rebel rebelled in the loftiness of his spirit, / and against that command which created him he poured out every scorn and contempt. / He calls himself by the name of the Living One, though dead in his sins, / and divinely displays his riches before the eyes of those who behold him. / He said that he is Christ and King, anointed in sin, / and he calls his ministers apostles of righteousness. / He sends demons as heralds to every region, / and they go out sowing the hateful report of the day of his coming. / They cast confused voices into the ears of their hearers, / and there is no hearing that is not troubled by their deeds: / 'The time of mysteries and types, which cried out curses [?], has passed, / and the truth has come that was depicted spiritually in the books. / Arise, come out, receive the truth revealed, you children of the kingdom, / and take the good things that the Good One has promised for your desires. / Cease from meditating on and studying the fulfillment of the mysteries, / and seal up the books of bodily observances. / Why do you need to display types to your minds? / Look, and examine closely the truth itself. / Cease from the toil of righteousness, for great is its toil:

and rest in the harbor [?] of the things to come, hidden in my person.' / O the mouth that speaks unspeakable wickedness! / How it exalts itself and is not ashamed even a little! / O the impudent one, whose nature is more shameless than a dog, / who barks without ceasing and does not perceive at whom he barks! / O the wrestler who wrestles with himself when no one presses him, / and casts strife among those on earth and those in heaven! / The wrathful one stirs up angels and men with his wrath, / and spews his bile upon spiritual and bodily beings alike. / He dwells in a man as he once dwelt in the serpent at the beginning, / and through him he bites mankind as through a viper. / As in a garment he covers his nature with bodiliness, / as he covered himself with the serpent in Eden, and erred and led astray. / The body becomes an instrument for his subtle nature, / and through its members he gives utterance to voices full of wickedness. / He and his legions enter and dwell in an unclean temple, / and through him they receive the worship of iniquity from the wicked. / He invites all his host to dwell in the assembly of his body, / so that the vile ones may come and escort the one viler than they. / He hurries all the demons before him, the demon embodied, / so that they may proclaim the utter deceiver as the genuine one. / All the demons throw the earth into turmoil on the day of his revelation, / so that the fame of his deceit may run swiftly. / Over all and in all they spread the nets of his snares, / so that by his cunning they may hunt the created world for him.

Woe to our nature from our oppressor, how fiercely he contends [?] against us, / leading us astray from the truth while we do not perceive it! / Woe to our race from the robber who lurks beside it, / who robs it and is not detected in his craftiness! / Woe to our kind from the kinsman of the spiritual beings, / who mocks it and delights in his mockery [...] in his mind! / Woe to us from that evil neighbor within our borders, / who wrestles every day and is never sated with wrestling! / Behold, for a little less than six thousand years he has been wrestling, / and once more he has resolved to take away even the ordinances [?] of our life. / He wishes to snatch our life from us at the end of times, / and that Will which called us His image does not permit him. / For this reason he hunts with a man from among us, / so that through our own nature he may catch our nature as in a trap. / That man becomes a trap for that hunter, / and he enters and lurks within our body to hunt us with it. / He saw that through a man the Good One redeemed us from his wickedness, / and behold, he schemes to turn us back to himself through a man. / He saw that he could not fight against us by himself alone, / and he hired men so that through them he might wrestle against our freedom. / In the hand of a man he sharpens the sword of his bitterness, / and he lays waste the ranks of mankind without pity. / He enters and lurks within a visible body, / and through it shoots the arrows of his wrath at the nature of men. / The crafty one does not fight with us openly:

nor does he compel our nature by force to be subject to him. / Through a man he utters crafty words against our freedom, / and like a hunter draws us down into the trap of his deceits. / It is a man who raises his voice on earth and calls to men: / 'I am the man who redeemed mankind, and I redeem again. / Come, take from my hands life [...],' cries the crafty one, / while his gift is death, wholly without end. / He wills our death, and by every pretext longs to kill us, / and had the fence of the command not stood before him, he would have destroyed us. / A hidden command restrains his harsh wrath within a boundary, / and when it lets him loose it restrains him again, so that he does not destroy us. / He lets him loose to accomplish his desire, which thirsted for blood, / and He restrains him to make known His love toward our race. / From our race He sends His command and restrains his wrath, / so that he may see and be put to shame that in our race there is one who goes out to meet him. / He sends one messenger from among us against his wickedness, / and he silences its turbulence by the sound of his words, / like the dawn from the sun that rises suddenly / and drives the darkness of his abominations away from mankind. / Like a mighty warrior the Tishbite goes out to meet him, / and by the power of the Spirit snatches from him the captives of mankind. / By the power of the Spirit the prophet of the Spirit comes at the end, / to go out and fight with the rebel who speaks falsehood. / Spiritually the bodily man fights with the false one, / and shows him that in our body there is the power of the Spirit.

At the time when he supposes he has accomplished his desire among bodily beings, / a bodily man appears [?] and exposes his deceit. / On the day when he reflects that at last he has come to reign over all, / a single man raises the word of his mouth and strips him bare. / From among us a man goes out to meet the one full of boasting, / and grapples with him openly before the eyes of all creatures. / From our camp the Spirit arms a mighty warrior, / and sends him to wage war with his vileness. / Through our body he fought against our freedom and defeated it, / and through our body he too is defeated, and all mock him. / Through the body which he saw being corrupted by his desires, / through that same body Elijah shows him his might. / The body that rebelled against the corruption of greedy death / wages war with the rebel who brought death in. / A great war takes place on earth at the end of times, / in which two bodies wrestle, with two powers [?]. / Truth and falsehood put on armor over their senses, / and hurl the arrows of their words at one another. / The Tishbite is armed with truth from head to foot, / and the son of perdition is wrapped in the form of deceit. / The son of the right hand is clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, / and the son of perdition patches together the loathsome rags of iniquity. / The prophet of truth has put on the helmet of faith, / and the crafty worker has overlaid his head with a plate of falsehood. / The righteous one fights mightily in the name of righteousness:

and the wholly iniquitous one hurls words of lying. / Falsely the evil one fights alongside the evil ones of his company, / and truly the truth conquers by the mouth of Elijah. / Lying is the whole armor of the son of perdition, / and the Spirit girds the preaching of the pure-minded one. / Through the Spirit the prophet of the Spirit cries out like a trumpet, / and the children of spiritual service listen to his voice. / The crafty apostle babbles illusion together with the liars, / and they obey him as that 'left hand,' Eve, obeyed the serpent [?]. / The prophet comes to undo the deceit of the crafty one, / so that his illusion may not take root [?] in the minds of men. / He comes at the end to fulfill what is written, / to turn the hearts of the hard-hearted to understanding. / The voice of the herald of truth sets its seal on the word of truth, / for he first cried out, 'Behold, Elijah has come, and is coming.' / Elijah, he said, is coming to proclaim the way of truth; / it is plain, then, that in him all that is written is sealed. / The chaste one comes to confirm the words of prophecy, / and he toils greatly and exposes the false one openly. / Like an athlete he goes down and stands in the midst of the demons, / and grapples with the strong one and his hosts. / All the demons grapple with him in a harsh struggle, / and he alone against them all, and they do not overcome his might. / The power of the Spirit strengthens his body and the movements of his soul, / and he does not slacken in the struggle for his Lord.

That commandment which gave him victory in the war against the priests of Baal / gives him victory also in the battle with the rebel. / For this reason power was given him in the days of Ahab: / to mark out the way for that victory at the end. / The sword he wielded against the priests of Baal was a pledge / that this sword is going to take vengeance on the camp of the demons. / The command that chose him for prophecy depicted in him a mystery: / that he is going to fulfill the truth of his words through deeds. / In a mystery the prophet of truth killed the prophets of falsehood, / that as it was then, so it would be at the end of times. / With his own hands he slaughtered the worshipers of demons, to the shame of the demons, / and through him the master of deceit too is exposed. / The righteous one exposes the deceit of that deceiver, / and makes him loathsome before angels and men. / At the height of his deceit he fights with him, / and accuses him of deceitfully pouring out scorn in fury [?]. / He alone shames the boasting of his tyranny, / and makes known to him the power of the Creator placed in our nature. / The Creator looked upon his evil nature from the beginning, / and beforehand placed in us the power of His help to fight with him. / Through Elijah our whole race fights with him, / and condemns his might through our weakness. / He holds the chaste one's form before him like a target, / and empties all his arrows into it, and does not harm him. / All the demons encamp against him [?] together with the son of perdition:

and not one of their crafty devices reaches him. / A great wonder is the war that the Tishbite wages, / that he alone, against thousands, does not slacken. / Worthy of wonder is the power of the Godhead that strengthens him, / that one man prevails over so many. / How mighty, then, is that help in his members, / that the demons, possessors of power, cannot harm him! / How firm is the mind and the word of the bodily man's mouth, / which silences the turbulent voices of that camp! / Come, let us marvel at that struggle before it takes place, / so that when it comes we may not be weakened by the harshness of its report. / Come, let us wonder with discernment at the man from among us / who wages war with spirits harder than himself. / Come, let us examine closely the armor upon him, / which is stronger than ranks of warriors and is not diminished. / Who ever saw a man like Elijah, / whom thousands of demons surround and cannot harm? / Who has considered the man who conquered greedy death, / and turned his trampling even upon the crafty one who brought death in? / Death and the evil one are put to shame before the son of mortals, / and cannot trample the greatness of the rank in which he is honored. / A great disaster falls suddenly upon Satan / when he sees him coming in strength against his host. / Blows [?] strike his hosts at the sound of his words, / when they hear him raise his voice against their ranks.

It is not the voice of the mortal man that the wicked fear,
but the power hidden within his words.
Great mourning comes upon the children of darkness
when they look upon the light in the words of this mortal man.
On the day of his victory the abject are defeated by a son of the lowly,
and they marvel at him, how he [?] their [?].
All of them together join in league against one man,
and lend one another aid, yet cannot overcome one man.
One man I have called Elijah the Tishbite,
and the other I have named the son of perdition, who destroys utterly.
Man against man they wage war, one against the other:
the prophet by [?], and the son of perdition by the power of Satan.
For that man who comes to deceive is a man,
and through his hands the hater of mankind carries out the deceptions that bear his name.
Without a man he cannot deceive mankind;
for this reason he chooses a man for wickedness, to do evil through him.
Great wickedness he works through the hands of that man,
and for the deeds and the works of his hands he is called to account.
Harsh iniquity his mouth belches against the Divine Being,
and with his lips he blasphemes the Name that is holier than all.
The holy Name he seeks to snatch, the unclean one of the unclean;
the worship due the Lord he longs to receive, the servant of servants.
Into the holy temple he enters and sits, that dwelling of demons,
and he speaks and says: “I, I am the Christ and the Son of God.”
His ministers, too, cry this out wickedly:

“This is God!” — [?] from the master and from his disciples.
In the name of God he goes astray and leads astray those who stray after him,
and, hating Him, he hides beneath His name the hatred of his soul.
The hateful one seeks to appear fair in the guise of the Pure One — not that he may become fair,
but that by his own hideousness he may make the comeliness of His beauty hateful.
The hateful one does not make the Good, who never changes, hateful;
it is himself he makes hateful by acting with presumption.
It is presumption for a servant to snatch the name of the Maker,
and utter wickedness for fashioned clay to despise its Fashioner.
Against his Fashioner the accursed one speaks accursedly,
and to the accursed one he gives the rank of headship.
The crafty one, the prince of the air, he calls the head of all things,
and to him he declares due the worship of men — to the murderer of men.
The murderer of men it is who guides him, that destroyer of life,
and he spurs him on to slay men with the sword of iniquity.
The sword of iniquity is gripped in the hand of one full of iniquity,
and he lays waste the ranks of mankind wickedly.
In the guise of peace he steals peace, he who hates peace,
and like a medicine of life he sows his word in the ears of men.
He proclaims peace on the day of his revelation, he who is clothed in envy,
and in the likeness of a friend he shows the face of falsehood.
All the teachings that were sown on earth the defiled one abolishes,
and then turns and builds the edifice of his falsehood with cunning.
Skilfully he sets up his great teaching of error,
and no one knows how to see through it, so skilful it is.

He abolishes priests, and fasts and prayers too,
and compels men to sacrifice their wills to him.
He deposes kings and removes the orders of rule,
and he alone calls himself king and lord.
Beneath his lordship he yokes the necks of the freeborn,
and they offer him their thoughts in place of tribute.
A crown of praises they plait and set on the head of the accursed one,
and they crown him as a king with their words.
The righteous alone do not bow beneath his authority,
nor are they swayed by the clamour of the crafty one’s tumults.
Tens of thousands of snares he hides deep to catch them,
and by every stratagem he strives to catch the righteous.
The accursed one stirs up the men of his party against the righteous,
and through his ministers he shoots arrows at the servants of truth.
Through the nations he wages war against the just,
and through visible members he oppresses the upright.
Through a body the bodiless one makes war on those who have bodies,
and with the sword of speech he lays waste the possessors of speech.
A great war he wages against all who do not submit to him,
until he hears that voice which destroys him.
He marshals battle against everyone who does not confess him,
until he is put to shame by the command that rules over all.
Above all he exalts himself, and at all he scoffs, haughty of mind,
until the King who is over all [?] and exposes him.
To every region flies the report of his turmoil,

until the hosts on high cry out and ask about him.
In every corner he spreads the snares of his cunning,
until he sees the heavenly ones coming forth to meet him.
On earth he lingers, goes astray and leads the earthly astray,
until the ensign shines out in [?] and he trembles before it.
He and Elijah wage war one against the other
until the appointed term of the span of time is fulfilled.
In this contest the righteous man holds out against the wicked one,
until the hidden sign opens the gates of the height.
In this battle the True One is engaged with the deceiver,
until the throne is made ready that is fit to judge all.
In this struggle earthly and heavenly beings are engaged,
until one command brings rest to all the ranks.
Watchers and men cry out together in their thoughts,
longing for the war against iniquity to be ended.
The righteous and the chaste bear the excessive weight of suffering,
and more than anyone they are pained by the wickedness of the evil one.
Harsh pangs strike their thoughts every hour,
and like a woman in labour they wait for the coming [?] of the raising of the dead.
Heaven and [earth?] and all that is in them are clothed in mourning,
waiting for the coming of that renewal which does not change.
Like a dead woman creation weeps for her own self,
waiting for the day she will live that life which does not perish.
Like a corpse her suffering is laid before her gates,
and she gazes upon Him, waiting for the day she will see Him in new life.

A sound of groaning rises from every mouth on earth,
and the dumb creatures weep bitterly over the one endowed with speech.
All of them alike look together to one hope,
until they find rest; [?] they are not comforted.
They long to hear the sound of that last trumpet,
and [?] they are not consoled from their grief.
They have only heard [?] that it is to sound at the end,
but the day of its sounding is hidden and concealed from all creatures.
The One alone knows the day on which it will be heard,
He in whom is hidden the hidden will that reveals all.
He, with the Hidden One, knows the day of its revelation,
and when He wills, He reveals His power and displays it.
Until the number of the years of the span of time, His sign tarries,
until it is complete; and so He fulfils the promise of His words.
Suddenly He dawns, like [?], upon the inhabited world,
and covers height and depth with the light of His words.
A great light beyond telling flashes from Him,
and light becomes as no light beside His light.
He opens the height by His descent, and so descends,
and calls the hosts on high to escort Him in procession.
All of them together gather to Him from every place,
and escort Him with a love befitting the greatness of His rank.
Thousands upon thousands cry His praise without satiety,
and myriads upon myriads recount His praise without ceasing.
Praise and holiness they all bear in their every movement,

and they offer Him a crown of victory befitting His name.
“Blessed is the Victor!” all the ranks cry to the ranks,
and they shake the earth with the sound of their “Holy.”
“Praised is He who has smitten all!” cry the orders of their companies,
and they strike the world with awe at the wonder of their words.
Great wonder fills the [?] of their beauty,
and no mouth can recount its intensity.
Fearful indeed is the sight of the face in which it appears,
and the light of fleshly eyes is too weak to look upon it.
Flashes of light go forth from the fiery beings,
and sight [?] at gazing on the power of their faces.
Fear and love fill their aspect and the sound of their speech:
fear for the wicked and goodness for the good — blessed is he who loves!
Blessings and woes [?] in the guise in which they appear:
blessings for the righteous, and woes for those who sinned — woe to those who did not repent!
Good tidings of the renewal of all they sow on the earth,
and as with seeds they gather bodies to the threshing floor of life.
Before the person of the One Person they gather and stand,
waiting for Him to exercise His power through their authority.
Beneath His authority all are yoked as beneath a yoke,
and the taste of His name is sweeter to them than to every other mouth.
On the chariot of the Spirit sits the King of kings,
and yoked to it are thousands of spirits without number.
[?] number to the hosts that escort Him,
and [?] to the sound of the “Holy” with which they hallow Him.

In great glory He shows Himself to the eyes of all creatures,
and men and heavenly beings give praise with His praise.
The ensign of His suffering and of His victory goes before Him,
and how greatly creation is lifted up in wonder at the Crucified Man!
At that hour the demons are put to shame, together with the crucifiers,
when they see the ensign which they mocked when it was held up to scorn.
In great amazement demons and Jews stand,
gazing at the Man they crucified, now reigning over all.
A groan of anguish falls suddenly upon Satan,
for the Name that he blasphemed, heaven and earth cry its praise.
Harsh is the mourning, beyond consolation, for the son of perdition,
who perishes utterly before the eyes of angels and men.
A fearful voice proclaims to him the Name he denied,
and denies him life in his soul and his body.
Wholly and entirely the wicked one whom He destroys perishes,
and no remnant [?] of him remains among the immortals.
One cry Christ the King shouts at him,
and he is [?] wholly, and the pride of his crafty master is put to shame.
A new thing watchers and men behold on the day of his destruction,
and they marvel greatly at the power of the Maker, whose power can do all.
A new thing the Lord shows His servants in the work of His hands:
though something was able, He makes it as nothing.
From nothing He created all things as it pleased Him,
and as it pleases Him He turns something into nothing.
Fittingly did You bring all things into being from nothing,

and fittingly You destroy the son of perdition without pity.
The Good One makes rational nature wise through his destruction,
that it ought to keep the order of its creaturehood.
The presumptuous one went outside the order of creaturehood;
for this He destroys him and banishes him from life.
Double mourning comes upon his master through his destruction,
and harsh punishment is added to him by the ruin of his life.
Better would it have been for him, too, to perish utterly with his disciple,
and not to be harshly tormented without end.
Wisely the will of his Creator dealt with him,
and no one knows how to tell how great is the tenderness of His love.
Great love, full of deeds, is that which He wrought there,
in that He does not consume the company of the wicked as He did that one.
In destroying one He shows that He is just and merciful too,
for as He destroyed one, He could have destroyed many as well.
Not for destruction did He will the destruction of the son of perdition,
but that His justice and His kindness might be revealed.
Both He makes known to both parties, the good and the wicked:
that while the Good is good, justice too is mingled with His goodness.
By the Good every rebellion against the knowledge of Him is punished,
and those who know His love know only how to praise Him.
Fittingly He chastises those who hate the riches of His kindness,
and fittingly He gains those who keep the mystery of His faith.
[?] just judgment examines iniquity and righteousness,
and sets rational beings before His sign with their deeds.

Into the furnace of testing He brings all through one Man,
and through His hands gives blessing to the good and punishment to the wicked.
For this He set Him apart from the beginning of His fashioning,
that through Him the ranks of the just and the wicked might be divided.
For this He appointed Him when He formed Him without wedlock,
that through Him He might renew creation, grown old in mortality.
His sign renews all creation through His mediation,
and makes her wise to know herself and her Maker.
Like a handmaid He sets her before Him on the day of His revelation,
and she escorts Him with a voice of praise beyond attaining.
The whole world with its inhabitants He brings out to meet Him,
to plait for His name a crown of praises befitting His name.
The holy Name of the Offspring who is from Him, hidden in His appearance —
by it He is hallowed by spirits and by bodies.
Glorious is His revelation, and beyond telling the sight of His body,
and the mouth of those endowed with speech is too small to say how great it is.
Thousands of watchers and angels bear His ensign,
and escort Him and glory in Him as is fitting.
On the face of the height they stand ready, appearing,
and they receive Him with the pure voices of their “Holy.”
Like the [sun] He dawns from on high upon the face of the earth,
and the world shines with the rays of the greatness of His light.
The sun sets, and the moon hides, and its rays as well,
and the course of the morning star and its fellows ceases.
The air rests from the motion of its lightness,

and the sea rests from the turbulent tumult of its waves.
The dumb creatures return to the dust from which they came,
and the world becomes as it was at the beginning of its being.
The nature of rational beings alone remains and is not destroyed,
and it alone enters the furnace where His creature is tested.
For the testing [?] of all, the Judge of all comes at the end,
and cries on the earth a single cry full of [?].
To the four quarters His voice runs like a messenger,
and creation shakes off its heaviness as from sleep.
The power of life He sows in the earth by the word of His mouth,
and the dust stirs and acquires senses for its sensing members.
Like seeds, bodies spring up from the dust,
and the aspect of their minds shines brighter than the sun.
Every body returns to life that knows no death,
and not even the smallest portion of a hair is forgotten in it.
Whole and entire it rises together, every limb that had fallen,
and not so much as a leaf of it remains in the earth.
The sign of its Fashioner [?] dust from within the dust,
and assembles it with skill, so that it will perish no more.
He holds judgment with Satan and Death on man’s behalf,
and demands of them the reckoning for his disgrace and his subjection.
Into the prison of darkness He casts the demons who trampled him,
and with chains of flame He binds the wicked.
His enemies He binds, and sets on their mouths the muzzle [?] of silence,
but man He releases from the chains of mortality.

In the waters of mercy He washes off the filth upon his limbs,
and adorns him with the robe of glory that never decays.
Corruption and death He scours from him who was corruptible,
and in place of the body He makes his body fly to the height above.
At his glory the spiritual assemblies marvel,
how heavy nature flies, though it was never used to it.
He too marvels at himself without satiety,
by what power his feebleness has gained the power of flight.
And the nature of mortals says to its own nature:
“Am I that same nature, or is this perhaps another in exchange?”
If it could have reasoned, it would already have reasoned it out;
but its unknowing cannot be uprooted.
He who raises its mortality [?] from the dust
strengthens it so that it does not waver over its transformation.
With its renewal it gains a power stronger than all,
and sufferings cannot gain mastery over its thoughts.
At the greatness of the power given to it I too marvelled,
and turned my word from its course toward its greatness.
Over the story of the erring one my thoughts were stirred from the beginning,
and I wished to meditate on the tale of the son of perdition.
Against his pride I wished to arm myself with weapons of words,
but when I saw that he would be exposed, I rested from him.
I wished to tell of the loftiness of his spirit with the voice of my words,
but first I looked at the end of his fall, how harsh it is.
At the presumption of the lawless one I marvelled greatly,

and at his endless torment I was utterly amazed.
His [?] urged me to recount his craftiness,
but my heart turned away from it at the sentence of judgment prepared for him.
Before the harshness of his punishments my word was blunted by their harshness,
and I said to myself: Who am I, to speak ill of the wicked one who has perished?
Let us then leave aside the indictment of the one who was indicted,
and resolve within ourselves not to grow slack in the war against him.
A great war he is about to wage against us;
come, let us forge for ourselves armour strong against his tyranny.
Arrows of wrath he makes ready to shoot at the camp of our race;
let us hold before our faces the shield of [?] faith.
With the sword of his malice he longs to destroy the life of our life;
let us set the helmet of good hope upon the head of our mind.
With the spear of his fury he has resolved to uproot the building of our soul;
let us put on love as a breastplate, so that we do not grow slack.
In every art it has been made plain to us how we may conquer;
come, let us arm ourselves, so that the arrows of the evil one do not wound us.
The end. Glory to Your power, our Saviour, by which You conquered the Accuser.
Another: You who make wars cease from the ends of the earth, make the wars of the crafty one cease from us.
On the Revelation of Our Lord
Twenty-Third Homily: On the Revelation of Our Lord and on the Way of Life of the World to Come

The good hope of the world to come has worn out my mind, / and I have sought to know when the world of time will end. / Time hinted to me about that world which brings the times to their end: / “Look, O man, how the world gives way to the world.” / Swiftly the world of time gives way to the world, / and there is no lingering between the one and the other, not even for a moment. / Like a shadow the world that is full of time passes away, / and the timeless world, in which there is no toil, endures. / There is no toil in the world that comes at the end of times, / no trading, nor any wearying over gain. / Without end is the world that carries the toiler across into the world, / and without limit is the span of the life that is bound up in it. / There is no reckoning the course of that life and the years of its living, / since there is not even a counting of days by sun and moon. / There is but one day, in which that way of life is brought to ruin, / and no change brings to an end the course of its perpetuity. / On its perpetuity, which is without end, my thoughts have pondered, / and they have risen to tell of the breadth of that which knows no end. / It brings this earthly way of life to its completion, / and gives rest to the weariness of heavenly and earthly beings. / It is a great harbour full of peace, in which there is no fear, / and in it the ship of the world, which toils have worn out, comes to rest. / Wearing toil has worn out the world and its inhabitants, / and see, it longs to rest its weariness in the harbour of peace. / Of that world which gives rest to the weary I long to speak,

and I long to reveal in words the kinds of its story. / The kinds of its story I hasten to reveal to men, / so that they may picture the beauty of its love in their minds. / The mind can picture an image that has no composition, / and the intellect can see what is not revealed to the eyes of flesh. / Of unrevealed things I tell in revealed words: / come, listeners, hear hidden things by means of revealed things. / Come, hear the account of the world that ends the world of time, / and reveals hidden things and shows them to the eye of those who see. / Come, consider the day that is the end of days, / and grants no other day to come after its day. / Come, gaze well upon the fitting beauty of its glories, / which is wondrous and glorious, and adorns men with the fitness of its beauty. / Listen carefully, like the discerning, to the report concerning it: / when it comes and how it comes, in great order. / A great order comes about on the day of the great day: / the world ends, and a world dawns in which there is no toil. / World for world the day of that revelation exchanges, / and no other day will ever come that resembles its day. / The greatness of its day our Lord also revealed in the revelation of His words: / that its day is more fearful than all the days that have been and are. / The powers on high are shaken by it, as it is written, / and they honour it as a day beyond all comparison. / The King’s standard is borne by the chief of the ranks of the heavenly ones, / and it shows the victory of His power to the eye of all creatures. / Before the One on high the hosts on high stand ready / to receive the King on high with great splendour. / Before these things, it is said, things will happen on earth, / and so that revelation which reveals hidden things will be shown. / There will be wars and earthquakes, famines and pestilences, / and men will lay waste to men in their strife. / Iniquity increases, falsehood prospers, sin grows strong, / love shrinks, and hope and faith come to an end.

Openly falsehood, the most abhorrent of falsehoods, triumphs, / and condemns the truth that is plain among the true. / An evil time is found evil, matching its own evil, / and helps the Evil One to fulfil the purpose of his bitterness. / All his will the deceiver belches out before the deceived, / and he deceives and leads astray up to the day of his time. / In a known time the time of that deceiver is fixed, / so that he may not boast that his own will establishes his deceit. / The power of the Creator brings him forth at the end of times, / and brings into the open that scheme which had been hidden in him. / The evil of his wickedness the God of all brings to light, / and shows it to the eye of earthly and heavenly beings. / For this reason He does not restrain him from his evil: / that everyone may know how evil is the wickedness of the deceiver. / The evil of his wickedness slew our race from the beginning, / and he has drawn out his wrath until the time of the end of times. / At that time the herald, the apostle Paul, looked ahead, / and revealed and examined the hidden mystery of his iniquity. / The mystery of iniquity the truthful one laid open, exposing falsehoods, / and showed that wickedness is destined to be revealed through a man. / Through a man the slayer of men fulfils his desire, / in the same manner in which he went astray and led astray in the place of Eden. / The hater of man chooses a man from humanity, / and speaks through him, as the Creator did through the Man who is from us. / Into a temple of flesh the accursed mind enters and dwells, / in imitation of the Word of the Father in the temple of our body. / In a man the Evil One conceals wholly the evil of his wickedness, / and in that very man he seizes the rank of the Creator’s name. /
