With the Creator’s name the evil servant names himself, / and he presumes to say, “I am the Messiah, the renewer of worlds.” / This blasphemy Paul, the excellent hearer, had heard, / and he foretold it before the blasphemer had blasphemed. / The sound of his blasphemies the sects of every doctrine hear, / and they acclaim him as the great master of falsehood. / To the four quarters the report of his falsehood goes out, / and his hunters catch distinct peoples of every tongue.

In every form of falsehood he speaks with them, / and eagerly they listen to the words of his lying. / Crafty schemes he contrives and hides before their eyes, / and with the death of the snare he scatters words full of wickedness. / Kinds of false signs he displays on earth, / and by illusions and the bewitching of eyes he establishes his deceit. / All his desire the deceiver fulfils upon the deceived, / until the Tishbite goes out to do battle with him. / The Tishbite goes out to meet the son of perdition, / and carries through the contest in the power of the Spirit. / The Spirit arms the man of flesh with the armour of the Spirit, / and sends him to wage war with Satan. / Men and heavenly beings watch in great astonishment / as demons and men contend against one man. / He alone takes up the fight against many, / and the warriors are defeated by him in their contests. / Like an athlete he goes down and stands among their ranks, / and lifts up his voice, and the hosts of the Evil One tremble at him. / Creation becomes a stadium for his athletic struggle, / and the world gathers to see the combat of one against thousands. / In the midst of the theatre of the contest he stands at the centre, / and earthly and heavenly beings gaze upon him. / Oh, the spiritual contest that takes place on earth, / in which thousands of spirits are defeated and men triumph! / Oh, the victory that comes about in a world full of sins, / in which truth triumphs and the party of error and her children are defeated! / Oh, that voice which the righteous one cries out before the wicked, / at which the hostile throngs of demons and men tremble! / Like a sword the word of the Tishbite flashes, / and the hater flees and cannot stand firm before his sayings. / Sharp arrows are his words, full of zeal, / and they tear apart the camp of demons that surrounds him. / Thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads gaze upon him,

and they flee and hide like foxes in their holes. / A fearsome battle he wages with the hosts of the Evil One, / until the King on high dawns and comes to his help. / The King on high looks out from the height of His kingdom, / and by His [?] brings the embattled world to its completion. / Like lightning His light dawns among the earthly, / and creation beholds and sees a new sight. / A new sight men and heavenly beings behold: / the gates on high opening before His revelation. / The trumpet-call of the heavenly beings sounds suddenly, / and the world cannot bear to hear the voices of their “Holy.” / Thunders of voices are all of them, as many as they are, / and they honour the King who reigns over their ranks. / Great order and a fearful vision are displayed on earth, / and the gaze of their minds hangs upon the command. / They long for the King’s command and are counted worthy to fulfil His words, / and the word of His mouth is sweeter to them than all good things. / By the word of His mouth He makes an end of the deceiver, the son of perdition, / and destroys and blots him out completely, body and soul. / Utter destruction that man receives suddenly, / and he perishes utterly, wholly, from life. / Great disgrace the demons see in his destruction, / as the breath of life is taken away from the life of the soul. / In astonishment and amazement creation stands at that hour, / and the pangs of the labour of the new birth confound it. / The trumpet-call shakes the earth and its inhabitants, / and after them all comes a fearful voice that commands them to rise. / In one instant the King over all cries out suddenly, / and all things are renewed and changed swiftly. / First all the dead rise from the dust, / and then the living, who are alive, are changed into that likeness. / In a single glance the dead rise and the living live, / and there is no interval between the one and the other, not even a moment. / A single moment raises the dead and gives life to the living, / and in that one sight the righteous and the wicked rise. / Good and evil alike the command that rules over all raises up,

and so they are separated one from another in the testing of judgment. / The testing of judgment separates the righteous from the wicked, / and treads out a way to the kingdom on high and to Gehenna. / In a small moment all the things of that day come about, / and the swiftness with which it is accomplished cannot be told. / There is no likeness to the swiftness of that command, / except the likeness of that [?] by which the worlds came to be. / That command which created creation from nothing / is the one that commands and renews it in the twinkling of an eye. / In the same manner in which He commanded and it came to be from nothing, / He commands it to become something better out of something. / Better is the renewal He works for it at the end of times / than the establishment He wrought for it at the beginning of times. / That greatness at the beginning is as nothing / when compared with the glory at the end. / Its end is more glorious than its beginning beyond measure, / and the nature of its glory cannot be told by those who speak. / He alone knows how both of them came about, / and in Him was hidden the coming-to-be of the world and the renewal of the worlds. / Seen by Him were the things that came to be, and how they would come to be, / and their renewal at the end was also depicted before Him. / Great order He kept in their coming-to-be and in their renewal, / and the mouth of His creatures is too small to tell how great He is. / He alone knows the things that are and those that are to come, / and they existed out of His being, which has no beginning. / Without beginning they were hidden in Him while not yet created, / and He created them and renews them as it pleased Him. / It pleased Him, and He showed His love toward His creatures, / that by their establishment and their renewal His power might be proclaimed. / From His creatures His creatures learned about His hiddenness, / and had He not created, His works would not have known His power. / I did not say this because He was in need, that they did not know,

but because there were no works to bear witness to His greatness. / His power He showed by His working to the work of His hands, / that from His fashioning they might learn His love toward what He fashioned. / For the benefit of His handiwork He did this, that He made us, turned to us, and renewed us, / so that through both it might learn the power hidden in His labour. / The greatness of His love He revealed in our coming-to-be and our renewal, / and He taught us how bound His love is to the work of His hands. / To the work of His hands He revealed His will, first and last, / and from His own labour He made a mediator toward His creatures. / Through the mediation of one man He renewed the world, / not because He was in need, but to magnify what is His by what is His. / He magnified what is His by what is His, one out of all, / and through His hands He renewed the world that had decayed in mortality. / Mortality wore out the work of Him who fashions all, / and by a mortal He renewed the world that had died in sin. / One mortal He chose from the whole nature of mortals, / and made him lord over earthly and heavenly beings. / His own image He [?] upon the nature of man when He fashioned him, / and now He has given him the exalted name of His divinity. / In His name he comes at the end to renew all things, / and by the might of his power he turns all toward the knowledge of Him. / He silences the name of error among mortals, / and brings to an end the demons’ battle against the truth. / He abolishes the Antichrist, the chief of the deceivers, / and no longer does he err and lead men astray by his struggling. / It is He who opens the gates on high on the day of His revelation, / and draws after Him the whole rational nature. / It is He who tests the good and the evil by the decree of His judgment, / and gives reward according to deeds, whether good or evil. / It is He who makes that separation between the one and the other, / and one is exalted and the other sinks into the pit below. / Two, then, will be at the same labour,

and they are separated suddenly from one another in the twinkling of an eye. / Oh, how fearful is the fearful hour of that separation, / and there is no comparison that resembles its fearfulness! / Oh, how hateful is the hideous sight of those left behind on earth, / and nothing is as hideous as the hideousness of their persons! / Oh, how harsh is the remorse of mind by which they are judged, / and there is no one to comfort, nor to offer words of persuasion! / Harsh is the punishment with which they are punished in body and spirit, / and its punishment is harsher than all punishments that are inflicted. / Weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth and the sound of groaning, / fire beyond nature [?], the worm that does not [?], and the darkness that does not [?]: / these, it is said, are what punish the party of the wicked, / and if the truth be told, the punishment is worse even than these. / How is it not bitter for the wicked who did not turn from wickedness, / when the gates on high are shut before their faces? / How is it not bitter, as they gaze at the company of the righteous / flying through the air, while they sink into the depth of the earth? / The earth becomes the dwelling place of the children of earth, / and they weep and wail, who have been left out of the bliss of the heavenly ones. / The bliss of the good they see at every moment in their minds, / and they long for it, and the desire within them is never fulfilled. / From them and within them springs remorse over their sins, / and they become the judges of their own thoughts. / The mind within them multiplies their punishments, / and as they are punished, they are punished again without end. / Their minds become a fountain of punishments there, / and flow at every moment upon their persons without ceasing. / With discernment they ponder it discerningly, / and they reproach their hideousness without ever being sated. / That knowledge which the good possess in the dwelling above / is the very one the sinners also possess in the dwelling of the earth. / They are equal in knowledge, since their resurrection too is equal,

and there is no difference in their minds’ love of the good. / There is no difference, neither in resurrection nor in knowledge, / for alike they rise and alike they know the kinds of wisdom. / Only in place are the companies separated from one another, / and the wicked are not permitted to mingle with the good. / Inequality has separated them from equality, / and stripped them of the delight that is with the righteous. / Their deeds have estranged them from the blessings of the good, / and they were not worthy to be heirs of heaven. / On earth remain the earthly, who loved the earth, / and the righteous, who longed for heaven, become heavenly. / Up to heaven ascend the righteous, the lovers of truth, / to where Christ is, the King of righteousness. / Christ the King does these things on the day of His revelation, / and it is He who gives gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked. / In Him things unrevealed and hidden are revealed, / and the testing of His judgment shows to each the kinds of his deeds. / Naked and exposed stands the whole nature of rational beings, / and there is no thought that is not revealed and laid bare before His testing. / A furnace of testing is the day of His revelation, / and it chooses and rejects as the testing of His just judgment does. / In one instant a voice is heard on earth before all creatures, / and creation is startled as if from a heavy sleep. / The voice of His command the senseless dead hear, / and they strip off the garment of mortality and acquire life. / Life without corruption corruptible bodies acquire, / and the suffering of death no longer comes near their limbs. / Suddenly the nature of mortals becomes immortal, / and it marvels at itself because of the renewal it suddenly acquires. / The Son of Adam raises up the whole human nature, / and the dead and the living put on the garment of immortality. / All the senses of the dead body acquire life, / and not one of its members is left behind in Sheol.

That very body which fell and decayed in mortality / is the one that rises and acquires immortal life. / That very soul which put on the body and did all things through it / is the one that returns and dwells in it without change. / In body and spirit the whole man rises entire, / and in his members and the movements of his soul he is repaid for the wrong he did. / In the very nature in which he worked the good and did the hateful, / in that he receives gifts of glory or abundant punishments. / In that same composition of body and soul, / body and soul are renewed with all that they acquired. / In the same manner in which Christ, the head of our life, rose, / so the visible body and the hidden soul rise. / In body and soul our Life-giver and Renewer rose, / and by His resurrection He drew for us the pattern of the day of our renewal. / This too is the reason for the resurrection of the firstfruits of our life: / to confirm us in the hope of immortal life. / For just as through Adam we became mortal, / so again in the second Adam we become immortal. / The second Adam trod out for us the way to new life, / and He first opened the door of the kingdom on high. / Into the kingdom on high our firstfruits entered in body and spirit, / and He promised us that we would enter with Him as He entered. / For this reason He descends to us at the end of times: / to raise our race to where His kingdom is. / Like the sun the light of the day of His revelation dawns, / and covers the light of the sun with the greatness of His light. / The powers on high run through the air before His coming, / and honour Him as the King who reigns over all. / He is King over all because the King gave Him His rank, / and as Creator He creates creation a second time, new. / With the power of the Creator the second Adam creates creation— / not to create it, but to give rest to what was created. / Great rest He gives to rational beings and to dumb creatures, / and they are no longer worn down by the wearing of this world.

There the kinds of passions of body and soul cease, / and they no longer desire the hateful desire of hideous things. / There the kinds of passions of body and soul cease, / and they no longer desire the hateful desire of hideous things. / There the harsh war of the tyrannical demons ceases and is ended, / and they no longer err and lead men astray in the mystery of error. / There insatiable death ceases from swallowing, / and sin no longer tramples man with the sting of iniquity. / There the nature of mortals mocks death and the Evil One, / and men say, “Where is your sting, insatiable death?” / There equality comes about between the Watchers and men, / and they are not held back from the confession of the one Creator. / One confession, without division, they confess there, / and three times they repeat the “Holy” in their minds: / one Being, which is three at every moment, / and as often as they repeat it, they repeat it again without ever being sated. / Through the Mediator who is from us their heart repeats its thanksgiving, / and with the Being they count Him also in name and in rank. / It is He who comes to do these things that have no end, / and as Mediator He fulfils the order of the hidden nature. / It is not the Being that comes to us by moving, / since it has no kind of movement from place to place. / It is not the Creator who judges those being judged, / but Christ, who also received all judgment. / It is He who comes by moving from place to place, / and opens the door of the Holy of Holies before those who enter. / All creation gazes upon Him when He appears, / and glorifies Him together with that Power which gave Him glory. / Glorious is His revelation, exalted His examination, and proven His judgment, / and the mouth of all creation is too small to recount His praise. / In the wonder of His glory men and spiritual beings are enlightened: / how He commands and renews all things in a small moment. / In a small moment He commands the earth, and she gives birth to men, / like that moment when He commanded her in the beginning and she bore Adam. / The voice of His command every soul hears, wherever it is,

and turns back and enters the temple of the body from which it went out.
It too is like that command by which He breathed it into Adam,
and He gathers it from every quarter into the limbs.
It too is like that command by which He breathed it into Adam,
and He gathers it from every quarter into the limbs.
Body and soul He joins together and forms a single human being,
in the very shape in which man came to be at the beginning of time.
Complete and perfect does the whole of nature become,
by that perfection with which the Anointed One too was perfected.
In Him, in Christ, all things are renewed and all are made perfect,
and He subjects all things beneath the authority of His headship.
In His hands the hidden will reigns over all and in all,
and there is no mind in which the fear of truth does not dwell.
To the divine will He turns everything,
and makes it ready for the side of the good, for the kingdom on high.
Into the kingdom on high He brings with Him Watchers and men,
all those who loved the day of His divine revelation.
On earth the wicked among men and the raving demons remain,
as they are called to account for the debt of the sins they sinned, and are brought low.
Neither mortal nor subject to suffering are any of them,
the children of the kingdom and the children of the earth alike.
In this alone are the wicked equal with the good:
that they put off mortality and the passions.
There the passion of the soul and the desire of the body cease,
and the spring of shameful things dries up in its course.
One spring wells up from the whole of humanity:
love of mankind and perfect love toward the Creator.
One Creator do they all call upon there alike,
and they contemplate in Him Three in One and One in Three.
There the good and the wicked learn the book with skill,
and they expound the power of the Creator in His work of creating.
Truly all things come to be through our renewal,
for in the creation of the immortals there is nothing that is lacking.
Only one thing is lacking to them alike, and nothing else at all:

the great boundary between the righteous and the sinners.
A great boundary marks off the two sides there,
and no one can cross the abyss of its depth.
There is a mountain stretched out from the earth to the face of the heights,
and its distance cannot be measured by surveyors.
At its distance the mind of earthly beings is astonished;
they gaze at it and cannot cross its great boundary.
A crushing longing constantly crushes their minds,
as they yearn and the longing within them is never fulfilled.
This is the longing that torments them more than any torment:
that they see glory and do not draw near to the gate of glory.
O how great is the glory of the glorified,
and how base the baseness of the shame of the tormented!
O how bitter is that torment of Gehenna,
and how sweet that delight of the kingdom on high!
O how hideous the hideous sight of the children of darkness,
and how fair the fair sight of the children of light!
O how harsh is that sentence, "Go to Gehenna,"
and how beloved that one, "Come, receive the kingdom on high!"
O for that hour when the just are separated from the wicked,
and one is lifted up and one sinks down: it is a great calamity!
A fearful calamity falls suddenly upon the sinners
when they gaze upon the flight that the just obtain.
It is a great wonder how crushing labours
make wings of flight sprout for those who perform them.
Wings of the Spirit the just obtain on the day of resurrection,
and like spiritual beings they fly through the air to the face of the heights.
Spiritually they journey on the spiritual way,
and this is the wonder: suddenly they obtain flight.
It is a great wonder, and its wondrousness cannot be told:
that though the good and the wicked are one, they are not one.
One is the nature of the good and the wicked on the day of resurrection;
and what is this, that out of it one flies and one remains behind?
Wickedness is the cause of this separation of one from another,
and it sinks a man to the side of the wicked, into the abyss of wickedness.

Righteousness it is that gives the just their flight,
and by it chaste bodies are lifted to the height above.
Sin it is that binds the limbs of those who are not true,
so that they do not run on the way of the kingdom on high with their companions.
Because of it the weight of wickedness has torn them away from justice
and sunk them in the hateful abyss of their deeds.
As if from sleep, the good and the wicked rise up there,
and they marvel and wonder at the swiftness of that separation.
All of them put off the weight of the body and the passions of the soul,
and though they do put them off, the likeness of their persons is not the same.
Their appearance itself distinguishes them from their fellows,
and by it they learn the kinds of conduct of good and wicked.
There they learn the kinds of good deeds and of shameful ones,
and there is no one who needs to ask or to learn the course of another's life.
On the limbs are spread the garments of the soul's labours,
and from what is revealed each one learns the kinds of hidden things.
The testing of judgment brings deeds and words to light,
and, as in words, men gaze at the blemishes that are on them.
Their blemishes judge them along with the guilty,
and condemn them together with the debts of their own selves.
O how exact is that testing which tests all things,
so that even the guilty justify His judgment, that His judgment is true!
O for that power which strengthens mortal nature
to know itself and to recount its blemishes before the eyes of the onlookers!
O for the wisdom that teaches men through the renewal of men,
and makes wise the childishness of men with the wisdom of truth!
The wisdom of truth it is that makes them wise by the power of its wisdom,
and it teaches them to accuse every kind of hateful deed.
With love and with suffering they judge their own selves,
and they justify the decree of judgment upon their debts.
Along with their debts they ever judge themselves, each distinctly,

as they are tormented by remorse of soul more than by any torment.
Remorse of mind is harsher upon them than all torments,
and harsher still when the gates of the height are shut.
That grief cannot be told at that time,
when they gaze upon that separation which comes suddenly.
With the eyes of the body and of the mind they gaze upon it,
and bitterly they weep and wail over their separation.
Heaven is high and the earth an abyss that cannot be crossed,
and so they repeat that saying of the rich man.
Precisely do they consider that word,
and they know that the gate of forgiveness is shut before their faces.
The gates of the height the King opens before those who enter,
and they enter and rest in that delight which does not perish.
Wonder and glory do the children of the kingdom see there,
and they marvel and wonder at glories that cannot be told.
That delight cannot be told by the tongue of men,
nor can spiritual beings recount it as it is.
The mind cannot gaze steadily on the loveliness of its beauty,
for the more it looks, the more its appearance shifts from one form to another.
Its account proves bitter to the eager who have sought out its account,
for the more they sought it, the more they turn to seek it as if they had not sought it.
The inquiry into it has urged me too to summon up my strength,
and I sought to know, and it reaches far beyond knowing.
It reaches far beyond the telling of the kinds of good things
of that delight which the Good One prepared for the lovers of His love.
In words I thought I could paint the image of His love,
but words gave out and could not portray its exactness.
Who can paint images that have no likenesses,
and who can liken a likeness to a likeness that has no likeness?
That spiritual order has no likeness,
just as there is no comparison for the One who Is beyond His works.
There is nothing comparable to the Godhead that made all things,
nor is there any likeness that resembles that dwelling of the heavenly ones.

The dwelling of the earth does not resemble it, though it too is a dwelling,
for the form of this one's way of life passes away, but that one does not pass away.
For it is not in its matter that this world, which I said passes away, passes;
it does not itself pass away, but only the order by which it is run.
He dismisses its order, the order of this earthly way of life,
and makes the order of that way of life reign which does not change.
That way of life does not change from what it is,
and Paul bears witness, who called it a house that does not perish.
Into this house He entered ahead of us as High Priest,
and He promised us that we would enter with Him on the day of His revelation.
On the day of His revelation He opens the gate of the Holy of Holies,
and brings in with Him those who loved the day of His revelation.
Of this day I wished to tell before those who listen,
and behold, I hope to reveal its beauty before the beautiful.
Its beauty has drawn me and draws me on toward its story,
that I may at last bring the ship of my speech to rest in a calm harbour.
It is a great harbour, full of calm without end,
and in it the ship of the world that the passions have battered comes to rest.
The sea of passions has battered the earthly dwelling,
and behold, it hastens to bring its ship to rest in the dwelling above.
One dwelling and another dwelling the Creator created from the beginning,
so that when one has grown weary, it might rest from its weariness in the one that abides.
For that which abides He prepared it, and invited those who would abide in it,
the race of men and the spiritual beings who are without composition.
In this world and beyond He bound up the hope of the promise,
as they await the reward of their hopes.
A good reward He promised to the hopes of the good,
and He gave it into the treasury of the trust of His words, to one from among men.
One from among men He made treasurer over that dwelling,
and made Him the dispenser of gifts and the inflicter of torments.
Into His hands He placed the whole treasury of the will of His love,
and gave Him rank, the exalted name of His Godhead.

In His own name He comes at the end to judge all,
and as Creator He renews the world worn out by error.
Evil error battered the world from the beginning,
and the world forgot the name of the Creator who fashioned all things.
That error Christ dispels on the day of His revelation,
and He turns all to the knowledge of the one Creator.
The name of the Creator reigns there over all and in all,
and no longer do creatures go astray after the name of what is not God.
This name they hallow continually in their minds,
and there is no end to the constancy of their hallowing.
With this refrain spiritual and bodily beings respond,
and the more they meditate, the more they long to meditate well.
This is the labour of that spiritual way of life:
holiness and praise, with a constancy that is never sated.
That glorifying of those who glorify is never sated,
for there is no weariness there, nor failing of the soul.
The evil inclination of the tempted ceases there,
and the passion of desires too comes to an end and falls silent.
Sin is uprooted, death is undone, the struggle is at rest,
and the war of crushing passions and raving demons is abolished.
There is no memory of evil there at all,
nor does anyone even think of pondering anything hateful.
The whole creation becomes a new creation there,
and the old name is wiped from every mind.
Abolished there too is the distinction of ranks and degrees,
and no one asks who is a slave or a free man.
There is no distinction of Jew and uncircumcised,
nor anyone who is reproached or who reproaches with shameful blemishes.
There is no blemish in that order, nor even the name of blemishes,
since mortality, which is full of blemishes, has passed away.
Among the immortals there is no name of blemishes or of harms,
for a new nature does not admit old things.

Old things have ceased in Christ, the King of all,
and He has renewed the world with a new and immortal world.
In that world there are no names or words of mortality,
nor any memory of desires and earthly things.
One memory abides there constantly in all minds:
the name of the Creator and love of mankind, without division.
In love and compassion men and spiritual beings are bound together,
and they do not slacken from the bliss of love's goodness.
Love alone remains in that order,
and by it the inclination of the soul is bound and does not slacken.
Our inclination has no power there to slacken,
and two thoughts do not persuade it to waver.
Only the spring of fair things flows from it,
and the kinds of evil are not remembered at all.
There is no evil, nor even the name of evil, in the land on high,
nor in the minds of the wicked who dwell in the land below.
That mind which the good obtain in the kingdom on high
is the very one that the sinners in Gehenna obtain as well.
One mind do the righteous obtain, and the sinners too,
and there is no division between mind and mind.
With one mind they glorify the name of the one Creator,
and love Him and honour Him without ceasing.
There is no ceasing or weariness at all,
nor any slackening from the bliss of the name of goodness.
Goodness alone is spoken of in that way of life,
and constantly they meditate on it and speak of it.
Great wealth of great understanding they obtain there,
as they call to mind the first things and the last.
Before their eyes is pictured the way of life of the two worlds,
and neither the things that have been nor those that are to come escape them.
They know the things of earth and of heaven exactly,
and they expound the power of the meaning of this world and that.
They are convinced of how creatures came to be from nothing,
and what the reason is that He renewed them at the completion of the times.
They know how to gaze across the great expanse of the four quarters,

and they comprehend it, in height and in depth, in their minds.
They see the blemishes; they examine wickedness and discern the truth,
and not one of the things that have been and will be escapes them.
Swiftly their sight runs along with their movements,
and they are not hindered in their course by the mountain stretched out.
Equally they gaze on things far and things near,
and together they see the visible and the invisible.
A wondrous sight they suddenly obtain in their senses and movements,
and they see the blemishes of themselves and of their fellows.
Each one knows the one he knew and the one he did not know,
and no one asks who someone is, or whose son, or where his place is.
All receive one knowledge that does not pass away,
and there is no tongue that does not expound the power of the Creator.
All tongues come there to a single level,
and no one needs to learn anything from his fellow.
The Adamic nature sees the whole of its nature,
and in its mind it grasps the sum of all Adam.
From Adam a man begins to count to Adam,
and he comprehends the whole of nature within his mind.
And why do I say he completes the number by which men are counted,
when even the number of the spiritual beings is reckoned among them?
Man becomes the sum of all things in that order,
and that which was said of him fits him well: that he is the hidden image.
Like the Creator he examines there the kinds of hidden things,
and his sight reaches so far as to see the nature of spiritual beings.
It is a great wonder, whose wonder is hard to believe:
that a composite nature obtains the elevation to see what is without composition.
And so his soul too sees itself as it is,
and comprehends its own simplicity by the likeness of its mind.
And if anyone objects that this is hard to believe,
I ask him whether Christ sees the spiritual beings.
And if He does not see the nature of spirit, which is without composition,
how does He judge those under judgment who are hidden from Him?

And if He does not judge the spiritual beings who sinned,
where then is that which is written, that He judges all?
It would be a great disgrace that He received the judgment to judge all
and had no power to see the natures of those He judges.
That He has received the office of judge over all is certain for us,
and that He sees those He judges is beyond dispute.
And if He sees what is without composition, as indeed He sees it,
then this sight is given to us as well.
For we see the nature of spirit, and our own souls,
and the soul marvels at the wonders that befall it.
It is a great wonder that our nature sees what has no fixed nature,
and that our sight runs swiftly over all creatures.
And if this is hard to believe for the one who hears it,
I will tell of another sight of his, far greater than these.
Christ the King, who reigns over all and rules over all,
we see exactly as He is.
Shall we see the King who is over all,
and not see the ministers of His service?
Yes, we see Christ the King and the spiritual beings,
and there is nothing in creation that is hidden from our mind.
One alone we do not truly see:
Him who raises the nature of His glory above all beholders.
Him alone we do not see at all,
because the eye of anything that is made cannot see Him.
The Godhead is not seen by the things it has fashioned,
neither by mortals nor by the spiritual beings who are without composition.
The spiritual beings too are made, however high they may be,
and they have no power to see the nature that fashioned them.
We have the power to see their nature, and they ours,
because we are equal in the one order that comes from the Creator.
From the Creator the sight of wonder is given to us,
and we gaze upon that order with the eyes of the Spirit.
A great wonder do men see there in men,
and they are not hindered from seeing height and depth.
They stand on high and see where the sinners dwell,

and the sinners too, their sight runs up to the height above.
In this sight the side of the wicked suffers greatly,
and it is more bitter to them than the torments of Gehenna.
Heavy torments increase upon the children of the earth
when they gaze upon the greatness of the glory of the heavenly ones.
And if anyone demands to know how the impassible can suffer,
I demand of him how the nature of demons suffers.
And if again he says that not even the demons suffer there,
I say to him: what then is the testing of judgment?
If there is judgment, there is also suffering for those judged;
and if there is no suffering, judgment is abolished, and the very name of justice.
And if there is no judgment nor justice that tests men,
then the race run by the just and by the angels is in vain.
If it is so [?] for earthly and heavenly beings alike,
then the Creator has not dealt justly with those He has dealt with.
It is not just that He held out the reward of labours as a promise
and then turned and made the good and the wicked equal alike.
Why then did He multiply the kinds of warnings about evil deeds,
and prove them false, with no punishments for the sinners?
Ah, untrue is the thought that presumption has brought forth,
and presumptuously I too have reproached the just decree.
Just is the discernment of that Judge who judges all,
and truly He bestows blessings and inflicts torments.
Blessings and torments make up His testing, as it is written,
and there is no letter in His books that is not justly inscribed.
Presumption has given the lie to things that are true,
for it is accustomed to reproach presumptuously.
Truly true are the accounts of the day of judgment,
and in deeds they will be revealed just as they were spoken.
The day of judgment reveals the power of their meaning,
and the fools who presumptuously reproached them are put to shame.
And so in their own selves they learn the power of just judgment,
as they are condemned for the guilt of their reproaches.
Cease, you presumptuous, from reproach full of boasting,
and listen properly to the account of the judgment that comes at the end.
Just is the judgment, and the manner of its justice cannot be told,
and the just and the wicked alike bear witness to its justice.

Its justice the good and the wicked together acknowledge as just,
and they seal the decree of its judgment in their minds.
Their minds become a furnace of testing there,
and they judge their own selves without leniency.
The word they heard judges along with them, as it is written,
and it demands of them the talents that they buried and so defrauded.
The Chief of judges sealed it and spoke with the word "Amen":
that whoever speaks a word that is not right, his speaking comes into judgment.
The judgment is just; just is the One who tests all on the day of judgment,
and by His justice He separates the just from the wicked.
One, it says, is taken and another left: this is what He does;
one to heaven and one on earth: it is a great calamity.
Where the body is, it is said, there the eagles will be:
the body is Christ, and the eagles are the just who enter with Him.
To where the body, Christ, is, the just enter,
and He gladdens them in that delight in which there is no toil.
There is no toil in that spiritual delight,
and spiritually body and soul are nourished in it.
Body and soul rest there from their toils,
and no longer do they toil in the manner of body and soul.
In spirit they are nourished with that nourishment which is no nourishment,
and they have no need of the uses of body and soul.
Spiritually they live a life without end,
and with the angels they sing and labour at spiritual things.
On spiritual things they meditate there like spiritual beings,
for there is no crushing toil of earthly things there.
It is a great rest in which those crushed on earth rest there,
and they abide in it, and its constancy never cloys.
Constantly they marvel and wonder at their rest,
how restful and how glorious their rewards are.
And so they repeat the word of Paul together with Paul:
that the sufferings of time are not worthy of the gifts of our glory.
Small are our sufferings when they are compared with our reward,
and the world of time is nothing compared with our glory.

Glorious and surpassing is the reward that the children of the kingdom receive; no one can recount it, nor can it be recounted as it truly is.
With their senses and their motions they see the glory of the glory that is in them, and they glorify their Glorifier in body and in spirit.
They see their Glorifier at every moment, unceasingly, and they offer him sacrifices, the pure sacrifices of their thoughts.
It is the one who is from among us that they see with their eyes and their mind, not the Being that has never been seen and is not seen.
The Being who is cannot be seen by a creature that was made, because in its nature Being is exalted above those who see.
They see as visible the high priest who is from among us, the one who fulfils the high priesthood on behalf of our lives.
In this figure the herald called him apostle and priest, true and [?] to the One who made him, more than Moses.
For this [?] the One who governs all chose him out of all, that he might fill his place toward the works of his hands.
He fills the Lord's place for human beings and for spiritual beings, and when they saw him, their motions came to rest through his body.
In the temple of his body their sight rests as in a temple, and through him they perceive [?] one Being, the one Creator.
The Creator longed for his works to see him, and since they could not, he gave them rest in the image of his image.
As an image he fashioned the image of Adam the second, and set him on high in the kingdom of the height in his own place.
He fills his place for heavenly and earthly beings, so that they would not wear themselves out searching for the Hidden One, who cannot be comprehended.
The search after the Hidden One asks of a creature where he is and how great he is, and he checked the course of its inquiry by means of a visible one.
He built him like a house in the city of his royal house, so that the temple of his body might suffice for those who worship him.
The Being is worshipped by the creatures that came into being from the Maker, and he, like a temple, is honoured with the name of Maker.

Together with the Maker he is honoured in name and in authority, since the Son of God is called God.
We call the Son who is from among us the Son of God, and we count him together with the Being, without division.
We understand one Being that is three: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one equality.
We count him in the number of one person together with the One who is, as the One who is without beginning.
This is the reason for the greatness of that man's rank: that by his greatness he might raise creatures up to the Creator.
Through him all creation is honoured together with the Maker, for when it worships him it knows that it too is worshipped in him.
He who receives the worship of all is a portion of it, and that is why he is worshipped together with the Creator.
Together with the Creator, creation receives the worship of love, and this is the wonder: that when it worships him, it is worshipped in him.
A great wonder the Creator worked toward his creatures, for he made them partakers in the glories of his divinity.
By what he did he revealed the greatness of his love to his works, so that they would know how much he loves the works of his hands.
Beloved is the Good One who made the works of his hands, he who orders all things, for he made them heirs of the glory of his body.
He made humankind heirs of glory together with the man, and they glorify him and are glorified in him by the power of the Maker.
It is the power of the Maker that made him glorious and glorified; were it not for this, [?] he would have exalted the children of his race.
God gave him the rank of his divinity and made him Lord, and also Judge of all creation.
He it is who judges spiritual and bodily beings; he it is who distributes gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked.
He it is who brings the children of the kingdom into the kingdom on high; he it is who leaves the children of darkness in the outer darkness.
Through his love he gives rest to those who loved his love, and in Gehenna he torments the wicked who despised his commandments.
With his glory he glorifies those who glorify his preaching, and by the sentence of judgment he humbles the arrogance of those who despise him.
In his royal house the King on high gladdens his friends, and before the eyes of all he makes the light of their conduct shine.

The light of the children of light shines forth from them, and they marvel and are amazed at the light of the glory of their own persons.
The glory that is in them shows the labours of their conduct, and the appearance of their persons shines according to their labours.
And though all of them are clothed in glory that does not perish, they are not all alike in a single appearance, but each is as he is.
The glory in them is less and greater, one than another, just as the shining of one star is less than that of its companion.
It is the will of the soul that does this in that state; it is the will that magnifies and diminishes the degrees of glory.
It is the will that shows itself in the case of the wicked as well, and the punishments of those punished are not all equal.
According to the will with which a man did evil, the punishments are many and severe, and according to the soul that judged itself, its torment is lighter.
A great wonder is what the will of our soul does: it glorifies us, and it condemns us on the day of resurrection.
It raises us to the kingdom on high, which is higher than all, and it sinks us under the weight of our debts in the land below.
Well then did our Lord, the Lord of all, say that it is not he who judges, but a person who judges himself.
It is a man himself who judges himself on the day of judgment, and from himself spring the kinds of good things and the harshness of punishments.
He himself sets the crown of victory before the eyes of the onlookers, and he himself brings about the shame of his face before many.
His are the precious things and the despised things, and it is he who makes us children of the kingdom and children of darkness.
And since it is evident that our will has power over both, let us not complain about the harshness of the punishments laid up for us.
Let us rather blame our will, like the painter who distinguishes between the two, for not proving worthy of the light of its discernment.
Great in its nature is the light of discernment, and its rays run to the four quarters more swiftly than the sun's.
It is a second sun that runs continually in the sky of our soul and shows us the kinds of good things and of hateful things.
As by light, we see by it the two ways of conduct, and by it we learn what is the cause of this world and of the world to come.
See then, O people, how great is the being that is in man:

he knows how to look upon things far and near.
Come, consider how unbounded is the freedom of his soul, and that he has power to do things beautiful and things hateful.
It is very easy for him to judge himself with precision, and to choose the good and reject the evil according to his own testing.
Testing is a furnace for things beautiful and things ugly, and better than a furnace it cleanses hateful blemishes from us.
Come then, let us scour away the kinds of our ugliness in the furnace of our soul, before the testing of the fearful judgment comes.
Come, let us seat the will of our soul as judge, and present to it the account of the debts we have incurred.
Come, let us engage the mind [?] as our advocate, and let it bring our case before the Judge who examines all.
Let us make the mind a marvellous orator [?] for the pleadings, and set out the passions of body and soul one after another.
Let the mouth take the part of mediator between the one and the other, and let the motions call out to the members to listen in good order.
Let the soul say to the senses of the body that serve her: "Take care not to run wildly like beasts."
Let the eye be like a guide to visible things, and tread out a path before the members so that they may run well.
Let it keep the gate of wisdom, the treasury of the soul, so that the kinds of evil do not plunder it like brigands.
Let the whole body keep the order proper to its bodily nature, and let the hidden soul interpret in it the kinds of wisdom.
Let the senses be like horses in her service, and let her stand above them like a charioteer upon a chariot.
Let her cast the bridles of order on the visible senses, so that they run well to the goal of love and faith.
Let soul and body keep the order of one human being, and not slacken in the conduct proper to humankind.
Humankind is one human being in body and in spirit, and must know the reason for its name and why [?].
Its name is interpreted "body and soul", a twofold vessel, one bodily and one of the soul, the dwelling place of all.

The human being, by his constitution, is the dwelling place of all, and in him the creation of the mute and the speaking is summed up.
And since he holds the sum of all things as it is, he must then also bring good things to completion in himself.
Let him form in his own person a good likeness for those who see him, and let them contemplate him as a divine image.
God called him the image of God in the beginning, when he created him, and gathered rational beings [?] to him, that they might be established in him.
Come, O man, see how greatly your nature has been exalted, that from dust you have acquired the name of god.
Come, consider the greatness of the rank that was given to you, and repay with goodness the One who honoured the lowliness of your clay.
See: your making at first, when you came to be, was from clay, and now it reigns over earthly and heavenly beings.
From you is the King who reigns over all creatures, and heaven and earth and all that is in them obey him.
The son of your race has become King and Lord and Judge as well; take care not to wrong the One who honoured the lowliness of your clay.
See that you are destined to enter the judgment whose testing is just, to pay there the debt of the debts you have incurred.
See that there, before the eyes of all, the blemishes of each one shine out, and people look upon one another's blemishes as in the sun.
Hear that the wicked who loved evil remain on the earth; keep away from iniquity, so that you do not remain on the earth with the wicked.
Hear that the good ascend to the height of the kingdom on high; enter with the good into that delight full of blessings.
See that the just and the chaste are destined to see Christ; purify your soul of hateful things, so that you too may see him.
See that those whose souls are hateful do not enter where he is; scour your soul of hateful things, and enter and see him.
Hear the sound of weeping and gnashing of teeth in Gehenna; tremble and be afraid of that report, so fearful to hear.
Hear that that spiritual delight never ends; despise everything, and enter and delight in it without end.
Behold, I have set out for you the kinds of good things and the name of evil things: flee from evil and love good, for its reward is good.
Behold, I have shown you that the labour of this world passes away:

do not be absorbed in it beyond due measure, lest you be put to shame.
Behold, I have taught you that there is another dwelling in heaven: love its business, so that you may be an heir with its heirs.
Behold, I have trodden out for you a path to run to the goal above: prepare your soul to run well toward the heights.
Behold, I have told you that the steep road demands labours: make your labours ready, and set out with those who journey on it.
You have heard well that there are two ways in creation: take care not to travel with the many on the broad one.
You have heard that it is written that the way of life is very narrow: constrain yourself, and receive the life that does not die.
All these things, and many more than these, are recorded in the writings of the books of the Spirit.
It is from the scriptures that I too have recounted what I have recounted, so that everyone may know that my thoughts ran in the way of the books.
The books showed me how to run in the way of their words, and they taught me to teach the truth of their meanings.
On the parable of the seed and the tares

[?] ... of the seed and the tares ...
Again, by the same author: the sixty-ninth homily,
which he composed on the parable of the seed and the tares.

Christ called the word of his teaching
the good seed;
the tares that grow with it
he called the teaching of the Accursed.
He likened the world to a field,
and called himself the master of the house.
The good seed is his teaching,
which the soil of the soul received.
But the one who sowed the tares
is the hater of our nature,
who sowed the word of his teaching
and raised up rifts and divisions.
He said that while people slept,
because they neglected what was right,
like a farmer who grows slack,
weeds multiplied in the field.
The faithful servants, when they saw
tares among the wheat,
put a question to their lord:
"Did you not sow good seed?"
The lord answered the servants,
he who knows all trials:
"The Enemy has done this,
to ruin the seed of my teaching."
The servants were stirred with zeal
and said to the good lord
that he should go and gather the tares,
so that they would not disturb the growth of the wheat.
But the lord said to the servants,
he who is gentle toward the zealous:
"Let them grow side by side
until the end comes,
so that the wheat is not uprooted
along with the bitter tares."
In this he made known the change
by which some turn away from wickedness.
Do not let them lead your understanding astray, my friend,
by saying that a tare cannot change,
because its bitterness belongs to its nature
and it cannot [?] its [?].
This seed, he says, was rational,
and had power over its will,
and it lay within it to change
according to the choice of its freedom.
Take the proof of this
from those who came before you:
tares that were bitter
changed and became wheat.
Abraham was a tare,
but he changed his will,
became a fruit full of sweetness,
and through him the bitter were made sweet.
Zacchaeus the tax collector was a tare,
gathering up the plunder of others;
he became wheat by his own will,
turned round and sowed righteous deeds.
The robber was a tare
and had grown up in human blood [?];
but when he saw the wonder on the cross
he mingled himself among the wheat.
Paul the great was a tare,
choking the wheat as he grew;
a zealot against the truth,
who turned and became a zealot for the truth;
a farmer who multiplied and sowed
his teaching in the four quarters,
tilled the soil of souls,
and filled the world with his fruits.
Here are tares that changed
and became choice wheat.
Now turn to those who strayed
and would not return to knowledge.
Marcion was the first tare,
sprouting in the plot of wheat;
he drank the rain of teaching
yet stayed in the bitterness of his will.
He was a dog that broke loose and ran mad
and barked at his own Maker.
He proclaimed three first principles:
the just, the good, and also the evil.
Another tare is Mani,
wrapped in the guise of wheat;
a wolf hidden in a fleece,
passing himself off as a lamb;
a serpent who sucked bile

and gave it to his neighbours to drink;
a scorpion, a killer of men,
growing up among the wheat.
He is like a painted bird
that changes into every colour.
He was a partner in sorcery
and a close neighbour of magic.
He cut away the order of our nature
and wronged the body by denying it life.
Out of his own mind he invented
the idea that the resurrection is of the soul alone.
The whole sum of his teaching
rests on two principles,
which he called good and evil,
after the deeds of the two.
Bardaisan was wheat
that turned and became a tare;
when the Church saw how he had changed,
she uprooted him from among the wheat.
He was one of the lambs of the flock,
but he turned and bit the flock;
the shepherds drove him out,
and he joined himself to the wolves.
He sought to prevail with bows,
but turned and shot at himself:
an archer aiming at his fellows,
whose teaching turned and fell short.
He made a searching inquiry into everything
and brought in many self-existent beings;
and while he thought he had gained, he lost,
and became a stranger to the truth.
Wheat whose growth turned bad:
Paul [of Samosata], who became a tare.
He was brought low through a woman,
like Samson who ground at the mill.
He too had been invited to the banquet,
but he went out and became a stranger.
He cut off his hope of life
and spoke iniquity against heaven:
that the Son had no hypostasis,
that there was no Son beforehand with his Father,
but that he was like the bare sound of a word,
which has no hypostasis in its nature.
He ascribed to him a beginning
from his birth of Mary,
to him who is equal with his Begetter
and is not younger than he in his being.
And what will the insolent man do
when John rebukes him:
"In the beginning he was,
the Only-begotten with his Begetter.
He was there in the world,
and the worlds were established by his hands.
He came to his own,
and his own did not receive his word.
Those who heard his teaching
he made heirs of his glory,
and gave them a share in honour
in the name of immortality."
Here is a proof that shines
like the sun before those who know;
yet those who see, as though short of sight,
stumble over the words of the Spirit.
Then Valentinus the tare,
who denies the resurrection of the body,
and regards the scriptures of the words of the Spirit
as alien.
But his great wickedness is this,
in which he openly takes pride:
that the Word, he says, was changed,
and did not take a body from Mary.
In the field of wheat Arius grew up,
who wronged the truth;
he was hidden in a disguise
so that his bitterness would not be found out.
He was a wolf dressed in a likeness,
hidden in a fleece.
But when the shepherds perceived it,
they drove him out of the flock.
Then he brought his thoughts into the open
and laid bare the falsehood of his mind.
He poured out lies from his heart,
and his lips spoke iniquity.
He called the Son a creature of the Father,
and the Spirit a thing the Father made.

"He alone, he says, truly is,
and the Son and the Spirit are his servants.
The Father, he says, is without beginning,
and the Son and the Spirit came from him afterwards.
And because he created them,
there was a time between him and them."
But if he made the Son a creature,
as the blasphemer's word has it,
what is to stop everything
from being called son of God?
Gabriel and Michael too
were fashioned by the Father's will;
and though the Spirit is good,
they are without the name of divine being.
And if the making of the Son
and theirs is all alike,
then the name he alone bears is borrowed,
and he is far removed from it in his deeds.
Another tare, Arius's companion:
[?] his name from [?].
But the Knowing One told him apart
by the fruits [?].
He too corrupted the confession
of the true faith,
and sought to tear down the building
whose foundations cannot be overcome.
He said that the soul was not taken up
along with the body by our Saviour,
but that the Word took a mortal body
and dwelt in it.
But when he knew that he would be found out,
he brought his following into the open.
He contrived another device
to hide behind for a time:
he turned round and confessed this too,
that our Lord took both body and soul,
but he left out the mind alone,
though it too is one of the three constituents.
Then why did all the Scriptures
not search this out for us,
and above all Moses,
who wrote about how we were made?
Has the contemptible man become wiser
than the son of Amram,
and found something more,
the mind, as a third constituent?
Here is the seed of the murderer,
which he sowed in the souls of those he dwells in;
he stirred up the earth with his tares
and cast rifts into heaven.
At first Satan sowed
his tares among the wheat,
and raised up rifts and divisions
like battle lines against the truth.
But when he saw that his camp was defeated
and that the truth prevailed through its ministers,
he contrived another device:
he went in and lay hidden among the wheat.
He saw that he could not win in the open,
so he began to fight from ambush,
and became like one of the household.
Like a teacher of truths he went about,
for he saw that the gospel had reached
all peoples and tongues,
that laws had taken hold in every quarter
and had bound up the snares of paganism.
So he put on the guise of a disciple,
so as not to show his falsehood openly,
for he knew his teaching would be rejected,
and that openly it would not be received.
He saw that the lamp was shining,
lighting up the eyes of souls
and turning sinners to repentance.
It [?] the way to the kingdom,
so he covered the hatred of his thoughts.
In the fair garment of the name of light
he went in and hid among the wheat,
and the simple did not perceive him.
He spread a veil over the soul
and blinded it to the light of knowledge.
He silenced the mind and cut it off from the senses,
so that it would not perceive what is right.
He darkened the light of the eyes,

keeping them from reading the Scriptures,
and stopped up the ears that hear,
so that they would not listen to the words of the Spirit.
The tongue, a spring of words
whose flow never ceases,
he made stammering and lame,
so that it would not speak of spiritual things.
The heart, the king of the members,
the fountain of all wisdom,
he stripped of its treasures
and cast his ruins into it.
O how cunning are his schemes,
and how deep his crafts!
O deadly poison of death,
with sweetness mixed into it!
"It is not good, he says,
to meditate on the divine Scriptures;
the reader gains nothing
except to learn vainglory.
So-and-so read a great deal, he says, and mastered it,
and began to probe and go deep;
he busied himself much with the Scriptures,
and went astray and left what is right."
O unspeakable iniquity,
which the Evil One proclaimed through the mouth of sinners!
Teaching is the light of the soul,
and [these] made it darkness.
The well-trodden path of the Scriptures
they filled with stumbling blocks.
"Do not listen to an explanation,
and do not heed the word of the preacher.
Be like a blind man before Scripture
and like a deaf man before its interpretation.
Flee from the waters of the zealous,
lest their streams lead you astray.
This alone is enough:
to believe without inquiry."
Where did you learn this,
you haters of the words of the Spirit,
that you have trodden a new road
and wandered off on the path of falsehood?
Satan has busied them
with the errors he sowed in their ears,
so that they are lulled by oracles
and tell foolish dreams.
It was not enough for him to lead them astray
with stumbling blocks while they were awake;
he also shows them visions,
so that these will be believed as true.
O enemy of our nature,
how skilled you are in battle!
Paul bears witness to this,
when he makes known his crafts:
that our struggle is not
with flesh and blood like ours,
but with the rulers of the air,
the spirit that wars against the flesh.
For at the beginning of the war
he would devise every kind of stratagem,
and renewed his armour every day,
since he was fighting the wise.
Now, he says, no crafts
are needed for his skill:
if he only beckons,
the foolish do his will.
If he wants to hunt us down
with the snare of the love of money,
our will is ready for him,
and gold is written on our hearts.
If he brings in the love of glory,
a drug pleasant to look at,
we desire it more than he does,
and he has already learned it from us.
If he wars with us through lusts,
their bridles are fixed in our nature,
and he reigns, he alone reigns.
And he brings into the open, as deeds,
the three heads of all the passions.
These are the ones we have named,
and whoever enslaves us through them
stands as the victor.
With these passions he fought
against the first of our nature,
and he trusted that he would win by them
as in former times.
For he knew the rebel,
who had been taken in temptation,

and that in these passions
the whole nature of mortals is bound.
He put them on like armour
for the struggle against our Lord,
the insolent one supposing
he could lead him astray as he had Adam.
But here his devices did not hold,
nor the stratagems of his skill,
for his opponent was armed
with the armour of the Spirit in secret.
After that victory
which our nature won with our Lord,
height and depth perceived it,
and it was proclaimed in every quarter.
Yet now we give him our hearing,
and he comes in and dwells in us as he pleases.
He has become as though he were one of us,
and the household do not treat him as a stranger.
The soil of our soul is ploughed for him,
and our hearing too is dug for him;
he casts in the seed of his teaching,
and its fruits come up a hundredfold.
We have uprooted the seed of the teaching
of Christ from our minds,
and received the seed of the Evil One,
and his tares please us.
We are insiders in name,
and outsiders in our conduct.
We are called workers of Christ,
and we work for the Enemy.
The hateful desire for sin:
its drink delights us greatly.
The love of money, the root of evils,
has planted its root in our hearts.
The love of glory, a deadly poison,
a snare that kills from ambush:
we are bound in its nets
and do not feel its bonds.
Envy, a murderous sword
that kills soul and body alike,
dwells within us like a great commander,
and our bosoms take pride in it.
Anger destroys good order;
a friend kills those he loves.
We wear it like a garment,
and our minds delight in it.
Slander, which the Accuser
brought forth at the beginning:
our tongue has been made its messenger
and serves it in its deeds.
We have strayed from the order of discipleship
and left what is right.
Each person is great in his own eyes,
conducting himself as he pleases.
Perverse writers have sprung up among us,
who teach from perverse books,
and are far from what is right,
from what the Scriptures taught us.
The way the ancients trod
was smooth in faith,
and all of them proclaimed it alike;
but Satan, through his tares,
raised in it divided rifts.
From one spring of teaching
all the teachers drank,
and like streams to the four quarters
they watered the earth with their words.
They were like light in creation,
and lit the world with their rays;
like a mirror [?], through their words
they turned sinners to repentance.
They put on armour against the Evil One,
so that the ranks of truth would not be shaken,
and by the sufferings of their own persons
they healed the wounds of our nature.
But when the end came
of the lives of those warriors,
and they slept the sleep of rest
after the toil of their labours,
Satan came in with ambushes
and cast the net of his teaching,

and troubled the whole flock.
With the bitterness of his tares,
when he saw that the watchful slept,
he began to uproot openly
and to make rifts and divisions
among the many.
The one fair body of the Church,
which is made up of many,
he divided into portions
through the variations of his teachings.
The field that the diligent tilled
with the sufferings of their afflictions
he defiled and filled with his tares,
and raised up a hateful thicket in it.
The straying flock that
the great Shepherd gathered:
wolves came in looking like lambs
and trampled the bodies of the flock.
The sweet spring of the Law,
which used to water the soil of the soul:
the heretics changed its words
so as not to receive it.
And who would not weep over this:
that the laws the Holy Spirit established
have become a dwelling for the unclean spirit,
since they gave a hearing to the Harmful One?
Captives who had come back through the cross
from the captivity of the Accuser
have turned and enslaved themselves to the Harmful One,
willingly and not by force.
The guests whom goodness invited
to the feast of the heavenly Bridegroom:
look, they have gone out and become strangers,
so that they will not delight in the wedding.
Who would not lament over this,
and over the hope of life that we have lost?
The substance of the things to come
we have exchanged for earthly things.
And who can set right
the hateful things in our days,
for evils have taken root in us
through long habit?
Our pain has grown too strong for medicine,
and the physicians shrink from it;
those who know cannot apply
a dressing to the wounds of our soul.
Teachers have put on haughtiness,
and learners a stiff neck,
and the gentle and easy yoke
they have made hard for those who bear it.
Novelties have sprung up in our day
from unlearned teachers,
who lay down a law for us
to keep hours and days.
They have abandoned the way the righteous trod,
in which the wise also walked,
and gone off walking in the paths
of error that the wicked taught.
They fenced in the whole law
with the observance of days,
and renewed Judaism for us
with new laws that they handed down.
They rejected the scriptures of the Spirit
and the profit of their words,
and out of the inventions of their own minds
set up alien laws.
They have stopped speaking of love,
of hope and faith,
and are busy all the time recounting
doubtful and foolish dreams.
And if someone who knows rebukes them
and restrains the inventions of their words,
they whet the sword of their tongues,
and all of them slay him with envy:
"This man, they say, is a meddling prober,
divided in his mind about God;
he teaches a new teaching,
and does not believe that the dream is true."
Who is it, then, who teaches novelties,
or who is blind to knowledge:
the one who recounts what is written,
or the one who sets up inventions?
They have blinded themselves to the light of knowledge
and do not wish to come to repentance,
and the proud man lacks the will

to humble himself and come to the truth.
So on every side
Satan's wishes are being fulfilled.
Among the outsiders he raised rifts,
and among the insiders disputes.
The Knowing One did not foretell
the ruin of our days:
that the Evil One has choked
the good seed of Christ with his tares.
Who, then, will rouse [?]
to stand and weep for us in its woes?
For he would know how to recount
the evils of sinners.
Good gold is now rejected,
and falsehood is openly received.
The precious are despised and scorned,
and the honour of the fool shines bright.
Come and see, righteous son of Amoz,
the iniquity of the nations become that of the people.
The evil they have called good,
and the good they have named evil.
They have mixed the sweet with the bitter
and the false with the true,
for anger confounds all order,
so that what is right is not tested.
Arise, tiller of souls,
Paul, great and glorious,
and see the field of your teaching,
which the Evil One has filled with his thicket.
Wise master builder, who built and completed
churches in the four quarters,
come and see the height of your building,
while the unlearned tear it down.
Sailor who steered on the sea
and kept your ship safe from the waves,
arise and see the ship of the Church,
which shadowy winds are wearing away.
Simon, the great one of the apostles,
fisher of fish and of men,
come and see the net of your teaching,
which the Evil One has torn with his disputes.
A thousand in a day you used to catch
by that power of apostleship,
and the Accuser has scattered many of them
with his envy.
Twelve shining apostles,
who lit the world with your rays,
arise and drive away from our humanity
the darkness the Evil One has spread.
Messengers whom the King sent
for the peace of the whole inhabited world,
come and mend the rifts that the Accuser
has cast into the churches.
Tillers of the land of the nations,
who uprooted the thicket of paganism,
arise and cleanse the field of the Church
of the tares of the Deceiver.
Salt that purified the insipid,
so that they gained a sweet taste by it:
let the thoughts the Evil One has corrupted
be purified by your sayings.
Come, my brothers, let us turn to the way
that the truth trod in the apostles,
and not stray on the path of falsehood,
where stumbling blocks are many.
Come, let us draw near to repentance
through the sayings of the Scriptures,
and heal the blemishes of our persons
with the words the Holy Spirit wrote,
and take medicine for our pain
from the root of their words,
for they know the passions of our nature
and can heal its scars.
Let us show the wound of our nature
to the diligent physicians,
and not be ashamed to confess
the hateful blemishes of our sins.
Let us draw near and ask for mercy
from the great sea of mercies,
who poured out the treasure of his gift
on the wicked and the wrongdoers.
Let us shed tears from our eyes
over the stains of our sins,
and wash away our baseness
from the snare in which we stray.
Let us drive pride away from us,

and root envy out of us,
and plant love in our minds
together with hope and faith.
Let us root out of ourselves the tares
that the Evil One raised up with his envy,
and receive the good seed
that the word of life has sown in us.
Let us till the soil of our souls
and root out the thicket of our sins,
and make our hearing ready
for the living teaching of the Spirit.
Here are the healers of Scripture:
come, let us draw near to them,
and with tears of remorse of soul
heal the pains of our wounds.
Here are the apostles, the physicians
who bound up the pain of our humanity:
let us show them the pains of our soul,
so that they may help us in our sickness.
Here is our Lord, a sea of mercies:
let us draw near and ask for help.
The purpose of his coming is this:
that sinners should turn to him.
How shall we win over justice,
so that the court does not accuse us,
when there is no room there for tears,
nor for remorse and repentance?
The time of his coming has drawn near,
the Bridegroom who has invited us to his wedding.
Let us make our garments ready for the feast,
so that there will be no mockery there.
Now is the time to trade
with the talent our Saviour gave us.
Let us not hide the silver of his word,
lest we be called wicked servants.
Let us put oil in our lamps,
so that we lack nothing when he comes,
and with the five virgins
may enter with him into the bridal chamber.
You who are sunk in sin,
rise from the sleep of your sickness,
for look, the great dawn is near,
and rebukes the idle.
Labourers whom grace has hired
at the close of the day's work,
look for the wage of his gift,
that you may be made equal with the first.
Look, he has opened the door of his grace:
let us call on his mercies to help us,
that he may help us in the contest
of his struggles against the Accuser.
The parable of the seed of the tares,
which the Truth spoke, drew me on,
for I saw that the teaching
sown by the Deceiver's word had flourished.
And while I wished to accuse
the bitterness of his tares,
the pain of the insiders grew stronger in me
than the iniquity of the outsiders.
The outsiders tore the flock apart,
went out and became strangers;
and the insiders strayed after them,
yet think they are still within.
They have left the way of the Scriptures,
where the words that guide are set,
and gone off wandering on paths
full of the terror of robbers.
Their bodies were devoured and trampled,
and they did not feel the blows,
for the Deceiver led them astray
with the greedy wiles of his snares.
Zeal for these has stirred me up
to recount the pain of our wounds,
for the dressing has already grown stale
for those who sleep, sunk in sin.
With weeping I sought to linger
over the severity of our fever,
for a pain grown old through habit
is healed by a strong medicine.
Christ, who renewed your creation,
do not neglect our prayer.
In your mercy you called us your heirs:
do not count us among the strangers.
On the Feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross

Thirtieth Homily
On the Feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross
Refrain:
Blessed is Christ, who by his cross gathered his Church and scattered
his crucifiers. My brothers,

Through the crucified Man the Creator revealed to the whole world
the name of His Being and the great power of His Godhead.
Like the sun He lifted Him up on the top of the wood,
and by Him the whole earth, which had been darkness, was filled with light.
Through the crucified Man He caught the world as in a net [?],
and brought His flock under the laws of His preaching.
On the top of Golgotha He stretched out the standard of the power of His victory,
so that by it He might gather together those of heaven and those of earth.
Through a man the beginning of sin came to mankind,
and they sinned and fell into the pit of mortality.
Through a man the Lord willed to give life to humankind,
and He fixed Him to the wood so that by Him He might abolish the sin of humankind.
By His crucifixion He crucified our whole race with Him,
so that by Him He might set free mortal nature, which breeds sufferings.
By His death died death, the greedy slayer of humankind,
and by His resurrection He shared out life to our whole race.
For our sake the Lord of the world came into the world,
and in the form of our body He showed His compassion toward humankind.
By the very judgment through which Adam sinned in Eden, within Paradise,
the second Adam conquered and reigned on the top of Golgotha.
By His crucifixion He put the archons and the powers to shame,
and by the stripping of His flesh He exposed them to the eyes of the onlookers.
Therefore, because in the wisdom of the God of all

the whole world did not perceive the power of His wisdom,
the Creator willed, through the simplicity of the preaching,
to give life to mankind and save them through the raised-up Man.
The world did not grow wise from the creatures in which He had set His sign:
the heaven above in its stretching out and its spreading forth;
the firmament drawn from the waters like a canopy over humankind,
which by its standing firm shows the glory of Him who established all;
and the luminaries too, set for the seasons, for the light of humankind,
which by their risings and their courses show His power.
The air, likewise, by its changes and its mingling,
shows mankind one Maker through its motions.
At times it thickens, and clouds come from it,
and from it lightnings and thunders appear with might.
Harsh thunders give forth their voices on high,
hail is formed and snow lightly settles.
The earth, by its expanse, its stillness and its springs,
brings forth and displays every form to the eyes of the onlookers.
For the surging of the sea He set a boundary of fear as a sign,
and cast into it a strong ordinance, that it should not be thrown into turmoil.
The earth is preserved and is not dissolved by the pressure of the waters,
and those waters are not lost from within the earth.
The order of the whole creation is kept as it was,
and the natures within it do not consume one another.
Yet through wisdom the world did not perceive its Lord,
nor did it become aware of the Governor who holds all things.
By the knowledge set in the understanding of mankind
they did not learn of one Creator who established all.
The whole creation shows His glory like a book,
and teaches humankind one doctrine concerning one Being.
Yet the whole world, in the dullness of its heart, did not become aware,
nor did it grow wise from the creatures so as to know its Lord.
Therefore the Creator willed, at the end of the times,
to give life to humankind through the simplicity of the preaching.
Through the crucified Man, despised by unbelievers,
He willed to give life to all, so that by His crucifixion He might give life to humankind.

His death was despised and His suffering made light of by the insolent,
yet by the simplicity of His preaching He saved the lost.
The orators were put to shame, the wise fell silent, the rebels fell,
and now they are under the lordship of the raised-up Man.
Where are the philosophers of the house of the Greeks,
who used to boast of the subtleties of their teachings?
For they supposed that by their meditations the world was enlightened,
but the Crucified shone forth and overshadowed their understanding.
When they perceived the power of the greatness of the crucified Man,
they abandoned their own, and all ran and clung to Him.
Their schools and their teachings vanished from the inhabited world,
for the Crucified dissolved them by His dawning in the midst of the earth.
So the word of Paul, the herald of the Spirit, was fulfilled:
that even the wise among the Greeks have come to nothing and perished.
The Hebrews too, who prided themselves on their books,
the Crucified whom they crucified brought down from their rank.
He dissolved the laws and the teachers of the Jews,
and scattered them by His great power to the four quarters.
Why, then, did the Jews, dull of heart, ask for a sign,
like the one they saw in the days of Moses when He redeemed them?
Let us say to the Jews: which is greater,
the whole world, or the signs that Moses performed?
Ten plagues, they say, the righteous man wrought in the land of Egypt,
yet not one Egyptian turned from his dullness.
The report of the power of his signs went out through all the land,
yet not one human being drew near to his teaching.
Not only did the uncircumcised peoples not turn to him,
