but not even his own people kept his laws.
He performed signs and showed mighty works in the name [?] of the Creator,
yet the dull people provoked him in the shadow of death.
They forgot Moses, went astray after idols, worshipped molten images [?],
and they all perished by the decree of judgment from God.
See what the Crucified accomplished at the end of the times:
though He was thought despised, He drew the world after His glory.
The Jews ran and hid from His preaching,
and the remnant of them is now scattered to the four quarters.
All the peoples together took up His yoke,
and now they worship the crucified Man in sincerity of heart.

By His dawning the Cross became a sign of peace for our nature,
and set it in the harbor of life that knows no death.
In the mystery of righteous Noah He gave rest to the worn-out world,
and by His crucifixion He delivered humankind from destruction.
In righteous Noah the world found rest from evils,
and through the ark he became a new beginning for the whole world.
The Noah of truth, Christ our King, who brings peace to all,
has set the world in the harbor of the peace of His crucifixion.
His living cross became like an ark for our nature,
and by it we were delivered from the flood of the decree of judgment.
Come, let us examine the greatness of the mighty works the Cross has wrought,
how it gained hope for humankind through its revelation.
The race of mankind had fallen into a multitude of evils,
and had become estranged from the worship of God.
For they had been stripped of the knowledge of the name of the Creator,
and so they ascribed His glory to the work of His hands.
In error, people served and bowed down before created things,
and did not perceive the Creator who had established them.
They worshipped carved images and honored senseless statues,
and robbed the Maker who created them of His glory.
All the demons were praised by unbelievers,
and honored by those in error as God.
The praise of the God of all had ceased
from the mouths and tongues of mankind,
for their tongues were wearied with vanities,
with the praise of demons and the worship of unclean devils.
It was not enough for them to honor the demons, their tyrants,
with the blood of animals and offerings of grain;
but in all this craving they grew so frenzied
that with the blood of their own children they appeased the slayers of humankind.
Shamefully, people served wicked and accursed demons,
and with pure blood they satisfied those who thirsted for blood.
Into this pit, the depth of iniquity, our race was cast,
and the accursed devils trampled it underfoot in their rebellion.
The hope of human nature was cut off from all good things,
and with its hope cut off it served its lusts in bondage.
Therefore He who knows all gave them up

and handed them over to the lusts of the emptiness of their hearts.
In their lust they defiled and dishonored even their own bodies,
and clothed themselves in shame through the perversity of their contempt.
In the mystery of demons they corrupted the order set in nature,
and perversely they coupled like beasts.
Male and female defiled the marriage bed
through promiscuity and corruption with many.
They practiced adultery and fornication beyond all order,
in drunkenness and contempt without law.
All these things the wicked carried out in the mystery of demons,
and the light was darkened for them in the eye of reason.
Streets and cities were filled with defiled altars,
and in every house they set up carved images and arranged statues.
Without number were the gods they worshipped,
and without order the goddesses that were served.
There was a great division between houses of priests and other priests,
and each one loved his own error through the evil of his inclination.
Quarrels and divisions multiplied among the peoples,
and countless wars raged in every generation.
From the wickedness of accursed demons came evils,
and people became accursed, shedding the blood of their fellows.
The sin the world committed of old cannot be told,
nor can the wickedness it practiced in every age be explained.
Words are too small to tell the kinds of iniquity
that all people committed before the coming of the crucified King.
All these things the Cross abolished by its revelation,
from within the People and also from the peoples throughout the inhabited world.
Now all the peoples together worship
the one God who turned them back through the crucified Man.
All of them renounce the names of the gods of their error,
and confess Jesus, who gave them life by the power of His victory.
All of them cry out with one confession in their tongues
to Him who by His cross made peace reign on high and in the depths.
Hail to the Cross, by whose crucifixion He slew death,
and proclaimed peace to all, to those far off and to those near.
He is our peace, who made the two one together,
and broke down the wall that stood before humankind.

He abolished all laws by one of His commandments,
and reconciled all to God by the sacrifice of His body.
Hail to the Cross, by whose revelation the dead came to life,
and through which spiritual and bodily beings were made one.
Hail to the Cross, which overturned and abolished all blasphemies,
and uprooted error from the People and from the uncircumcised peoples.
Hail to the Cross, which overturned and abolished all blasphemies,
and uprooted error from among the People and the uncircumcised peoples.
Hail to the Cross, which made the family of the human race worthy
to become, from the earth, heirs of the kingdom on high.
This is the Cross which washed creation clean of filth,
and wiped from it the hateful stench of abominations.
This is the Cross by which the family of humankind was gathered
into one Church, a harbor of the peace of the one God.
If you wish to learn the power of the crucified Man,
look in your mind to where His preaching has reached.
See in the East how the power of His rays has shone,
and Persia, which was darkness in idolatry, has been enlightened.
Let your mind rise to the regions of the West,
and see there the greatness of His power through those who worship Him.
All the kings and warriors, lo, are caught in His net,
and He has established them on the foundation of His faith.
Go in your thoughts as far as the South and examine it,
what the Cross accomplished by its dawning among its inhabitants.
Rise in your knowledge also to the whole region of the North,
and see the power of the name of the victory of the raised-up Man.
Go and marvel at all the teachings that were on the earth,
how the crucified Man consumed and destroyed them.
Before the pure rays of His living standard the idols fell,
the demons fled and were put to shame, and their ministers ceased.
For four thousand years Chaldeanism held sway,
yet it was not able to subject all to its teaching.
And though its rule held long on the earth in its antiquity,
the Cross by its dawning uprooted it, cast it down, and exposed its falsehood.
For a thousand and five hundred years
the law of Moses, the firstborn of prophecy, also held sway.
And though prophets, priests and kings were its heralds,
not one of the peoples turned and came to its teaching.
It is now a thousand years since Magianism also began,
and the law of its madness held sway among many.

Yet it did not prevail, though kings rose up to help it,
together with judges who aided it in the fury of their persecutions.
With dreadful tortures and harsh deaths they slew beyond all measure [?],
yet they could not find a way to turn a single person to their teaching.
And when they dared to draw near against the people of Jesus,
countless numbers turned from their own and believed in Jesus.
They tasted from the Church the sweet spring of baptism,
and became advocates for the confession of our faith.
The tortures of bloodthirsty, cruel men were defeated,
and the children of the holy Church multiplied beyond number.
Thus the whole error of Magianism held sway
through the harsh rulers and kings who sprang from it.
But the Cross, in somewhat less than five hundred years,
has brought all the peoples near to its teaching.
Its power has dried up the spring of Chaldeanism,
and exposed the wickedness of its falsehood to the eyes of the onlookers.
The city of Zion, which did not receive Him, it swept away from the earth,
and took from it prophet, priest and ruler.
He destroyed the temple of the house of the crucifiers, the ungrateful people,
and raised up in its place temples of His own in every place.
He dissolved the law, which had acquired bodily observances,
and taught the simple of heart by the power of His wisdom.
He brought to nothing the murmurings of Magianism, the emptiness of error,
and uprooted the altars that error had built for the Slanderer.
He cleansed the air of the dark smoke of sacrifices,
and purified the waters of the washings done in the name of demons.
He showed the children of darkness the manifest truth,
and trained them by the glorious light of His preaching.
By His dawning He showed the might of His power for the redemption of our life,
and by His crucifixion He filled creation with the name of His victory.
The Cross, which by the decree of His judgment had become a curse for humankind,
underwent a change and set humankind free from curses.
The Cross, which was reckoned a reproach by the peoples and the Jews,
abolished reproach and the decree of judgment from the guilty.

Sin was extinguished and death undone by the raised-up Man,
and life without end sprang forth for the race of Adam.
By His cross the Bridegroom on high opened the bridal chamber on high,
and brought those of the earth up to delight in it.
The whole creation bears the figure of this standard,
and points to His standard as with a finger.
The whole of it carries and adorns the standard of our Lord,
and in its order bears the mystery and the figure of His glory,
to the shame of the faces of adversaries who will not be persuaded,
and to the joy of all the children of the holy Church.
The whole world by its forms bears the victory
of the crucified King, revealed at the end for the redemption of humankind.
The world is held fast by His figure through its corners,
and serves this mystery by its very existence.
Its frame is composed in the likeness of the cross with its four sides;
the world shows in the body of its being that it bears His standard.
The year stands upon four elements in the likeness of the cross,
and if it falls short in any one of them, it is not completed.
The luminary too, which sheds its light on the whole world,
is not fulfilled without the pattern of the standard of the cross.
By the ascent and descent of its stages
it shows the standard of the crucified Man in four months.
On the twenty-fourth of June, over against December,
the one on high and the other in the depth, on two sides;
on the twenty-fourth of the month of March, over against September,
the two sides together bear an even measure.
On the four twenty-fourths the sun shows
the standard of the cross by its descent and its ascent.
East and West, North and South, facing one another,
together bear the complete figure of the cross.
But if one of them is split off from its fellows,
an astounding dissolution befalls them all, and nothing remains standing.
Look at the flight of the bird in the air, how it traces
the cross with its body and displays it to the eyes of many.
It stretches out its head, extends its feet and spreads its wings,
and so the clear air adorns it above its back.

This is the mystery: everyone who confesses the standard of Jesus
will fly up, ascending on the day of resurrection to the height above.
But whoever is not baptized and sealed with the cross on his face
will remain on the earth, and the door of mercy will be shut in his face.
Trees, too, and seeds of every kind
bear the four-sided standard of the crucified body.
Let us draw near, then, to the books of the Spirit and see His standard
as it was traced from generations of old by the hand of the righteous.
Abraham testifies how he received the promise of the land
from God, who poured out His love upon his household.
Abram received the inheritance of the land through promises,
so that, being confirmed in faith, he might become its lord.
He left his land and his father's house in Ur of the Chaldeans,
and went after the voice that called him to its promise.
All the land of the Amorites He promised to give him,
He who knows all, whose love is true and does not deceive.
By His revelation He made Abram walk through the land to see it,
commanding him to walk in it as its lord.
He taught him to traverse its length and its breadth,
so that by this the standard through which he would inherit it might be revealed.
By his walks he was tracing a cross as he inherited it,
so that He might make known to him that by this standard he would inherit the land.
See, you Jews, how the head of your tribes traced
the great figure of the standard of the cross on the land he inherited.
The land Abram inherited bears a likeness of the height,
that pattern which was to be revealed in the crucified Man.
The King on high made heaven a place of rest for the two,
and there He willed to give His flock rest in the harbor of blessings.
Everyone who signs the standard of the cross upon his forehead
will enter that kingdom which is never dissolved.
Like this, too, is the wonder concerning Isaac,
whose birth came from old age and from barrenness.
He went up to the burnt offering like a lamb, according to the command,
and before he died a ram from the tree delivered him.
By the decree of judgment, of evil and death, mortals were condemned,
and the living Lamb set them free by His crucifixion.

Isaac was redeemed by a ram caught in a tree,
and creation was redeemed by the living blood of the Crucified.
Old Jacob saw in a revelation a ladder
set upon the earth, with its top above in heaven.
This revelation is the mystery of the crucified Man,
by whose cross people ascend to the height above.
Jacob blessed as he had learned from the revelation,
and showed the mystery of the cross in the sons of Joseph.
Joseph set his two sons before his father,
Manasseh at his right and Ephraim at his left.
He crossed his arms one over the other in the likeness of a cross,
and by the standard of the cross he made one of Joseph's sons great and the other small.
Father Jacob made Ephraim great with his right hand,
and with his left made small his brother, who was the firstborn.
This mystery, lo, is explained in the crucified Man,
who made great the despised peoples who were baptized in His name.
The people that had been firstborn, glorious above the peoples,
was made small at the cross and became despised in its insolence.
By the cross itself old Jacob traced his blessings,
so that all might learn that without the cross they are not fulfilled.
When he had finished all that he said, he rose from his bed,
gave thanks to his Lord, and paid worship upon the top of his staff:
a manifest mystery which our Lord too carried out in His own person,
when He fulfilled and completed the whole course of His preaching.
He bowed His head on the top of the wood and gave up His spirit,
and on the cross itself He completed the mystery of the redemption [?] of humankind.
Come to the staff of Moses, the prophet of the house of the Hebrews,
and see how the mystery of the crucified Man was depicted in it.
For when Moses laid it flat [?] on the ground,
its working lay fallen and was void;
but when it was raised on high in the hand of Moses,
all natures, rational and dumb, obeyed it.
When it was lifted up in the hand of Moses over the land of Egypt,

countless signs multiplied against the Egyptians.
The Creator wrought great mighty works through the staff of the righteous man,
which bore the mystery of the wood of His crucifixion.
Moses lifted the staff in his hands toward the sea,
and divided the sea, and the waters stood like a wall.
The people walked in the depths of the sea, an unheard-of thing,
and received [?] complete freedom beyond all hope.
And the Egyptians, who dared to pursue the people,
he drowned in the midst of the sea by lifting his staff.
So too, the moment the Cross was raised on Golgotha,
all the devils sank by the Cross as in the sea.
Like the Egyptians, the rebels sank in the crucified Man,
and His great power destroyed them from the world.
Judaism and Samaritanism, together with paganism,
the adored King dissolved by His cross, and He reigned over all.
At the time when there was a great war with the Amalekites,
Moses raised the staff in his hand against Amalek.
When the staff in his hand was lowered, Amalek prevailed,
and when it was lifted up, the people grew strong through victory.
The hands of Moses, they say, were raised in faith,
and by the uplifting of the staff in his hands the children of his people conquered.
Joshua son of Nun, in the mystery of Jesus, conquered Amalek,
and put them to shame by the might of the weapon of Moses' staff.
The Son of God, Jesus our King, conquered by the cross,
and by His crucifixion Satan was defeated and death abolished.
Moses, who was a servant, bore the mystery of the cross,
and Jesus, who is the Lord of mysteries, bore it raised up.
These mysteries the son of the Hebrews traced in his staff,
and by the crucifixion of the Son of God they received their fulfillment.
With a piece of wood Moses sweetened the waters at Marah,
and the people drank and found relief from their thirst.
The cross of Jesus sweetened the peoples who had been bitter,
and gave them the sweet taste of the name of the Creator.

What shall we say of the serpent that Moses set up in the wilderness,
which shows the mystery of the revelation of the crucified Man?
The serpent, then, that was fashioned was of bronze,
and by being lifted up it gave the people life from the vipers.
By the stretching out of the mute serpent the Hebrews lived,
and through it they were delivered from the bites of the serpents.
The serpent bore the great mystery of the Man lifted up,
who by His crucifixion heals pains and sufferings.
On Golgotha He too was lifted up in the likeness of the serpent,
to save mankind from the sickness of the demons' venom.
The race of Adam, which the serpent bit among the trees,
looked upon the Cross and gained a life that does not die.
Look at Elisha, the prophet of the Spirit: what did he accomplish
when he revived the only son of the Shunammite?
It is said that the prophet lay down upon the boy,
and stretched out his legs and extended his hands in the likeness of a cross.
Elisha rose from the dead boy when his flesh grew warm,
and began to trace the Cross of Jesus with his steps.
In the house he walked once this way along its length, once along its breadth,
so that by this sign he might deliver the dead from the hand of death.
The prophet stretched himself upon the dead boy again three times,
and so the dead boy gasped, and lived, and stood on his feet.
Three times he marked the Trinity upon the boy,
a great type by which all the dead are revived.
What is said, that the prophet stretched himself upon the dead,
is the mystery of our Lord, who was to be stretched upon the wood.
Through these types the prophet was able to revive the dead,
to show us that by this mystery the dead rise.
Greater still than all these is what happened
when the iron fell from the sons of the prophets into the depth of the waters.
It is written that the prophet cut a stick and threw it there,
and the iron that had sunk floated up above the waters.
See the wonder that was shown through Elisha,
who by the mystery of his Lord multiplied mighty works among the Hebrews.
Like the iron, our nature had sunk into the pit of death,
and the Cross went down and raised our race up above death.

The Son of God went down by His Cross to the sea of Sheol,
and the dead came up from the depths of mortality.
By the wood of the Cross mortals who had fallen by a tree were victorious,
and in place of the debt that came from the tree they lived by the Cross.
Whoever is insolent and contends against these mysteries,
let him know that his contention is not with us,
but with the Lord, who traced His mysteries in all generations;
the stranger joins battle with Him against His types.
Let us speak, then, against the pagans and the Jews,
who in their wickedness together mock our preaching.
The erring ones supposed that the holy Church worships wood,
and honours it as God instead of God.
Because they worshipped things made instead of the Maker,
they rose up in malice and slander us over the wood of the Cross.
The accursed err through the falsehood of the Accuser,
and bitterly belch out iniquity against the truthful.
It is not visible matter that the Church worships,
but the sign of the crucified King who conquered by the wood.
But if the Church worships wood, as they supposed,
why is the Cross also made of other materials?
From every material, lowly and great and precious too,
the Church makes the visible image of the hidden King.
In His living sign it gains victory for the inner heart,
and kisses it with pure love, without doubting.
The Church has not gone astray, neither after trees nor after images,
nor after matter and materials that came to be for mankind's sake.
When it worships the living sign wherever it is traced,
it worships our Lord and not corruptible matter.
The ungrateful people of the Jews worshipped idols,
and honoured images and provoked the Lord who had redeemed them.
Thus they spoke before that calf which they made at Horeb,
as they worshipped it and honoured it as God:
“This is your Lord, O Israel,” said the wicked,
“and this is he who redeemed you from slavery in Egypt.”
The people honoured carved things and images, as it is written in the Scriptures,
and see, their wrongdoing stands accused from within the books.
The heart of the wicked people ran wanton after demons,

and for this reason it loved images in place of its Life.
The pagans all turned aside from the smooth and pure way,
and worshipped stones and beasts, and trees as well.
They honoured them as God in their worship,
and served them with lusts full of wickedness.
They saw the luminaries that He created by His might to order all things,
and went astray and worshipped before the silent things as God.
To this wickedness the children of error went down, and did not hold back [?],
and worshipped and served what had been given for mankind.
To this wickedness the children of error went down, and did not hold back [?],
and worshipped and served what had been given for mankind.
Far be it from the Church to confess these things like the unbelievers,
and far be it from it to take on the hateful likeness of the children of error.
The sign of our Lord, by which it was betrothed, it praises with glory,
and honours it as the seal of the King of kings.
Whatever the king honours above all for the king's sake,
even if it is despised, is honoured for the king's sake.
The wood of the Cross, though lowly in its nature,
is precious through its good cause, for the sake of Jesus.
The Cross of Jesus is a seal upon our faith,
by which His dispensation for our redemption was fulfilled.
Even a denarius that bears the image of an earthly king,
see, the people of the realm receive it as the king's own.
Because of the king's stamp it is precious above all,
and whoever despises it despises the king whose it is.
In the same way the worshipful sign of the Cross
bears in its appearance the great image of Christ the King.
The king's seal and the figures on his letters
people kiss and honour as they would the king.
Despised clay, and paper too, things of little value,
are despised by nature and counted as nothing by the wise.
But when the king writes his words on paper,
everyone honours it as though it were treasure and refined gold.
Despised clay, a feeble clod from within the earth,
when the kings of the earth stamp it, gains glory.
When the king's letter is sent with the seal of his hands,
everyone rises and kisses it as they would the king.
By the seal of his name the king shows that his words are binding,

and nothing is sent by his hands without his seal.
How much more, then, is the seal of Jesus our King true,
who sealed His words with the great seal of His crucifixion.
He walked on earth and fulfilled all His dispensation,
and by His being lifted up He showed that His words were true and binding.
If the seals of the kings of this age are honoured on earth,
how much more should the crucified seal of the King on high be honoured.
If the nations kiss and worship the seals of kings,
it is far more fitting that everyone honour the Cross.
Kiss and worship the sign of Jesus for Jesus' sake,
for by it you will be set free from the harms of the Accuser.
The seal of our Lord, the Cross, is what wins the victory,
by which death fell and error vanished from the world.
This sign the worshipful King set in His Church,
so that they might draw near to it as to the image of the King of kings.
By it the uncircumcised nations are sanctified and circumcised,
and become a people for the great King who reigns over all.
All who wish to be baptized are signed with it,
and without His sign they are not called the Church of Jesus.
The priesthood too is signed with it for the celebration of the mysteries,
and in His name it performs the rites and mysteries in the holy Church.
With it all the temples are signed, together with the fortresses,
and when they are sanctified by this sign, the Spirit dwells in them.
The priest imprints the seal of Jesus in the holy temple,
so that it may be a vessel full of life for the human race.
By this Cross the mysteries of the Church are sanctified too,
and in His name they become a pledge of undying life.
All these things the Cross accomplishes in the holy temple,
and through it He forgives and sanctifies mankind.
Through it the truth of Jesus is spread abroad among the people of the earth,
and by the image of His sign they receive blessings that do not fail.
By it unclean demons are driven from their dwellings,
and they are distressed by its rays and hide like bats.
By this sign the chills [?] and the power of demons are brought to nothing,
and by it all sicknesses and all harms are healed.
This weapon the righteous took up, and by it they prevailed,

and threw down the Evil One and pierced him with the spear of the sign of the Cross.
They became warriors, and the champions took up the Cross of Jesus,
and Satan and his angels were defeated before them.
This is the great banner in all our lands,
and it made the martyrs shine in their contests.
This is the one whose beautiful light has shone in all the world,
and it has gathered mankind to see its glory.
It is like an ark with us at the head of our camp,
and it steers the ship of the Church to the haven of peace.
Before the Ark cities shook and walls fell,
and all the kings of the Amorites were defeated and brought low.
But once the Cross of Jesus came to reign over creation,
the foundations of the walls of Sheol shook and fell to the ground.
By it the dead arose, and by it the faint of soul were upheld,
and by its revelation it gave hope to the hopeless.
It brought low the might and strength of the demons, the murderers of men,
and made them weak and despised before its worshippers.
It showed its glory to those in heaven and those on earth:
on high its sign, and on earth the image of its lifting up.
Constantine saw the Cross above in heaven,
shining like the sun in great glory.
And on its arms were written words, set in order:
“By this sign you will conquer, King Constantine.”
This sign he carried and went out at the head of his camp,
and before its appearance the enemies who made war on him fell.
The king and his armies raised a cry of praise
to Him who by His Cross put an end to wars on every frontier.
The king's mother searched for the worshipful wood,
and it was revealed to her by a fragrance that rose from within the earth.
A sweet fragrance of fine spices breathed out from the earth,
and the people and the nations who had gathered there saw its glory.
For this reason Helena, the king's mother,
built splendid temples in its honour and adorned its feasts.
From the day the worshipful wood was buried,
men had journeyed as if in darkness until it shone forth.

And now that it has shone forth, its light has gleamed in the four quarters,
and gladdened those in heaven and those on earth with its beauty.
O wood, when you were hidden in the earth by the wicked,
your sign was shown above in heaven, in the place of light.
Who will not marvel at the greatness of the mighty works our Lord performed,
who came in His love and gave the world peace by His crucifixion?
In the temple of His body on Golgotha He shone forth, lifted up,
and lit the world with the glorious light of His glory.
His rays spread like the sun into the four quarters,
and drove the darkness of idolatry from creation.
At His shining forth heaven and earth and all that is in them rejoiced,
and He filled them with the riches of His glory through His heralds.
This is the Shepherd who bore the Cross for His flock;
believe in His name and worship His sign without doubting.
Come, take refuge in this King, O mortals,
and trace His Cross constantly upon your bodies.
In His name accomplish your deeds and your goings,
and do not set about tasting anything without His Cross.
With a pure heart believe in His living sign and confess it,
and He will guard you from offences hidden and open.
His Cross is fearsome to those above and those below,
and when they see it, all the demons tremble before it.
This sign the holy Church adorns with glory,
and honours it, and receives from it grace and mercies.
In it all the faithful glory, and in it they take refuge,
for He set them free from the slavery of mortality.
See, they worship it and honour it with songs,
and assemblies of Watchers and men praise it.
Come, let us give thanks with one thanksgiving, together with the spiritual beings,
to Him who by His Cross exalted our race: to Him be glory.
On the Bronze Serpent

By the same author again.
The thirty-ninth homily,
on the bronze serpent;
it is suited to the feast of the Finding.

The Lord made a covenant of love with Abraham
and promised him that He would redeem his seed from slavery.
His seed was to be enslaved in the land of Canaan,
but He showed him beforehand that He would free it by the might of His greatness.
The might of His greatness He showed in Egypt to the Egyptians,

and against their will He fulfilled His will toward Abraham.
With power and with riches He brought them out of Egypt,
and settled them, without fear, in the fearful wilderness.
In a place of desolation He made them dwell, for the sake of peace,
so that through the desolation the desolation of their thoughts might be stilled.
For the sake of peace He made them dwell in the outer wilderness,
until they should grow estranged from their pursuit of loathsome things.
He saw that in peace they did not turn away from ugly deeds,
so He drove them to a place far from humankind.
By a change of place He thought they would change their deeds,
but their madness did not forget it, in desolation or in peace.
An evil habit made them used to what was unseemly,
and they did not resemble the fair likeness He had shown them.
With good things He was eager to win over their thoughts,
and He multiplied life and mighty deeds so that they might change.
With manna and quails He fed them, though they did not toil,
and from the rock He made drink flow and delighted them.
A cloud of dew He spread like a tent over their heads,
and like a lamp He set up a pillar full of light.
Light filled the place where they lived, night and day,
and with the visible light was the light of truth.
With light upon light those who were ugly of soul were delighted,
and though it was most fitting, they were not as fitting as was fit.
The visible light was fitting for the eyes of the body,
and the truth was more fitting still for the eyes of the soul.
Body and soul were tried by two lights,
and though they saw, they did not truly see.
In great peace they lived there, such as it was,
and there was no desolation as harsh as the desolation of their minds.
The wilderness in its peace rebuked the love that was in them,
for it had grown peaceful, while they did not turn back from evils.
The wilderness too had been evil before the people dwelt in it,
and through the people peace reigned over its evil.
Its peace was desirable, and men longed for its peace,
and there was nothing to trouble or even to strike its peacefulness.
Tasteless was the venom of the serpents that lived in it,
and though they bit, they did not bite to harm.
Without harm the seed of Abram was embittered by it,
and did not discern who was guarding it from harm.
With great wrong the wrongdoers wronged the goodness shown among them,
and when the wilderness saw it, it returned to the habit that was in it.
An evil habit compelled it to be like what it had been,
and its calm did not keep it at peace so that it would not be stirred [?].
The voice of blasphemy roused the sense that dwelt in it,
and hateful murmuring opened its mouth to bite.
The bitterness of want [?] broke open the lair [?] of the serpents' venom,
and roused the serpents to subdue the speaking creatures.
Sin opened the door of the command before the silent creatures
and set them upon the speakers to rise against them.
The people sinned, as is written in the book of great Moses,
and the Lord stirred up the serpents to bite them.
The Scripture lays upon God the harm done by the mute creature,
to make known to the rebellious the might of His lordship.
His might made wise the undiscerning serpents,

and He sent them and stirred them up as it pleased Him.
It pleased Him, and He set the seal of silence on their mouths;
again it pleased Him, and He loosed them to bite.
Not that this which I called His pleasure truly pleased Him:
the people's unseemliness compelled Him to change course.
That wholly fair Will saw the people's loathsomeness,
and it did not please Him to be tried by its loathsomeness.
He saw the fever of iniquity in the camp where He dwelt,
and gave it as food to the despised serpents, as with a word.
Not by its own nature did the silent creature cry out to the speaking ones:
"Look at me: this is not mine, but the power's that bound me and loosed me.
The power that created me held me back from harming your lack of discernment,
and because you did not discern it, it loosed me to come upon you for your ignorance."
The serpents put on the armor of wrath against the undiscerning,
and the venom began to pour out its arrows among the ranks of the people.
Like a sword the bold creatures drew their tongues,
and without pity they stabbed those whose souls were condemned.
A hard battle they waged against body and mind:
one they killed, another they drove out of his life.
The silent creatures exacted from the speakers the wages of iniquity
and silenced them from blaspheming the Creator.
The Creator Himself taught the undiscerning
to avenge upon the discerning the wages of the insult done Him.
The undiscerning discerned very well how to discern,
and still the possessors of speech do not discern as they discerned.
By their discernment He made wise the people slow of mind,
and by their venom He purged the venom of their thoughts.
An evil venom of idolatry filled their hearts,
and the Good One made it tasteless with the venom of evil creatures, out of their venom.
Venom with venom His might made tasteless, wisely,
and the serpents' venom overcame the venom of man.
Great order He showed in a thing that had no order,
and through confusion He set in order the order that the inclination had confused.
His will held the whip [?] of wrath in the mouth of the silent creatures,
and with a mouth instead of a hand He scourged the rebels.
He stretched out the people, heavy of heart, for harsh scourgings,
and made its scourgers accursed creatures, cursed by Him.
To torturers stripped of mercy He handed them over,
that by their accursedness He might soften the hearts of those hardened in iniquity.
Like creditors they prowled through the camp
and tracked down iniquity wherever it was hidden.
Like debtors the transgressors of iniquity hid themselves,
for they sensed that the serpents were demanding their debts.
The debtors had sinned and could not stand before the creditors,
and they raised their fingers to the Lord of the debt: "Spare us, do not destroy!"
The Gracious One spared, not because He was persuaded, but out of love,
and called His servant and taught him to apply a remedy to His people.
"Make yourself a serpent," the Lord said to Moses His servant,
"and set it up as a sign and a reminder to heal the people.
Fashion bronze in the shape of the serpents,
and let it be like a living serpent in every way."

He made a dead serpent in a form resembling the real one,
so that by its deadness the venom of the serpents might be stilled.
The humble man obeyed the voice of the command that spoke with him;
he believed, consented, prepared, and made a wrought serpent.
He forged [?] against the deadly bite of the serpents, for which there was no relief,
and raised it and hung it up in the camp of the tribes of the people.
In the midst of the people he hung the crafted likeness,
so that the bitten might look at it and seek its cause.
By the laws of holiness he mixed its remedy, the remedy of life,
and turned toward it the gaze of everyone, that they might study it.
Like a mirror he fixed it on wood before their eyes,
so that its appearance might be plain to body and mind.
A new sight Moses showed the children of his people,
and by that sight he showed them how to be healed.
"Look and be healed" was proclaimed aloud,
and they marveled and were amazed that a sight could heal.
At first they stood in doubt as they examined it,
until they learned by experience, and so believed.
By trial they gained comfort and grew wise,
and believed that a mute thing could stop the serpents' venom.
From those who gazed [?] they learned the working of the wrought serpent:
that truly it trampled the serpents by the power that came from it.
They saw that the sight of it ended the struggle of their distress,
and they scorned and mocked the weapons that had bitten their brothers.
The bitter bites became as nothing,
for the serpent by its sight made tasteless the venom in them.
When a living serpent bit a living man,
he looked at the dead one, and its venom turned back from his limbs.
When the condemned were embittered, they looked at it [?],
and that calm, lifeless sight calmed them.
They had toiled, and they found relief, lest the venom in them pour forth,
so that, bitter as it was, its bitterness was not felt.
However many bit, and bit bitterly,
it was as if no venom were felt in the senses of the body.
As long as a man's eye was fixed on the dead one,
the serpents' venom was not even thought to be there.
Constantly the eye stayed fixed on its appearance
and was never sated with studying its silence.
O silent one, whose silence astonished the rational creature
and drove its gaze after the power hidden in its appearance!
O lifeless one, wholly stripped of life,
who gave men life from the deadliness of the serpents' venom!
O voiceless and senseless one that raised a voice,
that rebuked the mute creatures and stilled them from their attack!
O you who do not see those who see you, nor whom you resemble,
yet became a sight that drove away the sufferings and pains of men!
O you who do not discern the might of greatness that spoke through you,
which set in order the venom of the undiscerning serpents!
O you who do not even know that you are what you are,
yet made men know how to search out the might of the Creator!
Who are you, serpent? You are no serpent—not even a serpent are you—
that you could become a cause of life for whoever looks at you.
Was it your sight, then, that made the serpents' venom tasteless,

or perhaps is there another sight in you that is not seen?
Did grace flow from you to the people,
or perhaps from Him who created the people and all things?
Did the healing that came from you happen by chance,
or perhaps a mystery of the Physician of truth is hidden in you?
What is it, then, that though you are silent you are stronger than the living?
By what power do you overcome the living and bring the dying to life?
The question about you is full of questions, serpent without a bite,
and a great wonder is hidden in the help that flowed from you.
The question about you has called me to question you,
and it has urged me to flow in words because of your story.
Your story presses me to retell your story before the hearers,
and behold, I am eager to reveal the power hidden in your silence.
Come, hearers, ask with me the cause I wished to know,
so that what we know we may know well, and ask about hidden things.
Let us ask for whose sake the forged serpent was made,
and by whom it was made, and how, and in whom it worked what it worked.
By what power did it conquer the serpents by its sight
and put to shame the strength of the deadly venom they cast?
How could a dead, lifeless sight
drive pains out of corrupted limbs?
How, again, was it pleased to heal through the eyes alone,
while the other senses gained nothing from its help?
Why was its grace given out by looking,
and its body not brought near to the wounds?
If the power that overcame the serpents was its own,
why were the bitten not brought near to it?
If it had no power to give life to men,
why [?] its sight, dead and lifeless?
Who used the senseless for those with senses,
and who made calm bronze profitable to the possessors of speech?
If a silent nature could do this,
why did the holy vessels in the holy house not do it?
Fair were the books, and glorious too the ark;
why, then, was there no healing in the sight of them?
One of two things fills the working of the forged serpent:
either it is something itself, or [?] something is hidden in its appearance.
There is some cause behind its cause and its healing,
and it seems to be greater than all the causes in the Law.
The books could not do what its sight did,
nor even sacrifices and burnt offerings and the blood of calves.
Its sight did a work that came about through a senseless thing,
and it was exalted and lifted even above Moses who fashioned it.
How is it not greater than Moses and his book too,
since it did what neither Moses nor his law did?
The bitten looked to Moses and his book
and were not helped against the harm of the serpents.
The appearance of great Moses was more awesome than anything,
yet to the serpents it was more despised and scorned than anything.
The whole of Moses, had he been laid upon the bites,
would not have healed unless a man looked at the serpent.
The sight of the mute thing was more precious to the condemned
than Moses and the divine law.

It is good, then, to ask its cause—what it is, and for whom,
and why it grew great and was honored above Moses.
At the greatness of its rank I marveled much, and still I marvel:
how did it give out the healing of life, though it was dead?
Its very deadness has constrained me to speak about it,
and here I stand like a woman in labor because of its story.
Like a woman in travail, its story has pressed my mind into labor,
so that it may come forth and proclaim the power of the search hidden within it:
the search for the divine power that is searched out in it,
which was to do a new thing on earth, as it did through it.
It trod a way in mystery before the deeds,
so that it would be easy for men to come to their life.
The life of men is hidden in its sight and its healing,
and the likeness of what is hidden through it is yet to be compared [?].
Spiritually the healing flowed from its calmness,
and so it still comes to men through the Son of Man.
God was to dwell among men and to give life to men,
and beforehand He did it by means of the serpent that healed men.
He portrayed His mystery in the sight of the silent one—He who was to come—
so that when He came His appearance would not be strange to men.
For men were going to marvel at the newness of His power,
and by the power of the serpent they would not doubt Him who was coming.
By its sight alone it gave healing to the stricken,
so that no one in faith should demand the sight of [?] approach.
By faith the Hebrews too were healed,
and not by a remedy that was seen and applied.
By that same faith He was to give life to men through a man,
and He laid the foundation of His faithfulness in faith.
In the death of men it was set for Him to undo death,
and He taught men to ask life from one wholly dead.
On the top of Golgotha they were to hang Him on the top of the wood,
and He taught Moses to hang His mystery in the midst of the people.
When the iniquity of the peoples grew great, it was a blow to Him,
and in that same likeness He revealed the likeness because of iniquity.
Because of iniquity the condemned creatures attacked the Hebrews,
and iniquity did not cast [?] the serpent's weapons against the pains.
By the impassible He loosed the passions from their sufferings,
so that when He redeemed through the passible one, no one would object.
By a dead thing that bears no name of life He gave life to the world,
so that when He gives life to the dead by a dead one, no one should dispute how.
Whom did the Judge rebuke beforehand by what He did,
so that if the Judge judges, He may judge what happened and this as well?
Whom did the doubter [?] expose beforehand by the healing of the serpent,
that if a silent thing gave healing, how much more a speaking one?
Which of the contentious did He rebuke by the sight that drove away pains,
that if this happened through bronze, how much more through the Son of Man?
Why then, man, are you amazed at the salvation of men,
when behold, through bronze there came a wonder like this?
Circumcised one, why do you not consent to the search of your mysteries,
when behold, this which happened among the uncircumcised peoples is portrayed in you?
Is it true to you that the serpent healed you freely,
and yet how a man gave life to men you will not accept?
Did the sight of the mute thing redeem you from the mouths of mute creatures,
and the redemption through the speaker you will not confess?

Did it, then, if it did not reveal it, tell me the cause of the serpent—
what it is, and for whom, and why you were healed by it?
If it is true to you that it healed your pains, as it did,
why do you doubt a healing greater than that?
Greater is the redemption that came through a man than through the serpent,
as much as the greatness of man is greater than that of the beasts.
Be silent, then, Israelite, blind with envy,
and do not deny the open truth with your lies.
Calm yourself too, heretic, double poison [?];
do not throw the course of our discourse into turmoil with your madness.
The band of your madness is to me the same as the Jew's,
for you have mingled the name of your wickedness with that of your like.
One is the confession of your faith and of the Jew,
for you have defiled the mystery of the incarnation just as he has.
He does not accept the redemption of men that came through a man,
and you do not confess that it was truly through a man that He redeemed humanity.
Through a man humanity is redeemed—O madmen!—
and Moses bears witness, who raised the serpent as a mystery of your redemption.
"As Moses raised the serpent in the wilderness,
so too the Son of Man must be lifted up."
The command that healed the people's pains through the serpent
is the same that gives life to men through the Son of Man.
The will that exalted the mute thing through its help
is the same that exalted a rational man above all.
In the mystery of the exaltation of the speaker the silent one grew great,
and by His authority it gained authority to drive away pains.
In this both its making and its lifting up were set forth,
that it might tread a way for the exaltation of the Man who is in the Son of Man.
The might of the Creator exalted man through the serpent and through a man,
and healed his sickness through the mute and through the speaker.
Through the serpent He healed the visible pains in the limbs;
through the Son of Man, the visible pains and the hidden sins.
Through the gaze of the eyes the healing of life was given out,
and the redemption of man through faith in the mind.
The power in the silent one was less than in the speaker,
for it could not wipe away sins and stains.
It could cleanse only the blemishes of the body;
to forgive the debt of sins was too hard for it.
The senseless physician healed half of man,
for it was not its part to make man whole, since it was not a man.
A man was to make men whole by the might of the Creator,
and beforehand He trod the way to His wholeness with what was less than He.
Like a guide He sent the serpent before His coming,
that by a contrivance it might heal the pains of the bitten.
To shame the demons He did this through a serpent and a man,
so that by the very thing through which they harmed man He might give life to man.
Through a serpent the head of their ranks overthrew [?] the head of humanity,
and through a serpent He healed the pains caused by serpents.
He was pursuing them through the mystery of the healing that came from the silent one,
to let them know that the time was near when they would be exposed.
Already they grew sorrowful as the serpent drove away pains,
just as they wailed when Christ drove out the Legion.
Already they were stricken [?] as they saw the healing done by the mute thing,
as at the time when [?] they were tormented before Jesus.

Already they were brooding with the hateful brooding of their thoughts:
"What is this new thing that has happened in the house of the dead?
How did it come about that the serpent which brought death in by its hand
has turned and given life to the deadness of man by the sight of its face?"
They put on mourning because of the serpent and because of our Lord:
how could pains and sins be healed without medicines?
Because of our Lord they mourned all the more,
for body and soul were healed by the word of His mouth.
At Him and at the serpent they marveled and were amazed,
how closely the mystery resembled the truth through its works.
And if the demons were amazed and astonished at the truth and at the mystery,
let the Jew and the heretic stay outside the door.
Outside the door of faith let the perverse stand,
since they do not wish to enter with us into the confession of truth.
Let the mystery and the truth put the stubborn [?] to shame,
and let truth shut its door in their faces.
Let the serpent by its silence argue the case against their words,
since they will not allow the Man who is from us to be exalted.
Did the lifeless serpent grow great and become honored,
while the second Adam—why do you withhold Him from exaltation?
Did the bronze that men forged heal man,
and the Man whom the power of the Spirit forged, why does He not heal?
Did they give Him the power to help, as they did the mute thing,
and leave it standing at a rank that brings it level with Being itself?
Is its rank greater than [?] the free-born,
and is the punishment harsh for whoever belittles the height of its rank?
Because of its rank the feeble, forged serpent grew great,
and were it not for Him [?], it would have been reckoned as nothing.
It would be nothing, were something not hidden in it,
and its healing would not be believed without something.
The something I spoke of is Christ, something true above all,
and everything is reckoned as nothing in comparison with Him.
And Paul testifies that it is the shadow of something [?]:
the Law possessed only the shadow,
and was not the reality of bodily things.
The body is Christ, who is true and complete in body and soul,
and His shadow is the serpent, which served the mystery of His redemption.
The mute thing served the mystery of His redemption among the Hebrews,
and like a herald its calmness cried out His coming.
To the discerning the speech of its silence was plain,
for without a voice it conversed with its hearers,
and eyes instead of ears listened to its proclamation.
O herald neither discerning nor speaking,
who proclaimed on earth the new good tidings of the renewal of man!
O messenger lame of word and of step,
who outran the possessors of speech in his swiftness!
O you in whom the might of the Creator whispered, though it did not whisper in you,
and men listened to it, though they never heard its voice!
O how beautiful is your story, serpent who are not beautiful!
Though you are ugly, men were made beautiful through you, away from ugliness.
O ugly one, who made man ugly from the beginning,
yet turned and made beautiful the beauty you had made ugly in the land of Eden!
Ugly you are, serpent, and still more so for being of bronze,

and the good that comes from you is not yours but the Good One's.
The Good One in His love made you a vision of fair things,
that through you He might shame the Hateful One who made men ugly by your hands.
So it is not you who are praised where you are praised,
but the Mighty One who shows His might even through feeble things.
The might of the Creator gave life to the people through the mystery of the mute thing,
and again it gave life to the dead peoples through the living truth.
In truth let us confess that His might worked both this and that:
His are the first things and the last.
Blessed is He who by His cross trod for us a way to the kingdom on high,
and by it redeemed us from slavery to the Evil One and to death.
On the Incarnation of Our Lord Christ

and the Consecration of the Church.
Another, by the same author again.
The fortieth homily,
which he composed on the incarnation of our Lord Christ;
it is suited to the Consecration of the Church.
Response:
Church of the peoples, worship Him who betrothed you,
who planted you on earth and wrote your name in heaven.
My brothers…

The Church, full of distinctions, / mistress of treasures and of wisdom: / the teaching that flows from her / has gone out to the four quarters. / Peoples divided in their tongues / and far from all agreement / she has yoked together with one yoke, / which teaches love to those who bear it. / A great mystery that was hidden / from generations and from ages: / its truth has been made plain in knowledge / to those above and those below. / The Son who is with his Begetter, / whose likeness was hidden and concealed: / the Church has learned the commandment / that he is the Existent One, born of the Father. / The Spirit who is from the Father / and not less than him in being: / within the Church he divided his wealth, / and she received it as [?]. / In the name of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, / three holy names, / she received power and authority, / and learned that the being is one. / One God Israel proclaimed, / as it had been commanded; / but the Church learned the interpretation, / to confess him in three hypostases. / The Son was hidden with his Begetter / from those above and those below, / and in mysteries and in figures / the prophets wrote down his symbol. / But when the fulfilment came / of the time decreed in his knowledge, / God sent his Son / to come and renew our frame. / He went forth from where he was, / and came to where he already was. / He went forth from the Father and did not move, / and his will came into the world. / For it is not possible that in his nature / he should pass from place to place, / since times and worlds are within him / and creatures do not confine him. / He came wholly in his will, / and remained wholly in his nature; / for his nature is in every place, / while his will goes and comes. / He came to the dwelling of mortals / to renew our worn-out image, / and from our despised nature / he made himself a temple and dwelt in it, / which the Spirit fashioned without seed / within a womb without union, / that by it he might renew creation / and reconcile those above through it. / He sent a messenger of peace / to announce his conception on earth, / and by the door through which death had entered / life entered and changed mortality. / "Peace to you, full of grace," / the Watcher said to Mary; / "the Lord is with you, daughter of mortals, / for from you the Saviour will shine forth." / Behold the place where they stumbled, / the heretics, the contentious, / and made it like an arena

for the dispute of their questions. / "The Word," they say, "was changed / and became flesh, as it is written; / he did not take a body from Mary, / but he himself became flesh." / But if the Word was changed, / then he received composition; / and if he received composition, / he became a beginning for his own frame; / and if he began through formation, / he is equal in his creation to every man, / and is Maker in name only, / while far from the deeds. / Let this blasphemy turn back / upon the head of the heretics, / who tore the robe of the confession / of the faith of the apostles. / Come, you who are perverse in persuasion / and blind beyond understanding: / why this contention, / and over what this strife? / What do you gain from this, / that you make the Existent One suffer, who does not suffer, / and call him who is equal with his Father / a creature of flesh? / Hearer, do not be troubled, / nor divided over what you have heard. / Come, draw near to persuasion, / and hear and learn aright. / It was not the Word that was changed / and became flesh in his own hypostasis; / rather the Word put on flesh, / to set mortals free by it. / The Word did not become flesh, / but took a man, / who was complete in every respect, / in body and soul alike. / It was a man who was tested / in womb, birth and upbringing, / in hunger, thirst and suffering, / and in death that fulfilled the time. / But sin did not rule over him, / and Paul testifies to this, / for he was the dwelling of the Godhead, / sanctified by the Holy Spirit. / And let the hearer not suppose, / because I have called him a man, / that I speak of two sons, / as the foolish have imagined. / One is the Son, the Son of the Being, / he who is equal with his Begetter, / who was hidden in his Father's bosom / until the time of his coming. / And because of his love toward us / he took a complete man / and made him one with himself / in lordship and authority. / From the day the Spirit fashioned him / within a womb without union, / he is Lord and heir and ruler / in height and depth alike. / Mortals could not / gaze on him in his nature, / and for this he took a man, / that his splendour might be hidden in a human being. / And by this he gave us a pledge / that he would put on our despised nature / and raise it with him to heaven, / to the honour at his right hand. / In his image he had called our nature / in the beginning, when he formed it, / and this image was corrupted / through the counsel of the Accuser. / But now he willed in his grace / to renew our worn-out image, / and took from us a firstfruits / and raised it to himself in glory. / This is our whole confession, / which we learned from the books of the Spirit: / that God does not change / and does not fall under sufferings. / The sufferings are a man's, / that passible one of our race, / who shared in the glories / through the love of the one who took him. / The womb and the birth are a man's, / circumcision and sacrifices are a man's, / food and thirst are a man's, / weariness and sleep are a man's; / prayer and suffering are his, / apart from God the Word. / Jesus the child grew / in stature and wisdom, with distinctions, / and increased in grace

before God and men. / Whose, then, are / all these distinctions? / The Maker's, who is not lowered, / or the man's, the son of our race? / Contentious ones, do not err: / it is the growth of the son of our race, / who came to perfection / in the union with the Word. / Not that his authority was less / from the day of his birth, / but this was fitting, / that his exaltation should keep pace with his growth. / Let us speak now of his temptation / and his struggle with Satan: / that at the end of forty days, / Scripture says, he hungered and was tempted. / Come, interpret this for us, / you new scribes who challenge us, / and explain to us its meaning: / who is it that hungered and was tempted? / Here they take refuge in silence, / and raise a finger against the truth; / for the plainness of the reading / rebukes the wickedness of their words. / For the Evil One would not have dared / to bring temptation near / to him who knows all things, / for he knew he could not be tempted. / But he brought temptation / to the one who had members, / for he saw that at the end of his fast / he craved food; / and as with Adam, the first man, / who craved food, / he saw that he had put on his nature, / and supposed he would accept his word. / In all these things he was tempted, / the son of our race, not the Maker; / for the nature of the Maker is exalted / above sufferings and above temptation. / He grew weary from the toil of the journey, / and sat and rested from his toil, / and asked the Samaritan woman for water / to ease the pain of his thirst. / Here is the weariness of a man, / and the hunger and thirst were his. / And while the Word dwelt in him, / he was tested in what was his own. / By means of water he turned / the erring woman toward his teaching, / and by the knowledge of his Godhead / he brought her deeds into the open. / To his disciples he said, / when they brought him food: / "I have other food / that you do not know." / And that food was / to do the will of his Father, / to show how much he longed / for the repentance of sinners. / He slept in the boat and they woke him, / and he rose, rebuked the sea, and it grew calm. / Sleep belongs to mortality, / and the calming of the sea to the Maker. / "Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, / and I rejoice that I was not there." / In his humanity he was not there; / in his Godhead he was there. / And as he went to raise him, / he shed tears of suffering, / grieving for the dust, / for the dusty one, the son of his race. / Whose are these words, / you perverse ones who have strayed from the way? / Surely his who put on members, / who was in need in every respect. / And in the Spirit, they say, he was strengthened, / and with a loud voice he called Lazarus: / "Come out, dead man, and see for yourself / the dwelling of life you had put off." / Here the voice was the Maker's, / which called Lazarus and he lived; / as one wakes sleepers from sleep, / he raises the dead from corruption. / Openly he spoke / of the lowly things concerning himself, / when he said to his disciples: / "I am going to my Father and my God." / Fabricators of books will say to us: / "Has God a God, / and has the Hidden Existent One a Maker, / through whom all things came into being?"

He called God his God, / for God is his Maker and the Maker of all; / and the Exalted One he named his Father, / who granted him this by grace. / "Now," they say, "my soul is troubled" / by the sufferings I endure, / "and I am grieved even to death" / by the harshness of the cross. / Whose soul is it that is troubled, / you contentious ones without understanding? / The Word, Existent from the Father, / he who is equal with his Begetter? / Do not err, you presumptuous ones: / the Existent One is exalted above sufferings. / The sufferings are a man's, / that passible one of our race; / these belong to the man, / him who became Son by grace. / Not that the Word, the Only-begotten, / who exists eternally with his Father— / I did not say that the Word / acquired sonship by grace, / lest Arius boast / that I am pleading his case. / "My Father who sent me," he says, "is greater than I" / in being and in authority. / The one made was not begotten / to be compared with his Maker; / he is greater than him in being, / for his nature is without beginning, / and whatever has a beginning / is less in its building than the Existent One. / We have, then, a high priest / who was faithful to his Maker, / like Moses in all his house, / and greater than the son of Amram. / Who is this high priest, / and whom do you call his Maker? / For he was trustworthy over his house / and had power over the works of his hands. / Jesus is the high priest, / and his Maker is the Hidden Existent One, / who made him a dwelling for the Creator / and made him lord over his possessions. / "One," they say, "is the Mediator / of God and of men, / the man Jesus," who grew / and became king and ruler. / Here he calls mediator / him who was from David; / and he became mediator by his death / and reconciled us with the Creator. / He tasted death, they say, in his nature, / apart from God the Word; / and while the Word dwelt in him, / suffering did not come near his nature. / Suffering and death belong to the passible one, / who has death in his nature; / resurrection and life belong to the Creator, / who has life in his nature. / Everyone who came to be through him has lived, / and he gives life and light. / He is a spring full of life, / whose flow never ceases; / for he does not diminish in his nature, / nor grow beyond what he is, / nor fall under sufferings, / for his nature is exalted above sufferings. / Sufferings belong to the son of our race, / who was small, grew and was exalted: / he was lowered in that he tasted death in time, / and grew in that he came into lordship. / Let not the hearer think / that in this I have separated the lowly things, / so as to speak of two persons, / the Word and the temple he chose for himself. / I confess one Son, / and I proclaim two natures: / the nature worshipped and glorified, / the Existent Word with the Father, / and our nature, which he took / by his own counsel and to which he pledged himself. / He is perfect in his Godhead, / being equal with his Begetter, / and perfect also in his humanity, / in the body and soul of mortals. / The two became, in the union, / one love and one will: / the Only-begotten Word from the Father, / and the likeness of the servant that he took.

And because of the love of the one who took, / he honoured the one taken together with himself, / and lowered himself in names, / though in his nature he is not lowered. / The dusty one became by grace / heir of the lordship with the Word, / who honoured him with his nature in all things / and subjected height and depth to him. / And the Word took his lowly things, / which belong to the dusty one, by a borrowed name, / and the mortal too was honoured / with the glories of the Only-begotten. / Not at the fulfilment of time / was he honoured with glories, / but from now and for ever, / for his authority has no end. / Once he offered himself / as a sacrifice to God, / and became priest in heaven, / and his priesthood is not dissolved, / in the heavenly Holy of Holies, / to make atonement for all; / and he obtained by his hand redemption / for the whole race of mortals. / He did not enter with the blood of animals, / after the order of the high priests, / but he himself became the sacrifice, / and his blood was poured out for everyone. / To him he said, "Sit at my right hand / until all things are subjected to you," / as he reigns over all that has come to be / together with God, who took him. / His too is the coming / that is to be at the end. / In the form in which he suffered on earth / he will be adorned when he comes. / At the voice of his word are raised / those who have slept from Adam until now, / and those who loved his appearing / fly to meet him on the clouds. / By the breath of his mouth he destroys / him who comes to deceive in his name, / and by the rebuke of his word he breaks / the authority of the Accuser. / He is adorned by thousands of Watchers / and by myriads of angels, / and seraphim without number / repeat the holiness of his greatness. / On the manifestation of his body gaze / those of heaven and those of earth, / while his Godhead is hidden / within the doorway of his humanity. / In him mortals behold / face to face, openly, / and, as through an image, by his manifestation / all are drawn to that Hidden One. / Not without the one he took / does he do these things when he comes; / with him is he who is without change / from beginning to end. / One is the Son and one person, / two kinds that became one: / the Only-begotten Word from the Father, / and the likeness of the servant which he took. / And it is not because they became one / that the natures were mingled in the union; / let the hearer not suppose / that he became a mixture in his nature. / The Being is not mingled, / and the Maker is not changed, / for his is a nature hidden and concealed / and beyond all changes. / Nor did his holy dwelling, / the likeness of the servant which he took, / undergo change, / for its nature is preserved with the Word. / But in thought are distinguished / the glorious things from the lowly, / and they are attributed to one Son, / of two natures that became one. / The weaknesses are a man's, / of him who was born of Mary; / the glories are of the Word, / the eternal Offspring of the Father, / who willed in his love / that our race should be honoured by him. / Here the conclusion has been reached / of that by which he called us his own image: / not in the image of his nature, / but in the image of his honour. / For he has no composition, / nor form nor likeness; / for the Creator is without composition / and not bounded by sight. / The prophets named him with names / suited to the hearing of humanity.

And though he is neither lessened nor increased, / they said that he was lessened and also grew; / and though in his nature he is in every place, / they said that he descended and ascended. / But the foolish who heard these things / were not properly instructed: / they applied them as weaknesses / to the Maker in his nature. / Nor was presumption enough for them, / though they strayed by it beyond measure, / but they composed fabrications / and armed themselves against the truth. / Come then, O hearer, / be a disciple of Scripture, / walk in the way of uprightness, / and do not stray onto a false path. / Believe in the Father without beginning, / the Existent One who precedes all that has come to be, / whose being is not bounded / by the thought of things made. / Confess the Son, who is from the Father, / begotten of him without passion, / Lord and Existent One and Maker, / equal with him in his nature. / Glorify the hypostasis of the Spirit, / who is from him by nature, / and not less than the Father and the Son / in lordship and authority. / One nature equally / is the Father's and the Son's and the Holy Spirit's: / three distinct hypostases, / one being without beginning. / This nature the prophets proclaimed / in mysteries and figures, / while the distinction of the hypostases / was kept to be revealed in the Son. / And when the time of his dawning came, / of him who was hidden from generations, / he revealed this distinction to us, / that we should confess three hypostases. / Behold the true confession, / not worn out with long discourses, / nor laden with a weight of words / to trouble the hearer. / The descent of the Son to us / was no going forth and moving, / but love and will, / while he was not lessened from what he is. / For I said in what I repeated / that the Maker is not diminished, / nor does he go or come, / for his nature is in every place. / It is the bodily one who was lowered and grew, / through the suffering and death of the cross, / and after these was honoured / by resurrection and ascension, / and became a true dwelling / for the Godhead, without separation, / for he was honoured with the Being / in lordship and authority. / "The Father," they say, "judges no one, / for he has given all judgment to him," / as by the decree of his judgment he examines / those above and those below. / It is he who gives reward / to the diligent for their labours, / and by him the wicked are condemned / to shame and to Gehenna. / And for this he chose him out of all / and made him a temple for his honour, / that mortals might gaze on him / as he examines their deeds. / And because the nature of his glory / is not subject to sight, / through a visible one he comforts us, / as one whom we see. / Here, in mysteries and figures, / we look as in a mirror; / and there, with unveiled faces, / we shall see his very self. / Not of the hypostasis of the Word / is this possible, / but of the son of our race, / the firstfruits of our nature. / For it is not possible / for mortals to see God and live, / and Paul testifies to this, / that no one has seen him or sees him. / And for this he took a man / and made him the image of his honour, / that mortals might be comforted by him / in place of the hiddenness of his being. / Thanks, O Good One, for your gift, / that you have loved our nature so much / and honoured it with your glories, / though our nature is not worthy. / Through the firstfruits you took from us / our whole race has been honoured, / and with us were renewed together

heaven and earth and all that is in them. / And what is more, those far above us, / spiritual beings in their natures, / learned of you through us and confessed your name, / and with us were renewed together. / Through the Church, it says, was revealed / the hidden wisdom of the Creator / to the authorities of heaven, / which had been concealed from the beginning. / Through us the spiritual beings learned / that the Father had a Son, though hidden; / and with us they received the confession / that the Spirit is Existent like the Father. / Through us they learned also the mystery / of two natures that became one: / the Existent Word from the Father, / and the man, the son of our race. / With us they received the knowledge / that in Christ all things are renewed, / and in our freedom they find rest / from the bondage of their toils. / And creation too, it says, with us / is set free from servitude, / when they receive the redemption / of the mortality of our nature. / Come, you who err, turn back to the way / while there is still time for persuasion. / For us the creatures wait, / to receive renewal with us; / to us the spiritual beings look, / to gain transformation with us, / and they wait for the redemption / according to the promise of the Maker. / The love of those who cherish teaching / roused me to say these things, / and the zeal of those who were presumptuous / compelled me to distinguish the natures. / And yet, even as I distinguish the natures, / the glorious from the lowly, / I have made no rent in my confession, / for I confess one Son. / One lordship I believe, / and one authority I know, / as I worship equally / the Word and the dwelling he chose for himself. / I confess the King who put on / the purple of Adam's body, / and I worship the Lord who united / our nature with his greatness. / I distinguished these from those, / not with a divided mind, / but so that the fools may not think / that the Son is a creature, as they imagined— / those who drew out their words at length / and lowered the Existent One to despised things, / and robbed our nature / of the honour of the one who took it. / For their thoughts are sick / and their minds diseased, / and they do not accept words of truth, / for sin has blinded their sight. / They are not equal to perfection, / for they are sorely broken in knowledge, / and like infants they are brought down / to fleshly food. / They laid the foundation of their words / on sand, and it did not hold. / They began to build a building / [?] destined for ruin. / They are drunk with murderous envy / against the holy books, / and they cover their hatred / with the name of God in which they wrap themselves. / Simple are they, without understanding, / who are led after their words; / they have abandoned the way of uprightness / and now stray after falsehood. / The truth that shines brighter than the sun / is darkness to their minds, / and to them falsehood, a dark night, / seems an upright confession. / The faith, the anchor / that holds the ship of the Church— / the fools abandoned it and sank / in the deep, as in the sea. / The sweet spring of teaching, / by whose drink the upright were reared— / they recoiled from it as from something bitter, / and the drink of the Evil One pleased them. / They are sick and lie in fever / in their minds rather than their limbs, / and they are proud as though healthy, / and do not perceive how diseased they are. / They stand erect against the truth / like zealots of the law,

and haughtiness is their garment, / as though it were their due. / They have not yet become disciples / nor studied the Scriptures, / yet in the impudence of their minds / they want to be teachers. / Come, submit to the truth, / you contentious ones, and learn the truth; / lay aside your hardness / and take up the yoke of humility. / It is not from envy that I wish / to pull down the edifice of their words, / but to turn, if I can, / your minds toward the truth. / For you ought to learn, being unlearned, / yet you want to teach; / and whoever teaches within the Church / you have counted as a stranger. / You have wronged prophecy / and rejected the words of the Spirit, / and you have received a new fabrication / from unlearned teachers. / And here has been fulfilled in deed / what is written in the Gospel: / if a blind man leads a blind man, / the end of his road is a pit. / In what does he differ from the blind man, / who is blind in knowledge? / He who [?] does not know the truth / promises to teach his companions. / Though sick and sunk in fever / in body and soul alike, / behold, he promises healing / to members afflicted with sin. / Do not do the will of your own soul, / you fool who have no understanding. / Humble your light mind / and hear the words of the Scriptures. / Teaching is a sweet spring / that gives life to its hearers, / and a light that turns souls / to the level road of uprightness. / Not that I wish to boast / in what I have repeated and said; / I call the truth as witness to my word, / for it is the truth I honour. / Not that I am lifted up in my own eyes / above the members, my fellows; / for I am a member of the body, / and in their pains I suffer. / And this befits those who know: / that in this order they should resemble / the joy of a single member, / which the whole body shares. / Christ, the head of the members, / made his Church one body, / and proclaimed good news concerning death in time, / because of the love of the one who took him [or: of his members]. / Behold the physician who knows the pains, / both hidden and revealed. / Sick ones, come, take healing, / that you may not die in your sins. / Wake up, you who sleep in sin, / and cast off the weight of your debts, / for behold, the morning has drawn near that wakes / the sleepers from the sleep of death. / Sick ones laid low by fever / of the hidden diseases of the soul, / behold, the Merciful has prepared a free medicine / that heals afflicted bodies. / Members of the household who have strayed outside, / turn back to the way while you live, / and do not trust in this, / that you are called members of the household in name. / For who sins more / than one who is named with the name of truth? / A borrowed name is a stumbling block / when it is far from deeds. / What did it profit Judas, / the apostleship he obtained from Jesus? / And what help did he gain from the power / of the mystery of the Body that gives life to all? / Because his purpose was not straight, / he became a stranger to his election; / and because he changed his will, / envy slew him instead of a sword. / Let no one boast in names, / but let him draw near to deeds; / for deeds can justify / even one who is far off in name.
