Come, you who err, take refuge / in the anchor of our Lord's body, / which can [?] our souls / and bring them in hope into heaven. / For the gift bestowed on our race / cannot be repaid by deeds: / let us repay goodness in return / with a confession without division.
On the Construction of the Tabernacle of Meeting

Memra 41. / On the Tabernacle of Meeting. / By the same author: / the forty-first memra, / which he composed on the construction of the Tabernacle of Meeting, / and which he applies to the sanctuary of the Church.

The creation that the Creator created a second time by the hands of Moses,
so that man might learn that it was He who created creation in the beginning.
His will depicted a twofold world before the steward of His house,
that the power of His craftsmanship might be proclaimed to the hosts on high.
He gathered the hosts on high upon Mount Sinai,
that they might see His power as they had seen it when the beginning came to be.
In the same manner in which He had created creation, before their assemblies
He sketched the likenesses of the tabernacle of time and showed them to His servant.
In the tabernacle of time He willed to reveal His greatness,
and in its arrangement He traced the order of the height and the depth.
After the pattern of the beauty of two worlds He depicted it on earth,
earthly and heavenly, a twofold radiance.
At a twofold wonder I have marvelled greatly: that the Fashioner of all
created something when there was nothing, and renews it.
From nothing He created all creatures in the beginning,
and He turned a second time and renewed them by the hands of Moses.
He called Watchers and men to look upon the building of His work,
that they might be witnesses to its renewal and to its order.
A likeness of what does not exist He depicted on the mountain as though it existed,
so that without anything they might see something from nothing.
Skilfully He depicted likenesses without composition,
so that by their composition He might confirm His servants in His creatorship.
The truth of His name He traced in the vision and showed them,
that they might not be divided concerning His being, which has no beginning.
His name He set first as the foundation for the building of His work,
and upon it He completed heaven and earth and all that is in them.
His name again He held like an iron tool in the hands of Moses,
and He hewed words and built upon them the truth of His name.
With words He taught him to build His power in writings,
and as with roots He made them firm by means of letters.
He built a house of something real, a building of the fear of truth,
and likened it to the order of that ordering made from nothing.
From nothing the world's Fashioner had created it,
and without anything he too imitated and made something.
The dwelling that was the world He depicted for him as a symbol,
that he might imitate it and make a tabernacle in the likeness of the worlds.
That Will which created creation from nothing
showed him a beautiful vision that resembled something.
"See, and make," His Power said to the craftsman,
"according to that spiritual likeness which I depicted before you.
See, depict well the beautiful form of the two worlds,
and set it on earth before beholders, that they may cleave to it.
Make one tabernacle after the pattern in which I made heaven and earth,
and when it is set in order, divide it into two that are without separation.
Spread a veil between the one and the other and separate them,

as the firmament separates, which is stretched between the two orders.
As by a partition of the waters I divided it to make two dwellings,
so you too make a fixed partition and divide your work.
Stretch curtains over the earth and fasten them,
and instead of a wall surround them with crafted boards.
Tabernacle and tabernacle shall there be in the tabernacle that you set up,
in the same manner as world and world out of one world.
The world of time and the world to come my will has set in order;
set in order you too a tabernacle and a tabernacle in the same manner.
For the world of time, whose time is full of passing things,
look with order, and set each thing to correspond to something.
In the outer tabernacle put earthly things,
and in the inner put the conduct of spiritual things.
Spiritual and bodily things arrange and make,
that the work of your hands may resemble the work of my hands."
O Craftsman who made the worlds from nothing,
who teaches His servants to imitate Him in making something!
O Fashioner who formed creatures when they did not exist,
who turned a second time and traced them before the son of Amram!
O He whose eternity is hidden within His eternity,
whose power whispered revealed voices before His ministers!
O you, you too, the man who is fashioned from earth,
whose mind ascended to imitate your Fashioner!
O you, Moses, frail clay drawn from the waters,
who attained, like the Creator, to creating creation!
O you stammerer, lame in uttering the words of the mouth,
whose word outran the course of men and of heavenly beings!
With the Daughter of the divine Voice the slow one ran,
and his tongue flew over things that were not visible to him.
The word of the Spirit whispered with him spiritually,
and depicted it in his mind, that he might fulfil words by deeds.
By deeds he fulfilled everything that was shown to him,
by the power of that Power perfect in His being and His creatorship.
The tabernacle of time he made upon earth as he was commanded,
and divided it in two like the division of the height and the depth.
In the order of the worlds, this one and the one to come, he arranged his work,
and gathered and filled it with the pattern of the conduct of here and of there.
Two conducts he showed to man by means of his ordering,
and taught them to keep the order placed in the two of them.
In the outer one he arranged them in bodily things,
and in the inner one he made them wise in spiritual things.
Bodily and spiritual things he set in the two of them,
corresponding to the composition of the human being, of body and of spirit.
The body he permitted to enter at all times into that outer one,
and the inner one he allowed to the soul of everyone through the high priest.
With the high priests all entered by way of thought,
since the body could not enter, being earthly.
Spiritually was that inner tabernacle fashioned,
and the high priests too entered it in the guise of spiritual beings.
Mystically was traced the likeness of that outer one,
corresponding also to the entry made by faith.

That one alone the body was permitted to see,
and it was barred from cleaving to spiritual things.
With the conduct of the body that outer tabernacle was filled,
and bodily things and the sustenance of the body were placed in it.
Dead sacrifices were sacrificed in its burnt offerings,
and rows of bread were set in order on its table.
A golden lampstand, [?], was fixed in it,
and above it the pattern of the luminaries and the reckoning of days.
The whole course of the year's sustenance was signified in it;
the power of the elements was hidden in the figures depicted in it.
Corresponding to the inhabited world the tabernacle was stretched out on four sides,
and it was arranged according to the order of the months of the year.
A great [?] filled its arrangement for whoever looked on it,
and its components too were set up to correspond to the world.
Along with the world the order of its course was carried,
and its objects were arranged in it like the alternations of the seasons.
In the north were set the altar of sacrifices and the table of bread,
which revealed the forgiveness of sins and the change of the seasons.
The changes of the seasons were signified by the rows on the tables,
and the months of the year revolved among their rows.
In six rows twelve months were shown,
and each of them was set up in two months.
The months bring about the sprouting of seeds and the growth of fruits,
and so also the rows were arranged in this order.
By bread the life of man subsists as long as he is earthly;
for that reason bread alone was placed on the table.
In this manner the rows were arranged on the north,
that they might face toward the order of the luminaries.
In the mystery of the luminaries the lampstand looked to them with its lamps,
and they were beside it like seeds turned to meet the sun.
In the south He who set the law placed it as a symbol,
and its face toward the north, after the pattern of the sun's orbit.
With the sun it revolved, not in substance [?],
but in the order of the working of its rays.
The whole order of the luminaries was arranged in it,
and the reckoning of days and the change of months was signified in it.
The week of days was depicted in it, and it itself was in the week,
and seven lamps, in the number of the days, were on its top.
By the number of the days the order of the lamps upon it was counted,
and it was arranged in the likeness of a week that lacks nothing.
Six branches were received into it, and it was in the middle,
like the days of the ordering of all things, and the Sabbath at the end.
That ordering of six days was bounded in it,
and it was holy like the Sabbath day, which the symbol hallowed.
The week of the two [?] was reckoned in the tabernacle of time,
and the lamps upon it were like the luminaries in the face of the height.
In the outer tabernacle alone was its light shown,
just as the sun too shines only in the dwelling below.
The Holy of Holies had no need of the light from it,
just as the dwelling above has no need of a luminary.

After the dwelling above that inner tabernacle was depicted,
and in its likeness it was barred from entry.
In the likeness of the height it was served while it was still on earth,
and its objects too told of things to come.
By the sacrifice of incense and the house of spices placed in it
they prophesied of the confession of purity of soul.
With the incense of spices the high priest too entered it,
and once a year he made atonement in it for himself and for the world.
Atonement of debts and a spirit of revelation he received in it,
and fear and love filled his going in and his coming out.
Fear filled him, because he was afraid on account of his sins,
and love filled him because he entered to receive mercy.
Mercy and judgment were revealed by its objects,
and they spoke of the deeds that have been and that will be.
The jar and the rod were a memorial of the things that had passed:
the food of manna and the choosing of the priests of the house of Levi.
Through the ark, the mystery of the heavenly ministries,
and through the seraphim, the perfection of immortal life.
By the golden object whose name was interpreted "propitiatory"
the atonement of debts that is in our Life-giver was interpreted.
By the name "propitiatory" that object was called,
not because it made atonement, but because it was the mystery of the Atoner.
The mystery of the propitiatory was hidden in the order of the law,
and it waited for when the Atoner of debts would be revealed.
The mute plate longed for the speaking Plate,
for when He would come to fulfil its mystery by deeds.
It longed for the atonement of debts that comes by deeds,
since by the power of sin it could not purify men.
Its power was too weak to lessen the iniquity of men,
and it was not able to loose death from mortals.
The name "propitiatory" of the Atoner was all it possessed,
and it shone like images that have no life.
In borrowed names without deeds it was wrapped,
a silent plate, a propitiatory of the mystery of propitiation.
Of Him who was to come it prophesied by its titles,
and as with a finger it pointed to the day of His revelation.
By the name "plate" His bodily nature was told,
and by "propitiatory" the power of the Being that dwelt in Him.
There was no power of atoning for debts in its silence,
nor could a man give life to men.
The power of the Creator strengthened the mystery and its fulfilment,
and by the power of His power He gave life in mortality.
The mortality of man was proclaimed in the silence of the plate,
and in the revelations that came about through it, the Word in the body.
A spirit of revelation breathed in it, in its silence,
like the divine will in the Man who is from us.
Through it the priest of the people learned the mystery of hidden things,
just as we learn the power of the Being through our Kinsman.
In the Holy of Holies a mute thing was placed upon the ark,
as its Lord too was destined to dwell on high.
Mute cherubim glorified its silence,
in the manner of the heavenly assemblies, for the Cause of our life.

For the Cause of our life the overlaid gold was honoured,
and its Merciful One too, because of the propitiatory on which they gazed.
But let the learned Jew, minister of mysteries, tell us
what the reason is for this silent propitiatory.
Why was it placed in the Holy of Holies as a holy thing,
and why did it reveal the mystery of hidden things and the atonement of debts?
Why did the priest need its silence when he entered,
and why did he learn through it to search out mysteries?
Why did the cherubim not speak, though they were mute as well?
For lo, it is written that from it a voice of revelation was conveyed.
Why did the priest not enter to it at all times,
and when he entered, why did he enter only with incense?
Why was a voice conveyed from a mute thing to his side,
and not from the height, from where [?] the power of the Being is?
Why was everything wholly through the mediation of a dead plate,
and why did the Speaking One bow His head before a silent one?
Look, Jew, with the power of inquiry and by the power of your books,
and see that my thoughts have rightly sought the [?] of the mystery.
My word asks also for the account of the tabernacle of your sacrifices:
for what reason was it called holy and holy?
Why was the outer one served with the blood of animals,
and that inner one only with incense, and once a year?
If the mystery of that entry brought profit,
why was it not performed every day, that it might profit every day?
Every day it would be fitting for those full of debts to be atoned for,
and at all times to hear the voice that blots out iniquity.
No, Hebrew, it is not so, as it is written;
another power is hidden in the signs, and the Voice that has dawned.
Your outer sanctuary: in it the dwelling of the earth is revealed,
and that inner one is the mystery of the spiritual order.
The altar of your sacrifices is the mystery of that Sacrifice offered for our life,
and your propitiatory is the shadow of Him who is the atonement of our debts.
That from that plate the voice was spoken at your side
was the power of the Helper who guides man through a Son of Man.
The cherubim of wood that hovered over the propitiatory
are the heavenly ones who serve the Head of our life.
That once a year the high priest entered it:
the entry of the Head of our life was depicted in it.
Into the sanctuary on high the mystery of our redemption was to enter,
and that entry was a rehearsal of His entry.
The priesthood of your people was a messenger before His coming,
and it announced Him with the sacrifice of lambs and the blood of calves.
Your tabernacle of time gave guidance through its division,
and showed two orders, of this world and of the world to come.
But why tabernacle and taber[nacle] for one conduct,
and why holy and Holy of Holies, revealed and hidden?
For what reason in the one a libation of the blood of animals,
and in the other incense and the manner of spiritual Watchers?
Why were you kept back [?] at the door of your Holy of Holies,
and did not enter to delight in praises?
Why did your priest too not enter by faith,
and when he entered, why did he not bring sacrifices in with him?
Your sanctuary testifies that what I have said is revealed in it,

and your Holy of Holies seals my words by deeds.
In all of it, it proclaims the preaching of our life,
and as with a finger it shows in its mysteries the truth of Him who has dawned.
It greatly longed for His dawning, that your books might receive radiance;
and now that He has dawned, why do you prevent them from looking on Him?
See, contentious one, how bright is His brightness,
which chased away the darkness of idolatry, and it vanished and ceased.
Then, fool, lift the veil from your mind,
and see the world that walks in the light of His preaching.
Then, obstinate one, come down from the height of contention,
and look on creation, which glorifies the banner of the Crucified.
All creation cries out His praise without ceasing,
and the four quarters weave a crown of victory for His name.
All the just were comforted in the mystery of His coming,
and the books of the Spirit told of His revelation.
Priests in His order were adorned in their persons,
and kings were honoured by His rank in their authority.
By the greatness of His rank the law and its commandments grew great,
and were it not for Him, it would not even have been renowned by name.
By His name it was honoured with the spirit of revelations,
and the revelations too told of His revelation.
To Him the priest bowed in mystery before that plate,
and that plate too filled His place for Him.
With the blood of animals the sprinkling of His blood was [?],
and who, I ask, was being revealed, but He who makes atonement?
In the counsel of the righteous His truth was confirmed,
and in their sacrifices His passion and His death were celebrated.
For Him that hope of the law was waiting,
and Moses testifies that he set up the tabernacle in the mystery of His revelation.
With the pattern of His revelation the tabernacle was filled [...],
and as with a finger it pointed to Him by [...].
[...] to Him the holy and the holy and all that was in them looked,
for when He would come and fulfil them by His holiness.
For the holiness that comes from Him the dead sacrifices longed,
for when the living Person would be sacrificed and release them.
The lamb by its sacrifice interpreted His sacrifice,
and louder than thunder its voice was raised in the mouths of those who ate it.
In the eating of the mute one the food of His body was revealed,
and in its despised blood His precious blood was interpreted.
The sprinkling of its blood guarded the people from harm;
and if the blood of a mute one sufficed to guard, how much more that of the Speaking One!
By the blood of the Speaking One the Good One was to redeem men,
and He sent the mute one to tread the way before His coming.
In the temple of His body the All was dwelling, and that by His will,
and He set up a tabernacle and called it the holy and the Holy of Holies.
In the mystery of the ordering of His body and His soul the tabernacle was depicted,
and it was served bodily and spiritually.
Bodily and spiritual things were placed in it,
since Watchers and men were to draw near to Him.
[?] led every one of the people,

and as with a guardian it bound them by hope in Him.
Until His dawning the banner of His commandments stood upright,
and as with a star it looked to Him in the beauty of its light.
An ordered arrangement filled the holy and the Holy of Holies,
and corresponding to the world it was fixed on the earth toward the four sides.
The place of the sun was filled in it by the lampstand of branches,
and by its lights the dues of the sacrifices were completed.
The sun by its heat ripens fruit and makes seeds sprout,
and in that same likeness it was in the tabernacle, the world of the two [?].
In the outer tabernacle it was fixed, it and its lamps,
since the sun too has its course bounded in the dwelling below.
Very close is the likeness that the son of the Hebrews imitated,
and no one can imitate better than this.
"See, and make after the pattern of the likeness that I depicted before you":
and this is the wonder, that when there was nothing he imitated with something.
There was nothing in the likeness that He depicted for him on the mountain,
and who will not be amazed that he imitated a likeness that has no likeness?
In his mind he examined what he had seen spiritually,
and the wonder-filled thing that he saw in his inner movements he completed [...].
The seer of hidden things saw a vision of light,
and it was far greater than earthly thought.
Many, again, were the measurements of the tabernacle of time,
and its divisions too were interwoven and mingled.
As with measurements of things that do not exist he made things that exist,
and as with divisions that are not real he made its order firm.
In order he made it, according to the orders he saw on the mountain,
and exactly and precisely he traced its likenesses without change.
O how exactly the son of the Hebrews painted your likenesses,
and made its likeness resemble that 'nothing' which was shown to you!
O how glorious the [?] with which the Spirit traced in your words,
and how its colour took on the beautiful colour that painted the worlds!
O how beautiful the path that you trod among earthly beings,
and so too that Voice which spoke with you trod it by your mouth!
O how true the name of the Being that you proclaimed on earth,
which spread abroad and exposed the [?] of the no-gods!
O how the word of your mouth ran, you who were heavy of tongue,
so that it rose above the worlds and came down to the order of the Fashioner of the worlds!
O how fine is your mind, O man, to see hidden things,
for you raised its movements to cleave to Him without sight!
Who will not marvel at your word, Moses drawn from the waters,
who instead of waters filled the earth with words of the Spirit?
Who will not say that the Spirit interpreted well by your mouth,
since according to His will you expounded His mysteries among earthly beings?
Who will not acknowledge the strength that strengthened the movements of your soul,
that it is He who created creation in the beginning and laid it open through your mouth?
Who will not believe that He caused the power of [?] to dwell in you,
and that by the command of His mouth your word was fulfilled upon mute natures?
Who will not call you a god,
an earthly one, as you were named, since works on earth were accomplished with your word?
Fitting is the renown that became yours, son of mortals,
and well was the word at your side fulfilled by deeds.

By a borrowed name the name of God was given you as a title,
and in deeds He came to be the one whom you called the great Prophet.
For all your words there was fulfilment, as they were prophesied,
and not one sign fell short that was not fulfilled.
He it is whom you called the great Prophet who fulfilled your words,
and He stamped your writing [?] with the stamp of the blood from His limbs.
Because of Him the Spirit whispered hidden mysteries in you,
and they were waiting for Him, for when He would come to reveal them.
To Him also looked the ordering of the tabernacle of time,
for He was to be the pure temple for the power of the Being.
Until the fullness of time the tabernacle served the name of the Creator,
and He who has no end is served in it in holiness.
In the sanctuary of His body the Hidden One dwells by His will,
and in it He is hallowed by spiritual and by bodily beings.
All creation worships its Fashioner in His body,
and cherishes Him as a divine temple.
The sanctuary is His body, and the Holy of Holies the movements of His soul,
and in their likenesses the holy and the Holy of Holies were depicted.
Holy and holy the tabernacle of time was called,
as if one were to say that it was to be in body and soul.
In the outer tabernacle bodily nature was revealed,
and in the inner the hidden soul was proclaimed.
By body and soul a man becomes a complete man,
and in that same likeness the tabernacle was depicted in two tabernacles.
In the ordering of a man Moses ordered that ordering;
come, let us see in it the ordering of the Man who came to be in a man.
On the vision of the seraphim that Isaiah saw

Homily Thirty-[?]
On the vision of the seraphim that Isaiah saw,
suitable for the Consecration of the Church.
Response:
Blessed is He who revealed worship to us through His true ones, my brothers.

Praised be the Creator, who magnifies his servants by his revelation,
and by visions shares out his wealth among the children of his house.
Worthy of praise is he who, lacking nothing of glory,
gives his glory to those who praise him, so that they may praise him.
In him is his glory, and no glory is added to his glory;
and if he is praised, his glory makes his praisers great.
He is wholly glory, and his perfections are full of his glory;
he lacks nothing, and from his bounty he provides for all.
Though he is without composition, he is wont to show himself in likenesses;
though he has no voice, he makes his voice heard through the voice of the senses.
In every form he shows himself to the work of his hands,
and in every likeness he paints his mysteries before the seers.
The greatness of his love he shows in visions of many likenesses,
so that by degrees he may draw man to come near him.
To Adam he showed an appearance that resembled the senses of his body,
and called him as one calls a child, that he might cover the nakedness of his body.
He spoke with Noah by a bodily voice,
and taught him to make an ark of rescue for himself and for all.
He called Abraham and conversed with him in his own tongue,
and sealed him with his name, so that his offspring would be called by his name.

He placed his strength in Jacob's hands in the form of a man,
and showed him how to grasp the Hidden One [?] through visible senses.
With Joseph he played a game like that of the sheaves,
and gave him power to discern hidden things.
On Mount Sinai he revealed his greatness to the eye of the son of Amram,
and filled him with the Spirit to recount his perfections.
Before Elijah he portrayed a showing of his sweetness,
so that he would know how to liken it to the gentleness of his mercies.
Now too he put on a fair form and stood in the sanctuary,
to reveal to men the greatness of his incomprehensible glory.
In great glory he willed to show himself to man,
and he brought one human being near him, that he might gaze on him.
To the eye of Isaiah he revealed his greatness in the holy temple,
and set up ranks of heavenly beings to sanctify him.
He moved from the height and dwelt in the depth, though not by nature,
and stood upon the earth, not in reality but in name.
He gathered the Watchers, called the angels, signaled to the cherubim,
and clothed them with an appearance full of manifold wonder.
The winged ones flew, the fiery ones, the swift ones ran;
they thought he had arrived, but his signal reached the earth before them.
The fair ones cried out, arrayed their ranks, ordered their legions,
and instead of weapons they put on the power of the Spirit to be made strong.
They were seen running across the face of the height without steps,
and the power of Being was among their ranks without change.
The host of the King was seen with the authority of the King of kings,
yet no path could be traced on the ground beneath their feet.
The Commander of the hidden power and of the hosts came down,
and no one perceived the sound of his descent but one.
One man out of all humanity was granted his share in it,
and stood and gazed on the greatness of his power and on his ministers.
One man saw his appearance, not with the eye's sight
but with the mind, as far as a creature is able to see.
With his hidden mind he saw the unseen appearance,
and in thought he entered with the Watchers into the holy temple.
Into the holy temple entered the Commander who rules over all,
and his ministers stood to serve him in holiness.
They adorned the throne of glory and set it up as for a king,
and laid out a veil of fire between him and themselves.

The ministers spread veils of glory before their eyes,
so that they would not gaze on the face of the King who dwells in glory.
Their wings became a covering for their persons,
and covered the senses they had suddenly acquired, beyond their wont.
They showed senses that were not bodily to a bodily eye,
and hid them from the glory of the greatness of the vision.
They wrapped their wings over their faces like veils,
so as not to be blinded by the dazzling splendor of the vision.
The appearance of splendor was seen before their eyes,
and they were afraid to look on it with open eyes.
It was most fearful, and yet there was nothing in it to fear;
it was beloved, and the sound of their sanctifications bears witness.
The wings were to them like partitions between him and themselves;
with them they offered him gifts of the holiness of their thoughts.
Six wings they suddenly brought forth, without composition,
and divided them into portions for their forms.
With two they covered their faces, which have no features,
and with two they hid their feet, though they have none.
With two the wings rose to fly swiftly,
and they began to cry out in holiness the sounds of holiness.
“Holy, holy, holy, Lord,” cried their ranks,
and the foundations of the holy temple shook at their sanctifications.
Three holies they cried alike, one authority,
and in their three they showed one lordship over all.
“Lord of hosts” they called the nature that holds all things,
and so they revealed that Being is to be proclaimed threefold.
They proclaimed the Trinity on earth by their sanctifications,
and in due order paid the confession they owed.
Three times they repeated the glorification in a wondrous voice,
and trod out a path for mankind to call on three names.
Three names were hidden in the name of that Holy One,
and the Watchers came first and revealed them by their sanctifications.
But why is it that they sanctified three times only,
and did not add more, nor fall short of the number?

If their service is truly holiness,
why did they not sanctify without ceasing, as they are wont?
They ought to have sanctified without number;
what is the reason they slackened and fell silent from rendering it?
If thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads were to give praise,
the praise would be small for that glory which was being praised.
If heaven and earth with their assemblies were to shout aloud,
they would not suffice to praise as is fitting.
Were all creation to stand up with its troops,
it would fall far short of offering the gifts of glory.
Beyond all measure is the Creator greater than creatures,
and they are immeasurably smaller than his greatness.
And if it is so, as their varied ranks bear witness,
why did the Watchers bring the “Holy” to an end at three times?
It was not to keep silent that the spiritual beings ceased from glorifying,
nor did they withhold, or were withholding, the payment they owed.
They showed a great order on earth by their sanctifications:
that in the hidden nature three hypostases [?] are hidden in its Being.
One Being they learned when creation was established in the beginning,
and after a time they gained understanding through the disclosure of the hypostases.
He revealed to them a hidden mystery, hidden and not in the open,
so that each one would seek out the meaning of the mystery.
In mystery they repeated the glorification three times,
and did not perceive the power hidden within their words.
They spoke words and did not grasp their meaning;
they sanctified the Holy One, and could not comprehend its reason.
They trod a path of peace for creation toward the Creator,
that it might walk well to the meeting of Father, Son and Spirit.
They arranged the holies in three and set them on it like milestones,
so that whoever travels by their sanctifications might not go astray.
“Holy is the Lord,” they cried upon the earth, and the earth shook,

and they taught it the order of the power of the infinite Being.
The power of Being taught them to sanctify,
and through Isaiah they taught a great wonder.
The son of Amoz saw a great wonder among the heavenly ones:
how glorious they are, and how they tremble as they sanctify.
At the wonder of them the thoughts of the son of the Hebrews were amazed,
and he gathered his mind from every quarter to meet the vision.
At the wonder of the vision and of its ministers the seer was amazed,
at how fearful the revelation was that spoke with him.
At their fear he was greatly amazed within himself,
that though they were spirit, they feared the spiritual vision.
“Who, then, has shaken the reeds [?] of the host, that it is so astonished,
and from whom do these glorious-faced ones hide their faces?
Who, then, gathered them and set them up, troop by troop,
and laid on them a yoke and fear, so that they are terrified?
To whom, then, do they cry the sounds of holiness in fear,
and why can they not lift their gaze to meet the vision?
Why do they hide their faces within their wings,
and why do they cry three cries and repeat no more?”
The prophet stood divided over what he saw,
for the wonder of the vision was dividing his mind.
“Is the thing I see real, or is it not?
Is it shown to me alone, or perhaps to others too?
Is it a body, and do I look on it bodily,
or is it perhaps a shadow that is not real?
Did I enter in the body and stand within the sanctuary,
or perhaps I see it in the mind, while not seeing it?”
“It is, and it is not,” the Israelite pondered,
like his father, who was granted a vision like his own.
Israel too was granted an appearance higher than himself,
and he was given the name Israel: “he saw God.”
The vision of the son of Israel resembles the vision of his father,
and it is one Power that showed its power there and here.
That Commander who placed himself in Jacob's hands
showed Isaiah too an appearance of wonder.
The seer, son of seers, saw a great wonder,
and stood and gazed without senses as though with senses.

Without satiety he gazed on the beauty of the vision,
and however much he looked, he looked again with delight.
Very sweet to his thought was the sight of the vision,
and his mind had no wish to look away from the fairness of its beauty.
The more he gazed on the seraphim, how they trembled,
the more fear and love grew within his thought.
The more their wings were folded over their faces,
the more he spread himself out within himself to hide.
The more the voice of “Holy, holy” was heard,
the more he counted himself unworthy even to hear it.
The more the appearance was seen in the Holy of Holies,
the more he pondered that the power of the Creator dwelt among his works.
In the Holy of Holies he saw the vision shown to him,
and the holiness of those who sanctify could not reach its end.
Far greater than all visions was the vision he saw,
and the appearance of the spiritual beings bears witness that they were not equal to it.
Beneath their cries their wings grew weary and their wits wandered,
and they had not the strength to gaze on the splendor of the vision.
They grew weary and were spent with covering their faces,
and though they covered them well, they were not covered as was fitting.
The vision filled the one who looked on it with fear and love,
and it terrified and alarmed him wisely.
By both of these the seer stood to gaze,
and he was afraid, and he longed to draw near and remain.
Hard pangs were striking his discernment,
and it was in labor to bring forth the vision shown to him.
Like a babe the vision pressed upon his nature,
to come forth through his senses and proclaim the greatness of his power.
His mind received the good seed of the Spirit of revelation,
and he was greatly amazed that, unworthy as he was, he was made worthy of such.
He remembered the lowliness of his race and the greatness of his iniquity,
and with discernment he marveled at what he saw.
The pain of his sins was pricking the mortal man,
and he was ashamed to lift his gaze toward the vision.

Though he longed to look well on the fairness of its beauty,
he looked at himself, felt pain, and groaned over his offenses.
Though he longed for the voice of the Watchers crying “Holy,”
he remembered the uncleanness of his people and covered his face.
Though he longed for the voice of the Watchers crying “Holy,”
he remembered the uncleanness of his people and covered his face.
When he perceived that the vision was of a spiritual nature,
he despaired and concluded that it would destroy him from life.
In a struggle of pains the prophet lay cast down before the revelation,
and longed to hear the voice of the forgiveness of iniquity.
The pain of his own iniquity and his people's pricked him,
and he groaned bitterly within his mind.
“Woe is me, wretched one!” the just man said to himself,
“for I am defiled by the shameful deeds of the people's iniquity.
Woe is me, for my face and my thoughts are hateful to look upon,
and yet I stand to look on the beauty of the vision of the power of Being.
Woe is me, for my dust is lowly and worn out by sins,
and yet I am made worthy to see the Sign that has been fitted to the lowliness of our dust.”
In just judgment the just prophet accused himself,
and before the judgment he condemned himself, that he might not be condemned.
The righteous man stood like a guilty one before the revelation,
and before he could be swallowed up, he hastened to confess, “I am guilty.”
As if with thongs he stretched himself out in repentance of soul,
and scourged himself before the scourges could reach him.
He decreed hard scourges on himself, though none had required them of him,
and with discernment he paid the debt owed by guilty humanity.
In place of the guilty he condemned himself, though not guilty,
and by his groanings he warded off [?] the blows from the insolent.
He became a good advocate for his people before Righteousness,
and by his supplication he quieted wrath and turned away anger.
At his advocacy the Judge and those of his rank were astonished,
at how well he knew how to compose sweet pleas.
The Commander hidden in the vision heard the persuasion of his words,
and sent his comfort through a spiritual messenger.
The vision sent a man of spirit to the son of Amoz,
to sound in his ears the good news of the forgiveness of iniquity.
The Watcher brought good news to the son of the Hebrews,
full of peace, bearing a sign of the pardon of sins.
The spirit carried the pardon of sins in the hands of its motions,
and gave it to the prophet, that he might be cleansed by it from his stains.

The Sign beckoned to the spiritual one concerning the ember of fire,
that he should go and take it with tongs of fire and bring it to him.
Fire with fire: he commanded the fiery one to take it,
and with it burn the forest of iniquity that had grown up in man.
The forest of iniquity had grown in the field of Adam's sins,
and the Hidden One sent against it, by the hand of the heavenly one.
He showed him a sickle of fire, to thrust in among the sins,
to reap the forest and leave the seed unharmed.
Like a reaper the spiritual one came to the son of Amoz,
and reaped his iniquity with the sickle the Sign had placed in his hand.
He saw the ember of fire lying on the holy altar,
and went and took it with a hand of fire, as he was commanded.
With tongs of fire the fiery one grasped the fiery ember,
and brought it and set it on the fleshly lips.
O the wonder that took place with the son of Amoz,
that though he was of flesh, he was not burned by the burning!
Fire could not take hold of fire without something between,
yet lowly flesh took it in its mouth and was not scorched.
The one who could suffer did not suffer from the heat of its fierceness,
and the one full of pains felt no pain in his body when it touched him.
O fiery one, who could not take the appearance of fire!
O body, which the flame did not hurt!
It was not fire that the Watcher took with tongs of fire,
nor was it an ember that came near the prophet.
It was not with the body that he saw the vision shown to him,
nor was the vision shown in bodily form.
The Creator is not confined in the holy temple,
nor did the seraphim bring forth wings perceptible to the senses.
It was not with a perceptible voice that the spiritual beings cried out,
nor did Isaiah listen to the voice with the senses of the body.
Spiritually the revelation came upon the man of flesh,
and he saw what he saw with the mind and not with the eyes.
With the eyes of the mind he saw the unseen appearance,
and with his thought he listened to an imperceptible voice.
With hidden motions the hidden Sign conversed with him,
and subtly the revelation played with his thoughts.
With motions too the spiritual one brought the ember to his motions,

though it was not an ember at all, but an appearance.
For it was an appearance that was truly seen,
not in body, but in a vision without composition.
Without hands the spiritual one grasped an ember that did not exist,
and without tongs brought it to a mouth clothed with a body.
With nonexistent tongs he grasped the unseen ember,
and brought it to a visible mouth, though not by sight.
With a bodiless voice the incorporeal played with the corporeal,
and revealed and showed him the forgiveness of iniquity, freely received.
“Behold, this has touched your mouth,” said the Watcher,
“to take away your iniquity and loosen the bonds of your soul's sins.
Behold, your iniquity is forgiven and the bond of your guilt is blotted out;
arise, go out, proclaim the word of forgiveness to the children of your race.
Behold, the hidden Sign that dwells in the vision has sent me
to bring you the medicine of mercies, not by hands.
Behold, it showed me with what I should heal the pain of your soul,
and how I should blot out the bond of debts that lies upon your limbs.
With fire it taught me to scour from you the filth of sins,
and by it revealed to me, that I might reveal the truth of the faith.”
Why, then, did he purify the pure soul by a sign of fire?
For fire is harmful to things that can be harmed.
Why, then, did the Watcher grasp it with tongs and not with his hand?
For the power of the spiritual one is stronger than mute [fire].
Why did he take fire from the altar of burnt offerings?
For it was the sacrifices that purified, not fire.
By the sacrifices of lambs the Israelites were purified;
why, then, did he not take from the sacrifices and bring it to him?
By the blood of calves the stains of the soul were cleansed;
why, then, did blood not reach his mouth and cleanse his sins?
It has never been heard that anyone sprinkled fire on limbs,
nor that a spiritual being, who has no senses, took hold of fire.
This atonement is utterly foreign to the Law,
and there is nothing in it like the order that Moses handed down.
Moses and Aaron sprinkled blood on sinners,
not on the mouth but on the ears and the thumbs.
New is this thing that the seraph of the Spirit did for Isaiah,

and it has no parallel in the whole order of the Law.
Come, explain to us, you priest who still ministers with blood:
what is this that the Watcher did for our kinsman?
Come, show us, Israelite, “who saw God”:
what is the power hidden in the vision your prophet saw?
Come, reveal to us, you who atone for iniquity with the blood of animals:
why did the spiritual one not blot out your brother's iniquity with blood?
Why did he not sprinkle blood on his ear or on its lobe,
as Moses and Aaron taught those who were to be atoned for [?]?
Why was the great order that walked among you changed,
and the Watcher taught you to walk in a way you had not seen?
Is something, then, to be hoped for in the vision your prophet saw?
Surely it is not a mystery, but the truth that makes mysteries pass away.
The mystery proclaims the manifest truth through its transformation,
and beforehand trod a smooth path ahead of the events.
The abolition of the sacrifices of the Law is depicted in the ember,
and the forgiveness of iniquity, made true by that One, fills out its meaning.
Great wealth that never grows poor is hidden in its appearance,
and the promise of life higher than the earth is revealed by it.
The pure “Holy” proclaims the voice of the heavenly ones,
and it was never heard that they sanctified in this way until now.
The Trinity fills the cry of their sanctifications,
and in threefold manner they teach man to sanctify.
Three cries they composed, and they cried out three times,
teaching the order that in Being there are three in one.
As with a finger they pointed them out to the earthly ones:
“Look, mortals, and sanctify well, as our voice does.”
Three equal hypostases they proclaimed in their sanctifications,
and interpreted them through Isaiah's mouth as true.
Their truth they revealed to the prophet in mystery,
and he took it and placed it in the Scriptures as in a treasury.
In the treasury of the books he placed the mystery revealed to him,

and sealed it in silence until it should be explained by events.
He laid silence upon the “Holy” like a seal,
so that the eyes of flesh and their simple folk might not look into it.
The pure “Holy” was kept for its own time, to be revealed;
for this reason the prophet covered it in silence from the seers.
In a mystery the revelation disclosed it beforehand through the mouth of spiritual beings,
and showed man how to keep the order of the fullness of times.
At the fullness of times he was to reveal the mystery of the “Holy,”
and beforehand he placed it as a pledge in the Scriptures.
The spiritual beings, too, sanctified thrice and then fell silent,
so that each one might ponder what the reason is for three times.
The atonement, too, that he gave the prophet, he gave in a word,
so that whoever marvels at the atonement may consider what it was for.
The ember, too, that carried away iniquity bears a full meaning:
how it touched a mouth of flesh and did it no harm.
Who, then, put the power of atonement into a thing without discernment,
and how did a dead thing give life to one who had died through his sins?
Fire is a dead thing, however much heat it has,
and without discernment, however much the heat of fire is in it.
The mystery of the gift of bread and wine is within it,
which, though they are dead things, give life to those who receive them.
In bread and wine the Good One was to give life to mankind,
and beforehand he gave life to one human being by the vision of fire.
The divided mind has shut the door in the face of nature [?]:
if the life given by the bread troubles it, let it look at the ember.
Did a mute ember blot out sins,
and can the body and blood of the Man not atone for sins?
If the word that iniquity was forgiven is true to you,
why do you falter over the forgiveness that comes through events?
If you wish to take hold of the appearance of the shadow,
why do you not take hold of the body, the truth of the shadow?
The shadow was the mystery of the atonement of the son of Amoz,
and this is the truth that atones for all through bread and wine.
A type of the truth was depicted in the vision of that revelation,
and it drew mankind to come near to its interpretation.

And [?] fashioned them as though in the likeness of an image, / and brought them in and set them in the Holy of Holies of the law. / In the manner of the law they traced spiritual likenesses, / and though these were splendid, the vision far surpassed the law. / Very bright were the colours with which it was painted, / and no blood of silent beasts was mixed into them. / The sacrifice of that image was not like the dumb sacrifices, / nor was the praise of its praisers like the glory of Moses. / It was exceedingly glorious, and no glory could compare with its glory, / for even the glory of the holy temple grew dim at the sight of it. / In the holy temple the Watchers portrayed the image of truth, / and cried glory to Him as to a king in His royal palace. / At the splendour of the glory of its praisers the son of Amoz was amazed, / and the world and its glory became as nothing in his eyes. / Beside that glory he did not even reckon that the world existed, / nor that it was such as he had once thought it, still less anything more. / The prophet supposed that he was in another world, / and he rose to accuse the iniquity of the people in his own person. / He entered into true judgment with himself on behalf of all mankind, / and saw that the whole of nature was imprisoned under sins. / He composed a “Woe” in the sound of his words, like laments, / and with them he wept loudly over the sufferings of mankind. / “Woe is me,” he said, that is, “Woe to human nature, / which iniquity has shut up in the prison house of mortality!” / He grieved over mortal nature more than anyone who had ever lived, / for the bodily armour with which it struggles is weak. / The Judge saw that he was judging himself rightly, / and in the mercy that is His He had pity on the lowliness of all nature. / He saw him accusing in himself the faults of his race, / and sent him to be an advocate at the trial of iniquity. / He saw that he would not take it upon himself to make light of its iniquity, / and sent him with the Spirit to purge through him the iniquity of the people. / He saw that he knew how to judge truly, without [?] contempt,

and He gave him the rod of prophecy to chastise the wicked. / Like a firstborn He tested the truth of his faith, / and made his mouth the searcher of hidden mysteries. / He who [?] made a voice heard among the members of His household, / who were wondering who was worthy to proclaim His words. / “Whom shall I send, and who will go?” cried the Revelation, / and he answered truly and lovingly, “I will go.” / Why then did the One who knows all ask, as though He did not know, / when He already knew who was ready for His service? / He asked so that the one being sent might listen with an eager mind, / and choose for himself to serve his Lord’s command. / In love he accepted the task of proclaiming the truth in stubborn ears, / and of his own will he chose toil on behalf of sinners. / “I will go,” he answered the Revelation that spoke with him, / “and I will make known the truth of Your name openly. / I will proclaim the power of Your being in the house of earthly men, / and abolish the name of the gods that error has made. / Give me the seal of Your great name, which does not lie, / that by Your name I may blot out borrowed names that are not true. / Write me a document that bears the hand of Your faithfulness, / that I may read it before all, and everyone may know that all is Yours. / Place in my hands the straight rod of the Spirit of Your will, / that with it I may shatter the dumb idols that demons have fashioned.” / O how the prophet, glorious among prophets, ached / to bear the honour of the preaching entrusted to him! / O [?] of nimble mind, how swiftly his mind ran, / so that before he set out his will had reached the place where they sent him! / O how beautifully the seer of beautiful things gazed, / and his thought flew toward the Revelation that is higher than his strength! / O how well the upright one knew how to judge with discernment, / for he looked at himself and condemned the iniquity of the whole world! / Come, let us set before ourselves a mark like the son of Amoz, / and present ourselves before Him by accusing our faults. / Come, let us groan over our hateful deeds after his likeness, / and judge our iniquity before the coming judgment judges us.
Let us confess that we have sinned, as he confessed before the Revelation, / that we may be found worthy to hear the voice of forgiveness, as he heard it.
On the Church and on the Priesthood

Memra Thirty-Two / On the Church and on the priesthood, suited to the Sunday / of the fourth week of the Sanctification of the Church / Response: The Bridegroom who has invited us to the bridal chamber of his kingdom: do not be parted from him, my brothers.

The Creator built a holy temple for the earthly,
that in it they might offer the worship of love in the spirit.
A holy place and a holy of holies he willed and established:
the holy place on earth, and the holy of holies above in heaven.
In the holy place of the earth he commanded them to serve as priests in mysteries,
and in the heavenly one by works that never cease.
Two ways of life he set apart by his knowledge, which cannot be grasped,
and filled them with the riches of time and of what has no end.
The dwelling of the earth he called the earthly sanctuary,
and the holy of holies that order hidden on high.
Through a holy place and a holy place he showed his love to the members of his household,
and taught them to hallow him in mysteries.
In the holiness of his name he willed to give the work of his hands a share,
that those who hallow the name of his holiness might themselves be hallowed by it.

He has no need of the sounds of their hallowings,
for he is holy, and by his purity he hallows the defiled.
By means of causes he draws his own to become like him,
to make them heirs of the glory of his Son.
For this reason he built a sanctuary and a holy of holies,
and urged mankind to serve as priests in it for the sake of their life.
To them he granted the forgiveness of the iniquity of their deeds,
and to their freedom he gave the power to be justified.
Over them he set stewards for the treasure that is in them,
that they might increase the riches of righteousness as they wish.
He made their nature the treasurer of glorious things,
to keep the glorious goods for itself and for its fellows.
The treasure of life without end he promised and pledged,
and laid it up above, in a place hidden from onlookers.
By what is hidden he showed [?] the hidden thing that is hidden in the soul,
so that the eyes of its impulses might gaze upon it and see its beauty.
He cast upon the earth the desire for spiritual riches,
so that the earthly might long for them and hate what is of the earth.
He showed them a new path, to walk after him,
and he trod it in sufferings, the one victor who conquered by the Spirit.
Like a guide he went ahead on the path of life,
and journeyed on and reached the goal of perfection.
He promised and pledged to the members of his race that they would be with him,
and through his mystery would walk with him in perfection.
In his own likeness he taught them to serve as priests,
he in heaven and they on earth, in mysteries.
To them he gave a rank greater than the rank of the law,
and instead of sacrifices he taught them to sacrifice love.
He fulfilled the law with the law of the words of his preaching,
and gave priesthood in place of the old ministry, that he might win all.
Twelve priests he chose for himself first, by the number of the tribes,
and instead of a single people he called all peoples to be his.

He gave into their hands the power of the Spirit to overcome all,
and they uprooted error and sowed the truth of the Creator's name.
They forgave iniquity and cleansed blemishes by his help,
and taught mankind to hate the iniquity of their deeds.
They served as priests on earth in the mystery of the order of the kingdom on high,
and in things revealed they portrayed images of things to come.
Through them the word of life was proclaimed among mortals,
and mankind began to walk on new paths.
They began to serve as priests in the spirit,
as they had received from the High Priest who hallowed them.
After his pattern they served, and grew into his likeness,
and handed on the rank of their works to their disciples.
After this pattern he gave priesthood to new priests,
that men might be priests to forgive iniquity on earth.
For the forgiveness of iniquity priesthood came to be among mortals,
for mortality always needs to be forgiven.
The pains of iniquity are born in human nature,
and are not cleansed without the medicine of holiness.
No one can walk the road without stumbling,
and whoever stumbles needs the mercy that heals his iniquity.
Mortals are struck down in body and soul by the pains of iniquity,
and they need a physician who knows the pain within and without.
For the healing of hidden and visible pain priesthood came to be,
to heal iniquity by spiritual skill.
The priest is a physician of hidden and visible things,
and to his skill is entrusted the healing of body and soul.
With the medicine of the Spirit he scours iniquity from the thoughts,
and men strip off the garment of iniquity and put on truth.
With his lips he treads out a path toward knowledge,
and as with fire he tests the truth and casts out iniquity.
He is the messenger of the Lord and his minister, as it is written,
and through him the service toward mankind is fulfilled.
As a member he is chosen from the body of the members of his race,
and as a head he is charged to govern his fellows.
He fills the office of the head for the impulses and the members,

and by him men examine iniquity and righteousness.
In him they see, as with an eye, the true and the false,
and like a mirror he shows the form of beautiful things.
Like a tongue he interprets the truth before learners,
and makes the power of hidden things shine before simple folk.
Spiritual teaching is hidden within his lips,
and he always sprinkles the dew of mercy on the ground of mankind.
Abundantly he sows hope and love and faith,
and reaps good, sweet fruits that do not perish.
He brings the hearing of the word of life into the bodily senses,
and the mind listens to the sound of words of sweetness.
The impulses need the fragrance of the sweetness that gives life to the dead,
and he sweetens the dead body with the voice of resurrection.
Like a trumpet he sounds always in the ears of mankind,
so that people may not grow slack about what has been promised.
Like a guide he shows the way to travelers,
so that mortals may journey in the company of the promise of life.
On the sea of mankind he sails continually by his words,
and earnestly warns each one to guard the treasure of his soul.
In the ship of the church he stands and warns night and day,
and guards her from the harms of the spirit of the wicked.
He is a helmsman, highly skilled amid the storms,
who knows how to steer to the haven of life without end.
With the sails of the Spirit [he drives?] the ships of speech,
and [steers?] them to the harbors of life hidden on high.
For the hope of things to come he endures labors,
and is anxious for each one, lest he run short of oil in his lamp.
He received a talent of the Spirit from his Lord to trade with,
and he must lay the silver of words on the table of the soul.
[?] the forgiveness of iniquity he learned from the King,
that he should not be grudging in forgiving his fellows.
The treasure of the Spirit is entrusted to his hands to administer,
and it befits him to provide wisely for those who look to him.
His Lord gave him rational sheep to govern,
to pasture them in the meadows of life, the words of the Spirit.
He is charged to govern sheep and lambs and ewes,
and all the ranks of men and women and children.
For the tilling of mankind the command that called him to his Lord appointed him,

to uproot error and sow the Creator's name on earth.
"Go then, make disciples, preach, and baptize all the peoples
in one Being of one Creator, three Persons."
The names of the Three he must proclaim in the ears of mankind,
and baptize them in the name of the Being hidden from all.
For this purpose priests are appointed on earth to serve,
to turn mankind from error to knowledge.
By their words people see the light of life,
and by their deeds they taste the sweetness of truth.
He is like a mediator in the house of God for mankind,
and through him the sacrifices of the soul are offered before the Lord of all.
Through him the riches of the Spirit are distributed to the [?],
and they call for strength, to be strengthened for the tilling of truth.
He opens to everyone the door of mercy before the onlookers,
and abundantly grants forgiveness of iniquity to the members of his race.
In water and Spirit he recasts them as in a furnace,
and strips off iniquity and clothes them in garments of righteousness.
He calls and entreats the hidden power to come down to him,
and to endow the water with a visible power to give life.
The births take place as in a womb,
and the power of grace is like the seed that begets life.
Body and soul go down together into the womb of the waters,
and are born again, made holy from uncleanness.
O the marvel shown to our race, how great it is,
that through sinners it willed to justify sinners!
O the gift of the God of all, which cannot be grasped,
that through the poor it distributed its riches to the poor!
O the command, how it rules over all creation,
that gave authority to the work of his hands to become like him!
By the hand of men he opened his treasure to mankind,
and men grew rich from the treasures of his divinity.
The keys of his mercy he gave to the [?] as to trustworthy men,
and they open the treasure of his mercy at all times in faith.
Mortality holds keys in its lips,
and with a tongue of flesh opens and shuts the doors of hidden things.
He buries men in the womb of the waters as in a tomb,
and raises up and brings to new life those dead in iniquity.

By the Creator's power he buries the dead and gives life to the dead,
and as from a belly he begets men spiritually.
He rears spiritual infants by the power of the Spirit,
and to those who have grown he holds out the food of perfection.
With the food of the Spirit bodily men are nourished,
and as the birth is, so is the nourishment of those born.
He always prepares a living sacrifice before those who eat,
and mixes a drink of life-giving power for body and soul.
He makes ready a table of life and sets it before their eyes,
and portrays the mystery of death and life in bread and wine.
Through visible things he shows the power of hidden things,
and people live by eating bread and drinking wine.
The outward senses see bread and wine,
while the hidden impulses receive the power within the visible things.
The priest stands like a tongue to interpret,
and his voice proclaims death and life to mankind.
In bread and wine he shows the body and blood of the King,
who died for all and lived, and gave life to all by his cross.
In fear the bodily man stands to minister,
and asks mercy for himself and for his race, that he may be worthy of mercy.
And he calls the Spirit to come down upon him with power from Him,
to give power to the bread and wine to give life.
In bread and wine, visible things, life dwells,
and they become food for mortality, which lacks life.
In the name of the Being, three Persons, he concludes his words,
and teaches men to cry "Holy" with the spiritual beings.
The people answer after his words, "Holy, Holy,
Holy the Mighty One [?], hidden from all and revealed to all."
Then he stretches out his hands and breaks the spiritual bread,
and signs the type of the body and blood that died and rose.
With his hands he gives the body of the King to his fellows,
strengthened by the power of grace to give life.
He gives the bread and says, "The body of the King Messiah,"
and gives the wine to drink and names it "precious blood."
O bodily man who carries fire and is not burned!
O mortal who, though mortal, distributes life!
Who allowed you, despised dust, to hold fire?
And who made you, son of the poor, a distributor of life?
Who taught you to hold fire in palms of flesh,

and who searched out for you the wisdom hidden from you?
It is not yours to do these things that are higher than you;
it is the power of the help of the God of all, who raised up your lowliness.
He made his hidden power dwell in you and strengthened your impulses,
and through you he interprets the power of his hidden things in ears of flesh.
From his help you have received a gift to give life,
and though you are dust, you hold the treasure of spiritual things.
For the treasure of the Spirit the priest of the Spirit was made treasurer,
and spiritual things are placed in his hands to distribute.
Mortality holds the keys of the height like a ruler,
and binds and looses by the word of its mouth like the Creator.
He binds iniquity with the chain of the word of his mouth,
and looses it again when men turn from iniquity.
After his words he seals the sign of the Creator's power,
and binds the wicked and the good as they have deserved.
A great wonder of the great love of the God of all,
who gave authority to the work of his hands to become like him!
The command belongs to him alone, who rules over all he created,
and it is his to bind and loose as he wills.
In his grace he gave it to mankind, to wield the authority of his command,
to make known his love, how he loves the members of his household.
In wisdom he acts to give his own a share in what is his,
that by means of causes he may draw his own to become his.
With glorious things he [?] men as one does children,
that by his words they may attain the rank that gains life.
In the name of priesthood he opened the treasure of his great riches,
that each might receive forgiveness of iniquity through one of his own race.
In the sanctuary on high he is ready to gladden the earthly,
and he gave the ministry as a pledge of the promise of his words.
Priests in the holy place of the earth figure the mystery of that dwelling,
and like a mirror they show the image of things to come.

Like guides they are set on the road toward the heights,
and no one travels without them to the haven beyond.
In place of light they fill the earth for those in darkness,
and as with salt they give taste to the tasteless.
They always cast the rational nets of their words,
and catch men out of deadness into life.
Through them the dead in iniquity, whom error had buried, are raised,
and see in their words the light that gives life to the dead.
By them the dead and the living are judged in two dwellings,
and to their authority the examination of men and Watchers is reserved.
They judge spiritual and bodily beings,
and put demons to shame by the splendor of their conduct.
But if the splendor of their conduct accuses iniquity,
how will those be acquitted who have wronged their words?
If spiritual angels are judged by them,
harsh judgment awaits whoever despises them.
Each one must pay them the debt of love,
for on behalf of everyone they ask mercy from him who pities all.
Let the reward of love be repaid to them by their hearers,
for they bear the spiritual needs of life.
Like fathers let them show their love toward their children,
and with the food of the Spirit nourish the impulses rather than the members.
They are called by our Lord shepherds of rational sheep,
and as the flocks are, so is the spiritual nourishment.
To them was spoken that word addressed to Simon,
that they should pasture the sheep and the rational lambs and the ewes.
Let the priests of the church hear the voice of that examination,
and show the love that Simon showed toward our Savior.
Let them pasture carefully, according to the command of the Good Shepherd,
and tend the flocks with the great love that befits his love.
Let them look and consider that he bought the flock of mankind with his blood,
and on the top of the wood wrote its freedom from slavery.
Let them see how much he suffered from wrongdoers for the sake of his flock,

and despised and made light of all sufferings, that it might not perish.
After his pattern he longed for the lovers of his love to become like him,
and to walk in his footsteps on the path of his preaching.
The Father promised and pledged a reward to whoever loves him:
that he will be with him in the delight of life without end.
Who, then, is the one whose love is true and whose nature is wise,
and who knows well how to govern his fellows?
"Truly, Amen": whoever acquires these things and does them,
all the riches of the kingdom on high are entrusted to his hands.
And together with the reward of him who administered his riches well,
threats are decreed against the wrongdoers who received and wronged.
But if the evil servant says that the judgment is far off,
his master will come and require his wrongdoing at his hands.
Come then, you servants bought with blood more precious than all,
listen to the word of the Liberator from the slavery of our race.
Come, consider the power of the meaning hidden in his words:
that with the reward there is also punishment without end.
The good he heartened [?] with the name of the reward of things to come,
and on the insolent he cast the fear of harsh scourges.
Let us fear his words, then, as true,
and not grow slack, lest we be condemned with the guilty.
His judgment is true and the promise of his words does not lie;
let no one waver over his promises, lest he perish.
It befits priests to keep these things more than anyone,
as the rank they have received is more glorious than anyone's.
Whoever knows his master's will and does not do it
deserves scourges in proportion to the knowledge he had and wronged.
But if whoever does wrong does it insolently,
he wrongs himself of the good things promised him.
By his own will he [has forfeited?] the reward of things to come,
and he is scourged as one who knew and understood.
The priest who understands, great is his indictment and harsh his scourge,
and in proportion to his rank are both his punishment and his exaltation.
I wished to praise the greatness of the rank of the name of priesthood,
but a pain struck me when I saw it diminished through ignorance.
I marveled when I saw the greatness of the glory of those who triumphed,

and I suffered and grieved at the disgrace of those who degraded it.
As great as their dignity was above all ranks,
so much has it sunk beyond measure below all ranks.
The treasure of the Spirit was entrusted to them to administer,
and fools despised it, not knowing how to discern the power of its greatness.
The hidden command gave the keys of the height into their hands,
and accursed priests shut the door in the face of those entering.
They were permitted to forgive the iniquity of men,
and the iniquity of the forgivers grew stronger than that of the defiled.
The High Priest called it light and salt when he gave it,
but its light grew dark and its taste turned insipid through those who received it.
He prepared it and called it to give life to mortality,
and see, it has died through shameful deeds.
It received good seed to cast upon the earth,
but the farmers ceased from tilling the word of truth.
It went out to meet the spiritual Bridegroom,
but the ministers slept and the light of their lamps went out.
The oil of mercy ran short in the vessels of their deeds,
and they did not receive mercy, because they did not pity and forgive wisely.
Those without compassion he named foolish virgins,
who kept the body but were not sanctified from harshness [?].
What will it profit one who keeps his body in purity,
if his mind is not cleansed of hatreds?
How will the minister clothed with the name of priesthood be helped,
if he does not make the work within match the name without?
The name of priesthood is a great work, not an authority,
and whoever would draw near to it must do so with deeds.
Paul teaches whoever desires it how he should draw near:
that whoever desires the presbyterate desires a work.
Priests wronged the word of Paul, the chosen one,
and desired authority and hated the labor that gains life.
They loved the name for love of earthly things,
and despised precious deeds and honored what is false.
They honored the false more than the truth that honored them,
and falsely appeared fair and were praised in the eyes of onlookers.

They received a gift that is not sold for earthly things,
and those who received it sold it for deceitful silver to the unworthy.
For dead silver they gave [?] the gift full of life,
and took in the dead who had died in sin and were not forgiven.
They put the rod of spiritual things into the hands of fools,
and simple men stood at the head of the flock to govern it.
An ignorant shepherd raised his staff over his fellows,
and one childish in mind became head over a broken people.
The weakling thought he was pasturing mere sheep, not rational beings,
and he governs them in earthly ways, as though they were dumb.
The fool imagined that lordship rules on earth,
and began to demand dues from the sheep like kings.
He did not know what the pattern of the name of his authority is,
nor did the flock gain understanding of how it should live.
A blind man, blinder in knowledge, led the blind,
and they began to walk a path of confusion without understanding.
Without knowledge the fool governs his fellows,
and walks a path without knowledge, as in darkness.
Upon him was fulfilled what is written in Scripture:
"The priest shall be without knowledge, like the people."
Priests and people alike became unseemly,
and strayed from the road and ceased from running toward righteousness.
Justice too, seeing that they had strayed outside the order,
sharpened her sword against the iniquity of their deeds.
She saw the iniquity of the ministers and of the flock and grew grim,
and shut the door, so that mercy might not plead on our behalf.
Outside the door mercy stands, seeking mankind,
and mercies are held back before the door of the just command.
Come then, all of us, let us plead for our iniquity while we live,
so that we may not be condemned by the decree of judgment without end.
Come, let us build ourselves a fence of mercy before Justice,
until she is appeased and blots out our iniquity from her book.
Let priests be like mediators through their words,

and as a gift let them offer up the sufferings of their minds. / It is theirs to offer sacrifices of love, / and to pardon the iniquity of humankind and their own. / They are permitted to open the door before sinners, / like treasurers of the great treasury that has no limit. / They shall be like a tongue that interprets, / and win relief before the Judge who examines iniquity. / Let the priest speak this word to his flock: / “Repent, you sinners, so that mercy may heal all your debts.” / Let him sow the hope of life at every hour in everyone’s ears, / and lay the medicine of the mind’s repentance on the pains of the soul. / Let him suffer for all and grieve for all, as one who discerns, / and count the sufferings of his companions as his own, like Paul. / A bond is written against him for the debts of the children of his race, / and he is bound to repay the debt of love to the One who honoured him. / Mercy brought him to a high rank above his companions; / let him show labour that matches his rank and is worthy of his name. / His name is a test: he was appointed to be priest on behalf of humankind, / and it is right for him to fulfil his name by his deeds. / The silver of mercy is placed in his hands to distribute, / and if he holds it back, he hears the cry: “Wicked servant!” / So too the one who took the talent and hid it thought he had escaped, / but the hidden mystery of judgment caught him in the answer he gave. / His master called him a wicked servant, as his wickedness deserved, / for he received freely and did not give freely as he had received. / To that voice let the priests listen with discernment, / and cast the silver of the word of life into their hearers. / And let the hearers receive the seed of their words, / so that they are not condemned with the wrongdoers who took and defrauded. / In love let them listen to the voice of correction in their words,

so that they are not reproached when they are disciplined for their sins. / Let each one gladly accept the setting-right of his trouble, / and not be ashamed before the physician who puts medicine on his sore. / The priest is a physician who heals the pains within the soul, / and every sick mind should run to him at all times. / He knows how to lay the medicine of the Spirit on the thoughts, / and he cuts away iniquity with the iron blade of divine mercy. / Come, then, you who are sick of soul, draw near to those who know, / and show the blemishes of your minds to the hidden mystery. / Come, then, you who are weak on the way, join yourselves to the wise, / and run well to the meeting place of life that has no end.
On the Consecration of the Church

Memra Thirty-Three
Again on the Consecration of the Church
Response: Church of the peoples, worship Christ, who planted you on earth
and wrote you in heaven, my brothers.

A great wedding the Son of God made for his Church,
and he invited and called all the peoples to the day of her banquet.
The daughter of darkness the Sun of Righteousness betrothed to himself:

and his fair beauty shone on her face, and she put on light.
The Rich One who never grows poor loved the daughter of the poor,
and quickly placed his great wealth in her hands, that she might be exalted by it.
Christ the Bridegroom in his great love bowed down his height,
and willed to be joined in marriage to mortals, and he exalted them.
The Lord who is on high bowed his height toward the lowly,
and became Bridegroom to the defiled peoples and sanctified them.
The Son of the Most High, the Bridegroom, betrothed the Church of the peoples,
and bound her to himself in his love and lifted her head among her enemies.
A lone exile, forsaken, worn down and humiliated,
became the consort of his Son who dwells on high.
A lone dark one, wrapped in the darkness of the fear of demons —
the Light loved her and called her to himself and filled her with light.
The scattered one, who wandered among vanities,
the Son of God called and gathered and made his own.
That straying daughter of foreigners the Lover of all loved,
and gathered her to himself and sowed in her ears the teaching of life.
That lost one, who had been lost amid the hosts of error,
the Finder of all sought, and he led her into the fold of life.
The one held up to shame and scorned the Honored One betrothed,
and made her modest with his splendor and covered her disgrace with the robe of his glory.
The companion of demons and handmaid of devils the Holy One chose,
and made her shine in his love and washed away from her her great iniquity.
He saw that she was black and bore filth, and he hated her appearance,
and brought her down to the waters and washed her and scoured her of her filth.
A bath full of life he prepared for her,
and washed her, rinsed her, and scrubbed her face of all that was hateful.
In living waters he washed away the filth of the stained one,
and poured the oil of holiness on her head and made her face glad.
With oil and water he washed her body and cleansed her soul:

and he gave her a name, Church of Holiness, full of beauties.
He stripped from her the name of her hatefulness, together with her offenses,
and clothed her in beauty, and gave her the title “the chosen Church.”
By the fair name that the prophets gave her in their revelations,
by that the glorious Bridegroom called her on the day of her bathing.
The prophets of the Spirit called her “Church” in their words,
and by that name they sang praise to her Lord from all the peoples.
The faithful prophets gave her the name “the Great Church,”
and the Bridegroom came and confirmed her name in baptism.
In water he washed her, with oil he sealed her, with love he made her shine,
and he took the robe of light and clothed her in holiness.
In his living name, and in the name of his Father and of the Holy Spirit,
he sealed the bride and completed her spiritual beauty.
A crown of light he set on the head of the glorious one,
and broke his body for her and mixed his blood for her and gladdened her heart.
By his suffering he freed her, by his slaying he redeemed her, by his death he bought her,
and by his resurrection spiritual life dawned for her.
A bridal chamber he wove for her from the rays of his Father's light,
and he, the giver of life, called worlds and generations to her wedding.
The Church, bride of the Crucifixion, put on light,
and from her rays her beloved ones, the children of her inheritance, shone.
The love of the Bridegroom cannot be reached by speakers,
and the affection of the bride cannot be set down in writings.
The love of the Bridegroom for the bride fixed him to the wood,
and the affection of the bride pursued her after the crucified Bridegroom.
Who is the bridegroom who for his bride endured the cross,
if not Christ, whose great love cannot be told?
And which is the bride who loved a bridegroom hung on the wood,
