if not the Church, whose story is too lofty for speakers?
For his Church the Son of God died on the cross,
and for his death the Church loved him and clung to him.
A slain Bridegroom and a redeemed bride have cleaved to one another,
and lo, at their wedding the generations rejoice together with the tribes.
On the height of heights the Bridegroom set the bride of his love,
and showed her beauty to the heavenly and the earthly.
He invited the generations, he called the tribes to the wedding of life:

and seated them before the King's daughter, the bride of holiness.
Faithful prophets, radiant apostles, priests and kings,
and slain martyrs he called to the wedding of the Church of holiness.
A great wedding: the Bridegroom is Christ, the bride the Church,
the guests apostles, prophets and martyrs, priests and kings.
All peoples, worlds and generations recline at her feast,
and all rejoice in the body and blood of the anointed Bridegroom.
The body of the Bridegroom is living food at the wedding of his Church,
and his blood is spiritual drink at his banquet.
This is the great wedding at which all the worlds recline,
and the hosts of the height serve at it.
This is the living feast at which life flows through its ranks,
and its guests drink the new life that the Bridegroom has mixed.
The singer of the Spirit — lo, his voice rises at the wedding of life,
and his delight shines with ineffable joy.
The guests sing the beauty of the Bridegroom without ever being sated,
and with their praises they make the crown of holiness glorious.
The voices of men and of angels are mingled,
and the house of the banquet is filled with the songs of the Spirit.
The chief of singers, David the king, takes up his lyre,
and plucks it and sings the blessings of the Church and the beauty of the Bridegroom.
Christ the Bridegroom and the Church the bride are on his lips,
and lo, the guests delight spiritually in his song.
“Hear, O Church, bride of light,” said David,
“and let me tell you of the beauty of the Bridegroom whom your heart loves.
Fairer in his appearance than the sons of men is Christ the Bridegroom,
and grace is poured upon his holy lips.
Blessed is he forever, whose majesty and glory have overcome tyrants;
his arrows are sharp, and his enemies he slew by his cross.
Sin and death, and Satan too, he cast down by his death,
and in victory he returned from battle, and his bow is lifted high.
His throne is established at the right hand of his exalted Father,
and he is clothed in righteousness; his dominion does not change.”

With the good oil of his divinity his humanity was anointed,
and with joy his body shone, the giver of life.
With sweet fragrance the garments of his embodiment are perfumed,
and at the right hand of his Father the Hidden One dwells on high.
“The Lord” — he is the Bridegroom — “and the Lord said: Sit at my right hand
until I make all your enemies a footstool for your feet.”
He is priest and living sacrifice that pardons debts,
and he does not change from his priesthood or his priestly office.
In the splendors of holiness he was born of his Father before the ages,
and in his humanity he was born of Mary in holiness.
All kings worship him with their offerings,
and all peoples serve him with an everlasting service.
His holy name endures forever, together with his dominion,
and before the sun his name was, and it does not change.
In him all peoples are blessed and praise him,
since from them is the Church of holiness, the bride of light.
David marvelled at the ineffable beauty of the Bridegroom,
and began to sing his exalted glory together with the children.
He saw him on earth, clothed in our body, and was amazed at him,
and began to cry out and proclaim his glory and his dominion:
“O Lord, our Lord, how glorious is your name in all the earth!
For lo, in heaven your glory thunders from on high.”
These words full of wonder David sang
to the Church of holiness, the betrothed of the Sun of Righteousness.
The beauties of the Bridegroom filled the hearing of the bride of light,
and the fire of his love kindled a burning coal within her mind.
Isaiah rose and began to cry out at the wedding of life
that Emmanuel is the Bridegroom whom the Church has loved:
“Beyond nature a virgin bore him without union,
and he is the Lord, mighty in power, who does not change.
Peace and tranquility his dominion bears to all the peoples,
and there is no end to his great peace and his kingdom.”
Old Jacob gave forth a voice amid the rejoicing:

“This is the Bridegroom for whom all the righteous have waited.”
This is he who came and brought to an end the prophets and the kings of the people;
this is the Bridegroom who suffered on the cross for his Church,
and with his pardoning blood washed the robe of his embodiment.
This is the Bridegroom whose teeth are whiter than milk,
and all of him blossoms with the glory he put on from the resurrection.
All the prophets, stewards of the household, rose up with their songs,
and the beauties of the Bridegroom filled the hearing of the bride of light.
One was crying out: “Lo, a ruler will come forth from Ephrathah,
who will shepherd the people and redeem the peoples and reign over all.”
Another shouts that Christ will come and bear death,
and uproot Zion and build the Church by his crucifixion.
Another sings: “Arise, shine, O bride of light,
for lo, your great light has come, Christ the Bridegroom.
Lo, his light has dawned and lit your eyes and gladdened your face,
and lo, his glory rests upon your head and adorns you.
To you the kings of the earth will come with their offerings,
and the hosts of the peoples, lo, run to you lovingly.”
Another cries aloud: “Rejoice, daughter of the peoples, in place of the daughter of Zion,
for lo, your King comes to you, Christ, and he gladdens you.
Righteous and upright and humble in his love, full of salvation,
he loves you in place of the Hebrew woman who played the harlot against her husband.”
The song grew strong, and the voices of prophecy multiplied
at the wedding of the Church, the betrothed of Jesus the fair Bridegroom.
The diviner heard a voice of joy and began to cry out
that he is the great Star, the Bridegroom who exalts the Church of holiness.
He is the exalted Head who arose from the seed of the house of Israel,
and he is the Head of all the peoples of whom she is made.
David changed to other words in his song,
and began to sing the beauty of the bride bought with blood:
“Lo, the King's daughter stands in glory at the right hand
of the glorious Bridegroom who came and redeemed her by his crucifixion.”

O King's daughter, all of whose glory is from the house of the King,
adorned in her chastity, decked out and full of beauties!
The beauty of the King's bride is not from without;
from within she is adorned with the beauty of the Bridegroom who died for her.
In the love of the Bridegroom the Church is adorned and full of beauties,
and faith and hope and love shine on her face.
Her garment is decked with the fine gold of faith,
and on her head is set the fair crown of holiness.
The daughter of the peoples, who forgot her people and her father's house too,
inclined her ear to the voice of the Bridegroom who died for her.
The Bridegroom saw that she burned truly with his love,
and he desired her fair beauty and made her his own.
She worshipped her Lord and clung in love to her Redeemer,
and lo, the kings of the earth seek her face with offerings.
The son of Jesse saw the perfect love of Bridegroom and bride,
and added words to his song about the Church:
“The great Church from the nations will surround you, O Bridegroom,
and for love's sake you will return on high above her.
From you is my praise in the great Church,
and in it all the tribes of the peoples you redeemed will worship you.
The foot of the peoples stands firm in you in uprightness,
and within your Church they bless you righteously.
In your great Church I will give you thanks, Lord, rejoicing,
and among the assemblies of the peoples round about I will sing to you.
I have proclaimed, our Lord, your righteousness in your great Church,
and I have not held back my lips from your salvation and your faithfulness.
I have not, Lord, despised your righteousness and your faithfulness
before your great Church from among the peoples, bought with your blood.
Worshipped are you, O Bridegroom, who remembered your Church, which you acquired of old;
do not, Lord, turn the right hand of your love away from your Church.
Your faithfulness, lo, is proclaimed, O fair Bridegroom,
in the great Church whose beauty shines in the saints.
God stood in the great Church among the holy ones,
great and fearful, glorious and exalted over all around him.
[?] in the Church, praise him in the Church, the Church of the peoples —
the Bridegroom, Christ, who redeemed the Church of the peoples by his cross.”

“I will give you thanks, Lord, righteously, with all my heart,
in your great Church in which the upright are gathered with praise.”
“Sing to the Lord a new song,” he said,
“for lo, his praise is in the great Church of the righteous.”
The son of Jesse saw the assemblies of the peoples in the Church of holiness,
and taught them a new song at the wedding of the Church:
“All you peoples, come, clap your hands in the Church your mother,
and sing praise to him who in his mercy redeemed your lives.”
With these beautiful words of the Church the son of Jesse sang
at that banquet which the Son of God made for his Church.
Lo, glorious voices thunder in her, in the Church of holiness:
prophets and apostles who sing in her spiritually.
The voices of prophecy and of apostleship are mingled,
and the Church is filled with glorious thunders of songs.
The great Paul — lo, his voice is raised like a trumpet,
and he cries out and proclaims the exalted beauty of the Church of holiness.
On his tongue her spiritual orders are woven,
and in his [?] her beauties, full of life, are drawn.
Lofty is the song of the herald of the peoples in the Church of holiness,
and at his melodies angels and men marvelled.
All the apostles sing with him in their tongues
at this wedding which Christ the Bridegroom prepared for his Church.
The Bridegroom's gospel thunders life at the wedding of his Church,
and from it the Bridegroom's guests drink new life.
Great is the wedding, wondrous the feast, and sweet the drink;
the Bridegroom rejoices, the bride dances, and the delight runs high.
High priests and radiant priests, guests of the Church,
fill their mouths with songs of the Spirit at the wedding of life.
O you, Church, betrothed of the Sun of Righteousness,
lo, your glory is lofty, and among the stars your crown shines!
Lo, your wedding flows on with the generations, full of delights,
and worlds and peoples in every quarter delight in it.
Fixed on earth is the Church of holiness, bought with blood,
and her exalted head, lo, is in heaven, in the house of God.
Every day her great feast grows, together with her delights,
through the peoples who come from every quarter to rejoice in her.

On the foundation of faith her building is set,
and the thoughts and words of all her enemies do not shake her.
Kings threatened her, and they did not shake the steadfast one,
and lo, in victory the head of the blessed one is crowned.
Among pagan crucifiers the Church of holiness stood,
and on her right and on her left she put on glory.
She overcame the doctrines and put an end to the factions of the children of error,
and lo, her head is lifted high, and beneath her feet her enemies are cast down.
The doors are open before everyone who comes to take refuge in her,
and she is full of light, and her children thunder with songs.
Kings tremble and run, bowing at the footstool of her feet,
and all peoples are gathered at her doors with offerings.
High are her walls, and they are not overcome by persecutors,
and lo, the promise of her great peace is inscribed in hope.
By a redeeming slaying, by blood, the Church of the peoples was bought,
and under the wings of the crucified Light her beloved ones dwell.
Upon the rock of faith our Redeemer built her,
and the gates of Sheol and the devourers of death do not overpower her.
On the confession of the chief of the disciples her building is set,
and her walls are raised high with good hope and pure love.
She is fixed on earth, and lo, her completion is in heaven,
and height and depth are held by the dominion of the bride of light.
A Church on earth and a Church on high, and one Church:
the Church of holiness and the Church of the firstborn, which is to come.
For it is one Church whose beauty shines in two worlds,
since the Bridegroom who betrothed her in two worlds has magnified her name.
She shines on earth and gathers peoples into her house of mercy,
and lo, in heaven her walls stretch out in structures of fire.
In the passing world she is a harbor for all tribes,
and in the world to come Watchers and men rejoice in her.
Once this mortal race is complete,
her beauty will blossom in the high place where there are no mortals.
Here she delights in the body and blood of the Bridegroom, her Lord,
and there she exults in his fair splendor, wrapped in a burning coal.
Here, by the sacrifice of his body and blood, she pardons her children:

and there she shows the nature of his humanity to all her beloved.
Here and there the Church and her children will delight in him.
Here she thunders with the books of the Spirit that the righteous wrote,
and there she rejoices in their persons clothed in light.
Here are the books of prophecy and of apostleship,
and there the assemblies of the persons of the children of light.
Here they thunder through their books within the sanctuary,
and when they are raised they gather to her in the place of light.
Above she is exalted in that ineffable praise,
and the assemblies of her children delight in her together with the spiritual beings.
My mind is amazed at the exalted beauty of the Church of holiness,
and I have no word sufficient to speak of her fairness.
Her story is too lofty for the wise and for speakers,
and she is the source of all the wisdom of the house of God.
Wrapped in light and clothed in light, betrothed of light,
shining light, and her fair light cannot be told.
In her the worlds and the peoples have gloried from the beginning,
and of her the books of the Spirit thunder in all generations.
The Lord of the prophets laid her foundations and set up her building,
and in his blood wrote the charter of her peace and her victory.
The apostles built her by their preaching, full of life,
and died for her and raised her walls through their slaying.
Priests and kings increased the beauty of the mistress of treasuries,
and all peoples thundered their voices in her songs.
Great is her bridal gift, and abundant the wedding of the King's bride,
and her treasuries are full of great wealth that cannot be plundered.
In the bridal chamber, when she entered the house of God,
the Bridegroom bestowed on her his body and blood and his great love.
The groomsmen too, the apostles, gave her their gifts:
the sufferings and deaths they endured from persecutors for her sake.
The prophets laid down their revelations concerning her,
and with their books they danced before her spiritually.
The martyrs lovingly poured out for her the blood of their necks,
and the priests came and laid down their ranks in the house of pardon.
Kings gave her their dominions as a gift:

and with their crowns they bowed at the footstool of her feet, rejoicing.
Men and women, old and young, and all ages
took up and brought her voices of praise as a gift.
Great is the wealth of the Church of holiness of the Son,
and from it all the ranks and companies of her children grow rich.
Those who have passed, those who are present, and those who are to come —
in her great beauty the ranks of their dominion shine.
Her lofty temples blaze with light full of delight,
in the house of pardon, wrapped in radiance and holiness.
Fixed in her is the altar, the mystery of the tomb of Christ the Bridegroom,
and set in her is the cross, the sign of the slaying of the giver of life.
In her are distributed the body and the blood for the pardon of debts,
the living sacrifice of that High Priest who bought her with his blood.
The Redeemer of the pledge, who paid his own price, gave her blessedness,
so that without end she is made complete in the blessings of the house of God.
The priests of the type gave honor to the priests of the truth,
for the type has passed, and the truth of the Church of holiness has shone forth.
The dumb sacrifices of the Law bowed from afar
to the rational sacrifice of the Church, the bride, the betrothed of the Son.
The dead sacrifices found their end in the living sacrifice
within the sanctuary of the Church, the mother of truth.
The Synagogue went out, who hated the Bridegroom to whom she had been betrothed,
and the Church entered and became the bride whose love is true.
The Synagogue crucified, and the Church of the peoples lived through his cross,
and lo, she delights in his body and blood that pardon debts.
Lo, the dowry of the bride of light is on her lips:
the body and blood of the living Bridegroom, the Son of the Most High.
In the four quarters, lo, the King's bride holds sway,
and height and depth are held by the dominion of the praised one.
The four quarters bear the name of her who is full of beauties,
for in four letters the Bridegroom, her Lord, set her title.
Blessed are you, O Church, for your Lord loved you and redeemed your life,
and great peace has shone on your paths and on your ways.
Blessed are you, O Church, for the Sun of Righteousness loved you,
and exalted light shone on your palaces and filled you with glory.

Blessed are you, O Church, for the incorruptible Light chose you,
and raised you to the lofty height above the heavens.
Blessed are you, O Church, for the Bridegroom, the good Lord, betrothed you,
and called two worlds to your wedding, full of blessings.
Blessed are you, O Church, for the Son of God bought you with his blood,
and redeemed your life from the slavery of the worship of idols.
Blessed are you, O Church, for the Father took pleasure in you and the Son betrothed you,
and the Holy Spirit completed your spiritual beauty.
Blessed are you, O Church, for above the daughters of kings he gave you blessedness,
for the Bridegroom whose are heaven and earth loved you.
Blessed are you, O Church, for lo, your bridal chamber is prepared in heaven,
and in it are laid out promised blessings beyond all measure.
Blessed are you, O Church, for though your race is lowly, from the earth,
lo, in heaven your beauties are portrayed in the house of God.
Blessed are you, O Church, for all beauties were poured upon your head
by the Lord of blessings, who loved you and betrothed you and magnified your name.
Blessed are you, O Church, for your feasts thunder in the four quarters,
and his holy name is exalted in you according to his promise.
Bride of blessings, receive my words as a gift,
and under your wing shelter my life from harm.
Our Lord, grant me not to be estranged from that blessedness
for which the Church and her children wait on the day of your revelation.
Glory to you, anointed Bridegroom, from your Church bought with your blood!
On Genesis and on the Being of God

Memra Thirty-Four
On Genesis and on the Being of God

"In the beginning": I heard that Moses wrote this before anything else,
and through his words I wished to look toward the beginning.
I saw five letters that he inscribed at the head of his account,
and my mind counselled me to meditate on the newness of his book.
Like stones he hewed the letters with the chisel of the Spirit,
and on them he built a great house of height and depth.
Like a painter grinding pigments he grinds the mystery in the words of his mouth,
and depicts creatures he never saw while they were being made.
Like a portrait he composed the world that came to be in the beginning,
and took up his colours before the onlookers, so that they might gaze on it.
The painter brought great order to his craft:
he depicted the creatures, and so also the form of the Creator's name.
He showed the King's order first to the King's servants,
and so he lifted the curtain of the gate of the royal palace.
He laid down that word "In the beginning" like a foundation,
and on it God built like a builder.
"In the beginning," he said, "God created the heavens and the earth":
up to that point is creation, and beyond it is the Lord of creation.
He spoke of creation before the Creator, and then of the Creator,
not because creation came first, but to make known the time when it came to be.
By writing "in the beginning" first he made known its coming into being,
and about the Creator he revealed that He exists without beginning.
He is the Being without beginning who brought creation into being,
and He abides without end in the order of His eternity.
The mind can say only that He is, and that He is;
but how He is, the gate is shut before any search into Him.
Among the works of His hands there is no eye able to see His nature,
nor can His works gaze on Him as they desire.

He is without composition, without limit, beyond sight,
and He does not change from what He is, nor turn to the contrary.
His nature is exalted above change and above all who look,
and no creature has a mind able to say how great He is.
His is a nature that holds every law in height and depth,
and within Him is enclosed everything that came from Him.
From Him comes the fullness of the creation He made from nothing,
and this is the wonder: when there was nothing, He created everything.
At His beckoning the great world stands upon nothing,
and behold the marvel: everything is set upon nothing.
By the power of life He reaches natures that speak and natures that are mute,
and behold, in them, in these natures, is shown the greatness of His power.
Natures cry out about His greatness, which cannot be grasped,
and by their deeds they show the power of their Maker.
His craftsmanship cannot be grasped by those who investigate it,
for however much they search, the inquiry into Him lies beyond the limit.
He has no limit, and inquiry into Him has no end of words,
and the one who inquires about Him grows weary.
Stop, inquirer, do not overreach in searching into the Hidden One;
know your own nature and give greatness to your Maker.
Seek, if you must seek, the inquiry fitting for the One without limit:
how is He one nature, equal in three persons?
Seek how there are in the nature without beginning
Fatherhood, Sonship and Procession.
Yet even this one should not seek by inquiring "how,"
but with love, which befits one who is learning.
It is fitting to inquire about the Being with love,
and meditation on what is hidden is beautiful when there is no prying.
So the one who seeks to learn properly is not to be blamed,
but the one who puts words together for contention.
To learn, I entered the house of laws of the King of kings,
to see the order of the royal palace, which I had not seen.
I did not enter where I entered in order to gaze on what is hidden,
but to hear a new discourse about hiddenness.
A certain man wrote a new discourse with the reed of the Spirit,
and I wished to learn the power of understanding hidden in his words.

"In the beginning": a certain herald proclaimed it in the house of the [?],
and I wanted to know the reason for his proclamation.
At the head of his words I saw the name "In the beginning" running,
and beyond it the name of the Creator who created in the beginning.
I heard the name of God, who created creation in the beginning,
and my mind urged me to seek with love an understanding of His name.
His name heaped up in me a fire, the fire of His name, so that I might know His name,
and behold, I make ready to call Him by a name worthy of His name.
The son of Amram called Him God and Creator of creation,
and behold, I purify myself to call Him so, I too, as he called Him.
That He is God of all, I agree with the son of the Hebrews;
that He is the Creator, I acclaim Him to the works of His hands.
That He is the Being without beginning is true to me,
and that His eternity has no end, I do not deny.
That the nature of His being has no bounds, I accept;
that He does not fall under the sight of onlookers, I believe.
That He does not change from what He is, my mind bears witness;
that He does not suffer under blows, my tongue cries out.
That together with His being He possessed knowledge of all that came to be,
this is written in my mind as on tablets, and is not erased.
That He knew how everything would be before it came to be,
this I proclaim before earthly and heavenly beings.
That in His nature there are equal persons, equal with Him,
heaven and earth will cry out with my mouth that so it is.
That He is Father and Son and Spirit, one Being,
beings that speak and beings that are mute will set their hand to the bond of my words.
That He is Father, and the Son is Begotten, and the Spirit is truly Being,
men and spiritual beings will be led by my confession.
That between Father and Son and Spirit there is no boundary or mark;
if there were, there would be another, lesser creation to confess it.
They are not divided from one another by any separation;
among creatures there is none who can say how great that equality is.

Since they are three and are also one,
there is no tongue able to praise that Being.
I did not speak of three beings in the Three,
but of three persons who are equal in it, in the Being.
I said, and I say again, that there is one Being,
and in it, in the Being, three persons who are not divided.
To examine the persons, they are counted one after another,
so that everyone may know that the order of their persons is true.
Manifest truth proclaims the order of their names:
whatever the Father has, the Son and the Holy Spirit have also.
One nature, one authority and one will,
and no distinction of greater or lesser between one and another.
Nothing in the Being is less than the Being,
for whatever is Being has no rank of greater or lesser.
The Fatherhood of the Father is not prior to His Begotten,
nor again is the Son's [?] less than His Begetter.
The Spirit falls short neither of the Father nor of the Begotten,
neither in Being nor in authority over all creatures.
They are one, even though they are placed one after another;
they are three, even though the nature in them is one.
They are three because of the order of their names,
and again they are one because the nature is equal in its nature.
One is not parted from another by cutting or separation,
but by [?] and by number, without confusion.
And behold a demonstration of what I have said about their constitution:
there is something which, while it is one, has something within it.
Look at the disk of the great sun that shines on everything:
though it is one, it has light and heat within it.
The nature of the sun's disk and of its rays is one,
and neither is it prior to what is its own, nor what is its own prior to it.
Light and heat are bound together in it, and it is with them,
and while they are one, they are three in their [?].
The disk of the sun, the light and the heat are three,
and again the three are known as one, without separation.

The disk has never been seen without rays,
nor have the rays shone forth from its bosom without heat.
It is as it is, in the order of its constitution,
and the powers that are with it abide in a permanence that is not divided.
Like the Begotten, the ray goes forth from within its bosom,
and though it goes forth, it does not go forth from it by being cut off.
Like the Spirit, it possesses the power of heat,
which dwells in it and goes forth from it without change.
Praise be to You in height and depth, hidden Being,
who created the worlds above and below at the beckoning of Your power.
Behold, You have shown in creatures the power of Your Godhead:
they travel forth and yet abide, without moving from place to place.
Two powers travel forth from the disk while not travelling,
and abide beside everything while not moving from their place.
The power of their working passes over all and through all,
and their swiftness is not hindered by the great distance above all.
If this sun, a thing made, is so wondrous in its constitution,
who would not marvel at the power of the Maker who has no bounds?
His limit is not bounded by the limit of bounded things,
nor can investigators grasp the inquiry into Him.
And if there is anyone who wants to inquire into words of disputation,
let him inquire, then, and explain to us these things of our own.
Let him explain how the soul dwells within the limbs,
hidden from all, yet revealing the power of its working.
How it, too, possesses two powers in its nature,
and they are within it and outside it, without separation.
How the power of its life runs through all the senses,
and its swiftness is not hindered in coarse bodies.
How its word goes forth from it outside the body,
yet departs neither from beside it nor from beside everything.
How it is within itself and outside itself, whatever the inquiry,
and however much one seeks, it is not grasped by scrutiny.
Who has ever seen it with the sight of the outward senses,
and who has grasped it and gazed on it with eyes of flesh?
And if there is something in us too hard for us to test,
why do we weary ourselves seeking to inquire into what cannot be inquired into?
Hidden inquiry into the Being cannot be pursued,
for even if the seeker seeks, he will surely go astray.

Let one seek by faith alone, as one believes,
and even then not by inquiry but by love.
With love it is possible to inquire into the hidden nature:
how He is, and how there are in Him three equal persons.
That the Father is, the seeker does well to seek,
and it is fitting to confess that He has a Begotten and a Spirit from Him.
It befits creatures to confess at all times the power of the Maker,
who established them from nothing when they were not.
There was nothing when He established everything from nothing,
and because He willed it in His love, everything came to be from nothing.
He alone was before all and beyond all,
and when it pleased Him, there came to be for Him something, something great.
With His Being were all the things that came to be,
not in nature but in love were they inscribed in Him.
In Him were portrayed the worlds that came to be after time,
and He counted how many they would be, and how, and when.
It was not newly, after time, that He thought to establish them,
nor did He look into time in time and so make it.
He ordained for the work of His hands when it would come to be,
and from beside Him it was already made and complete before it came to be.
From the beginning without beginning it was set for Him
that the power of His craftsmanship would be revealed in the work of His hands.
Wisely He made all that He made, the All-wise,
and no one knows how to gaze on the power of His wisdom.
Lovingly He showed His love, a fountain of love,
and among creatures there is none able to repay the debt of His love.
Skilfully He established the world, full of knowledge,
and there is no tongue able to give His craftsmanship its due.
Great wonder fills the beginning of His work,
and the world is too small to look closely and gaze on it.
Even if there were thousands upon thousands of crowded worlds,
they would be too few to see creation as it was being established.
If the hosts of the height had been created before it was established,
they would have been dumbfounded as it was established from nothing.
If they had been permitted to see how everything came to be at once,
the power in them would have [?] to marvel.
How great, then, is that command which He commanded and they came to be,
and its swiftness was not hindered by the great expanse!

How, then, did heaven and earth stand from nothing,
and how can that nothing bear anything?
It was not nothing that bore the weight of what came to be,
but the beckoning of that command which He commanded, and it was.
Out of silence He commanded, a hidden beckoning that rules over all,
and everything stood upon nothing when there was nothing.
He stretched out the heavens like a garment above everything,
and spread out the earth like a foundation beneath everything.
He made spiritual beings possessing power beyond number,
and counted them, though they are very hard to count.
He beckoned, and the expanse of the air, light of wing, was established;
at once it took flight and kept its law in the four directions.
He made the waters flow, kindled fire, spread darkness,
and covered His work through the hours of the night as with a garment.
With a garment of darkness He covered the earth in the beginning when it came to be,
like a painter who paints a picture and then unveils it.
In the evening the Lord of the world painted the world;
in the morning He uncovered the veil that lay over it.
Like a picture He composed and made heaven and earth,
and called rational beings to come and see the fitness of its beauty.
All night long He covered the beauty of His craftsmanship,
and did not wish to reveal how He spoke and everything stood.
A great silence lay over everything while He established everything,
and the natures that speak and the silent ones were awestruck.
For twelve hours silence lingered over everything,
and when it was over, He sounded a voice: "Let there be light."
The Lord of creation cried a new voice in creation,
and the ranks of the heavenly beings trembled at the greatness of His voice.
Like a trumpet His voice rang out within the dwelling,
and the spiritual beings gathered and came to listen to it.
For their sake He sounded a voice, though He has no voice,
to teach them that His beckoning had established them and everything.
Through an echo of a voice He made them wise and able to speak,
so that they might know that He had established everything from nothing.

He made them hear a voice resembling the stirring within them,
and roused them to gaze on the establishing of the light.
All night long they had been sunk as if in sleep,
and they started out of the silence at the voice that cried out over the earth.
Great amazement fell upon them before this voice,
and they marvelled at how they had come to stand when they were not.
By the stirrings within them they pondered themselves and everything:
who, then, had willed that they and all things should come to be?
The voice of the Creator that cried out over the earth was a great thing to them,
and it taught them a new book that they had not known.
As for children, the voice wrote in place of letters,
and made them spell out in the writing, "Let there be light."
Like a tablet He set the voice before their eyes,
and they began to cry out, "Blessed is the Creator who created the light!"
"Let there be light," cried that voice which has no voice,
and the word went forth into deed without delay.
The light dawned out of silence, beautiful, from nothing,
and pursued the darkness like a mighty man chasing one he despises.
The darkness fled and was lost in the narrow places at the ends of the earth,
and the Watchers marvelled at the greatness of the power that gave it power.
They marvelled not at the light itself but at the power of its light:
how it overcame the darkness and drove it out swiftly.
Swiftly the darkness fled from the dwelling,
and swiftly the shining one entered and reigned over the earth.
Like a bridegroom it rested in the bridal chamber of height and depth,
and lit up the world with the beautiful colour of its brightness.
Host upon host of spiritual beings rose to see its beauty,
and could not have their fill of praising its Maker.
The sight of its light was pleasant to their minds,
and more pleasant to them than its light was the beckoning that made it.
They gazed without being sated on the fairness of its beauty,
for He too, with them, was praising for them the work of His hands.
He created it from nothing as it pleased Him,
and then turned and praised it, not that He needed to praise, but that He might teach.
To instruct the heavenly hosts He praised the light:
if He praised it, how much more does it befit them to praise!

They praised and marvelled, extolled and magnified its Maker;
they confessed and worshipped, believed and affirmed the power of the Being.
Through the lights the spiritual beings learned the power of the Being,
and all agreed that everything came from one power.
He extended the dominion of the light for twelve hours,
and turned back the darkness to come and enter where it had been.
In the evening the spiritual beings marvelled, as they had in the morning,
at how the light withdrew in the same order in which the darkness had withdrawn.
The onlookers saw a wondrous sight, wondrous as it was:
mute natures keeping order like beings that speak.
In darkness and light they gazed on the power of the Creator,
how wise He is in ordering the work of His hands.
They too acquired great order through the silent things,
and bent their necks to bear the yoke of the Creator's name.
One day was completed, [?], in darkness and light,
and at once He cried out a voice like that first one.
Like a messenger the command went forth from beside the Hidden One:
"Let there be a firmament," a heaven like that first one.
It came to be in deed: the firmament came to be in the midst of the waters,
and stood in the middle like a canopy above the earth.
He established it from the element of the waters and made it hard,
so that it would be able to bear the waters on its back.
[Lacuna]
and on the earth there remained a portion equal to that which is above.
Here too the spiritual beings saw a great wonder:
a garment of waters bearing waters and rising swiftly.
They were astonished and marvelled at the skill of the beckoning that spread it out,
how it was stretched swiftly over the [?] directions.
Wisely they marvelled at a wonder worthy of it:
how He hardened the soft waters and they bore waters.
Then He stretched it out below, over the face of the earth, and so raised it up;
and then angels and light and air went up with it.
And if it is from the ends just as it is,
nothing was left that He did not enclose within it on high.
And how, then, was the hard vessel raised up,
and coarse natures pass through it, and it is not split?

The inquiry into how it came to be and was raised up is very hard,
and apart from the beckoning that spoke and it came to be, no one knows it.
My mind urged me to seek how, and I could not grasp it;
and again it urges me that perhaps it is possible to grasp something.
I considered it in thought, as far as a created being can consider:
perhaps He stretched this vessel out in the place above.
Or perhaps the command took up the whole portion of the waters,
and when He raised it, His beckoning hardened it, and it bore them.
Perhaps when it went up it was stretched out at once above everything,
and everything below remained on the earth as it had been.
Its establishing came swiftly, without delay,
and no mouth can say how great its swiftness was.
Swift indeed was the command that stretched it out on high,
and if there is anything swift, it is far slower than that.
That echo of a voice which spoke, and the heavens above came to be,
it was this that established it after the pattern of what came from nothing.
The first came to be from nothing at a small beckoning,
and this one from something, in its likeness, swiftly.
He made for His creation a beautiful order befitting His Being,
and wisely He created both from something and from nothing.
To the work of His hands He showed the order of His craftsmanship,
and for their instruction He stretched out His work over six days.
He could have created everything He created in a single hour,
but then His servants would not have learned the power of His greatness.
It was for their benefit that He took His time in creating creation,
that He might complete what was His in the perfection of His Godhead.

On the first day He made the heavens and the angels,
and the earth and the waters, the darkness, fire and air.
In the morning He prepared the light from nothing,
and the Watchers learned that they too had come from nothing.
On the second day He made the firmament from substances,
and taught them that it is easy for Him to create from something as well.
On the third He gathered the waters into the basin of the seas,
and made known to them that His beckoning rules over His creations.
On the fourth He made the lights, the sun and the moon,
and showed them how to keep the order of His craftsmanship.
On the fifth He paired the waters, and they brought forth creeping things,
and He made known to them that even silent things fulfil His word.
On the sixth He created from the earth the kinds of mute beasts,
and roused them to gaze on their variety.
As if with a finger He was showing them the power of His Being:
"Look, angels: I am the power able to do all things."
As if with a reed He was writing a book for them in their minds,
and making them read in it what was written of the establishing of everything.
Like a [?] His beckoning stood at the head of their ranks,
and recounted to them the power of the understanding of His hiddenness.
Like a picture He painted the world before their eyes,
and set them to gaze on it diligently.
Like a palace of the King of kings He built creation,
and brought them in to see the beauty of His royal house.
Through revelations He taught them the power of His Being,
so that they would not be driven to inquire into His hiddenness.
He was hidden from them, and they did not know the greatness of His power,
so He made it known to them through His creations, one after another.
Like a guide His command ran before their hosts,
and led them toward the teaching of the hiddenness of His love.
He revealed His love to them, how much He loves the work of His hands,
and how very eager He is to guard His work from harm.
Lovingly He created everything, hidden and revealed,
and without toil He fulfilled His will and showed His love.
He set His power in the powers of the height that came from Him,
and strengthened them to keep the order of His craftsmanship.

He set them as rulers over all that he had created, / that they might know how to govern heaven and earth.
With great love they too gave themselves up to the will of his love, / and gladly they bowed their necks beneath his command.
Like a king he gave command and arranged the ranks of their authorities, / and each of them took up the task that had been shown to him.
There is one whom he commanded to stir the air like a general, / and to drive the waters aloft through the midst of the wind that moves freely [?].
There is one whom he allowed to send forth the lightnings swiftly, / and to make the sound of harsh thunders heard with might.
There is one to whom he gave the sphere of the sun to hold by its motions, / and it runs on continually, night and day, without ceasing.
There is one to whom he entrusted the little moon that passes through its changes, / and lo, he orders the span of time for it, so that it is not thrown into confusion.
There are some who move the swift stars to run their course in order, / and by their courses they make wise the human beings who possess reason.
As they were commanded to govern the dominion of the nations, / so they toil at every hour to uphold their dominions.
There are some who stir up wars on earth against the guilty, / and some who draw harsh calamities away from the innocent.
There are some who subdue rebellious nations by means of their neighbours, / and some who hold back the strength of the wicked before the humble.
There are some who drive the thunders and lightnings mightily, / and some who bring down rain and dew pleasantly.
There are some who purify by means of the changes of summer and winter, / and some who guard bodily creatures from harm.
There are some who each govern a single human being, / and watch over him so that the wicked demons do not harm him.
They all serve the hidden will with eagerness, / and according to his will they run along the path of their ministries.
Toward the goal of his love they strive at every hour to become like him, / and they do not slacken in awaiting the recompense of their reward.
Like athletes they have been cast into the contest from the time they came to be, / and they await the victory at the end, together with all.
Wondrous is the contest in which the impassible strive, / and the greatness of its toil cannot be told by a tongue of flesh.

How great, then, is the strength in them to hold all things together, / for lo, for a little less than six thousand years they have not slackened.
How long, then, they have laboured in the heights of the height, night and day, / and have not grown weary or ceased from the course they run with the luminaries.
How they bear the weight of time that rests upon them, / and no weariness is born in their thoughts.
How they burn with the love of affection toward the Creator, / and have not grown cold or turned away from the goodness that accords with his will.
Yet let us marvel far more at the power of his will than at them, / for he is able to strengthen the work of his hands to keep their order.
Let the mighty ones [?] of his household praise his power, / and for his help let us weave at all times a crown of thanksgiving.
On the ordering of creation, and it also makes known about [?]
Discourse Thirty-[?] / On the ordering of creation / and it also makes known about the hypostases of the Trinity

The son of Amram opened for us
the great treasure-house in his prophecy:
the great power of the Creator
when He began to make.
This had been hidden from all:
how He began the creatures,
and by whose power were established
heaven and earth and all that is in them.
The Creator wished to make known
to rational beings the work of His power;
He chose Moses for Himself as a disciple
and taught him a spiritual book.
On Mount Sinai He showed him
a vision full of wonder,
and made him hear His voice
as He drew him on to learning.
In human fashion He wished to show

Himself to Moses, the Creator;
and because of this Moses longed
to see His nature.
"If You have chosen me for Yourself
as a disciple, and You love me,
show me the glory of Your nature,
that I may gaze upon Your hidden splendour."
"You err greatly, O Moses,"
the Lord said to him.
"No mortal sees Me,
for My nature is exalted above all who see.
I called you to Me for teaching,
that you might learn that I am the Creator;
not that you might learn of My hiddenness,
which creatures cannot attain.
I am the Lord and God,
and this is My name: I am who I am.
By My power I set up
heaven and earth and all that is in them.
And since mortals are not persuaded [?]
that My lordship rules over all,
I make you a messenger
and a mediator, to teach them.
By your hands I wish to reveal
My being and My works of making;
through you I wish to make wise
the whole race of rational beings.
See, Moses, I reveal to you
the hidden mysteries of My creations;
go down and proclaim among mortals
that I am the Maker of all that has come to be."
In forty days the Master
perfected His new disciple,
and the mind of a mortal was enough
to grasp the sum of all that came to be.
The power of the Spirit dwelt in him
and sang in him wondrous strains,
and at the sweetness of the melodies
the beings above and below marvelled.
The heavenly voice became like thunder,
and the mute and the rational heard it,
and his words, like trumpets,
proclaimed the power of the Maker.
"In the beginning," he says, "the Creator
began and created all that came to be,"
and in His knowledge He set the bounds of the times,
of beginning and of end.
And though in His being He did not begin,
for His nature is without beginning,
He began creation in its time,
as He Himself knew.
For it was no new thought
that drew Him to create the creatures,
since this had been set from eternity
in His knowledge, together with His being.
Nor again was it for His own rest that He established
heaven and earth and all that is in them,
but in love and mercy
He revealed His will to His creatures.
For He is good in His nature,
a nature that is full of goodness,
and in His goodness He willed, and brought
everything out of nothing.

For this befitted the Maker:
that by His works He should proclaim His power,
and that through the making of His creations
creatures should acquire knowledge.
His being is without beginning,
and His lordship is without end;
but to His works belongs a beginning,
and time and order to His creations.
His being is not grasped
by the thought of creatures,
nor is it seen by sight,
for His nature is exalted above this.
His being cannot be measured,
how far it precedes the beginning,
and there is no time when He was not,
for before all things He was.
He was without beginning,
an eternal and perfect nature:
Father and Son and Holy Spirit,
three persons, one power.
The perfect Father without beginning,
who begot the Son without suffering;
and the Son who is from Him, His like,
for there is no time between Him and His Father;
and the Spirit who is from Him, of His nature,
an eternal and true person,
whose equality of nature
bears witness that He is eternal with the Father.
The Father's Offspring resembles Him,
for He is with His Father from eternity;
and because He is with His Father,
times do not confine His Offspring.
The Father's Offspring resembles Him
and is with Him like radiance;
for as radiance is with fire,
so is the Offspring with His Father.
The radiance of fire is with it,
and there is no fire without radiance;
for fire is seen together with its radiance,
and radiance shines out together with it.
In the Father, too, is His Offspring,
and the Son is with Him without beginning;
there is no Father without His Offspring,
and no Son without His Begetter.
Yet the Son does not subsist from the Father
like radiance, without a person of His own,
but He is a true person
and an image that resembles His Begetter.
The Father is not named Son,
nor is the Son called Father,
for the distinction of their names
proclaims the truth of the persons.
The Spirit is a person from the Father,
equal to Him in everything;
as the Son is equal to the Father,
the Spirit is equal to Father and Son.
The difference of their names
does not oppose [?] their equality;
the names are taken for the sake of order,
and the persons are equal in being.
In our own soul He has portrayed for us
an image of the three persons of being:

for the Son and the Spirit are from the Father
as word and life are from the soul.
With the soul are born
word and power and life;
and with the Father are
the Son and the Spirit without beginning.
Two powers accompany the soul,
word and life, together with it;
and two powers are with the Father,
the Son and the Spirit without beginning.
The Son, an Offspring without beginning,
and the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father:
one begotten and one proceeding,
one equality in nature.
The Spirit is from the Father,
yet is not called by the name of Offspring;
for He is not alien in nature,
nor is He so in the order of names.
Eve was formed from Adam,
yet she is not his daughter or his sister;
and though she is from him in nature,
she is called only his wife.
In our nature, as in mysteries,
He has portrayed for us the type of His being;
and whoever is divided over the Offspring,
let him see its demonstration in what is ours.
By our very nature He has made us wise,
that we may contemplate His greatness;
for if what is ours is not revealed to us,
how much more hidden is the inquiry into what is His!
His creations are not comprehended,
and His works are too hard for us;
how then shall we dare to search
into His being, which is without beginning?
A creature cannot search out
the being of the Maker;
however much it seeks how He began,
it finds Him without beginning.
And however much thought seeks
to search out His being,
in this alone it finds Him:
that He is not seen in His nature.
Let this suffice our inquiry:
that we search into His works alone,
and let the inquiry into His being
be honoured by us in silence.
Let us hear rather about His creations
and praise the work of His hands;
for the creature is bound to give thanks
to the Creator for all that He created.
That He began creation in the beginning,
this we have heard from Moses;
and that He was before the beginning:
how and how long, let us not ask.
Let us ask rather, as those who know,
the question that befits creatures:
what is the reason He made heard

a heavenly voice over His works of making?
In the beginning, then, He began and created
heaven and earth first,
and five other natures,
which He did not call by names.
In this word, however, are included,
within the making of "In the beginning",
fire and water and darkness,
and angels, both rational and mute.
In this word "In the beginning"
he included the making of the angels,
and He, the Creator of all,
created them out of nothing.
At this making of "In the beginning"
it is not said that He made a voice heard,
for there was no creature to hear,
able to receive teaching.
But when He began the natures
that came to be one after another,
with a heavenly voice He wished to inform
the angels of His making.
The reason for the heavenly voice is this:
that He might teach the spiritual beings
that the Lord who establishes all things,
He it is who set up their hosts.
O voice, stronger than all,
that was spoken in "In the beginning",
and drew the knowing natures
towards Him in love!
Darkness covered
height and depth alike,
and the earth was hidden in the waters
until it should receive its making.
Without sight and without form
was the earth in the beginning,
and he calls it unformed
because it was not yet adorned with trees.
"The Spirit," he says, "was borne
above the waters of the deeps",
calling the air "spirit"
because of the blowing of the fine wind.
Then the word of the Maker came to pass
for the sake of a work of teaching,
and He made the angels hear a voice:
"Let there be light, illumining all!"
O voice that out of nothing
brought light into being!
O light, at whose hearing
a nature that was not was established!
The light drove away the darkness
that was spread over the creatures,
and the spiritual beings all alike marvelled
at the power that gave it dominion.
And over the word that created the light
He made yet another voice heard,
which praised His work,
that it was beautifully made by Him.
O wise craftsman,
how careful He is in His making!
He set a boundary for the luminous,
how far it should rightly rule.
He divided between light and darkness,
so that neither should trespass on the other,

and set a law for their courses
in the hours of night and of day.
He called the light day,
and the darkness He called night,
and by these names He designated them
according to the services of their hours.
There was evening and also morning,
one day, as it is written,
and He called it the first day,
for there had been no other like it.
He set the night also
as the beginning of the first day,
to keep the order of His creation,
for darkness had come first.
The first day was completed,
night and day, one day.
And again He cried out another voice:
"Let there be a firmament from the waters!"
O voice that held authority,
for with the word came the deed!
O power that out of soft things
compressed and made hard ones!
From the waters He created the firmament,
that it might bear waters above it,
and called it by the name of heaven,
that first heaven of "In the beginning".
Like a canopy close at hand
He made the firmament in the middle,
that it might be near to sight
and divide between waters and waters.
O balance that does not waver,
that divided the waters equally:
half for the earth, for its need,
and half for the stability of the firmament!
O craftsman who establishes all,
whose knowledge is not grasped!
For before He began the work
He knew what it would need.
The luminaries were to be hung,
a nature of fire, in the firmament,
so He laid waters above it,
that it might not be harmed by the fire.
The Creator knew too,
before He created all that came to be,
that rational beings would need
another dwelling at the end of times.
And for this He created the firmament
like a canopy in the middle,
that at the end it might be for us
in place of the earth, for our rest.
There was morning, as there was evening,
and the second day was completed,
and He turned and praised His work,
that it was beautifully made by Him.
There was the evening of the third day,
not different from the first,
for one power was commanding,
"Let something be," and it was.
"Let the waters be gathered," He said,
"and become seas in one place,
and let the face of the earth be revealed,

that it may be fit for habitation."
O command that does not weary!
O word that is not hindered!
For as soon as He commanded His will,
the waters were gathered into seas.
The earth shone and rejoiced,
and a command went out over it:
"Let the earth bring forth," He said, "and sprout
grasses and seeds and trees."
The command became deed,
and the earth was adorned with fruits,
and there were seeds and trees,
and the Good One praised His work.
There was evening and also morning,
the complete third day.
And another command went out,
and He commanded that there be luminaries:
"Let there be luminaries
in the firmament above the earth,
that times and months and years
may be known by their courses."
The word went out into deed,
and the luminaries came to be, suspended.
And He set a law that does not pass away
for the course of night and of day.
O craftsman who adorns all,
whose will has power over all!
For from something and from nothing
it is easy for Him to make everything.
From light He created the luminaries,
from that first light,
dividing it into portions
for the moon and the stars and the sun.
He did not fix them in the firmament,
lest their courses be hindered,
but hung them like lamps
and ordered the course of their hours.
The fourth day was completed
within the bounds of evening and morning.
And another command went out,
that there be creeping things from the waters.
And the waters brought forth living creatures,
kinds without number:
creeping things and fishes and sea monsters
and deadly creatures.
O power to which deeds are easy,
as He wills!
For from waters He composed and made
kinds without number.
From waters He created the birds,
a nature that swims upon the air;
and though it is from waters like the creeping things,
the air carries it and it journeys on.
O Good One, how great is His love,
who keeps His sign for His possessions!
For at the completion of their making
He furnished them with blessings:
"Be fruitful," He says, "and multiply on the earth,
in sea and on dry land alike,
your kinds being preserved

in succession, one after another."
On the fifth day was completed
the creation of creeping things and birds,
and on the sixth He began
to create wild beasts and cattle.
"Let the earth bring forth," He says, "and produce
living souls of every kind:
wild beasts and cattle
and creeping things, offspring of the earth."
O mute nature, that put forth
living creatures from its womb!
For though it is a clod, despised to the sight,
it bore the beauty of every kind.
It did not bring them forth by its own nature,
but by the power of its Maker:
He who spread out the earth in the beginning
commanded it, and it bore living creatures.
On the sixth day were created
cattle and wild beasts together with Adam,
so that those fit for his service
should receive their making with him.
On the sixth day was completed
the making of all that came to be,
and the Creator showed His power
in His works, for He spoke and they were.
On the seventh day the Maker
rested from His works,
and He blessed the seventh day
and called it a holy day.
For that power does not weary,
nor is His will hindered;
something came from nothing,
everything, in six days.
It was not that His will found it hard,
that He did not create everything at once,
for in one day or in many
it is all the same to Him to make everything.
He made an order for His creation
as He Himself knew,
and for the teaching of rational beings
He completed all things in six days.
For the angels were watching His making
and gazing upon it,
and whenever He spoke a word and it came to be,
the spiritual beings cried out praise to Him.
In knowledge He was visiting all things,
that Knower who knows all,
and from something and from nothing
He brought creatures into being.
The light He created from nothing,
to show His greatness;
and our soul too from nothing,
to show that He has power over all.
He created the luminaries from light,
sun and moon, the lamps,
and the hosts of angels gave
praise to the power that establishes all.
In these intervals the Creator
was looking on as He established all,
and He made His works a wonder,
to teach His power to rational beings.
With holy blessings
He furnished the seventh day,

so that it should not be a stranger to Him,
since He did not wish to create anything on it.
That day too was a day,
one of the first days,
and because no making took place on it,
He called it holy, lest they despise it.
The meaning of its holiness
is this: that it rested from labour,
so that whenever we hear the name of the world [?],
we may learn who is the Creator.
This day was to become
a teaching for the seed of Abraham,
that whenever they keep it free from labour
they may learn its reason, from whom it comes.
Over everything that came to be from Him
He made a voice heard as it came to be,
and He Himself praised His work,
that it was beautifully made by Him.
Up to this point there is sameness:
one voice over all that came to be;
but at the completion of His works
a new voice was spoken:
"Let us make," He says, "a rational man
in our own image and likeness,
and let him rule over all that came to be,
which was made for his sake."
O craftsman, how wise!
O Good One, how abundant His love!
For He created and adorned everything,
and then He formed the heir.
He built a house for the earthly one,
and stocked it and filled it with good things,
and mute and rational beings alike
He made subject to his service.
In all things He honoured the mortal:
in his making and in his authority,
in that He called him His own image
and subjected to him all that came to be.
In all that came to be and was established
He made only a voice heard;
but here, in the making of Adam,
there was counsel and new thought.
"Let us make man in our likeness,
and let him be ruler like us,
so that through the image of His revelation
he may proclaim His power to creatures.
Through him I reveal My hiddenness
to the knowing natures,
and through him I make known My lordship
to mute and rational alike.
As an image I set him
for creatures, that they may gaze on him,
so that through love towards him
everyone may come to know Me through him."
Wondrous is the making of Adam,
and different from that of the creatures;
for all that came to be He made by His word,
but of him He said in counsel, "Let Me make."
Glorious is the forming of the earthly one,
and hidden mysteries are concealed in it;
for He did not say, "Let him be like Me,"
but, "in our image and our likeness."

O mortal being, in whose forming
hidden mysteries are concealed!
O earthly one, who shows us
in his making three persons!
In the making of the image of Adam
He taught us, as in a mystery;
for "in our image and our likeness"
made known to us three persons.
The being without beginning
of Father and Son and Holy Spirit
was honoured in the image of Adam,
as in a mystery, by all that came to be.
Otherwise, whom was He calling
to equality with His greatness?
For "Come, let us make in our image"
He was not saying to the angels.
By "our image" He taught us
about the distinction of the persons,
and by "our likeness"
about the equality of nature.
"Come," He says, "let us make man,
and bind in him all that came to be,
so that through their kinship with him
they may supply his needs in love."
And God made in His image
Adam, dust from the earth,
and breathed into him a soul of life,
a living and rational nature.
O love towards our race!
O honour of our making!
For the life He made to dwell within us
He willed out of His love, and breathed into us.
O nature without composition,
whose being is not measured!
For while He establishes our nature,
He made us with hands and mouth.
He did not make us like the animals,
which came to be male and female;
for Adam came first in his creation,
and then Eve from his rib.
He established Adam first,
and then the woman from Adam,
so that she might learn the power of her Maker,
that it is He who adorned her making.
"The Lord God," he says, "formed
Adam, dust from the earth,
and placed him in the paradise of Eden,"
that the heir might be within it.
In a fitting and desirable dwelling
He placed Adam, as His image,
so that through one who is near
creatures might call upon the Maker in love.
His image resembles the Creator
in name, not in nature;
for He gave him authority over all that He established,
as the Creator has over what is His.
He becomes the father of what he begets,
and begets an offspring that resembles him,
like the Father who begot the Son
in His nature, without beginning.
But he becomes a father in time,
and in time begets an offspring;
the Eternal begot without time,
and there is no time between Him and His Offspring.
Man makes something out of something,
and when it is not, he brings it into being,

like the Maker who brought all
into being out of nothing.
He makes something out of something,
and so resembles the Creator.
All that is on earth he surveys,
yet his own gaze is towards heaven,
for in one glance of his gaze
he seeks his place on high.
In these things the earthly one resembles,
as in mysteries, the Creator;
for he too, with word and life,
gives commands to the natures.
With the name of image, as on loan,
He named the first Adam;
and the image came to be in deed
in Christ, the second Adam.
Here received its fulfilment
"Come, let us make in our image";
for the Creator took up His image
and made it a dwelling for His honour.
In Christ the promises made to Adam
came to be in deed;
for He called him His image, and it was corrupted;
He turned and renewed it in Christ.
Because of the image of Adam
he recounts the greatness of paradise,
so that Adam might know his honour,
that He places him in a glorious place.
"The Lord God," he says, "made
a paradise in Eden, in the east,
and caused to sprout in it trees
that were very fit for food."
One of the trees
He set in the middle of the paradise,
and called it the tree of life,
that by it Adam might gain life.
Another tree He planted
and called it the knower of what is fitting,
so that the knowledge hidden in Adam
might be revealed by its fruit.
He tells of the spring that went out
from paradise and watered it,
from whose abundance there divide
four springs to every quarter.
The first river, Pishon,
which surrounds the land of Havilah,
where there are gold and beryls,
and gems and shining pearls.
The second river, Gihon,
which waters the land of the Cushites,
and by a channel from it revives
the Egyptians and the Midianites.
The third river, the Tigris,
which was made a messenger to Assyria,
and all the peoples around it
take delight in its sweetness.
The Euphrates, the fourth river,
which passes through the midst of the land
and gives itself to the husbandmen,
that they may till the lands with it.
It was not to praise paradise
that the prophet recounted these things,
nor to extol its greatness:

of the rivers within it.
He magnified the power of the Creator,
whose deeds are hard to explain:
how the spring of Paradise
passes through the sea toward us.
Waters pass through the seas,
and the waters do not mix with the waters.
And this bears witness to his greatness,
that his power has established everything.
What a sign it is, that keeps waters
within waters as in a vessel,
so that the waters of Eden do not mix
with the turbulent waters of the deep!
Mute and silent creatures
cry out at every hour about his power,
teaching rational beings
that here is the Maker in his works.
The teaching that is full of life
has revealed to us the story of Paradise,
and the account of the tree
has brought us near to reason.
Through causes the Creator wished
to make our reason wise,
and, as with children, by a threat
he made known to us the freedom within us.
To the spiritual beings, through his works,
he taught that he is the Existent and the Maker;
and us he taught through our nature,
for in us he revealed his hidden being.
In the beginning he established
the earth and the heavens when they did not exist,
and together with the power of the beginning
came knowable powers into being.
He created lights, making a voice
sound to the companies of spiritual beings,
and by the coming-to-be of light he taught
that it was he who adorned their persons.
He made the firmament out of waters
and loaded waters above it,
and adorned it with shining natures,
an adornment fitting for rational beings.
He gathered the waters from the earth
into the basin of the seas and deeps,
and adorned it with seeds and trees
for the life of man and beast.
The waters swarmed with living creatures,
and the earth brought forth every kind.
And by silent works
he taught the rational much wisdom.
He made our nature out of the earth
and breathed into us the breath of life,
and out of love toward our race
he bound mute and rational together.
All these works
had been hidden from eternity in his knowledge,
and he brought them out to be revealed
and showed his love to his creatures.
His will was prior
to his works, together with his being,
and before he created he knew
how many natures he would make.
He had resolved upon two works
that were suited to rational beings:
a dwelling on the earth for mortals,
and heaven for the immortals.
He knew the thoughts

of rational beings before they came to be,
and the hidden things were revealed to him
that would be accomplished after time had passed.
He examined everything that came to be
before it came into being,
and the works that were to come from him
were contemplated in his knowledge.
It was not to fill his own need
that he brought creation into being;
he showed his hidden will,
how much he loves his creatures.
He is the spring full of life,
who possesses life by his nature,
and out of nothing he established all things
and gave life to the rational.
His wealth is his will,
and his great treasury is his thought;
and though no receivers asked him,
he opened his treasures and enriched all.
His love is spread over his creation,
and every day he visits his creatures,
and his command preserves the natures,
rational and mute alike.
He set a law for mortals,
that if they keep it they will live by it,
and he appointed his spiritual host
to minister to their needs.
These things had been ordained from eternity
to be accomplished according to his will,
and with a knowledge that cannot be grasped
he set the bounds of time for his works.
All of them proclaim his hidden being
through the visible things his hands have made,
as the sun and the moon in their courses
recount his greatness.
His works owe him
thanksgiving for his gift;
since he adorned them in mercy,
let them confess his being in love.
His need is not filled
by the thanksgiving of what he has made;
thanksgiving is our gain,
and for himself it is not required.
Who praised his nature
when he existed from eternity?
And who offered him glory
before he had created his creatures?
His glory lies in his nature,
and his exaltation is with his being;
it was neither lessened nor increased,
for his nature is higher than these things.
It is he who makes us great when he calls us
and brings us near to the knowledge of him,
so that, when we know him, he may give us
the kingdom in return for thanksgiving.
With the love of our soul let us give thanks
to the Maker for his works,
for he established all things for our sake:
to him be thanksgiving in full measure.
On the Ordering of Creation
Thirty-Sixth Homily / Again on the Ordering of Creation

The Being who adorned height and depth by the sign of His power
willed, by means of a word, to make His works known.
In the beginning He fashioned heaven and earth, and water and air,
and the hosts on high, and light, and the darkness spread over all.
He created creation from nothing by a slight sign,
and its face was covered by darkness as with a garment.
A great wonder the Creator wrought at the start of His works:
He built a house, stopped up its windows and filled it with darkness.
By means of causes He willed to make His works known,
and His works astonished rational beings, to instruct them.
The heavenly hosts were created in the beginning that came to be,
and for their instruction He made a voice heard: "Let there be light."
"Let there be light!" the Creator cried out to all,
and He gathered the heavenly ones to hear a wonder.
O the beauty of the Creator's voice, which cried out suddenly
and made the hosts on high hasten at the sound of its melodies!
O command whose deed came together with the word!
O Craftsman whose sign laboured in all that He made!
"Let there be light," a bright garment that adorns all,
and by it let height and depth and all that is in them be covered.
The deed was complete with the command, and light came to be;
it drove away the darkness and gladdened the air, which had been gloomy.
The ranks of the hosts on high cried out: "Blessed is the Creator,
who created and adorned a fair light and gladdened all!"
Glory to Him for His work, for His deed is beautiful!
And the sound bore witness to the greatness of Him whose power can do all.
O Word, which from nothing made something!
O command, which no want of anything held back!
By means of a word the Creator willed to teach

the rational powers about His Being.
They did not perceive that He exists, eternal before His creatures,
nor did they know who had adorned their own persons.
By the voice that cried "Let there be light" they gained understanding,
and with the deed they cried out praise to the Maker of all.
In this manner He who has no voice made a voice heard,
to teach the spiritual beings the power of His hiddenness.
Great for them was the voice that spoke first upon the earth,
and it taught them that one Creator created everything.
They tuned their voices in perfect love and worshipped before Him,
and all of them gave voices of holiness to the King on high.
The coming-into-being of the light taught them the Creator's power,
and He yoked them to the easy yoke of the voice of His thanksgiving.
One day, night and daytime, was completed with the ending of the light,
and darkness began to tread the road toward the second day.
He set a great order for the two of them in their dominions,
that they should not be confused with each other in their courses.
On the second day the command went forth: "Let there be a firmament,"
and it divided the waters, half above and half upon the earth.
"Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters," a hard vessel,
"and let the waters be borne upon its back, that it not [?]."
O command that hardened the waters, a soft nature,
and made them a hard nature to bear the waters!
O Weigher who divided the waters, a great mass,
and gathered them into two seas, the height and the depth!
Like a roof for the house below He stretched out the firmament,
that it might take the place of ground for the house above.
Like a garment, white of hue, the sign wove it,
and drew figures on it: the sun and the moon, lamps of light.
Two luminaries, lamps of light, He hung in the firmament,
that by their shining they might gladden the earth for the sustenance of man.
From that first light which came to be He made the luminaries,
and from it He apportioned to the sun and the moon lesser lamps.

A fair portion He fixed in the great sphere,
and a [?] of light He set in the sphere of the moon.
The portion of the great and bright one He gave to the day,
and that of the small and dim one to the quiet night.
He bounded the course of the sun and the moon to twelve [?],
so that when one has finished it gives place for its fellow to travel.
In two directions He set the course of the great sun,
that the order of the small moon's path might not be disturbed.
In the dwelling of man it travels its path during the day,
and gives place to the small moon to travel its path.
In a constant course it runs mightily in two directions,
as it circles the vault of heaven night and day.
At the time it rises, then, it is like a bridegroom,
and with the white rays of its brightness it gladdens the earth.
At evening it departs and is strong like a mighty man,
so that when the darkness perceives it has gone, it enters and holds sway.
The small moon makes its course by phases,
and in a single month it climbs and descends twelve steps.
The moon's light does not hinder the great sun
when it meets it in the dominion of the height, because of its rising.
For the life of man the Creator willed a great house,
and laid its foundations on many waters and made them firm.
He stretched out its roof from the softness of soft waters,
and spread waters above its back like a vault.
He hung lamps, the sun and the moon, in the roof of His house,
and the sign of His power poured oil and kindled them.
Praised be the Creator, wondrous in His works and great in His thought,
who knew beforehand, before He made it, what it would need!
An abundant dwelling the Fashioner of all made for creation;
two dwellings He adorned and built for two worlds.
He made the lower one to be fitting for mortality,
and stored and filled it with fruits that bodily beings need.
He made the upper one, a fair dwelling full of good things,

that spiritual beings might delight in it spiritually.
For the earthly He made earthly desires,
and to the heavenly He promised heavenly good things.
He who knows all was gazing upon two dwellings,
and before heaven and earth came to be He beheld them.
For the will of His love was prior to His work,
and the works He made were depicted to Him by His will.
He completed and built heaven and earth, a spacious house,
and stored and filled it with great wealth for whoever dwells in it.
He gathered the waters and made seas, a great mass,
and the sign of His power paired them, and they brought forth creeping things.
The bosom of the soft waters brought forth thick bodies,
and from the heavy ones a bird whose wing is light.
He commanded the earth, and it conceived kinds and families:
the tame beast, the beast of the crags, and every kind.
He tilled the earth and cast into it the seed of life,
and the seeds sprouted, the trees rose up and put forth fruit.
The Creator's power completed and finished all that came to be,
and then He fashioned the heir and lord of all His possessions.
In all that He made He let His voice be heard about His work,
but when He fashioned Adam's dust, word and counsel.
In all that came to be, He spoke and it was;
but in the making of His image, man: "Come, let us make."
He stretched out the heavens and called no other power to help Him;
he spread out the earth also and took no counsel with sons of His counsel.
He made the hosts of the heavenly ones fire and wind,
and did not reveal the mystery of the power [...] of His Being in the [?] with Him.
In the making of Adam, new counsel and deliberation too,
as He let the height hear the sound of His thoughts:
"Come, let us make man in our image and our likeness,
and let him rule like a king over all that has come to be."
Who is this with whom You take counsel, O Creator,
now newly, and deliberate over the dust of Adam?
Whom do You call to help You in making Your image,
and who has been a counsellor to You in all that You made?
O dust, whose clay is despised and whose making is exalted,
in whose fashioning hidden mysteries are spoken!
O mortality, which revealed and made known by its making

three Persons, one Being without beginning!
