By the composition of Adam's image the Father made known
that the Son and the Spirit made everything in equality.
He hid the mystery of making the Persons known from all that came to be,
lest the spiritual beings suppose another power.
In Adam, His image, as in a mystery, He revealed to the prophets
that the Son and the Spirit are equal with the Father in the name of Being.
In "in our image" He proclaimed and taught an equal nature,
and in one likeness He revealed and made known to us three Persons.
In Adam the heir He taught and revealed the Trinity:
that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one equality.
This Power, hidden from all, created everything,
and at the completion of all that came to be He composed man.
One word He made heard, hidden from all that came to be,
but in the making of Adam, His image, He changed His speech:
"Come, let us make man, a rational being, in our image,
and by the kinship of his soul and his body let him bind all together.
Let him be kin to the heavenly by the life of the soul,
and near to the bodily by the composition of the body.
And let the image, by its manifestness, proclaim my hiddenness,
and let it rule over all that came to be, teaching my lordship.
In him I reveal the being of my hidden nature,
and by him I teach the spiritual beings my dominion over all.
I honour his fashioning above all that I have created,
for with hand and mouth I fashion him and breathe into him.
With a hidden hand I adorn his despised dust,
and from my living mouth I breathe into him the spirit of life."
O Being without composition, hidden from all,
who for the sake of a despised one made Himself small by the name of limbs!
The Lord took despised dust from the ground
and composed Adam, a rational image, out of clay.
And He breathed into his face the breath of life from the breath of His mouth,
and Adam became a living soul, a rational vessel.
Him alone, without a mate, He composed as His work,
teaching him that in everything His making was new.

He completed and finished the rational vessel, His living image,
yet there was no counterpart like Adam to be joined with him.
He cast the stillness of sleep, and Adam the infant sank down,
and He took a rib from his limbs and fashioned the woman.
For him He filled up his body again as before,
and from what was his He composed a body that resembled his.
A human being came to be from a human being, resembling man,
and was complete, body and soul, in the likeness of Adam.
The sunken one slept and did not feel the hollowing of his body;
then he woke from his sleep and saw a human being resembling his body.
He struck up a revelation by the Creator's Spirit on the lyre of his soul,
and his mouth spoke new words of prophecy:
"This time she is bone of my limbs;
by my name shall she be called, the man's woman, who upholds the home."
He called her also by a name in which the meaning of the deed is distilled,
and showed that she is the mother of the living, who bears the living.
He gathered to him all the kinds that were on the earth,
that he might set the seal of his word on them, that they be his.
He named them by their names as far as he was able,
and learned the power that had subjected all to him as to a master.
In a lowly place He had fashioned the dusty ones,
and then He set them in the place of Eden, wondrous and desirable.
The heirs entered Paradise and received laws,
and He wrote them the deed of His lordship by means of the commandment.
He gave into their hands authority over the desirable fruits of Eden,
and withheld them from the tree that brings forth death.
He called Adam, His image, then, and set him a boundary,
that he should not draw near to take the fruit that holds knowledge:
"Do not eat from the tree that brings forth death;
keep the commandment, and I give you the fruit of life."
Two trees the Creator set for the testing of His image,
and He created them: a tree of life and a tree of death.
Two works, as in a mystery, He set in the trees;
the dwelling of earth and the kingdom of heaven He made known to us in them.

The commandment became like a ruler to guard them,
lest Adam the infant should presume upon their fruit.
He revealed and made known to him, as in mysteries, by the commandment:
"New life I give you, if you do not sin."
And knowing of him that he would surely sin, like a sinner,
by the commandment He willed to test him as if He did not know.
And knowing that He had set mortality in his nature,
by means of the fruit He willed to make those who came after afraid.
By the commandment about the tree He tried the simple one,
and brought his discernment to light by means of the trial.
The commandment became like a furnace for the testing of man,
and the desire for the fruit like a boiling over the gold.
The desire for the fruit blew air upon Adam's gold,
and increased its refining in the fire of its eating, and showed its beauty.
The Fashioner of all created Adam good gold,
and its beauty was hidden by lack of knowledge, as by a covering.
By the commandment, as into a furnace, He brought his [?],
and by the trial He purged his filth and showed his beauty.
Mysteriously He gave the command to those of Adam's house,
that the hosts on high might not hear the voice of the commandment.
Between them, hidden from bodily beings, was this mystery,
and He did not let the heavenly ones share in it in Adam's affair.
The head of the air had not heard this commandment,
and did not know why they were withheld from the fruit.
The envious one troubled the serenity of his soul and was suddenly darkened,
when he saw Adam made lord over all that came to be.
Zeal kindled the slanderer like fire:
"Why has dust been made king upon the earth?
It was not enough for the son of clay that He called him His image,
but He subjected height and depth beneath his authority.
It did not suffice for the dust of the earth that He fashioned him with His hands,
but He laid the yoke of his toil upon the spiritual ones.
As for me, a spiritual one with authority in the ranks of my fellows,
not even by a word did He care to explain our making.
This despised dust of the earth, son of clay,
He adorned and fashioned with great counsel and deliberation.
He called him His image besides, magnifying him as a lord,

and yoked the heavenly ones to the service of his life.
If I approach him without a body, he does not see me;
if I approach him without composition, he does not answer me."
That envious one was not permitted, at the beginning of times,
to change himself and lead man astray by likenesses.
He chose the serpent, to hide his bitterness in it,
and like a lyre, on the strings of flesh, he played falsehood.
He drew the serpent, which had a body, to the daughter of man,
so that when she saw a fleshly one she would accept his word.
He played falsehood in the guise of flesh, deceitful words:
"Why are you withheld and kept back from food?
Perhaps the Creator set a boundary on the trees,
that you should not delight in their fruit like the beasts?"
Eve answered the fleshly one with a bodily voice:
"He has given us authority over the delight of all the fruits.
From one alone He has bounded and withheld us, which brings forth death,
and so that we may not die, for this reason He withheld us from its fruit."
The cause of death had been hidden from the spiritual ones,
and the crafty one rejoiced that he had found a place to cast his falsehood.
He tilled the ground of hearing, the ears of the soft rib,
and cast the slanderer's seed into her mind.
"It is not a drug of death hidden in the tree," the serpent explained;
"the fruit gives eyes of light to whoever eats of it.
The tree possesses great power through its food,
and it can change man and make him like gods.
A great spring of divinity is hidden in the tree,
and if you drink of its sweetness you will gain high rank.
And for this reason He has withheld you from it, that you may not resemble Him,
lest you reach the great height of His divinity.
Out of envy He begrudges that you should be partakers of His being,
and be called by the great name of His divinity.

Hurry to the fruit and eat of it and see light,
and behold, you will gain the power of wisdom, like gods."
The woman saw that the fruit was desirable and fair to look upon,
and she took and ate, and then gave it to her husband, and he ate.
She was the first to hear the word and pick the fruit,
and her mouth hurried to the food, that she might become a god.
By eating the fruit she willed to snatch for herself the name of God,
and take rank above her husband and become the head.
By the desire of eating they thought they would reach [?] above,
but the commandment brought them down to the depth of Sheol.
By eating the fruit the dusty ones gained understanding;
they looked and were ashamed of the nakedness of their limbs.
The food became like a mirror for the movements of the soul,
and the mind was ashamed of the outward senses, [clothing them] in garments of leaves.
The broken-hearted gained the understanding of discernment,
and covered the naked flesh of their limbs.
From the tree from which they ate they made a covering,
and with the leaves of the very one that stripped them they covered themselves.
At the turning of the day the Creator's voice [?] them,
as He made the sound of walking heard within Paradise.
How is the Spiritual One heard to make a sound without limbs?
How does He who knows all ask His image, "Where are you?"
He knows where he is, and asks him while seeing him;
He makes His voice heard and calls him, to turn him back to Himself:
"Where are you, Adam, manifest image that makes known my hiddenness?
Where are you, heir, whom I made lord over all my possessions?"
With thunderous tones He sought the lost one,
and abundantly, with a voice of lament: "Adam, Adam!"
"Where are you, Adam?" the Creator cried to the dusty one,
and the Maker turned a choked voice toward the one He had made.
"I heard the sound of Your walking, and I hid out of shame,
lest You look upon my nakedness, which I lay bare."
"Who stripped from you the garments of your glory, king of the earth?
And who has made you naked of covering?"
He seized a pretext of shame and took refuge in the rib taken from him,
thinking he would not be held guilty in the decree of judgement:
"The woman You gave to be with me, she gave me fruit and I ate,

and had it not been for her, I would not have transgressed Your commandment."
He bore with Adam for a full time, as with a child,
and asked the woman, "What is this iniquity you have done?"
And she too, like Adam, laid the cause upon the serpent:
"The serpent counselled me, and I ate the fruit not of my own will."
But He did not ask the serpent who led her astray why he had done so,
for it was not he who led her astray, but another who spoke in him.
The Creator pronounced a harsh judgement on the deceiver,
and bound him and cast him into a prison of curses:
"Cursed be you above all I have created that creeps on the earth,
and let the swiftness of your lightness be checked, that you deceive no more.
Despised dust from within the earth shall be your food,
and you shall not delight in the sweetness of fruit.
You shall be hateful to man, whom you led astray, all your days,
and they shall be to you enemies with no reconciliation.
They shall tread on your head and crush you as they overcome you,
and you, whenever they sin, shall strike them by guile."
By the decree of judgement on the serpent the slanderer was condemned,
and by the curses upon the fleshly one He cursed the crafty one.
He did not will to reveal anything about angels at the beginning of times,
lest the error of the name of gods should multiply on the earth.
In this matter He hid the story of the slanderer,
lest he be thought all-powerful like the Creator.
He too had been created with the spiritual ones clothed in light,
and had dwelt with the holy ones in the face of heaven.
He held the headship of the dominion of the air and moved it,
and because he envied Adam he fell from his rank like lightning.
And he was cursed in this: "On your belly you shall walk upon the earth,"
that he might no longer rise to the face of heaven by his lightness.

Him again He humbled, and decreed despised dust as his food,
as he rolls on the face of the earth among the dusty ones.
Him He named hateful, because man kills man,
and it is he who strikes man's heel with the crookedness of iniquity.
He chastised the crafty one with harsh blows to match his folly,
for he had raised his rod against the daughter of man, who heard his word.
With the pangs of childbirth He chastised Eve, who picked the fruit,
and because she exalted herself He humbled her head beneath a man.
Adam, His image, He cursed last in the decree of judgement,
for the harshness of the blows on the serpent and Eve had softened his bitterness:
"Cursed is the earth on your account, king of the earth!
Thorns it shall sprout and give you when you till it.
In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, worn down,
and your possessions shall despise you, as you despised my commandments.
Dust you are, from clay, and dust you shall become;
because you loosed my words, death shall loose the dominion of your life."
O Knower of all, who knew all before it came to be,
who showed His anger in His decree of judgement as if He did not know!
He had created Adam from clay and called him His image,
and made his dust in the likeness of the dust of mortality.
For this He set him from the beginning in the composition of his body,
that he might walk the way of mortality and seek life.
Not out of anger did He decree curses and the pains of childbirth,
nor in regret did He bring death upon mortals.
The natural things that He had set in mortal nature
He turned and set as a threat for the help of man.
He knew of Adam's dust before it came to be,
that death would dissolve and undo the composition of his body.
It was plain to Him that he would surely sin through desire for the fruit,
and He knew the evil inclination of his discernment.
By trial He willed to make his rational nature wise

so that his discernment would not be without training. / Through the commandment he set up means by which Adam might learn / that it was fitting for him to keep the order of his Lord's command. / Through the tree he laid bare what was hidden [?] in his discernment, / and by his eating of the fruit he showed the power of his reason. / The tree did not possess the power of discernment, / nor did a silent thing cause the rational one to know these things. / Death was not hidden in the tree, to enslave Adam, / nor did the commandment make sinners of those who came after. / The very make-up of Adam's body cried out that it was mortal, / and so did his partnership with Eve, which was full of sufferings. / The whole world bears witness to this by its ordering, / and fruits and seeds, for the continuance of the seed of mortality. / He called the tree "possessor of knowledge," not by its nature, / but so that Adam's wisdom would be tested by means of its fruit. / He called the other "giver of life," not of itself, / but because it pictured in mystery the kingdom full of life. / Through the one he bound up decrees of judgment full of threats, / and to the other he plainly gave the hope of life. / Adam, being a child, was not yet ready for perfection, / nor was he able to hear the report of the kingdom on high. / Little by little, as with milk, he received training, / and so he tested him through the tree with two designs. / For life on earth he set forth a figure in a fruit-bearing tree, / and in the tree of life he pictured the order of the kingdom on high. / He promised Paradise as a reward for the labours of the contest, / and guarded its fruits by the abstinence his commands proclaimed. / Glorious was its spring, which waters the four quarters with its course, / and like a channel passes through the sea without mixing. / Where is the command that keeps the waters as in a vessel, / so that the spring of Eden does not mix in the great deep? / Where is the boundary of waters that cuts through waters, / so that, though they are one, waters became strangers to waters? / The spring of Eden did not gain such power by nature; / it is the Creator's might that keeps waters within the yielding waters. / He who created all from nothing by the might of his greatness

signalled to the yielding waters not to mingle with their fellows. / The son of Amram too magnified his might when he recounted them: / that things easy and things hard alike lie open to the might of his will. / In this he recounted that he divided the waters of Eden, / so that they would bear witness to the greatness of the might of the All-Powerful. / Like heralds he sent them out to the four quarters, / to cry out, though silent, about his greatness. / In India the great Pishon proclaims the Creator's might, / and with beryls and pearls enriches the land. / Among the Cushites Gihon rejoiced at the sound of its abundance, / and though silent it lifts up its nature [?] and waters the earth. / The Tigris cries like a trumpet to the Assyrians / that here is the Creator: among silent things they heard speakers. / The Euphrates makes its voice heard like thunder in its great course, / and like a trumpet rouses the harvests with the sound of its watering. / Moses did not praise the greatness of the rivers; / he magnified the might of the Creator, who is able to do all things. / And though his will is his treasury and his nod is wealth, / he made them marvel at the work of his hands as though he lacked something. / In six days he prepared all things, he who prepares all, / and on the seventh he rested from his labour, he who completes all. / It was no hardship for the greatness of the might of him who created all / to make with a single nod all that came to be. / His arrangements took six days, not because he was lacking, / but to teach his might to the spiritual beings, that it was he who arranged all. / He was teaching them, when he created the beautiful light, / that the Creator can make something from nothing. / And to them he makes known the sphere of the sun and the ordering of the moon, / that from something too he can change and make something. / Their ranks cried out as they saw a great wonder: / that with the command the deed was not delayed. / They learned the power of the Creator through his works, / and believed that he alone is without beginning. / By his nod they received authority to govern all things, / and their companies took charge of the affairs of earthly beings. / To them he entrusted great riches, as to faithful ones,

and made them stewards of mortal things. / They received spiritual authority over all that came to be, / and the nod of his might strengthened them for giving praise. / The Accuser he made a chief, who stirs the air, / and as a commander he gave his companions into his hand. / Through his authority pride took hold of that rebel, / and he wished to exalt himself above the Creator in the arrogance of his heart. / And since the evil one could not harm the might of the One Who Is, / he wished to overcome the Creator's image in place of the Creator. / In Adam's childhood the rebel made war on the Creator, / thinking that through his image he was doing harm to him whose image it was. / He led Adam astray by desire for the fruit, so that he would eat and die, / thinking that when Adam died, God would be grieved [?] by Adam's death. / By Adam's death the rebel thought he was snatching from him / the precious name, the name of Being of the God of all. / The rebel sought to gain glory [?] through Adam's error, / and the nod swept him like lightning from his authority. / The mighty one fell from his greatness and was stripped of his glory, / and while he thought he would be comforted, his pain grew greater. / In the sentence of judgment that Adam received, the rebel thought / that from then on death would dwell in the make-up of his body. / But the evil one's desire did not come about as he wished, / nor did Adam die by eating the fruit as he had thought. / For his life was lengthened to nine hundred years and more beyond that time, / and his body drew out a fount of life for the continuance of his kind. / He trained him with a threat in the sentence of judgment, as one trains a child, / and through the threat he came to hate sin, the cause of his death. / The mortals received nothing new in the sentence of judgment; / these things that happened the Creator had placed in nature itself. / His Lord's commandment became great to him, and he grew wise, / and in his mind he wrote signs in place of the threat. / He hated the sin that had become the cause of mortality, / and gained love for the Creator who trained him and made him his own. / These things concerning Adam had been known to the Creator from of old, / and it was not out of regret that he brought in death, as if against his will. / For Adam's help he spoke of them as though they were new, / so that by testing Adam might learn his Lord's will. / All things that came to be he fashioned in Adam as he willed,
and in his make-up he bound up the love of all that came to be. / For all that came to be, Adam owes a debt of praise / to that Creator who showed his love toward his works.
On the Order of the Angels
Thirty-Seventh Discourse: On the Order of the Angels

A great wonder fills the creation of the One who fashions all,
and the power of the meaning hidden within it cannot be told.
A hidden power lies hidden in the search into his craftsmanship,
and it is not explained unless he himself explains it to those who seek.
Lofty is the search for him, hidden the gaze upon him, and hard is finding him;
and the more one seeks him, the more one must seek him well.
Deeper than all depths is the wealth of his wisdom,
and the fair order of his creating has no end.
His command is wider than his creation, which is beyond all measure;
it reaches every limit, yet has no limit to bound it.
Swift is his nod, strong his power, mighty his strength,
and too small is the mouth to recount the ways of his might.
A word would need a word above it for anyone to tell
how he spoke, and his works arose out of nothing.
Out of nothing he created everything when there was nothing,
and upon nothing he set everything that came from nothing.
One command he commanded concerning everything,
and with the word everything came to be from nothing.
Swiftly his command ran over his creation,
and at once the work came to be before him at the nod of his command.

The work did not wait upon the nod, not even for the nod,
nor did it delay to show the power of his greatness.
By a nod he signalled to creation to come forth into the open,
and it was fashioned suddenly, not knowing how it was fashioned.
Suddenly he spoke, and mute things came to be along with speaking ones,
and they wondered and were amazed at their nature, formed out of stillness.
The rational ones marvelled all the more at their nature, how it was constituted,
and how it rules over the freedom that dwells within it.
In wonder and amazement their companies stood when they were fashioned,
and without end they were astonished at the reason within them.
In their rationality they marvelled how rational it was,
and how light the power of the thought that moves within it.
In themselves and in all things they searched with discernment
who it was that had established them and all things when they were not.
"Did we rise up of ourselves?" they pondered in their minds,
"or perhaps another power fashioned us?
 What then is this that has happened?" they signalled to one another;
"Are we beings who exist of ourselves, or have we come to be from another Being?
Did we exist as we are now, or did we not exist?
Have we come to be just now, or is being far removed from us?"
A great inquiry arose among them at the beginning, when they came to be,
and they marvelled greatly at their own making and at the making of all.
In the greatness of the expanse of height and depth they searched
how great was that command which had made them great.
They marvelled at the darkness of the newly created world,
and though it was very dark, it was not dark to them as darkness is dark.
In its darkness their sight was [?],
how it ran on and was not hindered by its gloom.
They saw a wondrous sight in its blackness,
and could not have their fill of searching into its workings.
Very great was the greatness of the wonder cast upon it,
and endlessly they strove to know its cause.
In the contest of wonder at the making of all they struggled,
and longed to learn the cause that had wearied them.
In the arena where the worlds came to be they persevered,
and did not cease from the struggle of the hidden inquiry.

They longed to see openly the Hidden One who was hidden,
so that what was being searched out might give rest to the toil of their minds.
In this hope the hope of their reasonings laboured,
to hear something that would resolve the inquiry that wearied them.
In ranks of hosts their orders stood, one facing another,
and like a woman in labour they travailed to bring forth what they sought.
All night long they toiled at the searching of this search,
until they heard the voice that cried, "Let there be light."
At dawn they heard a voice that was no voice,
spoken according to the hearing of their minds.
In a spiritual way that Nod which had fashioned them cried out,
and in a spiritual way they too heard with a hearing of the spirit.
An unheard hearing the hearers heard, listening well;
and though they heard it well, they could not hear it as it is.
They heard the One who makes all hear calling, yet not as one who calls,
for his voice did not resemble a bodily voice.
At the sound of his voice the hearers of his voice were amazed,
how he made the voice of his will heard while his nature was hidden.
At the openness of his voice and the hiddenness of his being they marvelled,
and they grew weary of searching into his hiddenness.
In weariness they remained until they saw the coming to be of the light,
and when it was fashioned they found rest in the harbour of its brightness.
In the harbour of peace they rested at the coming to be of the beautiful light,
and they rejoiced and praised its Maker, who had made it beautifully.
They cried out praise to that voice which created the light,
and gloriously they recounted the glory of the One who made the voice heard:
"Praise to him who made a voice heard to our hearing, which knows no voices,
and by visible works showed us the power of his hiddenness!"
Through works the spiritual ones saw the One hidden from all,
and found rest from weariness and from the search into his hiddenness.
At the coming to be of the light they looked on the coming to be of their own selves:
that as it had come to be, so they too had come to be from nothing.
From nothing the luminous one came to be, like everything else,
and at its making the spiritual ones marvelled at their own ranks.
In their ranks they stood before the One who had set them in order,

and beneath his glory they yoked their voices to give praise.
"Praised be the Creator!" their companies cried lovingly,
"for by his works he has revealed of his being that he is the Fashioner of all.
Worshipped by all is the Maker of all from nothing,
who through something has taught us the power of his divinity."
In a godly way they sang holy praise before the God of all,
and rendered him glory befitting his glory.
Like debtors they paid the thanksgiving they owed,
and acclaimed and magnified his creating, so beautifully wrought.
Very beautiful to their minds was the creation that had come to be,
and they marvelled greatly at its Maker and Preserver.
Wisely the wise ones gazed upon the wisdom of the Hidden One,
how skilful he is at fashioning and preserving.
Through his wisdom the spiritual wise ones learned,
and by his thought they gained the thought to search out hidden things.
He brought them into the house of learning like children,
that they might meditate on the name of the Creator and on his creating.
On the name of the Creator and his creating they meditated,
and marvelled at the variety of his utterances.
At that word, "Let there be light," they marvelled,
and they pondered that by a word they too had come to be.
That word stirred up an inquiry in their minds,
and they searched well and learned well about its beauty.
Come then, let us search with the spiritual ones the search they searched,
and learn with them the cause of the voice and the power of its meaning.
Come, let us consider, by the power of the thought that gave them discernment,
how and about what he made them wise through a voice.
Why a voice, then, for him who by nature has no voice,
who is hidden, as it were, from any audible voice?
He is without voice whose nature is without composition;
and if so, the cause lies hidden in the sound of the voice.
By a voice he taught that he made all things from nothing,
and that his are heaven and earth and all that is in them.
Within two visible vessels he enclosed everything,

so that no one should think there is within his creation a creation belonging to others.
Heaven and earth, water and air he created first,
and together with their making, the making of the spiritual beings as well.
Like a wall he created the heaven, and spread out the earth,
and within them he enclosed everything, rational and mute.
He built a great city as a dwelling for the works of his hands,
and laid up in it all that was required for the needs of his workmanship.
The rational ones he nourished all the more with good things,
and revealed and showed them the power of his being and his creating.
To the rational ones he made himself known through a swift creation,
yet for their instruction he drew out his work over six days.
In six days he taught them the order of his power,
and made them skilled scribes of the works of his hands.
As skilled scribes they learned from the creation before their eyes,
and in their skill began to bring order to the creatures without reason.
Through their discernment they gained understanding of the undiscerning,
who gave their hand to be subject to their rulers.
To that authority which set them in authority the silent creatures submitted,
and though without perception they perceived and knew that there is a Creator.
Through the speaking ones the silent learned to keep order,
and through the silent the speaking marvelled at the power of the Creator.
Both orders were enriched, each by the other, through one Lord,
and to that lordship they rendered thanksgiving with one hand.
They became a good cause for one another, rational and mute,
and abounded greatly in the fear of the Lord who fashioned them.
They learned that they were one creation of one authority,
and were not divided, as though there were another power that rules.
Their very making strengthened them by the power of the Creator,
and through their works they fulfilled the tasks of their service.
Now that rational and mute have submitted to one authority,
come, let us search into that authority which made them wise.
Come, let us consider the varied wonder of his creating:
that though it is one, it is not one in the things that are seen.
With the mind let us listen to what is inscribed in the Scriptures,
and with understanding look into Scripture and its writings.
Scripture has revealed to us about our own making and that of all things,
but about the making of the spiritual beings it did not wish to reveal to us.
Moses did not write of their making in the book he wrote,
until he came to Abraham and made mention of them.

He did not discuss their nature with us at the beginning of his narrative,
until he discussed their being sent to Hagar.
He did not make known to us that they had received anything to govern,
until they showed their care for the Egyptian woman.
He did not tell us that they are our brothers and companions,
until they taught order to Sarai's handmaid.
In silence he passed over the great story of their works,
and as if they did not exist he neglected them and kept silent about their making.
Silence he cast upon the labour of those who labour for our life,
and under a veil of unthinking he hid them.
Why did he neglect to mention them, he who records everything,
when all that came to be is recorded in his writings?
Why did he cover over the plain story of what happened to them,
and not reveal it before us as he revealed to us about our own making?
Why did he not say whether they came to be with all things or after all things,
as he said of man that he came to be last?
Why did he not reveal, he who revealed about everything,
that there is within his creation a creation exalted above harm?
Their nature is exalted above bodily harms,
even though it is said of man that he is exalted above all.
Why did he not show the power of the thought and reason within them,
nor discuss the freedom of their wills?
Why did he not teach that they are spirit and without composition,
so that we too might learn that their nature and the nature of our soul are one?
The Artist who formed them gazed upon their nature,
and seeing that it was beautiful, he hid them from those who look.
He saw their glory, that it is more glorious than all he had created,
and that if it were revealed, people would go astray over its glory.
He searched out the error concerning them before they existed,
and forestalled it by silencing it with the silence he cast over their making.
He saw that human inclination lusts after whatever is desirable;
therefore he hid the desirable story within silence.
Silence he cast over the desire of the sons of Adam,
so that an evil desire might not [?] in their minds.
Upon their minds he cast the bonds of not knowing,
lest by what they knew they be thrown into confusion over the course of his creating.
By his foreknowledge he had seen the woeful course of their thoughts,

and he forestalled them before they began to rebel in confusion.
A fence of silence he set before the faces of the brutish,
lest they trample the works of his hands with their blasphemies.
The sound of their blasphemies he had heard from eternity, before they existed,
and once they were made he stilled it with the stillness of the heavenly beings.
As though they were mute, he silenced them on account of error,
so that error, which was to reign on earth, might find no place.
The strife of error he stilled by the silence concerning them,
so that no one might be turned brutish and troubled by its frenzy.
He knew that it is brutish and kills people;
therefore he bound it with silence as with a weapon.
Into a prison of forgetfulness he brought it and shut it up,
so that the name of its wickedness might not be remembered on earth.
The name of its wickedness he blotted out of his books by the hand of Moses,
so that no one might meditate on the tales of its drunken folly.
For it was eager to seize the name of his Being and turn it toward itself;
therefore he expunged the hateful name from his Law.
It was falsely stealing creatorship for itself,
and prophesying a fiction of beings that were not true.
By the power of the angels the feeble one sought to strengthen itself,
and with their beauty it was covering its own ugliness.
It called them beings who had brought creation into the open,
and said that on their help creation depends and the world is preserved.
To the lofty rank of divinity it was raising them,
and naming them makers of all and preservers of all.
Not that the angels were being exalted to this height,
but error was taking refuge in their names.
Nor again was error raging of itself,
for it has no substance that subsists through deeds.
The will of demons and the inclination of man craved this,
and the One who held back the angels together held back their wickedness.
Upon the wickedness of the wicked that Good One, who is wholly good, looked,
and hid the goodness that is in the spiritual ones, so that it might not be defiled.
From blasphemy he kept back the making of those bright of soul,

and placed it in silence as in a treasury, so that it might not be profaned.
With the seal of silence he sealed the treasure of the members of his household,
so that wicked servants who stir up rebellion might not destroy it.
The order of demons was stirring up rebellion against his Being,
and their rebellion made all the greater the fortress he built against their lust.
A lofty fortress he built out of silence about the spiritual ones,
and within it he placed their making with care.
Wisely that Nod which makes all wise acted,
hiding goodness from the wickedness of the wicked.
Woe to you, evil! How evil is the bent of your insolence,
that even the Creator hides from you the goodness of his good gifts!
Woe to you, error! How insolent you are among those who err,
that the Maker of all guards his works from your blasphemy!
Woe to the hatred that makes hateful the gaze of whoever looks with it,
so that the Good One hid the beauty of his work from its eyes!
Woe to the loathsome thing whose very report disgusts the hearers,
so that the Maker of creation fled from it from the beginning!
From the beginning he saw how loathsome its look was,
and turned his face away, so that it might not gaze upon the making of the Watchers.
And if the Creator did not wish the loathsome thing to see it,
who would dare to search into that thing with a loving face?
It is not fitting for us to look upon it with a loving face,
lest we become hideous to behold in its likeness.
Its likeness hid the likeness of the Watchers from our minds;
had it not been for it, that likeness would have been revealed to our eyes from the beginning.
And if its gaze is so evil, as indeed it is,
who would not turn the sight of his heart away from contemplating it?
Flee, then, O people, from contemplating evil, which is evil,
so that you may not be robbed of contemplating the good, which is good.
See what it has done from the beginning, from the very beginning of time,
so that it has not allowed us to see the making of the heavenly beings.
Their making is more beautiful than the creatures that came to be with them,
and the order of their service testifies how beautiful it is.

Desirable is their appearance and swift the course of their works,
and who is able to look well into their ordering?
In a beautiful order the Maker of all ordered them,
so that by their ordering the brutish world might be set in order.
For the ordering of the world he ordered them with reason,
so that its creation might not be confused and without order.
Not that he lacked the means to order everything himself did he set them in order,
but to make known that his making too is ordered with order.
Along with the silent creatures he fashioned them,
so that they might not exalt themselves and stray from the order of his creating.
Along with those without speech he brought them into the school,
lest they boast as though they had no need of instruction.
By an open voice he made them hear the power of his hiddenness,
so that they might know there is a Being hidden from them.
Like children he made them wise through his creating,
so that they might not be thrown into confusion by the splendour and glory of their own selves.
By a small nod he spoke, and they came to be like all that came to be,
and he made them equal with everything else in servitude.
Servants they are, then, even if it is said that they are spirit;
and from one power they gained the nature to fly in the air.
The power of the Creator empowered them to do mighty deeds,
and he made them good servants of his ministry.
With the life of immortal life he furnished them,
and richly endowed them with freedom of soul.
Life and freedom of soul he set in their nature,
and by nature he gave them life and set them free.
With life exalted above harm he honoured them,
and with freedom that lacks nothing he enriched them.
Great wealth of discernment he placed in their hands,
so that they need not borrow anything from the silent creatures.
Without need he made them dwell in a needy world,
and without fatigue he occupied them with the needs of our life.
Fire and wind he named them by the mouth of the son of Jesse,
yet the subtlety of their minds is far lighter than these.
Fiery and spirit-like they fly through the air,
and are hindered neither by fire nor by wind.
Amid opposing elements they stand in the middle,
and are troubled neither by cold nor by heat.

Within the count of days and months they are enclosed, like everything else,
yet they have no need of the alternation of one with another.
This world is reckoned as one day before their eyes,
for it is one day that turns over all the days.
It is one day that has run its course in the world from the beginning,
and with its course they run without ceasing.
Their minds are not cut short by the passing of time,
for the Lord of time has empowered them to keep time.
O mind possessing the abundance of might,
which is not weakened by the opposites that surround it!
O the power of the divine might in the spiritual ones,
which holds the world and governs it through the members of his household!
O works made by the One who made all,
who do what is beyond the power of their own selves!
O nature which, when it was not, came forth into the open,
and once fashioned began to resemble its Fashioner!
O gift not contained by those who receive it,
which gave itself so that the limited might contain it!
O greatness which, from the divine greatness,
revealed its splendour in something small among its creatures!
A small thing is the nature of the heavenly beings,
and this is the wonder: that in its smallness it governs all.
Small is their nature beside the greatness of dense bodies,
and they are not to be compared with plains and lofty mountains.
Their nature is finer than the sphere of sun and moon,
and yet without them these cannot [?].
O nature that makes the light run with its brightness,
and bears something greater than its own measureless power!
O luminous ones that fly through the air with the luminaries,
whose brightness is not hindered by darkness!
O flying ones that possess wings without composition,
who fly and soar without wearying in their works!

O creation from the immortal Creator,
which possesses immortal life like the Creator!
O Creator, living in his nature and exalted in his Being,
who made his servants partakers in the glories of his divinity!
O Everlasting One, whose everlastingness
gave his creation a continuance that does not cease!
O how great is the abundance of your love, Maker of all,
that you made your work, too, a companion in the greatness of your glory!
Glorious is your making, yet not like you—God forbid, it is not—
for you are the Creator, and the work of your hands you made in grace.
Your works are filled with the praise of your glory,
and they are in you, yet are not mingled with your Being.
You are, and you are outside what is yours and within what is yours,
and your everlastingness is not grasped by those who search.
You are not grasped by the speakers who speak of you,
since there is no word able to say how you are.
Who is able to recount the glory of your gloriousness?
For even if he were able, the glory that comes from us is superfluous to you.
Out of abundance does whoever praises you give praise,
since your glory is above praise and above blame.
To your Being glorious praise and contemptible insult are alike,
and to you the voice of acclaim and the voice of blame are one.
Through praises you seek glory from your making,
so that whoever praises may be glorified by his praising.
No one praised you before creation came forth into the open;
it is plain, then, that not even now are you praised for your own sake.
The Watchers did not praise you with praise before they existed,
for had they not come to be, they would not even delight in your glory.
Being comes before the praisers, not praise;
so the praise of the praisers is for the sake of glory.
O how glorious is that Being who glorifies his works,
who made them possessors of glory for the sake of his glory!
Glorious is the making of the heavenly beings, how glorious!
And this is the wonder: that when they were not, they came to be and were glorified.
It is a wonder how beautiful things came to be from nothing,
and how their beauty became beautiful without anything.
Since [?] something is the cause of whatever comes to be,

and who would not marvel that the Watchers were made fair out of nothing?
The command that spoke, and they came to be, in place of any matter,
filled for them the place of the craftsman's work.
His sign became word and labour and craft as well;
it began and it finished, needing no other helper.
No Hyle was there to help him, as Mani invents,
nor an archon riding on the forgery of Bardaisan.
No Evil helped him, an Evil that begot a world full of evils,
nor gods that are no gods, whom the fabricator names.
Brazenly the fabricator gives demons the name of self-existent beings,
and falsely the deceiver said that Hyle is coeval with all.
The invention of the Manichaeans, with its two powers, is a lie,
and brazen is the teaching of Bardaisan's school about the Seven.
Two did not fashion creation in the beginning, you Manichaeans,
nor again did seven elements create it, you Bardaisanites.
There is no Evil, Mani. Why, evil one, are you so obstinate?
Nor do the archons your fellow invented hold any dominion.
Cease, you brazen ones, from your strife with the Creator;
do not defile his truth with the name of liars.
Liars are you, and falsehood fills your hearts,
and the beings your thoughts have begotten are not true.
One is the Being who is, and is as he is,
and he it is who fashioned creation in the beginning out of nothing.
The Being has no need to borrow help for his making,
nor can his making be exalted beside his Being.
Beyond all things is the Being who is without beginning,
and from him come heaven and earth and all that is in them.
Outside all and within all he is, and is,
and the might of his power is not bounded by the works of his hands.
Within his making the Hyle of the Manichaeans is confined,
and the beings of Bardaisan's school serve at his command.
All is bounded by him, since his nature suffices for all,

and there is no limit that bounds his craftsmanship.
Truly he is, and is in his very Being,
and beside his power there is no other power, alien to his name.
He created a creation filled with kinds beyond number,
and many as they are, they were counted in his knowledge before they came to be.
He made spiritual beings spirits,
and appointed them to minister before his will.
Paul bears witness to the service in which they stand firm,
in that he calls all of them by the name of ministers:
“Are they not all spirits and ministers?”
And they too live in the hope of the redemption of our lives.
In their very coming to be they received this from the Maker,
and the Maker ordered them for this and established them.
For the order of his labour he made them labourers,
so that as they toil they might know that they are made.
The labour in which they toil proclaims that they were made,
and points humankind, as if with a finger, to the fact that they are not self-existent.
Like a trumpet the course of their works cries out:
“Look, you who dwell on earth, how hard the heavenly host is toiling!”
The labour within them bears witness to their labours,
and they set their seal to its witness, that it is true.
True witnesses are the works of the Watchers, and the Watchers themselves,
that they came to be like everything else, to govern all that came to be.
They came to be, and are not makers of things made;
rather they are made servants to the things made by the Maker.
O wonder full of amazement at the one Maker,
who shows himself and yet is not shown as he is!
O how much greater his workmanship is than our thought,
and how small, beside his greatness, is what is beyond measure!
What is beyond measure is great to us and lowly to him,
for behold, he measured it before measures were ever laid upon it.
He had measured how great it would be before it came to be,
and he had weighed its weight in the scale of his sign.
The coming into being of the spiritual hosts was revealed to his sign,
and he had counted how many they would be and why they would be.
The whole creation had been created by him in his will,
and he created it a second time through works, when he willed.

This will he had possessed from of old with his Being,
and he brought it to light at the time that pleased the wisdom of his love.
In great love he accomplished the will in which he had willed,
and wisely he set in order the order he had traced out.
Heaven and earth had been traced by him on the palm of his hand.
Ah, what have I said? It was not by a hand but by a sign.
The worlds had been written by him in the book of his eternity,
and rightly I say that they stood firm in his steadfastness.
The earth and its dust he had measured with the full span of his hand;
he has no span, even though the prophet said that he has.
The high mountains and their rocks he had weighed,
weighed them in a balance not held by hands.
The wind and the waves he had held in the hollow of his power,
and the gathering of the waters he had bound in the cloth of his sign.
The visible border of the elements he had set,
and he had commanded how they should run without wrong.
The path along which sun and moon would travel he had made known,
and the race of the hours of light and darkness he had fixed.
The stars were numbered and ranked before his knowledge,
and allotted the course each of them should run.
The deeds of Watchers and of humans he had examined too,
and had scrutinized the good and the evil of their deeds.
The hosts of demons he had separated from the angels,
and it was decreed concerning them that those set apart should be set apart from their fellows.
All these things, and others like them, if there are any,
were hidden in him, seen by him, and counted by him.
It is not right, then, to call him by feeble names,
for behold, his creatures show the might of his power.
Let no one grow proud and suppose that some limit holds his bounds,
for behold, his making is not bounded by our thought.
Let no one babble and bring in another power beside him,
for behold, even the Watchers who are spirit are his works.

His works they are, and like everything else he fashioned them,
as David testifies, who said that he made his angels spirit.
He calls them his angels, not merely angels,
so that everyone may learn that they are his, since they were created by him.
They are his creatures, and they are all bound beneath his sign,
and they do not forget that he is their Creator and the One who cares for them.
The deceivers went astray and called them hidden self-existent beings,
and here the upright among them are grieved at this wrong.
It is a great wrong that the Creator's name should be given to servants,
and here the good servants are angered at this outrage.
Only the demons rejoice, and yet do not truly rejoice,
for though they rejoice, they rejoice briefly and turn to grief.
For a short time the demons rejoice and lead humankind astray,
and after that time comes a remorse beyond telling.
Remorse punishes the insolence that did not repent,
while to the angels who grieved here it shows love.
They grieve much when people go astray in their name,
and they rejoice much when the Creator's name is hallowed.
The Creator's name is dearer to them than all the movements of their thoughts,
and they long greatly that everyone should hallow the name of his holiness.
In holiness they hallow together, in one accord,
and never slacken from the harmony in which they stand firm.
The good servants remind everyone that they were made,
and they do not grudge to render praise to their Maker.
In their very fashioning the mind within them is wakeful;
they do not let it grow careless and fall silent from praise.
A wakeful mind is theirs by the nature with which they were endowed,
and for this reason Scripture calls them Watchers.
Watchers they are, who have never slept and never will sleep,
and by their wakefulness they rouse humankind toward instruction.
In the house of instruction they stand in front like masters,
and make wise the childhood of humankind by their teachings.
From the Great One who made them wise they gained their wisdom,
and all of them gaze toward that goal of his mastery.
They are occupied with meditation on his word and labour night and day,
and with the passing times they search out what concerns him.
The concern of divine love is dear to the Watchers:

come, let us become their companions in the meditation in which they stand firm.
They serve the hidden will every day without ceasing:
come, let us stand firm in steadfastness beside our Maker.
For our salvation they have toiled and grown weary ever since they came to be:
let us help them, even a little, by the labour of our lives.
For our sake they stir the air in all its changes:
let us stir our minds to know the order of their changes.
For our sake they run in the spiritual stadium:
let us acclaim them, that they may be worthy of the reward of their crowns.
For the help of our souls they are thrown into the contest with their fellows:
let us encourage them, that they may succeed once more in winning our victory.
By their contests they put an end to the demons' war against us:
let us repay with thanks the good Lord who armed them.
They drive the devils from our camp so that they do not harm us:
let us praise the Name that girded them out of love for our souls.
On the Conduct of the Angels
Thirty-Eighth Discourse / On the Conduct of the Angels

I saw the world of time running on without pause, and I wished to learn who it is that makes its silence run. I saw its course and its stillness wisely ordered, and I said: who, then, taught it to journey in order? I marveled greatly at the changes of its seasons, at how worn out they become, and I sought to know who wears it out and alters it. I went in and stood among its changes as in an arena, to see clearly how they overcome and are overcome. My thoughts longed to walk alongside its course, that I might know where its road begins and where its race ends.

Its course and its order made me search and inquire about it, so that once I had searched it out I might know, and make it known to those who seek it. [?] for it wore me down like a hungry man longing for bread, and I yearn to fill my mind with its crumbs. Its beauty drew me to come near it and examine it, so that perhaps the ugliness of my speech, full of afflictions, might be made beautiful by it. Through words about it I long to share in its beauty, and I am ready to bring my mind's desire into the open. Longing for the world has worn down my mind beyond measure, and now it urges me to bring forth words as one brings forth infants. Like a woman in labor my understanding travails over its cause: when will it bring the infants of discourse to birth before the hearers? The cause of the world is the cause my thought is in labor with: who moves it and changes it, since it is itself mute? Who changes summer into winter and winter into summer, and who turns its cold into heat? Who makes the sun's sphere rise at morning, and who hides the beauty of its light at evening? Who makes it run swiftly across the face of the heights, and who holds it so that it does not slacken and fall to the earth? Who makes the moon small when it is one day old, and who raises it to its prime in the middle of the month? Who puts the reins of order on its silence, so that the great order of night and day is not thrown into confusion? Who makes the stars run in order, one after another, and shows them the path of a course that never ceases? Who moves the mute air to serve us, and who makes its silence cry out in bodily sounds? Who hardens and thickens its fineness, and who loads it with floods of water so that it sprinkles them on the earth? Who lifts it like a rod above the sea, and casts down its stirred-up mass with its whirlwinds? Who calms its tumult when it rages, and who turns it about and makes it rage when it is calm? Where is its harsh blast when it does not blow, and from where does it come so suddenly with a harsh onslaught?

Who kindles the fire of the lightnings out of its quaking, and who makes the sound of thunder heard out of its stillness? Who mingles its cold with heat, so that from it there may be drink for the fruits of the earth? Who preserves it when it is mingled in dense bodies, so that it is not destroyed by elements foreign to it? These things made me inquire into their changes: whether the power of change is their own, or belongs to others. Do these mute things possess reason in their nature, or perhaps do rational beings move the irrational? Do the possessors of reason have power to do this, or perhaps are they in turn empowered by the might of the Creator? Reflection on these things cast this thought into my mind, and I reflected that it is One who accomplishes them by the power of His will. One is the Power who works by His power through spiritual beings, and He orders the work of His hands by the work of His hands. Through rational beings He moves the insensate natures, and through spiritual beings He fulfills His love toward His creatures. To their rationality He entrusted the world from the beginning, that they might keep the changes of the seasons without confusion. He made the angels treasurers of His goodness, to distribute the treasure of His mercies to the dwellers on earth. He appointed them stewards over His service, to give provision in its season to the children of His house. He gave them the world like a child to a master, that they might train it from childhood to maturity. To their tutelage He entrusted its swift course, that they might restrain it from frivolous deeds. He made them tutors to serve as a mind for the foolish one, so that they would not [?] it to walk as it pleased.

It was far too foolish for understanding, foolish as it was; therefore He set those shrewd of mind over its service. To their authority He committed the wealth it needed, that they might care for its wants day by day. It was gluttonously greedy to eat and [?], so He placed its food in the hands of sober stewards to distribute it. By the hands of sober ones He wished to discipline its gluttony, lest, eating gluttonously, it should die a miserable death. Exceedingly wise is the Lord of the world toward the brute creation, and wisely He made it wise by the reason of rational beings. He set rational beings over the service of what has no speech, that by their shrewdness they might make its brutishness wise. Through them, the rational ones, He governs all and arranges all, and there are no works whose course He does not complete through their hands. Through them He completes the course of the mute and of the speaking, and through their word the Hidden One makes known His ordinances. Through their mediation He shows His love and also His threat, giving blessings and inflicting stripes on those deserving of stripes. Through their embassy the Lord of all accomplishes all, choosing and rejecting as ever befits His will. He sends them as envoys to the dwellers on earth, and they return and report to Him, as He knows. From them He requires the number of mankind and the changes of the seasons, and they are diligent indeed to keep the order entrusted to their hands. Through them He carries out the ministry of His providence, now chastising and now winning over, so as to help. Through them He redeems the lovers of His love when they are oppressed, and through them He chastises the scornful when they grow proud. Through them He governs the dominion of kings and the division of peoples, and by their zeal He arranges wars and brings wars to an end. Like a charioteer His command rides upon their motions, and like horses they are yoked and fly through the air. O spiritual chariot of the God of all, to which spiritual horses are yoked with spiritual reins! O Charioteer who holds the world without hands,

who drives the hosts of the heavenly ones across the face of the heights! O Rider whose riding is higher than all riding, who runs a course without visible limbs! Who has ever ridden upon what cannot be ridden, and yoked beneath him a nature that is not subject to the senses? Who will not marvel at the great course of this great mountain, for lo, six thousand years, less a little, are but its single race? Who will not say that He who created all is the one who drives it, and that His power strengthens the weakness of the work of His hands? His power drives the heavenly ones under His command, and by that same command He drives the world under His ministers. O the wonder that teems with amazement: that the world is yoked under the Creator and its fellow creatures! Watchers are yoked under the command that established them, and the world is yoked under the authority He gave them. In the yoke of His love creation is yoked under spiritual beings, and their authority sits upon its back like a charioteer. With the reins of the spirit they grasp the bodiless air and drive it as the will that governs all directs. Everything together is yoked and subjected to their authority; with all things they run, and all things they guard from harm. In portions of their authority He divided the world, and each of them is careful in the work committed to his hands. Some hold the sun with hands that are not compounded, and show it the path of an unwavering course. With the mute one the watcher runs swiftly, and orders it so that the path of its course is not confused. Alongside its feebleness the swift mind flies continually, and helps it to circle the earth night and day. Some carry the moon on a bodiless shoulder, and guide it through its phases like a child. They carry it with the mind, becoming the discerning faculty of the undiscerning one, and guide it so that it is not driven brutishly. They set orders and steps before it like a pupil, that it may know how far to descend and to ascend. Some hold the brightness of the stars like torches, and by their brightness they chase away the darkness of the nights.

Rational beings level a straight road in the air for the mute ones, and these walk it continually and do not slacken from their course. Rank upon rank the insensate ones travel the road, with the heavenly ones at the head of their ranks as guides. They are like a king's camp, the ranks and those who array them, spiritual commanders of hosts beyond number. Some are appointed to stand over the moving air, and they move it with the hidden motions of their minds. With motion the bodiless move the bodiless, and compound it, though its nature is uncompounded. Incorporeal beings take hold of the incorporeal and [?] it into portions as though it were bodily. From what is not dense the incorporeal make a body, so that in its density it may bear the burden of heavy waters. Out of its fineness they weave thick felted garments, so that in their felting they may hold back waters that would pour out. They spread the clouds in the midst of the circle of height and depth, and above them they cover the waters like a roof. With water and wind they roof over the house of our life's need, and from its roof they bring down waters and sprinkle them on the earth. Some give the thunders a power whose voice is fearful, and they shake the earth with the sound of its swiftness. Out of that very air they make cisterns for the waters, and they give a sound when water is poured into water. The sound of the wind passes suddenly through the hollow of the waters, and scatters the mass of waters that is in the clouds. Loose waters fill the cloud, a wineskin of wind, and when the sound of thunder passes through it, it is torn and poured out. O the conflict of two mute ones and one rational one, in which is hidden the cause of peace for watchers and for men! For the sake of peace the watchers teach battle [?], so that the agreement of the elements may not destroy the peace of fruits and seeds. Skillfully the rational ones teach warfare to the mute ones,

and out of the air they forge the armor with which they are armed. They forge arrows of fire from it when it thickens, and send them across the heights with a harsh onslaught. As with iron, they strike its blows with a harsh blow, and from it shining sparks fly out. Brilliantly it shines out suddenly amid the light, and swiftly it shows its light and hides it. Wonder fills the sight of its light for the one who beholds it, for its end comes with its beginning, without delay. It does not let the one who sees it look at it well, for as soon as he sees it, it has gathered its light back from his eyes. O swift one, that does not itself see its own swiftness! And us who see it, it does not let look well. Leave us, mute one, to gaze at the beauty of your silence; do not alarm us with a swiftness that is not your own. It is not the lightning's own to run swiftly; it is a rational being who makes its silence run, while it perceives nothing. It is a watcher who swiftly bends the clouds down to the sea, and they carry waters and are not sunk by the weight of the waters. Like a ship the cloud carries its treasure of waters, and rises and stands on the face of the heights, and so it is opened. The spiritual one holds the rudders of the wind and steers it, so that it does not sink in the flood of waters within it. O sailor who drives his ship of air through the air, and instead of oars carries it with spiritual motions! With motions the spiritual one carries the wind of the air, and when it is shaken it gives a sound that shakes the earth. Like a dove he holds the wings of its swiftness, and brings it down to the face of the earth even though it does not wish it. O swift one, that has no desire to stay on the earth, but always travels the face of the heights like a noble! O how great is the good solicitude toward our race, which compels natures beyond their order for our sake! The nature of the air possesses flight in its very nature, and this is the wonder: that it rises to the heights and descends to us. The power of an angel compels the force of its flight, and brings the lofty runner down to our lowliness. One angel is made commander over its camp,

and governs it through changes of every kind. One it is who exercises headship over its changes, while there are with him members of the service who obey him. In place of Satan, who strayed and fell, a holy one was appointed, and the servants with him in place of the legions of rebellious demons. He and those with him order the brute air, and the [?] companies govern what is entrusted to them. In ranks the rulers divide their authorities, and in good order they walk the road of their deeds. Some are charged to order kings and their dominions, now enthroning and now removing them from authority. Some apportion battle and give it to warriors, and according to their judgment they acquit the good and chastise the wicked. Some guard men every day from harm, and drive away from them the hosts of rebellious demons. One angel accompanies every person as an escort of love, and is with him from the day of his birth to his death. With the life of the one whose life is short the living one runs, and at the side of his bed he stands steadfast on the day of his departure. He separates the soul, his sister, from the members, for he conducts it to the place appointed by the Creator. He is yoked and subject under the Creator's command, and it is not his own to do what is done through him. He does not give the span of life or a short time, nor has he authority to add an hour or take away an hour. Nor does he govern a man's life by compulsion, and he cannot compel him either to do good or to do evil. A person possesses freedom of soul in his likeness to God, and he can sin, or be justified, as a being of discernment. The freedom of the soul in a person is not constrained, nor is it driven to do anything against its inclination. One is the nature of the soul of man and of the spiritual beings, and it is not mastered save as it masters itself. By a perfect law it has possessed its being from the beginning, just as the constitution of the heavenly ones is also perfect. They are its siblings, and it is of their kind,

and they love their kinship with it always in their deeds. That voice which called man by the name of the Hidden One they honor through the honor they show toward man. In man they show their great love toward the Creator; therefore they toil in our life's sustenance and in serving us. For our sake they are worn out greatly, and wear themselves out, and they do not rest until they rest in the haven [?]. For our sake they are thrown into the contest of the changing seasons, that by their changes we may remember a life without end. For our sake they toil and labor with labors, and they do not grow weary with us until we find rest. For our sake they move the air with their motion, so that through its breezes the seeds of our life's sustenance may be established. For our life they order the course of the months of the year, so that the order of our discernment may not be confused and go astray. For our sake they show the path to the sun and moon, so that the path of our own course to the Creator may not go astray either. For us they divide the hours between light and darkness, so that we may not be divided against the Creator who created them. For the sake of man's rank they took on the authority of ranks and orders, and showed that they command and are commanded, so that his rank might be great. For his honor they honor the orders of their authorities, and for his ordering an order reigns among their ranks. A great order dwells in the orders of those who set in order, and though they are one, there are those who command and those who are commanded. Their command the great herald of the nations proclaimed, and he named them by the names of their authorities. And because of our suffering he wrote that they groan and also travail, until passibility is put off and glory is put on. All creation travails with them, and they with it, until the day comes of birth out of the house of the dead. With the silent creatures they respond and labor, on account of that passage which was the hope of its perishing state. On the hope of its hope creation hangs, and the watchers even more, since they are persuaded by the greatness of the hope prepared for it. In the good hope of our life's redemption they wait always,

and they are sure that they will receive it through their deeds. Because of its hope he wrote that it was subjected to futility, and the world received a pledge of reward on the day of its renewal. True is the labor that the watchers labor on man's behalf, and lo, the proof of its truth is in the changing of the seasons. The seasons bear witness to the labors of the heavenly ones, and instead of a mouth they cry out in silence how worn out they are. In silence the mute natures cry out to man: "Look, man, how the watchers are worn out for your sake! For your sake rational and mute alike are thrown into toil, and man does not perceive how much they are worn out on his behalf. Look, man, at their labor, even a little, and labor your soul in the good discipline of the watchers, your brothers. See how for your sake they are greatly worn and wear themselves out, and as they rear you they rear fruits for your need." Theirs is the rearing of fruits and the growing of seeds, and by their word the course of the months of the year is ordered. Swiftly they run through the air with their motions, and the [?] in their labors is pleasing to them. Gladly they serve all and keep all, and in their service they render glory to the Maker of all. Glory they cry out even as they are sent on their service, and this is the wonder: that with service there is also praise. Two things at once each of them accomplishes without hesitation: service on behalf of men and glory to the Hidden One. O servants of divine service, who are not hindered from fulfilling two things at once! O ministers of the Lord of all, who minister to all, whose love is perfect toward the Creator and toward His creatures! O envoys of the immortal King of kings, by whose embassy the life of mortals is preserved! O peacemakers and lovers of peace for all and among all, who strengthen the peace of men by the love that is in them! O heralds of the Creator's power toward His creatures, through whom mute natures hear a voice that is no voice! O how great beyond telling is the speech that is in them, that even the silent hear the sounds of their interpreting! For without a voice they converse, each of them, with the silent ones,

and without speech they accomplish words through deeds. In secret they converse with the insensate elements, and these give forth perceptible sounds as though they had senses. As though with hands they grasp the air by its four corners, and spread the onslaught of its swiftness to the four quarters. By its gentle breezes they refresh men and also animals, and by its moisture they soften the earth to yield fruits. Skillfully they bind up the wounds of the sick world with cold and heat, two opposites. They temper its cold continually with heat, and so they tend it as physicians tend painful wounds. O bodiless healing by bodiless beings, which the spiritual ones temper and which benefits our body! To their skill the Lord of the world entrusted the world, for He saw that they know how to bind up the wounds of its sickness. The power of His will He placed in their nature from the beginning, that they might be able to tend the world sick with sin. From Him they learned the art, and so they have prevailed, and the power of His help [?] with them to the end. With them the power of the Creator runs swiftly, and with Him they travel without measured steps. Subtly He gives His sign without a voice, and they hear His voice without bodily hearing. According to the hearing He gave them He speaks with them, so that they are able to hear the hidden voice with the mind. With the mind they hear that voice which is all of this, and with understanding they grasp it, marveling. O how great is the greatness of wonder in the spiritual beings, and how small is the mouth of all creation to recount their wonder! O how keen is the mind of the beings of mind, which can hear a voice subtler than every mind! O how swift is that understanding by which they understand, for though nothing visible is before them, it is true! O how hidden is that Hidden One who is above them!

and how plain their ministry stands before their eyes! / O how true is the hidden truth of their thoughts, / and they never cease to seek that hiddenness in prayer. / It is hidden from them as it is hidden from all creatures, / and this is the wonder: however hidden it is, to them it is as if revealed. / By faith they see a sight that cannot be seen, / and without sight the mind of their thoughts gazes on it. / By faith they listen to a voice that is no sound, / and they receive it without the senses that perceive. / By faith they completed the race of faith, / and believed that one may trust in the name [?] of the Creator. / By faith they completed the race of faith, / and believed that one may trust in the name of the Creator. / By faith they stood to set in order the power of the elements, / and by it they strengthened the hard strength of their struggle. / By faith they took up the service of humankind, / and did not dispute that voice which called man His image. / Faith yoked them to the labour of his life, / and they nourish him, so that he will not despise faith. / Faith sent them to be his brothers, / and through it they searched out the hiddenness of his spiritual soul. / They believed that it is spiritual and not mortal, / just as they too are spiritual and immortal. / Its kind is from that kind which brought forth the kinds, / and it too is without composition and without visibility. / Its origin descends from that origin which is not by succession, / and it too comes into being in that same manner, from nothing. / O the nature of the soul of man and of the spirits, / which possess immortal life like their Maker! / Alas for man: though the soul in men is immortal, / in their disputes they called the One who created it mortal! / Alas for the iniquity whose iniquity is plain even to the heavens, / which the children of dispute cover with a show of love! / O error, which error has sprouted in the children of error, / whose likeness resembles that error in Paradise! / One is the aim of the cunning of that one and of this one:

he was the deceiver who deceived there and leads astray here. / Very like is this error of mortality / to that error of envy and wickedness. / Out of wickedness he said, 'Eat the fruit for food'; / and with love he now leads astray: 'He consented to die.' / 'Out of love,' they say, 'He died, to set man right for man's sake.' / Behold an error full of error beyond measure! / Hard is it to measure this error with any measure, / and however far I lengthen the course of my words, they fall short of it. / Its enormity urged me to multiply my words about it, / and I left the discourse on the angels and spoke about it. / I saw its enormity, how it has disturbed the peace of humankind; / for that reason I mingled its discourse with the discourse on the heavenly beings. / I saw the heavenly beings, who are exalted above all sufferings, / and I grieved greatly that fools ascribe suffering to their nature. / In the suffering over Him I suffered much and was filled with suffering, / and I left the road and went down the road the wayward walk. / Turn, my soul, to your discourse, to the way of the word about the spirits, / and do not stumble on the path of the falsehood of those who love suffering. / Tread rightly and soberly the right course of the right-minded, / and search out well, with fitting inquiry, their ministry. / Inquire, then, how they are able to move the mute natures, / and by what strength they fortify the strength of the power of the elements. / How do they give body to the air, which is not bodily, / and then turn back and make its bodily state spiritual? / How do they mix its cold with heat, / and then separate it again and set it in its former order? / How does their fineness pass through its fineness, / while on them hangs the glory of the sun and the moon? / How long does the radiance that is in them endure in their ministries, / and the balanced order of the luminaries is never disturbed? / How far do they fly from where the circuit of the earth lies, / and how do they reach the other circuit by evening? / How do they weigh out the hours of the night and of the day, / and have never strayed, nor stray, from the order they received from the beginning? / How great, then, is the number of the thousands of their legions, / who are with each and every one, and each one with them, and everything in their hands? / Who can number the stars and the count of mankind,

since every star and every human being has one of them with it? / Who knows how to look well into all the changes, / since not a single change comes about without their being in it? / Who considers the authority of kings and the governance of peoples, / and how the ordering of these is committed to their ministry? / Who has heard David's word about their holiness, / which named them sanctifiers and praisers? / In one word the Holy Spirit revealed them, / and revealed that they are able to give praise in that they praise. / Who, then, can grasp the order of their ministries, / when the portions they apportion are beyond number?
