/ One alone counted and reckoned them before they existed, / and as their number [?], so was the measure of their ministries. / He knew of them how many they would be and what they would be, / and He arranged it before they took up their authority. / They were tried by Him in the furnace of His testing before they came to be, / and the truth in them and the falsehood in them were plain to Him. / The inclinations were plain to Him: how many of them would remain with Him, / and how many would go outside the bounds of His command. / The tyrant demons were driven out from Him before they went astray, / and the watchers on high were entering His household. / Satan, the head of the air, was loosed from his authority, / and Gabriel's company were being set up in the place of his rank. / They were honouring Him in order and in rank, as the times required, / and there was no order lacking its arrangements. / These things I have recounted were with the One who Is, / not in existence, but in the mystery of what was to come. / They were among the things to come, not among things made, / and they were known and granted as He knows. / They were known to that knowledge which created them, / for the time when it knew they would be needed, at the fitting time. / At the fitting time the Creator created the creation He created, / and showed it the way, through angels, so that it might walk after Him. / Through angels He taught the world of His lordship, / for through them He governs it and directs it until the end. / Together with His creatures they tend the life of those whose life is short, / and He does not leave man to do anything without them.

The world has nothing that is hidden from the angels, / and the angels have no authority outside His course. / They run, they run the race for the crown of victory, / and they long eagerly to fulfil it without reproach. / The Lord of the world occupied them with the labour of the world, / so that they might grow rich from the poor man whom they nourish. / For their own need they supply his needs at every moment, / and what they give him they receive from him, like the needy. / It is not God's need they meet when they accomplish all things by His hands, / for it is not He, but the world, that needs their course to be set in order. / The power that created creation from nothing / is not too weak to govern the work of His hands without the watchers. / Him and His servants they honour, through His hands: He helped by their hands, / and their low estate He exalted and raised up beside His greatness. / By grace the assemblies on high repay in their ministries; / and what am I saying, that they repay? They cannot repay! / Small is the repayment if it is compared with grace; / what am I saying, 'small'? It is small indeed, since it is nothing at all. / With the Creator there is no repayment of reward, / and if there is, it is by grace, not by labour. / Not by labour are the watchers worthy of recompense, / but by grace they receive a reward from grace. / I said that they receive blessings freely; it is not freely, / but because the world cannot measure up to the measure of the blessings. / Very beautiful, too, are the labours of the heavenly beings, / and no one can portray the beauty of their thoughts. / The Lord of beauty made them beautiful, / and were it not for Him, they would not be pleasing to the Giver of beauty. / The greatness of their love brought them near to the King, / and to the King Himself it was most pleasing to make them great. / O wonder of greatness, worthy of the Maker, / that made servants have acquired the authority of the Maker! / By the power of the Maker they move all things, as the Maker's hand, / and they do not mistake that it is by the power of His might that they strengthen all things.

They did not mistake the name of the Maker by whom they are made strong; / it was men who erred and were confounded by the fancy within them. / With the name of the Maker they named made beings, and erred, / and to their authority they gave the authority of the Maker. / Among their names they divided the great name of Godhead, / giving to each of them a share in creatorship. / You who err, do not be confounded and err so greatly: / the One who Is is one, and from Him all things came to be. / One is the Creator, to whom creatorship belongs, / and one the Creator, to whom the name of Being rightly belongs. / The name of the Maker does not befit made servants, who erred, / nor does it befit the Maker to give His rank to the work of His hands. / The spiritual beings find no rest in this error; / and why do I speak of their resting in it or not resting in it? / In their ministries they show the power of the Maker, / and if they could, they would cry aloud that the One who Is is one. / They knew one Maker from the first, when they were set in order, / and they know no other power but Him alone. / By the will of His love the love of their thoughts is bound, / and they take great care not to grow slack in the task He gave them. / In that task with which He occupied them they are occupied at all times, / and there is no time when their thoughts are not meditating on it. / A good meditation is set among them night and day, / and the more they meditate, the more they meditate on it without being sated. / By good hope they were bound to the blessings that come from Him, / and this is the wonder: however much they move, they do not grow slack. / The love of blessings is never sated in the good ones among them, / while our nature has strayed from the love of blessings through the slackness of our nature. / Good blessings the Creator has promised them and humankind; / blessed is he who keeps the remembrance of the blessings in his mind. / To the kingdom on high He has invited our race with their assemblies; / blessed is he who is found worthy and enters with them where they enter. / Come, you mortals, let us become companions of the immortals, / and be with them heirs of the promised blessings.
On the excellence of the soul, and how it governs
Thirty-ninth Discourse: On the excellence of the soul, and how it governs the body, which is its house

The beginning of wisdom is the wisdom of truth, which is the Creator's power,
who out of nothing created all things, hidden and revealed.
The beginning of understanding is to consider his work of creation:
that he did not create the creatures for his own rest, but in his love.
The beginning of discernment is to examine the greatness of his power,
who carries the world and governs it as he wills.
The beginning of knowledge is to know his love toward his creatures,
that when they wrong him he takes no vengeance on those who wrong him.
The beginning of faithfulness is to justify the testing of his judgment,
so that one who truly believes is not led astray by the sign of the eyes.
The beginning of goodness is to delight greatly in his sweetness,
for mercy truly springs forth, mingled even in the harshness of his blows.
The beginning of the discernment of discernment is to distinguish well
what befits reason, the mistress of the mute creatures.
The beginning of all things is to know the order set in nature,
so that the nature of rational beings may submit to the word that is in them.
The beginning of the law is to meditate on the law of the Spirit,
to fulfil all that is written from the mouth of the Hidden One.
The beginning of repayment is to repay love to the Maker of all,
who honoured the image of man above all, and called him.
Everyone owes love to his Maker,
who gave the law and made him lord over his possessions.
Manifold praise he is bound to repay, more than all that exist,
for he alone is called by a name exalted above all.
It is fitting for him to know the power of the command of his Creator,

who arose and took counsel over his formation, and so fashioned him.
It is fitting for him to justify the power of his Fashioner,
who fashioned him with his hand and breathed a soul into him from the breath of his mouth.
A vessel of dust his Maker skilfully composed:
a visible body and a hidden soul, one human being.
In the likeness of an image the power of his creating formed in him
the mute creatures in his body, and the rational ones in the make of his soul.
In his body he bounded the nature of all that is visible,
and within his soul the hosts of the height that are without composition.
He made him kin to the heavenly and to the earthly,
and as in a temple he made the crowned and the mute dwell in him.
A tabernacle of love he wisely pitched upon the earth,
and furnished it and filled it with the power of wisdom, to dwell in it.
In his soul he set the great treasury of his creative power,
from which every creature in need of its life may ask.
The soul of man is set as a treasury of hidden things,
in which the power of the boundless Creator is contained.
Hidden mysteries are hidden in the inquiry into its make,
and they are not searched out except by the power of its Creator.
A mystery for searching out the name of Being lies within its kind,
and its make is depicted threefold, in word and power.
Its likeness resembles, in a small way, the distinction of the Persons:
its being the Father, its word the Son, and its life the Spirit.
Not in its nature does its nature resemble the nature of the Hidden One,
but in a mystery, as a demonstration of its honour.
It falls far short of the Being that has no measures,
as the shadow of a body falls short of the body.
He is the Existent One, and there is no beginning to his eternity;
but it is limited [?], and its composition is confined beneath time.
The Creator's power gave it the power of reason,
that it might live and give life to the mortal body in which it dwells.
Like a spring that makes life flow he set it in the body;
through it the mute senses are watered to bear fruit.
By the irrigation of its rationality the body is composed,
and it yields the voice of thanksgiving to its Maker.
By the power of its life he lives and walks in the life of time,
and with it he waits to inherit the life that does not die.

By its light he sees the light that befits the name of the Creator,
and along its paths he is strengthened and reaches unto Being.
By its skill he acquires the sense to discern well,
and as a rational being he orders the course of his reason.
It is a sun which, in the two heavens of the corruptible body,
labours upon the earth with its rays and guides it on the way.
Its mind is salt for the insipidity of his desires;
by it a man is humbled and so becomes useful.
Its nature is wealth for the poverty of his despised dust,
and by its wisdom it provides for his life like a rich man.
By its word he raises the sound of his voice over the creatures,
and by its authority his authority is extended over all.
By its sign he commands the earthly creatures [?] to obey him,
and by its understanding he bends his gaze toward the heavenly ones.
By its lightness he crosses the sea as on dry land,
and the weight of his body does not sink amid the billows.
Like [?] it hangs upon the ship of his bodily being,
and guards him from harms, lest he be destroyed.
To its meeting-place he journeys like a sailor by the star of light,
and it sets straight for him the path that leads to the harbours of peace.
By its craft it teaches the mute creatures to serve him,
and by its discernment it gives order to what has no order.
By its cunning he grows wise over the silent creatures,
and by its devices he casts bridles upon the wild beasts.
Like a charioteer he rides upon the wild world,
and guides it so that it does not run wild beneath his goings.
The soul has subjected all creation to him, under his authority,
and it has seated him like a king upon a chariot.
By the reins of its motions he holds heaven and earth in his hands,
and turns the will of his lordship wherever he wishes.
O man, whose name is the dust of all,
how your despised rank has been raised above all!
O Creator, great and exalted above all creatures,
how the will of your love has stooped down to our lowliness!
Your sign has lifted our lowly rank above all,
and you have made us hold the sceptre of your sign, to rule over all.

The power of your wisdom you set in our nature, poor in life,
and the banks of words began to flow in your likeness.
Yours is the treasury of words within the soul,
and through you it learns to liken its words to your Word.
Your Word you made heard in the beginning, when you created it and all things,
and it leapt and rose at the voice of your command and acquired life.
Life you joined to its make when you fashioned it,
and you hid it in the garment of the visible body.
Your will built the temple of the body for it,
and it entered and stood like a king within the palace.
Like a lyre it composed the visible senses,
and the finger of its skill plucked them in speech and in hearing.
Like a flute the mouth that breathes out breath became for it,
and on it it played the sound of sweet melodies.
On the hollow reed it plays at every hour longed-for sounds,
and gladdens it, lacking life, with the life of its [?].
By the breath of its life the dead thing sings sweet sounds,
and boasts, as though of its own, in another that speaks through it.
It is like a reed stripped of voice and of life,
and when the living soul plays upon it, it acquires life.
The soul is his life, and it keeps him in the life of time,
and when it lets him go he returns to his nature and becomes dust.
Of all that he possesses he possesses nothing that is not its,
and he does not stand without the power of its working.
Like a mistress it dwells within him, and he does not see it,
and he, like a servant, serves and makes requests before its freedom.
Well, then, did the Creator build him as a house,
and then it entered to dwell in him like a king's daughter.
In the forming of a man the sign first composes the body,
and after a time it forms the soul and makes it dwell within it.
The builder sketches the royal palace on the face of the flesh,
and when it is finished he calls its inhabitant to dwell in it.
In the veins of the body he builds a bodily house,
and into the house of its joints he casts salt for whatever is moist.
Like a foundation he lays the seed in the womb of the body,
and raises it like a building to completion.
The fluid becomes seed for the body, and so it comes to be,
and from the body there sprouts a body that resembles the body.

The soul has no seed from which another might sprout,
nor does its nature sprout from its fluid among the members.
Out of nothing the hidden sign forms it,
in the same pattern by which it formed Adam's by the breath of his will.
Out of nothing its nature comes to its formation,
however much it is akin to the Watchers and the spiritual beings.
It too is spirit, like the spirits that have no composition,
and its nature and make are equal to that which was in him.
Out of nothing the spirits came to be in the beginning, when they came to be,
and out of nothing its coming-to-be runs through all generations.
After the body its formation takes place, as in the formation of Adam,
and that same order runs every day in it and in the body.
The great Painter first forms the image of the members,
and then breathes into it the breath of life, and it becomes a living soul.
The garment of flesh he weaves with a spiritual hand,
and then spreads it like purple over the soul.
Within darkness he composes the body and creates the soul,
just as he created in the beginning and set it in darkness.
As in a mystery he shows man, in the forming of man,
that order of his creation out of nothing.
The greatness of his power he proclaims at every hour in our fashioning,
through the forming of body and soul that takes place every day.
By the composition of the body he shows the creation of the beings of sense,
and by the coming-to-be of the soul, the coming-to-be of the hosts of the mind.
All creation he renews at every hour through our formation,
and gladdens it like a mother on the day of our birth.
In us the natures of the mute and of the rational are searched out,
by the power of the Maker who renews their natures in us.
A great wonder we see at every hour in our fashioning:
that human beings sprout in the likeness of a human being from seeds.
We see a seed that a man casts into the earth of a human being,
and though it is despised and contemptible, it turns and becomes a glorious vessel.
We see the body as it is composed like that first one,
and again the soul that dwells within it like Adam's.
And these bear witness to that voice of the sixth day,
as it is spoken on all the days: "Let us make man."
It is the very command that fashioned Adam
that fashions the body and breathes into its face the breath of life.
The living spirit creates in the body as it is composed,

and life that does not die stirs within its mortality.
Nine months it dwells in a house that resembles darkness,
and after a time it comes out and sees the beautiful creation.
Out of darkness a human being comes forth from within a human being,
and shows light, and makes a voice heard, and pours forth words.
At his [?] the hosts of the height marvel at how precious he is,
just as they marvelled on the first day, when light came to be.
Like the light he gladdens the earth that was dark,
he who also drives away the darkness of pain from her who bore him.
In body and soul a human being comes forth from the womb:
a visible body and a hidden soul, a twofold vessel.
Skilfully his composition is depicted in two likenesses:
the body dust and the soul spirit, two, one human being.
One human being they call man, as body and soul,
because of the love of the Creator who coupled them.
One is the body and one the soul of one human being,
and one is the sign that forms man in man every day.
From a body the sign forms another body,
and like the soul of one human being are all souls.
Body much resembles body, and soul soul,
just as each day's coming-to-be resembles the first day.
Not anew does the Maker of all create man,
for see, from the man he created in the beginning human beings go on.
From one body came all the bodies that were and are,
and souls too are one in nature, like the one that was.
One is the sign that created body and soul in the beginning,
and its power runs with its formations until the end.
Its formation is the same every day as it was at first,
and the body testifies that body resembles body, and soul soul.
Like a herald the soul cries out within the members:
"See, O men, how much men resemble man!"
Confined in the body and not seen bodily,
its voice shines brighter than the sun to the eyes of the body.
Within the body its precious appearance is hidden,
and it keeps itself modest toward it, lest it grow cheap to the eye of the beholders.
It dwells within it and is hidden from its inquiry into it,
and though it sees it, it does not see how or what it is.
Its nature is within itself, and its working outside in deeds,

and though it is truly in him, he is separate from it, and it again from him.
The make of its subtlety was not mingled through all of him,
for he is one thing and it is another, without mixture.
Hidden it lies concealed among the members in one place,
and the power of its life is spread over the senses, inside and out.
In the heart it dwells as in a temple in the middle of the house,
so that all the senses may listen to the converse of its love.
In the middle of the house the mistress of the house sits in her house,
and the senses of the body gather round her like children.
The body, child of thought, sucks the milk of its motions,
and as on her knees it is reared by it without ceasing.
Like a nurse it carries the infants of a childish heart,
and gives food according to his strength, to nourish him.
With his measures it too grows, though it does not grow,
and like a child its love dandles his childhood.
Its make is complete from the beginning even while it is being reared,
and yet in its completeness it can do nothing without the body.
In it is the word of its reason from the day it came to be,
but the course of its lightness is lamed because of the members.
It knows how to play the sound of sweet melodies,
but as long as the flute of flesh is weak, it too is weak.
It holds the skill to play well on its own lyre,
and fears lest it stretch the strings of the body and they snap.
It possesses the power of discernment to consider,
but the senses of the body do not answer it so that it can play well.
Wisely it keeps its treasures put away in silence,
until the child body grows up and inherits his possessions.
Like fathers it too takes care of the members,
who, as long as their heirs are young, do not give them authority.
It resembles the God of all in the [?] of its working,
who leads man from low states to high.
With his growth it rises to the rank of youth,

and with his old age it sinks to the rank of weakness.
With his health the testing of its discernment is healthy,
and with his sickness its understanding is sick, as is fitting.
On the day of his good fortune its thought is at rest and its voice is bright,
and on the day of his mourning its mind is darkened and its voice small.
It is filled in his fullness, though its nature does not receive food,
and hungry in his hunger, though it has no need of eating.
It is awake in his labour when he is busy with earthly things,
and it sleeps in his sleep, though its mind does not sleep but is awake.
It rejoices in his life, though he is dead and without life,
and is distressed again on the day of his departure, though it is alive.
His love inflames it, though he is quite dull in understanding,
and it hates his sufferings, though it does not suffer in his passibility.
It suffers with its beloved by love, not by nature,
for its nature is exalted above all bodily sufferings.
In love it bears the trouble of the pain of his mortality,
and like a grieving woman it laments on the day of his affliction.
In love it is yoked within his senses as in a yoke,
though the labour of his desires does it no good.
Because of his love, earthly love is dear to it,
and though it is spirit, bodily things please it.
Because of his love it goes down with him to despised things,
though it needs nothing alien to its name.
Its nature has no fleshly desire for intercourse,
yet when flesh desires flesh, the desire comes upon it from him.
It cannot eat coarse food like the body,
yet if he hungers, it hungers with him and eats with him.
Its mind cannot fall asleep at all, nor does it sleep,
and when his senses sink into sleep its thoughts wander.
The body sleeps, and it sleeps with him while not sleeping:
its voice sleeps, but its thought is awake and its mind flutters.
For sleep belongs to the body, and food, and marriage,
and under a borrowed name its nature shares in what is not its own.
Distinct are the sufferings that belong to its nature and to the nature of the body,
and yet because of love, see, they are called one human being.
Its own is envy, gnawing, crouching in the house of thoughts,
and its own is wrath, stretched out like a venomous asp.
Its own is pride, a wild ass that rebelled against servitude,

and love of glory, a fox that walks among lions.
Its own is murmuring, a moth that eats away the garment of love,
and slander, a snare that hunts the pure of heart.
Its own is grudge, its own is anger, its own is murder,
and it strives to repay injuries to whoever harms it.
Its own is suffering and repentance of soul over its deeds,
and it pleads, asking mercy for its sins.
The body's is food, the body's are sleep and intercourse,
and it is he who is bound to earthly things by his need.
His are the sufferings and pains of mortality,
and he again turns and becomes dust on the day of his departure.
He is with the soul and is not mingled with its subtlety,
and the soul is in him and is not compounded with his composition.
He carries it in his senses and does not perceive where it is, not knowing,
and it carries him and is not searched out in its lightness.
Like beasts his senses are yoked under its authority,
and he does not perceive what the cause of his yoking is.
Like a charioteer its will rides above his body,
and wherever it wishes it steers the ship of his bodily being.
As with reins it holds the path of his deeds by its motions,
and guides him so that he is not weighed down by desires.
A word from it it casts into his mouth like a bridle,
and does not let him harm himself or his fellows.
The rod of judgment is raised at every hour over his childhood,
and reminds him of the battles and the chastisements of the world beyond.
The book of remembrance of blessings and chastisements it holds in its hand,
and reads to him of hidden things that he cannot see.
The fear of death cries out in his mouth and warns him:
"See, the torment that has no end is kept for the wicked."
In love it urges on itself and its partner,
lest they slacken in the struggle for the truth.
Like a watchman it cries out to the senses and the thoughts:
"Arise, be diligent in the labour of fair deeds!
How long will you sleep, O body and inclination? Awake!
Arise, be zealous, and behold the dawn of righteousness!"
With the call of battle it rouses itself and the members,
lest they sink into desires as into sleep.

It drives the sleep of iniquity from itself and from its beloved,
that they may be awake to gather the fruits of reason.
In its rationality is its meditation, night and day,
and its motions pour forth the power of life without end.
A spring of life the Lord of natures set in its nature,
and the flowing of life never ceases from its life.
The leaven of immortal life is hidden in its creation,
and it draws the dead body toward life.
The power of its life runs along the banks of his mortality,
and makes flow strange words that are foreign to him.
Like a rational being the mute one speaks with what is not his own,
and bears the fruits of reason on the branches of his body.
The silent one bears the fruits of the soul on the top of his members,
and from him wafts the fragrance of a life that he cannot see.
The finger of life plucks at every hour the frame of his body,
and gladdens the darkened world with the sound of wisdom.
O lyre of strings of corruptible flesh,
which, though it is flesh, plays spiritual sounds!
O flute of a frail reed full of knots,
through which simple sounds are carried without hindrance!
O tunic full of the moth of despised sufferings,
which the living soul, kin of the Watchers, has put on!
O life which, though it needs no covering,
is wrapped in a corruptible garment and boasts in it!
O bird whose wing is lighter than the birds',
which dwells in the body and has no desire to fly from it!
O you who are confined in a prison full of darkness,
and the hard chains of passibility please you!
O command that confined the living one in a dead house,
and the fragrance of the life of bodies wafted forth, and it acquired a voice!
O Craftsman who formed life in a slack garment,
and sealed its face so that bodily beings might not see it!
O Painter, how wise is your creating,
who in man revealed your greatness to the work of your hands!
As on a tablet you depicted the world in his body and soul,
so that heaven and earth might search you out through his revelation.
In him the earthly and the heavenly behold you,

and though You are far off, in him You are worshipped as one near.
With body and soul You formed him and raised him into the image of Your image, / and from all creatures You drew together [?] Your sign with his ordering.
A tabernacle of love You fashioned on earth of two parts [?], / so that earthly and heavenly beings might dwell in it.
With body and soul You built and completed him as the temple of His life, / so that rational and mute beings alike might offer in it one thanksgiving.
Your finger wove the garment of his body out of dust, / and like a seal You stamped on it Your soul, the realm [?] of life.
By the life of his soul the dead world lives and walks, / and by its light it journeys toward the goal of the haven of peace.
Like a lamp the soul hangs in the temple of the body, / and burns with the oil of rational, immortal life.
An order of light fills the life of the dead body, / and when it is taken away, darkness reigns over its limbs.
Its word is a lamp that shows him the light of life, / and at the top of his tower its voice burns like a torch.
By its light he sees, by its voice he sings, by its words he interprets, / and by its skill he works on earth in every craft.
By its strength he brings his passions into subjection, / and by its help he overcomes the sufferings of his mortality.
Through it he is victorious in the contest of the labours of righteousness, / and it gives him the crown of victory in return for his toil.
It teaches him to take up the contest in the spirit, / and encourages him not to grow slack before the adversary.
It holds in its mind a crown of immortal life, / and draws him on as if toward a hope: “Come near and receive it.”
With him it goes down into all the battles of the passions, / and like athletes it anoints his senses so that they are not seized.
Death alone can part it from his company, / and without its partner it cannot take up the contest.
The executioner of the hidden command suddenly looks in, / and terrifies it like a woman in labour on the day she gives birth.
Pangs of terror strike it too at the hour of death, / as they press it to come out from within the body.
Like a captor, death enters the temple of its dwelling, / and strips it out from within the body of its home.

Naked it goes out from within its house, this mistress of the body, / and like an exile it moves its belongings to another place.
On the day of its departure its mind bears a great mourning, / as it sees its dwelling being destroyed by hasty death.
With a voice of lament it weeps for itself and for its beloved, / for he is being destroyed, and the voice of its own melodies falls still.
It weeps thunderously in silence over what has befallen it, / that it will no longer sing tender songs on the lyre of its love.
It is sorely distressed that its senses are being cut off from it, / and that in place of its mind the moth sings within his limbs.
It grieves deeply at its separation from the side of its love, / even though it knows well that hope stands firm that it will return to him.
The sign of its Creator gave it the strength to know these things, / and He loosed in it the power of the wisdom that it will endure.
That commandment which brought it in and shut it within the limbs / is the one that brings it out unharmed, just as it entered.
It is not brought low by the suffering of the body's pains, / nor is it destroyed when the garment that covers it is destroyed.
It is exalted far above death and above harm, / and it is neither seen nor seized in bodily fashion.
It is a living spirit, light of wing to fly through the air, / and it is not seized in the captivities of death as the limbs are.
One of the Watchers comes down beside it on the day of its departure, / and conducts it to the place commanded by the Creator.
Like a guide, spirit leads spirit, / until it enters the house of resting-places, among its companions.
That angel who guarded it in the life here / shows it where it is to dwell until the resurrection.
Lands are appointed on the earth for all souls to dwell in: / some in Eden, and some in the place to which each is sent.
In the region of Eden dwell the souls of those who love truth, / and those of the wicked in places beyond it.
Within paradise the righteous dwell in spirit, not in body, / longing for that ordering of the kingdom on high.
He willed that the children of the kingdom should dwell in a fitting place, / so that everyone might learn that the hope awaiting him is true.
It is not that they receive a reward there for their labours, / but that the distinction which will come at the end might be revealed.

Nor are the wicked tormented in the place outside, / but this is to make known that they will not enter into the height.
He gave paradise as a pledge to confirm His words, / so that by simple things He might confirm the power of His glorious things.
In keeping with the childhood of temporal life He made its time precious, / so that through it man might be drawn toward the things to come.
Paradise is a portion of the earth, however beautiful it may be, / and the food of its fruits perishes like all fruits.
Envy embittered the house of mortals through its doings, / and urged them to desire immortal life.
For this reason [?] our Saviour opened its entrance, / so that He might first tread the way before those who enter.
The first Adam shut its door in the face of man, / and the second Adam opened its door, and the robber entered.
Two souls entered it first, as in a mystery, / in the same manner as Eve and Adam had gone out from it.
Two dwelt in it at the beginning of the earthly order, / and two entered it in a true mystery that does not perish.
Two He brought out for transgressing the command, through desire for the fruit, / and two He brought in for keeping the commandment of righteousness.
Sin shut it before sinners who resemble Adam, / and righteousness opened it for Adam and for the robber.
With the Righteous One a sinner entered paradise, / to give the guilty a hand toward becoming upright.
Through the robber He showed that it is possible to be justified, / and that the greatness of one's wickedness is no hindrance from above.
By the one soul that entered with Him He revealed to everyone / that those who are willing are not hindered from above.

The soul of our Lord and that of the robber entered first, / and so the way was trodden for the journey to the region of Eden.
Into Eden enter all the souls that have endured sufferings, / and there they rest as on a bed of comfort.
As in sleep, they cease there from activity, / and do not act in reason with the power that is in them.
They cease even from discourse on what is fair and what is hateful, / and do not strive in the contest of the labours of righteousness.
It is not that the power in them has ceased from life, / but that there is no bodily instrument to convey words.
It is not that the stream of discernment has been cut off and dried up, / but that there is no tree of the body leaning upon the watering.
It is not that the craftsman has lost his skill and squandered his treasures, / but that there is no steward to place them in his hands.
It is not that the mind has ceased from the swiftness of its lightness, / but that there is no vehicle of the body to carry it.
It is not that the movements of the rays of light have darkened their burning, / but that the pupils of the eyes no longer respond to see beauty.
It is not that the word has fallen silent and the beauty of its voices is stilled, / but that death has shut the mouth that conveys words.
It is not that its freedom, daughter of the free, forgot itself in that silence, / but that the body of its love fell silent in that silence.
It holds mourning for its beloved who has parted from it, / and is not stirred by earthly passions.
Wisely it keeps silence over his departure, / until it hears the voice that calls to his mortal nature.
For it cannot do anything without him, / just as he too can do nothing without it.
The Fashioner of all fashioned them as one man: / can half of a man be made complete without its other half?
The soul is half of a man, though it is living, / and its activity cannot stand without the body.
The Creator willed that it and the body together be called His image, / so how could it perform its activities without the body?
He gave it the body in which to show the power of its wisdom,

and did not allow it to do anything even during his sleep.
The body sleeps, and the soul with it, though it does not sleep, / for until he rises it is not roused to its work.
And if, while he slept, it could not do anything, / how can it now, when he is sunk in the sleep of death?
If it did not sing in him while the frame of his body was sound, / how will it sing now that he has become a contemptible dwelling?
If, while it was in him, its running was lamed by the sleep of pains, / how much more does it rest now that it has gone out from his limbs!
It rests, I said, from activities, not from life, / for its nature does not allow the power of life to cease from it.
Wealth is in it, though it has gone out from its house; / there is no poor man for it to provide for as before.
The word is in it, though it rests from activities; / there is no tongue through which to interpret the power of its wisdom.
The mind is in it, an eagle that has gained the power of flight; / there are no limbs to serve as wings for its lightness.
The pilot is in it, skilled in the house of the waves; / there is no sail to hold the wind within its bosom.
In it are the motions of its bosom, possessors of the wind; / there is no sailor to look well to their destinations.
In it is everything that belongs to its nature, without change: / nature, word, and the power of life, though they are silent.
Though silent, they are not wholly like the body, / but rest from the activities carried out through movement.
They rest, not with a rest without discernment like the limbs, / but are awake and even think, though there is no work.
Without work the soul remains once it has been led away, / since there is no instrument of craft with which to act.
There is no carpenter who can work without an adze, / nor a smith who works with his hands without a hammer.
There is no sailor who travels the sea without a ship, / nor a fisherman who catches fish without nets.
The soul has no ship of bodily timbers, / since it rests from the voyage on the rational sea.
It has no fleshly adze dipped in blood, / since the framework of the timbers of its discernment has ceased.
Its craft remains in it, as it was in the body,

like a craftsman who keeps his mind on his craft.
Thus it pleased that Master of master-craftsmen / that without the body it should not trade in earthly things.
For it and the body He ordained reward and decreed judgment, / and together they will inherit the good things of the height and the punishments of the earth.
It and its beloved together await that reward, / and as long as the body is silent in the grave, so is it, though it lives.
In a lame life it now rests without movement, / in the same manner as when they are infants in the womb.
It is the same power that it possesses in the womb and outside, / and as long as the door of exit is held shut, it too is held back.
It is the same in the womb, in sleep, and in the grave, / and wisely it keeps its own order and his.
It cannot sin, nor be justified, except in him, / nor compose repentance [?] and words without him.
If it alone could be justified, / then long ago the wickedness of the first generations would have been repaid.
If Adam's soul had been sentenced to pay for what he sinned, / no account would remain of the folly in paradise.
And if the bond of the debts of those who have departed had been paid, / there would be no judgment and no claims against the ancients.
For until the judgment the books cry out like trumpets,

and creation testifies that the soul by itself has no works.
Therefore body and soul are bound to repay what they have sinned / before they are parted from each other and work ceases.
Therefore it is right for every man to become righteous / before greedy death comes and swallows his body.
Come, mortals, trade in righteous deeds while you are alive, / for after death there is no working of good or evil.
Come, let us entreat with body and soul the mercy of Him who fashioned us, / that He may save us from the torment that has no end.
On the blessings that Noah gave to his sons
Another, by the same author. / Memra fifty-one. / On the blessings that Noah gave to his sons.

The mystery of God's goodness toward mankind I have seen in the Scriptures, / which the prophecies scatter abroad by the Spirit in mystery. / The Spirit of revelation revealed to the son of Amram spiritually / that he should reveal to men the mystery that was hidden in their limbs. / In their limbs was hidden the mystery of their freedom, / and with their succession it was carried on from one to another. / In them was laid up the treasure of life for their need, / and through their life the life that was in them was preserved. / The Creator kneaded the vitality of life into the clay of Adam, / so that when it was corrupted, his mortal nature might live by its life. / With his clay the vitality flowed down from his limbs, / until it became a fountain of immortal life. / In mystery it flowed down hiddenly before the seers, / and though they saw, they did not see the power of its vitality. / Its appearing shone out brightly in Adam and in Seth, / and after a little in Enoch, and in Lamech, and in Noah his son. / In Noah was revealed the power of the life that is in human nature; / through him the sentences of judgment pronounced in Paradise were reversed. / Lamech prophesied that through Noah the worn-out world would find rest, / and that by his purity he would cleanse the earth of the curses. / By deeds his father's word concerning him was fulfilled, / for he gave the earth rest through the blessings with which he blessed his sons. / His limbs were a dwelling of peace for the peace of mankind, / guarding the life of the children of his kind from harmful things. / At the end of his body's life the succession of the treasure of life came to rest, / and he gave it to his sons, that they might carry it on to those after them. / Wisely he guarded the treasure of his fathers' house, / and with discernment he opened its hiddenness before his offspring. / The Spirit made him wise to guard his wealth with care, / and it also taught him to set his sons upon their courses. / His strength strengthened the weakness of the movements of his soul, / and his mind poured forth a discourse of righteousness. / His limbs were like channels for the flowing of the Spirit, / and like drops the waters of the blessings trickled forth. / Drops of words flowed from his mouth, from the mouth of the Spirit, / and in place of earth was the hearing of the children of his womb. / The righteous man sowed good seed in the field of his sons, / and he was eager that they should receive it with purity of soul. / His heart was pure, and the word of his mouth was simple, / and with joy he lifted up his voice to bless. / "Blessed!" the son of the household of faith cried aloud, / "is He who has strengthened my faculties to bless my offspring in His name. / Blessed is He who has stored up in me wealth befitting the work of His hands, / and has made me a fountain that pours out life for mankind. / Blessed is He who in me has revealed His goodness, the Lover of mankind, / and has made known by my hands the truth of His name, that He is the God of all. / Blessed is He who has made to dwell in me the abundance of the compassion He has for His servants, / and through me has kept alive natures both mute and speaking.

"Blessed is He who has set me up as a sign of peace before the seers, / that they might imitate me in calling upon His name with purity of soul. / Blessed is He who has made to dwell in me the power of the wisdom of His divinity, / that from my mouth might pour forth a discourse that gains life for mankind. / Blessed is He who has made me a second Adam for the children of Adam, / so that in rank I resemble the one whom He fashioned in the beginning. / Blessed is He who through me has created a second creation out of the one that was, / that the world might go on in the order of His creative work. / Blessed is He who has set me in a high rank that bears the image of His image, / and has stretched out my dominion over the lands in His own likeness. / Too small is my tongue to bless the name of His being, / who has granted my mind the power to understand the things to come." / With a view to the future the just man blessed the sons of his womb; / therefore he blessed the name of his God, and so his sons. / "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem": behold, the future! / And why "of Shem," and not "yours," O righteous one? / You are the elder; of all your offspring you are the just father; / upon you first should be placed the name of your God, and then upon your offspring. / It is a new thing that you did, just son of Lamech, in the mystery of your blessings, / and therefore the manifestation of something new is revealed in it. / "Blessed be the God of Shem," the prophet of truth prophesied, / and he made his sons partners in the greatness of the wealth that he bequeathed to his son. / "May Japheth be enlarged and dwell in the tent of Shem the elder, / and Ham shall be made a servant to his brothers, to serve them." / To Shem, "Blessed be the Lord"; to Japheth, "May he be enlarged"; and to Ham, "servant": / three forms which in a single word are both distinct and equal. / One name of the Lord, one beginning, and one servitude, / and all three from one mouth, in three words. / The eloquent speaker divided his sayings into three measures, / and yet they are bound equally in the [?] of a single word. / The just father handed three rods to his sons; / one he made long, and of the other two, one longer than its fellow. / Beneath the elder he set the youngest and the middle one, / and made them dependent on his inheritance in two forms. / In a form of words he hid the power that lay within his words, / and set the name of blessing upon the first without blessing him. / Shem the first has no blessing, if one looks for it. / For behold, "Blessed be the Lord," his father said, and Shem was not blessed; / nor again did the curse he pronounced fall on the last, who was near to it. / For behold, he cursed Canaan, who is the son of Ham, and it was not on Ham. / Shem's blessing he gave to the name of the Creator who is above all, / and Ham's he gave as the curse due [?] to Canaan his firstborn. / Laborious are your words, O righteous one, and deep is your story, / and no one can attain to the meaning of your blessings. / Your meaning is hidden, and it greatly confounds those who search, / and the searching out of your words is not easy for whoever searches. / Your blessings do not cleave to the name of those who are blessed, / nor do your curses distress the soul of those who are cursed. / You wished to bless Shem, and you hung it upon the name of God, / and when the blessing reached its place, you gave it to its Lord.

You also wished to curse Ham the hot-tempered, for Ham grew hot in sin, / and when you meant to grieve him, you grieved his son with the grief that was his. / No one knows what to call you according to your deed, / neither one who blesses nor one who curses, as it appears. / You seem to me like one who is not master of his own will, / as if it were not you who speaks, but another. / It seems that another constrains your strength wherever He wishes, / and your mind is drawn by force wherever He pleases. / [?] O righteous one, that the words you spoke are higher than you, / and if you were required to reveal them, they would be too hard for you. / [?] they are hard for you, not because they are hard, but because they are hidden, / and this is the wonder: that you recount something [?] hidden from you. / A great mystery is hidden in your word, O just man, / and therefore the lowliness of your kind [?] the lowly is destined to be exalted. / Your sayings are full of the sweetness of life, O son of mortals, / and therefore their [?] wipes death away from humanity. / A wonder is the discourse that your heart poured forth [?] blessed, / for you mingled curses with the blessings and hid them. / You resemble the God of all, O man, in the freedom of your [word?], / for at His nod good and evil alike are interchanged. / His nod made you wise to resemble [?] His likeness; / in Him, so to speak, you are imaged in the interchanging of your words. / His is the word [?] that spoke in riddles in the word of your mouth, / and through you He interpreted distinct sounds of a single meaning. / A single meaning [?] is hidden in the word of the just son of Lamech, / and to a single goal the search of his sayings is directed. / The goal [of] truth: truth set it aright for the lover of truth, / and he turned toward it as befits [?] the fear of truth. / The manifest Truth signaled to him to reveal the truth of His name, / that men might see His truth by the mouth of a man. / By the mouth of Noah came down the word of truth that had been worn away, / and on his lips murmured the sounds of mankind's restoration. / With humanity it came down from Adam, the head of humanity, / and its course did not rest until it reached the end of his life in the body. / In his body and soul dwelt the life that is hidden in men, / and like a spring its stream overflowed upon the head of his offspring. / Christ dwelt in him, so to speak, mystically, / and he gave Him to his sons in the form of the waters of the blessings. / To his firstborn he handed over the treasure of life that was hidden in him, / for he saw that he knew how to guard its treasures from harmful ones. / His brothers he subjected under the authority of his headship, / that by their subjection he might make them partners in the treasure of life. / He shared out life from his own life to the sons of his womb, / and taught them to keep the mystery of the life that was in them. / In mystery they saw the life that was in them, / lest, being openly seen, it be despised unworthily. / For this reason he [?] Ham and Japheth beneath Shem the great, / so that even against their will they would honor the mystery in the elder.

He honored the firstborn, not to honor what is natural, / but to magnify the One who renews nature that had worn out. / Not to nature did he who was full of justice grant honor, / but to the Mystery that perfects all mysteries by its perfection. / Not without discernment did he divide his words into three measures, / but so that he might build up the minds of his offspring by a single word. / He spoke a word, and though he spoke it well, it was not he who spoke it, / and he took great care to say it in due order, according to the One who spoke it. / And the Master of the word, the Being who has authority over [?], took great care, / and Noah the righteous, the keeper of mysteries, carried it. / In His truth the Creator looked, the Creator who reveals all things to him, / and He revealed and showed him the great mystery of mankind's salvation. / By testing his soul He saw that he was steadfast in faith, / and He set in him the hope of being given the words of faith. / In faith he too received the word of his Lord, / and lifted up his word and proclaimed the truth that had been revealed to him. / With love he received the mystery of the revelation that was revealed to him, / and he was greatly enlightened by the greatness of God's goodness toward mankind. / In great wonder the righteous one stood at the beginning of his word: / how could a man see the sons of men? / Like the son of Jesse, the father of the son of Jesse also marveled, / that one without rank, lowly and despised [?], rose to the head. / With a wonder like that in the psalm of "the Lord to my Lord," / Noah too stood at the time when the mystery was revealed to him. / David marveled and set words on the harp of words; / Noah was astonished and brought forth a discourse that pours out life. / At the life of his offspring he marveled and was discerningly astonished, / for how far higher it was than the life of the children of flesh! / The wise man marveled at the giving of life, not at life itself, / and he turned his word from the gift to the Giver. / He opened his lips and meant to say, "Blessed is my son, the firstborn," / but he turned the word around and said, "Blessed be the God of Shem." / Out of his readiness he was about to bless his son; / wonder held him back, and he blessed the Name that is full of blessings. / "Blessed be God," the just man said to the Just One who created him, / and he enclosed his son within the word addressed to his Lord. / With the blessing of his Lord the righteous one mingled the blessing of his son, / for he believed that the name of God is wholly blessing. / "Blessed be the God of my son, who delighted in him and called him by His name, / and blessed too is my son, within whom is hidden one who is his Lord and his son." / At what was hidden in his son he marveled; he gave thanks and said, / "Blessed be the Lord, who will reveal His lordship in my son." / What was to come his Lord revealed to the good servant, / not openly, but mystically, in mystery. / From his offspring was to come the liberator of mankind; / therefore he marveled at who would set free, and whom. / From Shem was to arise the King who rules over all; / therefore beforehand he bound his brothers to the yoke of His name. / But why did he not give separate blessings, to Japheth that he be enlarged, / and not to Ham, that he be a servant of servants?

Why did he not give Japheth an inheritance as he did the just one, / but granted him only to be enlarged and to grow great in his brother's inheritance? / Why, when he cursed Ham, did he not drive him away to a distant land, / but enclosed him within the inheritance of his blessed brothers? / Why did he not cut him off by a sentence of judgment, as he did Cain, / and why did he permit him to mingle with his kin? / Why did he not confirm the curse upon him, as one might say? / And why did he not serve his brother, as is written? / Scripture teaches that the seed of Ham did not serve in bondage, / neither the sons of blessed Shem the firstborn nor the sons of Japheth. / Of the sons of Ham it is said that they were the first to rule in headship, / and Scripture testifies that Nimrod is truly a son of Ham. / Nimrod received headship and the kingdom of his time, / and Scripture sets his might before the Lord. / This Nimrod, they say, was a mighty hunter; / as one might say, headship was given to him. / And if the Lord made Nimrod a mighty warrior, / then the curse was not true as it was spoken. / The Egyptians and the Canaanites too are sons of Ham, / and Scripture does not show that they were subjected, but that they subjected others. / The Israelites and the sons of Abraham are sons of Shem, / and against the law they served in slavery to the sons of the accursed one. / Where, then, was the word fulfilled as it is written? / For behold, the deeds were contrary to what was spoken. / They were contrary to what was spoken, but not in truth. / In its meaning, however, the speaker and his speech are true. / The manifest truth dwelt in the story that the just man interpreted, / and it needs understanding to show it to the eyes of the mind. / Without understanding the sight of its beauty is not seen, / and without labor its truth is not tested. / A story that is laborious in its hidden things requires labor, / and if one labors, he can see it clearly. / It is very clear to one who labors over it lovingly, / and very dark to one who does not toil with the steadfastness of his love. / With love anyone can see it as it is, / and with discernment one can recount it to others as well. / With love I heard it, and with care I long to recount it, / that lovers of love may discern it and love it. / Beloved is the story that the just man interpreted about his beloved ones, / and everyone ought to gaze into it lovingly. / The profit for men is full of the meaning hidden within it; / the righteous one too marveled at this, how profitable it is. / Toward its profit the wise man looked, and he spoke it with wisdom, / so that its preciousness would not be despised in the eyes of fools. / The eye of fools is accustomed to despise what is open; / therefore he cast a veil of words over all the words. / The Sign who spoke in Noah looked to the aim of fools, / and hid the words of his mouth in a garment of words.

He could have revealed openly the hidden mystery that He revealed to His servant, / and He could have shown His love plainly. / But He did not show it, not as though He fell short in benefiting men, / but because men were not able to profit from it. / Not even to Noah, into whose hands He divided the wealth of the mystery, / did He show its power exactly as it is. / He saw the shadow of truth bodily in the body of his son, / and gave thanks to his Lord who had shown him the mystery before the deeds. / Like a mirror He fixed the type before his mind, / and he embraced it lovingly, without having his fill. / Without having his fill he repeated that voice: / "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem, who has blessed us in His name." / As at an image he gazed at the rank of his son, / and called his two brothers: "Come, gaze!" / Blessing and curse he pointed out to the sons of his womb, / that they might acquire the gaze of their minds in the mystery that he saw. / Japheth he taught to enlarge his mind and the movements of his soul, / that he might be able to take hold of the wealth flowing down from Shem. / Ham he warned to bow the shoulder of his insolence / and take up the yoke of service to the life hidden in his brother. / With blessing and curse he urged them to keep his word, / that when it was fulfilled through deeds they might acquire its wealth. / Before the deeds he longed to do what was fitting, / that when they were revealed, it might befit the comeliness of his offspring. / He was looking ahead at the comeliness and beauty of the mystery that he saw, / and he urged his sons to picture it before their eyes. / With the eye of the mind the seer saw the comely mystery, / and he longed to see it in a body, without a veil. / In the body of his son he sought the One who would be embodied, / and he believed that consolation was hidden within him. / Shem was set before his eyes like a mirror, / and however much he looked, he looked again without having his fill. / On Shem he fixed the gaze of his eyes and of his mind, / like one who, in equal bodily love, was absorbed [?] in his story. / Twice he doubled the account of the blessings, / and this he did out of love for his offspring. / A servant of servants he made Canaan, twice over, / and this is the sign of the repayment of a father's love for his sons. / Out of love for his son the just man bound his sons, / that they might be yoked under the lordship of his Lord and his son. / To his Lord and his son he subjected the world through Ham and Japheth, / as one who allows all to be held [?] by their succession. / All, together with all, were destined to serve the offspring from him; / therefore he bound the necks of his sons to the yoke of his son. / In the service of the King who comes from his line he made his sons serve, / and he stamped them with two stamps of varied words. / The stamp of words the son of Lamech set upon Ham and upon Japheth,

and he varied them according to the number of the sentences. / The forms of blessing and curse he gave to both of them, / for they are quite distinct in name, but in power they are equal. / One is the power in the two, and one the meaning, / because it is also one who divided two in one. / Two in one the just man divided, from one to two: / the good that came from Shem, to Ham the despised and to Japheth the lowly. / To the servant he lowered it, as to a servant of his master's house, / and to the freeborn, as to one in need of sustenance. / From the treasury of abundant Shem both Ham and Japheth were enriched, / and they were subjected to him, lovingly and by force. / Japheth out of love received the stamp of service to his brother, / and Ham his begetter compelled by force to serve his brother. / In the name of freedom he gave freedom to the humble soul, / and in slavery he yoked the insolent one beneath freedom. / Something like this Paul also did in his letters, / subjecting slaves and freeborn to the Lord Christ: / "For every slave is a freedman, redeemed from bondage [?], / and the freeborn too is a slave of the Lord Christ." / And if Paul bound two groups under one Lord, / who will dispute the word of Noah, saying it is not right? / That it is right, as it is written, Scripture testifies, / and the righteous who came after it also lend their support. / After Noah, Abraham received the promise of life, / and sealed the book of the covenants through his two offspring. / Two he begot from his limbs, full of blessings, / and he gave them to drink of a stream of words like that of Noah. / To Isaac he handed down the headship he had received from Shem, / and the son of Hagar he bound to the yoke, to serve like Ham. / The just man looked to Noah, who blessed one and subjected one, / and he too complied, to fulfill the words through deeds. / To this same goal Isaac, son of the promise, also looked, / and closely resembled him in words through deeds. / Like Noah and Abraham he spoke words to his offspring, / and in that same form he repeated the blessing of wondrous words. / He honored Jacob with seniority, though he was not the elder, / and set the elder beneath him in the rank of the house of Ham. / To Esau he said, "If you repent, you will be set free"; / and from whom, then, was he to be set free, since behold, he was free? / Esau was not subjected to Jacob in all his days, / nor did his seed serve in slavery to the Israelites. / Wondrous are the just words set down in the Scriptures, / and no one knows how to marvel properly at their meaning. / The power of understanding strengthened them to perceive / how they might depict the meaning of words on the page of words. / Like painters who paint images of things to come, / they painted likenesses of things not manifest by means of what is manifest. / O seers, seers of something that cannot be uttered, / who, though it was not seen by them, recounted its likenesses before the seers!

O heralds who proclaimed mysteries before the deeds, / and before it came revealed the mystery of rest for the race of earthly ones! / O guides who trod the road for the coming of the King, / and set milestones along it, words full of the sign of peace! / Words of peace were the words of those full of peace, / and by the levelled ways [?] of their sayings travelers find rest. / They built an inn of love in the Scriptures for the journey of men, / that they might not be worn out by the cutting off of hope, the ruin of [?] the two. / To the one will of the one Creator they consented alike, / and they were not divided over the expectation of the hope they had heard. / They heard good hope interpreted in their tongues, / and acquired hope, to hope for the hope that is to come. / Noah first trod the road before their eyes, / and all of them walked in the footsteps of the word of his mouth. / Through his mouth the mind travels lightly on the road of hope, / and by his tongue it runs along the path of the promise of life. / O traveler, whose mouth traveled in place of his steps, / and whose tongue, without walking, measured the earth! / O guide who showed a road without steps, / and set milestones along it that are not measured by footsteps! / O you, the man who ran well on the course of life, / for your word reached the house of rest that gives life! / The Giver of life was hidden in your seed mystically, / and beforehand He showed you the power of His vitality in one of your offspring. / In your firstborn dwelt the dwelling of immortal life, / and your mind marveled as it gazed at the life of your son. / In great wonder your thoughts stood still at the fruit that came from you, / for you saw at the end of his body the life of mankind. / With your mind you looked at that Life who gives life to all, / and called your sons to look upon it with delight. / With humility your word looked at the mystery in Shem, / and toward its appointed place you gathered the [?] gaze of his brothers. / By the comeliness of its beauty you made the sons of your womb marvel, / and even against their will they painted its likenesses before their eyes. / As at an image they gazed at the word of your mouth, / for the image of their life was depicted in the name of God. / As one who holds a pen, your mind grasped the name of your God, / and inscribed with it that voice: "Blessed be the Lord." / Bless the Lord, who painted in you, the Lord, Master of painters, / that you might paint in your sons the image of the duties [?] they owe Him. / By the debt of love toward your Lord you bound your offspring, / that they might repay grace to the Good One who set them in order. / The Good One hid in you good leaven from His goodness, / and you cast it into the body of your sons, that it might keep them. / Wisely, O wise one, you dealt with your offspring, / for you hid the wealth they would need within their limbs. / The One who makes men wise made your movements wise to do this, / that the life of your kind might flow on with your succession. / The Lover of your kind placed in your kind the treasure of life, / and hid it in your earth, to be kept until the end of times. / Like merchants, the senses that carried it bore it along, / and brought it in love from one to another, until Mary.

O the wonder that comes from the Creator toward man, / that though he was mortal he became the keeper of the life of his life! / O the knowledge of the One who orders all things, how deep it is, / who placed in His creature wealth that suits its need! / O Artisan who made everything out of nothing, / who loaded and filled His handiwork from His wisdom! / The wisdom of truth from His wisdom He placed in our nature, / and that wisdom made our kind wise to know His name. / It revealed to Adam openly the hiddenness of the One who formed it, / and it made him know that he has a Lord, the Lord of all. / It bound Abel the pure in the love of his Lord, / and through things manifest he repaid the thanks befitting the Hidden One. / Through it the fair Enoch was made wise to make his soul fair, / and because he was very fair he remained in immortal beauty. / It revealed to Lamech about the offspring who came from him, / that he would give rest to the earth and take away the mourning of mankind's sorrow. / It spoke a new tongue in the son of Lamech too, / and his mouth interpreted new sounds of mankind's renewal. / Everything that wisdom said was from God, / and it made all wise, and it makes all wise until the end. / From its wisdom the first ones learned to be wise, / and it again perfects the others who come after them. / Noah, more than all, was made wise in it to reveal its mysteries, / and it too, more than all, drew him near to its intimacy. / As to a beloved it revealed to him the mystery of its hidden things, / and he too in love kept the commandment of its truth. / The lover of truth kept truth for the fear of truth, / and it too in truth repaid him a reward better than his labor. / A good reward it paid to the just man who labored with it, / and he took more from it and gave it to his sons, that they might be sheltered in it. / The enjoyment of immortal life it placed in his hands, / and he too placed it in the hands of his sons, that they might live by its food. / The just man ate its living food and fed his sons, / and set its life [?] in our nature, keeping it alive. / The life that flowed down from Noah came down with our kind from Noah onward, / and it goes on until the course of time is complete. / From us life began to flow from the beginning, / and with us it remains in a nearness that has no end. / The Power that created us created life in us and hid it, / and when it pleased Him, He showed it to the eyes of all and in all. / In our very fashioning He hid the life that comes from His life, / and after a time He revealed His will that had been hidden in us. / In hidden and manifest ways He showed His love toward our humanity, / and wisely He accomplished His will through us toward all. / Through us He fulfilled His care toward all and in all; / come, let us give thanks to Him more than all, for He has loved us more than all.
On the Tower of Babel and on the division of tongues
Memra 52, on the division of tongues. / By the same author. / Memra fifty-two, on the Tower of Babel and on the division of tongues.
The sign of peace the Creator gave to the nature of men, / so that they should not be terrified by a flood that destroys mankind.

A covenant of love he established with the children of flesh, / that he would no longer be angry and pursue their deeds with waters.
By manifest signs he showed them the greatness of his love, / how much he loves the children of his household and hates iniquity.
The sign of the bow he stretched in the clouds before their eyes, / that they might look on it and hate the iniquity that had destroyed them.
By the bow he revealed to them his severity and his kindness, / that he is the one who pursues and he is the one who is jealous, both at once.
A bent bow he showed them, with no string on it, / to teach them that he does not shoot arrows of water at them.
Without a hand and without a string he displayed the bow, / to make known to them that he has no wish to shoot at men.
Not to shoot did he stretch it in the air and display its appearance, / but to cast fear and love into the mind of men.
Fear and love he fixed in the clouds like a mirror, / that they might look on it, hate iniquity and choose love.
The appearance of blood and the brightness of fire were painted in it, / to make known how angry he had been with the wicked.
Peace and patience and the might of his being were hidden in its appearance, / for he had taken hold even of the bow and the arrows of his wrath.
As if with a finger he was showing them by the signs of the bow: / “This is what I held in my lofty arm on the day of the flood.
With this I bent the bow of my will, as with a string, / and loosed and aimed it against the iniquity of the tyrants among you.
This I gripped mightily in the hand of my will, / and shot arrows of rushing waters at the ranks of men.
With this I reaped the field of the wicked that was full of thickets, / and the waves became my gravediggers and fulfilled my will.
It is I, I who reaped the beasts together with mankind, / and made them a causeway of crumbling clay.
It is I, I who spared a remnant along with Noah my beloved, / and kept alive with Noah the dumb kinds for the service of men.
It is I, I who preserved the life of all in dead timber, / and they were not drowned among the planks and the rushing waves.
My will stood like a sailor within the ark, / and like a helmsman it steered it to the haven of peace.
My will drew it to peace, hidden, as if with oars, / and brought it out and set it in the midst of the earth unharmed.
Behold, I have brought you out to the haven of peace, as I promised; / see that you do not despise my commandments like those before you.
Behold, I have shown you the severity of the scourges that swallowed the wicked; / keep far from iniquity, lest you be scourged like the wicked.
Behold, I have taught you the ways of righteousness and the name of goodness; / see that you conduct yourselves wisely in both.
Behold, I have set a covenant of peace between me and you; / do not loosen it through the slackness of iniquity, lest I turn and be angry.
Behold, see the bow I have stretched across the face of the heights: / there is no string on it, nor even a hand to guide it.
Look and understand: on the day of battle a bow is needed, / but I, behold, have made it a sign of peace between me and men.
I long for peace, and not for war with mankind,

and that is why I have put no string on the bow I have shown.
Behold, I have shown you the desire of my will, that I am a lover of men; / do not force me, against my will, to carry out wrath.
Let heaven and earth be witnesses between me and you / that I have no desire to kill men where there is no folly.”
These words the Hidden One proclaimed in secret to men, / and wrote them in the covenants of the sign of the bow.
By them Noah and his sons were kept watchful, as in a book; / but after a time his offspring went astray after error.
For a full span of time peace remained among the earthly ones, / and after a little while rebellion came in and reigned on the earth.
The remnant that had escaped from the waters turned back to its corruption, / and began to walk in the way of wickedness like those before them.
They abandoned the inheritance of the commandment of peace they had received from Noah, / and forgot the sign the Creator had given between himself and them.
They went out from the place and the neighbourhood beside the ark, / and began to wander about to choose themselves lands.
They set out from Qardu, where they had come out to the haven of peace, / and took the road down to Babel, whose name is confusion.
They departed from the peace of the Creator, rich in love, / and went out seeking an inheritance of earth, which impoverishes its own bosom.
Out of desire for land the earthly ones went out from peace / [?] to lands that were fertile and fair.
They were all of one accord as they went down to the region of Babel, / and they were one people, one tongue and one mind.
One will led them as far as Babel, / and within Babel they lusted with a desire for toil and iniquity.
A hateful desire the insolent desired insolently, / like Adam, who desired and [?] rank and station.
Foolish arrogance drove on the sons of Adam, / and by its error they too went astray like their father.
The very thought Adam had, of becoming God, / came to his sons as well: to seize the divine rank.
In the way of Adam his offspring also walked insolently, / and sought to raise a rebellion of iniquity against the Creator.
Against the Maker the dusty children of clay rebelled, / and prepared armour to fight against their Life-giver.
The wicked wickedly put on the armour of iniquity, / and began to shoot the arrows of arrogance against the truth.
The fools put on foolish arrogance like armour, / and set vainglory like a helmet on the head of their understanding.
They supposed that height and depth were subdued beneath their hands, / and that they would ascend and stand at the lofty rank of divinity.
Simple-mindedly the simple thought what they thought, / and did not look well to the end of their deeds.
Without discernment they set out from the place where they were living, / and without order they sought to begin the building of iniquity.
What, then, was the desire that blazed in their thoughts, / and who conceived the idea that they should undertake a labour without measure?
Against whom, then, did they lift their thoughts toward the heights, / as the worldly ones set out on a road too hard for mortals?
An evil desire wore them down, the dull of heart, / and the earthbound sought to lift their wings toward the heights.
The want that was in them roused them as from sleep, / and they began to ponder their thoughts in an unseemly way.

As though in sleep their senses sank from what was fitting, / and like diligent men they rose and hurried to work with earth.
They abandoned the divine service that wins life, / and took on a labour without profit for body or soul.
They despised the oaths of God, the Lord of all, which cannot be broken, / and gave the lie to the sign, full of peace, that he had shown them.
They thought that he deceives and does not keep his word as he promised, / and might turn and bring fearful waters and destroy us.
The fools reckoned untrue the One who is truer than all, / and on that ground they began to build a rebellion against the Creator.
On this condition the proud of heart made a compact with one another, / and took on a labour that was never to reach completion.
This was the thought the senseless fools gave birth to: / to build a house in which to be saved from the flood.
With this intention they armed themselves, as with armour, / to wage war with the Maker across the face of the heights.
Three things the witless, whose minds were very dull, devised, / and for their sake prepared the armour with which they thought to win.
One, that they might be saved from the flood, should one come; / another, that they might hold a dwelling on high with the Creator;
and the third, that if they fought and won and reigned, / they would leave on earth a name of glory, like victors.
The guilty were striving for victory, / and did not know that they were condemned and guilty like their father.
They desired and planned to win with the armour of pride, / and brought out into the open the hidden cunning of their thoughts:
“Come, let us make bricks of clay and fire them, / and build a tower whose top reaches the height above.
Come, let us strive with labour for the salvation of our lives; / come, let us make for ourselves a name in creation greater than anyone's,
that the generations to come may tell of it, as befits our might.
Come, let us prevail in the struggle with the Maker, / and wage a fearsome war with him across the face of the heights.
Come, let us arm ourselves with armour fit for battles, / and shoot arrows at God, the Lord of all, who destroyed our race.
Come, let us avenge the blood of our kin, / whom he slew without sparing with the sword of the waters.
Come, let us do to him as he did to the children of our people: / let the blood of our kindred, which he shed for nothing, be required at his hands.
Come, let us tell him, as in a lawsuit, how we are in the right: / why did you destroy the dumb creatures along with mankind?
With lawsuit and armour let us do battle with him mightily, / and take his rank and the name of his authority, and it will be ours.
Let us make bricks and fire them in flames, / so that they do not dissolve when waters are poured on them.
Let us build a fortress and storehouses and fill them with armour and provisions, / so that it will be enough for the day of battle that awaits us.
Let us broaden its foundations and enlarge them to match its greatness, / so that the waves of the waters and the blasts of the wind cannot shake it.
Let us make it firm and build it skilfully, as befits us, / so that our craftsmanship is not put to shame after a time.
Let us build the whole of it with baked bricks, as with stones, / and instead of mud let us put lime between its courses.

Lime and bricks let us mix together in the building of our work, / so that the changing seasons of cold and heat may not harm it.
And along with our building let us also make our resolve firm together, / and not grow slack before the one who comes to fight us.
See that no one falls silent before his fellow in time of war, / lest we be scattered over all the earth by the one who opposes us.”
Woe to the proud, who without meaning to spoke and prophesied, / and foretold in advance the scattering that came upon them after a time!
O the blind, who without seeing saw accurately, / and looked and foresaw what was to come as if it had already happened!
O those who were of one mind in the building of iniquity, / and set their hand to it without the agreement of their tongues!
They proclaimed, unwittingly, their own guilt, / and revealed and declared their change to every quarter.
They set their hand, wrote and sealed that they would be scattered, / and took no heed of the sentence of judgment to which their own mouth had given ear [?].
They wrote their bond with the unbridled pen of their tongues, / and did not stop or fall silent from the foolish thought they had conceived.
They dug deep and laid foundations as if for ever, / and did not know that the time was near when they would be overthrown.
They fired bricks, burned lime and began to build, / and as their building rose, their thoughts rose with it.
As high as the building rose toward the heights, / so much higher did their heart rise in pride.
