As day by day it was added to in its measurements, / so the iniquity in them grew beyond all measure.
Their heart was awake and did not sleep night or day, / and though they were weary they did not feel how weary they were.
They were impatient for the time when it would reach the top of their purpose [?], / and longed for the moment when they would see the work completed.
Their desire to build was insatiable, / and their senses and movements never rested from the work.
The Maker, who sees things before they come to be, saw / that they were building in vain and multiplying their sins.
He saw that, even if they built, they could not build as they supposed, / and he spared them, so that they would not wear themselves out with toil and iniquity.
He pitied them and had compassion, as is his custom to show mercy, / and began to utter words of love and of threat.
Love tamed the course of the insolent, / and with pity cut short the pain of their thoughts.
For the Merciful One had pity on that senseless labour, / and in the guise of wrath gave them rest from the flood.
The guise of anger filled the voice he made them hear, / yet within it lay hidden a love beyond words.
Suddenly he made a manifest voice heard by those who have voices, / that he was taking counsel, he and those with him, to come down.
With the children of his counsel the Knower of all took counsel, / and as if for help he called them to come down with him:
“Behold, men have become one people and one tongue, / and have gathered together to contend against my will.
Behold, the sons of Adam have assailed my lordship like their father,

and seek to ascend to the lofty rank of divinity.
Behold, mortals have feared death by the flood of waters that guilt brings, / and have built a fortress to hide in from the flood.
Behold, the earthly ones have prepared armour and bound themselves in a conspiracy / to go up and stir up strife on high between me and them.
Behold, they have made a compact not to be divided one against another / until they conquer and height and depth are theirs.
Behold, they have prophesied their own scattering without meaning to, / and it is right that the word they spoke be fulfilled in deeds.
Come, then, let us go down and divide them one from another, / so that they may no longer understand the speech and utterance of their tongues.
Come, let us cast strife among them silently, while they do not perceive it, / and steal from them the sword of speech in which they boast.
Come, together let us go down to the earth without change, / and make war on the fleshly ones without blows [?].
Come, let us give them a separate utterance for every tongue, / and behold, they will be divided, and the war of their thoughts will cease.
Come, let us cast among them a new voice that they cannot understand, / and drive them out into exile among the lands.”
O Creator, who is this with whom you are conferring, / that your sign proclaims new words about your being?
Whom are you calling to come down with you among the earthly ones, / and whom do you wish to be a help to your strength?
With whom have you taken counsel, that he should be with you a giver of speech to men, / and to whom do you say, “Come with me, let us go down and divide them”?
Who was it who counselled you in the beginning when you created, / and with whom did you order the hidden mysteries of your divinity?
Who was your helper when you were creating heaven and earth, / and who was your strength, that he should lend strength to the work of your hands?
Whom have you ever called or brought near to speak with you, / and whom have you made your equal to pass judgment as you choose?
Your voice is like that first one on the sixth day, / when you were forming the image of Adam with the finger of your sign.
There alone did you make heard a voice like this one: / “Come, let us make man in our image, in our likeness.”
One is the voice and one the meaning, of that and of this: / “Come, let us make” there, and “let us go down” here, alike and true.
One is the sign that proclaimed them, that one and this, / and one the nature that fashioned there and divided here.
The children of his counsel he called, in “let us go down” and in “let us make,” / and they are the ones who made man and divided men.
It was the Father who called the Son and the Spirit at the fashioning of Adam, / and summoned them to the division of what they had created.
In the fashioning of men and the dividing of men the Creator willed / to reveal the mystery of the Persons hidden with him, that it might be searched out.
Outwardly, then, there is nothing among created things greater than man, / for behold, the hidden things that are hidden from all are revealed in him.
But let us ask what the reason is that he said “Come” / at man's fashioning and his dividing, he who alone is Sovereign.
If it was not the Son and the Spirit who are from him that he called on both occasions, / who then is his equal, that he should take counsel with him?

To the heavenly beings that utterance was not fitting, / “Come with me, let us make” and “Come with me, let us go down,” as to his partners.
Had he said, “Go, go down, divide the tongue of men,” / it would indeed have seemed that he called and sent spirits.
So it is beyond dispute that “Come, let us go down” / was said to the Son and the Spirit, the Persons who are with him.
To the Son and the Spirit belong both fashioning and dividing, / and with the Father they created everything and divided men.
They fashioned and they divided wisely, / Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one equal nature.
They are the ones who came down now without change, / to take away speech and give speech to the nature of men.
In the division of men they sketched the mystery of their Persons, / and at the last expounded it through the gift of tongues.
They called one another at the fashioning and at the dividing, / so that everyone might learn that the nature of the three is one.
They came down to divide, not by a descent involving change, / but by a sign whose swiftness cannot be told.
He sent the sign like a messenger to the insolent, / and it cried out suddenly and startled them, the sailors of arrogance.
It was the sign that came down and took from them the armour of speech, / and clothed them in another armour of other words.
With a hard sword it cut off the speech of their tongues, / and put in them a speech that differed from the first.
He took away the first, to teach them that he fashioned all things; / and gave the second, to make known that he rules over all things.
Graciously he waged war with them, as they had wished, / and instead of with the body he made the contest with the mind.
Skilfully he joined the struggle with their very movements, / and bound them with the hard bonds of their tongues.
Wondrous was the war the Hidden One waged with the earthly ones, / and the mind cannot recount its marvel, however much it recounts.
What, then, were those shears that he held in his hand, / that cut away speech instead of limbs, and the body did not feel it?
How, then, did he enter by a hidden sign into their thoughts, / and strip away and take the treasure within them, and they did not perceive it?
How did the Possessor of power snatch away the word from their mouths, / and make them dumb and stammering to one another?
How did he cut off the living fountain, the first speech, / so that words no longer flowed on the lip of the mouth as they were wont?
How did he cut off the course of the one tongue, / and tread out a path for the mind to travel in new words?
How, and how much, shall we say that what happened happened, / that he cut off speech and bestowed speech by a change of voice?
To that sign which did this let us ascribe its power, / for it alone knows how it did it so swiftly.
To it is revealed how it stripped away the speech of men, / and how it gave again another wealth, distinct from that.
His is the wealth of the other speech and of the first, / and he cut off speech and gave a taste of speech in nature itself.
The finger of his sign suddenly struck the lyre of the soul,

and it began to sing new sounds that were strange to it.
The command that breathed on it in the beginning, so that it gave forth sound, / spoke with it now in another speech, and it listened to its own voice.
He did not change its nature and make another nature, / but its speech took on a change within its very law.
The command dyed the word with another dye, / and it took on a colour, changed its voice, and was astonished at itself.
That voice which said “Let us go down” came down, he and those with him, / and terrified them, the ranks of men in their agitation.
He came down without coming down, for he has no place to walk in; / his command came down and fulfilled his word, and he remained as he is.
He came down, though he is with all and in all without limit, / so that by his descent he might bring man low from his haughtiness.
He came down and shook to the ground [?] their pride and their thoughts, / and took from them the armour of arrogance they had put on.
Great astonishment fell suddenly on the insolent, / and they sat marvelling at the hand that had touched them.
They looked at one another, each astounded at the other, / whether they were themselves or perhaps some other likeness.
They spoke to one another in a sound strange to their speech, / and the ear could not grasp the force of the sound.
For they heard with the ear's hearing but without understanding, / and again they saw the moving of the mouth without discernment.
Amid the divisions the feeble stood, [?] that had come about, / and in the nature of the body they observed what seemed not to be themselves.
The appearance of the body was true to the eyes of the body, / but the sound of the word was utterly strange to the hearing of the ear.
Eyes and ears marvelled at one another, / for the one saw and the other was blind to understanding.
The mouth marvelled in silence at its companions, / how they uttered distinct utterances and it did not know them.
Bewilderment and wonder were cast into movements and limbs, / and the soul marvelled at the body and the body at the soul.
The soul in the body was astonished that it heard and was at a loss, / and the body in the soul marvelled at its strange speech.
The soul was even more astonished at itself: / who, then, had changed the sound of the tones of its eloquence?
“Am I myself, the soul, or am I not myself?” it said to itself, / “Have I perhaps lost my first self and died into another?”
O wonder, great beyond measure, and wholly amazement: / that the soul heard the sound of its own tones and did not understand!
Or were new things happening among mortals, / that while they were in soul and body they were [?]?
Or speakers who lost speech and found words, / and from the one speech of one tongue acquired many!
New sounds were spoken among the earthly ones, / and men marvelled at men through the change of sounds.
Man called to man, and no one listened, / and speech became like no speech to the speakers.
The Syrian cried out to the Greek who wanted a word, / and the word of one mouth gained no answer from the mouth of its fellow.
The Roman spoke with the Egyptian in the tongue of flesh,

and could not make out the speech of his fellow of flesh.
The Mede beckoned to the Alan at his side, / and he kept silent and was still, as one who hears nothing, for he did not understand.
The Indian approached the Hun to converse with him, / and his words were in vain and found no hold [?].
Each one translated within himself according to his own tongue, / and to him was interpreted the force of the meaning the sign had put in him.
They grew weary and were worn out as they cried out to one another, / and the word of the mouth gave no return, voice for voice.
In the pangs of suffering they laboured like a woman in childbirth, / and the soul could not bring forth the infant of the word.
Like an infant the speech [?] turned within the soul, / and the doors of the mouth were shut before its coming forth.
That command which begot the word in the mind of the soul / was the one who shut the door in its face, so that it should no longer come out.
The word fell silent within the thoughts, and a word was given: / the same that fell silent was the same that came out in another colour.
One was the word that was divided into portions, / and from it the tongue of the peoples branched out like a shoot.
Like a vine it spread its branches to every place, / while it, as it is, kept its strength in the root of the soul.
As a root, the speech remained with one people, / and it alone was retained [?] in that first one.
As if by lots the hidden command divided them, / and each spoke by the lot of speech that fell to his name.
Love and mercy were mingled in that which he divided [?], / and though he divided, he did not tear apart the love set in nature.
For one lot fell to fathers and to their children, / and in one speech a man, his wife and his sons spoke.
With wisdom and love the Fashioner of all did this, / so that nature and the order of fellowship might not be corrupted.
With great order he divided them and settled them, / like a father who bequeaths to his sons the wealth he has acquired.
In the guise of wrath he gave the wealth of his kindness, / to put fear into the heirs who received the power of his wisdom.
And though the voice “Come, let us go down” was full of anger, / it was peace that he fitted [?] to mankind by his descent.
The sign of peace had been promised to Noah and his seed, / and he changed his voice into the guise of anger to frighten men.
The voice was clothed in the guise of sword and spear, / yet he who raised it as if to kill spared in mercy.
Not to kill did he raise his sword and show it to them, / but to make known that it does not please him to see iniquity.
Not because they built a building of iniquity did he divide them, / but to drive out the iniquity in them by means of division.
From the beginning what he did had been determined by him, / and he did it with wisdom, as he is wont to do well.
For he knew, before the word was formed in the soul, / that from it, in time, the lip of words would proceed.
This division he had determined before all things.

and he had his eye on it before heaven and earth came to be. / It was no new thought that drew him to the division, / nor was it anger that overcame him so that he came down and gave out tongues. / He is used to frightening the members of his household by putting on a show of anger, / as he did from the beginning with the house of Adam. / For there too he brought in death because of the fruit, / to teach them [?] together with the generation. / [?] and the Flood too, he said, he made because of iniquity, / to put bridles on human nature so that it would not turn brutish. / Because of iniquity he cursed Canaan and made him a slave, / so that no one would brazenly mock the father who begot him. / On these same terms he now came down to the earthly ones too, / so that by a voice that seemed to divide humanity he might bring humanity peace. / His will came down for the sake of peace, as though he himself came down, / and he brought peace to the people who had gathered as if to provoke him. / He saw that they were eager to build a rebellion brazenly, / and he came down and tore down the building of iniquity before it grew strong. / He saw that they were hurrying to storm the height and climb up to him, / and he made a voice heard and scattered them, so that they would not be crushed. / Like a king he ordered judgment on the wrongdoers, / and cast them into exile[?] across the lands. / The command of the hidden sign went out like a ruler / and bound them with the harsh weapon of their own tongues. / He put a different speech into their mouths like a chain, / and shut them up in the prison of their tongues. / As if to fortresses he sent them off to the lands, / so that they would never again raise a rebellion of iniquity against his lordship. / The sign held a new speech like a rod, / and drove them out of Babel as if in anger. / How closely this command against the presumptuous / resembled the command that drove Adam out of Paradise! / As if in anger [...] he drove them out, as he did Adam, / so that through Adam and through them he might make the earth peaceful for human life. / On these same terms he scattered them through the lands, / so that the earth's settled places would not be thrown into turmoil by a mounting toll of killing. / Had they stayed together in one place, as they intended, / they would have multiplied greatly and shed blood out of lust for land. / Had they remained in the land of Babel, the tower of rebellion, / they would have rebelled there against justice as they pleased. / Had he not issued the decree for their scattering, / dense iniquity would have piled up where they lived. / So he did well to confound them and scatter them, / so that their gathering would not multiply iniquity and disturb the peace. / They went out from Babel to divide up the land to which they were sent, / and each of them was brought to the place the sign appointed for him. / The divine sign became like a guide to them / and showed them the road to travel to every quarter. / The command that had divided them went along with them, / and moved with them to the lands where they would dwell. / The sign became like a teacher to them, simple-hearted as they were, / and made them wise to dwell in the land to which they had been sent. / Like a skilled scribe it wrote on the tablets of their minds, / and taught them to read well in the speech within them. / They read and pondered the writings of their thoughts

and interpreted the hidden power in the speech of their tongues. / They became masters of the new speech their hearts brought forth, / and laid down rules for the conduct of earthly life. / Along with speech they gained the further gift of living in good order, / and began to give thought to what is good for body and soul. / So what happened under a show of anger turned to our advantage, / and the Good One wisely worked it out in the face of our wickedness. / It is all full of love and mercy, though no one realizes it, / and it is the cause of peace for human beings and for spiritual beings. / The division of tongues gave the word of peace, / and both earthly and heavenly beings were enriched by it. / The spiritual beings saw the love the Good One showed our race, / and took hope that there was hope for us in our lostness. / They saw that the voice of threat was changed into gentleness, / and the scourges were turned and became a delight to those who were scourged. / That voice, "Come, let us go down," was full of harsh scourges, / but mercy turned it around, and they came down and handed out gifts of peace. / The Lover of mankind handed out peace under a show of anger, / so that the children of the adversary would not imagine that he loved iniquity. / He mixed the pledge of life into the voice and gave them to drink, / to portray the mystery of what was to come at the end of time. / In this division, made under a show of anger, he portrayed the mystery / of the gift he would give the apostles in the form of fire. / He tried out beforehand, in what happened then, what was still to come, / so that when it was fulfilled it would not seem strange to the eyes of those who saw it. / He was about to reveal in human language the persons who are with him, / and he gave tongues as a pledge. / The voice that divided humanity trod out for us the road of peace, / so that one might travel toward[?] the harbour of the peace of the Godhead. / It disclosed and taught us the persons of the Son and the Spirit: / that together with the Father they divided the peoples and gave out tongues. / They made that division under a show of wrath, / and they in turn gave power from themselves in the appearance of fire. / From both events mortals learned the power of the One who Is: / that the first things and the last are his. / To him, who orders all things, we owe one hymn of thanksgiving, / for he showed his love and made them wise in his hidden ways.
On Job the Righteous

Homily Forty
On Job the Righteous
and on the trials he endured

For the benefit of humankind the Creator recorded the memory of men, / so that by remembering the just who triumphed people might grow wise.
And though the will of the just was plain to Him, as One who knows all, / He did not wish to hide the wealth they had gathered by their labours.
He recorded the memory of their names in the book of His words, / and like guides He placed the road to life in their hands.

Like seals He set the names of the victors in His Scriptures, / and wove them a fair crown for the head of victory.
He laid their labours like a foundation in the books of His words, / so that people might build their own conduct on their labours.
Like lights, like sun and moon, He set their labours in place, / so that by their shining they might show light to the hidden soul.
As milestones of peace He set the names of the righteous in His Scriptures, / so that everyone might know how to walk in the labours of the soul.
By their conduct they became a mirror for the eyes of the heart, / so that each might polish away the ugliness of his soul through their labours.
The Creator did not weave praises for the just whom He loved; / He set up their conduct as a target for those who come after them.
He watched them as they suffered the sufferings of the body, / and He tested their endurance as they were struck down.
His strength strengthened their minds in their contests, / and by His help they won victory in their struggles.
It was not against flesh that they waged a fleshly struggle; / they went down to the contest against the prince of the air in the movements of their souls.
The Creator wrote down their victories and placed them in the archives, / so that everyone might learn about the struggle of flesh and spirit.
In this struggle with spirits Job too triumphed, / and he defeated the Accuser in the contest by his endurance.
And so that flesh conquered the prince of the air and the spiritual one was found guilty, / the Creator recorded a man's victory and the defeat of demons.
He wrote the memory of righteous Job in the book of His words, / and called him a "man", so that all might learn that he was a bodily being.
He made his country known and showed his people, that he was an Edomite, / so that all might know that he was earthly, formed from the ground.
He recounted his conduct: blameless and upright, just and perfect, / and greatly honouring his Lord's word in simplicity of soul.
He recalled his possessions and the greatness of his wealth, how he prospered on earth, / yet he was not distracted by his possessions towards earthly things.
He showed the fair crowns of his sons, ten in number, / and love for his children did not dull in him the love of his Lord.
He praised and extolled his care for his children, / how by sacrifices he made atonement for each of them, in case they had sinned.

Because of Job He brought in the account of the love of the just, / that they come at all times to pray [?] the Just One.
There came, it says, a day, as the sons of God were wont, / and they came to stand before God in simplicity of soul.
He brought in the account of the Accuser who came with them / and stood among them before God, but not to pray.
Two opposite things from two sides the Creator revealed: / the will of the just man and the Evil One's desire against the just.
It does not say they came in their nature or in visible form, / for created beings cannot see the One hidden from all.
He wished to examine their thoughts, of the just and of the wicked: / why they are always so eager for the gate on high.
The just do not see the Hidden One by their coming, / nor can Satan speak with the Divine Being.
And if the righteous see the Hidden One only in simplicity of soul, / how could the Accuser look upon God?
So it is right that one should not form the meaning from what the words sound like, / but seek within and not stumble over outward things.
In this way, it says, the sons of the Just One came / to pay the vow of simplicity of soul to Him who sees all.
The Evil One came to slander righteous Job, / not to offer sacrifices of love as the righteous do.
He wished to lay bare the scheme of his cunning concerning Job, / teaching us that this is his constant concern against the just.
The Hostile One [?] saw how great righteous Job's wealth was, / and the envious one was troubled that he prospered and flourished on earth.
The envious one heard of the fame of his conduct, blameless and upright, / and the voices of all who recounted Job's works goaded him.
The Accuser was lashed by the Creator's voice, / which proclaims at all times his righteousness and blamelessness.
The goodness of his works and his righteous deeds flew through creation, / and like arrows envy pierced the Accuser because of his good deeds.
A zealous fury kindled that envious one: / "What is this, that he has good conduct as well as possessions?"
The Accuser was scorched in the fire of wrath, / so that by these means he might bring his hidden cunning into the open.
He bound up a secret within himself and devised a scheme, / so that the Accuser might be able to overthrow the works of Job.

In this way, it says, he came before God / to slander the just Job as one who was not righteous.
He spoke and said this to himself, not to the Hidden One: / "I have gone round the earth and spread my nets to hunt mankind.
"Job alone has cut my nets and broken my snares, / and has not been entangled in the traps and knots of iniquity.
"He prospers on earth, his body is healthy, his mind is resolute, / and the goodness of his fair deeds shines in the four corners of the world.
"His Lord's sign does not permit me to approach and test him, / for like an athlete he is clothed and armed with the strength of His help.
"The Creator's power holds me back from approaching him; / had it not, I would long ago have made him suffer like everyone else.
"But who will give me the opportunity to strike him through his possessions, / so that everyone may learn that he is of mortal stock, clothed in sufferings?
"In his prosperity his mind is healthy along with his limbs, / but if his possessions were afflicted he would grow slack.
"Poverty and want have not humbled him, / and that is why he does not stumble into grumbling in his words.
"Death has not snatched from him the beloved offspring [?] of man; / if grief for his children broke him, he would be filled with outcries."
The Evil One accused Job in his prosperity, / saying that his wealth, not his will, had woven him crowns of victory.
The Creator revealed the schemes he had devised against the righteous man / through what He wrote: that He questioned him as though He did not know.
The Creator did not question the Evil One in order to learn his way, / nor did the Rebel ever see or speak with the One who knows all.
With such words the Creator is accustomed to condescend, / and He always questions His creatures as though He did not know.
He asked Adam, "Where are you, Adam?" while He saw him, / and He asked Cain, "Where is your brother?" while knowing where.
He made His voice heard in anger at Sodom: "I will go down and see / whether they have done altogether according to the report that has come to me."
Here He asked the Evil One where he had come from, / teaching us that he goes about on earth and leads mankind astray.
By the question He wished to examine the Evil One's cunning, / how the Accuser is always scheming against the righteous.
"Have you set your heart on my servant Job?" He revealed His thought:

"that there is none like him, blameless and upright and honouring me."
The Evil One answered the Creator, though not with an audible voice; / Scripture wished to write down for us his cunning scheme through his reply.
"You, it says, have shielded his possessions with a hand of mercy, / and by your help he has gained health and prospers on earth.
"By your power his name shines in creation as a blameless man; / take away your help and see, he will be reproached by everyone.
"By your power his name shines in creation as a blameless man; / take away your help and see, he will be reproached by everyone.
"A garment of mercy is spread over Job as a covering; / lift your right hand and see, the ugliness of his soul will be exposed.
"The gold of your word is plated over the counterfeit metal of his ugly soul, / and because of it his hidden bronze passes as though it were gold.
"Give me leave to test him by the loss of his goods, as in a furnace, / and I will expose the counterfeit of his slack soul, that he is not genuine.
"In his prosperity his mind is healthy and does not slacken; / in the abundance of his goods his spirit is lofty, as if he were genuine.
"He is of mortal stock, clothed in sufferings, formed from dust, / and if the river of my wiles passes over him, his dwelling will crumble away.
"Open the door for me to enter in to him by my subtlety, / and I will stun him with evil tidings, and his heart will tremble.
"There is no mortal who is not grieved at the loss of his goods, / and no sufferer who does not slacken at evil news."
These were the things the Accuser was thinking about him; / that insolent one was not answering or speaking with his Lord.
The force of the words is recorded in the Scriptures as it happened, / but the Hidden One never spoke with the Rebel.
By a sign He gave the Evil One leave in hidden movements, / just as He deals with the spirits when they are sent out.
He revealed the sign to the Accuser subtly: / "Behold, I hand over to you all that Job has acquired on earth."
The Rebel saw that the Good One had let go of His own household servant, / and he gathered his forces as if for battle against Job.
The insolent one supposed it was his possessions that made him bold, / and by the loss of his goods he sought to weaken the building of his soul.
He did not know, troubled as he was by envy against the just, / that the sound of loss does not disturb Job's simplicity of soul.

He looked on him as a sufferer, slack of mind, / and did not know that his sufferings were made strong by his endurance.
For he does not examine the hidden things of the heart as the Creator does, / nor search out the thought of the soul as the One who knows all.
Had he been granted to know before the struggle that he would surely be defeated, / he would not have gone down to the hard battle with the righteous man.
Without knowing, he armed himself and entered the battle, / and began to shoot the arrow of his wrath at the just man's possessions.
There came, it says, a day on which Job's children were gathered, / and the Evil One's messenger brought news that a raiding band had fallen upon them.
A messenger came to the righteous man, his voice urgent, / to stun the steadfast heart suddenly with hurried news.
"Raiders, it says, fell on us and carried off the oxen with the she-asses, / and the ploughmen and herdsmen died in fierce violence."
The Evil One contrived a pretext to deceive under the name of raiders, / and showed demons as if they were captors who fell upon them and carried off the spoil.
"I alone escaped from the raiders who fell upon us, / and I have come to report what happened without mercy."
And while the first was still finishing the news of the raiders who had fallen, / another arrived bearing news of the flocks that had perished.
"Fire from on high fell from heaven like lightning, / and burned up the flocks and the shepherds in a blaze.
"I alone was left there to bring the news, / that the Creator has not dealt justly with your possessions.
"Your Lord has repaid your righteousness with evil ruin, / bringing down fire and consuming the flocks without pity."
O the cunning that laid snares and hid them, / so that they would not be noticed by one who walks blamelessly!
He stirred up the air, gathered fire and burned the flocks, / and set out to make it seem that Job's Lord had dealt unjustly.
"He, it says, sent down His fire and it burned up the flocks, / and He took no account of the pure sacrifices you used to offer."
He had scarcely finished the news of the burning of flocks and shepherds / when another came, bearing news of the camels that had perished.
"The Chaldeans, it says, formed three bands on three sides, / carried off the camels and killed the men, and I alone am left."

Three arrows the Rebel shot with three tidings, / and not one [?] pierced Job's armour.
Three grievous reports he cast into his ears, / and his simplicity of soul was not troubled by the Evil One's [?].
Three times he changed the affliction and struck him with three reports, / and no bitterness at all broke out in Job's body.
Three times he put him to the test in the furnace of trial, / and showed how bright the beauty of the gold of his soul was.
He carried off the oxen, burned the flocks and took the camels: / three nets, and Job cut through them with ease.
Three times the champion of iniquity came down to the contest, / and from all three he came away ashamed, without victory.
His wiles proved futile against the blameless man, / and he was not entangled in the snares of his cunning.
The Accuser was defeated in the three contests he waged, / so he changed weapons and renewed the battle to win at last.
That envious one was scorched in the fire of his wrath, / because by these means the athlete was not shaken into grumbling.
The zeal of his anger inflamed his bitterness, / and he burned to add his fire against Job's children.
After the news of the camels that perished he brought fresh news, / bitter to hear, overturning love and troubling the soul.
"Your sons, it says, the seven of them with their sisters, were feasting in delight, / gathered in concord at the eldest brother's house, as was their custom.
"A fierce wind blew from heaven without warning, / shook the foundations of the house, and it fell and buried them.
"The roof fell and buried all ten of them, / and mingled their blood with their cups on their couches."
The Rebel put on a mask of pity to deceive Job, / and like a friend presented himself as he told the news of his sons.
"Such a thing, it says, has never happened among the righteous, / nor has the Good One ever paid such a reward to one who loves Him.
"Towards you, Job, the Creator has overturned the order of His mercies, / and mercy did not restrain the anger He has brought upon your possessions.
"It was not enough for Him to burn your flocks and carry off your camels; / He poured out His wrath on your heirs and killed them."

"The Creator did not deal justly in wronging your labours; / even if others had sinned, could He have [?] your children?
"If His love for you is genuine, why has He neglected you? / And if He repays works justly, why has He wronged you?"
O the cunning, for which the sword of man was not enough, / and which began to pour the gall of its anger upon the Creator!
"He, it says, blew a wind of anger and killed your children, / and the One who helps you seeks to afflict you through your heirs."
Through the battle over his sons the Rebel supposed he would make him suffer, / that love for his children would overpower him and bring forth grumbling.
The Accuser kept this hard battle for the end, / for he knows that human love is bound up with one's children.
Three battles the Rebel waged with the righteous man, / and in the fourth he spent his arrows and stood there ashamed.
On this struggle his hope hung, and he was waiting / for a cry of lament to be heard just once, so that he might defeat Job.
But the desire of his soul did not come to fulfilment, / nor did that blameless man give him the satisfaction of a cry of lament.
O athlete of righteousness, how steadfast he was, / and how he was not loosened by the wiles of the enemy!
O mortal clothed in limbs, who conquered sufferings! / O flesh that took up battle with a spiritual being!
O son of Adam, dust of the earth, who forgot his nature, / and in whom love for his children did not dull the love of his Lord!
O mind joined to the sufferings of mortality, / which was not loosened into grumbling by the suffering of his sons!
O adamant, which the Evil One hewed with harsh blows, / and which was not softened by grievous reports!
It was not that the mortal forgot his nature in the sufferings he bore, / nor that he did not grumble because he hated the love of his sons.
For he did feel the sufferings of his sons and his possessions, / but he was comforted by the love of his Lord and did not slacken.
Job weighed love against love like one who discerns, / and the love of his Lord's affection outweighed the love of his sons.
He grieved greatly over his possessions, yet did not grumble; / he suffered over his children, and soothed his suffering with the love of his Lord.
He tore the robe spread over his body and shaved his hair, / but he did not tear his heart by division against his Creator.

"Naked I came out when I was born," said the just man, / "and naked I shall return, without covering, as I came.
"My God gave to me and has taken back; His will has power. / May His name be blessed by His creatures for all that He has made."
The blameless man paid a voice of thanksgiving in return for his heirs, / and set his Lord's seal upon his endurance, neither complaining nor grumbling.
The struggle over the death of his sons and his possessions was over, / and the Accuser began to renew another battle, for the ruin of his body.
He was tormented by the fire of his anger against Job: / "What deep pit can I hide for one so nimble?
"It will be a great sorrow if the dust of Edom defeats me, / and the son of the trodden earth mocks and laughs at a spiritual being.
"I carried off his possessions, and he strengthened his soul with trust in his Lord; / I killed his sons, and he blessed the name of Him who gave and took.
"Now I know that he does not slacken through outward things, / and the pain of his children does not touch him as his own person would.
"It is now the temple of his body that I must approach and overthrow, / for if he does not suffer in his limbs he will not slacken."
These were the wicked plans he was devising against him, / to bring into the open the desire of his cunning that he longed for.
The Creator revealed his hidden cunning through what He wrote: / that he too came with the righteous before God.
The sign laid bare the scheme of his cunning through questioning, / and he betrayed himself by saying, "I have gone round the earth."
"Have you set your heart on my servant Job?" He made him hear, / "that he is blameless and upright, and there is none like him who honours me.
"He has not slackened from righteousness and blamelessness, / and you have incited me to destroy the good servant at your hands."
Cunning replied to the hidden sign that came from the Creator: / "It is not his own skin that has been struck by the arrows of my blows.
"All, it says, that a man has he will give to save his life, / for a man loves his own life alone above everything.
"And if you wish to learn this," answered the insolent one, / "stretch out your hand and strike him a little, and see, he will deny you.
"And if you strike his limbs with the rod of your hand, / he will stand before your face and blaspheme you without shame."
He who knows all saw into the desire of the Accuser's soul:

and He gave Job to him, so that he might go down with him to the battle over his body.
"Behold, it says, I hand Job over into your hands," the Hidden One signed to him; / "only his life I do not permit you to take from him."
The Evil One perceived that the Good One had let go of His own household servant, / and he drew his bow and filled it with arrows of the fire of his wrath.
The Evil One went out, it says, and struck Job with grievous sores, / from the top of his body to his feet, without pity.
He poured a foul sore over his body as in a furnace, / and by its fierce boiling purged from him the dross of sufferings.
He spent the arrows of his wrath with the fire he had kindled, / and Job's body was made truly beautiful in the flame.
Two opposing warriors went down to the arena: / the prince of the air, and a bodily man clothed in limbs.
The bodily one conquered the spiritual by the strength of his will, / and the spiritual one was defeated by the body through slackness of soul.
The athlete of righteousness stood in the stadium, / and flesh took up battle with a spiritual being.
The spectators of the contest gathered, the hosts on high, / and marvelled together at the bodily man who conquered the spirit.
O new struggle that came about unexpectedly, / in which the one struck down is rewarded with the crown of victory!
The bodily man was struck by the spiritual one and his body was crushed, / yet in his ruin he took the victory as one who is genuine.
The Rebel tore down the building of his body but built up his soul; / he crushed his limbs but strengthened his movements through endurance.
The Evil One and Job set up a target in the arena: / whoever hits it by his will takes the crown.
The bodily man drew his will towards the target they had set, / while the spiritual one spent his arrows and could not hit the target.
O bow that triumphed and conquered in every contest, / though an earthly man shot it, sitting stripped of his armour!
O mortal of lowly nature, whom demons trampled, / who rose though fallen and cast them under his feet!
O bodily athlete whom spirits seized, / who, heavy of body, rescued his soul from the light ones!
O sailor who steered on the sea in a harsh winter, / whose faith the turbulence of the waves did not sink!

The Evil One stirred up the sea of his body together with his mind, / but he bound the ship fast with the endurance of his soul, so that it would not sink.
Tidings blew against him like tempests, yet he did not slacken; / the pain of his sons' death beat upon him, yet he was not divided.
The Evil One struck the field of his body with a hail of pains, / and he opened his mouth with a voice of praise instead of blasphemy.
The Accuser carried off his possessions to take his heart captive, / but he stored the wealth of his hidden soul within the truth.
Because he did not slacken at the loss of his goods and the pains of his body, / his Lord wove him a crown of victory in return for his afflictions.
Because he trod the path towards righteousness with discernment of soul, / He made of him a path, so that people might walk in the likeness of his works.
Because he took on the target of true victory against the Evil One, / He inscribed his memory like an image within His books.
As a mirror for simplicity of soul He wrote down his memory, / so that each might polish away the ugliness of his soul by the beauties of Job.
In this way the Good One praised the just, / so that by their works they might be an image of hidden truth.
He did not weave earthly praises for His athletes; / He cast upon the earth a zeal among people for righteousness.
In Job's sufferings He opened the arena for contest, / and flesh began to take up battle with spirits.
His victories became like heralds in everyone's ears: / "Be strong, O men, and do not slacken in the sufferings of the body."
Like a trumpet he cries out to everyone about his victory: / "Short is the time, small the pain, and great the reward."
With all and to all he testifies by the sufferings he bore / that the sufferings of this time are not worth the glory to come.
Let Job be like a mirror for our slack souls, / for though he was bodily, in the body's sufferings he conquered the spiritual one.
Let us walk always in the path of his works without grumbling, / and by his endurance let us run straight to the target of our faith.
On Joseph, When His Brothers Sold Him

Homily Forty-[?]
On Joseph, when his brothers sold him; it is suited
to the Passion and is recited on Tuesday.
Responsory:
He who [?]

Love of the righteous has called me to look upon the path of the righteous,
and to walk in mind along the fair road of their way of life.
Love of them has drawn me, as a child is drawn to learning,
[saying,] "Rise, idle one, look upon the company of the diligent."
The fair growth of their way of life has set a goal for me:
that I should show its like through my words, if I am able.
My thoughts are amazed at their spiritual victories,
at how strong they were and did not give way before their oppressors.
I used to search into the nature of those clothed [in flesh]:
how does a despised body conquer and stand firm in its sufferings?
Earthly nature has no power of its own to conquer;
how then did bodily beings prevail in the contest of the spirit?
Flesh cannot win the victory by the strength of its limbs;
who then gave the weak one strength for victory?
The image He formed from the dust and called His image,
He Himself made strength dwell in it against afflictions [?], and it stands firm in its sufferings.
The Lord who made it to be lord over its fellows
gave it strength in its weakness and made it victorious by His strength.
By the strength of divine help the athletes triumphed,
and the Good One gave the strength of His help to their will.
For His own sake He made the children of His house victorious, who loved His love,
and in love He allotted the greatness of His strength to their labours.

He cast a word whose motion is hidden into the motions within them,
and urged them to trade with the silver of His words.
He fixed a denarius for Abraham and Isaac and his son Jacob,
that they might labour spiritually in the vineyard of His love.
Three labourers the Creator chose for the work of His vineyard,
and by their number He revealed the evidence of the name of His Being.
He taught them to labour with Him according to His will,
and they set His silver on the table of the motions of the soul.
They gathered spiritual fruits through their words,
and handed on their labours to their sons, and died, though they did not die.
Abraham handed on his course to Isaac to trade with it,
and Isaac showed the path of his labour to Jacob the chosen.
Jacob brought forth from his members twelve fruits
and offered them as firstfruits to the Most High.
Twelve he begot from the same root of his body,
and while he was even, the heart of the fruits that came from him was divided.
Some of them resembled him and walked in the way of the labour of his toils,
in expectation [?] of the reward named the denarius of life that had been promised.
Joseph laboured spiritually after the pattern of his father,
and stamped himself with the stamp of the Spirit, to contend.
In the rank of the Spirit the son of Rachel desired to serve,
and like his fathers he was like them in his love toward the Creator.
In them he took his likeness in running his course toward righteousness,
and in their paths he trod in the search of faith.
Love set before him a goal for spiritual labours,
and he leaned in hope toward the expectation of things to come.
By faith he was strengthened as by armour,
and in his mind the sword of his Lord's word was girded on.
His begetter too saw him armed in his own likeness,
and poured out love and anointed him with tender mercies, that he might grow still mightier.
With mercies he anointed him, as with oil, to take hold of the contest,
and he overcame the sufferings of the body's desire by the love of his Lord.
Why then did the righteous man divide his love among his offspring,
and anoint one with the oil of love more than his fellows?
Why did he break apart the harmony of love that is set in nature,
and cast envy among the twelve fruits of his womb?
Why did he honour one member and call him his own,

when the whole body of his offspring's make-up was his own?
Why did he tear apart the bond of mercies that is equal,
and to one bequeath an overflow of love that surpassed his brothers?
"One is the nature, O righteous one, and one the offspring,
and one the image that your Maker fashioned in the potency of your seed."
"That nature is one I know, and my nature bears witness;
but the will of the soul is not the same as [nature's] ordering.
It is the will of the soul that alters love that is equal,
and it causes one to be hated and one to be loved.
A great power of discernment is set in nature,
and leads it like a bridle wherever it wishes.
The strength of our will compels love by the strength of its will,
and draws it like a tow-rope to the haven of peace.
This power hinted to me in secret, with discernment:
'Look carefully and see a nature that is equal and divided:
equal in its nature, for the nature is one, and the image of its fashioning,
but torn and divided is the will of its soul through its freedom.'
It is master, then, of its will, in so far as it is rational,
and by its freedom it chooses and rejects whatever it wishes."
The righteous man's love for his offspring revealed and made plain to me
that the discernment within us is master over motions and desires.
The love of righteous Jacob was not divided and torn;
it was the strength of [his sons'] will that drew his love, not his own preference [?].
It was the unevenness of his offspring's wills that tore his love apart,
and he loved and hated by the discernment of his soul's will.
He cast zeal into the minds of his offspring toward righteousness,
that if they became righteous they too would be loved, like Joseph.
Joseph's love made him beloved to his father's will,
and because he loved truth the righteous man loved him more than his brothers.
His love set the youngest of his brothers above his brothers,
and raised him to a hidden rank as the repayment of a reward.
The love he showed to his begetter and his Maker
returned to him a crown of victory woven of mercies.
Nature prompted him to love his father and his Maker,
and by his way of life he repaid God and his begetter.

In equal measure he shared his love, the love set in nature,
and the love of his soul constrained his nature to love greatly.
The love his begetter bore toward Joseph is like
the love of Christ toward John, whom his Lord loved.
Our Saviour too begot twelve, spiritually,
and one of them He honoured in His love more than his fellows.
After the order of Jacob, who begot tribes according to the number of the months,
our Lord also chose disciples for the teaching of mankind.
According to the number of Jacob's sons He arranged them,
that they might match the mysteries of the People for the salvation of the nations.
In the mystery of our Saviour Jacob begot twelve tribes,
and portrayed in figures the twelve whom Christ chose.
He was like our Head in his love toward Joseph,
whose love prevailed toward the will that loves love.
In the love for his son he traced the type of the Bridegroom's beloved,
for He too loved one of His offspring, in the mystery of John.
Love made chaste Joseph beloved by his father;
love also raised the apostle above his fellows.
Joseph's love drew his father after his love,
and revealed and made plain that it is love that repays love with love.
In Joseph, then, let whoever asks for mercies look:
because he loved his Lord, love repaid him more than his own.
His begetter too for this reason loved him greatly,
because he saw that the love of his soul was bound to his Maker.
He loved him much more than his brothers, and stirred them to zeal,
that they might run to the hidden door, so that He would love them.
And though there is one Father and one Creator of body and soul,
the will of one member held fast [?], and the many went astray.
Joseph was eager and constant at all times at the hidden door,
that love and mercies might return to him as the reward for his labours.
With love and mercies his love was yoked in the yoke of the Lord,
and in his begetter he honoured the word of the Hidden One.
He took thought for his father's honour; he repaid him
for his love with the love that always repays the one who sets it in order.
He went ahead early with the will of his soul, before the Law

which after a time was to lay down the warning of its words.
It is clear, then, that the Law did not teach the righteous;
rather they were a law for the work of truth.
Well did the herald of the word of truth also explain
that the Law was laid down for the wicked, not for the righteous.
For the righteous, from the first, their minds were a law,
and they showed the path of the Law by their way of life.
The nature of discernment comes before all laws;
it is the great one that writes and spells out rationality.
Nature wrote a book for Joseph upon his mind,
and he read it with his understanding and interpreted the book of the worship of the Hidden One.
Two things he learned from the law of discernment:
that a man owes the repayment of love to his Lord and to his father.
Two things he too repaid in his love, as one who discerns:
the worship of love to the Lord who made him and to his begetter.
And when his father saw that he was eager to repay it as a debt,
he too repaid him the reward of love, according to his will.
He loved him in secret, when he saw that he was hidden in his love,
and honoured him openly, because his feelings were chaste along with his will.
With garments he adorned his body for his will's sake,
and in his thoughts he adorned his soul, full of love.
The Creator too loved him much more than his brothers,
for He saw that the love of his soul was bound to His hiddenness.
From His hiddenness He gave him strength to see hidden things,
and strengthened his motions to search into things to come.
The Hidden One interpreted the sign of His power in the motions of the soul,
and made it plain openly by the power of His hiddenness, which reveals all.
In his dream He revealed to him his exaltation and the humbling of his brothers,
and showed him in secret that his staff would be raised above those who hated him.
Joseph, then, saw a dream in secret and told his brothers,
and taught them about his rule, that he would govern and judge.
"I saw," he said, "that I and you were at work on the land,
while we bound sheaves in the field for the season's food.
I saw that my sheaf rose up and stood upright,
and I saw your sheaves bowing down to me."

By the sheaves He showed him the famine that would come and press hard on all,
and by their bowing, the subjection of his brothers, who bowed before him.
Eleven sheaves bowed their heads and did homage to one,
and a hand stretched out, ruled over them and prevailed over them.
O wonder, that through sheaves it was shown,
that famine and plenty, twelve, were being signified!
They are the number of the eleven months that sinned and were brought low,
and the hidden sign raised them up through one rich one [?].
O provider, who while he provided was asked for provision
through the twelve sheaves that bowed in entreaty and went hungry!
They are a type of nature, which is all equal and all divided,
and from which both famine and provision come, lacking and complete.
One is the nature, and wholly equal in all that it possesses,
and wholly divided through the will of its discernment.
From one spring the members flowed like streams;
eleven ran dry, and one overflowed in the flow of his love.
Like the Gihon he showed forth his stream in the land of Egypt,
and gladdened [it] with the drink of his rationality, more than drought [could parch it].
The Gihon ran dry, which iniquity had held back from its great flow,
but Joseph made a sweet abundance flow by means of food.
By the dream he saw he made both things plain to his brothers,
that they might be abashed [?] by the proof given through the sheaves.
Yet the disclosure of the mysteries only added to the wickedness of their inclination,
and they did wrong to the hidden things he had revealed through the sheaves.
Joseph's brothers were not helped by what he disclosed,
but added bitterness of soul against his dreams.
They hated him the more for his beauty, like envious men:
why, along with his beauty, was his mind also so excellent?
And the more they hated him for his exaltation,
the more his Lord made him a spring pouring forth the power of hidden things.
He turned again and revealed in him, in a vision, a second, different mystery,
which cries out in its power like a herald concerning his rule.
"I saw," he said, "a dream"—he repeated it, humbly, to his father and his brothers—

"and lo, the luminaries, the sun and the moon, were bowing before me.
With the orb of the great sun and the lovely moon
I saw eleven stars yoked in the yoke of homage to me."
His begetter saw that his dream was a sign of the name of his rule,
and marvelled greatly at how far beyond him was what it showed.
He revealed to his son the power hidden within the parable:
"I," he said, "and your mother and your brothers will come and bow down before you."
In great amazement the righteous man stood at what he heard,
and pondered much lest envy should hinder love.
He searched his brothers' will like a man of knowledge,
lest bitterness and the wickedness of deceit should settle upon the dreams.
And as closely as Jacob searched, in the manner of a righteous man,
so cunningly did the nature of his sons contrive deceit in secret.
The insolent envied and greatly hated the blameless soul,
because they saw he was raised up through spiritual revelations.
He grew up with his brothers, and his brothers with him,
and though he was even, the heart of his brothers was divided and torn.
He was bound in love to his father and to them,
but they, children of deceit, uprooted the building of love.
He and his father held firm in agreement about their needs,
but they tore down the love of him and of his begetter.
A blinding envy blinded the brothers of Joseph,
and they did not see the light of righteousness hidden in his dreams.
Envy became to them like a veil before their eyes,
and they did not perceive that the purpose of the dream was a help to them.
Envy is a dead thing that has died yet not died, that lives yet does not live:
dead to truth and alive to sin; it is not, and it is.
What evil is so evil, and thrives on its own evil?
And what is so bereft of light as its folly?
Jacob called and said to his chaste son Joseph,
"Come, go and see how your brothers and the flock are faring."
The blameless one hastened, as his begetter had commanded,
and with his limbs his mind too, in simplicity.
They saw him coming, the righteous one, humble and generous,
and whetted the sword of their minds to kill him.
"Here," they said, "comes the dreamer of dreams," the insolent answered;

"come, let us remove him from life, and his dreams will come to nothing.
Let his life be silenced, so that he muses no more on glories,
lest he reign and enslave us, as he saw."
The blameless one approached and greeted those full of wrath,
and they did not return him the manner befitting the love of brothers.
They received from him provisions for a time, for the life of the time,
and sealed his body with the treachery of death, to kill him.
He greeted them in love and mercy and kissed them,
but they did not return to him the greeting he gave them, as was fitting.
They ate the bread their father had sent them,
and began to contrive crafty schemes to make away with him.
When all his brothers saw him, thus they said:
"Look, here comes the dreamer of dreams, who makes mysteries known.
This is the heir whose fragrance is sweet before his begetter;
let us keep mourning for him among our [?] and before his father.
This is he who is to become lord and enslave us,
and, as to a lord, we shall bow before him and serve him."
Joseph's brothers took counsel, saying,
"By these schemes we will drive him from his father's house."
And when Joseph saw that his brothers were downcast,
he drew near to them and asked them, "What grieves you?
Has a lion fallen upon the herd and carried off a beast?
Or have wolves broken into the flocks and scattered them?
Has a raiding band cut off some of the sheep and driven them away,
and because this has happened today, you are grieved?
Do not grieve, if this is the thing that has happened,
for in our father's house there is great wealth beyond measure."
With contempt the contemptible burst out at this,
and fiercely they returned him a wicked word:
"Son of a thief, why do you speak galling words?
For because of you ten men are vexed.
Call to them, those dreams you have dreamed all your days,
and let them rescue you from the troubles that have come upon you."
Judah ran and drew a sword to kill him,
and Reuben made ready an empty pit for him to be hidden in.
His brothers threw him in, as he wept and lifted up his voice:

"What have I done, and what is my folly, that you repay me so?"
Joseph prayed at the bottom of the pit and called to his Lord:
"Judge in truth, judge righteously between me and my brothers."
Joseph looked to the height and the depth, and there was none to help,
and lo, merchants were made ready for him by God.
Righteousness itself brought them to the mouth of the pit,
that they might come upon it there and be amazed on his account.
The merchants approached the mouth of the pit and were struck with wonder;
the wicked ran to the mouth of the pit to deal with them [?].
They brought Joseph up out of the pit and led him away,
and began to seek company on the road, that he might go with them.
The wicked approached the merchants and asked them,
"If you want to buy a slave, there is one with us:
a young boy, fair to look on and very pleasing,
wise, and knowing how to serve both traveller and townsman.
We will bring him and you shall see him; fix his price;
give us the price and lead away the slave, and go in peace."
The insolent ran upon the humble one to sell him,
just as the Jews too ran upon our Saviour.
Joseph's affair greatly resembles that of our Saviour,
for, though he had committed no folly, the wicked hung him upon the wood.
Cruelly the insolent treated that blameless one,
and without pity they dragged him and brought him to the merchants.
The merchants saw Joseph's beauty and desired him,
supposing that they wanted a great deal of silver for him.
The insolent answered, "We want twenty of silver for him,
and that is not much; it is but a day's food. Give, and take him."
When the boy Joseph saw that they had settled this upon him,
and that he was being made a stranger to his father's house and his brothers' house,
he knelt and bowed down before his brothers, weeping,
and his tears poured down upon their shoulders as he begged them:
"Let me die here, by your hands, at this time,
and let me not be sold and become a slave in the house of strangers.
I adjure you by the God of the house of Abraham,
do not send me to places I do not know.
For Jacob's sake I grieve, that I am leaving him,

and his old age, and my youth with it, cry out to you.
Reuben, firstborn, beloved heir, have pity on your brother,
and do not bring our aged father down to Sheol in grief.
Simeon, hear me, and have pity on your brother at this time;
let me not be sold and become a slave to the house of strangers.
Judah, valiant one, your mother's lion's whelp, let your compassion shelter me,
and do not afflict our aged father with bitter grief."
Reuben dragged him, Simeon pushed him, Judah shouted at him,
and Naphtali made ready and brought fetters for his hands.
Zebulun said, "There is no need for many words;
bind the boy and hand him over and be rid of him."
When the boy Joseph saw that there was no more to be said,
he raised his eyes to the height and spoke thus:
"Who will make me like a bird light of wing,
that I might fly and alight and see the face of that old man?
Who will give me a voice of thunder, stronger than all,
that I might cry out from where I am, and our father hear the voice of my thunder?
Who will go and fall upon the ear of that old man:
'See, the son of your vows is being torn apart in foreign lands'?
Who will bring this great outrage before the Most High [?],
and show that tunic before Jacob?"
The wicked took Joseph's tunic and slaughtered a kid,
and rolled the tunic in the blood and sent it to his father.
When that tunic was brought in before Jacob,
they said to him, "Take it and examine the tunic.
Whether it is your son's or your beloved's we do not know,
for we found it in the wilderness as we wandered.
We know nothing about Joseph's tunic,
and if it is his, do not be angry with us for bringing you the news."
Jacob saw Joseph's tunic dyed with blood,
and grief seized him, and he wailed and wept bitterly:
"Who has broken the staff of my old age, his father's support,
so that from now on I fall and there is no one to hold me up and help me?
Who has quenched his father's lamp, whose light was wonderful,
so that in its absence I stumble as in darkness?

Who has plucked the lovely blossom whose fragrance was sweet,
and woven for me a crown of thorns for all my days?
Who has decked for me a bridal chamber of mourning at this time,
so that instead of dancing, see, I lament and weep?"
He tore his garments and put on sackcloth and sat in mourning,
and spread Joseph's tunic out before him and gazed upon it:
"How to think of your going out I do not know,
and by what schemes you were parted, son of my vows, from your father's house.
If it was a lion that broke you on an unsafe road,
why was your death not made plain along with your tunic?
Perhaps a raiding band parted my beloved from his father's house;
but it has not been heard that a raiding band came to this place.
Perhaps envy parted my beloved from his father's house;
there is trust in righteousness, which will require what is its own."
Jacob sent and brought his sons from the flock,
and asked them about Joseph, what had happened to him.
He shook and laid bare his white hairs before their eyes,
weeping, pleading and begging them:
"I adjure you by the God who does not lie:
what happened to Joseph, who came to the pasture?"
They answered him, making it up deceitfully,
and with oaths they denied it to him: "We do not know."
Wickedly they wept before their father,
and old Jacob believed them that they did not know.
Jacob raised his eyes and looked to the height,
and prayed before God and besought Him:
"You, O God, who answer the righteous according to Your goodness,
answer my beloved and keep him wherever he is.
Spread Your wing over him, that he may be hidden in it from harm,
and while I still live, grant me to see his very face.
Before I go down to the departed, grant me to see him,
and I will lay my lips upon his lips, and then I will die."

The merchants went into the land of the Egyptians, and Joseph with them, / rejoicing and marvelling because of him. / "We have found peace on our road since the day / this slave came into our hands to travel with us. / The works of the Lord go along with this boy, / and because of him we are kept from harm. / He is no slave—this we truly know— / and it is not right that he should serve as a slave." / The merchants went before Joseph and begged him: / "Eat, Joseph, and drink with us, and put away your mourning. / Do not be grieved over the sale by which you came to us, / for you are a son of free men; we do not dispute it." / Potiphar came out and saw Joseph with the merchants, / and he longed for his lovely beauty, and began to say: / "If this boy is a slave, give him to me, / and I will pay a great price for him with great joy." / The merchants said, "If he is willing to go with you, / who would stop him? For twenty pieces of silver he will go with you." / The merchants took Joseph's price from Potiphar, / and came up to him, kissing him and pleading with him: / "Do not be grieved over this, young Joseph, / and do not be vexed that we took your price, for we are in need." / Joseph said, "O merchants, go in peace; / may the Lord bless your journeys for ever." / It was Righteousness that called Potiphar out of his house / to come and buy a slave who would rule over the Egyptians. / Potiphar led the slave out of the market / and handed over his whole house into his hand to manage. / He gave him charge of all the treasure he had at his command: / "See to it, and manage it wisely as you think fit." / He hurried to tell the members of his household, saying to them, / "Come out and see the lovely slave we have acquired. / His appearance is fair, his complexion wonderful, his face radiant; / he is like the rose and the lilies in the days of Nisan." / The foolish woman saw Joseph's beauty and longed for him,

and like fire, lust for his body consumed her. / Like a lioness she sprang upon the innocent one, / to tear his body and his soul with her wantonness. / She painted her eyes with stibium that gleamed brightly, / braided her hair with skill, and stood before him. / She smoothed her body, put on her perfume, hung herself with gold, / and stood before him shamelessly in her wantonness. / She dressed in fine linen, with bracelets and three necklaces, / and ran to meet him, caressing him and saying to him: / "Look at me, Joseph, for I am beautiful and very lovely; / I am desirable—forget your people and your father's house." / She invited him to eat, but he had no wish to eat with her; / she mixed wine and set out meat, but he cast aside her wantonness. / When she called and he did not answer her, she stared at the ground; / when she spoke to him and he gave no reply, she shut her mouth. / When she gazed at him, his gaze was lifted to the heights; / when she beckoned to him, he bowed his head and went out to his work. / He came in and went out, set down and took up, and she was at his side, / and could not bear to be parted from him even a little. / That shameless woman began to speak, / unashamed of her wantonness before those who heard: / "Joseph, do not despise me, for I am your mistress, / and do not be vexed that you are our slave beyond dispute. / If you will be persuaded and do my will as I tell you, / I will make you lord of my possessions and my property. / If you are afraid of Potiphar, the master of the house, / I will make another plan for you, and you need not fear. / I will send him poison and kill him outright, / and you shall be my husband and lord, and my heir as well. / I will tell you another secret, between me and you: / I have a great treasure beyond measure." / Joseph heard this speech and his soul trembled, / and he began to shake out his garments and cry out despite himself: / "Wealth for which blood is shed is no gain to me, / and I will not acquire unjust property that is not holy.

Wealth of iniquity is to be renounced; it beggars those who pursue it, / and treasures paid for with blood are not holy. / I will not plot a wicked deceit against an innocent man, / nor defile the pure bed of marriage. / I have a glorious King who dwells on high, / and if He sees me do this, He will surely despise me." / Joseph lifted up his eyes and looked toward the height, / and prayed before God and entreated Him: / "You brought me up out of the pit into which Reuben cast me, / and You saved me from the sword that was sharpened. / You brought me into the land of the Egyptians by Your great might; / rise up for me now and help me against the Egyptian woman." / Joseph went into the chamber to pray, / and the foolish woman went in after him and held the door shut. / She embraced him and kissed him, weeping before him and pleading with him: / "If you love me, take care—do not reject me, son of the Hebrews! / If you will not be persuaded and do my will in what I tell you, / I will shut you up in the great pit of the prison. / But if you are persuaded and bow your head to my words and my urging, / I will make you head and lord over all Egypt." / Joseph looked to the height and the depth, and there was none to help, / and lo, help was made ready for him by God. / He shook her off and threw her to the floor [?] with the strength of his body; / he let go of her, flung her aside, opened the door and escaped from her. / The lioness saw that her prey had escaped her, / and she began to roar with choking cries within the chamber. / The slaves and the freeborn heard her loud voice, / and all gathered and asked her, "What has happened to you?" / That shameless woman began to speak, / unashamed of her wantonness before her companions: / "Look at the slave who was bought, whom the master of the house brought in! / He took me for a harlot and wanted to make sport of me. / I was sitting modestly in the chamber, / and he opened the door to come in upon me and disgrace me. / I saw him open the door to come in upon me, / and I began to scream, and I howled at him like a jackal. / When the deceitful slave saw that he was caught,

he left his garment, opened the door and went out like an innocent man. / See how this slave has repaid a good master / for the honour and the whole house he entrusted to his hands!" / Potiphar said, "Who is your witness that he did this? / For I do not wish to judge him unjustly. / His garment is in your hands, and here you are crying out—you are the guilty one; / I do not wish to believe you, for you are not truthful." / Yet the Egyptian heard his wife's words, grew jealous and was enraged, / and he shut Joseph up in the prison like a vile man. / The righteous one fell into the cruel pit that deceit had dug; / his body sank, but his love did not sink beneath the cruelty of his sufferings. / Joseph entered the house of darkness and gladdened its inmates, / and lightened for them the weight of their sufferings and their grief of soul. / Joseph alone did not deserve this lot, / and it was for nothing that blind envy imprisoned him, without consolation. / The chaste one was imprisoned and dwelt among the wicked, / like our pure and spotless Saviour among the thieves. / Two eunuchs, servants of the king, were with the righteous one, / like the thieves on the right and on the left. / The servants had been thrown into prison because they had offended, / like the thieves whose own deeds crucified them. / Joseph alone was imprisoned there without guilt, / a type of the Giver of life to all, whom envy crucified though He had not offended. / Both Egyptians dreamed, on the same night, different dreams: / in one, deliverance, and in the other, death at the top of the gallows. / They were downcast beyond measure by the dreams they had seen, / and the Hebrew went in to cheer them with the wisdom of his words. / He saw that they were sad at the memory of the dreams they had seen, / and from their faces he perceived the pain of their thoughts. / He questioned them as though he did not know, though he was not ignorant, / and he learned from them, and taught them by the spirit of revelation. / In the pouring of the vine and its wine he saw the cupbearer's deliverance, / and Joseph cheered him, as with wine, by the gladness of his words. / For the baker too, in the king's food he saw his end, / and the just one taught him that through food he would become food. / In the three branches, he said, the righteous one portrayed three days,

and in the three baskets three days, of life and of death. / O the Wisdom that lodges what is hidden in the members of His household, / and through their revelation displays the power of its hidden sign! / Joseph's words were fulfilled in deed just as he had interpreted: / the cupbearer lived and the baker died, as their words had said. / The cupbearer forgot the upright one, as an ingrate forgets, / until a dream woke the king, and then he remembered him. / Pharaoh, king of Egypt, saw a dream and was astonished, / and he asked his servants, but they gave him no interpretation of its words. / He saw fat cows on the bank of the river, / lovely and very fine to the eyes of those who looked on them. / Seven fat cows he saw first, / and after them seven that were very ugly. / He saw the lean ones eat up and swallow the fat ones; / they went in and vanished, and nothing was left of their bodies. / Again he saw seven ears of grain growing on the top of one stalk, / and they were fat like the first cows. / At the end of his dream he saw again ears that were blighted, / and their appearance was like that of the lean cows. / He saw ears swallowing ears, food swallowing food, / like cows whose flesh swallowed the flesh of their fellows. / Pharaoh the king was astonished and amazed at the dream he had seen, / for in its bewildering strangeness it surpassed all dreams. / He called the magicians and the soothsayers and asked them, / but the sign hid the power of understanding from their eyes. / The king was grieved and sat in mourning without consolation, / for he saw that the meaning of his dreams had eluded the magicians. / The king's cupbearer saw the king's grief and remembered, / and despite himself began to recall his offence. / The servant disclosed to his master his offence and the dream he had seen, / and told him about the Hebrew who had interpreted his dreams: / "My lord Pharaoh was angry with his servants because they had offended, / and he shut them up in the prison, a house of great suffering. / My companion and I saw dreams full of suffering, / and we brought them to a certain Hebrew, and he interpreted them.

True and good to our ears was the force of his interpretation, / and his word was fulfilled in the events of life and of death." / Pharaoh was roused, as if from sleep, toward the Hebrew, / and urged his ministers to hurry and summon Joseph. / The dream he had seen was drawing him after its meaning, / and like hunger it drove him on toward understanding it. / The son of Ham sent and summoned the son of Shem—the slave summoning the master— / that the blessed one might come and reveal to the cursed the meaning of the riddles. / The son of Abraham went in to the Egyptian and saw that he was downcast, / and with the sound of his words he drove grief of soul from him. / The son of Ham recounted to the son of Abraham the dream he had seen, / and told him too that his magicians had failed to explain his dreams. / Joseph began, by the spirit of revelation, to interpret for him, / and to make the meaning of hidden things shine before his mind: / "Hear, O king," he said, "and learn the power of the Creator's might, / for it is His to show dreams and visions. / It is not mine to reveal the meaning hidden in your dreams; / He has shown me, so that I may teach you the meaning of His hidden things. / Hear the meaning of your dreams from Him, through me as a mediator, / and know and understand that His sign makes wise the members of His household. / The seven cows are years—seven good years— / and the lean ones are seven bad years of famine. / The seven fat ears, too, are years, / and the seven withered by the scorching wind are a famine of seven years." / By the fat cows he revealed plenty, / and by the lean ones that swallowed them he showed famine. / In the same way he portrayed the fat ears also, / which, fine as they were, vanished into the lean ones. / By the ears of the field he signified both plenty and famine, / and taught men that they cannot live except by the Sign. / For if bread gave life by its own nature, / why was its power not the same in plenty and in famine? / Bread does not give life to mortals by its own power; / rather, the Sign gives its power through the means of bread. / Joseph showed the plenty and the famine that were to come / by the power of that Sign which gives life and puts to death by means of causes. / "See," he said, "there will be great plenty," the righteous one revealed,

"and famine will come after the span of years I have named. / As the cows that were lean swallowed the seven, / so the famine will swallow the plenty and make it vanish. / That is why the dream was repeated twice: / He is hastening the matter, which is about to come to pass. / Now let Pharaoh look for a man," said Joseph, / "who knows how to provide in the famine from the plenty." / The Egyptian who wore the crown fell down before the Hebrew;
