/ the son of Ham bowed to the son of Abraham, despite himself. / "There is no man," he said, "wiser or more skilful than you, / and no one knows how to provide as your wisdom does. / You shall be lord and ruler over my house, / and the word of your mouth shall reign and judge slaves and free. / Only in the title of kingship will I be greater than you, / and you shall have authority to govern as you will." / The king of Egypt fulfilled his promise and made him lord, / and adorned him in garments of royal attire like a king's son. / The son of Jacob rode in the chariot of the king of Egypt, / and the son of Abraham began to give orders to the sons of Canaan. / The dreams he had dreamed in his fathers' house were fulfilled in deed, / and his sheaf stood like the sheaf that had raised itself upright. / He received the fulfilment and the riddles of the interpretation of his words: / the plenty and the famine were revealed, as had been promised. / The famine was the cause that fulfilled that voice which came to Abraham: / "Know for certain that the children of your seed will be slaves." / For this the son of Jacob too was sent, / to go down and prepare a wonderful place for the seed of Abraham. / Though his brothers cast him away for evil, as if to evil, / yet it was the Sign, to whom all is revealed, that wrought this. / Evil filled the desire of their thoughts, / but the Lord of all accomplished the purpose of His working. / What He wrought by the hands of Joseph was plain to Him, / and He interpreted it through a member of His household, as one who is wise. / He made famine reign over all the earth, and it held its sway, / and He raised the sons of Abraham above the Egyptians. / The cruel famine forced the sons of Jacob,

and unwillingly they went down to pay the debt of the dreams. / Because they had given the just one no reward for his riddles, / they paid him principal and interest, twice over. / Twice they paid for the showing of his two dreams, / in the stars and the sheaves that had revealed them in mystery. / The Hebrews went down to the Egyptians to buy bread, / and the Righteousness they had wronged in Joseph caught them. / It bound the sellers before its beloved, / and drew the sword whose cruel stroke hung over their necks. / He who had been slain by envy made himself known to his sellers, / yet did not repay them the harm their deeds deserved. / The righteous one put on a stern guise to meet his brothers, / and brought them in as into a furnace to test their words. / "You are spies," Joseph said to the buyers; / "you have come down to spy out the land, not for bread." / "By the life of Pharaoh!" the chaste one swore, and terrified them, / and they trembled and were dismayed, for they had no more hope of escape. / "We are honest men, not wicked," answered the envious ones, / and even as they took refuge in the name of truth, it caught them. / They revealed that they were eleven, and had one father, / "and one," they said, "who was lost, and by his loss the number of the months fell short. / Ten of us came down to buy bread, and one, the youngest, stayed behind; / inquire and see that it is as we have said." / They fell into the snare they had laid with their own words, / and the hidden Sign bound them on every side. / He pressed them on their words, just as they had declared, / and showed that he was a just man who also feared the Lord of all. / "Let it be as you have said," answered the righteous one; / "show proof of your conduct, and you will be set free. / Go, bring me your youngest brother who you say exists, / and I will send you back with your brother to your father. / Leave a pledge to match the charge you have fallen under, / and you, carry bread to the hungry in your houses." / He kept back one of them and bound him in fetters for the full time [?], / and supplied them with silver and bread in their loads. / They turned back from Egypt and came home to their father, / and told him everything that had happened, and what had befallen them.

The righteous one was astonished and amazed at their words, / and he reproached his sons: "Why did you reveal this? / Why did you tell him the number of my children, how many there are, / so that the man will demand of you even the one who was lost?" / They fell silent, but the famine did not relent in its harshness, / and it forced them to return to Egypt against their will. / They took their brother with them as they had promised, so as not to be found liars, / and prepared gifts for Joseph the just, that he might be appeased. / They took of the good things of the land of Canaan, balm and honey, / and double the silver beyond the first, which they had paid and had returned to them. / They went back trembling at what had happened and had held them captive, / lest it be repaid in deeds and destroy them. / They were full of fear as they went, like guilty men, / lest pleading and words should not be enough before the court. / The nearer they came to Egypt, the more they were in anguish, / and their thoughts were thrown into confusion by what had happened. / They reached the place, and the pangs of death came upon them; / they were in anguish and dismay like a woman in labour gripped by her pains. / They prepared their gifts and went in to make their plea before the court, / and brought Benjamin in with them to confirm their words. / Eleven speaking sheaves fell to the ground, / and the dreams the just one had dreamed were fulfilled in deed. / The envious paid, despite themselves, the debt of love, / and fulfilled the mystery of the revealing mystery in the sign of the sheaves. / He spoke with them wisely, as a wise man, / for he saw that deeds had come to match words, plainly before his eyes. / He asked them about their father, whether the just one was alive, / and he saw his brother and said, "Is this the one you spoke of?" / Compassion seized him, but he mastered his nature in order to test them, / and by trial to learn the aim of their thoughts. / He honoured them kindly, as they desired, / and showed them that he knew the order of eldest and youngest. / He ordered his steward to send them off with a show of love, / and to put a cup in the mouth of their loads, and so bring them to distress.

His own cup he ordered to be put in his brother's load, / so that by all these things he might test the love of the deceitful brothers. / They turned back from him rejoicing, like innocent men, / and while they were still rejoicing, a command came running and terrified them, / and mourning wrapped itself about their minds like a garment. / "Why have you repaid the harm of disgrace in return for honour, / and not behaved as befits freeborn sons?" / He searched them as one who did not know how it had come about, / and found the cup where he had put it, with Benjamin. / They turned back weeping, with mourning spread over their heads, / for that mourning had turned their gladness of heart into grief. / They fell down and rolled on the ground, pleading over what had happened, / and confessed and said, "There is no innocence to answer for our guilt." / The righteous one saw the anguish of his brothers and suffered with them, / and could no longer endure the grief that wore away his soul. / For the natural love planted in his nature compelled him, / and his tears became a kind of release for his grief. / He wept for them as much as they had suffered without knowing, / and showed his love in not repaying them their deeds. / Compassion pressed on him like birth pangs before the court, / and he made known to them that he was the one whom deceitful envy had sold. / "I am Joseph, the slave of the envy that was in you, / and lo, the hidden will to which all is revealed has exalted me. / I am the envied one whom deceit drove out from peace, / and lo, the Lord of all has given me peace among a strange people. / I am the limb you cut off from your body; / come, let us be reconciled even now, and be one again. / I am the one who saw eleven sheaves, and one of my own, / and lo, the meaning of my words has been interpreted in your bowing down to me. / Go to Jacob the just: 'Joseph is alive! / Come down quickly, and you too pay the debt of the dreams.' / Go and tell him that the staff that supported him is alive: / 'Come, take in your hand the staff of my very self, and lean on it.' / Go and show him my honour and my authority in the house of the Egyptians, / and give his soul rest in the good harbour of my life."

Go, tell him that my God has made me lord of Egypt, / and established my authority, so that I rule over slaves and free men. / Go, reveal and show him too the hidden power that moves me, / and that the wisdom of the truth of secret things has come to dwell in my mind. / Go, tell him that the famine still has five years to run; / come, provide for yourself, lest you perish, you and all that is yours. / With these words Joseph also comforted his brothers: / “My God has sent me to be the one who feeds you in the famine.” / In this, again, he was urging Jacob his father on, / so that by his coming down he might seal the words spoken to Abraham. / By confessing the prophecy he persuaded his brothers / not to hold back from coming to his love. / He cast on them the fear of the famine and alarmed them, / for there still remained five years of the scourge of famine. / With these words he pressed them to come down to him, / and wrote them on their minds as on tablets. / Pharaoh, king of Egypt, heard of these things that had come about, / and rejoiced greatly at the goodness of the family of the Hebrew. / Then Pharaoh called Joseph and said: Do this: / bring your people and settle them among the good things of my kingdom. / Supply your brothers with provisions and send them to their father's house, / so that he may come and see, and rejoice in your life and your authority. / Joseph's brothers accepted what had come about and consented to it, / and set out for the land where they dwelt, rejoicing. / The true tribes went on and reached their father, / laden with the riches of the sale and the token of peace. / They gladdened him with the gifts that Joseph and King Pharaoh had sent, / and brought him the news that his son was alive and in authority. / He was astonished and amazed at what had happened beyond all expectation, / and he wavered and said: It is a great thing indeed, if it is true. / He saw the wagons that Pharaoh had sent, and his mind was set at rest, / and he took hope that what he had heard would be fulfilled. / Great it is, then, that Joseph is still alive, said the just man; / I will go down and see him, and rejoice in his life before I die. / I will go and give my eyes rest from their sufferings in the sight of his body, / and lay aside my grief through the answer of the words of his mouth.

I will go and pay the debt of the dreams that I owe him, / and render him the homage of love that he saw in the sun. / I will go and see him honored by the house of the Egyptians, / and the promise to Abraham and Isaac will be confirmed again in me. / Israel set out on the road on which the Hidden One had set his father, / and with his offspring he entered the land of Egypt and confirmed the promise. / Father and son saw each other, just man and just man, / and they repaid love and fulfilled the mysteries given through the dreams. / The just man bowed down before the just man, he and his children, / and bent his neck under the yoke of service to his lord, his son. / By the homage paid to Joseph the Creator bowed down crowned heads and sorcerers, / in a mystery of our Savior, who received the homage of love from all. / In this, again, he honored the just man through the homage of his family, / so that no one should be amazed at the homage of all paid to our Head. / In Joseph he taught the homage of all paid to a man, / for cities and peoples alike bow down to the image of a man. / A man the Hidden One was to take, and through him govern all things, / and in his person receive the homage of all. / In this he also portrayed the wonders in the conduct of the just, / so that the truth of its revelation would not seem strange when it was made plain. / He revealed his sacrifice through the sacrifice of the ram that saved Isaac, / that so he too would save his race by the sacrifice of his body. / He showed in Joseph that the homage of all is offered to him. / He portrayed his greatness and sketched his mysteries in the just and in kings, / and displayed it at the end, and in it explained all things, the last and the first. / Who would not marvel at the conduct of the just and at their zeal, / who by their labors searched out the way to the One who Is? / Who would not assent to the mysteries and types embodied in them, / and confess the power that strengthened them for the things to come? / Who would not confess, in keeping with the thought of their minds, / that they believed and loved and hoped, and assented to that for which they waited? / Who would not knock at the door of love by which they entered and reigned, / and reign himself in the likeness of chastity that they showed on earth? / Let anyone who wishes to be chaste look at Joseph, / and see himself in him, so as not to be defiled by the lust of the body.

Let anyone who runs the spiritual race gaze at him, / and throw off the fetters of his bodily senses, so as not to become like a beast. / Let the generation, young people with the rest, take his likeness as their own, / so that the fire in their limbs may be quenched by the vigor of his soul. / With him let them go down into the arena full of sufferings, / so that with him they may go up to the victory and its reward. / Glory to the Lord, who through his love fulfilled and brought to completion / the mystery of the wonders that his servants saw in the name of the One who Is.
On the Flood

Memra 16: On the Flood. / Also by him: the sixteenth memra, on the Flood. / It is recited during the Fast. / Refrain: / Blessed is he who exchanged our dwelling on earth, / and in his goodness gave us a dwelling in heaven. / [?]

Wise and glorious is the Creator, / who out of nothing fashioned all things. / He showed His power in His works, / for He spoke, and they came into being. / His wealth lay hidden in His knowledge / before the fashioning of His creatures; / His love revealed it to His will, / and He poured out His gifts upon all. / In due order He fashioned all of it, / and made nothing lacking; / for since He is perfect in His nature, / His craftsmanship is perfect and complete. / A fixed time was in His knowledge / for when He would create the creatures, / and His providence was hidden / with the hiddenness of His nature. / He revealed His hiddenness in His works, / and showed His power in His fashioning.

And the hosts on high cried out to Him: / “Glorious is the Creator in all that He has made!” / Through the fashioning of His works / He taught the rational beings / that one is the Power who fashioned all, / and nothing exists apart from Him. / He made one body and composed it / of rational beings and silent ones, / and bound His whole creation together / in the composition of the image of Adam. / He made the image a mirror / in which His creatures might look, / that in a visible image they might see / His hiddenness, which cannot be comprehended. / By His image He taught the rational beings / how greatly He loves His creatures; / and by the sentence of judgment on folly / He showed that He loves justice. / He was angry with Adam, who transgressed the commandment, / and He rejected Cain because he killed; / and He showed His love and His justice: / that He chastises, and keeps, and does not destroy. / He showed them, He showed them His justice, / that He hates iniquity and sin; / and He showed them His goodness, / how greatly He loves the penitent. / Like children being led to knowledge, / by the rod of the transgressed commandment / He drew along the simple; / and by suffering and renewal of mind [?] / He taught them what was fitting. / The Merciful One comforted them / through spiritual revelations, / coming down to them / in visions and likenesses. / Through one who made his conduct fair / He turned them toward His love, / and through the hope of his translation / He soothed the bitterness of the embittered. / In Enoch, who was pleasing and was translated, / He showed them His love: / that He did not hate nature, / but iniquity and sin. / He kept the righteous one back in life, / that through him the abolition of death might be proclaimed; / and by his translation He promised life / that would have no end for them. / He showed them His love in Enoch, / for He made him a hope for their [?]; / but by the iniquity of their deeds / they drew Him from mercy to wrath. / In Enoch His justice was at rest, / and He exchanged His wrath for calm; / but by the wickedness of their provocations / they sharpened His sword for vengeance. / The iniquity of men grew great on the earth / like the waters of the deep, / and the whole earth overflowed with sin / before the flood of justice. / They grew hot with the lust of the body / and confounded the order of nature. / Like wild beasts against one another / they gored and wronged one another; / like lustful stallions / they neighed after one another's wives. / Neither did a woman keep to her partner, / nor a man to his wife: / they ran outside the path / in a lust that lusted for excess, / and their thoughts were clothed / in wrong as in brass. / The flood of sin swelled / and wickedness rose up like a mountain, / and the surge of iniquity, like a sea, / hated the peace of humankind. / The cloud of their error spread out / and covered the face of the inhabited world, / and the rays of the light of the mind's eyes / flickered and went out. / They sank in the sleep of iniquity / and did not perceive that they were sinning; / and though their mind did not sleep, / their stirrings sank low together with their limbs.

One alone did not sink / into the depths of iniquity and evil; / for the stirrings of his soul were awake / and chased away the sleep of sin. / Noah alone was pure in his soul, / and did not defile his body with iniquity; / for his stirrings were like oars to him, / and he did not sink in sin. / The storm of the wrongdoers' iniquity / did not trouble the calm of his soul, / nor did he stumble as he ran / in the darkness among the wicked. / The stirrings of his mind became / wings for the weight of his limbs, / and discernment bore him up / above the waves of sin. / And because he kept the calm of his mind, / and his soul was pure of iniquity, / he was found worthy of spiritual revelations / that search out the wickedness of the evil. / In revelations God spoke with him / and bore witness to the purity of his soul, / and disclosed to him that by a flood / He would wash the earth clean of iniquity: / “The wickedness of man has stained / the beautiful garment of creation. / Behold, I will wash it with a flood / and cleanse its filth. / You alone, then, have kept / your thoughts pure of hateful things, / and your mind has not been defiled / by the mire of the earth's iniquity; / for you have not mingled your love with the wicked / in the intercourse of [?]. / You alone will be saved / from the vengeance of justice.” / He revealed and disclosed to the blameless one / the wickedness of the children of his people: / “Behold, justice will wipe away / the filth of your deeds.” / He revealed to him the iniquity of the sons of Seth, / who had mingled with the daughters of Cain, / though they were set apart from one another / by the sentence of the Creator's judgment. / The seed of righteous Seth mingled / with the race of Cain the murderer; / the lofty came down to lowliness / and became partners [?] with the wicked. / The glance of the eyes ensnared / the rational beings and bound them fast, / and the beauty of fair faces / ruined the beauty of their knowledge. / The sons of God, then, saw / that the daughters of men were beautiful; / they desired them and took them, / and begot giants of iniquity. / It was not greatness of stature / that the Creator wished to make known: / it was greatness of iniquity that was written down for us, / for they grew mighty over the first principles [?]. / The beauty of the daughters of Cain opened / the hateful spring of sin, / and drowned the sons of the righteous one / in the flood of bodily lust. / The murderer's daughters mixed the cup / and gave the simple its poison to drink, / and they troubled the mind of the wise / through the [?] of their faces. / The lofty ones forsook their dwellings / and came down to the land of groans. / The iniquity of their deeds went up / and brought justice down to the earth, / for they did not remain near / the beautiful dwelling of Paradise. / The flood of iniquity swept them away, / and wickedness multiplied upon the earth, / and God regretted that He had made man, / for men had corrupted and torn down His ordinances. / Yet it was no regret that overtook Him / who holds the end of all knowledge. / To them He made a voice heard, / that they might turn back from iniquity; / voices full of threats / were spoken to them, / so that perhaps they might wake, / the sleepers sunk deep in sin.

Like a trumpet the Creator's voice / sounded in their ears: / “Behold, I will wipe out from the earth / the men who have confounded My ordinances. / The end has come upon the earth, / and the sentence of wrath has gone forth.” / And He made a voice heard: “No longer / shall My Spirit dwell in man forever.” / Again a second voice spoke / to gentle Noah and said to him / that he should make an ark of timber, / to be hidden in it from the flood: / “Make yourself an ark of wood, / and coat it with pitch, so that it does not sink, / so that it may hold firm against the storms / when waters mingle with waters.” / He showed him its length and its breadth, / how great its measurements should be, / and taught him the division of the decks / and the cells that were needed: / “Make its length three hundred cubits, / and its breadth fifty cubits, / and its height thirty cubits, / with compartments within its decks. / It shall have three decks, / so that every kind may dwell in it: / beasts of the field and cattle, / winged birds, and men.” / How the Lord who bears all / teaches resourcefulness to the righteous! / For though He was able to save him, / He made him wise in the needs of his life. / He could have preserved the blameless one / with the remnant of all that lived, / and it was in His power that Noah be hidden / without any ark at all. / But it was for the repentance of the bold / that the ark was planned, / that by a visible sign they might be reproved / and judge their own deeds. / Through the labor of a silent house / He wished to make the rational beings wise, / so that the living might ask the dead things / why they were being worked upon. / Voiceless things were pressing / the rational beings to turn from iniquity: / “Behold, in our building is proclaimed / repentance, if you are willing.” / Like a herald / the sound of the work on the ark cried out: / “Arise, be rid of the weight of your debts, / you sleepers sunk in sin!” / Many were the voices toward them / from the building of the ark; / but the weight of wickedness stopped / the hearing that lets understanding in. / Noah alone was listening / and awaiting the fulfillment, / while the bold mocked him, / saying that his building was not to be believed. / The blameless one built himself a house / as the command that made him wise directed, / and the revelation spoke with him / that he should prepare provisions for himself: / “Bring in and carry food / for yourself and for every kind.” / And while the command was keeping him, / it taught him to make ready what he needed. / It was not food for fullness / that the righteous one gathered and carried, / for he knew that the food would not suffice / without the command. / On little were they nourished / for sustaining the life of their bodies, / and the command of the Creator's power / kept them alive on little. / Noah, then, did as he was commanded, / and the Creator spoke with him: / “Enter the ark, you and your sons, / and your sons' wives, with your own. / Bring in with you the beasts, / and cattle together with birds, / to keep seed alive on the earth, / that the kinds may inherit in succession. / Bring in males and females,

two by two of the unclean kinds, / and of the clean, seven by seven, / males and females alike.” / The blameless one did not know / how to tell the unclean from the clean, / until the command showed him / through the number of every kind. / It brought in the clean in greater number, / for he would need them when he went out, / since he was permitted to eat flesh / and to offer some of them as a burnt offering. / O command, which gathered the kinds, / the fierce and the wild, / and made them at peace with one another, / and subjected them before Noah! / That command which made them pass / silently before Adam / was the one that subjected and tamed them / to the yoke of the blameless one's word. / Kind upon kind came forward / as the command drew them, / and males and females came, / clean and unclean, and calm. / Bits of iron were put / into the mouths of beasts and silent creatures; / lion and bull were yoked together / under the yoke of the Creator's command. / The winged birds bowed / and came down from the height to the depth, / and doves and hawks ran / to the meeting at the ark's door. / A great peace reigned / at the door of the righteous one's house, / for kinds that devour one another / kissed one another in love. / In Noah was renewed the dominion / that belonged to the honor of Adam's image; / for the kinds that had rebelled against Adam / turned back and were subjected into Noah's hands. / The command went out like a messenger / and gathered them from every place, / and tamed them, so that in harmony / the separate kinds were made at peace. / He set a term of seven days / until the beasts were gathered, / in that order in which He fashioned all / and rested from His labor on the seventh. / There His creation filled / the hosts on high with wonder, as a lesson; / and here again He delayed, to show / that He has no desire to destroy. / For a hundred years goodness / cried out like a herald, / that sinners should turn from iniquity / before justice went forth. / After the long-suffering of the years / He set a term of seven days, / so that for a hundred years, and for an hour more, / He waited for repentance: / “From now on, for seven days, / fulfill My command in deed, / and I will bear with you in goodness / within the wall of justice. / From now on, for seven days, / I am shutting the door of My mercy, / and I will open the sea that is gathered / above the vault of the firmament.” / At five hundred years He disclosed / the revelation of this to Noah, / and at six hundred of his life it was fulfilled, / the providence that had been decreed. / In the six hundredth year of Noah's life / justice sharpened its sword, / and with the weapon of waters struck down / all the strength of the inhabited world. / In the six hundredth year of Noah's life / the sea crossed its boundary, / and the waters gathered above were changed / beyond the order of their station. / In the six hundredth year of Noah's life / the flood came upon the earth; / and Noah went in, with his sons and their wives, / and all the kinds of beasts. / The roar of the waters shook / the inhabited world upon its dwellers, / and the gloom of the waters above / covered its face with darkness.

Noah and those with him were waiting / for the command that had gathered them / to close the door of the ark / with the key of the command of His power. / That entering was a wonder: / that they should be hidden from the flood. / The rational beings scorned the voices / and despised the labor of the ark, / but the senseless beasts believed that by entering / the flood would not overcome them. / All were equal as they entered, / males and females alike; / not one was there over / and none lacking from the number. / For the bold saw / the kinds gathering at Noah's door, / yet they did not consider why / these had left the wilderness and loved peace. / Through all these things the Creator proclaimed / repentance in the ears of the dull: / by the building of the house of the ark / and by the gathering of the beasts of the field. / For a hundred years revelations / cried out like trumpets, / and like a rod of discipline / the voice of the flood resounded. / Even up to seven days / He set the limit of their sentence; / for the Lord of the seven days [?], / but not the heart [?] of those sunk deep. / Noah went in and brought in the beasts / as the revelation had commanded him, / and the command shut the ark, / and the power of the Creator sealed it. / The deaf went in, and [?] / those who were deaf by their own will; / and justice reproved them / by silent creatures that heeded the command. / And after seven days, / in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, / in the second month / the voice of justice cried out in the world, / and on the seventeenth day by count / it set the seal on the calamity of its sentence. / Against them all a host went forth, / the very lot of vengeance. / The springs of the deep burst open, / and the sluices of the heights were opened, / and with a sword of waters / the command laid waste the whole inhabited earth. / The waters of the depth rose to the height, / and the waters above came down to the earth, / and in a net of waters justice bound / the iniquity of the wicked. / The deep met its fellow, / sluice pressed hard on sluice, / and waters called to waters / to strike down the head of the bold. / The dumb deep roared / like a speaker as it rose, / and with the sound of its waves it rebuked / the rational beings who had transgressed the command. / The [?] above was judging / the wicked with the sound of its descent, / for iniquity had brought it down from the height / to the earth and troubled its calm. / For iniquity had brought it down from the height: / waters pressed on waters / as they rose toward the face of the height, / and those above met those below / like messengers of justice. / The voice of the command was proclaiming / to the waters above that they should come down to the earth, / and the dreadful command was urging / the waters below up toward the face of the height. / The descent and the rising of silent things / accused the rational beings, / for though deaf they heeded the command, / and rose up and came down for vengeance. / [?] was filled to the full, / and the mountains [?] of drownings; / and between height and depth there was / the strangling of every creature.

The infants were tossed about / as their lives came to an end; / they clung to their fathers, / and there was none to help the distressed. / They rose toward the face of the height, / and the flood brought them down; / they went down toward the face of the depth, / and the deep roared to meet them. / On this side and on that, / the war of the waters against the mighty hemmed them in, / and not one armed man or valiant warrior escaped / from all the strength of humankind. / For forty nights and days / rain came down upon the earth, / and the deep rose upward / as waters pressed on waters. / In forty days the waters reaped / the earth like a [?] of tares, / and with a hard sword they cut through / the hard neck of iniquity. / In forty days wrath stripped / the ruined vineyard, / and the waters, like treaders in the winepress, / trampled humankind and beasts. / The deep in its rising proclaimed / the great power of the Creator, / for His command stirred it / and it rebuked the rational beings. / The waters grew strong above the earth, / and the high mountains were covered; / beasts and cattle came to an end, / winged birds and men. / The waters destroyed every creature, / young and old alike; / since their deeds were alike, / the waters made their deaths alike. / In a single grave the flood gathered / and buried all the kinds, / and in a garment of waters it covered / humankind and beasts. / Noah and those with him were saved / out of all that breathed upon its face. / The command kept their lives safe, / not silent timbers. / The deep bore up the ark / and lifted it high on its waves, / and it was carried along upon the waters, / and the command held it fast. / It passed over the heights, / above the height of the cliffs; / the storms blew upon it, / yet its rider was not shaken. / The waves beat beneath it, / and it passed over them gently. / The surge of the mighty wind / rocked it this way and that; / beyond all order water and air / ground against each other, / and amid their battle the ark / dwelt in peace and quiet. / The deep carried it and rose, / bearing it proudly upon its shoulder, / and the waves bowed before it / and gave way for its course. / O ship without oars, / which crossed the sea as if dry land, / and no pilot steered it / through the turmoil of the storms! / O vessel that carried / the whole world from its end, / and its course had no need / of sailors to steer it! / The command became its sailor, / and the decree its pilot, / and the divine will took the place of a star, / steering it to harbor. / By the anchor of trust / its cable was made fast, / and goodness rested [?] in it / in place of a wind in linen sails. / For forty days in darkness / it journeyed like [?], / for the sailor who stood within it / had no need of light. / At the end of the forty [?], / justice [held back?] its sword, / and at a hundred and fifty there appeared / the sign of mercy on the mountaintops. / After a hundred and fifty days

the command went forth like a messenger, / carrying the letter of peace / which mercy had written to wrath. / The waters came to rest at a hundred and fifty days, / and the tops of the mountains appeared. / The command trod upon the silent waters / and gathered them into the deep. / For a hundred and fifty days / the ark crossed the sea, / and its course was set straight / for dry land and the middle of the earth. / From a place close to Eden / it set out at the beginning of its course, / and it ended the race of its journey / on the top of the mountains of Qardu. / At the end of the way it kept watch, / as did the command, over its rider, / that it might carry the race of the house of Adam across / to settle them in the middle of the earth. / Beyond the sea had dwelt / that generation which corrupted the earth, / and as yet the middle of the earth / had not been seen by mortals; / the sea was a fence before them / until the flood came. / But the command opened its fence / and carried them across to the middle. / In the vicinity of Paradise / those generations [?] had dwelt, / and the whole earth was empty / of humankind and beasts, / and it was as though desolate / from sea to sea; / no human voice spoke in it, / nor did the foot of beasts tread it. / For this second reason goodness fashioned / the ark as well: / that it might be a bridge for the house of Adam / and carry them across to the open land. / Because of the flood they trod / a road on which no man had passed, / while it lay determined in His knowledge / that the Maker would accomplish this. / It was not in anger that He drove them / from the place where they had dwelt, / nor in regret that He cast them / into the region in the middle of the inhabited earth. / For this wealth was laid up of old / in His knowledge before the creatures, / and He brought it out into the open through causes / for the dwelling of mortals. / So too in this, that He destroyed / and wiped out His creatures with water: / it was not wrath that made Him act suddenly, / for He is not swayed by a hand that [?]. / He knew before the flood / the things that have been and are to come, / and He consented to it in His fashioning, / that death would [?] and dwell there. / Iniquity corrupted His creation, / though His knowledge does not err; / for before He created sinners / He knew that they would surely sin. / He consented to leave a remnant / of humankind and of every kind, / and for this He ordered and brought / into the ark pairs upon pairs. / He knew that it would be asked / in the thinking of the bold / whether, because He hated His creation, / He destroyed it and made another. / He looked into the mind of the sowers of tares / before He destroyed, / and He forestalled the opinion / of the tares of their thoughts. / Of the first creation / He left a remnant of everything, / to show that it was not evil, / the creation His hands had made. / He looked upon all that came to be / before it came into being; / it was not in regret that He destroyed all, / and in His mercy He pitied and spared. / He showed His justice, that He is just [?]; / He is good in His deeds. / He showed that He is just when He chastises, / that they might not think He loves iniquity. / And He mingled mercy with His justice

so that they would not call Him harsh.
In both He showed His power:
in that He chastised and in that He spared.
He proclaimed the authority of His lordship,
that His will governs what is His own.
With rods of raging waters
He scourged the wickedness of the insolent;
and with the rod that overwhelmed the wicked
He preserved the order of life.
The waters envied the remnant
that mercy had rescued from wrath;
but He carried its remedy [?] across to the middle land,
so that its seed might multiply in every direction.
In the seventh month the ark [?]
entered and came to the haven,
and on the seventeenth by count
it came to rest on the mountains of Qardu.
In the second month it had set out
from its place on the seventeenth,
and in the seventh month it entered
the haven on the seventeenth.
For four [?] months in the haven
they were shut in and kept,
and it did not open the treasure-house of its riches
until the second month.
In the second month the master of the ark
sent out a messenger,
to go out and see whether the fury of the waters
had subsided from the earth.
The unclean raven was sent,
greedy and fond of food;
lust for flesh took it captive,
and it did not turn back to bring word.
He sent a second messenger,
of a kind that loves peace;
the dove went out and surveyed the dwelling-place,
and returned to him.
He waited again seven days
and sent the messenger once more;
and the dove came, carrying
the good news of peace in her mouth.
She showed him an olive leaf
that the divine Sign had sent by her hands,
as a pledge of reconciliation,
that the Judge's wrath had subsided.
The righteous man rejoiced and was comforted
by the letter of peace she brought.
Again he sent the messenger,
and saw that He had confirmed His promise.
Three times the dove went out,
and by all three she assured him.
He opened the door of the ark
and saw the land, and was comforted.
He saw light and heard a voice
through spiritual revelations:
"Behold, mercy has become mediator
and has calmed the wrath of the Judge.
Behold, grace has persuaded Him
to open the door before you.
Come out, you prisoners, and be comforted
by the fair sight of the earth."
After six hundred years of Noah's life,
at the close of the year that followed them,
the Sign commanded the righteous man
to go out onto the earth with his household:
"Go out," He said, "you and your sons with you,
and your wife with your sons' wives;
and bring out with you the birds,
the cattle and the wild beasts."
The just man received the command;
he went out and brought out every kind.
Not one of those confined was left
who did not go out to the land of the living;
according to the number that had entered it,
they came out from there complete.
For the Sign had kept them all
and sustained their lives.
The prisoners came out rejoicing
that their lives had been preserved.
In the second month the command
had shut them up in the prison-house,
and in the second month it opened
the door of mercy before them.
On the seventeenth by count
justice buried them,
and on the twenty-seventh of Iyar
grace raised them up.
In Iyar He brought about the Flood

when the elements were dry,
lest the insolent should think
that an excess of rain had happened by chance.
In Iyar He brought about the going-out,
in the month that is fair and adorned,
so that by the sight of crops and fruits
He might gladden the hearts of the distressed.
O the depth of the great riches
of the wisdom of the God of all,
who prepares for His creation
a fitting season for its restoration!
In Nisan He established the creatures
and adorned the earth with trees,
and men and animals found
a bridal chamber fair and adorned.
In Iyar He opened the ark,
in the month in which He had shut it before them,
and He prepared a table of nourishment,
a fitting season, before them.
In Nisan He brought out of Egypt
the congregation of the house of Israel;
He pitched a bridal canopy for it in the wilderness
and wove for it a crown of flowers.
In Nisan, again, He renewed
the creatures through our Firstfruits,
so that in the season in which He had established them
He might renew the ruin of His creation.
In the joyful season, with Noah too,
He completed and fulfilled his consolation:
He brought him out in the month of flowers,
and with him He gladdened everything.
All kinds went out with Noah
and dwelt with him on the earth,
and he offered firstfruits from them
to the Sign that had kept their lives.
Noah built a freewill altar
and offered sacrifices of reconciliation,
and the Creator accepted his sacrifice
together with the readiness of his will.
The Being who needs nothing
smelled the pleasing scent,
and was appeased from the fury of His wrath,
that Nature which is never angered at all.
"I will not again," He said, "curse
the earth because of man,
for I know that his inclination
is set on evil from his youth.
From now on, all the days,
seedtime and harvest and produce,
summer and winter shall go on
in the order of their alternations."
He blessed the earth with the changing seasons,
as it yields fruits for men;
and men He blessed
with conception and birth for succession:
"I lay the fear of you upon all,
upon wild beasts and cattle,
and under the yoke of man's dominion
all kinds shall be [?]."
Together with the blessings of birth
and dominion over everything,
He taught them to eat
the flesh of animals as they ate herbs.
He showed them the distinction
of how they should slaughter animals:
when they have poured out their blood on the ground,
then they may eat their carcasses.
"Only blood," He said, "you shall not eat,
for the blood is the life of the beast.
Do not eat flesh with its life,
lest you be liable to requital."
The ancients did not know
to eat the flesh of animals,
until the command revealed to Noah
that he might eat, and how to eat.
The promise He laid down for nature
became a law;
had the ancients known it,
Noah would have kept it all the more.
By laying down the law for him,
He showed that the law was new;
had it been laid down for the ancients,
He would not have renewed its covenant.
On the occasion of the killing of animals
He warned them against murder:
whoever kills a human being,
for that human being his blood shall be shed.
Man is the image of his Creator
and the lord of all creatures;
in proportion to the greatness of his honor

is the severity of the requital for his murder.
New laws the perfect Master
laid down for His disciple,
and wrote them on his heart
with the reed of the sign of His will.
Again He entered into a covenant with him
and confirmed the peace with oaths:
"I will not again blot out
men from the earth by the waters of a flood.
This is the sign of the covenant
that I establish between Me and the earth:
the sight of the bow, seen
amid the waters of the clouds."
This sign had existed
from the establishment of all things,
but He did not wish to show it to the ancients
until He revealed it in the days of Noah.
He honored Noah with the sign of peace,
that it should endure until the end,
so that when mortals see it
they may be comforted by the sign of peace.
He made the simple wise
by the new laws He wrote,
and gave them, as a consolation,
the tilling of the earth [?].
Noah began, it says, to work;
he planted a vineyard, and it yielded fruit.
He drank of its wine and became drunk,
and erred through the newness of its strength.
He had had no experience of it,
that its drink leads the mind astray,
nor did he know how
its drinkers ought to use it.
Noah drank and forgot himself,
and the wine overcame [?] the venerable man;
and the insolence of the will
of frivolous Ham mocked him.
The just man cursed the insolent one
because he had shamelessly mocked him,
and yoked him with the yoke of servitude,
to put fear into others through him.
By the curses upon the insolent
he set fear among the many,
lest they be like Ham the accursed
and become accursed in his likeness.
It was not by nature that the word of the just man
bound him to servitude.
There is no servitude by nature [?],
but only that of the wickedness of the will:
it was Ham's will that made light
of the venerable man who erred through his wine.
And He made him a sign to the insolent,
that they might restrain themselves before the venerable.
The Creator recorded the story
of the venerable Noah who was exposed,
to make those who know wise by it,
so that they would not show off their prowess over wine.
Alongside the purity of his members
He recorded the lapse in which he erred through wine,
to warn the more strongly
that its drinkers should use it in moderation.
He showed that he was worthy of revelation,
he who kept his mind clear,
to urge the pure by his example
that the word of life may dwell in them.
He recorded for us the victory of his endurance,
how strong he stood among the wicked,
in that he was not drawn away into imitating
the doings of his fellow men.
He kept him safe in the waters of the deluge
and made him a successor for creation,
and He peopled the desolate earth
with the companies [?] of his descendants.
He brought him out of the ark
and hid the ark from him,
lest his offspring go astray over it
and call it by the name of God.
For this reason justice
hid it from onlookers,
so that the cause of life
should not become an occasion of error for others.
He hid the ark in the earth,
in the same way that He dealt with Moses,
for He knew that the people of the Hebrews
would go astray over his tomb.
To Him belong all kinds of knowledge,
to Him who holds the sum of all wisdom,
whose knowledge does not forget
the things that have been and that are to come.
He examined everything beforehand,
and knows all before it comes to be;
and His works are encompassed in His knowledge
before they come to be.

Worthy is He to be praised by all,
He who knows all things,
who, knowing the wickedness of our inclination,
still [?] us through the produce of the earth.
On the calling of Moses, and on the fire that he saw

Forty-second memra / On the calling of Moses, and on the fire that he saw / in the bush, and on the deliverance of the Israelites / It is recited on the Thursday / of the Pasch / Response: Blessed is he who by his own killing killed death, and gave life to our nature / on the day of his resurrection, my brothers!

The son of Amram saw a new sight on the mountain top:
fire in the bush and the bush in the fire, and it did not burn.
He saw a frail nature standing in the mouth of the blaze,
and its heat did no harm to the bush's moistness.

Like a lioness the mouth of the flame stood open,
and the bush lay before it like food, yet it did not touch it.
Devouring Sheol, which the more it eats the more it craves,
was made to fast on Mount Horeb, against its custom.
She who confounds all order, who finds everything fit for her vast belly,
kept order before the divine revelation.
In a divine manner it appeared to the eyes of Moses;
though it could harm, it did not harm what could be harmed.
In the form of fire it appeared to the son of the Hebrews;
it was fire, and yet it was not fiery fire.
He saw the likeness of fire dwelling in the branches of the bush,
and marvelled greatly at who had put on it the bridle of stillness.
The untamed beast, whose greed had never been subdued,
had its strength bowed as under a yoke, beneath a command.
A hidden command rode upon the visible form
and set the flame's bridles in the mouth of its chariot.
On the mountain top he reined in the charger of its swiftness,
and the fire, beneath his strength, neighed like steeds.
Moses heard the neighing of the fire in the mouth of the bush,
and wished to learn the reason for the vision shown to him.
"I will turn aside and see this great sight," said the stammerer,
"why the bush is burning and yet does not burn."
The command that had shaped the vision called him secretly
to draw near and ask what the cause was, and why.
It drew him with delight to approach the face of the sight,
and then made him afraid to come near while he was not sanctified.
"Moses, Moses," it called him, speaking to him as one who knew him,
"loose your sandals, and only then come near to where I am.
I am holy, and the mountain is sanctified by my presence;
do not defile with the sandals of your feet the place I have made clean."
He counted the sandals on his feet unclean — not that they were unclean,
but to magnify the greatness of the vision before His revelation.
He taught him to approach the revelation in holiness,
so that he would know how to sanctify the children of his people.
For this reason He showed him the sight of the flame:

that he should blow the fire of the Creator's name into the forest of error.
By the fire He made known the might of His greatness, whose might can do all things,
and through the bush He revealed the wealth of His kindness.
The mystery of His severity and His kindness He painted in the sight,
and set them up like an image before His household servant.
He was sending him to the Egyptians and to the Israelites,
to chastise and to redeem, as His just judgement discerned.
It was as though by the fire He explained His sign: that it would come upon Egypt;
and He showed by the bush that He takes no pleasure in human ruin.
From within the fire He spoke with the one of halting speech,
saying to him: "I have authority over all and in all.
I am He who created creation in the beginning out of nothing,
and by my might the made world stands, which was made by my hands.
I, I am He who chose Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, my servants,
and honoured them with the great name of my glorious name.
I, I am He who promised the land of Canaan to the seed that came from them,
and I have come to fulfil in deeds the promise of my words to them.
The cry of their suffering in the land of the Egyptians has come before me,
and I have come down to deliver them in their wrongs from their oppressors.
I know the pain of their heart, how bitter it is;
therefore I have prepared the medicine of the vision to bind up their wounds.
I am persuaded of the wickedness of their oppressors, how great it has grown;
therefore I have drawn the sword of the Spirit to lay them waste.
To you I give the weapon of my word, which cannot be overpowered;
go, humble with it the sons of Ham the slave, who have enslaved the free.
Go, say to him, the slave of slaves, cursed by his father:
'Why have you enslaved the sons of the just one, whom his father blessed?'
Go, proclaim freedom of soul to the son of Shem the firstborn,
and cast off from him the yoke of slavery of despised Ham.
I have remembered the promise of my true words that I made with Noah,
which the seed of Canaan has falsified in the pride of its heart.
I, I am He who blessed, and I, I am He who cursed, as their dispositions deserved;
and I, I am He who decreed that Canaan should be slaves to the sons of Shem.
Wisely I blessed and cursed the two sides,
and the accursed one who has overturned my blessings, I shall overturn.
Reveal, then, the power of my blessings to the Israelites,

and reveal and show the scourge of my curses to the Egyptians.
Go, bring the good news to the children of my friends,
and remind them of the promises I promised him.
Sow the name of the God of their fathers in their ears,
and they will be roused at the call of their freedom."
The Hebrew heard of his people's freedom, and his soul revived;
then he turned uneasy, lest it be mere hearsay without deeds.
"Behold, I go," the humble one answered the voice that called him,
"and I will bring the Israelites the good news of your name.
Behold, I proclaim the name of God in the people's ears,
and they will demand of me the exact name — and what shall I say?
There are names of gods without number in creation,
and if I bring them the name of God, they will say, 'Which one is he?'
First they will demand the name from me, and then the deeds;
how then shall I name you before the inquirers who ask for your name?"
The Creator saw that he pressed hard his demand for His name,
and He revealed and showed him the name of Being, which has no beginning.
He taught him to reveal the name of His Being before the Hebrews:
that He is without beginning and without end.
"For I am not named by a mere name, as fools are,
but by the power and the deeds of my creating.
I am the One who Is, and the name of my Being is beyond comprehension;
no one has given me a foreign name, other than that I Am.
If you wish to learn the name that proclaims my lordship,
I am called God alone, and also Maker.
But Ehyeh asher ehyeh is the name of my Being,
and it is doubled, said twice over, so that it may stand firm."
The son of Amram heard the name of Being, which is and is hidden,
and pondered how the people would believe in something hidden.
"Go, and say this too," He repeated, telling the one being sent,
"'I am the God of your fathers, of Abraham and of Isaac.'"
These things that the stammerer heard were too much for him,
and he did not want to go, lest he go and not be believed.

"See, the people will not believe my words," the stammerer replied,
"nor will Pharaoh listen to the voice of the name of Being."
The Creator saw that he was looking to devise excuses,
and shut the door against the pretexts of his simplicity.
He saw that his faith had sickened with doubts,
and laid the medicine of mighty signs upon his mind.
"What is this in your hands?" He asked, as if He did not know;
and he said, "It is a staff," not knowing why He asked him.
He asked him so that he would confess that the staff in his hand was something real,
so that, once it was changed, he would not think it was nothing.
"Throw it on the ground," the Lord said [?] to the holder of the staff;
and he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent and began to writhe.
The Hebrew saw his staff transformed, and he trembled and was dismayed,
and he feared it, lest it bite him and put an end to his life.
The voice that spoke with him, seeing he was downcast, gave him courage
to take hold of the serpent as of a staff, and not be afraid.
He mastered his trembling and seized it in his hands, as he was commanded,
and the serpent turned back and became a staff, as it had been.
He spoke again and said to him, "Put your hand in and place it in your bosom";
he put it in and drew it out, and saw that it was leprous like snow.
He commanded him to put his hand in again, a second time;
he put it in and drew it out, and it was restored and became as it was before.
By his staff and by his hand He taught him the power that would work through his hands:
that He chastises and redeems, and [?] wickedness and silences it.
By the staff He showed him the hard plagues that would fall upon the Egyptians,
and by his hand that grew leprous, the ugliness of his own people's iniquity.
They were pure when they went in, free of paganism, that leprosy [?];
but once they mingled with the Egyptians, they became leprous with sin.
Through their going out from Egypt they would be cleansed,
in the same way that his hand grew leprous and was made clean again.
The Egyptians too had once been harmless, like the staff,
but in time they became venomous through sorcery.
Because of them He changed the staff and it became a serpent,
so that by its discipline He might strip them of their evils.

With two signs He marked out the way for the one being sent,
though the difficulties were plainly before his mind.
His thoughts stood amid doubts about his going,
and he turned and framed another excuse: the stammer of his speech.
The voice rebuked him: "Who is it that made a mouth for man,
and who gave a mouth to the power of speech that seeks for words?
Does not the staff that became a serpent teach you
that it is easy for me to have you proclaim my greatness with your stammer?
Why do you line up excuses and words against my will?
For whether you are willing or not, go you shall.
Go, and do not grieve as though what you have heard will not come to pass;
stretch your thoughts toward the outcome, and see that it is true.
I will be a fluent word in the stammer of your mouth,
and I will interpret for you to the Egyptians and to the Hebrews."
The son of Amram saw that He had finished His words, and that go he must;
and he took with him his wife and his sons, to go and to remain.
On this understanding he set out from Midian for the land of the Egyptians:
if He would redeem, well; and if not, he would stay with his kin.
The Searcher of hearts saw that he had resolved to slip away into hiding,
and He exposed and laid bare the hidden deceit in his heart.
In the guise of wrath He met the wavering man on the way,
and raised His sword and cut off the deceit of the deceiver.
The sword flashed against his life as if to kill,
and his wife saw it, and set before Him the circumcision of her son.
She held up the circumcision like a shield before the command,
and kept the sword from her partner, so that it would not come near him.
"I have a bridegroom of blood," she said, as she understood it,
"and I am kin to the faith of the house of Abraham."
The daughter of diviners held Abraham's seal in her hand,
so that when the Lord of Abraham saw it He would be reconciled to her.
And the All-Knowing saw that she had taken refuge in the house of Abraham;
He showed her favour, spared with His sword, and held back from killing.
It was not to kill that He raised His hand, though raise it He did,
but to lay bare the deceit that Moses had devised in his heart.
Like a raider the command fell upon his camp,
and took his company from him and sent him on stripped bare.
He gave the shepherd only the staff to hold in his hand,

so that by it he might show the might of signs to the people and the nations.
He put the sword of the Spirit into the warrior's hand,
to go and do battle with the sorcerers clothed in error.
Like an exile he went into Egypt, from which he had gone out,
and he raised his staff and the word of his mouth, and Egypt trembled before him.
He went in and told the children of his people the vision he had seen,
and they were comforted, yet without comfort, for they did not truly believe.
Pharaoh too heard the name of God, and he trembled without trembling,
for he thought there was no god mightier than himself.
Moses gathered the tribes and taught them the word of the promise,
and went in to the king to declare to him the name of God:
"The Lord who is over all has sent me to you as an envoy,
to redeem His people from bondage, that they may worship His name.
The Israelites are the children of His Godhead,
and to Him they owe the debt of love due to a father and lord.
He said to me, 'Go and say to Pharaoh the king:
Send me my firstborn son, whom I begot by the work of my hands.'"
"My firstborn son," said Moses, the firstborn of the Spirit of revelations;
but the promise of his words found no welcome in Pharaoh's ears.
"Who is the Lord, and who is His people? I do not know;
nor can anyone redeem Israel from slavery.
Go away, Moses; do not lead the children of your people astray,
lest you lay a double yoke upon their necks.
Go away, stammerer; you have babbled long enough before His Majesty;
speak no more, lest you come to grief."
Moses did not tremble at the Egyptian's threat,
nor did he slacken in setting forth the Creator's might.
The son of Abraham answered the son of Ham the slave:
"I am an envoy whom the Hidden One has sent to the earthly ones.
He gave me a decree bearing His name to bring to the children of His people;
read it, consider it, and see that what I have said is true."
Moses unrolled the edict of the name of Being,
and began to read out its first line: the changing of the staff.
The Israelite threw down the staff before the Egyptian,
and it became a serpent, not in appearance but in truth.
Pharaoh did not tremble when the staff changed and became a serpent,
for he was used to the illusions of sorcery.

For he thought that Moses, like the sorcerers, was deceiving with delusion,
and showing human eyes a sight that was not real.
He called the sorcerers to come and deceive with their semblances;
they threw down staffs, but the divination of their schemes did not succeed.
They too did as Moses had done, but not in truth;
and the truth rose up and swallowed their semblances.
The serpent of truth swallowed the counterfeit, and it vanished and was gone;
yet the counterfeiters were not put to shame by what was real.
The sorcerers thought that Moses was deceiving by their own sorceries,
since he had been schooled in their craft from his youth.
The hard of heart hardened their hearts and did not heed his words,
and he went back and brought another decree, of another plague.
He raised his hand in the Creator's name and struck the river,
and the sweet waters of the river became bitter blood.
The severity of the plague turned the waters into blood,
that Pharaoh might learn that it was on his account the voiceless creatures were struck.
O Creator, whose judgement upon the works of His hands is exact,
why do you punish those who have not sinned in place of the guilty?
Pharaoh deserves a double scourge, for he did not heed your words —
not the voiceless creatures, who do not even know who you are.
Raise your rod and strike the one who sinned, for his folly,
so that he will sin no more nor mock you insolently.
O mind, do not boldly reproach
that Wisdom whose judgement is just in the order it keeps.
He does well to punish the voiceless in place of those who speak,
to make known to them the greatness of His love toward humankind.
As for His saying, "I have hardened Pharaoh's heart,"
it was not that He hardened it, but that He bore with him in long-suffering.
He could have punished him and ended his life in a single hour,
but this did not befit His kindness.
In kindness He bore with the incorrigible wicked man,
until he sank himself in the abyss of iniquity.
The ill-minded man had gone out to the river to offer sacrifice,
and Moses met him and showed him the plague by which he was destined to be swallowed.
Before scourging them, the Treasury of plagues revealed His plagues,
to teach those being scourged that it was by Him they were struck.

He raised his hand and struck the ground, and it was filled with swarming things,
and frogs without number came out and covered its face.
The insolent one saw it and was enraged, and called on those who are not God,
and they made frogs falsely, though there were none.
Those of Moses were real in truth, like a body;
those of the sorcerers were like a shadow, which is nothing.
The land of the Egyptians stank with the frogs of Moses,
and the rebel was in pain, and begged and pleaded — but not in truth.
"Name a time for yourself," the humble one answered the arrogant of soul;
he said, "Tomorrow," and the just one prayed, and the frogs vanished.
The rebel turned back, and his heart went dead to uprightness;
and Moses returned and showed him a plague full of lice.
He told him first, "Behold, I will do it," and only then did he perform it,
so that he would know it was no delusion, but truth.
By the mute staff the earth was struck by the one who spoke,
and lice swarmed over people and beasts.
The lice that the Israelite made clung to bodies,
until even the Egyptians wailed at their torment.
The Egyptian was struck by a hard plague from the Hebrew,
and the sorcerers were defeated and pointed a finger before God.
"This is the finger of the God of all," they said to Pharaoh;
but the heavy of heart did not listen to the children of error.
The Creator turned again and sent to him a fifth time:
"Send me my people, or else receive another plague.
Behold, I send upon you a swarm of every kind,
mixed and confused, destroying all without pity.
And so that my word, running ahead of its coming, may prove true:
behold, I set my people apart from your people, so that it will not come near them.
Behold, I give great order to its confusion,
and though it has no discernment, it will discern better than you."
The swarm sprang up and covered the face of the whole land,
and ravaged alike the crops and the fruits of every tree.
The rebel suffered in due time, hardened though he was,
and called on Moses to hold back his hand from striking:
"Stop your plagues, son of the Hebrews; you have chastised me enough;
I will give you the people you asked for, to go with you."
Moses lifted the rod of the plague from the insolent one,

and he turned and lied, and did not give up the people as he had promised.
And the Lord said to Moses His servant, "Open the storehouses,
and bring out plagues upon the insolent who have scorned my threats."
A swift death went out with the word of the son of the Hebrews,
and all the cattle of the land of Egypt perished suddenly.
The beasts died, but the wickedness of the wicked did not die;
and the Lord saw, and raised His hand through His household servant.
He commanded him to strike the stiff-necked with evil boils,
so that through his body he might humble his soul from its pride.
He scattered earthly ashes toward the heights,
and troubled the air, and boils broke out upon people.
The insolent, clothed in pride, fell under the boils and blisters,
yet they would not put off the evil boil of their minds.
They were struck with hard plagues, and their limbs were tormented,
and while the blow of the blisters still lasted, another followed on its heels.
To suit their sickness the Physician prepared harsh cauteries,
to cut away from them the pain of the iniquity that tormented them.
He signalled to the air by the hands of Moses to rain down hail,
and with the word came the deed, without delay.
The man of dust lifted his right hand toward the heights,
and down came hail, and mingled with it the fire of wrath.
Hail and fire, two opposites, mingled with one another,
and came down and made war on the wicked on the Creator's behalf.
The voiceless things waged fierce battles with the wicked,
and exacted from them the reproach and insult to the name of God.
Ah, that contest, so unlike all other contests,
in which enemies loved concord for its sake!
Who ever saw two opposing elements
that, though alien to each other, loved concord against their custom?
Who has had authority over created things like the son of Amram,
who constrained natures and subdued them by the word of his mouth?
Here was fulfilled what He had said to him: "You shall be a god";
and like God he commanded the natures, and they heeded his command.
The mute things heard him and did not find it hard to fulfil his words,
but those endowed with speech rebelled with a rock-hard obstinacy.

Against their rebellion He varied plagues of every form,
and arrayed them swiftly, one after another.
After the hail He brought locusts, fierce and harsh,
and they covered the land as with a garment, so that it could not be seen.
It was exceedingly fierce; there had been none like it, nor will there be again;
and without pity it ravaged and destroyed fruits and crops.
The land of Egypt was laid waste and stripped of every good thing,
yet the heart of her children still stood firm in tyranny.
So the Lord of all raised His hand against their pride,
and after the locusts He overwhelmed them with the plague of darkness.
For three days there was darkness where they dwelt,
and the hours of night could not be told apart from those of day.
In the great darkness of ignorance the benighted sat,
bereft of light and of comfort.
At the end of the plagues the Command raised a hand through Moses,
and scourged them with the death of the firstborn, whose mourning is bitter.
By night the angel of death passed through the land full of iniquity,
and slew alike the firstborn of man and of beast.
The spiritual Watcher flashed his sword before their eyes,
and the soul trembled, and departed, and fled from the limbs.
Swiftly he flew over the bodies like lightning,
and like a thief broke into the limbs and plundered the soul.
All the firstborn died, of the free, of slaves and of the poor,
and no house was left that was not robbed by a sudden death.
Bitter wailing rose throughout all Egypt,
and they howled and wept like thunder over their firstborn.
They raised choking laments and cried out over the dead,
and grieved and groaned like thunder over their offspring.
The night of mourning plunged them into grief over their firstborn,
but it gladdened the Israelites with the mystery of salvation.
With the blood of the lamb He sealed the redemption of their freedom,
so that the angel of death would have no power over their firstborn.
Those who could speak sprinkled the mute blood on their doors,
and the Watcher saw it, turned aside, and passed over their houses.
Tell me then, mute one: by what power did you overcome the spiritual being?

and how did fire and wind humble themselves and fear you?
All Egypt shook and trembled at its harshness,
and you, silent one, by what power did you overpower the mighty?
What you have done, weak and silent one, is not your own:
the Watcher saw in you the type of the One who is coming, and turned aside [?] before Him.
When the Word was about to set all the nations free,
He first portrayed in you the type of His coming, at the departure of the people.
The mystery of truth set the sons of Jacob free
and taught them to carry it until He comes.
On the fourteenth of the month of Nisan He marked His memorial,
so that they would not forget this redemption that freed them.
From the beginning the mystery of this day had been kept;
He knew it before He set creation in order at the beginning.
On it He redeemed the sons of Abram from slavery,
and wrote His name before their eyes, that they might look upon it.
At the power of the Israelites' redemption the rebels were astonished;
they raised a finger and gave the victory to the name of the Creator.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Rise, go out from here,
and take your people; let them go and serve before their God."
"Go out from among my people," said the son of Ham to the son of Abraham;
and though unwilling, he pleaded, put to shame for his wickedness.
For just as he had resisted the truth from the start,
so now, at the end of the plagues, he pressed the people to go out.
Quickly he hurried them to depart;
yet it was not his own doing, but the Sign that was compelling him.
A hidden Sign was hurrying him to send them out,
so that the day of the mystery being commemorated would not be delayed.
In haste the Hebrews went out from Egypt,
and there was no time for the dough of their provisions to rise.
They went out rejoicing that they had plundered the wealth of their persecutors,
and Pharaoh bitterly regretted that he was left poor.
Foolish envy goaded the fool who had no understanding;
he armed his host, set out [?], and went out after the people.
The whole rebellious people went out with him,
so that with him his hosts might receive the requital of judgment.
The wicked who perished were guilty of the [?] of their wrongs,
and a hidden Sign gathered them for one destruction.
With a sword of water the wicked were slain utterly,

and for that very requital He made them ready, just as they had done.
With horses and armor they went out to hunt the Israelites,
and swiftly they pursued them as far as the sea.
The Hebrews saw their pursuers and were dead with fear;
they gave up hope that they could ever be saved.
They saw the terrible sea roaring before their eyes,
and Pharaoh the king, like a dragon, behind them.
They turned to Moses to persuade him—not in love,
but with murmuring and with divided minds:
"Why did you bring us out of Egypt to die here?
Better for us to be slaves of men than to die."
Moses prayed when he saw the murmuring of the foolish people,
and the Lord answered him—He who had answered him before he prayed.
He made darkness like a wall behind them,
and before them a great light like a pillar.
For the eyes of the pursuers He made the darkness a thick darkness,
and for their eyes He doubled the light in the hours of darkness.
All night the darkness stood behind them,
and all night the pillar before them shone.
That night was a night of darkness and of lights:
light for the people, and thick darkness for the Egyptians.
In fear both sides were encamped before the wonder,
and the people and Pharaoh alike were longing for victory.
Moses, in his hope in the power of the signs, took courage,
and his gaze of faith was fixed upon the Creator.
And the Creator too inclined toward him alone,
and as one would a child, He was instructing him in secret.
The Sign saw him, saw how earnestly he had entreated,
and spoke with him as with a friend whose love is true.
"Why are you praying?" the Lord said to His servant.
"Lift up your hand and divide the sea, and let the people cross.
With the rod with which you chastised the hard-hearted Egyptians,
strike the turbulent sea, and let it learn order.
Through you I am teaching order to the mute and to those who speak,
so that they may know the power of the Maker who set them in order.
Strike the sea with it, and let the turbulent rush of its waves be stilled,
and let the Israelites and the Egyptians see My greatness.

Cry out with it to the mute one, and see, it will listen to you as though it could speak;
speak My name to it, and see, it will perceive the power of My being."
[?] with the silent one, as he had been commanded,
and the mute one heard him and carried out his word in deeds.
It made a broad road through its midst for the people to cross,
and the waters stood like a wall on either side.
A great wonder Moses worked—yet it was not Moses,
but the Sign of the Creator's power that spoke through him.
A new vision the seers saw at the hand of the seer:
mute nature keeping order and not breaking it.
Commands of silence were laid upon the irrational creature,
and it no longer kicked with the feet of its waves as before.
That command which had gathered the waters in the beginning
now divided them and made them keep order.
The silent ones heard that Voice which had created them,
and made room for the people to cross amid their waves.
In a visible rod they saw a hidden power and feared it,
and stood like servants on the right and on the left.
Those who speak, too, seeing the mute obey the command,
took heart in the power of the Maker who is able to do all things.
The feeble people saw that a road had been trodden through the waters,
and began to walk with confidence among the deeps.
As on dry land the sons of Abraham walked through the deeps,
and as they walked, they could not have their fill of walking.
The walkers saw a new kind of walking, beyond all custom;
to their minds it was real and yet not real.
As in a dream they beheld that crossing,
and at its strangeness they pondered whether it was or was not.
The Egyptians too stood divided, amazed at the wonder:
whether the sea had been divided or perhaps not, they could not reckon.
The hidden Sign that had done this urged them on:
the people to cross, and the Egyptians to be drowned.
The Hebrews did not cross with the confidence of faith,
nor did the Egyptians fear as they went in between the waves.
As if with drugs, the Sign was drawing them on [?],
and they could not discern so as to perceive the power of the wonder.
Ignorance spread over Pharaoh and over his camp,

and the fools went in and stood among the snares, and did not understand.
Like a hunter He drew in the simple-hearted,
and surrounded them with nets of water on every side.
The vile one [?] went in with all his host, and they stood in the deep,
and he did not consider the cause: that his sins had bound him round with harsh cords.
The division of the sea held in its order until morning,
and at the hour of morning He signaled to Moses to lift up his hand.
The Egyptians saw a harsh sight at that hour,
and the wheels of their chariots were clogged, as if to drown them.
When they went into the midst of the sea, it was not they who went in;
nor did they even perceive this: that they had been humbled and made afraid.
A hidden command brought them in against their will,
and it, in turn, cast a terrible fear into their minds.
The son of the Hebrews turned his face and looked upon the deep,
and the waters went and covered the horses and their riders.
The nobles sank like lead in their sins,
and not one of them was left as a survivor who was not destroyed.
They all perished, because they had agreed with one mind
to drown the children of the Israelites in the waters of the river.
In the plunge of the waters the wicked died, with no shroud to wrap them,
in the same way that the infants had died without wrappings.
As they had done, so He did to them, measure for measure,
and the snares they had cast over their fellows recoiled upon their own hands.
The Hebrews saw their corpses on the shore of the sea,
and these reminded them of the corpses of the infants that had floated on the river.
The sons of Abraham rejoiced and were comforted in the Lord of Abram,
who had fulfilled and accomplished the promise of His words to Abram.
They praised and magnified the power of the Creator who had set them free;
they believed in His name, and loved and honored Moses His servant.
On Samson the Mighty Man
The Forty-Third Homily: On Samson the Mighty Man

In the Scriptures I saw the image of a just man's victory,
painted on the page of the Law in two kinds of likeness.
At the start of the passage I saw beautiful pictures,
and at its end I saw signs that were not beautiful.
In the first section I read the triumph of his great strength,
and in the second, shame, disgrace and weakness.
The beginning of his story is a great wonder to anyone who considers it,
and the end of his story is truly hateful to anyone who hears it.
No consistency is seen in the story of the just man,
and the course of his path is confusing.
The inconsistency in the contest of his labours puzzled my thoughts,
and I sought to learn the reason for these two things in one man.
My mind led me to search out the meaning of his glory and his shame,
and drew me in through the door of the books of the Spirit.
Into the house of written signs I entered and stood,
and began to search the section where the Nazirite is written of.
I saw the name of election inscribed at the beginning of his story,
and a spiritual being speaking of him before mortals.
I saw a man of the Spirit announcing his conception and his birth,
and marking out his chosen name with the name of the Creator.
By the name of the Creator the spiritual one named the bodily one,
that he might be a servant and minister of his Lord's word.
He set a holy name upon his head like a seal,
so that he would know whose he was and whom he served.
The command chose him for the service of the King hidden on high,
and girded him like a servant with the armour of the Nazirite vow.
With the Nazirite vow as his armour the bodily servant was equipped,

so that everyone might know that his armour was of the Spirit, and not of the flesh.
