It was in the spirit that he was destined to wage war against the hostile people,
and beforehand he was given the armour of the Spirit, with which to conquer.
He was destined to wage a great contest against iniquity,
and not to let his honour be brought low among ranks that stood above him [?].
The Watcher was sent and announced his conception and his birth,
and set on his head the great crown of the Nazirite vow.
As a great champion he was chosen from a people slack of mind,
that by his zeal he might strengthen them with good hope.
The people had grown slack in their trust in God,
and through Samson he roused their heart to the fear of the truth.
He set the power of his help on his head like a crown,
and gave him authority to judge his companions without fault.
He called him and set him up to judge the people and to contend with the nations,
so that by every means he might drive back iniquity and keep it from prevailing.
The divine sign sent him against the iniquity of the people and the nations,
and sent him in might to fight at the forefront of the struggle.
Against the nations he first showed his own will,
and made it plain that the counterfeit teaching of demons was thriving among them.
He saw the teaching of demons prevailing among the uncircumcised nations,
and he was zealous and braced himself to wage a hard contest with them.
The zealous servant made himself ready for the contest with the nations,
and devised pretexts for how he might fight on behalf of justice.
For justice he set himself a goal to strive for,
and showed it plainly in all his movements against iniquity.
Mightily he gave himself to the struggle,
for by every means he wished to exalt the name of justice.
In his heart he wisely devised crafty stratagems,
and in the guise of love he contrived to expose the lie.
The wise and crafty one put on the guise of love to make war,
and like a spy he entered the camp of the uncircumcised and spied out their affairs.
He took himself a bride from those who hated the name of his God,
so that by one woman he might humble the error of the name of gods.

A hidden sign strengthened his movements to act wisely,
and he said to his father, "Take for me a wife from the daughters of the uncircumcised."
His father and mother did not know that it was from God,
that he was seeking vengeance for the sons of his people on the Philistines.
He sought vengeance for his people on the nations by means of a daughter of the nations,
and faithfully showed that his will was bent on his Lord's purpose.
He set out from his people to go and betroth a foreign woman,
and on the way his Lord set a mark before him to test his strength.
A lion's whelp met him on the road, a roaring lion,
and he tore it apart and flung down its tough body like a kid's.
With the lion's strength He tested the strength of the champion,
and Samson knew that he could undertake the contest against the uncircumcised nations.
Without sword or staff he killed the lion,
and knew that he had no need of the help of weapons.
He went into the house of the uncircumcised, betrothed the woman and gave a pledge,
and returned to his people, planning how to carry out his affairs.
The thought of the woman pressed upon him, yet not for the woman's sake;
rather his soul longed to act against the Philistines.
He was most eager to fulfil his Lord's command,
and longed to seek vengeance for the sons of his people.
Swiftly the swift one went out to take the woman,
and prepared gifts in which shame and disgrace lay hidden.
The champion went down on the road to Timnah about his business,
and turned aside to see whether the lion's carcass still remained.
He saw that the destroyer of men lay rotting, cast on the ground,
and that in its bones the bee had made its nest.
He saw that a feeble insect was mocking it in all its might,
and he believed and was assured that in the same way he would mock the Philistines.
He saw honey flowing from a body full of harm,
and gained hope that he would save his people from oppression.
The Nazirite by choice stretched out his hand to the unclean body,
and took food full of life from out of the bitter.
The pure one ate unclean food and was not defiled,
and he gave some of it to his parents too, without revealing where it came from.
Wisely he concealed the mystery of his great strength,
lest what is passed around in the mouths of many should come to be despised.

He made a feast, prepared it and invited the uncircumcised of Philistia,
and at their banquet he composed a riddle about the slaying of the lion.
For he was thinking that through its slaying he would slay them;
that is why he composed the riddle of the lion and of the food from it.
He propounded a riddle full of insight before simple men,
and they could not tell the force of the meaning hidden in it.
"Out of the eater," said Samson, "came forth food,
and out of the bitter flowed sweetness, against all custom."
The uncircumcised of heart were astonished and amazed at the Hebrew,
at how wise and how hidden was the meaning of his words.
He held them in great wonder by the composition of his words,
and bound them as with armour without their knowing it.
They stirred up his wife to learn it from him and teach them,
and when she had learned it well and taught them, still they could not overcome him.
His betrothed pressed him to explain to her the secret of his riddle,
and his will gave way under the troubling of that daughter of the erring.
Beyond measure she harassed him with her distressing words,
and he revealed and showed her the secret he had hidden from his parents.
Out of vexation he revealed and explained to her the secret of his heart;
she in turn explained it to the sons of her people, the crafty ones.
On the seventh day the guilty got the better of the champion,
and before the meal they disclosed the food hidden in his riddle:
"What is there whose taste is sweeter than honey,
or what is there bitter and harsh like the lion's mouth?"
The wise one saw that the [?] had overcome him by means of the woman,
and he was zealous, braced himself, and armed himself for the contest with them.
Thirty men he killed as payment for the solving of his riddle,
and took their garments and paid them off as one pays fools.
He traced out a path for himself through the woman and his riddle toward the struggle,
that he might advance well toward the victory of his Lord's word.
Through the woman and the riddle he drew them on to the struggle,
and by every pretext he displayed the power hidden in his soul.
By pretexts he stirred up a hard contest with them,
and taught them that it was no ordinary way he fought them.
Three hundred foxes the hunter of the fear of the truth captured,

and with the silent he made war on those who speak.
With feeble foxes he humbled those full of pride,
and they could not stand before the will with which he fought.
The contentious put on wrathful zeal over their ruin,
and began to seek vengeance for the disgrace with which he had disgraced them.
They made ready to make war on Israel,
so as to hunt down in battle Samson, who had humbled them.
They thought to exact vengeance for their blood from the son of Abraham,
and did not know they would be caught in the snare they had hidden.
Foolish pride drew on the dull of heart,
and they prepared weapons to fight against Israel.
The crafty foxes, whom feeble foxes had brought into subjection,
began to boast against the kingdom that is likened to a lion.
With open voice the ranks of the Philistines cried out:
"Either come out and fight, or hand over to us Samson the great!"
The slack people heard the sound of trumpets blaring in their ears,
and they were afraid, humbled themselves, and bowed the shoulder to be enslaved.
They abandoned their trust in the name of the Creator who had exalted them,
and gave up their will for the impure of soul to make sport of.
They chose to make appeasement by giving up the marvel of power among them,
and turned away from the word full of the grace of the Gracious One.
They gave an oath to hand the just man over to the uncircumcised,
and the fools were not ashamed to condemn their saviour for nothing.
"Do you not know, Samson," said the divided of heart,
"that the Philistines rule over us at this time?
Why have you brought this evil on us with our enemies?
See, they are planning to destroy us in their wars.
Come down, appease the Philistines whom you have angered,
and take from us the war you have stirred up against our families."
"Swear to me by the Lord," said the just man to the sons of his people,
"that you will not strike me, and I will come down without dispute."
The fools bound the head of their people like a captive,
and gave him into the hands of the uncircumcised of heart to make sport of him.
The champion went down and stood among the shields of the warriors,
and he did not fear or flinch, though death was set right before him.

Courageously he went down, bound, to his slayers,
and had no doubt of the help that went with him.
A great wonder, full of confidence, was the son of Manoah,
for he did not lose heart before the killers who pressed upon him.
His heart had put on faith like armour,
and he was strengthened by good hope in his Lord's promise.
His hope was set on that power which had given him strength;
that is why he went down, bound, to his slayers.
He took courage from the power of the sign on the crown of his body,
and he gloried in the hair of his Nazirite vow more than in armour.
The uncircumcised saw him with his body bound, just as they wished,
and the fools thought that now his life was ending.
The fools counted as dead one who was alive in his God,
and did not know that they themselves would fall into the pit they had dug.
At the very hour they thought his life was ending,
he rose up from stillness and wiped them out of life.
They raised a whetted sword above his head,
and the power of the help within him raised it above their heads.
They stood eagerly to make sport of him,
and the fearful Name displayed its power and put them to shame.
The power of the Spirit stirred the soul of the champion,
and he snapped the visible harness and cast it from his limbs.
Scripture bears witness to the power of the Spirit hidden in him:
the chains became like threads before his greatness.
Like threads he snapped the hard iron and cast it off,
and stood and fought without weapons, with a feeble bone.
The hidden sign made the feeble bone ready for battle,
and with it, as with a sword, he laid waste the ranks of warriors.
The holy of soul took the unclean bone in his hand,
and the armoured could not stand before his right hand.
The wicked saw a fearful sight in the just man's hand,
and fled and hid in terror at what they had seen.
The son of the Hebrews held the bone like a sword,
and it flashed for him, and the ranks of the uncircumcised were terrified.
Fearful indeed was the sight of the bone; yet not of the bone,

but of the power that showed its appearance in its appearance.
Hard death was dealt out from its hardness,
and its blow was sharper than a sword's.
By its hardness the hard of heart were confounded,
yet not by it, but by the one who held it.
The bone and the hand that held it were truly fearful,
not by their nature, but by the power that held them.
A hidden power held the hand, and the hand the bone,
and it laid waste the proud and the dull of heart.
It was sharper than a two-edged sword,
and whatever it laid waste it hacked down, felling bodies.
Its edge had only to come near the uncircumcised bodies,
and they were swiftly consumed as if by fire.
The Nazirite had only to raise his hand against the ranks,
and they were dragged down until body lay heaped upon body.
O bone, how you conquered beyond all measure!
Not to you do I say it, but to the hand that held you.
O hand, how you were strengthened without measure!
Not you, O hand, but the sign that urged your will.
O man, how great was the strength of the senses of your body!
Not of your body, but of the power that strengthened your movements.
O Samson, a name in which the name of his God was hidden,
how the power of your name was made plain by deeds!
Was it not your hand, O man, that held the bone?
Or did that bone not suffice in that struggle?
How strong was the bone in your hand, and you in the bone!
It did not perish, nor did your hand fail from it.
How did it stand before a thousand men,
and by what power did it humble the power of those who possessed strength?
A thousand men a man killed with you, O feeble bone,
and this is the wonder: neither did the man grow weary nor did you perish.
A great wonder, full of deeds, was wrought with you,
and no one knows how to recount its greatness.
Samson, the skilled reaper, held it like a sickle,
and reaped the field of the Philistines in a single hour.

O reaper who reaped bodies with a sickle of bone,
and whose iron was not blunted on these thousand stalks of grain!
A thousand stalks the swift one cut down at a single stoop,
and did not straighten up until he had completed the number of a thousand.
With one he began, and with one he finished the contest he waged,
and not even one of his limbs was harmed.
Without harm he remained, whole in body and soul;
his strength did not waver, nor did he slacken in his trust.
Like an athlete the athlete came up from the struggle,
and on his head was set the crown of the number of these slain.
At the end of the contest the champion was thirsty and distressed,
and began to ask for a drink at that moment to sustain his life:
"Are you not the Lord who gave me victory by the power of your help?
Give me drink, as you gave the victory you worked by my hands.
You gave me victory in the hard contest, and now I am thirsty;
do not delay, lest my victory be lost at the hands of the uncircumcised.
Give me drink, as you also gave me victory,
lest I die and the fools mock your great name."
The good Lord heard the petition of his just servant,
and gave him drink from within the bone by which he had conquered.
With the feeble bone the Lord gave his servant victory in the contest,
and from it gave him sweet drink to refresh himself.
Sweet drink flowed from the bone, against all custom,
and the just man marvelled that by the power of the Maker all things are easy.
The bone was unclean, and bare of drink besides,
and over both of these the will that rules over all prevailed.
From where did water flow within dryness?
Or who made it a fountain of life, wholly unclean as it was?
The command that made water flow from the rock
is the one that stored in it a moisture that was not in it.
The will that made the rock a spring of water
also made the unclean bone a drink for the just man.
The angel who sustained the Israelites on the way
gave water from the silent to the mouth of the speaking.
One of the Watchers embraced the bosom of rock and bone,
and brought forth from them longed-for [?] offspring, against all custom.

The spiritual one took from the elements of moisture
and joined them with the elements of dryness.
Subtly he combined them, one with another,
as one practised carries out what he is commanded.
In the same way that water is borne up above the air,
he set it subtly in the rock and in the bone.
To us this thing that happened against all custom is hard,
but to the heavenly beings it is very easy, according to their orders.
They received great power from the power that ordered all things,
and theirs is the working of the height and the depth.
They wrought this, which happened along with all that has happened;
they wrought it by the power of the Maker who strengthened them.
By the power of the Maker water flowed from the bone for Samson,
and by his help he won and conquered without a sword.
Without a sword the conqueror of the sinful won,
and without dispute received drink from the mouth of a bone.
Pure water the pure one drank from the mouth of the unclean,
and by his drinking he showed that nothing is unclean.
So there is nothing unclean in anything made by the Creator,
for see, even what was unclean to us has shown that it is pure.
Let everyone skilled in faith look at Samson's drinking,
and not doubt, as though anything were unclean in food and drink.
The bone was unclean according to the command of the Law,
but was entirely pure according to the divine will.
The hidden will purifies and defiles as it purposes,
and who can judge the Lord who rules over all?
The will of his love worked lovingly toward his servant,
and gave him victory in the contest and gave him drink, as pleased him.
Wondrous was the contest the son of the Hebrews waged on earth,
and at its wonder Satan and his hosts were astonished.
Astonishment seized the prince of the air, blinded by envy,
at the struggle a man had waged by the power of the Maker.
By the arrows of his own nature the hater of man was consumed with envy,
when he saw Samson overcome the force that had been gathered against him.
He counted the war waged against the Philistines as waged against himself,
and laid his own disgrace to the guilt of his ministers.
For everywhere his name was being defeated among the uncircumcised,

and since he saw that he was shamed in the error of his name, wrath clothed him.
Satan put on the zeal of wrath against Samson,
and began to devise crafty stratagems to fight against him.
The crafty of mind devised stratagems against the righteous one,
for he saw he could not wage a contest with him in the open.
He dug deep snares of desire and hid them before his steps,
to hunt by them the swiftness of the Nazirite gazelle.
He put on the weapons of his cunning, shamelessness,
and began to lay his snares through women, as is his custom.
He sent a woman like a spy to the blameless one,
and spied out his strength by the weak rib by which he had spied out Adam.
With love of a woman he bound the just man as with fetters,
and by her troubling she dulled the force of his valour.
Samson, lover of the fear of the truth, loved a woman,
and by his love for her she loosed the bond between him and his Lord.
The son of Abraham made love with a daughter of the nations,
and in his desire for her forgot the concerns of his fathers' house.
As though taking him captive, the woman captured the captor of nations,
and yoked him like an ox in the yoke of her desires.
In every way she wore down the heart of the sound of mind,
that he might tell her what the power was by which he conquered.
Beyond measure she pressed the mind of the lofty of soul,
until he showed her the great secret of his Nazirite vow:
"I am a Nazirite, and a great name is hidden in my Nazirite vow,
and if I remove the crown that is on my head, I am brought low.
My God gave me a crown of victory, the crown on my head,
and if I shave it, the power of his help departs from me."
The foolish woman saw that he had shown her all his heart,
and she plotted, and revealed to the sons of her people the secret of his humbling.
She called him, as one calls a sleeper, and lulled him to sleep on her knees,
and began to plunder the treasure of power hidden in his head.
Like a simpleton the wise one sank in the river of sleep,
and did not stir or feel the plundering of the treasure of his Nazirite vow.
As if from a draught of strong wine he was stupefied and lay silent,
and became wholly sleep's portion, beyond all measure.
She, full of iniquity, shaved his head without mercy,

and with his hair the power of his help was taken from him.
She called and roused him clamorously, as if from love,
and the sunken sleeper stirred and saw that his crown had been taken from him.
The uncircumcised seized the one pure of body and Nazirite of soul,
and blinded his eyes mercilessly, without pity.
The blind of mind made the bright of mind blind,
and brought him into the mill-house and thrust him in like one accursed.
The weak foxes made the enfeebled lion grind at the mill,
and in darkness they silenced the voice of his valour.
Beyond measure they mocked and scorned him and his Lord,
and when his Lord saw it, he pitied his humiliation and repelled them.
The erring held a great feast for their god of error,
and summoned Samson to make sport of him before a no-god.
The just man came, whom iniquity had blinded, to the buildings of the uncircumcised,
and began to dance, humbled in mind, before the despicable.
The profane accompanied the dance with the clapping of their hands,
and he danced in silence, groaning over his humiliation.
A great sorrow pained the discerning one within his mind,
as he saw how degrading was the enslavement of his honour.
He saw the worshippers of [?] mocking him at the feast of demons,
and he called on his Lord to restore to him the power he had lost.
"I beseech you, my God," said the just man to his God,
"hear me and answer me, and avenge for me the wrong done to my eyes.
Pity my lowliness, pass over my folly and forgive my sins,
and do not hold against me the sin I sinned against the secret of your gift."
With moving cries the just man sought pardon for his folly,
and his Lord heard him and gave him strength as before.
The help that had once accompanied him returned and dwelt in his senses,
and he began to test its truth by trial.
The champion grasped two pillars in his two hands,
and pulled the house down on its occupants, with himself in the midst.
"Let my soul die," he said, "with the Philistines, the uncircumcised of heart,"
and his word was fulfilled in deeds, just as he had said.
By a crushing death the just man died with the wicked,
and was not overcome in the way the course of human life runs.
Mightily the mighty one died along with the weak,
and his victory on the day of his death surpassed that of his lifetime.

The dead he killed on the day of his death were many more than those he killed in his life;
and from start to finish he carried out the sword's purpose against the wicked.
Against the wicked he had set his will from the beginning;
yet though he was good, he acted foolishly, did not persevere, and neglected what was proper.
He acted foolishly in revealing the mystery of his gift to a foolish woman,
and he suffered and groaned bitterly over his folly.
Let the righteous man's folly be a rod for the rebellion of our souls,
and by its exposure let it draw out the evil hidden in our hearts.
Let us look closely at his zeal and the humility of his soul,
so that we do not boast of the fine things we possess.
The nature we are clothed in is weak and full of passions;
it easily shines with fair things, then turns and fades.
It is right to guard our lives from harm with fear,
and with freedom to guard the treasure of our souls' freedom.
On David and Saul
55. On David and Saul. / Again by the same author, his own: / Homily fifty-five, / which he composed on David and Saul.

My mind has found a fitting companion in the conduct of the righteous, and it longs to journey with it in the discourse of words.
It saw that the road of their labors is straight, and it has made ready words to cast itself as a companion [?] into their riches.
It saw that in their conduct they resemble the goal of the King, and it has brought words to the lyre of the mouth to [?] the truth.
On the road of truth the merchants of the word of truth set out, and through trial they gathered spiritual wealth.
My thoughts have gone out [?] after the wealth of their conduct, to see the beauty of their victories and whom they resemble.
The sound of their struggles has roused my mind as if from sleep; I have gone out to see how men overcome sufferings.
Love of them has drawn me, like a child, toward their labors, and I wish to paint the image of their beauties with the colors of my word.
I wished to read in the writings of the books of the King, and I saw a line in which the story of kings is inscribed.
King after king I saw inscribed among the records, and the stamp of each one's name differed from his fellow's.
Crown did not resemble crown upon their heads, nor did scepter agree with scepter in the hands that held them.
In one, the line of his story ran with blood across the pages; in another, the name of his dominion was proclaimed as a burden [?].
In the book of the Spirit Saul was inscribed as preeminent, but the Command turned it around, read him rightly, and blotted out his name.
It was not by mistake that the Writer erred and wrote his name;
He Himself inscribed it, to teach by his name that no one should go astray; He came and set it among the paths of the lines of the Spirit,
so that people might see and not be led astray in the wilderness of his way.
On the page of the book He drew the image of the slack king, to show in him the ugliness of iniquity, how ugly it is.
At the head of the record of the election of kings He inscribed Saul, so that whoever reads might look carefully and read accordingly.
On the second line He wrote the election of chaste David, and painted the triumphs of his soul's purity before the beholders.
The hidden Command anointed both of them, and not by error; it chose and rejected according to the testing of their wills [?].
He chose them knowing their deeds before they came to be, and showed His love, that it overflows even upon the wicked, if they are willing.
In Saul He showed how much He hates wickedness of the will, and in the son of Jesse He revealed His pleasure, that He loves the just.
Saul's iniquity rejected him and cast him out of the kingship, and David's love set upon him the crown of leadership.

The commandment blotted out the name of Saul from the archives, and the Doer of justice wrote David in place of the wicked one.
The hidden Command set its hand to his dominion, and with an oath sealed the rank of his leadership.
The God of all, who does not lie, swore and confirmed that David's throne shall be established forever, without end.
His seed shall run its course with the luminaries, sun and moon, and shall not be cut off from the succession of the name of kingship.
"Once I have sworn by My holy name, and I do not lie, that as long as I endure David shall reign, and the seed that comes from him.
"A kingdom in time I give him as a pledge, and by his deeds I will seal it at the fullness of the ages.
"A good reward I pay him for his struggles: a kingdom in time, and a kingship on high that will never be dissolved.
"Because he did not grow proud and despise My commandments as Saul did, I will exalt him before the eyes of beholders in the offspring that comes from him.
"Shall I not give him heaven and earth to govern, so that his scepter may reign over those above and those below?
"In the name of My being from the beginning I make him a sharer, and I make him heir and lord of all that I have created."
David received the promise of life at the beginning of his reign, and he believed, and held the far-off things as firm as if they were near.
Through things revealed he saw hidden things that are not seen, and in earthly things he traced the figures of things to come.
In expectation of the reward of things to come he endured labors, and for love of the Creator's name he kept the commandments.
He heard that God is the God of all and possesses all, and he set nothing beside His lordship, giving thanks to none but Him.
From the divine commandment he learned His being, and confirmed by His works that His eternity has no beginning.
On the law of the Spirit he meditated night and day, and on its hidden things he pondered evening and morning.
He was nourished like an infant on the milk of its words, and by its meanings he advanced to perfection.
Like a mirror it was fixed at all times before his mind, and in it he saw the fitting likeness of beautiful things.
With the outward senses he saw earthly things in it, and with his mind he contemplated the Endless One.
By his love the image of the Being without composition was painted in him, and though It is hidden, to him It was revealed through faith.
By faith he contemplated things not revealed, and they stood before him as though they had come to pass in deeds.
As if with a finger he pointed out the power of the Creator, so that people might see the God of all through His ordering of the world.
From silent things he taught rational beings: "Look, you discerning ones, at the silent course, and give praise."
With the clarity of his voice he stirred the hosts of heavenly beings to render praise to the Power that gave strength to their beings.
Rational beings and mute creatures he invited and called to the thanksgiving of the Hidden One, as debtors who have received life and owe thanksgiving.

With the voice of thanksgiving he trained the childhood of mankind, and raised it from the lowlands to the heights.
On the lyre of words he composed melodies to render praises, so that all might listen, through the readings, to the searching out of mysteries.
With songs he lured them as with bait, and so he cast the net of life over his hearers.
With the snares of the Spirit he hunted the perverse people, and shut them up within the strongholds of the word of life.
He put the bridle of love upon the brutish man, and set in order the course of his impulses away from ugly things.
Like a charioteer his voice rode upon every mouth, and drove them along the smooth road of the Creator's name.
Comely was his voice as he proclaimed in the ears of all: "Hear this, all you peoples, and listen to my words."
He longed to bind all the peoples with the yoke of love, so that they might serve under the lordship of the one Creator.
With the armor of the Spirit he fought against error, tearing down the name of paganism and building up the truth.
He was clothed with zeal like a breastplate for the one Creator, and contended against the gods that men had fashioned.
With the sound of his words he exposed the godless, who say in their thinking [?] that there is no God.
In every contest he was victorious, in hidden and in open things, and he was exalted over every god by the name of the Creator.
In every land the might of his victory was spoken of, and among all peoples the triumph of his labors was recounted.
Only one there was who mourned over his triumphs: the Hater of mankind, to whom the victory of man is not pleasing.
He was clothed with grief at the beauties of the chosen king, seeing that his love shone forth and won over everyone.
The rebel put on the jealousy of wrath against David, and wished to multiply crafty schemes, as he had against Job.
Long before, he had kindled the fire of wrath against the possessions of the just man, so that he might hear the sound of blasphemies from the righteous one.
Here he set a snare for the lion that terrified the peoples, so that if he fell he might raise his voice against the righteous.
He wages a hidden war always against the just man, and buries countless snares deep, to see how he may prevail.
The Evil One devised an evil plot against the son of Jesse, and caught him in a snare pleasing to the sight, as he had Adam.
He showed desirable bait to the swift-winged eagle, and it left its height and came down to the earth to take food.
Desire took captive the king who took peoples captive, and like an exile he went out and was enslaved to wantonness.
The tyrant shut him up within the dwelling of wantonness, so that he might no longer [?] his armies with the voice of his victory.
With a weak rib he struck [?] him and cast him down as if with a weapon, and shut the door [?] in his face so that he could not escape.
With the same chain that he had cast upon Adam he bound the just man,

and, as with the fruit, he enticed his desire with the beauty of a face.
With fruit he killed the king who first reigned on earth, and with enticements he overthrew David into the pit of iniquity.
Adam was lovely and David comely, before they sinned [?]; but the Evil One by his scheme disgraced the fairest of all.
He clothed the lovely kings in garments of iniquity, and stained them with the desire for food and the desire of the body.
He mixed the poison of death into food and bodily desire, and gave them to drink the draught [?] of the venom of his bitterness.
A cup of filth he mixed with sin and gave it to David, and he drank of it, and his mind, wiser than all, went astray.
As one does a child, he enticed him and drew him toward amusement, and set a snare before his pupils and caught him by his eyes.
The slack eye saw the comeliness of the body's features, and kindled a fleshly fire [?] in its kindred flesh.
Flesh lusted after flesh with the desire of the flesh, and like a hungry man he longed to eat the fruit.
The hunger of the eyes wore down chaste David, and he contrived how he might fulfil the desire of his lust.
The inner impulse signaled to the outward eye: "Look and see how sweet is the food of the flesh."
The eye was fixed upon the eye without being sated, and it pleased it to look again until its gazing was complete.
Desire of the body took the eye captive, as it had Eve, and it was not sated with gazing at the face, as she had been with the fruit.
Eve marveled at the fruit, how pleasant it was, and David's eye at the features of the body, how desirable they were.
The fruit, by its eating, blotted out the commandment of the Hidden One from Eve, and the beauty of a face blinded David to understanding.
There was nothing lovelier to Eve than that fruit, and the son of Jesse thought no beauty could compare with hers.
One was the snare that caught them both, David and her: David by a face, and her by [?].
The cunning hawk saw the bird that desired food, lay in wait on the ground, and caught it suddenly through an ugly gaze.
The young dove came down to take food for her belly, and the Enemy spread the birdlime of iniquity and plucked her wings.
The son of Jesse went up to look upon the beauty of the land, and the rebel set before his pupils a languid sight.
He slackened his will from the strength of the love of truth, and bound his mind with the face of a rib, soft of body.
As he gazed he did not consider at whom he was gazing, nor did he remember the voice that says, "You shall not covet."
That lyre that sang of truth forgot its wisdom, and began to play upon the strings of the body, heavy with the senses.
The pipe of the Spirit, sweet of melody, changed its voice, and composed fleshly tunes full of sorrow.
He who hated iniquity coveted and longed for what was not his, and broke down the fence that the law had set before the covetous.
A guest came to David, and lodged with David unawares [?]; and he spared his own, and robbed another, and offered up what was another's.

The just king sent and brought his servant's ewe, and made her a sacrifice to the crafty iniquity that lodged with him.
David ate the food of iniquity with the deceiver, and busied himself with the [?] in a foul drinking.
He who hunted peoples with the unbreakable net of the Spirit was caught by his own eyes in the flimsy nets of his household.
He who put the bridles of modesty in the mouths of the wanton let his own soul go into the ugly gaze of fleshly desire.
He who sealed the bond of fellowship with the seals of his words blotted out by his gaze the bond to which the finger of the Spirit had set its hand.
He who charged men that no one should wrong his fellows removed the boundary that the Creator had set in human nature.
He who rebuked the covetous not to long for what belongs to others
gave rein [?] to his will to rob his fellows of their wives.
The clear eye through which people used to see the Hidden One suddenly grew dark, and [...] darkness upon the beholders.
The trumpet voice that proclaimed the name of Being ceased its sounds, and people no longer listened to the word [?] of life.
He who interpreted the voices of hidden things for the ignorant fell mute in his understanding, and did not perceive his own deed.
The fair ray that showed the path of righteousness flickered and went out, and its course toward righteousness ceased.
The salt that gave a sweet savor to insipid things lost its savor and became like [?] things that have not been seasoned.
The reed of the Spirit, with which the skilled scribe used to write, gave itself into the hand of his inclination to write falsehood.
He who roused spiritual beings with the sound of his melodies to sing praise fell asleep in sin, and his senses sank into the sleep of iniquity.
He who invited the mute to the thanksgiving of the God of all saw his lyre fall idle, and iniquity snapped the strings of its movements.
He who was strong in battles, who conquered kings and plundered peoples, was defeated by a rib weak in strength and despised in body.
The athlete who triumphed in the crown of his labors was overpowered by his lust, and it trampled his might to the ground.
He who joined battle with spiritual foes and with bodily foes was seized by iniquity, which bound him and cast him down like a contemptible man.
The pure temple of divine revelations [?] defiled itself in the foul drink of its neighbor's spring.
The lion's whelp who killed the lion and tore apart the bear trembled before the face of a beast whose fang is soft.
Lion and bear did not shake him from his trust, but a tame bear growled suddenly and he trembled before her.
The son of Jesse lusted, and his inclination fulfilled the desire of his body, and he began to ponder shameful things unfitting for him.
He saw that his hidden lust had been exposed by her visible womb,
and he began to devise crafty schemes that bring about murder.
He abandoned the meditation on spiritual things in which he had been engaged, and busied himself reading in the book of the man-slayer.
The Evil One wrote a harmful book for him upon his thoughts, and he began to meditate like an ignorant man on unfitting things.
In the twisted line of the great deceiver he read craftily, seeking how he might contrive cunningly to shed blood.

He read, and was confirmed in the writings of the master [?] of falsehood, and he too learned to hold the pen as [?] he did.
With guile he sent, like a spy, to the member of his household, and summoned him to himself under the guise of love, while deceiving him.
Uriah saw the deceit hidden within the words, and he too hid the thought of his heart under the guise of words.
He heard the king command him to go and rejoice in his house, and he spurned comforts under the guise of love for his lord:
"No, by your life, good king, [?] king, I will not exchange your love for the pleasure of a moment [?]."
The son of Jesse saw that his snares had been defeated, and he plotted in secret with his thoughts to write iniquity.
His limbs took up the [?] that evil lust had sharpened, and he began to inscribe innocent blood upon the paper.
He who was the reed of the Spirit held in his hand the reed of death; he reversed the order and began to write from Taw to Alaph.
While the Holy Spirit wrote with it, its line was straight; but once the finger of the Evil One took hold of it, it threw its order into confusion.
He sealed the poison of death in a letter and gave it to Uriah, that he might go and drink it far from the king, so that it would not be revealed.
The guileless man took the sword that crafty lust had forged, and went and brought it to the executioner to cut off his own head.
O messenger who carries death upon his shoulders, and hastens it along like a gift to the ruin [?] of his own life!
He went proudly with the king's seal placed in his hands, not knowing that death lay sealed within the seal.
Uriah set out from the king with his death beside him, and walked with his murderer rejoicing and glad.
He arrived and reached the camp of his lord's servants, went in and presented himself before the commander who led the people.
He gave him greeting, and the king's seal in which death was depicted, and rejoiced that he had been found worthy to bear the king's word.
The poor man thought he was receiving gifts for his errand, and did not know that he was giving up his life like a condemned man.
The commander broke the king's seal that was placed in his hands, and marveled greatly how the just man had turned from the way.
He read the letter and saw the deceit hidden within it, and he sealed it up again and hid the deceit within his thoughts.
He saw death blazing in the lines of the writing, and knew in his heart that the king had decreed a sentence and sent it forth.
David had shut it up within the cage of the writing and sent it to Joab: "See, and release it wisely.
"Inspect the people," he says, "and set in order the ranks of the armies, and under the guise of battle hide the deceit, so that it may not be found out.
"Put Uriah at the head of the camp as a champion, and turn your face away from helping him, so that he may be struck [?] and die."
Joab fulfilled the king's will as he had been commanded; Uriah died, and the innocent was condemned, and iniquity prevailed [?].

The commander wrote and informed David of all that had happened: "Behold, your servant is dead; now fulfil your soul's desire."
The son of Jesse heard that Uriah was dead and was relieved of fear, not knowing that his death would multiply fear for his own life.
The just king accomplished his will through adultery and murder, and sent and took his neighbor's wife as though rightfully.
The wise man thought he had done wisely what he did, not knowing that it was folly before the One who knows all.
The king reasoned: "Who searches out the secrets of the king? And who [...] the head that is set above the body?"
His thoughts wove crafty schemes like a garment, and he hid his iniquity from beholders and from the One who sees all.
And who hid the image of the Hidden One from his mind, that vision in which the Hidden One was painted before his memory?
Who silenced the trumpet voice of his prophecy, he who said that the Hidden One is in the height and in the depth?
Who cut the strings of the lyre of the Spirit, and stilled the song of its sweet melodies?
Who hindered the course of his way, which ran so well, so that he ceased and sat idle from the labor of spiritual things?
Who caught the swift gazelle in the nets of iniquity, and gave it as food to the insatiable desire of the body?
Who shut up the mighty lion within the cage, so that contemptible foxes mocked and laughed at his humiliation?
Who put the bridle of silence upon the thunder of the voices that [...] praise to the Hidden One with the spiritual beings?
Who confounded the shrewdest of all through enticements, so that he who gave savor to insipid things became a child?
Who, then, broke the arms of the mighty warrior, so that he fell short of the goal he aimed at with the impulses of his soul?
Who, then, blinded the clear eye of his faith, and darkened his mind so that it could not see the Hidden One in His works?
Who, then, killed the body and soul of him who was wholly sound, so that he became sick through the wounds his inclination inflicted on him?
David had fallen into ugly iniquity as into a disease, and the king was ashamed to reveal his sore to the eyes of beholders.
The Physician on high saw the member of His household lying in iniquity, and sent to him the prophet, his companion, to heal his sore.
The Physician of the Spirit sent to the temple of the Spirit, to drive out iniquity and bring the Spirit back to the sanctuary of his soul.
With the sound of the lyre of prophecy He wished to awaken the sleeper, who had sunk under the weight of iniquity as into sleep.
[...] gave the medicine of the Spirit to the physician of the Spirit, [...] to go and heal the body that iniquity had made sick.
Nathan came to the son of Jesse as he had been commanded, and put out his hand and felt the sore, and saw that it was grave.
He saw that it was not fitting to bring a harsh incision near it, lest the pain reach the soul and it depart.
He wished to mix a gentle medicine by means of a parable, so that the swelling of iniquity might be softened by the medicine of the Spirit.

Nathan began to compound words like drugs, while David lay sunk as in sleep and did not perceive.
"There were," he says, "two men in a city, one beside the other; one rich and one poor, a king and his servant.
"That rich man possessed a multitude of sheep and oxen, and that poor man possessed only one ewe.
"A traveler came to that rich man who possessed much; he took the poor man's ewe and slaughtered it before him.
"Judge justly, with the discernment of your wisdom: condemn iniquity and vindicate truth, as you are accustomed to do.
"See that you show no partiality in the case that has been brought to you, for I have brought it to you trusting in your just judgment.
"A hidden Command has sent me to you in a figure, so that I may learn from you how iniquity is judged and how truth prevails."
The son of Jesse heard of the wrongs that men commit on the earth, and he grew zealous and fierce against the oppressor who wronged his neighbor.
He passed just judgment upon himself without knowing it: "As the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die."
He pronounced a just sentence upon himself according to the law, and sealed his tablet with the living name of the Creator.
He decreed the harsh threat of death upon the oppressor, and set his hand to the sentence that ended his life.
And what will you do, son of Jesse, after your words? For behold, you stand condemned by the decree of judgment that your own mouth pronounced.
Behold, you decreed death in your writings and placed it in the archives, and set your hand to the indictment that you deserve to die.
The prophet of the Spirit saw that the king stood condemned by his own words, while his heart was sunk and he did not perceive that he was judging himself.
Nathan lifted his voice and said, at the command of the Hidden One: "You are the man who did this, O king and prophet.
"You are the one who seized what was not yours, though you had much; and you are the one who shed innocent blood by your cunning.
"You have wives who possess beauty and wear crowns, yet your lust was not sated until you snatched your neighbor's wife.
"The desire of the flesh took you captive and led you outside the bounds of order; your eye lusted, your will coveted, and your inclination killed.
"Why did you forget that voice in the books, 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife,' so that you might not be exposed?
"Why did you blot out from your mind that saying, 'Whoever sheds blood, his blood shall be shed in return for the blood he shed'?
"Why did you hide the corruption of your soul from the One who knows all, and did not remember what you yourself prophesied, that He is the searcher of hearts?
"Was it not you who said that He is in all things, in the height and in the depth, and that the work of His hands cannot hide from its Maker?
"Where is your voice that used to resound in men's ears: 'Blessed is the one who has not joined with the wicked'?
"Did I not choose you as a just man and reject the wicked one? Why did you not hold fast to the election of your anointing?
"You sinned and hid yourself from righteousness like a fugitive, not knowing that it was following close behind your iniquity.
"You were ashamed before men, and you were not ashamed before My Name, which is holier than all,

"and you covered your iniquity with a thick garment of wronged blood.
"Because you hid yourself like a fugitive from correction [?], behold, I reveal the schemes of iniquity to the eyes of beholders.
"Because you shamelessly took liberties with your neighbor's wife, behold, I give the wives of your bed over to shame.
"Because you killed and shed innocent blood that had not wronged you, the sword of death shall never again depart from your offspring.
"Because you humbled truth and raised the horn of wantonness, your seed shall no longer lift its head before its persecutors."
The son of Jesse saw that the Command, to which all things are revealed, had caught him, rebuked his iniquity, and exposed his sin against his will.
He saw that justice had seized him firmly, and he lowered his voice like a debtor who has incurred guilt and been brought low.
He saw that the deceit he had devised within his thoughts was exposed, and [...] he condemned himself, that he had sinned unjustly and hidden it.
With a loud voice he accused his iniquity before the One who knows all: "It is I who coveted and committed adultery, who killed and hid my corruption.
"It is I, I, upon whose mind the guest of iniquity came and lodged [?], and enticed me and drew me toward the delight of wantonness.
"It is I, I, who refrained from rejoicing in a lawful companion, and hid my disgrace [?] by an unlawful slaughter.
"It is I, I, who hid snares to trip the guileless of heart, and it is I, I, who shed innocent blood that had not wronged me.
"Evil lust hid a snare for me in the outward senses, and iniquity caught me in the net of the face of a weak rib.
"Iniquity blinded me to the understanding of discernment, and I did not consider as I walked on the path of falsehood.
"I have sinned, then, and I cannot make repayment, and countless labors cannot be weighed against my folly.
"The waters of the great sea are too few to wash me, and the iniquity of my person is not pardoned by earthly things.
"Great is my folly, and the sin I have sinned cannot be measured; the sea is too small to wash away the filth of my iniquity."
The Will that had seen him before he sinned saw that he was scourging himself, as a judge scourges a man condemned to death.
It saw that he was humbled and that his heart had fallen from its confidence, and It gave him a hand, lest he cut off the hope of his life.
The Command signaled to the physician who had come to heal his sore, to lay upon his stains the medicine of soothing words:
"Speak with him gently with the sound of your words, and let fall into his ears the good news of life, that He is gracious freely.
"Reveal it and tell him: there is a medicine that heals iniquity, if you pay the price of repentance and the sufferings of the soul."
The Spirit spoke with the son of Jesse through Nathan's lyre: "Behold, mercy has persuaded the Hidden One to be reconciled to you.
"Behold, He has intimated [?] to me in secret that your iniquity is forgiven, and you will not die for your folly as you supposed.
"Behold, the Command has restrained the lawful executioner, so that he sheathes his sword within the divine mercies.
"A terrible death had been prepared for you by the law, but He has shown you favor, so that the Enemy might not boast over your death.
"For it was he who caught you through his deceptions, so that he might rejoice in your downfall [?].

"And if you die, envy will grow against the righteous.
I will not give room for his envy to grow great,
lest he grow used to shedding blood because of iniquity.
In you I tread a new road for repentance,
so that the Evil One may be put to shame when sinners are shown grace by the mercies of goodness.
In you I paint a fair image of the name of goodness,
to be an advocate for sinners until the end of the ages.
In you I proclaim a good hope to the hopeless:
that mercies abound toward human iniquity and give life freely.
I know the evil inclination of human nature,
how very weak it is to stand firm before rebukes.
In you I set the leaven of life that heals humankind,
and from your shoot I raise up the fruit that blots out iniquity.
By this stipulation your folly is quenched by the medicine of mercies,
so that I may tread the way before the One who comes to forgive iniquity.
From you will dawn the One who tears up the bond of debts,
and see, I have shown the mystery of his coming in his father's iniquity.
By the law of his words he abolishes the cries of vengeance,
and [?] writes grace and mercies within his books.
With his blood he writes a bond of freedom for the children of his race,
and tears up the deed of humanity's slavery.
And so I did not give death the opportunity
to kill your life because of the iniquity of the slaves' servitude.
Because of iniquity slaves were made subject to death;
see, I draw up the bond of debts by sparing your life.
See, son of Jesse, how much favor your sin receives:
I have relaxed my law so that you will not become a slave to death.
Yet I have not cancelled my law's demand;
I gave mercies as a ransom for you and settled it for you.
Nor was justice deceived, nor did it forget its record:
the statute of your iniquity is written in its book with all who have sinned.
Here the name of your folly is wiped out of the law;
it was not hidden from that writing which is inscribed in my knowledge.
See, your iniquity is forgiven in the fullness of time, according to the law.
Go, prepare for yourself sacrifices of love for the life to come.
See, I have shown you the path of pity that mercies have trodden;
hold to it with toil, and teach people to walk with you.
See, I have given you a hand of hope to return to life:
support the lost, and encourage them with the word of forgiveness.
See, I have delivered you from the law that held you bound:
rescue the wronged from the wrongdoer, show grace and have mercy."
The sinner who was dead in his sin heard the word of forgiveness,
and stirred from death as from sleep, and returned to life.
He saw that he had advocates at the judgment on behalf of his folly,
and began to strive to return to the rank of his authority.
He grieved that the bond of his forgiveness was not yet sealed,
and was ashamed to raise his hand to the divine Nod on his own behalf.
He turned to setting mournful strains on the lyre of his limbs,

in the hope that he might return to the boldness he had before his Lord.
He lived in fear, even though he had received forgiveness for his iniquity,
and did not cease to gather advocates on his behalf.
It was clear to him, though he had received release from his folly,
that he was not yet worthy [?] to sing praise in the Spirit.
Of this too he was ashamed: with the sound of laments
to strike [?] on the lyre of his soul as he had before.
The Creator saw that his inmost being longed to give voice [?] to it,
and restored to him the power to search out things to come.
He took up the gift that had dwelt in him before his folly,
and began to sing mournful strains in the Spirit:
"How long, Lord, will you forget me, as one [?]?
How long will you turn your face away from the son of your house?
How long will you set anxiety within my thoughts,
while I see the reproach of fools who mock me?
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me to my persecutors,
and put my help far off because of the hateful word my lips have spoken?
For I know that iniquity has taken my innocence from my head,
and for that reason the enemy has pursued my life without pity.
It is not hidden from me that my afflictions come because of my folly,
and it is true that my companions [?] have stirred up war against me.
It was not that the help which should have gone with me grew small and failed;
I am the one who fell short of the reward of the love of truth.
I confess that I have sinned, and that for my folly I am chastised.
I am ashamed not of my scourgings [?] but of my iniquities.
This alone I urge upon the Nod that chastises me:
that my correction may not be harsh, but merciful.
Do not, Lord, rebuke me in fierce anger,
nor show me a face of wrath that has no door.
Discipline me with gentle chastisements, as befits your sweetness,
lest the pain of my correction give birth to hateful murmuring."
The righteous man bore great suffering in his mind,
even after he had heard that voice from heaven: "Your iniquity is forgiven."
O righteous one, to whom the Nod handed over the bond of his debts,
yet who turned and placed himself under justice like a debtor!
O athlete who failed in the contest, yet the Nod held him up,
and he would not wear the crown of forgiveness without merit!
O ever-watchful one, who sank for a little while into the sleep of iniquity,
yet did not cease his glorious labors against iniquity!
Come, sinners, see a sinner who sinned and remained [?],
and stand like him at the door of mercy of the faithful Nod.
Come, righteous ones, see a righteous man who failed through sin,
and guard the treasures of your thoughts from the thief.
Come, discerning ones, see a seer who looked and was blinded,
and close the eyes of your thoughts to hateful things.
If the seer of hidden things went astray in his looking,
who would not cast a veil of modesty over his own eyes?
If the holy one defiled his soul by the sight of a face,
who would not restrain his eyes from running toward stumbling blocks?
If a mighty man was swept away by the rib of a soft body,

who would not arm the impulses of his soul against the serpent?
Let David be like a mirror before those who look,
and in him let the traders, righteous and sinners, take note.
Let the righteous man not boast like the one who reigned,
and let the one who has sinned not lose heart like the one who perished.
Let the righteous man guard the treasures of his soul from boasting,
and let the sinner too bind up his pain with repentance.
Toward the goal of truth let everyone strive with impulses and senses,
so that he may be worthy to receive the crown of victory that never perishes.
On Solomon, on his election, and on his judgment

56. On Solomon.
By the same author.
The fifty-sixth memra,
which he composed on Solomon, on his election, and on his judgment.

King David took the authority of the everlasting kingdom
and gave it to his son, so that the promise of His words might not prove false.
The son of Jesse saw that the royal throne would pass along his line,
and he charged his son not to grow slack and lose his rank.
He had heard that the sceptre of his headship was stretched out for ever,
and beforehand he gave his crown to his son in readiness.
In his lifetime he gave him the crown that the King over all had given him,
for he saw that the Evil One was ready to snatch away the greatness of his rank.
He sealed his crown with the seal of anointing, so that it might not be changed,
and so that the Evil One would see it and not rejoice in plundering his Lord's promise.
With the holy oil the prophet-king sealed his crown,
so that the crafty wiles of the Deceiver might not harm it.
The just man was convinced that his son had taken up a struggle with the Evil One,
and he anointed him beforehand, so that the hand of the Evil One would slip off him.
To Solomon he gave the crown and the rank of headship,
so that his name, the peace of mankind, might be fulfilled in deed.
Great peace lay hidden in the name that was given to him,
and David revealed it by the crown and the rank he quickly placed in his hands.
His first name, “Beloved of God,” revelation gave him,
and his other name was “Lover of peace among men.”
These names were given him through prophecy,
one by Nathan and one by David, singular prophets.
Nathan the prophet called him Jedidiah, “the Lord loved him,”
and David named him Solomon, the peace that brings peace to men.
Fittingly they set names upon one who would keep the law,
that first he should love the God of all, and so also His servants.
Love of truth and love of peace are his names,
and by both of them the son of Jesse wished to bring his son to perfection.
Wisely the wise man acted at the close of his life,
in making his son king and teaching him the power hidden in his name.
To his son the just king handed over his crown and his rank,
so that the promise of His words might proceed along his line.
The true man loved the promise of his Lord more than anything,
and his Lord in turn repaid him with a love greater than his own.
Through deeds he sealed his words to the son of his house,
that he might honour his son with the wisdom of truth, like his father's.
The wise son resembled his father at the outset of his reign,
and like his begetter he pursued justice and humbled iniquity.

Against iniquity he armed himself valiantly,
and like an athlete went down into the contest of righteousness.
The young lad took up the sceptre of headship
and raised his hand to scourge tyrannical iniquity.
He stretched out harsh cunning against the iniquity of the people of his nation,
and at his severity the wicked among the nations were afraid.
At the severity of his scourges both the wicked and the just were astonished,
at how much the speech of his mouth resembled his father David.
The wisdom of truth that was innate in him they heard from his mouth,
and good and wicked alike feared him and obeyed his commands.
The mystery of his election cast fear into their thoughts,
and though unwilling, they submitted to his election and honoured his rank.
That mystery, moreover, strengthened his movements with the power of wisdom,
and his mind became a treasury of hidden proverbs.
Like a treasure-house he opened his mind to the needy people
and enriched them by his discernment of judgment between good and evil.
The people were in need of the discernment of his judgment,
and he drove the darkness of partiality out from among the people.
Through a case of killing the mystery of his election first tested him,
and saw that his purity portrayed his beauty to the eyes of onlookers.
Through contemptible harlots it tested his truth,
and by deeds it explained his name, that he was a lover of peace.
Two foolish women lived together, though they were not alike,
and they conceived and bore like infants in a [?] succession.
The unlike women conceived alike at the same time,
and came and reached the order of childbirth that is set in nature.
Their unlikeness laid bare the covering of their deeds
and brought them into the furnace of testing of just judgment.
Contemptibly the foolish women slept, as was their custom,
and the heaviness of sleep overpowered them, so that they neither stirred nor sensed anything.
For one slept and killed her son [?],
and the other sank into sleep and did not wake at the smothering of her child.
The one full of iniquity slept, killed, rose, and stole;
the one full of compassion lay down, was silent, rose, and was dismayed.
Beyond the course of nature sleep overcame the [?] woman,
and she did not wake at the cry of her child as he was crushed.
The weight of her wickedness fell upon her infant and silenced his life,
and when she awoke, her wickedness did not awaken.
Her body alone stirred from the heavy sleep,
while her soul sank under the weight of iniquity, which is beyond measure.
Harsh iniquity wished to profit by the death of her son,
and in place of her child she conceived and bore a twofold iniquity.
The foolish woman saw that she had become a disgrace through her negligence,
and she conceived deceit and bore iniquity to heal her pain.
She saw that she was cut off from rearing the rational fruit,
and she wove a garment of thefts to cover herself with.
Like a robber she fell quietly upon her companion
and snatched the living infant from her and put the dead one in its place.
Infant for infant the woman full of iniquity wished to exchange,
and wickedly she took the living and put the dead in its place.

She took the living and put the dead in its place, the shameless one,
and though she thought her pain would be healed, her pain only grew.
With the living infant she wished to adorn the hatefulness of her soul,
and by her dead son she wished to disgrace the beauty of compassion.
She brazenly disowned her own child, saying it was not hers,
and what was not hers she called her own, though it was not.
The one not hers she held in her bosom until morning,
not knowing that the light would come and expose him to her.
At dawn it woke the contemptible women,
and they rose to tend children not their own as though they were their own.
Theft had overturned the order of birth:
they were theirs, and yet not truly theirs.
Both carried children not their own, falsely,
until the hour of dawn reproved the falsehood.
The dawn showed the falsehood in the faces of the infants,
and by their features exposed and revealed the deceit.
By the infant's face the mother of the living infant saw
that the dead child lying in her bosom was not hers.
Grief seized her at the lawless deeds,
that her infant had been stolen and another infant laid in her bed.
Lawlessly the quarrelsome woman had attacked her companion
and cruelly stolen the living infant from her.
The armour of impudence clothed the mind of the shameless woman,
and she began to contend that the dead infant was not hers.
As if in a [?], the two fell into grief and impudence,
and they quarrelled over the right to the living infant.
The mother of the living fought with the weapon of love,
and the mother of the dead with the crafty weapon of contentiousness.
The mother of the living was urged by compassion to claim what was hers,
and impudence drew the shameless woman to snatch for nothing.
The foolish women waged a great war over their infants,
and their struggle did not cease until the king and the people heard.
The son of David heard the report of the killing that reached his ears,
and he was zealous and strengthened himself to explain his name in deed.
For the peace of mankind the command of the Ruler over all had chosen him,
and he too began to make peace among men by his name.
Through deeds he wished to display the peace of his name,
and he summoned and called the tribes of the people to hear his judgment.
All the tribes gathered to hear a new judgment,
that at one stroke they might see the power in the son of David.
The power that the Power of wisdom had placed in him gathered them,
that through manifest things they might see the power of hidden things.
Assembly upon assembly stood, all the crowds, to listen to him,
and they waited for the moment when he would open the door of his mind.
Like [?], young men and elders were longing
to hear a word from the mouth of the youth who had quietly become king.
With hidden longing all stood [?] at the hour of judgment,
waiting for when the king's heart would bring forth the judgment of the infant.
The king, too, was pressed by the birth pangs of truth,
until the hidden case of the infant should be revealed before the onlookers.

Like a woman in labour stood his mind, which brings forth proverbs,
and it was in travail to bring forth a word beyond reproach.
The wise man gave command concerning the foolish women, and the court was convened,
and they began, one out of love and the other with impudence.
The mother of the living told the story gently,
and the mother of the dead struck out with brazen insolence.
She who loved her child claimed her child [?],
and she who had killed her son cried out wickedly, without shame.
At the impudence the son of David marvelled, how far a heart can go,
and he looked and considered how he might strip off her audacity.
He saw her heart, the harsh insolence of contentiousness,
and that without witnesses her falsehood would not be reproved.
He saw that if he said the dead infant was hers,
she would contend against him, king though he was, that it was not hers.
He considered that if he ordered the infant to be given to the cruel woman,
the people would think that, as one showing partiality [?], he had done her wrong.
He saw that if he dismissed the women's quarrel without a trial,
the wisdom of truth that dwells within him would not be revealed.
Wisely he examined the case that was brought before him,
and by a trial he searched it out and revealed it to the eyes of the onlookers.
Through a trial the wise son of the wise commanded
that a sword be brought and the dispute of the two women be settled.
Into the furnace of the sword he would bring the contemptible women,
and see which was the mother of the living and which the mother of the dead.
“Let the sword be a clear witness concerning the hidden infant,
and let it search out for us whose the living infant is.
Let it reveal to us the hidden things of the crafty inclination,
and recount to us how infant was exchanged for infant.”
In great astonishment the Hebrews stood at the king's command,
and they were amazed at the new and unaccustomed judgment.
His hearers stood divided when he asked for the sword,
pondering whether his judgment was true or not.
The dull of heart reckoned the word he spoke a joke,
while the lovers of truth thought that a truth lay hidden in the command.
Through the disagreement of their thoughts the son of David looked,
and he asked for the sword to test them along with the harlots.
Like the women, he brought them into the furnace of testing,
and purified them of the restless counterfeit of disagreement.
The sword was brought, and the executioner stood in the court,
and the king ordered that the living infant be cut in two.
“Cut the living infant in two,” commanded the son of David,
“and give half of his limbs to one and half to the other.”
The contemptible women who had been contending over his life cried out:
“Let his life come to an end, and see, we are rid of the strife!
In the struggle we were casting lots for which would win possession of his life;
let them take him from us in equal shares, and the struggle is over.”
The mother of the living saw that the king's command was hastening,
and she thought that he truly meant to kill her son.
She saw that the executioner had raised the sharpened sword,
and her compassion ran and seized his hand, to keep him from killing.
Nature urged her to claim the love that is set in nature:

and it taught her to hold back the hasty death of the king's command.
“No, son of David! Your judgment is not just,” she cried out in the court,
“and not justly have you commanded that the living infant should die.
Examine well, just king, and only then kill,
and do not hasten to shed blood without a trial.
Look, just son of a just father, and be like him,
and honour the truth that is hidden in your name, like your begetter.
See that you do not breach the just boundary your father set,
and do not learn to wrong a person through partiality.
Do not give iniquity room to grow arrogant
when it sees that you are walking in the way of deceit.
Do not destroy the living infant when he is not guilty,
and do not stain yourself with innocent blood that is far from sins.
Give him whole to the shameless woman and let him be hers,
and do not divide him into portions to no purpose.
I cannot bear to look upon his death as he is cut in pieces,
and if I see it, death is better for me than life.”
Oh, how zealous nature was, and how it claimed what its love demanded,
and did not slacken in the hour of contest with its adversary!
Oh, how valiantly she drew near to face the sword,
and gave no room for the order of her ardent love to be shaken!
Oh, how strong she was to contend in love,
and did not shrink or cower before the command of the king and his power!
Oh, the compassionate harlot, how her compassion was revealed,
for she gave the infant to the shameless woman so that he alone might live!
Oh, the cruel foolish woman, how she showed no pity,
for she asked that the living infant die so that she would not be exposed!
Oh, how brazenly she had acquired a heart of stone,
which did not soften when the sword confronted the child!
Oh, how the shameless woman cried out before the son of David:
“Let him be neither mine nor yours; divide him as has been decreed!”
At her impudence Solomon marvelled, the peace that brings peace to men,
and from her impudence he learned the deceit hidden in her heart.
At the love and compassion of the child's mother the son of David marvelled,
and from her pangs he discerned and understood that she was his mother.
“She is his mother, and her love testifies that he is hers;
give him to her alive, and let her rejoice in his life, as she asked.”
The harlot was vindicated, and the king set her infant on her as a crown,
and the impudence of the shameless woman was put to shame, and she went out naked.
The onlookers wove crowns of praise for the just king,
that he had rightly acquitted and rightly condemned, with wisdom.
In a hidden case he revealed the justice of the eye of his mind,
and the people testified that his judgment was true and his trial just.
By the judgment they learned that he had the power to administer justice,
and they feared him and honoured the rank of his headship.
As in a furnace he tested himself in the trial of the women,
and showed the people of his nation the beauty of his soul's purity.
The Creator too, seeing that he had been purified by testing,
adorned him with a vision and discoursed with him the power of His wisdom.
In a vision of the night the Watchful-eyed One spoke with him:

and commanded him to ask for the wisdom [?] of truth for just judgment.
“Ask,” He said to him, “as one who knows what he wants,
and I will fulfil the request of your soul in deeds.”
“Give me a heart and also understanding,” the son of David answered,
“that I may pursue truth and rebuke what is counterfeit without fault.”
Just judgment the son of David asked of the Creator,
and the Creator filled him with comfort and confirmed His words.
First He gave him wisdom of heart to hear judgment,
and then He added the riches of this age and abundance.
With two kinds of riches He adorned the rank of his headship:
with wisdom of soul and the beauty of bodily adornment.
In things spiritual and things bodily the son of David was rich,
and spiritually and bodily he was fair and adorned.
In body and soul he was pleasing to God and to men,
and he built and adorned a holy temple for the [?] of his Lord.
He built a house for Him of whom heaven and earth are full,
and though He does not dwell in the work of hands, He dwelt in it through love.
Through manifest things He showed His love toward the son of His house,
for though He is in all things, He chose for Himself a dwelling in a house of time.
The greatness of His great love for David was revealed in the son of David,
and He fulfilled the promise of His words in deed, as He had promised.
He had promised the everlasting kingdom to the son of Jesse,
and He made his son king and gave him wealth and wisdom of heart.
At the greatness of his wealth and the wisdom of his soul all peoples marvelled,
and the report of his judgment went out to the ends of the earth.
Through all regions the report of his judgment went round,
and among all peoples they recounted the [?] of his judgments.
The kings of the nations desired and longed to hear his judgments,
and they sent gifts to persuade him to let them see his face.
The awe of his name hastened the wealthy to him,
and they trembled and were dismayed at the greatness hidden in his name.
The name hidden in him cast fear upon the mighty,
and unwillingly they bowed their necks beneath the yoke of his name.
The Egyptians feared, the Cushites marvelled, the Indians were amazed,
and they loaded and brought fine gifts to offer him.
Those far off desired, strangers gathered, the people of the land pressed in,
to hear from him the wisdom of truth that had been given to him.
Truth was openly honoured [?] at the door of his house,
and the name of the Creator was glorified in his headship.
The God of all was praised by every mouth,
and the no-gods were despised by every tongue.
Through the gifts of kings the King over all was honoured,
and the idolatry of demon-worship was held in contempt.
“Blessed is God, who dwells among His people!” all the peoples cried,
and the Rebel shuddered, for the voice proclaiming the name of his gods had ceased.
All the peoples paid their debt of praise through the son of David,
and calamity seized the Envious One, for men gave praise through a son of man.
The name of the Creator triumphed through a son of man,
and the Envious One burned with rage: why should one made of dust become great?
The Envious One put on great mourning at the honour paid to his Lord:

and he began to contrive cunning devices to bring his name into contempt.
The heart of the Deceiver prepared the weapon of deceit,
to wage war against the Creator through a son of man.
The Rebel forged every weapon of his bitterness,
to stir up rebellion against the righteousness of the son of David.
He prepared all his host and called it to the struggle,
to bring down by every device the height of the fear of truth.
He gathered his demons, roused his legions, called his ministers,
to help him in the harsh struggle that had come upon him.
He dug his pits, hid his snares, spread out his crafts,
to hunt the man by whom the name of the Creator was honoured.
The Counterfeiter set the net of iniquity for the true son,
so that his mind, led astray, would be entangled in it and he would lose his rank.
With the crafty bonds of the daughters of Eve he bound his prey,
so that he could not escape the hooks of his bitterness.
Like a robber the Envious One lay in ambush on the road of women,
for he saw that King Solomon was always passing that way.
On the king's road the Captor and his confederates lay in wait,
and they leapt out quietly, caught the king, and stripped him of his adornment.
All his adornment of the Creator's name he snatched from his head,
and left him naked, without the covering of the fear of truth.
The trap that brought down his father, the lion who terrified the nations—
as he had caught David, so he caught him too through the love of women.
Through the love of women the Evil One caught the man of reason,
and in their affairs he held his mind back from righteousness.
With the bond of women he fettered the strength of the mighty hero,
and put his captive into the prison of ignorance.
In ignorance the crafty one bound him who was wiser than all,
so that he was not free to struggle against his wiles.
He sent women like spies and spied out his freedom,
and he persuaded them to persuade him to grow slack in his mysteries.
Through women the crafty serpent hid his bitterness,
and with their tongue stung him with their errors as with a sting.
The sorcery dealt a grievous blow to the man of sound soul,
and the venom of its cruelty spread through all his senses.
Like a dragon, deceit peered out from the house of women,
bit him in the soul, and made the hair of his mind's head fall out.
Like [?] it spread its venom over his limbs,
and it spread and reached to the hidden movements of his soul.
The Rebel, a [?] fowler, scattered [bait] before his eyes,
and as with a bird, drew his foot [?] toward his snares.
The contemptible one spread out the light snares of contempt,
and with them he caught his levity, so that Solomon would fall.
Oh, the swift one whom contemptible eyes caught,
and who put his captive into the harsh yokes of idolatry!
Oh, the hero whom feeble ribs overpowered,
and who took the weapon of the Creator's name from his mind!
Oh, the fair one who was loved, who was so beautiful in body and soul,
whose beauty was defiled by the hateful course of contempt!
Oh, the wise one at whose knowledge even spirits marvelled,
who busied himself with foolish women, and they made him a fool!
Oh, the knowing one who searched out the mysteries of hidden things:

so that the tyrant demons mocked and laughed at his wisdom!
Oh, the wise one who healed with his words the sick of soul,
who made his own soul sick with the restless pain of idolatry!
Oh, the true one who silenced the errors of the no-gods,
who left the way of the word of truth and walks in error!
Oh, the upright one who raised the head of [?],
who bowed the head of his truth before false gods!
Oh, the musician who amazed the nations with the sound of his melodies,
whose fair songs fell silent before deaf idols!
Oh, the lyre that once sounded forth the wisdom of truth,
whose strings, the strings of his soul, crafty demons cut!
Oh, the flute through which the will of his Lord was sung,
which demons broke, so that it could no longer carry the voice of the Spirit of revelation!
Oh, you king, more glorious than the kings who were and who will be,
who disgraced your rank in the eyes of those on earth and in heaven!
Who will not marvel at the abasement of him who was honoured above all,
that he himself despised his honour for no gain?
Who will not grieve at the humbling of him who was lofty in his counsel,
that he gave up meditation on spiritual things and expounded vanities?
