Who will not suffer at the change in the great sea,
whose wisdom was cut off and whose spring of discernment dried up?
Who will not weep over the craftsman, the composer of proverbs,
who became a proverb, and see, his disgrace is told everywhere?
Who will not fear the slips of ignorance,
that without knowing it a man slips and falls into abominations?
Who will not be wary of the hidden things within the soul,
that without one's noticing, passions assault and plunder one's riches?
Who will not be watchful in the battle with his deceiver,
who has dug and hidden many pits before his mind?
Who will not guard his soul from the Captor,
who day by day is constantly watching the gate of his treasures?
If the passions of his soul plundered the wise man's wisdom,
who can guard his treasures from the plunderers?
If the swift one was caught by the [?] of the demons of women,
who will not flee from dealings with the daughters of Eve?
If the hero fell into the nets of their enticements,
who will not flee to the love that lies beyond their devices?
On the translation of Enoch and of Elijah

Again by the same author.
The fiftieth memra,
which he composed on the translation of Enoch and of Elijah.

Sin and death fell upon Adam like raiders,
and stripped him and left him naked, with nothing to his name.
Naked the head of our race went out from Paradise,
and the kindred of his soul sat in mourning over his going out.
In great mourning the spiritual beings sat over man,
for they had heard that death was destined to undo the fabric of his body.
They pondered the sentence passed upon his folly,
and were distressed at how the image of the Creator had perished.
"Image of the Creator" the Creator called him when He fashioned him;
and when they heard the news that he would return to his earth, they turned and sighed.
His return to his earth saddened the heavenly ones,
and they gave up hope that he would ever turn back to life.
In the [?] of his life they had been [?] when he was fashioned,
and they grieved greatly over his parting from them.
The corruption of his body grieved them beyond measure,
that they should be parted from converse with the rational image.
They had marveled at his reason, how glorious it was,
that his soul uttered rational words through the senses of the body.
The sound of his songs had been sweet to them before his folly,
and when he acted foolishly and sinned they were shattered and stunned at his fall.
Sin overthrew the image, the brother of the heavenly ones,
and gave him as prey to greedy death, which ravaged his body.
As on a dead man they gazed on him, dead through iniquity,
and did not cease from grieving over his death.
They reckoned him dead from the moment he ate the fruit,
and all the more from that voice: "To the earth you shall return."
To the earth that command sent back the earthly one,
and he went out to dwell beyond the bounds of Paradise.
Outside the place where he had dwelt, the mortal dwelt,
and a wall of fire encircled the way before him, so that he might not enter it.
At the wall of fire the spiritual beings gazed,
and were astonished at what desire for the fruit had done.
Desire for the fruit drove Adam out of Paradise;
the demons rejoiced, and the hosts of the heavenly ones grieved.
All creation sat in mourning over his going out,
and bitterly bewailed the death his iniquity had brought.
The world had become like a house of mourning over man,
and the sound of its laments was uttered from every mouth.
Rational and mute creatures wept over his mortality,
and did not cease from sighing over his corruption.
His guilt built before his face a hedge of fire,
and he longed, yet could not enter his place.

The divine command cast him into exile,
and like a wretch he wandered in a land of thorns.
On thorns and thistles the king of the earth was fed,
and he sighed deeply over his humiliation.
Wearisome was his toil, worn down his course, scant his food,
and the changing seasons of his days troubled him.
In the sufferings of his soul rational and mute creatures suffered,
and they recounted the kinds of his afflictions with voice and with silence.
With voice and with silence the kinds of his afflictions were told,
and generation handed down to generation the grief of his life.
Through experience he learned the name of mortality,
and death began to destroy his offspring without pity.
Among Adam's sons the death that Adam brought in began,
and it swallowed Abel, the beloved firstling of righteousness.
By the death of the just one, death established its reign over its mortals,
and men became slaves to death and to the Accuser.
In deed the sentences passed upon the guilty were fulfilled,
and mortal nature was condemned and brought low in mortality.
As a pledge sin seized the body of Adam,
and gave it to death to feed upon greedily.
Greedily the devourer devoured him as food,
and without pity the destroyer plundered him as a captive.
Through all people passed the corruption of the corrupter,
and no one was left whom the claw of death did not seize.
Over his corruption heaven and earth mourned,
and they sighed and labored in pain.
The pangs of death struck all creation,
and it waited for when it would bring forth a hope of life [?].
These sufferings the Creator saw, He who sees all,
and suddenly made those without hope hear good hope.
Good hope the Creator sowed in human ears
through one who was not enslaved to the bondage of death.
One man He kept with care, free of corruption,
and consoled the world in its grief over man.
To console mankind, the Lover of mankind translated Enoch,
and kept him alive, that in him hope might be kept for mankind.
Hope He proclaimed through the translation of that fair one,
who pleased Him greatly, and He made his beauty a hope for mankind.
"The just one was pleasing"—so it is written of the just one in the book of Moses;
and because he was pleasing, He kept his beauty in the treasury of life.
As in an image He portrayed the image of his virtues,
and anointed him with immortal life [?], that he might not be corrupted.
He revived [?] the fitting beauty of Adam's image,
and renewed in Enoch that form which death had corrupted.
The corruption of death the Creator undid through Enoch's life,
and consoled people, so that they should no longer grieve over corruption.
Over their corruption Adam's offspring had mourned,
from Adam until Enoch pleased God.
With the scourges of death the children of mortality were scourged,
and there was no hope to herald hope to mortal man.
For six generations the scourging of the scourged stretched on,

and in stillness they heard a voice announcing life.
In the seventh generation mortals heard the good news of life,
and though they heard it well, they could not grasp it exactly.
They did indeed hear the report of Enoch's life,
and they wondered what it was, and why He had kept him alive.
All of them heard the good report of the just man's translation,
but they did not know how to [?] the [?] of the reviving of the dead.
Not openly did they learn the cause of death's abolition;
rather its report was spoken in a mystery, and its power was hidden.
In mystery the spiritual beings heard this,
and in mystery they pondered its meaning.
Through this mystery the lovers of mankind put off their grief,
and began to rejoice at the good news of mankind's renewal.
In great mourning they had sat over man,
and when they all heard the news of his life, they rejoiced and were comforted.
Enoch's life comforted the heavenly ones,
and spurred them to go on in the order of their ministry.
The transgression of the command had slackened their love toward mankind,
and they had no wish to set the motions of the air in their courses.
They reckoned their labor on mankind's behalf a vain toil,
and it was hard for them to go on in the way of their ministry.
A hidden sign bound them to labor greatly,
and they accepted and submitted to the command that bound them.
To the command of the Hidden One the spiritual ministers of men submitted,
and all the more from Enoch's translation onward.
Enoch lifted the sentence of mortality,
and reconciled men and heavenly beings by the translation of his life.
His life cut off the road of death in mystery,
before the time when it would be cut off in deed.
As a hostage of peace the Lord of the world took him to Himself,
and kept him alive to proclaim life to the children of his race.
The children of rebellion had raised rebellion against their Lord;
He chastised them with the harsh scourges of mortality.
With death He scourged the hardness that raised rebellion,
and in compassion had mercy on it by preserving the life of one man.
One man He chose in one span of ten generations,
and kept him with Himself as a pledge for the debtors.
Debtors was the whole race of Adam,
and they acknowledged it, yet did not repay the debt of debts.
For this reason He took Enoch as a pledge,
that they might remember to repay their debt to the Fashioner of all.
A bond of debts they had owed from the beginning,
and what they had not paid, they paid in Enoch, though unwilling.
The fair one became like a surety for the children of his race,
that they might pay the bond of debts of their deeds.
Through occasions He taught them to repay the debt,
and the love of His kindness pressed Him toward the righteous.
It was not the righteous who pressed Him to make peace for mankind,
for He knew, before He made peace, the works [?].
His love had foreseen the peace He made in Enoch's time,

and He had prepared his translation even before He translated him.
He knew this which He did at the beginning of the times,
and what was to come in the second time was plain to Him.
All times were seen beforehand by the Fashioner of times,
and their changes were set in order before they came to be.
He had allowed for the errors of Adam and his sons before they erred,
and stood ready to undo death and put away error.
Through occasions He revealed His will, that He willed our life,
and gave us hope through the translation of a man from among us.
He translated Enoch and kept him in immortal life,
and by his translation He gave hope to ten generations.
Good hope the first ones gained through Enoch's life,
and his translation became like a guide for those who came after them.
On the road of life his descendants walked in the hope of life,
and began to recount the mystery of their life from generation to generation.
Lamech splendidly expounded this mystery,
recounting the kinds of good things in store for mankind.
Noah, like thunder, made the voice of his blessings heard,
showing that the time of mankind's renewal had drawn near.
Through his blessings the righteous man revealed his Lord's will:
that He stood ready to redeem mankind through a man.
With Abraham all the voices that bore hope came to rest,
for in the harbor of his love the longing of twenty generations found rest.
Twenty generations journeyed from Adam to Abraham,
and their courses reached the harbor of peace of one man.
Abraham was one, and single was his love for his Lord,
and because of his love He made him a harbor for his fellows.
Abraham became a harbor of peace for the children of his race,
and in him the ships of the Spirit of divine revelations came to rest.
From Abraham onward people began to live in the love of truth,
and the Creator too revealed His will toward mankind.
God had a single will toward man,
and He tested it in the just through occasions of every kind.
To Abraham He said that through his seed He would bless the nations,
and to the son of Jesse that from his line He would establish a kingdom.
One after another they handed on the promises of His words,
and there was no time in which He did not show the kinds of His will.
To the good He showed the great love [?] of His kindness,
that they might sow good hope in human ears.
In every age He sowed the seed of mankind's redemption,
watering it, instead of with raindrops, with kinds of revelations.
Through revelations He made men and heavenly beings wise,
that they might know how to walk in the way of the name of the Divine Being.
A great road He trod out through the prophets, for walking toward Him,
and showed it above all in the Tishbite, prophet and priest.
A prophet and priest He chose for Himself in the middle of the times,
to show the kinds of His will to humankind.
All the power of His governance He placed in his hands,
to discipline the children of his people and win them in the fear of truth.
He made him a divine steward on earth,
to feed his Lord's servants from his Lord's house.

The just one justly provided for his Lord's servants,
and wisely gave sustenance in famine and in plenty.
With the scourge of famine he chastised those who rebelled against his Lord,
and taught them not to exalt themselves against the Creator.
The rebellious sons of Abraham had grown a stiff neck,
and the Tishbite subdued them as with a yoke.
A hard yoke was the voice of that zealous one,
and it subdued those brutish men against their will.
Against their will they chose the lordship of the name of God,
and reluctantly they rejected and cast off the worship of demons.
Under the constraint [?] of the Creator's name they came to love the Creator,
and from the foulness of idolatry they came to hate its practice.
The Tishbite's mouth had become a fountain of scourges,
giving them to drink every kind of severe blow.
He held his Lord's command like a rod,
and with it he chastened the perverse people, lover of straying.
In every way the just one subdued the perverse,
and by every device they broke the yoke of his words.
A hard yoke is the [?] of the words of prophecy,
and it skillfully subdues people in the fear of truth.
Elijah was choice among laborers in his prophecy,
and because he labored much he came to rest in a harbor raised above fear.
In the harbor of peace raised above fear the diligent one rested,
and he trod out a road for good laborers, that they might walk with him.
On a smooth road without stumbling-blocks the righteous one walked,
one trodden by the just Enoch in the beauty of his soul.
The beauty of that fair one's soul the Creator saw,
and He kept him for life, so that the beauties of his soul might not be corrupted.
In this very beauty of virtues Elijah was pleasing,
and He did with him what had been done with the fair one.
To one reward He made the pure of soul equal,
and gave greedy death no place over their bodies.
Above death He raised the good servants,
to cast into human minds a zeal to be good.
He taught people through two men whom He translated to Himself,
that they should not be divided over the pledge of the reviving of the dead.
The treasure of life was laid up with Him to reveal to mankind,
and He showed it beforehand in two men, Enoch and Elijah.
Enoch and Elijah became guides for human nature,
that people might walk on the road of immortal life.
Enoch He translated in the first span of ten generations,
and the Tishbite in the second, in the middle of the times.
In the middle of the times He made the translation of the good servant,
that it might call to mind the first things and the last.
Into three times the Lord of the world divided the world,
and from each time He took one man and kept him alive.
In the first He translated Enoch, the just man,
and in the second Elijah, the chosen prophet.
In the third—the word concerning Him is too lofty for us,
and no mouth can say how glorious His translation was.
As if by steps His will advanced through the course of the times,

and led people step by step from lowly things to glorious ones.
Lesser was the time in which He translated Enoch than Elijah's,
and the Tishbite's was lower than the Messiah's.
Of Enoch it says only that he was translated,
and does not explain to us where He translated him or where He placed him.
In mystery Moses hinted to us of his translation,
and did not explain to us the cause for which he was translated.
As to little children he lisped [?] these things about Enoch,
because the way of life at the beginning of the times was childish.
Far more childish was Enoch's time than Elijah's,
and the manner of his translation was lesser than the other's.
A plain voice the first ones heard in Enoch's story;
but in Elijah's, the full voices of prophecy.
Full voices told of Elijah
that the time had drawn near for him to be translated from among mankind.
Prophet told prophet the report he had received,
and they passed their revelations from one to another.
From one to another the day of his translation was passed on,
as they wove for him a crown of praises from their revelations.
With the voice of revelation the athlete of the Spirit was praised,
and the prophets of the Spirit celebrated his contest.
Like an athlete he went from place to place,
and though he knew it, he kept the day of his translation hidden.
The modest one did not wish to reveal his glory,
lest the crafty snares of vainglory should catch him.
Wisely he managed what was hidden,
until the spirit of revelation of [?] tested him.
The spirit of revelation pressed him to reveal even hidden things,
and though unwilling he disclosed the time when he would be translated.
With pretexts he framed reasons before his disciple:
that the Lord had sent him on an errand—spoken in mystery.
In mystery he showed him the mystery of his translation,
as befits the children of divine mysteries.
The God of all was making the good servant wise,
to set in order the passage to immortal life.
To incorruptible life the son of mortals was being translated,
and wisely he honored it before mortals.
He was about to travel a long road that has no milestones,
and he stretched his mind toward that measureless expanse.
With the eye of the Spirit the seer saw that delight,
and the world became as no world before his thoughts.
Another world he saw in a vision without body,
and he despised everything and loved what is not corrupted.
He saw how great was the way of life to which he was being translated,
and he was astonished and amazed at his Lord's love, how much He loved him.
The true one saw how great his Lord's love was,
and how He makes the children of His house shine with glories.
Glorious was the day on which the Tishbite was translated,
and splendid were the kinds of revelations along the course of his journey.
A wondrous sight he saw portrayed above the earth:
the form of a fiery chariot racing through the air.
Horses of fire he saw yoked to wheels of fire,
and above them stood a fiery charioteer.
Fire upon fire he saw, bound with reins of fire,

and he marveled at the greatness of the glory shown to him.
At the greatness of the glory of the day of his translation he marveled,
and could not have his fill of gazing on the beauty of those fair things.
He saw as much as a man can see of spiritual things,
and he left off his wonder and turned to speak with his disciple.
He revealed to him openly, "I am being translated"—truly—
and bade him ask whatever a master may fittingly give.
"Ask of me," said the faithful [?] master to his disciple,
"and take for yourself something that will be with you and adorn you."
The disciple asked for a double measure of prophecy,
and his master taught him how to ask and how to receive.
The asker asked and the giver gave, both at once,
and the prophet set out to travel a road he had never seen.
The one of dust sat upon the spiritual chariot,
and held in his hands reins of fire, and was not burned.
Gently [?] the Spirit [?] beneath the one of dust,
and the body was guiding the spirit, and the spirit the body.
In the wind the prophet of the Spirit flew wherever he was going,
and it seemed that he was being lifted toward the heights.
Toward the heights the sign drew him to go—
not to heaven, but to a place higher than the earth.
Not to heaven did Elijah ascend on the day of his translation,
but to where Enoch, his kinsman, had been translated.
The very sign that translated Enoch translated him also,
and He settled them in one place, that they might be together.
One was the cause for which they were translated from among mankind,
and it was fitting that they should share one place and one converse.
Only in glory did He make a distinction as they were translated,
according to the way of life, from childhood to maturity.
Childish was the time in which the fair Enoch was translated,
and the manner of his translation was lesser than Elijah's.
More mature was the Tishbite's time than Enoch's,
and glorious, too, were the likenesses of the day of his translation.
Through spiritual likenesses He distinguished them,
to reveal to people the distinction that will be at the end.
The day of the consummation He portrayed in the vision of the translation of the just,
and above all on the day of the Tishbite's translation.
To the height above He was destined to raise the human race,
and beforehand He portrayed that ascent in the translation of His servant.
Toward the height was lifted the gaze upon the course of that chariot,
to where all nature is destined to be raised.
For this reason it is said that the Tishbite ascended—
not that he ascended, but to portray the mystery of the ascent.
The mystery of the ascent He portrayed in the vision in which he was translated,
that thus mortal nature ascends in the mysteries of his ascent.
The road of life the just Enoch and Elijah trod out for us,
and they came to rest in the harbor at the end of the road of the immortals.
In incorruptible life they are kept in the place to which they were invited,
and in their nature [?] they live on something meager.
On something meager the just live, as they are,
by the power of that Spirit for whom even hard things are easy.

By the power of His command earthly men are kept in that land,
without being subject to the hardships of earthly men.
In that very nature, full of harms [?], they live unharmed [?],
and this is the wonder: that they are not weakened [?] by harms.
A great wonder it is that they live thus a human life,
and are not worn down by the turnings of the wearying spheres.
In them are the kinds of turnings that belong to human life,
but the command that translated them sets them free of these.
That command takes from them the kinds of turnings,
and they do not slacken from converse about glorious things.
Glorious is their converse, and fitting the course of their way of life,
and who is able to recount the meditation in which they persevere?
Unspeakable is the meditation of those fair meditators,
and Paul bears witness, who went there once and listened to their converse.
In the converse of the immortals the mortals converse,
and with the bodiless they sing praise with spiritual voices.
Like spiritual beings the earthly are destined to become,
and beforehand He translated two embodied men to confirm it all.
To confirm it all He translated the two men,
that by their translation mankind might be confirmed in the things to come.
As hostages of peace He received the pure of soul,
that mankind's peace with the Creator might stand firm.
A slack nature is the nature of mortals from the beginning,
and without order they constantly stray through their desires.
The hateful straying of their thoughts the All-Seeing saw,
and took from them two pledges to be with Him.
As a sign of peace He translated them from among mankind,
that people might keep their love toward His hiddenness.
The peace of mankind the two true ones confirm at every hour,
and strengthen it by the good meditation of their minds.
The image of man the Lover of mankind also loved,
and by every means He seeks this: that people should live.
For the sake of human life He spared two mortals from death,
that by their life they might remind people of their own life.
To all nature immortal life is promised,
and the witnesses of this are the two sureties [their life became for their mortality], Enoch and Elijah.
Their life became like sureties for our mortality,
that it might not slacken in its trust in the promised life.
Incorruptible life the Good One prepared for human nature,
and wrote it in two documents, with three witnesses.
In the first document Enoch and Elijah set their hand,
and in the second, one Surety and chosen Witness.
A chosen Witness the Creator chose from among mortals,
to bear witness to the good things in store for the children of His race.
By human custom every testimony on earth is given,
and people regularly seal a bond of debts with three witnesses.
A bond of debts the Creator wrote between Himself and mankind,
and sealed it in earthly and heavenly fashion.
Three witnesses He made witnesses in the bond of our life:
Enoch and Elijah, and third, the Messiah who is from us.
The Messiah who is from us sealed with His blood the bond of our life,
that the promise of life might be sure for all His race.
By His death He freed us from bondage to the Evil One and to death,
and by His resurrection He promised us immortal life.
Immortal He became in His nature after His death:

so that his life might be a proven witness for the human race.
For the life of mankind the Creator chose that Son of Man, and raised his rank to the lofty rank of his divinity.
Not by the order of his divinity was his rank natural to him, but by the order of that Ordainer who has no equal.
The rank to which the head of our race attained has no equal, and his headship is not to be compared with that of things made.
He did not make him like a servant, to grow great by portions,
nor did he make his translation like that of Enoch and that of Elijah.
Enoch and Elijah he translated from among men, and made them dwell in another place, which is on the earth.
On the earth dwell the earthly ones, Enoch and Elijah, and in that same mortal nature they are kept on the earth.
Into the region of Eden the true ones entered to dwell,
where Adam dwelt, the head of all our race:
Adam, [?] its gate [?] before the face of men; and he brought men into the place that had been fenced off by a decree of judgment.
By a decree of judgment men were barred from that place, until one Son of Man loosed it and set men firm.
One Son of Man, Christ who is from us, entered it first, and gave his entry to all men through their souls.
Enoch and Elijah alone entered it in body and in spirit, and they are in it until the time of the passing of the ages.
Before the passing of the ages he entered it first, in spirit, not in body, and went out from it and ascended to the place that befits him.
To the place of the height that is higher than the height our Head ascended, to the Holy of Holies, which the foot of man had not entered,
before the Divine Being, so that our priest might serve as priest in the place that is pure of harms and of those who harm.
With the blood of his own soul he served as priest once among earthly beings, and the sacrifice of his holiness sufficed for all creatures.
For all creatures the Creator chose him from among creatures, and he accepted his death as a redemption for mortals.
The iniquity of mankind had stained the world with filth, and the Good One turned and cleansed it by the death of one Son of Man.
By the very thing through which death entered and corrupted mankind, by that same thing life entered and abolished death from humanity.
Adam trod the path of death through desire for the fruit, and death passed into the whole of Adam's nature.
He transgressed the commandment and enslaved men to the slavery of death, and men supposed that the race of mankind would never live again.
For the hope of mankind the Creator chose three men, and made them witnesses who testify to the life of mankind.
To the life of mankind Enoch and Elijah testify on earth; [the Head?] of our life, above in heaven, confirms our life.
Two true ones testify on earth to our renewal, and one in heaven seals the words of above and below.
Two, like servants, give assurance on earth, Enoch and Elijah, and one, like a king, dwells in heaven and commands on earth.
The King who reigned does not have his portion with the servants, nor is his authority like the authority of the children of earth.
I have not called him a common son of man, like a mere human,

nor his translation like the translation of the children of flesh.
Let not the heretics [?] against us, as they are wont,
for I am not wont to give room to their wrongdoing.
I know them: they set traps like hunters, and it has not escaped me how cunning they are at hunting words.
The hunters of words hunt the words of faith, and when they have caught them, they fly off like a bird from their hands.
Our faith is not caught in the hands of fools, because they cannot grasp its power in their minds.
They are far too weak to fight even a single bout in the open, and the course of their arguments is cut short for lack of understanding.
They cannot catch words with words as they intend, nor can they offer plain persuasion about hidden things.
Hidden from them is the sound word of faith, and when it was revealed by the mouth of those who know, they were astonished and amazed.
The sound word of faith tells of a marvel, and it has not escaped me that it is received crudely.
Not crudely, not foolishly, have I arranged my words for you, you untrained ones, since you are not trained in the discipline of words.
You do not know how to walk on the path of faith, and the words set within its meaning are beyond your measure.
Without discernment you stumble as over a stone, and you cannot tell the difference so as to choose the fair over the foul.
Rightly did I speak in the account I gave of the Son of Man, that it was a Son of Man who was exalted above men.
It was a Son of Man who proclaimed hope to the children of men, and sealed the words that Enoch and Elijah had sown on earth.
It was a Son of Man who ascended and reigned above in heaven, and trod the way for men to become heavenly.
It was a Son of Man who became a witness to the bond of our life, and set his hand to it and sealed it with his blood, so that it might not be falsified.
It was a Son of Man, and again I say it was a Son of Man; and if the heretics are angered, let them cry out all they like.
Let them cry out all they like, until Legion hears, who wails along with them, like that cry he raised before our Lord.
Bitterly Legion wailed at his overthrow, and the cry of the disciples closely resembles that of their master.
The foolish heretics resemble that great fool, and they do not consider that they are guilty [?] by the sound of their words.
They resemble the mole, which is forever burrowing with evil burrowing; and when they heard the sound of the word of truth, they grew insolent and inflamed.
The noise of their insolence does not let me keep quiet about them, nor does it allow me to pass them by without blame.
Like a target their thinking is set before my thoughts, and it urges me to strike them with the arrows of my words.
With words I long to strike them on every side [?], because they do not cease from striving against my words.
I had a theme to ponder in the meditation of words, and while I was pondering it, the noise of the heretics troubled me.
Ask me, O men: I have cried out to them in every way, and the more I thought they would be quiet, the more they were stirred up and enraged.
Their agitation I see even now in this discourse,

and I left my discourse to rebuke the words of their blasphemies.
The blasphemies of the blasphemers turned my discourse aside, and it left its theme and went down the path of answering the perverse.
The perverse it rebuked, trading word for word in reply, and the untrained I urged on with the persuasion of truths.
Truly do I speak the truths: what is the reason that death held sway over men of our own kind?
Men of our own kind I have seen exalted above death,
and I have put together words to reveal in words what is not revealed.
What is unrevealed I wish to recount before my hearers, and to teach them, so that they may know the kinds of hidden things.
The kinds of hidden things were hidden in the story of those of whom I have told, hidden not from the mature but from the childish and the ignorant.
To the ignorant I reveal the reasons for the translation of men: what is the reason they were translated from us to another place?
To another place Enoch and Elijah were translated from us, and by their translation they portrayed for us a type of the change of our life.
A new life the Lover of our race promised us, and he sealed it with three seals, of three men.
Three men I have called them, all three of them, not by rank but by the order of human nature.
The three have one nature, in body and in spirit;
their ranks are not equal, for servants are not like their lord.
Enoch and Elijah are servants, however long they live; Christ who is from us is Lord over all, though he is a man.
Enoch and Elijah are kept on earth until the resurrection; Christ is in a lofty place, exalted above mortals.
He is not mortal, since he has become immortal, and he alone has received this, on behalf of mortals.
On behalf of mortals the Creator chose him from among mortals, so that he might fulfil the station both of servants and of the freeborn.
He too is a servant, in that he is a servant made by the Maker; and again he is also Lord, in that he received a divine rank.
He is divine because his rank is higher than all, and he inherited and reigned, not by his nature but by his rank.
By his rank that Son of Man from our humanity inherited, and all this because the One who willed it willed it.
The God of all willed to name him with the name of his own greatness, and see, foolish men are angered at the greatness of our rank.
Is it then grievous to you, you fools, that we are exalted, and do you not wish to accept our King?
Then rejoice, O men, that you have become divine, through a Son of Man who became God with God.
The Word, the Son of God, dwelt in a man from among us, and called him by his name and gave him the rank of the name of Being.
He gave him names, and also deeds that rise higher than himself; and though the Good One gave them to him, he does not forget that he is from us.
He is from us, and for our life he ascended and was exalted, and we are bound to give thanks to the Good One who exalted our race.
Let the whole nature of mortals say, "Thanks be to the Good One, who exalted our race in one Son of Man whom he took from us."
On Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael
Homily Forty-Four / On Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael / Responsory / The martyrs asked for mercy upon the world, which has taken refuge [?] / in your bones, my brothers.

The sons of instruction went down in captivity to the land of the Babylonians,
and did not slacken in their trust in their instruction.
Lovers of peace, kinsmen, went off to the region of the wrathful,
and the warmth of their love for truth did not cool in their minds.

Bearing the sign that the Creator had stamped upon their senses,
they dwelt among pagans, and did not become like them in their customs.
Men of savor went in and mingled with the savorless,
and the savor of their thoughts did not lose its proper taste.
Clothed in the armor of the law, forged by the Spirit,
they stood among the ranks of warriors and did not falter.
Runners in the race of righteousness, without negligence,
they lived among the defiled, and did not stop or grow slack in their labor.
Athletes who grappled [?] with trials,
the hands of those who seized them slipped from their bodies.
Sons of Abraham, the chosen lover whose love was true,
they entered the contest, conquered, and came out like their father.
Into the contest of sufferings went the victorious, sons of the victorious one,
and they waited for and fulfilled that heavenly voice that came to Abraham.
They were like Abram in waiting for a hope that does not deceive;
they believed, and trusted what was far off as though it were near.
Like a sign they fixed his trial before their eyes,
and it showed them much about the help that comes from God.
Abram the just did not waver at the death of his son,
nor did the sons of Abraham fear their own death.
In mind they gazed on him as he offered up his son as a burnt offering,
and gave their bodies to the flame so as to be like him.
They put on faith like armor upon their limbs,
and believed that the strength of his help could overcome the fire.
By faith they scorned and despised the Babylonians,
for they saw that the promise of the words of Chaldean lore was feeble.
By faith they chose to die the death of time,
rather than be robbed of the hope of the true teaching.
They reasoned that it was easier for faith to despise death,
and did not reckon on being delivered from the burning.
They remembered that if they died, they would walk the road of death like everyone,
and if they did not die, they would die in any case, like all mortals.
They gazed upon death, and despised and scorned earthly things,
and before death came they loved to die the death of hope.

Hope became for them like a guide on the road of sufferings,
and showed them a path of endurance in which there is no fear.
In the place of fear the steadfast stood, clothed in hope,
and bravely bore the sufferings of their afflictions.
Like a lion the Babylonian roared to terrify them,
and they reckoned his voice as the voice of a gnat buzzing in the air.
Like a [?] his command crept out to [?] them,
and they reckoned his strength as a mole that burrows and cannot harm.
He made a great image, skillfully wrought in sin,
to snare everyone by it into the error of Chaldean lore.
The Spirit of revelation had shown him an image, great and glorious,
and he wished to set up an image of his error after the mystery of what he had seen.
He saw that the image he beheld was artfully set up,
and sought to exalt his own headship to match its greatness.
A dream portrayed for him the image of his power, that he might contemplate it,
but he changed it and portrayed a conception contrary to truth.
He saw the dream, then in turn forgot it, so that its meaning had to be sought;
and once it was interpreted, he turned and contrived to go astray in his vision.
The prophet revealed to him that he was the head of fine gold,
and he reasoned that he would rise to a lofty rank by fashioning an image.
He showed him that he would perish by the decree of judgment from God,
and he raised a rebellion so as not to be subject to the words of the Spirit.
The fool put on the armor of pride against truth,
and began to make war on justice wickedly.
The wicked one, full of wickedness, readied his heart for war,
to destroy the ranks of the children of truth with the sword of his wickedness.
He commanded, and the image he had forged in his mind was made,
and he invited peoples and cities to the worship of the idol.
He forged it in his heart, and likewise persuaded men to forge it;
he portrayed it in his mind, and likewise the bodies of the images portrayed it.
Demons counseled him to fashion an image after their desire,
and they showed him how, and how great, he should make its height.
They also taught the craftsmen who assembled it
to carry out their wishes in the beauty of its appearance.
The deceivers, together with the Chaldeans, devised a mystery,
so that men would be led astray after error by the shape of the image.

Sixty cubits, then, they gave as the measure of its height,
so that its sight would be a wonder to everyone, even from afar.
Six cubits again they made its width, as they wished,
so that its structure would be firm in proportion to its height.
And already the demons had counseled Chaldean lore
to enlarge the image, so as greatly to magnify the king's authority.
Already he said: "Despise the teaching of Judaism,
so that the sons of the exile may not be exalted over the kingdom."
Already, too, the image was constructed with this purpose:
that by it they might snare the lovers of truth as with traps.
For they were convinced of the love the just bear toward justice;
therefore they enlarged and spread out the nets of the great image.
And like a trap they set the forged gold upon the ground,
so that by its splendor men would come to hate the beauty of a splendid soul.
The beauty of the just stirred envy in Chaldean lore,
because the truth in them had grown and triumphed.
The demons added the fire of rage through demons in bodies,
to banish by it the name of the God of the sons of Abram.
As with firewood they kindled the rage of the tyrant king,
so that the command of his word might blaze hotter than fire.
They gave the king of anger the cup of anger to drink,
and he drank and was drunk, and his mind strayed in the mist of error.
He completed the image, full of ruin, according to his will,
and made a festival so that men would celebrate it wickedly.
He issued a command full of the undoing of the fear of truth,
and wrote a decree by which falsehood would be established.
He sent messengers to every region, to all peoples,
and they began to proclaim tidings full of the ruin of the soul.
The peoples heard the king's command; the heralds cried out:
"Go out quickly, complete the ruin of your own selves!"
Thus, then, the chief king, the head of gold, commanded:

"Come, render me the worship of love in the image I have made.
You owe me the worship of love; pay it to me.
Repay your debt, lest you be dragged off like debtors.
I wish to bring you all to a test by means of the image,
to see who loves the power of my lordship most.
My lordship, which is over all and which I have exercised, I wish to test,
to learn who defies it presumptuously.
And behold, I command and I seal the document of my word:
raise your hand and seal after me by your worship.
And behold, I say and I testify before all and to all,
that whoever despises the command of my word shall burn in fire.
See that you do not trample the command I have laid upon the earth,
lest you be condemned by the decree of a judgment without mercy."
The rulers went out and gathered the peoples to the festival of the image,
and they carried out and fulfilled the king's command as they were commanded.
Each bowed his head, out of love or out of fear,
and the rational honored and worshipped the mute thing without discernment.
The king's command quickly terrified them,
and they did not delay to bend the knee before the silent one.
The command became a cloud of hail over their heads,
and struck them mightily, without pity.
Like a whirlwind the blast of his rage blew among their ranks,
and sank the ship of their thoughts in the worship of the idol.
All the Babylonian ships it sank in sin,
and only three Jewish ones remained, through vigilance.
All the ears of grain in the field of Assyria the scorching wind blasted,
and three of them, Hebrew ones, were not broken.
Throughout the whole vineyard of the sons of Nimrod the blight clung,
and the shoots of the house of Abraham remained, being sound.
The Chaldeans saw the beauty of the fruit on their branches,
and were grieved that their fruit too had not been spoiled.
The arrogant put on envious anger against the blameless,
because they had defied the command of the king who had honored them.
Through them they heaped stumbling blocks on the hard of heart:
"See, O king, how the captives whom you honored have despised you!
You honored them above all, and they despised you above all;
you gave them authority, and they have raised their heel to trample you."
The troublemakers stirred up the fierce one against the wise,

and he raised his voice and cried out in rage, without understanding:
"Where are the exiles, sons of the captivity, who spurned my authority?
Why have you rejected the word of my command before my armies?
Where are the debtors who were filled with bread from my provisions?
Why have you repaid evil wrongs to the one who honored you?
Where are the Jews whom I surnamed with the name of my gods?
Why have you despised the worship of the image that my will has honored?
Where are the freeborn who did not understand the honors given them?
Why have you belittled the greatness of my kingdom's rank, which is over all?
Where are the fools whom their own worship did not save?
Why have you mocked the festival I made for my great god?"
The victors did not tremble at the threat of the arrogant one,
nor did they slacken in their trust in the fear of truth.
They sought no help against the harsh war of his rage,
and did not stoop to placate him even with a word.
"We have no need of persuasive words for the king," they answered,
"nor do we need our spirit to go out to meet your threats.
Do your will and vent your rage, as you are accustomed;
we cannot be led astray into the error of worshipping your image.
Heaven and earth cannot persuade us to do this,
and neither Watchers nor men can overcome our courage in it.
Far be it from us to forget the great name of the house of Abraham,
and to despise the covenant of the Creator with our fathers.
Far be it that we should bow our head before a silent thing,
and call 'god' a no-god that a lie has put together.
Far be it from us to be slaves of a thing made, which slaves have made,
and to say that the made can take the place of the maker.
For neither height nor depth nor angels,
nor any other creature, if there be one, shall change our word.
Behold, we testify to you: leave off words and show deeds;
test our will in the fire of your rage, and see that it is true."
The Babylonian heard words full of the nullifying of his image,
and he grew bitterly agitated beyond all measure.
The gall of his bitterness surged within his thoughts,

and he called his servants and armed them to kindle a fire.
"Kindle the furnace sevenfold!" the tyrant commanded,
"that I may kill in it the exiles who have despised my commands.
Mix with the wood whatever can make it burn more,
and avenge on the Hebrews the insult to the image of my god.
Invite all the peoples who have come to the festival of the image's worship;
let them come and see the burning of the men who despised my honor.
Before the multitude I will humiliate those who have scorned me,
so that everyone may see and not grow insolent against my words."
The Chaldeans fulfilled the will of the king, eager for destruction;
they kindled the fire and invited the peoples, as they were commanded.
The Garbdaeans [?] gathered, and the Tibetans [?], in crowd upon crowd,
and the Medes and Alans stood, troop upon troop.
A great throng gathered to watch the Israelites,
to see the wonder of the endurance of men who would conquer fire.
Every eye was fixed on the furnace,
yet none could bear to gaze upon its heat.
The tyrant gave command to the [?] devoted to him,
and they bound the mighty men in their clothing.
In the fine garments [?] upon their bodies they bound them,
so that the fire would quickly consume their limbs.
In anger the wrathful did this to the blameless,
to appease by it the harsh rage in their minds.
Strong men tyrannically carried those full of peace,
and wickedly threw them into the midst of the fire.
The steadfast went down and stood in the furnace calmly,
and a Watcher of fire received them lovingly.
The Creator sent one angel to his faithful ones,
to guard them from the harms of the flame.
A breeze of dew brought relief within the furnace,
and blunted the force of the heat with coolness.
The fiery one held a rod of fire in his hand,
and drove the fire back so that it would not come near their limbs.
Fire saw fire, and was terrified, distressed, and hid,
and its strength could not bear to look upon the sight it saw.
It saw a fearful sight burning in the hand of the spirit,
and forgot its order, and began to run beyond its order.
The Watcher cast bridles of fire into the mouth of the fire,

and set the course of its frenzy, so that it would not run wild.
It kept order discerningly before the discerning,
and did not grow greedy to devour much, as is its custom.
Who ever saw a wonder like that of the just:
a greedy mouth with food placed in it, and it did not touch it?
Who was ever preserved in the flame of Sheol, the devourer,
which [?] has never been sated since the day it came to be?
Who put a curb in the mouth of the destroying lioness,
so that the blackness of the fire did not come near the bodies of the victors?
O nature that forgot its nature against all custom,
and left its order and walked a way not fitting for it!
O devourer, which grows greedier the more it devours,
that it decreed a fast and stopped its mouth from food!
O burning one, whose strength grows the more it burns,
that it cooled its rage in the very hour of the battle of its might!
O flame, which again grows greedier the more it consumes,
that it consumed much, and yet its craving [?] did not grow greedy!
O how, and in what way, shall we say that this thing happened as it did,
that straw was placed in the mouth of the burning one and was not harmed?
O how bold were the righteous victors to look upon its strength,
and the appearance of their bodies was not harmed by the coals!
O how eyes of flesh endured to see a wonder
at which even spiritual beings marveled and were amazed at the greatness of its wonder!
Forty-nine cubits the flame rose,
and as it rose, so it came down, beyond measure.
Who, then, cast a measuring line into the air and measured its measure?
For nothing can measure anything without something.
Where is the hand that held a reed above the fire,
and measured the line from the furnace to the end of its leap?
That command which put the bridles of silence in its mouth,
that was its measure, through the spirit of revelation, in the mouth of Daniel.
He who told it to keep its order against all custom,
he revealed to his servant how many cubits it rose into the air.
Beyond all other days it showed its leap at that time,
so that the slanderers who had kindled it for nothing might be burned by it.
It judged them by means of its rising toward the height,

so that men might see how high it rose, and yet kept order.
Look, Chaldeans: the silent one cries out to the speaking:
"Though I am fire, I became no fire before the bodies.
You held out food of flesh to me to be fed with,
and behold, it is set before me, and it terrifies me so that I do not approach it."
The fire in silence, and the Watcher facing it, examined the case,
and acquitted and condemned the two sides with discernment.
The just they guarded, and the wicked they pursued harshly,
so that everyone might learn that the power of the Maker dwelt in his servants.
The flame saw the power of the Maker in the works of his hands,
and shrank back from it, and did not approach it as is its custom.
Its custom is this: to harm all who approach it;
and here it was silent and did not harm bodies that could be harmed.
As in a bridal chamber of delight the just reclined in it,
and it, like a handmaid, served in the order fitting for servants.
The furnace became a beautiful bridal chamber for those beautiful of soul,
and the Watchers and the fire waited upon them.
As in the temple of the Holy of Holies they stood in prayer,
and there they offered the pure sacrifices of their thoughts.
In great suffering the victors prayed fervently;
with loud voice they asked and pleaded for their lives.
With a holy voice they rendered thanksgiving to him who kept them alive,
and with discernment they composed words of hymns.
"Blessed is the Creator," the holy ones cried out in holiness,
"who has kept our lives from the harms of the flame.
Blessed is he who revealed in us the sign of his mercy and of the decree of his judgment,
and proved through us the strength of his greatness, mighty over all.
Blessed is he who trod through us a path for men to the knowledge of him,
and made us witnesses of the greatness of his power in the land of the Babylonians.
Blessed is he who armed the Watcher of fire with the armor of his name,
and made a shield against the burning one for our limbs.
Blessed is he who taught order to the fire, frenzied in its feeding,
and by its discernment put to shame the pride of the undiscerning."
At the order of the fire the Babylonians, void of order, were amazed:
"Who then has put the bridles of silence on the brute?"
Its calm drew the heart of the one who stumbled toward understanding,
and he began to ask what power it was that had overcome his power.

Great dejection fell on the king and his armies
when they saw that the fire had no power over the food they had given it.
They saw that it was bound and did not come near the Israelites,
yet loosed its mouth to destroy the slanderers.
They saw that within it was calm and idle from its work,
and outside it was furious and roared like a beast.
They saw that it held back its fierceness within the furnace,
and went out and showed the might of its power on those who had prepared it.
Through its discernment it turned the festival of the image into mourning,
and turned the sound of hymns into wailing.
All Babylon had been rejoicing on the day the king held the festival,
and when it saw that the king's words were not true, it wept and mourned.
At the king's mourning the armies mourned,
for they saw that the haughtiness of his heart had fallen from its confidence.
The fool had been confident that he would grow great through the image,
and when he saw that captive youths despised it, he was ashamed and grieved.
The witless one thought his authority was exalted to the measure of its height,
and because the sons of the exile mocked it, dejection seized him.
Dejection seized him when he gazed and saw the youths in the fire,
walking about, and their limbs not burned.
"Are these really they, or perhaps I am not thinking clearly?
Are they walking about alive, or perhaps it is not true?
It is a new thing that has happened in the land of the Babylonians, and I cannot believe it;
and if it is true, the hope we waited for is false.
We waited to grow great through the greatness of the image we made,
and behold, we have become smaller than all, for three men have overcome our strength.
Three men were thrown into the furnace as if to death,
and behold, I see that they trampled it, and stood, and were walking about in it.
Three we gave to be food for the flame,
and they bound its mouth from their bodies and let it loose upon us.
Three branches we cut from the shoot of the house of Abraham,
and behold, I see that another, glorious one, has sprung forth from them.
Great glory fills the appearance of the fourth,
and the radiance of his face surpasses that of created beings.
His appearance overpowers even the appearance of the flame,
and already the fire has drawn back from him with discernment.
Already he has driven it from the bodies of the sons of the captivity,
and taught it to go out and destroy the ranks of our armies.

Already he has given it discernment, though it has none,
and by his command it has gained authority to give life and to kill.
What is this that has befallen our land and our days,
that it lashes us with a lashing of our soul, as though we were possessed?
We wanted to scourge the sons of the captivity for having despised us,
and it has turned on us and scourges us mightily.
By fire we thought to avenge on them the insult to us,
and behold, it has come out and avenges on us the insult of their blood.
Come, let us approach the furnace, fearful though it is,
and persuade them to persuade it not to destroy us.
Come, let us take refuge in the fear of truth to which they hold,
that we too may be delivered from the burning of the flame.
Come, let us all together ask them lovingly
to come out quickly from the furnace, so that the fire may cease."
In fear and in love the king and his counselors drew near,
and asked and pleaded with the scourged ones, whom we had greatly wronged [?]:
"Come out, servants of God, all of you, from the furnace,
and take away from us the rage of the fire that oppresses us.
Come out, you just ones, servants of truth without negligence,
and be advocates for us in judgment before justice.
Come up, victors, from the contest of righteousness;
great you are, and you have condemned Babylon of Assyria.
Come, innocent ones, rest from the war with our wickedness,
for behold, our guilt has been revealed before all creatures.
A war of wickedness we wickedly waged against you,
and the Just One saw, and turned our wickedness back upon our malice.
Just is your God, and true is his love toward his servants,
and according to his justice he acquitted his servants and condemned the wicked.
False is the fable of Chaldean lore to which we held;
if it were true, where is its power, that it did not stand up for us?
By what has happened let everyone learn truly
that there is no god who can save except One.
Let what he has done be the sign of his might,
that among the gods there is no power to help except in him.
By this let all peoples and their gods look on,
and see the error of their idols, how contemptible it is.
Contemptible is every god who cannot save the one who worships him,
and honored above all is he who has shown his power in his servants."

"You are servants of the God of all, who rules over all,
and see, the testimony of His divinity is in the members of His household."
The proud-minded king said these things against his will,
for he saw that the power of the Maker he had mocked had overcome him.
With great mockery he had opened his mouth against the Maker,
and it turned back, and against his will he praised Him before all peoples.
In the land of Judah he had profaned and scoffed at His lordship,
and in his own land He repaid him with an injury worse than the one he had done.
In the very house he trusted in He struck him down and threw him from his confidence,
and showed him how feeble was the power of help he had prided himself on.
He thought that by his own power he had overcome His people and put an end to its festivals,
but He rebuked him on his own ground: that victory had not been his.
He was musing proudly after he had uprooted the holy temple whose coals had gone out,
and He taught him wisdom through His servants, so that he would not boast insolently.
Through His servants He wisely judged his insolence,
so that he would not think that He was contending with his wickedness on equal terms.
He moved His servants to trample on him as one contemptible,
so that he might know how feeble was the power he boasted of.
Already His purpose had stirred the king's heart to make an image,
so that by means of the image He might portray His hidden purpose before the king's gates.
Already He had led him to summon the eloquent to the worship of sorcery,
so that when they strove He might make known to them the power of His greatness.
Already He had spurred on the slanderers to kindle the fire,
so that once it was kindled He might proclaim His power through His household.
Perhaps it was for this that He did not avenge it from the beginning,
so that His rebuke would not be without benefit.
It was not under constraint that He did, or does, these things I have spoken of;
rather, He waited and did not avenge them from the beginning.
He could have avenged the shame of His name and of His household,
yet He waited and kept silent until the wickedness of the wicked was revealed.
For in the wickedness of the wicked the power of His greatness is ever victorious,
so that the great wealth of His patience may be revealed to mankind.
In His patience He bore with the wicked Nebuchadnezzar,
and when He saw that he had done evil beyond measure, He rebuked him in measure.
Like a fisherman He stood upon the sea of His patience
and gave him the hook, as to a fish, until He had caught him.

He placed the net of His love in the hands of His household,
and spread it out, as fire instead of water, over the Babylonians.
In fire and water the divine fishermen stood,
and skilfully they caught Babylon, the huntress of peoples.
Like fish, they thrashed about at first in their struggles,
and when they saw that they had fallen into the nets, they were ashamed and fell silent.
They had been in great turmoil as they swam in the waves of the storm,
and when the decree drew them to dry land, their lives were snatched away.
As food for the fire they gave their bodies, those speaking fish,
and they wailed and cried out as they were roasted in the flame.
With a loud voice the Babylonian fish of dry land cried out:
"Come, fishermen, come up from the sea of flame!
Come up, O men, fishers of men without hands,
for you have caught your hunters with the bait of fire!"
Crowd upon crowd the peoples had gathered to watch
as the chosen martyrs came out from the midst of the fire.
Troop upon troop stood all the ranks, men and women,
to gaze upon the greatness of the power that had given them the victory.
In great amazement they gazed at what had happened,
and it was true, and yet not true, to their minds.
"It is, and it is not," the clear-minded kept pondering:
"Are these the men themselves, or a shadow that looks like a body?"
The divided of heart fell into confusion,
and as in a dream they were astonished at the plain truth.
In truth the true ones remained in the fire without harm,
and until they came out the truth was not confirmed to the unbelieving.
The true ones came out, standing firm in the truth,
and the unbelieving saw them and so were made firm.
They came out whole in their limbs and in their clothing,
and not a hair was missing from their heads or from their garments.
They came out with the radiance of their truth shining brighter than gold,
and the eyes of those who beheld them were dazzled by its brightness.
They came out wrapped in a visible garment and a hidden glory,
praising the living Name that had glorified them.

They came out of the fire treading it beneath their feet,
and this is the wonder: not even the smell had come upon them.
The prophet bears witness, he who became a witness at the mouth of the beasts,
who testified and said that the smell of the fire had not come upon them.
Wondrous is the contest these earthly men waged on earth,
and the mouth of earth's children is too small to tell how great it is.
Great is the victory of the endurance of the sons of the captivity,
and the pen of a tongue of flesh is too weak to capture its beauty.
Their Lord alone knows how to paint the image of their beauty
and to tell of the endurance of their minds.
It was He who engraved the power of greatness upon their tongues
and wrote in His books the day of victory on earth.
Like a mirror He set their victory in the Scriptures,
so that those who run the race of righteousness may look into it.
Through their labours He cast zeal into those who came after them,
so that they might long for the upright goal of their way of life.
It was for good that He took them captive to the land of the Babylonians,
so that through their sufferings those who were lacking might gain discernment.
He did well to bear with them while they became slaves,
so that by their servitude He might show the glory of His might.
Wisely He kept silent while they were going into the furnace of testing,
so that by their testing He might expose the fraud of Chaldean lore.
Skilfully He composed the story of their victories,
so that as it is told everyone may learn to be victorious.
Mightily He helped them in the contest of sufferings,
so that those who are tried by suffering might gain hope.
Just, too, is the punishment His purpose inflicted on their persecutors,
so that no one may dare to rise up against the humble.
Just is His judgment, upright His testing, and wise His purpose,
and no one knows how to recount well the kinds of His wisdom.
He took the people He had chosen for His name captive to the land of the Babylonians,
and by its servitude He humbled the error of Chaldean lore.
His providence brought about a twofold benefit:
through His people He taught the peoples that He is Lord over all.
His purpose made both the people and the peoples wise by what He did,
for He chastised them and won them, each by the hands of the other.
As with a rod, He raised them up one against another,

and chastised the people by the hands of the peoples, and the peoples by the people.
Come then, let us learn the power of His wisdom through His discipline,
and give Him the great glory that befits His name.
Response: Glory to the Power that strengthened the martyrs, so that they conquered and won the victory in the contest.
On the Rebuke of Priests
Homily Forty-Five: On the Rebuke of Priests, and Fitting for a Troubled Time

An evil time compels me to speak of its evil,
and its disorder has made me tell of its confusion.
Outside all order I saw it confound the order of its course,
and my mind hastened to examine its confusion.
Savagely I saw it going on the path of turmoil,
and I was greatly amazed at its lawless audacity.
Like vicious beasts it was raging,
and it would not let a man lay a hand on it to come near it.
At its affliction my thoughts wandered as in a dream,
and I pondered that perhaps its course was a dream and not reality.
A dream I reckoned the changing of the times that came in my days;
yet it was not of a dream, but of falsehood, worse than a dream.
Its disorder compelled me to call it the wandering of a dream,
for as in a dream it makes a man stray from what is fitting.
As in sleep it has sunk the world in its heaviness,
and no one wishes to shake off from himself the heaviness of iniquity.
It is like the darkness of night, the darkness of ignorance,
and it is very hard to walk well in its gloom.
Darker is the season of this time than all times,

and indeed there has been no other time darker than it.
Over all and in all its dominion is stretched out in darkness,
and its bitterness has withheld the light of discernment.
Travellers journeying to the goal of peace have halted,
for the time has stood like darkness before their eyes.
All measures have ceased from the pursuit of good things,
and each has shut up his disposition within himself as in winter.
The discerning have wrapped up their minds as in a cloak,
and have gone in and hidden, lest they be worn down by the harshness of the time.
Listlessness has seized them like a fever,
and they have no wish to interpret hidden sayings in the ears of men.
With one sickness of ignorance all the ranks have fallen,
and there is none to soothe his neighbour's pain with a word of truth.
The pain of their wounds is like an inflamed swelling,
and no one knows how to bind it up well with faith.
Hard is the sickness, for into it men fall from every pain,
and there are no medicines able to heal its wounds.
Into the hidden soul the sickness of this time has crept,
and lo, it weakens the nature of man like a moth.
By its sickness all ranks are cast down, with all measures,
and this is the wonder: everyone is sick, and no one perceives it.
Kings are sick, and the crown on their heads is ailing,
and there is no authority sound in its rank and walking in order.
Priests are sick, and the staff of their command is weakened,
and there is no canon standing beside them as health of the spirit.
Spiritually sick are the priests, the physicians of the soul,
and in their souls they are cast into the fever of the body's passions.
Hateful passions of every kind shine out from them,
and one catches the sickness from another and corrupts with shameful deeds.
Envy bites, pride kicks, harshness burns,
and though there are no causes, causes are knotted and not loosed.
Wrath rages, strife kindles hatred into fighting,
and each one strives to destroy his fellow as by fire.
Snares in deceit, nets in falsehood, ambushes in secret:
and who is able to escape the hardships?

Swords sharpened, arrows pointed, spears whetted,
and hardly a man is left who is not wounded.
War is prepared, battle made ready, ranks drawn up to fight,
and this is the calamity: for whom, and against whom, is the struggle?
Come, marvel, you natures, rational and silent alike,
at the hard battles which priests array one against another.
Come, spiritual beings, look and examine with discernment
how far our audacity has grown in this time.
Come, O nature of [?], groan over yourself,
and wail and weep over your lawless evils.
Lawlessly your evils have grown strong, O despicable nature,
and without order you have walked in the paths of coarseness.
Audaciously your will has gone against the truth,
and lo, the proof of your audacity is in the heads of your people.
The heads of your people have torn apart the concord that was set in you,
and they have divided you into portions of every shape.
The sowers of peace have troubled peace by their strife,
and have cast contention between the earthly and the heavenly.
An evil strife they have cast [?] among each and all,
and lo, the world is in turmoil, struggling with itself.
An evil zeal they have put on like armour, one against another,
and pitilessly they have shot words like arrows.
Arrows of insult the learned have shot at their own members,
and they did not consider whom they strike with the words of their mouths.
Blind envy has blinded them from understanding,
and they did not discern whom they have wounded with their blows.
Foolish pride has led them astray from understanding,
and they did not discern and know what befits their great name.
Love of money has bound them in earthly things,
and they did not long for the kingdom of the life to come.
Avarice has inflamed them in the fire of covetous desires,
and the world has grown too small in good things for their wants.
Love of glory has caught them in the snare of glory,
and like a bird they have fallen from the height of their conduct.
Gluttony has entered and crept into their thoughts,
and they gathered from everyone, and their desire was not filled.
Though not in want, they were in want of everything,
and though all that was theirs [?] their hands in everything.
The owners of wealth have come to need [?] from their own,

and lo, they are not ashamed to beg for alms like beggars.
Their greed has made them needy of everything,
and their stinginess has withheld good things from their own mouths.
They have despised their own persons in an unseemly way,
and they have lowered the lofty rank in which they stood.
Shepherds of rational beings they were called,
and they left mankind and went out wandering after the dumb.
The discerning loved the undiscerning more than the discerning,
and for the silent they acquired the possession of their gain.
For love of the earth they forgot the pursuit of spiritual things,
and for despised things they exchanged the wealth of precious things.
To lofty humility the Bridegroom on high invited them,
and they falsified His true words.
Truth will be witness at the judgment between Him and them,
and will exact from them the vengeance for the insult to His truth.
In true judgment He will rebuke them, the deceitful priests,
who despised His gift and insulted the mysteries of His precious things.
He will pronounce judgment on their deceits, the deceivers,
who sat upon His wealth and did not dispense it for the needs of men.
To them He gave His word, that by it they might share out life to mankind,
and they hid it within the cloak of their deeds.
To them He spoke that saying He spoke to Simon,
and they heard it, and were silent about the meaning hidden in it.
To them He entrusted the care of the flock of mankind,
and they ate the flesh of the fat and despised the weak.
Upon them it is fitting that the word of prophecy be applied:
“O priests, ignorant and foolish shepherds!”
Not rightly did the shepherds tend our nature,
and pitilessly they scattered our lives on the mountains of error.
Like a flock that has no shepherd our humanity has become,
and wild and evil beasts came in and destroyed our race.
Among the paths of ignorance the speakers have wandered,
and no one has turned his mind to the Scriptures.
The shepherds have ceased from aiming at the fear of truth,
and the flock has strayed on the false path of their deeds.
By their deeds they have confused the way of faith,

and by their deceits they have filled it with the dread of rough ground.
Roughness they have thrown like stones before the travellers,
and dread has grown, and no one walks straight.
The milestones of peace they have shifted and removed from their place,
and the way of hope and love has been confounded.
Like robbers, minds lie in wait against minds,
and man has stripped his fellow men of good things.
Great wealth filled the treasury of faith,
and men plundered it, not in love but in deceit.
The deceivers have joined deceit to the Deceiver,
and have plundered the undivided confession with their words.
Mysteries of iniquity the audacious have bound upon the rebellious,
and have troubled the peace of the Creator's name between us and them.
Wicked priests have become partners in disorder,
and have set up a course so as not to be persuaded by the word of peace.
As vessels of peace the word of peace appointed them,
and they drove peace from within peace into the desert outside.
In the desert outside wanders the peace of the Creator's name,
and it has no place to enter and dwell among those who know it.
Like a poor man driven from the dwelling that is truly his,
while a false intruder enters the house of his inheritance and plunders his goods.
The abode [?] of peace strife has seized and dwells in it,
and raises its voice and burns with pride against righteousness.
The desert does not so dread the robbers who dwell in it
as the side of peace dreads strifes.
Those who dwell in the desert do not so tremble at wild beasts
as the lovers of love shudder at craftiness.
A great calamity has come upon our bitter-natured generation:
that the cause of peace has become the cause of all evils.
For the cause of peace the priesthood was set among the earthly,
and the priests have turned the order of peace into strife.
In place of light and instead of salt it was given to us,
and its light has grown dark, its taste has grown insipid, and it has turned to earth.
“It forgives iniquity and gives life,” its Giver called it,
and its iniquity has grown, and its fragrance of life has gone stale.
The keys of the height the divine command gave it,
and it neither entered itself nor opened the door to the penitent.

The priests have shut the door of mercy in the face of mankind,
and have not accepted the repentance and tears of the suppliants.
The priests have hidden the word of life from the dead,
and have not given a hand to the dead in iniquity, that they might live freely.
Pitilessly they have decreed oppression upon sinners,
and have not laid the medicine of repentance on their wounds.
Sluggishly they approached the work to which they had been appointed,
and begrudgingly they rendered the thanksgiving they owed.
Servants the Herald of the Spirit called the rank of priests,
and they have turned it into a title of earthly dominion.
In earthly fashion they imagined the orders of the Church to be,
and like men of the world they demanded their dues from mankind.
Like a judge the priest sits at the door of his house,
and like a ruler he raises his voice and demands fees.
The title of authority the commoner flaunts over his hearers,
and does not perceive that his rank is far from authority.
Your rank is not authority, fool — how you err!
You are a servant and a minister of your fellows.
You were not appointed to exact payment, man — what do you want?
To give life freely you were called, as mercy at the King's door.
The great treasury that is brought into your hands is not yours;
why do you boast of what is not yours as though it were yours?
You are a treasurer, a member of the household of the King over all;
do not take pride in what you give from your Lord's house.
Your Lord has given you from His treasury to dispense;
see that you do not wrong your fellows by partiality.
Hear the voice of your Lord accusing the wicked servant;
administer well, lest you become his companion in judgment.
In true judgment the Creator will test His servants;
woe to him who has hidden his Lord's money from those who should receive it.
With fear and trembling one enters the court of His judgment;
woe to him who did not show mercy to his fellows in love.
With fire He tests the works and words of body and soul;
woe to him who did not build sound works into the building of truth.
Without disregard He brings judgment on all ranks,
and is not held back by the authority of priests and kings.
On priests He refines His punishment more severely,

in proportion to the gift and the greatness of the power they received from Him.
On them He hardens a double punishment without pity,
because they were given power to forgive, and did not show mercy and forgive.
Before angels and men He enters into judgment with them,
because they were honoured in the eyes of the earthly and the heavenly.
In the eyes of the earthly and the heavenly He honoured them,
and they despised His honour in an unseemly way.
Above the hosts of the heavenly He honoured them,
and they did not discern and know to what a rank they, the debtors, had risen.
To a lofty rank, higher than the Watchers, He raised them,
and they did not perceive how greatly the lowliness of man was exalted.
The rank they received bears witness how far they were exalted above all,
for even the spiritual beings who are higher than they are lower than they.
The Watchers are not permitted to ascend to the rank they have received,
nor are they able or sufficient to minister it in their own persons.
The hosts of the heavenly and their powers stand in fear,
and by comparison they are far less than the priesthood.
Gabriel is glorious and Michael great, and their names bear witness,
and yet their nature is less than the priesthood.
The title of priesthood — its nature is greater than all things,
and if there is anything greater than anything, it falls beneath its office [?].
The priests have despised the lofty rank to which He honoured them,
and defiled its beauty with the shameful things of their deeds.
In every way they have despised the name of His honour,
until the despicable mocked and laughed at its debasement.
For prices they have sold that gift which is not to be sold,
and though the world does not suffice for its price, they have fixed prices for it.
For passing things they have exchanged the rank that does not change,
and though there is nothing equal to its name, they have set a valuation on it.
O covetous greed that cannot be restrained,
which has set prices on a thing that is hard to sell!
O priesthood, which has exchanged its name for trifles,
and, though all things are its own, has given away its own for no gain!
For what is not its own it has sold its own like a common thing,
and lo, it is mocked between buyer and seller.
One brings it in, paying contemptible prices for it,
and another despises it, taking it in foolishness.

Between buyer and seller its contempt grows,
without their perceiving what the power hidden within it is.
O ignorant ones, who do not discern between good and evil,
why have you sold height and depth without knowledge?
O proud ones, whom foolish pride has led astray,
why have you exchanged heavenly things for a worthless clod?
A pearl is not sold to those who do not know it,
and this is the mockery: that fools have bought the priesthood.
Signet-gems are found only in the treasuries of kings,
and this is the wonder: that the Holy of Holies is cheap in the markets.
The ranks of the world are not conferred without examination,
yet for the wisdom of truth there is no inquiry about its stewardship.
This alone the priest asks: what will one give for it?
If there is gold, well; and if not, he does not trouble to sell.
According to the gift the priest looks, and so he bestows it:
if the gift is large, he too enlarges and increases it.
Because of his loss the buyer too trades in it,
as he contrives to recover what he lost in his dealing.
Its practice is reckoned by its seller as a trade,
and like merchandise its buyers too pass it around.
There is no limit set to earthly trade
like the limit to the taking and giving of spiritual things.
There is no such strife over corruptible possessions
