as the struggle that has set men against one another over things to come.
Kings and tyrants have not waged such wars one against another
as priests have waged furiously against priests.
Furiously the priests have burned against the priesthood,
and pitilessly trampled one another in their strife.
By their strife they have troubled the world that was at peace,
and lo, it struggles night and day without end.
By their divisions they have torn the garment of faith,
and faiths without number have multiplied on the earth.
By their envy they have cast, cast rifts among the churches,
and lo, everyone is divided and no one agrees with his fellow's word.
One is the united body that Christ gathered by His passion,
and the priests have divided it into innumerable portions.

One is the body that became a sacrifice for our [?],
and the foolish have rejected it by mixing one thing with another.
One is the nature that is, and is as it is,
and the perverse have mixed it with the creature His hands have made.
Complete in body and soul was the sacrifice for the redemption of our lives,
and the accursed have made it lacking a soul and without a mind.
One is the Word, the Son of God, with His Begetter,
and pride has torn that equality, though it could not tear it.
Without limit and beyond sight is the nature of Being,
and the senseless have confined it within members, though they could not confine it.
Distinct natures became, in Being, one person,
and the dull of heart do not consider the manner in which they came to be in Him.
They came to be in Him, I said, not by nature but by love,
and even so each is distinct from the other, inasmuch as it is distinct.
The Creator is distinct and is not mingled with what His hands have made,
and the creation is lower than the greatness of the power that created it.
A creature, a creature it is, however much it is magnified through its causes,
and the Being is the Being, however much He is lessened by a borrowed name.
By a borrowed name the Maker was lessened, if — God forbid — He was lessened,
for even this, that the name is borrowed, is an audacity.
It is audacity for anyone to attach change to the Being,
and madness to say that He was lessened even in name.
Being can never be lessened from what it is,
neither in borrowed fashion, nor in deeds, nor in any way at all.
The disposition of the wicked has tried to lessen the hidden nature,
and for this insult no one is to blame but the priests.
If these priests had rightly built one confession,
the foolish would not be building a dwelling within the building of truth.
If these priests had directed their movements to the right goal,
the dull of heart would not be uttering words of insult.
If these priests had loved the harmony of the body of Christ,
rifts would not be springing up within the churches.
If these priests had set their minds to meditate on spiritual things,

the love of mankind for the things to come would not have grown insipid.
The priests have become for us the cause of life and the cause of death,
and had they remained in the order of life, blessed would our race have been.
The cause of death has now prevailed through their deeds,
and lo, everyone hastens to kill his fellow without pity.
From them men have learned to envy men,
and lo, everyone has put on the zeal of anger against his neighbour.
They began it by demanding vengeance,
and lo, everyone is eager to exact vengeance from his companion.
They have confounded the right orders that walked among us,
and lo, our life is confused, and there is no order in us befitting mankind.
It was fitting for them to make wise the childishness of mankind,
and to give taste to the tasteless through their words.
It was their duty to walk well toward the goal beyond,
and by their labours to show the path of the kingdom.
The kingdom on high the Creator promised to the nature of man,
and the priests have barred the lofty way, and no one walks it.
The charioteers have ceased from the race of good things,
and no one drives on the path of the hope of faith.
And if there is anyone who drives, whether out of love or by nature,
the warfare of the priests does not let him run well.
The great dread of their struggles has fallen on everyone,
and there is no one who trusts even one whose love is true.
Everyone has been cast between division and disorder,
and no one has trust in his fellow, not even in a word.
If there is anyone who trusts, his trust is no trust,
for snares lean in from every side before his trust.
With a word man hunts man as with snares,
and perhaps silence and quiet, and no answer, would be better.
The word is the sign of the reason that is in our nature,
and what can it do when envy holds back its working?
The envy of the priests stands up like a wild lion,
and lo, it bites reason with the tooth of anger.
The teeth of a beast the priesthood, the anointing of mankind, has acquired,
and it has begun biting and kicking mankind without discernment.
In it was bound the peace of men and of spiritual beings,

and lo, Watchers and men are afraid to come near it.
A great calamity has come upon our generation, full of sins:
that from the very thing we trusted dread has sprung up for us, and hope has been cut off.
On the priesthood our hope and our faith had been set,
and lo, it has fallen, and with it has fallen the trust of our souls.
Like a foundation it bore the building of our life,
and the winds of desires blew, and it shook and tottered.
It was not the priesthood that shook and tottered, as I said;
the feeble priests shook at the sound of the wind of covetous desires.
It was not the priesthood that shook in these things I have recounted of its ministers;
their minds grew small and fell short of what was fitting.
It was not the priesthood that troubled the word of peace that dwelt in it;
the sons of its right hand did not wish to remain in the building of its love.
It was not the priesthood that despised its honour before outsiders;
the keepers of its treasury squandered its stores by their deeds.
I saw the debasement of its mysteries as the mouths of fools recount it,
and amazement overwhelmed me: who is it that openly [?] reviles whom?
I sought to avenge the insult to it through my words
upon the audacious who despised its freedom and insulted its ranks.
In the greatness of its [?] I saw the dull of heart mocking,
and I was greatly zealous to bring forth words of audacity.
It is audacity for anyone to rebuke those in authority,
and I who have rebuked do not know how I came to rebuke.
Zeal for the priests compelled me to rebuke their deeds,
for they have left the way of faith and trodden the path of falsehood.
It was their lawless deeds that my words rebuked,
and though I have rebuked, I do not despise the order that is in them.
Not out of envy did I rebuke them, in all that I rebuked,
and not out of malice did I slander their deeds.
Truth bears witness that I did not hate them, and do not hate them;
I hated the iniquity in them that cast evil strife among us.
They are dear to me because of the rank set in their hands,
and hateful to me because of the iniquity they have cast upon the earth.
I love them for love's sake — love — and for the sake of order,
and I hate them for their iniquity and their partiality.
I do not consent that anyone exalt himself above their ranks,

so that they are not despised, however evil their conduct may be. / Love owes it to them to repay them with wondrous love, / and even if we are unworthy, let us not withhold what is fitting. / The Greatest of the great set a canon over their ranks, / and he does not allow us to despise the order of their canons. / Let the scorner scorn their lawless conduct, / but without neglecting the duty owed to their name. / The honoured name of the One who is above all is set upon their head, / and it is not right for us to despise them as though they were laymen [?]. / The keys of heaven are held in the hand of their minds, / and without them no one enters that place of glory. / So let us honour them with love, / as treasurers and keepers of the love of spiritual things. / That is also why I have held back from accusing them, / so that no one would dare to mock their high rank. / My accusation was not slander either. / It came from a purpose full of love, and it bears witness to the harm done. / My love bears witness that I rebuked them lovingly, / and it is love that allowed me to contend with them from his laws. / I contended lawfully with the priests of the Church, / because I saw that they had turned aside from the lawful canon. / From the beginning my words drew their strength from his words, / and I will not stop repeating them to the end. / Fellowship in his love has pleased me more than anything, / and God forbid that I should forget it, neglect it, or fall silent about it.
On Reproof
Homily Forty-Six / On Reproof

Man is shut up in the prison-house of mortality,
and does not wish to leave it, not even by his death.
The weakling is cast into the snare of passibility,
and has no care to escape from its harshness.
With the hard cords of desires he is bound and thrown down,
and finds no respite to rise from the fall of his desires.
Love of the lust of desires dwells within him,
and clings to him like fire to the timber of the forest.
In the fire of lusts he burns all over, at all times,
and there is no time when he is not inflamed by one of the passions.
The fire of his desires lies hidden within his limbs,
and it is not quenched until his mortality is quenched.
Like a chain, love of money is cast upon his soul,
and it is not loosed until death looses his body.
The motions of his discernment are yoked in the yoke of vainglory,
and he will not be freed from it before the day of his departure.
The hard fetter [?] of fleshly lust is cast upon his limbs
and enslaves him like a beast without discernment.
Mortality is a hard weapon, yet to him it is not hard;
it is the prison of passibility, yet to him it is not counted so.
Death lies hidden in love of money, yet to him it is like life;
love of glory is a scourge redoubled, yet to him it is delight.
Fire and worm spring from the lust of the flesh,
yet the torment set down in the Scriptures he counts as a dream.

Like a mute he walks the road of reason,
and like a silent creature he tramples the order of his discernment.
In his ways and his turnings he is like a beast,
falling short of the animals by little, or rather by nothing.
Yet he is like a beast not because he resembles one, but because he chooses it;
for one who chooses is not compelled, as a dumb animal is.
He is not bound like the dumb beasts in the toil of earthly things,
nor does he stray without perception in the straying of desires.
He is convinced that he is rational, yet is not persuaded by his reason;
he knows that he is shrewd, yet is not shrewd against his passions.
Shrewd at doing harm, and simple when it comes to refraining from harm;
skilled at lying, and untaught at expounding truths.
Eloquent in saying whatever helps his weakness,
silent and mute when it comes to rebuking the ways of his wickedness.
Discerning and careful in choosing what is good for himself,
[?] and distracted, so that he disregards the blemishes of his shameful deeds.
Proud of his knowledge, he blames the dumb who know nothing,
yet never once blames himself for the things he blames in others.
Blamed by all, he does not consider why he is like this.
He judges the wrong outside himself strictly,
but does not examine the hateful things within him.
O judge, who judges everyone in the furnace of his testing,
look at your own grievous faults as at the open faults of your fellows.
He condemns his fellows for what they owe as the debt of sins:
condemn yourself for the guilt of the debt of your sins.
He orders the dumb beasts to imitate him in reason:
order your life so that it resembles rational beings.
He compels natures without discernment to follow his discernment:
compel your own nature to discern well the things that are good.
He teaches his habits to creatures that do not know human speech:
train yourself in what your free nature has acquired.
He puts bridles in the mouths of the silent beasts so that they go well:
bridle your own motions, so that the course of your way may be smooth.

He ploughs the earth and cuts through mountains by his skill:
plough your mind, so that the fruits of the fear of truth may be planted.
He subdues the waves and holds back the winds by his craft:
subdue your mind, lest it be churned up in the flood of wrongdoing.
He hunts reptiles and hides snares for the wild beasts:
hunt the hateful habits of your soul as you hunt the beasts.
He roots out thorns from the silent fields:
root out your evils like tares from the field.
He brings peace to the world by the word of peace that dwells within him:
bring peace to your own inclination by that same pattern of peacemaking.
You are the cause of peace, O man, an honoured name:
honour your name, so that peace is not troubled through your name.
By the peace of your name the world of time is guarded and kept at peace:
guard your freedom, lest it be despoiled by unfreedom.
You have a hidden war with all, and all with you:
do not grow slack, lest you be condemned and condemn all.
Your war has pressed me to address a discourse to you,
and it was not your vigour that drove me to reproach you, as though for slackness.
Come, hear the account of your guilt from my own guilt,
and judge truly whether you truly condemn yourself.
In the furnace of your discernment's testing examine my words,
and see clearly the exposure of the counterfeit of your falseness.
As at a trial, let the hearer stand beside the speaker,
and let the one who has sinned not busy himself making light of his wrong.
Hear, then, and speak the discourse about yourself, O man:
why is your life in turmoil and your course idle?
Why does the conduct of your life resemble the beasts,
an order foreign to the strong order of reason?
Why is creation steeped in the drop of your bitterness,
so that there is no food whose taste is sweet in the mouths of those who eat it?
Why does the change of the seasons vary from all times,
with no likeness to the seasons that came before them?
Why is the course of their changes not level and even,
and why do they prevail, or are prevailed upon, beyond their order?
Why does summer resemble summer, and winter winter [?],
and why are cold and heat now excessive and now deficient?
Why, though the course of months and days is one,
are the measures of our lives not filled out as before?

Why do earthly things fail in the life of man,
and no good reward is returned for wearying labours?
Why is the lifespan of time [?] together with that of eternity,
and there is no one in our generation who possesses that of earth or that of heaven [?]?
Why are the ailments of body and mind so many,
and there is no one among us healthy in body and in spirit?
Why is ignorance spread through all the orders,
and there is no wise man to heal the ailments of ignorance?
The remedies of body and soul have ceased from among us,
and there is no one who cares for our health, not even in word.
Those who knew the sufferings of passibility have been taken from us,
and our race is near to being dragged off by sufferings and pains.
The world has grown dark in the darkness of ignorance,
and so in a stupor we despise remedies, as it is written.
The understanding of the fear of truth has passed from our mind,
and nothing remains that has not come to nothing.
O how hard is the hardness of our heart, harder than all that is hard,
that it does not grow wise through the hardships that chastise it!
O how blind is the eye of our soul to what is fitting,
that it does not bend down to see the blemishes that abide in it!
O how dear is the hearing of our mind, so dull of hearing,
that it hears and forgets, and does not let us hear what is fitting!
O how dulled is the nature of our freedom, fallen from its freedom,
that it does not make known to us the rights that befit the free!
O how hateful beyond measure is our inclination,
that it does not persuade us to turn back even a little from our evils!
It swallows our body and does not grieve at its disgrace;
it overthrows it to the ground and does not consider what the cause is.
We do not ponder what the cause of our body's scourges is,
and we do not make supplication over the sufferings that oppress us.
Our heart is like a hard rock before the blows,
and, as one who feels nothing, behold, many sufferings afflict it.
Pains are many, sufferings oppress, and death hastens on,
yet it seems as though it had heard none of these things.
Famine oppresses, captivity carries off, and the sword destroys,

and our mind lounges as though on a bed of pleasure.
War presses hard, slaughter abounds, how it overflows!
And to our mind everything is counted as nothing.
Divisions in the Church, tumults among the pagans, and strife in every place;
and if anyone demands that we feel it, we do not feel.
There is no remembrance of our body's scourges in our mind,
and if there is, it is not truly kept by anyone.
The remembrance of true things is not kept in truth,
since the words of the mouth do not agree with the mind within.
There is one who repeats the remembrance of words in words alone,
and wipes from his mind the remembrance of good things.
There is one who is skilled in recounting the ways of good things,
while in his thoughts the acquiring of shameful things abounds.
There is one who is zealous to avenge wrong vigorously,
yet cannot reproach the wrong of his own soul, not even in word.
There is one who denounces adultery and theft,
and both are in him, and he is not reproached for them by his freedom.
There is one who is clothed in the habit of chastity and gentleness,
and no one is as base as his mind.
There is one who shows a face of love to his friend,
while his inner inclination whets the sword for blood.
There is one who grieves over afflictions when he does not grieve,
and is like a wolf clothed deceitfully in the likeness of a sheep.
There is one who knows how to [?] shameful things,
and the shameful things within him are not shameful to him.
There is one who reads in the books of the Spirit like an orator,
while his mind stammers at fulfilling the words in deeds.
There is one who expounds even the meaning of hidden things,
and does not perceive the hidden deceits in his own mind.
There is one who reminds others of the reckonings of the coming judgment,
and to him it is not even true that there is a Lord of judgment.
There is one who warns that no one should do wrong by taking what is not his,
and he hides many snares of deceit to defraud his fellows.
There is one who reproaches love of money valiantly,
and it is planted in him like a root in the depth of the earth.
There is one who rebukes love of glory skilfully,
and it lurks in him like a scorpion in the clefts of a rock.

There is one who defiles himself in the lust of [?] as though he were innocent,
and sinks in it as in a mire that cannot be crossed.
There is one who shuns the envious and the crafty,
while the fire of anger clings within him against his fellows.
There is one who mocks hateful pride and haughtiness,
and the haughtiness of his own spirit cannot be measured, so high it is.
There is one who scorns the irascible and the wrathful,
and what rages in him is no wrathful man but a demon.
There is one who accuses those who keep a grudge against their neighbours,
while he, for generations, does not let go the grudge of his anger.
There is one whose eyesight is sharp to see the motes,
and he does not examine the beams in his own eyes.
There is one who grieves and mourns and is distressed over hateful things,
and the memory of his own wrong never once comes up in his mind.
There is one who groans loudly over evils,
and over his own evils has not grieved since the day he was born.
And there is one who even distinguishes alms from necessities,
and if an orphan meets him in the market, he raises his staff.
There is one who expounds spiritual things before hearers,
and is bound and strangled in bodily things through insatiability.
There is one who strains out the despised gnats, the faults of his fellows,
and swallows the camels, the shameful sins his heart begets.
There is one who supposes that good things are brought to completion in him,
and he is as far from them as a distant mountain is far.
There is one who is falsely praised by liars,
and if the stones had a mouth, they would cry 'Woe!' at him.
How many there are who grew great and gained the rank of headship,
who were not worthy to be slaves to the slaves of slaves!
How many there are who lived in the priesthood and in health of body,
when it was not fitting that the sun should rise upon their lives!
How many there are who deceived in the parts of one guise after another,
and a day is coming when the falsehood of their guises will be revealed!
How many there are who became a house of oaths [?] for the broken-hearted,
and on the day of judgment they will be a laughing-stock to those who see them!
How many changes beyond number among men,

and there is no one who considers the wrong of men.
Men are sick with the hateful ailments of hateful wrong,
and they do not tend the bruises of their minds.
In their minds the pain of their minds lies hidden,
and they are not persuaded to put on it a healing drug.
Ignorance has blinded them to what is fitting,
and they look at one another while being ruined by their fellows.
Come, you silent ones, see how many speakers have been silenced,
who died in sin, and did not stir or feel at their departure.
Who ever died a death like the death of the dead of our generation,
which strikes everyone, while no one knows what his death is?
In what generation did evils grow as strong as our evils,
which, many as they are, do not satisfy those who commit them?
Insatiability is a beloved evil to the mind of the wicked,
and this is the wonder: how evil it is, and how beloved.
The evil of its evil has compelled me to inquire into its evil,
so that by its exposure men may see themselves.
The ugliness of its evil has made men ugly to look upon,
and I have painted it in words so that they may see how ugly it is.
My word has reproached its shamefulness, and my mouth reproaches it,
so that everyone may know how to reproach the ways of evils.
I saw the ways of evils, how they disgrace men,
and I suffered greatly over the disgrace of our great lineage.
The Creator called our lineage a great lineage,
in that he raised it to the name of the greatness of his being;
by this name he made it the head of the beginning of our life,
foreseeing that it would go and reign in the country on high.
A man, he says, whose lineage was a great lineage,
went to a very distant country to reign there.
In the country on high our race reigned through the Son of our race,
and our race forgot the promise of words made to our race.
It is said that he raised us up and seated us with him above in heaven,
and there is no remembrance of this ascension in our mind.
What he seeks on our behalf, the herald of his preaching has written,
and if anyone should ask, no one knows where it is written.
There is no remembrance of the Scriptures in anyone's mind,
and if there is, it is only half of a person that is occupied with repentance.
With half of themselves men meditate on the words of the Spirit,

with that part of a person whose portion is despised and whose meditation is slight.
It is the body, the despised part, that busies itself with meditating on precious things,
while the soul, whose task it fittingly is, stays clean and idle of the labour.
Woe to our race! To what depth its honour has descended,
that it has left what is above and busied itself with earthly things!
Woe to our people! What has become of the goodness of its good,
that it has forgotten the covenant of things to come for things that are seen?
The mortals have loved the things that are seen, lovers of vanity,
and have counted as nothing the advantages of true things.
O perverse ones, who have overturned the order of good things,
who have hated blessings and loved scourges without end!
O rebels, who have driven out peace by their quarrels,
and have begun to wage a hidden war with their brothers!
The Merciful One taught us the way of peace through one of mankind,
and little by little they forgot the goal he showed them.
Without their willing it he turned them back from errors [?],
and by their own will they despised the commandments he gave them.
Love and peace he taught them to keep toward him,
and cast them upon their senses as though by nature.
By these, he said, the world will know that you are my disciples:
by the love and peace that you show one to another.
Let us inquire, then, whether these are found in the conduct of our generation,
and see with whom the goal of love and peace abides.
Let us seek in the Church this matter of love and peace,
where that Teacher of good things bestowed it.
From the household let us learn the purpose of the master of the house,
for they know how to examine good things well.
Reveal to us, O Church, the mysteries you learned from your Betrothed,
that we may teach them to those who ask us about you.
Betrothed of the King, whom the King betrothed by the sacrifice of his body,
explain to your children the wonder that took place at your betrothal.
You have forgotten, O Bride, the covenant you made with your Betrothed,
and have been false to the gifts of the Spirit he gave you in his love.
With glorious gifts and fearsome powers the King honoured you:
where are they? Show something of what he established with you.
Where is the robe he wove and gave you, set with jewels?
It has been stained with the foul stain of your shameful deeds.

Where is the seal of the Spirit of revelation he placed in your hands?
It has fallen and been lost, not on his part, but on yours.
Where is the crown and the lofty dominion he was bringing you?
It is not with you, since you did not abide with him in love.
Who has plundered your wealth, you who had gained divine wealth?
Passions as robbers and demons as brigands: alas, what has befallen you!
Passions and demons have plundered the treasure of the children of the Church,
and now they go about like beggars to ask for alms.
Like raiders their passions entered their minds
and stripped them, and they did not stir or feel their stripping.
In the sleep of wrongdoing their motions sank, together with their senses,
and they lost love and hope and faith.
Three kinds of riches they possessed in the land of their dwelling,
and they lost them through the ignorance of their deeds.
There is no one who believes, no one who hopes, nor one who loves;
and if these are not with us, the hope of our race is lost.
By faith and hope and love our mortality lives;
how then shall we live, when our life is far from us?
Our life-givers saw inequity and fled from us,
and our humanity remained like a man in whom there is no soul.
Men live without the life of faith,
and walk in their deeds without hope and love.
The deceit of their heart has torn the garment of faith,
and they stand like Adam, naked and without covering.
The children of the Church stand naked, without modesty,
and demons mock them as they mocked Adam in Eden.
The beginning of Adam's race was a great laughing-stock,
and this is the laughing-stock: that after receiving our life we died in sin.
Sin and death held us as a pledge,
and one of us arose and pledged his body, and set our body free.
In the fullness of time he pledged his body, though not wholly:
three days he remained in death, and he lived and gave life.
Three days he determined to remain in pledge,
and he returned and took back the pledge of all his race.
By the resurrection of his body he raised the bodies of his fellows,

and made them partakers in the blessing of immortal life.
The Life of life mingled with our nature, full of mortality,
and immortal life [?] in our mortality.
By this life our humanity lived in the Son of our humanity,
and then turned and died again in human things, as before.
A double death the mortals die in this time:
one of nature and one of sin: woe twice over!
In body and in soul the dead of our days are dying,
and no one cares for the resurrection that is the soul's repentance.
The repentance of the soul raises up bodies and limbs,
yet the soul is idle and does not repent of its deeds.
Woe to you, soul, and greater woe to you, soul of the priests,
that you are not roused to have mercy on the children of your race!
The priests will bear the double judgment of these dead,
for had they remained in faith, everyone would have lived.
They stripped off faith, the desirable garment,
and when the demons saw it, they ran to everyone to strip him.
They tore apart even love by their unevenness,
and cut off the way of peace by their [?].
From them mortality sprang up within the life of our life,
when they dared to say that the Giver of life died on the cross.
That Life which gave life to him who gave us life
the priests put to death with their lawless blasphemies.
This blasphemy has troubled the earth and its inhabitants,
and behold, everyone rises against whoever says that the Living One does not die.
A double death kills its fellow and kills God,
if it does not confess according to the confession of its perversity.
Well then, fool, where did you see that the divine Being dies,
and who taught you to kill your fellow who does not kill you?
You who are slain by your sins, why do you kill the One who does not die?
Mad with pride, why are you driven mad to destroy your fellows?
The sword of fools, persecutors of peace, has ruled upon the earth,
and behold, the world is being laid waste by the sword of mortality.
The sword of the passions carries a wounding edge on the tip of its tongue,
and destroys the ranks that do not agree with it about passibility.
A new war over passibility has now struck me,

and it provokes me to hurl my words at those who prepare it.
I long to hurl words at the ranks of those who prepare it,
that perhaps they may be scattered from their agreement on passibility.
Their struggle does not let me neglect them,
and compels me to mix their name into all my tales.
In the tale of the sufferings of our passibility my word grew strong;
I heard of a suffering, and mixed its tale into the tale of our sufferings.
In our sufferings I suffered, and composed words full of sufferings,
and the tale of a suffering greater than all sufferings met me.
The wicked turned me toward the great suffering ascribed to the Maker,
and I left off reciting the sufferings of our souls and was amazed at it.
Amazement seized me at this suffering ascribed to the Godhead,
and beside it the thought of our own sufferings grew small in me.
But now we are seeking the cause of this suffering,
over which the war has grown fierce and darker than at any time.
Perhaps it is that humiliation of passibility which they have hidden in his Being
that hastens famine and captivity upon our souls.
Perhaps the blasphemy of the injustice against the body that is from us
rouses diseases and stirs up pains upon our limbs.
Perhaps the mixture that mixes the natures one with the other
is what makes the change of the seasons fall out of order.
Perhaps the outcries that fools have raised against those who know the truth
are what drive us out in every form.
The pure blood that the wicked have boldly shed
hastens death to carry men off lightly.
The foolish zeal with which the ignorant were zealous in their cunning
rouses anger, stirs up wrath, and brings the locust.
These are the things that have troubled peace through our anger,
and behold, the world is in tumult like the sea by storms.
Hard sufferings strike the ship of our mortality,
and there is no sailor who knows the way to the harbour of peace.
Our race stands in a place of storms of ignorance,
and there is no pilot in our race to still the turmoil.
There is no one to calm the turmoil of sufferings against mankind,
and no one to soften the hard pain of hard wrath.
In hard wrath men crush their fellow men,
and he is praised who knows the means to carry out his anger.

By cunning the cunning win, and are praised as well, / and the one who is most crafty is most honored among liars. / In our evil time falsehood prospers better than truth, / and lying is loved more than honesty. / There is no honesty, not at all, not in a single rank, / for even the truthful are not as truthful as they are thought to be. / A blemish governs every rank, the good and the bad; / even the good is mixed with evil along with its goodness. / There is no truth in truth that is clean of stains, / since there is no man who is not a son of man, with his passions upon him. / With passions the whole race of Adam is stained, / and what man is there whose body is not ruled by the earth? / One alone is the Man who was not stained by his humanity, / he over whose embodiment minds are confounded. / One alone overcame the hard battle of passibility, / he in whose suffering wounds were struck upon the Impassible. / One alone was pure, and his own mouth testifies that he is pure, / so it is plain that there is none pure but One. / There is none pure, and least of all in this time, / when everyone sells truthfulness for partiality. / Through partiality each man stands before his neighbor's face, / and like a shadow words pass by, pass by, without deeds. / Words are what a friend gives his friend for provision, and a companion his companion: / “Peace to me, peace to you,” yet there is no deed in which there is peace. / With the mouth, [?], mouth greets its fellow mouth, / and the mind does not even feel when mouth has greeted mouth. / Such is love in our cunning generation: / craftily it dwells and shows itself in every deed. / With this sign, though my speech has painted the image of our conduct, / still it could not match the likeness to the likeness. / There is no painter able to paint the likeness of our iniquity, / since the kinds of its evils are more than his colors. / The shares of our hideousness cannot be numbered, / for there is no scribe who could hold their sum within his fingers. / Hardly can a hand grasp the bow of our evil generation, / and the mouth is too weak to recount the words of its falsehood. / Falsehood is full of words without deeds,

and the one who does not lie finds no credit for his falsehood. / Envy and arrogance have clothed the customs of every land, / and there is no deed in which they are not, and it is their prey. / Malicious, they show themselves and dwell in their deeds, / and they wish the world and its labor to stand according to their will. / The proud mind does whatever it does in arrogance, / and envy is full of envy toward everyone. / Two brute lions dwell together with man, / and no one knows how to take proper heed of their ways. / Great ruin they have wrought in creation, and still they work it, / and there is none who discerns, ponders, and grieves over their ruin. / Brutishly everyone roars in their ravages, / and they stir and shake among mankind like wild beasts. / The roar of lions is not so terrible to the beasts / as envy and arrogance are feared by humankind. / No wild beast ever so destroyed a fellow beast / as the destructions with which man has destroyed mankind. / Nor again was a bird ever harmed by a bird / as friends have inflicted harm on those they love. / The silence of the speechless is better than the speaking, / and love is kept in their natures better than it is with us. / Strange is the word I have spoken, if it is true: / that love abides among the dumb, and in us it is not. / And again let it be made plain in the word about us, even now, / and let us bring sufferings upon the deeds of our passibility. / Through suffering let us scorn the passions of our soul and the blemishes of our body, / so that we may be healed of the sins of body and soul. / In truth let us pronounce a true judgment with our own mind, / so that we may escape that judgment which has no end. / The judgment of our soul, it is written, annuls the judgment to come; / so our nature holds a court of judgment here and beyond. / Come, mortal king, who holds two courts of judgment: / loose your deeds and free your soul from accusation. / In the judgment here condemn yourself as you will, / that you may not be condemned in the judgment where your soul's will has no say.
On the reproof of the daughters of Eve and [?]
Homily Forty-Seven: On the reproof of the daughters of Eve and [?], and the schemes and wiles they practice

Eve, the fountain from which life flowed for mankind,
turned the drink of her sweetness into the bitterness of death.
The rib that had become a help for solitary Adam
became a bow in the hands of the Evil One against Adam.
He named that commandment, in which He had placed life, “Life”,
and she changed the name of life into mortality.
“Flesh of my flesh” Adam called her in prophecy,
and she spurned his prophecy without propriety.
“Woman” he said that everyone should call her, a name of equality,
and she tore apart the peace of mankind by her strife.
With Adam she entered Eden in the beginning, when she came to be,
and with him she received the commandment of life concerning the tree.
Full of life was that commandment which the Creator laid down,
and by her slackness she made it a spring that flows with death.
She became the cause of death and the companion of the Evil One from the time she came to be,
and from her limbs snares and traps sprang up for us.
Impropriety appeared in her from the very beginning;
her thoughts conceived bitterness, and her heart gave birth to it.
She hid the insolence of impudence in her face in the place of beauty,
and was not ashamed to speak with the deceiver.
Like a harlot she stood in Eden, naked,
and when the Evil One saw her he ran to look at her and committed fornication with her.
Through her open senses the Slanderer committed fornication with her,
and his seed reached even to the soul, and she was corrupted by it.
Through what she heard she committed adultery, the King’s bride betrothed to Adam,
and before the day of her wedding feast came she conceived iniquity.
Loathsome iniquity her soul carried from the Destroyer,
and she did not wish to keep the fitting order of discernment.
Evil desire took her mind captive, basely,
and without shame she stretched out her hands to the tree.

She contrived deceit with the deceiver, falsely,
and did not reveal to Adam the secret of his wickedness until she had eaten.
She sought, in her audacity, to be raised above her husband;
for this reason she ate, and gave also to her husband, and he ate.
Her will consented to her destroyer more than to Adam,
and that is why he counselled her to eat the fruit first.
She has obeyed his counsel from the beginning until now,
and her heart has not parted from his shameful converse.
She struck up an evil companionship with him who kills mankind,
and she has no wish to part from him to the end.
With him she longs to fornicate in shameful things,
and her nature will not rest so as to share in things that are beautiful.
Insatiably she loves the love of the corrupter,
and without restraint her heart runs after his company.
In every form her mind can take she hunts for converse with him,
and on every occasion she longs for the lust of her soul to be gratified.
The lust of the Evil One is dearer to her soul than Adam,
and her mind embraces his shameful things insatiably.
With a mind that fornicates with the killer she is stripped of understanding,
and does not perceive that fellowship with him is the bitterness of death.
On the lust of the flesh her mind is fixed night and day,
and her thoughts are taken up with base talk.
A hateful meditation on baseness is always cast upon her,
and talk of spiritual life does not please her.
The whole of her, altogether, has become baseness,
and there is no place in her where holiness might dwell.
The Evil One dwells and lives in her continually,
and gives no room for truth to come near her.
There is no profit for one who wearies himself over her dwelling,
for the Evil One continually empties his labour.
A beautiful dwelling the Maker of all made her in the beginning,
and she defiled the beauty of her soul with shameful things.
Wondrous was her appearance, and desirable she was before she sinned;
but after she sinned, Watchers and mankind loathed her.

At her beauty the hosts on high marvelled when she was created,
and when she was defiled they turned and were aghast at her shameful deeds.
The spiritual beings saw the hatefulness of soul and fled from us,
and were unwilling to remain in their brotherhood toward our race.
Because of her they came to hate converse with our humanity,
and withdrew and dwelt in the heights so as not to look upon us.
They reckoned their labour on our behalf a vain labour,
and were unwilling to serve the hidden will.
The more they examined the iniquity of our shameful deeds,
the more they armed themselves with the armour of wrath against us.
The more they remembered Eve, who plucked the fruit,
the more they took vengeance for her iniquity on fruits and seeds.
The more her daughters came to resemble her in her impudence,
the more they withdrew from serving us.
The more iniquity grew among them day by day,
the more their zeal was kindled beyond measure.
The more the Creator was grieved by their deeds,
the more mightily they made ready for war against us.
The more they were corrupted by the idols that demons set up,
the more they resolved not even to bring rain and dew.
In great mourning they sat over our evils,
and waited for us either to be destroyed or to be renewed.
Their discernment was gripped by the birth pangs of suffering,
and they were in labour, waiting for the birth of our death or of our resurrection.
The Creator, who sees all, saw the severity of their suffering,
and sent His sign and comforted them in their grief.
He sent His sign to the daughter of Eve who brought in death,
and fashioned in her an infant and filled Him with life for mortals.
Life purifies, in the forming of the Child from her,
so that by His life He might wipe death away from our humanity.
For the sake of peace He fashioned in Him an image that renews peace,
so that Watchers and mankind might be reconciled in Him with His majesty.
In Him all earthly and heavenly beings are reconciled,
and in the [?] of His body the creatures that had been worn out found rest.
For as soon as death sprang up, greedy, destroying men,
there sprang up the medicine of life that heals the children of men freely.
From a daughter of mankind death began to destroy,

and from a daughter of mankind life began to renew.
Where sin abounded exceedingly, beyond measure,
there righteousness grew strong beyond all measuring.
Where the Slanderer sowed the bitterness of his deceit,
there sprouted the ear of life that gives life to mankind.
Through Eve the Hater of men corrupted the children of men,
and through a daughter of mankind mercy hunted them spiritually.
The one clothed us in a garment of fig leaves that perish;
the other covered us with a robe of glory that does not perish.
The Sign full of compassion took pity on her contemptible state,
and wove a garment within her limbs and covered her shame.
A garment from her His will put on willingly,
and in His hands He renewed the creation that had been corrupted by transgressing the commandment.
Behold the goodness of the Good One, who created creation in His goodness,
who renewed us through ourselves, reconciled us through ourselves, and showed us pity through ourselves.
Let us then compare the conduct of our life with His gift,
and see whether there is any likeness to His mercies in the labour of our soul.
Let us test our works in the furnace of the trial of our discernment,
and behold, our wrongdoing will be revealed, how much it has wronged.
The works of Eve let us test first, with discernment,
and let us purge her hatefulness with words as in a furnace.
Into the furnace of words let us bring the daughters of Eve,
and instead of boiling, let us refine them in the fire of our speech.
Let us join words to their deeds, which are lawless,
and set ablaze the forest hidden in the adornment of their limbs.
Their deeds dragged me to go down the road of words,
and they compelled me to speak about them for the sake of truth.
Truth constrained me exceedingly, beyond measure,
to reveal the falsehood of their guises to the eye of the beholders.
Loathsome falsehood is hidden in the appearance of their limbs,
and if it is laid bare, there is no discerning person who would not groan.
Unclean iniquity fills the chambers of their thoughts,
and if it is examined before beholders, they loathe it.
Baseness, a beast of two [?], dwells within them,
and if it comes out, even the wild beasts flee from it.
Their mind is clothed in a garment of white and sealed with it,
but if it is torn, they stand naked in the likeness of Eve.
In anger they are kindled, they stir up zeal and rage,
and who can measure the onslaught of their battles?

Bold for insult, keen for folly, ready for reproach—
who is the upright man who could withstand their revilings?
Greedy in eating, gluttonous in drinking, shameless in lust—
and who that possesses freedom of soul would blush and keep silent?
In the house their quarrelling, in the market their uproar, in the church their ambush;
let him who wishes to escape flee on wings by night [?].
Their mouth lies, their gaze is wanton, their hearing deceitful,
and who is equal to recounting their blemishes?
Their insolence is shameless, their talk arrogant, their encounter sinful,
and who would not grieve over their passions, how loathsome they are?
Their clothing is base, their shoes contemptible, their gait unclean,
and that is why the very earth finds them heavy to bear.
Deceits they contrive, snares they hide, nets they spread,
and where shall he flee who hates their company?
Souls they take captive, minds they hunt, impulses they bind,
and how can one escape their wiles?
The chaste they belittle, the upright they lead astray, the steadfast they weaken;
woe to him who falls into the snares of their tumults!
The pure they trouble, the clean they stain, the shrewd they fetter,
and what shall he do who wishes to live in purity?
Their warfare is strong, their armour mighty, their yoke hard;
woe to our nature from the harms that constantly beset it!
Nature makes its demands, the inclination stirs up the desire of the heart;
Lord of natures, restrain [?] our nature, lest it destroy us.
Nature is hunger; our nature is a contemptible thing that eats and hungers,
and however much it eats, it grows greedy again and demands food.
The lust of the body that dwells within it is food of a second kind [?],
and as with eating, the body demands food for its body.
Eve, more demanding than all, demanded this food,
and with the persistence of insatiability she is occupied in pondering it.
She makes war if she does not satisfy the lust of her soul,
and with the struggle of insatiability she seeks what she desires.
Her daughters wage a hard war with us every day,
and arm themselves against us with their tumults as if with armour.
As if in battle they shoot at us night and day,

and hurl at us the sharp arrows of their tongues.
Their mouth is sharper than a two-edged sword,
and their blow enters even to the soul and is not stopped.
Those slain by the sword are not as many as those slain by them,
nor is the harm of a fanged beast like the harm they do.
Their harm is worse than that of venomous beasts,
and the cure of their bite is hard for the upright.
They corrupt the soul and set blemishes in the mind,
and except by the Spirit the sores they cause are not healed.
David bears witness how grievous is the blow of their pain,
for the wound of adultery lingered with him until his death.
With the tooth of adultery Eve bit the man healthy of soul,
and he grew sick, and his whole body was afflicted in all its vitals.
He fell into a long sickness and fever from her bites,
while he cried out and lamented every day because of his sickness.
“All my wounds stink and fester,” he repeated,
“and behold, I groan with the roaring of the pain of my mind.”
And if Eve broke David, the harp of the Spirit,
who can stand firm before her struggles?
If the seer of hidden things looked and was thrown into confusion,
let everyone close the eyes of his soul to her converse.
If he who [?] terrified the nations trembled at her voice,
let us stop our ears, lest they be terrified at the sound of her tumults.
See what the daughter of Eve did to the son of Adam;
let everyone beware of meeting her, lest she meet him.
See what the feeble rib did to a mighty hero;
let a man say to his fellow: Fear Eve!
Let everyone fear the daughter of Eve, and the upright still more,
lest their thoughts grow slack as David’s did.
She is an abhorrence to our race, even though she comes from it,
and her truth is not true, however pure she may be.
Let no one trust and believe her words without testing,
for there is no upright man who listened to her tumults whom she did not bring down.
She is full of iniquity, and falsehood dwells within her,
and there is no trusting her trustworthiness, not even a little.
Sweet are her words to him who does not know her bitterness,
and her talk pleases him who does not discern her folly.

Beautiful is her appearance to him who has not tested the deceit of her heart,
and desirable is meeting her to him who has not endured the trial of her passions.
Harsh passions come forth from her like wild beasts,
and bite us with their [?] as if with teeth.
And although passions are found throughout the whole nature of mortals,
in Eve above all they display the power of their workings.
In her they rage to do battle against freedom,
and her nature cannot stand firm before their onslaughts.
It is quickly weakened before the impulses of the passions of the body,
and has no strength to engage in the war of the desires.
She is worn down by desires more than men are,
and the war of the passions grows strong against her [?].
Upon her they drive the hard goads of intercourse,
and easily arouse the lust of the flesh in her.
The passions of the body overcome her by trifles,
and she herself bears witness how worn down she is by their battles.
Her guilt cries out to everyone about her struggles,
and points out, as if with a finger, the battles that are constant to her.
She is very weak in struggling with her impulses;
therefore she is guilty, and by her guilt makes us guilty.
In love of money she is gripped insatiably,
in love of glory she is bound beyond measure.
In lust of the flesh she is unrestrained, without shame,
and by her impulses she is ensnared, without consolation.
Hateful envy coils in her like a dragon,
and cruel pride rears up in her like a lion.
Mockery is poured out upon her like water,
and fraud flourishes in her like Mount Lebanon.
She knows how to defraud, and there is no fraudster who can defraud her,
and Naboth bears witness how unjustly she defrauded him.
Ahab was a fraudster, yet did not know the devices of fraud
until he learned from her the arts of shedding blood.
She is exceedingly crafty, and there is none among the crafty craftier than she,

and exceedingly foolish, and her ignorance cannot be measured.
Very shrewd she is at covering up her deeds,
and very foolish when it comes to remembering repentance of soul.
For evil alone are her heart and her nature wise,
and that is why even the demons are nursed on her arts.
She taught the chief of their ranks how to lead astray,
and she opened to him the door of her mind, and he cast in his seed.
From her he learns the kinds of evil and how to do evil,
and through her he arms himself, as if with armour, against truth.
Her armour he put on in the battle against Joseph,
and with her limbs he took up the contest against his purity.
With the hand of the flesh he seized the spiritual man in bodily fashion,
but the hand of the flesh, and the spirit, slipped free [?] of the carnal one.
He went down into the arena of desires with the chaste man,
who subdued his impulses through the senses of his body, and she could not overcome him.
Like a lioness the foolish woman roared at the holy one,
but her base claws took no hold on the pure body.
Like a wolf the corrupting she-wolf howled,
but the sound of her wantonness did not move the man strong of soul.
Only his garments did the leopardess snatch from him;
the jaw of her wantonness did not reach his limbs.
Like a gazelle the nimble one leapt and passed over her snare,
and she gnashed her teeth because the prey of her body had escaped her.
Is it not, then, without cause that I have slandered Eve as a beast?
No—her deeds cry out against her that she is a beast.
It is not I who called her by a strange name for the sake of speech;
her baseness has made her resemble a fanged beast.
But let her speak against my words, if she can,
and say that these things I have recounted about her wickedness are not so.
Speak, Eve, if you have the strength to speak,
and I will accept the answer of your words, if they are true.
Is Moses truthful or not truthful in your view?
Is it truth that he wrote, or a tale of falsehood?
He wrote of the war your sister waged with the son of Jacob,
and he recounted how brazen and shameless her mind was.
With him all the books also cry out against your wickedness,
and reproach your audacity in many ways.

Great Samson—who bound him by the armour of his hair,
and who brought low his might into the hands of the uncircumcised?
Was it not you who struck down the strength of his might before his pursuers,
and was it not you who blinded the light of his eyes and of his mind?
Did not your insolence defile the holiness of his Nazirite vow,
so that those unclean of soul laughed at his purity?
Did not your wantonness yoke him to the mill in disgrace,
so that he became a sport in the assembly of demons, to demons and to men?
A thousand men the mighty man slew with a contemptible bone,
yet a drawn-out rib struck him, and he fell and could not rise.
The lion he tore apart, and the chains he snapped and cast off,
yet a feeble thread bound him and threw him down like a thing of no account.
Hear, you mighty; listen, you righteous; marvel, you wise,
at the fearful calamities Eve has wrought from generation to generation.
Joseph she imprisoned, Samson she bound, David she pursued,
and behold, the account of their afflictions is in the books of the Spirit.
And if the truthful and the possessors of strength fell in her battles,
who can stand firm before her harms?
Evil is the harm she does, and she strikes hard whoever she strikes,
and the Evil One is not as evil as her wickedness, evil though he is.
The Evil One strikes a man in secret, since he is loathed,
but she without shame strikes everyone, the good and the wicked.
Through her the Evil One himself does evil whenever he does evil,
and for that reason he could not do much evil were it not for her.
Through her he did evil to us from the beginning, when he did us evil,
and with her tongue he pricked us with the goad of her bitterness.
She armed him with the armour of iniquity against us,
and behold, he lays us waste with her baseness as with a sword.
“Alas for Eve!” let our race say, the children of her house,
for she is with us, yet her love is bound up with our killer.
The company of the Evil One is very dear to her mind,
and at the door of his divinations her heart knocks night and day.
From him she asks for womb and child, she who is stripped of understanding,
and to him she makes entreaty to turn the fruits of the womb toward her.
On the support of a broken reed she has placed her trust,
and it is not apparent to her that it was he who swept her away from the beginning.
O how blind she is, bereft of the consolation of discernment,

and unable to perceive how to tell the hateful from the beautiful!
O wretched woman, why do you not judge with discernment,
and why is no upright judgment set before your mind?
Why do you falsely call the Evil One good,
and why do you ask help for your life from your deceiver?
How can one full of afflictions give help,
and how can he who hates mankind look for the good of mankind?
Eve strays utterly in the error of his deceit,
and vainly takes refuge in him, an empty refuge.
She loves error, because she strays after straying,
and it is her habit to wander in the error of the desires.
She loves wandering, and her eyes gaze on vanity,
and if anyone watches her, he finds wandering within her mind.
In doorways and streets she is eager to stand basely,
and her ears incline to listen to a report of falsehood.
She busies herself with adornment, and her heart muses on beauty,
not that she may be fair, but that by her fairness she may make the fair ugly.
For vanity she adorns herself, the hateful one [?],
so that by means of adornment she may hunt the prey of desires for herself.
To hunt mankind she spreads adornment over her limbs,
and men fall by the adornment of her face as into snares.
Like a hunter her nature lies in wait within her limbs,
and the adornment of her face is like bait above the snare.
He teaches her to hide snares in the senses of the body,
and shows her how to spread nets by the signal of her eyes.
It is he who sharpens in her the hateful gaze of baseness,
and he who fixes the shameless sign before her doors.
He paints hateful desire before her so that she may resemble it,
and she leans with all her senses toward shamelessness.
Toward baseness her senses and the impulses of her soul incline,
and like one who hungers her heart longs for shameless food.
On the lust of the flesh her heart muses continually,
and she eats every day, yet the lust of her soul is not filled.
She is exceedingly greedy, and however much she eats, she grows greedy again,
and after eating her fill she eats and denies it: “I have not eaten.”
Like the insolent mother [?], the shameless daughter
who stole the fruit and contrived excuses: “The serpent deceived me.”

Her mother's habit goes with her through all generations, / and she cherishes it as the wicked cherish loathsome wickedness. / She longs to stand above the man, as her mother did, / and if she could, she would wish to be a man herself. / She seeks to seize the authority of men by insolence, / and to throw into confusion the proper order of creation. / Paul, the chosen herald, saw her insolence, / and he was quick to shut the door in her face, so that she would not rule. / "Let a woman learn in silence from the teacher," he said, / and let her not stand insolently in the rank of men. / With the weapon of his word Paul bound her insolence, / and yet even so she does not leave off her lawlessness. / He also set bounds to her wanton adornment and held her back from it, / but instead of heeding his word she busies herself with lavish adornment. / Now she has heaped up her adornment far beyond what is fitting, / so that she has overturned the order of seemly things in every respect. / Perhaps, if she knew how to read in the books of the Spirit, / she would blot out of them the sentences passed upon her offenses. / Perhaps, if she had the chance, she would roar against me too for exposing her blemishes, / as Jezebel did against the sons of the prophets. / Perhaps, if she knew who I am, or how weak I am, / she would never have her fill of hurling the arrows of scorn. / Perhaps, if someone painted the likeness of my person and showed it to her, / she would stone it with stones of mockery, as was done to prophecy. / Perhaps even now she is unsheathing the sword against my words, / and cutting them off like the head of the Bridegroom's friend. / Go away, woman! I am not a righteous man, nor the son of righteous men; / why are you jealous of me as of a righteous man, when I am not righteous? / Do not shoot the arrows of scorn at me, as you are accustomed to do, / and do not take vengeance on my words for the reproaches of your disgrace. / It was not out of malice that I exposed the shamelessness of your disgraceful deeds, / nor out of envy that I spread out your blemishes before the eyes of onlookers. / With my own eyes I saw that you were stained with disgraceful deeds, / and my mind counseled me to wash the filth of iniquity from you. / I saw hateful iniquity staining your limbs,

and I wished to sprinkle the waters of my words upon your impurity. / I saw that you were sick with the hard pain of wantonness, / and I ground words like medicines, so that perhaps you might be healed. / The desire of the flesh grips you like a fever, / and with my words I wished to cool the fire of your burning. / I saw the sword of your word laying waste the ranks of humankind, / and I went out to hold it back, so that at least a small remnant might be left to us. / I saw the gaze of your eyes hiding snares for our race, / and I held men back, so that they would not be caught in your nets. / I saw the adornment of your face spread out like nets, / and I raised my voice, so that the prey might hear and flee from you. / I saw your evil lust running over sea and dry land, / and I was zealous to restrain it, so that the world would not be thrown into turmoil by its running. / I saw your lawless envy stirring up good and wicked alike, / and I considered whether I might perhaps restrain it, so that it might abate a little. / Because of you priests and kings have fallen in battle, / and see, they still struggle, and there is no end to their battles. / I marveled greatly at the harm that comes through you, how strong it is, / and that is why I called you the cause of all evils. / Yet the evil of the inclination is not bound up in you by nature; / it is your will that sins and causes others to sin, as it wills. / It is your will that leads you wherever it wishes; / you were not created by anyone under compulsion to hunt after evils. / All the good and all the evil hidden in you are your own, / and you have power over both, as a free woman. / For it is in your freedom to do good and to do evil, / and if that is so, you have no ground left for excuse. / The way is open to you, then, to walk in the path of repentance, / and it is right for you to pay off your debts by penitence of soul. / Come, if you are willing, follow the counsel that I give you, / leave off the turmoil, and walk in the way that I show you. / I will walk ahead of you, if you are willing,

and I will bring you into the harbor of peace, where there is no dread. / Listen, if you will, to the story of the deeds of the daughters of your sex, / who were strong in sufferings and did not grow slack before temptations. / Paint in your mind the image of the way they lived, / and with their purity scour the filth from your thoughts. / Look at Sarah and Rebekah and consider them carefully, / how they endured the pains of barrenness of body without ceasing. / Let Hannah be a mirror to the eyes of your soul, / and through her patience gain patience in the day of trial. / You are of the race of these women, O daughter of man; / walk in the path of their endurance and leave dread behind. / And why do I say that you are of the lineage of noble women? / For see, from you is the woman who bore Life for humankind. / From a daughter of your race sprang up for us life without end; / we shall not die, since we have come to life by the Life that is from you. / Spare your soul, which is the vessel that carries life; / do not defile the fountain of life with disgraceful deeds. / Abandon the concerns of vain things that have grown old beside you, / and occupy your soul with good meditation on the word of life. / Flee from the errors of divinations, enchantments and the teaching of demons, / and inscribe upon your heart the three names of the one name of the Godhead. / Set the name of the Godhead before your mind as a target, / and see, you will learn to aim truly toward purity. / Let your mouth recite the Trinity instead of every other word, / and render thanksgiving three times over to the One who sets all things in order.
On “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”
By the same: a homily of [?], which he composed on “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

A new path has the Word that John wrote down traced for us;
he went down on it first and became a guide for us all.
He traced the path toward the Being and showed that there is one equality:
that the Father and his Offspring are one, and there is no time between him and his Child.
His voice became like thunder and cried out to the four quarters,
and fittingly he was called son of thunder, for he proclaimed the Word that was in the beginning.
“Hear, O peoples, and listen, O nations, to the new tidings I proclaim:
the Father begot from his bosom a Son who is not younger than his Begetter.
In the beginning was the Word, and he was with God,
and that Word was God, in hypostasis and in authority.”
O mystery that was hidden from generations and from families!
And the son of thunder has scattered it abroad and revealed it to those above and those below.
O John the herald, wonder of the race of Adam,
to whom the Holy Spirit gave keys!
He opened the treasury of the Being, rose up and reached the height of heights,
above the hosts of the spiritual beings,
and the power of goodness brought him near to speak of the Being.
He received power and authority and proclaimed the Word that was in the beginning:
that the Son was in the beginning, eternally with his Begetter.
He is everlastingly with his Father, as the radiance is with the sun,
for the sun does not precede its radiance, nor is the sun before its sphere.
The radiance of the sun was with it;
the Son is with the Father, and there is no time when he was separated from him.
The Father is a true hypostasis, and the Son a hypostasis like his.
And since he is called Father, there is no time between him and his Child.
He is a nature that is from eternity, and there is no beginning to his Being.
Neither did the Father begin to be, nor is there a time for his Child.
The Father is eternal, everlasting, for there is no time when he was not Father;
and the Son is perfect, lacking nothing,
for there is no time when he was not united [with him].
The Eternal is far removed from times, and times and ages are within him.
How could the Eternal be bounded by times that are made?
However far thought may search beyond the times, it finds him there.
The Father did not begin in his Child, nor is there a time for the Father's Child.
John called him his Word, for he is everlastingly with his Father,
like the word with the soul, which is from it and is with it.
The Son was with his Father, and came to the world, and was with him.
The word never goes out from the soul so as to depart from it,
nor did the Son go out from his Begetter and distance himself by departing.
The word goes out to every quarter and does not depart from the soul;
and while it is on its errand, it is in the soul, even as it is [there].
So too the Word went out from the Father and came to the dwelling of mortals,
and while he dwelt in our nature,

he was wholly in his Father.
The word is not seen openly, because it is from the soul,
and when it is inscribed by ink it is seen by means of letters.
And when ink has confined it in letters and bounded it in garments of ink,
in letters it exists in name, but all of it dwells within the soul.
The inks look mean when they are examined as letters,
yet the word does not let its nature be bounded by pages.
The Son was hidden with his Begetter from those above and those below,
and he showed himself to us by his will in the ink of Adam's body.
And when he put on the garment of our nature, he remained wrapped in his divinity.
His will dwelt in our nature, and his nature remained in its hiddenness.
The body he put on did not bound his nature, which cannot be bounded,
and the eye of flesh did not see the hiddenness of his divinity.
Through him, said John, all that came to be was made,
and nothing came to be without him, for he willed and ordered all that came to be.
He is the fountain full of life, who possesses life in his nature,
and from the life that is in his nature he distributed life to his creatures.
The life is light, which drives the darkness away from the light,
and the darkness of error did not overtake it to hinder the course of the light.
He was in the world always, and the world was made by his hands;
and though the world is his, the world did not wish to acknowledge him.
The Creator came to his own, and his own did not receive his word,
but those who heard his commandments acquired the authority of sons.
He called us his own children, in the mercies he showed toward our race,
for he begot us spiritually in the baptism of water and Spirit.
He showed us his good will in honouring us with the name of sons,
and he confirmed the name of sonship, for he chose for himself a dwelling in his sons.
The Word, said John, became flesh and dwelt among us,
and we saw the glory of his majesty at the door of humanity.
He became flesh for us and dwelt among us, and showed us his hidden glory;
and while he was hidden in his nature, he showed his glory through our body.
He did not descend into becoming, in that it says he became flesh;
rather he joined flesh to himself and dwelt in it by his will.
For the Creator cannot come into a new becoming,
nor can a time of birth set bounds to the Being that has no beginning.
If he always existed, how did he come into becoming?
And if he came into becoming, that is far from his having always existed.
There is neither beginning nor end to the Being that is everlasting,
whereas a thing that comes into becoming has its becoming before its nature.
If he was eternal with the Father, he is not bounded in his nature;
and if he bounded himself in a womb,
he was not eternal with his Begetter.
If he is everywhere
and has now come into becoming,
how did he receive formation — a part of him, or all of him?
If all of him was bounded, he does not have that which is unbounded;
and if he was bounded in part,

and if he has something that can be bounded, either all of him or in part,
then the Father too can be bounded, for from him is the nature of the Son.
How was he in his Father, and dwelling in the womb of flesh?
This is the question to be examined: how he received a dwelling.
And if, as the contentious say, he was in the womb and on high,
because he was able to divide himself so as to be on high and in the depth,
then his will comes before his nature, which is everlasting,
for behold, his will controls him and bounds his nature.
And if his will is able to override and overcome his nature,
then he changes every moment, as his will wishes.
And if his will directs his nature as it wishes,
where then is the Being which possesses its nature eternally?
Let this boldness go off after the band of the contentious,
who bring the Eternal down to lowly things and bound him in the womb of a daughter of man.
O you whose eyes are bereft of light, who walk on the path of darkness,
how can the eternal nature be bounded in his works?
By the word of the heretics, his creation is far greater than he,
for it can bound his nature!
How did a nature finer than spirit receive composition,
while he was in his own nature, or in a [?] that is not his?
Come, explain your mysteries to us, uncircumcised ones whose hearts are not circumcised,
and teach us how we should confess the Word that became flesh.
Or explain to us how the Word dwelt within limbs.
Or make ready weapons to fight, and let us see whose is the victory.
Gather all your arrows and stretch the strings of your bows,
and set up “the Word became flesh” as a target, and let us see who hits it.
Over “the Word became flesh” is the whole battle,
and I am convinced that for this you have prepared weapons against us.
With the weapon of your master you wish to wage battle with us,
for he forged the weapon and clad you in it against the Word that is from the Father.
Come, with your master the Egyptians, and let us seek the force of the expression,
and let us see the becoming: how
the Creator began to be,
whether he compounded himself while he existed, or began to be only now;
or perhaps another was compounded, and he is far from composition.
If he came to be, he did not exist; and if he existed, he did not [come to be] now,
for the Eternal cannot receive becoming after his being.
He became flesh, according to your words — a part of him, or all of him?
And how can a nature that has no composition be divided?
If all of him was compounded, then all of him was bounded,
and he was absent from everywhere and dwelt in the womb alone.
And if these things are so, where is that which is unbounded?
For behold, the womb of flesh has bounded him, by the craft you have compounded.
And if part of him was compounded, and part of him remained in his nature,
where then is the equality? For behold, his nature has been divided.
If the Word became flesh,

let us ask whose the flesh is:
did he bring it down with him from on high, or is it the flesh of a human being?
If his own hypostasis became flesh and he did not take flesh from Mary,
how has he helped our nature,
by becoming a flesh that is his own?
Then void is the promise
that was pledged to David,
and it is by a borrowed name that he is called Son of David, though he is not.
Which mortals have been helped by the Word that became flesh,
if he became flesh in his own nature and our nature remained in its lowliness?
Where then is that which cancelled the decree of death against us,
if he did not take a body from Mary?
The Word took it to himself and dwelt in it,
and this befits the wise, and the truth bears witness to their words.
The Eternal, then, cannot become flesh in his own hypostasis,
and becoming, as flesh, is far from the Being that has no beginning.
What arrogant shamelessness you have crafted in your words!
Reveal the target of your thoughts, and interpret in the manner of Arius.
Your words make him strong, and your expressions support him —
him who denied the being of the Son and called him a servant and minister.
This is the whole battle of Arius, disciple of the wolf,
who makes the Son less than the Father and puts him on a level with his creatures.
At his target you too are aiming, O contentious ones,
and in a disguise you portray the wickedness that is hidden in your words.
Come out of the flock, you arrogant ones; do not stray about in the guise of lambs!
For you have corrupted it into a division
of the two natures that became one.
The wickedness of their blasphemies has grown and risen to the height of heights;
they have brought the Eternal down from his limit and bound him in the bonds of limbs.
Heaven and earth, listen and hear
the wickedness the arrogant have spoken!
The Being that cannot be comprehended they have bounded and confined within a womb.
Like a shield in battle they have seized on this saying:
that the Word compounded himself and became flesh, as it is written.
Where did you get “he became,” O teachers of novelties?
You have gone astray over “he dwelt among us”
and have not examined its meaning.
“He dwelt among us,” said John:
who was dwelling in whom?
Behold, he has plainly spread out before us the dwelling of the two that became one.
If he spoke of dwelling, then “he became among us” must be examined,
for one can dwell, then, even without being the thing that comes to be.
If he dwelt in another, then becoming is superfluous,
and this befits his nature: to dwell without being bounded.
Come then, O hearer, examine my words, whether they are just,
and with the measure of your knowledge weigh my expressions, whether they are fitting.
Do not let the hearing of words
spoken perversely trouble you.
They are not of [?],
but are a dove's egg:
it is the egg of the Word who brings help, and hidden in it is the hope of our life,
which brings our nature near to the honour of the image it had lost.
Our battle is over this:

that the Word was not diminished by the dwelling,
but that he took up our nature and honoured it with the glory of his majesty.
This is the question of the dwelling which we dispute with the arrogant:
that the Being was not lessened
by the dwelling with humanity.
“He became” means this: that he dwelt; and “he dwelt” means that he took a man,
and hid the splendour of his majesty in the garment of the mortal body.
The eternal Word joined to himself the temple of the body and dwelt in it;
it was not he who received composition, as the wickedness of the heretics [holds].
What is not bounded in its nature does not descend to composition,
nor was the temple he joined to himself enough to bound his nature.
He was not dwelling by his nature
in the man he took from us;
rather it was an indwelling of will
and a union without separation.
The Word wove the garment of the body to hide his majesty in it,
so that men might see in a man the image of the glory of his majesty.
The promise that does not lie
he promised to Abraham and to David,
and now he has fulfilled it in deeds, in the first-fruits from the house of David.
The Word is not the Son of David — O contentious ones, whom are you fighting?
The Son of David is a son of our race, whom the Word took and dwelt in.
The Word fulfilled all his will in a body and dwelt in it,
and while his will was bounded in it, his nature was not bounded in it.
He was wholly in it by his will, and by his nature both in it and everywhere,
for this befits the Maker: that he not be bounded by his works.
The body was his work, which he willed to be a dwelling for him,
and since it did not bound his nature, he dwelt in it wholly by his will.
Yet the contentious are already fighting with my words, as though [?]:
“How can you call the made thing and the Maker
one person?”
I call “made thing” the temple that the Word joined for his dwelling,
and “Maker” the Only-begotten, who willed to dwell in his work.
Like soul and body, which agree together and are called one person:
the soul is a living nature, and the body a mortal nature,
and they are called one person,
though they are two and distinct one from the other.
The Word is the nature of the Being, and the body the nature of humanity;
one a Maker and one a made thing, yet they are one in union.
The soul is confined within the body, yet its activity is outside the body,
and while the body is in one place, the movement of the soul is in every quarter.
The Word was dwelling within the body
and was on high and in the depth;
his humanity was bounded,
but his divinity was in every quarter.
The soul does not suffer in the body when the limbs are scourged,
nor did the divinity suffer in the sufferings of the body in which it dwelt.
And if the soul, which is made like the body, does not suffer,
how could the Being suffer, whose nature is exalted above sufferings?
The soul suffers with the body by love, and not by nature,
and the sufferings of the body are ascribed also to the soul in a borrowed sense.
He made one with himself in glory the man whom he took from us,

and for the sake of his love toward us he took bitterness upon himself.
The soul dwells within the body, and onlookers do not see it;
and though it is bounded in its nature, the eyes of flesh do not grasp it.
So too the Word dwelt in our nature and was not bounded in our nature,
for it was an indwelling of will and not an indwelling of nature.
Behold, in our nature, a demonstration
of two natures that became one:
one living and one mortal, one hidden and the other manifest.
Come then, O contentious ones, let us search with a fitting inquiry.
Lower the height of your words and know your weak nature.
Let go of the question of the Being, the Being that cannot be comprehended,
and let us speak of the son of our race, whom the Eternal took and dwelt in.
He dwelt in him and did not bound himself, for his nature has nothing that can be bounded.
The mortal suffered in his nature, and the sufferings did not come near the Being.
He joined to himself a rational image, to show his authority through it,
so that rational beings, seeing him,
might honour the hidden through the manifest.
In the holy of holies of his hiddenness the Eternal dwelt in him hiddenly,
and through the mediator, the son of our race, we see the image of his glory.
For this he chose him and dwelt in him: that the hidden might be spread out in the manifest,
and that at the door of his hiddenness we might worship his hidden nature.
He made him lord over his house and ruler over his possessions,
and subjected to him height and depth, the rational and the dumb alike.
In him the creation was renewed, the image that had been corrupted by sin,
and there was fulfilled toward us in deed
that which called us his image.
To him angels and men bow down, as to the visible image of the king,
marvelling at the sight of him in place of the hiddenness of the Only-begotten.
Hear with understanding and perceive, O hearer, these things that I set before you.
Do not let thoughts trouble you about the Word that became flesh.
Behold, I have trodden the path before you;
come, walk in the track of my expressions,
for you will find the fountain of life
at the end of the path I have trodden for you.
Leave the Eternal in his hiddenness, in the manifest one he took for his dwelling,
and honour the king through his image,
for the king is honoured in his image.
For hard is the path to walk
toward the Being without beginning.
In the son of our race, as a guide,
he has trodden for us the path of hiddenness,
since the nature of made things cannot
examine the perfect Eternal.
The image he joined to himself has shown us the glory befitting his hiddenness.
Through the faithful one whom he took from us he bound creation into one,
and through the mediator, the son of our race, he made peace for us with his majesty.
This is the reason for his coming:
that he might come and renew our creation,
and bind up the peace that had been loosed,
through the mediation of our Head.
For our consolation he joined to himself the temple of flesh and dwelt in it,
so that we might worship in the outer sanctuary him who is hidden in the holy of holies.
The outer holy place of his body

we see with the eyes of flesh,
and the holy of holies of his hiddenness with the spiritual movements of the soul.
By the veil of Adam's body
those above and those below are held back,
and made things have no authority
to see the holy place of the Being.
Behold, the path is trodden for the weary: come, contentious ones, walk in it,
and do not stumble on the road of the division of your thoughts.
In the confession of the Being let no division be mingled,
for the Son is equal with his Begetter.
Let us not bring him down to weaknesses;
let us confess that the Word put on flesh, and willed, and dwelt in our nature,
while the temple of flesh in which he dwelt did not bound his nature.
He dwelt in it wholly by his will, and remained wholly in his Being,
and he took up its lowly things into his name and made it share in his praises.
Come, debtors, sons of Adam, let us repay goodness in return
to the Good One who made our nature share in the praises of his majesty.
Another by the same.
